Title: A correlation to compute the thermo-diffusive instability effect of lean hydrogen flames at engine-like conditions
Abstract: Lean hydrogen mixtures are a valid alternative to conventional fuels for internal combustion engine. Lean hydrogen flames are characterised by a low effective Lewis number, which triggers flame instabilities. Therefore, being able to correctly quantify the effect of such phenomenon on the flame propagation is important. However, the computation of the flame instability second order growth rate (ω2), which is widely used to model the laminar flame speed increase due to instabilities, is not straightforward, as chemical kinetics must be considered. In this work, a comprehensive correlation for modelling thermo-diffusive instabilities at engine-like conditions is presented, and an easy-to-implement correlation for the enhancement of the flame speed is proposed. As a first step, one-dimensional freely propagating flame simulations are used to compute the thermal expansion parameter σ of lean hydrogen flames. Secondly, by imposing the Sutherland’s Law to describe the mixture thermal conductivity, the terms that include the stabilising (or destabilising) effects of heat diffusion (B1), molecular diffusion (B2), and viscous diffusion (B3) are computed, and a fitting function is found for each of them. Thirdly, the computation of the Zel’dovich number β is performed, and a fitting procedure carried out. Finally, by the resulting fitting functions, an ω2 correlation dependent only on the local thermodynamic conditions of the mixture is developed within pressure, unburnt temperature and equivalence ratio ranges of 10–50 bar, 500–900 K and 0.2–0.7, respectively. Furthermore, reasonable results can be found through extrapolation up to 100 bar and 1100 K. The flame speed enhancement values obtained with the developed correlation differ by less than 6% from those reported in literature at relevant light-duty engine-like conditions. Larger discrepancies are observed only at low unburnt gas temperatures (300 K) or for very lean mixtures (Φ = 0.2). © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: The influence of initial pressure and methane blending ratio on the explosion characteristics of methane/ammonia/air premixed gas in open-ended pipeline
Abstract: To investigate the influence of initial pressure on the explosion propagation characteristics of methane/ammonia/air premixed gas in an open-ended pipeline, we systematically conducted premixed flame propagation experiments on a self-built visual rectangular pipeline platform under different initial pressures (0.8 atm, 1.0 atm, 1.2 atm) and methane blending ratios (100 %, 90 %, 75 %, 60 %). Through high-speed photography and synchronous collection of dynamic pressure, using the seven characteristic time points defined for the flame propagation process, the changes in flame morphology evolution, propagation speed, and explosion overpressure were quantitatively analyzed. The results show that an increase in initial pressure generally promotes the growth of flame propagation speed and explosion overpressure, and significantly advances the time nodes of each characteristic stage; ammonia blending generally delays the flame propagation process, but when 10 % ammonia is blended at a low pressure of 0.8 atm, the flame propagation speed and explosion overpressure in the mixed gas condition show abnormal increases compared to the pure methane condition. The essence is that the promoting effect of thermal diffusion instability exceeds the inhibitory effect of the decrease in reaction activity. The sensitivity of explosion overpressure to initial pressure is much higher than that of flame propagation speed. Especially the peak overpressure under the pure methane condition increases by as much as 398.4 % when the initial pressure rises from 0.8 atm to 1.0 atm. The influence of initial pressure and ammonia blending ratio on explosion characteristics shows a significant nonlinear coupling feature. The research results provide important experimental basis for the safety assessment and explosion prevention design of ammonia-methane mixed fuel in pipeline transportation and industrial applications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Trace metals, morphology and characteristics of particulates from methanol-diesel dual-fuel genset engine
Abstract: Methanol is a potential alternative fuel that reduces particulate emissions in the engine exhaust. This experimental study compared particulate matter (PM) emissions from a dual-fuelled genset engine and a baseline diesel-fuelled genset engine. In this experimental investigation, different fractions of methanol were used to displace mineral diesel on an energy basis in the dual-fuel combustion mode. The experiments were conducted using the Genset engine at a fixed speed of 1500 rpm and varying engine loads. Results showed that PM emissions were lower for dual-fuel combustion than for baseline diesel combustion. The particulate number-size distribution was higher in baseline diesel combustion. One key observation of this study was lower emissions of nanoparticles, nucleation-mode particles, and accumulation-mode particles from the dual-fuel engine compared to the baseline diesel engine. PM morphology investigations revealed that the baseline diesel engine emitted more agglomerated soot. The concentrations of trace metals in the PM were nearly similar for dual-fuel and baseline diesel combustion, which was another important observation of this study. The parametric characterisation of engine exhaust emissions showed the elimination of PM-NOx trade-off in dual-fuel mode. The maximum reductions in NOx, particulate mass, and particulate number were ∼79%, ∼62%, and ∼84%, respectively, for the methanol-diesel-fueled engine compared to baseline diesel. Soot reduction was ∼89% for the methanol-diesel-fueled engine. Soot, particulate mass, particulate number, and NOx emissions were lower from the dual-fuel engine, and methanol emerged as a superior alternative fuel for compression-ignition engines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Inhibition of spontaneous combustion in low-rank coal by facultative anaerobic microflora: reducing oxidizer, increasing retardant and modifying coal structure

Title: A fluorescent/colorimetric/electrochemical tri-modal sensing platform for cross-validated dynamic monitoring of endogenous glutathione in plants under stress
Abstract: Glutathione (GSH) serves as a core cellular redox regulator for plant abiotic-stress responses. Reliable quantification of endogenous plant GSH remains challenging owing to complex matrix interferences, as well as dependencies on specialized instrumentation or transgenic plant materials. Herein, we design and synthesize RFNSP, a resorufin-based molecular probe functionalized with a 2-fluoro-4-nitrobenzenesulfonyl ester recognition moiety, and further construct a fluorescence-colorimetric-electrochemical tri-modal sensing platform for cross-validated GSH quantification in plant samples. Upon reaction with GSH, RFNSP undergoes a two-step sequential activation pathway to generate the conjugated adduct Re-GSH, simultaneously triggering three independent signal outputs; this kinetic feature enables effective discrimination of GSH against cysteine and homocysteine. A graphitic carbon nitride/single-walled carbon nanotube modified carbon-paper electrode (CP/SWCNTs/g-C3N4) is adopted as the electrochemical sensing interface. Benefitting from complementary analytical performances, the platform achieves ratiometric fluorescence detection with a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.5 μM (0.01–1.5 mM), visual colorimetric readout, and electrochemical measurement reaching an LOD of 0.1 μM (2–200 μM). Title: Microstructural organization and functionality of transglutaminase-crosslinked casein micelle-based emulsions under pH variation: insights from X-ray microtomography
Abstract: This study investigated the potential of X-ray microtomography (μCT) to characterize a simple emulsion model, as the transglutaminase (TGase) treated casein micelle emulsions under different pH conditions (3.5-9.0). The results showed that pH significantly modulated protein conformation, leading to distinct microstructural organizations and macroscopic behaviors of TGase-treated casein micelle emulsion. At native and alkaline pH, increased electrostatic repulsion and molecular flexibility promoted efficient interfacial adsorption, resulting in finer droplet dispersion and high emulsifying activity. In contrast, near the isoelectric point (pH 4.6), extensive protein aggregation led to the formation of dense and interconnected microstructures, which enhanced emulsion stability despite reduced emulsifying capacity. Furthermore, the studied microstructural parameters showed strongly correlation with emulsifying properties (emulsifying activity, emulsifying stability, and destabilization indices) and rheological properties, confirming the key role of droplet organization in governing global emulsion behavior. Moreover, these relationships revealed that pH-dependent molecular changes directly govern the development and stability of the emulsion network. These findings demonstrate that X-ray microtomography is a powerful and suitable tool for characterizing fat droplet volume, spatial distribution, shape, and network organization in simple emulsion systems, comparable to more complex food emulsions. The study provides new insights into how pH governs the structure–function relationships of TGase-treated casein micelle-based emulsions. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Phase-field model and experimental study of acid fractures coupled with hydro–mechano–reactive flow and strain-softening
Abstract: Acid fracturing is a key technology for stimulating carbonate reservoirs and enhancing the production of oil, gas, and geothermal energy. The coupling among fluid flow, rock mechanical deformation, and chemical reactions during acid fracturing is a central scientific issue in the reconstruction of carbonate reservoirs. Existing acid fracture propagation models typically treat the rocks as linear elastic materials and neglect the strain-softening behavior induced by acid dissolution, which leads to deviations in the prediction of fracture morphology, breakdown pressure, and acid-etched wormhole development. In this study, a hydro–mechano–reactive flow coupled phase field model incorporating strain-softening plasticity is developed based on unified strength theory. A chemical damage variable linking porosity increase to Young's modulus degradation is introduced, together with the theoretical framework and numerical implementation. Through triaxial compression tests, nuclear magnetic resonance measurements, and X-ray diffraction analyses on acidized cores, the variations in mechanical parameters, pore structure, and mineral composition under different acidizing durations are obtained, clarifying that acidized rock exhibits strain-softening mechanical characteristics. Numerical simulation results show that, after accounting for strain softening, the propagation length of the main acid fracture is significantly shorter than that predicted by the elastic model, the fracture width increases, and the fluid pressure exhibits a gradually declining trend after breakdown. With increasing injection rate, the fracture propagation mechanism gradually shifts from chemical dissolution driven to fluid-driven. Within the investigated simulation conditions, increasing acid concentration shifts fracture propagation from fluid pressure dominance toward joint hydraulic–chemical control as chemical dissolution becomes more important. At high concentrations, rapid wormhole development enhances matrix acid leakoff, reducing the driving force at the main fracture front and limiting further propagation. This study reveals the key controlling role of acidizing-induced strain-softening behavior on acid fracture propagation patterns, providing a theoretical basis and optimization direction for acid fracturing engineering design. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Dong J.; Pei H.; Qi X.; Gao Y.; Guo Q.
Title: Influence of structure on the interfacial behavior of debranched maize starch-fatty acid-β-lactoglobulin complexes
Abstract: The influence of structure on the interfacial behavior of debranched maize starch-fatty acid-β-lactoglobulin complexes remains unclear. Understanding the correlation between the structure and interfacial behavior of the complexes is essential for designing emulsions with high stability and tunable digestion behavior through structure-driven precise regulation of interfacial behavior. In this study, the structural characteristics and interfacial behavior of the complexes formed among debranched maize starch (DMS), β-lactoglobulin (βLG) and various fatty acids, including lauric acid (LA), myristic acid (MA), palmitic acid (PA), and stearic acid (SA), were investigated. The total enthalpy change and relative crystallinity of DMS-PA-βLG complexes were lower than those of DMS-LA-βLG and DMS-MA-βLG complexes, but its enthalpy change remained higher than that of DMS-SA-βLG complexes. All complexes displayed well-defined V-type crystalline structures with comparable crystallite perfection, and DMS-PA-βLG complexes exhibited the highest short-range molecular order. In contrast, DMS-PA-βLG complexes exhibited the most favorable interfacial adsorption behavior, with stronger interfacial tension reduction, faster diffusion and reorganization, greater adsorbed mass and a more robust interfacial membrane. Correlation analysis showed that total enthalpy change was negatively associated with interfacial membrane viscosity, whereas short-range molecular order was positively associated with interfacial membrane elasticity. Relative crystallinity was negatively associated with interfacial affinity, whereas V-type crystallite perfection was positively associated with interfacial tension reduction. These findings revealed the influence of structure on the interfacial behavior of debranched maize starch-fatty acid-β-lactoglobulin complexes, providing a basis for the design of emulsions with high stability and tunable digestion behavior through structure-driven precise regulation of interfacial behavior. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Wang J.; Zhang Y.; Yang Y.; Ma H.; Hong R.; Chu H.
Title: Effect of the oxygen index on the microstructure and nanostructure of soot in a laminar diffusion flame of ethylene/ammonia
Abstract: As an effective technology for enhancing combustion and reducing emissions, oxygen-enriched combustion can significantly modulate soot formation characteristics in laminar diffusion flames of hydrocarbon fuels blended with ammonia. In this study, the effects of 24% oxygen index (OI) on the flame shape, temperature and OH* radicals in a laminar diffusion flame of ethylene/ammonia were comprehensively examined. Additionally, comprehensive characterization and analysis were conducted on soot particle size, fringe length and tortuosity ( L a and T f), and graphitization degree at the flame centerline and wing. Both ammonia addition and the switch to a 24% oxygen-enriched co-flow raised the flame centerline temperature and the peak OH* chemiluminescence intensity. The size of primary soot particles decreased at normalized heights above burner (NHAB) = 0.5 and 0.7 upon 20% ammonia addition. Notably, introducing a 24% OI co-flow altered the radial differences in primary soot particle size, leading to an axial reduction but a lateral augmentation in particle size compared to the 21% OI flame. Furthermore, under the examined conditions, soot sampled from the 24% OI flame exhibited lower graphitization than that from the 21% OI flame, characterized by shorter L a, higher T f, and a higher I D1/ I G. At the flame centerline (NHAB = 0.7), the difference induced by ammonia on soot graphitization was less pronounced under 24% OI than under 21% OI. In contrast, at the flame wing, the 24% OI condition coincided with greater soot structural disorder when combined with ammonia. Unlike previous studies, which focused on macroscopic parameters, this study focused on the microscopic characteristics of soot. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li W.; Gul S.; Chen Q.; Zhou F.
Title: Gradual machine learning for semi-supervised medical image classification via feature optimization
Abstract: Semi-supervised medical image classification (MIC) typically relies on the i.i.d. assumption when utilizing limited labeled data and abundant unlabeled data for model training. However, variations in populations and imaging devices can lead to differences in data distributions, which may introduce confirmation bias into model learning. In this work, we investigate gradual machine learning (GML) for semi-supervised MIC. By modeling inter-sample relationships, GML reduces reliance on the strict i.i.d. assumption. It uses a small set of labeled samples to construct feature factors for test samples and iteratively infers their labels through factor graph inference. Additionally, to provide complementary factors, we define two types of factors: class-centroid distance (CCD) and K-nearest neighbors (KNN), and propose a novel evolutionary multi-task (EMT) method to optimize them. Specifically, we first use two deep learning architectures to extract feature vectors from medical images and concatenate them to form the basic feature vectors. Then, two tasks are defined: the feature enhancement task (FET) and the feature selection task (FST). FET performs continuous optimization on the basic feature vectors from the CCD perspective to capture subtle feature contributions, whereas FST performs discrete optimization from the KNN perspective to enhance model robustness. These two tasks are jointly optimized by the proposed EMT to refine the feature representations and generate two sets of high-quality factors for GML to perform gradual inference. Extensive experiments on two widely used medical image datasets demonstrate that our method achieves competitive performance compared with existing semi-supervised methods. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhou L.; Li P.; Wang Y.; Chen H.; Li S.; Chen R.; Zhao J.
Title: Artificial optoelectronic neural synapses enabled by Co-sputtered Ti-doped Ga2O3 high-endurance memristor
Abstract: In this work, a sandwich-structured W/Ti-doped Ga2O3/Pt resistive random access memory (RRAM) device is fabricated. In contrast to previously reported Ga2O3-based RRAMs suffering from limited cycling endurance, the device prepared under optimal Ti sputtering power exhibits highly stable high- and low-resistance states, delivering an outstanding DC endurance of 56,000 cycles and multi-level storage capability enabled by compliance current modulation. The superior resistive switching performance is ascribed to the synergistic effect between efficient oxygen exchange of interfacial Ti ions and the oxidation-inert property of the W electrode. Meanwhile, I-V curve fitting verifies that the carrier transport mechanism in the high resistance state transitions from space-charge-limited current (SCLC) to Poole–Frenkel emission. XPS deconvolution confirms that Ti doping moderately increases the density of oxygen-vacancy-related defects to mitigate LRS degradation, while the reduced oxygen vacancy formation energy near Ti sites facilitates the directional growth of oxygen-vacancy conductive filaments. Finally, when applied to a convolutional neural network, the memristor-enabled optical pulse potentiation and electrical pulse depression yield a high pattern-recognition accuracy (92.8%). These results present an effective optimization approach for wide-bandgap oxide memristors, with remarkable potential for brain-inspired neuromorphic computing and optoelectronic synaptic applications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wei M.; Zheng G.; Xia B.; Zhou H.; Ding L.; Du Y.
Title: A comparative investigation of physics-driven machine learning architectures for consolidation analysis
Abstract: Physics-driven machine learning has emerged as a powerful framework for forward and inverse modeling of partial differential equations (PDEs), with increasing applications in geotechnical engineering. However, the relative performance of different physics-driven learning strategies remains problem-dependent, and their suitability for typical geotechnical problems has not been systematically established. This study systematically compares four physics-driven machine learning paradigms for consolidation analysis by combining Multi‑Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) and Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) with physics-informed neural networks (PINN) and the discrete-time deep energy method (DTDEM). The paradigms are evaluated for forward and inverse consolidation problems in one and three dimensions, with particular attention to convergence, computational cost, parameter inversion, accuracy, and robustness to noise. For forward problems governed by PDEs, although the energy-form DTDEM converges in fewer epochs than the strong-form PINN under both MLP and KAN architectures, its higher per-epoch cost results in a longer total wall-clock training time. A similar trade-off applies to KAN relative to MLP where the higher per-epoch cost can offset the benefit of faster convergence in terms of epochs. In terms of solution accuracy, replacing MLP with KAN improves both accuracy and training-loss convergence under the strong-form PINN framework, while under the DTDEM framework this advantage is not consistent. For parameter inversion, the DTDEM-based energy formulation is ineffective for parameter inversion because treating material parameters as additional optimization variables make the functional unbounded from below, resulting in divergent training. In contrast, within the strong-form framework, KAN substantially improves parameter-inversion accuracy and robustness to noisy data compared with MLPs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Effect of heat treatments on fatigue behavior and fracture of Inconel 625 additively manufactured by Laser Powder Bed Fusion
Abstract: This investigation examined the impact of Heat Treatments (HT) on the fatigue and fracture characteristics of additively manufactured Inconel 625. Following the fabrication of net-shaped specimens by the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) technique, the material underwent four distinct heat treatments: Stress Relief (SR), Direct Aging (DA), Solubilization and Aging (S + A), and Annealing (AN), all conducted in a high vacuum furnace. The effects of HT on microstructure, porosity, and residual stress state were comprehensively examined utilizing metallographic methods, X-ray diffraction, and computed tomography. The specimens, which included a batch retained in as-built (AB) condition for comparative analysis, underwent fatigue testing for up to 2E7 cycles. In all cases, HTs led to improved fatigue properties; however, AN produced the most significant enhancements, exhibiting the highest fatigue strength and a flatter slope of the S-N curve in the finite life zone. Post-fatigue residual stress measurements indicated that the heat-treated conditions with better fatigue performance were generally associated with a more favorable final compressive stress state; however, these measurements should be interpreted mainly as qualitative support, since cyclic loading and crack propagation may have modified the initial residual stress field. The examination of fracture surfaces by SEM and quantitative assessments of surface topography yielded additional insights into the relationships between HT-induced microstructures and fatigue failure processes. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Advances in pressure-enabled pyrolysis for waste-derived fuels: a review of reactor performance and product selectivity
Abstract: Designing thermochemical pathways that convert solid waste into value-added fuels is central to resource recovery and circular-material strategies. This review examines pressure-enabled pyrolysis as an alternative to conventional atmospheric pyrolysis for plastics, biomass, and composite wastes. Elevated pressure alters thermodynamic equilibria, transport phenomena, vapor residence time, and radical-reaction pathways, thereby changing product yield and selectivity. Pressurized operation suppresses rapid volatilization and intensifies secondary reactions. At moderate pressures, these effects can favor light hydrocarbons, hydrogen-rich gases, and more stable liquid fuels with reduced wax formation. However, excessive pressure or long vapor confinement may increase tar accumulation and secondary char formation, demonstrating that pressure effects are non-monotonic and strongly dependent on operating conditions. The review compares batch autoclaves, continuous tubular reactors, and auger or moving-bed systems, focusing on heat transfer, solids handling, sealing, and operational stability under severe conditions. It also evaluates in-situ sorbents and catalysts, including CaO, dolomite, HZSM-5 zeolites, and Ni-based materials. Their performance is organized around five interacting factors: thermodynamic equilibrium, contact efficiency, physical integrity, surface chemistry, and halogen management. These mechanisms govern deoxygenation, halogen capture, and in-situ fuel upgrading. A unified framework linking temperature, pressure, and vapor residence time is proposed to guide reactor design and process optimization. Overall, the review integrates reaction mechanisms, reactor configurations, and catalytic/sorbent design to clarify their individual and combined roles in determining product distribution and fuel quality in waste-to-energy systems. Title: p-Toluenesulfonic acid functionalized Fe–Zn MOF@MWCNT mesoporous composite as an efficient electrocatalyst for water splitting
Abstract: Developing efficient bifunctional electrocatalysts is essential for sustainable hydrogen production through water electrolysis. Herein, mesoporous Fe–Zn p-toluenesulfonic acid (PTSA) metal–organic framework (MOF) and multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) nanocomposites were synthesised via a facile solvothermal approach with different MWCNT weight percent (5, 10, and 15 %). The Fe–Zn PTSA@10 % MWCNT exhibited superior bifunctional electrocatalytic performance, requiring overpotentials of −169 mV for HER in 1.0 M H2SO4 and 190 mV for OER in 1.0 M KOH at 10 mA cm−2. The corresponding Tafel slopes were 59 and 106 mV dec−1, respectively, indicating favourable reaction kinetics. Enhanced activity was attributed to the synergistic interaction between Fe–Zn active sites and the conductive MWCNT network, which promotes charge transfer and increases electrochemically accessible active sites. The optimised catalyst also demonstrated excellent electrochemical durability for 25 h, highlighting its potential for efficient water splitting. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Ternary metal oxide engineering of screen-printed electrodes for wearable morphine sensing
Abstract: Reliable, in-situ detection of opioid drugs remains a critical challenge for healthcare, forensic analysis, and public safety. Herein, we report for the first time a morphine sensor based on a newly designed ternary metal oxide (TMO) with the formula of Mg0.50Ni0.25Zn0.25O. The TMO stabilizing six-coordinated Zn-O in rock-salt MgO and NiO matrix by short-range disorder, exhibits excellent sensitivity, selectivity, and long-term stability towards the electrochemical detection of morphine. The TMO-based morphine sensor shows robust performance across variable environments, in particular a two-fold higher sensitivity than the bare SPCE and achieves a limit of detection (LoD) as low as 0.11 μM with a dynamic range of 0.24 − 54.22 μM. By introducing a hydrogel interface to solvate and diffuse solid-state morphine to the TMO-modified flexible sensor electrode, our sensor is further integrated into a small form factor wearable platform capable of in-situ, non-invasive detection of solid-state morphine on surfaces such as skin, showing low sensitivity of 2.56 μA cm2 nmol−1 and LoD of 0.28 nmol cm−2 in the dynamic range of 1− 6 nmol cm−2. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Du S.; Cai W.; Wang Z.; Qiu G.; Li Q.; Wu W.; Cai W.
Title: Multiscale elucidation of the crystallization-condensation competition in CO2-alkane systems for pressurized liquefied natural gas technology
Abstract: The unclear competitive mechanism between CO2 crystallization and condensation of condensable alkanes constitutes a core bottleneck restricting the safe application of pressurized liquefied natural gas (PLNG) technology. In this work, the pressured low‑temperature visualization experiments are tightly combined with multi‑scale computational simulations (density functional theory (DFT) / molecular dynamics (MD). By using C2H6 to represent condensable alkanes in natural gas, this study systematically reveals, for the first time, the phase-change coupling mechanism under conditions with CO2 concentrations of 0.03–0.4 and C2H6 concentrations predominantly ranging from 0.1 to 0.15. It is found that the phase-change priority exhibits a concentration-dependent inversion. At the tested high-CO2-concentration compositions (0.3–0.4), CO2 crystallizes preferentially, whereas at medium-to-low CO2 concentrations (0.03–0.2), C2H6 condenses first. The condensed C2H6 liquid suppresses CO2 crystallization via strong solvation effects, and higher C2H6 concentrations lead to lower CO2 crystallization temperature. At low temperature, the reduction in dissolved‑state CO2 content and the increase in dissolution kinetic resistance drive CO2 precipitation from the condensate and facilitate crystal growth. This work elucidates, for the first time, the thermodynamic‑kinetic principles governing the phase‑change competition between CO2 and alkanes. It provides potential mechanistic insights for the anti‑blockage design of PLNG low‑temperature heat exchangers, offers new microscopic understanding of multiphase competitive behaviors in CO2‑alkane systems, and bears important guiding significance for the development of low‑temperature carbon‑capture technologies in natural gas liquefaction processes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhao K.; Dou Z.; Zhao Z.; Bai S.; Sun K.
Title: Morphological characteristics of soot from a heavy-duty non-road diesel engine under lean combustion at various operating conditions
Abstract: This study investigates the influence of operating condition parameters on the structural morphology of soot in a heavy-duty non-road diesel engine. Engine operating conditions were designed focusing on temperature and turbulence intensity, with the excess air coefficient for all operating points being greater than 1.7. Soot sampling was conducted upstream of the diesel particulate filter using a dilution sampling system, and the structural characteristics were analyzed via transmission electron microscopy. The analysis methodology relied on statistical data analysis and image fitting, and the concept of the “soot aggregate control volume” was further proposed. Statistical data indicate that, across the operating conditions investigated, the fractal dimension of soot aggregates ranges from 1.746 to 1.912. The primary particle diameter, maximum aggregate length, number of primary particles, and control volume density all follow log-normal distributions, with geometric mean ranges of 21.26 ∼ 25.53 nm, 1.07 ∼ 2.10 μm, 565 ∼ 3356, and 20.74 ∼ 47.82 kg/m3, respectively. In contrast, the control volume flatness and projected porosity conform to normal distributions, with arithmetic mean ranges of 0.54 ∼ 0.69 and 0.52 ∼ 0.68, respectively. Analysis reveals that increases in both in-cylinder combustion temperature and turbulence intensity reduce the mean primary particle diameter; moreover, elevated combustion temperature also leads to decreases in both the maximum aggregate length and the number of primary particles. However, as turbulence intensity increases, the maximum aggregate length, number of primary particles, flatness ratio, and control volume density each exhibit a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing. This suggests that the morphology of the soot control volume undergoes an evolution from an initial enlargement and fluffy structure toward a more elongated, branched configuration.These experimental results reveal the correlation between diesel engine operating parameters and soot structural morphology. Authors: Zhang W.; Zhao B.; Qin L.; Chen W.; Han J.
Title: A DFT study on the SO2-resistant mechanism of Hg0 oxidation over Fe-doped OMS-2
Abstract: Sulfur dioxide poisoning remains a critical challenge for mercury oxidation over manganese-based catalysts in coal-fired flue gas. Fe-doped OMS-2 catalysts exhibit excellent Hg0 oxidation activity under high concentration SO2 conditions in our previous experiment. However, the underlying mechanism responsible for their mercury removal and sulfur resistance remains unclear. In this study, focusing on the Fe-OMS-2(110) surface, both the mercury removal and sulfur resistance mechanisms of mercury oxidation over Fe-OMS-2 were systematically investigated through density functional theory calculations. The results indicate that Fe doping generates spatially differentiated Fe and Mn functional centers on the Fe-OMS-2(110) surface. The Fe sites can preferentially capture SO2 with an adsorption energy of −1.818 eV, while Mn sites exhibit stronger O2 activation and Hg0 oxidation capabilities. Specifically, the rate-limiting step for O2 dissociation at the distal Mn2 site is O–O bond cleavage, with an energy barrier of 1.07 eV. Under sulfur-containing conditions, SO2 and its oxidation product SO3 participate in the conversion of Hg0 into HgSO4 at the Mn2 site. which lowers the product-release barrier relative to the HgO pathway. Overall, the superior mercury removal and sulfur resistance performance of Fe-OMS-2 arises from the spatially differentiated functions of Fe and Mn centers, with Fe sites preferentially capturing SO2 and Mn sites facilitating Hg0 oxidation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yuan B.; Huang W.; Li J.; Chen Y.; Wu J.; Wang Y.; Gu J.; Hu Q.; Wang Z.; Qi S.; Wu Z.
Title: Planar gamma radiation field reconstruction from ultra-sparse measurements using a measurement-consistent dual-attention residual U-Net
Abstract: Reconstruction of planar gamma dose-rate fields from ultra-sparse measurements is important for decommissioning inspection, emergency response, and routine radiation surveillance. This work presents DARU-Net, an application-specific residual U-Net that combines squeeze-and-excitation channel attention, attention-gated skip connections, and deep supervision. A two-channel input represents the sparse dose-rate map and its sampling mask, while a measurement-consistency loss enforces agreement at observed locations. Training data were generated with a simplified point-kernel model for three scenarios: a single unshielded source, multiple unshielded sources, and multiple shielded sources, giving 30,000 samples. At a 1% sampling rate, DARU-Net achieved mean absolute errors of 1.60×10−5, 3.68×10−5, and 4.27×10−4 for the three scenarios, with corresponding R2 values of 0.9831, 0.9805, and 0.9216. Across sampling rates from 0.5% to 10%, the median R2 remained above 0.97, and under relative measurement errors of 5%–30%, R2 and FAC2 were 0.9942 ± 0.0017 and 99.23%±0.45%, respectively. Ablation reduced the mean absolute percentage error from 7.90% to 2.88%. The unmeasured-region accuracy varied by less than 0.001 in R2 over more than an order of magnitude of the measurement-consistency weight, whereas grid and serpentine-trajectory sampling reduced it by at most 0.01 relative to random sampling. A dual-source field experiment, for which a simulation dataset matching the experimental scale was generated and the network retrained, yielded Pearson’s R=0.9546, RMSE = 81.9 nSv/h, and MAE = 42.6 nSv/h. The results support the feasibility of measurement-consistent deep reconstruction for fixed-height gamma dose-rate mapping, while the simplified transport model that neglects the buildup factor and the small-scale experiment define the present scope of validation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yang Y.; Li K.; Gao Y.; Li Q.; Cai X.; Wang J.; Huang Z.
Title: Study on swirl combustion characteristics of iron particles in a thermal atmosphere generated by methane combustion
Abstract: As a zero-carbon fuel, iron combustion in burners suffered from issues such as incomplete combustion. The use of swirl combustion was found to improve the combustion performance and enable more efficient combustion of iron particles. In this study, the combustion characteristics of iron swirl flames in a methane-derived thermal atmosphere were investigated using a high-speed camera, thermal couples, and thermal radiometers. Experimental results showed that the iron particles exhibited a discrete combustion state, and combustion persisted until the iron particles detached from the methane flame, resulting in an increase in the overall flame length. The overall combustion efficiency of the iron particles exceeded 90%, indicating good combustion performance. The iron combustion under different methane flow rates was investigated. It was found that increasing the methane flow rate promoted iron particle combustion, manifested as an increase in self-luminescent particles and enhanced flame thermal radiation. The apparent axial equivalent ignition delay time of the iron particles prolonged. When the methane flow rate was increased from 3.5 L/min to 4.5 L/min, the combustion efficiency increased by 3.5%. Furthermore, the combustion behavior of iron particles under different swirl numbers was investigated. It was found that as the swirl number increased, the dark region related to the recirculation zone gradually grew, and the apparent axial equivalent ignition delay time exhibited a shortening trend. However, an increase in the swirl number did not contribute to the improvement of the overall combustion efficiency of the iron particles. The results indicated that the high-temperature environment generated by methane combustion was the main factor affecting the swirl combustion performance of iron particles. Copyright © 2026. Authors: Gong Y.; Huang X.; Nong H.; Ren H.; Huang Y.; Tang Q.; Zhang K.; Liao X.
Title: A G4-nanotweezer/DNA tetrahedron-confined dual-mode ECL/SERS biosensor for ultrasensitive rabies viral RNA detection via CRISPR-Cas12a-regulated hemin switching
Abstract: Reliable detection of low-abundance rabies viral RNA (RABV RNA) requires sensitive readouts that tolerate interfacial and matrix-associated signal variation. We developed a DNA tetrahedron-confined G4-nanotweezer biosensor combining electrochemiluminescence (ECL) and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). A Ti3C2/CsPbBr3@PDA@AuNPs nanocomposite (PAM) provided the dual-mode transducing interface, with hemin serving as both an ECL-modulating species and a SERS reporter. CsPbBr3 served as the ECL emitter, PDA improved interfacial stability, AuNPs provided SERS hotspots and DNA anchoring sites, and Ti3C2 acted as a conductive scaffold. Without target RNA, the bridging strand (ST) promoted a closed G4/hemin configuration, producing high SERS and low ECL signals. RABV RNA-triggered binding-induced isothermal amplification generated single-stranded DNA activators for CRISPR-Cas12a. Subsequent ST cleavage prevented nanotweezer closure and reduced interfacial hemin enrichment, producing an ECL-on/SERS-off response. Control experiments linked hemin-associated ECL modulation to the interfacial configuration without establishing a unique microscopic quenching pathway. The ratiometric signal R = IECL/ISERS enabled quantification over 1 aM to 50 fM. Additional low-concentration calibration yielded an estimated detection limit of 0.0675 aM by blank-threshold inverse prediction, extrapolated below the lowest measured nonzero standard of 0.10 aM. At 10 fM, matched-channel comparisons gave ratiometric relative standard deviations of 2.49% for ten successive readings and 2.87% across six independently prepared electrodes. In tenfold-diluted human serum at 10 fM, the ratio showed an 8.20% absolute deviation from phosphate-buffered saline, indicating partial matrix-effect compensation. This shared-reporter architecture links programmable DNA switching to complementary optical readouts for sensitive ratiometric viral RNA analysis. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: GFNet: Gated feature fusion network for underwater object detection
Abstract: Underwater images frequently suffer from color distortion, low contrast, and haze-like blur caused by light absorption and scattering in water. These degradations introduce inconsistent signal quality across feature scales, giving rise to cross-scale semantic competition during multi-scale fusion in feature pyramid networks, where heterogeneous feature streams compete unevenly and impair detection performance. To mitigate this issue, we propose a Gated Feature Fusion Network (GFNet) comprising two complementary modules: the Gate-guided Feature Fusion Module (GFFM) and the Multi-scale Feature Supplement Module (MFSM). The GFFM employs a Softmax-based competitive gating mechanism to perform instance-adaptive feature selection, dynamically regulating the relative contributions of multi-source features based on their discriminative statistics under degraded conditions. The MFSM aggregates multi-level backbone features into a structured cross-scale representation via dimensional modeling and injects supplementary semantics into the high-resolution branch, improving small-object representation without modifying the backbone architecture. Experiments on the URPC2020 and UTDAC2020 benchmarks demonstrate that GFNet consistently improves detection accuracy over FPN-based baselines, with notable gains for small-object and high-IoU metrics. The modular design facilitates integration into various mainstream detection frameworks with moderate computational overhead. Authors: Báthori A.-M.; Cormos C.-C.
Title: Energy and exergy assessment of an agricultural waste biomass-to-liquid (BtL) plant based on low-temperature iron-based Fischer-Tropsch synthesis
Abstract: Biomass-to-liquid conversion is a promising route for producing biomass-derived synthetic liquid fuels by integrating biomass gasification and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis. This study presents the thermodynamic assessment of an 18 kt/y liquid fuel capacity production from agricultural waste plant employing low-temperature iron-based Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, with particular focus on energy and exergy performance. The kinetic models for the Fischer-Tropsch and hydrocracking reactors were implemented in Fortran using literature-derived kinetic formulations, explicitly representing C1-C30 hydrocarbon species, and integrated into the overall process flow model. The investigated plant has an overall exergy efficiency of 30.28 % and an energy efficiency of 47.17 %, considering the final fractions of the hydrocarbon species, internal net electricity generation and recovered purified hydrogen. Water-gas shift reactions and pre-combustion CO2 capture were employed for syngas conditioning, achieving specific process CO2 emissions of 128.51 kg CO2/MWh of liquid fuel. The water–gas shift activity of the iron-based catalyst enabled hydrogen self-sufficiency for hydrocracking without external hydrogen input. Sensitivity analyses showed strong coupling between syngas conditioning, Fischer-Tropsch off-gas recycle, and plant energy integration. Title: Effects of main-stage swirl matching on ignition characteristics and large-scale pressure fluctuations in a centrally staged combustor
Abstract: Triple-swirler centrally staged combustors are used in advanced aero-engines to achieve efficient fuel–air mixing and stable combustion over a wide operating range. However, the influence of main-stage swirl direction on ignition characteristics has not been fully clarified. In this study, experiments were conducted to determine the ignition boundaries and examine the transient flame development. The measurements show that differences in droplet-size distribution, spatial spray distribution, and flame-propagation path are closely associated with the observed ignition behavior. Large-scale pressure fluctuations were repeatedly observed during ignition. The ratio of cumulative fluctuation duration to ignition delay time was used to characterize their temporal occupancy during the ignition process. This ratio increased with FAR for both configurations and remained higher for the counter-swirl configuration than for the co-swirl configuration at the ignition boundary, indicating a closer temporal association between large-scale pressure fluctuations and flame development. Compared with the co-swirl configuration, the counter-swirl configuration produced smaller droplets and lower Mie-scattering intensity, providing more favorable conditions for fuel evaporation and mixture preparation. Authors: Zhang T.; Philip Chen C.L.; Luo X.; Yang C.; Li J.
Title: Robust adaptation of visual representations for few-shot class-incremental learning via geometric calibration
Abstract: Although foundation models demonstrate proficiency in visual representation learning, effectively adapting them to Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL) is precarious in realistic visual scenarios. The intersection of data deficiency and erratic visual distortions results in a statistical impasse. This vulnerability is primarily based on the anisotropic characteristics of vision transformers, where slight perturbations can quickly shift embeddings over fragile decision boundaries. To overcome these limitations, Geometric Rectification And Calibration Embedding (GRACE) is proposed as a training-free framework that achieves robust adaptation by intrinsically rectifying the feature space geometry. Departing from computationally expensive active adaptation, GRACE operates through a dual mechanism. First, a power transform acts as a soft truncation to suppress heavy-tailed outliers induced by corruption. Second, a stationary geometric calibration transfers isotropic geometric priors from the abundant base session to novel classes. By constructing a statistically stable and isotropic metric space, this approach ensures that even single-shot class prototypes remain highly reliable against environmental distortions. Extensive experiments on MiniImageNet, CUB200, and CIFAR100 show that GRACE performs significantly better than other methods. Furthermore, tests on CIFAR-100-C and MiniImageNet-C reveal that the framework effectively enhances the few-shot incremental capabilities of the original models under diverse visual corruptions. Finally, by evaluating the approach across different model scales, we demonstrate its broad applicability, showing that the robustness gains are well-preserved when scaling up to larger network backbones. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Chen Y.-T.; Dai X.-J.; Xu X.-Q.; Liu P.; Zhang W.-R.; Liu X.-J.; Wang P.; Gong C.-H.; Yang Y.
Title: Oxygen-vacancy-rich amorphous MnO2@MOF-808 nanozyme for dual-mode colorimetric and smartphone-assisted determination of Sr2+ and H2O2
Abstract: The rapid and specific monitoring of toxic strontium (Sr2+) contamination is critically important yet challenging, as it typically relies on non-portable and expensive instrumentation. Herein, the crystal-phase dependence of MnO2 nanozymes was systematically investigated by in situ growth of five representative polymorphs, α-, β-, γ-, δ- and amorphous (A-) MnO2, onto a Zr-based MOF-808 scaffold. XPS and steady-state kinetics revealed that the dual peroxidase-like (POD) and oxidase-like (OXD) activities are proportional to the Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio and surface oxygen-vacancy density, both of which peaked in A-MnO2@MOF-808. The hierarchically porous MOF-808 framework reinforced the resistance of the amorphous shell to H2O2-induced reductive etching, supporting dual OXD and POD catalytic modes on the same nanozyme platform under independently optimized conditions. Capitalizing on its POD activity, a colorimetric H2O2 assay was first established (LOD = 0.3 μM), simultaneously providing a quantitative validation of the catalytic competence of the platform. Authors: Xing J.; Tang C.; Liu X.; Xiong D.; Huang S.-D.; Ju W.; Lv J.; Qiao Z.
Title: A Composite Path and Answer Self-Scoring reward mechanism for test-time reinforcement learning
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for advancing Large Language Models (LLMs), achieving remarkable performance in complex reasoning domains such as mathematics and code generation. However, current RL methods face a fundamental scalability bottleneck due to their heavy reliance on human-curated preference data or labeled datasets for reward modeling. To overcome this limitation, we explore RL on unlabeled data where models learn autonomously from continuous experience streams. The core challenge in this setting lies in reliable reward estimation without ground-truth supervision. Existing approaches like Test-Time RL address this through self-consistent consensus, but risk reinforcing incorrect pseudo-labels derived from majority voting. We introduce COMPASS (Composite Path and Answer Self-Scoring), a novel test-time reward mechanism that operates without external supervision. COMPASS integrates two complementary components: the Dual-Calibration Answer Reward (DCAR), which stabilizes training by establishing trustworthy pseudo-labels through confidence and credibility calibration, and the Decisive Path Reward (DPR), which directly optimizes the reasoning process quality beyond mere outcome supervision. By jointly reinforcing trustworthy consensus answers and highly decisive reasoning chains, the COMPASS systematically enhances the model's analytical capabilities. Extensive experiments show that COMPASS achieves significant and consistent performance gains across diverse reasoning tasks and model architectures, advancing a more scalable direction for LLMs to learn from continuous experience. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: LIMA-Mamba: A lightweight and distribution-robust Mamba network for PPG-based biometrics
Abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a promising modality for wearable biometric recognition because it enables non-invasive acquisition and contains identity information in pulse morphology and temporal dynamics. However, motion artifacts, physiological variability, sensor placement, and acquisition changes can increase intra-class variation and reduce inter-class separability. The model combines a dual-resolution one-dimensional backbone with parallel identity-aware Mamba encoders to capture fine-grained morphology and long-range dependencies with linear sequence complexity. Key-channel selection performs hard binary gating using a straight-through estimator, while semantic-aware patch refining uses identity-supervised gradient saliency, batch-wise difficulty ranking, and same-identity contextual injection with stop-gradient control. Intra-Class and Inter-Class Margin Learning (ICICML) further regularizes the embedding space. We evaluate LIMA-Mamba on CAPNOBASE, BIDMC, PPG-DaLiA, and PTTP-PPG under a validation-controlled, test-blind protocol with five matched seeds. It achieves the lowest mean EER on all four datasets: 0.46%, 0.96%, 3.89%, and 4.82%, respectively. Title: HCl emission prediction in municipal solid waste incineration using a Transformer–XGBoost hybrid model with deep feature extraction and SHAP-based interpretation
Abstract: Accurate prediction of hydrogen chloride (HCl) emissions plays an important role in efficient control of deacidification systems in municipal solid waste incineration (MSWI) plants. However, accurate prediction remains challenging due to the dynamic nonlinearity, multivariable coupling and time series characteristics of MSWI process. This study proposes a Transformer–XGBoost hybrid model to predict HCl emissions in MSWI process. Firstly, a feature extractor based on Transformer model is designed to capture target-relevant temporal dependencies and complex interactions among process variables, extracting features and generating auxiliary prediction. Subsequently, a weighted feature fusion strategy is introduced to integrate the extracted features with auxiliary prediction result, thereby enhancing the representational capacity of features. Finally, the fused features are input into the XGBoost predictor to predict the HCl emissions at time t + 3. The proposed model is trained, validated, and tested using real industrial data from the MSWI plant. Additionally, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis reveals model behavior and the importance of combustion air distribution and deacidification operating variables to HCl predictions. Comparative experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves optimal prediction performance, with an R2 of 0.974, a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.388 mg/m3, a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.262 mg/m3, and a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) of 8.14 % on the testing set. Authors: Zhu J.; Wang Z.; Chen S.; Jiao L.; Gong G.; Qi J.; Wang H.
Title: Amorphous NiMoP with synergistic Ni–Mo electronic interaction for efficient urea-assisted hydrogen production
Abstract: The development of low-cost, high-efficiency electrocatalysts for energy-saving hydrogen production via urea-assisted water splitting remains a significant challenge. Herein, an amorphous NiMoP electrocatalyst is successfully synthesized on nickel foam (NF) via a one-step electrodeposition method at room temperature. The NiMoP/NF electrode exhibits a unique three-dimensional flower-like nanoflake architecture, providing abundant active sites and facilitating mass transfer. Owing to the synergistic electronic interaction between Ni and Mo, as well as the amorphous structure, NiMoP/NF demonstrates excellent catalytic activity toward hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), and urea oxidation reaction (UOR) in alkaline media. Specifically, NiMoP/NF requires overpotentials of only 224 and 327 mV to achieve 50 mA cm−2 for HER and OER, respectively, and a low potential of 1.358 V for UOR at the same current density. Authors: Deng H.; Wang J.; Yin X.; Min X.
Title: MCP-Net: Multidirectional correlation-propagating network for progressive 3D medical image registration
Abstract: Medical image registration poses unique challenges owing to complex physiological and anatomical property. Pyramid-based methods partially alleviate these difficulties using hierarchical decomposition, yet they only coarsely separate deformation fields across scales, leaving complicate motion patterns inadequately decoupled at each resolution level. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces MCP-Net, a multidirectional correlation-propagating network for progressive 3D medical image registration. It comprises two core components: a multidirectional correlation (MC) estimator that builds multiple motion scenarios across feature subspaces and exploits directional cues to refine correlations, and a correlation propagation mechanism that integrates low-resolution correlation priors with high-resolution MC outputs, jointly forming a comprehensive multi-level correlation representation. Massive experiments on public 3D datasets, including lung CT (NLST), brain MRI (LPBA40, Mindboggle), hippocampus T1-weighted, and multimodal abdomen CT-MR, validate the superior performance of MCP-Net across modalities. Authors: Xia Y.; Jia Y.; Liang Y.; Wu T.; Yang S.; Yang P.; Yang B.; Lei Y.
Title: Oil film cavitation detection of thrust bearings based on acoustic-reflection-driven neural network
Abstract: Cavitation is recognized as a primary cause of lubrication failure in heavily loaded thrust bearings. However, cavitation detection remains a challenge due to the random coupling between cavities and the oil film. Ultrasonic reflection can physically respond to both the oil film and cavities. However, it fails to theoretically decouple these two physical mechanisms during real-time measurement. To address this challenge, a Physical Echo Reconstruction (PER) model is proposed to reconstruct an identical overall echo waveform. Initially, the ultrasonic field within the oil film is discretized to calculate the reflection waves from distinct units of air cavities or oil films. Subsequently, the overall echo is reconstructed by summing all individual reflections. Compared with the Finite Element Method (FEM), the effectiveness of the PER model is validated with a high determination coefficient (R2) exceeding 0.96 and computation time reduced to approximately 0.14% of that required by FEM. Furthermore, a PER‑driven CNN model is constructed to extract both oil film thickness and cavitation fraction simultaneously. This model is characterized by a physics‑informed loss function incorporating the residual between predicted and measured waveforms. Training samples include images of air bubbles and ultrasound signals collected simultaneously from a transparent test rig. Compared with traditional CNNs, the prediction accuracy is boosted from 0.88 to 0.93. Title: Coal gasification fine slag-assisted regeneration of sulfur-poisoned V2O5-WO3/TiO2 catalysts and its mechanism for enhancing NH3-SCR performance

On the other hand, the porous carbon fraction in CGFS also plays a crucial role: it promotes the adsorption of more reactive nitrate species (i.e., nitrite and bridged bidentate nitrate), facilitates the formation of adsorbed oxygen, and enhances the generation of NH4+, thereby synergistically improving deNO x efficiency. Title: CuO/SnO2 p-n heterojunction quantum dots: Enhanced photoelectrochemical properties and photocatalytic degradation of tetracycline hydrochloride
Abstract: Quantum dots (QDs) heterojunction photocatalysts exhibit considerable application potential in antibiotic degradation due to their high charge carrier separation efficiency and extensive specific surface area. Multiple parameters are systematically investigated to optimize photocatalytic performance. Title: Microstructural evolution and oxidation behavior of lignite pretreated in methane-bearing oxygen-deficient atmospheres

Title: Selective laser-induced etching enabled study on geometry and surface structure effects on liquid ammonia flash-boiling in micro-scale nozzles

Title: Local-global stiffness regulation in morphing tensegrity structures considering buckling
Abstract: Morphing tensegrity structures enable variable-stiffness adaptation, wherein the global stiffness is governed by the internal prestress state. While existing studies employ ideal axial truss models, the effects of buckling-induced bending in bars are often neglected or oversimplified. Local bar softening can reshape the global weak-stiffness subspaces and modify the system sensitivity to prestress variations. Buckling influences the global stiffness through mechanical paths depending on the deformation regime. An equivalent axial tangent stiffness captures post-buckling softening under axial-dominant shortening, while the full bending-dominated mode is retained for transverse-deformation driven responses. This work develops a local-global stiffness formulation for morphing tensegrity structures incorporating buckling members. A reduced-order discrete bar model is utilized, which switches between a smooth equivalent axial law and a full discrete element representation based on the prevailing deformation mechanism. From the state-dependent stiffness matrix, weak-stiffness directions are identified via a null-space decomposition. A load projection ratio is introduced to quantify the alignment between external loads and weak modes, serving as a metric to guide prestress redistribution and rest-length adjustments. Studies on a 4-bar tensegrity and its stacked extension demonstrate buckling behavior and validate the projection-guided regulation strategy. Title: NOx emissions in a high pressure non-premixed partially decomposed ammonia fired combustor: effects of decomposition ratio and secondary air staging, and stability-driven deNOx

A reactor network model of the combustor revealed a narrow secondary zone temperature window where NH3 efficiently reduces NO, with thresholds that are NH3/NO ratio dependent. At mid-to-high DCR, NOx exhibited the characteristic non-monotonic behaviour: increasing with DCR and peaking near mid-range values. Mapping of ϕpz showed a monotonic NOx decrease with increasingly rich PZ, but the curve shape depended strongly on secondary air distribution and associated PZ heat losses, which also govern mixing intensity. Title: Temporal regulation of electrolytic H2/O2 gas as a secondary fuel for coke combustion enhancement and heat redistribution in iron ore sintering

Title: Deoxygenation of waste oils and oxygen-containing plastics toward aviation-fuel-range hydrocarbons and sustainable aviation fuel pathways: Recent catalytic advances, industrial progress and future perspectives
Abstract: Driven by the global transition toward low-carbon energy systems and increasing environmental pressures associated with waste accumulation, the valorization of waste-derived carbon resources has attracted growing attention. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deoxygenation −based conversion of these waste feedstocks toward aviation-fuel-range hydrocarbons and potential SAF components, with particular emphasis on reaction pathways, catalyst design strategies, process optimization, and industrial development. Particular attention is given to the deoxygenation pathways of waste oils and oxygen-containing plastics, as well as the effects of catalyst properties, reaction conditions, and feedstock characteristics on product distribution. Furthermore, the current industrial implementation of waste-oil-derived SAF and the emerging potential of waste-plastic-derived aviation-fuel-range hydrocarbons are critically evaluated and compared. Key challenges associated with catalyst stability, feedstock complexity, process scalability, economic competitiveness, and fuel qualification are highlighted, and future perspectives toward efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable deoxygenation technologies are proposed. Authors: Zhou Y.; Shi J.; Luo S.; Zhou T.
Title: Universal Incremental Learning: Mitigating Confusion from inter- and intra-task distribution randomness
Abstract: Existing incremental learning (IL) methods rely on strong assumptions: incoming tasks either introduce exclusively new classes or new domains (i.e., Class IL and Domain IL), or increment by a fixed scale in a class- and domain-agnostic manner (i.e., Versatile IL, VIL). These assumptions severely limit their applicability in dynamic, unpredictable real-world scenarios. In this work, we investigate Universal Incremental Learning (UIL), a more realistic setting where the model has no prior knowledge of which new classes or domains will appear across sequential tasks, nor the scale of these increments within each task. This uncertainty hinders the model's ability to confidently acquire knowledge across varying task distributions and to learn uniformly from imbalanced intra-task distributions. Consequently, UIL introduces a more general IL scenario, where the model must cope with confusion stemming from both inter-task and intra-task distribution randomness. To mitigate both sources of confusion, we propose MiCo, a simple yet effective framework for UIL. At the inter-task level, we employ a multi-objective learning scheme to enforce accurate and deterministic predictions, further enhanced by a direction recalibration module that alleviates conflicting gradient updates. At the intra-task level, we introduce a magnitude recalibration module to address asymmetrical optimization caused by imbalanced class distributions. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that MiCo significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both the proposed UIL and existing VIL scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Jaikaew P.; Qian Y.
Title: DEM investigation of geogrid location effects on the depth-dependent micromechanical behavior of loose railway ballast
Abstract: Railway ballast can remain relatively loose after initial construction, renewal, or maintenance, resulting in increased particle mobility and susceptibility to deformation. Although geogrids can effectively improve ballast stability, how their vertical location governs stress transfer and particle-scale behavior remains insufficiently understood. This study employs three-dimensional discrete element method (DEM) simulations, validated against large-scale triaxial tests and particle-rotation measurements, to investigate the depth-dependent response of loose railway ballast stabilized with geogrids at different elevations. Eleven configurations are examined, comprising an unstabilized specimen and single- and dual-layer geogrid arrangements. The results show that stabilization effectiveness depends strongly on geogrid position relative to the active deformation region. Single-layer geogrids placed near or slightly above the specimen mid-height effectively alter the internal load-transfer path, increasing stress mobilization in the upper and middle zones while reducing stress transmission to the lower zone. For the centrally placed geogrid, particle displacement at 10% axial strain decreased from approximately 25 to 13 mm in the middle zone and from 14 to 7.5 mm in the lower zone relative to the unstabilized specimen. Effective geogrid placement also delays dilation, suppresses lateral deformation, promotes contact-network development, and restricts particle rotation. In contrast, geogrids positioned below or farther from the specimen center interact less effectively with the dominant deformation region and provide weaker restraint. Dual-layer configurations further enhance confinement and stress redistribution when positioned close to the specimen center, but their effectiveness diminishes as the layers move away from the active deformation region. Overall, the results establish a micromechanical link between geogrid location, geogrid mobilization, stress redistribution, and particle kinematics, demonstrating that stabilization efficiency is governed by the interaction between geogrid placement and the dominant deformation zone. These findings provide new micromechanical insight into the role of geogrid location and a mechanistic basis for future track-scale evaluation of geogrid placement in railway ballast. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Chehrmonavari H.; Ahmadabadi A.; Kakaee A.
Author full names: Chehrmonavari, Hamed (57217164764); Ahmadabadi, Ata (60378112800); Kakaee, Amirhasan (10539319500)
Title: Advances in Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI): Synergistic integration of piston bowl geometry, hybridization, and water/ozone injection
Abstract: The growing demand for efficient and clean internal combustion engines (ICEs) emphasizes the importance of disseminating knowledge about alternative fuels, particularly in facilitating transitions within hard-to-abate applications. Among advanced combustion concepts that utilize these fuels, Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) emerges as a prominent candidate. RCCI is characterized by low-temperature combustion (LTC) and is recognized for its intrinsically restrained operating range, with optimal efficiency observed at mid loads, demonstrating superior thermal efficiency relative to comparable LTC strategies. Thus, its commercial adoption faces challenges due to inherent limitations, such as a restricted operating range, combustion instability at extreme loads, and heat transfer losses. While fuel reactivity serves as the primary control mechanism, this review posits that a multi-tiered optimization strategy is essential to address these challenges. The current review critically evaluates three distinct layers of control: (1) Passive Hardware Optimization, where piston bowl geometry is assessed not only for its mixing capabilities but also for managing the balance between heat transfer losses and air utilization, directly affecting CO and HC emissions; (2) System-Level Strategy, which investigates hybridization as a means to decouple engine operation from road demands, thus circumventing low-efficiency zones; and (3) Active Thermo-Kinetic Control, which employs water injection as a combustion stabilizer to reduce pressure rise rates at high loads and ozone addition to enhance ignition reactivity at low loads. By integrating these technologies, this review offers a roadmap for expanding the stable operating range of RCCI to fully realize its potential as a viable powertrain. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Huang X.; Yang H.; Feng R.; Li Y.; Zhu S.; Huang D.
Title: Structural differences of starch-proteolyzed peptide complexes dictate in vitro fermentation behavior: Selective regulation of gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid production
Abstract: This study investigated the influence of distinct multi-scale structured starch-proteolyzed peptide complexes on starch degradation, peptide release, gut microbiota composition, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production during in vitro fermentation. The complex with a loose hydrogen-bond network and low crystallinity (5.87%) fermented rapidly, with rapid peptide release. It enriched the fast-growing Lachnospiraceae NK4A136 group (4.8%), and butanoic acid concentration peaked at 0.49 mmol/L within 24 h. The complex with an amorphous aggregate structure and moderate short-range order (R1047/1022 = 0.69) exhibited partial peptide release. It moderately increased the Bacteroidota (42.3%) and Firmicutes (33.1%), with slightly elevated Bacteroidota and Faecalibacterium. Acetic and propanoic acid production peaked at 24 h (0.08 and 0.19 mmol/L). The complex with a dense V-type crystal structure, high crystallinity (20.44%), and thick layers (16.11 nm) exhibited sustained substrate degradation and slow peptide release. It selectively enriched Roseburia (8.7%), Faecalibacterium (6.2%), and Bifidobacterium (5.3%), increased the Bacteroidota (46.8%), and reduced the Firmicutes (33.1%), lowering the Firmicutes/Bacteroidota ratio to 0.71. It also produced the highest butanoic acid concentration (0.60 mmol/L at 48 h) as well as sustained accumulation of isobutanoic acid and isopentanoic acid. This study would provide a theoretical basis for designing specific multi-scale structured starch-peptide complexes to selectively regulate the gut microbiota and SCFAs production. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yang J.; Li Y.; Cheng Y.; Wang X.; Zhang L.; Zhang H.; Yu Z.; Ni D.; Zhang J.; Zhang D.; Liang P.
Title: Hierarchical dual-branch CNN–Transformer fusion for joint discrimination of white tea types and production years from near-infrared spectra
Abstract: Rapid, product-based verification of white tea type and production year is important for label authentication and market supervision. Near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy provides fast, reagent-saving chemical fingerprints and is well suited to this task. This study aimed to develop a unified NIR method for simultaneously identifying three white tea types and six production years, forming an 18-class joint discrimination task, and to clarify the spectral and physicochemical basis of classification. NIR spectra were collected from Shoumei, Baimudan, and Baihao Yinzhen produced in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, and 2024, forming 18 joint classes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first NIR study to jointly resolve these type and production-year labels within a single classification task. To address this joint task, we developed a task-specific hierarchical dual-branch CNN–Transformer framework that integrated Min–Max and SNV–SG views from the same FT-NIR measurement through a shared convolutional backbone, a parallel CNN branch, and a six-segment local–global Transformer branch, followed by decision-level fusion. Unlike CNN-based tea models, Transformer-based spectral models for grain, drug, or protein spectra, NIRS-based origin traceability, transfer-learning tea classification, multispectral fusion, or SERS-based vintage/grade evaluation, this framework jointly addresses type and production year within one NIR framework and uses two views from the same measurement rather than fusing heterogeneous signals. Baseline comparisons, ablation experiments, spectral-segment occlusion, and physicochemical correlation analyses were conducted. The model achieved 99.17% test accuracy and 99.15% Macro-F1, with accuracies of 97.5% for Shoumei and 100% for Baimudan and Baihao Yinzhen. Macro-F1 exceeded the best baseline by 2.56 percentage points, and removing the CNN branch produced the largest performance loss. These results indicate that the joint task benefits from both local spectral detail and cross-segment integration, which single-branch or single-view models cannot fully capture. Spectral-segment importance and most physicochemical trajectories were tea-type-dependent, whereas gallic acid increased with nominal storage duration across all three types. These type-dependent patterns indicate that a shared chemical trend, such as increasing gallic acid, does not translate into a universal spectral marker, supporting the need for an integrated multisegment NIR fingerprint. These findings demonstrate that the proposed task-specific dual-view, dual-branch framework with integrated multisegment NIR fingerprints provides a promising approach for rapid verification of white tea type and production-year labels under controlled conditions, offering a product-based complement to production and distribution records for market supervision. Authors: Qi G.; Chen C.; He Y.; Sun J.; Li X.; Lu M.-H.
Title: Deep indentation behavior of soft materials under axisymmetric power-law indenters
Abstract: Deep indentation of soft materials is common in biological and engineering systems, yet how indenter geometry, material nonlinearity, and interfacial conditions collectively govern the transition from shallow to deep indentation remains incompletely understood. Here, we experimentally investigate the large-deformation indentation of soft materials using axisymmetric power-law indenters with systematically varied tip geometries. The force–depth response evolves through three regimes: a geometry-dominated linear-elastic regime, a transition regime with a non-monotonic local force–depth exponent, and a deep parabolic regime approaching F∼Ed2. In the deep-indentation regime, normalization by Ed2 reveals that the response is nearly insensitive to the power-law shape exponent, whereas the parabolic indentation coefficient is strongly correlated with the Ogden strain-hardening parameter α . Moreover, contact-surface observations and DIC measurements reveal pronounced sink-in and lateral material flow during deep indentation. The deformation field becomes nearly insensitive to indenter geometry, while stress concentration shifts toward the indenter sidewalls and shear deformation becomes increasingly pronounced. Together with dimensional analysis, these observations provide a physical interpretation of the approximately quadratic response. In addition, interfacial friction has little effect on the shallow-indentation response but increases the force at large depths and markedly alters the critical penetration behavior. Nevertheless, the near-quadratic scaling remains robust. These findings provide new physical insight into the large-deformation mechanics of soft materials under deep indentation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Jia W.; Liu X.; Li S.; Li S.; Sun C.; Zhao Y.; Lu W.; Cao Y.; Li X.; Fang Y.
Title: Comparative study on the extraction and fibrillization properties of whey protein from cow, buffalo, goat and camel
Abstract: Whey protein from different milk sources has evolved from by-product into commercially important ingredient of food industry, yet its functional properties (such as fibrillization) remain insufficiently compared. This study extracted and purified whey protein from cow, buffalo, goat and camel milk, and systematically compared their physicochemical properties, fibrillization behavior and fibril structure and functions. Pasteurization better preserved whey protein extractability than high-temperature sterilization, and pH 4.1 was identified as a common casein precipitation condition. Cow, buffalo and goat whey protein mainly comprised β-lactoglobulin and α-lactalbumin, whereas camel whey protein naturally lacked β-lactoglobulin. Buffalo and goat whey protein fibrils exhibited morphological features, assembly patterns and functional properties similar to those of cow whey protein fibrils, with fibrillization accompanied by conformational transitions from random coil/α-helix to ordered β-sheet. In contrast, camel whey protein failed to form fibrils under the same conditions, suggesting that β-lactoglobulin is the main component involved in fibrillization under applied conditions (90°C, pH 2). This study reveals the high similarity among cow, buffalo and goat whey protein fibrils in structure and functions, and highlights the species-specific composition of camel whey protein. These findings provide a theoretical basis for high-value utilization of specialty whey protein. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Zheng, Yuqiao (53867664800); Dong, Fugang (57219710394); Cao, Yongyong (58059170100); Wei, Jianfeng (58836820700); Shi, Chenglong (58745196000)
Title: A piezoelectric energy harvester integrating large-amplitude excitation conversion and passive directional adaptability
Abstract: In the ultra-low-frequency, large-amplitude, and multi-directional vibration environment of wind turbines, cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvesters are prone to structural damage induced by large-amplitude excitation, and their unidirectional sensitivity also limits the ability to adapt to multi-directional vibrations. This work proposes an L-shaped slot piezoelectric energy harvester (LS-PEH) that integrates large-amplitude excitation conversion and passive directional adaptability. Large-amplitude excitation conversion and passive directional adaptability are achieved by an L-shaped slot mechanism. Magnetic coupling enhances the ultra-low-frequency electrical output, whereas stopper beams constrain excessive piezoelectric beam displacement. Based on Lagrange's equations, dynamic models of the L-shaped slot mechanism and the piezoelectric substructure are established and experimentally validated. Numerical results show that the directional response level of the L-shaped slot mechanism is regulated by the excitation direction and the magnetic force within the slot, whereas the excitation conversion performance of the mechanism is determined by the excitation frequency and direction. Dynamic bifurcation analysis reveals that the constraint imposed by the stopper beams suppresses excessive displacement of the piezoelectric beam and limits the expansion of complex nonlinear motion regions. Under the synergistic effects of excitation conversion by the L-shaped slot mechanism, magnetic-coupling enhancement, and amplitude truncation by the stopper beams, the LS-PEH reaches a peak output power of 0.97 mW, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed configuration for ultra-low-frequency, large-amplitude, and multi-directional vibration energy harvesting. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS
