UV–visible and fluorescence spectroscopy showed the characteristic photophysical properties of the porphyrin chromophore, with fluorescence quantum yields of 0.02 and 0.03 for MNP-PEI and MNP-SPM, respectively. Both conjugates generated singlet molecular oxygen and promoted superoxide anion radical formation under irradiation. In PDI assays against Staphylococcus aureus , both materials exhibited strong antibacterial activity, with MNP-PEI achieving complete eradication after 30 min of white-light exposure. In addition, MNP-PEI produced a 2.7 log reduction in the viability of Escherichia coli under the same irradiation conditions. The photoinactivation efficiency was retained over three consecutive reuse cycles. Authors: Su C.; Xie Y.; Xu Z.; Cheng H.; Qin J.; Liu J.; Zhu J.; Liu X.; Liu H.
Title: Numerical investigation of flammable cloud evolution and spatiotemporal hazard persistence in a marine engine room
Abstract: Hydrogen leakage in tightly enclosed and geometrically complex marine engine rooms poses a critical safety challenge for hydrogen-fueled ships, where combustible mixtures may persist near potential ignition sources. Existing studies have mainly focused on concentration distribution, ventilation performance, or sensor response, while the coupling between flammable-cloud evolution and local exposure near high-temperature components remains insufficiently quantified. In this study, a three-dimensional transient computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model of a marine engine room with the main internal equipment retained was developed. A small-hole pipeline leakage source was introduced using a compressible-gas source-term model, and the release, source-isolation, and ventilation-removal stages were analyzed. The assessment combined the flammable-cloud volume ( Vflam ), the duration of exposure above the lower flammability limit (LFL), and the first arrival time to the LFL near potential ignition sources to distinguish compartment-scale cloud development from local hot-surface exposure. The results show that leakage height produced a non-monotonic response governed by local equipment blockage, with an intermediate-height leakage case generating the largest peak Vflam among the height cases. Higher initial pipeline pressure and ambient temperature enlarged the flammable cloud through increased release intensity and thermal expansion, respectively, whereas stronger ventilation reduced the global cloud volume but did not uniformly suppress local above-LFL exposure. The integrated comparison further shows that the largest flammable cloud does not necessarily correspond to the earliest local LFL arrival. These findings provide a basis for cloud-scale ventilation control, targeted monitoring, and local protection of high-temperature regions in hydrogen-fueled marine engine rooms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Wet gas measurement method of inner cone based on phase-isolation
Abstract: Wet gas is a common gas–liquid two-phase flow encountered during oil and gas production, transportation, and processing. Accurate measurement of gas and liquid flow rates is important for production management, economic evaluation, and process optimization; however, liquid-phase measurement remains challenging because of the strong dependence on upstream flow patterns. This study proposes a dual-parameter wet-gas measurement device consisting of a vane swirler and an inner cone. The swirler reorganizes the incoming gas–liquid flow into a gas-core/liquid-film phase-isolation state. Under this condition, radial and axial pressure-tapping configurations were investigated. The relationships among the radial differential-pressure ratio W, axial differential-pressure ratio M, gas Froude number Frg, over-reading coefficient Φ, and liquid-gas mass flow ratio were analyzed. Based on these relationships, radial and axial wet gas flow measurement models were developed and experimentally evaluated. The results showed that the radial pressure-tapping model provided better predictive performance than the axial model. Within the experimentally validated range of XLM = 0–0.30 and Frg = 0.664–2.325, the radial method achieved relative errors within ±3% for the gas-phase flow rate and ±10% for the liquid-phase flow rate. The applicability of the proposed correlations beyond the investigated operating range requires further experimental validation. The proposed method provides a feasible approach for wet-gas flow measurement in oilfield production. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Kim D.; Yang I.
Title: The decomposition of primes in nonabelian extensions of Heisenberg type and an analogue of Euler's criterion
Abstract: For primes p and ℓ such that ℓ divides p−1, Hirano and Morishita constructed a nonabelian Galois extension of the function field Fp(t) whose degree is ℓ3 and Galois group is of Heisenberg type. Here we analyze how primes of degree one decompose in such extensions. It amounts to investigating the decomposition of the principal ideal (t−a) for a∈Fp−{0,1} and our main result determines when it decomposes completely in terms of an explicit polynomial in a . It is reminiscent of Euler's criterion. The proof relies on both the group structure of the mod- ℓ Heisenberg group and the arithmetic of field extensions. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Das R.; Das S.
Title: Far-field surface and acoustic-gravity wave profiles from vertical motion of an ocean floor block of arbitrary surface
Abstract: Surface and acoustic-gravity waves (AGWs) generated by arbitrary but separable spatiotemporal motion of the ocean floor, mimicking a complex, non-planar submarine fault with a non-uniform slip rate, are analytically studied using linearized water-wave theory for a mildly compressible ocean. The arbitrary motion-induced bathymetry is approximated using slanted blocks, each of which yields a boundary value problem solved using the double Fourier transformation technique. The complete solution is obtained by superposing the solutions of the individual blocks. The stationary phase approximation is applied to obtain the far-field properties of the tsunami mode, AGWs, and surface pressure. The model is validated against results from the literature. Four test cases of complex faults are considered for the study. A graphical error analysis with respect to the number of discretization points is performed to assess solution convergence. The numerical computations reveal that fault geometry significantly influences wave characteristics, including pulse formation, packet broadening, and directional asymmetry. A comparison of the dimensionless amplitudes of surface and bottom pressure shows that bottom pressure is substantially larger, suggesting its utility for early detection. The far-field spectral energy distribution shows distinct signatures of gravity and AGW modes. The first AGW mode dominates at high frequencies, while the pure gravity mode controls the low-frequency range. Bottom profile variations modify spectral minima and oscillatory patterns. This study establishes that both fault complexity and ocean compressibility fundamentally alter tsunami characteristics, necessitating the use of arbitrary motion models for reliable hazard assessment. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Transient large amplitude internal waves from the framework of ‘long wave-short wave’ resonance
Abstract: The resonance among long waves and short waves for a stratified fluid with a region of rapid density change is studied theoretically. The sharply peaked buoyancy frequency profile is modeled by the square of the hyperbolic secant. The criterion of resonance is that the phase speed of the long wave must match the group velocity of the short wave. For a given long wave, this configuration permits resonance with many lower order short wave modes. The eigenfunctions of the Taylor-Goldstein equation are calculated for internal wave modes 1 through 12. Coefficients of the long wave-short wave evolution system are computed explicitly. The known rogue wave solution of such equations is taken as a measure for displacement amplitude in extreme events. The resonant short-wave number depends nonmonotonically on the short-wave mode number. More importantly, the amplitudes of the various possible rogue wave modes display a wide range of variations. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Toward 30%-efficient CdZnTe/perovskite tandem solar cells: stable device architectures explored via SCAPS-1D simulation

Accordingly, a regular (n-i-p) configuration was adopted for the PVK bottom subcell. By jointly optimizing individual layer thicknesses and the absorber layer defect density, the n-i-p PVK subcell achieved a PCE of 22.67%. Title: AnoCalib: Unified anomaly-aware feature calibration for zero-shot industrial anomaly detection
Abstract: Zero-shot industrial anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to localize industrial defects without requiring training data from target domains. Its performance hinges on powerful vision foundation models (VFMs), coupled with scoring mechanisms that measure either cross-image region discrepancy (e.g., MuSc) or image-text similarity (e.g., WinCLIP). These scoring strategies ultimately depend on the extent to which VFM features can discriminate anomalies from normal ones. However, VFMs are primarily optimized for semantic recognition of common object categories, and they lack the inherent capability to perceive and represent the wide variety of visual anomalies existing in industrial scenarios. To address this issue, we propose Anomaly-aware Feature Calibration, short for AnoCalib, a plug-and-play and test-time learnable method for boosting ZSAD via enhanced normal-abnormal discrimination. It integrates three key parts: (i) a test-time trainable adapter that injects anomaly awareness into VFMs; (ii) a calibration loss with three objectives, namely, aligning features with prompts, distinguishing different anomalies, and enhancing hard-sample discriminability; (iii) a label-free cold-start strategy that automatically selects pseudo-normal images and synthesizes pseudo-anomalies for test-time training. Extensive experiments show AnoCalib consistently improves multiple ZSAD frameworks, raising F1 and AUPRO by 22.9% and 11.0% for AnomalyCLIP, and by 4.4% and 1.4% for MuSc. Title: Two-dimensional LBM–Lagrangian mesoscopic modelling of sparse particle-laden flow around a circular cylinder: Particle deposition and wake evolution
Abstract: Mine air-conditioning condensers are commonly exposed to dust-laden airflow, and particle deposition on tube and fin surfaces can deteriorate heat dissipation, increase flow resistance and threaten the safe operation of underground thermal-control systems. To clarify the relation among carrier flow, sparse particle transport and numerically represented wall deposition near condenser-tube-like obstacles, this study develops a two-dimensional LBM–Lagrangian mesoscopic model for sparse particle-laden flow around a circular cylinder. The carrier flow is solved using a D2Q9 lattice Boltzmann formulation, whereas particle motion is described by a Lagrangian tracking model with a geometric wall-capture rule and a numerical surface-accumulation procedure. The particle volume fraction is evaluated from a site-specific mine-air dust concentration, confirming an ultra-sparse suspended phase for which direct particle-to-fluid momentum feedback can be neglected. Separately, the accumulated numerical height can enlarge the solid mask and thereby modify subsequent carrier-flow steps. The model is assessed against reported clean-cylinder drag coefficients at Reynolds numbers of 50–150, and the observed discrepancies are treated as quantitative accuracy bounds. The results indicate a transition from a comparatively symmetric wake at Re = 50 to an unsteady Kármán-vortex-dominated wake at Re = 150. This transition governs point-parcel migration, producing predominantly windward capture at moderate Reynolds numbers and broader lateral and leeward contact distributions at higher Reynolds numbers. Because direct suspended-particle momentum feedback is not implemented and the numerical morphology variable is not calibrated to physical deposit thickness or mass, the analysis is limited to carrier-wake evolution, parcel transport and threshold-induced boundary modification; no quantitative long-term fouling rate or deposition-induced drag increment is inferred. Title: Microenvironment-aware adversarial refinement with semantic coupling for predicting mutational effects on protein–protein interactions
Abstract: Protein–protein interactions play a crucial role in many biological processes, making accurate prediction of protein–protein binding affinity changes (ΔΔG) caused by amino acid mutations. While deep learning-based intelligent prediction methods have made some progress in recent years, they still face three key challenges: (1) neglect of cross-scale semantic coupling; (2) insufficient reliability of microenvironment reconstruction; (3) heavy computational burdens. To address these issues, we propose MARS-DDG, a microenvironment-aware adversarial refinement framework with a mixed-semantic codebook for protein complex ΔΔG prediction. MARS-DDG constructs mutation-centered local patches and uses a mixed-semantic codebook to jointly organize residue-type, local torsional conformation, and spatial conformation in a unified latent space, enabling multi-scale semantic fusion for mutation pattern representation. Hierarchical adversarial refinement is further introduced to improve the reliability of reconstructed microenvironment representations. The refined semantic codes are then injected as prompts into wild-type and mutant complex encoders to guide downstream ΔΔG prediction. Title: Metamaterial-based wearable nanosensor for continuous cardiovascular health monitoring

Title: A robust MoS2 catalyst engineered via two-step K modification strategy for the high‑temperature reverse water‑gas shift reaction

Title: Content of free amino acids and biogenic amines during the maturation of Casín cheese: Feasibility of using VIS-NIRS spectroscopy for their quantification

Title: Bimetallic nanoflower MOF-derived magnetic porous carbon for extraction and quantitative analysis of phthalate esters in environmental water samples

Title: Fast anchor-based multi-view clustering via collaborative learning
Abstract: Anchor-based methods improve the scalability of multi-view clustering by constructing anchor graphs. However, existing methods often fail to adequately capture intra-view local structures and inter-view complementary information. Specifically, the ℓ1,2-norm regularization enhances intra-view local structure preservation by suppressing redundant anchor connections, while the adaptive weighted graph fusion strategy dynamically assigns view-specific weights according to their contributions to exploit inter-view complementary information. The anchor graphs and consensus representation mutually guide each other. Title: From pore-scale mechanisms to hydraulic-work analysis: a microfluidic study of CO2-EOR via WAG, FWAG, and PWAG
Abstract: To mitigate severe gas channeling and poor volumetric sweep during CO2 flooding in low-permeability conglomerate reservoirs, WAG and its enhanced variants, FWAG and PWAG, are widely used for mobility control. We introduce cumulative hydraulic work, Wh, calculated by integrating the differential pressure over the injected volume, to quantify the magnitude and persistence of hydraulic resistance during each displacement stage. CO2-WAG improves conformance through intermittent liquid-phase snap-off and a transient Jamin effect, but the resistance decays as water slugs become unstable. CO2-FWAG provides more persistent resistance through foam-lamella regeneration and restructuring, while independently measured AOS-induced oil–water IFT reduction at 65 °C and ambient pressure is consistent with the observed breakup and dispersion of larger remaining-oil bodies. Title: Co-combustion of anthracite with raw biomass and flue-gas-torrefied biomass: Kinetic characteristics, pollutant release and ash transformation behaviors

Title: Numerical investigation of premixed hydrogen/air combustion in a stepped micro planar combustor with splitter plate
Abstract: A stepped micro planar combustor incorporating a splitter plate is proposed to improve the thermal performance of micro-thermophotovoltaic (MTPV) systems. Title: Three-dimensional CFD simulation of non-premixed combustion in a full-scale cement rotary kiln: effects of primary air ratio on NOx and CO emissions
Abstract: Cement rotary kilns face critical challenges in balancing carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions. Title: A numerical framework for hot spot formation on railway wheels during tread braking
Abstract: Thermo-elastic instability (TEI) is widely recognized as the underlying mechanism for hot spot formation on tread-braked railway wheels. However, existing TEI models are largely limited to disc brakes with rectangular cross-sections and structured meshes, making them inadequate for wheel–brake shoe systems with complex geometries. This study presents a comprehensive numerical framework based on the Galerkin finite element method and isoparametric transformation, which preliminary enables the prediction on the quantitative correlation between critical speed and hot spots on the tread-braked wheels. The framework integrates a thermo-elastic contact solution extended from idealized planar interfaces to realistic curved contact surfaces through a local coordinate transformation that accommodates arbitrary tread profiles, an intermittent contact modification accounting for the arc length of the brake shoe, and comprehensive field thermal boundary conditions including convection (air/rain), radiation, and the rail chill effect, which have been largely overlooked in previous TEI analyses. The results reveal a nonlinear variation in critical speed for the tread brake system, with one or two minimum values depending on the wheel geometry. Structural parameters primarily govern the critical speed for low-order hot spots, while rail chill effectively increases the critical speed for medium-order hot spots. Title: Cross-representation hierarchical alignment and refinement model for point cloud completion
Abstract: Point cloud completion is a fundamental task aiming to recover complete and structurally coherent shapes from sparse observations. Existing methods often rely on point-wise coordinate regression or loosely coupled cross-representation fusion, leading to redundant feature assignment and degraded recovery of fine-grained structures under severe occlusion. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Cross-representation Hierarchical Alignment and Refinement Model (CHARM) for high-fidelity point cloud completion. CHARM first generates self-augmented multi-view depth observations from controllable virtual viewpoints to enrich structural priors without requiring external images. It then introduces a cross-representation alignment mechanism that utilizes geometry-aware view weighting to establish balanced and precise structural correspondences between visual priors and 3D geometric representations. Building upon this initial structural scaffold, the Hierarchical Shape Refinement Module (HSRM) progressively refines the reconstructed surface through a multi-stage coordinate deformation pipeline. By integrating anisotropic vector-field guidance, cross-domain detail retrieval, and localized confidence gated fusion, the network adaptively harmonizes macroscopical shape priors with local geometric observations. This design effectively eliminates feature collapse, preserves global topological consistency, and enhances local detail recovery. Title: Low-frequency guided region-to-pixel refinement network for multimodal building damage assessment
Abstract: Disasters can cause damage to buildings and inflict catastrophic losses on human life and property. To achieve all-weather and all-day responses, multimodal building damage assessment (BDA) using pre-event optical and post-event synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images has become a pivotal research direction. Current methods mainly focus on designing and improving nonlinear comparison operators to analyze multimodal features for damage classification. However, multimodal feature heterogeneity leads to reduced comparability between optical and SAR features, posing a significant obstacle to accurate damage classification. To solve this problem, a low-frequency guided modality-agnostic information comparison (MAIC) block is proposed, where learnable low-frequency filters are designed to explore modality-agnostic semantic information from optical and SAR features, thereby bridging the modality gap. Based on the block, an MAIC decoder is designed to hierarchically aggregate damage cues, thereby acquiring representative damage features. Then, to address the difficulty of identifying damage categories under complex backgrounds and diverse feature distributions, a region-to-pixel refinement (R2PR) method is proposed to enhance the discriminability of damage features. This method introduces damage-region priors and aligns pixel-wise damage features with global dynamic prototypes, to improve feature discriminability across different damage categories. Combining the MAIC decoder and R2PR method, a low-frequency guided region-to-pixel refinement network (LFR2P-Net) is proposed to bridge the cross-modal discrepancy and obtain representative damage features with high discriminability, thereby alleviating the difficulty in BDA under multimodal heterogeneity. Title: Unitary dilation based coherent realization of nonnormal measurement blocks in quantum weighted state algorithms
Abstract: Estimating expectation values associated with nonnormal local measurement blocks is a fundamental primitive in quantum algorithms, especially in weighted-state frameworks for nonlinear quantum state transformations. Existing approaches rely on randomized decompositions into normal components, introducing additional sampling overhead and lacking tight operator-independent guarantees. To address this limitation, we propose a coherent measurement strategy based on Sz.-Nagy unitary dilation, which embeds a nonnormal measurement block into a larger unitary operator using a single ancilla qubit. Unlike randomized decomposition methods, our approach exactly recovers both the weighted reduced operator and the resulting scalar expectation value without stochastic branch sampling. We establish three theoretical results with explicit scope. First, among exact compression-form coherent normal realizations, the Sz.-Nagy dilation minimizes the spectral-norm factor controlling the operator-independent variance upper bound. Second, its bound is noninferior to that of any convex randomized normal decomposition. Third, against the canonical Hermitian/skew-Hermitian split, the improvement factor ranges from one to two, depending on the operator structure. We then specialize the construction to the Holmes quantum state polynomial (QSP) primitive and characterize when the coherent strategy applies and can offer a practical advantage. To bridge theory and practice, we introduce a compilation-aware proxy evaluated on basis-transpiled circuits under a simulated depolarizing-noise model. At the primary CNOT budget of ten thousand, its correlation with the finite-budget mean-squared-error ratio is approximately three times that of the operator-level ratio. Title: Nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvesting from subway rail vibrations: In Situ excitation characterization and optimization of a monostable Duffing harvester

Title: Experimental investigation of multiaxial fatigue behavior and life prediction using Transformer-PINN in Q355E steel welded joints

Title: A hierarchical scheduling strategy for achieving multi-source energy complementarity in self-powered systems

Title: Data-driven hydrodesulfurization of heavy feeds: from model compounds to refinery-relevant catalyst design, soft sensing, and process optimization
Abstract: Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) remains the primary industrial route for sulfur removal, but increasingly heavy and complex feedstocks make deep desulfurization more challenging. This review examines the evolution of HDS from model sulfur compounds to refinery-relevant heavy feeds, including vacuum gas oils, residues, biomass-derived oils, and waste tire and plastic pyrolysis oils. The distribution and reactivity of inorganic and organic sulfur species are discussed, with particular emphasis on refractory thiophenic compounds, and the competing direct desulfurization and hydrogenation pathways. The effects of temperature, hydrogen pressure, liquid hourly space velocity, and feed sulfur content are evaluated in relation to sulfur conversion, hydrogen consumption, catalyst deactivation, and process economics. The emerging role of machine learning (ML) in HDS research is assessed. ML enables quantitative mapping of catalyst descriptors, feedstock properties, and operating conditions to catalytic performance, enhancing catalyst screening, structure–activity analysis, sulfur-content prediction, soft sensing, multi-objective optimization of operating conditions, and catalyst lifetime prediction. The review further highlights hybrid physics-aware models, explainable ML, digital twins, and adaptive learning as promising approaches for bridging laboratory-scale models with dynamic refinery operation. Unlike conventional trial-and-error approaches, these data-driven methods can reveal complex interactions among catalysts, feedstock, and process variables while reducing experimental effort and enabling real-time decision support. Some barriers remain, including data quality, training-deployment data mismatch, model transferability, interpretability, and limited long-term industrial datasets. Integrating mechanistic HDS knowledge with ML promises a pathway toward faster catalyst development, optimized operation, improved catalyst utilization, and more sustainable heavy-feed desulfurization. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Electroactive bacteria in soil microbial fuel cells for petroleum hydrocarbon degradation: system performance, extracellular electron transfer and microbial engineering
Abstract: Petroleum hydrocarbon (PH) contamination of soils poses a significant environmental challenge due to its persistence, toxicity, and detrimental effects on ecosystem functioning. In recent times, Soil Microbial Fuel Cells (SMFCs) have emerged as a promising bio-electrochemical technique capable of simultaneously degrading PHs and generating electricity through the metabolic activity of electroactive bacteria (EAB). This review critically explores different SMFC reactor configurations used for PH remediation, the functional insights of the microbial communities involved in the removal of PH, highlights the bioelectricity generated by different electrogenic microbial populations during the degradation of PH, and elucidates the molecular mechanisms, particularly extracellular electron transfer (EET) pathways, that govern their electrochemical activity and degradation efficiency. Cutting-edge advances in synthetic biology, particularly the engineering of genetically modified electroactive microorganisms, the development of synthetic microbial consortia (SynComs), and the design of biosensors and regulatory circuits, have been critically discussed as promising strategies to enhance the efficiency and stability of SMFC. Further, this review explores the application of multi omics technologies to unravel microbial functions underlying SMFC performance and examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in performance prediction, process optimization, and intelligent design of SMFC systems. Finally, the applications related to SMFC technologies has been critically evaluated for its commercial viability. By addressing challenges and proposing solutions, this review provides a comprehensive outlook on SMFCs future, aiming for its successful application in sustainable energy production. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A tetra-dicyanovinyl-based sensor for fluorescent “turn-on” detection of glyphosate
Source title: Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology A: Chemistry
Abstract: Glyphosate is a widely used herbicide whose residues in agricultural and environmental matrices require rapid and reliable monitoring. Herein, a tetra-dicyanovinyl-based fluorescent probe ( TECN ) was synthesized and combined with Fe3+ to construct a fluorescence “turn-on” sensing ensemble for glyphosate. The TECNFe system exhibited a pronounced response toward glyphosate over most tested pesticides and common interferents, although aminomethylphosphonic acid produced a weaker fluorescence enhancement. Fluorescence titration provided a linear concentration-dependent response and a limit of detection of 2.81 × 10−7 M. More than 90% of the final fluorescence recovery was achieved within 10 s after glyphosate addition, demonstrating a rapid sensing response. Job's plot analysis indicated a predominant TECN :Fe3+ stoichiometry of approximately 1:2 and an apparent interaction ratio close to 1:1 between the preassembled sensing ensemble and glyphosate. FT-IR spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support a competitive coordination mechanism in which glyphosate weakens the Fe3+-mediated fluorescence-quenching interaction with TECN . Spike-recovery analyses in cabbage, potato, and soil samples afforded recoveries of 98.33–99.50% with relative standard deviations of 2.95–3.99%. Furthermore, time-dependent measurements of glyphosate-treated vegetable surfaces showed a gradual decrease in extractable residues while retaining a detectable response after 24 h. Authors: Lyu M.; Zou R.; Luo G.; Zhang H.; Xiao Y.; Li X.; Yao H.
Title: Co-combustion characteristics and decomposition kinetics of recycled papermaking solid wastes under various operating conditions and blending ratios
Abstract: The use of waste paper as a feedstock for papermaking can significantly reduce both virgin wood consumption and CO2 emissions in the paper industry. Nevertheless, this process produces large amounts of solid wastes, including recycled papermaking residue (RPR) and recycled papermaking sludge (RPS), which urgently require appropriate disposal. Incineration offers an alternative approach for both thermal energy recovery from these wastes and environmentally sound disposal. However, the individual combustion behavior of these two solid wastes is poor. In this study, we proposed a co‑combustion approach to improve the combustion performance of the two wastes, and we systematically investigate their co-combustion characteristics and decomposition kinetic. The results showed that RPS had high volatile contents and abundant CaCO3. The weight loss of the mixtures occurred in three stages: moisture evaporation, volatile release, and residue decomposition. Interactions during co‑combustion exhibited promoting effects in the later volatile release and the residue decomposition stages (450–789 °C). The comprehensive combustion index increased mainly with the increase in RPR ratio and heating rate, with its values ranging between 1.81 × 10−7·%2·min−2·°C −3 and 13.62 × 10−7·%2·min−2·°C −3. The kinetic results indicated that the best-fitting models for the volatile release and residue decomposition stages were CR4 and CR2, respectively. The mass-loss-weighted apparent kinetic index was mainly determined by the mixing ratio. As the RPR proportion increased from 25 % to 75 %, the index decreased from 127.4 kJ/mol to 108.2 kJ/mol, and R75S25 was also one of the better-performing blends among the mixed samples in terms of the comprehensive combustion index. The findings of this paper are expected to provide valuable guidance for developing treatment technologies for recycled papermaking solid wastes, and to contribute to close the loop of the paper recycling chain. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Study on the pilot fuel injection strategy for a large-scale diesel/methanol dual-direct injection engine at high methanol substitution ratio
Abstract: The diesel/methanol dual-direct injection (DMDDI) engine attracts wide attention because of its high methanol substitution ratio (MSR). Results indicate that excessively low or high PFIP weakens work output and fuel economy, whereas PFIP60 achieves the best power and economic performance. On the basis of PFIP60, PFPI reduces NOx, and delaying the post-injection timing (PIT) further suppresses NOx. At PIT14, the engine maintains higher performance while reducing NOx by about 12.39%, and it shows a favorable compromise for incomplete-combustion emissions. Furthermore, decreasing the post-injection mass ratio (PIMR) continues to reduce NOx; at PIMR10, the reduction reaches about 18.42%, and compared with the performance-optimal PIMR70, the differences in indicated power (IP) and indicated thermal efficiency (ITE) are only about 6 kW and 0.06%, respectively, although CO, HC, and CH2O emissions remain relatively higher. Title: An efficient spectral method for the internal transmission eigenvalue problem with an isotropic inhomogeneous medium in a complex domain

Abstract: In this paper, an efficient spectral method is proposed and studied for the internal transmission eigenvalue problem with an isotropic inhomogeneous medium in a complex domain. A rigorous mathematical proof of the error estimates is provided and spectral accuracy is derived for the approximation solution when the considered domain is an ellipse. Title: Leonurus cardiaca L. polysaccharide-stabilized Pd-Au nanozymes for NIR-responsive doxorubicin delivery and combined chemo-chemodynamic-photothermal therapy
Abstract: Traditional cancer therapies are limited by severe side effects and therapeutic challenges, while noble metal nanozymes offer promising enzyme-like therapeutic potential but remain constrained by poor aqueous stability. Title: Experimental and numerical study on laminar burning velocities of methane/ethane/propane blending with partial cracking ammonia
Abstract: Ammonia is regarded as a promising carbon-free hydrogen carrier for low-carbon combustion applications. Nevertheless, its practical deployment is constrained by inherent drawbacks, including low laminar flame velocity, inferior combustion stability, and high ignition energy. This study explores the effects of natural gas components on the laminar burning velocity of cracked ammonia fuels using the heat flux method and chemical kinetic simulations under elevated pressures. The experimental and numerical results show that, at a fixed ammonia blending ratio of x NH3 = 0.5, S L increases nearly exponentially with the elevation of the cracking ratio γ from 0 to 1. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to hydrogen generated from ammonia cracking, which substantially facilitates the H-radical dominated chain-branching reaction. For a constant cracking ratio of γ = 0.6, S L presents a non-monotonic variation trend, decreasing first and then increasing as x NH3 rises from 0 to 1. Such behavior is governed by the inhibitory effect of NH2 radicals as well as the promoting effect of cracked H2. Across all tested operating conditions, S L of mixed fuels declines with increasing pressure, and normalized S L/ S L0 collapse onto same trend under different pressures. The growth slope of S L with respect to γ and x NH3 follows a descending order of CH4 > C2H6 > C3H8. Among the tested fuel mixtures, the C3H8/NH3/H2/N2 mixture exhibits the lowest sensitivity to H2 addition and ammonia cracking ratio compared to CH4 and C2H6 blending mixture. This behavior is primarily attributed to the relatively low C–H bond energy and superior inherent dehydrogenation capacity of propane, which reduce the reliance on exogenous H radicals generated from ammonia cracking. Title: Chemical looping and conventional partial oxidation of methane for syngas production: A comparative thermodynamic and techno-economic assessment
Abstract: Conventional Partial Oxidation of Methane (POM) for syngas production is associated with significant energy penalties due to the requirement of an energy-intensive Air Separation Unit (ASU). Chemical Looping Partial Oxidation of Methane (CLPOM) offers a promising alternative by utilizing an Oxygen Storage and Release Material (OSRM), that supplies lattice oxygen for methane oxidation while inherently separating oxygen from air. In this study, a unified process-level benchmark of CLPOM and conventional POM integrated with an ASU was performed through a comparative thermodynamic and techno-economic assessment using Aspen Plus. Independent process flowsheets were developed for both configurations and simulated using the Peng Robinson (PR) thermodynamic model, which was validated against experimental data to ensure model reliability. The influence of temperature (400 – 1000 °C) and pressure (1 – 30 bar) along with ratios of NiO/CH4, O2/CH4 and air/Ni ranging from 0.1 to 2, 0.1 – 1 and 0.1 – 2.5, respectively on the equilibrium reactant conversion and product gas compositions was systematically investigated for each process as applicable. The CLPOM simulations predicted a syngas H2/CO ratio of 2.06, comparable to that obtained from the conventional POM simulation runs. Under optimal operating conditions, the net energy consumption of CLPOM was estimated to be 2.5 kWh/kmolsyngas compared to 11.8 kWh/kmolsyngas for POM integrated with an ASU. The corresponding energy and exergy efficiencies were found to be ∼12 % higher for CLPOM, while the syngas unit cost was ∼53 % lower than that of conventional POM. Title: Development of structural correlations and predictive models for NH3 emission in an amine-based post-combustion CO2 capture process
Abstract: Amine-based post-combustion CO2 capture is a promising technology for reducing CO2 emissions; however, oxidative degradation of amine solvents can generate ammonia (NH3), an important secondary emission. Oxidative degradation experiments were conducted under controlled conditions, and molecular descriptors representing structural, electronic, steric, and hydrogen-bonding characteristics were evaluated. Multiple linear regression (MLR), Ridge regression, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were compared using 30 repetitions of family-stratified five-fold cross-validation, with inner cross-validation used for tuning Ridge and XGBoost. XGBoost showed the best out-of-sample performance, with mean MAE and RMSE values of 0.477 and 0.630 log10 units, respectively, followed by Ridge regression. Authors: Liu Z.; He X.; Zhou X.; Li J.; Han J.
Title: Systematic effects of Transport-Parameter uncertainty on the laminar burning velocity of NH3/H2 mixtures
Abstract: Transport parameters, the Lennard-Jones well depth ε/k, collision diameter σ and dipole moment μ, are an essential part of every combustion mechanism file, yet unlike the rate constants they are largely inherited from mid-century empirical correlations and have never been independently validated. Taking NH3/H2 as the core system, this study quantifies on the Cantera platform how that uncertainty propagates to the laminar burning velocity (S_L) and to the extinction strain rate. An audit of mainstream mechanisms reveals two systematic biases: the ε/k of H, H2 and OH is underestimated by 73–88 % relative to first-principles values, and the dipole moments of polar species such as OH, NH2 and HNO are missing. The same entries recur, numerically identical, across mechanisms of independent kinetic origin, showing the bias to be inherited rather than incidental. Its consequences are not constant but evolve with the effective Lewis number, being amplified in hydrogen-rich flames (Le < 1) and negligible for pure ammonia. Isolating transport strictly within one mechanism, with kinetics, thermodynamics and numerics held identical, correction of the H/H2/OH parameters shifts S_L by up to + 6.8 % on the rich side; the shift is systematic and direction-consistent, but it lies within the experimental scatter and can be reproduced by an admissible change of a single rate constant, so it is reported as a quantified uncertainty rather than as improved accuracy. The extinction strain rate responds on the same order, rising from 26.4 to 4719 s⁻1 as the hydrogen fraction increases from 0 to 0.7. Extended along an n-alkane series computed within a single mechanism, the influence of the fuel’s own transport parameters decays monotonically with molecular weight, because the fuel is pyrolyzed before reaching the reaction zone; two independent diagnostics, the sign change of the pyrolysis lead distance and the 1 % sensitivity threshold, place the onset of this shielding in the C4–C6 interval. Title: ApolloWave: Rethinking time–frequency bases and spectral preferences for non-stationary time series forecasting
Abstract: Forecasting non-stationary temporal dynamics is essential in domains such as finance, where fluctuations are rapid and irregular. However, existing approaches mainly rely on normalization tricks or domain transformations to project non-stationary signals into stationary spaces, often resulting in substantial distortion of fine-grained temporal–spectral details. In response, this paper proposes ApolloWave, a novel forecasting framework designed to enhance dynamic-signal modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Learnable Redundant Wavelet Transform (LRWT), which provides an adaptive time–frequency basis for fitting non-stationary components. Meanwhile, we develop a Dynamic Time–Frequency Saliency (DTFS) module that automatically learns task-dependent spectral preferences and enhances representation quality in complex scenarios. Experimental results across real-world datasets spanning industry, transportation, and financial domains show that ApolloWave achieves competitive performance against ten state-of-the-art methods in non-stationary time-series forecasting tasks. Title: Hydrothermally synthesized MnO2/g-C3N4 photocatalyst for efficient cephalexin degradation: Reactive species, stability assessment and thermodynamic insights

Title: Light-regulated, cofactor-free amperometric biosensor for ultrasensitive TNT detection based on XenB-modified electrodes

Title: Enhanced DOA estimation using complex acoustic intensity quaternion polarization filtering for vertical line array with vector sensors
Abstract: The polarization characteristics of acoustic vector signals provide additional information for distinguishing target signals from noise. Next, based on quaternion theory, an unpolarized projection filter and a Wiener polarization filter are designed to suppress unpolarized background noise and correlated noise, respectively. Title: Theoretical analysis of the time-dependent response of roadway surrounding rock under energy-driven conditions and the synergistic control of support structures
Abstract: The mechanical response of rock mass after excavation is a non-equilibrium, continuously evolving process driven by energy and influenced by time-dependent effects. Traditional approaches based on stress or deformation cannot consistently characterize its mechanisms and associated risks. The analysis reveals the spatiotemporal evolution of energy accumulation, migration, and dissipation, and identifies key energy distribution features, including peak rings of elastic energy and closed zones of dissipated energy. Furthermore, the energy absorption mechanisms of support structures, including rock bolts, cable anchors, U-shaped steel frames, and shotcrete, are analyzed from the perspective of energy transformation, clarifying the staged cooperative effect of the RAUS support system in regulating rock mass energy. Comparative analysis between numerical simulations and field data demonstrates that the proposed model accurately captures the full-range deformation process of surrounding rock. Title: The effects of oxygen addition and nitrogen dilution on soot formation in PRF80 laminar diffusion flames
Abstract: This study employed color-ratio pyrometry to systematically investigate the effects of increasing the oxygen concentration in the co-flow and the nitrogen dilution flow rate in the fuel on the structure of PRF80 laminar diffusion flames and their soot formation characteristics. The experimental results indicate that when the co-flow oxygen concentration is increased from 21 % to 30 %, the visible flame height decreases from 5.37 cm to 3.24 cm. When the nitrogen dilution flow rate is increased from 200 mL/min to 350 mL/min, the visible flame height increases from 5.20 cm to 5.44 cm. Both changes lead to higher soot temperatures. Regarding the distribution and evolution of soot, soot is primarily concentrated in the two wings of the flame, with formation and oxidation processes dominating in the upstream and downstream regions, respectively. The addition of oxygen significantly enhances soot concentration and intensifies both its formation and oxidation. The maximum soot volume fraction increases from 3.47 ppm at 21 % co-flow oxygen concentration to 4.91 ppm at 30 %. The peak yield soot index first increases and then decreases, while the soot loading shows a monotonic decreasing trend. In comparison, nitrogen dilution markedly reduces soot concentration as well as its formation and oxidation rates. The maximum soot volume fraction decreases from 6.14 ppm at a nitrogen dilution flow rate of 200 mL/min to 3.11 ppm at 350 mL/min, with a significant reduction observed in both the peak yield soot index and soot loading. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wang D.; Zhou T.; Yang J.
Title: Frequency Separation and Aggregation-induced contrastive learning for ultrasound thyroid nodule segmentation
Abstract: Accurate segmentation of thyroid nodules is crucial for guiding treatment decisions and evaluating intervention effectiveness in thyroid disease. Despite advancements in the field, several challenges remain. Firstly, thyroid nodules, especially malignant ones, often lack clear grayscale boundaries with surrounding tissues, posing difficulties for segmentation algorithms to accurately locate nodule contours. Secondly, normal thyroid tissue structures or adjacent structures may exhibit ultrasound echo characteristics that resemble those of certain types of nodules, potentially resulting in the misclassification of non-nodule areas as nodules. To address these issues, in this paper, we propose a novel Frequency Separation and Aggregation-induced contrastive learning Network (FSANet) for thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound images. Specifically, in the encoder, we propose a Spectral Attention Module (SAM) to separate image features by frequency. They are then aggregated to form more discriminative combined features. In the decoder, a State Space-induced Interaction Module (SSIM) is presented to facilitate the interaction and mutual enhancement of different frequency features, allowing the model to flexibly utilize spectral features for segmentation at various decoding stages. Additionally, we employ a Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL) strategy to optimize feature representation within and across different spectra. This improves the model's ability to distinguish between nodules and background, thereby enhancing both segmentation accuracy and generalization. More importantly, we establish a new benchmark for comprehensively evaluating the thyroid nodule segmentation task. Authors: Guo T.; Huang Y.; Yu H.; Xu M.; Ma G.; Wang K.
Title: UCM-Distill: multi-teacher distillation with uncertainty modeling and contrastive learning for weakly supervised medical image segmentation
Abstract: Weakly supervised medical image segmentation aims to reduce the reliance on pixel-level annotations but remains challenged by noisy pseudo labels and unreliable supervision. Existing methods typically rely on single-model predictions or prompt-based strategies, lacking effective mechanisms to model uncertainty and inconsistencies among different models. We propose UCM-Distill, an uncertainty- and contrast-aware multi-teacher distillation framework that generates reliable supervision under weak annotations. Our method introduces a Consistency-regulated Uncertainty-aware Pseudo-label Generation (CUPG) module to suppress uncertain regions and enhance consistent predictions across heterogeneous teachers. In addition, a Mask-Guided Contrastive Distillation (MGCD) mechanism is designed to improve feature separability via foreground-background contrastive learning. By jointly optimizing pseudo-label quality and feature representation, our framework achieves robust and accurate segmentation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method performs consistently well on two public brain tumor datasets (2D and 3D) as well as a private pituitary microadenoma dataset, showing strong generalization across different imaging settings. Authors: Miyajima K.; Yamada T.
Title: Level set-based topology optimization of unimorph cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvesters with electrode-layout design under microfabrication constraints
Abstract: This paper proposes a reaction-diffusion-based level set topology optimization framework for unimorph cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvesters that is formulated for consistency with a planar thin-film microfabrication route. The piezoelectric thin film is kept continuous, and only the electrode layout is patterned. The electrode pattern is represented by an internal interface that partitions the film into electrode-covered and uncovered piezoelectric subdomains, while the substrate topology is optimized simultaneously using an extended level set formulation. Cross-sectional uniformity and substrate-support conditions are incorporated into the level-set evolution as process-consistent formulation constraints that define the admissible design space. Title: Electric field-enhanced trace hafnium detection in zirconium using 532 nm and 1064 nm LIBS: A comparative study
Abstract: In this study, the detection of hafnium in a zirconium matrix using laser induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) enhanced by an externally applied electric field under both 532 nm and 1064 nm laser excitations is reported for the first time to our knowledge. The impact of laser pulse energy, delay time, excitation wavelength and the strength of externally applied DC electric field were systematically explored to improve the limit of detection (LOD) and signal reliability. Under optimized conditions (100 mJ & 1 μs), the 532 nm excitation outperformed the 1064 nm through improved laser-plasma coupling, enhanced mass ablation efficiency and reduced plasma shielding, which improved signal to noise ratio (SNR) and relative standard deviation (RSD). An optimal electric field (175 V/mm) enhanced plasma confinement and excitation efficiency, yielding ∼2.4 times emission enhancement, while the SNR increased by ∼33% and the RSD decreased ∼50% under 532 nm excitation. Plasma diagnostics were found to confirmed local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) under all conditions, with an increase in electron temperature and density at optimal field strengths. The LOD values for Hf II 263.87 nm line under 532 nm and 1064 nm with 175 V/mm electric field assistance were 14.3 ppm and 34.2 ppm, respectively. However, this study has a few limitations such as, spectral congestion between zirconium and hafnium and the limited availability of interference-free hafnium lines, which restricts the quantitative analysis to two hafnium lines. Title: Nonlinear dynamic response analysis of ACCWDs based on a deterministic numerical source-to-structure simulation
Abstract: The source-to-structure simulation framework amalgamates earthquake rupture kinematics, seismic wave propagation through heterogeneous materials, site-specific geological conditions, and structural dynamic response, offering a physics-based methodology for producing realistic ground motions and evaluating the seismic performance of essential infrastructure. This research establishes a multiscale computational framework that integrates the spectral element technique (SEM) with the finite difference method (FDM) for thorough seismic analysis of earth dams. The SEM is used to do physics-based 3D simulations of seismic sources and wave propagation, producing site-specific ground movements that include intricate rupture kinematics and regional geological formations. Thereafter, the FDM is used to model the nonlinear dynamic response of the dam system, accounting for material nonlinearity and significant deformations. This comprehensive platform allows complete simulation from fault rupture to structural reaction. The approach is proven by its application to the Dashimen asphalt concrete core wall dam (ACCWD) in northern China, using six sample seismic scenarios. The results indicate that the domain reduction technique (DRM) successfully establishes one-way coupling between the regional-scale SEM and the structure-scale FDM models. The linked method effectively simulates seismic wave propagation in the foundation and properly delineates the deformation patterns and stress–strain progression in the dam, consequently serving as a reliable framework for the seismic safety assessment of ACCWDs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Han L.; Liu J.; Jiang Y.-L.
Title: A variable-step Crank-Nicolson and preconditioned fast quadratic spline collocation method for option pricing with jump-diffusion models
Source title: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
Abstract: In the field of financial derivative pricing, option pricing under stochastic market environments has long been a core focus of both academic research and practical application. However, traditional numerical methods often face severe challenges in balancing computational accuracy, efficiency, and stability when dealing with the partial integro-differential equations (PIDEs) derived from jump-diffusion models, especially under non-smooth initial conditions. In this paper, we consider the stochastic Merton's jump-diffusion model for European option pricing, which can be transformed into a PIDE. In view of the non-smoothness of the initial data, a variable-step Crank-Nicolson (CN) method is proposed for temporal discretization, and the quadratic spline collocation (QSC) method is used for spatial discretization. The prior estimate and convergence of the variable-step QSC-CN method are presented. Since a spatial non-local integration is handled implicitly, which leads to dense algebraic equations. Then a matrix-free fast Krylov subspace iterative solver is proposed to increase the computational efficiency, and preconditioning technique is applied to further accelerate the convergence. We show that the preconditioned fast QSC-CN method significantly reduces the computational cost from O((M+2)3) to O((M+2)log(M+2)), and the memory requirement from O((M+2)2) to O((M+2)), where M is the number of spatial discretization grids. This numerical method is further generalized for American option pricing. Numerical experiments are attached to verify the theoretical convergence order and the effectiveness of the fast computing technique. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: CRISPR-based point-of-care platform for EBV DNA screening and monitoring in nasopharyngeal cancer plasma
Abstract: Plasma circulating cell-free Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA is a clinically validated biomarker for early nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) detection and longitudinal disease monitoring. However, current quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays require sophisticated instrumentation and specialized laboratory infrastructure, constraining their accessibility in resource-limited settings. Here, we present two point-of-care testing platforms integrating the RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a system and oil-phase magnetic bead transfer (OMT) method for POCT detection: dμCRISPR, a droplet microfluidic chip for digital quantification, and idCRISPR, an integrated lateral flow device for visual screening. The OMT method achieves efficient and stable EBV DNA extraction from plasma within 8 min. The dμCRISPR platform provides absolute quantitative results within 60 min with an analytical sensitivity of 1 copy/μL. In parallel testing of 24 clinical plasma samples, dμCRISPR were consistent with qPCR. Additionally, the idCRISPR platform enables naked-eye screening within 50 min with a detection limit of 10 copies/μL, showing results consistent with qPCR in the 30 clinical samples evaluated. Together, these platforms form a dual-track strategy for precise quantification and rapid screening, supporting the end-to-end management of NPC across diverse healthcare environments. Authors: Li J.; Wang W.; Liu Y.; Li Q.
Title: MaskCL: Mask-driven Cross-Modal Collaborative Learning for multimodal anomaly detection
Abstract: Multimodal industrial anomaly detection has recently advanced by leveraging the complementary nature of 2D textures and 3D geometries. Among existing strategies, mapping-based paradigms have emerged as a prominent solution for establishing cross-modal alignment. However, such methods often suffer from a mapping shortcut, where the model gravitates toward point-wise numerical fitting instead of exploiting complementary information across modalities. To address this issue, we propose Mask-driven Cross-Modal Collaborative Learning (MaskCL), a novel multimodal anomaly detection framework that formulates cross-modal anomaly detection as collaborative representation learning under incomplete observations. To realize this framework, we first introduce a Foreground-aware Random Masking (FRM) module that constructs an information bottleneck by masking foreground regions, thereby reducing the reliance on direct point-wise correspondence. To effectively process incomplete feature representations induced by masking, we further develop a Collaborative Feature Learning (CFL) architecture that reconciles intra-modal structural reconstruction with cross-modal feature recovery. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal industrial anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that MaskCL achieves strong and competitive performance across different metrics, with robust anomaly localization in few-shot scenarios. Title: Experimental investigation of lean burn H2ICE: A comparison of PFI and LPDI
Abstract: Hydrogen internal combustion engine (H2ICE) is one of the promising technologies to fulfill the goal of carbon neutrality and sustainable transportation. This work experimentally compares port fuel injection (PFI) and low pressure direct Injection (LPDI) concepts on the same single cylinder heavy duty engine platform. Both PFI and LPDI strategies are investigated under varying excess air coefficient and spark timings. The study explores the effects of lean hydrogen combustion at stationary operating condition, and spark timing optimized to balance combustion efficiency and emission characteristics. The results demonstrate the high potential of H2ICEs for ultra-low engine-out NOx emissions. A maximum gross indicated efficiency (GIE) of 41.9% is achieved with the PFI configuration. Both PFI and LPDI meet the proposed Euro 7 NOx limits at λ = 2.5, while NOx approaches the analyzer detection limit at λ ' 4. PFI generally shows lower NOx emissions than LPDI due to improved mixture homogeneity. GIE exhibits a parabolic dependence on λ and spark timing, independent of injection strategy. Title: Investigating the mean stress effect of residual stress on rolling contact fatigue through a damage-coupled elasto-plastic framework
Abstract: A damage-coupled elasto-plastic model is established to investigate the effect of residual stress on the rolling contact fatigue of M50 steel. Residual stress is incorporated into the damage law through mean stress correction based on Basquin's law and the Goodman equation. The non-uniform compressive residual stress distribution in nitrided M50 steel is represented by a Gaussian function. The results show that higher compressive residual stress prolongs fatigue life within the investigated range by retarding crack initiation. Fatigue resistance improves when the depth of maximum compressive residual stress is close to the highly stressed region. Title: Portable fluorescence sensing coupled with smartphone-based image analysis for visual quantitative detection of streptomycin sulfate
Source title: Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology A: Chemistry
Abstract: Streptomycin sulfate (SM), a representative aminoglycoside antibiotic, is widely used for the treatment of tuberculosis and Gram-negative bacterial infections, but residues in water and food-related matrices may pose risks to human health. Here, we developed a portable sensing platform for on-site antibiotic residue monitoring. The platform uses carbon dots prepared from 4-aminobutyric acid and 5-amino-o-cresol by a hydrothermal route as a composite fluorescent nanoprobe. The probe showed a quantum yield of 3.8% in water and enabled both visual recognition and quantitative detection of SM. As the SM concentration increased, the probe color shifted from blue-green to yellow, allowing direct visual readout. The fluorescence assay showed a linear response over 0–500 μM with a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.47 μM, whereas the smartphone-assisted colorimetric readout was linear over 0–600 μM with an LOD of 0.21 μM. Title: Experimental study on inhibition mechanism of composite inhibitors for coal spontaneous combustion at critical temperature
Abstract: To elucidate the inhibition mechanism of composite inhibitors during coal spontaneous combustion under a selected critical-temperature condition, three coals with different ranks were investigated. Temperature-programmed oxidation coupled with gas chromatography, in-situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (in-situ FTIR), and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) were employed to evaluate the effects of individual inhibitors (MgCl2, TEMPO, and PX4B) and PX4B–TEMPO composite inhibitors on coal oxidation behavior and reactive structures at 70 °C. The results showed that the inhibitory effects of the inhibitors became more pronounced after treatment at 70 °C, with PX4B exhibiting the strongest overall inhibition. The inhibitory effectiveness of TEMPO increased with increasing coal rank. PX4B and TEMPO exhibited a distinct non-additive synergistic effect, as evidenced by CO emissions lower than the theoretically weighted values, with a maximum inhibition efficiency of 61 %. The optimal PX4B:TEMPO mass ratio was 7:3 for low- and medium-rank coals and 5:5 for high-rank coking coal, indicating a coal-rank-dependent matching relationship. FTIR analysis showed that the composite inhibitor altered the evolution of hydroxyl hydrogen bonds and reactive oxygen-containing functional groups, whereas EPR measurements revealed a decrease in residual free-radical concentration after inhibitor treatment. Based on these results and the known inhibition characteristics of the individual components, a complementary synergistic mechanism is proposed: PX4B mainly regulates reactive functional-group structures, whereas TEMPO suppresses the propagation of coal–oxygen chain reactions through free-radical scavenging. Title: Deformation characteristics of energy piles under combined loads
Abstract: Energy piles are simultaneously subjected to mechanical and cyclic thermal loads. Yet, the coupled effects of vertical load, horizontal load and thermal cycling on their thermo-mechanical response remain insufficiently understood. This study develops a validated three-dimensional thermo-mechanical finite element model to investigate the response of a full-scale energy pile under combined vertical and horizontal loads and repeated heating–cooling cycles. Parametric analyses were conducted by varying the combined load level and cyclic temperature change gradient. The results show that increasing the vertical load primarily enhances axial load transfer and vertical settlement accumulation, thereby reducing the pile tip load sharing ratio and promoting shaft resistance mobilisation. Increasing the horizontal load primarily amplifies the bending response and lateral deformation of the upper pile segment. A larger temperature change gradient intensifies restrained axial thermal deformation and residual vertical settlement. The migration of the vertical displacement neutral point further reveals that vertical loading promotes deeper axial load transfer and downward migration of the neutral point. In contrast, horizontal loading enhances upper-pile bending and shifts the neutral point upward. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Dianyu E.; Yang Y.; Weng L.; Jiang Z.; Liu Y.; Liu L.; Cui J.
Title: CFD-based optimization of hydrogen-enriched fuels for heating performance and emissions in a metallurgical heating furnace
Abstract: Metallurgical heating furnaces typically utilize a mixture of blast furnace off-gas (BOG) and coke oven gas (COG) as fuel. The high hydrogen content of COG makes it crucial for carbon reduction. A comprehensive 3D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model was developed to simulate the complex thermochemical states and multiscale heat transfer within the furnace. The model was verified via literature data, and a mesh sensitivity test was conducted to guarantee its reliability. Optimal COG blending ratios were evaluated based on four key aspects: furnace thermal state, slab heating performance, pollutant emissions, and fuel economy. While increasing the COG ratio significantly enhances carbon reduction, it also leads to a sharp rise in NOx emissions. To balance these effects, the COG proportion should be maintained below approximately 68%. The preferred operational zone, considering production intensity and emission standards, was identified, with quantitative correlations established between operating conditions and heating costs. Title: Topology-dependent adsorption and diffusion mechanisms of CO2 capture from humid flue gas in zeolites: A molecular dynamics study
Abstract: Zeolites are promising adsorbents for CO2 capture from industrial flue gas, but competitive adsorption and intracrystalline diffusion under humid conditions remain poorly understood, hindering the rational design of high-performance adsorbents. To clarify these mechanisms, we investigated LTA, MOR, and CHA zeolites with distinct framework topologies. Ab initio calculations were performed to refine the CO2-zeolite interaction parameters, and isothermal CO2 adsorption experiments were used to validate the results. Relative to the original UFF, the calibrated force field reduced the mean deviation between simulated and experimental CO2 uptakes from more than 15 % to less than 5 %. Further Grand Canonical Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (GCMC-MD) simulations using the resulting force-field parameters revealed an adsorption-diffusion trade-off: the 3D cage networks of LTA and CHA favored CO2 uptake through stronger confinement, whereas CO2 migration in topologically two-dimensional MOR was dominated by the 12-MR main channels, giving rise to effectively quasi-one-dimensional transport and faster intracrystalline self-diffusion. Under the simulated ternary conditions, H2O and N2 modified CO2 adsorption and intracrystalline mobility through competitive site occupation, short-range CO2-H2O contacts, and changes in the local pore environment, with the responses depending strongly on framework topology and gas composition. The 3D interconnected pore network of LTA offered persistent CO2 transport pathways under humid conditions, illustrating how framework topology can mitigate moisture-induced transport limitations. Title: Modulating liquid metal flow by IN718 addition to improve surface quality in laser direct metal deposition of SS 316L
Abstract: The surface quality of cladding layer (CL) in laser direct metal deposition (LDMD) is strongly related to liquid metal flow. Improving the surface quality by modulating liquid metal flow is an effective strategy. Hence, a three-dimensional thermo-fluid dynamic model is established to investigate the influence of IN718 addition rate on the liquid metal flow and morphology evolution process of the formation of SS 316L CL during LDMD. The standard deviation and fluctuation amplitude of surface height of CL in central longitudinal section (LS) are defined to analyze the two-dimensional surface quality. The three-dimensional surface deviation of CL is calculated to discuss the three-dimensional surface quality. With the IN718 addition rate increasing, the temperature coefficient of surface tension is reduced and the surface tension gradient is decreased, which leads to the weakened Marangoni flow. The height of molten bulge is reduced due to the weakened Marangoni flow and then the difference between the heights of the solidified bulge and depression on the CL surface is decreased. As a result, the standard deviation and fluctuation amplitude of surface height of CL in central LS are reduced significantly and the three-dimensional surface deviation of CL is decreased greatly. The results can provide valuable reference for improving the surface quality in LDMD of SS 316L. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Ball-milled biochar as a water-based nano-additive: Linking dispersion stability, composite tribofilm formation, and tribological performance
Abstract: Developing efficient and sustainable nano-additives is critical for advancing water-based lubrication under boundary and mixed lubrication conditions. In this work, nano-biochar (NBC) was prepared from commercial biochar by a simple ball-milling and centrifugal fractionation process without chemical modification, and its performance as a water-based nano-additive was systematically investigated. Ball milling transformed the pristine biochar into a finer carbon material with reduced particle size, retained local graphitic nanodomains, and slightly enriched oxygen-containing surface groups, which markedly improved its aqueous dispersion stability. Under the optimum condition of 2.0 wt% and 200 N, the NBC suspension reduced the average friction coefficient and wear volume by 74.45% and 89.58%, respectively, relative to pure water, while also outperforming unmilled biochar and graphite. Surface and interfacial analyses showed that NBC lubrication led to the formation of a carbon/iron-oxide composite tribofilm on the worn surface. Raman and XPS results revealed the coexistence of carbonaceous species and iron-oxide-related components, and cross-sectional FIB characterization further confirmed the presence of a distinct interfacial film with a thickness of about 106 nm. The excellent tribological behavior of NBC is therefore attributed to the coupling of stable aqueous dispersion, stable-dispersion-enabled particle delivery to the sliding interface, and tribofilm formation during sliding. These findings highlight ball-milled biochar as a simple, effective, and sustainable nano-additive for aqueous lubrication systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Structural and thermoluminescent characterization of Cu, Mn Co-doped LiF nanophosphors for potential dosimetry applications

Title: Effects of hydrogen addition on laminar burning velocity and nitrogen oxide emissions of ammonia flames
Abstract: Ammonia-hydrogen binary fuel blends are receiving increasing attention as carbon-free energy vectors capable of supporting decarbonisation of combustion-based power systems. Title: Logit-guided feature denoising distillation for model compression
Abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective strategy for compressing deep models by transferring knowledge from a large teacher network to a lightweight student network, which is particularly valuable for reliable deployment in resource-constrained industrial environments. Traditional distillation methods usually align features as a whole, ignoring that they often contain background activations unrelated to the target as well as scattered noisy responses. To address this problem, Logit-Guided Feature Denoising (LGFD) distillation is proposed, which integrates the logit discriminative encoder (LDE) and the feature denoising mask (FDM) into a novel framework to guide the student toward acquiring the truly discriminative feature of the teacher. Specifically, the LDE encodes the teacher’s logit discriminability for feature denoising, thereby aligning features along semantic directions. Based on the LDE, the FDM highlights the attentive regions related to label class, which can help suppress redundant and noisy activations in the feature maps. Title: RCDF-Net: Retinal-cortical dual-pathway fusion for medical image segmentation
Abstract: Medical image segmentation aims to accurately extract lesion regions from complex backgrounds, making it critical for intelligent clinical diagnosis. However, this task faces two critical challenges: the intermingling of salient and non-salient objects generates interference that induces erroneous model responses to non-lesion regions, ultimately degrading segmentation accuracy; existing methods fail to capture orientation-selective texture features of lesions and lack global modeling strategies that are adapted to the radially symmetric geometry of lesions, resulting in incomplete lesion structure modeling. The cortical pathway captures orientation-selective textures and establishes geometry-aware spatial context modeling of radially symmetric lesion geometry. Title: A simple weak galerkin finite element method for the reissner-Mindlin plate model on Non-Convex polytopal meshes

Title: Sustainable NOX scrubbing with lignin-based materials: Lignin sulfonate and vanillin as model compound
Abstract: Pretreatment of flue gas prior to CO2 capture via amine scrubbing is important for maintaining CO2 capture efficiency and avoiding formation of toxic byproducts due to the presence of NOX. One flue gas cleaning method for that has increasingly gained attention is NOX scrubbing, in which NO is pre-oxidized to NO2 which can be absorbed using aqueous solutions containing suitable additives. While commonly used sulfur-based additives achieve high absorption efficiencies, they suffer from high consumption rates due to oxidative consumption. A recent study on phenolic additives demonstrated that e.g. 4-methylaminophenol could be used as efficient additive which has much lower consumption rates. This compound however is limited for industrial application due to environmental concerns. The present study aims to demonstrate the usage of bio-based phenolic polymers for NO2 absorption which should be more suitable for industrial usage on the example of lignin sulfonate. Additionally, vanillin was studied as a model compound to better understand NO2 absorption chemistry with such additives. Tests were conducted using lignin sulfonate at different pH values and additive concentrations with 50 ppm inlet NO2 at a total gas flow rate of 2.3 NL/min. Lignin sulfonate at 500 mg/100 mL and pH 9 maintained high NO2 absorption efficiency of approximately 90 %. Vanillin at 5 mM showed efficiencies of 91 % and 94 % at 50 and 100 ppm inlet NO2, respectively, at the same gas flow rate. With vanillin, absorption efficiency remained at a high level even after more than 1 mol NO2 per mole additive was absorbed, while sulfur-based additives showed a much lower ratio than 1 when fully consumed. NO2 absorption by the sulfur-based additives was successfully modeled, highlighting the lower chemical consumption of vanillin. Title: Macroscopic yielding of periodic porous materials with anisotropic matrix and cylindrical voids: A static lower bound and the transition to localized plasticity
Abstract: This work investigates the macroscopic strength of ductile porous materials with a matrix obeying Hill's anisotropic yield criterion and containing a periodic distribution of long cylindrical voids. The primary objective is to formulate an analytical homogenized yield function that captures the combined effects of porosity and plastic anisotropy. Restricting the analysis to transverse isotropy under axisymmetric loading, a static limit analysis on a cubic elementary cell yields a rigorous lower-bound estimate of the homogenized strength, expressed as a simple parabolic function of the mean lateral stress and Hill's equivalent stress. Unlike classical Gurson-type hollow-cylinder models, this geometry provides a more accurate representation of periodic microstructures. Reference solutions from finite element analysis assess the model predictions in terms of both macroscopic stress responses and local stress fields. These reveal that at high stress triaxiality the plastic field loses cylindrical symmetry and localizes in the transverse plane, producing a nearly vertical asymptote of the yield locus that limits the mean lateral stress. The stress triaxiality marking the diffuse-to-localized deformation transition is observed to depend on the material porosity and plastic anisotropy. The proposed lower-bound model is accurate in the longitudinal and hydrostatic regimes, while a multi-surface criterion that combines the Benzerga-Besson kinematic model with the present hydrostatic solution closely matches the finite element results across the full range of stress triaxialities. Title: Decoupling of ash deposition and high-temperature corrosion during combustion of waste-sludge-derived fuels
Abstract: Fuels derived from hydrothermally treated sludge are promising waste-to-energy resources, but ash deposition and high-temperature corrosion limit their practical use. This study evaluates whether these risks follow the same trend. Three fuels with distinct ash chemistries were examined using combustion deposition tests, SUS 316 corrosion experiments, thermogravimetric/differential thermal analysis (TGA/DTA), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). SS-B had the highest ash content (54.5 wt%), SS-C the lowest (17.2 wt%), and SS-A an intermediate content (26.5 wt%). Deposit ratios for SS-A, SS-B, and SS-C were 0.278, 0.339, and 0.221, respectively, giving the order SS-B > SS-A > SS-C. By contrast, specific mass changes of SUS 316 after 24 h at 1000 ℃ were 22.17, 4.78, and 80.00 mg/cm2, respectively, giving the corrosion-severity order SS-C > SS-A > SS-B. Specific mass changes remained low at 600 and 800 ℃ but increased sharply at 1000 ℃, indicating that severe ash-induced corrosion occurred only at the highest temperature. The TGA/DTA residual-mass order was SS-B > SS-A > SS-C and therefore did not explain corrosion severity.
