Title: Integrating human–stream interactions into ecological stream assessment: A novel rural–urban socioecological sustainability framework
Abstract: Current assessment tools for streams and rivers focus on ecological functioning while ignoring the social dimension, which varies across rural and urban ecosystems. This study presents the rural–urban socioecological stream sustainability index (hereinafter, RU-SESSI) for assessing stream function across the rural–urban continuum. This index is based on the stream ecosystem services (ES) and biodiversity index (SESBI), which was developed in our previous study to assess stream health. The SESBI was extended into a sustainability subindex by adding two economic indicators, and the framework was complemented by a stream–society interaction subindex comprising accessibility, public safety, and community involvement. Together, these subindices capture stream function through both sustainability performance and human–stream interaction patterns. The framework was refined and validated using the Delphi method, revealing significant differences in the relative importance of most RU-SESSI indicators between rural and urban segments. Applied to the Yarkon Stream in central Israel, the index revealed higher biodiversity and regulating services scores in the rural reach, whereas economic, recreation, and accessibility scores were higher in the urban reach, while public safety and community involvement were comparable between reaches. The urban reach achieved a slightly higher RU-SEES score than the rural reach (6.22 vs. 5.76), with no significant difference in the distribution of weighted indicator scores. The RU-SESSI offers a context-sensitive framework that accounts for unique socioecological dynamics, providing policymakers with valuable insights for tailoring stream management to rural–urban settings and contributing to global water security and sustainability. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Liu J.; Xia H.; Wang X.; Wang Y.; Geng L.; He R.; Liu C.; Qiu J.
Title: Brain dynamics differentially predict originality and appropriateness of creativity: The role of error sensitivity
Abstract: Background Originality and appropriateness are the defining characteristics of creative thinking, yet the dynamic neural processes associated with these two facets remain incompletely understood, and the cognitive processes linking brain dynamics to creative output have not been fully elucidated. Error sensitivity, referring to individual differences in detecting and responding to performance discrepancies, may provide insights into creative cognition. Methods The present study integrated resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, hidden Markov modeling, and behavioral measurements to investigate whether error sensitivity mediates the relationship between brain dynamics and creativity. A sample of 746 participants completed a stop-signal task to assess post-error slowing (PES) as a behavioral proxy for individual differences in error sensitivity and an Alternate Uses Task (AUT) to assess originality and appropriateness of ideas. Results Hidden Markov modeling (HMM) decoded four recurrent brain states, including two key states with antagonistic network activity patterns: State 1 was characterized by salience network activation and default mode network deactivation, whereas State 3 showed the opposite pattern. The fractional occupancy of and transition probability to State 1 were positively correlated with appropriateness, whereas State 3 dynamics correlated positively with originality, and both were positively associated with error sensitivity. Critically, error sensitivity partially mediated the relationships between State 1 and appropriateness, and between State 3 and originality. Conclusions These findings suggest that distinct intrinsic brain-state configurations may be differentially related to originality and appropriateness of creativity, and that error sensitivity may play a context-dependent role in these associations. The present findings provide evidence that individual differences in error sensitivity may be relevant to how dynamic neural characteristics are associated with different dimensions of creativity. Authors: Yang Y.; Li J.; Li Y.; Zhang S.; Guo K.
Title: Facilitator or hallucination trap? A social-cognitive account of AI-generated misinformation handling in GenAI-assisted L2 writing
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has demonstrated remarkable potential in second language (L2) learning, yet it is prone to hallucinations. Empirical research on how GenAI-generated misinformation is handled in educational contexts remains scarce. Accordingly, little is known about how these practices shape learning processes and outcomes. Guided by social cognitive theory, the current study frames students' GenAI-assisted L2 writing (using a tailored GenAI writing agent) in a hallucination-prone context in which misinformation was implanted. We examine AI literacy, higher-order thinking resources (i.e., critical thinking and creativity), L2 writing resources (i.e., L2 writing grit and self-regulatory writing strategies), English writing self-efficacy (EWSE), AI-generated misinformation detection (AI-MD), and L2 writing performance within this framework. Using a multi-method approach, combining a qualitative interview study (N = 35), two lab experiments (N = 140), and a large-scale questionnaire survey (N = 406), we find that critical thinking positively predicts GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance via AI-MD, and that negative priming on AI hallucinations significantly improves students’ AI-MD and their GenAI-assisted L2 writing performance, relative to neutral or positive priming. Furthermore, the cross-sectional survey focuses on personal factors and shows that AI literacy significantly predicts EWSE both directly and indirectly through a cognitive–generative pathway involving higher-order thinking resources and a motivational–regulatory pathway involving L2 writing resources. These findings extend social-cognitive accounts of GenAI-assisted L2 writing and inform instruction that helps learners evaluate AI outputs, manage misinformation risks, and sustain their own writing processes. © 2026

Authors: Wang Y.; Wang Z.; Zou Y.; Song Y.; Xia G.; Chen S.; Guo H.; Cao C.; Yang X.; Deng Z.; Li J.; Gong D.; Wang W.; Lyu X.; Tao Z.; Huang X.
Title: Self-disclosure to intelligent virtual agents: A scoping review and the disclosure affordance–actualization–governance framework
Abstract: Intelligent virtual agents (IVAs) have become digital social objects to which people disclose personal, emotional, health-related, and other sensitive information. Yet similar cues—including anthropomorphism, social presence, empathy, gaze, anonymity, and structured questioning—are associated across studies with greater disclosure, refusal, impression management, socially desirable responding, or discomfort. Searches covered four bibliographic databases without publication-year restrictions through March 17, 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar searching on May 20, 2026. This review, reported with reference to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), maps 88 empirical studies and introduces the Disclosure Affordance–Actualization–Governance (DAAG) framework as a middle-range account linking specific empirical findings with broader explanations of IVA-mediated disclosure. DAAG distinguishes sociotechnical interaction ecology; perceived safety from judgment, relational receptivity, expressive latitude, and boundary agency; disclosure actualization; affective, relational, and functional consequences; governance; and evidential reach—the extent to which studies observe perception, behavior, consequences, time, and governance. The literature is most developed for disclosure onset, sensitive reporting, emotional expression, and immediate system acceptance, but remains thin on persistence, reciprocity, subjective–behavioral divergence, correction, revocation, and downstream data use. Recurrent patterns are consistent with IVA cues being interpreted through evaluation risk, partner responsiveness, observability, topic sensitivity, competence, privacy, and control. DAAG is not presented as a validated causal model, but as a framework for explaining when digital social interaction supports, redirects, or appropriately constrains self-disclosure. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Ranucci, Immacolata (59471306000); Abay, Kibrom A. (55539635400); Tiberti, Luca (35184161100)
Title: Perceived need and measured well-being: How well do subjective rankings capture relative poverty?
Abstract: Subjective well-being rankings are widely used to target social protection programs, yet their ability to capture relative welfare and wealth remains debated. This study compares three commonly used subjective ranking methods: self-, peer-, and elite-based poverty rankings, against consumption- and wealth-based measures using a large household survey in Ethiopia, where about 20 households per village were ranked from most to least “needy” by themselves, their peers, and community leaders. We assess concordance between subjective and conventional welfare rankings and explore sources of divergence. Subjective rankings align more with relative wealth than consumption and with total rather than per capita welfare, suggesting they overlook household composition. Among the three subjective ranking methods, elite-based rankings best capture conventional measures, although overall concordance between subjective and welfare-based rankings remains weak. Subjective rankings also better reflect relative deprivation among households exposed to covariate shocks. A composite index combining all three modestly improves concordance with standard metrics. We find suggestive evidence that information asymmetry, favoritism, and welfare dynamics partly explain discrepancies between subjective rankings and conventional welfare measures. These findings offer important insights to improve targeting in data-scarce settings. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Wang Z.; Yang J.; Qiao X.; Lei L.
Title: Online collective aggression in algorithmic environments: The roles of algorithm awareness, moral outrage, and negative descriptive norms
Abstract: In algorithmic social media environments, filtering, ranking, and recommendation systems shape which online events, comments, and group reactions become visible. However, little is known about whether awareness of these algorithmic processes can reduce online collective aggression. Drawing on a focused application of value-added theory and a multidimensional framework of algorithmic literacy, the present research tested a moderated mediation model in which algorithmic awareness may reduce aggressive participation through attenuated moral outrage, with negative descriptive norms as a boundary condition. Across three experimental studies with emerging adults aged 18–28, participants completed self-developed online collective aggression scenarios. Study 1 (N = 158) showed that experimentally induced algorithmic awareness reduced individuals' tendency toward online collective aggression. Study 2 (N = 306) further found that moral outrage mediated this effect, suggesting that algorithmic awareness may reduce aggressive participation by weakening immediate moralized emotional responses to online events. Study 3 (N = 289) revealed a significant index of moderated mediation: the conditional indirect effect through moral outrage was significant when negative descriptive norms were low but not when they were high. Together, these findings identify algorithmic awareness as a potentially protective cognitive factor whose effects depend on the normative climate inferred from visible cues. They clarify how algorithmic curation, moralized emotion, and normative cues jointly shape aggressive participation. Practically, these findings underscore the need to develop algorithmic literacy education and platform interventions that address both users’ recognition of algorithmic curation and the normative cues conveyed by visible comment environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Pu Y.; Chen H.; Guo Y.
Title: Autonomy-supportive mediation and scam susceptibility: The role of literacy among middle-aged and older adults
Abstract: Although online scams increasingly threaten middle-aged and older adults, existing research has largely focused on individual literacy and short-term interventions, leaving the development and application of scam literacy in everyday contexts less understood. Drawing on parental mediation theory and self-determination theory, this study conceptualizes autonomy-supportive mediation (ASM) as a family-based socialization context for developing aging parents' scam-related literacy. It also considers face concern, a personal orientation reflecting individuals’ motivation to protect their social image from potential social judgment. This study tested two complementary models that distinguish between the foundation of scam literacy (scam knowledge) and its activation (cyber-risk beliefs). Data were collected through a cross-sectional vignette-based survey of 404 middle-aged and older adults in China between February 13 and February 27, 2025, using a volunteer-assisted convenience sampling strategy. The results indicated that higher levels of ASM were linked to lower scam loss, with this association mediated by scam knowledge and moderated by face concern. Moreover, ASM was positively related to cyber-risk beliefs, which were subsequently linked to greater systematic information processing and suspicion toward potential scams. These findings suggest that effective scam prevention depends not only on what individuals know, but also on whether they recognize and respond to risks in real-world situations. This study highlights the importance of autonomy-supportive family communication in combating online scams. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Management: Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
Abstract: This study presents an examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in the disaster management (DM) cycle to support human decision-making systems. There is an urgent need for holistic application strategies that support disaster risk reduction given the increasing frequency and severity of disaster events. This stems from the growing adoption of AI technologies, including machine learning (ML), deep learning, and natural language processing in transforming disaster management. This is to enable the development of high-performance tools for assessing disaster impacts and addressing un-met human needs. This study reviewed journals and conference proceedings articles from three different academic databases: Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Article selection and query refinement were conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to support methodological approach. The review explored scholarly perspectives on AI application in DM phases to support human-centered decision-making processes in reducing disaster impacts on human lives. Findings from the review indicate that most existing studies focus primarily on the AI application in the response phase. Despite its potential, integrating AI into disaster management remains challenging, particularly due to widespread misconceptions about adoption of AI, as well as ongoing ethical, trust, and security concerns. This study emphasizes the comprehensive application of AI to enhance planning, encourage proactive measures, and improve response and recovery efforts during disaster events. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Author full names: Toda, Rizu (59253380400); Toda, Nazu (59253559700); Hagihara, Hiromichi (57191920922); Kanakogi, Yasuhiro (36102980500)
Title: How do children intervene in transgressions? The influence of apology and intervention costs
Abstract: When norms for maintaining cooperative networks are violated, humans try to cope in various ways. However, knowledge is limited regarding how children respond to transgressions. Across two experiments, we examined how 82 six-year-olds, predominantly of Japanese ethnicity (97.6%), choose among punishment, forgiveness, and non-intervention when addressing transgressions from a third-party perspective using a novel paradigm. In addition, we examined how an apology from the transgressor and intervention costs influence children’s moral intervention behaviors. In Experiment 1, Japanese children (N = 41) were presented with a transgressor who either did or did not apologize. Contrary to the previous assumption that children are highly inclined to moral intervention even when it is costly, punishment was the least selected option and non-intervention was the most selected. Children who initially showed reluctance to intervene in transgressions then flexibly adjusted their choice to show forgiveness in response to the transgressor’s apology. In Experiment 2, as in Experiment 1, Japanese children (N = 41) avoided costly punishment and predominantly chose non-intervention. However, when punishment involved no personal cost, children were more likely to choose punishment and less likely to choose no intervention. These findings demonstrate that, when presented with multiple options, 6-year-olds engage less actively in punishment or forgiveness than previous work has suggested, and their intervention strategies are sensitive to social cues and personal costs. This research provides novel insights into the development of moral decision-making in early childhood. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Sesele K.
Title: Holding the periphery: Women, territorial holding labour, and the post-extractive labour-sending economy
Abstract: Post-extractive scholarship has focused predominantly on mines, mining towns and industrial transition, with limited attention to labour-sending territories historically incorporated into extraction through labour circulation and social reproduction. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 21 participants engaged in informal livelihood activity in Viljoenskroon, South Africa, this paper focuses analytically on nine women to examine how such territories continue to function after extractive employment contracts. The findings identify seven interlocking mechanisms through which women sustain households, livelihoods and community continuity under conditions of constrained accumulation, weakened institutional incorporation and infrastructural decline. The paper conceptualises the territorial condition produced through these relations as the extractive periphery and the feminised work through which its continuity is maintained as territorial holding labour. It argues that as extractive employment contracts, reproductive labour that historically subsidised extraction through the reproduction of labour increasingly subsidises its territorial aftermath through the reproduction of continuity. This extends post-extractive analysis beyond sites of production and social reproduction analysis beyond households and labour power to the reproduction of territorial continuity. The findings also challenge continuity as evidence of successful transition: apparent resilience may conceal the transfer of unresolved adjustment costs into women’s income, time and labour. Transition policy must therefore account for labour-sending territories and for who bears the costs through which their continuity is sustained. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Qi Y.; Yan Y.; Xiao X.; Xiao R.; Shi K.; Guo X.; Wang S.; Wang X.; Dong X.
Title: Social–ecological interactions from a carbon-neutrality perspective: Evidence from 30 Chinese provinces
Abstract: Human activities and climate change have profoundly disrupted the equilibrium of social–ecological systems (SES), underscoring the urgency of achieving carbon neutrality. However, existing SES frameworks have largely neglected the critical dimension of carbon flow dynamics and interaction relationships in the context of carbon neutrality. Addressing this gap, this study is the first to systematically construct an integrated SES analytical framework by incorporating interspecific interactions from a carbon-neutrality perspective. Using this foundation, we identify the interaction patterns between social and ecological subsystems, including mutualism, parasitism, and competition. Applying this framework to 30 Chinese provinces from 2003 to 2022, we reveal that the social low-carbon development index initially declined but then increased gradually, while ecosystem services and environmental carrying capacity indices rose. The pressure exerted by the social subsystem far exceeded the feedback capacity of the ecological subsystem across most regions. Importantly, higher SES development does not necessarily imply mutually beneficial interactions. Based on the multi-year mean classification, four provinces were classified within the mutualistic regime, although annual interaction states varied over time, whereas most regions exhibited competitive or parasitic patterns. The study offers new insights into socioecological interaction patterns relevant to current carbon-neutrality goals, and provides differentiated policy recommendations for regional governance, ecological compensation, and cross-sectoral coordination. © 2026

Authors: Chies M.
Title: River Crossings at the Yangtze’s Headwaters: Mapping Hydrosocial Mobility Infrastructures across the Sino-Tibetan Borderlands
Abstract: This article investigates river crossing spaces and practices as key features of past and present human-river relationships along the fluvial landscapes of today’s Three-River-Source (TRS or sanjiangyuan) region of the Qinghai Tibetan Plateau (QTP), which includes the sources of the Yellow, Yangtze, and Mekong Rivers. Through an ethnographically informed analysis of Western travel literature about the Sino-Tibetan borderlands (1850–1950), this study contributes to the environmental history of the QTP by mapping the main pre-1950s river crossings within the Yangtze’s headwaters region and examining how they inform contemporary state-led infrastructural and heritagization processes. This essay draws on critical infrastructure and hydrosocial theory to present river crossings as “hydrosocial mobility infrastructures” (HMIs) enabling connectivity within the wider system of historical trade routes linking China and Tibet in the headwaters region. The HMI framework highlights the ecological and relational character of pre-1950s river crossings, which are shaped by human and non-human interactions, local ecological knowledge, overlapping authorities, and frontier geopolitics, as well as by hydrological, geomorphic, and seasonal changes. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Fostering creativity through interdisciplinary teaching: A meta-analysis of effectiveness
Abstract: Interdisciplinary teaching is widely promoted to cultivate students’ creativity, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. This meta-analysis synthesized 55 quantitative studies (70 effect sizes, 7490 students) from 2013 to 2024, applying random-effects models using Hedges’ g. Creativity outcomes were decomposed into three theoretically grounded dimensions: creative thinking process, creative practice ability, and creative personality and psychology. Results indicated a large overall positive effect ( g + = 1.090, 95% CI [0.913, 1.266]), with very high heterogeneity ( I 2 = 96.017%). Dimensional analysis revealed significant variations: the strongest effects on creative practice ability ( g + = 2.164), followed by creative thinking process ( g + = 1.253), while effects on creative personality and psychology were smaller ( g + = 0.478). Moderator analyses revealed that educational stage, dominant subject, pedagogical approach, intervention duration, and group activities significantly influenced outcomes, while class size and instructional setting did not. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Clemente A.; Penacchio O.
Title: Computational models of hedonic evaluation: An explanatory–predictive framework
Abstract: Hedonic evaluation underlies preferences across domains ranging from food and social stimuli to art. Increasing evidence suggests that these diverse judgements rely on common computational and neurobiological principles, motivating a unified perspective on how hedonic value is constructed. Computational modelling has become central to this endeavour by transforming conceptual theories into quantitative, testable accounts of how sensory information, prior experience, internal states and contextual factors give rise to subjective value. However, the rapid expansion of computational approaches has produced a heterogeneous landscape of models that differ in their assumptions, computational principles, explanatory ambitions and predictive performance. Here, we propose an explanatory–predictive framework for organising, comparing and evaluating computational models of hedonic evaluation. The framework characterises models according to two complementary dimensions: mechanistic explainability and empirical predictive performance. We also organise models into six broad families defined by their dominant computational principles. Finally, we argue that progress will depend less on competing modelling traditions than on integrating complementary computational principles into a general computational theory of hedonic evaluation. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Does artificial intelligence improve social stability risk performance in China?
Abstract: This paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to improving the social stability risk level in China. Against the backdrop of rapid digital transformation and increasingly complex governance challenges, AI has been widely adopted in areas such as public security, social management, and risk monitoring. However, its actual effectiveness in mitigating social stability risks remains underexplored. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions in China, this study constructs an empirical framework to evaluate the impact of AI policy on social stability risk levels. The analysis integrates indicators of technological capacity, governance performance, and socio-economic conditions, and applies quantitative methods to identify both direct and indirect effects. The findings suggest that AI policy significantly reduces social stability risks by promoting digital economy development, increasing wage levels and investment in education. At the same time, the results reveal notable regional heterogeneity. The AI policy significantly reduces social stability risk in the central and western regions, and areas with moderate digital economy development, but has no statistically significant effect in economically developed and digitally advanced areas. The study also highlights potential challenges, including data governance concerns and uneven technological access, which may offset some of AI's benefits. This research contributes to the literature by linking technological innovation with social governance outcomes and provides policy implications for leveraging AI to promote social stability. It suggests that policymakers should not only invest in AI infrastructure but also address institutional and regional disparities to ensure inclusive and effective risk management. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Efficacy of group-based acceptance and commitment therapy in reducing anxiety and improving mental health among adults recovering from COVID-19: a quasi-experimental interventional study
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Background: Survivors of COVID-19 frequently encounter persistent psychological distress. While Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) aims to enhance psychological flexibility, its clinical utility and underlying mechanisms in post-pandemic recovery within diverse cultural contexts require further empirical investigation. Objective: This study evaluated the efficacy of a group-based ACT intervention in alleviating anxiety and promoting psychological well-being and mental health among COVID-19 survivors in Iran. Methods: This study employed a quasi-experimental interventional design with a pretest–posttest and 6-week follow-up assessment, including a control group. Individuals meeting the preliminary eligibility criteria were screened using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and the General Health Questionnaire-28 (GHQ-28). A total of 40 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 and exhibited clinically significant anxiety and reduced general mental health were enrolled and randomly assigned to either the ACT intervention group (n = 20) or the control group (n = 20). The intervention consisted of eight weekly 90-minute sessions focusing on the core processes of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT). Outcomes were assessed using the BAI and GHQ-28 at baseline, immediately after the intervention, and at a 6-week follow-up. Results: Analysis of the 36 participants who completed the protocol revealed that the ACT group demonstrated significant and sustained reductions in anxiety and somatic symptoms, alongside marked improvements in social functioning and overall mental health compared to the control group (p < 0.001). These gains were maintained at the 6-week follow-up. High intervention fidelity (90%) and attendance (87%) suggest the feasibility and acceptability of this approach in a post-viral clinical context. Conclusions: Group-based ACT is an efficacious and feasible intervention for addressing the long-term psychological sequelae of COVID-19. The findings support the integration of ACT into rehabilitation programs to enhance resilience and quality of life in survivors. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive

Authors: Canpolat E.; Bakx J.; Cole M.
Title: Will this time be different? Just transition pathways in eastern and Southern Africa’s critical minerals sector
Abstract: The global energy transition is driving unprecedented demand for critical minerals required for renewable energy technologies like solar panels, wind turbines, and battery storage systems. However, the future translation of mineral reserves into equitable socio-economic development in the region depends on policy frameworks and governance systems that promote inclusive participation, recognition, and benefit-sharing. This paper examines pathways for inclusive economic transformation, analyzing the conditions required to ensure mining-affected communities benefit equitably from the critical minerals boom. We employ a justice-centered framework of distributional, procedural, recognition and restorative justice to analyze five countries (Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Zambia, Malawi, and Burundi) through stakeholder interviews with 43 actors and document and policy analysis, including Malawi and Burundi, whose emerging sectors are largely absent from the peer-reviewed record. Across the five cases the four dimensions are not encountered as separate problems. Findings suggest that employment opportunities do not always reach local populations, revenue mechanisms face transparency challenges, consultation processes have limited influence over outcomes, customary tenure is inconsistently recognized, and environmental legacies often persist without adequate remediation. Ensuring that the substantial economic opportunities created by critical mineral demand are realized inclusively will require simultaneous interventions across all four justice dimensions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Employment subcenters and polycentric urban development in the Greater Dhaka Region, Bangladesh
Abstract: Although a significant number of studies have focused on urban growth patterns in Dhaka, the spatial structure of employment and its roles in shaping polycentric urban development is poorly understood. Specifically, how employment subcenters (ESCs) emerge and organize under conditions of informal and infrastructure-led urban growth typical of Global South megacities remains unclear. Hence, this study poses the question of how ESC formation is related with the construction and development of a polycentric urban employment structure in the city and how their hierarchical spatial organization shapes intra-urban agglomeration. To answer this question, the spatial distribution of employment in the Greater Dhaka Region during the 2011-2013 study period was analyzed based on fine-scale employment data from the 2013 economic census together with Local Moran's I (LMI) within a grid-based framework. An optimal grid size and shape were used to detect ESCs, including their location, hierarchy, spatial extent, geographical distribution, spatial characteristics and processes. The study found 59 ESCs, including one rank 1 center, four rank 2 centers, 18 rank 3 centers, and 36 rank four centers. The findings reveal a core-dominant but dispersed polycentric employment structure, in which high-ranked ESCs concentrated within approximately 20 km of Dhaka's historical core and low-ranked ESCs developed along major transportation corridors in peripheral areas. The findings suggest that the employment structure observed during the study period reflected a hierarchical, corridor-oriented pattern influenced by market forces and infrastructure-led urban processes rather than by planned decentralization, with weak metropolitan coordination strengthening the continued dominance of the historical core. These findings refine polycentricity theory for Global South contexts and provide evidence to support data-driven spatial planning and more balanced urban development in rapidly urbanizing regions. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Family specific spatial borrowing in multimodal urban reconstruction: a leave one neighborhood out study of Cincinnati
Abstract: Urban spatial models often assume that nearby borrowing improves prediction across target variables, but this assumption is rarely tested across distinct urban feature families within a city. We evaluate this question on a citywide hexagonal grid of Cincinnati, Ohio (2016 cells, 60 features in 14 feature families) using multimodal masked reconstruction. We compare four models spanning linear, local nonlinear, shared-gate graph, and selective-gate graph architectures under full leave-one-neighborhood-out evaluation across 50 neighborhoods, with primary summaries for the 36 neighborhoods having at least 20 cells. Median held-out-neighborhood R2 is the primary comparison metric. Cross-neighborhood transfer is family-specific, and no single borrowing strategy dominates. Ridge performs best for street structure, indicating that some spatially regular families are best reconstructed from local linear combinations. The local nonlinear masked autoencoder (MLP-MAE) holds the highest median for most families with positive transfer, though these differences are not statistically distinguishable from the graph models, indicating that local nonlinear multimodal fusion is often sufficient. Graph-based models help most clearly for topography, while the selective-gate graph model wins many individual neighborhood comparisons for several families despite lower medians, reflecting different error profiles. Graph models also produce more neighborhood-structured representations: contextual embeddings from the selective multimodal spatial autoencoder (SMSA) recover neighborhood structure better than raw principal components or local-only embeddings. Learned gates are stable across folds and provide interpretable diagnostics of context reliance, but not a universal ranking of borrowing regimes. These results show that the appropriate spatial borrowing strategy is target-specific rather than universal. For neighborhood-scale interpolation, imputation, and urban monitoring, one spatial modeling recipe can systematically misrepresent some feature families even within the same city. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Jin X.; Cao X.; Li H.
Title: The effect of social robot authority on epistemic vigilance in early childhood
Abstract: Social robots are increasingly deployed as tutors and learning partners, yet their authority cues may discourage children from questioning or verifying information. We investigated whether robot authority influences Chinese children’s epistemic vigilance and which source of authority drives this effect. In Study 1 (N = 128, ages 4 and 6, Mage = 5.39 years, SD = 0.92, 66 girls and 62 boys), robots with high and low overall authority asserted that all aliens in a task had three eyes. Children’s verification behaviors were assessed in terms of the number of times they checked the information, the length of time they spent checking, and how much time passed between checks. Results showed that children engaged in significantly less verification in the high-authority condition, and 6-year-olds checked more often than 4-year-olds. Study 2 (N = 200, ages 4 and 6, Mage = 5.19 years, SD = 0.92, 97 girls and 103 boys) built on Study 1 by manipulating two sources of authority: role authority (teacher-like vs. peer-like) and cognitive authority (knowledgeable vs. unknowledgeable). The same task and outcome measures were used as in Study 1. The results showed that cognitive authority significantly decreased children’s verification behavior, but there was no significant effect of role authority or child age. Title: International supply chain drivers of forage-livestock conflicts in pastoral China
Abstract: China aims to eliminate forage-livestock conflicts (FLCs) in pastoral areas by 2035 to restore degraded grasslands and address related environmental, social, and economic issues. International trade affects grazing-induced FLCs in pastoral China through global economic supply chains. Here, we examine the crucial foreign consumption drivers, international supply chain paths, and global socioeconomic factors influencing FLCs in pastoral China from 2010 to 2020. The results show that foreign consumption caused two million tons of FLCs in pastoral China in 2020. During 2010–2020, foreign consumption contributed 0.1%–10.4% of FLCs in each pastoral province of China. Inner Mongolia, one of the vital ecological barriers against sandstorms in Asia, underwent a significant increase (92.0%) in its FLCs caused by foreign consumption over the decade. The final production sectors in critical international supply chain paths moved from non-pastoral provinces to foreign economies during 2010–2020. In addition, foreign economic structure transitions led to 660 kt of FLC increments during the decade, where foreign production structure transitions contributed 66.8%. Our findings highlight the importance of optimizing foreign production structures and fostering international cooperation to realize China's goal of FLC elimination. © 2026

Title: The effects of resilience-oriented workspace interventions: combining social network analysis and organizational quality indicators
Abstract: Although it is known that workspace influences the performance of healthcare teams, there is scarce evidence regarding how to evaluate its implications for resilient performance. This study demonstrates an integrated approach for evaluating the effects of relocating three acute response teams responsible for the same patients – the rapid response team (RRT), medical on-call team (MOC), and nursing supervision (NS) – from separate rooms to a shared workspace. The intervention was evaluated using two complementary sources of evidence. First, social network analysis surveys were conducted before and after the intervention with the same 30 participants. The surveys mapped advice-seeking relationships from which 22 social network metrics were derived. Second, seven organizational quality indicators were analyzed before and after the intervention. Five quality and 12 network indicators showed statistically significant improvements; except for two social network metrics, all 27 indicators changed in the expected direction for improvement. Notably, reciprocity between teams, which is crucial for resilience, increased substantially – e.g., RRT↔MOC increased from 57.5% to 80.0%. Changes in collaboration patterns and quality indicators provided complementary evidence that the conditions supporting resilient performance were enhanced. The evaluation approach can be adapted to other resilience-oriented interventions in which relational dynamics and patient safety are crucial. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Grinding Charcoal for Rock Painting: A Methodological Framework for Particle-Size Analysis in Rock Art Micro-Samples
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Research on the materiality of rock art has shifted attention from images as finished products to the technical and social processes involved in their making. Within this framework, pigment grinding is a crucial but still methodologically elusive aspect of painting production, despite its potential to inform technological choices, labor investment, and variability in painting practices. In this paper, we propose an experimental and archaeometric approach to the study of charcoal grinding in rock art micro-samples. By combining experimental archaeology, optical microscopy, and particle analysis, we develop a model linking charcoal particle area to grinding time. We apply this method to study black rock paintings from the Oyola archaeological site, in northwestern Argentina, where charcoal was identified as the main black pigment. The results show that microscopically measurable differences in particle areas make it possible to distinguish varying degrees of grinding among paintings that are macroscopically and chemically similar. Beyond the local case study, our findings demonstrate that pigment granulometry can provide access to otherwise invisible dimensions of rock art production, complementing the existing knowledge of technical variability, painting events, and the historical processes through which painted surfaces were made and transformed. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Exploring the evolution of public cognition toward generative AI through sentiment-topic mining and community detection in social graphs
Abstract: The swift advancement of Generative AI(GAI) improves content production efficiency and generates commercial value, yet it presents complex governance issues, including misinformation and technological misuse. To investigate the cognitive evolution of the public and the characteristics of the online opinion ecosystem regarding GAI, this study collected 105,384 GAI-related posts and comments from Sina Weibo between 2023 and 2026. A semantic-topological social graph(ST-Graph) was constructed from textual semantics, engagement feedback, and user profile features, and a Contrastive Learning-based Graph Neural Network(ConGNN) was employed for node representation learning and community detection. Additionally, StructBERT-based sentiment classification was combined with DeepSeek-based key attribute and trigger-word extraction to analyze emotional orientations and cognitive focuses across communities. Experimental findings indicate that ConGNN achieved the highest Silhouette, ARI, and NMI values among the compared methods, while the yearly community partitions yielded Silhouette coefficients ranging from 0.4002 to 0.4476. These results indicate relatively clear separation in the learned representation space and consistent clustering under the evaluated settings, supporting the effectiveness of ConGNN for the constructed ST-Graph. Sentiment analysis shows that public attitudes toward GAI are generally positive, but vary across publishing entities. Public figures garner the greatest number of remarks, with positive feedback from Enterprises constituting the predominant share(49.3%). Government mainly garner neutral feedback(70.9%), however Media and Organizations/Institutions observe a greater share of negative remarks(38.9% and 41.2%). Aspect-level analysis further indicates that public cognition is shifting from early technological expectations and substitution anxiety toward institutional concerns, especially demands for anti-counterfeiting, content credibility, and digital governance mechanisms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The evolving science of negotiation alternatives: New contexts, new perspectives
Abstract: We review the past decade (2016 – present) of empirical research on negotiation alternatives across multiple disciplines, including dyadic bargaining, international trade, and civil conflict interventions. Three themes emerged in our analysis: First, research has focused on how the effects of a negotiator's BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) are not person-invariant but are instead moderated by the characteristics of the party who “holds” the BATNA. Second, studies are establishing the conditions under which negotiation alternatives can backfire and hurt a negotiator's performance. Third, an emerging stream of research challenges our conventional understanding of BATNA by highlighting its perceptual nature and the possibility that it may exist on multiple levels within a given negotiation. We close by outlining future directions for each of these emerging themes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Nodding of virtual humans does not necessarily increase customer trust: a temporal analysis
Abstract: Virtual humans can potentially facilitate engaging customer interactions, but remain rarely used in customer service. Their embodiment enables virtual humans to use non-verbal listening cues like nodding. Nodding is theorized to increase trust in virtual humans, but literature on this effect is scarce, inconsistent, and only uses measurements after interactions. This study therefore aims to research how nodding of virtual humans influences customer trust, by (1) studying the following hypothesized mediation: nodding (social cue) triggers perceived responsiveness (social signal), which subsequently increases trust (social response); and (2) studying temporal trust dynamics within a customer interaction using exploratory analyses. An online experiment (N = 429) was performed, using a between-subjects design with two conditions: a virtual human either nodded during listening or did not. To isolate nodding optimally, participants watched a video of a customer interaction: a virtual human advised a customer on a wardrobe. While watching, participants used a slider scale to keep updating their temporal trust in the virtual human. Afterwards, participants answered questionnaires on trust and perceived responsiveness. Results showed that nodding did not increase trust or perceived responsiveness, nor did nodding build temporal trust. Temporal trust was built throughout the customer interaction, mostly when the virtual human was speaking. Exploratory analysis found that nodding increased anthropomorphism. Possibly, nodding did not influence trust because other social cues already caused trust-building. Virtual human developers should therefore be aware that nodding does not necessarily build customer trust. The temporal trust scale was useful for visualizing trust-building throughout customer interaction videos. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Driving sustainable development goal alignment through green consumption marketing and public mind
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Sustainable development demands synchronized efforts across socioeconomic and environmental domains, specifically targeting poverty alleviation, food security, and environmental stewardship. Although sustainable consumption patterns and ecological marketing act as established catalysts for environmental transitions, the specific socio-civic pathways translating micro-level pro-environmental behaviors into macro-level policy alignment remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, the study objectives were to evaluate the direct and indirect pathways through which green consumption behavior and green marketing drive local alignment with the sustainable development goals through the mediating role of the public mind among residents in Nonthaburi Province, Thailand. METHODS: A quantitative survey design was executed to gather data from 400 residents across administrative districts in Nonthaburi Province using proportionate stratified random sampling. The researchers collected primary data through structured questionnaires employing a 5-point Likert scale. Analytical procedures encompassed descriptive statistics, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling to validate construct relationships and assess overall structural model fit. FINDINGS: The results of structural equation modeling indicate that both green consumption behavior and green marketing significantly influence the realization of local sustainable development goals, operating through both direct pathways and indirect pathways mediated by public consciousness. The public mind demonstrated the strongest direct influence on sustainable development goals realization (β = 0.69, p < 0.01), followed by direct impacts from green consumption behavior (β = 0.35, p < 0.01) and green marketing (β = 0.28, p < 0.01). Additionally, green consumption behavior was the primary driver of public mind activation (β = 0.37, p < 0.01), surpassing green marketing (β = 0.27, p < 0.01). The validated structural model accounted for substantial variance in sustainable development goals alignment (R^2 = 0.97) and the public mind (R^2 = 0.77). CONCLUSION: Green consumption behavior and green marketing are critical precursors to cultivating a collective public mind, which bridges individual eco-conscious actions with macro-level alignment of Sustainable Development Goals. Municipal authorities ought to embed the mobilization of public ecological awareness into environmental governance policies. Furthermore, this structural framework offers a scalable model adaptable to other rapidly urbanizing provinces in Southeast Asia. Title: Vulnerable narcissism outperforms grandiose narcissism as a predictor of social comparison orientation, motives, and affect
Abstract: Narcissism is often characterized by feelings of superiority over others, yet little research has directly tested its relationship with social comparison. Existing work has focused mostly on grandiose narcissism, leaving the role of vulnerable narcissism largely unexplored. Thus, it remains unclear how the two dimensions of narcissism contribute to social comparison processes. Across four correlational studies, we tested how facets of narcissism predict frequency of making social comparisons (Study 1, N = 176; Study 2, N = 217), motives for making comparisons (Study 2), tendencies to make upward and downward comparisons (Studies 3, N = 228; 4 N = 300), and affective responses to upward and downward comparisons (Studies 3 & 4). We also explored whether associations between narcissism and social comparison varied across measurement approaches, using three measures of narcissism. Across studies, vulnerable narcissism consistently predicted greater social comparison orientation, self-enhancement motives, higher directional comparison tendencies, and more negative affect following upward comparisons. In contrast, associations involving grandiose narcissism were weaker, inconsistent, and dependent on measurement approach. These findings indicate that vulnerable narcissism is a more robust predictor of social comparison processes than grandiose narcissism and should be centrally incorporated into future research on narcissism and self-evaluation. Title: Complex adaptive governance for sustainable tourism villages: Explanatory insights from combined polycentric and chaos theoretical perspectives
Abstract: Sustainable tourism villages face complex governance challenges because they must simultaneously support economic development, protect local culture, preserve ecological resources, and respond to changing social conditions. Existing studies have examined sustainable tourism governance mainly from administrative, community-based, or institutional perspectives, but less attention has been given to how distributed authority interacts with nonlinear adaptive dynamics in village-level governance systems. To address this gap, this study develops an integrated framework that combines polycentric governance theory and chaos theory. Using a quantitative explanatory design, survey data were collected from 590 stakeholders involved in tourism village governance across four regencies and one city in Yogyakarta Province, Indonesia. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that institutional diversity has the strongest association with sustainable tourism village governance, followed by decentralization and local autonomy, bifurcation and cosmology, community participation, flexibility and adaptability, edge of chaos and the butterfly effect, and self-organization and strange attractors. The model yields a very high coefficient of determination, which suggests a close within sample fit between the proposed constructs and the observed perception data. This result is interpreted cautiously because the study is cross-sectional and several constructs are conceptually proximate. The study contributes to governance theory by showing that sustainable tourism village governance can be understood as both polycentric and complex-adaptive. Practically, the findings suggest that policymakers and tourism village managers should strengthen multi-actor coordination while maintaining flexibility to respond to uncertainty and local change. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Emotion Regulation in Language Learning: Strategies for Managing Foreign Language Anxiety among Iranian EFL Learners
Abstract: This study employed a mixed-methods approach to examine the utilization of two emotion regulation strategies, namely cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression, among a group of Iranian learners of English as a foreign language (EFL) at universities in Isfahan, Iran. The investigation was based on the Process Model of Emotion Regulation, a psychologically-validated theoretical model proposed by Gross (2015). The study also investigated the correlation between emotion regulation and levels of foreign language anxiety (FLA), and as an additional area of investigation, the impact of emotion regulation on the association between FLA and motivation for learning a second language. A total of 295 learners were questioned using a quantitative questionnaire. The qualitative research involved the selection of thirteen respondents from three levels (high, medium, low) of FLA. The primary component employed in this study was a stimulated recall interview. Data collection was undertaken online due to scheduling constraints. The findings indicated a low frequency of utilization for the two emotion regulation strategies, with cognitive reappraisal being more commonly employed compared to expressive suppression. Learners with low English proficiency exhibited a lower prevalence and preference for cognitive reappraisal. There was a stronger positive correlation observed between expressive suppression and FLA. The study found a negative correlation between cognitive reappraisal and FLA. It provides evidence that understanding the inner workings of learners’ emotion regulation may inform pedagogical practices. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. All rights reserved.

Title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
Abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: CasHyper: Modeling multi-factor interactions and asymmetric influence in cascade prediction via hypercomplex algebra
Abstract: Cascade prediction aims to forecast the future evolution of information diffusion and is an important task in social network analysis. Most existing methods represent users and cascades in real-valued Euclidean spaces, which may offer limited capacity to model multi-factor interactions and asymmetric influence in complex diffusion processes. To address these challenges, we propose CasHyper, a hypercomplex-based cascade prediction framework that integrates hypercomplex algebra with graph neural networks and Transformers. CasHyper organizes user and cascade embeddings into multiple hypercomplex components, with each component encoding distinct latent factors, and uses structured algebraic operations to model cross-component interactions. The non-commutative hypercomplex product further yields order-dependent interaction representations, enabling the model to learn asymmetric influence among users. In the network encoding stage, a static heterogeneous graph channel captures user-user and user-cascade relations, while a Neural ODE-based dynamic channel models the continuous evolution of node states and edge weights. A hypercomplex Transformer with norm-preserving rotary transformations is then introduced to incorporate relative positional information into cascade sequence modeling. Finally, an interaction-aware module and a linear projection module are combined to estimate the probability of each candidate user participating next. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that CasHyper achieves competitive or better performance than the compared methods under the evaluated settings, including relative improvements of up to 43.24% on Android and 18.43% on Christianity in Hits@50. Additional analyses of architectural variants, graph incompleteness, computational efficiency, and different Cayley–Dickson algebras further demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of the proposed framework and reveal dataset-dependent behaviors of different hypercomplex structures. Title: Can bigger cities be safer? Evidence from criminal indictment data in China
Abstract: This paper examines how city size affects the criminal indictment rate, drawing on panel data from Chinese cities spanning 2014-2021. The results show that bigger cities are associated with significantly lower criminal indictment rates. This finding remains robust after accounting for endogeneity concerns and conducting a series of robustness checks. Further analyses provide suggestive evidence that larger cities may reduce criminal indictments through higher opportunity costs, stronger punishment-related deterrence, and greater moral and social costs of crime. However, this crime-reducing effect is weakened by the presence of migrants, and supplementary evidence suggests that lower levels of migrant social integration in larger urban settings may help explain this moderating pattern. These findings highlight the importance of not only supporting urban development, but also ensuring stronger institutional capacity, effective public security governance, and more inclusive public-service provision. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Service-fund coupling for ecological compensation and payments for ecosystem services in transboundary watersheds within China: A systematic review and conceptual framework
Abstract: Transboundary watersheds within China cross provincial, municipal, regional, and other subnational jurisdictions, separating ecosystem-service providers from beneficiary jurisdictions and creating persistent mismatches among ecological benefits, conservation responsibilities, and funding. This review examines how ecological compensation (EC) and payments for ecosystem services (PES) address these mismatches and develops a service-fund coupling framework. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting principles, it combines bibliometric analysis and metadata-based thematic synthesis of titles, abstracts, and keywords from 1263 studies published during 1995–2025 (823 China National Knowledge Infrastructure; 440 Web of Science) with a purposively stratified full-text audit and qualitative evidence synthesis of 60 studies. The literature has shifted from compensation standards, valuation, and institutional design toward ecosystem service flows, policy attribution, and actor interaction, but ecological, financial, behavioral, and institutional analyses remain weakly integrated. Five gaps persist: biophysical-economic translation, funding-behavior feedback, spatiotemporal mismatch, attribution and adaptive feedback, and equity and institutional constraints. The framework connects ecology-to-funding and funding-to-ecology chains through three interfaces: ecological evidence to payment responsibility, funding arrangements to behavioral additionality, and monitored outcomes to adaptive rule adjustment. It treats temporal lags, uncertainty, power asymmetries, and equity as internal coupling conditions, supporting adaptive, transparent, and accountable governance rather than static transfers. Because the evidence base is weighted toward Chinese-language EC research, the framework applies most directly to transboundary watersheds within China; international transboundary-basin research provides comparative and conceptual reference, and transfer beyond this intranational setting requires separate empirical testing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How Changes in Elephant-Handling Practices Shape Human Perceptions of Their Wild Conspecifics
Abstract: Opportunities for direct experience with wildlife shape human perceptions and behaviors, influencing human-environment relationships. These perceptions vary across communities according to lived experiences and the assessed costs and benefits of living with wildlife. In a changing global context, a “perception-practice loop” emerges, where shifts in local practices directly affect attitudes toward wildlife. This study uses a mixed-methods approach - combining qualitative and statistical analysis of semi-structured interviews - to examine how evolving elephant handling practices in Laos influence direct interactions with and perceptions of wild elephants. Our findings indicate that owners adapt their strategies to diverse socio-ecological contexts driven by recent global pressures. These practices, often grounded in reciprocity, shape perceptions and levels of tolerance toward wild individuals. The results indicate that tolerance depends less on aggressive elephant behavior and more on the perceived balance of costs and benefits. While wild elephants impose psychological or delayed burdens, they also provide tangible and symbolic benefits, such as mating opportunities and conservation value. We conclude that fostering reciprocal relationships and integrating traditional knowledge can enhance human-wildlife coexistence, supporting both biodiversity and local well-being. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Narratives in the arenas of Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM) in indigenous lands in Brazil
Abstract: Narratives play a central role in structuring political arenas surrounding artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) in Indigenous Lands in Brazil. Drawing on qualitative evidence from field research conducted in the Brazilian Amazon with the Kayapó peoples—particularly the Mekragnotire and Metuktire subgroups—and the Munduruku people, this article provides an in-depth analysis of the narratives that influence alliances, mobilize actors, and guide decision-making processes within the arenas. The study relies on an extensive dataset collected between 2019 and 2020. This dataset comprises 93 semi-structured and unstructured interviews conducted primarily at local and regional levels, as well as direct observation, field notes, and documentary materials. The framework combines the concepts of political arenas and narratives as a theoretical and methodological lens with a focus on socio-environmental decision making processes. The findings identify four predominant narratives: (i) ASGM as a means of Indigenous integration or assimilation into national society; (ii) ASGM as a threat to ethnic continuity and environmental protection; (iii) ASGM as an activity amenable to regulation and sustainability; and (iv) ASGM as fundamentally incompatible with Indigenous territories. With respect to regulation, the analysis identifies intermediate positions. These positions indicate potential pathways for legitimation through the adoption of safeguards, including territorial governance, collective decision-making, and strengthened monitoring mechanisms. Based on narrative analysis, the article illustrates the coexistence of multiple interpretations of ASGM in indigenous lands, extending beyond the polarized positions in the debate. Copyright © 2026. Title: Blowing Leaves in Archaeology—The Multidimensionality of Technological Complexity in Human Origins Research
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Technological complexity has been a continuous trope in archaeological research from its beginnings in the nineteenth century. Based on a concept of unidirectional cultural evolution, archaeological material was ordered along a linear progression from simple to complex. While creating hierarchies of extant populations based on the complexity of their tools is not overtly practiced in archaeology anymore, the same is not true for the deep past. The concept of behavioural modernity and research on human cognitive evolution is still partly founded on technological complexity. The turn away from technological complexity to symbolic behaviour in pursuing questions surrounding behavioural modernity and humanness was less a reaction to criticisms of the concept but served to maintain the hierarchical ranking between modern humans and extinct hominins. Here, we propose an alternative view on technological complexity that attempts to overcome linear hierarchies and lingering progressivist notions. By reviewing several measures of complexity alongside their analytical units and underlying definitions, we show that technological complexity is not suitable for creating a single hierarchy of artefacts, assemblages, or hominin species. The multitude of existing definitions, methods, and measures does not imply a fundamental flaw in these approaches but exemplifies the multidimensionality of technological complexity. We propose a new way of understanding multiple, justified measures for technological complexity through a heterarchical structure that allows various kinds of ranking to exist depending on context, need, scale, or function, including the potential for competing or even contradictory hierarchies. A heterarchical perspective on technological complexity asks ‘How were technologies or hominins complex?’ rather than ‘How complex were technologies and hominins relative to another?’ This approach can shed persistent historical bias and overcome simplistic dichotomies such as ‘us’ and ‘them’ in deep-time archaeology that hinder our ability to engage with questions about the becoming of humans in a meaningful way. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Prolonged participation AI-based mindfulness school programme in primary education: Implications for AI practices, schools and developers
Abstract: Background: Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim: This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method: The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group (N = 91) and a control group (N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% (SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results: Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η2p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η2p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η2p = .025). Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion: The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. Title: Negative and positive emotional eating and food cravings related to weight loss during weight management
Abstract: Emotional eating and food cravings are common among adults living with overweight or obesity. This study investigated these in relation to weight-management success and reports on strategies for managing emotional eating. A quasi-prospective study design was used including an online survey completed by 3834 adults on a community weight management programme. Measures included negative and positive emotional eating (BEES) and food craving (CoEQ). Additionally, objectively measured body weight over the previous 12 weeks was obtained and participants were grouped into Higher (>10%, N = 962), Moderate (5-10%, N = 2156), and Lower (<5%, N = 716) weight loss groups. Open questions were used to explore strategies for managing emotional eating. Between-group differences were tested using univariate ANOVAs, with Tukey post hoc comparisons where significant effects emerged. Open ended responses were analysed using inductive thematic analysis and mapped onto the Behaviour Change Taxonomy. Respondents were mostly female (92.0%), mean age = 57.2 years, and BMI = 32.1 kg/m2. Results showed participants had lost 3.7 BMI units over the previous 12 weeks. Higher weight loss was strongly associated with lower negative and positive emotional eating, fewer food cravings and eating control difficulties. Prominent themes for managing emotional eating were distraction (31.7%) and physical activity along with healthier food substitutions, planning and positive mindset. Group social support was also highlighted. These data highlight the perceived importance of psychological and group-based social support in weight management. Authors: Wu E.L.; Kuo H.-C.
Title: The influence of gender, socioeconomic, and domain competencies on students’ creative thinking across four high-performing educational systems
Abstract: This study explores the multidimensional construct of students’ creative thinking by analysing the PISA 2022 Creative Thinking assessment data from four educational systems: Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Macao, and the Czech Republic. These jurisdictions are uniquely characterised by high student performance in reading, mathematics, and science, while their average creative thinking scores fall below the OECD benchmark. The study examines the predictive power of gender, socioeconomic status (SES), and academic proficiency in Reading, Mathematics, and Science on students’ performance across four creative thinking (CRT) domain contexts: Written Expression, Visual Expression, Social Creative Problem-Solving, and Scientific Creative Problem-Solving. Evidence shows that female students consistently outperformed male students across all four creative thinking domains, while SES demonstrated a modest but consistently positive association with creative thinking performance. Academic competencies also contributed significantly to CRT but exhibited distinct domain-specific predictive patterns. Reading competence was the strongest and most consistent predictor, particularly for Written and Visual Expression. Science competence showed stable positive associations across domains, whereas Mathematics contributed most strongly to Social and Scientific Creative Problem-Solving but was negatively associated with Visual Expression. These findings indicate that academic competencies contribute differently across creative thinking domains. Representative item-level analyses further illustrated task-specific predictive patterns, while the complete item-level analyses are reported in the Supplementary Material. These findings support a domain-sensitive view of creative thinking, in which academic competencies show differential associations with creative performance depending on the domain and task context, and further offer practical implications for creativity assessment and educational practice. Title: Measuring head motion across deceleration levels in automated driving: Quantifying comfort
Abstract: Passenger-centred comfort measures are needed to enable adaptive driving styles in automated vehicles, particularly where comfort begins to decrease. This study examined passengers' head motion during automated braking at a crosswalk. Data from thirty-four participants were analysed, who experienced three deceleration levels (−1.5, −2.5, −3.5 m/s2) and two pedestrian visibility conditions, reflecting how quickly the AV braked after the pedestrian appeared, rating comfort respectively. As expected, head pitch and translational acceleration increased with deceleration intensity, while pedestrian visibility had no effect on head motion, even though faster AV responses were previously found more comfortable, suggesting this reflects passengers' judgement of the AV's response rather than head stability. Head-motion measures did not add predictive value beyond vehicle kinematics, likely because comfort ratings were similar across conditions. In this scenario, head-motion mainly reflected physical response to braking rather than subjective evaluation. Future research should test head-motion measures in more complex driving conditions. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Wang Y.; Liu X.; Deng Y.; Xiao H.; Zhang Y.
Title: Gendering conversational AI in human–AI interaction: The role of interaction context and sexist ideology in shaping user evaluations
Abstract: As human–AI interaction becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, users often infer social identities from AI systems, including gender. Moving beyond the conventional view of AI gender as a static, designer-assigned attribute, this study conceptualizes AI gender as a user-constructed perception shaped by contextual cues. Integrating social role theory, the stereotype content model, and ambivalent sexism theory, we conducted a 2 (AI gender cues: male vs. female) × 3 (interaction context: service-oriented, warm-authoritative, vs. serious-authoritative) between-subjects experiment with Chinese participants (N = 833) to examine how interaction context, perceived AI gender, and sexist ideology jointly shape evaluations of AI competence, warmth, and trustworthiness. The results showed that interaction context significantly influenced gender attribution, with the serious-authoritative condition eliciting stronger gender categorization and a masculinization bias regardless of assigned gender cues. The evaluative consequences of perceived AI gender were also context-dependent: perceived femininity consistently linked with warmth, but was associated with competence and trustworthiness primarily in the serious-authoritative condition. Hostile and benevolent sexism further moderated these relationships in distinct ways. By shifting attention from designed gender to perceived gender, this study offers a more process-oriented account of AI anthropomorphism and demonstrates the value of integrating the stereotype content model with ambivalent sexism theory to explain bias in human–AI evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Assessment of Drinking Water Security and Waterborne Disease Prevalence in Imphal East and West Districts of Manipur, India
Abstract: Integrated assessment of drinking water security and the prevalence of waterborne diseases in the Imphal East (IE) and Imphal West (IW) districts of Manipur, India, using the water poverty index (WPI). WPI is evaluated across various dimensions, including the availability and accessibility of water resources and the use of safe, acceptable-quality drinking water; the socioeconomic capacity of the population to cope with water security challenges; and overall environmental challenges. The seasonal prevalence of waterborne diseases was assessed with respect to climate variables, specifically rainfall and temperature. The systematic, structured household questionnaire survey and focus group discussions were conducted to assess socioeconomic parameters of the representative population. Based on the integrated assessment, the study reveals a poor-to-moderate WPI, highlighting a significant challenge for people in accessing potable water in the region. This underscores the need to improve rural drinking water supply to ensure public health safety. Thus, the present study incorporates the interlinkage between climate variability, public health challenges, and their impact on the drinking water security in the region. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.
