Title: Gaze aversion and emotional mimicry deficits in individuals with schizophrenia during naturalistic interaction
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia exhibit a range of verbal and nonverbal impairments during social interaction, which contribute to reduced interaction quality and broader social dysfunction. To optimize clinical interventions, it is essential to identify the mechanisms underlying these deficits. Building on previous findings demonstrating reduced emotional mimicry in schizophrenia, the present study examined whether gaze aversion is associated with instances of failed mimicry during naturalistic conversation. In a within-partner design, interacting partners (n = 20) each engaged in one conversation with an individual with schizophrenia (n = 20) and one with a matched healthy control (n = 20). Prior analyses using OpenFace-based video coding revealed diminished emotional mimicry in the schizophrenia group. In the present study, the same video recordings were reanalyzed using FaceReader to extract gaze direction. We specifically examined gaze aversion during the interaction and, more critically, during episodes of failed mimicry, defined as instances in which participants did not reciprocate their partner's smile. Results indicated that although individuals with schizophrenia did not display significantly greater overall gaze aversion across the entire interaction, they exhibited significantly greater gaze aversion when their partner was smiling. This pattern was associated with a higher proportion of failed mimicry accompanied by gaze aversion in the schizophrenia group compared to controls. These findings suggest that reduced visual attention may represent one mechanism contributing to emotional mimicry deficits in schizophrenia. Clinical implications are discussed, along with the potential role of stigma in exacerbating these processes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Hutchinson J.
Title: The therapy room is not a classroom: Why emotional safety in therapy belongs to the client
Abstract: Emotional safety in the therapy room is a clinical resource that belongs to the client. A growing number of clinicians, particularly those trained in social justice frameworks, feel empowered or obligated to correct clients' use of language deemed offensive. This paper argues that such practices are ethically indefensible and clinically counterproductive. Drawing on meta-analytic evidence on the therapeutic alliance, countertransference management, and core conditions of change, the evidence indicates that corrective responses to client language damage the alliance quality, increase the risk of premature termination, and suppress the very kind of honest disclosure that therapy requires. This paper further examines structural ideological bias in the profession, the contradictions between activist training frameworks and foundational ethics codes, and the misapplication of harm-speech theory to the clinical context. The fiduciary obligation of the therapist, the clinical evidence base, and every major professional ethics code converge on the same conclusion: the counseling room is not a classroom, and the client's psychological safety is not the therapist's to withdraw. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yeleliere E.; Frimpong Boamah E.
Title: Locked in: How formal institutional design sustains extractivism and ecological decline in Ghana’s mining–water sector
Abstract: Mining-related water pollution persists despite repeated legislative reforms and regulatory interventions. Yet, existing explanations largely attribute this persistence to weak enforcement, political patronage, or socioeconomic pressures driving artisanal small-scale mining (ASM). We argue instead that the problem is fundamentally one of institutional design. Drawing on institutional theory and institutional grammar analysis, we examine how Ghana's mining-water legislation allocates authority and embeds incentive structures that shape environmental governance. We find that the legislative framework privileges regulative over constitutive institutional elements, producing governance arrangements that are procedurally elaborate yet functionally weak. At the same time, it embeds economic and political incentives that favor extractivism while providing comparatively weak social and regulatory incentives for environmental stewardship, reinforcing fragmented authority, symbolic governance, and executive overreach. These institutional arrangements generate intertwined common-pool resource and public-bad dilemmas that lock Ghana's mining-water sector into a gilded trap, in which short-term extractive gains systematically outweigh long-term socioecological sustainability. The findings suggest that persistent mining-related water pollution is not simply a failure of enforcement but a consequence of institutional architectures that privilege extractivism while weakening environmental governance. In reconceptualizing the gilded trap as an institutionally produced condition, the paper demonstrates how imbalances between constitutive and regulative institutional elements generate symbolic governance and position the state as an active producer, rather than merely a failed regulator, of extractivist outcomes. © 2026 .

Authors: Troath S.
Title: Deep sea mining, think tanks, and the politics of expertise
Abstract: Deep sea mining (DSM) is being contemplated in an environment of heightened geopolitical tensions. A confluence of factors has led to securitised framings of DSM, including the centrality of the Pacific as both a potential mining location and a perceived frontline of strategic competition, and the desire of western states to “derisk” from China when it comes to critical minerals. One of the factors shaping how strategic competition is understood and responded to is the role of experts. Within western states such as the US and Australia, think tanks play an important role in shaping narratives, perceptions, and policies relating to defence and foreign affairs. In this paper I will investigate how western security-related think tanks are approaching DSM.I will argue that think tanks are playing a significant role in contributing to narratives of necessity regarding DSM, and that security and strategic competition are the dominant framing of these narratives of necessity. Authors: Melumad S.
Title: Modality effects in human–technology interaction
Abstract: This paper reviews emerging research on how different interaction modalities influence information processing and behavior when using new technological devices. A conceptual framework of modality effects is proposed which argues that different input (vocal, haptic) and output modalities (audial, visual) can trigger both cognitive and affective processes that alter users' downstream behaviors. For example, information consumed audially from voice technology rather than visually on a screen can enhance both cognitive load (i.e., cognitive process) and one's sense of social presence (i.e., affective process), which ultimately shape the types of choices made through the technology. The work concludes with a discussion of future research directions in this domain. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: How social status shapes U.S. children’s beliefs about social mobility
Abstract: Children grow up within social hierarchies that shape their everyday lives. Social mobility is a core mechanism through which societies either challenge or maintain existing inequalities. The present study examined how U.S. children’s social status—both experimentally manipulated and measured at the neighborhood level—shapes their beliefs about social mobility for themselves and their high- and low-status peers. Children ( N = 130; 3–8 years; 70 girls, 59 boys, 1 non-binary; 12.3% Asian, 6.9% Black, 11.6% Latine, 20.7% Multiracial, and 48.5% White) were randomly assigned to either experimentally advantaged or disadvantaged groups. They were then assessed on their (1) general expectations about social mobility, (2) effort-contingent expectations for mobility, and (3) post-hoc explanations for upward and downward mobility. We found that compared to experimentally-disadvantaged children, experimentally-advantaged children were more likely to have higher expectations for themselves and high-status peers, but lower expectations for low-status peers. With age, disadvantaged children (experimental and neighborhood) exhibited higher expectations for themselves and lower expectations for high-status peers, whereas advantaged children’s expectations remained stable. Older children were more likely to believe working hard leads to upward mobility and attribute upward/downward mobility to individual effort. This tendency was especially pronounced for their own upward (vs. downward) mobility, but less so when evaluating the upward mobility of high-status peers (vs. themselves). These results suggest that children’s beliefs about social mobility develop throughout childhood, differ by target, and are shaped by their own social status. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Cash transfers and social preferences of children
Abstract: We study the effects of a large unconditional cash transfer program on social preferences of children in rural Kenya using a randomized controlled trial. We measure the social preferences of 4022 children with survey questions and incentivized behavioral games three years after the cash transfer. First, we find no persistent economic effects of the program. Additionally, we find no consistent evidence that children from the treatment group or that children from the spillover group are more or less prosocial than children from the control group. However, we find some evidence of reduced psychological well-being among adults and children in spillover households. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Rural occupational health in Colombia: policy–practice gaps among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca
Abstract: This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia. Authors: Wenhao W.; Qi H.; Zhaolun D.; Kulophas D.
Title: “Empowerment” or “Burden”? A study on the double-edged sword effect of university ethical leadership on faculty members’ creativity
Abstract: Higher education is entering a comprehensive and profound transformation stage, which is both an inevitable trend of societal development and a response to increasingly higher demands for talent cultivation quality. University faculty creativity is not only a core driver of their own career development but also of strategic significance to the innovation-oriented educational ecosystem in higher education institutions. As a widely endorsed leadership paradigm in universities, the influence of ethical leadership on faculty creativity remains insufficiently understood and requires systematic investigation. Grounded in social learning theory, this research develops a theoretical model to examine the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which university ethical leadership influences faculty creativity. Based on 487 three-wave time-lagged matched leader-faculty data, this study employed Mplus 8.3 to conduct bootstrap analyses. The results show that university ethical leadership enhances faculty creativity through increased perceived work meaningfulness, while simultaneously inhibiting creativity through heightened perceived ethical strain. In addition, faculty work centrality not only strengthens the direct effects of ethical leadership on perceived work meaningfulness and perceived ethical strain, but also amplifies the indirect effects of ethical leadership on creativity through both mediating mechanisms. This research extends the application of social learning theory in the field of higher education management and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for optimizing leadership practices and fostering faculty creativity in universities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Broken bodies in Domestic Spaces: Direct and Structural Violence in an Atypical Mortuary Dataset from Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: A major challenge for the understanding of violence in the past is that our main source of evidence comes from cemeteries, but a significant proportion of the victims of violence are not buried in cemeteries. Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia (c. 500 BCE–1050 CE) is infamous for its emerging warrior ideology and hegemony of violence. Yet, somewhat counter-intuitively, trauma rates have typically been found to be relatively low in cemetery populations. Not everyone was afforded formal burial in cemeteries, however. The BODY-POLITICS project examines a previously neglected mortuary dataset: disarticulated and semi-complete human remains deposited in and around domestic spaces such as longhouses, pits, wells, postholes, and hearths. We report on 12 individuals inscribed with 19 ante- and perimortem traumatic injuries, analysed through osteological, bimolecular and digital imaging methods. The unusual post-mortem history of these individuals, set within a historical context of raiding, enslavement, and ritual violence including potential ‘human sacrifice’, allows us to explore multiple scenarios for inflicted injuries: war-like events (extra-community violence), interpersonal and domestic violence (intra-community violence), and ritual violence. Finally, by integrating trauma patterns, mortuary treatment, and contextual information, we discuss the broader life histories of these individuals and argue that some may have been vulnerable to structural, ‘slow’ violence that compounded over the lifecourse. This study thus contributes to broader discourse on direct and structural violence towards potentially marginalised people, as well as connections between ritualised violence and divergent mortuary pathways. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Gümüştaş C.
Title: Masculine honor, social visibility, and safety non-compliance: intentions and approval judgments in high-risk sectors in Turkey
Abstract: Unsafe work in high-risk sectors cannot be explained only by knowledge deficits or weak safety management; workers may also attach reputational meaning to visible compliance. Drawing on honor theory and occupational-safety research on risk perception and social context, this study examined whether masculine honor values (hereafter honor values)—the belief that a man’s worth depends partly on a publicly defensible reputation—were associated with unsafe work intentions, lower perceived risk, and greater approval of safety-rule non-compliance among male workers in Turkish construction and shipbuilding. A worker survey (N = 244) was combined with a within-person vignette experiment in which the focal hazard was held constant while visibility was manipulated and audience identity and prior social comment varied orthogonally. Honor values were positively associated with unsafe work intentions (H1a) and approval of others’ violations (H1b), and negatively associated with perceived risk (H2). Perceived risk partially accounted for the honor–intention association (H3). The association between honor values and approval of non-compliance was stronger when the violation was public rather than private (H4), consistent with a reputational, visibility-contingent account. These findings identify a micro-level sociocultural pathway that complements knowledge- and risk-based accounts of safety decisions. They also suggest that safety communication and supervisory practice should address the social meaning of compliance, while the cross-sectional mediation and judgment-based vignette outcome limit causal and behavioral inference. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Viestad V.M.; Wintjes J.
Title: Teaching Through Making: |xam and !xun Material Culture of the Bleek and Lloyd Collection
Abstract: At Wits Art Museum (University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa) is a small collection donated to the former Wits Museum of Ethnology by Percival Kirby in 1952. A note in the accession register ties the items into the context of the renowned ‘Bushman researches’ of Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd in Cape Town in the 1870s and 1880s, an unusual cross-cultural collaboration with a small group of |xam- and !xun-speaking people against the backdrop of the extreme oppression of San peoples across the southern African region. These objects represent a rare instance of historical material culture of San (‘Bushman’) origin in museum collections being associated with named persons or specific communities of origin. We examine them according to object type—spoon, head ornament, firestick, plaything, arrow and bullroarer—to assess their provenance and approach them ‘biographically’, exploring their community origins and coming into being as specific things, and their being gifted to Kirby by Wilhelm's daughter, Dorothea Bleek. Our ‘relocation’, documentation and contextualization of the Bleek-Kirby collection enables some of the material linkages to be restored, complementing the better-known narratives, making the case for the objects as active participants in the conversations, and enriching understanding of the Bleek and Lloyd Collection as a whole. We examine the significant cultural know-how embedded in these objects and emphasize the creative agency of the |xam and !xun people—|hanǂkass'o, !nanni, Tamme among others—as primary authors and producers of knowledge within the broader intellectual project. The bullroarers in particular reveal some of the affordances of this detailed work, assisted by the ongoing digitization and digital curation of the archive. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Analogy Versus Behavioral Ecology in the Study of Human Evolution
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: In a recent critique published in this journal (Ben-Dor, M. & R. Barkai, 2026, Paleolithic dietary flexibility? Methodological considerations in analogy-based reconstructions of Paleolithic energetic returns, Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 33, article 47, pp. 1–27), the authors characterize behavioral ecology approaches to the study of foraging efficiency as being fundamentally constrained by their reliance on conventional analogy-based reasoning. This characterization, however, misrepresents the aims and theoretical and methodological foundations of these approaches. Rather than relying on simple analogies, behavioral ecology models evaluate how interactions among variables such as prey behavior, encounter rates and contexts, seasonal variation in the macronutrient composition of game tissues, technology, pursuit success rates, opportunity costs, and other ecological and economic factors influence foraging efficiency across diverse habitats and among a wide range of societies. By explicitly identifying and testing the mechanisms that generate variation in economic returns, these approaches provide a rigorous and theory-driven alternative to conventional analogy-based interpretations. We also identify several problems with Ben-Dor and Barkai’s claim that proboscideans constituted high-ranked prey during the Lower and Middle Pleistocene. These include a selective use of relevant data, assumptions that lack sufficient empirical support, methodological shortcomings in the treatment and interpretation of the available evidence, and reliance on inadequately controlled archaeological datasets. Given these limitations, we find little support for their claim that proboscideans represented a frequent and easily acquired prey resource during the Pleistocene. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Pastoral Belonging and Educational Opportunity for Mongolian Herder Women
Abstract: As part of the UN’s International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralism (2026) the Gender Working Group stresses the importance of equality in pastoralism. For herder women themes of family, work, schooling and marginality resonate across African and Asian drylands. As environmental, economic and development pressures impact herding women are essential to its continuity. In Mongolia, a prominent pastoralist nation, the role of rural women in household decision-making, livelihood production and community contributions has received little study. In a series of interviews in two rural districts this study explores the practice and knowledge of female herders with a focus on their daily lives. Findings reflect pastoralism in a time of social and livelihood transition. Nature, livestock and tradition were valued whilst family and work responsibilities were arduous. Reflecting perceived challenges and opportunities, experienced herders encouraged daughters to pursue education. Whether growing up in the socialist era or appreciating today’s conveniences, women’s commitment to herding is a vital part of the country’s past nomadic heritage and future direction. As social roles and environmental uncertainty reconfigure pastoralism, female herders are at the forefront of changing rural communities in Mongolia. Author full names: Jang, Daisung (33067714000); Welker, Christopher (58062267500); Le, Dai Quy (58168242400)
Title: Negotiation across the social sciences: An interdisciplinary review
Abstract: Psychological investigations have generated numerous insights into how two parties bargain. To build on this literature, we review recent research across multiple disciplines, focusing on aspects of negotiation that have received relatively little attention, namely individual differences, multiparty negotiations, and contextual factors. Insights into individual differences are observed in the developmental psychology, artificial intelligence, and social psychology literature. Investigations in these domains show that young children can think strategically about exchange, that individual differences shape the information negotiators obtain and how they utilize information, and that situational factors can constrain or facilitate the expression of individual differences. Insights into multiparty negotiations emerge from the social networks and political science literature. Investigations in these domains explore novel multiparty dynamics, highlighting the importance of structural position in bargaining, and demonstrating that relationship history can shape coalition formation. Insights into contextual factors emerge from the economic and public health literature. Title: Integrated system dynamics modeling for sustainable fisheries provisioning services
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Fisheries provisioning services deliver food production, livelihoods and ecosystem functions, but are increasingly under pressure from environmental degradation, declining fishery resources and socio-economic stressors. Traditional paradigms in fisheries governance often exhibit a deficiency in accounting for the multidirectional feedback loops linking ecological systems with socio-economic dynamics. The objectives of this study were to develop an integrated system dynamics model to assess interactions between these dimensions and identify management options to improve fisheries provisioning services through long-term scenario simulations. METHODS: A system dynamics model was integrated, consisting of social, environmental, and economic sub-models using primary and secondary data from 2018-2023. The model includes population, fishermen, floating net cages, alternative employment, willingness to be a fisher, water quality and aquatic conditions, fish restocking, capture fisheries production, fisheries productivity, fish processing innovations, income, costs, and fisher's income. The model was verified and validated using the mean absolute error and average variation error metrics. Subsequently, predictive simulations were projected to 2045 under current, moderate, and optimistic scenarios. FINDINGS: Actual capture fisheries production declined by 88.9 percent, from 588,100 kilograms in 2018 to 65,035 kilograms in 2023 and was projected to decline to 31,179 kilograms by 2045 under current conditions. Under the moderate and optimistic scenarios, the number of floating net cages was modeled with an annual reduction rate of 30% and 35%, respectively. Production recovery commenced in 2027 under the moderate scenario and in 2026 under the optimistic scenario. Furthermore, target water quality conditions were achieved by 2041 and 2037, respectively, while fisher's net income reached positive values by 2034. CONCLUSION: The integrated system dynamics model underscores the potential for the sustainability of fishery production services through coordinated actions across social, environmental, and economic dimensions. The faster realization of target outcomes under the optimistic scenario highlights that proactive, coordinated interventions effectively expedite ecological restoration, fisheries output, and socioeconomic progress. This model offers a decision-support framework for assessing long-term fisheries management strategies. © 2027 The author(s). Title: Investigating secondary school students’ shared epistemic agency with GAI in online scientific explanation writing
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used as a pedagogical assistant in online learning; yet how young students, such as secondary school students, enact epistemic agency (EA) when learning with GAI remains underexplored. In this study, we examined the types and levels of EA demonstrated by secondary school students with scaffolded GAI and investigated the relation among students' prior academic proficiency, self-efficacy in learning, and EA demonstrated. Participants were 122 seventh graders who engaged in an online bilingual inquiry unit on photosynthesis. The unit supports students in Taiwan in learning science inquiry and English as a foreign language, with GAI prompted and integrated to support students' scientific explanation writing in English. Data collected and analyzed included students’ prior academic proficiency through assessments, self-efficacy in learning through questionnaires, and student–GAI conversation turns through textual conversation logs. Results identified seven types of student–GAI shared epistemic agency (SEA), with at least 86% of students demonstrating such agency at least once. Correlation results indicated that the frequency of EA demonstrated by students was associated with their prior language proficiency. Cluster analysis with the retained four-profile solution further suggested that student–GAI SEA was likely to be activity-specific. The identified SEA categories provide a framework for examining student–GAI SEA, and the instructional design illustrates how GAI can be prompted to preserve opportunities for student contribution. Title: Effects of a design thinking education program for kindergarteners: A mixed-methods study
Abstract: Children as young as three can engage in oral and visual planning when creating tangible objects from materials, yet it remains unclear whether such design competencies can be systematically strengthened in early childhood to cultivate future design thinkers and innovative creators. To evaluate a research-informed design thinking (DT) education program, we conducted a mixed-methods study. The quantitative component involved a quasi-experiment with 133 children ( M age = 5.22, SD = 0.86) from a Chinese kindergarten (intervention group: n = 68; business-as-usual comparison group: n = 65), where the intervention group received an eight-week DT program. Each child’s DT competence was assessed immediately before and after the intervention, followed by play-based interviews with 12 children (six per group). Child-level analyses indicated a statistically significant improvement in overall DT competence favoring the intervention group (Cohen’s d=0.38). However, gains were uneven across specific DT dimensions. Children showed more apparent gains in Empathize, Define, and Prototype, whereas no significant gains were observed in Ideate and Test. Furthermore, the youngest children appeared to show larger gains, whereas gender did not significantly moderate the intervention effects. Qualitative interviews provided insight into the cognitive processes underlying these developmental variations. Together, these preliminary findings may inform DT education research and practice in early childhood settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Social-ecological resilience and environmental justice in Bangladesh: A multi-site analysis of sand mining governance
Abstract: As global demand for sand reaches an estimated 50 billion tonnes annually, the pressure on fluvial and coastal ecosystems has created a significant sustainability crisis. This study examines the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of sand mining in Bangladesh, a deltaic country where rapid urbanization has transformed sand into a multi-billion-dollar industry. Combining Social-Ecological Systems (SES) and Environmental Justice (EJ) frameworks, the research uses a qualitative case study approach across three ecologically distinct sites: Chandpur (river confluence), Sandwip (estuarine island), and Cox's Bazar (mainland coast). Data from 39 semi-structured interviews and field observations show that unregulated extraction is reported and observed as coinciding with a self-reinforcing (positive) feedback loop of increased riverbank erosion and habitat loss that respondents associate with harm to the livelihoods of marginalized fishers and farmers. The results reveal a triple failure of justice: distributive (unequal erosion burdens), procedural (exclusion from leasing decisions), and recognitional (marginalization of local ecological knowledge). Additionally, an analysis of the Balumohal and Soil Management Act (2010) uncovers critical institutional issues, including political patronage and poor coordination between the Department of Environment and local authorities. By highlighting community stories of adaptation and displacement, this study contends that sustainable resource management must shift from top-down, revenue-focused models to participatory, justice-driven frameworks that safeguard the resilience of rural social-ecological systems. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Cross cultural patterns of linguistic aggression and aggressive combat content enjoyment: A computational study of PUBG reviews across six continents
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: This study explores global patterns of linguistic aggression and appreciation for aggressive combat content as expressed in reviews of PlayerUnknown’s Battlegrounds (PUBG), analyzing over 18.7 million Google Play Store English language reviews from over 80 countries. Grounded in the General Aggression Model (GAM), it integrates media psychology, cross cultural communication, and computational social science to assess emotional expression in user generated content. Two indices, Aggression Score and Appreciation of Aggressive Content (AAC), were constructed using NLP, sentiment analysis, and lexicon-based tagging to capture hostile sentiment (anger) and positive reinforcement (joy, ratings, likes) in aggression-related reviews. Results reveal a significant increase in the average intensity of both scores over time, with reviews grouped under South America exhibiting higher average aggression and AAC scores within the dataset, while reviews grouped under Australia show comparatively lower levels of these measures. The study uses GAM as a conceptual lens to interpret large-scale, naturalistic expressions of aggression and enjoyment. Methodologically, it offers replicable framework for affective analysis; practically, it offers exploratory insights for game design and content moderation in digital environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Linear settlements: Morphological Patterns and Processes, Shaping territory, networks and urban fabrics. A case study in and around Vienna in a European perspective
Abstract: Linear settlements represent a distinctive village typology that is prevalent across numerous regions of Europe, encompassing both rural and more urban areas. In the context in and around Vienna, historical linear settlements are a defining feature of the built landscape. From historically grown structures to top-down planned settlements, these linear village types are defined by a range of factors, e.g. agricultural activities, geographical conditions or even internal colonisation processes by monarchs. Over the course of history, a canon of different village forms with distinct spatial qualities has developed. However, within the scope of this research on Vienna and against the background of the umbrellaing 15 mC project (emc2), the predominant types of Straßendorf and Angerdorf are the primary focus. In Vienna, these historic linear settlements are integrated into the urban fabric while still retaining varying degrees of permanence and persistence in the urban layout. By combining different methods - local morphogenetic analysis, urban network analysis, regional typological mapping and comparative analysis to regions in France and Italy - this study provides insights and findings on how linear settlement types in and around Vienna have developed morphologically, with a particular focus on the last two centuries. The objective of this study is to explore the influence of these linear settlements on the shaping of territories, networks and urbanisation processes, and their subsequent characterisation of contemporary urban and rural environments. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Khedhiri S.
Title: Predictors of Death Related to Drug Use Disorder and Interpersonal Violence in North Africa
Abstract: Fatal interpersonal violence and deadly drug use disorder are serious social issues resulting from criminal behavior, which require effective intervention policies. Prior research on African countries is limited, and the potential association between the two issues, as described in the literature, has not been investigated. In this study, a statistical analysis was performed with R packages to identify factors that predict the death patterns related to drug use disorder and interpersonal violence, and to show empirical evidence for the association between drugs and violence in North Africa. Data on annual counts of deaths attributed to drug use disorder and interpersonal violence between 1990 and 2023 were collected, and a bivariate copula modeling approach was adopted to account for the dependence of the two counts. The findings show that socioeconomic factors, including per-capita gross domestic product, youth unemployment rate, and urban population, are significant predictors of these death counts, and statistical tests show a positive relationship between deaths related to drug use disorder and deaths caused by interpersonal violence. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Characterizing Core Morphology and Scar Patterning Within a Unified Spherical Harmonic Framework
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Lithic cores preserve the most direct evidence of past reduction strategies, yet their analysis still relies largely on typological classifications that are subjective and difficult to reproduce. Recent 3D methods quantify core attributes more precisely, but morphology and scar organization are handled in separate mathematical frameworks, precluding joint analysis of how the two relate. Here we present a unified framework based on spherical harmonics that encodes both core morphology (M-SPHARM) and scar patterning (SP-SPHARM) within a single rotation-invariant, landmark-free space, the latter being the first application of spherical harmonics to scar orientation data. Co-inertia analysis examines their covariation, and harmonic reconstruction renders statistical axes back into interpretable three-dimensional forms. While the methods are complementary, validation on ideal models and experimental cores shows that the scar pattern descriptor resolves finer distinctions among core types than existing metrics, most clearly the radial subtypes others cannot separate. The exploratory analysis on experimental and archaeological assemblages reveals no detectable covariation between morphology and scar organization. We identify core type as the principal factor structuring variation at Sandinggai (Hunan, China). The methods are released as an open-source R package (spharmlithic) with a fully reproducible workflow. More broadly, the framework supports understanding core variability as a continuous techno-morphological space rather than a set of discrete types. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Accuracy is not enough: The roles of accuracy, reliability and personality in the trust process
Abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) systems are increasingly integrated into human–machine systems, making it essential to understand how specific performance characteristics shape user trust and interaction behaviors. Although system performance is known to influence trust, research has largely conflated accuracy and reliability, limiting guidance for applied system design. The present study experimentally examined the independent effects of AI/ML accuracy and reliability on trustworthiness perceptions, trust, and monitoring behavior in an image classification task. In addition, individual differences in propensity to trust technology (PTT) and risk aversion (RA) were examined to better understand variability in user responses over time. Changes in trustworthiness perceptions, trust, and monitoring behavior were modeled using growth analyses. Results demonstrated accuracy and reliability exerted distinct effects on user perceptions and behavior. Higher accuracy primarily influenced trust and trustworthiness perceptions, whereas reliability was more strongly associated with monitoring behavior over time. PTT predicted initial trust perceptions prior to task experience, whereas RA moderated changes in trust and trustworthiness as users accumulated performance information. Title: Continuity and Discontinuity in Artefact Distributions from Multi-Period Archaeological Sites
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Artefact finds recovered by metal detecting and reported by members of the public are a growing source of archaeological information, with over 1.2 million finds recorded to date by the Portable Antiquities Scheme in England and Wales. Heritage schemes in many other European countries where hobby detecting for archaeology is legal likewise report growing numbers of finds. Using point pattern analysis, this paper presents a worked-out set of computational methods to study diachronic processes within artefact assemblages at field or local (e.g. parish) levels. We present a simulated ‘toy’ example to illustrate the methodology and test it with two large artefact assemblages from the counties of North Yorkshire and Norfolk that differ in terms of finds record quality and known contextual archaeological landscape information. The proposed approach and example code can be reapplied to other archaeological point patterns. It formalises a spatial statistical workflow that produces an assessment regarding landscape persistence and reuse, and which can be used, for example, to assist fieldwork or planning decisions by identifying areas for further research. The case studies highlight the considerable need for formal analytical workflows in public finds research, which can be easily deployed at different sites and local assemblages. Title: “How can I help you learn?” Incorporating emotions into parents' support of young children's self-regulated learning at home and school during prolonged crisis
Abstract: Background: Parents apply their knowledge of cognition, emotion, and behavior (metacognition, metaemotion, and metabehavior) to provide children external regulation to achieve learning goals. Results: Mediation coefficients were estimated for parent metaprocesses associated with their children's SRL, mediated through external regulation. In distance learning, parental metaemotion, metabehavior, and co-regulation were positively associated with their children's SRL. Co-regulation was positively associated with emotion SRL-reappraisal for Cohort 2 and Cohort 3. Metaprocesses were linked to SRL, math, and language skills through other-regulation, whereas metaprocesses were associated with SRL strategies and social skills through co-regulation. Title: Bridging single-species models to ecosystem-based maximum sustainable yield for environmental sustainability in marine fisheries
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: Maximum sustainable yield remains a central biological reference concept in fisheries management. Its reliability is shaped by model assumptions, uncertainty, ecological interactions, and environmental change. The study objectives were to reconstruct the mathematical progression of maximum sustainable yield, from single-species deterministic models to ecosystem-based, multispecies formulations. The critical narrative review synthesizes the paradigm shift in ecological modeling, tracing its trajectory from equilibrium-based single-species frameworks to holistic, ecosystem-aware formulations. Classical production models are compared with age-structured, stock-recruitment, bioeconomic, precautionary, and multispecies approaches. The assumptions, data needs, uncertainty, and management implications are evaluated. Eight fisheries cases are used to illustrate contrasts in data availability, assessment methods, harvest rules, ecosystem awareness, and shared-stock governance. These cases are treated as illustrative examples rather than a representative validation sample. Evidence shows that trophic interactions can alter species-specific and system-level reference points. The direction of change depends on food-web structure, selectivity, interaction strength, environmental productivity, and management objectives. Environmental variation can also affect growth, recruitment, natural mortality, habitat capacity, and species interactions. Accordingly, biological reference points require adaptive updating when stock productivity exhibits nonstationarity, precluding their interpretation as rigid constants amidst shifting environmental conditions. Economic objectives, social needs, and conservation goals must also be distinguished from biological yield objectives. A five-dimension readiness framework is proposed as a preliminary hypothesis-generating heuristic. Alternative weighting schemes indicate that some borderline classifications are sensitive to assumptions. Independent validation and inter-rater testing are therefore required before operational use. While substantial data constraints persist across multiple Indonesian fisheries, these limitations must not be regarded as the sole impediment to comprehensive management. Governance, enforcement, fleet structure, socioeconomic incentives, habitat condition, and climate variability can independently affect performance. Greater use of adaptive monitoring, precautionary harvest rules, uncertainty analysis, and ecosystem indicators is therefore recommended. Multispecies assessment should be prioritized where trophic or technical interactions materially influence stock dynamics. Maximum sustainable yield is best retained as an analytical reference point rather than a literal catch target. Environmentally sustainable application requires precautionary, adaptive, and ecosystem-based governance frameworks dynamically aligned with local empirical data quality, ecological conditions, and institutional capabilities. Title: Cognitive appraisal of illegitimate tasks and research creativity: dual reflective processing pathways in graduate education
Abstract: Although graduate students frequently encounter illegitimate tasks—assignments perceived as inconsistent with their research roles—little is known about how such tasks influence research creativity and through what cognitive mechanisms. Drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory (CAT), a dual-pathway model is proposed in which illegitimate tasks influence research creativity through problem-solving pondering and affective rumination, with supervisor–student relationship quality as a moderator. Data were collected from 389 graduate students in Chinese universities using a two-wave survey design, and the hypothesized moderated mediation model was tested using hierarchical regression analyses supplemented by the PROCESS macro. The results indicate that illegitimate tasks exert opposing indirect effects on research creativity through distinct reflective cognitive pathways. Illegitimate tasks were associated with increased affective rumination, which interfered with sustained creative engagement. However, under high-quality supervisor-student relationships, illegitimate tasks were more strongly related to problem-solving pondering, which facilitated creative thinking. Supervisor-student relationship quality further shaped how illegitimate tasks were interpreted and which reflective pathway was activated. These findings clarify the cognitive mechanisms and relational conditions through which illegitimate tasks influence research creativity and contribute to understanding how task legitimacy shapes creative thinking in graduate research contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Enhancing college students’ reflective thinking through online visualized collaborative argumentation: An exploratory study
Abstract: In this era of technological advancements, how to better support students in argumentation-based computer-supported collaborative learning using emerging interactive technology to develop their reflective thinking has become an important issue in talent development. This study was embedded in the Cognition of Multimedia Learning course, and involved a pre- and posttest experiment with 56 college students to investigate the effects of visualized collaborative argumentation on their reflective thinking. The relationships between students’ argumentation and changes in their reflective thinking were also examined. Moreover, the differences in cognitive performance in argumentation among students with different levels of change in reflective thinking were explored using epistemic network analysis. The findings revealed that visualized collaborative argumentation significantly enhanced students’ reflective thinking. Especially, the higher the students’ level of engagement in rebuttal, the greater the impact on their reflective thinking. Moreover, according to the changes in reflective thinking behavior scores, K-Means cluster analysis determined a high-level change group (N = 33) and a low-level change group (N = 23). Title: Environmental qualities in green and natural spaces: Fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature as pathways to perceived visit-related health benefits
Abstract: Rising levels of stress and mental ill-health have intensified interest in nature-based public health approaches, including green social prescribing and nature as medicine. However, it remains unclear whether different environmental qualities are associated with different aspects of visit experience, and how these experiences relate to perceived visit-related health benefits. This study examined direct associations of biodiversity, safety, accessibility and cleanliness problems with perceived visit-related health benefits, and indirect associations involving fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature. Cross-sectional data from 19,814 adults in England who reported a recent visit to a green or natural space in the People and Nature Survey (PaNS) were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In the direct-effects model, biodiversity, safety and accessibility were positively associated with perceived visit-related health benefits, whereas cleanliness problems showed a negative association. Most of these direct associations were substantially attenuated when the two visit experiences were included, and both experiences were positively associated with perceived benefits. The pathway model also revealed differentiated associations across experiences, with safety most closely associated with fresh air / peace and tranquillity, biodiversity with feeling closer to nature, and cleanliness problems showing a negative indirect association through fresh air / peace and tranquillity. By considering qualities of the setting alongside experiences during the visit, the findings highlight the value of a quality-experience-benefit perspective in which different environmental qualities may show different patterns of association with perceived visit-related health benefits through particular visit experiences. This perspective may help inform the selection and management of natural settings used in nature-based public-health approaches, particularly where specific visit experiences are intended to be supported. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Compitus K.
Title: Categorical exclusion: Speciesism as a neglected dimension of prejudice in cognitive behavioral therapy
Abstract: While CBT and ABA have recently begun to grapple with their own internal biases, the field's ethical framework remains stubbornly anthropocentric. Scholarship increasingly addresses systemic prejudice in research, yet speciesism—the hierarchical valuation of life based on biological category—is still largely ignored as a socio-political ideology. This is a significant oversight: psychometric evidence suggests that speciesism is not a fringe belief, but is cognitively rooted in Social Dominance Orientation (SDO), much like racism and sexism. Consequently, the discipline's human-centricity should not be viewed as a neutral default, but as an active ideological framework that prioritizes control over clinical insight. This is visible in the pathologization of vystopia. By framing the profound distress caused by industrialized animal exploitation as a cognitive distortion, clinicians commit a form of microaggression that can fundamentally weaken the therapeutic alliance. Furthermore, the behavioral emphasis on mastery and compliance uncomfortably echoes colonial power structures, treating sentient beings as mere variables rather than autonomous agents. To evolve, the field must adopt a socio-ecological model that recognizes the agency of both non-human animals and neurodivergent individuals alike. Title: Collective Action and Efficiency Loss? The Role of Kinship in Multi-Household Grassland Management on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau
Abstract: By facilitating cooperation, the multi-household management pattern (MHMP) enables some household members to engage in non-agricultural employment and is often assumed to enhance production efficiency. However, empirical evidence on its actual efficiency effects remains limited. Drawing on survey data from 156 herder households in Maqu County on the QTP collected between November 2021 and March 2022, this study applies an output-oriented Data Envelopment Analysis combined with Tobit regression to examine the impact of MHMP on production efficiency. The results show that participation in MHMP is associated with lower production efficiency. Labor reallocation from animal husbandry to non-agricultural activities explains this negative relationship. Moreover, strong kinship ties intensify the efficiency loss, as households embedded in close kinship networks tend to adopt more lenient norms regarding effort. While kinship-based cooperation facilitates collective action, it simultaneously reinforces relational norms that weaken performance-oriented incentives. Title: Obsessive compulsive disorder and depression change in a residential setting with the added role of quality of life
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: Co-occurring depression is a common aspect of obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) presentation, however, there are mixed conclusions on how depression influences treatment outcomes. Many studies lack accounting for temporal precedence, and do not account for both within person and between-person effects. This study utilizes a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to examine changes in OCD and depression over the course of intensive/residential treatment for OCD in a sample of 311 adults. We build on past research by including quality of life in the model as well. Autoregressive paths reflected OCD symptoms predicting future OCD symptoms across time, and depression symptoms predicting future depression symptoms in the context of treatment. Contrary to past research on OCD and depression, there were no significant cross-lagged effects in either model except for a positive relationship between quality of life at week 1 and OCD at week 2. Authors: Vu L.H.
Title: From trust and generational education to climate action: Global empirical evidence on shaping climate beliefs and policies; [از اعتماد و آموزش نسلی تا اقدا مهای اقلیمی؛ شواهد تجربی جهانی دربارة شکلگیری باورها و سیاستهای اقلیمی]
Abstract: Public support for climate action depends not only on economic incentives and information, but also on deeper social and institutional foundations. This study investigates how trust shapes individuals’ climate change perceptions and their willingness to support mitigation policies, particularly through higher environmental taxes. Using individual-level data from the fourth round of the Life in Transition Survey, combined with country-level macroeconomic indicators from the World Bank, the analysis covers 37 countries over the period 2022–2023. We estimate baseline models using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), with all regressions weighted by national population to ensure cross-country representativeness. Authors: Begade S.
Title: Inferring Behavioural Landscape Systems in Palaeolithic Archaeology: Unsupervised Spatial Learning as a Framework for Formal Inductive Inference
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Interpretations of Palaeolithic landscapes have frequently relied upon a priori site typologies, functional classifications, and environmentally deterministic frameworks that risk circular reasoning, typological reification, and underdetermined behavioural inference. This study develops and applies an explicitly inductive framework for identifying behavioural landscape structure without imposing pre-defined functional or categorical assumptions. Using a multivariate dataset of 158 georeferenced open-air Palaeolithic occurrences from the Vidarbha region of eastern Maharashtra, India, the analysis integrates topographic, hydrological, and raw-material accessibility variables alongside a kernel-derived archaeological persistence measure within an unsupervised spatial learning workflow. Unsupervised spatial learning refers here to the application of clustering algorithms requiring no predefined class labels to spatially referenced archaeological datasets, distinguishing this exploratory inferential mode from confirmatory supervised prediction. Cluster robustness was evaluated through multiple internal validation diagnostics, including elbow analysis, silhouette optimisation, gap statistic assessment, sensitivity testing, and cross-algorithm comparison. Results reveal reproducible multivariate landscape configurations best understood as probabilistic behavioural landscape systems rather than discrete functional site types or deterministic settlement categories. These findings demonstrate that coherent archaeological landscape organisation can be detected inductively prior to typological assignment, while clarifying persistent zones of temporal palimpsest formation, proxy limitation, and interpretive ambiguity inherent to open-air records. The study argues that unsupervised spatial learning is most productive when positioned as an epistemic support framework that formalises pattern discovery, stabilises inductive reasoning, and preserves the interpretive centrality of archaeological expertise, contributing to a more transparent and methodologically accountable approach to behavioural inference in Palaeolithic landscape research. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Afrouz M.
Title: Automatic Detection of Grammatical Errors in English Translations: Assessing the Efficacy and Suggesting Some Recommendations for Boosting Grammarly Software; [تشخی ص خودکار خطاهای دستوری در ترجمههای انگلیسی:» نر مافزار گرامرلی « ارزیابی کارآمدیو ارائۀ پیشنهادهایی برای ارتقای آ ن]
Abstract: Grammarly is one of the most widely used software applications for the automatic detection of grammatical errors in texts translated from Persian into English. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of Grammarly and to propose suggestions for improving its performance. To achieve this objective, a corpus consisting of English translations of booklets introducing works of resistance literature was analyzed. After grammatical errors had been identified by the researchers (human evaluators), the electronic versions of the booklets were submitted to Grammarly for error detection. The identified errors were then categorized, and the results obtained by the researchers were compared with those generated by the software. Following the qualitative and quantitative analyses of the errors and the presentation of the findings, recommendations were made to enhance Grammarly’s effectiveness. According to the findings, of the 98 instances identified by Grammarly as errors, 16 were not actual errors. In four cases (4.9%), Grammarly failed to correctly identify the type of error. The software demonstrated its weakest performance in the detection of spelling errors and the misuse of masculine and feminine pronouns. Authors: Wei M.; Zheng R.; Song R.
Title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
Abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. Therefore, this study constructs a multi-source heterogeneous hypergraph with higher-order semantics, spanning the “Science-Technology-Industry” dimensions. By mapping the structural phase transitions of weak signals across an “Outlier-Mutation-Key Node” trajectory, we devise a quantifiable indicator system to shift the analytical paradigm from static retrospective detection to dynamic evolutionary tracking. Using a dataset of 145,316 papers, 79,050 patents, and 5941 project records from the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) fuel cell domain (2015–2024), we identify 226 candidate nodes exhibiting this trajectory. A two-round Delphi expert evaluation confirms 193 of these nodes as expert-confirmed weak signals, establishing Delphi-validated reference labels for subsequent model evaluation. We then employ Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Dynamic Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN), and Large Language Models (ZS-LLM and ICL-LLM) to prospectively predict weak signals with disruptive potential. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). This synergy between higher-order topology and semantic intelligence effectively filters stochastic noise and enables meaningful predictive capability of emerging technologies, providing an exploratory decision-support framework for technology foresight. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Stupacher, Jan (55683070400); Rosso, Mattia (57222089125); Vuust, Peter (16041024200); Keller, Peter E. (58008087300)
Title: Multiple pathways to social bonding through music
Abstract: Music is widely recognized for its ability to foster social bonding. Yet, while research has largely focused on interpersonal movement coordination, other ways in which music can connect people have received comparatively less attention. We argue that music-related social bonding extends beyond coordinated movement and emerges through multiple forms of imagined and shared social experience. We propose a conceptual framework comprising three interrelated pathways: interpersonal coordination, shared social experience without explicit behavioral coordination, and imagined social experience during solitary listening. Across these pathways, music recruits interacting mechanisms of temporal prediction, self-other integration, reward processing, and social-cognitive alignment that together promote social closeness, affiliation, and prosocial orientation. We further highlight how musical features and individual differences shape these processes. By integrating evidence from music psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and social psychology, this framework broadens current perspectives on how music promotes social bonding and identifies conceptual and methodological directions for future research. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Extracting secondary value from mine waste: Critical minerals, circular economy, and ESG governance for the energy transition
Abstract: Decarbonization depends on a growing supply of minerals whose extraction is itself carbon- and conflict-intensive. Four literatures address this paradox, critical mineral supply chains, circular economy and secondary recovery, ESG governance, and mineral carbonation, but have developed in isolation. This integrative review synthesizes 66 peer-reviewed and policy sources (2008–2025) to argue that mine tailings are an underexploited source of the secondary value the energy transition requires. Under the IEA Net Zero scenario, lithium demand rises ninefold and graphite fourfold by 2040, each ton mined leaving far more tailings behind. The sector's 2019–2022 ESG record is asymmetric: injury rates fell 29 percent and community investment rose 233 percent, while water use and waste per unit of output rose 25 and 22 percent and emissions intensity did not improve. End-of-life lithium recovery remains below 5 percent against a theoretical maximum above 90. We propose the Circular Value Nexus, which treats tailings as a single object of recovery and accountability: value realized through direct and accessory element recovery, bulk reuse, and, where mineralogy allows, carbonation coupled to permanent CO2 removal. Secondary value is bounded by four interacting constraints: mineralogical, economic, regulatory, and social, each able to foreclose a pathway alone, with community consent the one that cannot be engineered around; the framework is stated as four falsifiable propositions and a screening matrix. Coupling carbonation to co-product recovery lowers the viable carbon price, though the conditions are narrow. Priority gaps are full-chain life cycle assessment, benefit distribution design, and producing-country participation in standard-setting. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhang J.; Wang M.; Liu K.; Zhuang L.; Zhao Z.
Title: Assessment of horizontal ecological compensation in China based on ecosystem service flows
Abstract: Ecological compensation has been regarded as a key mechanism for promoting the coordinated development of regional social-ecological systems and addressing environmental justice. The scientific identification of compensation priorities and amounts is recognized as fundamental for the effective implementation of horizontal compensation schemes. The spatiotemporal dynamics of supply and demand for water, grain, and carbon ecosystem service values were assessed, together with coupling coordination and supply-demand balance. A national horizontal compensation framework for China integrated flow models for individual services, network topology analysis, and compensation accounting to link providers and beneficiaries across cities and estimate reference amounts. Supply generally increased, whereas demand rose for water and carbon but remained relatively stable for grain. Across 2000, 2010, and 2020, the average proportions of cities where local supply exceeded local demand were 80%, 86%, and 22% for water yield, grain production, and carbon sequestration, respectively. Substantial variations in network structure and node characteristics were observed among the compensation networks, with the number of modeled flow paths increasing for water and decreasing for grain and carbon. The numbers of ecological-provision and ecological-beneficiary cities decreased, while their respective average modeled net ecological benefits and net compensation payments were higher in 2020 than in 2000. Meanwhile, the number of cities with unresolved service deficits and no modeled compensation inflows or outflows increased. By linking supply-demand imbalances with flows of individual services, the framework provides a quantitative basis for identifying compensation partners and negotiating differentiated payment responsibilities using estimated amounts as references. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Qiao H.; Feng S.; Wang J.; Zhang F.; Li F.
Title: THDiff: Joint modeling of social and temporal factors in hyperbolic space for time-aware information diffusion prediction
Abstract: Information Diffusion Prediction (IDP) aims to forecast how information spreads among users on social platforms at a micro level. Most existing methods emphasize social relations while overlooking fine-grained temporal dynamics, even though both factors are essential to diffusion. Moreover, both social and temporal factors exhibit hierarchical and imbalanced structures, posing challenges for effective modeling via conventional Euclidean methods. In particular, our analysis of real-world diffusion data reveals highly irregular and heavy-tailed time-interval distributions, suggesting the need for refined representations that can accommodate such imbalanced patterns. While hyperbolic geometry has demonstrated strong capability in capturing hierarchical social influence, its potential for modeling temporal imbalances remains largely unexplored. Motivated by these observations, we propose a novel time-aware hyperbolic diffusion prediction model (THDiff) that jointly models social and temporal factors within a unified hyperbolic framework. Specifically, THDiff uses a rotation-assisted hyperbolic embedding to construct user representations that encode global hierarchical social influence. Building on these representations, it leverages hyperbolic attention to construct cascade representations from both social and temporal perspectives and fuses them through a hyperbolic Hawkes process, enabling comprehensive modeling of complex dynamic diffusion dependencies. By jointly modeling social and temporal factors, THDiff effectively predicts not only who will be activated but also when diffusion events are likely to occur. Extensive experiments across four real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing methods, achieving up to 8.2% and 10.9% improvements in Hits@1 and MRR, respectively. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Waiting for Uganda’s first commercial ‘Pearl Sweet’ oil: Discourses on social and environmental impacts and safeguards
Abstract: Uganda discovered approximately 3.5 billion barrels of commercially recoverable oil reserves in 2006 and is poised to become a major oil producer in Sub-Saharan Africa. In assessing progress towards full–scale oil production, expected by the end of 2026, Uganda’s President referred to the country’s commercial crude oil as “pearl sweet”, highlighting its medium-to-heavy, highly waxy characteristics, relatively low sulphur content, and ease of refining. Despite the anticipated economic benefits, considerable debate persists regarding the potential social and environmental impacts of oil development and the adequacy of safeguards ahead of full–scale production. Drawing on experiences from established oil–producing countries, this paper examines how environmental and social impacts are framed, how safeguards are prioritised, and what this implies for Uganda’s emerging oil sector. Anchored in environmental justice and political ecology, the study adopts a sequential integrative design combining a systematic literature review with empirical insights from twelve purposively selected stakeholders in Uganda’s oil-producing districts and national regulatory institutions. The literature review used Boolean search strings that connected terms within conceptual blocks using OR and combined blocks using AND, following a PRISMA-guided process across Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar and institutional data bases. Of 1800 records identified, 95 key sources were retained for analysis. The findings indicate that, although Uganda has initiated several safeguards measures including oil–spill preparedness training, buffer zone enforcement, afforestation, and resettlement programs – implementation remain fragmented, under–resourced, and heavily centralised. Comparative analysis further indicates limited integration of international climate frameworks, including the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, into national oil governance. We argue that Uganda’s challenge is not simply the absence of safeguards, but the persistence of centralised, uneven, and under–resourced governance arrangements that constrain the translation of international safeguard commitments into effective national practice. This study contributes to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land), while also intersecting with SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Domain-specific risk tendencies show little association, directly or indirectly, with domain-specific self-esteem
Abstract: Both risk taking and self-esteem have traditionally been considered general traits that apply across domains of behaviors, although each has separately been considered as multidimensional or domain specific at times. The domain specificity of both constructs is debated, though, and the theoretical relationships between self-esteem and risk-taking remain unclear. The present study (N = 191) looked at relationships across both domain specific self-esteem and domain-specific risk taking, as well as a theoretically hypothesized possible moderating variable of relative state (perceived ability/need). General self-esteem and general risk taking were assessed concurrently. Specific domains of self-esteem and risk taking were mostly correlated with, yet distinct from, the general constructs with a few notable exceptions. General self-esteem was not correlated with general risk taking, and—although social and physical appearance self-esteem differentially associated with evaluations of their relative state in those areas—domain specific self-esteem was largely not correlated with specific types of risk taking. Moderation analyses did not support an indirect relationship between self-esteem and risk taking. Better measures for the relative state model of risk and more firmly grounded theoretical models of self-esteem and risk taking may be needed in order to better understand if and how they are related. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: van Kleef, Gerben A. (6506205495); Cohen-Chen, Smadar (55970882000)
Title: Social consequences of emotional expressions in negotiation
Abstract: Negotiation is integral to social life. Whether we focus on exchanges between individuals, groups, organizations, or nations, negotiation is the most common and constructive way of making deals and solving disputes. Negotiations can spark intense emotions, which in turn shape negotiation processes and outcomes. Here, we review research on the social consequences of emotional expressions in negotiation. We summarize evidence regarding specific single emotions (e.g., anger, happiness, disappointment, sadness, fear, guilt, shame, pride, hope) as well as alternative (patterns of) emotional responses (e.g., empathy, emotional ambivalence, mixed emotions, alternating emotions, indifference) across levels of analysis (interpersonal, intragroup, intergroup). Our review indicates that emotions can have both favorable and unfavorable consequences, depending on critical moderators (e.g., information processing, perceived appropriateness) and the focal criterion (e.g., monetary gains, social outcomes). The richness of the empirical record underlines the importance of investigating discrete emotions (rather than positive vs. negative affect) and defies simple conclusions about the (dys)functionality of emotions. Emotional expressions can help or hurt negotiators’ outcomes depending on goal prioritization (e.g., maximizing individual outcomes vs. maintaining positive relations) and the social context. We call for research outside the lab to gain insight into real-world consequences of emotional dynamics in (intergroup) negotiation, mediation, and diplomacy. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: How could redistribution be possible? Effects of national identity and communion among Chinese youth
Abstract: Previous studies in Western countries demonstrated that the relationship between national identity and redistribution preferences was inconsistent, and few studies addressed the cross-cultural consistency about this relationship. Based on social identity theory, the present study aimed to explore the relationship between national identity and redistribution preferences and its mechanisms as well as boundaries through three sub-studies in Chinese youth. A cross-sectional study among 1791 young adults, a priming experiment among 182 college students, and integration of experimental manipulation and daily diary study among 51 college students were conducted respectively in study 1–3. We found that national identity of Chinese youth had positive effect on redistribution preferences and communion mediated this effect at the static and dynamic levels (study 1–3). Dark Triad strengthened the direct relationship between national identity and redistribution preferences (study 1), whereas weakened its indirect relationship (study 1 and 3). These findings indicated the positive effect of national identity on redistribution preferences and the mediating role of communion in this effect, and the well-adapted function of Dark Triad to some extent. These findings provided theoretical basis for the initiative for common prosperity from the perspectives of identity and personality in Chinese context. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Incentivized sadism: The impact of intrinsic and extrinsic reward on sadistic aggression
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: In two studies (one correlational, one experimental; total N = 419), we tested whether dispositional sadism is related to the anticipation of experiencing pleasure (instead of guilt) during and after aggressing, and whether this anticipation motivates aggressive behavior. We also tested whether individuals higher in sadism are less likely to use dissonance reduction strategies for behaving aggressively (and feeling pleasure while doing so). Study 1 looked at how dispositional sadism is related to the anticipation of intrinsic and extrinsic rewards of behaving aggressively. Study 2 looked at whether offering a meager extrinsic reward for behaving aggressively (i.e., financial compensation) increased the experience of pleasure and decreased the experience of guilt during and after aggression – a dissonance reduction strategy – and whether this effect was reduced for people high (vs. low) in sadism. Results revealed that dispositional sadism positively predicts (1) the expectation of reward and lack of guilt after behaving aggressively (Study 1), (2) aggressive behavior in an animal-killing paradigm (Study 2), and (3) hedonic pleasure and lack of guilt while doing so (Study 2). Notably, these affective correlates of sadism were not maintained after aggression, suggesting that hedonic gains are short-lived. The effects of introducing a financial incentive for behaving aggressively were inconsistent across the main studies and a preliminary pilot study (reported in Supplementary Materials), and should be interpreted with caution.
