Authors: Serema B.
Title: The Influence of Tswana Cosmological worldview and Sacred Beliefs on the Spatial Organization of Traditional Settlements: A Study of the Setswana Traditional Space kgotla
Abstract: This study examines how Tswana cosmology and sacred beliefs shaped the spatial organization, social structure, and geography of traditional settlements, focusing on the Setswana kgotla as the central sociopolitical, ritual, and spiritual space. Although the kgotla has undergone substantial functional and physical transformation through colonization, modernization, and contemporary planning, its historical development provides important insight into the principles underlying Tswana settlement planning. Using an interpretive qualitative approach based on historical documents, classic ethnographic literature, comparative spatial analysis, field observations, and oral accounts from six historically significant Tswana villages in Botswana—Kanye, Mochudi, Molepolole, Maun, Serowe, and Ramotswa—this study investigates the sacred and social principles governing settlement organization, including the location of the kgosi’s ward, the centrality of the kgotla, geographic setting, cardinal orientation, hierarchical ward structure, spatial configuration, and threshold treatments. The findings show that traditional Tswana settlements were shaped not only by practical and defensive needs but also by a cosmological order in which authority, ancestry, community, environmental relationships, and protection were expressed through space. Rather than serving solely as a traditional court, the kgotla functioned as the symbolic center where the moral, political, and sacred dimensions of Tswana society converged. The study argues that Tswana spatial organization is best understood as a dynamic system shaped by cosmology, environmental knowledge, and historical change rather than as a fixed symbolic structure. It further demonstrates that precolonial Tswana settlement planning embodied an Indigenous system of spatial knowledge rooted in concepts of hierarchy, enclosure, ecology, and social affiliation. Reconsidering the cosmological foundations of the kgotla therefore provides valuable insights into Indigenous settlement planning and contributes to broader discussions of culturally grounded, context-responsive approaches to spatial organization. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: The viral deviation: a quantitative analysis of social media engagement metrics on non-compliant flight deck behaviors
Abstract: Background Normalization of Deviance (NoD) is a well-documented organizational failure mode in aviation, yet its propagation through digital ecosystems remains unexplored. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) highlights a critical mentorship vacuum due to pilot retirements, and social media platforms increasingly serve as informal training environments. This study introduces the concept of Algorithmic Normalization of Deviance- ANoD, hypothesizing that recommendation algorithms systematically reward and amplify “gray-zone” cockpit behaviors that erode sterile flight deck protocols. Method We conducted a stratified netnographic analysis of 150 high-visibility aviation videos (N = 150) across Instagram Reels, split between algorithmically recommended content (n = 100) and curated influencer content (n = 50). A novel coding framework operationalized compliance (Compliant vs. Gray Zone vs. Deviant) and incentive structures. Engagement metrics were analyzed to quantify the algorithmic advantage of non-compliant behavior. Results The analysis reveals a directionally consistent “Viral Deviation” pattern rather than a statistically decisive one. Gray-zone recordings (i.e., technically legal but procedurally borderline) comprised 57% of the sample and attracted higher engagement than compliant content, although this difference was small and did not reach conventional significance (d = 0.24, p = 0.11). The clearest signal emerged between content sources: algorithmically surfaced posts showed significantly higher interaction rates than curated influencer posts (d = 0.31, p = 0.029), a small but statistically significant per-view advantage for content promoted directly by the recommendation system. Structural incentive analysis further indicates that monetization pressures co-occur with increased gray-zone production, structurally analogous to a parallel, shadow curriculum associated with conditions that may facilitate drift. Conclusion The study identifies statistical associations, not causal relationships, and the downstream behavioural impact on pilots is hypothesised from the algorithmic-pattern evidence rather than directly measured. Within those bounds, social media algorithms constitute a structurally unmonitored distribution channel whose observed associations with gray-zone content amplification are consistent with a normalisation-of-deviance feedback mechanism operating beyond current regulatory oversight — an association that warrants urgent empirical validation and proactive governance. We propose a shift from prohibition to risk-stratified governance, recommending that regulators distinguish between handheld (high-risk) and mounted (managed-risk) devices, and integrate digital algorithmic literacy into ab-initio pilot training to counter this new systemic threat. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Li X.; Yu N.; Chang X.; Zhang H.; Hu G.; Zhao H.; Dong Z.
Title: Spectral graph filter bank fusion for multimodal rumor cascade representation and detection
Abstract: Rumor detection on social media is inherently a multi-source information fusion problem that involves heterogeneous signals from textual content, user interactions, and temporal dynamics. Existing approaches often underexploit the global structural patterns encoded in rumor propagation graphs. In this work, we propose a unified multimodal fusion framework, termed Rumor Graph Filter Net (RGFN), which integrates multimodal representations with learnable spectral graph filtering. Specifically, post content embeddings derived from a pre-trained language encoder, user social relation representations obtained via self-supervised contrastive learning, and propagation timestamps are jointly transformed into the graph spectral domain using the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT). To adaptively capture discriminative propagation characteristics, we design channel-wise graph filter banks based on Chebyshev polynomial approximations, enabling frequency-selective enhancement and noise suppression. The filtered spectral responses are projected back to the spatial domain through the inverse GFT, followed by a simplified hierarchical multi-view graph pooling mechanism to obtain robust graph-level representations across scales. The final classifier operates on fused multilevel features for rumor identification. Experiments on two real-world rumor datasets, Twitter and Weibo, show that RGFN achieves the highest F1-score among the baselines and performs competitively on other metrics. Specifically, RGFN outperforms the best baselines on Twitter and Weibo by 4.9% and 1.4% on F1-score, respectively. The proposed framework offers a principled integration of graph signal processing and multimodal information fusion for social media credibility assessment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Traditional Ecological Knowledge of the Arhuaco People on Water Management in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta
Abstract: This article analyzes the role of Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) of the Arhuaco people in water management in the upper Ariguaní river basin, in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (Colombia), in a context of accelerated socio-environmental transformation. From an ethnohydrological approach, the study adopts a mixed-methods design that integrates community surveys, participatory techniques, spatial analysis of land use change (2000–2023), and dynamic socio-hydrological modeling. A TEK Index was constructed to evaluate three dimensions of water management: cultural management, indigenous norms, and government norms. Title: Lithium extraction and developmental embeddedness in Zimbabwe: Chinese-led investment and local development outcomes
Abstract: Zimbabwe’s rapidly expanding lithium mining sector, dominated by Chinese investment and integrated into global battery and electric vehicle value chains, presents significant opportunities for economic transformation. However, whether this investment generates development benefits for mining-affected communities remains uncertain. This paper examines the extent to which Chinese-led investment contributes to locally experienced development outcomes in Zimbabwe. Drawing on survey data from 230 respondents across six lithium mining sites complemented by stakeholder interviews, field observations, and documentary sources, this study assesses economic outcomes, social responsibility, environmental stewardship, governance and public participation, and physical infrastructure. The findings reveal limited local economic integration and infrastructure development, weak community participation, and significant environmental and social costs. These outcomes are shaped not simply by investor nationality, but by the interaction between corporate practices, globally integrated transition mineral value chains, and fragmented and weakly enforced governance frameworks. The article argues that Zimbabwe’s lithium sector remains weakly developmentally embedded despite rapid production and export growth. It advances the Community-Centered Developmental Embeddedness Framework as an analytical framework for assessing whether transition mineral extraction becomes developmentally embedded through inclusive governance and participation, local economic integration, and environmental and social accountability, supported by coordinated government action. Title: Assessing Urban Flood Resilience through the Lens of a Dynamic Flood Resilience Index: Systematic Review
Abstract: Urban flooding is becoming more frequent and damaging due to the combined effects of climate change and rapid urbanization, exposing the limitations of conventional risk-based flood-management approaches. Consequently, resilience-based strategies have gained attention for managing uncertainty, system complexity, and recovery capacity in urban flood contexts. Flood-resilience index (FRI) frameworks are widely used to operationalize resilience by integrating social, economic, infrastructural, institutional, and environmental dimensions into composite indicators. However, many existing FRI frameworks rely on static or snapshot-based assessments that inadequately represent feedback mechanisms, temporal evolution, and nonstationary flood regimes. This study presents a systematic literature review examining how geographic information systems (GIS), multicriteria decision-making (MCDM), and system dynamics modeling (SDM) have been applied individually and in combination to support urban flood-resilience assessment. Seventy-six peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2024 were analyzed using qualitative content analysis and frequency-based quantitative synthesis. The review synthesizes dominant methodological practices and identifies recurring limitations related to indicator aggregation, weighting, spatial representation, uncertainty treatment, and temporal dynamics. The findings show that GIS-MCDM approaches enable spatially explicit and structured resilience assessment but are commonly constrained by static assumptions and criterion independence. SDM applications offer strong potential for capturing feedback-driven system behavior and for the long-term evolution of resilience, yet are rarely integrated with GIS-based MCDM FRIs. The paper proposes a formalized synthesis-based framework that integrates GIS, MCDM, and SDM to support spatially explicit and dynamically informed urban flood-resilience assessment. Title: How Indigenous Socio-Cultural Systems Resist, Accept, or Direct Ecological Transformation: A Research Agenda
Abstract: Anthropogenic ecological transformations are challenging conventional environmental management paradigms, as maintaining historical ecological structures and functions becomes increasingly untenable. The resist–accept–direct (RAD) framework offers a strategic tool to navigate these shifts. However, as a product of the dominant socio-cultural system, the RAD framework risks perpetuating the same patterns of thinking that have contributed to unsustainable social-ecological dynamics. Indigenous socio-cultural systems, considered here through the lens of long-term coevolution with their environments, offer valuable empirical models for adaptive responses to environmental change. Such Indigenous socio-cultural responses, grounded in narratives, governance institutions, value systems, and other cultural elements collectively referred to as Indigenous Knowledge (IK), hold relevance for addressing today’s intertwined environmental and social challenges. We provide a targeted review of existing literature at the intersection of IK and the RAD framework, along with a broader conceptual overview of relevant insights across related fields. These reveal contrasting assumptions about Indigenous responses to environmental change, such as consistently resisting to preserve cultural fidelity or uniformly accepting, reflecting deeper cultural, temporal, and ecological complexity. We propose a structured research agenda to investigate Indigenous socio-cultural responses to environmental change through empirical research, theoretical synthesis, hypothesis development, and practical application. This agenda is grounded in comprehensive collaboration, emphasizing shared power and integrating both emic and etic perspectives throughout all stages of research and implementation. Title: Crops in Motion: Strontium Isotope Analysis of Cereal Provenance in a Foraging-Oriented Neolithic Economy

Abstract: Strontium isotope analysis offers a powerful tool for investigating mobility and provenance in prehistoric contexts, yet its application to archaeobotanical finds remains limited. Title: Development and validation of an ICD-11–based problematic social media use scale
Abstract: The present study aimed to address conceptual and measurement challenges in assessing problematic social media use by developing a scale grounded in the ICD-11 diagnostic framework for behavioral addictions. Item generation was based on core features including impaired control, prioritization of the behavior, continuation despite negative consequences, and functional impairment. Item Response Theory analyses showed that the scale demonstrates higher discrimination at low to moderate levels of problematic use, highlighting its sensitivity for early detection. Title: Assessment of a Role-Playing Game’s Effectiveness in Identifying Cattle Herding Strategies at a Wildlife-Livestock Interface in Zimbabwe
Abstract: Natural resource management at the interface between protected areas and communal lands varies across space and time, affecting wildlife and livestock movement patterns. In southern Africa, many communities bordering protected areas are partly agropastoral and rely on access to these areas to graze their cattle. However, farmers face complex decisions about whether to graze cattle inside protected zones or on communal lands, weighing factors such as increased predation risk or exposure to wildlife-borne diseases within protected areas. Authors: Li W.; Liao H.; Teng M.
Title: Extreme weather and human capital formation: evidence from Qing China
Abstract: Weather shocks can constrain educational investment and human capital formation. In Qing China, education spending rose and fell with weather-sensitive farm income. Adaptive measures such as the introduction of sweet potatoes, savings from surplus years, and flexible pricing mechanisms prove effective in mitigating drought effects. For robustness, we proxy regional recording capacity with the word count of meteorological entries and augment the baseline with controls for social unrest and epidemic shocks, with results remaining stable. By bringing long-run historical evidence to bear, this study enriches the literature on how extreme weather affects human capital formation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: STR-LBSN: Spatio-temporal Role-based Heterogeneous Hypergraph Embedding for location-based social networks
Abstract: Location-based social networks (LBSNs) contain rich social, spatial, and temporal information. However, most existing embedding methods overly simplify the underlying hypergraph structure, represent each user with a single static embedding, and fail to model the coupling between social relationships and mobility behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose STR-LBSN, a Spatio-temporal Role-based Heterogeneous Hypergraph Embedding framework for Location-Based Social Networks. STR-LBSN models users’ temporally evolving behavioral roles as hidden states in a Hidden Markov Model and constructs a role-centric hypergraph from the decoded role assignments. Based on this structure, STR-LBSN learns multi-role representations through biased random walks and heterogeneous sampling in cosine space, while balancing social contexts and spatio-temporal mobility patterns. Title: Academic self-handicapping in education: reconceptualizing it as a central psychological mechanism through a systematic review

Abstract: This study synthesizes empirical findings on academic self-handicapping (ASH) in educational contexts using a systematic literature review (SLR) of 30 articles retrieved from major international databases. The review aims to identify antecedent factors, examine the role of ASH as a psychological mechanism, and analyze its impact on academic and psychological outcomes. Although intervention-based research remains limited, preliminary intervention evidence suggests that cognitive- and emotion-focused approaches, including CBT, REBT, and ACT, may help reduce academic self-handicapping; however, the limited number of intervention studies precludes firm comparative conclusions. Title: Bone Surface Mapping: A New Method for Recording Detailed Human Bone Surface Variation

Abstract: Surface changes on bone can be indicative of a range of different processes affecting an individual, from palaeopathology and taphonomy to cultural modification. Authors: Carney M.
Title: Archaeologies of Indigenous Foodways and Collective Capacities
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Recent archaeological scholarship has embraced food security and food sovereignty frameworks to connect past foodways to present-day crises. However, these studies require critical examination of the colonial origins and ideological foundations of these frameworks, which emerged from industrialized western economic paradigms that do not align with Indigenous worldviews. Drawing on food studies scholarship, I argue that archaeologists must move beyond the uncritical adoption of food security and sovereignty frameworks to embrace culturally grounded paradigms developed by and for descendant communities. This paper advocates for reframing North American archaeological investigations of foodways through Indigenous philosopher Kyle Powys Whyte’s concept of collective capacities: webs of relationships among humans, non-human beings, and landscapes organized together to support responses to change and continuance. As a linking tool, collective capacities help archaeologists carry out the material and analytical work that Indigenous Food Sovereignty movements call for. An archaeology of collective capacities shifts our focus to understanding how food systems functioned as relational infrastructures of care, responsibility, and reciprocity that sustained communities across millennia. In this contribution I outline an archaeological framework identifying key material signatures of collective capacities. Applying this framework to the Pend Oreille Valley in northeastern Washington State, I demonstrate how paleoethnobotanical and archaeological data from the last 1500 years reveal Indigenous food systems were sustained through active management, coordinated labor, and intergenerational knowledge transmission across climatic and sociopolitical changes. I also consider how contemporary practices of reciprocity and relationality mirror the archaeological record of stability and stewardship. By centering culture-specific terminology and philosophies, an archaeology of collective capacities offers a methodological and theoretical approach that supports, rather than imposes frameworks upon, past societies while documenting the enduring systems that enabled communities to thrive across deep time. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Breaking the cycle of malice: Influence mechanism and intervention of social exclusion on malevolent creativity in adolescents
Abstract: Creativity is the core driving force for humans to break through existing boundaries and promote continuous social progress, and its positive impacts have been widely recognized. Study 1 conducted a field questionnaire survey (N = 1567). Title: Urban Renewal to Promote the Green Intensive Use of Land: Empirical Evidence from China

Abstract: Urban land green use efficiency (ULGUE), which directly impacts sustainable economic and social development as well as people's well-being, has garnered significant attention. The key findings include the following: (1) Urban renewal notably catalyzed improvements in ULGUE. Rigorous analyses of robustness further corroborated this outcome. On average, cities implementing urban renewal witnessed a substantial increase of 6.74% in ULGUE compared to those without such initiatives. (2) Urban renewal had a significant impact on ULGUE in the eastern and southern regions, large cities, and non-resource-dependent cities. Conversely, this impact was absent in the central and western regions, northern areas, small cities, and resource-centric cities. Title: Teacher professional development for creative data storytelling: A design-based research study
Abstract: With data increasingly central to contemporary professional and civic life, various data literacies have been put forth as necessary for individuals to cultivate. Title: Actionable Weather Communication Recommendations for Hard-to-Reach Populations Using Topic Modeling and Thematic Analysis

Title: Examining primary students’ mathematical communication through the lens of de Bono’s practical thinking processes

Title: An Analysis of Interactive and Interactional Metadiscourse Markers in Applied Linguistics Webinars: The Case of Top-Tier Native vs. Non-Native Speaking Scholars

Title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens

Employing models such as Moghaddam’s Staircase to Terrorism, Wiktorowicz’s Theory of Cognitive Openings, and Relative Deprivation Theory, it evaluates the structural and psychosocial conditions that fuel extremism and how locally-rooted programs neutralize them. The paper argues that the fusion of youth engagement, women’s empowerment, economic inclusion, and digital literacy has yielded a resilient counter-narrative that deserves formal integration into national policy frameworks. By analysing field-based insights and contextualizing global peacebuilding precedents, the study proposes a strategic reorientation toward grassroots-led deradicalization. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Limited 2026.

Authors: Winata I.N.P.; Radjawane I.M.; Nurdjaman S.; Radiarta I.N.; Sidik D.; Deby; Pratiwi S.K.; Makmur S.; Utama A.A.; Suman A.; Husnah
Title: Temporal water-quality variability and its implications for environmental management of sand lobster aquaculture
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Sustainable management of sand lobster aquaculture is often limited by monitoring approaches that summarize environmental conditions using long-term averages, obscuring short-term extremes and spatial variation. The study objectives were to characterize spatial and temporal variations in water quality within a floating net cage aquaculture system, identify their underlying physical drivers, evaluate whether longitudinal growth is governed more by culture duration, initial size, and stocking density than by environmental exposure alone, and translate these empirical relationships into a transferable environmental monitoring framework. METHODS: The study collected longitudinal growth and environmental data from floating net cage culture in Indonesia. Monitoring covered temperature, salinity, oxygen concentration, potential of hydrogen, and nutrient concentrations across three water depths and multiple sampling times. Non-parametric statistical tests were employed to evaluate depth-dependent variations in dissolved oxygen, while correlation and regression analysis assessed the relationships between wind speed, water temperature, and dissolved oxygen levels. Multivariate statistical ordination summarized dominant environmental gradients, and mixed-effects statistical models, compared through an information-theoretic model selection approach, captured longitudinal growth. FINDINGS: Dissolved oxygen concentration differed significantly among depths (test statistic 29.27, probability below 0.001), declining by close to a fifth from the surface to three and ten meters. Monthly wind speed closely tracked the concurrent decline in temperature closely (correlation coefficient -0.988, probability below 0.002) but exhibited no statistically significant association with dissolved oxygen, consistent with a wind-driven transition observed during this production cycle. Culture duration, initial size class, and stocking density together explained total length best, with an additive model carrying more than seventy percent of the statistical weight among six candidate models. Growth rate exhibited its strongest association with low-oxygen exposure, followed by temperature and potential of hydrogen condition, an interpretation that warrants caution given the limited independent exposure intervals available. CONCLUSION: Successful sand lobster aquaculture requires an adaptive environmental monitoring architecture that accounts for depth-related oxygen stratification and wind-driven seasonal variability, alongside coordinated management of culture duration, initial seed size, and stocking density. The analytical framework of integrated site assessment and management for lobster can be adapted to other marine aquaculture systems through the inclusion of species-specific biological indicators and management variables. © 2027 The author(s). Authors: Cheng T.; Guan C.
Title: When Cities Encroach: Urbanization Pressure on Basin Area Landscape in Eastern China
Source title: Journal of Urban Planning and Development
Abstract: The spatial configuration of land cover plays a crucial role in shaping the impacts of urban growth and guiding land-use management. However, quantifying these influences remains challenging. This study introduces a new framework to assess the potential influence of urban development on natural and seminatural landscapes, using the urban impact weighted interspersion and juxtaposition index (UIW-IJI), the bivariate Anselin local Moran's index analysis, and the landscape expansion index. Applying the China Land Cover Data Set at a 300-m grid from 2004 to 2019, we examine the spatial relationship between UIW-IJI and urban sprawl in major river basins in Eastern China. Results reveal three distinct patterns of urban influence comprising stable zones, declining peri-urban zones, and urban intensification zones, with the Taihu Lake Basin urban agglomeration particularly illustrating these dynamics. The analysis identifies a geographically uneven distribution of urban pressure, with persistence in central and eastern regions and emerging influences in the southwest. Furthermore, the transition from expansion-oriented to infill-dominated urbanization (>70%) has not necessarily reduced pressure on natural lands. Instead, it has shifted the impact from dispersed to locally concentrated, intensifying ecological pressure in northeastern cities. These findings provide insights into targeted land-use planning interventions to enhance both development efficiency and ecological conservation, demonstrating the importance of incorporating UIW-IJI into regional ecosystem management and sustainable urban development.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Vakilifard A.; Joola A.A.
Title: A Tale of Two Styles: Exploring the Compatibilities and Incompatibilities among Learning and Teaching Styles in Second Language Didactics
Abstract: The process of teaching and learning is a complex interplay of multiple factors, including teaching and learning styles. A mismatch between these styles can lead to negative outcomes. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the learning styles of non-Iranian Persian language learners and the teaching styles of their instructors. To explore the alignment and discrepancies between these variables, a quantitative method was employed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between them. This research was conducted with a sample size of 116 Persian language learners and 25 teachers, and data on learning styles were collected using the Perceptual Learning Style Preference Questionnaire (PLSPQ). The same questionnaire was adapted and validated to collect data on teaching styles. The study revealed no significant difference in the prioritization of visual, tactile, auditory, and kinesthetic learning styles between learners and teachers. However, a notable difference was observed in group and individual learning styles. Furthermore, academic background emerged as a crucial factor affecting teaching style, with teachers who had completed a teaching Persian program (AZFA) prioritizing group-style instruction. The outcomes of this research underscored the existence of discernible disparities between the teaching styles of educators and the learning styles of students. As such, it was recommended that teachers adjust their teaching styles to align with the learning styles of their students. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. All rights reserved.

Title: Offshore infrastructure decommissioning, just transitions, and the struggle for the right to the sea: Small-scale fishers’ perspectives from coastal Ghana
Abstract: Offshore petroleum infrastructure decommissioning is usually framed as a technical and environmental process requiring technical expertise. Yet, offshore infrastructure decommissioning could have deleterious consequences on adjacent coastal communities and livelihoods. Drawing on qualitative data from 65 respondents from Ghanaian coastal communities of Saltpond and Kormantse, this paper investigates small-scale fishers’ experiences of offshore oil and gas infrastructure decommissioning. The paper frames decommissioning as a critical phase of energy transition and interrogates its outcomes through the dual lenses of just transitions and the “right to the sea.” The findings reveal that decommissioning produces socio-ecological and economic disruptions. These include the creation of offshore safety zones leading to spatial exclusion of fishing activities, the erosion of socio-ecological knowledge systems, material precarity through asset loss, and ecological uncertainty linked to perceptions of pollution. While these processes are officially justified on grounds of safety and environmental protection, they are experienced locally as forms of livelihood dispossession and governance exclusion. The study argues that decommissioning represents an unjust transition, in which the challenges associated with post-extractive restructuring are disproportionately shifted onto vulnerable coastal communities. At the same time, it is a struggle over the right to the sea, as regulatory and security mechanisms reconfigure access to marine space in ways that privilege state and industrial actors over fisherfolk. The paper concludes that achieving socially just and sustainable decommissioning outcomes requires moving beyond technical compliance toward inclusive governance frameworks that recognise local knowledge, ensure equitable access to marine resources, and address the livelihood impacts of transition. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Shahmohammadian A.; Ghafory-Ashtiany M.
Title: Navigating housing system complexity – Part II: Quantitative analysis of the Housing System Abstraction Hierarchy (HSAH)
Abstract: Housing is a key component of urban systems, playing an essential role in shaping sustainable development and enhancing the resilience of cities. To achieve adequate housing, governments must adopt a systemic, integrated perspective on the housing system's structure, considering its complex interdependencies. Part I of this two-part study (the accompanying paper) introduced the Housing System Abstraction Hierarchy (HSAH), a conceptual framework for capturing the structural complexity of housing systems. Part II quantifies the HSAH, consisting of 176 nodes and 7822 interconnected links, using advanced network analysis metrics to identify the most influential components of the housing system and their functional dependencies. The results reveal that nodes with high Eigenvector Centrality, primarily within the economic, environmental, and technical domains, represent the most structurally influential parameters, whereas governance and social-related nodes with high Betweenness Centrality act as critical bridges facilitating cross-sectoral coordination within the housing system. Understanding these leverage points and network hubs provides policymakers with targeted entry paths for improving housing outcomes and driving system-wide transformation. Furthermore, the analysis traces cascading effects and systemic vulnerabilities, demonstrating how weaknesses in lower-level functional parameters can propagate and influence the system's higher-level objectives. Finally, the study highlights key insights from the policy paper on achieving adequate housing in Iran, developed based on the HSAH analysis, offering transferable insights for other developing and rapidly urbanizing contexts worldwide. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Transforming value of sustainability in urban development: Reconfiguring logistics service in the construction industry
Abstract: Urban development depends on construction activity to improve sustainability, yet the logistics required to move materials, equipment, waste, and workers remains insufficiently integrated into urban planning. This paper examines how construction logistics can be integrated into municipal urban planning by analysing how actor groups perceive its impacts and coordinate value creation across fragmented urban systems. The study applies a qualitative interactive research design based on a Swedish construction logistics project. Data were collected between August 2022 and March 2024 through eight semi-structured group interviews, joint workshops, actor-specific validation workshops, and a final synthesis workshop with developers, main contractors, suppliers, and trade organizations. The analysis combines iterative thematic coding with value configuration theory. The findings show that suppliers emphasize efficiency and climate savings, main contractors focus on project efficiency and safety, developers stress sustainability, accessibility and accountability, while trade organizations highlight knowledge-building and sector coordination. These differences create misalignment because societal benefits are often separated from project-level costs. Four conditions are identified as central: clearer procurement requirements, stronger logistics knowledge, scalable logistics service designs, and systematic follow-up of time, cost, and emission effects. The paper concludes that municipalities should use procurement, planning requirements and follow-up mechanisms to enforce construction logistics values in urban planning. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Self-report measures of mindfulness for children: convergent validity, predictive validity, and impacts of social desirability bias
Abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions have shown promise in supporting psychological well-being in children. However, mindfulness is commonly measured using self-report questionnaires, a method that might be problematic due to its reliance on children’s accurate self-perceptions of their own mindfulness and the potential influence of social desirability bias. In the current study, we examined the convergent validity, the predictive validity, and the influence of social desirability bias on three mindfulness self-report measures for children ages 9–13 years (N = 109). Results showed that children’s self-reported mindfulness demonstrated good convergent validity and predictive validity, as higher levels of self-reported mindfulness were positively associated with higher levels of parent-reported executive functioning. Self-reported mindfulness also covaried with social desirability bias. However, controlling for this bias did not substantively affect the convergent validity nor the predictive validity of self-reported mindfulness. These findings suggest that children’s self-reported mindfulness also captures social desirability bias, but this bias may not affect conclusions about mindfulness when assessed as a latent factor across multiple measures. Future work measuring children’s mindfulness with self-reports should account for social desirability bias when possible, as well as explore objective methods of assessing mindfulness in children. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Motivational Aspects of Teacher Feedback Practices: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire Based on Students’ Perceptions
Abstract: This study developed the Motivational Aspects of Teacher Feedback Practices Questionnaire (MATFP-Q), designed to examine students’ perceptions on six key types of teacher feedback—task-focused, specific, self-referenced, normative, next-step, and person-focused—from a motivational perspective. The instrument’s theoretical foundation integrates Hattie and Timperley’s (2007) feedback model with Koenka and Anderman’s (2019) principles for motivation-supportive feedback. Validation was conducted with a sample of 1,079 Chinese secondary school students. Student workshops were conducted to ensure ecological and cognitive validation, and expert reviews were used to establish content validation. Exploratory factor analysis was conducted to identify the underlying factor structure, and confirmatory factor analysis provided evidence for the structural validity of the proposed six-factor model (χ² = 902.49, df = 309, p < .001, CFI = .920, TLI = .909, SRMR = .059, and RMSEA = .042 [90% CI = .039, .045]). The internal consistency of the subscales (Cronbach’s α = .69–.86) ranged from acceptable to excellent. Furthermore, correlations among the MATFP-Q subscales indicated that the instrument captures related but distinguishable aspects of teacher feedback. In addition, the expected pattern of correlations with students’ perceptions of teachers’ goals and mindset belief provided evidence for convergent and divergent validity. The MATFP-Q is a reliable, theory-based tool for examining teacher feedback from a student motivation perspective. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Mining transitions in the Mid West of Western Australia: A regional transition knowledge system
Abstract: Mining transitions are typically understood as the shift from active mining to post-mining futures requiring technical planning and stakeholder consultation. This framing overlooks how mining regions experience continuous transitions throughout project lifecycles and marginalises the knowledge communities accumulate through navigating these changes. Drawing on social constructionism and knowledge systems, this paper argues communities in the Mid West of Western Australia experience mining transitions within a broader regional context. Through community-engaged methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted with twenty-two participants, including First Nations community members, across diverse sectors and sub-regions. Analysis revealed three interconnected knowledge forms: contextual knowledge situating mining within regional systems; observed knowledge from direct experiences of the mining industry; and practical knowledge of mining transitions and strategies to manage them. These forms constitute a regional transition knowledge system that already exists within communities in mining regions, distinct from industry expertise. The paper's contribution is identifying this knowledge system. Community knowledge operates across generations and addresses questions industry knowledge is not designed to ask about social disruption, intergenerational consequence, and the lived reality of being on the receiving end of decisions made elsewhere. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The psychology of AI-mediated communication across languages
Abstract: Communication across languages is increasingly mediated by artificial intelligence (AI). This creates opportunities for people with different language backgrounds to communicate in their respective native languages. AI-mediated communication can therefore reduce cognitive effort, disfluency, and social stigma associated with speaking a non-native language. At the same time, non-native language use influences cognitive, emotional, and social processes that go beyond the accurate transmission of meaning. By affecting these processes and introducing new cues, AI-mediated communication could also have unintended effects on communication effectiveness and social evaluations between interlocutors. We examine the conditions under which these effects may help or hinder cross-linguistic interactions and identify directions for research on the psychology of cross-linguistic communication as AI language tools become prevalent. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Towards a digital skills framework for the energy sector: Evidence from the Australian LNG industry
Abstract: Digital innovations have become increasingly widespread in almost every industry, and Australia’s energy sector has not been immune to this. It therefore follows that the coordination of energy exports like liquified natural gas (LNG) across government, industry, and community stakeholders will be largely dependent on the ability of these constituents to share digital information between and among each other in useful timeframes. However, the success of these integrated data systems will hinge on the ability of the energy sector’s workforce to use these technologies effectively, but it is increasingly coming into focus that the industry’s workers have very uneven levels of proficiency with digital technologies. By synthesizing earlier digital skills frameworks from other industries and adding qualitative evidence distilled from 42 interviews with a broad range of employees throughout a midsize Australian LNG company, this paper puts forward a digital skills framework for the energy sector which identifies five skill areas that will be required in 2030: (1) data analytics, (2) digital communication and collaboration, (3) digital security, (4) digital ethical and social responsibility, and (5) digital innovation. The required level of proficiency that will be required in 2030 for each of these skill areas is then assessed for different discipline groups throughout the industry. We conclude by explaining how the presented framework can be used as an assessment tool for identifying skill gaps throughout the energy sector, and exploring the policy-related implications of the findings. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: When many voices enter the dialogue: Trajectories of instructional conversations for equitable participation and creative thinking in a primary classroom
Abstract: Equitable classroom dialogue is often linked to creative thinking, but how the two develop together has rarely been examined lesson by lesson. This mixed methods study followed one Grade 5 English class in Taiwan through six lessons designed around Instructional Conversations for Equitable Participation (ICEP), a framework for inclusive dialogue. Two independent raters coded lesson videos across four ICEP domains (equitable participation, contextualized discourse, everyday language, and collaborative activity) to describe session level trends. Creative thinking was assessed before and after the intervention with a Taiwanese adaptation of the PISA based Social and Scientific Creative Thinking Test, and ten student interviews were analyzed thematically. The composite ICEP index rose from 3.5 in Lesson 1 to 4.0 in Lesson 6, with the clearest gains on the equitable participation and collaborative activity indicators. Creative thinking improved from pretest to posttest (t (20) = 4.37, p ' .001, dz = 0.95), with gains on idea diversity (dz = 0.71) and improvement (dz = 0.81) but no reliable change in originality (dz = 0.37, p = .107). Students described more dialogue, lower speaking anxiety, and a preference for small group discussion. Interpreted as parallel trajectories rather than causal effects, the findings are consistent with the view that dialogic equity may be a necessary but not sufficient condition for originality, which appears to require epistemic challenge not foregrounded in this implementation. Title: Bridging governance and sustainability in the Global South: NGO-led urban transition pathways in Mashhad, Iran
Abstract: Urban areas in the Global South face growing challenges of centralized governance, rapid urbanization and environmental degradation, which demand more inclusive and sustainable planning approaches. This article investigates how civil society organizations, particularly professionally oriented NGOs, can influence urban governance and contribute to sustainability-oriented transitions. The study examines the case of CharTabaqeh, a non-governmental organization in Mashhad, Iran, that contested the construction of the Southern Beltway and played an important role in the policy process that ultimately contributed to the project's transformation into the Mountain Park. Drawing on document analysis and observation, the research adopts a qualitative case study approach. The findings reveal that CharTabaqeh acted as a transition intermediary by creating participatory spaces, mobilizing citizens, and connecting community concerns with formal decision-making processes. The organization also promoted a shift toward more sustainable and resilient urban development by advocating for the preservation of ecological assets and the development of public green space in place of a car-oriented infrastructure project. Moreover, the NGO's strategic use of digital platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic facilitated civic mobilization, strengthened coalitions and amplified advocacy efforts at local and national scales. These results demonstrate that NGOs can act as catalysts of sustainable urban transitions by bridging community interests with policy processes, reframing development trajectories and leveraging digital technologies within centralized governance contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Effects of textual explanations and spatially augmented visual cues on spatial visualization and mental rotation performance in desktop VR
Abstract: Spatial ability is fundamental to STEM learning, as many STEM tasks require the mental representation and transformation of 2D and 3D information. Desktop virtual reality (desktop VR) has therefore been increasingly adopted for spatial training due to its interactivity and 3D representations. Textual and visual cues are widely used as instructional supports in multimedia learning, yet their distinct and combined effects on spatial training in desktop VR remain insufficiently understood. This study conducted a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment manipulating the presence of textual explanations and spatially augmented visual cues in a desktop VR environment to examine spatial visualization and mental rotation performance. Spatial performance, learning experience, cognitive load, and visual attention allocation were measured using tests, subjective scales, and eye-tracking data. The results showed no significant main effect of textual explanations or spatially augmented visual cues on posttest performance after controlling for pretest scores, but a significant interaction between the two. The textual-explanation-only condition outperformed the combined textual-explanation-and-visual-cue condition, suggesting that the effect of textual explanations depended on whether visual cues were also present. Conditions including spatially augmented visual cues showed comparable training-phase performance to the other conditions; however, this was not accompanied by better immediate posttest performance when the cues were unavailable. Eye-tracking results further revealed that the combined cue/interactive areas received more fixations than the text areas, but this attention pattern did not translate into better posttest performance. These findings inform the application of the signaling principle within desktop VR-supported spatial training and suggest that instructional supports need to be carefully coordinated rather than simply combined. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Cushioned but hollowed out: coal’s end and the demographic legacy of Spain’s mining communities
Abstract: Between 2018 and 2020 Spain closed almost its entire coal sector, abruptly and in a handful of mining districts, under a just-transition agreement that retired displaced miners early. I ask what the closures did to the population of the mining municipalities and whether the cleaner air they left behind drew anyone in Comparing the municipalities that the government classified as most affected by the mine closures with non-mining municipalities on the same pre-closure population path, I find that the two move together until the closures and then diverge: the mining municipalities lose about three percent of their population by 2022. The loss is larger where coal mattered more and survives randomization inference. It did not arrive as unemployment, which fell relative to controls because early retirement converted dismissal into pension, and it was not offset by newcomers: in-migration to the areas whose air improved most does not respond, an improvement that was small in this low-pollution setting. The transition therefore delivered justice to workers without securing the territory. Read through the lens of territorial justice, income protection for the displaced is necessary but not sufficient for the sustainable development of extractive regions, and the social and cultural costs of a hollowing community, together with the lagged effects on services and on the young, lie beyond what the quantitative record yet shows. Title: Do workers value formal jobs? Evidence from Brazil
Abstract: Informal employment, and the resulting lack of social insurance coverage, remains widespread in low- and middle-income countries. This paper contributes to the debate on the determinants of informality by estimating workers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for a formal job using a sample of 4997 Brazilian dependent workers. On average, workers are willing to forgo 15.1% of their wages for a signed work card, with higher WTP among formal and highly educated workers. Predicted eligibility for non-contributory social assistance lowers WTP, while predicted eligibility for contributory social insurance increases it. A simple calculation suggests that workers’ WTP may not fully offset employer contributions if passed on through lower wages. Providing additional information on formality raises WTP, but mainly among those already having a higher valuation of formality. © 2026 The Author

Title: How do Self-Compassion and Cognitive Flexibility Shape Pre-Service English Language Teachers’ Resilience? The Path from Self-Care to Strength
Abstract: The present study sought to examine the association between preservice second or foreign language (L2) teachers’ self-compassion (SC) and teacher resilience (TR), with the mediation of cognitive flexibility (CF). Results from a structural equation modeling analysis indicated that these three constructs are positively related. Specifically, SC was found to significantly predict TR, and CF significantly mediated the association between the constructs. The results also showed that the indirect effect of SC on TR through CF was significant, indicating that flexible cognition helps transform self-directed compassion into resilient professional functioning in L2 teaching. The findings imply that self-compassionate teachers of the English language are more likely to remain resilient in their profession, and this association is fostered when coupled with their flexible cognition in language teaching. Implications are offered for teacher education, including incorporating reflective practices that cultivate SC and activities that train flexible thinking and adaptive problem-solving. Title: From rejection sensitivity to phubbing: Self-compassion and self-uncertainty as serial mediators and a self-compassion writing intervention
Abstract: Phubbing—attending to one's smartphone in another person's presence—is widespread, yet its dispositional and intrapersonal correlates remain poorly understood. Drawing on the cognitive-affective model of rejection sensitivity (RS) and a self-regulatory resource framework, we examined whether RS is associated with phubbing through two intrapersonal processes: reduced self-compassion and heightened self-uncertainty, operationalized as low self-concept clarity. Across three studies with Chinese university students, we combined a cross-sectional survey (Study 1, N = 1202), an experiment crossing measured high- versus low-RS groups with a social-context recall manipulation (Study 2, N = 197), and a four-week randomized self-compassion expressive-writing intervention with one-month follow-up (Study 3, N = 87 completers). In Study 1, RS was positively associated with phubbing, with statistical indirect associations via self-compassion, self-uncertainty, and their serial combination. Study 2 replicated these indirect associations and showed that social context moderated the indirect pathway through self-compassion: relative to a neutral condition, it was larger after rejection recall and smaller after acceptance recall. In Study 3, self-compassion writing, relative to neutral writing, produced larger gains in self-compassion and larger reductions in phubbing, sustained at follow-up. The findings identify intrapersonal responses to rejection as correlates of phubbing and provide preliminary evidence for a targeted writing intervention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The Integration of Islamic Religious Values in the Ritual Mantras of Pinisi Boat-Making as Instructional Material for Literature Learning in Islamic Schools

Title: Enhancing Agricultural Extension Access: The Role of Different Extension Media in Climate-Vulnerable Areas of Bangladesh
Abstract: Enhancing rural productivity and resilience depends heavily on agricultural extension services, which support farmers in climate-vulnerable regions. This research examines how different farmer characteristics affect access to agricultural information through three channels: individual, group, and mass media. A cross-sectional survey of 820 farm households across the High Barind Tract and the southwest coastal and southeastern hilly regions of Bangladesh used random sampling for data collection. Researchers then analyzed the data with descriptive statistics and Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) and Tobit regression models to identify determinants across the three communication channels. According to the results, human capital (education, experience) and social capital (organizational participation) remain the strongest and most consistent drivers of farmers’ multi-channel access to agricultural extension services. Age negatively influenced engagement, while farming experience enhanced contact. The majority of farmers relied on informal networks, including progressive farmers and neighbors, but showed minimal interaction with official extension agents and digital resources. Older and less-educated participants displayed restricted use of mass media. The study establishes that effective extension strategies require educational development, organizational engagement, and demographic adjustments. The successful delivery of agricultural information requires both formal service expansion and digital literacy education, as well as reinforcement of community-based learning platforms in climate-vulnerable regions. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Is green product trade a pathway to better air quality in China?
Abstract: This study evaluates whether green product trade can serve as an effective pathway to improving air quality in China. Using panel data for 28 provinces from 2010 to 2021, we are the first to jointly examine the impacts of green trade on six major air pollutants (PM2.5, PM10, CO, SO2, NOx, and CO2) while simultaneously identifying both its temporal dynamics and spatial spillover effects within a unified empirical framework. We construct an integrated green-product trade database combining the APEC, OECD, and World Bank classifications and employ System GMM and the Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) to address spatial-temporal dependence. The results show that a 1% increase in green trade reduces PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by approximately 1.1%. Moreover, green imports in neighboring provinces generate strong spatial spillovers, lowering local PM2.5, PM10, CO, and SO2 emissions by about 5%. We also find that green imports exert significantly stronger pollution-reduction effects than green exports, suggesting an import-driven technology-upgrade mechanism typical of developing economies. These findings provide robust evidence that green trade contributes to China's environmental improvements and offer important policy insights for emerging economies seeking to leverage green globalization for sustainable, lower-emission development. Authors: Dinler H.
Title: Cognitive-affective profiles in AI adoption: Person-centered clustering of critical thinking, self-regulation, and ethical skepticism among teacher candidates
Abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational ecosystems necessitates that teachers restructure not only their technological competencies but also their cognitive and ethical frameworks. While existing literature has largely employed variable-centered approaches to examine these constructs, such methods often mask the heterogeneity within populations of teacher candidates and tend to reduce technological hesitation to a mere psychological deficit. Consequently, this study adopts a person-centered approach to identify distinct cognitive-affective profiles of teacher candidates based on their critical thinking, self-regulation, and multidimensional AI perceptions. The study group consisted of 341 teacher candidates from a state university. Data collection utilized scales demonstrating high internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha coefficients ranging between .84 and .92, and analyzed using K-Means clustering, ANOVA, and Chi-Square tests. The analysis revealed three statistically distinct profiles: Digital Pioneers , characterized by high cognitive regulation and high AI acceptance; The Disengaged Group , exhibiting low engagement across all domains; and Skeptical Intellectuals , a novel profile displaying high critical thinking skills yet the highest level of negative perception and informed caution towards AI. Effect size analyses revealed that perceived self-regulation and critical thinking played decisive roles in differentiating these profiles, evidenced by substantial effect sizes of .481 and .461, respectively. Furthermore, the distribution of these profiles showed no statistically significant association with gender and education level (p ' .05). These findings suggest that critical thinking alone does not guarantee technology acceptance; rather, it fosters a necessary vigilance against techno-solutionism. In this context, self-regulation functions as a pivotal mechanism strongly associated with candidates' critical engagement with AI rather than passive consumption. The study implies that teacher education programs should move beyond one-size-fits-all technology training in favor of differentiated strategies, emphasizing that sustainable AI integration requires strict institutional accountability alongside individual adaptability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zheng Y.; Cen Y.; Tao Y.; Zhang H.; Yu S.
Title: Group awareness in EFL students’ collaborative writing: A multiple-case study
Abstract: Despite a growing body of research on group awareness in computer-supported collaborative learning contexts, relatively little attention has been paid to students’ group awareness in naturalistic collaborative settings. This multiple-case study, informed by a conceptual framework of group awareness, investigates the key factors shaping group awareness and the ways students leverage group awareness in collaborative writing across behavioral, cognitive, and social dimensions. Analysis of individual interviews, group chats, and collaborative writing documents from 17 EFL students in four collaborative writing groups revealed that, behaviorally, students prioritized face-to-face interactions through regular meetings to ensure effective communication and idea-sharing. Cognitively, group leaders played a pivotal role in cultivating awareness, demonstrated by students’ understanding of member expertise and adept use of collaboration tools. Socially, group dynamics significantly impacted awareness, with students managing task responsibilities and relationships to enhance collaboration. Based on the findings, an empirically grounded conceptual model delineating group awareness in collaborative writing was developed, emphasizing the dynamic interplay of behavioral, cognitive, and social awareness. Authors: Chung Y.; Choi Y.-J.
Title: From facial synchronization to social conformity: A computational analysis of emotional contagion in online co-viewing
Abstract: This study examines emotional contagion and social conformity in online co-viewing environments, where viewers can observe one another's facial expressions during shared media experiences. Using a 2 (group size: 3 vs. 8) × 3 (emotional valence: happy, neutral, mixed) between-subjects experiment, we applied deep learning–based facial expression analysis (DeepFace) to capture participants' emotional responses on a frame-by-frame basis. Emotional contagion was operationalized as frame-by-frame facial expression synchronization between participants and co-viewers. The results showed that facial expression synchronization was significantly higher in smaller groups and in the happy-valence condition, suggesting that emotional contagion occurred even without direct interpersonal interaction. Contrary to predictions based on classic conformity research, synchronization was stronger in smaller groups, indicating that visual social cues may operate differently in online co-viewing than in face-to-face settings. Time-lag analyses further showed that facial expression synchronization was strongest with no temporal delay and declined as the lag increased, suggesting that emotional contagion emerged rapidly during online co-viewing. These findings extend current understanding of emotional contagion and social conformity in video-mediated communication by showing that visually mediated emotional cues can shape shared affective responses in ways that differ from established patterns of face-to-face social influence. Methodologically, this study illustrated the usefulness of AI-based facial expression analysis for examining dynamic emotional processes during shared media experiences. The findings also provide practical implications for designing online co-viewing platforms that leverage visual social cues to enhance shared viewing experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Sociotechnical imaginaries and acceptance of artificial intelligence in education: A longitudinal social media analysis
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a site of public debate on social media concerning the future of education, raising broader societal questions about human behavior, judgment, and accountability. However, how educational AI is publicly interpreted and contested in everyday digital discourse is still underexplored. Addressing this gap, this study examines how AI in education is publicly discoursed through a longitudinal mixed-methods analysis of user comments responding to TED Talk videos on YouTube that circulate influential public narratives about technological and educational futures between December 2022 and November 2025. The study traces changing public orientations towards educational AI and the future visions underpinning them. Multilingual sentiment analysis reveals a fluctuating three-year trajectory, with sentiment becoming more positive in the middle period before negative sentiment rose again in 2025. Thematic analysis of the public discourse further identifies three sociotechnical imaginaries through which commenters articulate competing visions of educational futures: (1) human-centered education in an age of cognitive displacement, where concerns focus on preserving critical thinking and human judgment; (2) educational transformation through literacy, governance, and accountability; and (3) teachers as mediators of competing AI-powered educational futures. The study contributes to existing scholarship by demonstrating how acceptance and resistance toward AI in education are socially and discursively constructed through competing visions of desirable educational futures in digital public spaces. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Sung Y.
Title: Translanguaging as an epistemic mechanism in Korean immigrant parents’ mediation of mathematical meaning
Abstract: This study investigates how Korean immigrant parents draw on translanguaging practices to mediate mathematical meaning with their elementary-aged children during home mathematics interaction. Using video-based, ethnographically informed observations of six sessions across three parent-child dyads, the analysis examines how parents coordinated Korean and English alongside gesture, diagrams, and tools to make mathematical relationships more visible, interpretable, and open to negotiation in real time. In this study, translanguaging is conceptualized as the epistemic mechanism through which mathematical meaning is mediated. The findings suggest that parents used translanguaging to diagnose procedural and structural mismatches, make unfamiliar terminology more accessible, bridge semantic and structural relationships across concepts, reorganize algebraic representations, and coordinate geometric action through multimodal guidance. The most salient form of this mechanism appeared in diagnostic interactions, where bilingual contrast and multimodal coordination made otherwise implicit mismatches visible and available for repair. The study contributes to translanguaging research in mathematics by respecifying translanguaging not only as a resource for participation but as an epistemic mechanism through which mathematical structure is made visible and available for reorganization. The study also suggests that Korean-English interaction provides an analytically productive context for examining how typologically associated linguistic resources become interactionally available in mathematical activity. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Makhetha E.; Maharajh R.
Title: Underground movements: Zama Zama Mobility, Precarity, and community resilience in South Africa’s Platinum Belt
Abstract: This article examines the lived experiences of unregulated artisanal miners, locally known as Zama Zamas, who mine within and around abandoned platinum mines in South Africa’s North West province, a region rich in critical minerals. While artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) in abandoned gold mines has been the subject of considerable academic inquiry, similar activities in platinum mining areas remain understudied. This study seeks to address this gap by situating ASM within the broader discourse on Africa’s critical minerals agenda and contributing to both academic and policy debates on its strategic role. Drawing on a mixed-methods approach, the paper investigates how Zama Zamas navigate precarious and often dangerous working conditions, patterns of circular and transnational migration, and exclusion from formal mining economies. It further reveals the social and economic networks and adaptive local strategies that foster resilience and community cohesion amid institutional abandonment and uncertain regulation within the critical mineral extraction sector of derelict mines. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: From trust to action under disinformation pressure: a sensemaking architecture of crisis social media effects on community protective response
Abstract: Crisis informatics assumes that improved information quality and institutional visibility enhance compliance and coordinated response. In plain terms, this study shows that institutional trust translates into protective action only when people retain the ability to make coherent sense of contradictory or overloaded information during a crisis. Yet recent evidence reveals a resilient guidance paradox: high engagement and elevated trust coexist with attenuated protective action and misinformed sharing. This study advances a mechanism-sequenced architecture in which crisis social media effects operate through a sensemaking converter (an interpretive process that translates trust and information into coherent understanding) that governs whether institutional credibility becomes actionable understanding. Using survey data from 712 residents in flood- and typhoon-prone regions of Viet Nam and consistent PLS-SEM with formative antecedents, higher-order constructs, and moderated mediation, the findings demonstrate converter dominance: institutional trust influences protective response primarily through sensemaking efficacy. Disinformation exposure is associated with converter collapse in the modelled direction, and need for cognitive closure amplifies disruption, producing conditional attenuation of quality-driven behavioural gains. The study reframes crisis communication theory from monotonic exposure logic to a boundary-aware, socio-technical conversion model, offering a decision-support framework for resilient digital crisis governance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: 'In Every River, in Every Lake': Impacts of Beaver Population Change on Indigenous Livelihoods and Wellbeing in the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Western Canadian Arctic
Abstract: Ecosystem transformation driven by climatic, environmental and societal factors poses interlinked ecological and social challenges for many Indigenous communities. For Inuvialuit communities in and around the lower Mackenzie Delta, in the western Canadian Arctic, recent changes in the population of beavers (Castor canadensis) have disrupted subsistence harvesting activities and travelling routes, exacerbating stresses linked to the cost of living and increasing the exposure of active harvesters to risk. Drawing on interviews with 25 Inuvialuit knowledge holders from the three communities of Inuvik, Tuktoyaktuk, and Aklavik, we investigated concerns around beaver population change in the western Arctic and the impact of this change on Inuvialuit livelihoods and wellbeing. Beyond the direct impact of beavers, the issues associated with ecosystem transformation pose challenges for Inuvialuit collective identity, the continuity of knowledge and connections to the land. While beaver population change was widely attributed to the local effects of a warming climate, participants also pointed to the effects of social transformations over recent decades. Ecological changes interact with social factors to produce complex and wide-ranging consequences for Indigenous communities. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Flexible ambition: How to make bold first offers without backlash
Abstract: One of the most vexing dilemmas negotiators experience is whether to make the first offer—and how ambitiously to do so. Although research finds that ambitious first offers lead to better outcomes on average, they can also incite extreme boomerang counteroffers, impasses, and resentment. We call these countervailing effects the first-offer double bind: Modest first offers produce poor economic outcomes, but ambitious first offers risk economic and relational backlash. To overcome the first-offer double bind, negotiators need to present their ambitious first offer in ways that invite conciliatory rather than competitive reactions. In this article, we introduce a generalizable solution to the first-offer double-bind: present ambitious first offers that signal flexibility. We highlight several strategies for producing flexible ambition: (a) frame ambitious proposals as offers vs. requests, (b) highlight how one's ambitious offer benefits the other side vs. oneself, (c) propose an ambitious range vs. point value, and (d) present ambitious multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs) vs. a single package offer. Each strategy preserves or strengthens the first-offer anchor, tethering counteroffers to the first offer, while guiding receivers to see ambitious offerers as less aggressive and more cooperative. We close by considering two research frontiers. First, we propose that the flexible ambition approach can mitigate other double binds more broadly, including the gender, social class, and low-power double binds; preliminary evidence suggests that MESOs work equally well for high and low power negotiators and for men and women. Second, we explore how ambitious and flexible first offers should be. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Ng, Yee Man Margaret (56957717900); Maslowska, Ewa (56830422700)
Title: Platform abandonment through push–pull–mooring: Trust, commitment, and generational patterns in U.S. social media
Abstract: Generational frameworks frequently explain platform adoption, but rarely platform abandonment. Through a stratified survey of 990 U.S. adults, this study examines how age cohorts (digital natives vs. digital immigrants) respond to platform change and what predicts abandonment across Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, and TikTok. Using the push-pull-mooring (PPM) framework, we found that cohort labels did not predict exit in pooled models. Distrust was the strongest pooled push predictor. Affective and normative commitment reduced abandonment odds, whereas need-based commitment increased them. Generation did, however, structure post-exit destinations: among Twitter/X leavers, digital natives were more likely to name Instagram and TikTok, and older cohorts were more likely to name Facebook. Abandonment is better explained by institutional distrust and multidimensional attachment than by cohort labels, but generation remains consequential for where users go next. Platforms seeking retention should repair credibility and cultivate wanted attachment rather than relying on lock-in or age targeting alone. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Artificial intelligence in negotiation research: From computational negotiators to psychological evidence
Abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence are reshaping how negotiation is conducted and studied. AI systems increasingly enter negotiation research in two broad roles: as part of the negotiation process, either as negotiators or as support for human negotiators, and as research instruments that annotate, standardize, and simulate negotiation at scale. As negotiators, these systems range from theory-driven agents to data-driven and hybrid agents, each embedding different assumptions about negotiation. As instruments, they promise scale, consistency, and control, but also raise risks of circular inference, in which AI appears to reveal patterns in human negotiation while actually reproducing patterns learned from its own training data. This review organizes emerging work on AI and negotiation around these two roles and argues that their scientific value depends on psychological grounding. Used naively, AI becomes a mirror of its own assumptions. Used carefully, with grounding in theory and calibration against human evidence, AI can become a transformative tool for advancing negotiation science. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Wu R.; Liu Q.; Zhang N.; Wang G.; Li X.; Wang H.
Title: Differentiated impacts of urban expansion patterns on ecosystem services and their socio-ecological drivers: Evidence from the Pearl River Delta urban agglomeration in China
Abstract: Urban expansion can alter ecosystem services (ES), yet the effects of different expansion patterns and their socio-ecological drivers remain insufficiently understood. The study focused on the Pearl River Delta urban agglomeration (PRD) to understand how different geometric expansion types influence regional ES. The Landscape Expansion Index (LEI) was used to identify interior-filling, edge-spreading, and leap-frogging expansion, while the InVEST model assessed changes in habitat quality, carbon sequestration, soil retention, water yield, and food production. A Random Forest model was further employed to identify the relative importance of ten socio-ecological drivers under different expansion patterns. The results showed a clear spatial gradient, with interior-filling concentrated in the urban core, edge-spreading dominant in the middle belt, and leap-frogging more common in peripheral areas. Carbon sequestration, habitat quality, and food production declined over 2000–2020, with net changes of −11.86 × 108 gC, −21.67 × 104, and −17.12 × 105 t, respectively, while soil retention decreased by 7.73 × 106 t. Water yield increased by 7.24 × 107 mm despite declines during the early periods. Edge-spreading generated the largest absolute ES losses because of its extensive spatial footprint, whereas interior-filling produced the highest ES loss intensity per unit area. The driving mechanisms also differed among patterns: edge-spreading was more sensitive to topography and precipitation, while interior-filling was more strongly associated with socioeconomic factors. Leap-frogging had smaller regional effects but may increase local risks such as habitat fragmentation, soil erosion, and reduced ecological connectivity. These findings suggest that urban growth should be managed according to expansion patterns, with ecological land around urban fringes protected during edge-spreading, ecological safeguards strengthened during interior development, and green infrastructure improved in areas affected by leap-frogging expansion.
