Authors: Obaidallah M.D.
Title: The American touch: Evaluating the reach of U.S. soft power in India; [رویکرد آمریکایی در ارزیابی دامنة قدرت نرم ایالات متحده در هند]
Abstract: The study assesses the reach and effectiveness of U.S. soft power in India from 2010 to 2025. It also explores how cultural, educational, economic, and diplomatic tools have shaped Indian perceptions of the United States. In this study, using Joseph Nye's soft power theory, qualitative content analysis was combined with quantitative data from Pew surveys and secondary indicators, including educational exchange, aid flows, and trade figures. According to the findings, U.S. influence in India is impressive but unbalanced, with it being strongest in the areas of technology, education, and entertainment, but limited by historical mistrust, cultural sensitivities, and geopolitical complexities. Initiatives such as Fulbright exchanges, immigrant engagement and economic cooperation have fostered goodwill, but apparent inconsistencies in U.S. policy and moral messages continue to limit deep appeal. In conclusion, sustained and creative engagement – based on credit, equality, and shared prosperity – is essential to transforming U.S. cultural appeal into a lasting strategic influence in India's evolving multipolar fabric. © 2026, University of Tehran. Authors: Li Q.; Ke Y.; Wang Z.; Zhao J.; Xu H.; Hong Q.; Liu C.; Zhu D.
Title: HyFora: Hyperspherical representation and frustration quantification for community structure discovery in complex information networks
Abstract: Complex information networks encode rich associative structural information about group organization, cross-group interactions, and information diffusion, making community structure discovery an important task in information science. However, existing methods mostly rely on Euclidean proximity or local structural features, making it difficult to balance global community separation with local relational consistency measurement. To address this issue, this paper proposes HyFora, a hyperspherical frustration-aware framework for community structure discovery in complex information networks. HyFora first constructs a background-corrected relation operator to distinguish community-relevant structural deviations from degree-driven connectivity patterns. Based on this operator, node relations are represented on the unit hypersphere, where directional consistency and angular separation jointly characterize intra-community cohesion and inter-community distinction. HyFora further quantifies the mismatch between local relations and global community organization as structural frustration, providing an interpretable consistency measure for community readout and boundary-node analysis. Experimental results show that HyFora achieves maximum relative improvements of approximately 21.2%, 27.3%, 15.4%, and 14.0% in terms of NMI, ARI, ACC, and modularity Q[jls-end-space/], respectively, while ablation, sensitivity, and node-ranking analyses verify the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed components. Author full names: Geiger, Eva J. (58849126700); Ditzer, Julia (58147707700); Joormann, Jutta (6602734156); Barnow, Sven (56276774100); Pruessner, Luise (57203399582)
Title: Alexithymia and everyday interpersonal emotion regulation
Abstract: Alexithymia, a multifaceted personality trait characterized by difficulties identifying and describing feelings and an externally oriented thinking style, is linked to social difficulties. Drawing on the extended process model of extrinsic interpersonal emotion regulation (IER), we examined whether higher (vs. lower) levels of alexithymia are associated with differences in how people regulate others' emotions, a pathway that may help explain why alexithymia is linked to social dysfunction. Across two ecological momentary assessment studies (Study 1: Germany, n = 129; Study 2: United States, n = 220; 6028 observations), results revealed distinct patterns of association across alexithymia facets. In both studies, the direction of associations suggested that greater difficulties identifying feelings were associated with higher IER strategy use, with this pattern most apparent for more cognitive and problem-focused strategies versus more emotion-oriented IER. In contrast, greater difficulties describing feelings were consistently linked to lower IER strategy use, whereas externally oriented thinking showed no consistent directional pattern. These findings suggest that alexithymia is associated with differential patterns of IER strategy use, underscoring IER difficulties as an interpersonal process that may contribute to links between alexithymia and social dysfunction. Our results emphasize the importance of considering the multifaceted nature of alexithymia in IER. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Chandran S.; Ramachandran T.; Sivakumar D.; Ambika A.
Title: The impact of environmental, economic, and social sustainability under intensive agriculture
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Intensive agriculture has substantially increased agricultural productivity but is increasingly associated with environmental degradation, resource depletion, and socio-economic challenges. The study objectives were to evaluate the sustainability impacts of intensive agricultural practices across environmental, economic, and social dimensions in Namakkal district, Tamil Nadu, India, with particular emphasis on resource utilization, ecological stress, and the factors influencing sustainable agricultural development. METHODS: Primary data were collected during 2025 from 663 eligible farmers selected through multistage stratified random sampling across eight taluks of Namakkal District using a structured questionnaire. Farms were classified as traditional or intensive based on cultivation practices. Relationships among the study variables were examined using correlation analysis, analysis of variance, regression analysis, and non-parametric statistical tests. FINDINGS: The findings revealed a strong positive relationship between landholding size and family size (correlation coefficient = 0.7214), indicating close structural and demographic linkages within farming systems. Intensive agriculture was significantly associated with land expansion (correlation coefficient = 0.658), environmental pollution (correlation coefficient = 0.519), and declining health conditions among farming communities (correlation coefficient = 0.412). Approximately 63 percent of respondents reported land degradation, while 65 –78 percent reported salinity and nutrient depletion, reflecting perceived ecological stress. The regression model explained 7.1 percent of the variation in agricultural production (coefficient of determination = 0.071), indicating modest explanatory power. Questionnaire reliability was satisfactory (Cronbach's alpha = 0.824), supporting the internal consistency of the survey instrument. CONCLUSION: Intensive agriculture is associated with higher short-term agricultural productivity but is also associated with environmental degradation, increases health risks, and places greater pressure on natural resources. These findings may inform strategies to improve the environmental, economic, and social dimensions of agricultural sustainability through sustainable soil management, balanced agrochemical application, efficient irrigation, and policy support. While the study is limited to a single district and cross-sectional data, it provides empirical evidence to inform future longitudinal and multi-regional investigations. ©2026 The author(s). Authors: He X.; Wu R.; Zhang L.; Yuan Y.
Title: Exploration of the impact of polycentric spatial structure on urban growth types from a generalized perspective
Abstract: Addressing the limitations of conventional narrow-sense polycentric spatial structure research and the practical demand for intensive growth in sustainable urban development, this study adopts the generalized polycentric spatial structure as its analytical framework and investigates its influence on urban intensive growth. Drawing on a sample of 287 prefecture-level cities nationwide, the study integrates nighttime light (NTL) data and LandScan population raster data to construct the urban nighttime light (UNL) composite agglomeration index, applies exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA) and geographically weighted regression (GWR) to delineate urban primary-secondary centers, and classifies four generalized polycentric morphologies along two orthogonal dimensions, namely the number of primary centers and the agglomeration-dispersion degree of secondary centers. A patch-based urban index (PBUI) is further developed to identify urban growth types from 2014 to 2024. The analysis identifies 205 generalized polycentric cities in total, and the structural effects exhibit pronounced heterogeneity. Cities with higher agglomeration-synergy levels, specifically the polycentric-synergistic and balanced-symbiotic types, effectively suppress extensive growth in distant suburban enclaves and facilitate intensive urban development. The monocentric-dispersed type exerts only a negligible and statistically insignificant restraining effect on disorderly expansion. The acentric-fragmented spatial configuration tends to generate functional overlap among centers and fragmented resource allocation, thereby exacerbating inefficient and extensive growth. Furthermore, this effect varies by development level: cities with stronger economic foundations and well-established infrastructure demonstrate more pronounced polycentric guidance toward intensive growth, whereas indiscriminate spatial dispersion in less-developed cities depresses land-use efficiency and impedes the realization of intensive growth. This study clarifies the temporal logic through which generalized polycentricity shapes urban expansion, and establishes a reproducible identification framework for generalized polycentric structures alongside compatible expansion measurement indicators. The findings offer empirical support for China’s differentiated formulation of polycentric spatial plans, the regulation of disorderly urban peripheral expansion, and the coordinated promotion of high-quality, intensive land use in both urban and rural areas. They also provide a reference for spatial optimization and sustainable urbanization in developing countries facing analogous challenges. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Systemic approaches in human factors and ergonomics for analysing team dynamics: A systematic review
Abstract: Team dynamics in complex sociotechnical systems are critical for safety and organisational effectiveness. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the utility and applicability of systemic Human Factors and Ergonomics(HFE) approaches for analysing team dynamics. Four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect) were searched for peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2020 and September 2025. Studies were included if they applied systemic HFE methods to analyse team dynamics in organisational settings. Studies focusing solely on individual performance or lacking methodological detail were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data, and methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Data were synthesised using thematic analysis. Seventy-seven studies were included, with healthcare being the most represented domain (n = 39). Most studies (51.9%) used adapted or combined approaches. Communication and coordination were the most frequently analysed dimensions of team dynamics. Established frameworks (e.g., SEIPS, FRAM) supported system-level analysis, while author-developed methods provided greater insight into local interactions. Hybrid approaches enabled integration across levels of analysis. Most studies were of high methodological quality (64.9%). These patterns informed a two-axis model positioning systemic HFE approaches by level of analysis and methodological integration, operationalised as a framework for method selection. Systemic HFE approaches are effective for analysing team dynamics in complex settings; however, no single method is universally optimal. Title: Supporting initial teacher education student creativity and critical thinking using active constraints in assessment: A scoping review
Abstract: Assessment design plays a critical role in shaping student learning in higher education, particularly in disciplines where creativity is both a learning outcome and a pedagogical approach. In Initial Teacher Education (ITE), this role is intensified, as assessment tasks often function as the primary site of learning for time-poor students and simultaneously model pedagogical practice for future teachers. While constraints are frequently embedded within assessment tasks, their role in supporting creativity remains under-theorised and inconsistently articulated in the literature. This scoping review examines how constraints are used within assessment tasks that aim to foster creativity and/or critical thinking in social sciences, humanities, education and creative arts courses in higher education in order to consider implications for enhancing creativity through assessment tasks in ITE. Using a scoping review framework, 28 empirical studies published since 2000 were identified and analysed thematically. Six key themes emerged: the role of prior experience, constraints as catalysts for creativity, task design and flexibility, rubrics and scaffolding as support structures, the domain-specificity of creativity, and the presence of “invisible architectures” in task design. Findings indicate that constraints function as powerful pedagogical mechanisms when they are intentionally designed, aligned with disciplinary practices, and calibrated to student readiness. However, many studies prioritise creative outcomes without sufficiently detailing the task conditions that shape them. Drawing on these findings, the paper positions constraints as active contributors to assessment design and introduces a design-oriented framework to support educators in making constraints explicit and pedagogically purposeful. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: From Herders’ Knowledge to Ecological Insight: Reindeer, Voles, and Food Caches in the Arctic
Abstract: This paper examines pistin, a little-studied forage resource for domestic reindeer previously mentioned only briefly in the scientific literature: underground stores of rhizomes made by voles on the Yamal Peninsula in the Russian Arctic. Drawing primarily on semi-structured interviews with reindeer herders and interpreting them alongside rodent trapping data, habitat descriptions, and genetic identification of rhizome samples from one available cache, we document a hidden trophic interaction among reindeer, voles, and tundra plants. Herders’ observations reveal reindeer’s seasonal use of pistin, its high attractiveness as forage, and its uneven spatio-temporal distribution across Yamal. Long known to Nenets herders in southern Yamal, pistin has only recently become visible in the peninsula’s northern part, where herders describe it as a new or still absent resource. We argue that pistin is both an overlooked seasonal forage resource and an indirect indication of vole presence across tundra subzones. The case highlights how herders’ knowledge can reveal connections between adaptations in reindeer foraging and vole range shifts, both shaped by climate-related change in the Arctic. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Gai P.J.
Title: How AI amplifies, mitigates, and creates social biases: A tripartite framework
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in social life, shaping how individuals perceive themselves and others and influencing social dynamics that bear directly on equality and collective welfare. Yet its relationship to social bias is paradoxical: the very systems that can entrench and amplify long-standing prejudices may also be leveraged to challenge them, and may simultaneously generate entirely novel forms of bias. This review synthesizes recent empirical literature within a tripartite framework organized around the core pathways along which AI shapes social biases: AI design, lay beliefs about how AI operates, and processes of social evaluation and attribution. Drawing on these pathways, I outline three corresponding avenues for intervention: more equitable AI design, targeted adjustment of lay beliefs about AI capabilities, and redesign of social evaluation processes to account for the attribution biases that AI introduces. Together, these findings underscore the urgency of a socially informed approach to AI development and governance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Investigating the interplay between public art, urban design, and national identity: Case of the UAE
Abstract: Public art and culturally responsive urban environment play a crucial role in shaping national identity, particularly in culturally diverse and rapidly evolving societies like the UAE. This study examines how different forms of public art, their integration into urban spaces, and digital platforms influence perceptions of national identity. Grounded in Social Identity Theory, Place Attachment Theory, and Public Space Theory, it employs structural equation modeling (SEM) and thematic analysis using data from 543 respondents across UAE emirates. The SEM model explains 40.3% of the variance in Perceived National Identity (PNI), emphasizing the significant role of public art and digital platforms in cultural engagement. Mediation analysis highlights the importance of interactive experiences in strengthening cultural connections, while thematic analysis identifies cultural integration, community involvement, and sustainability as key themes. Findings suggest that combining traditional Emirati artistic elements with modern digital technologies enhances inclusivity and engagement. However, the limited direct impact of urban design on national identity highlights the need for culturally relevant elements to maximize its effectiveness. By integrating quantitative and qualitative insights, this study offers clear implications for policy and practice by recommending participatory planning, integration of heritage-based design elements and use of digital platforms to enhance cultural visibility and engagement. It provides a practical framework for urban planners, cultural policymakers, and designers to develop inclusive public spaces that reinforce national identity in the UAE. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Yin B.; Wu X.-R.; Lian R.
Title: AI-assisted interactive narrative as an integrative-learning design task: Student appraisal in preservice teacher education
Abstract: Research on generative AI in education often asks whether these tools improve learning outcomes. Collaborative design raises a prior question: how should teaching organize AI-supported work so that disciplinary knowledge, creativity, collaboration, and human judgment come together? Integrative learning names that aim: connecting disciplinary knowledge with situated experience and synthesizing insights across cases. Integration matters in teacher education, where preservice teachers must apply principles to ambiguous professional situations. We examined an AI-assisted interactive-narrative (AI-IN) assignment in which preservice teachers designed branching professional-ethics games through a whole-part-whole sequence: course-wide orientation, collaborative development of a focal case with AI-supported possibility generation, and cross-case reintegration. We used self-reports from a 480-person primary cohort and an independent 257-person same-course cohort to ask how students appraised the design, whether the learning ratings shared residual covariance in a one-factor model, and which conditions accompanied appraisal. Allowing residual covariance between the two perceived-learning ratings improved the one-factor model in both cohorts (scaled Δχ²(1) = 11.99 and 14.20, respectively; both p < .001); the localized association was stable across sensitivity analyses. This localized covariance may reflect perceived-learning content or shared-method influences, including wording and placement; it establishes neither learning gains nor a distinct latent domain. In the primary cohort, favorable appraisal accompanied clearer roles, efficient collaboration, greater contribution, better challenge-engagement balance, and positive AI attitudes. Students reported challenges in translating ethics into plots, selecting platforms, and managing workload. AI-IN offers a testable design proposition for integrative learning: AI supports possibility generation while students retain responsibility for selection, verification, ethical judgment, and synthesis. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Herzlinger G.; Galanidou N.
Title: The Acheulean Large Cutting Tool Assemblage from Rodafnidia, Lesvos: A 3D Morpho-technological Cross-regional Comparative Analysis
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: The Acheulean, a key Lower Palaeolithic technocomplex characterised by iconic large cutting tools (LCTs), is one of the most extensively studied phenomena in prehistoric archaeology. Yet its vast chrono-spatial distribution, together with the persistent tension between technological homogeneity and variability, has hindered the construction of robust cultural phylogenetic scenarios for its evolution and dispersal. One way to address this challenge is to develop regional- and continental-scale syntheses of industrial traits based on standardised analytical protocols. Such protocols can help overcome differences in site context, artifact recovery, chronology and publication standards that reflect diverse geographic, chronological and academic traditions. In tune with this we integrate technological and computational archaeological analyses under open science principles to conduct a comparative study of Acheulean variability and cultural phylogeny at the Eurasian crossroads of the Aegean and the southern Levant. Our point of departure is Rodafnidia, a Middle Pleistocene locality on the island of Lesvos, Greece, where excavations have revealed stratified Acheulean knapped stone tool assemblages. We present a comprehensive morpho-technological analysis of an LCT assemblage composed of handaxes and cleavers from Rodafnidia. The analysis evaluates contextual integrity and examines the relationship between technological procedures and morphological features across well-provenanced stratified artifacts and surface finds. Given the scarcity of Acheulean assemblages in the Balkan Peninsula and western Anatolia, we compare the Rodafnidia material with five handaxe assemblages from ‘Ubeidiya, Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (GBY), Ma’ayan Barukh, Holon, and Nahal Hesi, as well as with nine cleaver assemblages from GBY. Together, these reference assemblages span different chrono-cultural stages of the Levantine Acheulean. The results reveal a high degree of homogeneity within the Rodafnidia assemblage, indicating consistent technological preferences and recurrent morphological outcomes. At the same time, the morpho-technological configuration identified at Rodafnidia differs from any pattern recognised among the studied Levantine assemblages. Our research protocol underscores the value of integrated comparative morpho-technological analyses for investigating the complex evolutionary and cultural dynamics of Acheulean hominin populations. More broadly, our findings contribute to a nuanced understanding of Middle Pleistocene Acheulean variability and cultural phylogeny in this part of the Mediterranean, while demonstrating a scalable approach that can be applied across the Acheulean world. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Amormino P.; Cameron C.D.
Title: Too many humilities: Construct proliferation and the measurement of a consequential trait
Abstract: Humility is among the most morally and socially consequential traits in individual-differences research, yet it is measured by more than 20 instruments spread across four traditions that differ in theoretical level and have developed largely on separate tracks: intellectual, relational, and cultural humility, and the Honesty-Humility factor of HEXACO. Two recent papers bring the costs of this fragmentation into focus. Costello et al. (2023) report that widely used intellectual humility self-reports track confidence more than error recognition, a failure of criterion-related validity against metacognitive calibration and error recognition. Pärnamets et al. (2026) show that consolidating measures within a tradition is feasible and clarifying. We argue that cross-tradition integration should become a priority for individual-differences science, and we outline what it requires: multitrait-multimethod designs; comparison of correlated-factor, higher-order, and bifactor models; attention to discriminant and incremental validity, and to measurement invariance; and validation against distinct classes of external criteria that have psychometric support of their own. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Negotiating the contested: A framework for studying social issue negotiations
Abstract: Negotiation research has yielded useful insights on how to manage economic and business interactions by highlighting the importance of information sharing, trade-offs, and integrative solutions in achieving mutually beneficial outcomes. However, these approaches inadequately explain why negotiations over social issues such as immigration reform and climate change can remain deadlocked despite sustained efforts to reach agreement. Drawing upon recent research, we introduce an organizing framework that identifies three common features of such negotiations: moralization, identity threat, and public contestation. Moralization frames issues as matters of right and wrong, reducing willingness to compromise; identity concerns transform policy disagreements into threats to group membership and self-concept; and public scrutiny increases reputational risks and constrains flexibility. Together, these dynamics hinder engagement, value creation, and the quality of agreements. We review emerging interventions—including moral reframing, perspective sharing, high-quality listening, informal dialogue, and third-party mediation—that may mitigate these barriers. We conclude by highlighting the need for research examining how moral, identity, and public pressures interact across levels of analysis to shape social issue negotiation processes and outcomes. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Fuchs C.; Granulo A.
Title: A two-layer model of technology lay beliefs and their societal and political consequences: The case of AI
Abstract: Modern technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to economic and societal prosperity. Yet, independent of their actual effects, consumers, workers, and the public often hold negative beliefs about these technologies, which can contribute to aversion to AI and technological change more broadly. This article examines technology lay beliefs, with AI as the focal case, and proposes an interconnected two-layer model to explain their societal impact. Layer 1 captures general psychological predispositions to technological change that provide a baseline for why technology lay beliefs often emphasize potential losses. Layer 2 captures specific contextual interpretations of AI that amplify or attenuate this baseline. We use this model to organize existing research and discuss the societal and political consequences of technology lay beliefs in the age of AI. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Kumar A.
Title: From distraction to engagement: An applied examination of the IMPACT framework in technology-rich management education
Abstract: Student perceptions of instructional effectiveness in technology-rich management education remain actively studied amid concerns about classroom distraction in digitally mediated environments. This study introduces IMPACT—an integrative pedagogical framework composed of Incentive, Measurement, Project-based Learning, Accountability, Critical Reflection, and Technology. It presents an exploratory, multi-course demonstration across four management courses spanning the MBA, Executive MBA (EMBA), and Executive Postgraduate Diploma in Management (EPGDM–VIL) programs, delivered in face-to-face and synchronous online modes. Implementation was examined using institutional course-evaluation data (N = 202 of 203 enrolled students), and a thematic close reading of open-ended comments informed by reflexive thematic analysis. Across all four courses, student perceptions of instructional effectiveness were uniformly high on standardized nine-item instrument (weighted averages ≥ 6.0 on a seven-point scale). Qualitative themes aligned with the framework's design intent: practical relevance, structured project workflows, visible progress indicators, and technology-mediated tools, alongside integrative configuration as a framework-level property. Findings support consistent implementation across heterogeneous settings and association with positive student perceptions, but do not support causal claims about engagement. The study contributes design-oriented vocabulary identifying integrative configuration, operational workflow, and multi-mode portability as the framework's primary contributions. Limitations include single-institution, single-instructor, construct–measurement mismatch, and the absence of comparative or pre/post designs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Symptom network structures of social media addiction and internet gaming addiction among school-aged youth: Undirected and Bayesian directed graph analyses
Abstract: Social media addiction (SMA) and internet gaming addiction (IGA) are increasingly recognized as important behavioral concerns among children and adolescents. However, little is known about whether their symptoms occupy similar structural positions across digital behavior contexts. This study compared the symptom structures of SMA and IGA among school-aged children and adolescents using network and Bayesian graph analyses. A school-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among 11,638 students aged 10–18 years from six public schools in Chongqing, China. SMA was assessed using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale, and IGA was measured using the Game Addiction Scale. Regularized partial correlation networks, Network Comparison Tests, and Bayesian Directed Acyclic Graphs were estimated to examine symptom associations, gender differences, and probable directional pathways. Both networks were densely connected but organized around different hubs. Tolerance emerged as the most central symptom in SMA, whereas Withdrawal occupied the central position in IGA. No significant gender differences were observed in the SMA network. In contrast, the IGA network showed significantly greater global strength among females, although no individual edge difference survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses yielded no directionally interpretable pathways for SMA, whereas the IGA network showed a small number of interpretable pathways, with Tolerance and Withdrawal both pointing toward Mood Modification. These findings revealed the different symptom structures of SMA and IGA, with implications for more targeted school-based assessment and intervention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Enhancing computational thinking through unplugged activities in elementary education: A systematic literature review
Abstract: This study aims to analyze the role of unplugged activities in enhancing computational thinking (CT) skills among elementary school students through a systematic literature review. Using the systematic literature review design guided by the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework, the study examines 34 relevant empirical studies. Data collection involved literature searches in multiple electronic databases using keywords related to unplugged activities and CT concepts. The data were analyzed using a coding scheme covering methodological characteristics, subject area, types of unplugged activities and tools, contextual factors, challenges and suitability. The findings indicate that unplugged activities can support the development of computational thinking skills, particularly in resource-limited environments. Reported contextual factors associated with variation in outcomes include learner age, year level, curriculum and school support. However, challenges such as inadequate teacher training, difficulties in curriculum integration, and the lack of standardized assessment tools persist. The implications of this study suggest that unplugged activities can serve as an inclusive and cost-effective pedagogical tool for teaching CT skills in elementary education. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Preschoolers use exploratory approaches to selective social learning
Abstract: Preschoolers evaluate many cues when making inferences about others (Harris et al., 2018). It is unclear whether children’s understanding of inference-making is sophisticated enough that they also seek out the most relevant cues for making specific inferences. Here, we tasked 4- and 5-year-olds and adults with a modified epistemic trust paradigm in which they were told to select one of two informants to help them learn about novel objects. However, before doing so, participants were told that they could learn up to three pieces of information about the informants: what they know (epistemic cue), how they play with their friends (benevolence cue), or what they look like (appearance cue). Of particular interest was which cue participants prioritized (picked first) and what strategies they used for seeking information. In Study 1, adults prioritized learning epistemic information and tended to employ efficient information-seeking strategies (selecting the fewest cues possible to make their inferences). Children, on the other hand, chose each cue first at relatively equal rates and tended to employ exploratory strategies for information-seeking (sampling broadly from the available information). This was even the case in Study 2, in which the informativeness of the appearance and benevolence cues was reduced. These studies raise questions about the way in which children make inferences about others and point to a tendency for children to employ exploratory strategies for learning about others (Gopnik, 2020). © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Storey K.
Title: The evolution of remote operating centres: Towards a new geography of mining
Abstract: In mining ‘remoteness’ was once a measure of isolation from other activities and communities. With the adoption of new digitalization technologies, ‘remote operations’ now more often refers to the management, monitoring and control of mining equipment, processes and infrastructure from locations which are geographically separate from the immediate extraction site. This paper reviews the evolution of remote operating centres in the sector and explores the nature and implications of the new geography of mining that they are helping to create. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Nature- versus non-nature-based recreation: A comparative assessment of self-reported anxiety alleviation
Abstract: Nature-based recreation delivers vital ecosystem services that shape human physical and psychological well-being, representing a core category of nature's contributions to people within urban and peri-urban social-ecological landscapes. While non-nature-based recreational activities can also improve people's quality of life by mitigating anxiety, the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based recreation to people's mental health, and the factors that influence them, remain largely unknown. Here, we conducted a survey of 15,522 respondents across China and applied structural equation modeling to show that nature-based recreation is associated with significantly stronger self-reported anxiety alleviation than non-nature-based recreation. A longer time allocation to nature-based recreational activities during holidays and weekends was also associated with greater self-reported alleviation of anxiety from nature-based recreation. Furthermore, predictors including environmental pressure, anxiety-related attributes, and socioeconomic status were associated with the relative contributions of nature- and non-nature-based anxiety alleviation, with these associations partly mediated via recreation engagement. This empirical evidence improves integrated landscape and urban planning frameworks by providing context-specific guidance for sustainable urban recreational space design and cross-regional governance focused on public health. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The blind spots of in-situ upgrading: Rethinking social infrastructure
Abstract: In-situ upgrading has become a preferred strategy for improving informal settlements worldwide, yet its focus on physical infrastructure often obscures the social infrastructures that sustain everyday life. This study examines how communal spaces—alleyways, rooftops, and other informally produced environments—function as urban commons and how they become vulnerable during upgrading processes. Drawing on Schlager and Ostrom’s bundles-of-rights framework, document analysis, field observations, and 105 interviews, the research traces changes in access, use, management, and ownership of communal spaces during a comprehensive in-situ upgrading project in Nantou, Shenzhen. The findings show that social infrastructure in informal settlements is constituted through shared routines, tacit norms, and collective practices rather than formal design, making it particularly susceptible to enclosure when upgrading prioritizes aesthetic, commercial, or heritage objectives. The study identifies governance displacement as a mechanism through which upgrading reconfigures rights and responsibilities, producing non-physical forms of dispossession even without relocation. By conceptualising social infrastructure as urban commons, the paper advances a framework for recognizing and protecting these often-invisible systems. The findings offer transferable insights for upgrading practices globally, highlighting the need for governance-sensitive, participatory approaches that safeguard the social foundations of community life. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Building on sand: state capacity, livelihoods, and the limits of environmental governance in Cabo Verde
Abstract: Cabo Verde has built an extensive environmental policy framework, ratifying major multilateral agreements and enacting decree-laws that formally regulate the exploitation of natural resources. Yet on Santiago Island, small-scale illegal extraction of development minerals by low-income households continues to cause severe degradation of beaches, watersheds and hillsides. Drawing on fieldwork in two northern municipalities (São Miguel and Tarrafal) and 25 semi-structured interviews with community leaders and sand and gravel extractors, this article investigates why extraction persists despite a dense regulatory architecture. We find that extraction is a survivalist strategy primarily undertaken by women heads of household, for whom environmental regulation represents a direct threat to precarious livelihoods. Mobilising the "environmental state" framework and feminist political ecology (Nightingale, 2006). We argue that state intervention has tightened coastal enforcement but displaced extraction into riverbeds and hillsides, intensifying rather than reducing aggregate environmental pressure. We characterise this as "governing through precarity", an environmental state present in law and on highly visible beaches, though absent in inland sites where the poorest extractors work. By centring the politics of enforcement and social reproduction, the article contributes to global debates on artisanal extraction, gender, and informality in African Small Island Developing States (SIDS). © 2026 The Authors.

Title: “Whose Death Killed Death, and Took Away His Sting”: Aemilia Lanyer-s Subtle Art of Death in Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum
Abstract: Historically grounded approaches to the Renaissance “death arts” can be used to illuminate Lanyer-s mobilizing and transforming of standard rhetorical tropes and poetic conceits—most notably the blazon—to reconceptualize and represent the bliss-imbued chiastic movement from Jesus-s incarnation and death by crucifixion to the resurrected Christ-s making possible the prospect of eternal life. Lanyer-s poem thus provides a rich case study in the death arts to promote a novel, reconfigured form of female piety predicated on a series of stunning memory images of the grotesquely maimed and blood-drenched male body. Title: Preparing nurses to engage with upstream social determinants of health: A scoping review of nursing educators' approaches and understandings
Abstract: Aims: To perform a scoping review to examine how nursing educators prepare nurses to engage with upstream social determinants of health (SDOH), and to explore educators' understandings of nurses' roles in addressing these determinants. Background: International policy frameworks increasingly position nurses as key actors in addressing the upstream SDOH. Nursing educators play a pivotal role in developing nurses' capacity to engage with health inequities at this level; however, little is known about how educators prepare nurses for this work or how they conceptualize this role within contemporary nursing practice. Data sources: CINAHL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched on 5 September 2026 for peer-reviewed primary studies published with no date restrictions. Review methods: Following full-text screening of 125 papers, 27 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final scoping review. Results: Studies (2010–2025) were predominantly from the United States. Fifteen examined educational approaches to teaching SDOH at all levels, while 12 explored nursing educators' understandings of SDOH in practice. No studies were explicitly designed to prepare nurses for upstream engagement as a central aim (e.g. policy engagement or structural and systemic advocacy). Nursing educators themselves held varied, and at times conflicting, understandings of the role of upstream engagement within nursing practice. Conclusions: This review identifies a critical gap in nursing education related to preparing nurses to address upstream SDOH. Title: A Holistic Framework for Paleolithic Projectile Studies: Insights from Swabian Gravettian Fléchettes
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Projectile technology and long-range weapons represent a major innovation in human evolution, shaping subsistence strategies, complex behavior, and advanced planning skills. Given the fast decay of organic remains, the Upper Paleolithic record is dominated by lithic implements, which are often classified as projectiles based primarily on morphological characteristics. However, such typological classifications frequently overlook macro- and microfractures that signal actual projectile use and may vary between different weapon systems. Here, we present the results of a detailed technological and functional analysis of 54 fléchettes from the Gravettian layers of the cave sites Hohle Fels, Brillenhöhle, and Geißenklösterle. Using a holistic approach including multiple analytical approaches spanning from lithic technology, traceology, projectile experiments, and statistics allowed a more comprehensive and robust analysis of possible wear patterns linked to projectile use. The technological analysis focused on the production sequence and morphological variability of the fléchettes, while use-wear analysis was employed to identify macro- and micro traces indicative of projectile use. The observed traces were tested against a reference assemblage of experimentally replicated fléchettes knapped from Jurassic chert and radiolarite, the two primary lithic materials used in the Swabian Gravettian. The experiments tested different propulsion modes, including spear-throwing and bow-and-arrow propulsion, as well as the influence of raw material variability on the formation of macro traces. The results reveal a high overlap of use-wear traces between Ach Valley fléchettes and fléchettes used in experimental spear-throwing while clustering with TCSA values of ethnographic arrowheads. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that fléchettes were likely adapted for projectile use in a long-range weapon system, complementing other Gravettian point types in a modular projectile design that reflects the versatile technological and subsistence organization in the Swabian Gravettian. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: One airport, four efficiencies: Comparing efficiency dimensions in airport benchmarking
Abstract: Evaluating airport efficiency through a single analytical dimension, whether operational throughput, airline response, service quality, or environmental sustainability, risks misrepresenting overall infrastructure performance. This study examines dimensional divergence by estimating four Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) models for Brazil's twenty-nine largest airports from 2000 to 2024: an operational infrastructure-conversion model, a tactical airline-response model, a two-stage network model accounting for flight delays and cancellations, and a socio-environmental network model incorporating pollutant emissions for the 2018–2023 window. Applying within-year Spearman rank correlations, Kendall's coefficient of concordance, and a percentile-based dissonance index evaluated via a double bootstrap that re-estimates the DEA frontiers within each replication, with airport and year fixed effects, we demonstrate that single-dimension rankings conceal fundamental operational trade-offs. While operational throughput and tactical airline responses exhibit close alignment (mean Spearman ρ = 0.85), correlation with social effectiveness drops to 0.55, and environmental agreement falls to 0.40. Furthermore, system concordance is highly state-dependent, collapsing from about 0.86 in pre-crisis years to 0.52–0.63 during 2020–2021, when regulatory clarity is most critical. Crucially, dimensional dissonance is associated with physical scale rather than with ownership structure; governance regimes fail to predict dissonance even under within-airport fixed effects, whereas large capacity-constrained hubs are associated with systematic penalties when operational delays and cancellations are priced. Ultimately, unidimensional benchmarking introduces predictable structural bias into performance assessment, which indicates that regulatory incentives and corporate benchmarking need multi-model architectures to capture hub saturation and regional network realities accurately. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Anglada-Tort M.; Lee H.
Title: Computing aesthetic taste
Abstract: Recent breakthroughs in computational and experimental techniques have produced major discoveries in the science of aesthetic taste. This paper reviews key findings from two complementary approaches: machine learning and large-scale human experiments. We argue that together these approaches represent a fundamental shift in computing aesthetic taste, from measuring preferences and choices to reconstructing the complex, high-dimensional representations that generate them. Using these representations, which we refer to as ‘taste spaces’, researchers can move beyond asking what people like to explaining why they like it, and how aesthetic taste is learned, structured, and transformed across individuals, cultures, and artificial systems. We conclude by discussing how these advances create new opportunities for addressing some of the defining scientific challenges of the coming decades, such as understanding the rich diversity of aesthetic taste across individuals and cultures, and the ways in which artificial intelligence increasingly distorts human taste. © 2026

Title: Uncovering creative metacognition patterns in TVET innovation education: insight from an epistemic network analysis of students’ self-reflective assessments
Abstract: Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) increasingly position creativity as a teachable competence in innovation and entrepreneurship education, yet little is known about how Creative Metacognition (CMC) elements are structurally interconnected and activated to facilitate creativity in TVET learners. To address this gap, this study provides an exploratory epistemic network analysis on structural mapping of CMC in TVET innovation and entrepreneurship course. Forty TVET learners completed a three-stage authentic Creative Problem-Solving task focused on venture design for a remote region. Their self-reflective assessments were segmented into 1,506 theory-driven semantic fragments and coded into Creative Strengths (CS), Creative Restrictions (CR), and Creative Contextual Knowledge (CK). Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was employed to model the co-activation patterns and relational intensity among CMC elements. Results show that students with high scores exhibited a stronger connection between CS and CK, suggesting that contextual knowledge was framed as creative affordances. In contrast, low-scoring students demonstrated a stronger connection between CR and CK, suggesting that situational reasoning was more often associated with perceived barriers and may reflect constrained idea development despite contextual awareness. The study also provides evidence of associations between reflective CMC configurations and creative performance, offering implications for reflective scaffolding and TVET entrepreneurship task design. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Motivation for cyberhate among Ukrainian youth
Abstract: While research on cyberhate has focused largely on prevalence and exposure, motivation underlying cyberhate perpetration remains under-researched. This study examines revenge and proactive motivations for cyberhate perpetration among Ukrainian youth during the ongoing war. Guided by the general aggression model, social identity theory, and social cognitive theory, we explored the mediating roles of revenge and proactive motivation in the association between cyberbullying victimization and cyberhate perpetration. Using exploratory structural equation modeling on survey data from 4149 youth aged 10–25, we found that victimization was significantly associated with cyberhate perpetration, partly through revenge motivation. Proactive motivation was related to victimization but was not significantly associated with cyberhate perpetration. Findings highlight the role of revenge motivation in cyberhate behaviors. In this war-affected population, the nonsignificant proactive pathway suggests that cyberhate may differ from forms of online aggression driven by entertainment or social reward. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Kazali E.; Kalliontzi E.
Title: Cognitive predictors of narrative retelling in early childhood
Abstract: This study examined the associations between inhibitory control, working memory, inductive reasoning, awareness, and children’s narrative retelling abilities in early childhood. A total of 212 children aged 4–7 years participated in the study. Executive functions were assessed through measures of verbal and visuospatial working memory and inhibitory control, inductive reasoning was assessed using a Raven-like matrix task, and awareness was assessed through perceptual and inferential awareness tasks. Narrative retelling was evaluated using a story retelling task that captured multiple aspects of narrative performance. Correlational analyses indicated moderate associations between inhibitory control, working memory, and several narrative retelling indicators. Narrative retelling performance also increased significantly with age, indicating clear developmental gains from the preschool to the early school years. Structural equation modeling further showed that inhibitory control and verbal working memory were significant predictors of the latent narrative retelling construct, whereas visuospatial working memory and inductive reasoning were not significantly associated with narrative retelling. Awareness showed small but significant associations with certain narrative retelling indicators. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Jiang S.; Stadtfeld C.
Title: The social embeddedness of learning: Social network formation and academic achievement in an undergraduate student community
Abstract: Background: Students play an active role in developing their social learning environment and peer relationships. Meanwhile, their academic behaviors are likely to be affected by their integration and individual positions in social networks. Despite the clear importance of social aspects on learning, the mechanisms shaping students’ social networks and the impact of emerging social ties on students’ academic performance remain underexplored. Aims: We investigate (1) the development of undergraduate students’ friendship and co-learning relationships, and (2) the influence of social embeddedness on students’ academic achievement. Sample: The sample consists of first-year students from two large STEM cohorts at a Swiss university: NA=225, NB=625. Methods: With longitudinal network data, we applied stochastic actor-oriented models to simultaneously examine the (co-)evolution of friendship and co-learning networks for each cohort while controlling for other network mechanisms on relationship formation. Furthermore, we implemented network autocorrelation models to examine the influence of social embeddedness on students’ first-year qualification exam GPAs. Results: The results revealed a mutual sustainability of co-learning and friendship ties, which were initially bridged by more generic positive social interactions. Furthermore, we found a significant association between students’ first-year grades and the average grades of their co-learners. This grade interdependency may be a joint outcome of peer selection and peer influence processes. Conclusion: Our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the co-dynamic processes of undergraduate students’ co-learning and friendship networks and highlights the importance of social embeddedness in students’ academic performance. © 2026 The Authors

Title: A comprehensive survey on multimodal sentiment analysis: Approaches, challenges and open issues
Abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to extract affective knowledge from various types of input media, including image, audio, and text. Given the significant impact of leveraging the vast amount of multimodal data from social networks and of fusing and integrating information extracted from different modalities on enhancing the validity and accuracy of the sentiment analysis process, MSA has become an important, fascinating, and widespread topic. The MSA methods presented in the literature exploit the latest advances in deep learning and transformers for multimodal feature extraction, fusion, classification, and polarity identification to enhance efficiency and performance. Despite various research having been conducted and recent articles presented with diverse approaches for MSA, the lack of a comprehensive study that examines several aspects of the problem addressed in these studies, including approaches, paradigms, methods, tools, and techniques, and evaluates them by considering related issues such as the datasets and benchmarks used, criteria and parameters for measuring results, and the extent to which intermediate and final objectives are addressed and achieved, is noticeable. In this paper, MSA and its various processes and phases are addressed within a comprehensive study framework. In this regard, techniques, tools, and datasets for feature extraction, multimodal fusion, and sentiment classification are thoroughly reviewed, categorized, summarized, compared, and evaluated, and for better comparison, some evaluation factors are proposed at each stage. Furthermore, a comprehensive overview of existing challenges, open research topics, and future research directions is provided along with a set of guidelines for conducting future studies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Faunal Evidence and the Duration of Occupation: A Statistical Approach to Neanderthal Archaeological Sites
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: The duration of Neanderthal occupations of caves and rock shelters is one of the most debated issues in prehistoric archaeology. Several disciplines, including lithic analysis, micromorphology, zooarchaeology, taphonomy, and spatial archaeology, have proposed criteria to estimate occupation length, but their reliability varies. This study focuses only on indicators derived from faunal assemblages and evaluates their effectiveness through statistical testing. Four features were analysed: number of taxa, hunting spectrum, anthropogenic modifications, and evidence of carnivore activity. These characteristics were applied to a dataset from Late Mousterian sites in Spain and south-eastern France (70–40 ka) that have previously been examined through multidisciplinary approaches. The results indicate that the four features do not provide equally robust signals. Anthropogenic modifications and the number of exploited taxa show the strongest correlation with occupation duration. In contrast, the number of taxa and carnivore activity, when considered alone, are less reliable indicators. Multivariate analyses reveal a clearer structuring of the faunal assemblages. Brief stopping places are consistently distinguished from longer occupations. However, long-term occupations and repeated short-term occupations tend to overlap, largely because of palimpsest effects. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and the limits of faunal criteria. They highlight the need for integrated, high-resolution approaches to reconstruct the duration and intensity of Neanderthal occupations. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Koebner I.J.
Title: Cura: The case for institutionalizing health and well-being in the arts & culture sector
Abstract: A convergent body of evidence from clinical trials, epidemiological cohort studies, mechanistic science and emerging economic analysis demonstrates that arts and cultural engagement is a meaningful determinant of health. Yet the organisational infrastructure of arts and cultural institutions has not kept up with this science. Drawing on the historical example of how education became a permanent institutional vertical in arts and cultural organisations during the twentieth century, this paper argues that the evidence base for arts and health now meets a reasonable threshold for a parallel structural change: the creation within arts and cultural organisations of a permanent, staffed and resourced health and well-being vertical. The argument is normative in its institutional commitments, but deliberately pluralist in form. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Hakki A.
Title: The reality of Dubai's property price index and a look at the foreseeable future; [تحلیل شاخص قیمت املاک دبی و پیشبینی آیندة آن]
Abstract: The real estate market serves as an important indicator of economic health, reflecting the complex interaction of numerous factors. The study provides a detailed assessment of the real estate sector in the United Arab Emirates, with a particular focus on the Dubai market. Using price data from 2012 to 2024 compared to a base index of 1.00 (equivalent to AED 934,524 for apartments and AED 1,646,567 for villas), the results show a steady upward trend in value. This growth will peak in 2024, when the index will reach 1.58 for apartments and 1.43 for villas. The study uses the Orange-ARIMA forecasting model, according to which the period of market stability will continue until 2028. At this stage, a slight correction is expected, with the forecast indices stabilizing at 1.57 for apartments and 1.37 for villas. As a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, the apartment price index fell to a low of 0.99 in the second quarter of 2021, while the villa price index reached its lowest point in the first quarter of 2020, recording 0.99. The research confirms that the Dubai real estate market has remarkable resilience and great potential for sustainable growth. This stability is underpinned by solid economic fundamentals and a predictable political environment. Key drivers include the increasing adoption of advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence, which enhances operational efficiency and market transparency. All these factors together reinforce Dubai's unique and leading position as a safe and advanced investment center in the region. © 2026, University of Tehran. All rights reserved.

Authors: Shen X.; Kong J.; Shen X.; Dai F.
Title: Parks as behavioral climate adaptation infrastructure: mechanisms and limits under extreme heat
Abstract: Urban parks are increasingly positioned as critical nature-based solutions for mitigating extreme heat. However, while their physical cooling capacity is well-documented, their role as infrastructure for behavioral climate adaptation remains underexplored. This study examines urban parks as behavioral climate adaptation infrastructure by integrating event-based mobility analysis, park-level adaptation performance assessment, and neighborhood-scale accessibility analysis in the City of Las Vegas. Using anonymized mobility records, extreme heat episodes were identified and linked to changes in visitation intensity, dwell time, and nighttime use. Event-level behavioral responses were summarized using the Park Behavioral Adaptation Index (PBAI), while longer-term park performance was evaluated using the Park Adaptation Performance Score (PACS). Accessibility to higher-performing parks was subsequently assessed in relation to neighborhood social vulnerability. The results reveal three key findings. First, adaptation occurs primarily through temporal reallocation. Second, adaptation performance varies substantially across parks and cannot be explained by park size, morphology, vegetation greenness, or amenity provision alone. Third, access to higher-performing parks is unevenly distributed across the city. Adaptation deficit zones are concentrated in lower-income, renter-dominated, and minority neighborhoods, indicating that opportunities for park-based adaptation are socially unequal. By linking behavioral responses, park performance, and adaptive accessibility within a unified framework, this study shifts attention from the cooling potential of parks to their role in enabling realized adaptation under extreme heat. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Sun D.; Mi X.; Hong J.
Title: From diagnosis to explanation: An integrated framework for examining spatially heterogeneous associations between temporary industrial-land use and neighborhood gentrification
Abstract: As Chinese megacities transition to post-industrialism, the socio-spatial consequences of temporary industrial land reuse—a pivotal urban renewal strategy—remain under-theorized. This study integrates Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR), Geodetector, and Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to examine associations between four functional types of temporary use and a Standardized Gentrification Index (SGI) capturing changes in educational and floating-population composition across 134 Beijing subdistricts. The results reveal differentiated and context-dependent patterns. Technology-oriented use density exhibits a stable and spatially widespread positive association with SGI. Cultural-use area is positively associated with SGI across most subdistricts, whereas cultural-use density is predominantly negative. Production-service area is significant only in a limited set of locations, while consumer-service measures show no statistically significant local MGWR coefficients. Cultural and technology clustering recur as the principal correlates of coefficient heterogeneity, whereas production clustering, transport-accessibility growth, and housing-price change matter in specific relationships. These findings suggest a state-mediated, technology-oriented pathway of demographic upgrading and a more conditional cultural pathway. Methodologically, the framework moves from mapping spatial non-stationarity to interpreting its contextual correlates, providing evidence for differentiated urban-renewal governance. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Tune J.W.; Miller D.S.
Author full names: Tune, Jesse W. (57147370500); Miller, D. Shane (59862559300)
Title: Foraging Theory and the Colonization of Unfamiliar Landscapes: Assessing Late Pleistocene Projectile Point Reduction Strategies
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: How humans perceive risk has long been of interest to the social sciences. The colonization of unfamiliar landscapes by Late Pleistocene hunter-gatherers is a valuable case study that required novel strategies of risk management, technological organization, and ecological knowledge acquisition. Here, we apply evolutionary theory to projectile point reduction in the Tennessee River Valley to model utility thresholds and assess resharpening versus replacement decisions. We evaluate attributes of Clovis and Cumberland points to quantify artifact use-lives and curation intensity using a dataset drawn from the Paleoindian Database of the Americas. Results indicate that Clovis groups practiced a more conservative lithic resource management strategy by resharpening points further to extract greater utility. By contrast, subsequent Cumberland groups more frequently discarded points with variable amounts of utility remaining, suggesting reduced emphasis on resource conservation. We interpret this difference as reflecting the resolution of landscape knowledge barriers. Clovis groups confronted higher search costs in raw material acquisition, whereas Cumberland groups inherited generational knowledge of local lithic resources and became more familiar with known resource distributions. More broadly, our study demonstrates that lithic artifacts, when modeled as patches of utility, provide archaeologists with rare opportunities to test predictions of optimal foraging theory and risk management. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Mislin A.
Title: Hidden dissatisfaction after agreement: Post-negotiation perceptual alignment
Abstract: Negotiations continue to have consequences after an agreement or impasse. When parties reach a deal, value is often created only later, as they implement commitments, adapt to uncertainty, or decide whether to negotiate again. This review introduces post-negotiation perceptual alignment, how accurately a negotiator understands the counterpart's post-negotiation experience. Integrating research on subjective value, interpersonal perception, and post-agreement outcomes, I distinguish four states: recognized satisfaction, recognized dissatisfaction, overestimated dissatisfaction, and hidden dissatisfaction. Hidden dissatisfaction is consequential because it creates a false sense of success where one party treats agreement as evidence that the negotiation went well while the counterpart carries forward negative appraisals that remain unrecognized and unaddressed. Recent research suggests tactics that appear successful at agreement can impose unrecognized social and relational costs. I review why misalignment arises, emphasizing how negotiators’ imperfect inferences about counterparts’ experiences can combine with social pressures that discourage dissatisfied parties from speaking up. I conclude by outlining directions for measuring alignment and testing how negotiators can recognize and respond to dissatisfaction after negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Adak B.; Tuna A.
Title: Pre-service teachers’ perceptions of mathematical creativity: a phenomenological analysis of their conceptualizations and reflections in task selection
Abstract: The purpose of this study is to investigate pre-service mathematics teacher perceptions of mathematical creativity and how these perceptions are reflected in their task choices. The study group for the research consists of 16 mathematics teacher candidates. The research combined a phenomenological approach with a qualitative document review. Two data collection tools were used in this research. First, the Mathematical Creativity-Focused Task Selection and Explanation Form (MC-FTSEF) developed by the researchers to obtain participants' task selections and explanations for these selections in a structured format, was administered. Additionally, semi-structured individual interviews were conducted to delve into pre-service mathematics teachers' perceptions of the concept of mathematical creativity, in addition to elaborating on the data in the aforementioned form. The data obtained were analyzed through deductive content analysis and phenomenological analysis. The findings indicate that pre-service teachers distinguish mathematical creativity from general creativity, interpret it within the disciplinary structure of mathematics, and relate it specifically to the dimensions of flexibility and originality. Furthermore, the task characteristics that pre-service teachers believe support mathematical creativity are not fully reflected in the selected set of unique tasks. Geometry stands out as a more favorable area in terms of mathematical creativity, while algebra and probability have been excluded from pedagogical preferences. Furthermore, group work, peer interaction, freedom of expression, and contexts related to daily life have been evaluated as elements that support mathematical creativity. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Informal urban regeneration through social capital: The Anousheh Street experience in a developing city
Abstract: While underprivileged neighborhoods are often seen as obstacles to urban development, their regeneration is essential for achieving sustainable urban development. Understanding the factors that influence successful regeneration experiences can guide action in similar neighborhoods. This study examines how the local community drove the informal regeneration of Anousheh Street in Ahvaz, Iran, transforming an underprivileged neighborhood into a vibrant street food hub. This study employed a Straussian Grounded Theory approach based on 24 in-depth interviews, triangulated with secondary socioeconomic data, to explain how the regeneration of Anousheh Street emerged. The findings show that vendor solidarity, rooted in social capital, acts as the central driving mechanism. This solidarity enabled informal creativity in attracting customers, supported by gradual institutional involvement from local authorities. This sequential process drives social, economic, and physical regeneration, evidenced by a 31-fold increase in commercial units and a halving of the local unemployment rate (from 35.27% to 16.81%) between 2011 and 2016. Unlike top-down models, this informal approach preserves cultural authenticity, fostering local identity and economic opportunities. This study develops a novel empirical model demonstrating how urban regeneration in developing cities can be achieved without reliance on large-scale physical investment, instead leveraging social capital and street food-based economies. The model contributes to theory by addressing a key gap in Middle Eastern urban studies and extends the application of Grounded Theory within urban regeneration research. From a practical perspective, this study proposes a context-sensitive yet scalable and transferable model based on three key conditions: vendor solidarity, vendor informal creative practices, and gradual institutional support. While the model demonstrates potential for application in other developing cities, its success depends on local socio-cultural and institutional contexts. These findings provide new policy-relevant insights for advancing inclusive and low-cost urban regeneration in the Global South. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Chimwanda A.; Mudefi E.
Title: Modern artisanal gold mining practices and livelihood dynamics in Shurugwi, Zimbabwe
Abstract: Artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) is increasingly central to rural livelihoods in Zimbabwe amid unemployment and declining agricultural viability driven by climate change. However, in a context characterised by uneven access to technology, capital, and contested resource governance, ASGM assumes a socially differentiated and politically contested character with far-reaching implications for livelihood trajectories. Drawing on qualitative data from interviews, focus group discussions, and archaeological surface survey walks in Shurugwi, Zimbabwe, this article analyses how everyday mining practices, technological adoption, and socio-political relations shape livelihood dynamics. Using a historical materialist lens, the study shows that differential access to processing technologies and means of production structures participation and reward within the mining economy. Informal arrangements function as adaptive governance mechanisms regulating access to labour, markets, and claims amid regulatory ambiguity. Overall, ASGM emerges as a contradictory livelihood system that simultaneously enables accumulation, survival, and precarity, underscoring livelihoods as contested processes embedded in evolving socio-technical and political relations of production. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Lee S.Y.
Title: The dynamics of climate change skepticism sharing on social media: Social identity, partisanship, and the impact of negative public opinion cues
Abstract: Social media has facilitated the rapid spread of incorrect information, including climate change skepticism. Drawing on Social Identity Theory, we investigated why individuals adopt skeptical views and disseminate them on social media. Study 1 (N = 316) revealed that Republicans were more likely to endorse climate change skepticism and that those with strong partisan attachments were particularly likely to share these views actively as a manifestation of their social identity. Furthermore, Study 2 (N = 120) designed through the lens of the Spiral of Silence theory revealed that explicit social media cues signaling opposition to climate skepticism (e.g., high number of “dislikes” on posts about climate change skepticism) effectively discouraged climate change skeptics from sharing their skepticism. The findings of the two studies highlight the psychological drivers of climate change skepticism dissemination on social media and demonstrate that explicit cues (e.g., number of “dislikes”) can reduce the spread of climate change skepticism in digital spaces. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From hostile feedback to withdrawal: Emotional exhaustion as a barrier to social media misinformation correction
Abstract: User-driven misinformation correction is essential for sustaining the integrity of democratic discourse on social media, yet the emotional costs that discourage engagement remain understudied. Drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, this study examines how the emotional tone of other users' feedback affects correctors' emotional exhaustion and subsequent willingness to engage in future corrections in a social media environment. In a cross-national experiment (N = 2001) across Austria, Bulgaria, Denmark, and Poland, utilizing a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design, participants corrected misinformation and received feedback varying in valence and arousal. Results show that angry, high-arousal feedback uniquely depletes emotional resources, producing higher exhaustion than civil disapproval or positive feedback. This indicates that critical feedback does not inherently exhaust correctors, but it is the hostile tone, not the negativity itself, that drives depletion. Emotional exhaustion, in turn, predicts avoidance of future corrective engagement. This exhaustion-driven withdrawal is amplified rather than buffered by correction confidence, suggesting that individual motivation alone is insufficient in hostile environments. These findings highlight emotional exhaustion as a key psychological constraint on citizen-led fact-checking and suggest that platform-level moderation targeting hostile comments is critical to protect the emotional resources required for a resilient democratic debate in digital environments. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Designing the future of consciousness: A components framework and speculative implications
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: As technologies increasingly converge with users’ psychophysiology and mental states, perception and mind-altering are emerging as plausibly designable components of user experience. This gives rise to emergent phenomena of digitally induced altered states of consciousness (DIAL) that find application not only in therapeutic and mental health contexts but also in communication and leisure. Modern consciousness-altering technologies primarily exist as early prototypes, and their empirical research tends to constrain the context of use to instrumental functionality. Fictional narrative analysis proposes to push these limitations by considering concepts of technology in imaginary contexts, thereby examining the experiences, social rituals, and ethical issues associated with their use far beyond traditional technical scenarios. This article employs a reflexive thematic analysis of popular science fiction narratives to expand our understanding of how ASCs are integrated into HCI, considering broader sociocultural and sociotechnical contexts. As a result, we identify key aspects of interaction (purpose and context) and combine their subcategories into a framework that facilitates rethinking traditional HCI, revealing potentials that remain inaccessible within clear consciousness. This framework was used to construct five themes, highlighting that the benefits of mitigating cognitive load and deepening technology-mediated communication with DIAL might entail sacrificing identity and autonomy and increasing the pressures of the modern, overcompetitive, hyper-individualistic lifestyle. Thus, the article contributes to the HCI agenda by expanding existing paradigms of interaction with mind-altering technologies and by demonstrating the use of science fiction as a powerful avenue for exploring the design space and critical inquiries about these types of interactions. © 2026 The Author(s).
