Title: Mental Health and Neurodivergence Disclosure Risk Mitigation in Private Higher Education Institutions: An Integrated Risk-Protection Framework to Support Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: This study examines mental health and neurodivergence disclosure risk mitigation in private higher education institutions through an Integrated Risk-Protection Framework to support Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted involving 297 academic and non-academic staff from selected private higher education institutions in Selangor, Malaysia. The data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Structural power asymmetry, institutional trust deficit, stigma anticipation, and absence of safeguards reduce psychological safety in disclosure. Perceived enforceability of protection moderates these relationships and strengthens the explanatory power of the model. This study highlights perceived enforceability of protection as a key risk mitigation mechanism for developing inclusive, psychologically safe, and sustainable higher education governance. © 2027 Bumi Publikasi Nusantara.

Authors: Almatar K.M.
Title: Modeling the historical relationship between waterfront development and transport infrastructure: Evidence from Jeddah’s coastal transformation
Abstract: The redevelopment of waterfronts is increasingly perceived as a transport-mediated spatial process as opposed to a design or land-use process. Nevertheless, limited information exists on the impacts of transportation infrastructure on waterfront integration over time, nonlinear dynamics and temporal lag effects, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions. This paper examines the history of the relationship between the evolution of transport infrastructure and waterfront spatial integration along the Jeddah coastline in a longitudinal, GIS-based study. The analysis combines network accessibility, pedestrian permeability, land-use intensity gradients, and a composite Waterfront Mobility Integration Index (WMII) across three historical development phases. Normalized indicator trajectories, sensitivity tests, and counterfactual situations are used to analyze the concepts of threshold behavior and time lag. It has been found that accessibility to transport grows more rapidly than other spatial dimensions, and that substantial growth in pedestrian permeability and the continuity of public space is achieved only after accessibility becomes critical, with a time lag. The findings reveal that accessibility is sufficient, though not necessary in waterfront integration, and that pedestrian infrastructure is the mediating variable in the transformation of transport investment into continuous, publicly accessible waterfront environments. The research adds to the transport-waterfront literature by offering a replicable analytical framework on evaluating waterfront change in fast growing coastal metropolitan areas and providing longitudinal evidence of threshold effects and lagged spatial response. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Digital Literacy of English Language Teachers in EFL Contexts: The Necessity of Teachers’ Development in the Digital World
Abstract: Digital technologies have significantly reshaped the landscape of language education, influencing both pedagogical practices and teacher professional development. This review article investigates the role of English language teachers’ digital literacy in enhancing teaching efficiency by synthesizing findings from recent empirical and theoretical studies. Drawing on a comprehensive analysis of peer-reviewed journal articles, books, and academic reports published over the past decade, the review explores how digital competence contributes to instructional effectiveness, classroom engagement, and ongoing teacher growth. The literature was systematically selected based on relevance, publication quality, and thematic focus on digital literacy and language education. The synthesis reveals that teachers with higher digital literacy are better equipped to integrate educational technologies, adapt to dynamic learning environments, and foster more interactive and learner-centered classrooms. The review highlights the growing importance of digital skills in teacher development and calls for structured digital literacy training in language teacher education programs. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Authors: Zentner M.
Title: Music in early childhood: Perception, action, and social experience
Abstract: Research on early musical development has expanded beyond perceptual abilities to encompass movement, social interaction, and broader developmental processes. This Opinion article highlights three themes that illustrate this evolution: the relation between rhythm perception and movement, the role of music in caregiver–child interaction and social communication, and the developmental significance of active musical engagement. Through the lens of these themes, musical development appears as an embodied and socially embedded process in which perception, action, and social interaction are closely intertwined. © 2026 The Author

Title: Designing a Data-Driven E-Learning Module for Teaching English to Young Learners: Integrating Needs Analysis and the ISAV Learning Model
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: This study designed a data-driven e-learning module for Teaching English to Young Learners by integrating needs analysis with the Interactive, Somatic, Auditory, and Visual learning model. Using a design-based research approach, the study focused on the analysis and design phases. Data were collected from elementary school English teachers and pre-service English teachers through a structured questionnaire addressing necessities, lacks, and wants. The findings identified vocabulary, reading, and oral communication as key learning necessities, alongside difficulties in sentence structure and broader instructional constraints. Respondents also preferred interactive and multimodal learning activities. These findings informed an ISAV-based e-learning module prototype integrating interactive, somatic, auditory, and visual features to support learner-centered, multimodal, and contextually responsive English instruction for young learners in digital environments. © 2027 Bumi Publikasi Nusantara.

Authors: Segura-Duque V.; Griffin L.
Title: Hand clearances in ergonomic design: A scoping review of types, methods, and measurements
Abstract: Hand clearances, the space available for hand access and operation, are essential for manual workspace design. However, clearance types lack systematic characterization, unified methods, and standardized criteria for defining adequate space during manual tasks. This scoping review analyzed 26 records published between 1960 and 2026. Ninety-four unique clearances were identified and organized into four categories: Openings, Operational Clearances, Object-Specific Clearances, and PPE Allowances. Four methodological approaches and eight methodological gaps were identified, including reliance on static measurements, inadequate treatment of PPE, small or outdated samples, and limited reporting standards. Widely cited clearance values originate from small, demographically narrow 1960s studies and have propagated with limited re-validation. The review introduces the functional clearance margin as a conceptual proposition describing the additional space beyond hand dimensions required for functional operation rather than fit alone. These findings provide a foundation for developing more representative, dynamic, and standardized approaches to hand clearance design. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Hapipi; Stylianides A.J.
Title: Students’ engagement with statements and their understanding of corresponding proofs by contradiction and contraposition
Abstract: Engagement has been shown to influence students’ understanding and achievement, yet little is known about how engagement with statements relates to students’ understanding of corresponding proofs. In this paper, we take a step towards addressing this gap by investigating whether engaging with statements is associated with better understanding of proofs by contradiction and contraposition. Eighty-seven Indonesian undergraduate mathematics education students, organized in four groups, participated in the study. Two groups (n = 43) were randomly selected to first engage with the statements—reflecting on their meaning, judging their truth, and attempting to prove or disprove them—before responding to an instrument designed to measure their understanding of given proofs for the same statements; the other two groups (n = 44) proceeded directly to the instrument. There were six statements overall, three proved by contradiction and three by contraposition. We found that students who engaged with the statements achieved significantly higher mean scores on measures of proof understanding than those who did not, with a medium effect size. Regression analyses confirmed engagement as a significant predictor of students’ understanding for both proof methods, and individual semi-structured interviews with 12 participants provided qualitative support for these findings. Overall, our findings identify engagement with statements as a meaningful factor in students’ proof understanding and suggests that selectively incorporating an engagement stage before introducing key proofs may enhance undergraduate mathematics instruction beyond the typical Definition-Theorem-Proof (DTP) approach. Authors: Zhang P.; Jiang N.; Wei Z.; Hui P.
Title: Exploring socioeconomic associations of crisis information processing via large language models and explainable AI
Abstract: Social media evolution has restructured corporate crisis communication, yet extracting regional intelligence from unstructured data remains a significant computational challenge. This study proposes an integrated AI-Spatial Information Framework to analyze provincial-level discourse patterns during a major corporate crisis. Using the DeepSeek R1 671B model with few-shot learning, we classified 225,515 social media comments from Douyin into five theory-driven categories and an “Other” category, achieving an overall accuracy of 85.67% against stratified human reference labels (Cohen’s kappa = 0.828). We then employed LASSO-based feature selection and FDR-corrected OLS regression to examine associations between provincial-level socioeconomic indicators and consumer discourse patterns across 31 Chinese provinces. Statistical results suggest that provincial socioeconomic factors account for a substantial portion of the observed variation in digital discourse. Life expectancy was positively associated with brand anthropomorphism, while tertiary education showed a tentative negative association with health risk perception. More importantly, these associations suggest that regional variation in brand-supportive discourse is closely related to socioeconomic conditions and is theoretically consistent with cognitive buffering processes. By integrating theory-driven LLM classification with spatial analysis, the proposed framework connects computational linguistics and spatial social computing, providing a replicable approach for examining regional heterogeneity in digital crisis discourse. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Macdonald, Wendy (8744367000); McCredie, Kate (58295516600); Oakman, Jodi (55180688400)
Title: Workplace management of musculoskeletal and mental health risks: translating evidence into practice
Abstract: There is a large body of research evidence identifying the biomechanical and psychosocial hazards that can affect work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) and stress-related mental health problems (MHPs). The APHIRM Toolkit was developed to facilitate more effective translation of this evidence into workplace risk management practices. Using APHIRM survey data from three occupations in the healthcare sector, this project compared hazard ‘riskiness’ profiles: (a) at occupational versus local workgroup levels, and (b) using hazard constructs versus individual hazard items. It was concluded that effective risk management is likely to require: risk assessment and prioritisation of control actions separately for each local workgroup; assessment of specific hazards rather than the generic constructs used by researchers. Results highlight the value of managing MSD and MHP risks together, because both were affected by both psychosocial and biomechanical hazards in combinations that varied widely between workgroups. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Do smiling faces change children’s minds? Testing evaluative conditioning in 3–6‑year‑olds
Abstract: This study examined whether preschoolers form preferences for shapes paired with happy or sad faces (evaluative conditioning) and whether the effect varies with age or with the number of different faces paired with each shape. Sixty-one children aged 3–6 years viewed four neutral shapes during a brief conditioning movie. Each shape was assigned to one of four conditions, in which it was paired with a single happy face, a single sad face, five different happy faces, or five different sad faces. Shape preferences were measured before and after the movie, along with memory for the pairings. Children showed clear pre-existing preferences for some shapes, and the pattern differed by age. After accounting for these starting preferences, two additive advantages emerged (for positive over negative faces and for multiple over single faces) and their combination in the shape paired with multiple smiling faces was the only condition to produce a reliable shift from zero. The other three conditions did not produce reliable change, and children’s exact age and memory for the pairings did not predict change. These findings suggest that evaluative conditioning in preschoolers is more selective than typically assumed, with the number of different faces paired with a shape emerging as a key factor. The results also highlight the importance of accounting for children’s pre-existing preferences when measuring acquired evaluative learning. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Integrating Computational Thinking and Islamic Values in Geometry Learning: Effects on Pre-Service Primary Teachers’ Conceptual Understanding
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: This study examines the integration of computational thinking and Islamic values in geometry learning for Primary School Teacher Education (PSTE) students. Using a quantitative descriptive approach, the research involved 70 PSTE students at Universitas Islam Riau. Data were collected through tests, observations, and interviews, and analyzed using triangulation to ensure validity. This integration significantly improves students’ conceptual understanding, as reflected in the increase in post-test scores. The one-sample t-test yielded a significance value, confirming a meaningful difference between pre-and post-test results. In addition, students internalized Islamic values such as honesty, cooperation, and spiritual awareness during learning activities. This study responds to the need for educational models that balance cognitive skills and character development. The integration of technology and Islamic principles creates a holistic learning experience, contributing to the development of competent, ethical, and responsible future educators. © 2027 Bumi Publikasi Nusantara.

Author full names: Morse, Ian (60851251000); Klinger, Julie Michelle (56710981000); Murphy, Gwendolyn K. (59391419100)
Title: Energy transition materials, climate knowledge, and the imagined supply chain: Escaping the productive paradox of necessary mining
Abstract: Much scholarship, public discourse, and policymaking on ‘energy transition materials’ (ETMs) imagines a supply chain from material production to climate mitigation, despite the absence of any mechanism ensuring that mined materials will become an electrification technology, let alone replace fossil fuels or avoid warming impacts. Scholarship about energy transition material (ETM) discourse, including criticism, largely neglects this material-discursive contradiction and truncates final analyses to paradoxes productive toward extractive futures. Leveraging a review of 99 peer-reviewed articles published between 2013-2025, this article brings mining scholarship into conversation with climate knowledge politics. It charts the dematerialization of climate knowledge from warming impacts to values negotiated along three spectra (urgency, scale, and sacrifice) and rematerialization reflected in extractive rationales (developmental, Indigenous rights, nature, and futures). Most ETM discourse is enclosed in three narrative boundaries, which lean on the imagined supply chain and foreclose non-extractive possibilities: (1) The contingencies that link climate policy and mining, such as materials science, technological manufacturing and use, are taken for granted; (2) Scalar formulations separate and compare anthropogenic climate change and mining impacts; and (3) ETMs wield climate knowledge itself as a supply chain, dialectically illustrating a problem to its own solution. Pathways to overcome the boundaries can center the materiality of mining and climate change over the abstractions of supply chains and imagined climate benefits, critically reflect on the relationships between material production and technopolitical knowledge, and take seriously actually occurring alternative livelihoods. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Xiao M.; Tian J.; Chen Y.; Dai W.; Zheng A.; Chen X.; Liu X.; Han J.; Liu Y.; Chen H.
Title: How is self-defeating humor associated with perceptions of the physical self? A large-sample resting-state fMRI study
Abstract: Self-defeating humor (SDH), characterized by self-ridicule to gain social approval, has been consistently linked to the body-image disturbance. However, its neural underpinnings remain poorly understood. The present study investigated the neural mechanisms linking SDH to negative physical self-perceptions in a large sample ( N = 1668). Participants completed measures of humor style and negative physical self, and resting-state functional MRI. Behaviorally, SDH was positively correlated with all dimensions of negative physical self. Whole-brain fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations analyses revealed that SDH was associated with decreased activity in the right parahippocampal gyrus, left caudate, right posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and right precuneus (PCUN), but increased activity in the right postcentral gyrus (PoCG). Resting-state functional connectivity analyses showed SDH was negatively associated with caudate–occipital and PCC–PCUN connectivity but positively associated with PCC–occipital and PCUN–occipital connectivity. Mediation analyses identified a negative indirect effect through PoCG activity, and a positive indirect effect through PCUN activity in the associations of SDH with negative evaluations of general appearance and fatness, respectively. These findings highlight the role of brain regions involved in self–other information processing in linking SDH to maladaptive self-perceptions, thereby advancing our understanding of the neural pathways through which humor styles influence psychological health. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Al Atok A.R.; Sayuti Hassan M.
Author full names: Al Atok, A Rosyid (59910255500); Sayuti Hassan, Muhamad (56217590700)
Title: Presidential Involvement in Legislative Processes in Indonesia: Constitutional Distinctiveness or Structural Anomaly Within a Presidential System?; [La participación presidencial en los procesos legislativos en Indonesia: ¿una particularidad constitucional o una anomalía estructural dentro de un sistema presidencialista?]
Abstract: The lawmaking process in Indonesia, as defined by the 1945 Constitution, features extensive presidential involvement in proposing bills, participating in deliberations, and enacting laws. This departs from most presidential systems, where the executive's role in lawmaking is more limited. This article examines whether Indonesia's model is a distinctive constitutional innovation or an anomaly that strains the separation of powers. Employing a normative legal methodology, it analyses constitutional provisions, implementing statutes, and comparative studies of presidential systems in the United States, South Africa, and Colombia. The analysis shows that Indonesia's model institutionalises intensive executive-legislative cooperation but also generates legal ambiguities, especially in agendasetting, budget formation, veto practice, and emergency legislation. These procedural uncertainties risk governance instability and blur classical boundaries between branches. The article argues that Indonesia represents a "colegislative presidency" that both departs from orthodox presidentialism and enriches comparative typologies of executive-legislative relations. Authors: Yurttadur O.; Irgatoğlu A.
Title: The Effect of Mindful Teaching on Job Satisfaction among L2 Instructors: Examining the Mediating Role of Teacher Self-Efficacy
Abstract: Teacher well-being has become an important concern in higher education due to increasing levels of occupational stress, burnout, and attrition, which may negatively affect instructional quality and student learning outcomes. These challenges are particularly evident in English as a foreign language teaching, where instructors frequently manage intensive workloads, diverse learner needs, and substantial emotional demands. Although previous research has linked mindfulness and self-efficacy to positive teacher outcomes, limited attention has been given to the psychological mechanisms through which mindful teaching contributes to job satisfaction in EFL contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study examined the direct effect of mindful teaching on job satisfaction and investigated the mediating role of teacher self-efficacy in this relationship. The participants consisted of 321 EFL instructors working in English-language preparatory programs in higher education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Mindfulness in Teaching Scale, the Teacher Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Job Satisfaction Index. The findings revealed a statistically significant positive relationship between mindful teaching and job satisfaction. Teacher self-efficacy was also found to partially mediate this relationship, indicating that mindful teaching contributes to job satisfaction both directly and indirectly through stronger efficacy beliefs. These findings identify self-efficacy as an important psychological mechanism underlying the relationship between mindful teaching and job satisfaction. The study extends current understanding of teacher well-being in EFL higher education by providing empirical support for a mediation model linking mindful teaching, self-efficacy, and job satisfaction. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Author full names: Pennell, Ashlinn (60930657300); Bishop, Olivia C. (59148497500); Fawcett, Jonathan M. (25627951300); Fawcett, Emily J. (36763521900)
Title: Fear of psychosis in an OCD analogue sample: Prevalence and associated factors
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) includes heterogeneous presentations, despite the disproportionate research and clinical attention on contamination and symmetry symptoms. Colloquially coined “schizophrenia OCD”, obsessional fears of having or developing a psychotic disorder (or “going crazy”) and associated compulsions have received growing recognition within psychoeducational contexts and patient communities. This preliminary study examined the prevalence and associated factors of fears of psychosis among a university student sample (N = 154). Participants completed an online questionnaire that included symptom checklists assessing psychosis-related unwanted intrusive thoughts and compulsive behaviours, alongside a series of validated measures. Fears of psychosis were commonly endorsed: 77.9% endorsed lifetime unwanted intrusive thoughts, 70.1% endorsed associated compulsive behaviours, and 83.1% reported at least one psychosis-related unwanted intrusive thought or compulsive behaviour. Fears of losing control of your thoughts or actions was the most frequently endorsed intrusive thought (50.6%), whereas fear of developing a psychotic illness (18.3%) was rated most distressing. The most frequently endorsed compulsive behavior was replacing “bad thoughts” with better thoughts (53.2%). Supporting our hypothesis, individuals meeting OCD symptom cut-offs were more likely to endorse psychosis-related fears. Finally, hierarchical regression analyses indicated that health anxiety and negative beliefs about losing control predicted psychosis-related unwanted intrusive thoughts, over and above demographic factors, OCD severity, or other clinically relevant variables. Findings underscore the need for recognition of fears of mental health issues in individuals with OCD and suggest that interventions targeting health anxiety and perceptions of loss of control may be particularly relevant. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Impact of Livelihood Capital on Farmers’ Adoption of Sustainable Crop Residue Management Practices: Empirical Evidence from Punjab Province, Pakistan
Abstract: Sustainable crop residue management can increase agricultural productivity and reduce farming-related carbon emissions, yet adoption of sustainable crop residue management practices (SCRMPs) remains limited. This study investigates how farmers’ livelihood capital shapes SCRMP adoption in Punjab, Pakistan, using survey data from 500 farmers in three agro-ecological zones. A multivariate probit model, weighted with the entropy-TOPSIS method, estimates the effects of human, social, natural, physical, and financial capital on practices including on-farm use, livestock feed, residue retention, and biogas production. Human, social, financial, and physical capital positively influence on-farm residue use, while all five forms of capital significantly promote biogas production. Although livestock feed remains the most common use, many farmers are willing to adopt alternatives such as biofertilizer production and biogas. These findings indicate substantial potential to expand sustainable residue management in the region. Policymakers should prioritize farmer training, credit access, rural infrastructure, biogas technologies, extension services, and farmer cooperatives to encourage environmentally and economically sustainable practices. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Cocco E.
Title: Understanding situational fear of crime in context: a virtual reality interview approach to studying victimization avoidance strategies in nocturnal urban spaces
Abstract: Most research on the behavioral dimension of fear of crime captures broad avoidance habits through surveys or retrospective interviews, leaving the in-situ risk management behaviors people deploy while actually present in a threatening space largely unobserved. This study uses Virtual Reality Retrospective Thinking Aloud (VR-RTA) to access this underexplored dimension. Sixty-one participants navigated a 3D replica of nocturnal Lausanne in scenarios developed with police officers. Analysis identified two types of in-situ avoidance strategies: anticipatory scanning and route management; reactive symbolic distancing from perceived threats, modulated by personal familiarity with the area as a dispositional factor, alongside three vulnerability dimensions (self, environment, others) reflecting the core components of Routine Activity Theory. Crucially, many routing decisions proved habit-driven rather than fear-driven (a distinction surveys cannot detect) and several behavioral adjustments operated below conscious awareness, recoverable only through VR-RTA video review of participants’ own behavior. Findings point towards a sequential process model of situational FoC: behavioral adjustment begins as routine cognitive appraisal and escalates to full fear engagement only when perceived risk crosses a threshold. They confirm and nuance existing qualitative typologies of avoidance behavior while identifying specific gaps in survey instruments for measuring the behavioral dimension of situational FoC. Based on these insights, new survey items targeting in-situ risk management behaviors are proposed to strengthen the measurement of fear of victimization events. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Suriano R.; Paonessa L.P.
Title: Science takes more than belief: Epistemic and cognitive predictors of scientific reasoning
Abstract: Belief in science and scientific reasoning represent related but conceptually distinct aspects of individuals' engagement with science: the former reflects an epistemic orientation toward science, whereas the latter concerns the ability to evaluate evidence, methods, and inferences. We examined actively open-minded thinking (AOT) and cognitive reflection (CRT) as theoretically complementary characteristics, representing an epistemic disposition and a reflective cognitive component, respectively. In a sample of 333 Italian participants, we examined the incremental associations of belief in science, AOT, and CRT with scientific reasoning and whether AOT and CRT showed similar or differentiated associations with belief in science and scientific reasoning. Belief in science was positively but weakly associated with scientific reasoning. AOT and CRT accounted for additional variance in scientific reasoning beyond sociodemographic characteristics and belief in science. AOT was associated with both belief in science and scientific reasoning, whereas CRT was associated with scientific reasoning but not significantly with belief in science. Overall, the findings indicate partly differentiated patterns of association across the two constructs. Given the cross-sectional design, no causal or temporal conclusions can be drawn. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Hatami Y.
Title: Populist urbanism and the speculation network: Discourse, conflict, and planning monopoly in Hamadan
Abstract: This article explores how populist discourse reshapes urban planning conflicts and legitimizes speculative development in Hamadan, Iran. Using post-structuralist discourse theory and qualitative analysis of 1248 local media texts (2017–2024), it shows how signifiers like “the people” and “justice” construct antagonistic narratives that erode planning authority. The study introduces the concept of a “speculation network” involving political, commercial, and media actors that exploit participatory rhetoric for elite gain. It finds that populism marginalizes expertise and reinforces monopolies, with media as a key discursive arena. The article advances agonistic planning theory and advocates media-aware, conflict-sensitive planning approaches. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Noncausal joint-action scenes facilitate Mandarin-speaking preschoolers’ interpretation of intransitive verbs with conjoined subjects
Abstract: Children learn novel verb meanings by integrating sentence-level cues with information from the surrounding event. Although sentence frames provide information about verb transitivity, success with intransitive frames varies across languages and tasks. In Mandarin, preschoolers have been reported to struggle with conjoined-subject intransitive sentences, raising the question of whether this difficulty reflects a limitation in syntactic bootstrapping or partly stems from how children construe the comparison scenes. In a forced-choice pointing task, Mandarin-speaking 3-, 4-, and 5-year-olds heard transitive or conjoined-subject intransitive sentences containing novel verbs and chose between a causal scene and a noncausal scene. Critically, the noncausal scene was either a parallel-action scene or a joint-action scene. In the joint-action scene, the two participants acted together in physical contact but without a causal asymmetry. Children at all ages reliably matched transitive sentences to causal scenes. For intransitives, 3-year-olds performed at chance in both scene conditions, 4-year-olds succeeded only with joint-action scenes, and 5-year-olds succeeded in both. Thus, performance with intransitives improved with age and was facilitated when the noncausal alternative was easier to construe as a single noncausal event. These findings suggest that previously reported failures with Mandarin conjoined-subject intransitives cannot be attributed solely to insensitivity to argument structure, but also depend on how candidate events are visually and conceptually represented. More broadly, the results are consistent with a multiple-factor view of verb learning, in which syntactic cues interact with semantic, and event-based information. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Xu Y.; Hao Q.; Li X.; Niu L.; Xia C.
Title: Reinforcement learning with experience sharing promotes collective cooperation on higher-order networks
Abstract: As a central form of prosocial behavior, collective cooperation is the cornerstone of social prosperity, and elucidating how it emerges among the self-interested population is of significant theoretical and practical importance. However, existing research of cooperative evolution on higher-order networks typically assumes that agents update decisions exclusively based on their own experiences, overlooking the pervasive diffusion of information within groups. In reality, decision-making is shaped not only by individual experience, but also by experiences acquired from neighboring agents. To this end, we develop a hypergraph-based reinforcement learning framework that integrates individual and neighborhood experiences to investigate how information sharing affects cooperation under higher-order interactions. Specifically, we utilize hypergraphs to characterize the interaction topology, within which agents update their strategies according to the Q-learning algorithm. Extending the standard learning paradigm, we introduce an experience sharing mechanism, where neighborhood information is aggregated to form a shared experience and subsequently fused with individual experience to guide decision-making. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that an intermediate level of experience sharing can significantly enhance the collective cooperation, particularly under severe social dilemmas, increasing the final cooperation level by up to approximately 0.43. In contrast, excessive experience sharing leads to behavioral homogenization among agents, thereby undermining the relative advantage of cooperation. Moreover, higher learning rates coupled with moderate discount factors are most conducive to cooperation. These findings shed new light on how experience sharing shapes cooperative dynamics in higher-order networks. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zou Y.; Lei Z.; Hao F.
Title: When the sea remembers: Ritual, emotion, and identity at the Mazu Festival
Abstract: The study examines how ritual participation in religious festivals generates emotional energy and reinforces cultural identity, using the Mazu Festival in China as a case example. Findings reveal that ritual engagement fosters affective synchronization and reactivates collective memory, enabling participants to reconnect with heritage, culture and negotiate evolving identities. Emotional energy emerges as a central process linking symbolic system to identity formation. The research contributes to festival tourism studies by advancing an integrated emotional and symbolic framework and by highlighting the role of festivals as dynamic platforms for cultural continuity and identity renewal. The findings also offer practical insights for destination managers and policymakers seeking to enhance cultural meaningfulness of festival experiences. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li Z.; Zhou H.; Wu Q.
Title: An adaptive-problem structure framework for survival relevance in temporal processing
Abstract: Research on survival-relevant cues and subjective time often groups stimuli into immediate-survival, reproductive, and social categories. These labels do not explain why cues within one category recruit different temporal processes across contexts and perceivers. The Adaptive-Problem Structure (APS) Framework characterizes the adaptive problem indicated by a cue through two separable appraisals: ecological urgency, the time sensitivity and cost of delaying a response, and interpretive indeterminacy, the extent to which adaptive meaning and the appropriate response remain unresolved. APS predicts when these appraisals recruit established arousal, attention, information-sampling, and memory processes, how diagnostic context changes those links, and which personality differences strengthen them. Temporal consequences depend on the timing paradigm, interval, and response format. We outline independent ratings, selective within-domain manipulations, process measures, and staged construct validation. Five predictions specify task conditions, personality mappings, comparison baselines, and non-supporting outcomes. APS offers testable constraints on mechanism recruitment and prediction for new stimuli; the framework itself remains to be empirically validated. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Desrizal; Widigdo B.; Yulianto G.; Kurniawan F.; Sulistiono
Title: Sustainability assessment for multi-activity coastal areas using an integrated hierarchical decision-making framework
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Sustainability assessments of multi-activity coastal areas generally evaluate each utilization activity independently, leaving interdependencies unaccommodated and risking biased contribution estimates under conventional hierarchical weighting. This constraint carries profound implications for settings where anthropogenic activities vie for finite ecological space, most notably within tropical coastal socio-ecological systems in developing countries. The study objectives were to develop an activity-based sustainability assessment framework integrating hierarchical and network-based multi-criteria weighting to estimate the relative contribution of three activities: small-scale capture fisheries, vannamei shrimp ponds, and coastal tourism, in the coastal area of Pariaman City, Indonesia. METHODS: Assessments covered 36 indicators across four sustainability dimensions: ecological, social, economic, and governance, with a 17-node interdependence network built from 14 indicators showing cross-activity dependencies through shared resources and identified causal pathways. Hierarchical weights for individual activities were derived independently by fifteen experts across three sectoral panels. Additionally, network-based weighting to account for inter-activity interactions was performed by a subset of five cross-sectoral experts. All pairwise comparison matrices satisfied the predetermined consistency threshold. The resilience of the regional index to weighting uncertainty was tested through sensitivity analysis. FINDINGS: Network-based weights ranked vannamei shrimp ponds above small-scale capture fisheries and coastal tourism, but far less dominantly than under hierarchical weighting, which treated ponds as an extreme outlier by ignoring their negative influence on shared water quality and spatial resources. With a near-uniform contribution value of 0.554 across all three activities, the regional index underscores that intervention prioritization requires integrating interdependent cross-activity contributions rather than relying exclusively on standalone activity assessments. The moderately sustainable category held consistently across sensitivity scenarios, although activity contribution order proved more sensitive to weighting uncertainty. Title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
Abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. However, critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on recent data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Halali E.
Title: Two automatic motivations, two control systems: A neuroscience framework for negotiation
Abstract: Negotiation often involves a recurring tension between self-interest and social preferences such as fairness, trust, honesty, and reciprocity. A central debate concerns which motive, self-interest or social preferences, constitutes the automatic default and which requires cognitive control to be expressed. Understanding these automatic processes is important because negotiations often tax cognitive resources, increasing reliance on automatic responses. Yet, the evidence remains contradictory: in some contexts, self-interest appears spontaneous and social concern effortful, whereas in others the reverse holds. This review argues that the inconsistency stems from a flawed premise. Drawing on converging evidence from social, affective, and decision neuroscience, I propose that both self-interest and social preferences are automatic motivational processes, driven by distinct motivational systems and regulated by separate prefrontal control mechanisms. The right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) is proposed to regulate reward-seeking motivation, facilitating prosocial behavior such as fairness and reciprocity, whereas the right ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (rVLPFC) is proposed to regulate socio-emotional responses, facilitating self-interested choice, together forming a proposed double dissociation within this motivational conflict. This dual-control framework reframes the central question from which motive is automatic to which automatic motivational system dominates a given context. It reconciles conflicting findings and explains why subtle situational shifts can reverse the apparent automatic response. The review considers emerging hormonal, neuromodulation, and hyperscanning evidence from dynamic interactions and discusses how changing circumstances may alter not only which motivation dominates, but also which form of control is needed to act in accordance with one's goals. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Brains on copy-paste mode? A mixed-methods study on the relationship between generative artificial intelligence use and students’ critical thinking skills
Abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools, such as ChatGPT, into higher education has raised important questions about their relationship with students' critical thinking (CT) skills. This study explored these associations among 398 undergraduate students using a mixed-methods design. Quantitatively, participants completed validated measures of critical thinking and a survey assessing frequency of AI use in academic contexts. Correlation analyses indicated a significant negative association between AI use and Analyzing/Organizing skills. Moderation analyses revealed that academic achievement moderated this relationship for Analyzing/Organizing and Evaluating, with higher achievers showing a stronger negative association. No significant effects emerged for gender and age on the remaining CT dimensions. Likewise, qualitative analyses of 200 open-ended responses identified three user profiles: (1) instrumental/uncritical, comprising younger low-achieving male students emphasizing AI speed and utility while reporting reduced verification effort; (2) stable/complementary, comprising older high-achieving students perceiving little change in their evaluative practices; and (3) ambivalent/skeptical-trusting, comprising women with medium achievement, divided between increased skepticism and greater reliance on AI outputs. Supplementary analyses linking Analyzing/Organizing and Evaluating scores to these profiles showed that lower development of both skills consistently aligned with the instrumental/uncritical profile. The interpretive consistency between both analytical strands suggests that the relationship between generative AI use and CT skills is nuanced and profile-dependent, limited in scope to specific dimensions and student groups rather than reflecting a broad negative impact, while highlighting the risks of uncritical reliance and the potential of AI as a complementary academic tool when used reflectively. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: The role of citizen science in engaging older adults with age-friendly green spaces
Abstract: This project addresses the global challenges of an ageing population and rapid urbanisation by exploring how citizen science can support the engagement of older adults in shaping age-friendly green spaces. Conducted in the City of Unley, South Australia, the study engaged 30 older residents (aged 60+) as citizen scientists to trial a multi-format audit tool and co-reflect on its use in practice for creating age-friendly environments, generating practical insights for future research and design practice. Integrating audits into participants’ daily routines and everyday life spaces ensured that findings reflected lived experiences. Citizen science was not merely a data collection tool but a sustained dialogue, with regular workshops and informal café sessions supporting motivation, peer learning, and collaborative analysis. Participants reported challenges such as sustaining long-term motivation, but also highlighted opportunities for empowerment, confidence-building, and strengthened community ties. Importantly, many older adults described shifts in how they experienced their environments—becoming more observant, extending their walking habits, and growing more confident in voicing ideas. Several participants continued their civic engagement beyond the project, illustrating the lasting impact of participation. The study contributes methodological insights into designing inclusive citizen science initiatives, offering guidance on recruitment, tool development, and engagement strategies tailored to older populations. Overall, this study demonstrates the power of citizen science not only to generate grounded data but also to empower older adults and co-produce inclusive urban knowledge. Findings provide process-focused insights into age-friendly engagement and illustrate the broader potential of citizen science in shaping equitable, community led public spaces. Overall, this research demonstrates how citizen science can move beyond data collection to become a co-creative process that empowers older adults and informs age-friendly urban transformation. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Affective Dimensions of Spanish as a Foreign Language (SFL) Education: Exploring the Interplay of Anxiety, Motivation, and Self-Esteem among Secondary School Students
Abstract: This study probed the associations among Spanish as a foreign language (SFL) students’ anxiety, motivation, and self-esteem. Beyond mapping the connections between these affective factors, the research also examined the extent to which students’ motivation and anxiety predicted their self-esteem. The data were collected from 118 secondary school students through three validated instruments, namely the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale, Foreign Language Self-Esteem Scale, and Motivation towards Foreign Languages Survey. The analysis indicated clear patterns of association, with higher levels of anxiety linked to lower levels of both motivation and self-esteem. The results highlighted the importance of addressing emotional factors in foreign language education and suggested that interventions targeting anxiety reduction and the enhancement of self-esteem and motivation could foster a more supportive language learning environment. By demonstrating how affective factors shape SFL learning, the study offered practical insights for policymakers and language educators seeking to promote students’ emotional well-being and engagement. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Title: From growth mindset to social-emotional skills in early and mid-adolescence: A educational-cultural examination of an integrated mind-body-behavior framework
Abstract: Background: Social-emotional learning (SEL) is a core educational goal, yet little is known about how adolescents’ cognitive beliefs, body-related self-perceptions, and everyday health behavior jointly relate to social-emotional skills across diverse cultural contexts and school stages. Objective: Based on mindset theory and self-regulation perspectives, we examined an integrated Mind-Body-Behavior framework in which growth mindset, positive body image, and health behavior show a theoretically specified pattern of associated with adolescents’ social-emotional skills. Sample: Participants were 62,105 adolescents from 15 regions where data were drawn from the OECD 2023 Study on Social and Emotional Skills. Methods: A two-stage quantitative design combined structural equation modeling and machine learning. Results: Growth mindset was associated with social-emotional skills both directly and indirectly associations via body image and health behavior. The direct association was substantially stronger than the combined indirect associations, indicating partial rather than complete support for the full proposed pattern. Scalar invariance across the seven clusters was not supported, so cluster-level comparisons were treated as descriptive. Associations differed between cohorts: the association between growth mindset and body image was stronger in the younger cohort, whereas the association between health behavior and social-emotional skills was stronger in the older cohort. Conclusions: The study contributes an integrated view of how beliefs, body-related self-perception, and health behavior relate to social-emotional skills. The framework shows that cognitive, body-related, and behavioral domains each relate to adolescents’ social-emotional skills and that these relations change between school stages. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Canbay P.
Title: Lexicon-guided representation learning with self-attentive transformer models: Enhancing offensive language detection in low-resourced languages
Abstract: Detecting offensive language in online social platforms is essential yet challenging in low-resourced, morphologically rich languages such as Turkish. This study presents an engineering-driven and innovative approach for offensive language detection in Turkish. The proposed method directly injects offensive lexicons collected from local sources by domain experts into transformer self-attention mechanisms. In particular, it leverages lexicon-guided representation learning within Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) variations to enhance attention toward offensive linguistic cues. DistilBERT and XLM-RoBERTa are enhanced with a lexicon mask that reweights attention toward lexicon-matched tokens by a factor of five, while maintaining end-to-end fine-tuning without architectural modifications. Using the OffensEval Turkish dataset (35,284 annotated tweets), the proposed method is evaluated against traditional baselines (MLP, CNN, SVM, LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU) as well as vanilla transformer models. The proposed Lexicon-Guided XLM-RoBERTa achieves an F1-score of 0.87, while Lexicon-Guided DistilBERT attains 0.85, outperforming vanilla XLM-RoBERTa (0.78), DistilBERT (0.76), and non-transformer baselines (0.66–0.72). Additionally, LIME is employed to provide local and model-agnostic explanations for both offensive and non-offensive predictions, demonstrating that lexicon-guided attention enhances the detection of morphologically complex and implicit offensive cues while reducing false positives in neutral contexts. The proposed method offers practical and multidisciplinary contributions through a lightweight plug-in attention mechanism based on linguistic resources, achieving state-of-the-art performance in Turkish offensive language detection while providing interpretable outputs beneficial for content moderation, human-centered AI, and computational social science. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Yang K.; Pauletto S.
Title: Sounding different: Exploring attitudes towards digital voice personalization in a conversational setting
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: With the rapid advancement of voice generation and conversion technologies, the application of voice personalization in everyday communication is becoming increasingly possible. However, current studies on voice personalization have largely focused on tool design, while relatively little is known about the impact of these technologies on self-presentation and social interaction. To explore this, we conducted a qualitative study with 14 pairs of participants (28 in total, 15 females and 13 males) that integrated a voice personalization tool into natural conversation. In pairs, participants first engaged in a conversation using their original voices, and then reflected on this experience. After that, they personalized their voices using a voice modification tool and took part in a second conversation with the same partner in which they heard each other’s modified voices in real-time. Finally, they participated in follow-up interviews. Our findings show that voice personalization prompted participants to reflect on their original and modified voices, to negotiate between authenticity and desired traits, and to consider both benefits and risks of voice personalization in different contexts. These insights indicate that voice personalization is intricately linked to self-perception while simultaneously functioning as a malleable social signal. Overall, this study contributes empirically grounded findings on how voice modification affects self-perception and impression management, and offers design directions for future personalization tools. © 2026 The Authors. Title: What motivates landowners to use prescribed fire in a wildfire prone landscape? Evidence from California, USA
Abstract: The use of prescribed fires on private lands is important to achieving landscape and community resilience goals, yet private landowner adoption remains low. This study examines the factors shaping non-industrial private forest and rangeland owner intentions to use prescribed fire in California. Using the Theory of Planned Behavior framework and Likert scale questions, we administered a survey to 4000 landowners, yielding 509 usable responses. We used multinomial logistic regression to model adoption intention (yes, maybe, and no) and binary logistic regression to examine preferred implementation approaches among landowners open to burning. Results indicate that 27% of respondents were willing to burn, 42% remained uncertain, and 31% were unwilling. Social norms were the strongest predictor of adoption intention. Past wildfire exposure, perceived wildfire risk, landholding size, perceived benefits of prescribed fire, and attitudes toward cultural burning positively impact adoption likelihood. Capacity to conduct burns strongly differentiated the willing adopters from uncertain ones, while prohibitive cost was the most consistent barrier across groups. Among landowners open to burning, community cooperative burning was the most preferred implementation approach, followed by agency-assisted burning, with preferences shaped by trust, liability concerns, and landholding size. Findings suggest that in California, making prescribed fire more visible may matter as much as making it feasible. Effective outreach should prioritize peer-based demonstration strategies, reduce cost and liability barriers, and build local burning capacity to bridge the gap between interest and action. Policy interventions supporting community burn networks and technical assistance could accelerate prescribed fire adoption on private lands. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Modelling Local Strontium Isotope Baselines from Human Isotopic Data Using Machine Learning: Implications for Past Mobility Studies
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Estimating bioavailable strontium isotope baselines is a critical step in archaeological mobility studies. Conventional proxy-based approaches, which rely on environmental samples, such as soils, fauna, plants, or waters, are not always feasible and may be affected by environmental, taphonomic, or sampling-related biases. Here, we introduce MobSr, a machine-learning-based model designed to estimate probable local 87Sr/86Sr baselines directly from human enamel isotope data. The model combines four first-layer classifiers—Naïve Bayes, k-nearest neighbours, support vector machine, and Random Forest—with a Bayesian ensemble layer that integrates classifier outputs and refines local/non-local probability estimates. MobSr was trained on a dataset of approximately 3000 human enamel samples from 86 archaeological sites, using published expert-derived local/non-local classifications. Local isotopic ranges are estimated by analysing posterior probabilities assigned to individual observations. Model performance was evaluated through general cross-validation and through site-specific case studies, including a La Tène period cemetery from the Czech Republic, an Early Medieval cemetery from Finland, and multi-period burial assemblages from Bahrain in the Arabian Peninsula. The results show 87–95% agreement with published local/non-local classifications, depending on the evaluation strategy and treatment of atypical cases. These values quantify concordance with the source-study labels. These findings demonstrate that MobSr can replicate and refine local baseline estimates without requiring additional environmental sampling. The model offers an efficient tool for preliminary mobility assessment and provides a complementary strategy to traditional baseline construction in bioarchaeological research. In addition, the use of a large training dataset enables broader exploration of expert-derived locality assignments across predominantly sedentary populations from different regions and periods. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Recognition of individual angry versus happy faces in 6- and 9-month-old infants
Abstract: With mixed evidence from adults, children, and infants suggesting either anger or happiness superiority in emotion detection, emotion recognition, and recognition of individual faces posing emotional expressions, the current research was undertaken to determine if one or the other emotion would result in higher recognition of individual faces by 6-month-old and 9-month-old infants. The infants were familiarized with an angry or happy face and then given a novelty preference test pairing the familiarized face with a novel face posing the same emotion. Recognition performance of both age groups in each emotion condition was above chance; however, recognition of angry faces was reliably higher than for happy faces. A simple exposure-frequency account of the findings is unlikely because infants experience more happy than angry faces. In addition, lower-level interpretations based on differences in salience, complexity, and discriminability were not supported by image analyses, infant looking times during familiarization, or adult ratings. An account based on the processing of facial expressions as social or communicative signals by infants is discussed, with a possible role for an early negativity bias. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Orgs G.
Title: The neuroaesthetics of liveness
Abstract: Live theatre, dance and music pervade to human culture. Building on a rich theoretical debate within theatre, performance and media studies, this review sketches out a psychological approach to understanding live experiences. It distinguishes physical liveness (presence in a here and now) from social liveness (sharing experiences with others). Recent mobile EEG studies on live dance performances and music concerts demonstrate that audience engagement during live performances is measurable as dynamic brain synchrony between co-present audience members or between audience members, music and movement. Differences in audience engagement between live and recorded performances (physical liveness) are measurable as looser or tighter slow wave neural synchrony. Conversely, social liveness can increase audience arousal, indexed by reduced power in the EEG alpha band during collective viewing of both live and recorded dance. These findings suggest that variable performance content and stable performance context engage dissociable neural mechanisms, attention and arousal respectively. Research on liveness originates in the performing arts but can be extended to the visual arts and to sport events. Physical and social liveness may facilitate those rare, memorable and transformative aesthetic experiences that are difficult to produce in lab-based environments. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: From Individual Reasoning to Collaborative Engagement: Continuity of Student Problematic in Grade 1 Mathematical Problem Solving
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: This qualitative study examined the continuity of student problematic from individual reasoning to collaborative engagement in a Grade 1 mathematics classroom within the Transformative Lesson Study Incorporating Open Approach (TLSOA) context. Seven Grade 1 students were followed across six lessons on addition and subtraction. Data were collected through video and audio recordings, students’ written work, field notes, and photographs, and analyzed using protocol analysis and analytic description. The findings show that student problematic remained observable when students re-engaged with the same mathematical problem in small groups. Student problematic appeared through proposing, questioning, explaining, checking, reconsidering, and coordinating mathematical ideas. Title: Meaning in the age of AI: Experiencing less, needing more
Abstract: What does it mean to be human when artificial intelligence (AI) can simulate human thought and creative labor with increasing fidelity? Unlike AI, humans experience meaning in life. Yet AI may create a paradox for meaningfulness. AI may reduce people's ability to experience meaning by disrupting selfhood (loss of effort and self-efficacy), social relationships (reduced mattering and connection), and culture (erosion of value and stability). At the same time, it may heighten people's need for meaning by challenging human exceptionalism and increasing the need for coherence amidst upheaval. This paradox—experiencing less while needing more—is what we term the AI Meaning Gap. Yet meaninglessness is not inevitable. If developed and used intentionally, AI could become a tool for reflection, understanding, and self-growth, thereby enhancing meaning. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Beyond the final product: AI-Enabled Learner Traces as Assessment Evidence in Project Management Education
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in project management education (PME), especially in digital learning environments where learner activity can be captured as process data. This matters because project management learning involves collaboration, coordination, decision-making, reflection, and professional judgement, which are difficult to assess through final outputs alone. This systematic mapping review examines how AI-generated or AI-mediated learner data are collected, analysed, and used for assessment-related purposes, and identifies the educational implications reported in the literature. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searches were conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and IEEE Xplore for studies published between January 2016 and November 2025. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The review identified five categories of AI-enabled learner data and assessment-relevant evidence: human–AI dialogue and prompt-based interaction logs, adaptive and personalised learning process data, project artefacts and revision traces, reflective, self-report, and course feedback evidence, and standardised task, output, and scoring data. These categories are treated as different layers in the data-to-evidence process rather than as learner traces in a narrow technical sense. Future-oriented conceptual data systems were identified as an emerging possibility but were treated separately from reported learner data and assessment evidence. Across the included studies, data were analysed using natural language processing, machine learning, rule-based techniques, learning analytics, and generative AI/LLM-based prompting, and were used to generate feedback, indicators, recommendations, and scoring support. Reported benefits mainly relate to formative feedback, improved visibility of learning processes, and more timely instructional support. However, the evidence base remains limited and uneven, with important gaps in validity, fairness, transparency, and longer-term educational effects. Overall, AI in PME is used not simply to automate assessment, but to broaden how learner activity is captured, interpreted, and used to support process-oriented assessment and pedagogical judgement. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Evaluating feasibility of an ACT group telehealth-delivered therapy intervention for adolescents with depression
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Increasing rates of adolescent depression call for efficient and accessible interventions that are well received by adolescents. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a third-wave psychotherapy that has been shown to be effective in treating depression in adolescents, delivered both individually and in group settings. Group therapy can help address service provider shortages by enabling a single provider to treat multiple individuals at once. Additionally, telehealth allows greater access to care for individuals who cannot readily travel to a clinic. Telehealth-delivered group therapy combines these two strategies to facilitate adolescents’ access to mental health treatment. We piloted a 10-week group intervention, adapted from ACT for Adolescents with Depression, and explored its feasibility. Adolescent patients with depression (N = 10) ages 14 to 18 (M = 16; SD = 1.49 years), seeking mental health services, participated in the program and completed pre and post assessments. The majority identified as female (70%) and White (60%). The groups were well attended; only one patient dropped out, and one was discharged. The patients reported overwhelmingly overall positive experiences with the program. Group means for depression and anxiety scores in this sample decreased from baseline to end of treatment, psychological flexibility increased by the end of treatment, and no changes were observed in flourishing scores. Overall, the intervention was well accepted. Title: The benefits of reading narrative fiction
Abstract: The benefits of reading are well-known and have been well-established by research. But does it matter what we read? Are there unique benefits to reading narrative fiction: stories about people, their goals, challenges, emotions, and interactions? Focusing on research published in the past few years, we review the empirical evidence of the benefits associated with reading fiction. This includes a wide range of domains, including language abilities, our ability to understand others, early social development, intergroup prejudice, meaning in life, cognition, longevity, and well-being. Several remaining research questions are also presented. Title: Unbowed: Raiding and Hunting with Paracas Spearthrowers and Slings and the Conspicuous Absence of the Bow in Western South America
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: New weapons such as the bow and arrow often emerge alongside rising population densities and interpersonal conflict. We test this generalization in southern Peru during the violent Final Formative (400–1 BCE) with measurements of 200 obsidian projectile points anchored to precise Bayesian chronologies from Paracas sites in the Palpa valleys. Based on Bayesian regressions against hafted archaeological projectile points, we conclude all Paracas points were spearthrower darts. This agrees with the lack of bows in Paracas burials and in imagery on ceramics and textiles. Conflict was limited to small-scale raids, based on a compilation of sites with slingstones, mace heads, skeletal trauma, and walls. Hunting and herding were focused in the highlands, mapped with a MaxEnt predictive surface of modern prey location. Based on spatial correlations, conflict did not drive settlement patterns; the key factors were hunting grounds, herding pastures, and agricultural suitability. Pending future research, the notable lack of the bow in the region may include later Nasca, Moche, and Chimú populations. This invites us to rethink the conditions that drive and limit the adoption and invention of bows, a uniquely human and purportedly superior projectile technology that no one bothered with during these violent centuries. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: The Fragility of Collective Action in Community Forest Management: Social Feedbacks, Trust, and Cooperation Dynamics
Abstract: In community forest management, cooperation is rarely a one-time decision. It depends on whether local actors continue contributing time, labor, and resources year after year. We examine this problem with a system dynamics model that follows changes in trust, reputation, reciprocity, perceived benefits, and free-riding. The model adapts an earlier structure to the case of ejido La Loma, Mexico. The case material guided several modeling decisions, especially the choice of variables and the interpretation of the scenarios. It did not, however, provide enough information for full empirical calibration. The simulations show that trust and reputation may sustain cooperation even as participation declines. Over time, however, the loss of active members can weaken monitoring and place collective action at risk. One result is particularly relevant: a favorable starting point does not guarantee long-term stability. Authors: Lai A.; Wu J.; Cao Y.; Lin T.
Title: Corporate environmental credit rating and social stability: Evidence from capital-labor conflicts in China's polluting industries
Abstract: Mitigating capital-labor conflicts is essential for maintaining social stability. Using China's Enterprise Environmental Credit Evaluation System (EECES) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study examines the impact of corporate environmental credit rating on capital-labor conflicts. The results indicate that EECES reduces capital-labor conflicts in polluting industries by approximately 17.63%, although its effect weakens over time. Channel tests show that EECES mitigates capital-labor conflicts by reducing workers' pollution exposure risk, improving corporate environmental information transparency, and enhancing social trust in corporations. Moreover, in cities with weaker social governance capacity, EECES exerts a stronger restraining effect on capital-labor conflicts, suggesting that it effectively compensates for deficiencies in social governance. Further analysis reveals that although EECES reduces industrial output, it significantly promotes economic transformation. Overall, these findings highlight EECES as an effective policy tool for safeguarding social stability. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Kesar P.; Ache P.M.
Title: Re-imagining visions as shared societal statements– empirical insights from Indian cities
Abstract: Visions in Indian cities lack commitment from actors and possess low normative power. To address these concerns, we take up the task of examining vision-making with a focus on institutional settings across 31 million-plus populated cities. Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework and ADICO grammar tool are used for analysis. We ask how rules-in-use within the vision-making settings are organized and geared towards collective action, and how they affect outcomes, i.e., visions. The analysis underscores three commonalities that hinder collective action, i.e., bureaucratic hegemony and allegiance to sectoral mandates, fragmented actor constellation and weak regulatory power of visions. Within visioning settings, facilitators serve as key agents for ensuring a level playing field. We found that when facilitators are external (i.e., consultants), stakeholder coverage is wider and documentation is exhaustive. In large metropolises and megacities, the visioning process acknowledges stakeholder consultation responsibly. Perhaps fair information exchange and informal monitoring of visions by civil society actors contribute to the politicisation of vision-making. In institutional terms, visions are closer to being a strategy and less to norm-setting. The paper argues that participatory discussions in diverse and heterogeneous settings with the scope of repeat interactions will build homophily and address concerns of structural fragmentation. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Territorializing the sea: fragmented operational control in offshore tin mining on Bangka Island, Indonesia
Abstract: The expansion of offshore tin mining transforms the sea into a space of extraction, yet territorial claims over this space do not necessarily translate into operational control. Studies of territorialization have largely focused on the formation of claims rather than on the processes through which such claims are converted into operational control. This article examines the territorialization of offshore tin mining on Bangka Island, Indonesia, through three interrelated analytical moments: territorial claims, securing access, and operational control. This qualitative study draws on fieldwork comprising interviews with 23 informants and observations, supplemented by a review of relevant literature and an analysis of regulatory documents, corporate reports, and news coverage. The findings show that exploration and regulatory arrangements produce epistemic and legal claims over marine space but do not, in themselves, enable mining operations. Companies and their local networks must still secure access by cultivating and representing support, engaging village institutions and local intermediaries, negotiating benefits, and making personal approaches to key actors. Their success varies across locations, shaped by local power relations, actor legitimacy, and fisher resistance. Consequently, operational control is contingent, partial, fragmented, and continuously negotiated: mining operations can proceed in some locations, whereas elsewhere territorial claims remain in force without being translated into operational control. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Chen M.; Li R.; Hu T.; Dong J.
Title: Community participation intensity on asynchronous biodiversity and human well-being responses to ecological restoration in global drylands
Abstract: Ecological restoration serves as a key strategy for addressing desertification and ecosystem degradation in global drylands. However, achieving synergistic benefits for both biodiversity and human well-being remains a significant challenge for sustainability. Although community participation is increasingly promoted, quantitative evidence remains limited on how participation intensity is associated with measured ecological and social outcomes in dryland restoration. A dataset encompassing 744 effect sizes from 41 independent studies across global drylands was constructed to conduct a meta-analysis. The synthesis indicated positive benefits relative to degraded baselines, while composite biodiversity and composite human well-being showed asynchronous responses across community participation intensity. For composite biodiversity, the pooled mean estimate corresponded to an average increase of 122.11% relative to degraded baselines. Limited community participation was associated with long-term positive patterns in the composite biodiversity (159.35%) and composite human well-being (130.71%), whereas extensive community participation showed an evidence-limited and marginally supported positive tendency in composite human well-being in the short term. Eventually, we propose an adaptive framework in which livelihood-support components may be emphasized during early restoration, followed by lower-disturbance stewardship considerations as biodiversity recovery stabilizes. Overall, our findings provide exploratory quantitative evidence for discussing how community participation may affect asynchronous ecological and social outcomes in dryland restoration. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Fukubayashi N.; Fuji K.
Title: From overloaded to unsatisfied: The short- and long-term effects of online career media exposure
Abstract: The contemporary career landscape is increasingly influenced by digital technologies. The widespread availability of online career information and the daily exchange of content via social media not only facilitate autonomous career development but also expose individuals to a vast array of career options. Although this abundance reflects greater self-determination, it may also lead to psychological challenges through choice overload. In this study, the possibility that online exposure to career information and options increases career choice overload, which, over time, may reduce overall career satisfaction, is examined. Using a combined contemporaneous and cross-lagged effects model, we found that greater online exposure to career information was associated with increased career choice overload, which was captured across three dimensions: career choice avoidance, disengagement from one's current career, and impatient career idealism. Longitudinally, elevated career choice overload predicted lower overall career satisfaction, and conversely, lower satisfaction contributed to greater overload, which suggests a potential negative spiral. Our findings provide empirical evidence that routine online media exposure can generate both conscious and unconscious career choice overload, which highlights the occurrence of choice overload in high-stakes career contexts and its multidimensional nature. © 2026
