Title: Teaching Persian derivational affixes to non-Persian speakers from a Cognitive Morphology Approach: A case study of nominal suffixes (kar, gar, ban, baz, -ande); [آموزش ونده ا و شب هوندهای اشتقاق ی فارسی به غیرفارس یزبانان از منظر صرفِ شناختی: مطالعۀ موردی پسوندهای اسم فاع لساز)کار، گر، بان، باز، نده (]
Abstract: The analysis of word formation plays a significant role in the development of learners' vocabulary knowledge (Vadasy & Nelson, 2012, p. 108). Therefore, teaching vocabulary through different instructional approaches can contribute substantially to vocabulary acquisition among language learners. This study investigates the effectiveness of teaching Persian nominal suffixes (-kar, -gar, -bān, -bāz, and -ande) in derived words to non-native learners of Persian through explicit and implicit instructional methods.In the explicit approach, the principles and findings of the Cognitive Morphology framework developed by Hamawand (2011) were employed. In the implicit approach, learners were exposed to texts containing derived words that incorporated the target suffixes. The participants consisted of sixteen advanced-level learners of Persian from the Azfa Center of Allameh Tabataba’i University and Shahid Beheshti University. They were assigned to an experimental group and a control group and participated in both a pre-test and a post-test.The results, based on descriptive statistical analyses, indicated that teaching nominal suffixes through Hamawand’s Cognitive Morphology framework and its three cognitive functions—categorization, configuration, and conceptualization—together with the concepts of prototype and periphery, can effectively enhance learners’ vocabulary knowledge. Overall, the findings suggest that raising Persian learners’ awareness of the lexical and semantic structure of derived words contributes positively to their linguistic competence and vocabulary development. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Authors: Hu S.-G.; Liu Y.-Y.; Wang X.-X.; Wu Z.-H.
Title: Beyond positive attitude: What motivates stem undergraduates to engage in classroom discussions?
Abstract: Fostering active participation in classroom discussions remains a persistent challenge in higher education, particularly in STEM fields where lecture-based instruction remains prevalent. While positive attitudes are often considered an important predictors of participation in classroom discussions, this study examines a broader set of psychological factors associated with STEM undergraduates’ intention to participate in classroom discussions. We propose and test an integrated model incorporating attitude, subjective norms, perceived need, and self-efficacy. Using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) on data from 550 undergraduates from engineering-focused universities, the study examines the motivational factors associated with participation intention and willingness to recommend classroom discussions. Perceived need and self-efficacy showed the strongest statistical associations with both outcomes. Subjective norms were positively associated with participation intention but not willingness to recommend, whereas attitude did not demonstrate a significant unique effect in the full model. Additional analyses suggest that this pattern reflects the stronger explanatory role of perceived need when considered alongside students’ general evaluations of classroom discussions. These findings highlight the importance of perceived learning value and confidence in predicting students’ participation in classroom discussions and provide context-specific implications for discussion-based teaching in engineering education. Authors: Neog B.; Gogoi A.P.
Title: Landscapes of extraction: Youth, coal and contested livelihoods in Tinsukia, Assam
Abstract: The article explores the diverse and intersecting forms through which youth encounter, experience, and respond to coal mining in Tinsukia, Assam’s easternmost resource-rich district. Drawing on qualitative ethnographic fieldwork in the Ledo and Margherita coalfields, it examines how extractive economies reshape youth livelihoods, aspirations and vulnerabilities in a landscape marked by environmental devastation, informalization of labour, and uneven development The article focuses on three connected processes: the erosion of traditional livelihoods and ecological relations; entry into precarious and informal mining-related work; and the emergence of critique and resistance. Rather than treating youth as a homogeneous category, the article analyzes how their positions are not fixed but fluid. It shows how their positions differ according to access to land, labour, networks, and political resources, while also shifting between economic dependence, negotiation, and opposition. The article contributes to political ecology and extractive-frontier scholarship by foregrounding youth perspectives from a Northeast Indian coal belt and by showing how development is experienced simultaneously as livelihood opportunity and socio-environmental harm. Authors: Zhang (Albert) H.; Liu Y.; Guan X.; Cai J.; Carroll J.M.
Title: Harnessing the power of AI in qualitative research: Role assignment, engagement, and user perceptions of AI-generated follow-up questions in semi-structured interviews
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Asking appropriate follow-up questions is an important aspect of semi-structured interviews, yet interviewers’ knowledge and skills may limit their depth and affect outcomes. While many studies have demonstrated the usefulness of large language models (LLMs) for qualitative analysis, their potential in data collection remains underexplored. We adopt an AI-driven/Reverse “Wizard-of-Oz” setup to investigate how real-time LLM support for generating follow-up questions shapes semi-structured interviews. Through a study with 17 participants, we examine the value of LLM-generated follow-up questions, the evolving division of roles, relationships, collaborative behaviors, and responsibilities between interviewers and AI. Our findings (1) provide empirical evidence of the strengths and limitations of AI-generated follow-up questions (AGQs); (2) introduce a Human-AI collaboration framework in this interview context; and (3) propose human-centered design guidelines for AI-assisted interviews. We position LLMs as complements, not replacements, human judgment, and highlight pathways for integrating AI into qualitative data collection. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The effect of gender on L1-L2 syntactic processing in Turkish-Persian balanced Bilinguals using fMRI; [شقنتیسنجردشزادرپیوحننابزلواومودردیاههنابزود نزاوتمیکرت–یسرافابهدافتسازاfMRI]
Abstract: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of gender on the L1-L2 simultaneously morphosyntactic processing in balanced bilinguals who learned their L2 at the age of seven. Using event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (ER-fMRI), Turkish-Persian balanced bilinguals (15 women and 15 men) performed an auditory grammaticality judgment task with an alternating language switching paradigm. Based on the Bilingual Dominance Scale (Dunn and Fox Tree, 2009), no significant difference was observed between the participants' proficiency in their L1 (Turkish) and L2 (Persian). Imaging results demonstrated strong neural similarity between men and women in two left-lateralized syntax-specific ROIs (Pars opercularis and posterior superior temporal gyrus), supporting the indistinguishable gender performance during L1-L2 simultaneously morphosyntactic processing. In addition, in EF-specific areas in right-hemisphere (planum temporale, supplementary motor area, superior parietal lobule and superior frontal gyrus), we did not observe differences in hemispheric recruitment by men and women, evidencing empirically for gender sameness in lateralization. Therefore, the present task and sample are not consistent with the previous claims that women show (a) superior language performance and (b) less lateralization. In general, our findings suggest that L1 and L2 simultaneously morphosyntactic processing in balanced bilinguals is not affected by the gender parameter. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Authors: Naemi Z.
Title: The Relationship between Second Language Learning Strategies, Learning Engagement, and Writing Skill in the Arabic Writing Curriculum; [رابطه راهبردهای یادگیری زبان دوم اشتیاق یادگیری و مهارت نوشتاری در برنامه درسی نگارش زبان عربی]
Abstract: Language learning strategies refer to deliberate behaviors, processes, and approaches through which learners receive, process, and use new information in a structured and purposeful manner, thereby promoting self-directed learning, self-regulation, and learner responsibility. Due to a lack of sufficient empirical research in this area, the present study aims to investigate the relationship between language learning strategies, learning engagement, and writing skills in an Arabic language writing curriculum. This study employed a descriptive-correlational design and included 70 female undergraduate students of Arabic Language and Literature at Kharazmi University in 2019. Data were collected using the Oxford Language Learning Strategies Scale (1990), the Learning Engagement Scale developed by Schaufeli et al. (2002), and a researcher-developed writing skills questionnaire. The data were analyzed using regression analysis.The results revealed a positive and significant relationship between language learning strategies, their components (except for the affective/emotional strategy), learning engagement, and Arabic writing skills. Furthermore, the findings indicated that language learning strategies and learning engagement together account for 17% of the variance in writing skills. These results suggest that the use of effective language learning strategies and higher levels of learning engagement can enhance students' writing performance.In practical terms, the findings of this study propose a pedagogical model for integrating language learning strategies and strengthening learning engagement within the curriculum. Specifically, the application of learning strategies alongside improved engagement is identified as a key factor in enhancing writing skills among Arabic language and literature students. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University All rights reserved.

Authors: Hosang M.L.A.; Susilawati; Alouw J.C.; Puspitasari M.; Senewe R.E.; Sujak; Rohimatun R.; Hutasoit R.T.; Subiyakto; Nurindah; Sunarto D.A.; Meththananda R.G.U.I.; Pinaria B.A.N.
Title: Environmental risks of pest management practices in smallholder coconut plantations
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: Oryctes rhinoceros, the coconut rhinoceros beetle, remains one of the most damaging pests of coconut (Cocos nucifera) across South and Southeast Asia, the Pacific, and increasingly, new invasion fronts in the Americas. Although climatic alterations may redistribute the geographic footprint of the hazard, predictive assessments underscore non-linear and variable outcomes. Regional expansions in vulnerable or suitable extents are largely contingent upon the analytical scenario and structural parameters of the model utilized. This reinforces the case for treating its management as an environmental, not solely agronomic, concern. The study objectives were to characterize how smallholder-level management choices translate into differentiated environmental and health risk. Smallholder coconut plantations, which supply most world coconut production, are disproportionately exposed because of fragmented land holdings, limited capital, and constrained extension access. This review evaluates the translation of management interventions into distinct environmental and health hazards by systematically reviewing evidence on coconut rhinoceros beetle biology, intervention efficacy, smallholder socioeconomic dynamics, and insecticide risk literature through a standardized four-tier risk framework. Smallholders commonly rely on chemical control options such as organophosphates and pyrethroids. These options carry documented risks: non-target toxicity, soil and water contamination, and occupational exposure. In the absence of beetle-specific metrics, elevated occupational exposure risks are inferred from prevailing normative practices in smallholder agriculture concerning the omission of protective equipment. Biological and cultural alternatives include O. rhinoceros nudivirus, Metarhizium anisopliae, Bacillus thuringiensis, botanical larvicides, and pheromone-based trapping. These present a substantially lower environmental risk profile: laboratory bioassays report 90 to 100 percent larval mortality for Metarhizium isolates from East Java, comparable to the up to 98 percent larval and 90 percent adult mortality reported for a granular carbamate alternative, indicating technical efficacy is not the limiting factor, with field-deployed monitoring documented in Jepara and Bengkulu. Uptake of these lower-risk options is nonetheless constrained less by technical efficacy than by production economics, extension access, and the fragmented governance of smallholder replanting and pest-management programs. The evidence suggests that attenuating this risk burden is predominantly constrained by the disparity between existing lower-risk technological interventions and their operational uptake, among other compounding determinants. Risk-management strategies must therefore be designed around smallholder economic and institutional realities rather than efficacy data alone. Authors: Doheim R.M.; Farag A.A.
Author full names: Doheim, Rahma M. (55954973500); Farag, Alshimaa Aboelmakarem (57203922690)
Title: Factors affecting public transport adoption in Riyadh- case study
Abstract: Riyadh's greenhouse gas emissions and urban climate risks are likely heightened by accelerated urbanization and profound dependence on private cars. Despite the government's investment in public transportation, societal resistance to giving up private cars and using public transit persists due to cultural and traditional factors. Within the Gulf context, this study is the first to investigate the unique socio-cultural and urban context of Riyadh to understand university students' mobility behavior, identify four factors that significantly are associated with their travel choices, and quantitatively rank the relative influence of these factors. Surveys (n = 710) were used to assess four key factors, analyzed via multiple regression, chi-square, and t-tests. Results indicate that, in descending order of influence, psychological factors (explaining 23% of the variance) have the most significant association with students' willingness to switch to public transport in Riyadh, followed by trip characteristics (13%), urban factors (12%), and socioeconomic and demographic factors (12%). The result suggests that, alongside infrastructure improvements, coordinated strategies are required to change social norms, enhance environmental awareness, and create culturally responsive incentives. The findings support the implementation of place-based policies for sustainable mobility. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Randall A.R.
Title: Intervening Impersistence on the St. Johns River, Florida
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Across 9000 years, shells were a common medium of terraforming along the St. Johns River in northeast Florida. In this regard, shell mounds nicely match definitions of persistent place. However, close attention paid to shells and their itineraries highlights how impersistent these places were. Shell, as a construction medium and an index of history, provided opportunities for re-establishing place in the context of change, even when used by settler colonists to build out Florida’s road networks in the twentieth century. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Arianpour M.; Mozaheb M.A.
Title: Assessment of Pragmatic Disorders in Persian­Speaking Adults with Acquired Brain Injury; [ارزیابی بیماران آسیب دیده مغزی بزرگ سال فارسی زبان از منظر اختلالات کاربرد شناختی]
Abstract: This study investigates pragmatic communication abilities in Persian-speaking adults with acquired brain injury (ABI), focusing on patients with right-hemisphere damage (RHD) and left-hemisphere damage (LHD). Pragmatic competence, crucial for interpreting metaphors and speech acts, depends on distributed neural networks, with increasing evidence highlighting the right hemisphere's critical role in processing non­literal meaning, inferencing, and social cues. Despite extensive research in non-Persian populations, evidence on pragmatic impairments in Persian speakers with focal brain injuries is limited. This study evaluates and compares pragmatic performance across RHD and LHD groups using the Montreal Protocol for the Evaluation of Communication (MEC). Results indicated that 60% of RHD patients exhibited pragmatic deficits compared to 30% of LHD patients, though group differences were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). Lesions in temporal lobe regions and adjacent areas were consistently associated with pragmatic impairments, suggesting a significant role for these regions in higher-level communication. These findings support a stronger role for the right hemisphere in non-literal meaning and contextual cue interpretation within the Persian language context. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University All rights reserved.

Authors: Ji L.; Chang Y.
Title: What prevents community gardens from long-term survival? A five-year case study in Suzhou, China
Abstract: Community gardens are increasingly recognised as important instruments of urban micro-regeneration, yet their long-term sustainability remains fragile under project-based governance. This study traces the five-year evolution (2021–2025) of maintenance barriers in a government-initiated community garden in Suzhou, China. Using a longitudinal mixed-methods design, this paper tracks the community garden across three stages (inception, growth and struggle) through three phases of Likert-scale surveys and semi-structured interviews, supplemented by Participatory Action Research (PAR). The findings reveal a marked divergence in barrier trajectories. Individual technical constraints declined as residents accumulated horticultural knowledge, with the mean score for ‘lack of gardening knowledge and skills’ falling from 4.00 in 2021 to 1.83 in 2025. By contrast, team and institutional barriers intensified: ‘lack of an internal leader’ rose from 4.07 to 4.83, ‘unclear garden tasks’ from 3.20 to 4.33, and ‘Inadequate support from local authorities’ from 3.53 to 4.83, reaching the ceiling value of 5.0 for several individual respondents in 2025. The withdrawal of external facilitators exposed a governance vacuum that residents themselves labelled the ‘Three-Ignores’ ( san-bu-guan ) condition, in which fragmented responsibilities among Residents’ Committees, Property Management Companies and Homeowners’ Committees, together with unfulfilled budgetary commitments, produced systemic deterioration. At the same time, a significant demographic shift towards a volunteer team composed exclusively of elderly residents weakened the garden’s collective resilience. Sustaining community gardens requires a shift in urban management from temporary ‘project logic’ to more durable ‘governance logic’, including formal exit strategies, clearer responsibility arrangements and the incorporation of community assets into established administrative and budgetary systems. Authors: Fitria D.; Nugraheni D.R.; Herdiansyah H.; Qamruzzaman M.
Title: Consumer awareness, participation, and accessibility in sustainable electronic waste management
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: The rapid increase in electronic waste has created increasingly complex environmental and health challenges, especially in developing countries like Indonesia. The study objectives were to examine how household awareness and accessibility of electronic-waste management facilities are associated with consumer participation, controlling for socioeconomic factors, demographics, and the region's spatial characteristics. METHODS: This study uses a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design to examine household consumers living near electronic waste management facilities in Indonesia. To analyze the data, Spearman's rank correlation was employed to evaluate variable relationships, ordinary least squares regression to estimate the associations of awareness and accessibility with participation levels, Kruskal-Wallis test to examine group differences, and Geographic Information System-based spatial analysis to describe the spatial patterns of facility distance, accessibility, and electronic waste management participation. FINDINGS: Consumer awareness of the consequences of electronic waste showed a significant positive correlation with the intention to manage electronic waste, with a correlation coefficient of 0.340, but showed no significant correlation with actual behavior, with a correlation coefficient of only 0.067. Accessibility showed a significant positive correlation with both intention and actual behavior, with correlation coefficients of 0.197 and 0.416, respectively. Accessibility had the largest reported regression coefficient for actual behavior ( β = 0.449 ), followed by awareness of consequences ( β = 0.182 ). The Kruskal-Wallis test confirmed significant differences in intention and actual behavior across accessibility levels, with chi-square values of 11.67 and 35.91, respectively. Spatial analysis using the nearest neighbor method produced a nearest neighbor ratio of 0.60 with a z score of -10.01. Spatial analysis revealed that highly aware and active residents are significantly clustered rather than randomly dispersed, with the vast majority residing within a functional catchment area defined by 10 to 30 kilometer distances or 10 to 30 minute travel times from e-waste facilities. CONCLUSION: The findings underscore the need for electronic waste management policies that prioritise facility accessibility and spatially based approaches to strengthen community participation within a circular economy framework. Title: Analytic hierarchy process-based criterion weighting for water resources management projects
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Prioritizing water resources projects requires decision-makers to balance hydrological performance, engineering feasibility, environmental and social sustainability, and economic value under limited budgets and implementation resources. Conventional evaluation frameworks are frequently bound to specific project typologies or geographical contexts, thereby constraining their direct applicability across heterogeneous project portfolios. The study objectives were to develop an analytic hierarchy process-based multi-criteria decision-making framework for deriving criterion weights for water resources management project assessment, using Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as the empirical context. METHODS: The framework was developed by synthesizing water resources management principles, practical project-assessment considerations, and relevant multi-criteria decision-making literature. The evaluation model comprised four principal dimensions and 18 operational sub-criteria. The Analytical hierarchy process framework was employed to analyze expert judgments elicited from six senior water resources and irrigation specialists, each possessing a minimum of 20 years of professional experience. Individual judgments were subsequently evaluated for consistency and aggregated using the geometric mean. Local weights were calculated using the eigenvector method and combined with the corresponding main-dimension weights to obtain global priorities. FINDINGS: Engineering and Implementation Feasibility received the highest main-dimension weight (32.58 percent), followed by Economic performance (25.84 percent), Environmental and Social Sustainability (21.87 percent), and Water Resource and Hydrological Performance (19.71 percent). At the global level, cost effectiveness ranked first (13.99 percent), followed by Structural Scale (11.58 percent), Foundation Suitability (10.60 percent), and Storage and Hydrological Adequacy (8.93 percent). These four sub-criteria accounted for 45.10 percent of the total weight. Accounting for 81.88 percent of the total weight and encompassing elements across all four dimensions, the top 11 sub-criteria demonstrate that comprehensive assessment necessitates an integrated approach spanning technical, economic, hydrological, environmental, and social dimensions. CONCLUSION: By establishing a transparent architecture for criterion organization and context-specific priority derivation, the framework facilitates water resources project evaluation. Integrated with empirical performance data and explicit scoring protocols, it underpins the formulation of robust project screening, portfolio comparative analysis, and budgetary prioritization procedures. The reported weights represent the judgments of the study panel and should be recalibrated for other locations, project types, and stakeholder groups. Subsequent applications of this framework should formulate a structured operational scoring rubric while comprehensively evaluating parameter sensitivity, model robustness, and project-ranking stability. Author full names: Ozbay, Yagmur (57217681757); Stamkou, Eftychia (57217604327); Oosterwijk, Suzanne (34768833700)
Title: Art as a scaffold for social cognition
Abstract: The idea that art connects us to others is culturally compelling, yet empirical evidence linking art engagement to social cognition remains mixed across paradigms, methods, and timescales. We develop the thesis that art functions as a scaffold for social cognition, rather than a direct intervention on social-cognitive abilities. From this perspective, art structures the conditions under which social cognition unfolds by shaping whether individuals engage with socially meaningful content, how deeply they become involved, and whether they return to similar experiences over time. The scaffold model identifies three interrelated components: a motivational gate, qualities of engagement, and reinforcement and habit formation. By integrating previously disconnected literature, the scaffold model reframes art's social-cognitive impact as a recursive process that creates repeated opportunities for social-cognitive practice across contexts, media, and timescales. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Nelson P.P.
Title: Adaptive stewardship of understanding: Artificial intelligence and intergenerational governance in mining
Abstract: Mining stewardship has traditionally focused on the governance of physical assets, operational performance, environmental impacts, and organizational decision-making. While these responsibilities remain essential, they assume that the understanding supporting stewardship is comparatively stable. In reality, understanding continually evolves as new observations emerge, assumptions are revised, stakeholders change, institutions adapt, and stewardship extends across increasingly long temporal horizons. Artificial intelligence further transforms this process by participating in how observations are integrated, interpretations are developed, assumptions are reinforced or challenged, and institutional knowledge is preserved and communicated. Stewardship must therefore address not only what decisions are made, but also how understanding itself is created, maintained, questioned, and renewed. This paper proposes adaptive stewardship as a framework for governing an evolving ecology of understanding throughout the mine life cycle and beyond closure. The framework distinguishes understanding from observation, examines the lifecycle of assumptions, introduces the concepts of time windows of understanding and observation boundaries, and argues that governance must preserve the conditions under which understanding can continue to improve across generations. Within this ecology, artificial intelligence is treated not as an autonomous decision-maker but as an evolving participant whose value depends upon transparent governance that maintains visibility of assumptions, uncertainty, evidence, and human judgment. The paper concludes that the long-term objective of stewardship is not to preserve today's knowledge, but to preserve society's continuing capacity to develop better understanding as mining systems, environmental conditions, technologies, institutions, and societal expectations evolve. Title: The role of mnemonic discrimination in symptom severity and treatment response of obsessive-compulsive disorder
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: Mnemonic discrimination, the ability to differentiate novel stimuli from highly similar past ones, has been evidenced as a compelling factor for fear overgeneralization in anxiety disorders. However, very limited research has examined mnemonic discrimination in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The current study provided an initial examination of the relationship between mnemonic discrimination to OCD symptoms and treatment response. Patients (N = 48) in an intensive partial hospital/residential treatment program for OCD completed the Mnemonic Similarity Task at admission and discharge, along with self-report measures of OCD severity, trait worry, intolerance of uncertainty, and threat estimation. Results showed no significant relationship between mnemonic discrimination and baseline OCD symptom severity. Over the course of treatment, mnemonic discrimination did not change significantly, nor was it associated with OCD symptom reduction. Notably, however, there was a significant interaction between poor mnemonic discrimination and high trait worry to predict more severe OCD symptoms at baseline. Findings suggested that while mnemonic discrimination alone might not be a risk factor for OCD severity or impact treatment response, it could be a potential transdiagnostic risk factor that exacerbates internalizing symptoms when co-present with other cognitive vulnerabilities. Future studies should continue investigating the mechanistic link behind these relationships in larger, more representative samples. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Cherif R.; Lawton P.
Title: Spatial analysis of the 15-minute city concept in three historically distinct urban areas across metropolitan greater Cairo
Abstract: This paper explores how the 15-min city concept plays out in Greater Cairo by examining three neighbourhoods: Agouza, Madinaty, and Badya. To do so, it draws on a systematic approach that includes selecting case studies, identifying key service categories, extracting POI and street-network data, mapping service areas in ArcGIS, and presenting the results through service area analysis and thematic mapping. To complement this, accessibility was assessed through four measures: cumulative opportunities, land-use entropy, functional redundancy, and space syntax (integration) metrics. The findings show that access in Cairo depends not just on distance but also on the diversity of available services, the degree of proximity between services, and the way streets connect different areas. Cycling makes a clear difference in widening reach and reducing accessibility inequalities and fragmentation. The findings suggest that, in addition to clinics and schools, social anchors such as souqs, ahwa, and cultural places emerge as vital parts of daily urban life. The paper argues that in Cairo, the 15-min city concept, whether built from scratch or adapted to existing urban fabrics, should not be treated as a universal recipe but as a flexible framework. The concept is part of a longer lineage of planning ideals, adopted in the planning of several areas of Cairo, from the Garden City movement to New Urbanism. It should build on the city’s own urban vocabularies, shaped through layered urban planning and lived experiences, which continue to define how urban spaces and services are used and valued within the 15-min radius or beyond. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Setyowati M.S.; Hanum R.K.
Title: The effect of agricultural taxes and local agricultural policies on enhancing food security and environmental sustainability
Source title: Global Journal of Environmental Science and Management
Abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Indonesia is currently working towards sustainability in line with Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger). Anticipated demographic growth to 10.8 billion by the year 2050 is expected to place unprecedented strain on global food security and production systems. The study objectives were to examine the biophysical factors, production inputs, economic conditions, socio-technological factors, agricultural business management, and agricultural tax policies regional agricultural policies and, ultimately, agricultural productivity. METHODS: This quantitative study employed structured questionnaires administered to a sample of 200 farmers in Surabaya. The instrument used a one-to-five Likert scale covering biophysical factors, economic factors, tax policy, tax morale, and agricultural productivity. Data was analyzed using partial least squares-structural equation modeling version 3. The analytical procedure comprised three distinct phases: first, evaluating the outer model for convergent and discriminant validity; second, conducting reliability assessments; and third, testing the inner model via bootstrapping to determine the coefficient of determination, the effect size, and hypothesis significance. Hypothesis significance was determined using t-statistic values of at least 1.96 and p-values of no more than 0.05. FINDINGS: Four hypotheses were rejected: economic factor on regional agricultural policy (p-value 0.557), agricultural taxation policy on tax morale (p-value 0.072), tax awareness on agricultural productivity (p-value 0.058), and tax morale on agricultural productivity (p-value 0.208). The findings reveal that regional agricultural policies are substantially driven by three key dimensions: biophysical factors (beta coefficient of 0.251, probability value of 0.000), production inputs (beta coefficient of 0.253, probability value of 0.002), and agricultural business management (beta coefficient of 0.228, probability value of 0.007). Agricultural tax policy significantly affects tax awareness (beta coefficient of -0.229, probability value of 0.000), while tax administration efficiency also significantly affects tax awareness (beta coefficient of -0.345, probability value of 0.000) and tax morale (beta coefficient of -0.634, probability value of 0.000), since clarity on procedures, benefits, and regulations fosters public responsibility and awareness of taxpayer obligations and rights. CONCLUSION: Elevating agricultural output demands comprehensive frameworks characterized by active farmer participation, supportive regulatory policies, targeted outreach regarding tax frameworks, and enhanced coordination between industry stakeholders and governmental bodies. Regional agricultural policies and tax awareness significantly influence agricultural productivity. These findings offer practical insights for policymakers aiming to strengthen agricultural governance and tax compliance frameworks in support of sustainable rural development. Title: Pastoral Nomads at a Crossroads: Investigating the Resilience of the Bakarwal Community to Climate and Socio-Ecological Challenges
Abstract: Environmental shifts influence the livelihoods of Bakarwal pastoral nomads as they traverse the varied terrains of the Western Himalayas. Climate fluctuations and socio-ecological stressors markedly affect their resilience. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study examines how environmental factors and livelihood pressures interact among these nomads. By integrating scientific analysis of long-term climate patterns with qualitative data from 239 Bakarwal families, the research investigates their adaptive strategies and internal capacity. Results show that a 1 °C rise in winter and early summer temperatures, coupled with decreased rainfall in winter and transit habitats, affects mobility and resource availability, including fodder and water. The study highlights the importance of traditional knowledge, flexible transhumance practices, and eco-friendly methods in enhancing resilience. However, socio-ecological challenges, including limited institutional support and marginalization, threaten the sustainability of their pastoral lifestyle. The research situates livelihood resilience within the dynamic interactions of environmental and cultural systems. By simultaneously evaluating climate and socio-ecological factors, it affirms the enduring value of traditional wisdom and the resilience of pastoral systems in preserving ecological integrity and fostering sustainable development. It underscores the need for inclusive, community-driven policies and adaptive strategies to strengthen resilience and sustain pastoral livelihoods. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Author full names: Alhakari, Redhwan Ayedh (60851095500); Wahab, Izudinshah Abd (57202044700); Alaradah, Mohammed Sultan (60851001400); Belitski, Maksim (55934938700); Al-Awag, Eman Ali (57722411600)
Title: Sustainable urban planning in conflict-affected cities: Governance, displacement, and hierarchical sustainability in Marib, Yemen
Abstract: Sustainable urban planning frameworks presuppose institutional stability and regulated development, yet their applicability to conflict-affected cities remains theoretically underexamined. This qualitative case study examines how sustainability is interpreted and prioritised in Marib city, Yemen, an urban centre experiencing rapid growth amid armed conflict and mass internal displacement. Drawing on a framing analysis of global sustainability frameworks, semi-structured interviews with 16 city stakeholders, and structured observations in seven neighbourhoods, the study identifies a structural mismatch between global sustainability paradigms and local planning practice. Whereas international models assume balanced domain integration, the evidence from Marib reveals a context-conditioned hierarchy in which governance capacity and essential service provision operate as preconditions structuring environmental management, economic activity, and technological uptake. Locally, environmental sustainability is reduced to basic service continuity; social sustainability is dominated by displacement-driven absorptive pressures; economic sustainability narrows to livelihood survival; and technological adoption is fragmented and institutionally constrained. The paper advances a context-conditioned, hierarchical model of urban sustainability that challenges the implicit universality of parallel-domain planning approaches and calls for planning paradigms that recognise institutional capacity as foundational in fragile urban contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Revisiting the Agropastoral Landscape of Çatalhöyük East Through Agent-Based Modeling (9100–8100 BP)
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: Understanding the complex interplay between external climatic forcing and internal socioecological dynamics remains a major challenge in the study of early sedentary societies. While unilinear frameworks frequently link systemic shifts to external climate triggers, these perspectives tend to neglect the internal dynamics and non-linear feedback loops of complex socioecological systems (SES). This research sheds new light on established narratives by investigating the 1000-year coevolution of agropastoral practices and landscape dynamics at Çatalhöyük East (ca. 9100–8100 BP). We employ a high-resolution agent-based model (ABM), integrating the MedLanD (MML) platform with the Macrophysical Climate Model (MCM) via an original sequential simulation design. This methodological novelty allows us to quantify how cumulative land-use legacies and their environmental costs shaped the community’s later options. Our results indicate that while the agricultural strategy effectively sustained high population density, it simultaneously pushed the system toward a rigidity trap. The model demonstrates how short-term adaptive successes generate structural limits in landscape capacity. These findings suggest that the settlement’s eventual reorganization was not a simple response to external climatic forcing but rather an emergent outcome of internal socioecological stress. By reframing the trajectory of Çatalhöyük through a complex systems lens, this study emphasizes that resilience must be understood as a dynamic process shaped by the long-term interaction of human agency and landscape evolution. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Forte M.; Ortoleva J.K.
Title: Performing Power and Transitional Space: the Use of Acoustics and Multimodal AI in Etruscan Painted Tombs
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: This article presents a new multimodal AI and acoustic methodology using two 5th c. BCE Etruscan painted tombs at Tarquinia, Italy, the Tomba del Gallo and the Tomba dei Demoni Azzurri as case studies. Via the integration of AI computer vision–based visual saliency analysis, architectural affordance modelling, acoustic data, and agent-based perceptual trajectories, the study suggests that each tomb affords distinct experiential strategies. The Tomba del Gallo privileges visual sequencing, threshold control, and gaze discipline, whereas the Tomba dei Demoni Azzurri potentially induces perceptual disorientation and immerses the visitor into a sensory and spatial environment that has the possibility of inducing trance-like experiences. A central contribution of the study is the reinterpretation of subterranean funerary spaces as possible transitional spaces, where architectural and symbolic devices mediate between life and death, order and chaos, memory and transformation, and sensory manipulation operate as core ritual technologies. Ultimately, we argue that when combined with scientifically documented acoustic data, AI enables archaeology to move beyond representational interpretation toward the experimental modelling of ritualised experiences in the ancient Mediterranean. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Metacognitive monitoring in Kenyan, Chinese, and U.S. children
Abstract: Theories of cognitive development propose that cultural values shape metacognitive skills. However, cross-cultural research on metacognition remains limited and often relies on verbal assessments that may lack validity across cultural contexts. The present study examined metacognitive monitoring in Kenyan, Chinese, and U.S. children (N = 95; 6–10-year-olds; 46% female) using a non-verbal problem-solving task in which children assembled objects according to a model. Across all three cultural contexts, children exhibited various monitoring behaviors (e.g., checking the model), and the frequency of these behaviors increased with age. Cross-cultural differences emerged in the specific monitoring strategies children used: Chinese children engaged in more thorough monitoring than Kenyan and U.S. children. These findings highlight both culturally-recurrent and culturally-variable patterns in children’s metacognitive monitoring. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Mountacer M.; Youssef N.
Title: Training and Institutional Guidelines in Teachers’ Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence: Bibliometric Analysis, Empirical Evidence, and Implications for Quality Education and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly shaping educational practice, yet teachers’ professional adoption remains uneven. This study examines the roles of AI-related training and institutional guidelines in teachers’ use of GenAI and situates the findings within the broader context of quality education and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A cross-sectional survey of 208 Moroccan teachers was analyzed using descriptive statistics, bivariate tests, and binary logistic regression, complemented by a concise bibliometric overview of GenAI research trends. AI-related training was significantly associated with professional GenAI use, whereas institutional guidelines were not significant after adjustment. Authors: Mansfield J.; Rennie L.J.
Title: The role of creativity and imagination in scientific endeavour
Abstract: Creativity and imagination (C&I) are integral, but often overlooked, aspects of scientific endeavour. If scientists aim to innovate and develop new knowledge about the world around us, C&I are essential, yet how C&I are used in science is poorly understood. This lack of clarity about how C&I are defined, and how they are used, results in uninformed views about the nature of scientific endeavour. Here, we propose a conceptual Framework for an informed view of C&I to support the understanding of science through both research and teaching. We define our understanding of scientific endeavour, then define creativity in science through the generation of new thoughts, processes and products in intentional and unintentional ways which are effective in the context in which the creativity was applied. Imagination complements creativity and is defined as the ability to form mental images in the absence of the senses. During scientific endeavour, C&I work in conjunction with critical thinking and manifest as dispositions and actions when questioning, planning, doing and reflecting in science. Nineteen aspects of scientific endeavour are identified and the roles of C&I for each aspect are illustrated. The result is a characterisation of the role of C&I in scientific endeavour that makes creative and imaginative thoughts and actions explicit. This conceptualisation of an informed view provides a Framework for science educators who are tasked with researching, teaching and assessing, students’ understanding about the role of C&I in scientific endeavour. We close with implications for science education and research. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Beyond the hotspots: Identifying public opinion blind spots and agenda-setting dynamics in crisis information generation
Abstract: During sudden crises, a structural mismatch between social media attention and governance value often marginalizes key crisis issues, creating public opinion blind spots that undermine effective emergency management. Using the 2021 Henan rainstorm as a case study (N = 40,160), this study proposes an integrated framework to identify public opinion blind spots and examine their agenda-setting dynamics. Methodologically, we combine grounded theory with Large Language Model (LLM) analysis for theme classification (92.7% accuracy), apply refined Importance-Performance Analysis (IPA) to identify blind spots, and use Vector Autoregression (VAR) models, Granger causality tests, and impulse response functions (IRFs) to examine agenda-setting dynamics. Bootstrap estimation further assesses the association between blind spots and agenda-setting effects. Results show that blind spots vary dynamically across the 4R phases, with Prevention Education, Disaster Causation, and Review and Improvement recurring most frequently. Bidirectional agenda-setting effects can emerge at a 1-hour resolution, and stronger agenda guidance from authoritative users is associated with blind-spot mitigation. Ultimately, these findings offer practical implications for optimizing crisis information supply and strengthening social resilience. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Dirksmeier P.; Göb A.
Title: Why conversations constitute neighbourhood cohesion: A mixed-methods approach to substantiating cause and effect
Abstract: Communicating is a meaningful practice for building neighbourhood cohesion by fostering a sense of connection, mutual support and belonging among residents of a geographically defined neighbourhood. In our paper, we highlight the role of regular contact and conversations with neighbours for generating neighbourhood cohesion. Following a mixed-methods approach, we combine qualitative instruments from two case studies focusing on neighbourhoods in Hanover with quantitative data from a panel survey conducted in Hanover and Magdeburg, Germany. The residents’ statements clearly show that talking to each other influences their socio-spatial orientation towards the neighbourhood as a point of reference, thus promoting attitudes and practices to strengthen neighbourhood cohesion. Based on these results, the causal model confirms the effect of conversations on neighbourhood cohesion, which is mediated by the factor of trust. Combining the two types of data helps to understand and explain why neighbourhoods are relevant for peaceful coexistence: they enable low-threshold interaction and thus the experience of belonging and integration. It remains open whether and to what extent neighbourhood cohesion can be scaled up, which requires comparisons with other cities and city types as well as different neighbourhoods to identify regional and international differences. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Safi H.
Title: Conflict minerals, institutional failure, and the limits of transparency: Resource governance in post-2001 Afghanistan
Abstract: Why did the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI) fail to generate accountability in Afghanistan, which was declared EITI-compliant in 2012 and suspended in 2019? This article treats Afghanistan's post-2001 extractive sector as an extreme case of resource governance under a contested political settlement and examines it through an embedded single-case design. Drawing on interviews with senior officials of the Ministry of Mines and Petroleum, the national EITI secretariat, and civil society, together with interviews with miners, community members, and academics, focus groups, and documentary sources, it traces how neopatrimonial governance and elite capture undermined transparency. Three mechanisms emerge: the colonization of mining institutions by patronage networks; the exclusion of mining communities from participation and benefit-sharing, which sustains customary and insurgent revenue channels; and the invisibility of artisanal, armed-group-controlled extraction to payment-reconciliation mechanisms. The article's main contribution is a sequenced governance framework, derived abductively from the conditional-transparency literature and the case evidence, which holds that in deeply captured, conflict-affected sectors, security provision, elite incentive restructuring, and community empowerment are preconditions for, rather than consequences of, effective transparency. The article specifies the framework's scope conditions and the evidence that would count against it. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Orozco Aceves R.
Title: The dialectic of the carrot and the stick in the expansion of the extractive frontier in Oaxaca, Mexico
Abstract: The expansion of large-scale mining in Mexico since the 1990s has been accompanied by intensifying socio-environmental conflicts, particularly in rural and Indigenous territories. While existing literature has shown that extractive governance frequently combines coercive practices with strategies aimed at securing local legitimacy, this article argues that these mechanisms are mutually constitutive rather than simply simultaneous or complementary. It develops the concept of the dialectic of the carrot and the stick to explain how corporate social responsibility (CSR) and coercion recursively reshape the conditions under which one another operate over the life of an extractive project. The article examines the San José silver and gold mine in Oaxaca, Mexico, operated by Fortuna Silver Mines (FSM). Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted between 2023 and 2024, including interviews, field observations, corporate publications, media reports, and civil society sources, it traces extractive governance over more than a decade of conflict. It shows that community programmes and relationships with local institutions produced differentiated and conditional forms of legitimacy, while repression, intimidation, and violence increased the costs of dissent and weakened resistance networks. Coercion thus transformed the terrain on which legitimacy was subsequently cultivated, while persistent limits to legitimacy generated renewed pressures to contain opposition. The dialectic therefore describes a recursive process through which coercion and consent reshape one another, enabling extraction to persist despite sustained opposition. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Khatibu S.; Kahimba J.
Title: Breaking Down Barriers to Conservation Conflict Resolution in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review
Abstract: The global commitment to conserve 30% of land and oceans by 2030 has renewed debate about the social consequences of protected-area expansion, particularly for resource-dependent communities in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This systematic review synthesises 26 studies published between 2010 and 2024, identified through Google Scholar, JSTOR, and Dimensions using a PRISMA-informed screening process. It examines the drivers of persistent conservation conflict, the performance of governance and conflict-management approaches, and the institutional conditions associated with more equitable outcomes. Across the reviewed studies, recurrent drivers included insecure land tenure, limited participation in decision-making, livelihood restrictions, human-wildlife conflict, and weak or inaccessible compensation arrangements. Community-based and participatory approaches were associated with more favourable outcomes where communities had recognised rights, meaningful decision-making authority, transparent institutions, and access to conservation benefits; however, elite capture and weak devolution often limited these gains. Enforcement-heavy and militarised approaches were commonly associated with distrust and resistance in the cases reviewed. The review highlights the importance of rights-based participation, equitable benefit sharing, tenure security, and context-sensitive governance in reducing conservation-related conflict. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Gavin C.; Temeljotov Salaj A.
Title: Navigating CSRD compliance: Challenges in sustainability reporting for the real estate sector
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the challenges faced by the Norwegian real estate sector in complying with the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), addressing a critical gap in understanding how these regulations impact sustainability reporting practices. The research seeks new insights into the barriers to implementing CSRD-compliant reporting, contributing to a deeper understanding of the sector's readiness and areas requiring improvement. The study employs a mixed-methods approach, utilizing a scoping literature review to map existing knowledge and semi-structured interviews with industry stakeholders to supplement findings. Data were collected from peer-reviewed articles, master's theses, and interviews with key stakeholders, and analyzed using thematic coding and qualitative analysis. The results reveal that the main challenges include limited knowledge of sustainability matters, difficulties in conducting Double Materiality Assessments (DMA), high costs, poor data systems, and administrative burdens. These findings provide evidence that while some companies proactively prepare for CSRD compliance, many, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), struggle due to resource constraints and a reliance on manual processes. This highlights significant implications for improving digital solutions and stakeholder collaboration. This research offers a novel perspective on sustainability reporting in the Norwegian real estate sector, providing valuable insights into the sector's preparedness and key barriers. The study's findings contribute to advancing digital reporting practices and support for SMEs, highlighting areas for future research and potential policy development to ease the transition to CSRD compliance. Authors: Chen Z.; Emery C.R.
Title: Divergent relationships between moral disengagement and cyberbullying bystander response behaviors: Examining the amplifying roles of humor and anonymity
Abstract: While bystander response behaviors are pivotal for cyberbullying (CB) intervention, prior research has yielded inconsistent findings regarding their correlates, partly because it has often treated diverse bystander responses as a monolithic construct and failed to distinguish constructive defense from aggressive defense. Furthermore, few empirical studies have examined how digital affordances interact with individual factors in relation to diverse bystander responses within a Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) framework. To address these gaps, this study examined the main and interactive associations of individual moral disengagement (MD), perceived anonymity, and humor of CB with four distinct online bystander responses (constructive defense, aggressive defense, inaction, and reinforcement). A final analytic sample of 1201 Chinese secondary school students, selected via multi-stage random sampling, completed a survey assessing MD, CB contexts, and real online bystander responses. Multilevel analysis indicated that MD, perceived anonymity and humor were consistently and negatively associated with constructive defense but positively associated with inaction. Conversely, MD and anonymity were positively associated with aggressive defense, whereas humor showed no significant link. Regarding reinforcement behaviors, perceived anonymity and humor were positive predictors, whereas MD exerted a non-significant association. Moderation analyses revealed that anonymity strengthened MD's positive associations with inaction and reinforcement, whereas humor amplified MD's association solely with reinforcement. These findings underscore the necessity of distinguishing constructive from aggressive defense and integrating individual moral cognition with contextual cues for both exploring correlates of online bystander response and designing CB interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Can leisure travel help combat loneliness in later life?
Abstract: Loneliness is a growing public health concern, particularly among older adults. Tourism research on healthy aging has largely centered on positive well-being; limited attention has been given to whether travel can alleviate loneliness. Drawing on longitudinal data from China and the United States, this study conceptualizes leisure travel as a form of activation and examines its relationship with loneliness among older adults. The findings indicate that greater participation in leisure travel is associated with lower levels of loneliness among this group over time. Travel also offsets age-related declines in daily social participation and the accompanying increase in loneliness, highlighting travel's activating role in later life. Leisure travel further serves as a compensatory resource for older adults with relational deficits. This mechanism varies across cultural contexts. By moving beyond the focus on positive emotion, this study demonstrates tourism's therapeutic potential for reducing loneliness and promoting well-being in aging populations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Impact of heritage status on market prices of townhouses in Central Rio de Janeiro
Abstract: This study investigates the effects of differentiated heritage protection regimes on townhouse property values in central Rio de Janeiro, contributing original evidence to a largely unexplored field in Brazil. Based on a sample of 86 townhouses, it applies a traditional hedonic pricing model (OLS), a Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), and a Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression with Spatial Autoregressive Error (MGWRSAR), which account for spatial heterogeneity and residual autocorrelation. To overcome data limitations, the analysis employs a bootstrap procedure to improve the robustness of inference. Results indicate that only properties under the least restrictive protection (“monitored”) display statistically significant price premiums. However, rather than reflecting a simple inverse relationship between restrictions and market value, this finding points to the importance of regulatory legibility, enforcement consistency, and perceived investment risks. The discussion highlights how flexible and intelligible protection regimes may foster market confidence, while ambiguous or overly rigid frameworks can undermine the effectiveness of heritage policy. The study also underscores a structural barrier to evidence-based policymaking: the lack of public access to transaction-level data in Brazil. This constraint limits empirical evaluation and transparency, both in academic research and in public administration. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Beyond compliance: Community development committees and the transformation of resource governance in Tanzania
Abstract: Resource-rich countries worldwide often face persistent imbalances in the redistribution of resource wealth. Although mineral extraction generates substantial revenues, these funds are typically centrally managed and redistributed, leaving host communities, who bear the social and environmental burdens of extraction, impoverished and marginalized. In Tanzania, despite provisions allowing Local Government Authorities to levy a 0.3% service charge on mining revenues and receive Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) contributions intended to support local development, means of engaging host communities remain a challenge. Community Development Agreements (CDAs) have been identified as potential instruments to safeguard the interests of host communities. However, despite their widespread promotion, a critical gap remains in understanding how communities can effectively engage in, negotiate, and implement CDAs, particularly in contexts marked by power asymmetries. Communities are often poor, with limited knowledge of mining and the broader extractive industry, and with no access to decision-making power. This study addresses the gap by examining Community Development Committees (CDCs) as an inclusive, participatory institutional mechanism through which communities can effectively articulate their development priorities. Using semi‑structured interviews with 36 key informants across the mining value chain, including central government officials, mining representatives, and local communities, the study finds the CDC model as an effective approach for strengthening community voice, enhancing transparency, improving negotiations, and monitoring project implementations. Although grounded in Tanzania’s mining sector, the study offers insights relevant to other resource dependent economies seeking to foster more equitable social contracts. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Connectivity in Written Personal and Fictional Narratives: The Study of Iranian EFL Learners and Native Speakers of Persian and English
Abstract: The present study aimed to examine the use of different levels of syntactic architecture in written personal and fictional narratives in both Persian and English across three discourse communities, namely Persian native speakers, English native speakers, and Iranian EFL learners. To this end, the participants of the study were selected based on convenience sampling and were asked to write one of their happiest memories. Also, an English fable from Aseop's fables and a Persian story, chosen based on comparative literature and having the similar plot, were given to them to read and write whatever they remembered; there was no limit on the number of words and paragraphs. To analyze the data, the Berman and Nir-Sagiv's (2009) model was followed. The findings showed that in fictional narratives written by both Persian and English native speakers, isotaxis, asymmetric parataxis, complement (CMP), and parataxis levels were frequently employed; however, personal narratives in Persian were dominantly isotactic, paratactic, and asymmetric paratactic, CMP, while isotactic, hypotactic, and paratactic levels were frequent in English written personal narratives. Also, after receiving explicit instruction on different types of English sentences, the use of adverbial and relative clauses (hypotaxis level) increased in Iranian EFL learners' written narratives. It can be concluded that explicit teaching of syntactic levels enabled EFL learners to arrange their sentences correctly to express their intended meaning. Teachers can benefit from the results to gain a more comprehensive understanding of narrative connectivity and help EFL learners elaborate clause linkage in their written narrative tasks. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Title: Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy for flashforwards: Randomized multiple baseline single case experimental design in social anxiety disorder
Source title: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
Abstract: Background and objectives: Negative mental imagery in social anxiety is common and can involve memories of adverse events or catastrophic future anticipations (i.e., “flashforwards”). Laboratory research has shown that such imagery can be modulated by dual-tasking interventions, which is used in Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) therapy. Methods: Using a replicated sequential single-case experimental design, we examined whether EMDR therapy for flashforwards reduces social anxiety and avoidance of fear-related situations, relative to baseline, in eight individuals with social anxiety disorder. Participants were recruited from a specialized treatment center after unsuccessful CBT or because of treatment complexity (e.g., comorbidity) and were randomly assigned to varying baseline durations before EMDR therapy. Outcome variables were daily social anxiety and avoidance. Randomization tests were conducted for each case separately to test whether EMDR therapy compared to a baseline phase resulted in less daily 1) social anxiety and 2) social avoidance for individual participants and for the total sample. Results: The preregistered randomization tests did not show statistically significant between-phase differences in daily social anxiety, daily social avoidance, or weekly social anxiety severity. Exploratory, unplanned permutation distancing tests, conducted to examine the possible influence of serial dependency, indicated lower scores during the intervention phase across all three outcomes. At the individual level, these exploratory analyses indicated reductions in daily social anxiety for six participants, in daily social avoidance for three participants, and in weekly social anxiety severity for five participants. Aggregated effect-size estimates were medium for daily social anxiety, small for daily social avoidance, and small to medium for weekly social anxiety severity. Limitations: Limitations include modest serial dependency, absence of an active treatment control condition, absence of long-term follow-up measurements, and inclusion of one participant without a clearly identifiable flashforward, although treatment adhered to the prespecified Stage 1 treatment protocol. Conclusions: The preregistered analyses did not provide confirmatory evidence that EMDR therapy for flashforwards reduced social anxiety or avoidance. However, the descriptive findings, effect-size estimates, and exploratory analyses showed a pattern consistent with possible reductions in social anxiety, while findings for avoidance were weaker and less consistent. These results should be considered hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered controlled studies. Title: Indonesian Teachers’ Perceptions About the Potential of Technology-Enhanced Language Assessment (TELA)
Abstract: Technology-enhanced language assessment (TELA) has significantly improved language evaluation by integrating digital tools to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and accessibility. This study aims to investigate the role of TELA in language assessment, particularly its advantages, challenges, and implications for pre-service teachers and learners. A mixed-method design was employed, combining closed-ended and open-ended questionnaire responses to provide both quantitative and qualitative insights. The findings reveal key trends in TELA, including the use of artificial intelligence, automated scoring systems, and adaptive testing. While TELA facilitates personalized and immediate feedback, concerns regarding digital equity, validity, and ethical considerations remain significant. This study concludes that a balanced approach is necessary for the effective implementation of TELA to ensure pedagogical effectiveness and ethical soundness. Future research should explore strategies to mitigate the challenges associated with digital assessments in language learning. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. All rights reserved.

Authors: Lopez-Lora L.; Vazquez-Cano E.
Title: Message scrutiny and claim verification: Changes in preadolescent reasoning about disinformation across AI-supported instruction
Abstract: Digital information environments expose preadolescents to misleading content before verification routines are fully developed. This study examined pre–post patterns in disinformation evaluation across a two-session instructional sequence combining media-literacy orientation, guided news-analysis activities, researcher supervision, and interaction with Pimpoyo, a generative-AI chatbot using Socratic questioning and a ZPD-inspired rationale. The sample comprised 152 Spanish students aged 10–14 years. Longitudinal evidence came only from the pre–post group ( n = 80); a baseline-only reference group ( n = 72) contributed baseline information. The primary outcome comprised 24 measurement-equivalent indicators expressed on a 0–25 scale. Indicator-level changes were differentiated: the clearest increases clustered around cues available within the focal message, including sensationalism, alarmist format, writing quality, tone/style, and timeliness, whereas triangulation/lateral reading did not change reliably and externally oriented verification remained mixed. The overall composite increased from M = 11.90 to M = 15.90, t (79) = 6.18, p < .001, d_z = 0.69. These indicator-level patterns are exploratory and are not formal comparisons between psychometric reasoning domains. Self-perceived competence changed, whereas perceived task difficulty did not; these secondary findings do not demonstrate metacognitive recalibration. Because only one group was followed longitudinally and the sequence bundled several instructional components, observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI, Socratic prompting, or any single component. The findings identify a potentially important distinction between focal-message scrutiny and external verification for future controlled research. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Conflict expression: A decade of group conflict research
Abstract: The conflict expression framework was developed to generate new practical and theoretical insights into how conflict communication affects group processes and negotiated outcomes. The framework proposes that conflict expressions vary along two dimensions: directness and oppositional intensity. The framework suggested that the effects of different types of conflict on group processes and outcomes likely depend on how the conflict is expressed, that conflict within groups is likely perceived differently by different members of the same social unit, and that conflict affects negotiation processes dynamically through reciprocated statements and responses. We review research building on the framework – including empirical tests of the main propositions, methodological advances, and as a theoretical foundation for conflict communication research more broadly – and identify directions for the future. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Enhancing Real-World Physics Problem-Solving Skills through Mind Map-Based Scaffolding: The Role of Metacomponents among Pre-University Students
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: Physics problem-solving is essential in physics education, yet many pre-university students struggle to apply concepts to real-world contexts. This study examines the effectiveness of integrating mind map-based scaffolding with metacomponents to enhance real-world physics problem-solving skills (RWPPS). A quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test non-equivalent group design involved 253 students at Universiti Malaysia Sabah. The experimental group used mind maps to define problems, organize information, and plan strategies with guided scaffolding, while the control group received conventional lectures. Data from open-ended RWPPS assessments showed that the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group, with improvements across all metacomponent sub-skills, especially monitoring. Normalized gain results indicated higher learning gains in the experimental group, highlighting the approach’s effectiveness in fostering structured and reflective problem-solving. © 2027 Bumi Publikasi Nusantara.

Author full names: Lagercrantz, Hedvig (59390899600); Asante, Kofi Takyi (57203149831); Mithöfer, Dagmar (15837023600)
Title: Declining cocoa and intensifying artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM): examining changing labour structures and livelihoods in rural Ghana
Abstract: Ghana’s cocoa frontier increasingly overlaps with mechanised artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM), creating competition over land and labour. This article examines how declining cocoa production and intensifying ASGM reorganise a local labour regime and reshape rural livelihood pathways in Juaboso District, Western North Region. It draws on 40 semi-structured interviews with cocoa farmers, ASGM workers and institutional actors, alongside observations at four ASGM sites, conducted in 2024. The analysis combines the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework for the 21st Century (SLF-21) with a labour-regime lens. The findings show that cocoa decline and political arrangements governing access to land, machinery, finance and licences create uneven openings for mining. Landowners and operators can convert cocoa land and capture mining rents, while young, often migrant, workers enter hazardous and insecure work. At the same time, ASGM expansion reduces labour availability for cocoa production, increases labour costs for cocoa farmers and degrades land and water used by farming households. Mining income can meet urgent household needs and, in some cases, support farming, but these gains coexist with risks that are shifted onto workers, non-mining farmers and younger generations. These risks are unevenly distributed across generations, with younger people likely to bear a greater burden through depleted land and water resources, and the health and educational consequences of mining-centred livelihood pathways. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Positive emotion dispositions and human values in a Brazilian sample: Structural evaluation and exploratory network analysis
Abstract: Understanding how positive emotions relate to broader motivational systems across cultural contexts is essential for clarifying their underlying structure. In this study, we examined the organization of positive emotions and their motivational correlates in Brazil, contributing to ongoing debates about the structure and foundations of positive emotions across cultures. Analyzing responses to the Dispositional Positive Emotions Scales (DPES; Shiota et al., 2006 ) in a Brazilian sample ( N = 435), we found mixed fit and reliability across individual scales, but neither the full seven-factor solution nor a previously reported six-factor model adequately fit the data. Following stability-based item pruning, EGA yielded four exploratory communities based on 18 items that cut across the original categories: Social Recognition, Awe & Happiness, Compassionate Caregiving, and Self-Contentment & Growth. We examined how these emergent communities mapped onto values as indicators of motivational goals. Value associations differed across communities, particularly between Compassionate Caregiving and Social Recognition. Overall, the findings identify exploratory item communities showing differentiated associations with several human values in this sample. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yasar D.; Öktem Erkartal P.
Title: Between indeterminacy and intervention: A field-based typology and design framework for interstitial Urban voids
Abstract: Urban voids are increasingly discussed as opportunities for urban transformation, yet they are often treated as a homogeneous category despite their diverse spatial, perceptual, and social characteristics. This study adopts a field-based qualitative research design that combines walking-based observation, standardized field coding, photographic documentation, and matrix-based comparative analysis to examine interstitial urban voids as heterogeneous spatial conditions. Using this research design, 61 interstitial micro voids were documented across four dense urban corridors in Istanbul. Data were recorded through a standardized protocol integrating morphological features, visibility and accessibility, informal use traces, sensory conditions, and perceived safety. The coded variables were then comparatively analysed to construct a typology and to support context-sensitive transformation decisions. Based on the combined evaluation of these variables, six void types were identified: circulation leftover, back-of-house void, residual structural gap, visual relief void, unintentional social pocket, and infrastructure-related void. Findings indicate that transformation potential differs across types and cannot be interpreted through a single factor. Unintentional social pockets and selected visual relief voids were associated with observed social or perceptual value, supporting preservation or light-touch intervention as analytically derived options rather than intensive formalization. By contrast, back-of-house voids and infrastructure-related voids combined poorer maintenance, negative sensory conditions, weaker public integration, and lower observer-based perceived safety, indicating a stronger need for safety-oriented redress before public activation. Circulation leftovers and residual structural gaps occupied an intermediate position, where transformation potential depended on access, visibility, ownership, maintenance, and existing use conditions. © 2026 The Author(s).
