Authors: Kumari P.; Mohanty R.N.
Title: Urban transformation in heritage cities through the perceptions of experts- A case of Varanasi, India
Abstract: This study presents responses to questionnaires submitted to 30 experts from diverse professional backgrounds about one of the oldest settlements in India, i.e., Varanasi. Expert interviews provided diverse perspectives on the challenges of urban settings and their transformation. To decipher the subjective responses, this data was analysed using MAXQDA24, a data analysis tool that facilitates quick analysis, coding, and presentation of large qualitative datasets. The expert highlights that the visual representation of the city, including its religious, educational, and historical significance, is highly prominent. Additionally, the study suggests the establishment of a city-level heritage body to a) maintain heritage properties, b) plan different neighborhoods for different perceptual experiences to segregate the footfall, and c) involve the local community. Overall, this study offers a unique expert-driven perspective on the current conditions and the transforming fabric of Varanasi. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Contesting Interests Between Institutional Pluralism and People-Centred Development in Natural Resource Management: Lessons from Selous Niassa Wildlife Corridor in Tanzania
Abstract: The debate on institutional pluralism (IP) in relation to natural resources management and people-centred development has become significant in Tanzania and many other developing countries. Mostly, the debates are related to the challenges of balancing conservation goals with people-centred development pathways in natural resources management. The theory of Self-Governance explains how the central government manages resources in community-owned areas. Data were gathered from national- and local-level government, non-governmental, and private-sector institutions relevant to the study, particularly those predominantly involved in natural resources management. The study utilized key informant interviews (KIIs), focus group discussions (FGDs), and household surveys in villages within the Selous-Niassa wildlife corridor (SNWC). The KII and FGD data were analysed using content analysis, and descriptive statistics were computed for the household interview data using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS). The results indicate that the evolution of institutional pluralism progressed through distinct stages, both before and after independence. During the pre-independence period, indigenous knowledge and practices for managing natural resources were destroyed, giving the colonial government power, even though it did not ensure sustainable management. This remained the same until the 1990s, when decentralization and Community-Based Resource Management were established (1990s - present). Tanzania saw increased recognition of the role of institutional pluralism in natural resource management. However, the increased recognition did not align with the current management status of natural resources in the SNWC, where degradation is accelerating due to increased human development. This paper concludes that natural resource management under institutional pluralism is influenced by communities’ development ambitions. This paper calls for strategies that balance the goals of natural resource management and development and recommends natural recovery measures. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Author full names: Escalada, Cecilia Soledad (60815640200); Ithuralde, Raúl Esteban (14626340200); Urdampilleta, Constanza María (57222406300)
Title: Socio-ecological Landscape Contexts and Ecosystem Services in the Argentine Dry Chaco: From Agroexpansion to Inhabited Forests (2000–2020)
Abstract: Landscape transformation driven by agribusiness expansion in the Dry Chaco is among the most pressing socio-ecological challenges globally, yet biophysical, ecosystem-service (ES), and sociodemographic dynamics are typically analyzed separately, obscuring how territorial configurations shape landscape change. To address this gap, this study proposes the Socio-Ecological Landscape Context (SELC) framework — a spatially explicit approach that integrates biophysical metrics with sociodemographic variables to define territorial units and interpret how they mediate ES supply over time. We applied it to Santiago del Estero Province in the Argentine Dry Chaco, analyzing landscape transformation (patch count and edge density) and ES supply (a rapid multicriteria assessment assigning potential supply values to land-cover types) over two decades (2000–2020), using satellite imagery (MapBiomas Chaco Collection 4), deforestation records, and census data. Cluster analysis identified six SELCs: First Wave Agroexpansion, Second Wave Agroexpansion, Concentrated Population, Inhabited Dry Forest, Hilly Arid, and Alluvial Plain. Closed woody vegetation declined by 12.6% points (from 66.6% to 54.0%), while the number of forest patches rose by 44%, indicating progressive fragmentation. Two contrasting patterns emerge: dynamic SELCs (First and Second Wave Agroexpansion, Concentrated Population) show marked declines in key ES, whereas persistent SELCs maintain higher ES levels over time. A sparse rural population shows a modest but consistent positive association with ES supply. These findings suggest that similar land-cover compositions can yield divergent socio-ecological outcomes depending on landscape configuration and modes of inhabitation, supporting biocultural conservation approaches that recognize peasant and Indigenous communities as active contributors to landscape multifunctionality. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Talebi Z.; Bafralı G.
Title: The Relationship between Classroom Justice, EFL Female Students' Attitudes toward Empowerment, and Their Self-esteem
Abstract: This study investigated the relationships between self-esteem, empowerment attitudes, and perceptions of classroom justice among EFL (English as a Foreign Language) learners. Relative stratified sampling was used to choose the 329 participants that make up the research sample. The Cronbach’s alpha was used to assess the reliability of questionnaire. This study used path analysis within the framework of structural equations, using a descriptive-correlational methodology, to analyse data and test research hypotheses. Software such as AMOS22 and SPSS22 were used to analyse the collected data. The results showed a significant correlation between students' perceptions of classroom justice dimensions and their feelings of empowerment and self-worth. The implications extend beyond the confines of the classroom, pointing towards a holistic approach to education that considers both the interpersonal dynamics within the learning environment and the individual empowerment of students. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. Authors: Hu Y.; Wang W.; Meng Y.; Liu Z.; Tang Y.; Bai Q.
Title: Characterizing the spatial correlation network of cultivated land system resilience: Nonlinear relationships between interregional production factor flows and node centrality
Abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying uncertainty shocks and increasingly frequent cross-regional factor flows, the spatial governance of cultivated land system resilience (CLSR) has become an increasingly important issue. Existing studies have largely treated CLSR as a localized attribute confined to specific administrative units, while paying limited attention to the evolution of its spatial correlation network. To address this gap, the Vertical and Horizontal Scatter Degree Method, Social Network Analysis, and the XGBoost-GeoShapley model were employed to examine the spatiotemporal patterns of CLSR and interregional flows of labor, capital, and technology across Chinese cities, and to identify the nonlinear relationships between interregional production factor flows and node centrality in the CLSR spatial correlation network. The results show that CLSR in China increased steadily and exhibited a clear east-west gradient, with higher levels in the east and lower levels in the west. Interregional flows of labor, capital, and technology continued to intensify, while spatial agglomeration and differentiation coexisted. The CLSR spatial correlation network in China was characterized by overall connectivity but sparse linkages. Network density fluctuated only between 0.10 and 0.14, indicating that substantive intercity linkages in CLSR remained relatively weak. All node centrality measures displayed long-tailed distributions, and cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Suzhou, Chongqing, and Qingdao occupied advantageous positions in terms of connectivity, accessibility, and bridging functions. Further analysis reveals a significant nonlinear relationship between interregional production factor flows and node centrality in the CLSR spatial correlation network. Overall, low levels of interregional production factor flows were associated with positive contributions to node centrality, whereas high levels were associated with negative contributions, which gradually stabilized at the upper end of the flow distribution. Moreover, fiscal support, geographical location, and their interaction emerged as important factors explaining heterogeneity in node centrality. From the perspective of relational geography, this study extends the analytical framework of CLSR and provides a scientific basis for the cross-regional coordination of CLSR enhancement and the optimization of resource factor allocation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Digital Learning of Regional Languages through the Bahasa Nusantara Application Based on Persuasive Systems Design to Support Language Revitalization
Source title: ASEAN Journal of Educational Research and Technology
Abstract: Regional languages in Indonesia face continuing decline as intergenerational transmission weakens and daily communication increasingly shifts toward Indonesian. This study aimed to design, develop, and formatively evaluate the Bahasa Nusantara application to support regional language revitalization in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. Using design science research, user needs from students, parents or guardians, and institutional employees in Tetun Fehan, Bunaq, and Adang communities were translated through Persuasive Systems Design into interconnected learning components. Formative evaluation with experts, teachers, and children showed stronger credibility and social support, while usability and independent use required further improvement. Effective digital language revitalization should combine trusted learning resources, teacher mediation, child-friendly onboarding, and community participation. The study provides a practical design basis for community-based regional language learning. © 2027 Bumi Publikasi Nusantara.

Author full names: Konaté, Ahmed Amara (56430719200); Hébélamou, Joseph (59980437500); Oularé, Fassidy (57561774400); Doumbouya, Ibrahima Kalil (58764117800); Kaba, Fanta (17338497200); Bah, Idiatou (57882467200); DembÉLÉ, N’dji dit Jacques (60822035500); Palm, Linda Maud Naa-Dedei (54781672200)
Title: Integrated assessment of the environmental and social impacts of bauxite mining in the Boké Prefecture
Abstract: Since the 2011 mining reforms, Guinea has experienced a rapid increase in bauxite extraction, particularly in the Boké Prefecture. While this growth has significantly stimulated the nation's economy, the aggregated socio-environmental and territorial consequences of bauxite extraction at the local level remain insufficiently documented in peer-reviewed literature, especially through comprehensive, community-level empirical analyses that links spatial transformations to residents’ experiences of displacement. This study argues that existing compensation and governance frameworks do not match the territorial extent of bauxite mining impacts, resulting in ongoing livelihood insecurity even in cases of formal resettlement. The research employs a mixed-methods approach, integrating field surveys, direct observations, interviews, and focus group discussions with 83 participants from four impacted communities. It also incorporates a diachronic analysis of land use and land cover (LULC) derived from Landsat imagery spanning 1973 to 2024. The study follows Cernea’s Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction framework. Findings indicate a marked increase in mining areas (from 0 to 68 km²) and exposed soils near Sangarédi, accompanied by a substantial decline in vegetation cover (–28%). These spatial changes align with local perceptions of deteriorating air and water quality, farmland loss, and heightened livelihood insecurity, despite observable investments in social infrastructure. In Kanfarandé, the expansion of port infrastructure has precipitated significant territorial changes, even absent direct mining activities. Overall, the research shows that current compensation and governance mechanisms remain inadequate to address the cumulative and indirect impacts of bauxite exploitation, underscoring the need for integrated, participatory, and territorially informed governance frameworks. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhao H.; Shi R.
Title: Why disaster experience does not always improve Preparedness: The role of disaster learning and heterogeneous effects
Abstract: The frequency and severity of natural disasters and public emergencies have continued to increase worldwide. Household preparedness plays a vital role in disaster risk reduction, yet the effect of disaster-related experience on preparedness remains inconclusive. Using survey data from 5,862 residents in China, this study separately examines the associations of past disaster experience and disaster learning with household preparedness. Conventional regression models and a causal forest approach are used to estimate average associations and explore heterogeneous effects across individuals. The results show that disaster learning, rather than past disaster experience, is positively associated with preparedness behavior, highlighting the importance of capacity building. In addition, both past disaster experience and disaster learning exhibit heterogeneous effects across individuals. Feature importance analysis further indicates that social capital, emergency awareness, and community infrastructure are important influential factors associated with preparedness behavior. By introducing a causal forest approach to distinguish the differential effects of past disaster experience and disaster learning, this study provides a more nuanced understanding of household preparedness and offers useful insights for developing more targeted household disaster risk reduction strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Kodom M.; Akonnor A.; Delali P.; Bugyei A.G.
Author full names: Kodom, Michael (57207358019); Akonnor, Augustina (57210918513); Delali, Peace (61023111000); Bugyei, Abraham Gyimah (57205127121)
Title: Living the paradox: community perceptions, drivers, and responses to illegal small-scale mining (Galamsey) in Ghana
Abstract: This study examines why illegal small-scale gold mining (galamsey) persists and how affected communities experience and respond to it in Ghana's Western and Western North regions. The qualitative study draws on 88 semi-structured interviews with traditional leaders, adults and youth, including active miners, across 30 mining-affected communities in six districts. Thematic analysis shows that galamsey provides employment, income and local economic activity, and sometimes finances education, household assets and community facilities. These gains coexist with polluted water bodies, degraded farmland and forests, health risks, school dropout, weakened traditional authority and social tension. Persistence reflects more than poverty and unemployment. Peer influence, the social normalisation of mining, restricted access to productive land and perceived protection by political and business elites reduce the social and legal costs of participation. Communities are therefore neither passive victims nor uniform supporters. Some have introduced bylaws, age and spatial restrictions, taboo days, pit-covering rules and local taskforces, although fear, livelihood dependence and elite involvement constrain these responses. The study shows how livelihood pressures identified by the sustainable livelihoods framework interact with unequal control over land, finance and enforcement emphasised by political ecology. It contributes community-level evidence that explains why enforcement-led interventions produce temporary disruption without changing the conditions that sustain galamsey. The findings support accountable action against financiers and complicit officials, feasible formalisation for small operators, non-mining livelihood and education support, and legal backing for locally developed environmental rules. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yao H.; Chen Z.
Title: How autonomy-supportive environments and growth mindset foster creativity efficacy in middle school students? Evidence from a large-scale survey in China
Abstract: This study examines the associations between multi-source autonomy-supportive environments, growth mindset, and creative self-efficacy among Chinese middle school students, with particular attention to the mediating role of growth mindset and individual heterogeneity in these associations. Using large-scale survey data from 6146 middle school students in Suzhou, China, and drawing on Bandura's (1997) social cognitive theory and Self-Determination Theory, we employed structural equation modeling and quantile regression to investigate these relationships. The SEM results indicate that teacher, parental, and peer autonomy support are all positively associated with creative self-efficacy, with teacher and peer support showing stronger total associations than parental support. Growth mindset mediated all three associations, with the indirect effect proportion being highest for teacher autonomy support, followed by parental autonomy support and peer autonomy support. Quantile regression analyses revealed meaningful heterogeneity across the creative self-efficacy distribution: teacher and parental autonomy support showed stronger associations at lower quantiles, peer autonomy support peaked at moderate quantiles, and all associations weakened at higher quantiles. These findings contribute to the cross-cultural understanding of how multi-source autonomy-supportive environments relate to creative self-efficacy in a collectivist educational context, and offer practical implications for differentiated educational interventions targeting students at different levels of creative self-efficacy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Imran A.; Li J.
Title: X-MCB-Net: Explainable multimodal Cyberbullying Detection Network using Swin Transformer
Abstract: Cyberbullying on social media represents a persistent digital safety concern, often conveyed through the interplay of offensive text and images. Existing detection systems largely treat visual and textual modalities independently and offer limited interpretability, hindering deployment in accountable content-moderation workflows. This study presents X-MCB-Net, an explainable multimodal cyberbullying detection framework that integrates the Swin Transformer for visual feature extraction with XLM-RoBERTa and a bidirectional GRU for textual analysis. A dynamic intermodal attention mechanism fuses visual and linguistic representations to capture implicit and context-dependent cues for abuse. Authors: Lundkvist M.
Title: Opportunities for mathematical reasoning within teacher-student interactions in a Thinking Classroom context
Abstract: Developing students’ capacity to reason mathematically is a key aim of mathematics teaching. However, how such reasoning is supported remains complex. This study examines teacher-student interaction and students’ opportunities for mathematical reasoning in a Thinking Classroom context. While Thinking Classroom is designed to increase student engagement and mathematical thinking through substantial changes to classroom organisation, relatively little is known about how teacher-student interaction unfolds within this instructional context. The study draws on 34 video recordings from five upper secondary mathematics classrooms implementing the first three practices of the teaching approach Thinking Classroom, which concern task selection, random group formation, and work at vertical non-permanent surfaces. A thematic analysis of 124 teacher-student interactions identified four recurring patterns of interaction. Drawing on selected concepts from a complex dynamic systems perspective, these patterns are interpreted as relatively stable. The analysis further examines the students' opportunities for reasoning within these patterns. Opportunities for mathematical reasoning differed across the four patterns and often remained brief, even in interactions where reasoning was most visible. The findings suggest that, in the observed classrooms implementing the first three practices of Thinking Classroom, opportunities for sustained reasoning within teacher-student interaction were limited. The present study highlights the challenges involved in supporting mathematical reasoning and the importance of teachers’ interactional choices in creating and sustaining opportunities for reasoning. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Gullibility, loneliness, exploitation or just bad luck? Exploring older adults’ perceptions of fraud risks, protections and victimhood
Abstract: Exploring older adult victimisation of cybercrimes, perceptions of risk and protections using semi-structured interviews and a mixed interactional analytic approach, this paper assesses the implications of isolation, technical knowledge and trusted sources of protection advice. It explores perceptions of personal responsibility, fraud risk, fraud protections, the interconnected and dichotomous narratives of blame and empathy relating to victimhood, and how judgement rests on whether victimhood is perceived as acceptable (just bad luck) or not (gullibility). Title: When tourism competitiveness becomes human development: The conditioning role of institutional quality in Central and Eastern Europe
Abstract: Why do destinations with similar levels of tourism competitiveness experience different human development outcomes? Integrating Sen's Capability Approach with the Tourism Competitiveness Theory Hypothesis, this study examines the institutional conditions under which tourism competitiveness becomes meaningful for human development. Tourism competitiveness is conceptualized as a resource-generating capacity, while institutional quality represents a macro-level condition shaping its conversion into human development. Using annual data for eleven Central and Eastern European countries (2000–2023), we estimate heterogeneous panel autoregressive distributed lag models, error-correction dynamics, and Granger-type causality tests. Results show a positive long-run relationship between tourism competitiveness and human development, with stronger institutional quality associated with larger developmental returns. A trajectory analysis identifies four tourism–development pathways and interprets their differences through institutional quality. The study extends tourism competitiveness theory beyond destination performance by explaining why comparable competitive capacities can generate different human development outcomes across institutional contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Data centres and the new strategic infrastructure governance: From cloud ESG to compute sovereignty
Abstract: Data centres have moved from the background of the digital economy to the foreground of energy, climate, industrial and national-security politics. Artificial intelligence is intensifying this shift through growing demand for compute, electricity, cooling, land, hardware and critical materials. Yet governance remains largely organised around facility-level metrics that treat data centres as bounded technical assets rather than strategic infrastructure embedded in grids, water systems, supply chains, communities and security architectures. This article develops the CLOUDS framework—Coherence, Lifecycle materiality, Operational locality, Utility burden, Digital sovereignty, and Social licence and public purpose—as a diagnostic architecture for evaluating data centres as system-shaping infrastructure. It also develops capacity extraction: the process through which heterogeneous inputs such as electricity, water, land, permits, institutional trust and community tolerance are rendered as a single quantity called capacity and converted into compute whose higher-value layers may remain controlled elsewhere. The framework is developed through an integrative review and tiered empirical design spanning Chile, Australia, Querétaro, Ireland and Singapore. It is proposed for testing rather than presented as validated. Two findings are central. First, instrument incoherence can arise without regulatory capture when no institution can govern trade-offs across electricity, water, planning and public value. Second, hosting is not sovereignty: physical location alone creates no assured claim on compute access, workload priority, crisis continuity or higher-value layers. The policy implication is strategic infrastructure bargaining over both system capacity and the institutions governing its conversion into compute. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Feelings of ease in generating ideas: My loyal companion that guides my mental action but does not help me generate more creative ideas
Abstract: The ability to generate creative ideas is an important skill for education. This study examined how feelings of ease in generating ideas act as a cue that allowed individuals to have information to monitor their mental action and make important metacognitive decisions while generating creative ideas. Participants were asked to generate four ideas to help deal with the problem of empty work offices during and after the pandemic of COVID-19. After generating each idea, participants reported their feelings of ease and evaluated the creativity of each idea. Participants then reported their confidence in the ideas generated and selected their most creative idea. Results showed negative, curvilinear trajectories of feelings of ease and self-evaluations of the creativity of each idea. Feelings of ease in generating ideas were positively related to self-evaluations and the decisions to continue generating ideas and negatively related to choosing the first idea as the most creative. In addition, feelings of ease were indirectly and positively related to post-task confidence through their relationship with self-evaluations. These findings provided initial, empirical evidence that feelings of ease acted as cues to inform relevant judgments and decisions in the process of ideation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: ACOPI-QGen: Implicitness-aware joint quintuple extraction for aspect-based sentiment analysis via contrastive and graph-based modeling
Abstract: In social media and online reviews, sentiments are often expressed implicitly through contextual, figurative, or indirect language, making them difficult to capture using traditional Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA) techniques. Many prior studies on ABSA treat implicit aspects and opinions as auxiliary cases or evaluation subsets, limiting their role during learning. To address this limitation, we propose ACOPI-QGen, a joint structured framework that extracts a five-element sentiment quintuple (Aspect Term, Aspect Category, Opinion Term, Polarity, Implicitness). Rather than treating implicitness as a post-hoc attribute, we model it as a supervised four-class variable: EAEO, EAIO, IAEO, and IAIO, where A/O denote aspect/opinion and E/I denote explicit/implicit realization. The proposed framework combines BERT-based contextual encoding, Supervised Contrastive Implicit Learning, and a Relational Graph Attention Network guided by a Surrogate Aspect-Opinion Dependency Tree to support implicit sentiment modeling when aspect or opinion spans are missing. A non-autoregressive set decoder uses parallel tuple queries to predict multiple candidate sentiment quintuples while preserving aspect-opinion alignment. We curate three datasets for quintuple extraction (Restaurant-ACOPI: 2584; Laptop-ACOPI: 4376; and Shoes-ACOPI: 3896 instances). ACOPI-QGen achieves Exact Match F1 scores of 55.68, 48.43, and 60.49 on Restaurant-ACOPI, Laptop-ACOPI, and Shoes-ACOPI, respectively, with corresponding improvements of 2.92, 2.53, and 5.45 absolute F1 points over the best-performing state-of-the-art models across the three domains. These results show that explicit modeling of implicitness improves joint quintuple extraction in implicit sentiment settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Mohammadi P.; Dahmardeh M.
Title: Gender Representation and Intercultural Competence in Iranian EFL Coursebooks from the 1960s to 2020s
Abstract: This study aims to investigate the representation of gender and intercultural competence in the images and texts of 15 Iranian secondary school English coursebooks, published over six decades. Gender representation was investigated using the framework proposed by Dahmardeh and Kim (2020), and the scale developed by Solhaug and Kristensen (2020) was used as the criteria for investigating intercultural competence. The data were coded and counted using manifest content analysis. The results showed that Iranian English coursebooks mentioned males and females unequally in their texts across different decades, with one gender being represented more in each decade. Regarding gender representation in the images, males were represented more than females in almost all decades. The representation of males and females in the books published in the 1970s was almost equal, followed by extreme and sudden changes in gender representation in the 1980s. However, the books published in and after the 2000s presented a balanced picture of males and females. The coursebooks dealt with intercultural competence in their texts and images very rarely, limiting this concept to religious issues and neglecting other aspects. In fact, the coursebooks addressed only one category out of the 11 categories. Finally, the study ends with implications for coursebook authors, materials designers, teachers, students, and teacher trainers. © 2027, Tarbiat Modares University. All rights reserved.

Title: Probable alcohol use disorder in the U.S. Veteran population: Results from the 2025–2026 National Health and Resilience in Veterans study
Abstract: Background Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a pervasive public health problem in the United States, and military veterans are at elevated risk. A prior wave of the National Health and Resilience in Veterans Study (NHRVS) estimated the prevalence of past-year probable AUD at 10.5 % in 2019–2020. Updated national surveillance data are needed given demographic shifts in the veteran population and evolving drinking patterns in the post-pandemic era. Methods Using data from the 2025–2026 NHRVS (N = 2,620), we estimated the weighted prevalence of probable AUD and compared it to that of the prior NHRVS wave. Multivariable analyses examined sociodemographic, military, trauma and mental health characteristics associated with probable AUD. Results The weighted prevalence of probable AUD in 2025–2026 was 12.1 %, compared with 10.5 % in 2019–2020 (difference, 1.6 percentage points; 95 % CI, −0.6 to 3.8), a difference that was not statistically significant. Independent correlates of probable AUD included younger age, unpartnered status, homelessness history, higher household income, and more adverse childhood experiences. When all lifetime psychiatric diagnoses were examined simultaneously, self-reported provider-diagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remained significantly associated with probable AUD (OR = 2.40). Veterans with probable AUD also had significantly greater odds of past-year suicidal ideation (OR = 2.02; 31.6 % vs. 11.7 %) and lifetime suicide attempt (OR = 1.67; 11.8 % vs. 4.0 %). Conclusions The prevalence of probable AUD among U.S. veterans remains elevated and is characterized by early adversity, co-occurring psychiatric conditions, and elevated suicide risk. Title: Evolution and Uses of Rock Art Sites: Contribution of Morphogenic Mapping of Rock Walls
Source title: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
Abstract: In this article, we present a new method for investigating rock art within the framework of site morphogenesis. Although numerous surveys of paintings and engravings have been conducted in archaeology since the twentieth century, few have taken into account the geomorphological characteristics of rock surfaces and their morphogenic evolution. Yet the processes responsible for these transformations directly interact with rock art. This approach therefore raises several questions: have the sites and their rock surfaces always been accessible? If not, from when until when were they accessible? Beyond parietal paintings and engravings, are there other traces of human activity? How are these related to the rock art? The method developed, based on the general geomorphological ground mapping’s codes, has been adapted for the analysis of painted and engraved rock walls at different spatial scales. The results demonstrate the relevance of such morphogenetic analysis of rock walls for the understanding of painted and engraved archaeological sites. At Rocher du Château (France, Savoie), phases of the rock wall’s evolution have been identified, which enable discussions about Neolithic and proto-historic frequentations contemporaneity with rock paintings, and their accessibility through time. At Bruguier rock shelter (France, Gard), seven phases of human activity, that are not visible on the ground, and numerous modifications were identified on the rock wall. The methodological and cartographic framework presented in this paper is grounded in an integrative approach to the study of evolving rock walls. Geomorphological analysis sheds light on the physical changes affecting the rock wall before, during, and after (pre)historic human occupation, while the cartographic framework is intended to be further developed through interdisciplinary collaboration. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Evaluating role-prompted LLM responses on autism-related Theory-of-Mind tasks
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform well on social-reasoning benchmarks, but it remains unclear whether role prompting can produce distinguishable response patterns on autism-related Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks. This question matters for developing neurodiversity-aware AI evaluation, but any such work must distinguish behavioral output patterns from claims about autistic cognition or lived experience. In this paper, we introduce a ToM evaluation covering 11 established task types and four instructional personas: neurotypical and ASD Levels 1–3, labeled using DSM-5 support levels as heuristic anchors rather than validated clinical profiles. We curate 460 multiple-choice items and test state-of-the-art LLMs of varying scales. Baseline results show that in the original experiments, even detailed persona prompts do not yield reliable accuracy differentiation across model families, with smaller models often failing to meaningfully distinguish the imposed personas. A prompt-specificity ablation shows that explicit speech, cognitive-style, and response constraints substantially strengthen persona differentiation. Native-thinking configurations enlarge full-profile accuracy gaps and improve role-only accuracy, while some role-only conditions retain weaker, model-dependent ordering. To improve role fidelity, we implement an actor–critic workflow in which the actor produces in-character answers and the critic enforces persona constraints. After actor–critic, higher ASD levels exhibit lower accuracy on advanced ToM tasks and produce shorter utterances with fewer mental-state terms, matching the prompt-specified profile constraints. We further examine scale and alignment: larger models tend to increase overall accuracy while preserving role fidelity in our experiments, whereas general alignment tuned for helpfulness via preference optimization raises average correctness but reduces persona separability, collapsing the prompt-induced gradient. Title: Emotional preferences in LoRA-driven AI-generated urban vitality spaces: A study using discrete choice models
Abstract: China's transition toward urban stock renewal has heightened the focus on the emotional quality of urban vitality spaces. While AI generative design offers new approaches, whether AI-generated images as visual representations for specific spaces can meet people's emotional needs remains insufficiently examined. This study examines whether AI-generated visual representations of such spaces evoke image-based emotional preferences comparable to those for real photographs, and identifies which spatial attributes drive these preferences. Using THE BOX in Beijing as a case, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)-fine-tuned Stable Diffusion models generated visual representations of seven chosen scenes. Emotional preferences were measured through validated scales completed by 115 participants. A discrete choice model was used to compare participants' preferences between photographs of the real space and AI-generated images and identified influential attributes. Results showed that participants with design-related backgrounds preferred real photographs. Positive affect toward AI-generated images was the strongest predictor of preference. Real-scene color, natural elements, and uniqueness reduced the odds of choosing AI-generated versions, whereas AI-generated form and structure, natural elements, and changeability increased them. The study contributes a replicable workflow linking generative AI with emotional preference measurement, offering a structured approach for evidence-based design review. The findings are preliminary due to the single case, modest sample, and reliance on static images. Future work should extend to diverse urban contexts and multimodal evaluation. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Defisherization: The political ecology of small-scale fisheries decline in Indonesia
Abstract: In many coastal areas, the decline of small-scale fisheries is a daily reality for fishers. However, it is still framed as a technical issue, leaving unaddressed the power relations in marine governance that gradually erode fishers' livelihoods. This article develops the concept of defisherization to analyze how conservation-oriented coastal governance and ecological pressures cumulatively erode the livelihoods of small-scale fishers. Based on research in fishing communities along the coast of Buton, Southeast Sulawesi, the study employs observation, in-depth interviews (including a structured household questionnaire), and focus group discussions to examine the dynamics of this transformation. The findings suggest that defisherization occurs through the interplay of four main mechanisms: the narrowing of fishing spaces through permanent conservation zones; ecological pressures that drive household adaptation strategies without fully exiting the fisheries sector; symbolic persistence without adequate material reproduction; and the cumulative interaction between the three that gradually consolidates fisheries as a cultural identity but increasingly marginalizes it as a livelihood. This article offers defisherization as an analytical lens to move beyond explanations that view the decline of small-scale fisheries as an unintended consequence of conservation or environmental crises, demonstrating that environmental governance is vulnerable to undermining the material foundations of livelihoods. In this context, successful ecosystem protection often comes at the cost of compromising the sustainability of small-scale fishers' livelihoods. By offering an analytical lens to understand fisheries decline as a cumulative political-ecological process, this study emphasizes the importance of linking conservation agendas to the sustainable social reproduction of coastal communities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A bibliometric and systematic analysis of artificial intelligence and the transition towards smart geotourism

Abstract: The rapid digital transformation of tourism has positioned artificial intelligence as a key enabler of destination intelligence, data-driven decision-making, and sustainable tourism management. Although artificial intelligence has become increasingly important in smart tourism research, its application to geotourism remains fragmented, particularly regarding geoheritage conservation, geodiversity management, and territorial planning. Employing a retrospective approach, this study delineates the developmental trajectory of artificial intelligence applications in sustainable tourism while interrogating their integration into the paradigm of smart geotourism. An integrated bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review were conducted to evaluate scientific developments and empirical applications of artificial intelligence within geotourism contexts. Such findings delineate a burgeoning field of inquiry structured through the convergence of three intersecting axes: technological advancement, analytical intelligence, and visitor-focused experiential paradigms. The review study identified four principal domains through which artificial intelligence contributes to geotourism: predictive analytics, smart destination management, geoheritage interpretation, and environmental monitoring and geoconservation. The findings further highlight significant regional differences in technological adoption and reveal a limited integration between artificial intelligence, geoheritage conservation, and sustainable territorial governance. Based on these findings, the study proposes a smart geotourism framework that connects artificial intelligence, smart tourism, geoheritage conservation, and territorial planning within a unified conceptual structure. By delivering an integrated appraisal of artificial intelligence within geotourism, this study contributes to extant scholarship by conceptualizing artificial intelligence beyond its technical dimensions—positioning it as a fundamental enabler of empirical territorial planning, destination analytics, and the sustainable preservation of geological resources. Authors: Bulgarelli F.; Rabideau M.
Title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers’ novel word learning
Abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning, sometimes benefitting learning and other times making it more challenging. However, all prior studies investigating effects of talker variability have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used a novel active learning paradigm wherein 3- and 4-year old preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, but that talker variability does not predict word learning. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children do seek out variability, but that word learning outcomes are most predicted by their relative vocabulary sizes and not talker variability choices. These results inform theories on the roles of both talker variability and active learning in language learning. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Intellectual overconfidence and susceptibility to anti-science misinformation
Abstract: Anti-science misinformation can undermine trust in science, and understanding who is most susceptible is important for combatting its influence. One relevant trait is Intellectual Humility (IH), associated with greater understanding of science and the reasoning skills required to reject misinformation. Three pre-registered experimental studies (total N = 1604) examined IH and susceptibility to anti-science misinformation in the context of consumer genetic testing. A central subscale of IH – Lack of Intellectual Overconfidence – emerged as the strongest predictor, with intellectually overconfident individuals most susceptible to misinformation, though effect sizes were modest. Title: The social implications of classroom seats: replicating and extending previous findings on seating arrangements and peer status
Abstract: This preregistered replication study examined how physical proximity in the classroom is associated with peer perceptions of social status, specifically likeability and popularity. We aimed to replicate and extend the study by van den Berg and Cillessen (2015) using data from 719 students across 33 elementary classrooms (grades 4–6; Mage = 10.27; 51.6% boys). We replicated previous findings by showing that classmates seated closer together concurrently rated each other as more popular and likeable. Furthermore, when given the opportunity to create their own seating arrangements, students placed classmates they found likeable and popular closer to themselves. We extended previous findings by showing that increased proximity between two classmates over time led to an increase in mutual liking, but not perceived popularity. Further, findings did not differ significantly between friends and non-friends. Finally, because extant studies differ in how proximity is measured, we tested an operationalization of proximity in terms of desk clusters. Title: Silent Valleys: Unraveling the Causes and Strategic Pathways for Reverse Migration in Hilly Regions of Uttarakhand
Abstract: This study examines out-migration and the prospects for sustainable reverse migration in the hilly regions of Uttarakhand, addressing three objectives: identifying the main drivers of migration, synthesizing reinforcement strategies to reduce distress migration and support return, and linking causes and responses within a human-environment systems perspective. We conducted a scoping review of 68 studies (2010–2025) using a structured screening and synthesis process. The study synthesizes an evidence-graded portfolio of interventions: livelihood diversification, agri-value-chain strengthening, digital access and skills, climate-resilient infrastructure, community-based and eco-tourism, and improved local service delivery and governance support, contributing an integrated conceptual framework linking drivers, feedback loops, and intervention levers for coordinated, place-based mountain-region planning. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Handedness, psychological characteristics, and social adaptation among Chinese college students
Abstract: Handedness may be associated with individual differences in information processing, but its implications for social adaptation remain unclear. This cross-sectional study examined associations among handedness type, openness, cognitive flexibility, multitasking preference, and social adaptation in 3798 Chinese college students. Mixed-handed students reported higher openness (η2 = 0.013), cognitive flexibility (η2 = 0.030), and multitasking preference (η2 = 0.007) than right- and left-handed students, with the largest group difference observed for cognitive flexibility. Left- and right-handed students showed broadly similar scores across these characteristics. Mixed-handedness was positively associated with openness ( r = 0.11), cognitive flexibility ( r = 0.17), and multitasking preference ( r = 0.08), whereas its association with social adaptation was weaker ( r = −0.04). Title: Bridging Conservation and Human-Wildlife Conflict for Coexistence
Abstract: Human-wildlife conflict (HWC) poses a significant threat to conservation, particularly in the region, where dense human settlements and recovering wildlife populations compete for resources. This study examines HWC patterns in the buffer zone of Parsa National Park, where growing populations of large mammals overlap in their use of shared resources. Elephants accounted for 45% of reported incidents, followed by leopards (29%) and tigers (13.5%). Title: Structural Determinants of Household Resilience in Earthquake-Affected Communities: A Case Study from Bawean Island
Abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic impacts of the March 2024 earthquake on household resilience in Bawean Island, East Java, Indonesia. Data for this study were collected through a survey with a snowball sampling technique, with a total of 221 valid respondents from affected regions. Using a household survey across 12 affected villages and partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), the study identifies critical factors contributing to household resilience, namely social, economic, human, and physical capital assets. The findings can be explained in two ways. First, the result confirms social, economic, human, and physical capital as critical resilience determinants. Second, higher household resilience could reduce the impact of natural disasters. Title: The Impact of Environmental Regulation on Air Quality: Empirical Evidence from the National Ecological Civilization Demonstration Counties Policy in China
Source title: Journal of Urban Planning and Development
Abstract: China faces increasing ecological constraints, and the National Ecological Civilization Demonstration Counties (NECDCs) policy may offer an effective solution. Using a sample of 1,963 counties in China from 2015 to 2021, which represents approximately 70% of all Chinese counties after screening for data completeness, this study treats the selection of NECDCs as a quasinatural experiment and employs a multiperiod difference-in-differences model to empirically examine its impact on county-level air quality. The results indicate that NECDCs experience a 2.4% reduction in the PM2.5 index, which is driven by mechanisms of promoting dynamic adjustments in firms, enhancing innovation capabilities, facilitating industrial upgrading, and increasing public environmental awareness. The impact is more pronounced in regions with higher digital financial inclusion, better ecological quality, and those in central and western China. This study also finds the spillover effects of NECDCs in surrounding areas. Title: Organizational safety and adaptive work practices in aquaculture
Abstract: The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Morse Y.L.
Title: Despite the odds: assessing Africa's new social welfare landscape
Abstract: Over the past decades more attention has been given to the growth of social welfare related programs in sub-Saharan Africa. However, to date there are still insufficient empirical observations, which makes it difficult to assess these changes or the factors behind them. This article introduces the Structure of Social Welfare (SSWA) dataset. Rather than rely on spending data, which is sporadically reported, the SSWA gathers data on the design elements of diverse social welfare programs for 44 African countries between 1960 and 2022. These data are used to create indexes of social welfare that take into consideration intended coverage as well as institutional and fiscal sustainability. The SSWA data demonstrates that despite difficult material conditions there is considerably more social welfare in Africa today, but that there is also important variation across countries in terms of the level of commitment. The utility of the SSWA data is then demonstrated by reevaluating the contested impact of democratization on welfare expansion in Africa. The results indicate a positive yet underexplored relationship. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Text-driven causal mapping of PET/rPET circularity in Australia: A dynamic factor–network analysis
Abstract: PET circularity is often evaluated by recovery volumes, although performance ultimately depends on whether recovered material can be converted into quality-assured outputs and absorbed by viable end markets. Yet the mechanisms connecting policy, markets, technology, and stakeholder behavior remain dispersed across heterogeneous evidence. We developed a source-attributed, time-stamped causal-network approach using 750 Australian government, industry and NGO, corporate, and media documents published during 2010–2025. Causal extraction, semantic normalization, sentiment assignment, and graph construction yielded 2794 factor nodes and 1588 unique causal edges. The network was strongly externalized: policy, market, and social factors were more numerous and highly connected than internal technical and operational factors. Persistent barriers combined cost and price volatility, inconsistent recyclate quality, infrastructure gaps, and weak policy implementation. Positive mechanisms clustered around standards and measurement, design for recyclability, operational capacity, and end-market development; their circular value depended on retained material quality and the end use reached. Source attribution revealed systematic framing differences, with media coverage concentrating negative implementation narratives. Temporal and regional analyses indicated a shift from limited attention to rapid expansion and subsequent consolidation, alongside national structural hubs and differentiated state pathways. A full-text academic shadow corpus preserved the broad problem domains but changed their hierarchy: academic evidence foregrounded material and processing mechanisms, whereas the primary corpus foregrounded institutional coordination and market implementation. The contribution is therefore not a universal ranking of Australian interventions, but an auditable framework for identifying how technical feasibility becomes, or fails to become, operational circularity under different institutional conditions. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Healthy crew, healthy life: The captain’s role in commercial fishing crew health
Abstract: Objectives Commercial fishermen engage in one of the most dangerous professions in the United States. This qualitative study explored how the internal priorities of commercial fishermen captains influence the health and well-being of their crew members. Methods Data were collected via semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted under the 2025 Southeast and Gulf Coast Fishing First Aid and Safety Training program. Commercial fishermen and individuals working adjacent to the industry (n = 10) were recruited using purposive sampling. Using a priori qualitative coding, two coders performed a thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti. Results Overall, participants reported that crew health and wellness were affected by the captain’s attitudes. Participants (40%) explored crew preparedness as a central theme in captains’ approaches to crew well-being, with the captain’s knowledge of pre-existing conditions allowing for a proactive approach to medication management and injury/illness reduction (30%). Some (20%) highlighted a conflict of priorities between crew productivity and well-being or observed that captains’ attitudes towards zero-tolerance policy against substance use would influence substance use onboard the vessel (20%). Authors: Babić A.G.; Halog A.
Title: A transferable methodological framework for using EIA documentation as a data source for sector-level environmental footprinting
Abstract: Sector-level environmental assessment of mining is frequently constrained by the limited availability of consistent and publicly accessible operational inventory data. Although Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) documentation contains detailed engineering information on mining projects, its potential as a source of life cycle inventory (LCI) data has received little attention. This study develops and demonstrates a transferable bottom-up methodological framework that uses EIA documentation as a source of operational inventory data for sector-level environmental footprinting. The framework integrates project-level information extracted from publicly available EIA studies with official national mining statistics to estimate extraction-stage greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, land-use intensity, and water use. Croatia was selected as the demonstration case because publicly available EIA documentation can be systematically linked with official production and concession data. A total of 68 EIA studies describing 75 mining operations prepared between 2015 and 2024 were analysed. The estimated extraction-stage GHG emissions of the Croatian mining sector amount to 0.164 Mt. CO₂-eq, corresponding to approximately 2–3% of industrial GHG emissions. Construction stone and aggregates dominate total emissions because of their production volume, whereas dimension stone quarrying exhibits the highest specific GHG emissions and land-use intensity. The results further demonstrate that production scale primarily determines total environmental burdens, while extraction technology exerts a stronger influence on specific environmental intensities. Beyond the presented case study, the principal contribution of this research lies in demonstrating how publicly available regulatory documentation can be systematically transformed into operational inventory data suitable for sector-level environmental assessment. The proposed framework complements conventional LCA and national environmental inventories by improving the visibility of extraction-stage impacts and provides a transferable methodological approach for jurisdictions where comparable regulatory and statistical data are available. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: The processing of word order is affected by verb subcategorization frequency: Evidence from electrophysiology
Abstract: This study investigated the influence of verb subcategorization preferences on sentence processing in Standard Indonesian. We examined how verb biases affect the processing of active and passive sentences by utilizing event-related potentials. Our findings revealed that passive sentences with active-bias verbs elicited a significant late positive shift (P600) relative to active sentences, which indicated increased processing difficulty. No such effect was detected for passive sentences with passive-bias verbs. The cost was observed only where the verb's preference conflicted with the passive structure, suggesting that verb-specific statistics, rather than word order alone, contribute to the difficulty of passive sentences. We highlight the need for a nuanced understanding of sentence comprehension that incorporates both structural and lexical influences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: SDE-IG: A robust malware family classification method based on graph invariance learning
Abstract: While existing malware family classification methods achieve high performance on in-distribution data, they often overfit mutable features when subjected to different compilers, optimization levels, and advanced code obfuscation. This vulnerability significantly degrades their generalization under complex distribution shifts. Furthermore, applying existing graph invariance learning methods, which typically rely on random topological sampling, disrupts the strict semantic dependencies inherent in binary code. Additionally, a naive concatenation of dynamic and static features introduces underlying system call noise, adversely affecting the model's ability to identify core family logic. In response, this paper proposes SDE-IG, a robust malware family classification framework based on invariant subgraphs. A cross-environment invariant subgraph extraction mechanism is designed from a static perspective. By integrating binary semantic priors with parameterized graph neural networks, this mechanism decouples the program call graph into an invariant subgraph representing core semantics and an environment subgraph capturing noise. This separation is designed to reduce reliance on environment-dependent structures that may vary across compilation, linking, and obfuscation settings. To address potential static topology failures caused by extreme obfuscation, SDE-IG incorporates a dynamic behavioral view as auxiliary semantic evidence. During end-to-end joint optimization, a collaborative mixup strategy is applied to simulate unknown variants and broaden the distribution boundary. Coupled with an asynchronous two-stage optimization and a gated residual calibration mechanism, this approach effectively minimizes the interference of dynamic behavioral noise on the static backbone representation. Experimental results show that SDE-IG achieves improved cross-period classification stability under the chronologically separated temporal distribution shifts evaluated in this study. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Developing a cyber-resilience framework for UAVs: insights from expert interviews on addressing cybersecurity challenges
Abstract: Rapid technological advances have greatly enhanced the development of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and their potential for beneficial uses. Such uses, however, have been limited by cybersecurity concerns. Despite considerable research attention, threat levels are increasing, and this is likely to further inhibit UAV use. A different approach is therefore required, one that marks a change from reactive mitigation to proactive prevention. This study proposes a holistic cyber-resilience framework for UAVs based on five resilience features, which are redundancy, flexibility, modularity, diversity, and tightness of feedback loops. Such a change, called for by several authors but yet to be achieved, can come through the components of a framework that are supported by expert perspectives. The study employs a mixed-methods design with in-person interviews of 32 expert professionals across eight sectors (aviation, military, security, insurance, aerospace, cybersecurity, logistics, and academia). A total of 261 vulnerabilities ranging across five threat categories are identified, with those related to communication facilitating a point of entry for cascading attacks. Drawing on expert evaluations of five resilience features, the novelty of this study is its proposed lifecycle-based framework that shifts UAV security from mitigation to embedded resilience. Practical trade-offs that include weight, power and relative costs as well as the position of the framework in relation to existing standards such as NIST CSF and MITRE frameworks are discussed. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Greenhouse gas emissions implications of hydrogen fuel cell technology for passenger trains
Abstract: The transportation sector contributes over a quarter of the greenhouse gas emissions in Canada. Rail decarbonization remains challenging where electrification is not feasible. Hydrogen fuel cell trains may offer an opportunity to mitigate carbon emissions in these areas. Their environmental impacts depend on hydrogen leakage, fuel distribution pathways, and the carbon intensity of hydrogen production. This study quantifies the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions of a regional hydrogen train compared with a diesel train using primary operational data from a pilot project in Quebec, complemented by secondary data. A well-to-wheel model evaluates scenarios of hydrogen leakage and fuel distribution pathways considering short- and long-term climate impacts. Uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo simulations, and critical thresholds are identified through environmental break-even analysis. The hydrogen train emits 3 g carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2-eq) per passenger kilometre (PKM) compared to 26 g CO2-eq per PKM for the diesel train at full passenger loads and optimal conditions using a 100-year global warming potential (GWP). High hydrogen leakage reduces the climate benefits by approximately 26% using a 20-year GWP with diesel trucks transporting fuel. Low leakage scenarios achieve 83–86% emission reductions using fuel cell trucks and pipelines over a 100-year horizon. The sensitivity analysis identifies key parameters, including the carbon intensity of electricity used for hydrogen electrolysis and the fuel consumption rate. A hydrogen emission rate of 6.6% or higher eliminates the climate benefit for diesel truck delivered hydrogen. The break-even electricity emission factor ranges from 0.14 to 0.26 kg CO2-eq per kWh across distribution pathways. These findings provide quantitative thresholds to guide hydrogen deployment in rail transportation and highlight key data gaps in life cycle inventories, supporting leakage mitigation and low-carbon electricity supply as priorities for decision makers. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Dynamic Diffusion of Legal Compliance and Ethical Conduct among Construction Project Owners: An Epidemiological Modeling Approach

Abstract: Construction industries worldwide face persistent challenges of ethical misconduct, contractual violations, and regulatory noncompliance, imposing substantial legal liabilities and undermining sustainable development. Although legal frameworks exist to govern owner behavior, their dynamic enforcement effects and interactions with market-driven compliance mechanisms remain poorly understood. An extended susceptible-exposed-infected-removed (SEIR) model was developed to analyze how statutory enforcement and voluntary market adoption jointly drive compliance diffusion, simulated via MATLAB. Title: Does fast mapping accelerate lexical integration? Evidence from spoken and written novel words
Abstract: Fast mapping (FM) is an encoding paradigm in which a novel label is learned incidentally by inference. Some studies have interpreted FM training as capable of bringing forward the integration of novel words into existing lexical networks relative to typical consolidation timelines, although the evidence is mixed. We conducted three experiments to investigate whether FM promotes faster lexical integration compared to explicit encoding (EE). Experiments 1 and 2 extended prior orthographic fast mapping work, testing whether the rapid lexical integration claim generalises to the auditory (spoken) domain. Participants learned novel spoken words through either FM or EE training. Lexical integration was assessed using a pause detection task immediately after learning, one day later, and one week later (Experiment 1 only). Neither experiment found evidence that FM led to more rapid lexical integration compared to EE. Experiment 3 was a direct replication of previous orthographic fast mapping research ( Coutanche and Thompson-Schill, 2014 ), using a semantic categorisation task to assess integration of visually presented novel words. Again, we found no advantage for FM in promoting rapid lexical integration. Across all experiments, EE consistently produced superior explicit memory for the novel words compared to FM. These findings fail to support claims that FM-based training allows novel words to bypass time-dependent consolidation processes and become rapidly integrated into the mental lexicon. The results are consistent with complementary learning systems accounts positing that lexical integration typically benefits from offline consolidation, regardless of encoding method. Title: CloudTrip: Exploring physiological data-enabled multisensory metaphorical narratives for everyday stress management
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: In modern society, an increasing number of people are suffering from the harmful effects of chronic stress, while data-enabled reflection has been shown to be an effective approach to stress management. However, most existing human–data interaction designs primarily focus on retrospective data review, often failing to foster engaging and meaningful reflection. In this paper, we present CloudTrip, an immersive application that represents the users’ data throughout a day as an experiential and interactive digital story for mental health self-reflection. Specifically, CloudTrip metaphorically conveys users’ daily stress-related physiological data into narrative experiences by dynamically mapping the data onto changes in visual and auditory elements of characters and virtual environments. Users can record reflective content during the experience and receive responsive feedback generated by a large language model, thereby forming an interactive narrative loop that further deepens reflective engagement. We conducted a 14-day within-subject study with 20 participants, comparing CloudTrip with a traditional line-chart visualization using a mixed-methods evaluation to assess its impact on the reflection experience and reflection support. Results show that CloudTrip was associated with a cardiac autonomic pattern compatible with higher arousal, increases in self-reported valence, arousal, and dominance, more favorable motivational ratings for the experience, stronger perceived support for reflection, and promise for repeated use. Title: A novel vector-based approach to measure the directional characteristics of urban expansion and its heterogeneity

Title: The relationship between product-based creativity and ADHD traits in children and the associations with later well-being
Abstract: Creativity is increasingly recognized as a positive aspect among adults with ADHD and those with high ADHD scores, but evidence in youth is limited, particularly regarding product-based creativity. It also remains unclear whether higher creativity benefits the lower well-being typically associated with ADHD traits. Title: Biofeedback in musicians: A systematic review and meta-analysis of its effects on muscle activity, musculoskeletal health, and performance

Title: Do non-governmental organizations contribute to urban green space equity? A systematic review of impacts and pathways

Title: Development and test-retest reliability of a laboratory-based shipboard firefighting simulation for controlled performance testing
Abstract: Understanding shipboard firefighting performance is critical for improving crew safety and vessel preservation during damage control events. While prior research has been conducted in naval spaces, controlled simulations that assess performance without requiring naval vessels, personnel or specialised equipment are lacking. This study was designed to both develop and test a laboratory-based shipboard firefighting simulation. Consistent with shipboard firefighting activities, the simulation included walking, stair climbing, hose dragging, simulated boundary cooling, extinguisher carrying and casualty dragging tasks, completed within 8 min. Twenty-seven participants (22 males, 5 females) performed the simulation twice, with good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.78; SEM = 17.6 s). Compared to Session 1, time-to-completion was 2.6% faster, RPE was 12.2% higher, HR was 5% lower, and core temperature estimate was 0.8% lower in Session 2 (all p < 0.05). This simulation provides a practical, low-cost solution for conducting shipboard firefighting research using minimal space, equipment, and untrained subjects. Copyright © 2026. Title: A longitudinal study of patterns of direct online harms victimization in six EU countries
Abstract: Addressing the ubiquity of online harms, such as threats of violence and sexual harassment, is a priority for citizens and policymakers globally. However, comprehensive cross-national insights about online harms victimization remain limited. Our study addresses this gap in the literature. Using three-wave panel data from adult samples from six EU countries (Poland, N = 731; Italy, N = 947; Ireland, N = 468; Germany, N = 736; France, N = 826; Finland, N = 924), we aimed to identify distinct patterns of direct online harms victimization and their longitudinal dynamics. Additionally, we sought to assess whether certain responses to victimization (e.g., assertiveness) predict persistent exposure to online harms over three years. Latent Markov Models highlighted four states of victimization experiences in all studied countries: non-victimization, which was the largest state, infrequent experiences of a small number of diverse harms, and infrequent and frequent confrontation with all nine assessed harms. While non-victimization was stable over time, this cannot be said for any of the three other states, which reflected qualities of poly-victimization. Predictors of ongoing victimization could – especially for the infrequent and frequent broad victimization states – not be confidently estimated. Acknowledging this limitation, we carefully conclude that there was no clear evidence that strategies for coping with victimization predict the stability of (or transitions between) victimization patterns over two or three years. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Effectiveness of exposure-based therapy through inhibitory learning via virtual reality in electronic gambling machines: Multiple baseline single-case experimental design
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Context: Electronic gambling machines (EGMs) can harm individuals and contribute to gambling disorder (GD). Empirically supported cognitive-behavioral interventions are effective yet associated with high relapse rates. One avenue for improvement is to target the urge to gamble through exposure. In the exposure approach based on the inhibitory learning model, the perceived self-efficacy (PSE) to refrain from gambling despite the urge serves as a proximal factor for change. The goal is to create a new learning association that overrides the pre-established link between gambling stimuli, urge to gamble, and PSE to refrain from gambling. Exposure can be done in virtual reality (VR) to promote self-control and reduce gambling behaviors. VR is a relevant exposure method because it allows reproduction of ecologically valid, realistic environments. Furthermore, researchers have more control over the course of the immersion experience than during exposure in vivo. Objective: This study evaluates the effectiveness of a VR exposure-based intervention for EGM players. Method:. The single-case, multiple-baseline experimental design includes six intervention sessions with VR exposure and daily journaling to measure PSE, urges, and gambling behaviors. This approach emphasizes building PSE to resist from gambling despite the urge. Four adult males who wanted to stop their gambling behavior participated in this study. Results: Statistical analyses demonstrate a significant increase in PSE across participants and a significant reduction in the urge to gamble in three of the four participants. This study highlights the potential benefits of using of such an exposure model. It provides grounds for a large-scale randomized controlled trial where exposure and its underlying clinical rational could be included in more traditional cognitive-behavioral therapy programs. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. Authors: Strambler M.J.
Title: Racialized psychotherapy: Understudied risks and the case for empirical scrutiny
Abstract: Racialized psychotherapy, a cluster of approaches centering race, racial identity, and racism in clinical work, emerged from legitimate concerns about cultural incompetence and minority underservice. The field has not tested the assumption that race-centering benefits racial minority clients. This paper identifies four mechanisms by which racialized therapy may harm clients: therapist-imposed racial salience that overrides client-defined concerns; hypervigilance induction through attributional training toward racial threat; externalized locus of control that undermines agency; and therapeutic deference that reduces the productive challenge clients from stigmatized groups may most need. The validation argument for racialized therapy is partly right but justifies responsive rather than proactive race-framing. The evidence base for culturally adapted interventions is modest, adverse effects go unreported, and the most explicitly race-focused protocols lack randomized trial evidence. Systematic research on conditions under which race-centered approaches benefit or harm clients is overdue. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
