Title: Empirical Stage-Damage Functions for SME Content Losses in Australian Flood Vulnerability Assessment
Abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SME) dominate Australian business activity, yet empirically calibrated functions for nonresidential flood-related contents losses remain limited. Postevent surveys of 185 SMEs across 12 business types and 14 towns affected by the February-April 2022 Northern Rivers floods were used to derive stage-damage functions for stock, equipment, and fit-out. Contents-specific damage indices combined peak internal flood depth (0-6 m, relative to finished-floor level) with self-reported losses and preevent replacement values. Pooled curves were fitted using LOESS and a beta-family generalized additive model (Beta-GAM); a hierarchical Beta-GAM (HBGAM) generated business-type functions under partial pooling, while random forest and XGBoost provided depth-only predictive benchmarks. Across the pooled models, performance on the corresponding within-event 25% holdout sets was moderate (R2=0.57-0.69; RMSE=0.23-0.27), and neither machine-learning benchmark consistently improved performance. The Beta-GAM was retained because it provided smooth, bounded, interpretable relationships, model-based and bootstrap uncertainty intervals, and extractable threshold depths. The fitted mean damage index reached 0.50 at 1.03 m for stock, 1.09 m for equipment, and 1.27 m for fit-out, with uncertainty generally increasing above 3 m as data density declined. HBGAM-derived D50 values ranged from 0.66 to 1.18 m for stock, 0.81 to 1.18 m for equipment, and 1.09 to 1.48 m for fit-out, indicating model-derived sector variation. These event-calibrated functions support screening-level relative SME contents-loss assessment and evaluation of loss-reduction options in comparable settings; application elsewhere requires external validation or local recalibration.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Daily affect profiles during addiction recovery: Transition dynamics and links to acute recovery outcomes
Abstract: Introduction As individuals in recovery from substance use disorder (SUD) find initial stability, the next milestone is developing the emotional wellbeing that will offer greater quality of life, making affect a critical target. Many investigations into emotion during recovery, however, fail to account for the significant heterogeneity in daily affective experiences. The present study leverages advanced person-centered methods to capture that heterogeneity by identifying types of affect days in recovery and examines their place in daily recovery. Methods 129 individuals in SUD recovery were recruited remotely to complete a 10-day daily diary protocol (1,177 days). A mixed-indicator latent profile analysis was conducted on PANAS items to identify distinct profiles of daily affect. Latent profiles were examined in relation to prior-day meaning, next-day binary, and conditional craving, using robust standard errors to account for the repeated measures data structure. Results A 5-profile solution was selected: Prevalent NA (14% of affect days), Prevalent NA-Mild PA (30%), High Arousal Affect (11%), Intense PA (17%), and Mixed Affect (28%). Compared to other profiles, Intense PA and High Arousal Affect days were associated with higher prior-day meaning, lower odds of next-day craving, and lower levels of next-day craving among craving days. Conclusion Not only do results demonstrate the prevalence of NA-PA mixed days in recovery, but a second dimension – arousal – was also uncovered in affect patterns. Types of affect days differentially predicted acute recovery outcomes, with High Arousal Affect promoting recovery, warranting consideration of arousal in future studies. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Safety and health of workers in post-disaster reconstruction: a scoping review and evidence map
Abstract: Post-disaster reconstruction (PDR) is essential for restoring damaged communities, yet the occupational safety and health (OSH) of PDR workers remains poorly understood. Although PDR involves many familiar construction hazards, these risks arise under distinct conditions, including damaged infrastructure, compressed recovery timelines, environmental contamination, fragmented governance, and pressure for visible recovery. This scoping review and evidence map examined peer-reviewed and authoritative gray literature on OSH among PDR workers. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, the review used a Population-Concept-Context framework to search bibliographic databases and targeted organizational sources for English-language literature published from 2005 to 2025. The final evidence base included 55 sources, comprising 40 peer-reviewed publications and 15 gray literature documents. The review identified a geographically uneven and thematically concentrated evidence base, with strong representation from the United States and multi-country sources, and greater attention to multi-hazard and earthquake-related contexts than to other disaster types. Findings show that PDR workers face overlapping OSH hazards and exposures. Evidence was strongest for early recovery tasks such as debris removal, demolition, and cleanup, while later reconstruction phases, informal labor, volunteers, undocumented workers, and self-recovery residents remained underexamined. The review also highlights major methodological, policy, and practice gaps, including limited longitudinal evidence, inconsistent outcome measures, weak surveillance, and insufficient worker-specific protections. By integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature, this review frames PDR as a distinct OSH context and develops Faster Reconstruction Syndrome as a concept, interpreted through Job Demands-Resources and safety-climate theory to explain how recovery-speed pressures may weaken worker protection in disaster recovery policy and practice. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Affective prosody and facial expression cues differentially augment spoken sentence and discourse comprehension for acute left and right hemisphere stroke survivors
Abstract: Comprehension for spoken sentences and discourse is differentially impacted by left- (LH) and right-hemisphere (RH) brain damage, such as that caused by stroke. Comprehension deficits can have disabling effects on one's ability to process information, participate in everyday life, and create and maintain relationships. This cross-sectional, observational study evaluated differences in sentence- and discourse-level comprehension between LH and RH stroke survivors across different prosodic conditions and examined relationships between comprehension and damage to key LH and RH regions. Participants included 43 LH and 46 RH acute stroke survivors and 39 controls. All participants completed an in-house clinical assessment that included short passages presented in three conditions: neutral prosody, affective prosody, and affective prosody plus facial expression cues. Stroke survivors also completed magnetic resonance imaging. Consistent with expectations, stroke participants achieved lower comprehension accuracy than controls across conditions. LH participants' accuracy in the ‘affective prosody plus facial expressions’ condition was greater than in the neutral prosody condition, and total LH lesion volume was associated with performance. RH participants' accuracy in the ‘affective prosody’ and ‘affective prosody plus facial expressions’ conditions was greater than in the neutral prosody condition. Overall, both groups' scores increased linearly from Condition 1 to 3. None of the prespecified LH or RH brain regions were significantly associated with performance. Findings suggest that some acute LH and RH stroke survivors with comprehension deficits can benefit from affective prosody and facial expression cues, but different or additional cues may be needed for greatest benefit. © 2026 The Authors

Title: When and why are negotiators overly pessimistic? The psychology of under-trust innegotiation
Abstract: Research on negotiation has devoted considerable attention to the risks of misplaced trust, particularly the possibility that negotiators may be exploited by deceptive counterparts. Less attention has been given to the opposite form of trust miscalibration: under-trust, and particularly, unwarranted pessimism regarding counterparts' honesty. This review focuses on such undue distrust and proposes a misperceived motivations account to explain its emergence. According to this account, negotiators' excessive distrust stems from an asymmetry between the motives that negotiators attribute to their counterparts and the motives that actually guide those counterparts’ behavior. When deciding whether to behave honestly, negotiators are driven not only by self-interest but also by concerns about moral self-image and anticipated moral emotions, which constrain dishonesty. However, when deciding whether counterparts are honest, negotiators assume that their counterparts are primarily motivated by self-interest and fail to foresee the constraining moral-identity concerns. We integrate evidence from the literature on negotiation, trust, and moral psychology to explain why pessimism is especially likely to emerge and persist in competitive bargaining contexts, highlight circumstances that may attenuate or amplify it, and identify implications for theory and research, alongside practical inferences for fostering truthful disclosure and credible honesty in negotiation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Creative or uncreative partner: Comparing humans and AI in collaborative creative tasks
Abstract: Creativity is fundamentally a collaborative process. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated into creative work, understanding how it reshapes collaboration becomes critical. This pre-registered study directly compares human-human and human-AI collaboration dynamics across two creative tasks: the Alternate Uses Task (AUT) and creative short story writing. Participants were randomly assigned to pairs in either human-human (N = 68 pairs) or human-AI (GPT-4o; N = 72 pairs) conditions, with partners alternating turns as first responders to examine how initiation order shapes the creative process. Our findings reveal that the apparent “AI advantage” in creative collaboration is illusory, driven primarily by increased AI verbosity rather than enhanced creativity. Critically, collaboration with AI partners negatively impacted humans' own creative responses compared to human-human partnerships, with human-AI collaboration failing to enhance idea originality or diversity relative to human-human collaboration. Human partners demonstrated higher collaborative creativity that strengthened over time, indicating that current generative AI systems, while producing more verbose outputs, do not replicate the collective creativity characteristic of human-human collaboration. These results challenge assumptions about AI's creative potential, with direct implications for AI system design and collaborative creative practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Followership, teamwork, and wellness among nursing students: A cross-sectional study
Abstract: Background: Effective followership is progressively acknowledged as an essential professional competency in healthcare. However, nursing education has traditionally emphasized leadership development, resulting in a limited understanding of how followership relates to teamwork and wellness during professional preparation. Evidence regarding effective followership among nursing students remains scarce. Objective: To examine the relationships among effective followership, teamwork, individual wellness, and organizational wellness among nursing students and to identify factors associated with effective followership. Methods: A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted among 325 nursing students recruited from universities in Jordan. Participants completed an online survey comprising measures of effective followership, teamwork perceptions, individual wellness, and organizational wellness. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and multiple linear regression were used to examine the data. Exploratory factor analysis was conducted to evaluate the construct validity of the investigator-developed measures. Results: Students reported moderate levels of effective followership and teamwork perceptions. Effective followership demonstrated strong positive associations with teamwork perceptions (r = 0.66), individual wellness (r = 0.59), and organizational wellness (r = 0.59). Multiple linear regression showed that teamwork (β = 0.576, p < 0.001), GPA (β = 0.210, p < 0.001), and academic level (β = 0.083, p = 0.041) were significant predictors of effective followership, with the model explaining 47.10% of the variance (R2 = 0.471). Students demonstrating greater active engagement, accountability, and independent critical thinking reported more positive collaborative and wellness experiences. Conclusion: Effective followership appears to be an important professional competency associated with teamwork and wellness among nursing students. The results support consideration of the inclusion of followership development alongside leadership preparation within nursing curricula. Educational strategies that promote active engagement, accountability, constructive communication, and shared responsibility may better prepare students for interprofessional healthcare practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The Resource, Users’ Socio-economic Status, and Governance in Coastal Marine Benthic Mollusk fisheries in Costa Grande, Guerrero, Mexico
Abstract: The mollusks caught by coastal fishing were analyzed as a resource, as well as the socioeconomic condition of the fishermen involved in this activity, who are members of the fishing cooperatives of the Costa Grande of the state of Guerrero. The objectives were to be acquainted with the list of species fished for human consumption, determine those of greatest economic importance, analyze the socioeconomic characteristics of the fishermen, and determine the current state of the mollusk resource based on the fishermen’s perception. The specimens were acquired from landing zones and restaurants, and a total of 27 surveys were conducted with fishermen, members of fishing cooperatives in the region. A total of 24 species of mollusks were identified; 10 were the target species for fishing, and seven species were not economically profitable for fishermen. Striostrea prismatica, Trochita trochiformis, and Hexaplex princeps generate more income annually. Five species have been excluded from the list of catches: Megapitaria squalida, Periglypta multicostata, Pinctada mazatlanica, Malea ringens, and the giant limpet Scutellastra mexicana. There was no evidence of generational replacement in the fishing activity. The fishermen’s income is sufficient to cover their basic needs and those of their families. The current regulations are insufficient. There is an urgent need to carry out technical-scientific and biological research to provide relevant information that can be used to implement measures for the appropriate use and regulation of mollusk fisheries in the region. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Lörch L.; Bonawitz E.; Brod G.
Author full names: Lörch, Lucas (57203911205); Bonawitz, Elizabeth (19933641800); Brod, Garvin (54917165400)
Title: The power of varying more than one thing at a time
Abstract: Background: Varying one thing at a time (VOTAT) is considered a universal approach for designing informative experiments. Its core idea is that controlled experiments can be designed by manipulating a single variable. However, we show that this single-manipulation heuristic can produce misleading evidence in contexts involving interrelated variables. We argue that varying more than one thing at a time (MOTAT) can be more informative when learners’ prior beliefs render alternative explanations implausible. Aims: To test these claims, we compared single-manipulation to MOTAT experiments in a Bayesian learning simulation and a pre-registered empirical study on children's learning about water displacement. Sample: Participants in the empirical study were 185 children aged 6–9. Methods: Learners predicted which of two spheres would displace more water and then observed an animation of the spheres being submerged. In the single-manipulation experiments, the spheres differed either only in size or only in material, leading to a confound of these dimensions with mass. In the MOTAT experiments, both size and material were manipulated such that the larger sphere was lighter. We investigated the formal informativeness of single-manipulation and MOTAT experiments (simulation study) and their effect on children's learning, as measured via a post- and transfer test (empirical study). Results: MOTAT experiments were most informative and led to the highest transfer test performance. Conclusion: These findings provide initial evidence that VOTAT's core heuristic has a narrower scope than is commonly assumed. When variables are interrelated, deliberately varying more than one variable may be the better choice. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The parent bereavement questionnaire: A measure of grief severity and prolonged grief disorder for parents of young children
Abstract: Background The death of a child causes severe, disruptive grief. Prolonged grief disorder (PGD) was formally adopted as a diagnosis in DSM-5-TR in 2022. The Parent Bereavement Questionnaire (PBQ), a bereavement measure developed specifically for parents, was validated prior to these criteria, and its performance under current diagnostic standards is unknown. Methods We conducted a secondary analysis of 244 mothers (>12 months post-loss) whose infants died suddenly and unexpectedly from SIDS or unascertained causes, recruited through a large-scale, multi-center prospective cohort study that investigated risks for sudden infant death syndrome and international parent-support organizations. Ten PBQ items were mapped onto DSM-5-TR PGD criteria and evaluated for internal consistency, factor structure, and criterion validity; nine additional items assessing parent-salient grief domains were analyzed separately. Results The 10-item PBQ core demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = 0.88), a unidimensional factor structure. PBQ scores showed strong concordance with the algorithmic classification of probable PGD (AUC = 0.93); 23% of mothers met this probable-PGD threshold. Supplemental items reflecting social disconnection, self-blame, and difficulty trusting others formed distinct but related domains. Conclusions We provide psychometric support for the PBQ core as a brief, DSM-5-TR-aligned tool for screening PGD-associated symptoms in bereaved mothers, a population often disconnected from healthcare. Pediatricians and community providers may use it to identify at-risk parents and guide individualized, trauma-informed support. Supplemental domains such as social disconnection, self-blame, and difficulty trusting others may serve as correlates of PGD risk and as targets for tailored intervention. Copyright © 2026. Title: Livelihood Diversification and Migration Amid Climatic Risk Perception in Slash-and-Burn Agroecology in Northeast India: A Case Study
Abstract: Slash-and-burn agriculture in tropical forests is widely debated in the context of net-zero carbon emissions and global warming. In India, approximately two million hill tribes practice slash-and-burn agriculture, locally called jhumming, across 11 million hectares, with a high concentration in Northeast India. The present study aims to assess climatic risk perception in jhumming in Northeast India, examine livelihood diversification and labor migration as part of livelihood strategies, and finally propose policy measures to address the crisis. This is a case study based on a field investigation of 352 tribal households in Manipur, one of the Northeast Indian states where jhumming is predominant. The study finds that soil erosion, declining soil fertility, monsoon vagaries, and summer temperatures are the predominant perceived risks in cultivation. There are also non-ecological issues, such as market inaccessibility and infrastructure deficits. Approximately 72% of households have ‘zero’ income diversification, specializing in a single activity—farming. Rural non-farm diversification is very challenging here; customary land rights and physiography are key bottlenecks. Labor migration—accounting for around 36% of households—to urban centers contributes substantially to non-farm income diversification. Vertical crop diversification—value addition to existing crops and market linkage—would be a policy suggestion. It will enhance farmers’ income and make farming sedentary, resulting in a longer fallow period and a well-developed secondary forest. Meanwhile, organized labor migration can be placed in the policy arena, which has double benefits—minimizing livelihood crises and reducing pressure on forest resources. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Beyond financial literacy: The role of trust and neuropsychiatric symptoms in fraud vulnerability in dementia
Abstract: Background: Fraud vulnerability is an increasing concern in aging populations, particularly as financial activities shift to digital environments. Individuals with neurocognitive disorders may be especially vulnerable, yet the relative contribution of financial literacy, behavioral functioning, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and interpersonal factors remains poorly understood. This study examined these determinants in individuals with neurocognitive disorders. Methods: 290 individuals with neurocognitive disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, semantic dementia, and mild cognitive impairment, were enrolled. Financial vulnerability was assessed using the Financial Frailty Battery, a caregiver-administered instrument evaluating financial behaviors before and after disease onset. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were assessed with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Regression models examined predictors of fraud occurrence, fraud type, and fraud frequency. Results: Behavioral changes in everyday functioning and interpersonal trust emerged as the strongest correlates of fraud vulnerability. Behavioral tendencies (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [1.01, 1.19], p = .030) and trust (OR = 1.11, 95% CI [1.04, 1.18], p < .001) significantly predicted fraud victimization. Higher trust predicted non-digital (OR = 1.12, p = .005) and mixed fraud (OR = 1.19, p < .001), but not digital-only fraud (OR = 1.08, p = .101). Trust was also associated with repeated victimization (χ2(2) = 42.2, p < .001). Conclusions: Fraud vulnerability in neurocognitive disorders appears to be driven primarily by behavioral and interpersonal factors rather than financial knowledge alone. Preliminary evidence suggests partially different vulnerability profiles for digital and non-digital fraud, highlighting the need for prevention strategies tailored to different forms of financial exploitation. © 2026

Title: Modeling internalizing symptoms and substance use comorbidity using causal network methodology
Abstract: The cooccurrence of internalizing and substance use disorders can be explained from several perspectives, yet most are modeled in isolation and limited to correlational evidence. Advancements on two common etiological perspectives – i) internalizing symptoms predisposing toward substance use disorder symptoms, ii) transdiagnostic factors predisposing toward both symptom domains – are therefore hampered by scarce multivariate and causal evidence. The present study addressed this gap by modeling direct (causal) links from internalizing symptoms to substance use behaviors and (causal) links from the transdiagnostic factors cognitive control, locus of control (LOC), and meaning in life. We analyzed data from wave 7 (2019–2023; N = 1725), the 15-year follow-up of the ongoing longitudinal cohort study the Netherlands Study of Depression and Anxiety, using a correlational network and a causal network based on the fast causal inference algorithm. The correlational network showed that depression and social anxiety symptoms were positively related to alcohol-related problems and negatively related to alcohol consumption. Cognitive control and external LOC correlated positively with alcohol consumption. Meaning in life was negatively associated with depression and social anxiety symptoms, alcohol consumption, alcohol problems, and drug use. The causal network showed causal relations of external LOC with depression and social anxiety symptoms. Although our correlational findings gave some support to both perspectives on internalizing and substance use comorbidity, the present findings do not support a causal, etiological interpretation of these perspectives. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Pan S.; de Vries W.T.; Yi D.; Yi J.; Chen W.; Guo J.
Title: Expansion toward risk: China's urban growth reshapes population exposure to compound environmental pressures
Abstract: Rapid urban expansion is altering the distribution of environmental benefits and risks. As cities grow outward, newly developed areas may face elevated exposure to multiple environmental pressures, raising concerns about whether urbanization is inadvertently exposing population toward more adverse environmental conditions. To investigate this, we use population-weighted exposure model to quantify three key environmental exposures in China's newly built-up areas from 2000 to 2018: blue-green space exposure (BGE), PM2.5 exposure (PME), and heat stress exposure (HSE). By integrating SOM–K-means clustering and Bayesian Networks, we identify the evolution of typical environmental exposure combinations and examine their conditional dependencies. Results show that, from 2010 to 2018, BGE slightly improves, PME shows greater balance but persistent risks, while HSE intensified significantly. Clustering analysis identifies three distinct environmental exposure types: Ecological Deficiency (ED), High Environmental Cost (HEC), and Eco-Advantaged under Heat (EAH). In 2010, ED is the most prevalent type (1133 counties; 55.5%), followed by HEC (792 counties; 38.8%) and EAH (115 counties; 5.6%). By 2018, EAH increases to 386 counties (18.4%), while ED and HEC decline to 1052 (50.1%) and 664 (31.6%) counties, respectively. Notably, 466 ED counties transition to HEC, making ED-to-HEC the largest single transition. 146 counties transition from ED to EAH, indicating ecological improvement accompanied by greater heat stress. Together, these changes reveal a pattern of urban expansion toward risks. Bayesian Networks further reveal a reconfiguration in the conditional dependency structure of environmental exposures, moving from a relatively constrained dependency pattern toward a more interconnected configuration, with BGE becoming more centrally embedded in the network. This study contributes a novel integrative framework for understanding how urban expansion reshapes population exposure to compound environmental pressures and provides insights to inform risk-aware and equitable urban governance. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: From the couch to the arena: Prefrontal cortex network dynamics of reward and loss processing during gameplay across internet gaming disorder symptom severity
Abstract: This study employed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) to investigate how gameplay contexts differing in sense of agency are associated with prefrontal cortex (PFC) network dynamics during reward and loss processing, and how these dynamics relate to Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD) symptom severity. Eighty-four college students participated in the experiment. Data-driven clustering identified three recurrent PFC connectivity states across active gameplay (higher-agency) and passive viewing (lower-agency) conditions. Compared with passive viewing, active gameplay recruited the high connectivity state more frequently during both reward and loss processing. Furthermore, IGD symptom severity was associated with context-dependent changes in the occurrence probability and network topology of PFC network states during reward and loss processing, with differential patterns emerging across gameplay conditions differing in agency. These findings indicate that agency-related gameplay contexts are associated with distinct patterns of PFC network organization during reward and loss processing, whereas IGD symptom severity is associated with context-dependent network organization. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhong W.; Luo J.; Yu S.; Lyu Y.; Guo J.
Title: Navigating AI affective support: The cognitive-affective pathway from appraisal to emotional well-being in learners
Abstract: As affective artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in educational contexts, understanding how learners emotionally engage with such systems is both timely and critical. Grounded in cognitive appraisal theory and the theory of affective bonding, this research examines how students interpret AI-delivered affective support during academic stress. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 202; N = 394), we find that AI affective support enhances emotional well-being via affective resonance, the perceived emotional alignment between learner and agent. Study 1 shows that affective resonance mediates the effect of AI affective support on positive and negative affect. Study 2 advances a process model in which learners' appraisals of task value and perceived AI emotional affordance are associated with emotional valence, which in turn is associated with affective resonance. Preliminary evidence suggests this indirect effect is stronger when tasks are perceived as personally meaningful. Our findings indicate that emotional responses to AI are not passive reactions to expressive cues but are actively constructed through motivational and cognitive appraisal. By clarifying how learners perceive and internalize AI affective support, this study extends theoretical understanding of human–AI interaction in education and offers actionable guidance for designing emotionally attuned learning technologies that support engagement, resilience, and well-being. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wald K.A.
Title: Self-awareness and negotiations
Abstract: How does directing attention toward oneself, or self-awareness, affect one's performance in a negotiation? This article reviews recent research on self-awareness and discusses the implications of these findings for a negotiator's actions before, during, and after a negotiation. Before a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's choice to negotiate in the first place, one's planned strategy, and one's preparedness to manage difficulties. During a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's ability to adapt one's tactics and make ethical choices, and outward expressions of self-awareness may affect one's counterpart's perceptions of oneself. After a negotiation, self-awareness may affect one's self-reflection and ability to improve. Altogether, these findings shed light on a variety of possible effects of self-awareness on negotiations, and point to directions for future research. © 2026 The Author

Authors: Esposito A.
Title: The EU challenge to make its ports more sustainable and competitive: The case of the Green Ports Project for the Port of Naples
Abstract: Today European ports have moved beyond their traditional role as logistical gateways to become strategic infrastructure for energy, supply-chain resilience and urban development. In this context, port competitiveness can no longer be understood only in terms of logistical performance but must be assessed within a governance model capable of integrating environmental sustainability and territorial resilience. Against this background, this research reconstructs the European framework on port competitiveness and sustainability and analyses its effectiveness in shaping governance conditions and supporting sustainability-oriented projects. In particular, Regulation 2017/352 and Regulation 2024/1679 are examined as legislative acts that establish an institutional bridge between competitiveness and environmental objectives. This approach is further strengthened by the 2026 Communications on the EU Ports Strategy and the Industrial Maritime Strategy. The research adopts a qualitative methodology grounded in regulatory assessment, combining a multi-level legal analysis of the EU and Italian frameworks with an explanatory case study focusing on the Port of Naples and its involvement in the Green Ports Project under Italy’s Recovery and Resilience Plan. To better understand the case study, the article first examines the evolution of Italian legislation on port competitiveness and sustainability: from Law No. 84/1994, which promoted reforms to reshape the Italian port system, to Legislative Decree No. 169/2016, which created Port System Authorities and introduced the Energy and Environmental Planning Document. The research argues that, despite the impact of these reforms, pronounced governance fragmentation is still compromising the development of a sustainable strategy for the port and the surrounding city. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: A longitudinal study of supervisor support as a moderator in maintaining work engagement during working from home: A moderated moderated-mediation model
Abstract: Maintaining employee work engagement during extended periods of work from home (WFH) is essential for sustaining productivity. Although prior research highlights the detrimental effects of job stress and imbalanced work demands on burnout and engagement, few studies explore how supervisor support mitigates these effects over time. This study examines such relationships as WFH progresses. Panel data from 145 participants, collected at multiple time points over a 10-month period, reveal that as the WFH period extends, supervisor support becomes increasingly effective in alleviating the negative impact of job demands and perceived stress on burnout. This reduction in burnout subsequently contributes to the sustained work engagement of employees. These findings offer valuable insights into the role of supervisor support during extended WFH periods and provide recommendations for managing burnout and maintaining engagement in remote work environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Thulin E.J.
Title: Prevalence and correlates of GenerativeAI chatbot use for mental health concerns in higher education students
Abstract: Background: Large language model chatbots are increasingly used for mental health help-seeking, with general-purpose systems like ChatGPT becoming popular among young adults despite concerns about accuracy and misinformation. High rates of mental distress in higher education attending emerging adults make them an important focal population to characterize and contextual the use of generativeAI models for mental health in. Methods: Data were collected from the 2024-2025 Healthy Minds Study at a large, public 4-year university. Of 12,000 students invited, 2071 participated; 896 bachelor-level students aged 18–24 years were randomly selected to complete a module with generativeAI questions, and 809 (90.2%) had complete data. Measures included chatbot use for mental health support, perceived AI trustworthiness, AI knowledge, mental health diagnosis, perceived need for help, past-year mental health treatment, barriers to care, other forms of informal help-seeking, and demographics. Weighted logistic regression models examined associations between these variables and chatbot use for mental health support. Results: 15.4% of students reported using generalized chatbots for mental health help-seeking. Significant correlates included greater perceived need for help, experiencing more barriers to clinical care use, higher perceived trust in AI for mental health information, lower AI knowledge, and identifying as Asian. Specific barriers of financial constraints, limited time, fear of clinician mistreatment due to identity and privacy concerns were linked to chatbot usage. Conclusions: GenerativeAI chatbots are a notable source of mental health support for college students, especially among those facing access barriers and who perceive AI as trustworthy. Future initiatives should educate young adults about chatbot capabilities and limitations and promote equitable mental health support. © 2026 The Author

Title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
Abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Chamberlain R.
Title: Teaching people to draw is teaching people to look
Abstract: Artists have long observed that drawing facilitates a way of looking at the world more attentively. Psychological research has sought to evaluate this claim by investigating the association between drawing abilities and training, and performance on visuospatial tasks. This body of research literature has shown that some visuospatial abilities are enhanced in those that have better drawing abilities, specifically those that require integration of stored perceptual and cognitive schemas, and flexible visual attention. Longitudinal research has further shown that learning how to draw leads to changes in the way that visuospatial tasks are approached, suggesting that drawing involves strategies designed to circumvent the limits of perception. Such insights are valuable in the context of an environment that often precludes looking slowly and closely, and suggest that teaching drawing may be an effective way of teaching people how to look. © 2026

Title: Structural heterogeneity and spatial clustering in mountain agriculture: Evidence from European compensatory payments in the Central-Southern Apennines (Italy)
Abstract: Mountain agriculture is characterised by marked structural diversity, yet comparatively less attention has been devoted to understanding how this heterogeneity is spatially organised across territories. While previous studies have mainly examined farm structural characteristics at the individual holding level, their territorial organisation has received comparatively less attention in the literature. This study investigates the spatial organisation of farm structural heterogeneity among beneficiaries of Measure 13 (M13) in the Molise Region (Italy), using total farm area and land fragmentation as complementary indicators of farm structure. Starting from parcel-level administrative and geographical information, farm centroids were reconstructed and combined with structural indicators to analyse local spatial association through Local Moran's I statistics. The results reveal clear spatial clustering for both farm size and land fragmentation, identifying distinct territorial configurations characterised by relatively large and consolidated farms as well as areas dominated by small and fragmented holdings. These findings demonstrate that structural characteristics are not randomly distributed but exhibit well-defined territorial patterns that cannot be fully captured through conventional farm-level analyses. The proposed approach provides a territorial perspective for interpreting structural heterogeneity in mountain agriculture and offers a methodological framework that may be applied to the analysis of agricultural structures in other geographical contexts. The results also provide useful evidence for the design of place-sensitive rural development policies capable of addressing the diversity of structural conditions within disadvantaged mountain areas. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Navigating the unspoken: A qualitative study of how clinical nurse educators transmit tacit knowledge to nursing students
Abstract: Background: In nursing education, a significant body of knowledge essential for professional practice is tacit—difficult to articulate, yet crucial for clinical judgment, ethical comportment, and professional identity formation. Understanding how clinical nurse educators perceive and transmit this tacit knowledge is critical for optimizing student preparation. Objective: This study aimed to explore the experiences of clinical nurse educators in identifying, conveying, and cultivating tacit knowledge among nursing students. Design: A descriptive qualitative study. Methods: The study involved in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 20 clinical nurse educators who were purposively sampled from 15 Chinese provinces and possessed ≥5 years of teaching experience. Data were collected from July to October 2025 and analyzed using thematic analysis, from which the key themes and subthemes were derived. Results: Four themes and 12 subthemes were extracted. The themes were The nature and expression of tacit knowledge in clinical nursing education, Strategies for transmitting tacit knowledge, Challenges in tacit knowledge transmission, Organizational support and cultural nurturing. Conclusions: Tacit knowledge is fundamental, not optional, to nursing practice. Its effective transmission hinges on deliberate pedagogy, supportive structures, and a reflective mentoring culture. These findings provide a foundation for developing clinical education frameworks and faculty policies dedicated to cultivating competent, compassionate, and ethically aware nurses. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Najib Nia N.; Alquist J.
Title: Rocky past, hazy future: Childhood adversity and adult prospection
Abstract: Two preregistered studies tested whether childhood adversity is associated with hazy future thinking, characterized by reduced clarity and detail in imagined future events and a more negative emotional outlook toward the future, and whether it is related to higher levels of intolerance of uncertainty. In Study 1 ( N = 232; 77.2% female, 22% male, 0.8% other or not specified), when asked to consider the future, participants with higher childhood adversity reported less vivid, detailed, and optimistic future thoughts, with more hopelessness and negative emotions. In Study 2 ( N = 262; 79.4% female, 19.8% male, 0.8% other or not specified), higher adversity was related to lower confidence, persistence, and commitment regarding goals. Separating adversity into harshness and unpredictability revealed that unpredictability was more consistently associated with both cognitive and emotional aspects of hazy future thinking, even when controlling for harshness. Also, higher childhood unpredictability was associated with higher intolerance of uncertainty in both studies. These findings provide evidence that early-life unpredictability is related to less cognitively clear and more emotionally negative visions of the future. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Role of community engagement in industrial disaster risk management: A systematic literature review and bibliometric mapping
Abstract: Community engagement in disaster management refers to the active involvement of local populations in planning, preparedness, and response activities aimed at reducing disaster risks. In the context of industrial disasters, such engagement is critical for enhancing resilience and minimizing cascading impacts. This study aimed to systematically review the role of community engagement in industrial disaster preparedness and response. The primary objective was to synthesize existing evidence on participatory approaches and their effectiveness in improving disaster risk management. Publications from 2000 to 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches of Scopus, Google Scholar and grey literature sources, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From an initial dataset of 578 records, 446 were screened after duplicate removal, and a total of 27 studies met the final inclusion criteria. These were analyzed using thematic synthesis and bibliometric mapping techniques with VOSviewer and R-bibliometrix. Findings indicate that community-based disaster risk reduction (CBDRR) and community-led disaster risk management (CLDRM) approaches are widely reported to enhance preparedness, trust, and adaptive capacity. Engagement strategies such as participatory GIS, scenario planning, serious games, and co-created early warning systems were identified as effective. However, challenges persist, including tokenistic participation, technological exclusion, and limited integration of local knowledge into policy frameworks. Triangulating the systematic and bibliometric findings further reveals a geographic divide, where advanced participatory tools are concentrated in high-income regions, leaving gaps in underrepresented industrial zones. The review underscores the need for institutionalizing participatory governance, fostering multi-sectoral collaboration, and leveraging technology inclusively. In essence, this article highlights community engagement as a cornerstone of industrial disaster resilience and provides actionable insights for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers seeking to advance equitable and proactive disaster risk management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Linking need for cognitive closure to cyberchondria among health information seekers: Disentangling the roles of uncertainty discrepancy, health worry and information processing evaluations
Abstract: Despite growing research on online health information seeking behaviors, the psychological factors through which dispositional characteristics are linked to maladaptive information outcomes such as cyberchondria remain underexplored. Drawing on the Theory of Motivated Information Management (TMIM), this study establishes a conceptual framework to examine how the need for cognitive closure is associated with cyberchondria through interpretive constructs (i.e., uncertainty discrepancy and health worry) and evaluative assessments (i.e., perceived health information overload and self-efficacy). The study examines the pattern of associations among these information management constructs as theorized by TMIM. Analysis of data from 581 adults using structural equation modeling demonstrates that the need for cognitive closure was directly associated with cyberchondria and was also positively associated with uncertainty discrepancy and health worry. Uncertainty discrepancy and health worry were associated with perceived information overload and self-efficacy, and perceived information overload and self-efficacy were associated with cyberchondria. This research offers insights into the information management constructs associated with cyberchondria by illustrating how dispositional factors are linked to maladaptive information management outcomes in a pattern consistent with the structure theorized by TMIM. Because the data are cross-sectional, this structure reflects a theoretical ordering assumed by the framework rather than an empirically established temporal sequence. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Jiang L.; Liu Y.; Zhao H.
Title: Spatial trajectories and land-use potential of China's utility-scale photovoltaic expansion toward 2035
Abstract: China aims to reach 3600 GW of combined wind and solar capacity by 2035, requiring substantial expansion of utility-scale photovoltaic (PV) deployment. Quantifying the geospatial footprint of this expansion is essential for sustainable land-use planning and ecological protection. This study develops a nationwide assessment framework that integrates multi-source remote sensing observations, Random Forest (RF) suitability modeling, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for model interpretation, and scenario-based spatial allocation. Historical PV data from 2000 to 2025 show that China's utility-scale PV farms expanded to 13,800 km2, with growth concentrated in northwestern mega-bases and emerging decentralized installations in central-eastern regions, indicating a dual-track spatial trajectory. Scenario projections suggest that Scenario B (NDC Update-Aligned Pathway) requires an additional 21,420 km2, whereas Scenario C (Wind-Slowdown Compensation) increases land demand moderately to 24,405 km2. Scenario A (Business as Usual) could require up to 63,990 km2 and would disproportionately affect croplands and forests. However, China retains more than 206,000 km2 of high-potential land, indicating that ecological conflicts are driven mainly by spatial mismatch rather than absolute land scarcity. These findings underscore the need for integrated spatial governance, optimized ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission, and distributed PV deployment. By linking observed spatial trajectories, interpretable suitability modeling, and capacity-to-land translation, this study provides a transferable framework for assessing the land-use potential of utility-scale PV expansion toward 2035. © 2026

Authors: Tinio P.P.L.
Title: Toward a greater understanding of profound and complex experiences during engagement with art
Abstract: This review focuses on two contemporary trends in the psychology of art. The first is a shift in research focus from hedonically based judgments of art, such as liking, preference, and beauty, toward more complex and profound outcomes of art engagement, such as experiencing self-transcendent emotions, experiencing a greater sense of meaning in life, and sensing personal transformation (awe, absorption, and being inspired and moved). The second trend involves new approaches to characterizing and conceptualizing art engagement. Examples include network analysis and latent profile analysis that help reveal the hidden and multidimensional nature of the aesthetic experience of art. Together, these trends suggest a shift toward understanding of art engagement as a multidimensional experience that can shape cognition, emotions, and the self. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The power of noticing the good: The mediating role of reward perception in the effect of mindfulness on depression and suicidal ideation

Abstract: Background: Although dispositional mindfulness is inversely associated with mental health problems and suicidal ideation, the behavioral mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear. This study investigated whether environmental reward perception mediates this association. Method: In a cross-sectional study of 407 Colombian adults, Kendall’s tau correlations and bootstrapping mediation analysis with 5,000 resamples and bias-corrected 95% confidence intervals were used to estimate indirect effects. Results: Mindfulness positively correlated with reward perception; both inversely correlated with depression and suicidal ideation. The model revealed a significant indirect effect of mindfulness on depression (ab = −0.281, 95% CI [-0.335, −0.226]) and suicidal ideation (ab = −0.367, 95% CI [−0.427, −0.308]) through reward perception. Conclusions: The findings were consistent with an indirect association between dispositional mindfulness and both depression and suicidal ideation through environmental reward perception. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted as theoretically consistent associations rather than evidence of a causal mediation process. However, these indirect associations illustrate the value of this analytic approach for identifying candidate mediators such as environmental reward perception, which can subsequently inform the design of future longitudinal and intervention research on mindfulness-based approaches to depression and suicide prevention. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. Title: Tracing locations from pixels: A survey of worldwide image geo-localization
Abstract: Worldwide image geo-localization (WIGL) estimates the geographic coordinates of a photograph from its visual content, without metadata on the query image and without a known search area. This capability supports practical applications, including cybercrime source tracing, disaster response, and autonomous navigation. In this manuscript, a comprehensive review of WIGL is presented, in which current methods are systematically organized into four paradigms: classification-based, retrieval-based, generation-based, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). For each paradigm, representative approaches and core design principles are examined, with their strengths and limitations compared. Training, testing, and fine-tuning datasets are also reviewed in depth. A spatial distribution analysis of these datasets reveals notable coverage biases in existing benchmarks. Standard evaluation metrics are consolidated, and the reported results on six test sets are aggregated, providing a common basis for comparison across methods. The comparative analysis of reported results indicates that RAG approaches currently achieve the highest accuracy on major benchmarks, though this advantage is partly confounded by larger backbone models and training data while generation-based approaches offer a promising alternative for zero-shot location inference. Finally, several under-explored research challenges that are rarely discussed in prior surveys are identified and outlined. These include the difficulty of disambiguating visually similar images captured at distant locations, as well as other open problems to guide future work. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Diagnosing systematic overestimation and feature dependencies in data-driven predictions of urban CO₂ emissions in China
Abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to simulate and predict complex urban phenomena, such as CO₂ emission patterns in cities. However, the effectiveness, biases, and uncertainty of these predictive models are not well understood. This study systematically evaluates 18 different machine learning algorithms using a rich dataset of county-level CO₂ emissions in China from 2001 to 2020, incorporating 41 diverse features spanning socioeconomic, environmental, and energy consumption factors. The analysis reveals a widespread issue: nearly all models, regardless of type, tend to systematically overestimate emissions in Chinese county-level cities across both space and time. By isolating the effects of feature selection and quantifying uncertainty through bootstrap resampling, the research demonstrates that aggressive dimensionality reduction often harms model performance, while retaining a high number of features is crucial for capturing the true complexity of urban emissions. Tree-based models, such as CatBoost and LightGBM, outperform others in accuracy and uncertainty quantification. These findings highlight the urgent need for the scientific and policy communities to prioritize diagnosing and correcting systematic biases in machine learning models, rather than focusing solely on improving accuracy, to ensure reliable guidance for urban carbon management and climate policy. © 2026

Authors: Hart E.
Title: Post-negotiation behavior and attitudes: We have a deal, now what?
Abstract: Negotiators often equate “winning” with securing favorable agreement terms, yet the agreement is only one outcome of the negotiation process—and may not be the most important, particularly when interactions continue after the deal. This review broadens the lens to encompass post-negotiation outcomes, including emotions, satisfaction, relational perceptions, contract implementation, and subsequent behaviors. Considering a wider range of outcomes deepens understanding of the costs and benefits of negotiation, and can shed light on negotiation initiation and strategy. Integrating post-negotiation behavior also reveals when and why economic and relational motives collide. Title: Identifying and Mitigating Legal and Contractual Risks in BIM-Enabled Construction Projects: A Conceptual Framework
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Building information modeling (BIM) is accelerating across Saudi Arabia's construction sector in support of Vision 2030, yet its legal and contractual integration lags behind technical adoption. This study investigates the legal and contractual risks associated with BIM-enabled project delivery and proposes a conceptual framework to guide risk mitigation in the Saudi context. A total of 21 BIM-related legal risk factors were identified from a comprehensive literature review and refined through a pilot study. An online questionnaire survey was administered to construction practitioners (consultants and contractors), yielding 87 valid responses for analysis. Principal component analysis revealed two latent dimensions: legal and regulatory ambiguities and BIM model management and technical risks. Mean-rank analysis identified the lack of coordination and control over the BIM model, lack of clarity regarding BIM standards and processes in the contract, and unclear rights and responsibilities related to BIM were ranked as the top risk factors. Synthesizing the empirical findings with mitigation strategies identified through an extensive literature review, the study developed a seven-pillar conceptual framework for risk mitigation: (1) standardization and legal infrastructure; (2) contractual clarity and enforceability; (3) roles, responsibilities, and liability; (4) ownership and intellectual property; (5) confidentiality and security; (6) data integrity and interoperability; and (7) collaboration and dispute resolution. The findings extend the limited scholarship on BIM's legal and contractual risks in Saudi Arabia and offer context-aware guidance for policymakers and practitioners to embed BIM-specific provisions aimed at mitigating dispute propensity in BIM-enabled construction projects.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Defining trauma-informed approaches and their purpose in nursing education: A scoping review
Abstract: Background: A focus on nursing student trauma has increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Scholars have turned to trauma-informed approaches to understand how nursing students can be better supported in their education and mitigate the effects of past, current, and future trauma exposure. Aim: To examine the current published literature on how trauma-informed approaches to nursing education are described in the literature. Design: We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute framework. We used the PRISMA-ScR guidelines for reporting of findings. Methods: We performed searches in June 2024 and then again in June 2025 in Medline via OVID, CINAHL via EBSCO, ERIC, PsycInfo, Education Research Complete, and Scopus. We included literature published in English in any year that focused on nursing students and/or nurse educators, included a definition of a trauma-informed approach (TIA) and involved any education context. Results: 35 sources were included, published between 2020 and 2025. Study types included 11 descriptions of implementing a TIA and 6 unstructured reviews supporting its implementation. 10 sources were primary research. Findings included descriptive categories of definitions of a TIA, sources of nursing students' exposure to trauma (in their education, personal lives, and specifically COVID-19), and the purpose of a TIA (success in education and the creation of a future workforce). Conclusions: TIA to support student learning and develop the future nursing workforce are increasingly prevalent and recommended in the nursing education literature. Terminology and definitions of TIA varied but often shared commonalities, with some specifically addressing structural inequities. Differences between definitions that highlight structural inequities specifically need to be examined for how they differ from more common definitions. The student perspective on resilience and TIA effectiveness is needed. Conceptualizations of TIA must also address how they might reinforce power structures within educational institutions, thereby avoiding the reproduction of inequities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Welfare analysis of electricity distribution: The Dignity Tariff in Bolivia
Abstract: We conduct an analysis of the demand functions associated with electricity distribution in Bolivia, focusing on the implications of price fluctuations on consumer welfare. This analysis requires the estimation of demand functions, which we achieve through the application of panel data with fixed effects and the use of instrumental variables. Additionally, we apply propensity score matching (PSM) to compare electricity expenditures between beneficiary and comparable non-beneficiary households, providing an independent welfare estimate grounded in observed household behaviour rather than structural demand parameters alone. In 2006, the Bolivian government introduced the Dignity Tariff, aimed at regulating electricity distribution costs for both urban and rural households. This tariff offers a 25% reduction in electricity prices for households that consume up to 70 kWh per month. Our key findings indicate that the Dignity Tariff effectively acts as a subsidy for electricity consumption. Estimates derived from demand functions suggest an average monthly welfare gain ranging from Bs 17.98 to Bs 21.12 (USD 2.58 to USD 3.03), while propensity score matching yields an average monthly saving of approximately Bs 47 (USD 6.75) for beneficiary households, providing significant financial relief to economically vulnerable populations. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Du Y.-W.; Shang Y.-X.
Title: Hierarchical DEMATEL-based key risk identification for urban public safety within grid management
Abstract: With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Nabi, Amim Altaf (59236287800); Nema, Arvind Kumar (6602915232)
Title: An adaptive methodology for determining the optimal transition point and reuse lifespan of photovoltaic panels considering degradation-adjusted energy yield
Abstract: End-of-Life (EoL) management of Photovoltaic (PV) panels is an emerging concern for waste managers and policymakers, given the high rates of PV deployment worldwide. Existing studies emphasize the benefits of PV recycling, but there are few assessments of panel reuse. Identification of the appropriate transition point from reuse to recycling that balances economic and environmental trade-offs is much needed. Studies that do engage with this domain fail to account for the operational and maintenance (O&M) and EoL costs incurred during the reuse phase. With the aims of sustainable waste management, the present study develops a dynamic techno-economic and environmental optimization framework for PV reuse, based on a scalarized multi-objective analysis, referred to as the Reuse Time Span Optimization Model (RTOM). RTOM integrates degradation-adjusted energy generation and monetized environmental benefits into an economic optimization model while accounting for O&M and EoL costs. Results indicate that, after a first life of 25 years, PV panels can be optimally reused for up to 13 years, yielding substantial net benefits. It shows that reuse boosts PV panel benefits by eight times (8×) compared to recycling. The study concludes that reuse is beneficial only within an optimal reuse duration; beyond which, it is no longer advantageous. A Monte Carlo-based sensitivity analysis is used to capture parameter uncertainty and evaluate robustness. The developed RTOM is a decision-support framework that is adaptable and transferable by modifying region-specific parameters. Overall, this work advances the discourse on PV waste management by repositioning reuse as a viable and preferable strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Author full names: Richardson, Corianne (58353321400); Langtree, Tanya (55794225600); Biedermann, Narelle (6603454236); McAuliffe, Marie (55871688800); Wicking, Kristin (57195763535)
Title: From clinician to coach: Immediate learning and experiences of mental health nurses following a coaching for clinical nurses (C4CN) workshop
Abstract: Background: Coaching is increasingly used to strengthen nursing leadership and reflective practice, yet limited evidence describes how workplace coaches are prepared or how coaching education supports capability and role clarity in healthcare environments. Aim: To explore mental health nurses' experiences of a Coaching for Clinical Nurses (C4CN) workshop and examine immediate learning in developing workplace coaching capability and emerging coach role. Design: Exploratory qualitative analysis of a preparatory workshop within a constructivist embedded case study. Methods: The two-day workshop was delivered to 13 clinical leaders working in a single adult inpatient mental health unit in Queensland, Australia, in preparation for a six-month workplace coaching intervention. Workshop material included written reflections and group discussions, anonymous real-time responses and facilitator reflective session notes. Inductive reflexive thematic analysis was used to examine immediate learning and understandings of workplace coaching. Results: Four themes captured participants' learning: personal and leadership commitment to coaching; integration of coaching into daily routines; practical application of coaching; and self-development and confidence building. Subthemes reflected an emerging coaching mindset, coaching in the moment, structured coaching processes, developing coach identity and role clarity, and self-reflection and self-management. Participants described clearer coaching purpose and boundaries and growing confidence in coaching conversations. Experiential practice, peer dialogue and structured frameworks supported movement from technique towards a developmental leadership approach. Implications for nurse education: Workplace coach preparation should combine experiential skills development, reflective learning, role-boundary clarification and opportunities to practise coaching. Continuing development and organisational support are important for translation into practice. Conclusions: The C4CN workshop showed how experienced mental health nurses began developing workplace coaching capability and making sense of their coach role alongside other nursing and leadership responsibilities. The findings support workplace coach preparation as an experiential, reflective developmental process and provide a foundation for subsequent examination within the broader case study. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The increasing sensory richness of digitally-mediated experience
Abstract: Digital interfaces were once sensorially sparse. Contemporary technologies have changed this dramatically, expanding the sensory richness of digital interfaces across visual, auditory, haptic, olfactory, and even gustatory modalities, collectively narrowing the perceptual gap between digital and physical worlds. We present findings from a growing, multidisciplinary body of evidence examining how these evolving sensory affordances shape individuals' perceptions, judgments, and behaviors. We conclude by offering a selection of future research directions with particular attention to those whose implications extend beyond any single sensory channel into more fundamental questions about human experience. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: PEFT: Evaluating parameter-efficient fine-tuning for clinical-note summarization across transformers and large language models
Abstract: The need to analyze and summarize critical information from electronic health records places a significant burden on clinicians. Clinical-note summaries are vital for making healthcare more efficient and helping healthcare personnel keep track of their paperwork. While transformer models and large language models (LLMs) are efficient in this task, the computational cost and stringent performance requirements in healthcare present major challenges. This work addresses these challenges by evaluating parameter-efficient fine-tuning with low-rank adaptations (LoRA) techniques for abstractive clinical-note summarization.We conducted a full evaluation on the MIMIC-IV-Ext-BHC dataset, comparing four transformer models (T5, PEGASUS-XSUM, BART, and FLAN-T5) and four LLMs (Mistral-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and Falcon-7B) across zero-shot, full fine-tuning, and LoRA fine-tuning strategies. We also integrated LexRank, TextRank, LSA, and Luhn with clinical NLP functionalities from cTAKES for graph-based extractive summarization. In our investigation, LoRA achieved higher scores than full fine-tuning on key metrics while reducing the computational resource burden. Specifically, our LLaMA-3-8B model, fine-tuned with LoRA, achieved a ROUGE-1 score of 0.7022, ROUGE-2 of 0.5312, ROUGE-L of 0.6718, METEOR of 0.6787, and BERTScore F1 of 0.9180 on the test set. This represents a 2.6× improvement in ROUGE-1 over the extractive baseline, though direct comparison is limited by fundamental differences between extractive and abstractive approaches.These results were accomplished using approximately 97%–99% fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning. The findings indicate that LoRA could facilitate the implementation of LLMs within resource-constrained medical environments, and has the potential to improve healthcare professionals’ access to information and support clinical decision-making processes. © 2026 The Authors. Title: When AI meets DEI: Employee AI-beliefs and their implications for workplace diversity, equity, and inclusion
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the workplace, its impact on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) has been examined primarily through the lens of what AI actually does (i.e., system design, outputs). This review shifts the focus to humans' subjective beliefs about AI, identifying mechanisms through which three dimensions of AI-beliefs (competence, warmth, and morality) may affect DEI goals: improving representation of underrepresented groups, closing career gaps across groups, and fostering inclusion. Our synthesis shows that, independently of what AI does, AI-beliefs can disadvantage underrepresented groups in some contexts, while creating opportunities for bridging human subgroups in others. This suggests that achieving DEI goals in AI-integrated workplaces requires attention not only to the properties and behavior of AI, but also to employees’ beliefs about AI itself. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Mittal S.; Jha K.N.
Title: Emotional Factors in Quality Negligence: A Study of Residential Real Estate Construction Professionals
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Quality negligence in the construction industry, a significant originator of legal crises, is predominantly attributed to technical and procedural failures. However, the pivotal role of construction professionals' emotions as a precipitating factor remains a critically unexamined research area. This study addresses this gap by investigating the influence of specific emotions on quality negligence and its subsequent escalation into legal crises for construction firms. The research employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design. Initially, a comprehensive literature review and unstructured interviews with industry experts identified seven prominent emotions (anxiety, guilt, pride, shame, elevation, injustice, and gratitude). Subsequently, a quantitative phase involved distributing a self-administered questionnaire to 162 Indian construction professionals within the Indian residential construction sector to assess their emotional states and quality negligence levels. Data analysis using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM) indicated a statistically significant positive relationship between quality negligence and five emotions. The effects, in descending order of magnitude, were elevation (β=0.406, p<0.001), shame (β=0.405, p<0.001), gratitude (β=0.321, p<0.001), pride (β=0.261, p=0.009), and anxiety (β=0.179, p=0.047). In the final phase, consultations and brainstorming sessions with industry experts were used to identify the resulting legal crises and to establish a novel emotion-quality negligence-crises framework. This framework models the pathway from emotional antecedent to quality negligence and its culmination in a legal crisis. The study provides a critical diagnostic tool for practitioners in the real estate sector to mitigate risk and offers a new theoretical model for academics analyzing this psycho-legal connection.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Wang X.; Liu W.
Title: Drought, women's time poverty, and the development costs of water collection in Sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract: Drought can impose development costs that are not fully captured by income, production, or formal water access indicators. This paper examines one such hidden cost in Sub-Saharan Africa by focusing on women's time poverty arising from household water collection. Combining harmonized Demographic and Health Surveys with geocoded drought exposure measured at the survey cluster level, we estimate how local drought conditions are associated with women's annual water collection burden and broader household adjustments. We find that drought exposure is associated with higher water-collection time for women, with larger estimated increases among women living in poor households, women with no formal education, and women living in households without piped-water access. Intermediate-outcome evidence shows that drought is associated with lower local water availability and a higher likelihood of very long collection trips, particularly journeys exceeding 60 minutes. These water-time burdens are also associated with greater engagement in flexible, household-based, family-based, and self-employed forms of work among women rather than with a simple expansion of protected paid employment. In addition, higher community water burdens are associated with poorer schooling outcomes among girls, including a greater likelihood of being out of school and larger grade-for-age gaps. Household-linked evidence further shows that poorer girls’ schooling outcomes are associated with larger household shares of adult women in unpaid or in-kind work, self-employment, and family work. The findings suggest that drought-related water insecurity can redistribute adaptation costs within households, making women's unpaid time a key margin through which climate stress produces hidden development costs. © 2026

Authors: Zaborowska O.; Kuhlmann B.G.; Symeonidou N.; Hanczakowski M.; Zawadzka K.
Author full names: Zaborowska, Oliwia (57193802851); Kuhlmann, Beatrice G. (36655914500); Symeonidou, Nikoletta (57222983751); Hanczakowski, Maciej (38561386300); Zawadzka, Katarzyna (55361418900)
Title: Context memory in younger and older adults: Insights from metacognition
Abstract: Cognitive aging is characterized by a deterioration of episodic memory functions. Since episodic memory requires retrieval of context, it has been proposed that older adults suffer from a specific deficit in terms of remembering context associated with to-be-remembered information. At the same time, however, it has been argued that providing context information at the time of retrieval can ameliorate age-related memory deficits. These positions can be reconciled if older adults show a deficit in encoding specific, not meaningful (i.e., not related) item-context associations but demonstrate a preserved ability to encode meaningful item-context associations and retrieve them when both items and contexts are provided as cues. In three experiments, we demonstrate such a pattern of deficits and preserved functions by asking younger and older adults to encode pairs of words embedded in contexts, then varying whether these contexts are reinstated when the same pairs of words are restudied. We then examine how this manipulation affects – via spontaneous retrieval of item-context associations – metacognitive monitoring of the effectiveness of restudy in the form of judgments of learning (JOLs). Experiment 1, using semantically unrelated contexts, showed the context reinstatement effect in JOLs only for younger adults. Experiments 2 and 3, promoting encoding of context for older adults by using semantically related contexts, showed effects of context reinstatement for older and younger adults. Together, these results show that older adults sometimes fail to encode specific contextual associations, but if they do encode them, they experience no deficit in spontaneous retrieval of these associations. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.
