Authors: Li Q.; Chen H.; Lin Y.
Title: Trust begins at home: The role of psychological distance in trust transfer for emerging technology
Abstract: The widespread adoption of emerging technologies holds substantial potential to benefit societal development. However, fostering public trust and acceptance of emerging technologies, which involve complex underlying principles and are in pre-commercialization stages, remains a critical multifaceted challenge. To address this issue, this study draws on trust transfer theory to identify an effective mechanism for enhancing people's trust in emerging technologies. Specifically, we propose and test that trust in emerging technologies can be transferred from that in familiar institutions of the public by reducing psychological distance to such technologies. Analyzing quota-sampling data, we find that greater consumption of news about local brain–computer interface (BCI) achievements was associated with greater trust in local technology institutions. Institutional process and purpose trust were, in turn, associated with lower psychological distance to BCI, which was associated with greater general trust in BCI and, subsequently, stronger BCI use intention. The corresponding pathway was not supported for performance trust. These findings extend trust transfer theory by introducing psychological distance as a vital mechanism. Practically, this study demonstrates a route through which practitioners can promote public acceptance of unfamiliar and emerging technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Uysal, Mehmet (61014496800); İşbulan, Onur (35423778300); Demirel, Ayşen (60531333700)
Title: Is knowledge a buffer or a burden? The mediating role of AI literacy in the relationship between medical AI readiness and AI anxiety in nursing education
Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare, yet AI anxiety remains a significant barrier to its adoption. Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between Medical AI Readiness and AI Anxiety among nursing students and to determine the mediating role of AI Literacy in this relationship. Methods: A descriptive, cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with a convenience sample of 302 undergraduate nursing students at a university in Istanbul, Türkiye. Data were collected using the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale (MAIRS), Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS), and Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), and analyzed using the Hayes PROCESS macro (Model 4). Results: The findings revealed a “Paradox of Preparedness,” where Medical AI Readiness was a significant positive predictor of AI Anxiety (B = 0.435, p < .001). Contrary to theoretical expectations that competence mitigates fear, students with higher readiness and literacy levels reported higher anxiety, with AI Literacy partially mediating this relationship (Indirect effect: B = 0.119, 95% CI [0.034, 0.218]). Conclusion: These results theoretically suggest that students may experience a state of “perceived incompetence,” where self-reported literacy grants awareness of AI's risks without the corresponding perceived technical skills to manage them. Consequently, nursing curricula must transition from passive AI awareness to active empowerment, integrating human-in-the-loop ethics and hands-on technical training to build professional confidence. © 2026

Authors: Sun Z.; Zhao X.; Wang X.; Li Q.; Ran Y.; Zhang D.
Title: Synergy threshold-guided ecological zoning: Evidence of the response of carbon-water-biodiversity nexus to human activity intensity
Abstract: Intensive human activities in rapidly urbanizing areas have altered ecosystem structure and function, undermining the stability of the carbon–water–biodiversity synergy network. This poses challenges for implementing sustainable ecological management. Therefore, this study develops a coupled analytical framework linking human activity intensity with the carbon–water–biodiversity nexus and applies the XGBoost–SHAP model to identify nonlinear responses and threshold effects of the interactions among carbon, water, and biodiversity in the central Yunnan urban agglomeration. On this basis, an ecological zoning scheme is formulated. The results show that (1) Human activity intensity exhibits a center-to-periphery decline, resulting in a spatial pattern dominated by low and very low intensity levels. A reduction in carbon–water–biodiversity functions is observed, with water yield showing the most significant decrease. (2) Pairwise and overall relationships among carbon, water, and biodiversity transition from synergy to trade-offs as human activity intensifies, although synergy continues to dominate in moderately disturbed areas. Spatially, the configuration characterized by high carbon storage, high biodiversity, and low water yield emerges as the dominant functional pattern. (3) The overall relationship among carbon, water, and biodiversity shifts from synergy to trade-off at human activity intensity thresholds of 0.34 in 2010 and 0.33 in 2023. The synergy between water and biodiversity weakens and shifts to a trade-off at thresholds of 0.32 in 2010 and 0.31 in 2023. In contrast, the synergy between carbon and biodiversity strengthens at thresholds of 0.35 in 2010 and 0.32 in 2023. No clear threshold is observed for the relationship between carbon and water. (4) Based on the estimated thresholds, five ecological functional zones were delineated: core protection zone, buffer regulation zone, critical synergy zone, optimization and enhancement zone, and repair priority zone, with corresponding management strategies developed. The ecological zoning paradigm developed in this study offers guidance for the precise governance of land space in similar regions. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Forty-year trends in heavy and high-intensity alcohol use among U.S. Adults: The national alcohol survey series from 1984 to 2024
Abstract: Background Attention to drinking beyond the binge threshold have primarily focused on young adults. Given recent increases in alcohol consumption across age and other demographic groups, this study examined trends in past-year heavy episodic drinking (HED; consuming 5 or more drinks in a single day) and high-intensity drinking (HID; consuming 8 or more and 12 or more drinks in a single day) for U.S. men and women by age, race and ethnicity, and socioeconomic status from 1984 to 2024. Methods Nine National Alcohol Surveys of general population samples of U.S. adults ages 18 years or older were pooled from 1984 to 2024 (n = 59,514). Weighted sex-specific descriptive and time-varying effect models of past-year any use (prevalence) and number of days (frequency) of 5+, 8+, and 12 + drinks on a single day were conducted to describe trends by age, race and ethnicity, and education level. Results Prevalence of any heavy episodic drinking (HED: 5 + ) and any high-intensity drinking (HID: 8 + and 12 + ) have declined since 1984. From 2010 to 2024, days of HED and HID (frequencies) have increased for women, but less so for men. Variations were found by age, with declines among young adults and increases among middle-aged and older adults. Conclusions While declines in excessive alcohol consumption were observed since 1984, increases in HED and HID frequencies since the 2010 s, particularly among women and older adults, require more tailored public health intervention to reduce alcohol-related consequences, morbidity and mortality. Monitoring heavy drinking trends is important to drive data-informed policy efforts to reduce alcohol-related harms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Firefighter turnout gear limits the ability to reach down for an object without flexing the spine
Abstract: The restrictive nature of firefighter turnout gear may influence firefighter's ability to lift low-lying objects using strategies aimed at mitigating low back disorder risk. This study examined the influence of each component of firefighter turnout gear on how far they could reach down for an object with their spine physically restricted from forward flexion. Wearing any component of fire gear restricted reach depth ( p < 0.001). The greatest amount of restriction, compared to wearing station fatigues, occurred when firefighters wore full gear with boots (12 cm, 95% confidence interval = [10, 14]). There was no statistical difference in restriction when firefighters wore only fire pants versus wearing only fire jacket and oxygen tank. Wearing boots only had a significant impact when firefighters wore full gear (average difference = 2 cm, 95% confidence interval = [1, 3], p < 0.001). Firefighter turnout gear limits the ability to lift low-lying objects without flexing the lumbar spine. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Who gets to negotiate? Tracing gender gaps in structural empowerment with people analytics
Abstract: Gender differences in compensation and career advancement are often examined through the lens of negotiation behavior, initiation, outcomes, and stereotyping. We shift attention to the organizational structures that precede and shape formal negotiations. Drawing on organizational gender research, we use structural empowerment as an organizing framework to review and synthesize the literature on organizational structures that may shape who gains access to negotiations and the negotiation power employees bring to them. Existing research documents gender differences in access to opportunities, information, support, and resources, yet their implications for negotiation access and power remain underexamined. We explain how people analytics can help scholars and practitioners trace these dispersed and longitudinal processes and outline directions for future research. We conclude with methodological, ethical, and theoretical considerations associated with using people analytics to examine these questions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Tell me what you read, and I will tell you what you remember: Evidence for personalized embeddings in memory modelling
Abstract: Computational models of memory have achieved considerable success by formalizing how traces are encoded, cued, and retrieved. However, the role that individual linguistic experience plays in shaping representational structure has been relatively understudied. Where the issue has been examined, most models assume that a common population-level semantic space suffices, effectively treating individual variation in language experience as noise rather than signal. We test the theoretical adequacy of this assumption. In a large-scale experiment ( N = 478), participants completed a cued recall task in which identical target words were paired with cues drawn from eight different genre-specific semantic spaces (mystery, fantasy, horror, literary fiction, romance, science fiction, thriller, and non-fiction). Participants reported their reading habits across the eight genres, and personalized semantic representations were constructed by weighting genre-specific corpora proportionally to each participant's reading profile. Two complementary analyses were conducted. In a model-free analysis, cosine similarity computed within each participant's personalized semantic space predicted recall and omission outcomes more reliably than similarity derived from generic semantic spaces. In a computational analysis, substituting personalized representations into the embedded Computational Framework of Memory improved cue–target-level predictions over generic alternatives, accounting for approximately 4 percentage points more explained variance. These findings provide proof of concept that variation in individual linguistic experience shapes semantic structure in ways that are both behaviourally detectable and computationally tractable. More broadly, they suggest that the predictive limits of memory models may reside not only in their retrieval mechanisms but also in the fidelity of the representations they assume. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Smart city governance and public value creation: an analysis in emerging cities
Abstract: Governance is a core component of smart cities, yet further research is needed to understand its internal structure and interactions. This study analyzes how smart city governance (SCG) is configured and the types of public value it generates in two emerging economy cities: Medellín, Colombia, and Buenos Aires, Argentina. Using an exploratory qualitative approach, the research draws on 70 interviews, non-participant observation, and over 40 official documents. It proposes a socio-technical SCG model with four components: strategic management, collective intelligence, technological intelligence, contextual conditions, alongside a public value outcome dimension, 12 subcomponents and 15 types of public value. These values fall into two categories: urban sustainability and internal efficiency and effectiveness. The model offers an integrative framework for understanding SCG and guiding policy and program design. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Alternative Dispute Resolution in Construction Projects in the Middle East: A Systematic and Bibliometric Review
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: The construction industry in the Middle East is undergoing unprecedented growth driven by megaprojects, strategic national visions, and large-scale infrastructure development. This expansion has intensified the complexity of contractual relationships, leading to frequent disputes that challenge project performance, cost control, and timely delivery. While litigation has traditionally dominated dispute resolution, alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods such as arbitration, mediation, negotiation, and dispute review boards (DRBs) have gained prominence as more efficient and relationship-preserving mechanisms. This study provides an integrated systematic and bibliometric review of ADR in Middle Eastern construction projects, synthesizing findings from 77 peer-reviewed studies retrieved from Scopus and screened through a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-based process. Employing PRISMA guidelines and VOSviewer mapping, the research analyzes publication trends, thematic clusters, authorship networks, and country-specific practices. The results reveal the dominance of arbitration and litigation, the underutilization of mediation and DRBs, and significant legal variations across jurisdictions. The study highlights cultural factors such as hierarchy, honor, and relational norms as critical mediators of ADR effectiveness. Emerging innovations [including digital platforms, building information modeling (BIM), and expert systems] illustrate a shift toward technology-enabled dispute management. By bridging bibliometric evidence with thematic synthesis, this review contributes a comprehensive overview of ADR practices in the region, identifies gaps in enforcement and institutionalization, and proposes a holistic improvement agenda that balances legal reform, dispute avoidance, and sustainability. Findings provide actionable insights for policymakers, industry professionals, and international investors seeking to strengthen dispute resolution frameworks and enhance project outcomes across the Middle East.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Progressive resource allocation outperforms uniform strategies in enhancing urban vegetation growth offset: Evidence from DSTFormer-SHAP modeling across China's 19 urban agglomerations
Abstract: Urbanization degrades vegetation through direct land conversion while simultaneously stimulating residual vegetation growth through indirect environmental modifications. The growth offset coefficient (GO), measuring the degree to which indirect enhancement compensates for direct loss, serves as a key indicator of vegetation-growth compensation capacity; however, the nonlinear response, temporal lag structures, and optimal management strategies governing GO remain poorly understood. This study develops DSTFormer, a spatiotemporal Transformer integrated with SHAP analysis, and applies it to panel data from 227 cities across China's 19 major urban agglomerations from 2001 to 2022. Results indicate that GO increased at 0.0043 yr−1, with indirect enhancement (Ind) strengthening (0.0065 yr−1) faster than direct loss (DI) deepening (−0.0021 yr−1), although the net urbanization effect on vegetation remained negative throughout the study period. SHAP attribution identified forest landscape cohesion (FLCOHESION) as the leading positive predictive factor and impervious patch number (IMNP) as the main fragmentation-related constraint associated with GO variation. Temporal lag structures differed systematically across agglomeration types: the full sample and Optimization-Upgrading Agglomerations showed stronger recent contributions, whereas Cultivation-Development Agglomerations retained stronger historical contributions. Under identical total adjustment budgets, progressive temporal allocation was associated with larger predicted GO gains than uniform allocation. Spatial clustering further identified three regulatory regimes requiring differentiated interventions: a landscape-composition and infrastructure-environment mixed regime, a connectivity-fragmentation constraint regime, and a built-environment morphology and management-environment coupling regime. Title: Are explainable AI (XAI) evaluation strategies aligned? Comparing subjective, objective, and mathematical evaluation measures using saliency maps
Abstract: The evaluation of explainable AI (XAI) approaches often relies on three families of methods: subjective measures (e.g., questionnaires on trust or satisfaction), objective measures (e.g., task performance metrics), and mathematical metrics (e.g., for faithfulness). Yet, it remains unclear how these families align or diverge in practice. In a preregistered between-subjects study (N=166), we use three established saliency map techniques (LIME, Grad-CAM, Guided Backpropagation) as a testbed to examine this issue. We find that each family of methods leads to different conclusions: participants reported no differences in trust or satisfaction, Grad-CAM improved user performance, while mathematical metrics favored Guided Backpropagation. At the same time, mathematical metrics were only partially related to user performance, and these relationships were sometimes counterintuitive. Our findings highlight the methodological importance of comparing subjective, objective, and mathematical approaches when evaluating XAI, illustrating both tensions and aspects that are aligned. We discuss implications for XAI evaluation frameworks. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Psychological vulnerability in conversational AI: How incentive and urgency manipulations alter trust formation and privacy behaviour across healthcare, financial, commercial, and security contexts

Abstract: Users increasingly interact with conversational AI systems in sensitive domains, yet little is known about how psychological manipulation techniques systematically alter privacy decision-making and trust formation across different contexts. Authors: Hu C.; Zheng J.; Lai N.; Wang Q.; He S.
Title: Can digital-real integration effectively curb urban sprawl? Evidence from China using double/debiased machine learning
Abstract: Urban sprawl (URS) has become a major challenge to China's sustainable development under the backdrop of rapid urbanization. Digital-real integration (DRI) provides a new pathway for urban spatial governance, yet its concrete impacts and mechanisms remain insufficiently tested. Based on panel data from 280 prefecture-level Chinese cities between 2013 and 2023, this study constructs a multidimensional DRI index and employs a partially linear double/debiased machine learning (DML) framework to estimate the effect of DRI on URS. Multiple robustness checks, including complementary instrumental-variable analyses, yield results consistent with the baseline finding. The findings show that a one-unit increase in DRI is associated with a 0.06-unit reduction in the URS index, and this conclusion holds under various robustness tests. The mechanism analysis provides evidence consistent with three potential transmission pathways: industrial structure upgrading, stronger aggregate city-level correspondence between employment opportunities and resident population, and reduced dependence on highway commuting. Further heterogeneity analysis reveals that the restraining effect of DRI is more pronounced in eastern regions, major national urban agglomerations, and cities at more advanced stages of urban development. This study not only provides empirical evidence on how digital technologies reshape urban spatial structures but also offers policy implications for implementing differentiated digital governance strategies and enhancing the effectiveness of spatial planning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Qu Q.-X.; Tang Y.; Guo F.; Duffy V.G.; Man S.S.
Title: Mitigating cognitive workload in automated driving takeovers: Effects of non-driving-related tasks, takeover request modalities, and lead times
Abstract: In Level 3 conditional automated driving, non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs) may reduce drivers’ readiness to resume control, while behavioral indicators alone may not fully capture concurrent changes in workload and psychophysiological stress. This study examined the effects of NDRT packages, takeover request (TOR) modalities, and TOR lead time (TORlt) on cognitive workload, cardiac responses, gaze behavior, and vehicle-control performance. A within-subject experiment used EEG, eye movements, cardiac interval measures, NASA-TLX, and post-TOR driving indicators. News reading and video watching produced larger post-TOR changes in selected physiological indicators and greater vehicle-control effort than the phone call task, while video watching also resulted in higher subjective workload. Visual TORs were associated with higher subjective workload, altered cardiac interval responses in the primary analysis, and greater control fluctuation than auditory and auditory-visual TORs. Shorter TORlt was associated with greater changes in cardiac interval measures, whereas its relationship with steering corrections was less robust across sensitivity analyses. Physiological and behavioral responses were not always aligned, as drivers sometimes maintained relatively stable vehicle control despite elevated workload or psychophysiological stress. These findings support the value of multimodal driver-state monitoring during takeover transitions. Under the present simulator conditions, auditory and auditory-visual TORs may warrant further evaluation when drivers are engaged in screen-based NDRTs or when lead time is limited. Overall, the results provide preliminary evidence for condition-specific adaptive warning design and suggest that combining physiological, visual-attention, subjective, and vehicle-control indicators may improve the characterization of driver state during automated driving takeovers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: De La Rosa Ruiz, Daniel (57209535876); Miró López, Susana (60803060700)
Title: Ethical training in artificial intelligence for communication students: A qualitative study from the perspective of anthropology and social responsibility; [Formación ética en inteligencia artificial en estudiantes de comunicación: Un estudio cualitativo desde la antropología y la responsabilidad social]
Abstract: Introduction: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence in higher education poses new ethical challenges for training future communication professionals, particularly regarding critical thinking, social responsibility, and the ethical use of digital technologies. In Schools of Communication, where content production and discourse analysis are central, it is essential to incorporate a humanistic approach that brings together anthropology, ethics, and digital culture. Methodology: This study follows a qualitative, interpretive design conducted at a School of Communication within the courses Anthropology and Social Responsibility. The intervention involved students producing academic papers, revising them with the support of generative AI, and subsequently carrying out a critical appraisal of the AI-generated suggestions. Students’ revisions were examined through qualitative analysis using Atlas.ti, based on a thematic coding process. Results: The findings indicate that critical engagement with generative AI fosters ethical reflection, intellectual autonomy, and professional awareness among future communicators, as evidenced by meaningful changes in how students reinterpret, partially adopt, or challenge automated recommendations. Discussion: Guided use of generative AI functions not merely as a technical tool but as a pedagogical device for developing critical thinking and social responsibility in digital communication contexts. Conclusions: Integrating generative AI through an anthropological and ethical lens contributes to the comprehensive education of communication professionals, promoting a conscious, reflective, and responsible use of emerging technologies in the university setting. © 2027, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Title: Mental healthcare contact and diagnoses prior to suicide among older adults in Norway: A register-based nested case–control study
Abstract: Background Suicide is a global public health concern, with the highest rates among older males in most countries. Access to mental healthcare is central to suicide prevention. This study examined mental healthcare contact among older adults who died by suicide compared with controls from the general population. Methods Using Norwegian national health and administrative registries, we conducted a nested case-control study of individuals aged 60 and older who died by suicide between 2009 and 2021. Cases were matched on age and sex to controls from the general population. Mental healthcare contact and sociodemographic characteristics were described for cases and controls, and mental health diagnosis of cases in contact with mental healthcare services. Results A substantial proportion of older adults who died by suicide ( N = 2002) had prior mental healthcare contact. Specialized mental healthcare contact decreased with age and was more common among females than males (60–69: 50% vs. 38%; 70–79: 42% vs. 22%; 80+: 33% vs. 13%). Primary mental healthcare contact showed small sex differences and remained relatively stable (24–30%) across age. Depression or depressive symptoms were common among cases in both specialized (35%) and primary care (36%). Among those without mental health contact, cases more often were males, not married, and living alone than controls. Conclusion Older adults who died by suicide received care across multiple healthcare levels and were often diagnosed with depressive symptoms, highlighting the need for prevention and treatment across mental healthcare settings. Improving prevention strategies, particularly among older males, may strengthen suicide prevention in later life. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Workplace responses to perpetration of family and domestic violence: a global scoping review
Abstract: Introduction Family and domestic violence (FDV), which includes intimate partner and family violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace interventions addressing the issue of FDV have predominantly concentrated on providing support to victim-survivors, while there is limited research regarding employer responses to employees who perpetrate such violence. Method A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources, and 28 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Practical applications Effective workplace responses to perpetration of FDV should consider work design factors, referral pathways and confidentiality protections which are guided by graduated accountability models and regulatory frameworks. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Goldstein T.R.
Title: Psychological perspectives on acting, redux
Abstract: Acting is everywhere - film, television, theatre, and everyday performances such as work presentations, leisure activities, and pretend play with children. Yet psychology has historically paid very little attention to what skills, physiological states, and psychological mindsets are needed to act, as noted in Goldstein, 2009. Happily, over the last two decades multiple studies on the major psychological components of acting have produced exciting discoveries, and new questions have arisen. For such a commonly watched activity that involves all the components of human behavior and emotion, it remains strange that acting as an empirical area of study continues to be underdeveloped. Nonetheless, the field is now ripe for nuanced work and interdisciplinary questions from multiple perspectives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and fear of missing out: Evidence from network analysis and a daily diary study
Abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and fear of missing out (FoMO) are common psychological vulnerabilities during emerging adulthood, yet their item-level organization and daily temporal associations remain underexplored. Study 1 ( N = 875) used item-level network analysis in an undergraduate sample to examine the conditional association structure of IU and FoMO. Study 2 ( N = 235) used a 14-day diary design and dynamic structural equation modeling to examine their within-person temporal associations at the construct level. In Study 1, IU and FoMO formed two communities with stronger within-community than cross-community connections. In Study 2, both constructs showed autoregressive continuity and positive bidirectional cross-lagged associations. Higher daily IU was associated with higher next-day FoMO, while higher daily FoMO was associated with higher next-day IU. Together, the findings describe complementary aspects of the IU-FoMO relationship: Study 1 identifies candidate item-level interface domains, whereas Study 2 independently shows temporal coupling between daily IU and daily FoMO at the construct level. These findings may inform future research and the development of interventions for uncertainty-related distress and socially specific missing-out concerns among college students. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A hybrid framework of LLM-based interaction generation and adaptive sampler for recommendation enhancement
Abstract: Data augmentation (DA) is a critical technique for addressing data sparsity. Existing DA methods suffer from several limitations: extensive parameter tuning, dependency on specific types of data, and the tightly coupled DA network in the backbone recommendation model. Consequently, there remains a notable absence of universal data augmentation frameworks capable of adapting to diverse recommendation tasks and backbone models. To address these issues, we propose a hybrid framework to mitigate data sparsity via DA in a more flexible and universal paradigm. Notably, we disentangle the data augmentation process into two modules, data generation and data fusion. Firstly, we prompt LLMs to learn collaborative filtering information from raw user–item interaction data in a CSV format, generating new reliable interactions. Specifically, we devise clustering-based data grouping and multi-round shuffling strategies to enable LLMs to capture comprehensive collaborative filtering information through limited context. Secondly, we design an adaptive sampler to obtain personalized fused data for backbone recommendation models dynamically, making the fused data satisfy the different data demands of diverse downstream recommendation models. Experiments on various recommendation models across distinct datasets demonstrate that our framework can consistently improve vanilla recommendation models and facilitate existing DA methods. Compared with vanilla recommendation models, our framework achieves an average performance gain of 7.10%, 23.54%, and 24.55% on MovieLens-100k, Book-Crossing, and Toys and Games datasets, respectively. These results highlight the effectiveness of our proposed framework in mitigating data sparsity in recommender systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A signaling-cognitive architecture for product rating as quality inference
Abstract: Current product rating prediction methods generally rely on algorithmic construction and data-driven approaches, often overlooking the nature of rating generation as a result of quality inference from observable signals. To bridge this gap, we propose ScoRE (Signaling theory-guided and COgnitive-driven Rating prEdiction), an architecture that reframes rating prediction as a quality inference task. This framework integrates signaling theory with a four-stage cognitive process, incorporating a product quality signal strength index to weigh the importance of product-side signals based on their credibility. Extensive experiments show that ScoRE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Specifically, compared with the strongest baseline on each dataset, ScoRE reduces RMSE by 14.85%, 7.17%, and 16.71% on the Clothing, Electronics, and Home datasets, respectively. Moreover, it surpasses the strongest LLM-based models by 34.25% on Clothing and 7.31% on Music. These results underscore the discrepancy between the generative objectives of LLMs and the requirements of numerical prediction, highlighting the necessity of task-specific and theory-informed designs. Title: Self-construal and the three flows of compassion: The role of dialectical thinking
Abstract: Compassion for self, others, and from others is increasingly understood as culturally embedded. Independent self-construal was positively related to dialectical thinking, which was associated with self-compassion and compassion for others, but not compassion from others. Title: Journey to the bargaining table: Signaling, seeking, and screening
Abstract: Negotiation scholarship has focused extensively on what happens at the bargaining table—how parties make offers, manage conflict, and reach agreements. Far less attention has been paid to how parties get to the table in the first place. In this article, we argue that the journey to the table deserves greater scrutiny. We organize pre-table dynamics around three behaviors: signaling (communicating whether and how negotiation might proceed), seeking (approaching a counterpart to propose bargaining), and screening (deciding whether to engage with or withdraw from a seeker). We review recent and foundational work bearing on each, identifying where the field has made progress and where significant gaps remain. Title: How does responsible governance affect firms’ Innovation resilience? A matching perspective on responsible leadership and responsible AI
Abstract: Innovation resilience has become a critical capability for firms to withstand risks and achieve sustainable growth. However, how responsible governance shapes firms’ innovation resilience remains underexplored. Drawing on signaling theory and conservation of resources theory, this study examines the effects of responsible leadership, responsible AI, and their congruence on firms’ innovation resilience. Title: LanMe: Exploration and evaluation of multilingual LLMs for low-resource finance in Southeast Asia
Abstract: Despite advances in generative AI, large language models (LLMs) struggle with financial NLP in low-resource Southeast Asian (SEA) languages due to limited data, complex terminology, and cross-lingual challenges. Our empirical analysis shows that existing benchmarks inadequately assess model capabilities, and translation-based methods cannot fully adapt mainstream financial LLMs. To address this, we present LanMe (Image 1), an open-source ecosystem integrating data, models, evaluation and open leaderboard. Title: Regulatory exclusion and occupational health risk in Turkish firefighting: a legal-epidemiological policy analysis
Abstract: Article 2(2)(b) of Turkey’s Law No. 6331 on Occupational Safety and Health excludes the intervention activities of disaster and emergency units from that statute’s scope. The exclusion concerns duties performed during response operations; it does not establish that firefighters lack every protection under other legal or administrative instruments. International evidence identifies occupational firefighting as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Group 1), links fire suppression with sharply elevated risk of fatal coronary events, and documents substantial psychological and musculoskeletal burdens. In the official sources examined, no nationally binding firefighter-specific instrument was identified that prescribed post-incident decontamination, detailed health-surveillance content, personal protective equipment performance monitoring, or structured psychological support. The judicial corpus was coded across eight analytical categories; its holdings concentrated on pay, personnel status, compensation, procedure, and jurisdiction rather than concrete preventive OSH duties. We interpret these findings through a structural accountability gap model, under which the statutory exclusion may constrain investigation, data generation, standard-setting, and regulatory learning. The model is interpretive, not a tested causal finding. Title: Urban park biodiversity preferences and trade-offs: A comparison between residents and professionals using Adaptive Choice-Based Conjoint analysis
Abstract: Urban parks are important biodiversity hotspots as well as recreational spaces in cities. It is desirable for urban residents to derive pleasure from parks that also embody biodiversity values due to their ecological and health benefits. Despite the evidence that urban residents are happier and healthier when they have access to green spaces of good quality, it remains unclear how residents prioritise biodiversity when considering the joint effects of other green space attributes, and how these priorities differ from those of landscape/ecology professionals. We used Adaptive Choice-Based Conjoint (ACBC) analysis to examine how biodiversity was prioritised in trade-offs with other important park attributes among residents and professionals. The ACBC study was conducted in Hangzhou (N = 187) and Shanghai (N = 194), two cities in eastern China. Utility values and average importances were estimated using Hierarchical Bayes (HB). While both residents and professionals preferred higher biodiversity levels, biodiversity improvements from poor to moderate yielded greater utility gains than from moderate to rich. Residents prioritised facilities over biodiversity when making trade-offs, whereas professionals prioritised biodiversity as the most important park attribute and valued it significantly more than residents. In both groups, preferences for higher biodiversity were associated with preferences for fewer facilities, denser tree cover, and low-maintenance, wild-looking landscapes. Title: Variance-based global sensitivity analysis of a stochastic Collision Risk Model: how wind turbine parameters impact seabirds
Abstract: To achieve the United Nation's goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, we must create a world powered by renewable energy. This will rely on large-scale infrastructure projects, which must be developed with consideration for the natural environment. Offshore wind farms (OWFs), in particular, must balance the collision risk that turbines pose to seabirds with green energy targets. Within the UK and most of Europe, collision risk modelling (CRM) is a required component of Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) and integral for developers and regulators to gauge the risk an OWF development poses to seabird populations. Despite this, how different combinations of OWF parameters may impact collision risk estimates is poorly quantified. We assess the sensitivity of the stochastic CRM to seven key OWF parameters. Using variance-based global sensitivity analysis methodologies, we quantify results for six seabird species deemed at high risk of turbine collision. We find that the estimate of annual bird-turbine collisions is most sensitive to variation in the number of turbines and the distance between blade tip height and highest astronomical tide (air gap), whereby increasing turbine number and decreasing air gap contributed to increased collision rates. A smaller number of large turbines with greater energy output (larger rotor radius) reduced collision risk per unit energy output. These results quantify the impact of OWF parameter variation on seabird collision risk, which could be used to inform design envelopes, focusing the number of turbine scenarios that developers consider within EIAs and maximising cost-effectiveness whilst minimising seabird collision risk. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: What impacts can intertemporal trading have on carbon markets across different development stages? An economy-wide analysis
Abstract: Carbon markets have encountered challenges such as limited flexibility and substantial price volatility. Intertemporal trading mechanisms, as one of the important ways of green finance, have been proposed as a potential solution to improve market efficiency. However, existing studies frequently overlook whether the intricate internal mechanisms of carbon markets are suitable for introducing intertemporal trading. To comprehensively analyze the effect of intertemporal trading, this study employs a computable general equilibrium model incorporating an intertemporal dynamic mechanism and a carbon market module. This study designs scenarios focusing on total quotas, sectoral coverage, quota allocation, and intertemporal trading to simulate and compare their macroeconomic impacts. The results suggest that intertemporal trading is particularly beneficial in carbon markets that prioritize later-stage reduction, experience rapid sectoral coverage, or have a high auction rate. Under these conditions, introducing intertemporal trading can help reduce long-term carbon prices while promoting the development of cumulative GDP and household welfare. It is noted that the output of sectors covered by the carbon market undergoes an initial contraction in the early stage, followed by a gradual increase in the later stage. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: A socio-technical maturity framework for design firms to enable the transition to design-out-waste in Indonesia's construction sector
Abstract: The construction sector remains a major driver of resource depletion and solid waste generation, with a substantial share traceable to early design-stage decisions. Design-out-Waste (DoW) strategies, including waste-efficient documentation, modern construction methods, and prefabrication, represent a proactive approach to enhancing lifecycle resource efficiency. However, their implementation remains fragmented, particularly in developing-country contexts, partly due to the lack of a structured framework for assessing organisational maturity. This study addresses this gap by developing an empirically grounded socio-technical maturity framework for DoW implementation in building design firms. The framework integrates five socio-technical dimensions into a single operational model encompassing processes & procedures, people & culture, industry structures, technology, and goals & incentives. Using data from 116 construction professionals, Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to validate the measurement and structural relationships, while Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) provided empirical importance values for weighting the maturity dimensions and attributes. These weights were subsequently integrated with a five-level maturity scoring scheme to operationalise the assessment framework. The results reveal an interdependent socio-technical structure, with Industry Structure emerging as the most influential dimension and an important upstream driver of other organisational capabilities. The resulting framework provides an empirically weighted basis for assessing organisational readiness, identifying capability priorities, and guiding DoW implementation towards circular construction. It also provides a structured basis for informing environmental assessment, project appraisal, and policy interventions aimed at improving resource efficiency and waste prevention. © 2026

Authors: Baggio M.
Title: When the state cannot police: EEZ enforcement, foreign fishing, and maritime piracy
Abstract: Maritime piracy and illegal foreign fishing are usually treated as separate problems, handled by separate agencies. This paper argues that they share a cause. Coastal states that cannot enforce their Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) lose fish to foreign fleets, and as fishing incomes fall piracy becomes the better-paid alternative for those at the margin. Piracy in turn raises the cost of operating in those waters and keeps part of the foreign fleet away, doing informally what the state cannot do formally. This implies a counter-intuitive test. If piracy substitutes for absent enforcement, unauthorized foreign fishing should fall more sharply at the 200-nautical-mile boundary in weakly governed EEZs, not less. Comparing satellite-tracked fishing immediately inside and immediately outside that boundary, a line at which legal authority changes but ocean conditions do not, confirms the prediction; geocoded piracy incidents around the same boundary show the corresponding pattern. This boundary comparison provides the study’s strongest evidence, and cross-country patterns and a model calibrated to Somalia corroborate it. The policy implication is that counter-piracy operations and fisheries governance are complements rather than substitutes. Naval deployment suppresses piracy but allows foreign fleets to return, leaving intact the enforcement gap that produced piracy in the first place. Durable reductions require investment in coastal states’ own monitoring and enforcement capacity, and access agreements on terms the coastal state can verify. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A systematic review of the maturation of selected cortical auditory event-related potentials in passive paradigms: Developmental changes from infancy to early adulthood
Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a unique window into the neural dynamics of cognition, particularly through event-related potentials (ERPs) that index sensory, attentional, and cognitive processes. EEG and ERP measures are widely used to study atypical neurodevelopment in children due to their sensitivity to disruptions caused by genetic and acquired brain disorders. We conducted a systematic review of the literature on the typical presentation of four core cortical auditory and language-related ERP components, extracted during passive paradigms, from infancy to early adulthood. These components reflect neural responses to the passive perception of discrete stimuli (N100), the automatic detection of deviant stimuli (Mismatch Negativity (MMN), sometimes in children referred to as the Mismatch Response (MMR)), the allocation of attention to deviant stimuli (P3a), and language processing of discrete stimuli (N400). Drawing from 61 studies, many of which reported on a single component within a specific age range, we chart developmental trajectories of ERP latencies, amplitudes, and scalp topographies. Across all components, latency tended to decrease with increasing age. Amplitude trajectories varied: N100 amplitude tended to decrease; MMN amplitude remained relatively stable or showed a slight decline; P3a amplitude typically increased during early childhood before decreasing in early school age; N400 amplitude consistently declined. Scalp topographical reports, among all components, revealed a shift toward increased focal activation with increasing age. Together, these findings provide a normative foundation for acoustic and auditory language processing in the context of the selected components in typical development, serving as a necessary reference point for understanding and assessing atypical development. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Highly inclusive teachers’ practices in responding to all students’ learning characteristics
Abstract: Background: Although inclusive education places strong emphasis on addressing all students’ strengths and needs, the understanding of student diversity in its broadest sense remains limited. Studies exploring how inclusion is implemented tend to focus on specific groups of learners (e.g., students with SEN or those from socio-culturally disadvantaged backgrounds). However, this methodological shortcut has been repeatedly highlighted in review studies as a limitation that distorts the findings of research on inclusive education for all. To successfully address the learning characteristics of all students in heterogeneous classrooms, teachers must use inclusive practices. Aims: The aim of this research was to explore how the practices of highly inclusive teachers address all students’ learning characteristics, enabling them to learn successfully in a heterogeneous classroom. Sample: The study involved six teachers, forty-two students, and two teaching assistants. Methods: Triangulation of hundreds of hours of ethnographic observation, contextualised through various types of interviews and complemented by products written by students, allowed us to identify diverse types of student learning characteristics and teachers’ inclusive practices. Results: Our findings indicate that teachers' inclusive practices aimed at supporting student engagement, as well as determining and facilitating students' learning progress, were among the most extensively employed and addressed a wide spectrum of students’ learning characteristics. Conclusions: The study unravels the complexity of highly inclusive teachers’ practices and proposes several implications for inclusive education. © 2026 The Authors

Title: PhDGPT: Measuring bias in academic mental health across quantised and uncensored LLMs
Abstract: We investigate bias in academic mental health as reflected by Large Language Models (LLMs). To this aim, we introduce PhDGPT, a synthetic dataset encapsulating the machine psychology of Ph.D. researchers and professors as perceived by OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 and GPT-OSS-20b. The dataset consists of 18,000 data points for each model, comprising 300 iterations repeated across 15 academic events, 2 gender personas, 2 career levels and 42 unique items responses of the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-42) across 2 LLMs. The PhDGPT dataset integrates these psychometric scores with their explanations in plain language. This synergy of scores and texts offers a dual, comprehensive perspective on the emotional well-being of simulated academics, e.g. male/female Ph.D. students or professors. We find that both GPT-3.5 and GPT-OSS produce higher levels of mental distress when impersonating Ph.D. students compared to professors, a direction that aligns with humans’ recent results about mental health in academia. Compared against more than 39,000 human psychometric responses, GPT-3.5 reproduces the canonical structure of anxiety, stress and depression, whereas GPT-OSS does so only under vLLM inference and not under the GGUF quantisation analysed here. This specific instance of GPT-OSS, run via LM Studio under GGUF quantisation, also produces markedly fewer linguistic patterns correlating with psychological dimensions of distress than GPT-3.5. A robustness check — encompassing prompt paraphrasing across four alternative formulations and 3 additional open-source models spanning a range of alignment strategies (Mistral Small 24b Instruct, and 2 uncensored variants) — confirms that psycholinguistic signatures are stable across surface-level prompt variation, while revealing that the relationship between safety alignment and psycholinguistic richness is more complex than a simple censorship effect. Authors: Lin S.; Liu Q.
Title: “Crossing the river by feeling the stones”: Sub-national agency in China's highway maintenance marketisation
Abstract: Marketisation reforms in China are often described as an extension of Western New Public Management (NPM), yet their meanings and effects vary substantially across regions and remain poorly understood from the perspective of policymakers themselves. Drawing on document review and interviews with sub-national officials and practitioners involved in highway maintenance in two underdeveloped provinces, this study examines how marketisation is interpreted, justified, and enacted through a "learning by doing" process shaped by administrative legacies, political incentives, and constrained market environments. The analysis shows that NPM-related principles, such as competition and performance management, are selectively adapted rather than directly transplanted, producing hybrid arrangements that combine bureaucratic control with quasi-market practices dominated by state-owned enterprises. The study identifies four narrative frames through which policymakers explain and evaluate reforms, as well as the recurring strategy of deliberate inaction, which emerges as a pragmatic response to tensions between central expectations and local socio-economic realities. It also considers the broader implications of marketisation for highway service performance, public satisfaction, fiscal sustainability, and technical capacity, pointing to uneven outcomes and persistent governance tensions. By foregrounding sub-national agency and context-sensitive adaptation, the article contributes to understanding policy transfer, the institutional logics shaping China's state-led market reforms, and the prospects for more sustainable infrastructure governance in less developed regions. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: “Looking at artifacts”: The development of visual aesthetic preferences
Abstract: Developmental aesthetics is an underexamined yet growing area of aesthetics research. Very few studies have investigated infants’ visual preferences for artifacts. Would a young child have visual preferences for artifacts, given their limited exposure to the world and with a developing brain? Revisiting our framework (Göksun et al., 2014), which was built on the aesthetic triad of Chatterjee and Vartanian (2014), we provide an overview of the current state of the field on early visual aesthetic preferences with a focus on art and architecture. After presenting evidence for perceptual primitives that may guide visual aesthetic preferences, we center on early artifact appreciation with infants and young children. We conclude the paper by charting new research directions required to examine early aesthetic appreciation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
Abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed feedback provision in writing practices. However, little is known about the mechanisms through which AI-mediated engagement and revision contribute to longer-term learning transfer. Research aims: Framed by theories of self-regulated learning (SRL), socially shared regulated learning (SSRL), and cognitive engagement, the study examined the relationship among engagement, immediate revision gains, and longer-term learning transfer in AI-assisted feedback. Methods: This 16-week cluster-randomized experiment involving 108 undergraduates in China compared two feedback modes: AI-assisted self-feedback and AI-assisted peer feedback. Analyses drew on 1100 writing samples (including pretests, four assignments with two drafts each, and posttests), and 432 reflection forms on AI feedback. Findings: Linear mixed models revealed a decoupling of learning and performance: while both conditions produced similarly strong second drafts, AI-assisted peer feedback demonstrated significantly greater learning transfer to subsequent tasks. In AI-assisted self-feedback, learning followed a performance-dependent SRL cycle in which AI engagement and revision improvements independently predicted learning. A threshold-like pattern further showed that benefits emerged only when students engaged constructively, measured by reflection forms, to internalize writing standards. Conversely, AI-assisted peer feedback was associated with stronger learning transfer that was less dependent on revision gains or engagement with AI, a pattern consistent with an SSRL perspective emphasizing interactive engagement and co-constructed understanding. Conclusion: These findings highlight the importance of revision mechanisms and depth of engagement across feedback contexts. The study contributes to theories of regulation and cognitive engagement and offers pedagogical and design implications for fostering meaningful learning through AI-assisted feedback. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhao Y.; Zhao X.
Title: Assessing urban carbon emissions from a water-energy-food nexus perspective: An intensity-structure-pressure framework for differentiated management in Chinese cities
Abstract: The classic Kaya identity lacks integration of water-energy-food (WEF) nexus elements, and conventional geographical zoning fails to capture the structural heterogeneity of urban carbon emissions. To address these gaps, this study extends the Kaya identity to construct an intensity–structure–pressure chain decomposition equation covering the energy-economy-agriculture-land-water system. A three-stage analytical framework, macro-driving decomposition, structure type identification, and conditional associations analysis, is then applied. Using city-level panel data from China (2000−2020) and integrating Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition, Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) clustering, and panel quantile regression, the study decomposes the structural factors of carbon emissions, identifies city clusters with homogeneous resource structures, and reveals heterogeneous factor associations across emission levels. The results indicate that: (1) Economic growth emerges as the dominant positive factor in carbon emission growth, with its decomposed proportion exhibiting significant north–south regional divergence; (2) cities can be classified into six distinct structural typologies in terms of resource use and emissions, high-emission clusters are typically constrained by a dilemma of improving efficiency while still expanding in scale, whereas low-carbon clusters have systematically entered a phase of decoupling economic growth from carbon emissions; and (3) regression analysis further suggests that the direction and magnitude of the conditional association of the same decomposition factor differ significantly between low- and high-carbon cities, with the marginal association of most factors diminishing as emission levels increase. This study provides a basis for transcending the limitations of geographical proximity and establishing intensity-structure-pressure-oriented, precise, and differentiated carbon management strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Training emotion regulation in Preschoolers: Preliminary evaluation of a Researcher–Teacher co-constructed program aligned with usual classroom practices
Abstract: This study evaluated the effects of a research-based, innovative training program targeting emotion regulation in preschool children. The program was co-constructed with teachers to ensure its integration into everyday classroom practices. Its effectiveness was evaluated using tasks assessing emotion comprehension, recognition, and identification, as well as Theory of Mind and emotion regulation (ERC-vf checklist; Nader-Grosbois, 2014, completed by teachers). The results indicated improvements in teacher-rated emotion regulation and reductions in teacher-rated emotion dysregulation associated with the intervention, as well as gains in the identification of emotional intensity (particularly at the highest levels). Across these domains, pre- to posttest gains were greater in the Intervention group than in the Non-Intervention group, with differences in emotion regulation and dysregulation between groups emerging only among older children (5–6 years) in the classroom-adjusted analysis, although the effect for emotion regulation was at the threshold of statistical significance. The potential role of emotion regulation in supporting emotional and non-emotional competencies is discussed. These findings might prompt new ideas and initiatives in the design of future educational programs. © 2026 .

Title: Differences in the orthographic expectation effect during auditory novel pseudo-character learning in Mandarin-speaking prelingually deaf children with cochlear implants
Abstract: While the orthographic expectation effect (OEE) is well-documented in alphabetic languages, its manifestation in logographic systems like Chinese, particularly among children with atypical auditory experience such as those with cochlear implants (CIs), remains unexplored. This study investigated whether Mandarin-speaking children can form orthographic expectations for Chinese characters through auditory exposure alone, comparing 36 prelingually deaf children with CIs and 36 age-matched children with normal hearing (NH). Using a novel-word learning paradigm, participants were auditorily exposed to pseudo-characters. Their reaction times in a subsequent lexical decision task were analyzed using Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Models (GLMM) to compare auditorily learned versus unlearned phonograms and non-phonograms, as well as predictable versus unpredictable phonetic radicals. Results revealed that both groups exhibited significantly faster reaction times for auditorily learned phonograms, and this expectation effect emerged robustly only when the phonetic radicals were highly predictable. However, children with CIs demonstrated markedly slower responses than their NH peers across all conditions. These findings demonstrate that Mandarin-speaking children can form robust orthographic expectations through auditory input regardless of hearing status. Although children with CIs exhibit slower baseline processing speeds due to underlying perceptual constraints, the magnitude of their orthographic expectation effect remains remarkably intact and comparable to their normal-hearing peers. Ultimately, this highlights the resilient nature of cross-modal reading acquisition, offering crucial neurocognitive insights for designing adaptive literacy interventions in clinical and educational settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A network approach to mapping responsibility in wildfire risk mitigation
Abstract: As wildfire risk escalates in the wildland urban interface/intermix (WUI), creating defensible space clear of flammable fuels is important for wildfire risk mitigation and management. By definition, defensible space is constrained to the property parcel's boundaries and wildfire risk assessments generally focus on individual parcels, but this overlooks any risk in neighboring properties. If we imagine defensible spaces as buffers that cross property boundaries and overlap, neighboring properties may share wildfire risk in the overlapping spaces. However, homeowners may not recognize these overlapping regions and spillover effects of mitigating risk, jeopardizing their properties and, ultimately, the entire neighborhood. To address this issue, we propose a novel paradigm to rethink defensible space management by mapping the homeowner's responsibility to mitigate wildfire risk in overlapping defensible space buffers with respect to their neighbors who may share or owe responsibility to mitigation. First, we develop three new spatial metrics (Personal Responsibility (PR), Shared Responsibility (SR), and Owed Responsibility (OR)) for each homeowner, computed as the product of wildfire risk and the corresponding area of responsibility. Here, we use a fire behavior model to generate rate of spread (ROS) as a measure of wildfire hazard and compute each responsibility metric. Second, we build the metrics into spatial responsibility networks, modeled using all the houses in a given neighborhood with nodes characterized by average PR and with links weighted by average SR (or OR) that are directed to designate who is responsible between neighboring properties. In our study site, we find that SR and OR networks are composed of multiple sub-networks. This information is important to inform homeowners about their individual responsibilities, identify properties with greater responsibility, and gather neighbors with interconnected responsibility. Subsequently, we simulate different mitigation strategies by iteratively removing network links and monitoring how the total responsibility may change in the neighborhood. We use three strategies (random, localized, and targeted) for link removal. Results demonstrate that the targeted strategy (removing links in descending order of highest responsibility) reduces the total responsibility most rapidly and fragments the network into smaller components, concentrating mitigation on the highest-responsibility links. Through this study, we provide a framework for wildfire risk management, which can be used with different metrics and for various neighborhood layouts. Ultimately, the spatial responsibility metrics and networks provide a scalable and spatially-explicit approach to map complex wildfire risk in the WUI, which can help inform defensible space inspections, guide efficient resource allocation, improve neighborhood-level planning, and empower individual homeowners to make more risk-informed decisions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Negotiation and relationships: Insights from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature
Abstract: Negotiations often unfold within ongoing relationships, making relationships integral to negotiation processes and outcomes. Yet, despite repeated calls for greater attention to relational dynamics, behavioral negotiation research has largely relied on paradigms that minimize the role of relationships. We review research from adjacent, psychologically-grounded literature (e.g., on close relationships, marketing, strategy, and operations) that conceptualize negotiation as embedded within ongoing relationships. We show that negotiations in relationships unfold under distinct starting conditions that shape negotiators’ interpretations, judgments of appropriateness and risk, and the interplay between negotiation processes, outcomes, and the longer-term relationship. As a result, negotiations in relationships often involve managing both objective and relational interests simultaneously, producing beliefs, behaviors, and outcomes that differ from dominant findings in behavioral negotiation research. We conclude by encouraging more dynamic, relationally embedded perspectives and methods that capture how negotiation unfolds across ongoing relationships and repeated interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Generative AI use and sustainable pedagogical practices as predictors of 4Cs skill development: The mediating role of digital literacy among international postgraduate students in China
Abstract: This study examines how Generative AI Use (GAU) and Sustainable Pedagogical Practices (SPP) are associated with international postgraduate students’ critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and communication (4Cs), with Digital Literacy (DL) examined as a mediator. Using survey data from 369 international Master’s and PhD students at China’s C9 League universities, this study applies Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN) analysis. The 4Cs were modeled as a higher-order construct comprising four lower-order dimensions. The results show that both GAU and SPP are positively associated with students’ 4Cs, with SPP showing the largest standardized direct association. GAU and SPP are also positively associated with DL, which in turn is positively associated with the 4Cs. Significant indirect associations of both GAU and SPP with the higher-order 4Cs construct were observed through DL. The ANN results provide complementary predictive evidence, with SPP showing the highest normalized predictive importance, followed by GAU and DL. Together, the findings support a technology–pedagogy–capability perspective in which pedagogical design shows the largest standardized direct association with 4Cs development, while DL functions as a learner-side information-processing capability linking AI-supported and sustainability-oriented learning experiences with competence development. For practice, the findings suggest that universities may benefit from embedding generative AI within structured, sustainability-oriented learning activities that emphasize information verification, responsible use, and collaborative problem solving. These findings should be interpreted in light of the cross-sectional, self-report design and the specific context of international postgraduate students at China’s C9 League universities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Nursing faculty perspectives on integrating emerging technologies in undergraduate nursing education: A qualitative descriptive study
Abstract: Background: Emerging technologies (ET), including virtual, augmented, mixed, and extended reality alongside simulation-based tools, are increasingly available for undergraduate nursing education, yet their institutional and pedagogical integration remains uneven. Nursing faculty are central to this process, but their own experiences and perceptions of adopting ET have received limited empirical attention. Aim: To explore nursing faculty's experiences and perceptions of integrating emerging technologies into undergraduate nursing education. Design: Qualitative descriptive study with a contextual quantitative component. Settings: Three university nursing faculties in Spain. Participants: Twenty-two nursing faculty members. Methods: Three focus groups were conducted and analyzed using template analysis, a form of thematic analysis. An ad hoc questionnaire provided descriptive data on participants' self-reported experience with specific technologies, used to contextualize the qualitative findings. Results: Three themes emerged: Resources and Integration, Teaching and Learning, and Navigating the Digital Divide in Nursing Education. Faculty recognized the pedagogical value of ET, particularly of well-established tools such as high-fidelity simulation, but identified limited institutional support, unequal training opportunities, and concerns about preserving humanistic and relational aspects of care as central barriers. Low-cost technologies already accessible to most institutions were seen as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, theoretical instruction. Conclusions: Nursing faculty view emerging technologies as pedagogically valuable but constrained by institutional support, training, and equity considerations. Because this study captures the perspective of faculty only, future research should examine how nursing students experience these same tensions. © 2026

Title: From tabbing to talking: LLM-driven conversational agents for web form interaction

Abstract: Web forms are a critical gateway to online services, yet they remain challenging for blind and visually impaired (BVI) users. Despite accessibility standards, screen reader workflows often prove frustrating and error-prone. Title: Regional disparities, source decomposition, and formation mechanisms of the water-energy-food-carbon system adaptability in urban China
Abstract: Addressing the structural imbalances within urban water-energy-food‑carbon systems is critical for sustainable development. The study analyzes the differences in the adaptability of the water-energy-food‑carbon system among cities, focusing on China, a developing country with prominent regional development imbalances. By integrating the Dagum Gini coefficient, variance decomposition, and Quadratic Assignment Procedure analyses, the study deconstructs these disparities spatially and structurally, ultimately explaining their formation through the system's internal mechanics. This research offers a novel, resource-centric approach to achieving urban sustainable development. The findings reveal: First, China's urban water-energy-food‑carbon system adaptability displays a distinct gradient pattern characterized as “higher in the east, lower in the west, with clustered improvement”. Cities in the eastern region exhibit the highest adaptability levels, followed by cities in the central region, while adaptability levels in the western and northeastern regions are comparatively lower. Second, regarding sources of difference, inter-regional disparity represents the primary spatial source of adaptability variation, accounting for an average of 75.58% of the total difference. Sensitivity represents the primary structural source of adaptability variation, accounting for an average of ~43% of the total difference. Third, the structural layer indicators all have a significant positive impact on the differences in adaptability. Among them, sustainability is the core driving factor, with a regression coefficient of 0.568. These findings indicate that policies aimed at enhancing the adaptability of urban resource systems should go beyond short-term emergency management. Title: Symptom-derived profiles and regional gray matter volume differences in youth with disruptive mood and behavior disorder
Abstract: Background This study aimed to identify symptom-derived profiles among youth with disruptive mood and behavior disorders (DMBD) based on dimensional psychopathology and to examine whether these profiles were associated with regional gray matter volume (GMV) differences. Methods Magnetic resonance imaging scans were acquired from 121 youth (59 DMBD, 62 typically developing controls [TDC]). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed using six continuous symptom indicators: irritability, callousness, uncaring and unemotional traits, and proactive and reactive aggression. Regional gray matter volumes were compared among the identified DMBD profiles and the TD group using voxel-based morphometry. Results LPA identified two symptom profiles that differed primarily in overall symptom severity: a severe profile ( n = 42) and a moderate profile ( n = 17). The severe profile showed higher levels of most symptom indicators, with particularly pronounced differences in aggression and callousness. Exploratory whole-brain VBM identified group effects in the bilateral anterior insula, right anterior prefrontal cortex, left posterior orbital gyrus, and right lateral orbital gyrus; however, none survived whole-brain correction for multiple comparisons. Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons of extracted GMV showed lower GMV in the severe profile than in the TD group in the bilateral anterior insula and right anterior prefrontal cortex. In the orbitofrontal regions, lower GMV primarily involved the moderate profile, although the pattern differed between regions. Conclusions The identified profiles primarily reflected differences in symptom severity rather than qualitatively distinct clinical subtypes. These severity-based profiles were associated with different regional GMV patterns, although the neuroimaging findings were exploratory. The findings support further investigation of dimensional symptom-based phenotyping as an approach to characterizing clinical and neurobiological heterogeneity among youth with DMBD. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Structural constraints and psychosocial eating behaviours associated with dietary quality among reproductive-aged mothers in urban slums of Bangladesh
Abstract: Dietary quality among women in urban slums may reflect structural constraints and eating behaviours, yet evidence examining both is limited. This cross-sectional study examined associations of food insecurity, work-time burden, and eating behaviours with dietary quality among 400 mothers aged 15–49 years in 20 urban slums of Dhaka, Bangladesh (two-stage stratified cluster sampling), and explored whether food insecurity moderated the emotional eating–dietary quality association. Dietary quality was assessed using the Bangladesh Healthy Eating Index (BD-HEI; 0–90) from a single 24-h recall, and food insecurity using the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES; 0–8). Multilevel models with slum random intercepts included linear and quadratic food insecurity terms (quadratic term improved fit, p < .001). Mean BD-HEI was 61.5 (SD 15.7), lowest for fruits and milk products. Predicted BD-HEI was 17.3 (95% CI: −24.2 to −10.5) and 18.6 points (−26.7 to −10.4) lower at FIES = 4 and 8, respectively, than at FIES = 0, mostly at low scores, with no statistically significant difference between FIES 6 and 8. Age (β = 0.375) was positively, and emotional eating (β = −0.872 per scale point; 95% CI: −1.696 to −0.048) negatively, associated with BD-HEI; work-time burden and residence duration were not significant after adjustment. The apparent food insecurity × emotional eating interaction was not supported with a quadratic term (joint test χ2(2) = 1.89, p = .389).
