Title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
Abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Fan R.; Lu C.; Liu X.; Yao Y.; Fan A.; Yang X.
Title: Spatial optimization of land use for synergizing economic development and carbon neutrality based on an efficiency-driven PLUS model
Abstract: Optimizing land-use allocation is important for achieving regional carbon-peaking and carbon-neutrality targets. Existing land-use simulation studies generally incorporate carbon objectives through ex-post assessment or macro-level land-demand optimization, leaving historical grid-level carbon–economic performance disconnected from future spatial allocation. To further address this limitation, we developed LUCE-PLUS, a framework that links grid-scale land-transition accounting and efficiency evaluation with PLUS-based spatial simulation. Using Jiujiang City, China, as a case study, we quantified conversion costs, economic-output changes, and carbon emissions induced by observed land-use transitions from 2010 to 2020 at a 30-m resolution. A single-stage mixed-integer linear programming super-efficiency range-adjusted measure (Sup-RAM) model treated carbon emissions as a weakly disposable undesirable output and enabled discrimination among efficient grid-level transition units while ensuring Pareto-efficient projections. The resulting surfaces of economic efficiency and carbon–economic synergy efficiency were incorporated into PLUS as scenario-specific predictors of land-use expansion probabilities. Land-use patterns in 2030 were simulated under natural-development, economic-dominant, and carbon–economic dual-objective scenarios while aggregate land demand and planning constraints were held constant. Mean carbon–economic synergy efficiency was 20.5% lower than mean economic efficiency, indicating that economic efficiency alone may understate the carbon-related environmental costs of land-use transitions. Compared with the dual-objective scenario, the economic-dominant scenario increased the projected GDP increment by only 0.04% but raised land-use-change-induced carbon emissions by 7.3%. Impervious-land expansion under the dual-objective scenario also showed a stronger tendency toward locations associated with lower carbon-stock losses. LUCE-PLUS therefore provides a performance-informed approach to low-carbon spatial allocation under fixed land-demand targets. From an environmental impact assessment perspective, the framework could support alternatives analysis in strategic environmental assessment of territorial spatial plans by enabling ex ante comparison of projected land-use patterns, carbon-stock changes, and economic outcomes under consistent planning constraints. © 2026

Authors: Zhu Q.; Zou N.; Cheng K.
Title: A dual-path model of employees' emotional reactions and behavioral consequences toward leaders' other-oriented perfectionism: The role of employee ambition
Abstract: Perfectionism has become increasingly pervasive and legitimized in today's workplaces. Although existing research has predominantly examined the intrapersonal consequences of perfectionism, its interpersonal implications—particularly how others emotionally and behaviorally respond to perfectionistic demands at work—remains largely unexplored. Drawing on appraisal theories of emotion, we develop and test a contingent framework explaining how leaders' other-oriented perfectionism elicits divergent emotional responses (i.e., vigor and anxiety) among employees, contingent on employee ambition. Furthermore, we propose that these emotional reactions differentially shape employees' leader-focused behaviors (i.e., leader-directed affiliative behavior and negative workplace gossip about the leader) and general work behaviors (i.e., work goal progress and work procrastination). Evidence from a scenario-based experiment and a multi-wave field study supports our hypotheses. Our findings illuminate the downstream interpersonal consequences of leaders' other-oriented perfectionism and offer insights for organizations that endorse the pursuit of perfection. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wu S.; Ma S.; Chen S.; Gu X.
Title: Dynamic engagement patterns during collaborative reasoning discussions and their relations to adolescents’ individual reasoning
Abstract: Background: Collaborative Reasoning (CR) is a dialogic, learner-centered instructional approach shown to promote learners’ higher-order thinking. However, existing research has paid less attention to how learners engage in CR processes and how the temporal dynamics of engagement relate to the development of individual reasoning. Aims: To address this gap, this study investigated the temporal development of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement during CR discussions and examined how evolving engagement patterns were associated with subsequent individual reasoning. Sample: The participants were 29 seventh-graders from a middle school in China. The students formed four discussion groups, and each group participated in seven CR discussions. Methods: The 28 discussions were video-coded for cognitive, emotional, and behavioral interactions (6868 codes). Process mining and epistemic network analysis were used to model shifts in engagement patterns. Individual reasoning was assessed through post-discussion essays. Results: Engagement patterns shifted dynamically over time, moving from socially shared regulation to sustained knowledge co-construction. Groups differed in the timing and trajectory of this transition: some groups shifted earlier, whereas others engaged in prolonged regulatory exchanges. The group characterized by later transitions produced fewer basic argumentative elements but more advanced elements in their individual essays. Conclusions: This study highlights dynamic engagement patterns as an important link between collaborative processes and learning outcomes and underscores the importance of understanding temporal configurations of regulation and knowledge co-construction in collaborative learning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Han Z.; Zhao H.; Ma L.
Title: Bridging the Cognitive Gulf: User Dialogue Repair Strategies and Effectiveness in Human-AI Interaction
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping how people seek information. Its probabilistic outputs can diverge from user intent, making dialogue breakdowns a persistent challenge. User-initiated repair strategies in naturalistic GenAI interaction remain under-characterized. Drawing on Norman's cognitive engineering framework, this study develops a taxonomy of user repair strategies and examines how repair strategies, observable breakdown signals, and context relate to observed resolution. Rule-based retrieval identified candidates from 117,283 conversations in the LMSYS-Chat-1M corpus. Large language model-assisted coding identified 45,861 breakdown instances, including 40,818 with observed repair attempts. Results reveal a Frequency–Efficacy Paradox: Diagnostics & Direct Feedback, the most common strategy, had an observed resolution rate of 40.1%, whereas the less frequently used Task Decomposition & Guiding reached 75.4%. Under Explicit Resolution alone, Task Decomposition & Guiding still had a higher adjusted probability, but the difference was smaller than under the broader criterion that also included Implicit Progression. Strategy use varied across topics and breakdown types. Generalized estimating equations indicated higher adjusted odds of observed resolution for User Evaluation Gulf than AI Execution Gulf breakdowns and lower adjusted odds at later turn positions. Exploratory analyses indicated meta-strategy-by-topic interactions. Topic Switch followed by Implicit Progression provided a conservative, non-exhaustive flag for potential pseudo-resolution, separating progress on a new task from evidence that the original request was resolved. These findings extend Norman's framework by relating repair strategies to breakdown conditions and clarifying the strength and task reference of outcome evidence. They inform design hypotheses for optional metacognitive scaffolding and task-based evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Jie Y.; Hu S.; Su J.; Wang J.
Title: From rules to reasoning: A systematic review of agent-based and LLM-empowered simulation of public collaboration
Abstract: Agent-based simulation of public collaboration is consolidating into a distinct research pathway, with rule-based agent-based modeling (ABM) and large language model (LLM)-empowered simulation emerging as two technological lineages. Whether they are competitive, substitutive, or complementary has not been systematically examined. Drawing on 1,064 public collaboration simulation studies, we apply a “2 × 4” framework to compare the two lineages across research agendas, theory–model relationships, simulation paradigms, and knowledge contributions. The comparison reveals a pronounced divergence: rule-based work concentrates on outcome explanation (79.5%) and policy evaluation (64.4%), whereas LLM-empowered work is overwhelmingly methodological (98.5%) and foregrounds deliberation and consensus building (35.8%), with meta-theoretical inquiry at 38.8% versus 7.5% in rule-based work. These headline differences persist under temporally controlled comparison against same-period, early-stage, and more strictly matched rule-based windows, with support attenuating in the smallest window, and they are consistent with paradigm expansion rather than substitution: simulation instruments not only answer research questions but shape the questions that can be asked. For information processing and management, the review supplies the evidence base and reporting standards needed to evaluate generative simulation as an instrument for studying collective information behavior, and identifies hybrid ABM–LLM architectures, behavioral validation protocols, and dynamic-network modeling as priority agendas. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Kurniawan W.; Muluk H.
Title: Temporal Constructs as an Open Frontier in Misinformation Research: A Bibliometric Mapping and Research Agenda (Scopus, 2005-2025)
Abstract: Research on misinformation increasingly invokes temporal processes – recency, delay discounting, time perspective, the timing of corrections – yet it is unclear how far these constructs have entered the field. This article maps the Scopus-indexed journal literature on misinformation that engages psychological, dispositional, or temporal constructs (approximately 900 records, search executed 4 July 2025, publication years 2005–2025) and sets out a research agenda for the constructs it finds missing. Annual output grew from fewer than a dozen articles per year before 2017 to 175 in 2024. The 2025 slice covers only the first 185 days of the year and shows no downturn: it runs at about 1.37 times the 2024 rate. Thematic mapping yields four quadrants organised around fake news and media literacy, conspiracy belief, political misinformation, and personality and individual differences. No temporal construct from categories 1, 2, or 4 appears as a theme; the only category 3 construct, continued influence, sits in the emerging or declining quadrant, and an evidence-gap map crossing four families of temporal construct against four misinformation outcomes leaves fourteen of sixteen cells empty. The dispositional side of the field is by contrast well developed, with associations involving conscientiousness, agreeableness, extraversion, and analytic cognitive style, though no quality appraisal was conducted and no claim is made about their strength or consistency. We argue that this is a gap of pairing rather than of theory or instrumentation – validated measures exist for every missing construct – and specify six studies that would populate the map, including a direct test of the widely repeated but untested proposition that delay of gratification confers resistance to misinformation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Life history strategy and the Dark Triad: A meta-analysis of trait-specific associations
Abstract: Life History (LH) Theory has been increasingly employed as an evolutionary framework for understanding individual differences in the Dark Triad. However, findings remain inconsistent regarding trait-specific associations between LH strategy and the Dark Triad. This meta-analysis synthesized 41 effect sizes from 18 independent samples reported in 16 articles. A three-level random-effects model showed a significant positive overall association between faster LH strategy and Dark Triad traits (Pearson's r = 0.26, 95% CI [0.19, 0.33], p < 0.001). Moderator analyses revealed significant differences among the three traits, with psychopathy showing the strongest association ( r = 0.36), followed by Machiavellianism ( r = 0.25), whereas narcissism showed the weakest association ( r = 0.11). The main effects of LH operationalization, gender composition, sample type, and cultural region were not statistically significant. However, the interaction between Dark Triad trait and LH measurement domain was significant ( Q  M  (4) = 11.90, p = 0.018), indicating that the pattern of associations across LH measurement domains differed among the three traits. By providing a quantitative synthesis of trait-specific associations between life history strategy and the Dark Triad, this study clarifies current evolutionary accounts of dark personality traits and highlights the importance of differentiating among the three traits. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Huang Q.; Ma Y.; Li C.; Sui L.; Zhou C.; Li M.
Title: Attribution, zonation, and simulation of spatiotemporal distribution of negative oxygen ions in mountainous megacity: A case study of Chongqing, China
Abstract: Negative oxygen ions (NOI) are key indicators of urban ecological quality. However, NOI dynamics in mountainous megacities remain poorly understood. A key challenge lies in translating complex environmental observations into interpretable knowledge for environmental planning rather than prediction alone. Therefore, we integrated few-shot learning, explainable AI (e.g., SHapley Additive exPlanations), and causal inference within an explainable GeoAI framework to identify NOI drivers and predict spatial patterns in Chongqing, China. Results revealed pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity, with low concentrations in southwestern urbanized areas and high values in forested mountains and river valleys of northeastern Chongqing. Attribution analysis identified elevation, curvature, relative humidity (RH), NO₂, and aerosol optical depth (AOD) as dominant drivers with model-derived nonlinear response thresholds (AOD > 273.67; NO₂ > 15.42; RH > 90.95%), beyond which predicted NOI responses changed markedly. Additionally, DML-based analysis estimated a positive treatment effect of middle elevations on NOI (+0.179 per unit, p < 0.001). Scenario simulations demonstrated that humidity enhancement and the integrated scenario yielded stronger responses than pollution mitigation or greening alone, and achieved a mean ΔNOI of 130.12 cm−3 with 76.25% of the area displaying gains. However, the integrated scenario increased inequality despite maximizing population-weighted benefits (106.99 cm−3), favoring sparsely populated mountainous regions (Gain = −28.76 cm−3, Gini = 0.0835). These findings underscore the capacity of explainable GeoAI for adaptive urban planning by linking environmental response interpretation, intervention evaluation, and spatial equity assessment. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Depressive symptoms, coping skills, and the perception of barriers to psychological treatment among college students
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: College students experience psychological symptoms at a concerning rate but infrequently access psychological treatment. However, research in this context has been incredibly limited, and the psychological factors related to perceptions of barriers to treatment are not well understood. We set out to provide an evaluation of the perceived prevalence of common barriers to psychological care, considering how perceptions of barriers are associated with depression symptoms and coping skills. Our findings were consistent with depressive symptoms being associated with greater perceived subjective and objective barriers. Interpersonal skills demonstrated small negative associations with stigma, treatment concerns, and perceived access barriers, and mindfulness skill was negatively associated with both stigma and perceived access barriers. Emotionally impaired coping was positively related to both stigma and treatment concerns. However, behavioral and cognitive skills were not correlated with any perceived barriers. We also considered how coping skills and depression symptoms interacted to predict perceptions of barriers. We found two significant interactions for perceived access barriers specifically. When cognitive or behavioral skills were greater, psychological symptoms were more strongly related to barrier perceptions. This suggests that those with greater coping skills perceive more barriers to treatment when experiencing elevated depressive symptoms compared to those with more limited coping skills. Findings from this study provide an initial characterization of barrier perceptions among college students and have the potential to inform efforts to increase treatment seeking among college students. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. Title: A digital serious game for brain health among first-year nursing students: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study
Abstract: Background: Brain health is increasingly recognised as a public health priority, with relevance to prevention, healthy ageing and person-centred care. Student nurses require opportunities to engage with brain health early in preregistration education. Digital serious games may offer a brief, interactive and repeatable approach to introducing complex public health concepts. Aim: To examine immediate educational outcomes and student experiences following use of a digital serious game on brain health with first-year preregistration nursing students. Methods: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used. First-year nursing students at a United Kingdom university used a digital serious game as an adjunct learning activity within a public health module. Pre- and post-gameplay questionnaires assessed attitudes towards brain health, self-efficacy and behavioural intentions. Post-gameplay evaluation assessed usability, satisfaction and relevance. Focus groups explored gameplay experiences and helped explain the quantitative findings. Results: Of 282 eligible students, 225 completed pre-gameplay questionnaires and 208 provided post-gameplay data; matched data were available for 197. Attitudes towards brain health increased significantly, with a large effect size (dz = 0.96, p < 0.001). Self-efficacy also increased significantly, with a small effect size (dz = 0.25, p < 0.001). Behavioural intentions showed a small, non-significant increase (dz = 0.12, p = 0.088). Post-gameplay evaluation was favourable, with a mean System Usability Scale score of 80.28/100; 76.9% awarded five stars and 97.6% agreed the game was useful for health promotion learning. Three focus groups with 25 students indicated movement from informal awareness to structured understanding, recognition of relational practice, and value of repetition and feedback. Conclusion: The game was positively evaluated and associated with immediate improvements in attitudes and self-efficacy, but not behavioural intentions. Qualitative findings connected gameplay with self-care, patient education, relational practice and emerging professional identity. Authors: Li S.; Li X.; Du X.; Xin Z.
Title: How local–global identity shapes physical-digital preferences through convenience preference
Abstract: Despite the functional advantages of digital products, consumers’ preferences between digital and physical formats remain highly heterogeneous in a marketplace where globalization and renewed localism coexist. Drawing on identity-based motivation theory, this research examines how local versus global identity influences consumers' preferences for physical versus digital products through convenience preference. Across three studies (five sub-studies), we demonstrate that a relatively stronger local-over-global identity is associated with greater preference for physical over digital consumption formats. Further analyses reveal an asymmetric effect that local identity drives stronger preferences for physical products, whereas global identity does not produce a corresponding increase in preference for digital formats. We further identify convenience preference as the underlying mechanism, showing that stronger local identity reduces convenience preference, thereby increasing preference for physical products. These findings reconceptualize physical versus digital preferences as identity-consistent choices rather than purely functional evaluations. By identifying convenience as an identity-contingent motivational preference, this research advances identity-based motivation theory and provides timely insights into how identity orientations shape consumer preferences amid ongoing digital transformation and heightened societal attention to globalization–localism dynamics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhong T.; Zhu G.
Title: Uncovering emotion dynamics across human–AI interaction modes in programming: Evidence from facial expression and electrodermal activity
Abstract: Emotions play a fundamental role in learning by shaping learners' cognitive engagement and influencing learning outcomes. In generative AI (GAI)-supported programming, learners interact with AI in different ways. However, limited research has examined how different interaction modes are associated with learners' emotional dynamics. This study investigated students' emotions across three human–AI interaction modes (i.e., AI-reliant, AI-independent, and human–AI hybrid) during AI-assisted programming. A total of 150 undergraduate students completed programming tasks with access to ChatGPT, during which video recordings of their facial expressions and electrodermal activity (EDA) were collected. Facial expressions were analyzed to examine both emotion distributions and temporal transitions using lag sequential analysis, while EDA was used to measure affective arousal. Results reveal that none of the seven facial-expression categories differed significantly across the three modes. Lag sequential analysis uncovers that the three modes shared reciprocal anger ↔ disgust, fear ↔ surprise, and neutral ↔ sadness transitions. Descriptively, the AI-reliant mode showed transitions between positive and negative emotions, the AI-independent mode showed a relatively neutral-centered transition network, and the human-AI hybrid mode demonstrated a relatively surprise-centered transition network. However, none of the transition probabilities differed significantly across modes. In terms of EDA analysis, the hybrid mode exhibited significantly more skin conductance responses (SCRs) in total and significantly more SCRs per minute than the AI-reliant mode. These findings suggest that emotion states can serve as signals for understanding how learners engage with GAI during programming. The study highlights the importance of designing emotion-aware AI-supported programming environments that balance technological assistance and learners’ emotional engagement in problem-solving. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhang X.; Sun L.; Chang L.; Sun Z.
Title: Natural Hazards, Critical Infrastructure Systems, and Resilience Enhancement: A Structured State-of-the-Art Review and a Synthesis-Based Rapid Assessment Framework
Abstract: Critical infrastructure systems (CISs) are increasingly exposed to natural hazards whose impacts are amplified by infrastructure interdependence, urban complexity, and the growing prevalence of compound and cascading events. Existing research provides valuable insights into individual hazards, infrastructure components, modeling methods, and resilience metrics, but these insights remain difficult to translate into preliminary decision support because they are organized across different hazard types, sectors, analytical scales, and decision contexts. This article presents a structured state-of-the-art review of natural hazards, CIS impacts, and resilience enhancement. A two-pathway review strategy was adopted. A Web of Science (WoS) core search was used to characterize the bibliometric landscape and identify WoS-sourced core synthesis studies, while a targeted anchor-search pathway was used to verify foundational concepts, hazard mechanisms, methodological approaches, resilience frameworks, and authoritative institutional sources. The review clarifies the conceptual distinction among dependencies, interdependencies, compound hazards, cascading failures, service disruption, and resilience; synthesizes cross-hazard infrastructure impact mechanisms; compares major method families for hazard-impact and resilience assessment; and develops a synthesis-derived rapid resilience assessment framework for preliminary screening and prioritization under constrained data and time conditions. The synthesis indicates that future CIS resilience assessment would benefit from moving beyond isolated asset-damage analysis toward integrated workflows that link hazard loading, component vulnerability, network functionality, service consequences, recovery capacity, uncertainty, and feasible intervention choices. The article contributes a more transparent evidence-source structure, an evidence-to-decision bridge, and a bounded decision-oriented framework for organizing future research and practical resilience screening.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Complex post-traumatic stress disorder in patients initially diagnosed with idiopathic hypersomnia: a case series

Abstract: Objectives: The etiology of hypersomnia remains largely unknown, while the concept of complex post-traumatic stress disorder has recently emerged in the field of psychotraumatology. This case series report aims at highlighting a possible association between hypersomnia and trauma-related disorders. Methods: We conducted a retrospective analysis of medical records conducted as part of routine clinical practice. This case series comprises 17 consecutive patients previously diagnosed with idiopathic hypersomnia based on clinical and neurophysiological evaluations, all of whom underwent psychological and psychometric evaluations. Results: Eleven of 17 patients (64.7%) met ICD-11 criteria for CPTSD. Inferential comparisons between the CPTSD and non-CPTSD groups were exploratory and did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons. Descriptively, patients with CPTSD showed higher trauma-related and anger-related symptom scores. Dissociative symptoms also showed a descriptive difference, although interpretation was substantially limited by missing data in the non-CPTSD group. Conclusions: This case series suggests that some cases of pathological hypersomnolence might be associated with traumatic disorders. Hypersomnolence may represent a response to traumatic memories, particularly in patients with complex traumatic histories, such as childhood abuse. The small sample size limits the generalizability of the findings. Authors: Mazalik P.; Halberda J.
Title: Successful modal reasoning depends on WHAT went WHERE
Abstract: Modal reasoning requires quantifying over possibilities (e.g., categorizing events as necessary, possible, and impossible). This suite of abilities matures during the preschool years, but toddlers perform better in some modal reasoning tasks than others. We propose that these mixed findings reflect a cognitive distinction: toddlers perform worse when reasoning about ambiguous locations of objects (WHERE) than when reasoning about ambiguous kinds of objects (WHAT). In Experiments 1 and 2, we directly compared these forms of ambiguity using matched tasks. Consistent with the hypothesis, toddlers performed substantially better when reasoning about ambiguous kinds than ambiguous locations. Experiment 3 revealed a similar asymmetry in language comprehension, with preschool children showing better comprehension of modal terms such as “can” and “have to” in a What-based task than in a Where-based task. Thus, modal reasoning emerges earlier than previously suggested, and diversity in results reflects differences in how kind and location information are represented and processed. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: A need for calibration: Self-reported cyber hygiene fails to predict task performance
Abstract: Cybersecurity research relies primarily on self-reports, yet these measures may not reflect behavior during security-relevant tasks. We examined the correspondence between self-reported cyber hygiene and simulated task performance in 433 participants. Participants completed the Cyber Hygiene Inventory, the Big Five Inventory-2, and a simulated task battery across five cyber hygiene domains: storage and device hygiene, transmission and browsing hygiene, file-sharing/media-related hygiene, authentication and credential hygiene, and email and messaging hygiene. Self-reported cyber hygiene did not consistently align with simulated task performance. Total self-report scores inversely correlated with task performance (r = -.26, p < .001), with similar negative associations appearing for storage and device hygiene, transmission hygiene, and authentication. Only email and messaging hygiene showed a small positive association. A signed standardized discrepancy score was then used to examine the gap between self-report and task performance. Personality traits explained 33% of discrepancy variance, and the full model, including demographic and cyber-experience variables, explained 56%. Agreeableness, online engagement, self-rated cybersecurity knowledge, education status, gender, and prior cyberattack experience emerged as predictors of this gap. Online engagement was associated with lower signed discrepancy, whereas self-rated knowledge was associated with higher signed discrepancy. These directions do not establish better calibration or overconfidence. These findings indicate that self-report and simulated tasks capture distinct aspects of cybersecurity behavior. Researchers should treat perceived behavior, task-based performance, and calibration as related but distinct outcomes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Examining the layered veil of pay transparency: Implications for perceived ambiguity, sensemaking, and negotiation
Abstract: In the last decade, pay transparency—making pay information more accessible and understandable—has become a defining workplace reform. We examine the common assumption that pay transparency reduces pay disparities by improving negotiation outcomes. Our cross-disciplinary review suggests that pay transparency's effects on negotiation hinge on three factors: (1) how transparency is operationalized (i.e., what type of pay information is shared); (2) how people interpret the information provided; and (3) whether transparency alone can motivate and equip individuals to leverage that information to negotiate effectively. We distinguish three interrelated negotiation-relevant layers of pay transparency—job offer, peer, and market—and then assess how these reduce ambiguity, shape negotiator sensemaking, and influence negotiation processes and outcomes. We conclude by outlining implications for future negotiation research and practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Bagheri-Nesami M.; Ahmadi F.
Title: The association between alexithymia and job burnout in nurses: A systematic review
Abstract: Alexithymia, as a deficit in emotional processing, may be associated with increased vulnerability to burnout. This systematic review examines the association between alexithymia and job burnout among nurses. Following PRISMA guidelines and the PICO framework, a comprehensive search was conducted across international databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, ProQuest) and Iranian databases (SID, Magiran, IRANDOC, Civilica), up to May 31, 2026. After duplicate removal, screening, and quality assessment using the JBI checklist for cross-sectional studies, 9 studies were included. Mean alexithymia scores fell within the possible alexithymia range in most studies. Regarding job burnout, the personal accomplishment subscale was low across all studies, whereas levels of emotional exhaustion and depersonalization varied among studies. All studies reported a significant positive association between alexithymia and job burnout, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.187 to 0.84. In two studies employing univariate regression analysis, 33% of the variance in job burnout was attributable to alexithymia. Studies utilizing multivariate models suggested that, in addition to its direct statistical association, alexithymia was associated with job burnout through mediating variables such as depression, social support, and optimism. One study also found that depersonalization was significantly associated with alexithymia. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the directionality and potential bidirectional nature of these associations. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Galeana F.
Title: Governing Indigenous territories: trust, moral economy, and the legitimation of Indigenous territorial authority in the Honduran Moskitia
Abstract: Formalizing Indigenous land rights is critical for environmental justice and sustainable development. Yet legal recognition often creates new territorial governing bodies tasked with managing collective lands, whose legitimacy cannot be assumed. This study examines how trust in Indigenous territorial authorities is built, contested, and withdrawn following the formalization of collective land rights in the Honduran Moskitia. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and household interviews in three villages across diverse socio-ecological settings, the study analyzes how residents assess their territorial authorities. The analysis treats trust as multidimensional and relational. The study examines different forms of trust—dispositional, rational, affinitive, and procedural—to identify the rationales that drive assessments of authority in each village. These rationales are interpreted through the lens of a Miskitu moral economy, framing trust assessments in terms of what residents expect of a territorial authority to be considered legitimate. A moral economy lens contributes analytically to a multidimensional trust framework by explaining why certain forms of trust feel more salient when evaluating authority performance and how they interact with one another. The central finding is that the socio-spatial configuration of land conflicts shapes which evaluative dimensions of trust become most salient. A multidimensional and relational trust analysis contributes a more granular understanding of this process: it shows how different forms of trust interact and shift through everyday encounters with authority, identifying the specific points at which legitimacy is strengthened, strained, or quietly lost. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Vrljić B.; Botički I.
Title: Explaining deceptive language in topical discourse: Integrating transformer models and explainable AI using LIME and SHAP for transparent text-based deception detection
Abstract: Detecting deception in textual communication is an important challenge in online environments where misleading information and deceptive narratives are increasingly prevalent. This study investigates the integration of fine-tuned transformer models, prompt-based large language models (LLMs), and explainable AI (XAI) techniques for interpretable deception detection. Its contributions include a statistically validated comparison of six BERT architectures, a factorial prompt ablation across five GPT models, and a quantitative evaluation of LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) explanation quality and stability. Experiments were conducted on two domain-specific datasets totaling 500 statements, with 264 related to climate change and 236 related to COVID-19. The results show that transformer models are effective for deception classification even when trained on relatively small datasets, with DeBERTa achieving 88.87% and 87.92% accuracy on topical datasets. LIME and SHAP were applied to analyze word-level attribution patterns in the best-performing model. The two XAI methods exhibited substantial aggregate-level agreement, converging on similar sets of influential words associated with deception across domains, whereas agreement on individual predictions was more limited. These findings align with prior research on recurring patterns in deceptive language and provide supportive evidence that linguistic patterns identified through explainability techniques remain consistent across topics, even under limited data conditions. Overall, the results demonstrate that combining contemporary language models with XAI techniques can provide both accurate predictions and interpretable insights into the linguistic characteristics of deceptive communication. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Zheng L.
Title: Teaching by example? Teacher ICT use and middle school students’ computer and information literacy across China and the United States
Abstract: Background: In the digital era, Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) has become a crucial educational outcome. While teacher Information and Communication Technology (ICT) use is widely promoted to enhance student digital skills, its effectiveness may vary significantly across different national education systems. Aims: This study investigates the impact of teacher ICT use on middle school students' CIL in China and the United States. It aims to compare these cross-national effects and examine the mediating roles of school ICT resources and institutional support in shaping these relationships. Methods: Using nationally representative data from the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS) 2023, this research employs regression models and instrumental variable (2SLS) methods to address potential endogeneity. Mediation analyses further explore how school-level factors transmit teacher ICT effects. Results: The analysis reveals striking cross-country differences: in China, all dimensions of teacher ICT use significantly improved students' CIL, whereas these effects were statistically insignificant in the United States. School ICT resources and support fully mediated teacher ICT effects in China but only partially mediated ability effects in the U.S. Additionally, student background factors consistently influenced CIL across both countries. Conclusion: While teacher ICT experience demonstrates universal importance, the broader impact of instructional ICT practices depends critically on national context and institutional support systems. The findings highlight the complex interplay between teacher practices, school resources, and national educational environments in shaping digital literacy outcomes. © 2026

Title: Linguistically responsive learning and teaching for non-native speakers in undergraduate nursing education: a scoping review
Abstract: Aims: To map the literature on linguistically responsive learning and teaching for non-native-speaking students in undergraduate nursing education, covering students' and educators' experiences, language needs and requirements, assessment instruments, and supportive measures. Design: Scoping review conducted in accordance with the JBI methodology and reported following PRISMA-ScR. Data sources: MEDLINE, CINAHL, ERIC, and MLA International Bibliography; grey literature via OpenGrey; archives of German second/foreign language journals; reference list screening. Searches conducted in June 2023 and updated in June 2025; English- and German-language sources without date restriction. Review methods: Titles, abstracts, and full texts were screened independently by two reviewers against pre-specified eligibility criteria. Data extraction was conducted by one reviewer and independently verified by a second. Findings were synthesised qualitatively and quantitatively per research question, with language-related challenges organised by core language skill and supportive measures by actor level. Results: 133 sources published between 1990 and 2025 were included, most from the United States (45%), Australia (30%), and Canada (8%); qualitative designs predominated (47%). Student experiences encompassed seven psychosocial categories and language-related challenges across reading, listening, speaking, and writing. Educators reported pedagogical, assessment-related, and institutional challenges, with insufficient preparation the most consistently documented finding. Formal admission requirements varied substantially across national contexts, with no unified standard identified. Twelve assessment instruments addressing six distinct constructs were identified, with limited contextual validation for clinical language performance. Supportive measures spanned student, educator, and institutional levels; linguistic modification of assessment items was the only measure for which experimental evaluations were identified. Conclusions: The literature documents a structural misalignment between admission language standards, programme demands, and available support infrastructure. Supportive responses have been predominantly reactive, educator-initiated, and infrequently evaluated. Priorities include validated nursing-specific language competency frameworks, systematic educator preparation, curriculum-integrated language support, and a conceptual shift from deficit-based to asset-based framing. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Song X.; Zhang X.; Mao F.; Yu Z.; Li J.; Geng Y.
Title: Potential spatial association of green transition performance in China's resource-based cities: Evidence from a city-level network analysis
Abstract: Green transition in resource-based cities (RBCs) poses a critical challenge, particularly in China, where these cities have long underpinned national economic development. Decades of resource extraction have left many of them facing resource depletion, environmental degradation, and industrial imbalance. Combining the DPSIR (drivers-pressures-state-impact-responses) framework with entropy weighting and GIS, this study assesses the green transition performance of 100 prefecture-level RBCs in China from 2003 to 2019, and builds a potential spatial association network with a modified gravity model to examine how the cities are positioned relative to one another. Transition performance improved in all four development stages, with revitalized cities improving the most, whereas seven cities, four in Gansu Province and three in the northeast, were still at the lowest performance level in 2019; cities in the eastern and central regions generally outperform those in the west. The binary network keeps a stable hub-periphery structure over the seventeen years, although the identity of hub cities depends on whether ties are treated as binary or weighted. QAP analysis shows that the model-implied associations are positively related to provincial co-membership but not to economic disparity. Block modelling further identifies four geographically coherent city clusters that barely change over time. Because the network describes potential rather than observed interactions, these findings indicate, rather than demonstrate, opportunities for coordination. They suggest building coordination channels across provincial borders, piloting central cities as demonstration sites, and tailoring transition standards to local conditions. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Author full names: Flores Jaimes, Flor Bella (60913140700); Villegas, Keila (60913293000); McGuire, Connie (56851348100); Allaire, Maura (55900903800)
Title: (Dis)trust in tap water: Consumer perceptions and behavior in California
Abstract: Tap water is not universally trusted in high-income countries, leading to tap avoidance and reduced public support for urban water infrastructure. This paper examines trust as a dynamic process that shapes drinking water perceptions and behaviors. We investigate how trust is built, eroded, and rebuilt using narratives from 91 semi-structured interviews in California. Results highlight that trust is built gradually through transparent communication and positive lived experience, yet can be quickly lost with sudden, unexplained changes in perceived quality. Utility compliance with water quality regulations is insufficient on its own to rebuild trust. Residents also value direct and frequent engagement from their utility and improved tap water aesthetics. Findings highlight why technical measures of water quality and public perceptions often diverge and offers actionable insights for urban utilities to enhance public trust by responding to residents’ lived experiences. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Sex differences in biodynamic response to seated whole-body vibration: A scoping review
Abstract: Seated whole-body vibration (WBV) exposure increases musculoskeletal injury (MSKI) risk, particularly for females. This review synthesizes the literature evidence for sex-differences in biodynamic response (BR) to seated WBV. Studies were included if they reported one or more BR outcomes, included both males and females, and exposed participants to seated WBV. Twenty-six studies met the inclusion criteria, fourteen of which reported significant sex-differences in one or more BR outcome(s) under various vibration and seating conditions. Experimental and data analysis methods between studies were found to be somewhat inconsistent and/or incompletely disclosed, making comparisons between studies difficult. This potentially led to the equivocal findings between studies with respect to sex differences. Most authors suggest that regional body composition probably contributes to differences in BR but no studies have assessed body composition by region. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Do you need to add (con)text to the equation? Subject-related, linguistic, and contextual factors in competence-oriented assessment
Abstract: Background: The growing emphasis on competence-oriented school assessments requires tests with more complex descriptions of real-life situations. However, few studies have systematically examined the associated changes in performance requirements, therefore, it is unclear how subject-specific and linguistic task characteristics (interacting) determine the level of difficulty of such tasks and the role of real-life context. Aims: This study examines how linguistic, subject-related, and contextual task characteristics influence the empirical difficulty of reality-based assessment tasks. Sample: The participants were 786 lower secondary school pupils from three comprehensive schools in a federal state in Germany. Methods: In the experiment, three different language versions and three mathematical tasks were developed for 15 German-language factual texts and used in paper-and-pencil tests with a rotational design. Results: The results of the generalized linear mixed models showed that mathematical and linguistic task factors significantly affect empirical task difficulty, although no interactions were found. The real-life context of the tasks proved to be relevant, as students' interest in respective contexts significantly influenced task success. Conclusions: The findings highlight the need to differentiate specific linguistic features in task construction and acknowledge the previously neglected but critical role of real-life contexts in competence-oriented assessments. © 2026 The Authors

Title: PLRA-KG: Pattern-derived latent relation augmentation for knowledge graph-based recommendations
Abstract: Knowledge graph (KG)-based recommendation has emerged as an effective solution to data sparsity by incorporating structured semantic information into user and item representations. However, existing KG-based recommendation approaches still face two core challenges: (i) over-reliance on explicit relations while insufficiently capturing latent connections between items, and (ii) feature degradation during high-order propagation, which leads to the dilution of informative signals in learned representations. To this end, we propose PLRA-KG, a pattern-derived latent relation augmentation framework for KG-based recommendation. PLRA-KG uncovers implicit item associations by generating syn-relations and syn-entities from global user preference patterns and relational structures. Specifically, PLRA-KG first performs relation-aware clustering via self-training to group items with strong association patterns. It then introduces a discernment-aware relation-pair selection mechanism to identify relation combinations that significantly influence user decisions. Based on the selected relation-pairs, a pattern-derived syn-relation generation strategy is designed to construct latent relations by jointly modeling global user preferences and relational value interactions. These generated syn-relations and syn-entities are subsequently integrated into the original KG, resulting in an augmented graph that better captures hidden semantic connectivity. Finally, PLRA-KG is optimized in a unified framework that jointly considers recommendation learning, KG embedding, and clustering objectives, enabling seamless integration with various KG-based recommendation models. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that PLRA-KG consistently improves both recommendation accuracy and diversity, achieving average improvements of approximately 6.64% in Recall, 7.83% in AD, 5.56% in Coverage, and 6.20% reduction in ARP. Authors: Ma C.; Du C.; Zhao X.
Title: Cognitive flexibility as a bridge between depressive symptoms and problematic smartphone use in adolescents: A two-wave network analysis across depression-severity groups
Abstract: The co-occurrence of depressive symptoms and problematic smartphone use (PSU) in adolescents poses a growing public health concern, but its component-level conditional associations, cross-wave patterns, and variation across depression-severity groups remain insufficiently understood. Using a two-wave observational design with a 12-month interval (N = 1200 students from one high school in a county of Gansu Province, China), this study integrated Gaussian graphical modeling (GGM), network comparison testing (NCT), and latent profile analysis (LPA). Cognitive Flexibility showed the largest absolute bridge expected influence at both waves, and the ranking was unchanged when the comparison was restricted to nodes measured at the same level of aggregation. NCT detected no significant global difference between the T1 and T2 contemporaneous networks, although several local cross-community edges differed between the two estimates. LPA retained four nearly parallel, severity-ordered classes at both waves, interpreted as depression-severity groups rather than qualitatively distinct profiles. Subgroup bootstrap analyses showed acceptable edge-weight accuracy; expected-influence CS coefficients ranged from 0.286 to 0.750, whereas all bridge-expected-influence CS coefficients were below 0.25, so the subgroup findings are confined to cross-community connectivity. Between-group differences in cross-community connectivity persisted after equal-n down-sampling. These findings should be interpreted in light of the observational design, single-school convenience sample, and reliance on self-report measures. Cognitive flexibility nevertheless emerged as a consistent cross-community correlate in the overall networks and warrants further longitudinal and intervention evaluation rather than being regarded as an established intervention target. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Survival of Contractor Consortiums in the Road Construction Industry during Economic Crisis
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Road construction industries worldwide are periodically exposed to economic crises, which are cyclical in nature and often characterized by high inflation, currency depreciation, resource shortages, and institutional inefficiencies. In such conditions, traditional procurement methods frequently struggle to maintain project continuity, prompting the emergence of local contractor consortiums as a more resilient alternative. This study examines how contractor consortiums in the road construction sector adapted to recent economic crises and sustained operations amid unprecedented challenges. A qualitative research approach was adopted, involving 14 semistructured interviews with industry experts. Manual content analysis identified key adaptive measures, including financial pooling, shared equipment and labor, agile internal coordination, and proactive engagement with public authorities. These mechanisms enabled many consortiums to continue project delivery despite severe economic and operational constraints. However, the effectiveness of these measures was constrained by rigid legal and contractual frameworks, limited digital integration, fragmented stakeholder collaboration, and delayed institutional responses. To enhance future resilience, the study recommends modernizing contractual systems, strengthening digital adoption, and improving public-private coordination. The findings contribute to construction management research in crisis contexts by demonstrating the viability of consortium-based procurement and providing practical guidance to support the long-term sustainability of local contractor consortiums in the road construction sector. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Perceived control and stress reactivity in algorithm-supported hiring decisions
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Algorithms increasingly determine who gets interviewed, flagged, or passed over in hiring, often without explanation, consistency, or any mechanism for response. Yet the psychological mechanisms through which algorithm-supported decision-making shapes stress responses remain insufficiently specified. This article develops a theoretically grounded framework linking diminished perceived control to stress reactivity in algorithm-mediated decision-making contexts. Drawing on self-determination theory, decision-making process frameworks, and psychological safety, the manuscript integrates empirical evidence from research on AI hiring practices, including findings on Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) individuals navigating applicant tracking systems. The framework identifies three primary mechanisms through which AI-supported decision-making may influence stress reactivity: limited transparency, inconsistent decision processes, and constrained opportunities for feedback. This work offers a foundation for empirical work on how technologically mediated environments shape cognitive appraisal, perceived control, and stress. These dynamics extend beyond hiring to any structured assessment context in applied behavioral and clinical settings. © 2026 Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive. Title: Institutional resilience and land-acquisition governance: Participation and conflict-management mechanisms in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project
Abstract: This study examines governance performance during infrastructure land acquisition and the role of institutional resilience in supporting implementation. Using survey data from 108 public-sector implementers involved in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project in Indonesia, the relationships among institutional resilience capacities, participatory governance, conflict-management mechanisms, and governance performance were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Learning capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to participatory governance, while buffering capacity was positively related to conflict-management mechanisms. Participatory governance showed no direct relationship with governance performance but its indirect relationship through conflict-management mechanisms was statistically significant. Buffering capacity and adaptive capacity were positively related to governance performance, while learning capacity showed no significant relationship. The findings reveal differentiated governance roles across resilience capacities and distinguish direct capacity–performance relationships from process-based relationships involving stakeholder participation and conflict-management mechanisms. In conflict-prone land acquisition, conflict-management mechanisms emerged as an important governance process linking stakeholder participation with governance performance. The study shows how different resilience capacities support different governance functions during land-acquisition implementation. © 2026

Title: Socioeconomic and circumstance differences in means of suicide among U.S. adults: Evidence from the National Violent Death Reporting System
Abstract: Background Suicide is a major public health problem. To our knowledge, few studies have examined how multiple socioeconomic and circumstance factors are associated with a comprehensive set of International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10)-defined suicide means; therefore, we evaluated these associations in a national sample of U.S. adults. Methods Data were obtained from the U.S. National Violent Death Reporting System from 2003 to 2023. Adults aged ≥18 years who were assigned an ICD-10 cause of death code that corresponds to a suicide means were included (N = 391,250). Suicide means were categorized as firearm, asphyxiation, medication poisoning, non-medication poisoning, non-firearm weapon, jumping, and motor vehicle. Multinomial logistic regression was used to regress suicide means by socioeconomic and circumstance factors, using firearm suicide as the reference outcome. Results Firearms were the most common suicide method (52.6%), followed by asphyxiation (26.9%) and medication poisoning (11.1%). In general, suicide by firearm was relatively less likely among those in older age groups, higher education levels, racial-ethnic minorities, females, and those with mental health and substance abuse history. In contrast, suicide by firearm was generally more likely among those who were married, military history, employed in the workforce, financial hardship, and those with physical health and relationship problems. Conclusions We identified socioeconomic and circumstance factors that may be associated with different means of suicide. These results may identify high risk individuals and guide clinical practice, screening guidelines, and policies based on which suicide means may be more likely. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The Symmetric and Asymmetric Impacts of Foreign Capital Inflows and Trade Openness on Africa’s Economic Growth: Evidence from Linear and Nonlinear Panel ARDL Models
Abstract: This study investigates the symmetric and asymmetric impacts of foreign capital inflows and trade openness on economic growth in 37 African countries from 2000 to 2021 using linear and nonlinear panel autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) models. To examine the dynamic panel threshold effect, the study employed dynamic panel threshold estimation for each of the independent variables. The results indicated that trade openness, foreign direct investment, and official development assistance have significant threshold levels at 24.24%, 23.44%, and 23.21%, respectively. This suggests that the effects of foreign capital inflows and trade openness operate across two regimes—base and high—defined by these thresholds. Comparative analysis of symmetric and asymmetric effects without threshold considerations showed that trade openness consistently exerts positive long- and short-term influences on economic growth, both symmetrically and asymmetrically. Conversely, foreign direct investment (FDI) does not demonstrate a significant symmetric effect but exhibits an asymmetric long-term impact on growth. Additionally, official development assistance (ODA) shows an asymmetric effect that surpasses its symmetric influence on economic growth, highlighting the vulnerability of African economies to financial shocks. Negative shocks in the interaction between FDI and ODA have a more pronounced effect on growth than positive shocks. In the long run, variables such as capital, the globalization index, and political stability positively and significantly impact economic growth, while the labor force has a negative effect. Overall, the findings underscore the importance of creating policy environments that strengthen the capacity to absorb foreign capital, manage trade openness effectively, and coordinate aid and investment policies to foster sustainable economic growth across Africa. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Buy now, pay later in e-commerce: Platform provisioning strategies and sharing intentions
Abstract: As an innovative financial payment tool, Buy now, pay later (BNPL) is profoundly reshaping e-commerce transactions. However, existing literature on BNPL primarily focuses on its impact on consumers through empirical research, paying little attention to the strategic decisions of stakeholders such as BNPL providers, e-commerce platforms, and third-party sellers (TPSs). We address this gap by developing a game-theoretic framework that reveals the decision-making processes of stakeholders regarding BNPL provision, adoption, and sharing. Our findings suggest that the e-commerce platform is more likely to introduce BNPL and sellers are more willing to adopt BNPL when it induces a relatively large incremental demand. However, this does not necessarily encourage the platform to share BNPL with the TPS. Our analysis shows that sharing BNPL emerges as an equilibrium strategy only when incremental demand and service fees are moderate. Under such sharing arrangements, a higher service fee is more likely to prompt the e-commerce platform to provide BNPL itself. This game-theoretic approach helps stakeholders identify optimal strategies and provides theoretical guidance for platform operational decisions and management information system optimization. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The road to hell is paved with good intentions: How does the construction of low-carbon cities affect corporate low-carbon technological innovation in manufacturing?
Abstract: Low-carbon technological innovation (LCTI) is crucial for decarbonization and global climate change mitigation. Taking China's Low-carbon City Pilot (LCCP)—a pioneering exploration for low-carbon development through policy innovation—as an exogenous policy shock, this study utilizes a staggered difference-in-difference-in-differences model and the data of China's manufacturing firms to examine the causality between the voluntary carbon regulation and LCTI. For the first time, the results indicate that the LCCP enactment significantly hinders corporate LCTI, contradicting the predictions of the Porter hypothesis. Mechanism analysis reveals that under the LCCP framework, local governments are authorized to design innovative policies tailored to their specific conditions and are responsible for their own assessment. Using a two-stage LLM-based approach to construct a climate policy uncertainty perception index, we confirm that this “bottom-up” approach introduces significant policy uncertainty faced by firms and weakens their motivation for LCTI involvement. Furthermore, the compliance costs associated with the policy crowd out the funds for LCTI, further hindering firms from engaging in LCTI. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the adverse impact is more evident among firms exhibiting high risk aversion, ones with high artificial intelligence (AI) technology exposure, ones situated in non-resource-based cities, and state-owned ones, and that the adverse impact is significant for emission reduction technologies and zero-carbon technologies, but not for negative-carbon technologies. Title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
Abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. This study provides context-specific empirical evidence on how formal just culture is translated into frontline reporting practice and offers practical insights that may inform efforts to improve near-miss reporting, reduce reporting concerns and strengthen closed-loop feedback in comparable organisational or cultural settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Datta R.; Ballard M.
Title: Women-Led Wildfire Disaster Adaptations within and from Indigenous Knowledge Perspectives
Abstract: This study examines Indigenous women-led wildfire disaster adaptations through traditional environmental knowledge and community-led strategies. Centering Indigenous traditional story sharing, intergenerational learning, and land stewardship, Indigenous women serve as key leaders in wildfire prevention and forest management. The research highlights the role of Indigenous fire governance in sustainable land management and the critical intersection between traditional knowledge and Western scientific tools in Chang Mai, Thailand. Using decolonial methodologies, the study highlights the necessity of Indigenous women leadership in climate-resilience efforts. Findings reveal that Indigenous women's practices contribute significantly to biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation, and community-led disaster response. The study calls for stronger academic engagement with Indigenous knowledge and policy reforms that center Indigenous women's expertise into global forest fire governance. The research provides a foundation for future transdisciplinary collaborations, advocating for Indigenous women's leadership in sustainable wildfire management.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Specker E.; Schino G.
Title: Different knowledge, different aesthetic experiences (and vice versa)?
Abstract: Do different kinds of knowledge lead to different aesthetic experiences (and vice versa)? This paper addresses this question by examining the role of (art) knowledge within an interactionist perspective. Contemporary theories increasingly conceptualize aesthetic experience as emerging from the interaction between perceiver, stimuli, and contexts rather than from isolated properties of artworks or perceivers alone. Despite this theoretical shift, empirical research still often investigates knowledge as a characteristic of perceivers. We argue for a broader and more integrative understanding of knowledge that distinguishes between internal knowledge, residing within the perceiver, and external knowledge, provided by the environment. Internal knowledge encompasses prior experiences, competencies, and beliefs, whereas external knowledge includes information embedded in contextual features such as exhibition settings, curatorial texts, and other environmental cues. Drawing on empirical literature and illustrative findings from museum and laboratory studies, we show that aesthetic experiences are shaped by the continuous interaction between these two forms of knowledge. External knowledge can activate relevant internal knowledge, guide expectations, and support interpretation, while internal knowledge influences how viewers engage with artworks, seek additional information, and construct meaning. This reciprocal process can generate new insights that become incorporated into future knowledge structures, thereby influencing subsequent aesthetic encounters. Our perspective aligns with phenomenological perspectives emphasizing situated and embodied engagement with the world. We conclude that variations in aesthetic experiences give rise to differences in knowledge (and vice versa), and more specifically, that this is due to the interaction between internal and external forms of knowledge during aesthetic experiences. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Not naive, just gullible: psycho-cognitive vulnerability and fraud victimization in Italy
Abstract: Fraud represents a growing and complex threat in contemporary societies, with consequences that extend beyond economic losses. Despite increasing international evidence, limited research has examined the psychological and cognitive factors associated with fraud victimization in the Italian context, particularly in relation to online scams. This study examines individual differences and fraud experiences among 600 Italian adults through an online survey assessing sociodemographic characteristics, fraud experiences, personality traits, gullibility, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy. Results revealed that more than half of the sample (n = 416) reported exposure to scam attempts, most of which occurred through remote channels (either exclusively online or in combination with offline channels). A smaller subset (n = 115) reported actual fraud victimization. A binomial logistic regression was conducted to identify individual factors associated with fraud victimization among exposed individuals. Gullibility emerged as the only statistically significant predictor, indicating that higher gullibility was associated with a greater likelihood of victimization, whereas sociodemographic characteristics, personality traits, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy were not significantly associated with victimization. These findings highlight that fraud prevention strategies may benefit from considering psycho-cognitive vulnerability factors alongside traditional financial and digital literacy initiatives. © 2026

Authors: Sajadi A.; Dadashpoor H.
Title: Explaining the relationship between urban land use per capita and residents’ perceived accessibility using a spatial justice approach: A case study of Tehran metropolis
Abstract: Land use per capita remains one of the most widely used quantitative indicators in urban planning for evaluating the provision of urban services. Despite its normative significance, its validity as a proxy for accessibility has received limited empirical examination. This study investigates the extent to which land use per capita provision corresponds to accessibility outcomes across seven neighborhoods in District 20 of Tehran. Using a spatial evaluation model, spatial equity is evaluated through observed service distributions and survey-based accessibility data. Accessibility is operationalized as a measurable variable derived from standardized survey responses. Statistical analyses and spatial diagnostics, including Global Moran’s I, are employed to explain the relationship between six categories of service-related land uses and reported accessibility levels. The findings reveal that higher land use per capita provision does not consistently translate into improved accessibility. The relationship is weak and spatially unstable, while service distribution exhibits a fragmented and non-clustered pattern across neighborhoods. These results suggest that land use per capita standards provide only a partial representation of accessibility outcomes. Spatial configuration and distributional structure emerge as key dimensions influencing the effectiveness of service provision. The study highlights the need for more robust, evidence-based evaluation models that integrate spatial and behavioral dimensions of accessibility. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Anger regulation scale for adolescents (ARS-A): Psychometric properties of the Portuguese version and its associations with emotion regulation, depression, and anxiety
Abstract: Adolescence is marked by difficulties in anger regulation, which are linked to internalising and externalising problems. Despite this, the instruments currently available to measure anger regulation in adolescents have a limited evidence base and require further investigation. The present study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the Anger Regulation Scale for Adolescents (ARS-A) in the Portuguese context. A sample of 432 adolescents aged 11 to 18 (M = 13.73, SD = 1.61) from different regions of Portugal participated in this study. The factor structure and model fit were assessed through Principal Component Analysis and Confirmatory Factor Analysis, using the Solomon method for equivalent sample splitting. All subscales demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and fit indices, confirming the original three-dimensional structure after two items were removed. Pearson correlations with other measures of behavioural and cognitive emotion regulation were consistent with theoretical expectations, although not all associations were as expected. Correlations between anger regulation, depression and anxiety corroborated the relationship between dysfunctional anger regulation and emotional distress. The ARS-A is a reliable and valid measure of anger regulation for adolescents. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Testing different metrics for syntactic and morphological complexity in aphasic discourse: A cross-genre comparison in Spanish
Abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study is to determine which of four tasks testing different discourse genres (descriptive, procedural, conversational, and narrative) is the most sensitive in detecting syntactic and morphological complexity deficits in Spanish aphasia. Additionally, we compare two approaches for measuring syntax in discourse to identify the most accurate set of metrics for discriminating group membership. Method: In this comparative cross-sectional study, we analyzed the discourse of an aphasia group (N = 20) and a non-brain-damaged group (N = 14). Data was preprocessed using manual and automated procedures. We measured syntactic complexity through proxies (mean length of utterance, noun-verb ratio, and verbs per utterance), in addition to a competing ‘syntactic structures’ metric. The latter includes variables of subordination, left branching, relative clauses, and word integration, while morphological complexity was measured through an inflectional index. Results: The descriptive and narrative tasks highlighted the most significant differences across syntactic complexity metrics between the groups. Additionally, nested binomial logistic regression models showed that the ‘syntactic structures’ metric predicted groups better than the proxies alone. Conclusions: A comprehensive assessment of syntactic complexity can be obtained through the administration of both descriptive and narrative tasks. The measurement of ‘syntactic structures’ in discourse proved a fitter and finer-grained approach for group discrimination than the incorporation of syntactic proxies alone. These findings provide guidance for a precise discourse assessment in Spanish aphasia. © 2026 The Authors
