Title: Experiences of after-dark urban forest walks when using head torches: off-the-shelf vs customised
Abstract: During the dark season, electric lighting in urban forests can facilitate recreational activities and psychological restoration. However, the permanent presence of electric lighting causes light pollution, with detrimental effects for people and wildlife. This study explored the extent to which head torches could support pedestrian needs in a Nordic context where daylight hours are reduced during the winter season. The aim was to compare the pedestrian appraisal of an urban forest path under different lighting conditions: daylight (DL); regular off-the-shelf head torches (OHT); and customised head torches (CHT), with reduced light distribution and thereby less light pollution. The 75 participants completed structured walks with observer-based environmental assessments on site by means of questionnaires under DL, OHT or CHT light conditions. The results showed that participants experienced (appraised) the urban forest path similarly in the two head torch conditions in terms of visual accessibility, perceived safety, and the restorative potential of the forest setting. The behavioural intention to choose the path did not differ between head torches, but the intention to avoid the path was lower with OHT. No differences in comfort aspects of the light could be identified. As expected, the urban forest was rated higher for the environmental appraisals in DL, but retained its restorative potential even in the two head torch conditions. Authors: Guan Q.; Gong T.; Wang Y.; Tang X.; Ji P.; Guo K.
Title: A Land-Sea integrated ecological compensation framework based on carbon sequestration service flows: Evidence from a Coastal City
Abstract: Ecological compensation (EC) is an important policy instrument for coordinating ecological conservation and economic development and promoting carbon neutrality. However, existing EC policies in coastal regions remain largely terrestrial-oriented, making it difficult to identify cross-regional dependence on land-sea carbon sequestration services (CSs) and the corresponding compensation responsibilities. Using Qingdao, China, as a case study, this study develops a land-sea integrated EC framework that combines random forest, the IPCC inventory method, and a spatial interaction model to identify land-sea CSs supply-demand patterns and carbon sequestration service flows (CSF), and to allocate EC responsibilities accordingly. The results show that: (1) from 2004 to 2023, the imbalance between CSs supply and demand continuously intensified, with pronounced spatial mismatches; (2) CSF exhibited clear land-sea coupling, with the sea area and coastal mountainous area (Laoshan District) serving as the major CSF sources. CSF outflows from the sea area accounted for 29.02%–47.81% of the total positive regional CSF and primarily flowed to the rapidly urbanizing area of Huangdao District; and (3) actual EC payments differed markedly from ideal responsibilities across county-level administrative units, while the sea area received 78.10% of total inter-county compensation receipts. The Ecological Compensation Priority Index (ECPI) further indicated that the sea area and key terrestrial CSs supply areas should be prioritized for compensation. By integrating land-sea ecological contributions, external CSs dependence, compensation responsibilities, and implementation priorities into a unified analysis, the framework can support more equitable and efficient EC decision-making in coastal regions. © 2026

Authors: Torpuş K.; Cengiz S.
Title: Development of flood fear scale and investigation of psychometric properties
Abstract: This study aimed to develop a flood fear scale. The study was designed as a methodological and cross-sectional study. The study was conducted with 1158 participants aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region between February 15, 2025, and May 15, 2025. SPSS 25 and Amos 21 programs were used to analyze the data. The flood fear scale consists of four dimensions and 26 items. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was 0.948, and the scale explained 62.644% of the total variance. The model fit indices were χ2/ df = 3.444, RMSEA = 0.065, SRMR = 0.056, CFI = 0.921, IFI = 0.922, NFI = 0.893, and TLI = 0.912. The findings indicated that the flood fear scale provided valid and reliable for adults aged 18–65 residing in Türkiye’s Black Sea Region. The total scores obtainable from the scale range from 26 to 130, with higher scores indicating an increased level of flood fear. Title: Empowering adaptive MOOCs: A learning path recommendation model based on multi-level knowledge graphs and rule-guided path constraint optimization
Abstract: Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) provide abundant learning resources, yet their fixed instructional structures and limited adaptive support constrain learning effectiveness. Second, building on this framework, we develop a rule-guided path constraint optimization method, which incorporates dynamic reasoning mechanisms, path constraint modeling, and learning gain simulation to deliver adaptive learning path recommendations. Implemented in a prototype integrating seven database-related MOOCs, KGRRec was evaluated through a one-group pretest-posttest study (34 students) and a randomized controlled study (59 students). Results showed KGRRec significantly outperformed eight baselines on Prerequisite, CogValidity-F, and expert ratings. Title: A multimodal framework for Linking perceived Affordances, Emotions, and behavioral Rhythms in urban parks
Abstract: Urban park experiences arise from the interplay of perception, emotion, and behavior, yet these dimensions are rarely examined in an integrated manner. This proof-of-concept research note presents a reproducible modular toolkit that links review-derived perceived environmental qualities, review-derived affective valence, and mobility-derived visitation behavior within a shared analytical structure. A pilot implementation across 109 public parks in Detroit, Michigan, combines 10,509 Google Maps reviews with Advan Research Monthly Patterns mobility data from January 2021 to May 2025, joined to American Community Survey 2019–2023 estimates. Interpretable gradient-boosting models reveal contrasting associations: visitation frequency is linked primarily to visitor demographics and functional amenities, whereas dwell intensity is more strongly associated with perceived comfort, safety, and positive emotions. Title: Transformations in nursing education: Voices of senior faculty members with decades of experience
Abstract: Background: Nursing education in Türkiye has undergone profound structural transformations over the past decades, driven by rapid program expansion, intensifying demands for research productivity, digitalization, and the erosion of academic-clinical continuity. Despite their centrality to educational quality, the lived experiences of senior nursing faculty members navigating these changes remain largely unexplored. Aim: To explore how senior nursing faculty members in Türkiye describe the major transformations in nursing education throughout their careers and how these changes have shaped their professional roles and academic identities. Design: Descriptive qualitative research design using thematic analysis. Settings: Multiple higher education institutions providing nursing education in Türkiye. Participants: Twelve senior nursing faculty members were recruited through purposive sampling with maximum variation, supplemented by snowball sampling to reach participants across diverse institutional contexts; the mean age was 54.67 years, with an average of 29.50 years of academic experience. Methods: Data were collected through semi-structured, in-depth, online individual interviews. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis framework. Rigor was ensured through reflexive researcher positioning, collaborative analytic discussion, and member checking with six participants. Results: Three themes emerged: the transformation of academic nursing identity, characterized by growing distance from clinical practice and competing academic demands; shifting student cultures and the transformation of teaching, reflecting pedagogical alienation and decreased depth of learning; and the transformation of academic production from quality to quantity, characterized by metric-driven academic value, disconnection from nursing practice, and the burden of academic productivity. Conclusions: Senior nursing faculty members in Türkiye are navigating interlocking structural pressures that have destabilized the professional foundations of nursing academia. Title: Terror management and antagonistic personality: A network analysis of the dark tetrad, self-esteem, and fears of death and dying

It also showed comparatively high strength but near-zero expected influence due to offsetting positive and negative edges. D4 traits showed distinct TMT-related profiles: Machiavellianism connected negatively to self-esteem and positively to FoDeath-Others, with lower strength and intermediate expected influence; narcissism connected positively to self-esteem but no fears, and showed the highest D4 expected influence; psychopathy connected negatively to self-esteem, FoDying-Self, and FoDeath-Others, but positively to FoDeath-Self, showing the highest D4 strength but lower expected influence due to offsetting positive and negative edges; sadism was unrelated to self-esteem and connected negatively to FoDying-Others, showing lower strength and intermediate expected influence. Title: Energy equity under crisis pricing: the vulnerability-responsiveness paradox in Norwegian residential electricity consumption during the European energy crisis
Abstract: Dynamic electricity pricing is widely advocated for demand-side management, yet its distributional consequences under crisis conditions remain poorly understood. Title: From uncertain preferences to reliable predictions: A hierarchical preference uncertainty propagation framework for rating prediction
Abstract: Rating prediction in review-based recommender systems requires both accurate estimates and reliable confidence scores. Existing review-based models often consolidate user review histories into a single preference representation, obscuring stable persona preferences and context-dependent situational preferences. Title: The sweet spot of seeing: A categorization-based account of visual aesthetic pleasure
Abstract: Aesthetic pleasure is shaped by many visual attributes, including prototypicality, fluency, complexity, symmetry, and self-relevance, but it is unclear why such diverse factors all influence liking. I propose that a major component of visual aesthetic pleasure is an epiphenomenon of categorization in the visual system, constrained by the metabolic cost of neural activity. In this view, successfully recognizing a stimulus as a member of a category is intrinsically rewarding because it supports perception, generalization, and planning, and aesthetic pleasure partly reflects the summed effect of many local rewards for successful categorization across the visual hierarchy. At the same time, neural activity costs energy, so that strongly driven, cluttered, or statistically extreme displays incur costs that can make them aversive even when they are easily interpretable. The “sweet spot of seeing” (3S) model formalizes visual pleasure as a compromise between categorization-based reward and metabolic expense. It offers a unifying explanation for prototype effects, fluency and mere exposure, mid-level regularities such as symmetry and good continuation, and visual discomfort. The model links classic inverted-U relations between complexity and liking to a concrete trade-off between information and cost, and it makes specific predictions for how aesthetic preferences change due to expertise or fatigue. Title: Self-regulated learning trajectories, predictors, and cognitive outcomes in animation-facilitated computational thinking: A growth mixture modelling study of primary students

Title: Industrial robotization and provincial green synergy performance in China: Coupling coordination, regional disparities, and dynamic responses

Title: When interface style meets personality: Big five differences in self-extension and emotional attachment in online shopping platforms

Authors: Öztaş İ.; Demir E.; Yava A.
Title: Closing the gap or transforming the crisis? A qualitative study on the mentoring model as a sustainable solution to instructor shortage in surgical nursing education
Abstract: Background: Pressures on the global nursing education workforce and a growing shortage of clinical educators in surgical settings have placed preceptorship models at the heart of education. Viewing nursing education as a “revenue-generating commodity” raises concerns regarding the erosion of academic identity and the risk of disciplinary expertise being reduced to a technical craft. Aim: This study aimed to describe the effects of the mentorship model in surgical nursing education on academic identity, pedagogical processes, and workforce sustainability, based on the perceptions of academicians and clinical mentor nurses. Design: A study using a qualitative descriptive design was conducted to gather in-depth perspectives from stakeholders in academic and clinical fields. Method: Data were collected through semi-structured individual interviews; audio recordings were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using a self-reflective thematic analysis framework. The study involved 10 academics from the Department of Surgical Nursing and 10 preceptor nurses who supervise students in surgical clinics (Total N = 20). Findings: The analysis revealed four main themes: a shift in academic identity, highlighting the transition of academics from clinical expertise to administrative coordination; pedagogical tension, pointing to the risk of surgical nursing education devolving into the mere transfer of technical skills—or a “watch-and-do” model; a sustainability paradox, describing the invisible labor undertaken by clinical preceptors and the accompanying sense of burnout; and institutional disconnect, revealing—through the participants' own words—the gap between theory and clinical reality. Conclusions: The findings indicate that participants perceive a significant risk regarding the sustainability of the current preceptorship model. Key implications arising from these findings include the development of defined collaboration protocols between the university and the hospital, the recognition of the educational contributions made by clinical preceptor nurses, and the piloting of clinical-academic hybrid staffing models. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhou D.; Gong Z.
Title: Organizational responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI versus human failures in government services
Abstract: Existing research provides only limited insights into whether, compared to traditional human service failures, artificial intelligence (AI) failures in government services lead the public to attribute more responsibility to the service organization, and whether outsourcing necessarily alleviates organizational responsibility attribution. To advance this debate, this study conducted three pre-registered survey experiments. Study 1 (N = 1112) reveals that citizens attributed more responsibility to the service organization for AI service failures than to human service agents. The effect was mediated by the perceived service provider's controllability, rather than by counterfactual thinking. Study 2 proposed and tested two distinct pathways, namely the responsibility-transfer and controllability-transfer pathways. The objective was to explain how diminished controllability perceived at the individual service provider level increases the attribution of responsibility to the organization. Empirical evidence (N = 1084) supports the responsibility-transfer pathway. When citizens perceive that AI agents have less control over services than humans, they assign less responsibility to the AI agent and transfer more responsibility to the service organization. Study 3 (N = 1007) examines whether disclosing that the AI agent was externally developed mitigates the attribution of organizational responsibility. Compared to in-house AI systems, outsourcing to either a state-owned enterprise or a private enterprise, rather than to other government organizations, reduced organizational responsibility. In this study, this reduction was substantial enough to eliminate the disparity between AI and human service failures. This study advances theories of responsibility attribution in the digital era, highlighting the nuanced role of outsourcing transparency and the responsibility-transfer mechanism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Xu Y.; Mi Y.; Wu Y.; Shen J.; Wang C.; Zhao G.; Liu C.; Qian X.
Title: From scoring to workflow: A survey of agentic recommender systems
Abstract: Agentic recommender systems (ARS) extend recommendation from one-shot item scoring to interactive, adaptive, and feedback-driven workflows. Yet existing surveys rarely examine the coupling between agentic mechanisms and recommender system pipelines. This survey provides a recommender-system-centered analysis of ARS by examining how agents restructure decision objects across the workflow. Through systematic literature search, this survey constructs an analytical corpus of 47 studies published or made publicly available between January 2023 and April 2026. It organizes current ARS research into four workflow stages: User Modeling, Adaptive Decision Orchestration, Candidate Optimization, and Exposure Refinement. Across these stages, this survey synthesizes representative methods, evaluation resources, design trade-offs, deployment burdens, cross-stage dependencies, and recurring failure modes. The analysis also identifies key challenges in simulator fidelity, memory scalability, strategy-candidate alignment, candidate provenance, explanation faithfulness, feedback reliability, and runtime governance. It also highlights future opportunities enabled by frontier agentic mechanisms. Overall, this survey offers an RS-centric framework for understanding current progress and guiding reliable, scalable, and governable ARS research. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhu J.; Jiang Y.; Zhu F.; Chai Y.; Liu Y.
Title: Target item identification for injection attacks in recommender systems via graph-enhanced user representations
Abstract: Recommender systems are increasingly threatened by profile injection attacks. However, most existing defenses focus on detecting fake users, which becomes unreliable as modern attacks generate highly concealed profiles and operational platforms often lack attacker labels or attack priors. To address this limitation, we propose TIGER (Target Item Identification via Graph-Enhanced Representations), a hybrid auditing-oriented framework that reframes the final defensive output from user-level fake user labels to item-level suspicious target item candidates. Importantly, TIGER does not eliminate user-side analysis; instead, it uses unsupervised suspicious user discovery as an intermediate support step for downstream auditing. Specifically, TIGER first leverages a small trusted reference set to learn stable item embeddings and aligns unknown data into a shared semantic space. It then constructs graph-enhanced user representations by integrating rating statistics, preference patterns, and item semantics, enabling the extraction of informative suspicious user candidates for target item auditing. Finally, suspicious target item candidates are flagged through a rank-shift auditing strategy that compares recommendation outcomes before and after reintroducing suspicious users. Extensive experiments on three widely used datasets under ten representative attack scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TIGER. Across ten attacks, TIGER achieves average DR@5/DR@10 values of 0.4430/0.6120, 0.5550/0.7500, and 0.2670/0.3400 on ML-100K, ML-1M, and Automotive, outperforming the average results of the best baseline selected for each attack by 106.20%/28.25%, 72.36%/64.84%, and 154.29%/111.18%, respectively. These results indicate that TIGER provides a reliable auditing tool for identifying high-risk target item candidates in adversarial recommender systems. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Afridi R.; Azfar R.W.; Waqas M.; Tanoli W.A.; Qureshi H.J.
Author full names: Afridi, Rowaid (60971524700); Azfar, Rai Waqas (57191163844); Waqas, Muhammad (60957528400); Tanoli, Waqas Arshad (57196245739); Qureshi, Hisham Jahangir (55750149000)
Title: Bridging Transparency Gaps in Construction Claims through Blockchain Integration
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: The construction industry plays a vital role in Pakistan's economy, yet it continues to face persistent challenges in claim administration that hinder project performance, transparency, and trust among stakeholders. This study addresses these challenges by identifying the principal shortcomings of conventional claim management systems and developing a blockchain-based claims management application to improve security, traceability, and procedural efficiency. A three-stage research design was adopted. First, a systematic literature review was conducted to identify deficiencies in traditional claim management practices. This was followed by semistructured interviews with fifteen contract specialists involved in extension of time (EOT) claims to validate and refine the identified issues. Second, a decentralized application (DApp) was developed using React.js front-end and Solidity-based smart contracts and deployed on the Polygon test network to enable faster and more cost-effective transactions. Third, the developed system was evaluated through expert review involving 32 participants drawn from contracting, consulting, client organizations, and academia, followed by statistical analysis. The findings indicate that the proposed blockchain-based claims management system (B-CMS) improves data integrity, transparency, traceability, and timeliness in claim administration compared with traditional approaches. However, the system is not intended to replace professional judgment in highly subjective claim situations and is not suitable for capturing oral instructions or unstructured design and work-pattern changes. Despite these limitations, the study demonstrates the feasibility of B-CMS for construction claim administration in Pakistan and offers insights that may be relevant to comparable project environments internationally.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Author full names: Bernardelle, Pietro (59412634100); Civelli, Stefano (59510569500); Fröhling, Leon (57223204695); Lunardi, Riccardo (59414092500); Roitero, Kevin (57191042663); Demartini, Gianluca (23087954800)
Title: Political Ideology Shifts in Large Language Models
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in politically sensitive contexts, raising concerns about their susceptibility to ideological biases. In this work, we examine how synthetic persona conditioning shapes ideological expression across seven open-weight instruction-tuned models (7B–72B parameters) using the Political Compass Test (62 statements) as a standardized behavioral probe. Across three studies involving 200,000 synthetic personas and more than 260 million model responses, we analyze implicit and explicit malleability, as well as theme-associated variation. We find that: (i) larger models exhibit broader implicit ideological coverage, increasing from 14%–35% for 7–8B models to up to 49% for 70B+ models; (ii) explicit ideological priming induces large and statistically significant shifts, with right-authoritarian cues moving all models in the intended direction and generally producing larger shifts than left-libertarian cues across model-axis comparisons; (iii) left-libertarian priming produces more heterogeneous responses, with counter-directional economic shifts in three of four 7–8B models and intended-direction shifts across all 70B+ models; and (iv) theme-associated semantic content in persona descriptions is linked to systematic and interpretable directional shifts in ideological space. While our results identify an upstream mechanism through which persona conditioning can alter model responses under a standardized ideological probe, we do not test whether such shifts affect users’ beliefs, decisions, or political behavior. Our findings are best understood as evidence of ideological malleability at the generation layer, highlighting the need to account for interactional factors when evaluating political neutrality, fairness, and safety in English-prompted, persona-conditioned language models. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Novotorzhentseva A.; Poon M.
Title: Cultivating high-reliable organizing: A holistic perspective
Abstract: High-reliable organizing (HRO) has long been associated with how organizations sustain reliable performance under conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and change. While Mindful Organizing (MO), and Resilience Engineering (RE) have generated important theoretical insights, guidance on how organizations can cultivate HRO in everyday organizing remains fragmented. This conceptual essay develops a holistic perspective that positions HRO as an ongoing accomplishment rather than a fixed organizational capability or the outcome of implementing isolated concepts. Through a systematic comparison of the five established MO processes and the four resilience potentials, we show how the two perspectives can be related while preserving their distinct analytical orientations. MO focuses on the collective organizing through which people notice, interpret, coordinate, and respond to emerging situations, while RE emphasizes organizational potentials to monitor, respond, anticipate, and learn under changing conditions. Building on this synthesis, we develop the holistic framework of HRO, identify two additional organizing processes— preoccupation with things that go right and self-awareness —and develop an approach to cultivating and operationalizing HRO through collaborative inquiry, driving forces, and situated practices. Rather than prescribing predefined practices, we argue that organizations can cultivate mindsets and directions of attention that guide how established concepts are translated to context-sensitive action while remaining grounded in the scientific foundations of HRO, MO, and RE. The essay contributes a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding and cultivating high-reliable organizing as an ongoing accomplishment in complex sociotechnical systems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Xin Z.; Qiaoyun Y.; Jixuan H.; Jiao W.; Li W.
Title: eHealth literacy levels and associated factors among nursing students: A global systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Background: The rapid digital transformation of healthcare highlights the importance of electronic health literacy (eHealth literacy) for nursing students. However, existing global evidence regarding their eHealth literacy levels and associated factors remains fragmented. Objective: To determine the overall level of e-health literacy among nursing students worldwide, analyze its associated factors and associations with health outcomes, and provide evidence-based support for nursing education reform in the digital age. Methods: A systematic search was conducted in eight Chinese and international databases, including PubMed, for cross-sectional studies published from the inception of each database through June 1, 2026. Study quality was assessed using the AHRQ scale, and random-effects meta-analyses and meta-regression analyses were performed using Stata 19.0. This systematic review protocol was registered in advance with PROSPERO (Registration No.: CRD420261418156). Results: A total of 20 cross-sectional studies involving 12,390 nursing students across 11 countries were ultimately included. The pooled eHEALS score for nursing students worldwide was29.51 (95% CI: 28.42–30.61), indicating an overall level slightly above average; however, there was extremely high heterogeneity among studies (I2 = 99.4%, P < 0.001). Senior-year students demonstrated significantly higher levels of literacy than junior-year students (SMD = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.41–0.59, P < 0.001); gender had no significant overall effect on literacy (SMD = −0.04, 95% CI: −0.35–0.27, P = 0.803). Regression analysis showed that living in an urban area (β = 4.24, P < 0.001) and having good economic conditions (β = 0.79, P < 0.001) were exploratory study-level indicators associated with higher literacy. Digital health literacy was moderately positively correlated with health-promoting behaviors (r = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.35–0.49, P < 0.001) and was significantly associated with lower levels of anxiety (OR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.92–0.99, P = 0.006). Conclusions: Overall, the digital health literacy of nursing students worldwide is acceptable, but regional digital divides remain prominent. Systematic nursing education may help enhance digital health literacy, which is associated with more positive health behaviors and mental health outcomes. Institutions need to refine their digital health curriculum systems, focusing on cultivating students' abilities in information evaluation and AI-assisted decision-making to meet the evolving demands of digital healthcare and artificial intelligence. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Stamkou E.; da Silva Pinho A.
Author full names: Stamkou, Eftychia (57217604327); da Silva Pinho, Ana (57705708800)
Title: Out of the picture: A multilevel framework of gender disparities in art
Abstract: Why do women artists remain a minority in museum collections and art markets, decades after becoming the majority in art schools? Talent does not explain it, since creative ability shows no meaningful gender differences, and audiences cannot tell an artist's gender from the work itself. The gap persists, we argue, because it is produced by a system rather than at any single stage of artwork production, selection, and reception. We therefore introduce a multilevel framework that treats the art world as an ecosystem. Artists, gatekeepers, and audiences act on artworks within three embedded levels of analysis (individual, institutional, and societal), and gender enters the ecosystem not only through these actors but also through the gendered content of artworks and the norms of the wider society. Actors, artworks, and norms interact across levels and over time. Societal beliefs in male artistic genius are internalized by artists and audiences and enacted by gatekeeping institutions; biased selections accumulate into a male canon; and the canon feeds that belief back to the next generation. The ecosystem is thus recursive, reproducing inequality without requiring discriminatory intent. Yet the same loop invites contestation, and excluded artists have answered with concealment, counter-institutions, and activism. Integrating evidence scattered across disciplines, this review derives a research agenda that treats the feedback loop, rather than any single stage, as the unit of analysis and as the lever of change. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Data-centric AI in disaster management: Scalable Named Entity Recognition via LLM-based stacking and pseudo-label generation
Abstract: This study presents a scalable Teacher–Student architecture for Named Entity Recognition (NER) that enables automatic information extraction from Turkish disaster-related social media texts. To reduce labeling costs, the collective intelligence of three large language models (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5) is combined through a learnable stacking meta-classifier. On a 500-tweet manually annotated dataset, stacking reached a token-level Macro F1 of 0.9313 (0.9219 under leakage-free tweet-level grouped cross-validation), on par with the strongest individual model (0.9245) and clearly above a BERT baseline trained on the same data (0.8335). It was selected as the Teacher for its learnable per-class weighting, its stability across meta-classifiers and its robustness to single-provider outages. The Teacher’s discrete predictions were transferred to a more efficient BERT Student through hard-label pseudo-labeling, and this Student was then used as a zero-cost proxy labeler to scale the corpus to 17,000 tweets. On a fully isolated 300-tweet blind test set, the final model obtained an entity-level Macro F1 of 0.9160, against 0.8648 for the baseline trained only on manual labels. A size-matched controlled experiment isolates the source of this gain: labeling the same 3000 tweets with the model ensemble instead of a self-training labeler improves entity-level Macro F1 by 0.033 in all five random seeds ((Formula presented) ), whereas scaling from 3000 to 17,000 instances adds only 0.006. Label quality, rather than data volume, drives the improvement, and the approach offers a practical, low-cost route to rapid humanitarian needs mapping when annotated data is scarce. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Narrative-driven VR exergames for active older adults: Examining the impact of narrative styles and themes on motivation and user experience
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Older adults often face the dual challenge of insufficient physical activity and unmet psychological needs. Although exergames can promote physical activity, they often struggle to sustain motivation or adequately support psychological need satisfaction. This work explores the potential of integrating narrative into a VR cycling exergame, focusing on how narrative design can enhance motivation and fulfill psychological needs. Two experiments examined the impact of narrative styles with varying interactivity demands and different narrative themes (hedonic, eudaimonic, mixed-affective) on user experience. Study 1 (N=15) suggested that interactive narrative styles were associated with enhanced autonomy and relatedness, facilitated attentional dissociation from bodily fatigue, and led to higher psychological need satisfaction and lower perceived exertion, albeit at the cost of increased cognitive demands. Study 2 (N=36) compared hedonic, eudaimonic, and mixed-affective narratives. Hedonic narratives appeared to support flow and motivation with relatively low cognitive demands, whereas eudaimonic narratives were linked to deeper emotional and reflective engagement but imposed higher cognitive and emotional demands, leading to reduced replay intention. Mixed-affective narratives, by contrast, presented a potentially more balanced trade-off between motivational benefits and competence satisfaction. Interpreted through a Self-Determination Theory-informed perspective, these findings provide insights into how narrative styles and affective themes may be leveraged to design VR exergames that better align psychological engagement with older adults’ physical capacities. Overall, these exploratory findings highlight both the promise and the limitations of narrative-driven exergame design, and they offer implications for the development of adaptive, psychologically informed exergames for older adults. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Using reusable ceramic vs. disposable cellulose-pulp plates in a wine tasting service in Italy: Findings from a life cycle assessment application experience
Abstract: Wine tourism, including winery visits, tastings, and cultural events, boosts sustainable development but generates environmental impacts ranging from food and wine production to tasting services. This study applies Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), focused on Carbon Footprint (CF), to compare the use of reusable ceramic vs. disposable cellulose-pulp plates in a tasting service in an Apulian winery. A cradle-to-grave analysis reveals that, in baseline scenario, reusable plates showed a slightly higher CF than single-use plates (0.0668 vs. 0.0635 kgCO₂eq/person served, respectively). Based on the results obtained, process optimisation solutions were identified: it was found that using photovoltaic-powered energy-efficient dishwasher may reduce the CF of reusable plates by 67%, reducing the impact to 0.0179 kgCO₂eq/person served in the best-performing scenario. Five service configurations were then tested over a total of 2500 customers served in six months, assuming a constant optimal dishwasher loading efficiency (i.e., operating exclusively at full capacity). Whilst the absolute reuse rate of the plate stock inherently scales with customer volume (averaging approximately 73 uses per plate in the baseline period), the results showed that, without technological improvements, the lowest-impact option was to serve 500 people with reusable plates and 2000 with disposable plates. Overall, this study extends the application of Life Cycle Assessment from conventional production systems to experiential tourism services. The findings demonstrate that the environmental performance of tableware is not solely dictated by intrinsic material properties, but is fundamentally driven by the systemic operational configuration, including dishwashing efficiency, service volumes, and the carbon intensity of the electricity mix. Consequently, this study provides a novel, scalable methodological framework to support wineries and tourism operators in designing scientifically grounded, lower-impact tasting services. © 2026

Authors: Wei W.; Hu Y.
Title: Extreme weather, long-term economic growth, and cross-border spillovers: Evidence from a multi-sector environmental DSGE model of China and the United States
Abstract: The rising frequency of extreme weather events threatens long-term economic growth. Few studies have integrated multiple extreme weather types, cross-country economic linkages, and sector-level dynamic adjustments in a single framework. This study fills that gap by developing a two-country, multi-sector environmental DSGE model linking extreme weather shocks to factor input allocation. It quantifies the long-term economic impacts of single and compound extreme weather shocks on China and the U.S., identifies mechanisms through factor and sectoral adjustments and cross-border transmission, and examines nonlinear economic adaptation under cumulative climate stress. The analysis includes baseline, single-hazard, and compound-shock scenarios. Results show compound shocks cause greater losses than single hazards, with storms having the largest impact. Cross-border spillovers from China to the U.S. are stronger than vice versa. Sectoral adjustments arise from capital and labor reallocation, while both economies exhibit nonlinear, threshold-dependent responses to cumulative shocks. By integrating cross-country linkages, sectoral adjustments, and adaptation, this study clarifies the dynamic mechanisms through which extreme weather affects long-term growth and provides policy-relevant insights for climate risk management and economic adaptation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Li T.; Zhai H.; Guo M.; Deng J.
Title: Escaping the AI cage: construction workers’ perceived risk with AI gives rise to unsafe behaviors
Abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Ried L.
Title: Contextualizing negotiation research: The unique dynamics of buyer–supplier negotiations
Abstract: Effective buyer–supplier negotiations are important for organizations to attain their goals and for wider society to have a reliable supply of goods and services. These negotiations also have distinctive characteristics that differentiate them from other negotiation settings, such as personal buyer–seller negotiations, which have attracted much of the attention in the negotiation literature. Given the differences between professional buyer–supplier and personal buyer–seller negotiations, some findings from personal negotiations may have limited applicability in supply chain settings, while others hold across contexts. These findings have important implications for both negotiation research and education, calling for careful contextualization based on the type of negotiation. By reviewing recent studies in the supply chain management literature, this article highlights several common dynamics of buyer–supplier negotiations and how they affect negotiation outcomes. These dynamics are broadly categorized into the non-exhaustive themes of power in ongoing buyer–supplier relationships, other relational factors (supply network complexity, cross-cultural relations, and AI adoption), and negotiation strategies in buyer–supplier relationships (distributive, integrative, and mixed strategies), providing scholars with an overview of selected recent research on buyer–supplier negotiations. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Hu L.; Yang A.J.; Deng S.
Title: Gender differences in early semantic trajectories and academic career persistence
Abstract: Gender disparities in academia are well documented in publication output, citations, and career attrition, yet relatively little is known about whether male and female scholars differ in the semantic development of their research. Using SPECTER2 embeddings derived from 67 million publications in OpenAlex, we characterize the semantic trajectories of 2.76 million scholars using three measures: semantic expansion (divergence from prior work), research coherence (consistency of prior research), and semantic alignment (continuity with prior research direction). On average, male scholars exhibit greater semantic expansion, whereas female scholars show higher research coherence and semantic alignment. These differences persist across career stages and productivity levels. Discrete-time hazard models further indicate that early semantic trajectories are associated with subsequent publication-based career persistence. Greater early semantic expansion is associated with a lower risk of dropout for both genders, whereas greater research coherence and semantic alignment are associated with a higher dropout risk, with stronger associations among female scholars. These patterns are consistently observed across major scientific disciplines. Together, our findings suggest that gender differences in academia are reflected not only in research productivity and career outcomes but also in the semantic organization of research development, and that early semantic trajectories are associated with subsequent patterns of career persistence. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Biscoe N.
Title: Remote video cognitive behavioural therapy for panic disorder with comorbid Crohn’s disease: a quasi-experimental single-case design
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: The current report describes the case of a man in his early 30s living with Crohn’s disease and presenting with a one-year history of panic disorder. The case study design was quasi-experimental single case, consisting of 14 sessions of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy − of which 11 were the intervention phase. The effectiveness of the intervention was measured weekly using the Panic Disorder Severity Scale (Shear et al., 1997) and the Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation (Barkham et al., 2013). Whilst symptoms of panic improved, the change in symptoms of general distress throughout treatment did not reach statistical significance. These outcomes are discussed in the context of complexity including physical ill health and comorbid trauma history. Authors: Lee H.; Lee J.S.
Title: Shaping street rhythms: Spatial context and the temporal patterns of pedestrian activity
Abstract: Urban streets provide spatial contexts in which pedestrian activity unfolds over time, yet previous research has seldom examined how these street rhythms differ across space or how they are associated with local street conditions. This study addresses this gap by examining street-level pedestrian rhythms across Seoul's commercial streets. Using mobile phone signal–based estimates of pedestrian presence for 110,574 street segments in 2022, we extract 11 temporal features from weekday pedestrian time series and apply fuzzy C-means clustering to identify five street rhythm types. Multinomial logistic regression evaluates how these rhythms relate to 16 indicators of commercial hierarchy, physical scale, accessibility, functional mix, and surrounding populations. The findings show that street rhythm types are systematically associated with multiple dimensions of spatial context, rather than reflecting simple differences in pedestrian-presence levels or land-use intensity. Even among commercially active streets, evening-peak rhythms were distinguished by concentrations of retail, leisure, and entertainment-oriented functions. Midday- and afternoon-peak rhythms, despite their similar daytime profiles, were also differentiated by their spatial contexts: midday-peak rhythms were associated with office- and institution-based workday districts, whereas afternoon-peak rhythms were linked to production-related commercial areas. By revealing these distinctions, this underscores the value of treating time as an integral dimension of urban spatial structure. © 2026

Authors: Cross E.S.
Title: Aesthetic perception is an embodied experience
Abstract: For at least the past century, philosophers have proposed a role for the human body in aesthetic perception. Scholars from experimental psychology, empirical aesthetics and human neuroscience joined in this endeavour in earnest at the start of the 21st century, following on from the establishment of neuroaesthetics as a formal scientific discipline as well as neuroscientific discoveries advancing our understanding of action–perception coupling in the human brain. The expansion of embodied accounts of aesthetic perception was most pronounced following the proliferation of research working directly with the performing arts (specifically dance), as such studies focus on the body as both subject and object, performer and observer. This piece charts the short history of scholarly thinking on aesthetic perception as an embodied experience and speculates on what the future of this line of inquiry might hold, especially given the increased involvement of disembodied AI tools in artistic practices and aesthetic experiences. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Choi J.
Title: Designing residential green electricity tariffs in a regulated retail market: Consumer heterogeneity and evidence from South Korea
Abstract: This study examines the design of a voluntary residential green electricity tariff in a regulated retail market where households cannot switch suppliers. In this context, the tariff functions as an administered rate-design instrument rather than a competitive retail product. Using a choice experiment and a latent class choice model (LCCM), the analysis identifies four preference classes in South Korea. The largest class (38.4%) is the most price-sensitive, with model-implied relative acceptability declining sharply as the premium increases. For the status quo-oriented class (21.7%), model-implied reservation premium thresholds are negative under all evaluated scenarios, indicating that none of the specified packages achieves utility equivalence with the status quo at a non-negative premium. Class membership is associated with trust in government energy policy and residential characteristics. No common ranking of tariff packages is observed across classes. These results support testing a limited menu of standardized tariff options rather than a single uniform design and using relatively low initial premium levels instead of treating the estimated thresholds as pricing targets. The size of the status quo-oriented class also suggests that voluntary premium payments alone are unlikely to achieve broad household participation. Any residential application would require regulatory approval, assessment of household bill impacts, and pilot testing. The findings are also relevant to other regulated electricity markets with limited or no supplier choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Economic consequences of climate change: Evidence from the Philippines
Abstract: This paper evaluates the economic implications of climate change in the Philippines. Data spanning two decades reveal that warmer temperatures increase out-migration, yet locations exposed to intense heat send fewer migrants to historically connected destinations. This pattern raises the question of how climate change affects the spatial allocation of economic activity when mobility is constrained. I employ a quantitative spatial equilibrium model in which rising temperatures and sea-level rise depress local amenities and productivity. Taking climate projections for 2100, I estimate aggregate welfare and output to fall by 15% and 12% respectively, with more prominent losses for high-skilled workers. Large-scale coastal protection can offset damages by up to 3 percentage points, but removing migration barriers attenuates welfare losses by as much as 13 percentage points. © 2026

Title: From disposition to action: The role of trait and state reactance in pro-choice protest participation in Poland
Abstract: Governmental restrictions on individual freedoms often elicit heterogeneous public responses. While some individuals mobilize collectively, others remain passive. The present study examines whether stable personality differences in trait reactance explain variability in protest engagement in response to abortion restrictions in Poland. Drawing on psychological reactance theory, we test a mediation model in which trait reactance predicts state reactance, which in turn predicts protest-supportive attitudes and collective action participation. Autonomy orientation and frustration with injustice were included as related dispositional variables to test the specificity of the proposed trait–state relationship. A sample of 586 participants completed measures of trait reactance, autonomy orientation, frustration with injustice, state reactance, and self-reported protest behavior. Structural equation modeling revealed that trait reactance positively predicted state reactance, which was strongly associated with favorable protest attitudes and higher participation. The indirect effect of trait reactance on participation via state reactance and attitudes was significant, whereas the direct effect was not. Autonomy orientation did not predict state reactance when controlling for trait reactance, providing evidence that the trait–state association was not explained by autonomy orientation. These findings suggest that sensitivity to freedom restriction is a key dispositional factor underlying collective action in response to political constraints. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Chen Z.; Shi Z.; Han Z.; Chen B.; Dong M.; Luo X.; Sun C.; Song Y.; Wang Y.; Wu L.
Title: Exposure–loss mismatch reveals regional and sectoral heterogeneity in flood-loss propensity
Abstract: Flood adaptation is often prioritized according to where economic assets are most exposed, although similar levels of exposure can be associated with markedly different losses. Identifying such differences is difficult because vulnerability is rarely observed directly at the sectoral and regional scales relevant to adaptation decisions. Here, we develop exposure–loss mismatch as an outcome-based diagnostic for identifying structural heterogeneity in how direct flood losses vary relative to economic exposure. Using China as a national case study, we reconstructed 116 historical flood events from 2003 to 2024 at 250 m × 250 m resolution, estimated inundation depth, mapped sectorally explicit economic exposure, and combined these estimates with event-level reported direct economic losses in a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Posterior estimates show that loss shares do not scale proportionally with exposure shares. Highly exposed provinces, including Guangdong, Sichuan, and Hunan, exhibit relative loss attenuation, whereas Hebei, Gansu, Ningxia, and Tianjin show stronger loss amplification in specific sectoral contexts. Commercial and service-oriented activities exhibit higher modeled loss propensity than industrial, construction, and residential activities. These patterns indicate systematic regional and sectoral differences in the relationship between economic exposure and direct flood losses, providing vulnerability-relevant information that is not apparent from exposure alone. The framework offers a potentially useful analytical approach for data-constrained settings where micro-level loss records are unavailable. By identifying where historical losses have been disproportionately high or low relative to exposure, it complements conventional exposure-based assessment and can help identify contexts in which more detailed vulnerability-focused evaluation may be warranted. © 2026

Title: Exploring the relationships between problem and responsible gambling behaviors across time
Abstract: Recent legislative and technological changes have transformed the gambling landscape in the United States, underscoring the need to better understand both problem gambling and responsible gambling behaviors. The Positive Play framework conceptualizes responsible gambling from the player’s perspective, yet little is known about how these behaviors change over time. The present study examined longitudinal changes in Positive Play scores and problem gambling symptoms among a sample of adult gamblers (n = 2,942). Participants completed repeated assessments of the Positive Play Scale and the Problem Gambling Severity Index across five waves over approximately two years. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the original four-factor structure of the Positive Play Scale. Latent growth models indicated that scores across all Positive Play subscales increased over time, while problem gambling symptoms decreased. Notably, increases in gambling literacy scores were associated with greater reductions in problem gambling severity, whereas changes in other Positive Play domains were not. These findings suggest that gambling literacy, in particular, may be associated with reductions in gambling-related harm over time. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wang Z.; Lai J.; Zhao Z.; Chen L.; Sun C.
Title: Hierarchical efficient anonymous authentication system for smart homes
Abstract: The proliferation of heterogeneous devices in smart homes poses significant challenges to secure and efficient authentication. Due to insecure communication channels, smart-home devices are highly susceptible to sophisticated impersonation attacks and are easily deceived by forged information from attackers, resulting in operational interference. While existing authentication schemes aim to isolate external attackers, they often struggle with high computational overhead or specific security vulnerabilities in dynamic IoT environments; notably, our analysis reveals that many remain susceptible to impersonation attacks. This paper proposes an anti-impersonation Hierarchical Anonymous Authentication (i-HAA) scheme supported by a tailored hierarchical architecture. Crucially, we construct a formal security model for i-HAA which rigorously defines and proves its resistance against the aforementioned impersonation attacks. By categorizing devices into high-performance administrators and low-performance data owners, the system offloads complex cryptographic computations to the former, significantly reducing latency for resource-constrained devices. Experimental results demonstrate that i-HAA achieves an authentication time of approximately 3.22 ms and a signing time of approximately 1.61 ms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Community Flood Perceptions in the Context of Flood Risk and Flood Hazard Indicators
Abstract: Floods have and continue to cause severe damage to property and loss of life globally and in the US. The perceived risk of flooding, defined as an individual’s subjective assessment of the likelihood and severity of a flood event, can influence their preparedness and response to flooding and proposed mitigation strategies. The current study investigated individuals’ flood risk perception using data from 700 responses to a telephone survey conducted in Harris County, Texas (Houston). Results indicated that individuals lack situational awareness (i.e., ability to perceive, understand, and effectively respond) of their flood risk but are well-informed and have opinions regarding proposed mitigation alternatives. The study correlated flood risk perception to select sociodemographic variables and demonstrated more corresponding perceptions of risk among older White and Asian communities. The study additionally pointed to the complexity of flood risk assessment and the lack of effective communication methods and tools to better inform individuals and communities. The study used data on flood hazard indicators such as past flooding and high-water marks after a flood to assess objective risks; it is proposed that such a framework presents an opportunity for more readily communicating flood risks to individuals and communities. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Author full names: Cruz, Miriam Ccarita (60823491600); Aziz, Ahmed Abdel (60263260400)
Title: Early Termination Provisions in Public–Private Partnerships: Synthesizing Institutional Guidance into Process-Based Benchmarks
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Early termination provisions (ETPs) are critical risk management mechanisms in public–private partnership (PPP) contracts, defining the conditions, processes, and consequences under which contracts may be terminated before their expiry. While leading institutional guidance documents provide extensive and authoritative treatment of ETPs, their coverage is dispersed across different mandates, drafting styles, and levels of procedural detail, making it difficult to extract a coherent, operational benchmark directly from the guidance. The objective of this study is to systematically synthesize institutional PPP guidance into a unified, process-based benchmark for early termination. Using inductive qualitative content analysis methodology, the study examines guidance issued by five widely recognized institutions: the World Bank, the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL), the European PPP Expertise Centre (EPEC), the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), and the US Federal Highway Administration (FHWA). The analysis identifies five principal ETP categories—private partner default, contracting authority default, voluntary termination, force majeure (FM), and uninsurability—and, where applicable, drives analytically grounded subcategories. These findings are translated into five benchmark flowcharts that operationalize early termination as a sequenced process structured around circumstances, procedures, and consequences. The results demonstrate that, despite differences in articulation and drafting depth, institutional guidance reflects a shared conceptual framework in which early termination is an exceptional outcome following the failure of cure, adaptation, or policy intervention mechanisms. The resulting benchmarks provide a practical reference for institutions to design, assess, and align ETP regimes in PPP contracts, supporting clearer risk allocation, improved governance, and more defensible termination practices. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Liu Z.-G.; Li X.-Y.; Qiao L.-M.
Title: Effects of China's Community Gridding on Coproduced Reporting of Rainstorm-Induced Emergencies: A Community-Wide Analysis
Abstract: Presently, the involvement of citizens in emergency management is inevitable and indispensable, but how to facilitate the participation of citizens remains unclear. Utilizing panel data from 174 communities in China between 2013 and 2023, this study investigated the effects of the community gridding policy (an important policy for facilitating citizen participation in public services in China) on citizens' coproduced reporting of rainstorm-induced emergencies (e.g., small-scale debris flow, water inundation, and trapped citizens) by integrating propensity score matching (PSM) and difference-in-differences (DID) methods. Statistical results showed that the community gridding significantly enhanced both citizens' reporting engagement (represented by the number of citizen reports) and reporting quality (represented by the ratio of the reports that have been accepted by communities to the total received reports). Mediating effect analysis showed that community gridding policy enhanced citizen reporting by increasing the capability of citizen training, reporting rule completeness, and technological maturity. In addition, the effects of community gridding on enhancing citizen reporting strengthened with the increase of the community scale. Furthermore, high risk perception increased the impact of community gridding on citizen reporting. The findings contribute to both the literature on and practice of emergency service coproduction and rainstorm disaster risk reduction. Moreover, those findings provide guidance of improving citizen participation for the jurisdictions that have similar rainstorm risk situations as China. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Zhang C.; Li Y.; Zhang B.
Title: Fintech, climate shocks, and agricultural land use transition: Evidence from farmers in China
Abstract: The expansion of non-grain production under climate change exerts big threat to national food security. This study investigates the nonlinear effects of climate change shocks (CCS) on farmers’ non-grain production decisions (NGPD) and the moderating mechanisms of Fintech. Using data from China Land Economic Survey (CLES) during 2020–2022, we find that CCS has an “inverted U-shaped” nonlinear impact on NGPD. Fintech significantly moderates this relationship by smoothing the curve and shifting the turning point leftward. Mechanism analysis shows Fintech achieves this by enhancing farmers’ factor allocation and risk decision abilities. Furthermore, Fintech acts as an effective substitute for traditional rural finance by overcoming constraints in formal supply and informal networks. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that Fintech strengthens agricultural resilience in major grain-producing areas but has insignificant effects on agricultural entrepreneur households, warning against profit-driven capital inducing NGPD. This study offers empirical evidence for leveraging digital finance to secure agricultural planting structures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Liss M.; Schweitzer L.
Title: Personality, cognition, and AI use profiles of college students
Abstract: This study seeks to better understand how different AI use profiles of college undergraduates vary in relationship to prompting and verification behaviors, personality variables, procrastination, and need for cognition. Using cluster analysis, three groups of students who approach AI in different ways were identified: power users, cautious users, and moderate users. Power users have high levels of trust, familiarity, and AI use for writing and low levels of distrust. Cautious users have low levels of trust, familiarity and AI use for writing, but high levels of distrust. Moderate users score at average levels across all of these variables. Power users tended to maximize their prompting for optimal results, but were less likely to verify AI output. They were more extraverted and agreeable. In contrast, cautious users were less likely to modify prompts for maximal results but were the most likely to verify. They were highest in openness and were higher in need for cognition than moderate users. The study demonstrates that subgroups of AI users can be identified and these groups differ in both cognitive style and personality which affects how they use AI in their academic lives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The mediating effect of nursing students' academic resilience between the clinical nursing internship environment and patient safety competency: A cross-sectional study
Abstract: Background: The clinical internship environment is crucial for developing nursing students' patient safety competency. While existing studies have confirmed their direct correlation, the underlying psychological mechanism remains unclear. Academic resilience, a key psychological resource for coping with clinical challenges, may serve as an important mediator, yet its specific role lacks empirical evidence. This study aims to address this gap. Objective: To examine the mediating role of academic resilience between the clinical nursing internship environment and patient safety competency among nursing students. Methods: From February to March 2025, we used convenience sampling to recruit nursing students from two tertiary grade-A hospitals in Kaifeng, yielding 298 valid questionnaires. We collected data using a general information questionnaire, the Clinical Nursing Internship Environment Evaluation Scale, the Patient Safety Competency Scale, and the Nursing Student Academic Resilience Scale. We performed mediation analysis using the SPSS PROCESS macro. Results: We obtained survey data from 298 nursing students. The total scores for the clinical nursing internship environment evaluation, patient safety competency, and nursing student academic resilience were 94.0 (91.8, 110.0), 117.0 (114.5, 138.0), and 70.0 (68.0, 78.0), respectively, all in the medium-upper range. Correlation analysis revealed significant positive correlations among the total scores of the clinical nursing internship environment, patient safety competency, and academic resilience (r = 0.933–0.960, P < 0.01). Nursing students' clinical internship environment and academic resilience can directly and positively affect their level of patient safety competence; nursing students' academic resilience partially mediates the relationship between clinical nursing internship environment and patient safety competence, with a mediating effect of 0.368 (95% CI: 0.1789–0.5108), accounting for 49.47% of the total effect. Conclusions: Nursing students' academic resilience mediates the relationship between the clinical nursing internship environment and patient safety competence. Nursing managers should focus on improving nursing students' academic resilience and adaptability to the practice environment during clinical practice to optimize the clinical practice environment, improve nursing students' safety competence, and ensure patient safety. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Age-related positivity bias in emotional processing: Investigating its neural correlates across early and automatic processing stages
Abstract: Emotional processing differs systematically across the adult lifespan, with older adults demonstrating a preference for positive stimuli, known as the positivity effect. However, it remains unclear whether this effect depends on controlled processing or can also emerge at early, automatic stages of emotional processing. The present study addressed this question using a deviant–standard–reverse oddball paradigm combined with event-related potentials (ERPs) and sliding-window representational similarity analysis (RSA). Younger and older adults were presented with schematic faces, in which neutral faces served as standard stimuli and happy or sad faces served as deviants, while attention was directed to a central task. Neural responses were indexed by the N170 component and expression mismatch negativity (eMMN), reflecting early perceptual processing and automatic change detection, respectively. The results revealed a clear age-related dissociation in emotional bias. Younger adults showed enhanced neural responses to sad deviants, whereas older adults showed enhanced responses to happy deviants. Critically, this pattern was observed at both early perceptual stages (N170) and later automatic stages (eMMN). These findings suggest that the positivity effect in aging is not limited to controlled processing but extends to automatic stages of emotional processing, supporting the view that age-related emotional biases may be partly driven by automatic emotion regulation mechanisms. Authors: Li Z.; Zheng Z.; Zhang S.; Yue X.; Zhang Z.; Zhu J.; Hu B.
Title: CCD-MAF: A Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram-driven Multi-Agent Framework for structured CBT dialogue generation
Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in mental health support, existing approaches often provide unstructured emotional responses and struggle to deliver structured, evidence-based interventions such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Existing CBT dialogue datasets also lack sufficient clinical depth and phase-specific patient resistance. To address these limitations, we construct the CCD-CBT Dataset, a multi-phase CBT dialogue corpus integrating expert textbook knowledge with real-world doctor–patient interactions sourced from Haodf Online and other medical consultation websites. The dataset contains 1314 samples covering the four standard CBT treatment phases, from initial assessment to termination, with an average dialogue length of 132.12 turns. The average utterance length is 61.34 Chinese characters for patients and 97.05 Chinese characters for therapists. Based on this dataset, we propose CCD-MAF, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework guided by the Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram (CCD). CCD-MAF decomposes the CBT counseling process into macro-phase planning, meso-state tracking, and micro-technique execution, enabling dynamic modeling of patients’ cognitive structures and targeted interventions. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B as the therapist component within CCD-MAF and conduct single-turn and multi-turn clinical simulations. The evaluation distinguishes system-level comparisons among independently operated systems from therapist-component substitution comparisons within the shared CCD-MAF framework. Results indicate that CCD-MAF demonstrates strong performance in Cognitive Therapy Scale (CTS)-based simulated evaluations. In the component-substitution setting, the fine-tuned therapist component achieves the best performance among the evaluated therapist components under the same CCD-MAF framework. Ablation studies further support the contribution of the proposed multi-agent mechanism. This study provides an interpretable and clinically structured framework for developing AI psychological assistants, with its effectiveness evaluated in simulated counseling settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Sleep regulation as a function of boredom proneness
Abstract: Boredom proneness has been cast as a challenge of self-regulatory control such that the highly boredom prone struggle to launch into action despite the desire to do so. This has typically been explored in the context of cognitive and affective dysregulation. Here, in two samples ( n = 256 and 309), we explored the relation between trait boredom proneness and sleep regulation. In both samples, higher boredom proneness was associated with poor sleep quality. In step-wise hierarchical regressions, boredom proneness reliably predicted poor sleep quality, but was only a significant predictor of bedtime procrastination in Sample #2. In our second sample, boredom proneness also predicted poor sleep hygiene. In that sample, we used mediation analyses to explore the role of rumination in the relation between both state and trait boredom (as predictors) and sleep quality and hygiene (as outcome variables). Results showed that the tendency to ruminate acted only as a partial mediator in these relations. Results are discussed in the broader context of self-regulatory models of state and trait boredom. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The role of masculinity in understanding gender gaps in negotiation
Abstract: We review empirical research on masculinity processes in negotiations. Studies to date are typically based on the precarious manhood thesis, which suggests that men seek to demonstrate their manhood to others, or on evolutionary psychology, which suggests that men are susceptible to evolutionary pressures to compete for mates. The current empirical literature on masculinity and negotiation suggests that men negotiate assertively, or even unethically, when they perceive their manhood to be threatened. Moreover, research repeatedly has shown that men's negotiation behavior is influenced by counterpart attributes, particularly the gender of the counterpart. Future research on the role of culture, the propensity to initiate negotiations as a criterion, power, and countermeasures for unethical negotiation behavior is needed. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Shi E.R.
Title: Sequencing thought into speech: Hippocampal functions in linguistic linearization
Abstract: The hippocampus has traditionally been understood as a memory system central to episodic representation, spatial navigation, and relational binding. Recent findings, however, suggest that its functions may extend beyond memory to the organization of sequential information. This raises the possibility that hippocampal mechanisms contribute to linguistic processes that require ordered expression, including the linearization of hierarchical syntactic structures. Linearization, defined as the mapping of parallel and recursive syntactic configurations onto a temporally constrained sequence of words, constitutes a fundamental problem for language production, yet its neurocognitive implementation remains insufficiently explained. Here, we advance the hypothesis that hippocampal sequence coding may provide one component of the neural substrate for this process. We review converging evidence from neuroimaging, patient studies, and developmental research that is consistent with hippocampal–prefrontal involvement during narrative construction, anaphora resolution, and temporal reference, as well as reports of disrupted discourse following hippocampal damage. We propose that these observations motivate testing whether hippocampal mechanisms help organize components of event representation into temporally structured relations within and across sentences. Building on proposals that sequence organization is relevant at both levels, we hypothesize that hippocampal indexing may interact with syntactic phases: syntactic phases define structurally bounded derivational domains, while hippocampal mechanisms may help relate event components and successive linguistic states across time. On this view, linearization may depend in part on a cross-modular interface between syntax and memory, with the hippocampus treated as a candidate contributor rather than as a dedicated linguistic linearizer. © 2026

Title: Narcissus under uncertainty: A network analysis of perfectionism, narcissism, intolerance of uncertainty, and psychological distress in young adults
Abstract: Perfectionism, intolerance of uncertainty, and narcissism have been linked to psychological distress in young adults, but their conditional associations remain unclear. The present study used network analysis to explore interrelations among these constructs in 535 young Italian adults (59.4% women; mean age = 23.89 years). A regularized Gaussian graphical model (EBICglasso) was estimated, alongside Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA) and sensitivity analyses. Depressive symptoms showed the highest strength, whereas vulnerable narcissism exhibited the highest expected influence and the highest bridge-centrality values under the four theoretically defined communities. However, its bridge strength was not statistically distinguishable from that of depressive symptoms and inhibitory intolerance of uncertainty. Centrality and bridge-centrality estimates showed adequate stability, and sensitivity analyses generally supported the main network pattern. EGA identified three communities, with socially prescribed perfectionism clustering with narcissism and intolerance of uncertainty, although this community showed limited bootstrap stability. Overall, the findings provide insights into the associations among perfectionism, narcissism, intolerance of uncertainty, and psychological distress, while highlighting the sensitivity of bridge-centrality estimates to community specification. Longitudinal and replication studies are needed to determine the stability and generalizability of these patterns. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Wu W.W.; Barasch A.
Title: Technology and the psychology of experience: A temporal framework
Abstract: Technology is increasingly central to how people experience the world, shaping not only what they do but when and how those experiences are psychologically constructed. We propose that technology does not merely backdrop experiences; it transforms them, stretching what were once bounded episodes into representations that are imagined before, lived through, and relived long after they end. In this article, we offer a temporal framework that synthesizes recent research on how technology reshapes experiences before, during, and after they unfold. Then, we use this framework to evaluate the current state of knowledge. We conclude by highlighting opportunities for future investigation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
