Title: The development of children’s mathematics achievement in primary school: the early and longitudinal links with perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety
Abstract: This longitudinal study investigated developmental trajectories of children’s mathematics achievement, especially the early and longitudinal effects of perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety. The participants included 1231 Chinese children (M T1age = 8.49, SD = 0.59; 40.29% female) assessed annually across four waves from Grade 3 through Grade 6. Latent class growth models identified three trajectories of children’s mathematics achievement: a low stable group (9.3%), a medium fast rising group (81.4%), and a high stable rising group (9.3%). Relative to the low stable group, early higher levels of mathematics anxiety were associated with lower odds of membership in the latter two groups both. In terms of the developmental trajectory of perceived teacher support, a higher initial level, a smaller early decline, and faster growth during the middle-to-late period were associated with a greater likelihood of membership in the high stable rising group. In contrast, the developmental trajectory of mathematics anxiety indicated that a higher initial level of as well as a slower subsequent decline were associated with a greater likelihood of membership in the low stable group. These findings highlight the distinct predictive roles of perceived teacher support and mathematics anxiety across diverse trajectories of mathematics achievement. Practically speaking, the present study emphasizes the need for differentiated instructional interventions tailored to children’s achievement levels, with attention to both environmental support and individual academic emotions. Authors: Sun X.; Cheng Y.; Zhao L.; Huang Z.; Guo X.; Xi W.
Title: Enhancing Empathy and Creativity through Embodied Cognition: The Application of a Hand Pain Intelligent Simulation Glove in Design Education
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Fostering students' empathy and creativity toward marginalized user groups is essential to achieving human-centered design in design education. Although experiential learning has gained increasing attention in recent years, there remains a lack of operable and perceptually engaging tools to support empathy instruction. To this end, this study developed a hand pain simulation glove and incorporated it into design instruction. Two quantitative experiments and one qualitative study were conducted to evaluate the glove's pedagogical potential. In the initial experiment, 30 students were subjected to three distinct pedagogical interventions: textual experience, video experience, and embodied experience, with the objective of comparing their respective impacts on empathy scores. A subsequent experiment engaged another cohort of 30 students in product design tasks under different experiential conditions, and their creative outcomes were evaluated by expert raters. Results showed that embodied simulation produced greater gains in empathy and design performance than text- and video-based instruction, particularly in innovative thinking and technical functionality. By translating otherwise invisible and action-dependent pain-related constraints into first-person sensorimotor experience, the glove supported students in reframing user problems and generating more context-sensitive design responses. These findings position embodied pain simulation as a pedagogical approach for empathy-oriented design education and provide a transferable framework for related learning contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Learning aircraft procedures through an immersive virtual reality environment
Abstract: Pilot trainees must familiarize themselves with a cockpit and master the associated procedures, i.e. specified sequences of interaction. Usually, this self-regulated learning relies on paper-based procedures and a cockpit poster, which can be monotonous and demotivating for trainees. In this study, N=36 pilot students tested the efficiency of a new Virtual Reality (VR) training tool for learning aircraft procedures. Results were compared with previously collected data from both traditional paper-based training and desktop training software embedded on a tactile screen. Participants were more motivated using the VR tool than with the two other methods. When tested in a realistic flight simulator, training effectiveness was better for VR than the traditional method, but similar to the tactile desktop tool. Moreover, study duration has not been shorten with the VR tool. Finally, open comments by participants provided useful directions on improving user interaction with the VR environment. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Low compliance with mandatory ecological mitigations in English housing developments – an overlooked threat to the integrity of onsite biodiversity net gain
Abstract: Globally, biodiversity no net loss or net gain (BNG) policies are potential key solutions to urbanisation's ecological impacts. The UK's 2012 National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) required developers to achieve BNG and mitigate losses to protected species. Under the NPFF, and subsequent 2024 metricised BNG policy, ecological enhancement and mitigation features are a condition of planning consents, or mandated by binding legal agreements. We assess delivery of ∼6,000 individual habitat (e.g. grassland creation) and species-based features (e.g. bird boxes) within 42 major housing developments, across five English Local Planning Authorities (LPAs) that obtained planning permission under the 2012 NPFF. We quantify compliance rates and use generalised linear mixed models to assess if delivery varies with year of planning permission, number of houses in a development, and developer type (local, regional, national, other). 54% of conditioned ecological features were delivered, varying from 0% (invertebrate boxes) to 75% (pond creation). The number of ecological features conditioned per house increased slightly over time, but compliance rates were largely invariant over time, development size, and developer type. Low-effort features were less commonly conditioned, especially in larger developments. There is a serious policy-implementation gap between conditioning of ecological improvements and delivery. Stronger governance and enforcement systems are urgently required to ensure delivery of BNG practices, otherwise biodiversity declines associated with increasing UK house building will continue. BNG style policies currently being developed in 100 countries must ensure they pay sufficient attention to the monitoring and enforcement of outcomes when designing governance schemes. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Jia H.; Lin B.
Title: Appliance-level energy assessment and its implications for the environmental impact of household energy conservation: Evidence from urban China
Abstract: Accurate appliance-level energy judgments may help households identify and prioritize meaningful electricity-saving opportunities, with potential implications for the environmental benefits of household conservation. Using survey and experimental data from 2592 residents in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, this paper assesses how accurately urban households estimate the electricity consumption of 11 common appliances, whether their judgments exhibit patterns consistent with availability-based reasoning, and whether a randomized heat-related information cue improves relative appliance-energy judgments. The results reveal substantial misalignment between perceived and benchmark electricity use: (1) respondents tend to overestimate the energy use of low-energy, frequently used appliances (e.g., televisions) while underestimating high-energy, infrequently interacted devices (e.g., water heaters); (2) appliance use frequency is positively associated with perceived energy consumption, a pattern consistent with greater cognitive accessibility of frequently used appliances; (3) random assignment to the heat-related cue increases perceived energy use for heat-producing appliances and improves respondents' measured relative correspondence with the benchmark; and (4) further analyses show that higher educational attainment is associated with closer benchmark alignment and that closer alignment is associated with lower reported household electricity expenditures. These findings document systematic deviations in appliance-level energy judgments and show that a targeted information cue can improve such judgments. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Flores-Mayorga M.-T.; Arámburo-Lizarraga J.
Title: Parental mediation and exposure to online grooming in primary education: Empirical evidence from Mexico; [Mediación parental y exposición al grooming digital en educación primaria: Evidencia empírica desde México]
Abstract: Introduction: Early access to the internet has transformed children’s communicative practices, but it has also increased their exposure to various digital risks, including online grooming. In this context, the present study examines the role of parental mediation in preventing conditions associated with digital grooming among children. Methodology: A questionnaire was administered to 251 primary school students (aged 10-14) from public schools in western Mexico. Parental mediation was operationalized across three dimensions: restrictive, active, and technical. Exposure to conditions associated with grooming was constructed as a dichotomous variable based on experiences related to ambiguous online contact with adults, requests for sexual content, and the sending or receiving of provocative images. Independent binary logistic regression models were estimated for each mediation dimension, controlling for gender. Results: The results indicate that active parental mediation is significantly associated with a lower probability of exposure to conditions associated with online grooming. In contrast, technical mediation did not show a statistically significant protective effect. Likewise, no significant gender differences were found in levels of exposure. Discussion: The findings suggest that parental mediation strategies based on communicative guidance and relational supervision may play a key role in reducing children’s exposure to situations linked to grooming in digital environments. Conclusions: This study provides empirical evidence from a Latin American context to the international debate on online child protection and highlights the importance of strengthening active parental mediation practices as a preventive strategy against digital risks. © 2027, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Authors: Shewark E.A.; Sivak C.J.; Sampson N.; Nassauer J.; Pearson A.L.
Title: Urban residential cues to care in Detroit neighborhoods: A validated lot level virtual audit tool
Abstract: High-quality built environments have potential to improve the mental and physical health of residents. Qualitatively, such environments are characterized by the visible evidence of human intervention and maintenance, including cues to care (CTC). However, to date, there has not been a validated way to quantify CTC that accounts for structure-inclusive lot types (i.e., residential, commercial). We present a validated tool that allows entire urban neighborhoods to be assessed (including occupied properties and vacant lots). We validated lot-scale physical CTC against measures of neighborhood conditions that have been widely associated with residents’ health. These measures include land use amenities and resident perceptions of neighborhood cohesion, attractiveness, and safety. We developed a novel coding tool that expands current geospatial CTC tools to quantitatively assess urban residential CTC. We applied Lot Level Cues to Care (LLCTC) to 781 lots across 245 street segments in Detroit, MI. We then investigated the relationship between LLCTC (where higher values indicate more CTC) and widely used as well as validated measures of neighborhood conditions, in a survey of 214 Detroit residents. We found negative correlations between LLCTC scores and signs of disorder and area deprivation. We also found significant associations between LLCTC scores and perceived neighborhood attractiveness. Although only approaching statistical significance, higher perceived cohesion and greater perceived safety were also associated with higher LLCTC scores. In conclusion, LLCTC is a valid quantitative geospatial measure of CTC in an urban residential environment, as validated by resident perceptions of their neighborhoods. © 2026

Title: Dear Diary, so far so good—The application works perfectly
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Approaching a development framework for the first time is like embarking on a journey, marked by mistakes, solutions, design choices, and key considerations. Tracking these aspects, much like keeping a diary, helps programmers understand implementations, revisit errors, and plan future strategies. Inspired by this analogy, we present Dear Diary, a tool integrated into the IDE that enables programmers to document their development journey. The tool allows developers to capture multiple versions of a project, functional or not, and to add rich explanations in their own words. These explanations can refer to all the components of a project, encompassing files, code, terminal commands, and dependencies, to create a holistic approach that provides richer context for understanding and learning from project evolution. A user study with 18 participants examined how Dear Diary was used during a framework-learning task, focusing on the capture phase of the development journey. Results showed that participants used the tool throughout the programming task to capture diverse forms of contextual knowledge linked to their development activity, while reporting positive perceptions of its usability, relevance, and potential usefulness. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Liu J.; An X.; Xu S.
Title: A framework integrating topological potential and semantic embeddings for identifying scientific research clusters in scholarly collaboration networks
Abstract: Multi-team collaboration is essential for addressing major scientific challenges. Previous methods focus predominantly on individuals or single teams, making it difficult to capture the structure of multi-team collaborative innovation systems. To address this, this study conceptualizes a research cluster as a multi-team system formed through inter-team relationships and related research goals within complex collaborative research environments. We further introduce a four-phase Topological Potential–Semantic Embedding Research Cluster Identification (TPSE-RCI) framework to identify scientific research clusters. First, research teams are detected and a team collaboration network is constructed. Second, team feature vectors are generated via topological potential–enhanced Node2Vec and initial clusters are identified with HDBSCAN. Third, team publications are analyzed using BERTopic with BGE-M3 semantic embeddings to derive hierarchical research goals. Fourth, validity criteria are applied to filter scientific research clusters. Using medical informatics publications as a case study, we detected 4262 research teams from 81,557 publications by 269,598 authors. At the structural level, 702 initial scientific research clusters were identified. At the thematic level, 319 topics were extracted from the team publications and consolidated into 21 secondary and 7 primary research goals. By integrating structural and thematic results, we ultimately identified 239 scientific research clusters. Comparative and ablation analyses indicate that incorporating topological potential improves team representation and structural-clustering quality within this empirical setting. The identified research clusters can provide decision support for practical tasks such as organized research management, major project coordination and optimization, domain expert identification, and research resource allocation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Kim P.H.; Ferragamo A.
Title: Repairing trust in AI: Attribution, anthropomorphism, and the illusion of difference
Abstract: Trust repair between humans and AI systems is an emerging area of inquiry that builds on a well-established literature in human–human (HH) interactions. This review examines how key HH findings, particularly the differential effectiveness of repair strategies following competence versus integrity violations, generalize to human–robot interaction (HRI). While some patterns hold, important divergences exist. The paper argues that better operationalizations of integrity violations and increased anthropomorphism can align HRI findings more closely with HH research. However, enduring challenges remain regarding the ethics of anthropomorphic design, the moral values AI should adopt, and how AI should extend trust to humans. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yin Y.; Zhou J.; Peng K.
Title: Online dating paradox: Why lonely hearts choose to ghost
Abstract: This study examines the differential associations of state and trait loneliness with ghosting behavior in online dating, considering self-presentation strategies and dating fatigue as potential explanatory pathways. Survey data from 881 Chinese mobile dating app users were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results showed that state loneliness was negatively associated with ghosting, whereas trait loneliness was positively associated with ghosting. Dating fatigue was positively associated with ghosting and statistically mediated the associations between both forms of loneliness and ghosting in opposite directions. Acquisitive self-presentation was positively associated with state loneliness and negatively associated with trait loneliness; unexpectedly, it was negatively associated with dating fatigue. Authentic self-presentation was not significantly associated with loneliness or dating fatigue. These findings suggest that temporary and chronic loneliness may correspond to different patterns of engagement and disengagement in online dating. The study contributes to mobile dating research by distinguishing state and trait loneliness and by identifying dating fatigue as an important correlate of ghosting behavior. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Li Z.; Tao Y.; Cui Z.; You Q.; Liu Y.; Yang C.
Title: Longitudinal associations between physical exercise and psychological resilience among college students: A random-intercept cross-lagged panel model
Abstract: Physical exercise is closely associated with psychological resilience, yet the temporal direction and within-person dynamics of this relationship remain unclear. This study examined the longitudinal association between physical exercise and psychological resilience among Chinese college students and tested whether it differed by sex. A three-wave longitudinal survey was conducted among students from universities in four provincial-level regions of China. Physical exercise and psychological resilience were assessed using the Physical Activity Rating Scale and the Connor–Davidson Resilience Scale, respectively. A total of 1451 valid participants were included at baseline, of whom 913 completed all three waves. At the between-person level, physical exercise was significantly and positively associated with psychological resilience. At the within-person level, physical exercise positively predicted subsequent psychological resilience across both time intervals, whereas the reverse association was small and observed only from T1 to T2. Multi-group analyses showed no significant sex differences in the autoregressive or cross-lagged paths. These findings extend the longitudinal evidence on the relationship between physical exercise and psychological resilience, reveal the dynamic nature of their within-person associations across the two time intervals, and suggest that physical exercise may be an important behavioral factor supporting the maintenance and development of psychological resilience among college students. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zeng T.; Zhang R.; Ke Q.; Yu Y.
Title: Does low-carbon policy improve the environmental performance in China?
Abstract: This study examines the impacts and driving mechanisms of low-carbon policy on environmental performance, with a focus on both direct policy effects and the underlying structural drivers. Drawing on panel data from multiple regions and years, the analysis employs a combination of econometric modeling and configurational approaches to capture heterogeneous and non-linear relationships. The results indicate that low-carbon policy significantly improves environmental performance, particularly in terms of emissions reduction, energy efficiency, and pollution control. However, the magnitude and direction of these effects vary across regions depending on differences in economic development, industrial structure, and governance capacity. Further analysis reveals that technological innovation, green investment, regulatory intensity, and public participation are key driving factors that jointly shape policy effectiveness. The study also identifies multiple pathways through which these factors interact to enhance environmental outcomes, highlighting the importance of synergistic policy design. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how low-carbon goals translate into measurable environmental improvements and offer practical implications for policymakers seeking to optimize policy implementation in diverse socio-economic contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Author full names: Kågström, Mari (55675992800); Biehl, Juliane (57203806059); Faith-Ell, Charlotta (8611254600); Geißler, Gesa (55382987800)
Title: Navigating context and complexity: pedagogical insights from environmental assessment teaching
Abstract: Teaching Environmental Assessment (EA) in higher education is both challenging and essential, given its applied, interdisciplinary nature and close connection to evolving practice. While previous studies highlight recurring challenges in EA teaching, such as dispersed course structures, weak links to research, and ambiguities in how EA is positioned within academic programmes, they tend to address these aspects separately rather than as interrelated conditions. Drawing on literature analysis and qualitative interviews with teachers in Sweden and Germany, the study examines what teachers aim to convey, how they teach, and the factors that shape their pedagogical choices. Conceptually, it proposes an analytical framework that integrates teacherrelated, subject-related, student-related, and contextual dimensions, emphasising how teachers perceive and navigate them. In this sense, EA teaching is understood as a navigated practice shaped by how teachers respond to the conditions within which they work. The findings show that EA teaching shares a number of common aims and understandings across countries. Nevertheless, the teaching is also diverse and at times fragile. Teachers' responses to constraints, including limited resources, uneven access to EA knowledge and networks, and context-specific demands, play a central role in shaping what is taught. At the same time, the interdisciplinary nature of EA offers significant opportunities for integrating theory and practice. The study highlights the need to move beyond prescriptive accounts of EA education towards supporting teachers' situated practices and their capacity to make informed pedagogical choices under varying conditions. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The Economic Value of Animals Traded for Traditional Medicine in Ghana and Its Effect on Biodiversity Conservation
Abstract: The trade and use of wildlife for traditional medicine are widespread in many developing countries and continue to expand. The increasing demand for high-value, endangered animals used in traditional medicine has raised important conservation concerns. In this first nationwide cross-sectional study of its kind in Ghana, we assessed the economic value of wildlife traded for traditional medicine through interviews with 133 vendors in 48 markets and examined its implications for biodiversity conservation. The mean annual sales per vendor were estimated at USD 15,123.6. Based on an estimated 1,074 vendors engaged in the trade of Animal-Based Medicine (ABM) nationwide, the annual economic value of the sector was approximately USD 16.2 million. We found that the vendors' sex, age and religious affiliation were not statistically associated with their annual trade values. However, vendors whose clientele consisted predominantly of females recorded significantly higher annual sales than those serving predominantly male clients (USD 247,852.8 vs. 59,765.6; p-value = 0.004). The most expensive animal parts included endangered species such as lion (Panthera leo), tiger (P. tigris), African savanna elephant (Loxodonta africana), and Home’s hinge-back tortoise (Kinixys homeana). Our findings showed that the ABM trade in Ghana provides employment and income for many actors along the supply chain, and contributes millions of dollars annually to the national economy. These findings highlight the need for stakeholders and policymakers to strengthen collaboration in regulating the harvest and trade of wildlife used in traditional medicine to promote both sustainable livelihoods and biodiversity conservation in Ghana and across sub-Saharan Africa. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Brattico E.; Marzano D.; Carraturo G.
Title: Music as a form of art: Current findings and challenges of music neuroaesthetics research
Abstract: In recent decades, empirical research on music, often grouped under the label of cognitive neuroscience of music, has approached music primarily as a biological, cognitive faculty, focusing on audiomotor predictive and reward mechanisms. More recently, the neuroaesthetics of music has expanded this focus to musical experience as a situated encounter with music as a performing art. From this viewpoint, three complementary accounts of musical experience can be distinguished: an audiomotor–reward account, closely linked to cognitive neuroscience and centered on prediction, reward and auditory–striatal connectivity; an appreciative–evaluative account, in which liking, being moved, and meaning can emerge without an explicit aesthetic stance; and an aesthetic–artistic account, involving reflective judgments of beauty, novelty, and artistic significance. We review recent advances in naturalistic listening, experimental concert research, and hyperscanning, showing how they move the field beyond isolated sounds toward culturally, socially, and bodily embedded musical events. Finally, we identify a theoretical challenge: future research should explain how musical experiences become meaningful, shared, and potentially transformative across diverse, non-elitist, and non-Western-centered contexts. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: From faux flipped to gamified flipped classrooms: scaffolding and cognitive load management
Abstract: Background: Students new to flipped classrooms frequently encounter challenges with motivation and comprehension when engaging with pre-class materials independently, particularly outside scheduled class hours. Aims: This study examined a scaffolded flipped-learning approach that helped students move step by step from a Faux Flipped Classroom (FFC) to a Regular Flipped Classroom (RFC), and then to a Gamified Flipped Classroom (GFC) over one semester. The goal was to support students in adapting to flipped learning, managing their mental workload, and improving their learning performance. Method: Mixed methods were employed in the data collection. For quantitative data, learning achievement was assessed with tests and self-rating scales measured cognitive load, while qualitative interviews provided more detailed feedback. Results: The results revealed that students in the experimental group who learned through the scaffolding strategy performed better than their counterparts in the control group. Meanwhile, both groups demonstrated a small drop in intrinsic cognitive load, likely because they became more familiar with the tasks rather than because the material got easier. However, the scaffolded group showed a larger drop in unnecessary cognitive load and a larger increase in germane cognitive effort, suggesting the intervention helped students focus more on learning and less on confusion or figuring out what to do. Intrinsic and germane cognitive load should be interpreted cautiously because they are closely related. Conclusion: This study contributes to Cognitive Load Theory and scaffolding research by showing that flipped classroom success depends not only on design but also on how students are gradually prepared to use it. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Nita A.; Zamorano M.
Title: An integrated multilayer environmental impact assessment framework for accelerating sustainable energy infrastructure permitting
Abstract: The deployment of sustainable energy infrastructure in the European Union is now limited less by technology costs than by the duration and unpredictability of permitting. Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), the main authorization instrument for energy projects, evaluates the impacts of a proposal. What it does not evaluate is the quality of the governance process through which those impacts are assessed and decided, so risks arising from institutional fragmentation, weak stakeholder coordination, or the exclusion of affected groups stay invisible until they surface as objections, litigation, and delay. In this paper we develop an Integrated Multilayer EIA Framework that repositions EIA as a decision-support system for energy infrastructure permitting. The framework organizes the assessment into four coupled analytical layers, physical-environmental, socio-economic, institutional-governance, and stakeholder, and places network analysis of stakeholder interactions and institutional relationships at its core. Governance quality is expressed through a small set of structural indicators, reciprocity of engagement, brokerage concentration, the connectivity of affected groups to decision-makers, all derivable from documentation that procedures already produce. We illustrate the framework's diagnostic logic with governance patterns observed across European energy permitting, from onshore and offshore wind to agri-photovoltaics, hydropower, biomass conversion, and cross-border hydrogen infrastructure. The approach allows permitting risk to be detected earlier, stakeholder engagement to be targeted where it matters, investment certainty to improve, and the acceleration of authorization that the European Green Deal and REPowerEU require to rest on a sounder basis. Although developed for the EU permitting context, the framework is defined over procedural records that EIA systems produce everywhere, so its diagnostic logic transfers to any jurisdiction in which multi-actor authorization governs energy deployment. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Muhlis; Halide H.; Ambo-Rappe R.
Title: Assessing seagrass climate risk and biodiversity vulnerability to support marine spatial planning in Indonesia
Abstract: Seagrass ecosystems support marine biodiversity, coastal resilience, and climate regulation, but are increasingly exposed to climate change and anthropogenic pressures. Indonesia contains globally significant seagrass resources and requires spatially explicit tools that translate ecological and climate information into management priorities. This study developed a quantitative framework for assessing seagrass climate vulnerability across 18 Indonesian study sites using ecological monitoring data, SST-based climate indicators for 1981–2018, and an independent emission-related pressure layer. Ecological condition and climate exposure were integrated into the Seagrass Climate Vulnerability Index (SCVI), and SCVI classes were combined with emission-pressure classes through the Seagrass Climate Risk Interaction Matrix (SCRIM). A symmetric sensitivity analysis across five ecological-versus-exposure weighting configurations showed high agreement among site rankings (Kendall’s W = 0.960), supporting the retention of equal weighting as a representative central estimate rather than an assumed reference. Results showed marked spatial heterogeneity: Ternate, Raja Ampat, and Karimunjawa were classified as relative high-risk sites, whereas Selayar, Makassar, and Sikka were identified as relative potential-refugia candidates under the low-SCVI–low-emission combination. The SCVI–SCRIM framework provides a transparent decision-support approach for preventive conservation, restoration targeting, enhanced monitoring, and pressure reduction in data-limited marine spatial planning contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Comparing AI chatbot users and non-users in Germany: Reasons for use, addictive AI chatbot use, mental health, and loneliness
Abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots is becoming increasingly popular worldwide. To prevent potential negative consequences associated with the use at an early stage, it is crucial to understand its associations with mental health. Therefore, the present study compared people who use AI chatbots with those who do not engage in AI chatbot-interactions in terms of mental health and loneliness. Moreover, we investigated potential mechanisms associated with addictive AI chatbot use. Data of 7,312 persons (3,729 users: 42.1% men, 57.9% women; Mage = 42.23, SDage = 13.33; 3,583 non-users: 42.6% men, 57.4% women; Mage, = 54.28, SDage = 14.49) from the German adult population were collected via an online survey. AI chatbot users had significantly higher levels of loneliness, depressive, anxiety and stress symptoms, and significantly lower levels of life satisfaction than non-users. Users primarily engaged in AI chatbot-interactions for informational and practical reasons, such as obtaining information and inspiration, and receiving text-related assistance. The frequency of AI chatbot use to escape negative emotions was significantly positively associated with addictive tendencies. Loneliness statistically mediated the association between addictive AI chatbot use and the mental health variables. Most observed effect sizes were small. The present findings show that using AI chatbots for emotion regulation is positively associated with higher addictive tendencies and lower levels of mental health. Title: Comparing Strava and survey-based data for coastal recreation accounting
Abstract: Coastal zones provide recreational ecosystem services across land and sea, yet spatial data for ecosystem accounting is limited. Strava over-represented activities along the coastal belt and across marine areas, while under-representing island visitation and leisure-oriented activities. Although Strava underestimated absolute recreation activity levels relative to PPGIS, the datasets showed strong agreement in relative spatial variation among municipalities. Our findings demonstrate that Strava data can support mapping of recreation patterns, but may misrepresent the magnitude and distribution of coastal recreation activity. These biases may influence the identification and prioritization of recreational areas in planning and accounting. Combining Strava data and representative survey-based approaches may improve recreation assessments for coastal planning and accounting for physical and monetary recreation services. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Cardillo E.R.; Chatterjee A.
Title: Aesthetic experience: Foundations, tensions, and new directions
Abstract: Neuroaesthetics is a young subdiscipline of cognitive neuroscience that investigates the psychological and biological bases of diverse aesthetic experiences. Emerging from the iterative interaction of perceptual, affective, and cognitive processes, aesthetic experiences are complex, dynamic, subjective states with considerable individual variability. Three decades of behavioral and neuroimaging investigation supports varied and robust theoretical accounts, with key points of debate including whether aesthetic experience constitutes a distinct psychological and neural phenomena or is sufficiently explained in entirely domain general terms. Foundational research conducted in lab settings has established general principles of experience, especially with respect to the engagements with visual art and architecture. Studies with culturally diverse stimuli and populations, and in ecologically valid contexts are growing, and important for testing the generalizability of such patterns. Moving beyond beauty and pleasure, characterizing the diverse and nuanced emotional dimensions of aesthetic experience is a major area of development. Promising applied approaches in neuroaesthetics include the health and wellbeing impact of aesthetic experiences, and how people respond aesthetically to nature and the built environment. Research in these areas has the potential to inform policy and practice in healthcare, architectural design, and urban planning. Contemplative neuroaesthetics has emerged as a new subdiscipline, expanding the interdisciplinary nature of the field. Immersive aesthetic experiences that encourage receptive, non-evaluative attention can expand our understanding of the transformative potentials of aesthetic engagement. © 2026

Authors: Hattori T.; Hoshino T.
Title: Perceived strategy fit in empathy regulation: Trait perspective-taking predicts usability advantages of third-party perspective-taking
Abstract: Emotion regulation strategies are typically evaluated by their efficacy, yet a strategy that works may still go unused if it does not feel usable. The present study examined whether two strategies for reducing empathy-induced partiality—third-party perspective-taking and cognitive reappraisal—differ in perceived usability, and whether this usability depends on dispositional empathy. Adults ( N = 212) read a prioritization scenario, regulated their response using one of the two strategies, and rated the usability of the strategy they had used. The two strategies reduced helping prioritization to a comparable degree, with moderate Bayesian evidence for no difference. However, third-party perspective-taking was rated as substantially more usable than cognitive reappraisal. Critically, this usability advantage was moderated by trait perspective-taking but not by trait empathic concern: among individuals high in dispositional perspective-taking, third-party perspective-taking was experienced as especially usable, whereas the usability of reappraisal was unrelated to either trait. Thus, the disposition that generates empathy-induced partiality was not the disposition that made its remedy feel usable. These findings indicate that the practical value of an emotion regulation strategy depends on the fit between its core operation and the perceiver's habitual dispositions, with implications for tailoring regulation guidance to individuals. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Do bilinguals avoid ambiguity or minimize processing effort? Insights from an online eye-tracking study in spoken Mandarin
Abstract: Previous research on anaphoric reference shows that bilinguals tend to choose more explicit referential forms (e.g., overt pronouns over null pronouns) compared to monolingual speakers. It remains unclear whether this tendency towards greater explicitness extends to other forms of referential uncertainty, such as lexical ambiguity, or whether it depends on specific processing demands of anaphoric reference tasks. Avoiding lexical ambiguity may be demanding because it requires speakers to inhibit a readily accessible shared (ambiguous) label and retrieve a less accessible, more specific alternative. By conducting two experiments examining lexical ambiguity in spoken Mandarin, we tested two hypotheses: Hypothesis 1 : bilinguals would rather be redundant than ambiguous in general; Hypothesis 2 : bilinguals are less likely to avoid ambiguity when doing so is too costly. In Experiment 1, L1 Mandarin L2 English speakers in the UK and more-monolingual speakers in China completed a picture naming task. We manipulated whether the preferred label was ambiguous in the visual context (Ambiguous Condition) or unambiguous (Unambiguous Condition) and tested whether speakers avoided ambiguous labels. Experiment 2 extended this task by incorporating online eye-tracking using WebGazer. Our results showed that, contrary to Hypothesis 1 , bilinguals were more likely than more-monolinguals to use ambiguous expressions for ambiguous trials. Eye-tracking analysis revealed that bilinguals tended to direct early attention towards image pairs with more accessible shared labels, indicating a preference for linguistic choices that are cognitively less demanding; by contrast, more-monolinguals showed proactive monitoring of ambiguity depending on their responses. These findings support Hypothesis 2 , suggesting that bilingual referential choices may be shaped by domain-specific processing demands rather than by a general preference for avoiding ambiguity. These findings also shed light on cognitive constraints in bilingual lexical access and early signs of lexical attrition. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: From tourism pressure to overtourism vulnerability regimes: A municipal impact assessment framework for sustainable destination governance
Abstract: Overtourism is increasingly understood as a multidimensional sustainability challenge, yet local decision-makers still lack replicable tools for assessing where tourism pressure may translate into territorial vulnerability. This paper develops a municipal impact-assessment framework for diagnosing overtourism vulnerability regimes. The analysis follows a two-step logic. First, a regional tourism-pressure screening index is constructed for Euro-Mediterranean NUTS-2 regions to identify broader high-pressure contexts. Second, an Overtourism Vulnerability Index (OVI) is implemented for the main tourism hotspots in Apulia, Italy, using eight normalized indicators capturing direct tourism pressure, air accessibility, accommodation platformisation, economic dependence and heritage attractiveness. Rather than treating the OVI as a ranking device, the framework decomposes vulnerability into three diagnostic dimensions: direct pressure, structural fragility and gateway/heritage amplification. These dimensions identify four regimes: critical overload and fragility, gateway/heritage pressure, coastal fragility and platformisation, and monitor-and-prevent contexts. Robustness checks and an external waste-based plausibility check support the diagnostic interpretation. The resulting toolbox links each regime to assessment, monitoring and candidate intervention priorities, helping planners move from regional pressure screening to municipal scoping and targeted environmental and carrying-capacity assessment. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Gesture benefits in second language learning take time to develop
Abstract: Background: Multimodal enrichment can enhance second language (L2) vocabulary learning, but most evidence comes from studies with extensive training; it is unclear whether similar benefits occur with limited exposure. Aims: This study investigated how ten brief instances of gesture- and picture-based enrichment influenced adults’ learning and long-term retention of concrete and abstract L2 vocabulary. Sample: Fifty-two German-speaking adults were recruited from teacher education programs at the University of Leipzig. Methods: Using a fully within-participants design, each learner studied abstract and concrete L2 nouns under three conditions: listening only (no enrichment), listening while viewing related pictures (picture enrichment), and listening while viewing and performing related gestures (gesture enrichment). Each word was presented ten times across five training sessions. Word learning was assessed using free recall, L1–L2 translation, L2–L1 translation tasks at three retention intervals (day 8, month 2, and month 6). Results: Both gesture and picture enrichment significantly improved learning of abstract words compared to no enrichment. For concrete words, performance did not differ across conditions. Gesture enrichment did not outperform picture enrichment at any time point. Memory performance declined over time, particularly for abstract words, while concrete word performance remained more stable. Conclusions: Even brief exposure to gestural and pictorial enrichment can enhance the long-term retention of abstract L2 vocabulary. More extensive training may be required for gesture-based benefits to exceed those of picture enrichment. The findings establish boundary conditions for multimodal learning and inform both theoretical accounts of sensorimotor enrichment and practical approaches to language instruction. © 2026

Title: Emotional Stability and within-person Big Five profile dispersion: Evidence for a U-shaped association in adolescents
Abstract: Personality traits are typically studied as independent predictors of behavior and well-being, yet less attention has been paid to their configuration within individuals. One approach to capturing this configuration is through intra-subject variance across traits which could reflect the consistency or divergence across the five traits. We operationalized intra-subject variance (Vi) as the within-person variance of direct Big Five scores. Across N = 3785 adolescents (14–17 years), we observed a robust U-shaped association between Emotional Stability (ES) and Vi: profiles were most homogeneous at moderate–high ES and more dispersed at both low and very high ES. This pattern held in polynomial regression models including a significant quadratic term. A robust non-linear (U-shaped) association was found between Emotional Stability and Vi: both low and very high levels were linked to greater dispersion, whereas moderate-to-high levels showed more homogeneous profiles. Other traits showed weaker nonlinear associations, with substantially lower explanatory capacity than Emotional Stability. Emotional Stability emerged as the strongest predictor. Findings suggest that Emotional Stability plays a distinctive role in the internal organization of personality and highlights the relevance of within-person approaches. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and further longitudinal and multi-method research is needed. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Seeing what matters: How signaling influences teachers’ noticing of classroom disruptions in scripted classroom videos
Abstract: Background: Noticing describes teachers’ ability to perceive and interpret relevant events. Regarding classroom management, noticing disruptions is particularly relevant. However, many teachers often misinterpret disruptions, perceive them too late, or not at all. While classroom videos can be an effective way to train noticing, they are often overwhelming and therefore less effective. Aims: This study examined whether highlighting disruptions in staged classroom videos through signals affects adult education teachers’ noticing skills and self-efficacy. Sample: One hundred and twenty-one teachers in adult education participated in this study. Methods: All participants watched a scripted classroom video in the practice phase with the task to perceive and interpret disruptions. One group received signals highlighting occurring disruptions, whereas the other group did not. Finally, the participants' noticing skills (perception and interpretation) were assessed in a test phase with a new video without signals. Results: Participants in the signaling group perceived more disruptions during the test phase but did not interpret more disruptions correctly than the control group. There was no difference in self-efficacy between the groups. Further, exploratory mediation analyses showed that the participants’ performance in the test phase was associated with their interaction with the signaled disruptions during the practice phase. Conclusion: The results indicate that signaling is a useful tool to support teachers in perceiving classroom disruptions, whereas interactions with the signals in the practice phase may be necessary to support teachers’ interpretation skills. Potential explanations for the findings and directions for future research are discussed. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Effects of AI-based chatbot coaching on goal attainment, self-efficacy, and stress: A longitudinal randomized experiment
Abstract: Students in higher education face a range of academic challenges, which leads to high levels of stress among many students. While coaching has been shown to help students address these challenges, it is resource-intensive and therefore not broadly accessible. AI-based chatbots may help broaden access by providing interactive and personalized guidance at scale, yet empirical evidence on their effectiveness remains limited, particularly from longitudinal experimental studies. Addressing this gap, we conducted a longitudinal between-subjects experiment with four measurement points across an academic semester, randomly assigning 101 students to one of three conditions: AI-based chatbot coaching, literature-based self-study (active control), or a waitlist control condition. Students in the chatbot coaching and literature study conditions engaged in repeated interactions with the intervention, averaging approximately 100 min of cumulative interaction time accumulated across four sessions of 23–28 min each. We examined how students’ goal attainment, university-related self-efficacy, and stress developed over the course of the study. Results showed that students in the AI-based chatbot condition achieved significantly stronger increases in goal attainment over time compared to students in both control conditions. Self-efficacy also increased in the AI-based chatbot condition over time; however, between-condition differences were not consistent across time points, suggesting that the intervention had a more limited impact on self-efficacy relative to goal attainment. Furthermore, no significant effects were found for university-related stress. The findings suggest that AI-based chatbot coaching can effectively support students in achieving university-related goals and strengthening their self-efficacy, while its impact on stress reduction may be limited. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Ye Y.; Arnold J.E.
Title: Does prediction error explain referential adaptation?
Abstract: Pronoun resolution is guided by various discourse cues. For instance, ambiguous pronouns are often assigned to the subject of the preceding sentence (e.g., Ana went shopping with Liz. She bought a hat). Studies have found that these discourse biases can be learned through exposure by tracking frequent pronoun-reference patterns (e.g., pronouns often refer to subjects), a process known as referential adaptation (e.g., Johnson and Arnold, 2023 ; Kaiser, 2009 ; Ye and Arnold, 2023b). Yet, the mechanisms underlying this learning remain unclear. Two experiments examined whether referential adaptation is driven by prediction error, which has been suggested to explain syntactic adaptation (e.g., Chang et al., 2012). This account predicts that learning depends on how surprising the input is, with more unexpected input leading to stronger adaptation. We tested this prediction by exposing people to discourse patterns within both contexts where the reference was highly expected (Exp. 1) and equi-biased (Exp. 2). Robust referential adaptation occurred in both experiments. These findings show that strong expectation violations are not necessary for referential adaptation and suggest that adaptation is not straightforwardly determined by the strength or consistency of prediction error. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Effects of internal and external coastal wetland conversions on soil organic carbon in China
Abstract: Coastal wetlands are critical blue carbon ecosystems, yet their soil carbon pools are subject to substantial uncertainties due to dramatic changes in landscape patterns. Although local studies have explored these changes, systematic national-scale quantification of their impacts on soil organic carbon (SOC) dynamics remains insufficient. This study conducted a meta-analysis to clarify the spatiotemporal evolution of China's coastal wetland landscapes and quantify SOC responses to internal wetland conversions and external human-driven land-use transformations. Results demonstrate a substantial reduction of natural coastal wetlands accompanied by a continuous expansion in anthropogenic land covers. During 1990–2020, wetland ecosystem internal conversions were dominated by mangrove restoration and Spartina alterniflora (S. alterniflora) expansion; these conversions contributed an increase in SOC storage of 1.04 ± 0.16 Tg C (mean ± standard error) and 1.87 ± 0.43 Tg C, respectively. In contrast, external conversions of natural wetlands driven by the expansion of coastal aquaculture ponds reduced SOC storage by 0.53 ± 0.17 Tg C. Notably, reclamation of tidal flats for cropland largely preserved carbon sequestration capacity, with 57,326.3 ± 729.4 km2 of transformed area contributing a net SOC storage increase of 1.22 ± 0.69 Tg C. SOC density changes correlated positively with conversion duration, with subtropical zones as hotspots due to favorable hydrothermal conditions. These findings contribute to the scientific assessment of blue carbon stocks and inform conservation, restoration, and sustainable management of coastal wetlands. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: “Can talking like you make it work?”: The role of linguistic convergence and maintenance in human–robot interaction
Abstract: As domestic robots become more integrated into everyday life, effective and socially attuned communication strategies are essential for enabling meaningful human–robot collaboration. Prior work has addressed robot errors, but less is known about handling user errors. This study investigates how domestic robots’ verbal coordination strategies shape user experiences when handling human speech errors. To establish the experimental framework, Communication Accommodation Theory (CAT) was applied to define two linguistic strategies (convergence vs. maintenance), and McGrath's Group Task Circumplex Model was utilized to establish four task types (Generate, Choose, Execute, and Negotiate). We conducted a video-based experiment using a 2 × 4 × 2 mixed factorial design, varying CAT strategy, task type, and age group. Results revealed that while convergence was generally perceived more positively, its advantage was task-dependent. In Generate and Choose tasks, convergence was associated with greater trust, while maintenance was comparably effective in Execute and Negotiate tasks. Participants’ evaluations varied by both task type and age, suggesting that communication strategies should be tailored to context and user characteristics. This study contributes design insights for adaptive, socially responsive domestic robots. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Distributionally-robust heterogeneous graph neural networks via relation-aware grouping
Abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a key challenge for heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs), which often exhibit substantial performance degradation under real-world distribution shifts. While Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) has proven effective in promoting OOD generalization in various domains, its application to heterogeneous graphs remains largely unexplored. This gap stems from a fundamental obstacle: the complex, multi-relational nature of heterogeneous graphs renders conventional group definitions, which rely on explicit node attributes, inadequate. To bridge this gap, we propose DroHGNN, a GroupDRO-based framework for OOD generalization on heterogeneous graphs. DroHGNN introduces a relation-aware soft grouping mechanism coupled with a two-stage optimization procedure to enhance OOD robustness. Specifically, DroHGNN learns soft group assignments through learnable prototypes over relation-specific node representations. These assignments serve as optimization-oriented group proxies for GroupDRO, which minimizes worst-case group risk. To encourage structural coherence of the inferred assignments, we further introduce a heterogeneous graph structural consistency constraint that regularizes the group assignments of structurally connected target nodes. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks show that DroHGNN consistently achieves strong OOD performance compared with competitive baselines. Notably, under degree-distribution shifts on the ArXiv dataset, DroHGNN outperforms NaiveDRO and the leading baseline CaNet by 23.3% and 6.5% in Macro-F1, respectively. Moreover, relative gains of up to 3.2% in average Macro-F1 under the inductive temporal setting further demonstrate its effectiveness under heterogeneous distribution shifts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Barriers and enablers to circular economy implementation in 3D concrete printing: A fuzzy decision-making approach
Abstract: The circular economy (CE) is increasingly emphasised in 3D concrete printing (3DCP), yet evidence remains limited on the key barriers to its implementation and the enablers needed to support practical uptake. This study addresses that gap through a sequential mixed-methods design combining a literature-informed review to identify initial barriers, ten semi-structured expert interviews to refine them and elicit corresponding enablers in the 3DCP context, and a questionnaire survey of 58 academic and industry specialists from multiple regions to prioritise their relative importance using a fuzzy synthetic evaluation approach. The findings show that CE implementation in 3DCP is constrained less by isolated technical limitations than by wider system conditions shaping approval, investment, knowledge translation, and supply-chain coordination. Regulatory and standardisation issues emerged as the most critical barrier theme, followed by financial and market constraints, while the gap between low-TRL academic research and high-TRL industrial implementation was identified as the most prominent item-level barrier. The most influential enablers were CE-oriented standards, cost-effective process maturation, targeted R&D support, and stronger validation and implementation pathways. By revealing convergence between academia and industry on the main priorities, the study contributes a context-specific methodological approach for investigating CE implementation in 3DCP and establishes a prioritised evidence base on the barriers and enablers shaping circular 3DCP. It also provides practical guidance for researchers, industry stakeholders, and policy actors by identifying where intervention is likely to be most effective, particularly in standards development, technology validation, investment support, and supply-chain coordination, to scale circular 3DCP in support of net-zero and zero-waste ambitions. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Yetişgin S.O.; Canan S.
Title: Traditional Ecological Knowledge in Sustaining Mobile Pastoralism of Türkiye
Abstract: Traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) underpins sustainable pastoralism by guiding livestock mobility, resource management, and climate adaptation. However, in Eastern Anatolia, Türkiye, TEK is increasingly marginalized by socio-economic change and restrictive land-use policies. This study documents the TEK held by mobile pastoralists in Eastern Anatolia, Türkiye, and examines how it informs herd mobility, pasture use, and weather-related decision-making. Ethnographic fieldwork was conducted between February and April 2024 across Diyarbakır and neighboring provinces, involving structured interviews, participatory observations, and focus group discussions with 20 mobile pastoralists. Qualitative and descriptive statistical analyses were used to identify patterns in decision-making related to migration, pasture selection, and weather forecasting. Within this small, purposive sample, pastoralists reported weighing pasture condition (75%), weather conditions (55%), and water availability (15%) when planning migration and grazing. Traditional forecasting relied on ecological indicators, including star density (65%), cloud formations around the moon (60%), and animal behavior (20%). These practices reveal an embedded ecological literacy that integrates environmental perception with kin-based decision-making. Yet declining interest in pastoralism among younger community members, land privatization, conservation restrictions, and other socio-economic constraints threaten TEK continuity. TEK functions not merely as inherited knowledge but as a living body of practice that supports pastoral communities within their own socio-ecological systems. Integrating TEK into contemporary rangeland management could enhance sustainability, climate preparedness, and the long-term viability of pastoral livelihoods in semi-arid environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Wu Z.; Zhang D.; Li Y.
Title: Respect your privacy: An identifiable and authorized privacy-preserving data retrieval protocol through decentralized identifier
Abstract: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires personal data processing to satisfy both the principles of lawfulness and data minimization. However, existing privacy-preserving data retrieval protocols rarely meet both principles, especially at the batch scale. To solve these problems, we present IAPDR, an Identifiable and Authorized Privacy-Preserving Data Retrieval protocol that builds on Decentralised Identifier (DID) that focuses on data-subject privacy under GDPR compliance. IAPDR uses DIDs to provide verifiable, globally unique identities while preserving anonymity and self-sovereign management. It uses non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (NIZKs) for anonymous authorization. The data controller can verify the lawfulness of each retrieval request without learning any personally identifiable data, thereby upholding data minimization. For scalable retrieval, IAPDR employs Private Set Intersection with Payload (PSI-Payload) to execute large-batch matching while keeping both identifiers and associated records confidential. We prove anonymity and unforgeability, and give a Universal Composability (UC) security analysis in the semi-honest model. Under the same dataset sizes and network settings on public benchmarks, IAPDR achieves an average 1.36 × improvement in computational efficiency and an average 3.62 × reduction in total communication compared with state-of-the-art schemes. These enhancements make GDPR compliant privacy-preserving data retrieval practically feasible. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A failure of food-specific inhibitory control training to affect food choices via a hypothetical food delivery platform
Abstract: Inhibitory control training (ICT) is a computerised intervention which requires individuals to repeatedly inhibit a pre-potent motor response to unhealthy food-related cues. In doing so the cues are devalued, which may in turn reduce the choice and/or consumption behaviour towards unhealthy foods. Whilst single-session laboratory evidence suggests ICT may be a promising intervention, online studies show equivocal results. In this pre-registered randomised controlled trial, we administered ICT online (vs a control group) to 512 individuals (47.6% female, mean age = 41.68). Immediately following training participants were asked to make a hypothetical food order from a mock pizza delivery website based on a popular UK chain. Devaluation of pizza, salad, and unhealthy but untrained images was also measured pre- and post-training. Our results demonstrated that ICT (mean = 1270 kcal) did not lead to fewer calories ordered vs the control group (mean = 1287 kcal: t(503.74) = 0.381, p = .703, d = 0.03 [95% CI: −0.14 to 0.21]: BF10 = 0.105), or fewer number of individuals ordering pizza-dishes (X2(1) = 1.93, p = .165; OR = 0.72 [95% CI: 0.47 to 1.11]: BF10 = 0.272). Overall, the findings of this study suggest ICT delivered online is unlikely to be an effective stand-alone intervention for changing food-ordering behaviours, however replication with real world outcomes is necessary. Title: Assessing the environmental–economic viability of expressway photovoltaics in China: A spatio–temporal life cycle perspective
Abstract: Expressway corridors are increasingly considered for distributed photovoltaic deployment, but their environmental–economic viability depends strongly on local solar resources, infrastructure availability, grid structure, and future decarbonization pathways. This study develops an integrated framework that combines spatio–temporal assessment with environmental life cycle costing to evaluate the deployment potential and comprehensive benefits of expressway photovoltaic systems across 351 prefecture–level cities in China. The assessment covers service areas, rest areas, and expressway slopes under business-as-usual and carbon-neutrality-by-2060 scenarios. Results indicate that expressway slopes provide the greatest installation potential, with 49.71% of cities supporting more than 200 MW. At the national-average level, expressway photovoltaic systems yield a net internal benefit of 317.05 USD/kW and a net environmental benefit of 249.48 USD/kW under the business-as-usual scenario. Inverter and monocrystalline silicon photovoltaic module production are the main contributors to environmental costs. Under the carbon-neutrality-by-2060 scenario, grid decarbonization reduces the avoided environmental burden of photovoltaic electricity and delays the transition to positive net environmental benefits from 2035 to 2037. These findings support a shift from capacity-oriented expansion to region-specific life cycle planning, prioritizing corridors where solar resources, expressway availability, grid displacement benefits, and recycling infrastructure are jointly favorable. © 2026

Authors: Martin J.; Elg M.
Title: Safety in military organizations –A scoping review
Abstract: Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Zhang L.; Xia T.; Chen N.; Wang Z.
Title: Spatial Spillover Effects of Drought Disasters on Grain Yields: Evidence from 31 Chinese Provinces
Abstract: Drought disasters are the most severe natural disasters affecting China's grain yields, characterized by prolonged duration and extensive impact. Under the integrity of the ecosystem and the interaction among factors, drought not only directly affects grain yields in the affected areas, but also further influences grain yields in neighboring regions by changing agricultural production conditions. Based on the panel data of 31 provinces in China from 1989 to 2023, this paper employs Moran's I to analyze the spatial autocorrelation and agglomeration characteristics of grain yields. The spatial Durbin model is further utilized to examine the spatial spillover effects of drought disasters on grain yields and their regional heterogeneity. The empirical results reveal significant spatial autocorrelation in grain yields, with local characteristics of high-high and low-low agglomeration. Drought disasters exert a significant inhibitory effect on grain yields and generate negative spillover effects that transcend administrative boundaries, impacting surrounding regions. These effects exhibit pronounced regional heterogeneity: from the perspective of economic development, significant spillover effects are observed in the eastern and northeastern regions, but not in the central region. In terms of industrial attributes, the intensity of spillover effects is greater in major grain-producing areas compared to nonmajor grain-producing areas. The findings of this paper provide insights for integrating disaster response into the national food security industrial belt planning, enabling a closed-loop management framework that encompasses "disaster impact, spatial transmission, and policy response." © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: TEMPO-DQ framework: A Temporal-Ensemble, multi-phase operational data quality approach for early multi-class prediction under heterogeneous big data
Abstract: Early multi-class prediction under heterogeneous big data requires data-quality (DQ) assessment that can determine whether partially observed, multi-source and temporally evolving inputs are genuinely fit for downstream deep-learning (DL) inference. Conventional DQ measures and existing DQ frameworks provide static, surface-level evidence, offering limited support for early-stage discrimination, temporal stability analysis and root-cause diagnosis. This study proposes TEMPO-DQ, a Temporal–Ensemble, multi-phase operational DQ framework for deployment-oriented early multi-class DL prediction. Its core contribution is the Temporal–Ensemble principle, which aggregates DQ evidence across observation phases and recurrent model families to reduce single-model bias and capture the stability of data fitness over time. The principle is operationalized by AccTEMPO, a three-level diagnostic mechanism providing a global monitoring indicator, phase-specific intervention summaries and fine-grained variant–model–phase evaluation. Validation uses two XuetangX-derived MOOC datasets of 3,297,128 and 2,324,524 instances under seven data variants, four cumulative phases and four recurrent architectures. Completeness and Consistency saturate at 1.000 for every processed variant, yielding no post-preprocessing discrimination, whereas AccTEMPOM1 still separates operational fitness across ranges of 0.1081 and 0.3370 in the two tasks. Ablating the aggregation mechanism shows that pooling the model committee alone reduces the spread of the DQ verdict for a data version by 54.6% and 65.8%, pooling phases alone by 45.2% and 27.5%, and only their combination yields a single-valued verdict, whereas a published performance-linked baseline recomputed on the same data returns mutually inconsistent per-configuration scores. © 2026 The Authors. Abstract: Objective Genu varum is a potential risk factor for the development and progression of knee osteoarthritis. This study aimed to investigate the immediate effects of kinesiotaping applied to the biceps femoris and vastus lateralis muscles on the external knee adduction moment and lower-limb joint power during walking in individuals with genu varum and healthy controls. Methods Thirty male participants, including 15 individuals with genu varum and 15 healthy controls, were recruited. External knee adduction moments and lower-limb joint power were assessed during walking under two conditions: without taping and with kinesiotaping applied to the biceps femoris and vastus lateralis muscles. Results Before taping, the genu varum group exhibited a significantly greater first peak of the external knee adduction moment than the control group (P = 0.029). Following kinesiotaping, this between-group difference was no longer statistically significant (P > 0.05). In the genu varum group, kinesiotaping was associated with significant increases in the magnitude of negative ankle joint power (P = 0.038), negative knee joint power (P = 0.025), and positive knee joint power (P = 0.012). Positive knee joint power also increased significantly in the control group (P = 0.017). No significant changes in hip joint power were observed (P > 0.05). Conclusion Kinesiotaping of the biceps femoris and vastus lateralis muscles was associated with immediate changes in knee adduction moments and ankle and knee joint power during walking, particularly in individuals with genu varum. These findings suggest that kinesiotaping may influence lower-limb joint mechanics; however, its clinical benefits and potential effects on knee osteoarthritis risk remain uncertain and require further investigation. © 2027 The Author(s). Authors: Arab A.
Title: Advancing smart school initiatives: A case study of Zahedan city
Abstract: This mixed-methods case study evaluates Iran's Smart Schools Project in Zahedan, a socioeconomically heterogeneous city, to identify barriers and scalable interventions for technology-enhanced schooling in resource-constrained contexts. Data comprise structured surveys (n = 150), semi-structured interviews with policymakers (n = 10), and classroom observations across urban, semi-urban and rural schools. Findings reveal stark infrastructure and access gaps (rural device-sharing 1:175; chronic power outages; intermittent urban connectivity). Targeted, low-cost interventions (solar microgrids, offline learning-management systems, and Raspberry Pi deployments) produced measurable gains (rural literacy +25%; STEM engagement +18%). Cultural resistance was substantially reduced through engagement with religious leaders, raising parental approval from 20% to 65%. Analysis is situated within TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) and SAMR (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) frameworks. Policy implications include tiered funding that prioritizes rural allocation (proposed 60% share), promotion of domestic low-cost device manufacturing, and decentralized, context-sensitive teacher training. The study demonstrates that equity-driven, culturally attuned strategies can align national smart-school ambitions with local realities, offering a replicable model for other resource-limited regions seeking to close the urban–rural digital divide. © 2026 The Author.

Authors: Li M.; Yang Y.; Wang X.; Su Y.
Title: Capitalizing on positive experiences: Receiving affective empathy fosters a better mood and prosocial waiting
Abstract: Interpersonal responses to emotional disclosures have potent effects on immediate affective states, yet their capacity to shape subsequent prosocial behavior remains unclear. Across two experiments, we investigated how the perceived empathy conveyed by facial responses influences both emotional outcomes and downstream altruistic choices. In Experiment 1, participants shared imagined positive or negative life events and received either an empathic, nonresponsive, or counter-empathic facial response from ostensible partners. We observed a context-dependent affective modulation: empathic responses maximally enhanced positive affect following positive disclosures, whereas counter-empathic responses most severely worsened mood following negative disclosures. In Experiment 2, we coupled this paradigm with an experiential intertemporal choice task in which participants chose between different waiting durations for rewards benefiting themselves or a charitable cause. Empathic responses to positive disclosures selectively increased charity-benefiting decisions, indicating a greater willingness to incur personal time costs for others. Computational modeling of choice data characterized this prosocial enhancement as being accompanied by a reduction in the weight placed on waiting time relative to reward, that is, a lower subjective cost of waiting. These findings demonstrate that receiving affective empathy, particularly in the context of positive experiences, promotes downstream prosociality by recalibrating the cost–benefit computations underlying altruistic choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Screening out ethics: How technology enables ethical fading in negotiations
Abstract: Negotiations are rife with opportunities and temptations to engage in unethical negotiating behavior. Such behavior is not always strategic or even intentional; rather, it can emerge from situational characteristics of the negotiation environment. One psychological process through which situational characteristics influence unethical behavior is ethical fading, a process that limits one's ability to recognize the ethical aspects of the situation and behave in line with one's ethical values. As technologies such as email, video conferencing, and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly common in negotiations, an important question is whether these technologies facilitate ethical fading. In this review, we explore the impact that technology and AI have on ethical fading and unethical negotiating behavior. We propose that technology and AI use in negotiations promotes three cognitive processes that facilitate ethical fading: psychological distance, cognitive offloading, and displaced accountability. We review how technology may serve as an antecedent to each of these processes and explain why these processes may facilitate ethical fading in negotiation contexts. Because research on the relationship between technology and unethical negotiating behavior remains limited, we conclude by identifying promising directions for future research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
