Title: The effects of an online mindfulness-based intervention for parents of children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
Abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have been identified as a complementary treatment for children with ADHD. While there is a growing interest in developing MBIs in online formats, its application in parents is largely based on healthy populations. A two-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) was designed to investigate the effectiveness of an online MBI (arm 1) compared with an online psychoeducation (PSY) program (arm 2). Outcomes were measured before the intervention, after the intervention, and at 3-month follow-up. A total of 248 parents whose children with ADHD symptoms aged 6 to 12 years old participated in the study, with 131 parents assigned to the online MBI group and 117 to the PSY group. Both groups indicated significant and lasting improvements in their children's ADHD symptoms, executive functioning, and parental well-being. In addition, parental stress levels and two dimensions of expressed emotion, including critical comments and initial statements, decreased significantly in both groups. Notably, a specific benefit of the online MBI was identified for insomnia. A small-magnitude improvement in parent-child relationship quality, as a dimension of expressed emotion, was observed in the repeated measures ANOVA but was not consistently supported by the sensitivity analysis. Future studies should verify the specific and sustainable treatment effects of MBIs, strengthening parental engagement and support. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Children’s vocabulary predicts their math abilities: The mediating role of verbal and visuospatial short-term memory
Abstract: This study recruited 131 Chinese children aged 4 to 6 years and measured their forward counting, symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitude comparison, arithmetic problems, shape naming, vocabulary, and verbal and visuospatial short-term memory to explore the relationship between vocabulary, short-term memory, and mathematical ability. The results showed that verbal short-term memory fully mediated the relationship between vocabulary and symbolic magnitude comparison, as well as between vocabulary and arithmetic problems However, no mediating effect of visuospatial short-term memory was found between vocabulary and current mathematical ability. In addition, for nonsymbolic magnitude comparison and shape naming, only the direct effect of vocabulary was significant. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: Classification of influential factors on mining machinery operators’ workplace safety performance: integrated PLS-SEM, TOPSIS-SORT and kNN framework
Abstract: Workers’ satisfaction and performance regarding safety in mining industry are far from desired, possibly because the dependencies between influential factors and workplace safety are not sufficiently researched. The purpose of this paper is to propose novel, hybrid framework for classifying different mining machinery workplaces on the basis of occupational safety factors and occurred injuries. The proposed framework integrates structural equation modelling with a multicriteria and machine learning techniques for further modelling and classification. The importance of the occupational safety (technical, human and organizational factors) is assessed using the PLS-SEM analysis, by surveying 546 mining machinery operators. Multicriteria decision-making Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), is advanced using a new sorting procedure to assess and sort operators’ workplace safety satisfaction by the working factors and the types of mining machinery. The PLS-SEM analysis confirmed human and organizational factors impact, while technical factors showed no effect. TOPSIS-SORT results revealed that operators with no injury history (particularly those working with loaders, bulldozers, and excavators) exhibited satisfactory safety satisfaction, while 70 % of workplaces fell into the lower satisfaction category, particularly those of operators with experience of previous injuries. Finally, a kNN classifier, with SMOTE oversampling applied within each cross-validation training fold, classified operators by injury history with a balanced accuracy of 0.650 and an injury-class recall of 0.72. Among the models, kNN achieved the highest balanced accuracy (0.650), Macro-F1 (0.564), and injury-class recall (0.72), despite lower accuracy (0.607). A permutation test confirmed above-chance balanced classification performance (p = 0.017). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Attenuated attention engagement and sensorimotor resonance to social events in first-episode adolescent depression: Evidence from EEG oscillations
Abstract: Background Depressive symptoms may disrupt social brain development during adolescence, resulting in adverse long-term quality of life. Yet, little is known regarding the cognitive and neural changes during the processing of social interactions in adolescents with first-episode depression, particularly from an allocentric perspective. Methods We used electroencephalography (EEG) to assess two neural indicators during the observation of others' interactions, including sensorimotor mu suppression and occipital alpha-band activity, in 22 adolescents with first-episode major depressive disorder (MDD) and 23 healthy counterparts. Participants observed animated motions wherein actions were directed toward animate (human-like) or inanimate (rock) targets, comprising social (giving) and kinematically matched control events (disposing, taking and acquiring). Results Healthy controls (HCs) exhibited stronger central-parietal mu suppression in the lower sub-band during observation of socially interactive giving events than disposing events. In contrast, adolescents with MDD manifested no corresponding difference in mu suppression. Additionally, depressive adolescents demonstrated significantly higher occipital alpha power when viewing social (patient) than non-social (rock) targets, and this alpha power was significantly higher than that observed in HCs. Exploratory correlation analyses revealed that attenuated sensorimotor resonance of social interactions was significantly associated with increased severity of depressive symptoms in the MDD group. Conclusions Adolescents with first-episode depression showed difficulties in efficiently encoding social information and implicitly extracting the social-relational meaning of observed social interactions. These findings critically extend current understanding of neurocognitive mechanisms underlying social cognitive alterations in this population, and provide potential avenues for early screening and targeted interventions of social functioning impairment in adolescence. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: LeBlanc R.; Zeigler-Hill V.
Title: Do I matter? The connections between borderline personality traits and mattering
Abstract: Borderline personality traits are marked by interpersonal vulnerabilities such as rejection sensitivity and fear of abandonment, but little research has examined their connections with mattering – the perception that one is important to others. We proposed that diminished mattering may be an important relational perception associated with borderline traits. Three studies of undergraduates used complementary methods: a cross-sectional survey (Study 1; N = 390), responses to ambiguous romantic rejection scenarios (Study 2; N = 186), and a daily diary design (Study 3; N = 576). Borderline traits were consistently associated with lower perceived mattering. Perceived rejection statistically accounted for the link with diminished mattering, and lower daily mattering accounted for borderline-related negative emotions. These findings suggest that mattering may be an important interpersonal representation for individuals with borderline personality traits. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Human behaviour in wildfire emergencies: insights from evacuation decision-making and timing across Canada, Australia, and the United States
Abstract: Wildfires often require rapid evacuation to save lives, leading residents to make quick and context-specific transportation decisions that may differ across countries and cultures. This study examines intended evacuation behaviours during wildfires, focusing on promptness, departure time, and cross-country differences. Surveys were conducted across Canada, the United States, and Australia (with sample sizes of 1,366, 1,490, and 1,173, respectively), and the data were used to run advanced choice modelling techniques to estimate factors influencing time-related decisions. The findings emphasized the importance of preparedness, reasons for evacuating, and risk perception in shaping responses to emergencies. Moreover, results identified country differences and similarities in evacuation preparedness time. For instance, employment, age, and income were factors relevant only in the U.S. context, while gender was significant exclusively in the Australian context. For all three countries, households with older adults were less likely to evacuate promptly, while households with children were more likely to evacuate promptly. The study also revealed that complex models showed minimal or no improvement in fit relative to simpler models. These insights on evacuation decisions and departure times, especially across jurisdictional boundaries, can assist in improving generalized wildfire evacuation plans and implementing more inclusive emergency communication strategies. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: What counts as urban smartness? A longitudinal thematic analysis of smart city indexes
Abstract: Smart city indexes increasingly influence urban governance, policy benchmarking, and investment narratives, yet their conceptual evolution remains insufficiently examined. This article investigates how major smart city evaluation frameworks changed between 2017 and 2022 through a longitudinal thematic analysis of six prominent smart city indexes selected from an initial inventory of sixteen. The findings suggest a shift in the smart city index landscape from more technocentric assessment frameworks toward more integrated evaluation logics that give greater attention to governance capacity, economic conditions, and societal dimensions. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
Abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Associations of one-to-one peer support service and intervention outcomes among older adults with depressive symptoms: Evidence from a community-based stepped care programme for late-life depression in Hong Kong
Abstract: Objective Evidence on the outcomes of peer support for late-life depression is limited. This study examined whether the presence of a peer supporter alongside intervention improves older adults' mental health outcomes and the differential impacts of different peer support types and contents. Method From January 2024 to July 2025, depressive symptoms (Patient Health Questionnaire–9), generalised anxiety symptoms (Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7), and loneliness (3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale) of service users in the community-based mental health programme were collected at pre- and post-intervention. Linear mixed models examined the interaction effects between time and the presence of a peer supporter, service type, content, year of peer support experience, adjusting for sociodemographic variables, on mental health outcomes. Result Among 1124 older adults, 591 received peer support. Those with peer support showed a greater reduction in depressive symptoms (b = −0.42, CI = −0.80 - -0.05) compared to those without. Home visits (b = −1.27, CI = −1.97 – −0.57) and sharing personal recovery stories and life experiences (b = −1.07, CI = −1.87 - -0.26) were associated with a greater reduction in depressive symptoms than those who did not receive any peer support service. Service users with a more experienced peer supporter had a greater reduction in anxiety symptoms (b = −0.29, CI = −0.47 - -0.11) and loneliness (b = −0.14, CI = −0.24 - -0.03) following treatment. Conclusion Employing older adults as peer supporters may be a promising approach to improve service outcomes and promote productive ageing. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Li X.; Guo X.
Title: Dynamic configurations and ecological fit: A fuzzy-set QCA analysis of effective data security governance in summer olympic games (1992–2024)
Abstract: Against the backdrop of accelerating digital transformation, Summer Olympic Games have become mega‑temporary events generating massive volumes of data, where data security governance is critical to smooth event delivery. Nevertheless, existing scholarship mostly adopts fragmented technology‑centric or management‑centric perspectives, overlooking the synergistic interplay among multi‑dimensional factors. Drawing upon information ecology theory, this study applies fuzzy‑set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to nine Summer Olympic Games held between 1992 and 2024. We examine how five antecedent conditions—data asset sensitivity, organizational management maturity, technological maturity, security deployment intensity, and external regulatory pressure—jointly shape high‑level data security governance. Necessary‑condition analysis shows that no single factor is indispensable for sound governance. Three equifinal configurational paths are identified: the Full‑Element Driven path, the Management‑Technology Dual‑Driven path, and the Low‑Risk Baseline path. Our findings demonstrate that effective Olympic data security governance arises from nonlinear multi‑element synergy rather than isolated single‑factor advantages, while governance failures stem from ecological mismatches among information‑ecology components. Building on these patterns, we derive a path‑contingent investment framework specifying what budget‑constrained hosts can compress and what they must prioritize. This paper extends information ecology theory to the temporary governance context of mega‑sporting events and delivers differentiated, resource‑constrained managerial insights for future Olympic host cities under the ecological‑fit principle. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From precarious work to occupational health outcomes in hotel housekeepers: a narrative review with meta-synthesis
Abstract: Introduction: Hotel housekeepers sustain the core functioning of the hospitality industry yet perform demanding, repetitive, and undervalued work associated with substantial physical and psychosocial risks. Understanding how working conditions shape health, motivation, and lived experience is essential for informing prevention strategies and promoting decent work. Methods A sequential narrative review and qualitative meta -synthesis were conducted to integrate and reinterpret evidence across disciplines and study designs. Searches covered five academic databases and gray literature without year or language limits. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and synthesized through narrative, tabular, and meta -analytical thematic analysis, with findings interpreted through the JD-R framework. Results Findings revealed employment precarity, work intensification, musculoskeletal pain, chemical and biological hazards, and elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Time pressure fostered coping strategies such as skipping meals and delaying bathroom use. Gendered labor divisions, discrimination, and negative supervision contributed to invisibility and limited autonomy. Workers also expressed pride, intrinsic motivation, and collective action to make their contributions visible. Conclusions This review demonstrates that housekeeping is characterized by structural precarity and cumulative health burdens alongside resilience and emerging activism. Improving occupational health requires organizational and policy transformations: realistic workloads, safer equipment, secure contracts, participatory risk management, and leadership practices grounded in dignity and fairness; rather than reliance on individual coping. Structural change is essential to advance safer, more equitable, and sustainable workplaces in the hospitality sector. The JD-R framework highlights the need to reduce demand and strengthen resources. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Research note: Method for delineating urbanized areas based on mean land parcel area
Abstract: The expansion of growing cities into neighboring areas, known as urban sprawl, is reflected in morphological changes to the land parcel pattern. This paper examines urban cadastral parcel patterns, assuming that population-driven land demand drives fragmentation, and that the degree of fragmentation is proportional to local population density. Adopting a radial analysis of cities, the study analyzes 21 urban systems across three continents to examine how mean land parcel area scales with distance from the city center. The results reveal that mean parcel area increases exponentially within urbanized areas before stabilizing in the surrounding non-urban zone, thereby providing a clear structural threshold for delineating the extent of urbanized land. The characteristic distance of this exponential regime scales with the square root of total city population, showing that the spatial extent of high-degree parcel fragmentation associated with urbanization increases systematically with city size. This result is consistent with radial-scaling findings for urban land use, but is derived here independently from cadastral parcel data. This analysis offers a new approach to understanding spatial urbanization and the morphological evolution of the land parcel pattern as cities expand, while highlighting cadastral data as a valuable source for studying the spatial urbanization. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: “Triggering autonomy, not just automation”: Design implications for LLM-based home automation assistants for people with intellectual disability
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Smart home technologies offer considerable potential to enhance autonomy, safety, and quality of life for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID). Yet, configuring and personalizing such systems remain challenging due to complex interfaces and the technical expertise required. Traditionally, End-User Development (EUD) is often proposed as a way for non-experts to autonomously configure home devices. This work investigates the extent to which Large Language Models (LLMs) can provide effective support to people with ID in applying EUD. It explores whether an LLM-powered conversational interface can support individuals with ID in shaping smart home behaviors through natural conversations. Insights from exploratory sessions involving users with ID, caregivers, and stakeholders demonstrate a positive attitude towards this approach and suggest that conversational interaction can foster accessibility of automation programming through iterative clarifications. We conclude by outlining design opportunities and broader implications that can inform future research towards LLM-based EUD interfaces for people with ID. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Dyremose S.C.S.
Title: Closing the offshore window? Prioritising the green energy transition in an insecure Europe
Abstract: Offshore wind power (OWP) and offshore energy hubs (OEHs) have recently become stable components of decarbonisation efforts across the EU. To this end, a plan to construct "Energy Islands" was institutionalised in Danish policy in 2020, alongside ambitions to scale up OWP capacity by 6 GW. However, in 2022, the Russia-Ukraine conflict altered the geopolitical landscape, rapidly changing prospects for OWP implementation. Inflation, uncertain energy market developments and annulment of an open-door scheme have negatively impacted OWP incentives in Denmark. This article utilises the Multiple Streams Framework (MSF) to analyse symptoms, barriers, and proposed solutions to this development. It identifies how offshore energy policy 'windows' in Denmark are affected by shifting geopolitical landscapes across the EU from 2020 to 2026. To assess this, a thematic analysis of discourses surrounding OWP development is conducted, utilising themes appearing in the Problem, Policy and Politics streams of the MSF to frame the analysis. Data was gathered from six public events focusing on OWP development and from two focus group discussions. A document analysis of relevant policies and literature is conducted to support findings. Results indicate that the OWP window of opportunity has been at risk of closing due to significant shifts in deployment capabilities. Policy adaptations and new regulations can help mitigate geopolitical uncertainty and keep it open. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Abubakar S.; Mhungu A.
Title: Academic assessment feedback in theoretical nursing education: A scoping review
Abstract: Background: Assessment feedback is essential in nursing education, supporting students' academic and professional development. While extensive literature exists on feedback in clinical placements, there is limited evidence on academic assessment feedback approaches within the theoretical component of nursing education. Aim: This scoping review explores existing practices, feedback models and their effectiveness in theoretical nursing education. Methods: The review is guided by Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) five-stage framework and reported in line with PRISMA-ScR. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across CINAHL and Medline databases, supplemented by Google Scholar and reference list screening, in March 2025. Inclusion criteria included peer-reviewed articles published in English language on academic assessment feedback in nursing education. Identified studies were managed using Covidence and data were synthesised using qualitative content analysis. Results: A total of n = 261 studies were identified, n = 7 studies met the review criteria following full screening. Findings show a predominant focus on formative feedback, provided using approaches such as written annotations, audio podcasts and Immediate Feedback Assessment Technique (IF-AT). There are inconsistencies in the feedback approaches and a limited application of structured feedback models among educators. Evidence on summative feedback approaches remains limited. Conclusion: Assessment feedback in theoretical nursing education is characterised by a strong emphasis on formative feedback. However, the practice lacks consistency and standardisation. The integration of structured, evidence-informed feedback models and enhancement of feedback literacy may improve consistency, quality and academic development value of assessment feedback. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Spatial wildfire risk assessment for Oahu, Hawaii, using swarm-intelligence-optimized CatBoost and the analytic network process
Abstract: Wildfires in the Hawaiian Islands are an increasing concern due to climate change and the spread of invasive species. This study thus assessed the wildfire risk on Oahu, Hawaii. Wildfire susceptibility was modeled using the categorical boosting (CatBoost) algorithm. To improve model performance, its hyperparameters were optimized through a comparative analysis of two swarm-intelligence (SI) metaheuristics: the pathfinder algorithm (PFA) and the sparrow search algorithm (SSA). These SI approaches automatically explored the hyperparameter space and maximized the prediction accuracy for the validation set, resulting in two optimized models (PFA-CatBoost and SSA-CatBoost). Socioeconomic vulnerability was then quantified using the analytic network process (ANP), based on eight socioeconomic and demographic indicators that were weighted, fuzzified, and integrated into a composite index. The wildfire susceptibility results showed that the hybrid PFA-CatBoost and SSA-CatBoost models outperformed the baseline CatBoost model, with SSA-CatBoost achieving the best performance, reaching an accuracy of 0.984 on the testing set. The ANP analysis identified annual household income, population density, and education level as the primary socioeconomic indicators associated with wildfire vulnerability. According to the resulting wildfire risk map, 11.7% of Oahu fell within the high or very-high risk categories. The high-risk areas were primarily concentrated in densely populated corridors such as Makaha, Waianae, Maili, Nanakuli, Ewa Gentry, Waipahu, and the Honolulu–Waialae-Kahala corridor. Overall, the proposed framework provides a robust approach to spatial wildfire risk assessment, supporting risk-informed decision-making for wildfire mitigation, land-use planning, and emergency management on Oahu Island. © 2026

Title: Personality engineering with AI agents: A new methodology for negotiation research
Abstract: According to canonical negotiation theory, people's success in a negotiation depends on how well they balance competing demands—empathizing and asserting, demonstrating concern for other and concern for self, being soft on the people and hard on the problem. Yet people struggle to manage these tensions, so researchers have lacked the ability to rigorously test the field's prescriptions under controlled conditions. AI agents do not face the same limitations, and their precision, repertoire, consistency, and scalability enable a new class of experiments to contribute to negotiation theory. In this article, we introduce personality engineering—a methodology that precisely parameterizes the personas of AI agents based on established personality frameworks—and propose how this method can be used to study the traits and behaviors of negotiators. Given its relevance to negotiation theory, we propose the interpersonal circumplex—and its two core dimensions of warmth and dominance—as a foundational coordinate system for the field. This approach offers both a rigorous methodology for testing classic negotiation theories and a practical guide for designing the personas of AI negotiation agents. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Suicidality during intranasal (es)ketamine treatment: A retrospective cohort study
Abstract: Background Intranasal (es)ketamine has shown efficacy in therapy of treatment-resistant depression (TRD). However, its effects on suicidality have not been fully elucidated. Methods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal cohort study of 80 patients affected by TRD and treated with intranasal (es)ketamine. Suicidality was assessed using item 10 of the clinician-rated Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) and item 9 of the Beck-Depression-Inventory-II (BDI-II). We measured patient- and transition-level fluctuations of suicidality, tested temporal clustering using mixed-effects logistic regression, examined associations between non-suicidal depressive symptom change and suicidality worsening, and explored baseline predictors. Results Mean suicidality ratings decreased modestly. Upward and downward category transitions occurred at similar frequencies across treatment (MADRS: 57 increases and 50 decreases across 767 valid transitions, 7.4% vs. 6.5%; BDI-II: 22 increases and 23 decreases across 741 transitions, 3.0% vs. 3.1%). At least one upward transition occurred in 38.8% on MADRS and 21.3% on BDI-II. Transient elevations were more frequent than sustained elevations. Sustained elevation occurred at 15.0% on MADRS and 7.5% on BDI-II. Increases did not cluster by treatment phase. MADRS, but not BDI-II, upward transitions were associated with concurrent and lagged worsening in non-suicidal depressive symptoms. Higher baseline suicidality showed the most consistent association with later worsening across both measures. Two serious adverse events occurred, including one suicide. Conclusions In this routine-care cohort, suicidality decreased on average, with no evidence of treatment-phase - specific worsening. Nonetheless, a minority of patients showed transient or, less often, sustained increases in suicidality, supporting necessity of continuous suicidality monitoring throughout (es)ketamine treatment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Moeyaert M.; Lou Y.
Title: Moderator analysis for single-case experimental design meta-analysis
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Moderator analysis in single-experimental design (SCED) meta-analysis allows for fine-grained analysis allowing explanation of variability in intervention effectiveness between studies in addition to between participants. This is desirable for the field of cognitive therapy as individual SCED study participant characteristics might explain participant's responsiveness to interventions. This stands in contrast to traditional group design meta-analysis in which moderator analysis is limited to exploring study level characteristics. If traditional meta-analytic techniques were to be used, as in group design studies (i.e., using study average moderators), then the unique benefits of synthesizing SCED studies are missed. In this manuscript, three-level meta-analysis for synthesis of SCED effect sizes with inclusion of moderators is introduced and an empirical demonstration using SCED studies focusing on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is provided. The goal is to provide applied SCED meta-analysis with appropriate methodology to conduct moderator analysis which can result in more fine-grained evidence. This approach can support a more comprehensive understanding of the conditions under which, and the participants for whom, interventions may be recommended. © 2026

Authors: Qiao Y.; Zhang X.; Zhou S.; Wu X.; Liu D.; Khan W.R.; Shi Y.
Title: Greener but not more balanced: Cross-scale divergence between carbon sequestration and nitrogen retention in urban green spaces
Abstract: Expanding urban green space is assumed to enhance carbon sequestration service (CSS) and nitrogen retention service (NRS) simultaneously, yet their responses to urbanization and spatial form may diverge. This study examined carbon–nitrogen functional imbalance in the Yangtze River Delta (YRD), China, by integrating long-term ecosystem-service assessment, city-scale morphology analysis, interpretable machine learning, and constrained NSGA-II optimization. CSS and NRS were estimated from 1990 to 2020 using CASA and InVEST-NDR, respectively. At the city scale, twelve green-space and building morphology indicators representing both two- and three-dimensional characteristics were linked to CSS, NRS, and CN_gap across four selected cities. Regionally, CSS first declined from approximately 700 to below 600 gC·m−2·yr−1 and then increased after 2000, whereas NRS peaked at 7.1–7.3 gN·m−2·yr−1 in the early 2000s before declining after the mid-2000s. This divergence produced a rising C/N ratio and persistent spatial mismatch, with high CSS concentrated in the southern and southwestern YRD and high NRS more evident in northern, central, and eastern plains. City-scale models showed moderate to strong performance (R2 = 0.61–0.83). SHAP analysis revealed both shared and distinct morphology responses among CSS, NRS, and CN_gap. ED consistently showed the strongest positive association with CSS, whereas NRS and CN_gap were more strongly influenced by city-specific combinations of green-space configuration and built-form intensity. NSGA-II candidate scenarios increased CSS by 16.28–17.38% and NRS by 5.15–12.31%, while reducing CN_gap by 43.59–77.06%. These findings suggest that increasing urban greenness alone does not necessarily improve carbon–nitrogen coordination, highlighting the need for morphology strategies tailored to local conditions rather than uniform greening targets. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Management of Disputes in the Construction Industry during COVID-19: Contractors' Takeaways for Future Pandemics
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic intensified construction disputes. While dispute management has been widely studied, limited research has examined pandemic-induced disputes globally, especially within the Sri Lankan construction context. Hence, this study aims to investigate how to manage the disputes due to COVID-19 in the Sri Lankan construction industry, considering the contractors' perspective. The study adopts an interpretivist philosophy and employs a qualitative Delphi technique involving two iterative rounds of semistructured interviews, thereby making a methodological contribution. The data were analyzed through manual content analysis. The findings reveal six positive impacts and 12 negative impacts of COVID-19 on the construction industry, along with suitable preventive measures to manage the 12 important causes of disputes arising from the pandemic. This is positioned as one of the limited studies identifying both positive and negative impacts and suitable preventive measures in managing the identified causes. The findings can be applied for developing contexts of a similar nature, particularly in managing disputes during future pandemics.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Authors: Liu L.; Chen J.; He Y.; Zhao C.; Cui Y.
Title: Diagnosing ecosystem service mismatches through service flows and explainable AI: evidence from the Weihe River Basin, China
Abstract: Ecosystem service flows (ESFs) connect ecological supply with human demand, yet the links among service transmission, supply-demand imbalance, and nonlinear response thresholds remain difficult to diagnose in rapidly urbanizing regions. To provide a transferable diagnostic approach, we developed an explainable AI-assisted supply-demand-flow framework. We tested it in the Weihe River Basin, a representative ecological-economic transition zone of Northwest China, from 2000 to 2020. We quantified the supply, demand, and ecosystem service supply-demand ratios (ESDRs) for water yield, soil conservation, carbon sequestration, and food provision; simulated service-specific flows; and used XGBoost-SHAP-PDP to identify dominant drivers and threshold intervals. Ecological sources in the Qinling, Longshan and loess hilly regions remained separated from demand centers on the Guanzhong urban plain. Water yield supply increased from 9.41 to 11.99 billion m3, and soil conservation supply from 4.36 to 5.93 billion t, while their respective demands declined by 21.5% and 24.1%. Water and soil conservation flows were concentrated along terrain-controlled river corridors, carbon sequestration showed strong outward spillover and weak internal inflow, and food flows shifted toward a multi-center network linking eastern Gansu and the Guanzhong Plain. SHAP identified population density as the leading driver of water and food ESDRs and forestland proportion as the dominant driver of soil and carbon ESDRs. By coupling service-flow mechanisms with interpretable machine learning, the framework offers a reusable basis for environmental impact assessment, ecological compensation, corridor protection, demand-side regulation, and threshold-based territorial planning in comparable urbanizing regions. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Wang K.; Pan Z.; Lu Y.
Title: Incompetence or deception: Unraveling the asymmetric mechanisms of AI hallucinations on trust and distrust
Abstract: Reliance on generative artificial intelligence (AI) for knowledge work is increasing, yet confidently presented hallucinations can elicit strong negative user reactions. Existing literature frames hallucinations as technical failures that reduce trust, conflating the decline of trust with the emergence of distrust. However, trust and distrust are theoretically distinct constructs rather than opposite ends of a single continuum. Drawing on information manipulation theory (IMT), this study reconceptualizes AI hallucinations as violations of conversational norms. It proposes a model linking hallucination cues to perceived communicative incompetence and perceived source deception, which are differentially related to trust and distrust. It further examines whether perceived AI autonomy moderates the relationship between hallucination cues and perceived source deception. The model was tested using a sequential mixed-methods design that combined qualitative semi-structured interviews with a two-wave survey of 506 GenAI users. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA). The findings revealed that hallucination cues were differentially associated with perceived communicative incompetence and perceived source deception, with the former more strongly associated with trust and the latter with distrust. Perceived AI autonomy moderated the associations between some hallucination cues and perceived source deception. The PLS-SEM–NCA analysis provided complementary evidence on net effects and necessary conditions that neither method could offer alone. Overall, this study extends research on AI hallucinations by conceptualizing them as distinct forms of conversational norm violations and explaining how different hallucination cues are associated with perceived communicative incompetence and perceived source deception, which are differentially linked to trust and distrust. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yan X.; Wu N.; Dai H.; Han D.; Nieuwenhuijsen M.; Ji J.S.; Zhao B.
Title: Global health benefits of urban greening across three decades (1990–2020)
Abstract: Urban greenness serves as a pivotal nature-based solution for mitigating heat islands and air pollution, while fostering both physical and mental well-being. However, despite documented regional potential health benefits, global-scale evidence regarding estimated historical gains from urban greenness variations and the potential for preventable mortality reduction remains scarce. Furthermore, little is known about the drivers of the changing health gap and disparities across age groups and city densities. This study systematically evaluates global urban greenness trends from 1990 to 2020, quantifying the estimated potentially averted premature deaths linked to historical changes, as well as the projected health gains under counterfactual scenarios. Our findings suggest that elevating global urban greenness to the provincial top 25th percentile benchmark could potentially expand the scale of preventable premature mortality, with estimated preventable deaths rising from 370,933 (95% CI: 220,465– 518,819) in 1990 to 1,744,656 (95% CI: 1,032,723– 2,449,854) in 2020. Parameter contribution analysis reveals that urban expansion and population aging are the primary drivers of this growing health gap. Furthermore, the estimated health benefits of urban greenness exhibit significant spatial disparities, with these gaps being particularly pronounced among elderly populations in megacities. These results underscore the need for future urban planning to pivot toward precision interventions that prioritize high-density and rapidly aging communities. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Boredom and creativity in classrooms: A latent profile analysis
Abstract: Background: Contradictory results have emerged from empirical research into the relationship between boredom and creativity. Theories suggest that states of low arousal and positive valence promote creative processes. Studies have differentiated students' experiences of boredom based on valence and arousal as latent profiles. Aims: We will examine whether latent profiles of boredom described in previous research can be found in a younger age group sample in a school context, and whether different latent boredom profiles vary in terms of their creativity value. Sample: A total of 111 ninth-grade secondary school students participated. Each student received 18–19 signals (a sum of 2057 momentary assessments, 345 missing, total number of completed momentary assessments k = 1712). Methods: We conducted an experience sampling study and analysed the assessed data (boredom, valence, arousal, creativity) using latent profile analyses. Results: In line with previous research, we identified five profiles of boredom. According to our hypothesis, the identified boredom profiles differed in their mean creativity scores. In particular, the boredom profile characterized by slightly positive valence and low arousal showed the highest mean creativity score. In contrast, profiles characterized by strongly negative valence showed lower creativity scores. Moments that were not perceived as boring had a higher creativity value on average compared to moments perceived as boring. Conclusions: Our findings help to clarify the controversy surrounding the relationship between boredom and creativity. We demonstrate that creativity varies considerably depending on the specific profile of boredom, and outline implications for research and practice. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Feasibility of an internet-based cognitive behavioral treatment for university students with depression and/or anxiety: A mixed-methods single arm repeated measures study
Source title: Journal of Behavioral and Cognitive Therapy
Abstract: Mental health problems are prevalent among university students, with anxiety and depression being the most common conditions. Despite available campus services, barriers to access persist, creating a substantial treatment gap. Internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (iCBT) offers a scalable alternative, although evidence in university settings remains limited.This study assessed the feasibility and preliminary effects of VIVIM, an adapted iCBT program delivered through interactive eBooks for Spanish- and Catalan-speaking university students with anxiety and/or depression. It also evaluated the feasibility of conducting a future randomized controlled trial (RCT).Feasibility was evaluated through recruitment, retention, adherence, engagement, and acceptability. Thirty-three students from Rovira i Virgili University accessed the intervention over eight weeks.Recruitment targets were achieved within the planned timeframe, whereas retention was limited, with 45.45% and 39.39% of participants completing post-treatment and follow-up assessments, respectively. Adherence was low: only 12.12% of participants accessed all six predefined core eBooks, and 6.1% remained engaged throughout the intervention period. Nevertheless, participants who completed post-treatment assessments reported moderate-to-high levels of engagement and satisfaction.Completers and intention-to-treat sensitivity analyses showed significant improvements in depression and anxiety, although the uncontrolled single-arm design does not permit attribution of these changes to the intervention. Exploratory analyses suggested a possible association between greater eBooks use and larger symptom improvements, although findings were based on small subgroups and partly LOCF −imputed data.The findings suggest that both the intervention and study procedures require further optimization before progression to a full-scale RCT, despite encouraging preliminary evidence of improved mental health outcomes. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Masson SAS on behalf of Association Française de Therapie Comportementale et Cognitive.

Title: Deepening the Conceptual Debate on Sportswashing: Institutional narratives of reputational projection of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo on Social Media; [Profundizando en el debate conceptual sobre sportswashing: narrativas institucionales de proyección reputacional de Ruanda y la República Democrática del Congo en redes sociales]
Abstract: Introduction: In recent decades, sport has become a strategic instrument within international politics, used by states to project national image, strengthen global reputation and enhance territorial positioning. At the same time, the concept of sportswashing has gained prominence in both academic and media debates to describe the use of sport as a reputational legitimization strategy in the face of political or social criticism. However, its widespread use has generated conceptual ambiguity and confusion with other sport-related strategies such as sport diplomacy and sport place branding. Methodology: This study adopts a quantitative approach based on digital content analysis of social media, examining 684 posts published in 2025 by institutional accounts related to the territorial promotion strategies of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Data were collected using the social media analytics tool Fanpage Karma and analyzed through three complementary dimensions: communication activity, digital engagement performance and lexical-discursive narrative analysis. Results: The findings reveal a clear asymmetry in the communication strategies of both countries. Rwanda displays a highly centralized strategy around the Visit Rwanda brand, where sport functions as a key instrument for international visibility and high levels of digital engagement. In contrast, the Democratic Republic of Congo presents a more fragmented communication strategy focused primarily on cultural and tourism promotion. Discussion: The results confirm the usefulness of the proposed political triangle of sport framework for interpreting these strategies, highlighting the predominance of sport place branding over sport diplomacy and sport for development narratives. Furthermore, the study argues that sportswashing can be understood as a critical interpretative outcome that may emerge across these strategies. Conclusions: The research contributes to clarifying the conceptual debate by proposing an integrative analytical framework that distinguishes legitimate territorial branding strategies from their potential reinterpretation as sportswashing in contexts of reputational controversy. © 2027, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Title: Regional heterogeneity in the relationship between temperature and household electricity consumption across rural South Africa
Abstract: In this study we examine the heterogeneous effects of temperature on household electricity consumption using combined hourly electricity consumption and temperature data across several rural areas in South Africa. We apply a panel data regression model controlling for temperature bin dummies to capture nonlinear temperature effects, as well as a set of fixed effects to capture the unobserved heterogeneity across households and over time. We find that the temperature–consumption relationship varies across geographical locations and is characterised predominantly by inverse J-shaped and inverse U-shaped patterns, which differs from the typical U-shaped curve in the literature. Title: Exploring Lean-Integrated Circular Economy in the Built Environment Setting: Implications for Project Governance and Compliance
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: The current study establishes how lean tenets contribute to the circular economy (CE) with exploration of lean tools with circular economy core principles and framework development. While there seem to be synergies between the concepts of lean and CE, the construction management research fraternity has not fully tapped the huge research potential in this domain. To address this gap, a two-phased exploratory qualitative research design is proposed. The first phase involves mapping lean tools with 10 dimensions of CE in the context of the built environment sector through content analysis and expert validation (n=3). Continuous improvement and added value tools of lean attained maximum realization of CE dimensions. The second phase involves semistructured interviews of experts (n=9) on an understanding of the synergies between lean and CE through thematic analysis (TA). The current study identifies predominant lean tools that realize CE dimensions and develops a conceptual model of a lean-driven circular economy (LdCE) framework for construction projects. Also, the lean tenets and their allied tools enabled value optimization through effective mapping of non-value-added processes and minimizing wasteful aspects. These findings are intended to inform engineers, construction managers, and legal practitioners about actionable strategies for promoting sustainable, legally compliant project execution. This study proves to accelerate sustainable construction through a lean and CE integrated framework in developing nations. Title: Quantifying energy–cost–carbon tradeoffs in China's onshore wind expansion: A life cycle-based turbine design optimization
Abstract: China's onshore wind expansion must reconcile electricity generation, life-cycle cost, and life-cycle carbon emissions across heterogeneous wind regimes. We develop a region-specific assessment and turbine-design optimization framework linking rotor diameter and hub height to annual energy production, life-cycle cost, and greenhouse gas emissions from component manufacturing to grid delivery. Spatial screening identifies 2.61 million km2 of eligible land, representing 27.2% of China's land area. Under a uniform-design assessment using the reference wind speed, maximum geometric capacity reaches 10.1 TW, with gross generation of 30 PWh/yr and 10.6 PWh/yr after an idealized infinite-array adjustment. Separate national optimizations select turbine configurations across wind-speed zones under generation, cost, and carbon constraints, assuming full development of eligible land and using gross generation. The minimum-unit-cost solution generates 38.2 PWh/yr at 0.25 CNY/kWh and a carbon intensity of 15.0 g CO₂-eq/kWh. Minimizing carbon intensity lowers it to 13.3 g CO₂-eq/kWh but raises unit cost to 0.75 CNY/kWh, with generation of 40.2 PWh/yr. Selected turbine dimensions and rated powers generally decrease beyond their respective peaks in low-to-intermediate wind-speed zones; the minimum‑carbon-intensity solution generally favors larger rotors and higher-rated turbines. By quantifying energy–cost–carbon trade-offs, the framework supports turbine selection tailored to regional wind conditions and economic or carbon objectives. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: The Dynamics of Poverty Transitions in Indonesia: A Multilevel Analysis of Household Entry Into and Exit From Poverty
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: Indonesia’s aggregate poverty rate masks substantial household-level mobility. This study investigates the determinants of entry into and exit from poverty using panel data from the National Socioeconomic Survey (SUSENAS) 2022–2024. Multilevel binary logistic regression is applied to model transition probabilities across 34 provinces. Results show that education level and employment sector are the strongest household-level predictors: higher-educated heads working in services or manufacturing face a lower risk of entering poverty and greater prospects of exiting poverty. Findings reflect associations from an observational design and should not be interpreted causally. The evidence points to the need for anticipatory social protection targeting near-poor households and sustained investment in secondary and vocational education as structural pathways out of poverty. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Authors: Gibbons S.; Hilber C.A.L.
Title: Caring in the time of austerity
Abstract: The years after the election of the UK's coalition government in 2010 saw a decline in central funding to local government and a fall in expenditure on a range of local services, including social services. These cuts were backed by a theory that individuals in the community would step in with voluntary action (the ‘Big Society’) to fill the void left by withdrawal of public support, a specific case of the argument that government activity crowds out that of private individuals. With borrowing costs in the UK sharply increasing and austerity debates resurfacing elsewhere in Europe, evaluating the consequences of the previous round of spending cuts is particularly timely. Using a large panel survey of individuals linked to detailed local government income and spending data for the period from 2008/9 until 2016/7 and exploiting central government funding cuts as an exogenous source of variation in Local Authority spending, we estimate how these changes in public support affected individual caring, voluntary and charitable behaviour. Our main finding is that spending cuts had no causal effects on these activities when considered in the aggregate, providing little support for the proposition that cutting public sector spending increases individual caring and philanthropic activities. The near-null results, however, mask spatial heterogeneity: rural communities show greater responsiveness to spending cuts than urban populations, consistent with thinner provision of formal public and third-sector support in rural areas. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Li M.; Tian M.
Title: Analysis of synergies and trade-offs in sustainable development goals at the local scale: A case study of 2,063 counties in China
Abstract: Understanding the potential synergies or trade-offs among the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is crucial for achieving the 2030 Agenda. This study systematically investigates SDG synergies and trade-offs at the local scale by quantitatively describing the monotonicity and linear characteristics of SDG interactions in Chinese counties from 2000 to 2020 and compares the findings with those of other multiscale studies. The key findings include the following: (1) China's local-scale sustainable development trends show overall improvement, although the SDG2, SDG3, and SDG17 indices exhibit declining trajectories. (2) The majority of SDGs do not have significant interactions. Among the classified interactions, synergies are clearly more common than trade-offs are, and linear interactions are more common than nonlinear interactions are. (3) Spatial location and land development intensity shape SDG trade-offs. Synergies are largely consistent across locations, while adjacent counties show stronger economic–ecological tensions. Counties with higher shares of construction land exhibit more active SDG interactions and intensified trade-offs between economic development and ecological conservation. (4) SDG1, SDG8, SDG9, and SDG17 serve as core goals within the local-scale SDG network, functioning as leverage goals to maximize synergies and advance sustainable development. Additionally, the network relationships among the SDGs tend towards simplification over a 20-year period. (5) The synergies and trade-offs among the SDGs exhibit significant spatial variation across the different scales. Compared with global-scale and regional-scale SDG interactions, local-scale SDG relationships demonstrate stronger spatial heterogeneity and structural stability. Title: Sleeper effects of a universal, school-based social and emotional learning intervention (Passport: Skills For Life) on internalising symptoms and related outcomes during the transition from childhood to adolescence: a cluster-randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Universal, school-based social and emotional learning interventions have been consistently shown to meaningfully improve a range of salient outcomes for children and young people in the short-term, but less is known about their longer-term effects. This study focuses on such effects in the context of a cluster-randomised controlled trial of the Passport: Skills for Life intervention in Greater Manchester, England. Passport is implemented by trained classroom teachers, who deliver 18 weekly lessons across 5 modules (emotions; relationships and helping each other; difficult situations; fairness, justice and what is right; change and loss). Mainstream primary schools (clusters, k = 62; trial cohort of N = 2,425 children, aged 8-9 years at baseline) were the unit of randomisation. Allocation took place following completion of baseline measures, with minimisation ensuring balance across trial arms in school size and the proportion of children eligible for free school meals. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses at immediate-post-intervention follow-up revealed no intervention effects for any trial outcome. Accordingly, the focus of this paper is on the potential emergence of so-called ‘sleeper’ effects at 12-month post-intervention follow-up, which coincided with the final year of primary school for the trial cohort. However, ITT analyses revealed no statistically significant impact of Passport on internalising symptoms (primary outcome; d = 0.06, 95% bootstrapped confidence interval, BCI -0.17, 0.27) or any of our secondary outcomes (emotion regulation, d = 0.00, 95% bootstrapped confidence interval, BCI -0.21, 0.21; wellbeing, d = 0.05, 95% BCI -0.18, 0.30; loneliness, d = -0.02, 95% BCI -0.24, 0.20; bullying, d = 0.01, 95% BCI -0.21, 0.23; peer support d = 0.05, 95% BCI -0.13, 0.25). Taken together with findings from related analyses of this trial, the present results do not provide evidence to support further scale-up of Passport. Our discussion focuses on whether the impending transition to secondary school was a sufficient or universally applicable catalytic event to trigger the application of skills acquired in Passport, or whether the intervention may simply have been insufficiently potent to provide a meaningful benefit over usual practice. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Domain-specific links between the better-than-average effect and self-reported depressive symptoms: Competence but not morality
Abstract: The better-than-average effect (BTAE), the tendency to evaluate oneself more favorably than the average other, has been linked to lower depressive symptoms. However, whether this association differs across evaluative domains remains unclear. This study investigated how BTAE in the moral and competence domains was associated with depressive symptoms. To further clarify these associations, we decomposed BTAE scores into self- and average-other evaluation components and examined their associations with depressive symptoms. A total of 285 adults rated themselves and the average person on moral and competence traits and reported depressive symptoms. Results showed that higher competence BTAE was associated with lower depressive symptoms, whereas moral BTAE was not, and these associations differed significantly. Component-level results suggested that depressive symptoms were associated more strongly with self-evaluation than with average-other evaluation in the competence domain. For morality, depressive symptoms were negatively associated with self-evaluation, but self- and average-other coefficients did not differ significantly. These findings indicate that BTAE is linked to depressive symptoms in a domain-specific manner. Competence BTAE may be more closely linked to depressive symptoms than moral BTAE, highlighting the need to distinguish evaluative domains when examining the psychological significance of BTAE. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The security–efficiency trade-off in ransomware networks
Abstract: Ransomware groups pose a threat to both the economy and national security, yet little is known about their structural dynamics. This study analyses the Conti group using leaked Jabber encrypted instant messaging chat data (similar to Messenger) and Relational Event Models to examine how preferential attachment and triadic closure mechanisms shape its communication network. Findings show Conti prioritised efficiency through centralisation but mitigated risks via compartmentalisation, creating a hybrid structure that balances speed and secrecy. This adaptive approach enhances both effectiveness and resilience. The research provides new insights into the evolution of ransomware groups and suggests that disruption strategies should target internal cohesion rather than external infrastructure. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Pyyhtinen O.
Title: From elimination to utilisation: the stabilisation of waste incineration and the transformation of mixed municipal waste in Finland
Abstract: Drawing on parliamentary debates and media coverage supplemented by documentary materials, the article traces the stabilisation of waste incineration as the predominant method for treating mixed municipal waste in Finland from the early 2000s to the present. It shows how waste incineration moved from controversy to normalisation in Finland during the 2010s, only to become contested again in the 2020s, particularly due to increasing problematisation of its sustainability at the EU level. The article argues that the transition of Finland’s waste infrastructure from landfilling to incineration enacted a fundamental transformation in the ontology and valuation of mixed municipal waste, as it came to be progressively configured not as unwanted residue but as a combustible, valuable, energy-bearing resource. By reconstructing how the understandings of both incineration and waste were transformed, the article contributes to debates in discard studies and STS on the making of waste, value and socio-technical order, illuminating how waste infrastructures become stabilised, how certain waste ontologies are normalised at the expense of others and how technologies of disposal may become reframed as technologies of resource recovery and utilisation. The Finnish case also demonstrates how difficult it may be to disengage from a socio-technical arrangement once it has become stabilised and infrastructurally embedded, even when that arrangement becomes dependent on the continued generation of the very waste it was intended to eliminate. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Reconceptualising the mobility capital model in an urban, car-lite, Asian context: A photovoice study of three Singaporean communities
Abstract: Introduction Older adults are more mobile than ever as they age in place. However, functional decline typically increases with age. This can significantly affect older adults' mobility, making it harder for them to get around the community as they wish. Musselwhite and Scott's (2019) Mobility Capital Model focuses on how infrastructure, social, cultural and individual capital contributes resources older adults need to maintain mobility without a car. Yet this model remains underexplored, especially in Asian contexts. Therefore, the aim of this article is to explore Musselwhite and Scott's model of mobility capital in the context of Singapore. Methods and context This article focuses on photovoice and focus-group discussions with participants from three unique contexts in Singapore: A touristic, but still residential and commercial area, a residential satellite town and a residential, green area. Results Using applied thematic analysis, we found that the data mostly corresponded with the Mobility Capital Model. However, the use of the Mobility Capital Model helped to accentuate some key characteristics in the Singapore context that foregrounded how social, cultural and individual capital often were driving forces in how mobile older adults were, while infrastructure played a crucial, but background role. The data illustrates that when infrastructure is mostly sufficient, other capitals gain prominence for older adults living in the community. Conclusion Ultimately, our article underscores the utility of the Mobility Capital Model, while also proposing a more milieu-based perspective that spotlights the holistic nature of mobility capital, especially in well-connected, urbanised contexts like Singapore. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Educational interventions to enhance emotional intelligence among nurses: A scoping review
Abstract: Background: Emotional intelligence plays a central role in the emotionally and socially demanding work of nurses, where compassionate and person-centred interaction is essential. As healthcare settings increasingly require advanced interpersonal and self-regulatory competence, emotional intelligence has become increasingly important in healthcare education. Existing evidence on related educational interventions, especially their educational content, remains limited and fragmented. Aim: To summarise existing research knowledge on educational interventions designed to develop the emotional intelligence competence of nurses, and to identify the competence areas and content included in these interventions. Design: A scoping review. Data sources: A systematic search was conducted on CINAHL, PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycArticles, Web of Science, Medic, ProQuest and MedNar. Methods: This study was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines and reported following the PRISMA-ScR framework. The Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework guided the search strategy. Each title, abstract, and full text was screened by two independent reviewers. Data were charted in relation to the review questions and synthesised narratively. Results: Emotional-intelligence educational interventions varied widely in type, duration, and delivery. Education ranged from single sessions to year-long programmes and was most commonly delivered face-to-face, although online and workplace-based learning environments were also used. Analysis of intervention content identified seven recurring competence areas: emotional intelligence fundamentals, emotional awareness, emotion regulation, empathy, communication, reflection and well-being. Discussion: Emotional intelligence educational interventions for nurses, address several competence areas central to person-centred and compassionate care, including emotional awareness, emotion regulation, empathy, communication, reflection and well-being. However, the interventions vary considerably in design, delivery and reporting, which limits comparison and synthesis of evidence. Future research should focus on developing clearly described, theory-informed interventions and using consistent evaluation methods to strengthen the evidence base for emotional intelligence education in healthcare. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Peer mentorship in health science doctoral programs: A systematic review
Abstract: Background: Doctoral training in health-related disciplines entails demanding academic, research, and clinical requirements that can contribute to isolation, burnout, and delayed degree completion. Peer mentorship has emerged as a promising approach to enhance student success, psychosocial well-being, and professional development. However, peer mentorship program designs and implementation vary widely, and no systematic review has comprehensively synthesized the available literature. Aim: To identify the theoretical frameworks, core components, implementation strategies, and outcomes of peer mentorship among PhD and DNP students in health-related fields. Design: Systematic review. Data sources: Five databases, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Education Resources Information Center (ERIC), were searched from January 2000 to June 2025. Review methods: This review was conducted in accordance with the JBI systematic review methodology and reported following PRISMA guidelines. Studies reporting components, implementation strategies, and outcomes of peer mentorship among PhD and DNP students in health-related fields were included. All included studies were appraised using the Quality Improvement Minimum Quality Criteria Set (QI-MQCS) for quality improvement projects, and Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) for quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-method studies. Results: Of 1267, 10 studies were included. Programs ranged from informal peer groups to hybrid faculty-student models, and included regular group meetings, workshops, and one-on-one mentoring. Across studies, peer mentorship was reported to support academic performance, confidence, and sense of belonging, while reducing stress and isolation. Institutional support, intentional matching, and consistent facilitation were key facilitators of program success. Conclusion: This review identified peer mentorship models, components, and implementation strategies present in peer-reviewed literature over the last 25 years. The findings underscore substantial variability in program design. Future research should employ more rigorous study designs, integrate both theoretical frameworks and pragmatic considerations into program development and evaluation, and examine psychosocial and academic outcomes longitudinally to strengthen the evidence base. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Breaking bonds, building mistrust: how coups reshape social capital in Africa
Abstract: Military coups have become an increasingly common yet understudied form of institutional shock across Africa, with consequences for social capital that remain poorly understood relative to their economic and political costs. This paper provides the first comprehensive causal analysis of how successful coups affect both horizontal (interpersonal) and vertical (institutional) trust. Using Afrobarometer data (2005–2015) from 24 African countries, we show that successful coups reduce interpersonal trust by 3.3 percentage points and institutional trust by 6.7 percentage points, after controlling for regional coup dynamics. These effects are specific to successful seizures of power: failed coup attempts have no significant effect on interpersonal trust and produce only a short-lived boost in institutional trust that quickly reverses. Temporal dynamics reveal a critical asymmetry: interpersonal trust recovers gradually over 15–20 years, whereas institutional trust follows a boom-bust cycle before entering a monotonic decline, driven primarily by deteriorating government performance evaluations rather than by economic disruption. Young adults and members of ethnic majority groups bear disproportionately severe institutional trust deficits, and the interethnic trust response is itself heterogeneous, with majority group members showing a temporary upward adjustment while minority group members show a much smaller gain. These findings challenge narratives that portray coups as corrective mechanisms, calling instead for sustained, targeted reconstruction that addresses both dimensions of social capital simultaneously. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Cognitive evaluation in drone delivery adoption: a satisfaction-based heterogeneity approach
Abstract: Drone delivery services are emerging as a promising last-mile delivery solution aligned with sustainable development goals through their potential to reduce carbon emissions and alleviate traffic congestion. However, their successful diffusion depends critically on understanding public adoption. Nevertheless, prior research has insufficiently examined how consumers’ cognitive evaluations shape adoption intentions toward drone delivery services, despite the important role of cognitive evaluation in technology adoption decisions. To address this gap, this study incorporates a cognitive evaluation perspective to better understand public adoption of drone delivery services. The framework incorporates multidimensional perceived risk as an internal personal cognition, social commerce constructs as external environmental cognition, and satisfaction with conventional delivery services as an experience-based moderator from a social cognitive perspective. To investigate public adoption of drone delivery services, a modeling framework integrating latent class clustering analysis and structural equation modeling is applied. Consumers are classified into two latent classes based on satisfaction with conventional delivery services, and structural equation modeling is applied to validate the developed extended technology acceptance model. Our results reveal that various factors influence public adoption heterogeneously between the two groups. Specifically, physical and social risks significantly affect adoption intentions among less satisfied consumers with conventional services. Privacy and financial risks, however, significantly influence more satisfied consumers. Also, less satisfied consumers rely heavily on social commerce constructs, with all three dimensions showing significant effects. In contrast, only recommendation and referrals are influential for the more satisfied consumers. By identifying effective strategies and policies based on the results, we aim to foster broader adoption of drone delivery services as a more sustainable alternative in last-mile logistics. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Authors: Shawar Y.R.; Shiffman J.
Title: Political factors shaping national priority and capacity to address child sexual abuse: a scoping review and framework
Abstract: Child sexual abuse (CSA) remains a low political priority in most countries, despite its high prevalence and severe consequences. Little research examines the political and bureaucratic factors shaping national responses to CSA. This scoping review identifies political factors shaping national priority and capacity to address CSA. The review is based on literature published between 2010 and 2025 in PubMed, PAIS, and SCOPUS. Eighty-four articles met inclusion criteria, spanning 36 high, middle, and low-income countries and territories. Findings indicate that national responses are shaped by three interrelated domains: historical and sociocultural context, priority-setting processes, and capacity-building efforts. For context, patriarchal beliefs, victim-blaming, and honor–shame norms create cultures of silence that discourage disclosure. Broader challenges—such as poverty, tourism, and digital technologies—heighten CSA risks, while colonial legacies and fragmented legal frameworks constrain justice and coherent policy responses. For priority-setting, advocacy by service providers, researchers, women’s movements, survivors, and political champions has been pivotal in many of the countries studied for reframing CSA as a public issue and for pressing governments to act. High-profile scandals and media exposure often catalyze attention, while legislative reforms, inquiries, and international discourses help sustain momentum and accountability. Regarding capacity for addressing CSA, most countries face workforce shortages, weak inter-agency coordination, unstable funding, and limited accountability systems. Although awareness is rising, stigma and misconceptions persist, hindering effective discovery, prevention, and protection. Drawing on these insights, we propose a framework of fourteen factors organized into three interrelated analytical domains—context, priority, and capacity—that shape national responses to CSA, and inform the need for future research, policy, and advocacy. Title: Water Management in Ladakh (India): Traditional and Contemporary Perspectives
Abstract: Ladakh, a high-altitude cold desert in India, represents a unique case of human resilience and adaptation within an ecologically fragile environment. Water, a scarce resource in this arid region, has historically shaped the livelihoods and landscapes of its communities. Over generations, traditional water management has evolved as vital strategies for sustaining life and maintaining ecological balance in this challenging terrain. This chapter explores the interplay between Ladakh’s geo-environment and its people, emphasizing the critical role of traditional water management systems in maintaining regional sustainability. Additionally, it gives a perspective on the contemporary urban water management in Leh town. By integrating survey data and GIS-based mapping, the study examines how these practices have created landscapes where water, land, and social systems come together. It also investigates the transformations in these traditional systems under contemporary environmental, social, and institutional pressures. Highlighting the relevance of these practices, the chapter emphasizes their importance in framing sustainable development strategies for this ecologically fragile yet culturally rich region. This study underscores the need for context-sensitive, community-driven approaches that bridge indigenous wisdom with modern water governance frameworks. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.
