Title: Cultural Beliefs, Family Decision-Making, and Health Literacy in Preeclampsia Prevention Among High-Risk Pregnant Women in Rural Indonesia
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: Preeclampsia remains one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings where social and cultural contexts beyond biomedical care strongly influence preventive behaviors. This study explored how health literacy, cultural beliefs and practices, including local food practices, and family decision-making influence preeclampsia prevention among high-risk pregnant women in rural Indonesia. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, using focus group discussions with 29 participants: high-risk pregnant women (n = 10), women with a history of preeclampsia (n = 8), health workers (n = 5), and government stakeholders from the health, agriculture, fisheries, and livestock sectors (n = 6). Data were analyzed thematically using NVivo 12. The findings revealed that maternal understanding of preeclampsia was generally limited and largely symptom-based rather than risk-oriented; traditional food taboos, cultural interpretations of pregnancy-related symptoms, and delayed healthcare seeking shaped preventive behaviors. Family members—particularly husbands and mothers or mothers-in-law—played a dominant role in decisions regarding antenatal care, dietary practices, and referral compliance. Although nutrient-rich local foods were available, their utilization was constrained by cultural norms. This study extends existing maternal health research by integrating health literacy, cultural beliefs and practices, including local food practices, and family decision-making into a unified sociocultural framework for understanding preeclampsia prevention. The findings support the development of culturally responsive, family-centered, and community-based maternal health interventions for rural populations. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Authors: Nishi M.
Title: Harmonising Indigenous and Local Knowledge in Climate Smart Agriculture: Practical Insights from the Satoyama Initiative
Abstract: The potential role of Indigenous and local knowledge (ILK) is increasingly gaining attention in achieving ‘triple-win’ goals of Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA): agricultural productivity, climate resilience and adaptation and climate mitigation. This study explores how to harmonise or effectively pair ILK with modern science and technologies for CSA. Drawing on the review of the case studies collected through the International Partnership for the Satoyama Initiative (IPSI), the chapter aims to address the following questions: 1) what ILK is used or applied for CSA, 2) how such knowledge is harmonised or paired with modern science and technologies and 3) what effects are derived from the use or application of ILK to realise ‘triple wins’ of CSA. The study finds that certain ILK (e.g. farmers’ ecological knowledge, local experiential knowledge) aids in promoting CSA, having multiple effects for sustainable development beyond ‘triple-win’ goals (e.g. biodiversity conservation, livelihood improvement). It suggests that the process for beneficial knowledge pairing and coproduction should be experimental and iterative with involvement of multiple stakeholders, beginning with local community mobilisation and consultation. Furthermore, for the complete achievement of the triple-win of CSA, a systematic monitoring and evaluation framework along with clear goal-setting would be required. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Schneider R.
Title: Green surveillance: the social implications of harnessing local communities for conservation law enforcement in Namibia
Abstract: In response to the social injustice and counterproductivity attributed to militarised conservation, anti-poaching efforts increasingly focus on ‘inclusivity’ and surveillance. This shift can be explained with the emergence of ontopower, a new form of environmental power that focuses on anticipatory and pre-emptive actions to avoid the virtual, future destruction of nature. This article argues that conservation’s novel combination of inclusivity, surveillance, and ontopower produces a particular mode of conservation governance which I call ‘green surveillance’. Green surveillance captures the open-ended use of military and criminal intelligence approaches to the collection of universal information on environmental crime which target local communities in the pursuit of conservation security. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork, the article examines what green surveillance looks like in north-west Namibia, where local people are being ‘harnessed’ for conservation law enforcement. By showing how local people experience green surveillance, the article responds to calls to investigate the social implications of community-focused surveillance efforts employed as part of militarised conservation. The analysis reveals that green surveillance can have severe negative social implications for rural communities, such as local instrumentalisation, exploitation of precarious livelihoods, physical and slow violence, social exclusion, breakdown in trust and social cohesion, and false reporting; all contributing to social conflict. Title: Contested Lines and Mapping Practices: An Introduction to the Relationships Between Cartography and Border Disputes in the Iberian Peninsula, North Africa and Latin America
Abstract: This chapter examines the relationships between cartography and border disputes across the Iberian Peninsula, North Africa and Latin America. It discusses the complex role of maps in defining fixed political boundaries within fluid physical and human environments and their use as persuasive tools in diplomatic, military and popular realms. By emphasizing mapping practices, the chapter aligns with methodological trends that challenge idealized and decontextualized histories of cartography. The persistent notion of cartography as a unified, progressive and neutral enterprise often parallels the ideal of the nation-state as a clearly bounded and sovereign entity. In contrast, this study approaches maps as geopolitical instruments that sustain and legitimize nationalist projects. The chapter first outlines historical connections between maps and border disputes, before exploring how these dynamics played out in the Iberian, North African and Latin American contexts. It concludes by introducing the volume’s case studies, which collectively illustrate diverse temporal, political and geographical perspectives ranging from the mid-eighteenth to the mid-twentieth century. By approaching a series of methodological challenges that encompass the study of mapmaking and boundary-making, the volume seeks to contribute to ongoing interdisciplinary debates in fields such as map history, historical geography and history of science. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Village shops and multiple ruralities in Sweden's sparsely populated north
Abstract: Villages in sparsely populated areas of northern Sweden have experienced long-term demographic, economic and service decline, contributing to dominant narratives of the region as hopeless ‘problem regions’ or temporary ‘pleasure peripheries’ for tourists. Such portrayals overlook more diverse ruralities that emerge through the ways in which different people, activities and experiences come together in everyday village life. This research explores how village shops as ordinary rural community sites reveal different ruralities through the interplay of physical spaces, people, practices and meanings. Drawing on an ethnographic study of 18 village shops in northern Sweden, we identify six recurring rural characters: traditional identity, cultural pluralism, seasonality and temporal rhythms, gateway orientation, social connectedness, and digital orientation. These characters combined in different ways, giving rise to multiple, coexisting and sometimes competing ruralities within wider relational communities. The characters were expressed across high- and low-amenity areas and in both private and community-owned shops, but varied with geographical, historical and mobility contexts. They also evolved over time as new practices, relationships and material arrangements were layered onto existing ones amid continued precarity. The study contributes to scholarship on multiple ruralities in sparsely populated areas and on village shops as multifunctional community institutions, while offering practical insights for rural service provision and local community development. Title: Experimental impact study on a micro-grid project in rural Madagascar: The Café Lumière project
Abstract: This paper evaluates the impact of a pilot innovative project aiming at promoting a replicable model to create access to distributed electricity in rural areas where grid extension is economically infeasible. The project proposes building solar-powered micro-grids to provide affordable electricity and basic electricity services to households, businesses, and public services. The pilot nature of the project was conceived to facilitate a rigorous testing of its developmental impacts, contrasting with the existing evaluation literature, which provides at best descriptive conclusions. The evaluation methodology is based on a randomized control trial (RCT) design, with data collected before and after project implementation through two waves of household surveys in 2017–2018 and 2023, complemented by locality data. The experimental dimension of the paper is based on a treatment implemented at the locality level. A dozen of comparable localities had been initially selected after a common pre-feasibility study as suitable for the project, and the project has been randomly implemented in only half of them. Findings reveal notable improvements in household access to electricity, particularly in the use of modern energy services like lighting and phone charging. The project has also triggered nascent new economic activities, especially secondary income-generating occupations, though the overall impact on household wealth remains limited. Social outcomes have seen mixed results, with only significant improvements in health and none in education. Complementary actions mentioned in the project's theory of change but not fully implemented may be needed to achieve the broader economic and social transformation initially anticipated. © 2026 International Energy Initiative

Title: Negotiations through the lens of situational affordances – A person-situation perspective on negotiating cooperation in social dilemmas
Abstract: We adopt a person–situation perspective on negotiating cooperation behavior in social dilemmas to examine when, and for whom, different forms of commitment (i.e., negotiation formats) increase cooperation. In a preregistered lab experiment (N = 244), we assessed individual differences in prosociality and experimentally varied the negotiation format in a voluntary negotiation preceding an incentivized public goods game. We investigated the likelihood to take part in the negotiation as well as the final negotiation offer, expecting individual differences in unconditional vs. conditional concern for others (i.e., Social Value Orientation, Honesty-Humility vs. conditional cooperation and HEXACO Agreeableness) to be expressed as a function of the negotiation format. As expected, the likelihood to participate in a negotiation increased with conditional cooperation when negotiating common minimum (vs. individual) commitments. Unlike expected, final negotiation offers in individual (vs. common minimum) commitments were not more strongly associated with Agreeableness but exploratory analyses revealed a stronger association with Social Value Orientation. Title: Impact of maternal postpartum depression on neurodevelopment of preterm infants during the first year of corrected age: A prospective longitudinal study
Abstract: Background Preterm infants are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental difficulties, and maternal depressive symptoms may further affect early developmental outcomes. However, their longitudinal relationship remains unclear. Methods In this prospective longitudinal study, 286 mother-preterm infant dyads from a tertiary hospital in Wuhan, China, were followed after discharge. Maternal depressive symptoms were assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at 2 weeks after discharge and at approximately 4–6 and 7–9 months postpartum. Infant neurodevelopment was assessed using the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, Third Edition, at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months corrected age. Cross-lagged panel modeling, group-based trajectory modeling, and logistic regression were performed. Results Maternal depressive symptoms declined over follow-up, with EPDS scores ≥10 decreasing from 41.96% to 31.81%. Infant developmental abnormalities decreased from 1 to 6 months corrected age and then increased slightly at 12 months. In the cross-lagged panel model, maternal depressive symptoms at the third assessment were associated with lower neurodevelopment scores at 12 months corrected age, whereas infant neurodevelopment at 3 months was associated with subsequent maternal depressive symptoms. Persistent maternal depressive symptoms were associated with a higher risk of overall developmental abnormality at 12 months corrected age (OR = 2.787, 95% CI 1.063–7.306), with stronger but exploratory associations observed in the gross motor, problem-solving, and personal-social domains. Conclusions Persistent maternal depressive symptoms were associated with adverse 12-month developmental outcomes in preterm infants, highlighting the potential value of repeated maternal mental health assessment and early developmental support after preterm birth. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: When does distress disclosure help? Anticipated stigma and the moderating role of perceived social support in depression and anxiety among individuals with multiple sclerosis
Abstract: Objectives Depression and Anxiety are pervasive in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the psychosocial mechanisms associated with these outcomes in this neurological condition remain insufficiently specified. Guided by the Disclosure Processes Model, this study examined how functional disability and anticipated stigma are associated with depression and anxiety indirectly through distress disclosure, and whether these pathways are moderated by perceived social support. Methods In a sample of 272 Iranian adults with MS diagnosis (79.4% women; Mage = 42.5 years), participants completed the Chronic Illness Anticipated Stigma Scale, Distress Disclosure Index, Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and Expanded Disability Status Scale. By Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), a mediation-moderation model was tested. Results Anticipated stigma was positively associated with anxiety and depression, whereas functional disability was positively associated with depression only. Distress disclosure partially mediated the association between anticipated stigma and anxiety and depression, with higher stigma being associated with greater disclosure, and greater disclosure being associated with lower distress. Perceived social support moderated several of these associations. Specifically, disclosure was negatively associated with affective outcomes under low social support but was positively associated under high social support, yielding robust crossover interactions. Conclusions Anxiety and depression in MS are shaped not by disability alone but by how stigma and disclosure are embedded within social contexts. This suggests that interventions may benefit from prioritizing stigma reduction and strategically tailored disclosure, rather than uniformly encouraging openness, to support psychological adjustment. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Lee D.S.; Kulesza D.
Title: When less is more: Unifinal framing promotes intention to use social media for social connection
Abstract: People often wish to rekindle their dormant relationships yet struggle to act on their intentions. This intention-action gap is notable in an era of rising loneliness and surprising in a time marked by unprecedented technological tools for social connection. We propose that one reason for this gap lies in how people evaluate the appropriateness of the means for achieving their social connection goals. Drawing on goal systems theory, we examined whether framing social media platforms as serving a single social connection goal (unifinality) versus multiple goals (multifinality) shapes evaluations of the means and intentions to reconnect with dormant ties. Across three preregistered studies (N = 1095), unifinal framing increased perceived diagnosticity—the sense that a means is well suited to a focal goal—which in turn enhanced intentions to reconnect. Diagnosticity was empirically distinguishable from perceived instrumentality and more consistently accounted for the effect of framing on intentions to reconnect. These findings highlight goal structure as a key determinant of when people view digital platforms as appropriate tools for meaningful social connection and when they intend to use them for such purposes. We discuss broader implications for how individuals navigate their social goals in increasingly multifinal digital environments and for how technology companies must balance emphasizing multifunctionality with highlighting specific relational affordances. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Public support for establishing marine protected areas: an Italian case study
Abstract: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are management tools aimed at protecting and restoring marine ecosystems and promoting the sustainability of social-ecological systems. Their success, however, depends on stakeholders’ relationships with marine resources and on the quality of the governance processes through which MPAs are designed, calling for research on stakeholders’ perceptions of MPAs long before they are established. This study focused on assessing support for MPAs among the general public, which constitutes one critical stakeholder group. The case study selected was the Conero Promontory Coast (CPC), Italy, which is an area of interest to become an MPA. In 2024, a questionnaire was distributed to 262 members of the public to investigate their environmental perceptions and general attitudes towards MPAs, including support for the establishment of the CPC MPA. The participants were concerned about local and global marine environmental issues and held positive views of MPAs prioritising conservation and education, but also appreciated the potential of MPAs to find a balance between protection and use. They ultimately supported the establishment of an MPA at the study location. Attitudes towards MPAs were influenced by environmental perceptions, views on management priorities, and perceptions of the objectives of MPAs. While acknowledging its limitations, especially the involvement of only one part of the larger pool of stakeholders normally affected by MPAs, this study still offered recommendations regarding the engagement of the public in discourses around MPAs. In particular, it demonstrated how public participation can provide insight into MPA planning, including strategies to design and implement successful MPAs through participatory governance. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Park K.; Song H.-D.
Title: Meaningful learning profiles in MOOC environments: A person-centered analysis of engagement, intention to persist, basic psychological needs, and learning presence
Abstract: Meaningful learning in massive open online courses (MOOCs) may vary across learners, yet this heterogeneity has received little person-centered attention. This study identified profiles based on active, constructive, intentional, authentic, and cooperative learning; compared behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social engagement and intention to persist across the profiles; and examined associations of teaching presence, learning presence, and basic psychological needs with profile membership. Survey data from 117 adult MOOC learners were analyzed using latent profile analysis and auxiliary procedures that accounted for classification uncertainty. A three-profile solution was retained based on statistical and substantive evidence. The low, moderate, and high meaningful-learning profiles differed primarily in overall level rather than in characteristic-specific patterns. Behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social engagement and intention to persist increased consistently from the low to the moderate and high profiles. In separate three-step models, design and organization, direct facilitation, cognitive presence, and emotional presence differentiated all three profiles. Social presence distinguished the high profile from the other profiles, but not the low from the moderate profile. Competence and relatedness were associated with high-profile membership relative to the lower profiles, whereas autonomy showed a limited pattern of association. The findings indicate that heterogeneity in meaningful learning was expressed mainly through overall level rather than sharply differentiated configurations. Given the cross-sectional self-report design, the observed associations do not establish causality. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Nursing students' motivations and expectations regarding study exchange: A document analysis of motivation letters
Abstract: Background: Despite increased recognition regarding the internationalization of higher education (IoHE), the motives for and expectations of study exchange for nursing students remain under-researched. Knowledge about students' motivations for study exchange can provide an understanding of their rationale for going abroad. This, in turn, can offer insight into students' values and expectations, making it essential for developing sustainable study-abroad programmes. Aim: The study aim was to explore the motivations and expectations of second- and third-year undergraduate nursing students applying for study exchange. Design: Qualitative design utilizing document analysis of motivation letters. Method: Document and reflexive thematic analysis were conducted on 56 motivation letters written by nursing students in Norway as part of their application to study abroad. The students applied for study exchange programmes in Albania, Australia, Cameroon, Cuba, Czech Republic, India, Madagascar, Netherland, Tanzania, Thailand and the United States. Results: Five main themes were found: (a) the constructing of the exotic otherness, (b) building cultural, social, and professional capital, (c) the ‘saviour complex’ narrative, (d) a journey of self-discovery and professional development and (e) reproduction of student mobility. Conclusion: Nursing students' motivations for study exchange extended beyond academic learning and included personal growth, professional development, and engagement with different cultures and healthcare systems. Many students were attracted to destinations perceived as culturally and environmentally distinct from Norway, highlighting connections between student mobility, ecotourism imaginaries, and constructions of ‘otherness.’ Exchange was also viewed as a means of building cultural, social, and professional capital through international networks and global health knowledge. At the same time, students' desire to help communities in lower-income countries underscores the need for critical reflection on power relations and privilege. Overall, the findings suggest that study exchange can foster understanding of global and planetary health, but should be accompanied by reflection on sustainability, equity, and global responsibility. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Stotten R.; Campbell H.
Title: Constructing relational resilience: Governance, power and the limits of transformation in Aotearoa New Zealand’s hill country farming
Abstract: This study investigates how resilience is relationally constructed within Aotearoa New Zealand’s hill country farming systems. Drawing on qualitative interviews with hill-country farmers, and applying a social relational resilience perspective together with the Resilience Capacities Framework, the research examines how capacities for persistence, adaptation, and transformation emerge through relationships among farmers, communities, markets, and governance institutions. The findings show that persistence is sustained through long-term trust, reciprocity, stewardship, and intergenerational social ties, while adaptive capacity depends on diverse social networks, collective learning, and the integration of heterogeneous knowledges. However, adaptive opportunities remain uneven and are shaped by unequal access to networks, markets, and institutional support. Transformative capacity was comparatively weak across cases, constrained by fragmented governance relationships, limited institutional trust, and power asymmetries that restricted collaborative problem-solving and cross-scale engagement. The study argues that resilience is not an attribute of individual farmers nor reducible to capital stocks, but an emergent and relational process shaped by everyday interactions, governance dynamics, and socio-political context. By operationalising the Resilience Capacities Framework empirically, the paper contributes to relational resilience scholarship and demonstrates the importance of relational infrastructures, inclusive governance, and co-produced adaptation pathways for rural sustainability transformations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Guo R.; Dong J.; Guo F.; Wei C.
Title: An integrated assessment framework for urban street-level green infrastructure development potential: Unraveling nonlinear effect via multimodal large models and explainable AI
Abstract: Street networks serve as critical corridors for expanding urban green infrastructure. However, existing assessments of micro-green space (MGS) development potential are predominantly based on static multi-criteria decision-making approaches. These approaches fail to capture the nonlinear spatial effects of complex built environments on MGS interventions, and lack street-level, predictive assessment capabilities at the urban scale. This spatiotemporal bottleneck hinders evidence-based future impact projections and scientific decision-making. To address this gap, this study develops an AI-driven spatial assessment framework. By integrating street view imagery, the zero-shot semantic perception of the Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) model, and an RF-SHAP model ensemble, this framework facilitates the automated interpretation of street-level visual features and enables the quantitative assessment of MGS development potential at the urban scale. Drawing on multidimensional built-environment indicators—spanning physical and socioeconomic dimensions—an empirical analysis of MGS sites in central Shenyang reveals distance to buildings (23.00% contribution) and distance to parks (14.34%) are the dominant drivers. Applying this framework's generalization capabilities identifies 3286 potential sites across the study area, objectively quantifying the greening capacity of street networks. Furthermore, SHAP-based clustering identifies four distinct MGS typologies, yielding a dual-oriented spatial map that aligns construction priority with functional suitability for MGS development. The results reveal significant heterogeneity in development potential for MGS across intervention levels: 71.0% of the 787 Ecological Connectivity and Microclimate Mitigation sites present high potential, whereas 81.5% of the 796 Social Vitality and Community Cohesion sites exhibit lower potential for MGS development. The remaining Flood Resilience and Health Promotion and Spatial Equity and Social Inclusion sites predominantly display moderate-to-high potential. Overall, these findings support predictive spatial interventions to transform marginal streets into inclusive and climate-resilient urban assets, directly advancing UN SDG 11.7. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Multi-scale asymmetric graph contrastive anomaly detection
Abstract: Graph contrastive learning has been widely deployed in graph anomaly detection (GAD) due to its powerful ability to extract discriminative information. However, existing methods fail to capture deviated consistencies of anomaly characteristics from graph topologies and overlook the influences of the quality of contrastive views, obstructing effective consistency learning. To this end, we propose a Multi-scale Asymmetric Contrastive Graph Anomaly Detector (MAC-GAD). MAC-GAD overcomes the drawbacks of traditional symmetric contrastive learning and develops a multi-level dominant view generation mechanism to enhance the contrastive learning performance. To capture comprehensive consistency of anomaly nodes, based on the dominant view, MAC-GAD introduces an asymmetric contrastive learning paradigm for local and global consistency. Theoretical analysis further demonstrates the superiority of asymmetric contrastive learning. Comparison experiments on six public datasets (Cora, Citeseer, Weibo, T-Social, T-Finance, and Pubmed) demonstrate the superiority of MAC-GAD over state-of-the-art baselines, showing average improvement of 1.81% in AUROC and 4.21% in AUPRC across five out of the six datasets except for Pubmed. Extensive validations, such as ablation, sensitivity, and robustness, further verify the advancement of MAC-GAD. Authors: Taylor S.
Title: The trial multiple: The ontological politics of a South African PrEP trial
Abstract: A growing body of research has problematised the multi-sited clinical trials that underpin the global bioeconomy. These accounts often oscillate between a narrow focus on ethical oversight and critiques of exploitation, leaving the lived and organisational realities of trials under-examined. Rather than evaluating clinical trials as more-or-less successful techniques for managing molecules and subjects, this paper approaches trial management as the work of coordinating multiple enactments of biomedical objects. It examines how clinical trial management is enacted through a case study of a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) trial in South Africa involving HIV-negative men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women. Working with and beyond extant research on relational materiality, the paper interrogates how PrEP’s apparent singularity as a prevention technology is sustained in practice, tracing how different enactments of PrEP emerge through situated configurations of practices, technologies, and narratives. It focuses on two particularly salient enactments – PrEP-as-investment and PrEP-as-salvation – and shows these are not simply competing perspectives but materially distinct realities that must be actively coordinated within the trial. Through strategies of translation, alignment, and equivalence, these divergent realities are rendered comparable while their differences are selectively maintained or marginalised. This paper contributes to geographical debates on relational materiality and biomedicine by showing that clinical trials function as spatially distributed assemblages in which coherence is actively achieved. This reframing foregrounds the practical work through which biomedical objects are made to cohere across contexts while highlighting the political implications of stabilising certain realities and excluding others. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Should I ride or not?: A conjoint study on young riders’ nighttime e-scooter use after drinking
Abstract: Alcohol-impaired riding is a leading contributor to e-scooter crashes and injuries, especially among young adults during nighttime hours. Yet, research on the decision-making processes underlying this risky behavior remains limited. Based on a stated preference approach, this study quantifies the situational factors influencing young people’s likelihood of riding e-scooters after drinking alcohol at night. An online conjoint experiment was conducted with 717 participants aged 16–35 from Switzerland, Germany, and Denmark. Respondents evaluated realistic scenarios varying five attributes: type and availability of transport alternatives, e-scooter availability, peer influence, and perceived security. Hierarchical Bayes modeling and choice simulations revealed peer influence and the presence of viable transport alternatives as the most decisive factors, each accounting for over a third of the decision weight. Scenarios where peers opted for safer alternatives or where public transport was directly available significantly reduced the likelihood of alcohol-impaired e-scooter use. Men and frequent e-scooter users showed higher risk propensity, and more permissive attitudes toward drunk riding associated with both past behavior and higher scenario-based e-scooter riding likelihoods after drinking alcohol. Implications include the need for social-norms campaigns leveraging peer dynamics, improved late-night transport provision, and restricted e-scooter availability in nightlife hotspots. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Augmentation strategies for intravenous ketamine in treatment-resistant depression: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Treatment-resistant depression (TRD) affects 30–60% of individuals with major depressive disorder and carries substantial morbidity and healthcare costs. Intravenous (IV) ketamine (KET) is a rapid-acting antidepressant, but benefits are often transient, prompting augmentation to sustain efficacy or improve tolerability. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of IV KET augmentation in adults with TRD. MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO were searched through October 29, 2025. Eligible studies compared KET plus augmentation with KET plus placebo/sham or active control. Seven RCTs (N = 346) met inclusion criteria. Strategies included glutathione, riluzole, lamotrigine, lithium, D-cycloserine and ketamine combined with psychotherapy (KCP) approaches involving cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and automated self-association training (ASAT). Across the included trials, IV KET was associated with antidepressant improvement, although augmentation strategies generally did not demonstrate additional benefit over their respective control conditions. Pharmacological augmentation strategies did not demonstrate additional benefit at primary endpoints. KCP approaches using CBT and ASAT yielded preliminary signals of improved maintenance of antidepressant effects, although each was evaluated in a single study. An exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of seven heterogeneous comparisons found no statistically significant overall difference in depressive symptoms between augmentation and control conditions (SMD = −0.12; 95% CI, −0.37 to 0.12; p = 0.323; I2 = 0.0%). No clear new safety signal emerged in the trials, although adverse-event reporting was heterogeneous across studies. Title: Welcoming behaviors in user experience: a design framework for human-computer interaction

Abstract: Welcoming behavior is a fundamental and indispensable component of human social interaction, necessary for establishing positive initial encounters and effectively conveying interaction intent. This study aims to gain a deep understanding and quantify such behaviors, thereby laying the foundation for designing more effective, contextually appropriate, and emotionally resonant welcoming behaviors for smart systems. We conducted a content analysis of welcoming behaviors observed in film scenarios featuring human and anthropomorphic characters (e.g., animated figures), identifying 13 terms that summarize various welcoming contexts. Subsequently, utilizing semantic differential scales and exploratory factor analysis (EFA), we identified five underlying dimensions of welcoming behavior: support and acceptance, energetic, ritualistic, resonance, and intimacy. These findings provide a foundation for a framework that enables Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) researchers and practitioners to apply these dimensions of welcome, derived from human and human-like behaviors to the design of smart systems that foster welcoming behaviors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Audience Perceptions of Social Media Influencers’ Role in Tourism Promotion in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates: A Comparative Survey Study
Abstract: Introduction: This study examines self-reported following of social media influencers for tourism related information among surveyed respondents in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates and explores respondents’ perceptions of influencers’ promotional role across four tourism categories: desert tourism, coastal tourism, medical tourism, and event based tourism. Methodology: The study adopted a quantitative descriptive survey design. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to a purposive sample of 2,400 social media users, with 1,200 respondents from Jordan and 1,200 respondents from the United Arab Emirates. The study does not claim national representativeness. Instead, it analyzes patterns within the surveyed sample. Results: The findings show clear differences between the two country subsamples in the degree of following social media influencers for tourism related information. Respondents in the United Arab Emirates reported higher levels of following, while respondents in Jordan were more likely to report moderate engagement. The results also indicate that respondents perceived influencers as having a notable promotional role in several tourism domains, particularly event based tourism and desert tourism, while coastal tourism and medical tourism showed greater variation across the two national contexts. Conclusion: Statistically significant differences were found in respondents’ degree of following social media influencers according to gender, age, educational level, and nationality. The findings also indicate statistically significant positive associations between the degree of following influencers and respondents’ perceptions of influencers’ role in promoting desert, coastal, medical, and event based tourism. Title: Social networks and active school transportation: Understanding how parents’ connections shape commuting decisions for their children
Abstract: Introduction Parental social networks influence decisions parents make for their children and active school transportation (AST) is a significant and underutilized source of physical activity (PA), however, it is unclear how networks influence AST decisions. Methods Data were gathered emailing Midwest elementary school children's parents (N = 531) a survey based on the interpersonal level of the social-ecological model, social capital, and diffusion of innovations theories including parental social networks, AST barrier perceptions, and AST decisions for their child(ren). Title: Do faregate replacements affect crime? Evidence from WMATA metrorail
Abstract: Public transit networks structure social and economic activities by bringing diverse populations together in shared spaces. This study examines the spatial relationship between faregate replacements and nearby crime patterns within the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) Metrorail network in the District of Columbia, Montgomery County, and Prince George's County, Maryland. Faregate replacements were implemented system-wide across all 98 Metrorail stations between July 2023 and September 2024; however, the rollout was staggered, and precise completion dates were not uniformly documented for all stations. This study therefore uses the seven stations with verified replacement dates as treatment stations and uses propensity score matching (PSM) to select seven control stations based on pre-intervention property and violent crime levels to assess changes in nearby crime patterns following the intervention. These stations constitute the earliest confirmed interventions, allowing for a before-and-after comparison and a quasi-experimental design with temporal precision. We use a spatial analytical approach employing the weighted displacement quotient (WDQ) and negative binomial difference-in-differences (DID) models to analyze property and violent crime patterns between the pre- and post-intervention periods (2022 and 2024). This approach examines Census blocks in street-network buffers of 0–400 m, 400–800 m, and 800–1,200 m around stations. The results indicate statistically significant reductions in property crime within the 0–400 m treatment area, with weaker effects at greater distances from stations. In contrast, violent crime exhibited no statistically significant changes following faregate replacement, suggesting that the effects of access-control interventions may differ across crime types. This study highlights the significance of considering interventions in the built environment and, more broadly, underscores the need for urban policy to account for the broader social consequences of transportation design. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Toward a Thai-Specific Generational Cohort Framework: A Basic Individual Values Perspective

Abstract: This study takes a step toward developing a Thai-specific generational cohort framework grounded in the country’s historical, economic, and social transformations. In particular, younger Thai cohorts place greater relative emphasis on Face and Conformity, while patterns in Achievement, Security, and Universalism diverge from those observed under U.S.-based cohort classifications. These findings contribute to the literature on generational analysis by demonstrating the value of context-specific cohort frameworks and highlighting the importance of incorporating national historical and socio-economic conditions when studying generational value differences. Title: Combining AI and corpus technology in language teaching: Professional development and knowledge co-construction using the CoI framework
Abstract: As established technologies (e.g., corpus technology) and emerging ones (e.g., generative AI) reshape language education, teachers need clear, evidence-based approaches to integrate both into practice. This mixed-methods study examined how over 150 language teachers co-developed AI-empowered TPACK for corpus technology (AI-TPACK-CT) during online professional development. The program was designed using design-based learning and guided by the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, which views effective online learning through learners' social and cognitive engagement. We analyzed discussion posts, lesson plans, and interviews to trace teacher engagement, knowledge building, and learning outcomes. To understand participation patterns at scale, we conducted social network analysis (SNA) to map interaction structures, and then selected participants for deeper investigation. We conducted case studies of one central participant and two peripheral participants to explore how these teachers' knowledge and design work evolved. CoI-based quantitative results indicated high social and cognitive presence, suggesting an environment conducive to shared inquiry and knowledge building. Title: The evolution of territorial agrifood systems between global and local dynamics: Insights from hazelnut production in Tuscia (Italy)
Abstract: Globalisation and industrialisation have over time generated profound changes in the agrifood system, producing multiple effects with strong spatial characteristics. These include de-territorialisation, accompanied by standardisation, specialisation and intensification. These processes have often determined significant impacts on rural territories and communities, due to the primacy of specific economic interests over the priorities of local socio-ecological systems. As a reaction to these dynamics, new paths have emerged, oriented to food re-localisation and sustainability transition and, more generally, seeking a more democratic approach in governing food systems and local development. Transitions of territorial agrifood systems indeed become the outcome of complex interaction dynamics established among different, multi-scale networks, reflecting their respective visions, objectives and power. Against such a background, this paper aims to contribute to the understanding of the transformations of specific territorial agrifood systems, marked by tensions between global forces and local dynamics. To that end it applies an analytical framework interrelating actors’ role and interactions, discursive components, and policies and governance issues. Focusing on the rural area of Tuscia (Italy), it analyses the expansion of the problematic hazelnut production. Tracing the long-term evolution of the territorial agrifood system and of governance dynamics, it reflects on the critical issues associated with the presence of global-scale economic activities in specific territorial contexts, and on the challenges faced by sustainable, locally tailored and community-driven development trajectories. The analysis helps deepen understanding of these processes and provides significant insights for the scientific debate, policy-makers and social groups involved in this type of process. © 2026

Title: Pretty privilege? Effects of perpetrators’ attractiveness and hate type on user responses against misogynist digital hate
Abstract: Digital misogyny is increasingly pervasive, making it vital to understand how users perceive and respond to it. Drawing on distinctions between incivility, intolerance, and threats and on the elaboration likelihood model as a framework for understanding when peripheral cues such as perpetrator attractiveness shape moral judgment, this preregistered online experiment (N = 884) examined how hate type (incivility, intolerance, threat) and perpetrator attractiveness (high, medium, low) shape users' cognitive, affective, attitudinal, and behavioral responses to misogynist hate. Results show that users’ responses broadly followed a normative continuum from incivility to intolerance to threat, with both incivility and threat reliably distinguished across all response dimensions, while intolerance proved more nuanced and outcome-dependent. Threats and intolerance were judged as less acceptable and more sexist than incivility, though cognitive evaluations plateaued between the two more severe forms, suggesting a ceiling in moral judgment once digital hate crosses a clear normative threshold. Negative emotions continuously intensified with hate type. Threats elicited stronger indirect intervention intentions and greater support for content moderation than incivility and intolerance. Readiness to intervene directly remained limited, pointing to a fundamental asymmetry between moral condemnation and visible action. Perpetrator attractiveness did not influence user responses across any outcome or hate type, marking an important theoretical boundary condition for appearance-based biases in moral judgment, where in morally unambiguous contexts, such as misogynist digital hate, content-based reasoning appears to override heuristic shortcuts such as the pretty privilege bias. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Drinking, cannabis use and mental health as predictors of within-person changes in aggression over eight weeks among youth involved with binge drinking
Abstract: Introduction Sequential, multiple assignment, randomized trials (SMARTs) are used to deliver behavior interventions to adolescents and emerging adults (A/EAs) involved with alcohol use and aggression. We examine with-in person markers of aggression from a recent SMART to inform future interventions for this population. Methods A/EAs (n = 400; ages 14–20; 22 % male) in the emergency department who reported binge drinking and aggression were enrolled in the SMART, completed a baseline survey, received a brief behavioral health intervention (SafERteens), were randomized to booster conditions over 8 weeks, and completed 8 weekly surveys to inform intervention components. We examined same week aggression occurrence in relation to weekly risk (i.e., alcohol consumption, any cannabis use, mental health symptoms, acting impulsively) and protective factors (i.e., excitement, hopefulness, fun activities, social support). Unadjusted and adjusted conditional logistic regressions examine within-person effects of weekly factors on an individual’s risk of aggression. Results In the unadjusted model weekly factors associated with increased likelihood of aggression in the same week included earlier survey week and any cannabis use; more alcohol consumption, mental health symptoms, and impulsive acts; and, less hopefulness and social support. In the adjusted model, earlier survey week, cannabis use, and more alcohol use and mental health symptoms were associated with increased likelihood of same week aggression. Title: Breaking the Silence: Factors Associated with Perceived Social Norms Regarding Sexual and Reproductive Health Among Adolescent Students in Monastic Schools, Myanmar

Abstract: This study assessed perceived SRH social norms, SRH knowledge, and associated factors among adolescent students in monastic schools in Myanmar. Data were drawn from the 2016 baseline survey of the Integrated Multi-Sectoral Approach (IMSA) project, involving 870 students aged 11–18 years from eight monastic schools in Magway Region. Title: U.S. children draw on personal experiences and perceived parental beliefs to form attitudes about immigrant groups
Abstract: Drawing on intergroup contact theory, this study investigated how 8- to 11-year-old American children’s (N = 262, 55% girls, 52% White, in 2024 and 2025) direct contact with immigrants (e.g., at school) and perceptions of their parents’ attitudes about them spending time with immigrants (comfortable or uncomfortable) informed their own attitudes about immigrant groups. More direct contact was associated with more positive attitudes, specifically, liking immigrants more and seeing immigrants as more American (βs = .16 and .20). At the same time, children who perceived their parents to be more comfortable with immigrants also liked immigrants more, felt closer to them, and were more interested in including them in their own activities (βs = .56, .28, and .40). These associations were comparable for children’s attitudes about peers from Mexico, China, India, El Salvador, Nigeria, and Poland even though the sample had, on average, more frequent contact with people from some of those groups than with others. In an increasingly diverse country with a complex history around immigration, this new evidence is a helpful first step to understanding how American children integrate their personal experiences and perceptions of their parents’ beliefs to form their own attitudes about immigrant groups. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Revealing exacerbated socioeconomic stratification of urban mobility: A case study in Beijing, China
Abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic recedes, urban life, economic activities, and transportation systems appear to have returned to normal. Yet latent post-pandemic impacts on shifts in socioeconomic stratification within human mobility remain under-explored. Using large-scale longitudinal mobile signaling data for nearly 8 million residents in Beijing between 2019 and 2024, weighted using census data and integrated with social attributes and housing price data, this study examines how socioeconomic stratification patterns and mobility behaviors evolve across socioeconomic groups. Here, we show that the potential stratification has intensified in the post-pandemic era. First, the place-level and inter-group contact-based socioeconomic stratification index increased by 34.83% and 32.34%, respectively. Counterfactual simulations reveal that shortened travel distances and homogeneous mobility preferences reduced opportunities for cross-group encounters. Second, residential proximity and shared social attributes significantly explain variations in opportunities for inter-group co-presence. Spatial disparities in urban infrastructure configuration can either mitigate or reinforce mobility-related socioeconomic stratification across locations. Collectively, this study underscores that spatial context, socioeconomic characteristics, and behavioral preferences shape mobility stratification, offering empirical evidence for understanding post-pandemic socioeconomic stratification dynamics. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Lithium during maintenance electroconvulsive therapy: Secondary neuropsychological outcomes from the open-label PRASED randomized controlled trial
Abstract: Background Lithium is commonly used for relapse prevention after successful electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). However, the combination of lithium and ECT has warranted caution in clinical practice due to concerns about cognitive tolerability, while evidence remains inconclusive. Objective To evaluate the neuropsychological effects of maintenance ECT (M-ECT), with and without lithium, in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) across all ages. Methods The Preventing Relapse After Successful Electroconvulsive therapy for Depression (PRASED) study was a multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial. Patients who achieved remission after an acute ECT course for MDD were randomized to receive symptom driven M-ECT and maintenance pharmacotherapy with or without adjunctive lithium. In this secondary outcome analysis, neuropsychological functioning was assessed repeatedly over six months using a comprehensive test battery covering global cognition, memory, attention, fluency, processing speed and subjective memory complaints. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to examine group differences in cognitive trajectories over time and associations between serum lithium levels and cognitive outcomes. Results No significant differences in cognitive trajectories were observed between the lithium (n = 50) and non‑lithium (n = 46) group. Neuropsychological performance improved over time in both groups across all cognitive domains except verbal fluency. Serum lithium levels were not associated with neuropsychological performance. Title: From lifestyle to citizenship: Social influence and political consumerism in egocentric networks
Abstract: Political consumerism has become a widespread form of civic engagement, yet the social mechanisms driving boycotting and buycotting remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates how perceived citizenship norms within individuals’ egocentric networks are associated with their own civic orientations and subsequent participation in consumer activism. Using a national survey of 543 U.S. adults reporting on 1822 social ties, we integrate social learning and social influence theories to examine how network environments cultivate engaged and dutiful citizenship norms. Results show a strong correlation between perceived network norms and individuals’ internalized norms, with engaged citizenship norms significantly predicting both boycott and buycott behaviors. Dutiful norms show no significant association. Structural equation modeling reveals that network influence operates indirectly through internalized engaged norms rather than direct social pressure. The study concludes with practical implications for advocacy groups and public relations practitioners, emphasizing how value-aligned messaging and network-based mobilization strategies can more effectively activate consumer activism. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Zaher H.
Title: Gender paradigms and women's empowerment in rural Morocco
Abstract: This article examines the evolution of gender and development paradigms in Morocco, from Women in Development (WID) and Women and Development (WAD) to Gender and Development (GAD) and empowerment approaches, to assess their capacity to address structural inequalities and gendered power relations. The study uses documentary evidence to examine how international gender frameworks have been interpreted and translated into specific socio-cultural, institutional, and territorial contexts. Despite significant policy advances and the progressive alignment of national policies with international gender frameworks, persistent inequalities continue to constrain women's access to land, productive resources, markets, and decision-making structures. Policy implementation remains constrained by institutional, socio-economic, and territorial factors, creating an implementation gap whereby many initiatives expand opportunities for women's economic and social inclusion in rural Morocco without leading to empowerment. Empowerment is best understood as a multidimensional process involving agency, collective action, social recognition, and the transformation of power relations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Trends in Research on Sustainable Development of Craft Village Tourism: A Bibliometric Analysis Using CiteSpace Software

Abstract: This study examines global research trends on sustainable development in craft village tourism from 1976 to 2024 using CiteSpace software, explicitly to address a critical structural and conceptual gap in the existing literature: a lack of a macro-level, systematic synthesis of the field. A dataset of 185 documents drawn from the Scopus and Web of Science databases was analyzed to identify key themes, influential authors, and collaborative networks. Results show an evolving focus-from early works on cultural preservation and traditional crafts toward multifaceted approaches encompassing economic sustainability, environmental management, and community-based strategies. Despite a recent surge in publications, co-authorship and keyword analysis reveal moderate to low network densities, indicating fragmented collaboration and limited thematic integration. Southeast Asia, particularly Vietnam and Indonesia, leads empirical research on heritage conservation and community empowerment, while China and developed countries often contribute frameworks for policy and technology adoption. Emerging topics include digital transformation, circular economy models, and post-pandemic resilience. Future studies should establish standardized sustainability criteria, strengthen cross-regional partnerships, and apply advanced digital tools to enhance stakeholder engagement. By converging cultural preservation, economic viability, and environmental stewardship, craft village tourism can be positioned as a resilient and equitable model of rural development. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Right-wing authoritarianism and support for restricting adolescents' access to social media: Evidence from Brazil's Felca Law
Abstract: Support for restricting civil rights remains a central concern in psychological science. Among these rights, access to information has increasingly been regulated, including through policies limiting adolescents' use of social media. Higher RWA and older age independently predicted greater support for the law, with no significant interaction between them. Support for the Felca Law appears to be shaped less by developmental maturation than by stable ideological mechanisms, even in a policy domain framed around youth protection. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The emotional aftermath of football: How national team performance during the UEFA Men's EURO 2024 shapes spectators' daily emotions

Title: Does school-based AI education narrow readiness gaps? The role of prior agency-related learning
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes part of everyday learning, preparing students to participate confidently and responsibly in AI-mediated environments is essential. Yet students enter AI classes with different prior agency-related learning experiences, indicated in this study by self-initiated AI learning before school-based instruction, which may shape how they benefit from formal curricula. All groups improved in both psychological and cognitive readiness after a year-long school-based instruction. However, while psychological gaps narrowed, cognitive gaps persisted, suggesting that school AI programs may foster psychological equity but not full cognitive parity. Title: Reciprocity and state capacity: Evidence from a national pollution control reform in China
Abstract: We propose a new approach to pollution control from the social contract perspective, which highlights the reciprocal obligations between firms and the government, in contrast to the conventional regulatory view. Combining granular data on Chinese industrial firms with a 2007 reform that sharply increased the government's incentives for pollution control, we show, in a difference-in-differences framework, that firms with prior government support achieved greater emission reductions than those without following the reform, primarily through costly clean technology adoption and output cuts. Alternative explanations—including government leverage, financial constraints, regulatory enforcement, and political connections—cannot explain our findings. We further examine the aggregate implications of firm-government reciprocity at the city level, exploiting quasi-random variation in city-level support induced by plausibly exogenous mayoral rotation and across-mayor variation in support preferences in an instrumental variable design. We find that such reciprocity translated into significant declines in regional pollution concentrations, thereby enhancing the government's capacity for pollution control. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Green grabbing and territorial displacement in the Andes: transhumant pastoralism, state power, and rural resistance in Argentina
Abstract: This article analyzes a paradigmatic case of green grabbing in the Argentine Andes, where 12, 351.66 ha of highland pastures historically used by transhumant pastoralists were transferred to a private tourism consortium to develop a “sustainable” ski resort. Conceptually grounded in political ecology and critical agrarian studies, the article introduces the notion of identity displacement to describe forms of exclusion that go beyond material dispossession, affecting cultural reproduction, social belonging, and intergenerational land-based practices. It argues that transhumant resistance −through legal mobilization, public protest, and everyday practices of territorial persistence- challenges dominant development narratives and reclaims space for alternative futures. The study contributes to current debates on green capitalism, land control, and rural governance by offering an empirically rich and theoretically grounded account of how green grabbing unfolds at the intersection of state territoriality, mobility and peasant persistence. It highlights the need to rethink environmental governance frameworks that erase mobile livelihoods and customary commons regimes in the name of sustainability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Social life cycle assessment of primary coffee production in Brazil: A risk-based identification of social hotspots
Abstract: With an estimated consumption of around 3 billion cups per day and global production of around 10 million tons, coffee is one of the world's leading agricultural commodities. Against this backdrop, this study aimed to identify social hotspots in primary coffee production using Type I Social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA), considering the case of Brazil. The coexistence of high generative capacity in the sector, evidenced by high embodied value added and high risks related to remuneration and trade union freedom, could indicate a possible structural asymmetry in the distribution of economic benefits. These findings suggest that high value generation capacity does not automatically lead to a proportional distribution of benefits along the supply chain. Finally, from an environmental and economic perspective, primary production appears to be relatively efficient in its use of land and blue water but presents a structural criticality in terms of climate performance, implying that, for the same economic value generated, the coffee sector may be more exposed to regulatory shocks than low-carbon activities. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Subjective Well-Being Inequality Among Thai Older Adults: Evidence From the Health, Aging, and Retirement in Thailand (HART) Survey

Abstract: This study examines subjective well-being inequality among older adults in Thailand using the 2022 wave of the Health, Aging, and Retirement in Thailand (HART) survey, comprising 3,607 observations. Subjective well-being is measured using respondents’ self-reported quality-of-life satisfaction scores. The study applies the mean log deviation (MLD), a decomposable inequality measure, and subgroup decomposition to assess how inequality is distributed within and between groups across the dimensions of demographics, socioeconomic status, health, family structure and support, and social participation. Results show that overall subjective well-being inequality is relatively low and is dominated by within-group variation, indicating substantial heterogeneity among older adults with similar observable characteristics. However, between-group inequality varies across dimensions. Health status, measured by self-rated health, has the largest between-group component, followed by geographic disparities, particularly provincial differences. Social participation explains a moderate share of inequality, whereas socioeconomic and family-related factors contribute only small shares. These findings suggest that subjective well-being inequality among older adults in Thailand is structured more by health status, geographic context, and social engagement than by conventional socioeconomic factors. The results support a multidimensional approach to later-life well-being policy, while noting that the analysis identifies patterns of inequality rather than causal effects. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Motivation, cognition, and emotion: Unpacking the pathways from fitness app gratifications to workout intention
Abstract: The rising popularity of fitness apps underscores the need to understand how their use translates into workout intention. However, a paucity of research has examined this issue from a user-centric perspective. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G) theory and the adapted Cognitive Mediation Model (CMM), this study develops and tests a process-oriented framework to explicate how gratifications obtained from fitness app use are related to workout intention through cognitive and affective mechanisms. Structural equation modeling based on survey data (N = 795) from Chinese fitness app users shows that all five examined gratifications are positively associated with cognitive elaboration, whereas four (excluding social interaction gratification) are positively related to the emotion of inspiration. Cognitive elaboration, in turn, is positively tied to both objective and subjective fitness knowledge. Inspiration is positively associated only with subjective knowledge. Importantly, although both forms of knowledge are positively linked to workout intention, subjective knowledge exhibits a significantly stronger association. By integrating motivational, cognitive, and affective perspectives, this study extends the CMM through the incorporation of context-specific gratifications and emotional components. The findings illuminate the distinct roles of objective and subjective knowledge and underscore the dynamic interplay between emotion and cognition in shaping health-related behavioral intentions. These results contribute to a more nuanced, user-centered understanding of human-fitness technology interaction and offer implications for the design and optimization of digital health interventions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Dierckx K.; Van Hiel A.
Title: A latent profile analysis of intergroup attitude patterns among four ethnic-cultural minority groups in the Netherlands
Abstract: Research on intergroup attitudes has focused largely on majority populations, while much less is known about how minority group members view other groups in diverse societies. To help address this gap, we examined the intergroup attitudes of members of four ethnic minority groups in a large, nationally representative survey conducted in the Netherlands (N = 4028), a country characterized by substantial ethnic diversity. Overall, respondents tended to evaluate both the national majority and their own ethnic group positively. At the same time, evaluations of other minority groups were somewhat less favourable, particularly when those groups were perceived as culturally dissimilar and having a higher societal status. However, this general pattern concealed substantial variation. Using latent profile analysis, we identified five distinct subgroups with markedly different combinations of attitudes toward the national majority, their own group, and other ethnic minorities. In addition, the subgroups varied meaningfully with respect to broader social attitudes and demographic characteristics. Exploratory follow-up analyses suggested that the profiles could be understood largely in terms of how people perceived Dutch society and their feelings of societal belongingness. Taken together, the findings highlight that minority populations are far from uniform in their intergroup views. Rather than a single pattern of attitudes, multiple perspectives coexist. These results underscore the need to pay greater scholarly attention to the diversity of minority viewpoints in increasingly multicultural societies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Peters P.; D'Souza A.; Van Der Gaast W.
Title: De-risking equity investment for productive use integration in mini-grids: Designing a first-loss demand-risk guarantee for e-mobility in Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya
Abstract: Achieving commercially viable mini-grid operations in remote areas of sub-Saharan Africa remains constrained by uncertain electricity demand, contributing to investor hesitancy, particularly among equity investors. Productive use of electricity can improve asset utilisation and strengthen revenue generation, but its integration requires additional investment that remains exposed to revenue risk when early-stage demand uptake is uncertain. This paper designs and evaluates a first-loss demand-risk guarantee for electric two-wheeler battery-swapping integration into the solar mini-grid of Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya. Methodologically, the case study is grounded in design science research and combines system sizing, financial modelling, scenario analysis, and guarantee stress testing. The system analysis identifies a technically feasible configuration of 200 electric two-wheelers and 140 spare batteries without additional generation or storage capacity, which is used as input for the financial model. The financial model shows that the business case reaches the equity investor threshold, defined as a 15% equity internal rate of return, only under high vehicle utilisation and with a 25% capital subsidy on charging and swapping infrastructure. The proposed guarantee addresses the resulting utilisation-driven revenue risk through partial first-loss coverage, a utilisation-based activation window, annual payout caps, and a cumulative exposure cap. Scenario results show that the guarantee improves equity returns across all eligible utilisation-shortfall scenarios. It raises the base- and best-case scenarios above the investor threshold and substantially reduces the return gap in the worst-case scenario. The study contributes a project-level design framework for developing demand-risk guarantees as development-finance de-risking instruments for productive-use integration, while highlighting the need for case-specific calibration, robust verification, and further testing across additional mini-grid contexts. © 2026 The Authors

Author full names: Hamann, Ralph (7003476701); Rapson, Mandy (60964046900); Ramarumo, Thanyani (60963643900)
Title: It takes two… How complementary intermediaries span institutional disjunctures during crisis
Abstract: Transition scholars increasingly attend to intermediary ecologies, but not to how these might address formal-informal institutional disjunctures and entrenched inequality. We conducted a qualitative, multi-sited study of eight intermediaries and 86 smallholder farmers in four South African provinces during the Covid-19 pandemic. We show how two types of intermediary – which we call bonding and linking – brought complementary bundles of resources to an emergency supply chain that enhanced farmers’ resilience and demonstrated the potential for more inclusive food systems. We characterise this as a crisis-enabled niche, whose niche orchestration came not from a dedicated central orchestrator but from a hub orchestrator: an intermediary within the supply chain it helped coordinate. We thus contribute to the intersection between transitions, management, and development scholarship, foregrounding institutional disjunctures and inequality as defining challenges for transition intermediation in postcolonial settings, and showing how collaborative intermediary ecologies may be better positioned than single intermediaries to meet these demands. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Yuan T.; Zhang J.; Zhang H.; Zhan B.; Kong L.; Chen A.
Title: Cross-modal social attention differs across emotional categories: Evidence from biological motion and gaze cues
Abstract: Humans are highly proficient at utilizing various social cues (e.g., biological motion, eye gaze) to guide their attention, even in the detection of stimuli from other modalities, a process known as cross-modal social attention. Here, we investigated whether this fundamental cross-modal social attention could be altered by the emotional information expressed in visual social cues. By presenting emotional (happy and sad) and neutral biological motion (BM) stimuli together with auditory targets in the modified central cueing paradigm, we found that happy BM cues induced a significantly stronger cross-modal attentional effect than neutral and sad ones. Moreover, this cross-modal modulation effect is similarly obtained with attentional effects induced by another type of social signal (i.e., gaze). Importantly, when the emotional information contained in visual social cues (i.e., BM, eye gaze) was disrupted through inversion, this modulation effect vanished, ruling out the potential confound of low-level features. Drift diffusion model (DDM) analysis showed that this effect was primarily associated with shorter non-decision time induced by happy cues (potentially reflecting preparatory attention), rather than with changes in the evidence accumulation rate (potentially reflecting sustained attentional resource allocation). Overall, these findings highlight the flexibility of cross-modal social attention to vary as a function of emotional categories. This cross-modal emotional modulation appears to involve preparatory attentional processing and is observed across perceptually distinct dynamic social signals (i.e., BM, eye gaze), suggesting a similar cognitive mechanism through which emotion perception interacts with cross-modal social attention. © 2026

Authors: Pin L.ü.
Title: Weaponizing intimacy: Emotional proxy repression against feminist activists in China
Abstract: How does the family become an instrument of authoritarian political control? This article theorizes Emotional Proxy Repression, a form of authoritarian control whereby states mobilize family members to pressure activists through emotional appeals, achieving demobilization while evading accountability. Drawing on 25 interviews with Chinese feminist activists, social media posts and movement archives, this analysis reveals three emotional mechanisms—the invocation of familial obligation, the weaponization of care, and the mobilization of shame—through which family members produce acute psychological harm, sustained exhaustion, and political withdrawal. These dynamics are shaped by patriarchal family structures and gendered expectations, making this form of repression particularly effective against Chinese women activists. The study contributes to understanding the expanding and evolving repertoire of authoritarian coercion, and the concrete manifestation of how public and private forms of oppression converge. © 2026 The Author.

Authors: Alegado P.J.
Title: A critical evaluation of the co-produced online pre-arrival course for international student nurses through a social justice lens
Abstract: As international student mobility continues to expand within UK higher education, international nursing students face complex transitions shaped not only by cross-cultural movement but also by the demands of academic socialisation into unfamiliar higher education systems. In response, a co-produced online pre-arrival course was developed with international student partners to support this transition. This paper presents a reflexive, theory-informed critical inquiry into the practice of co-production, rather than solely the course content, using Nancy Fraser's three dimensions of social justice—redistribution, recognition and representation. The analysis generates three key conceptual insights. First, co-production partially redistributes informational resources but remains constrained by institutional power structures that limit epistemic and decision-making equity. Second, while student narratives enhance recognition, they risk reinforcing assimilationist norms when positioned as testimonial rather than epistemic contributions. Third, co-production often operates as bounded representation, where student participation is enabled but not fully extended to governance and evaluation. The paper argues that co-production must be understood not as an inherently decolonising practice, but as a contested praxis requiring deliberate structural, epistemic, and power-related shifts. It offers a transferable framework for global nursing education to navigate tensions between professional standardisation and social justice agendas, and proposes principles for embedding genuinely transformative coproduced curriculum design. © 2026
