Title: Psychiatrists' perceptions of mandatory treatment orders in Singapore: a qualitative study
Source title: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
Abstract: Mandatory Treatment Orders (MTOs) are used in Singapore to manage offenders whose culpability is diminished by mental illness, yet guidance on their optimal application remains limited. This qualitative study explored psychiatrists' perspectives on the use of MTOs and their role within the broader mental healthcare and justice system. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 21 practicing psychiatrists at a tertiary mental health institution, and data were analyzed thematically. Participants described substantial variability in MTO practice, shaped by clinical experience and levels of forensic involvement. Three overarching themes emerged: determining appropriate MTO duration, distinguishing between criminal and civil use of MTOs, and balancing forensic assessor continuity with independence. Longer MTOs were generally favored for individuals with psychotic disorders and histories of non-adherence, while shorter MTOs were viewed as sufficient for milder conditions, minor offences, and individuals with established engagement and insight. Many participants expressed ethical concerns about extending MTOs to civil contexts, citing risks of coercion, weaker enforcement mechanisms, and prioritization of social control over therapeutic benefit. Although continuity of the forensic assessor was often preferred for clinical and practical reasons, concerns regarding impartiality were also raised. Overall, psychiatrists viewed MTOs as occupying a dual therapeutic–justice role, generating tensions that contribute to variability in practice. Clarifying policy objectives, strengthening training and operational supports, and defining assessor roles may help improve fairness, consistency, and treatment outcomes. Copyright © 2026. Title: Radio coverage of climate change in Spain (2020–2024). Longitudinal analysis of content, approaches and sources; [Cobertura radiofónica del cambio climático en España (2020–2024). Análisis longitudinal de contenidos, enfoques y fuentes]
Abstract: Introduction: Climate change communication constitutes a critical challenge for contemporary media, given its scientific and social relevance. Radio, as a medium with wide reach, low barriers to access, and high credibility, continues to play a strategic role in the dissemination of environmental information and the construction of public discourse. Methodology: This study analyses radio coverage of climate change in Spain between 2020 and 2024 through a longitudinal and quantitative approach. A total of 2,224 news items broadcast by 18 radio stations with different ownership structures and geographical coverage are examined, collected by Observatorio de la Comunicación del Cambio Climático (Spain), with the aim of assessing how radio addresses global environmental challenges, with particular attention to framing, sources and thematic emphasis. Results: The analysis identifies an increase in trends of media attention to climate change, the predominance of specific news frames, and the types of sources and voices employed. It also explores the dynamics of thematic structuring and narrative priorities associated with causes, impacts, and benefits. Discussion: Although coverage has improved in terms of volume and specialization, shortcomings persist in source diversity, gender equity, and thematic depth. Conclusions: These results underscore the significance of radio as an accessible and socially widespread medium, with the capacity to enhance environmental literacy and public debate based on scientifically grounded and critical discourse. © 2026, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Authors: Wang H.; Lin C.; Xu T.; Zhong Y.; Du S.; Zhao Y.; Lin X.; Li S.; Xue H.; He W.
Title: Decoding resilience-based urban decarbonization pathways: Dynamic simulation of CO2 reduction and emissions peaking in China's Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area
Abstract: Accelerating the development of green, low-carbon and resilient cities is essential for balancing urban socio-economic development with ecological sustainability, especially under emerging risks and uncertainties. This study develops a comprehensive “social-economic-institutional-ecological-engineering” urban resilience (UR) framework to simulate and optimize Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) carbon dioxide (CO2) emission reduction from a resilience perspective. UR is first evaluated using an entropy-weighted TOPSIS approach, and key resilience drivers are identified via a LASSO-SHAP interpretability framework. City-level CO2 emissions are then estimated by integrating nighttime light (NTL) data with a city-specific logarithmic regression inversion model, after NTL preprocessing supported by a PSO-BP model. Building on the assessed UR and emission profiles, standardized UR indicators are projected using a BP-Linear ensemble to generate bounded scenario baseline trajectories. UR-related transition pathway variables, including technological innovation capacity (TIC), energy efficiency capacity (EEC), and industrial structural upgrading capacity (ISC), are then reconstructed and used to condition the RCP-SSP-based CO2 emission scenario assumptions, while Monte Carlo simulation is employed to dynamically evaluate city-specific peaking status and mitigation potential under alternative pathway combinations, thereby informing the ex-ante assessment of UR-related transition pathways and differentiated decarbonization planning. The results show that: (1) Resilience development in the GBA is highly uneven across cities, although the regional average continues to rise, with social security and health-care resources emerging as decisive factors in strengthening UR. (2) From 2000 to 2021, total CO2 emissions in the GBA increased significantly at an average annual rate of 5.39%, with Shenzhen and Dongguan exhibiting the fastest growth; among the simulated pathways, the LCE-HURS is associated with the most favorable emission reduction outcome under the UR-related pathway-conditioned scenario setting, whereas the HCE-LURS performs the worst. (3) Under the pathway-conditioned scenario assumptions, most GBA cities show peak-year modes around 2021; however, despite Shenzhen peaking in 2021, its 2035 emissions remain far above the 2000 level and its post-peak decline is relatively limited, highlighting the need to guard against “false peaking” when formulating carbon-peaking action plans. This study offers valuable insights for optimizing urban CO2 reduction strategies and underscores the urgency of incorporating UR-related transition pathways into sustainable regional development and decarbonization planning. © 2026

Title: Interventions to address loneliness and social isolation in community-dwelling older adults: an umbrella review
Abstract: Social isolation and loneliness significantly affect the physical and mental health of older adults, contributing to cognitive decline, increased morbidity, and reduced quality of life. Addressing these conditions remains a public health priority, prompting the continued development and evaluation of interventions to reduce their impact. This umbrella review aimed to identify, synthesise and critically appraise the existing evidence on interventions aimed at reducing social isolation and loneliness among community-dwelling older adults. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search of systematic reviews, scoping reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2014 and 2025 was conducted in PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. The search identified 2068 records, of which 28 met the inclusion criteria and quality assessment. A narrative synthesis was conducted to categorise the interventions based on objectives and delivery formats. Five types of interventions were identified: psychosocial, technological, health promotion, multicomponent, and recreational. Psychosocial approaches, complemented by technology or structured leisure activities, appear most effective, particularly when they foster meaningful relationships and enhance coping strategies. Findings suggest that interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness can meaningfully enhance the wellbeing of older adults and should be integrated into community and healthcare service models. However, further research is needed to assess the long-term effects of these interventions, their cost-effectiveness, and their feasibility for large-scale implementation across diverse ageing populations. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Gurumayum T.
Title: Sacred waters, gendered labour and survival: Ngamee women in the floating village of Loktak Lake
Abstract: Loktak Lake in Manipur is more than an ecological resource — it is a deeply storied landscape embedded with material, cultural, and spiritual significance. Central to its ecological uniqueness is the phumdi , a floating biomass that supports both human habitation and rich biodiversity. However, state-led interventions like the construction of the Ithai Barrage in 1983 and the implementation of the Loktak Lake (Protection) Act, 2006, have disrupted the ecological balance and delegitimised indigenous lifeways by labelling native fisherfolk as ‘occupiers’. Within this contested landscape, gendered divisions of labour shape everyday life. While men typically engage in fishing, women perform dual forms of labour, managing household responsibilities and participating actively in the fish economy through tasks like preparing, smoking, and marketing fish. This paper explores how fisherwomen navigate their social and economic roles in a space marked by sacred meaning, political and ecological precarity. Drawing on extensive fieldwork in Champu Khangpok, a floating village on the lake, the study situates women's experiences within the framework of emotional political ecology, highlighting how gender, cultural cosmologies, state regulation, and environmental change are intertwined in shaping the lives and struggles of Loktak's fishing communities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The Spanish moral foundations questionnaire-2: Psychometric properties and predictive associations with intergroup attitudes
Abstract: The Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2 (MFQ-2) was developed to offer a cross-culturally applicable instrument to assess the core dimensions of human morality. The main goal of the current research was to study the psychometric properties of the Spanish adaptation of the MFQ-2. To this end, we conducted four preregistered studies to evaluate the scale's factor structure, reliability, and validity. In Study 1 ( n = 956), a Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was employed to test the hypothesized six-factor structure of the MFQ-2 ( Care , Equality , Proportionality , Loyalty , Authority , and Purity ). Study 2 ( n = 315) examined the convergent validity of the MFQ-2 by comparing it with the original Moral Foundations Questionnaire (MFQ-1). To assess the instrument's predictive validity, Studies 3 ( n = 287) and 4 ( n = 278) examined the relationships between MFQ-2 scores and negative attitudes toward individuals with obesity and toward migrants, respectively. Across all four studies, the Spanish version of the MFQ-2 and its subscales demonstrated adequate reliability. These findings suggest that the Spanish MFQ-2 possesses good psychometric properties, confirming its viability as a reliable and valid tool for the Spanish scientific community to investigate the complexities of moral foundations. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Tong R.; Mao Y.; Wang L.; Xu S.; Liang F.
Title: The redemption of accidental republic: a resilience-based study on the measurement and evolution of Chinese workers’ compensation insurance
Abstract: Against the backdrop of declining risk resilience and slowing development in the Chinese Workers’ Compensation Insurance (WCI) system, this study focuses on Henan Province, a representative region in central China, to examine the challenges associated with what has been termed the “Accidental Republic”. A resilience-based study has been adopted to address these issues. First, a “Resistance–Recovery–Development” analytical framework is developed based on the Pressure–State–Response (PSR) model to identify key influencing indicators. Then, using panel data from 18 cities in Henan (central China) from 2019 to 2023, kernel density estimation and the Tobit regression model are used to analyze the changes in resilience levels over space and time and to assess WCI resilience. Finally, recommendations have been proposed to address the associated challenges. As a result, WCI resilience is influenced by internal indicators such as participation rates, human capital, and policy support, as well as external shocks like population structure, economic growth, and urbanization. The evaluation of WCI resilience in central China has only gradually increased, with notable regional disparities. Based on these findings, targeted recommendations are proposed at the strategic, operational, and institutional levels to enhance the sustainability and adaptability of WCI resilience. This study provides a resilience-based analytical framework for measuring and evaluating WCI resilience at the provincial level, offering insights for the sustainable development of workers’ compensation systems in similar regions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A Sustainable Sufficiency Economy Model Based on Community Identity in Security-Challenged Areas: A Case Study of Thailand’s Southern Border Provinces
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study aims to examine current contextual and spatial changes in Thailand’s southern border provinces, assess residents’ quality of life amid persistent security challenges, analyze security-related environmental factors that influence everyday life, and develop a sustainable sufficiency-economy model grounded in community identity within security-challenged contexts. This study employed a mixed-methods design that integrated qualitative and quantitative approaches. In-depth interviews were conducted with 12 representatives from government agencies and a focus group with 30 community leaders. Semi-structured interview guides and focus group protocols were employed, and qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis. For the quantitative component, surveys were administered to 384 residents in the southern border provinces, and the data were analyzed using frequency distributions, percentages, means, and standard deviations. Findings revealed three significant contextual challenges: ongoing unrest and security issues; the spread of drug abuse; and the impact of large-scale infrastructure projects and Malaysia’s rapid development. Regarding quality of life, concerns emerged in four areas: rising chronic conditions such as office syndrome, increased cases of depression and anxiety, persistent economic hardship and unemployment, and heightened feelings of insecurity in daily life. Survey results confirmed that the environmental dimension of quality of life scored lowest, particularly with respect to financial sufficiency for basic needs. Despite these challenges, the findings indicate that substantial social and cultural capital remains in the region, reflected in high evaluations of several security-environment dimensions, except for the economic dimension. Based on these findings, the proposed model for a sustainable sufficiency economy consists of six mechanisms: network building, participatory research, knowledge-based learning, communication for change, behavioral incentives, and community-based development through integrated collaboration. The study highlights how community identity and the Philosophy of Sufficiency Economy can be mobilized to enhance quality of life, strengthen security, and promote sustainable development in security-challenged border areas. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Competing powers: An examination of the role of intra- and extra-household factors on fathers' leave take-up
Abstract: This article examines how intra-household resources and extra-household organisational contexts jointly shape fathers' parental leave trajectories under a gender-neutral individual entitlement. Using administrative social security register data (IGSS) from Luxembourg, we analyse first-time, parental leave-eligible heterosexual couples with one child born between 2009 and 2012, conceptualising parental leave as a two-stage process: (1) fathers' initiation (timing) and (2) couples' joint allocation of leave duration. We estimate Kaplan-Meier curves and parametric survival models for initiation and multinomial logistic regressions for joint leave-taking strategies. We find that fathers generally take parental leave relatively late, with the first months after childbirth remaining predominantly a maternal territory. Descriptive results show that fathers in couples with greater economic resources tend to start leave later, with initiation timing strongly patterned by workplace context, including workforce composition in both fathers' and mothers' workplaces. Fathers' earnings play a stronger role in determining how leave is allocated between parents, suggesting that the financial costs of leave matter more for leave duration. At the same time, workplace conditions, particularly whether fathers work in female-dominated workplaces, remain important for both when fathers take leave and how much they take it. Overall, the findings show that having a legal right to parental leave does not automatically lead to equal use of that leave. Fathers' leave-taking is shaped by both workplace norms and the practical constraints couples face when making decisions together. Policies that aim to increase more symmetrical allocation of leave among parents should therefore focus not only on leave entitlements and payment levels but also on creating workplace environments that support and normalise taking leave. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: A signal detection analysis of source effects on misinformation susceptibility
Abstract: Signal Detection Theory suggests that people may fall for misinformation because they are unable to discern true from false information (i.e., low truth sensitivity) or because they have a general tendency to accept information regardless of veracity (i.e., low acceptance threshold). While a large body of evidence suggests that characteristics of information sources can influence susceptibility to misinformation, it remains unclear how source characteristics affect misinformation susceptibility. Using a signal-detection approach, the current research investigated (1) whether source characteristics influence truth judgments of true and false information via truth sensitivity or acceptance thresholds; (2) potential differences between perceived reliability and perceived partisanship as distinct facets of sources; and (3) how the two facets interact with information content in shaping judgments of true and false information. Across seven preregistered experiments (N = 4,286), we found that (1) source characteristics affected susceptibility to misinformation via acceptance thresholds, not truth sensitivity per se; (2) effects of source characteristics were limited to conditions where comparisons of sources are salient; (3) source characteristics had no effect on partisan bias, in that acceptance thresholds were substantially lower for ideology-congruent than ideology-incongruent information regardless of the source; and (4) perceived reliability and perceived partisanship showed corresponding effects on acceptance thresholds regardless of information content, suggesting that both source characteristics might influence truth judgments via perceived source credibility. Together, the findings provide deeper insights into how source characteristics influence susceptibility to misinformation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Task structure and construct validity in the neurobiology of trust: A systematic structural synthesis
Abstract: The neuroscience of interpersonal trust has expanded across functional magnetic resonance imaging, electroencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, pharmacology, genetics, physiology, and brain stimulation. Although this literature implicates distributed reward-, salience-, mentalizing-, and executive-control systems, findings are often difficult to compare because nominally similar Trust Game paradigms differ in their task architecture and analytic definition of trust. Here, we provided a PRISMA-guided systematic structural synthesis of 198 empirical studies comprising 200 experiments. Rather than conducting an effect-size or coordinate-based meta-analysis, we coded paradigm architecture, economic structure, temporal dynamics, trustee information, control conditions, participant populations, measurement modalities, and analytic strategies to characterize conditions relevant to neurobiological interpretation. Our synthesis showed that trust neuroscience is dominated by standard and binary Trust Game variants, simulated partners, limited explicit controls, and decision- and outcome-phase analyses. Exploratory contingency analyses identified associations among task architecture, measurement approach, and analytic operationalization without testing neurobiological effects. These features may emphasize different trust-related processes, including valuation of expected reciprocity, betrayal aversion under vulnerability, social inference about partner intentions, executive regulation, and feedback-based updating. We therefore propose a structural–computational alignment framework in which neurobiological findings can be interpreted relative to the task features and analytic contrasts under which they are observed. This framework reframes heterogeneity in trust neuroscience as a construct-validity problem rather than simple theoretical fragmentation. Explicit alignment among task design, inferred computation, analytic choices, and neurobiological measures may support a coherent mechanistic account of interpersonal trust. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Bodily Practices and Subjectivities of Lao Migrant Female Sex Workers in a Thai Border Town
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study examines the bodily practices of Lao female sex workers in a Thai border town, focusing on how these practices are shaped by subjectivity and negotiated within a context of transnational mobility and legal ambiguity. Employing a qualitative research methodology, the study draws on in-depth and narrative interviews, as well as participant observation, with 20 Lao women. Findings show that bodily practices—such as cosmetic surgery, skin whitening, and emotional labor—are strategies of negotiation and identity-making within the ambiguities of borderland sex work. Title: How directionality emerges through frame layering: An analysis of Swedish research and innovation policy on agri-food
Abstract: Transforming agri-food systems is widely seen as necessary to address overlapping ecological and social crises. Public research and innovation policy is a central mechanism through which such transformations are steered, yet it is often articulated in ways that obscure the normative commitments legitimising particular pathways. Using critical frame analysis and drawing on debates around directionality and the contrasting paradigms of sustainable intensification and agroecology, we analyse Swedish agri-food research and innovation policy from 2017 to 2025. We ask how problems and solutions are framed across successive levels of policy articulation, and what this implies for directionality. The policies comprise two national strategies, two action plans, two strategic research agendas and 21 funding calls. The findings show that directionality is not the property of any single instrument or policy level but emerges through frame layering across levels. In this way, diversity at one level can partially compensate for closure at another. We argue that directionality is therefore a relational and partly emergent property of how frames are layered. Hybrid framings, whose paradigm alignment depends on operationalisation, define challenges and solutions in broader terms that ease political friction at the cost of directional clarity. The paper offers a layered account of directionality and shows how critical frame analysis can surface the normative commitments embedded in research and innovation policy. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Towards climate resilient cities: An adaptive zoning approach based on flood vulnerability assessment
Abstract: Coastal megacities face escalating threats from climate-induced hazards such as sea-level rise and extreme precipitation events, which highlight the limitations of static urban planning approaches relying upon historical data, as they struggle to predict and adapt the real scenario of future flood conditions. To overcome the limitations of static urban planning, this study proposes a rule-based adaptive zoning approach based on flood vulnerability assessment. The proposed approach aims to translate multi-dimensional risk data into concrete spatial planning strategies, in order to address the “assessment-to-action” gap that has long persisted in the field of flood resilience and spatial planning. Specifically, this rule-based framework integrates inundation scenarios simulation (generated by a Digital Elevation Model) and flood vulnerability assessment (by incorporating population density, building coverage, and green-space coverage), and consequently delineates three adaptive zones of “Core Protection Zone”, “Retreat Zone”, and “Buffer Zone”. A case study of Huangpu River region in Shanghai has been conducted to exemplify the effectiveness of the proposed framework. The framework has effectively delineated the waterfront into three distinct adaptive management units. The first unit is the “Core Protection Zone”, which concentrates extremely high population and building densities, making structural flood defenses a planning priority. Unlike the “Core Protection Zone”, the “Retreat Zone” captures areas where severe exposure or limited ecological buffering makes long-term risk reduction and ecological restoration more appropriate. The “Buffer Zone” occupies the largest area and provides a transitional space highly suitable for deploying hybrid grey-green infrastructure. By explicitly identifying the “Core Protection Zone”, “Retreat Zone”, and “Buffer Zone”, the findings of this research not only deliver an operational bridge between vulnerability science and actionable spatial planning, directly addressing the long-standing “assessment-to-action” gap, but also provide a replicable and transferable toolkit that enables coastal megacities to move beyond “one-size-fits-all” flood control toward more climate resilient urban development in complex metropolitan areas. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Shi P.; Zulkepli N.B.
Title: Dual-Track Digital Affordance Framework for Enhancement of Willingness to Communicate in Chinese EFL Contexts
Abstract: This study examines how WeChat and MOOCs differentially enhance Chinese EFL learners’ in-class willingness to communicate (WTC), addressing persistent gaps in comparing language learning between social-media-supported environments and learning management systems. Grounded in Affordance Theory, it proposes a dual-track framework that distinguishes between affective-social (WeChat) and cognitive-structural (MOOCs) pathways. A 10-week quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with 135 undergraduates compared three groups: a WeChat-supported group, a MOOCs-supported group, and a conventional instruction group. ANCOVA results (adjusting for pre-test WTC and English proficiency) showed that the WeChat group significantly boosted post-test WTC (M= 153.98) compared with the control group (M= 143.76, p=.023), whereas the MOOCs group yielded moderate, non-significant gains (M= 151.93). Qualitative analysis showed that WeChat’s low-social-presence features (voice messaging and asynchronous group interaction) reduced anxiety and built peer cohesion, benefiting learners across WTC levels. Conversely, MOOCs’ cognitive-structural affordances supported content mastery but imposed excessive load on lower-proficiency learners and lacked real-time social interaction, thereby limiting WTC translation into classroom practice. The findings advocate a sequenced integration: MOOCs for pre-class cognitive scaffolding and WeChat for post-class affective-social activation. This dual-track model advances Affordance Theory in EFL contexts and offers concrete pedagogical guidance for optimising mobile-assisted WTC development. Authors: Hu Y.; Jiang L.; Zhang Y.; Fu C.
Title: Current status and influencing factors of AI literacy among nursing students: A scoping review
Abstract: Background: With the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the healthcare sector, AI literacy has become one of the core competencies for nursing students. However, the existing evidence regarding the factors influencing AI literacy among nursing students is currently fragmented and lacks systematic synthesis. Objectives: To systematically review the factors influencing AI literacy among nursing students, identify research gaps, and provide a reference for nursing education interventions. Methods: This scoping review followed Arksey and O'Malley's methodology framework and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. We searched six electronic databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, CNKI, and Wanfang Data), covering the period from the inception of each database to 25 March 2026. Original studies reporting on the influencing factors of AI literacy among nursing students were included. Two researchers independently screened the literature and extracted data, using a thematic synthesis approach to classify and summarise the influencing factors. Results: A total of 19 studies were included, comprising 11 from China, 5 from Turkey and 3 from the United States; these included 17 quantitative studies and 2 qualitative studies. Nursing students' AI literacy was generally at a moderately high level, but significant individual differences and dimensional imbalances were observed. Nursing students' AI literacy is influenced by multiple factors, which can be summarised into four categories: demographic factors, psychological and cognitive factors, educational and environmental factors, and social and organisational factors. Conclusion: Understanding these multi-level influencing factors is crucial for enhancing nursing students' AI literacy. The dynamic relationships between these factors should be explored in depth to identify key drivers and formulate more effective management strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Psychosocial, behavioural, health, and productivity-related factors associated with public transport use and walking for transport among infrequent bus users in a regional area
Abstract: Background and aims Public transport (PT) users are typically more physically active compared with private vehicle users. This study aimed to determine the variables associated with objectively measured PT use and self-reported walking for transport among infrequent bus users in a regional area of Australia. Methods Analysis of cross-sectional baseline data of 109 infrequent bus users (defined as making an average of ≤ 2 bus trips per week over the past 6 months) in the Tasmanian Trips4Health study. Walking for transport (minutes/week), psychosocial, behavioural, health, and productivity measures were self-reported via questionnaire. Bus use was objectively measured via smartcard (average bus use/week). Multivariable linear regression assessed associations with bus use and walking for transport. Results Participants reporting greater self-efficacy (β = 0.44; 95% CI = 0.00, 0.87), family support for using public transport by catching the bus with them (β = 0.30; 95% CI = 0.03, 0.57) and planned daily travel (β = 0.86; 95% CI = 0.50, 1.22), demonstrated higher weekly bus use. Higher self-reported physical quality-of-life (β = −1.13; 95% CI = −1.86, −0.39) and being a woman (β = −0.54; 95% CI = −1.05, −0.02) were associated with lower weekly bus use. Moderate self-perceived general health was positively associated with walking for transport (β = 150.08; 95% CI = 13.84, 286.31) compared to poor/fair self-perceived health. Participants with regular access to a motor vehicle (β = −181.0; 95% CI = −272.0, −89.92) walked less for transport than those without motor vehicle access. Conclusions Individual and social variables are associated with adults’ PT use and walking for transport. Strategies to enhance PT use and walking for transport should consider self-efficacy, family support, skills to plan PT use, and gender in their design. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Ortega Puente G.
Title: CROSS-BORDER SURROGACY ARRANGEMENTS AND THE RIGHT TO KNOW ONE’S ORIGINS: TOWARDS AN INTERNATIONAL LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN’S RIGHTS?
Abstract: Surrogacy raises complex international legal challenges, particularly regarding the right of individuals born through such arrangements to know their origins and the conditions required to ensure its effective realization in practice. This article adopts a doctrinal and jurisprudential approach, conceptualizing this right as a core element of identity and human dignity. It examines recent developments within the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) and the International Social Service (ISS), including the Verona Principles. It argues that existing frameworks remain insufficient and calls for coherent international standards ensuring effective access to origin-related information as a necessary precondition for exercising this right. © 2027 Universidad de Jaen. Title: Diversity in how people use racial categories to generalize
Abstract: Generic statements, such as “Black people are strong”, can imply that there are racial essences. But what about generic statements like “Black people face barriers to career advancement”? Statements like these may instead imply the existence of systemic racism. In three empirical studies, we examined the beliefs and attitudes held by Black (N = 387) and White (N = 400) American participants who endorse generic statements, controlling for endorsement of non-generic statements about the same events. For both Black and White Americans, generic statements about ability and character predicted a belief in racial essences (and endorsing the racial hierarchy), whereas generic statements about experiences and outcomes in social institutions predicted a belief in systemic racism (and rejecting the racial hierarchy). Thus, there is diversity in how and why people use race to generalize, and generic language flexibly accommodates that diversity. © 2026

Authors: Lin J.-J.; Chien H.
Title: Spatial disparities in surf-resource sustainability: Implications for coastal policy and marine education in Taiwan
Abstract: This study situates global surf sustainability within the Taiwanese context, where recreational surfing has developed since the 1980s and expanded internationally after 2010, yet region-wide assessments of surf-resource sustainability remain limited. Little is known about how sustainability conditions vary across Taiwan’s coastal regions, which sustainability dimensions contribute most strongly to these disparities, and what implications such patterns have for coastal governance and marine education policy. To address this gap, a literature-based Surf Resource Sustainability Index (SRSI) is adapted through a novel integration of remote sensing, GIS, and open socioeconomic datasets, enabling consistent township-scale evaluation beyond data-rich surf sites. The framework incorporates indicator weighting and statistical validation to strengthen the diagnostic interpretation of sustainability differences and domain relationships. By integrating temporal demographic trends with spatial assessments, the framework provides additional contextual evidence for understanding longer-term social capacity and policy-oriented surf-resource management. Correlation analysis shows that social factors are most strongly associated with overall SRSI performance, followed by governance and economic dimensions, while environmental factors exhibit weaker relationships. Spatial analysis further reveals distinct sustainability patterns across domains, while the sustainability profile typology identifies different combinations of domain-level strengths and weaknesses that may occur even among townships with similar overall SRSI levels. Temporal demographic evidence further provides context for interpreting these spatial disparities, suggesting that longer-term demographic trajectories may influence the capacity of coastal communities to maintain social networks, local knowledge, and institutional continuity. These findings highlight the importance of place-based approaches that consider social, economic, environmental, and governance conditions together rather than relying on overall sustainability scores alone. Accordingly, reducing spatial disparities in surf-resource sustainability emerges as a key priority for evidence-based regional marine policy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Sun Y.; Keung J.; Yu H.K.; Cao Y.
Title: At the point of risk: Can AI-assisted decision support reduce digital fraud vulnerability across age groups and scam types?
Abstract: Digital communication has broadened fraud's reach and complexity, making detection more urgent and cognitively demanding. Yet most studies examine static risk profiles or single scams, leaving real-time support in realistic settings underexplored. To address this gap, this study examined an AI-assisted decision support framework for digital fraud prevention. Using a 2 × 2 online lab-in-the-field experimental design, we compared an AI-assisted condition with a control condition across a younger group and an older group. A total of 72 participants completed a 10-day study involving ecologically realistic simulated fraud scenarios across six scam categories: financial/payment fraud, cyber/technical fraud, social relationship scams, consumer fraud, government or institutional impersonation fraud, and social media scams. The AI system provided real-time risk assessments, explanations of suspicious cues, and recommended actions. The results showed that AI-assisted support improved fraud detection accuracy and reduced risky behavioral intention. Younger and older groups also showed different scam-specific vulnerability patterns, and AI support reduced participants’ willingness to engage in risky actions in response to fraudulent communications in the scam categories to which each group was most vulnerable. Post-study questionnaire ratings and semi-structured interviews further indicated that participants generally perceived the system as useful and realistic, while trust depended on whether the AI output was interpretable and actionable. These findings demonstrate the potential of AI-assisted decision support for digital fraud prevention and highlight the importance of interpretable and actionable support that accounts for age-specific vulnerability patterns, offering practical guidance for the design of digital safety interventions in everyday online environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Xie M.; Lim S.
Title: Are the blue and the green natural allies? Mapping the public foundations of just transition worldwide
Abstract: A Just Transition, with its dual goals of environmental sustainability and social equity, has gained global prominence and has been adopted as a formal policy agenda by governments and intergovernmental organizations. While broad and meaningful public support for both goals is crucial to effective implementation, research on public attitudes has largely focused on developed Western countries or specific vulnerable populations. To address this gap, we examine whether and how support for environmental protection aligns or conflicts with backing for progressive redistribution across a diverse range of developed and developing countries. We posit that access to economic safety nets enables broader alignment at the population level (i.e., breadth of support), while post-materialist values and lived endorsement of the welfare state foster stronger individual-level alignment (i.e., depth of support). Our analysis, covering 95 countries from 2005 to 2022, finds support for these expectations. First, the population share of Green-Blue progressives supporting both goals is notably smaller in developing countries with high economic insecurity. Second, one's environmental and redistributive attitudes in much of the Global South are unaligned or negatively correlated, in contrast to the positive individual-level alignment observed in developed countries, particularly among post-materialists and in generous welfare states. Regional variation is also significant: Europe ranks high in breadth and shows significant depth; North America shows strong depth but no significant breadth; East Asia demonstrates wide breadth but comparatively shallow depth. Sub-Saharan Africa lags significantly on both dimensions. This global variation calls for context-sensitive Just Transition policies that account for distinct socioeconomic realities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Re-embedding rural development: The multiscale enactment of “He” culture in China's Beautiful and Harmonious Countryside
Abstract: Rural transformation can unsettle the relationships that organize production and everyday village life. China's Beautiful and Harmonious Countryside (BHC) vision combines material improvements with social and cultural aspirations, yet their connection in practice remains unclear. Drawing on “He” as a cultural reference for mutual support and shared responsibility, this study develops a multiscale framework for examining re-embedding across family, neighborhood and village life. We draw on interviews, field observations, village documents and questionnaire survey data from Santuo Village, Chongqing. The findings indicate that (1) household production brings older members' cultivation together with younger members' seasonal participation in harvesting and sales, providing a basis for family cohesion (FC); (2) villagers use public spaces to exchange experiences and discuss village affairs, providing a basis for neighborhood amity (NA); and (3) residents and village organizations use village regulations to coordinate shared resources and responsibilities, providing a basis for village harmony (VH). These findings show that villagers and village organizations in Santuo organize changing production and collective affairs through local social relationships—a process examined here as re-embedding. For comparable rural initiatives in the Global South, the case suggests pairing investments in livelihoods and facilities with opportunities for household cooperation, regular neighborly exchange and residents' coordination of shared needs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: E-bike injuries and prevention strategies across social and built environments: A systematic review
Abstract: Background Electric bicycle (e-bike) injury incidence and severity are increasing. While prior studies describe e-bike injuries and outcomes, there remains limited synthesis linking injury patterns and healthcare burden to contextual determinants such as the built and social environment, rider demographics, and e-bike safety policies. This review addresses this gap by integrating epidemiologic findings with prevention-relevant context using a Haddon Matrix framework. Methods We conducted a systematic review (PROSPERO-registered), searching MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library to June 2, 2025. Eligible studies reported e-bike-related injury data and at least three additional e-bike-specific elements drawn from these 4 domains: injury context, severity, treatment, and outcomes. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Findings were synthesized narratively and stratified by country, with pooled descriptive summaries reported where feasible. Results Thirty-five studies met inclusion criteria, representing 23 unique datasets (6107 cases) from six countries. Injuries predominantly involved the head (18%-65.7%) and extremities (6.4%-74%). Pooled outcome estimates indicated substantial healthcare utilization, including surgical intervention (31.6%), ICU admission (13.1%), and mortality (1.64%). Single-vehicle injuries were frequently reported. Helmet use varied widely by setting, ranging from 1% to 1.7% in the Netherlands to 63%-73.1% in Switzerland, reflecting differences in policy and cycling culture. Reported prevention strategies most commonly emphasized helmets/protective equipment, education and training, enforcement/legislation, and infrastructure-based interventions. Based on NOS, 48.6% of studies were considered good quality, 11.4% fair, and 40.0% poor. Discussion E-bike injury profiles vary substantially across countries, consistent with differing rider demographics, crash scenarios, infrastructure, and regulatory contexts. Prevention will likely require context-specific, multi-component strategies and stronger surveillance and standardized reporting to support rigorous intervention evaluation. Copyright © 2026. Authors: Ryser M.; Mazzarella D.
Title: Let's play, but seriously: Joint commitment in children's pretend play
Abstract: Social pretend play offers a unique window into the early manifestation of commitment in development. When engaged in social pretend play, children actively cooperate to create a shared fictional world and hold normative expectations about how each participant should behave within it. Yet, previous research has been cautious in characterizing the nature of the commitments at stake in pretend play. In this article, we offer a fine-grained conceptual analysis of joint commitments in pretend play. Drawing on Bangerter et al.’s (2022) proposal to investigate joint commitment as a product and as a process, we identify several facets of pretend play that involve distinct forms of joint commitments and discuss how these may be established even in the absence of explicit linguistic expressions of agreement. We also highlight relevant gaps in the current experimental work on joint commitment in pretend play and their implications for future research. © 2026

Authors: Wangukkarangkul A.
Title: Mechanisms of Political Mobilization and Voting Behavior Change: A Structural Equation Modeling Approach to Local Elections in Surat Thani, Thailand
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: Comprehensive models capturing how campaign fundamentals translate into voter responses through mobilization, including reciprocal relationships, remain underdeveloped in Southeast Asian subnational contexts. This study examines how political mobilization patterns mediate the associations between electoral success factors and changes in voting behavior in the 2025 Surat Thani Provincial Administrative Organization (PAO) chief executive election. Drawing on mediation theory and dynamic campaign models, structural equation modeling was applied to survey data from 430 eligible voters selected through multi-stage sampling to test a model that integrates five electoral success dimensions, six mobilizat io n patterns, and multidimensional voting behavior. Model fit was acceptable (CFI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.058, χ2/df = 2.14). Electoral success factors were associated with voting behavior both directly and indirectly through mobilization, with the indirect pathway accounting for approximately half the total effect. Mobilization patterns showed bidirectional associations with success factors, with the forward pathway substantially stronger than the feedback pathway, suggesting an asymmetric reciprocal structure. These findings contribute to population and social studies by refining our understanding of how subnational electoral dynamics in consolidating democracies are shaped by traditional authority, digital communication, and institutional networks, with implications for mediation theory and dynamic campaign models. Findings are interpreted as patterns consistent with dynamic electoral processes rather than definitive causal evidence. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Children’s classroom experiences in pre-K and their social-emotional development
Abstract: Prior literature provides mixed evidence on the association between individual classroom experiences and social and behavioral skills and global classroom quality without accounting for the interrelated nature of these pre-K experiences for children’s social and behavioral development. The current study uses data compiled from two large, multi-state studies of pre-K student experiences ( n = 2,982 children) to address this gap by assessing patterns of children’s classroom experiences (i.e., time in activity settings, exposure to classroom content, teacher-child interactions) using Latent Profile Analysis and examining associations between these profiles and seven unique social and behavioral skills (i.e., assertiveness, peer social skills, task orientation, and frustration tolerance, conduct problems, internalizing behaviors, learning problems). This study also examines whether these associations differ based on the emotional and instructional quality of the classroom. Findings from this study suggest the emergence of five unique profiles of child experiences highlighting great variation between settings and contexts. No evidence was found of associations between these profiles and children’s growth in social and behavioral skills across the pre-K year or of variation in associations by measures of classroom quality. Overall, the findings of this study highlight the importance of considering the combination of activity settings, classroom content, and teacher-child interactions to most accurately understand pre-K classroom experiences. Additional implications and suggestions for future research are outlined. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Mishra J.
Title: The intergenerational clock: How advanced parental age shapes offspring biological aging, longevity and neurodegenerative risk
Abstract: Background: As delayed parenthood becomes a global demographic norm, understanding the biological consequences of advanced parental age or APrA (≥35 years in mothers; ≥40 years in fathers) is a critical geroscience priority. This shift represents a significant public health challenge, as parental senescence dictates implications far beyond immediate fertility. APrA is a key determinant of offspring healthspan, linked to increased risks of congenital anomalies, premature mortality, neurodevelopmental and metabolic dysfunction, as well as neurodegenerative diseases. This inherited biological legacy supports an "intergenerational clock" linking reproductive timing to the aging trajectories of subsequent generations. Scope: This review synthesizes molecular mechanisms connecting parental senescence to reproductive success and offspring longevity. It examines the divergence between maternal factors, such as declining oocyte quality, and paternal factors, including sperm DNA fragmentation. Crucially, it integrates cross-species evidence ranging from Drosophila and mammalian models to human cohorts demonstrating how APrA progeny exhibit distinct behavioral phenotypes, including social deficits and anxiety, alongside compromised metabolic vitality. Major Conclusions: Age-related modifications in DNA methylation, histone profiles, and non-coding RNAs serve as primary mediators, influencing gene regulation during early embryogenesis. These epigenetic processes interact with parental lifestyle and environment to alter germ cell programming. Propagated through intergenerational inheritance, these signatures increase susceptibility to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Ultimately, this reframes aging as a continuous intergenerational process rather than an isolated individual trajectory. General Significance: Bridging reproductive biology and geroscience, this framework decodes how parental age shapes offspring biological legacy, essential for refining reproductive counseling and informing public health strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Better at what cost? The contrasting effect of norm feedback on exercise behaviours and body image
Abstract: Descriptive norm feedback informing people they have performed below average on an exercise task can motivate improvements in their subsequent performance and exertion. However, no research has examined whether such feedback has concurrent negative effects. We addressed this in a pre-registered lab experiment. Participants (N = 120) completed a brief no-equipment exercise workout twice. Prior to and during Trial 2, participants either received no feedback (control condition) or feedback that their Trial 1 performance was 30% below (high norm condition) or 30% above (low norm condition) the average of fellow students. Mixed model ANOVAs indicated that participants in the high norm condition demonstrated significantly greater improvements in both their objective performance (vs. low norm: t(78) = 7.77, p < .001; vs control: t(78) = 9.36, p < .001) and exertion (vs low norm: t(78) = 2.41, p = .046; vs control: t(78) = 4.20, p < .001). However, participants in the high norm condition also demonstrated significantly greater reductions in their body satisfaction (vs low norm: t(78) = −4.43, p < .001; vs control: t(78) = −3.63, p = .001) and increases in their negative mood (vs. low norm: t(78) = 5.80, p < .001; vs control: t(78) = 3.38, p = .003). Moderation analyses indicated that the effects of the norm feedback on performance (F(2, 114) = 4.55, p = .13) and body satisfaction (F(2, 114) = 7.19, p = .001) were moderated by social identification such that its effects were stronger among those who strongly identified with the norm reference group. Descriptive norm feedback may improve exercise outputs but carries a psychological cost. Its use should be sensitive to potential negative impacts on body image and mood, with further research needed to examine ways to offset these unintended effects. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: From online demands to policy responses: optimizing China’s child protection policies based on public opinion on child abuse
Abstract: This study draws on comments about nine child abuse incidents on Sina Weibo and national-level child protection policy texts currently in force in China. Natural language processing and topic modeling are used to identify public demands and their characteristics in terms of responsible actors and intervention levels. Semantic matching assists in identifying relevant policies, while specific policy provisions and institutional milestones are examined to assess subsequent policy responses. The findings show that demands expressed by the sampled users are primarily directed toward the state and judicial authorities and concentrate on system-level governance and emergency response. Demands concerning employment entry requirements and occupational bans, police intervention, legal accountability, guardianship intervention, and mandatory reporting exhibit high semantic matching with policies, whereas those concerning criteria for criminal liability and penalties for abuse, the commercial exploitation of children online, oversight of women’s federations’ performance of duties, and case information feedback mainly exhibit partial matching. Further analysis of policy content and temporal order shows that employment entry requirements and occupational bans received relatively clear policy responses after concentrated demand expression, although related demands continued to appear in discussions of subsequent incidents. By contrast, although the partially matched demands included in the temporal analysis correspond thematically to relevant policies, their core requirements concerning changes to offenses and penalties, regulation of the commercial exploitation of children online, and oversight and feedback mechanisms have not received direct policy responses. A comparison of demands that received responses with those that did not suggests that demands with relatively focused regulatory targets, relatively clear identification of responsible actors, and specific measures that can be implemented through existing administrative procedures may be more likely to receive policy responses because of their greater operational feasibility and relatively limited additional coordination costs. By combining demand-side information from social media with policy content verification and temporal tracing, this study provides empirical evidence for identifying specific public demands for protection and differences in policy responses, thereby informing targeted improvements to child protection policies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Public transport barriers and unmet long-term care needs in England
Abstract: Introduction Communities and the built environment have a profound influence on people's access to care and support. This study investigates the relationships between reported public transport barriers and unmet long-term care needs in the English older population. Methods The data came from five waves of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA, waves 6-10, 2012-2023). The sample consisted of people aged 50 and over with long-term care needs (10,518 person-waves). We looked at five indicators of public transport access: availability, coverage/connections, affordability, reliability and frequency. We built three-level generalised linear regression models to investigate the relationships between public transport access and unmet care needs. Results People experiencing unavailability, unaffordability, unreliability, and infrequency of public transport services are significantly more likely to have unmet needs than those without such experience. These relationships remained statistically significant after a wide range of control variables and individual-level and local authority-level heterogeneity were accounted for, with odds ratios ranging from 1.37 to 1.63 in different models. Further analyses showed that those relationships are accompanied by reduced access to informal care but not by formal care. Conclusions Disparities in public transport access go in tandem with disparities in long-term care access. High-quality, affordable and accessible public transport services are vitally important to the production of care and the fulfilment of the rising care demand in the population. There is a strong case for social care and public transport authorities to tap into the synergies between their policies. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Cultural, organisational, and individual factors contributing to cyber incident reporting: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Incident reporting behaviour is a critical yet underexplored human factor in organisational cyber resilience, shaping how organisations learn from incidents and adapt to evolving digital threats. This systematic literature review synthesises evidence from 106 peer-reviewed studies across cyber resilience, healthcare, and aviation to examine how cultural, organisational, technological, and psychological factors influence employees’ reporting behaviour. The review identifies five thematic clusters of antecedents—organisational, psychological, technical, social, and motivational—and shows how their interaction can either facilitate or hinder incident reporting behaviour. Building on these findings, we propose a novel, integrative multilevel conceptual model that extends the Cybersecurity Culture–Behaviour (CSCB) framework of Sutton and Tompson (2024) by incorporating a widely used behaviour-change framework, perceived consequences of reporting, and the moderating roles of incident characteristics and reporter attributes. The results highlight the importance of multilevel, human-centred interventions that foster psychological safety, provide timely and meaningful feedback, and align managerial practices with principles of a just culture. This study advances understanding of incident reporting behaviour as a socio-technical behaviour and offers a unifying framework for designing interventions to strengthen cyber resilience through improved human reporting practices. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Beyond waste valorization: Environmental justice in Brazil's Sertanejo Biodigester Program - Evidence from two municipalities and multi-level stakeholders
Abstract: Circular bioenergy systems can improve waste management, energy access, and rural livelihoods, but their justice implications remain insufficiently examined. This study assesses the Sertanejo Biodigester Program as a circular rural-energy intervention, focusing on distributive, procedural, and recognitional justice and on the Transformative Innovation Policy (TIP) principles of directionality, inclusivity, and reflexivity. We use a qualitative case-study design that combines documentary analysis, 20 semi-structured stakeholder interviews, and five days of field observation in Mirandiba and Verdejante, Pernambuco. The evidence indicates perceived reductions in purchases of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and firewood, sanitation benefits, and productive use of digestate; these are reported or observed co-benefits rather than quantitatively estimated impacts. Participation is concentrated in installation and training, with limited evidence of upstream influence over technology design, beneficiary selection, or long-term governance. Evidence concerning women's participation suggests gendered exclusion from some decision-making spaces, while evidence on Indigenous and Quilombola inclusion is too limited for population-wide conclusions. The study contributes an operational qualitative framework that links Environmental Justice (EJ) dimensions to TIP governance criteria and shows that transformative potential depends on transparent allocation, participatory governance, recognition of local knowledge, and sustained post-installation support. Because field observations are confined to two municipalities, program-wide claims are made only where supported by broader documentary and institutional evidence. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The decay of impact with network distance in linear diffusion processes
Abstract: Many processes related to status, power, and influence within social networks have been modeled using forced linear diffusion models; examples include the highly successful Friedkin-Johnsen model of social influence, the status/power scores of Katz and Bonacich, and the widely used network autocorrelation model. While a basic assumption of such models is that the impact of one individual on another through any given path falls exponentially with path length, the total impact of the first individual on the second involves contributions from walks of all lengths; thus, while total impact is expected to decline with network distance, the relationship is not trivial. Here, we provide an approximate solution for the total impact of one node on another as a function of network distance, showing that the total impact is given to first order by a product of eigenvector centrality scores together with an expression in terms of the graph spectrum (eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix) that falls exponentially with distance. We also show how this solution can be refined using higher-order eigenvectors of the adjacency matrix. A numerical study on interpersonal networks drawn from educational settings verifies an average exponential decline in impact strength under the linear diffusion model, and shows that the first-order eigenvector approximation can often be a good proxy for total impact as obtained from the exact solution. This suggests a simple model that can be used to approximate total impact for social influence or status processes in a range of settings. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Interpersonal neural synchrony and parent-child behaviors during naturalistic interactions: A systematic review
Abstract: Interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), defined as the temporal alignment of neural activity between socially interacting individuals, has been proposed as an index of parent-child interaction quality. However, its relationship with moment-to-moment adjustment of parent-child behavior remains insufficiently understood. This systematic review examined associations between INS and observable behavior during naturalistic parent-child interactions, the factors influencing these associations, and the methods used to investigate them. Following PRISMA guidelines, systematic searches of Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect identified 15 peer-reviewed empirical studies involving children from preschool age to early adolescence. INS–behavior associations were heterogeneous across studies. Higher INS was most consistently associated with mutual engagement, shared positive affect, and supportive parenting, whereas findings concerning reciprocity, responsiveness, and child agency were more context-dependent. Time-resolved analyses further indicated that INS fluctuated in relation to specific behavioral events and revealed temporally asymmetric patterns in which parent or child neural activity preceded that of the interaction partner. However, these patterns do not establish causal directionality and may partly reflect shared exposure to task-related or interactional inputs. Task structure and the availability of direct social cues appeared to shape INS–behavior associations, while parental stress and child social functioning emerged as potential sources of variability in INS. Methodologically, the findings highlight the value of combining micro- and macro-level behavioral coding with time-resolved and directionality-sensitive analyses, alongside stronger controls for spurious synchrony and common inputs. Given the limited number and methodological heterogeneity of available studies, the findings should be regarded as preliminary and primarily hypothesis-generating. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The Role of Patios in Creating Equitable and Sustainable Cities
Abstract: Patios or inner courtyards have been part of Cordoba city for centuries. Today, they represent a retro innovation and disruptive technology to fight climate change and to create equitable and sustainable cities. Patios use plant evapotranspiration as an economical and affordable technology to cool the houses and boost health and well-being. The combination of plants, water bodies, architectural features and wind circulation might act as a passive cooling system that reduces energy consumption and GHG emissions. However, patios are also spaces for socialisation, creating places to meet and develop social activities in contact with nature. This chapter describes the functioning of patios, the features that made them more efficient and the role they might play in boosting urban equality and sustainability. The experience of Cordoba, whose patios are recognised as UNESCO intangible heritage, might be used for other cities facing similar problems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Han J.; Bao L.; Peng Y.; Liu S.
Title: Sustainable neighborhood regeneration for SDG localization: A systematic review and conceptual framework
Abstract: Under urbanization and multiple global crises, translating the sustainable development goals (SDGs) from global visions into local practices has become a central challenge of urban transformation. Sustainable neighborhood regeneration (SNR) has been widely regarded as an important spatial practice for advancing SDG localization. However, existing studies have largely focused on intervention performance, sustainability assessment, or SDG mapping, while paying less attention to the sequential process through which SDG-related goals enter SNR decision-making, are translated into specific intervention actions, and generate multidimensional effects under different conditions. To address this gap, this study conceptualizes SNR as a process mechanism for SDG localization and develops an analytical framework integrating goal translation, intervention actions, impact identification, and implementation conditions. A systematic review of 341 publications from 55 countries was conducted, using content analysis, SDG relationship coding, and structured narrative synthesis. The results show that: (a) knowledge production remains geographically uneven, and evidence from the Global South beyond China is still relatively limited; (b) multiple types of relationships are formed between SNR intervention actions and the SDGs, including direct positive contributions, indirect positive contributions, and negative effects; (c) SDG-related goals are selectively translated into local indicators, planning criteria, and negotiation agendas mainly through potential and performance assessment, modeling simulation and objective optimization, and participatory decision-making, while the translation of goals related to social equity and local context continues to be constrained by limitations in data, modeling, and participation conditions; and (d) financial, institutional, technical, data-related, and stakeholder conditions further shape both goal translation and action implementation. This study advances the understanding of SNR-SDG relationships from static goal correspondence toward a process-oriented, relational, and conditional explanatory framework for SDG localization, offering insights for risk-sensitive neighborhood regeneration decision-making. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: How personalization-privacy trade-offs influence Robotaxi adoption: Insights from mobile Third Places
Abstract: With the development of autonomous driving technology and the sharing economy, robotaxis are expected to transform from traditional transportation tools to the future mobile Third Places. The focus is shifting from mere mobility to the enhancement of comfort, with an emphasis on delivering personalized services across diverse in-cabin scenarios. However, accessing more advanced personalized services in robotaxis may require users to disclose additional personal information, thereby creating a trade-off between the desire for personalization and concerns about privacy. Therefore, based on the privacy paradox theory and privacy calculus theory, this study incorporates privacy-related psychological latent variables and attributes of personalized services for robotaxis to construct an integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) model. A stated preference survey questionnaire was conducted to investigate choice behavior and relevant attitudes, and a sample of 651 responses was collected for model analysis. The results reveal that in the context of robotaxi services entertainment enhancement services, and comprehensive personalization services have a positive impact on robotaxi choice, whereas environment adjustment services do not. Additionally, privacy invasion experience and privacy concern negatively influence the choice of robotaxis with a higher level of personalized services, while perceived usefulness and hedonic benefit have a positive influence. The findings provide practical implications for robotaxi system design, suggesting that personalized services and privacy-friendly human–system interaction designs should be jointly considered. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Machine learning in the prediction of binge drinking: A systematic review
Abstract: Background Binge drinking (BD) refers to episodes of excessive alcohol consumption, which are associated with various acute and long-term consequences. Despite its high prevalence and negative impacts, predictive features for BD remain lacking. This study aims to review machine learning (ML) research on BD, comparing different algorithms and types of data, trying to identify promising models and variables that may help identify individuals at risk. Methods A systematic search was performed in PubMed, Embase, and Scopus to identify relevant studies published before July 2, 2026. 21 studies were included in data extraction process. Results The results suggest that impulsive factors, substance-use variables, emotional distress, as well as demographic features, particularly gender and age, play a significant role in predicting BD. Moreover, emerging methods that use real-time data recorded via mobile apps showed promise. Conversely, findings from neural data yielded mixed results, with no single brain area consistently associated with BD. The qualitative comparison did not show any specific ML algorithm consistently outperforming the others across studies; however, the predictive performance of ML approaches tended to improve when different data types were combined. Limitations The analysis of the available literature was restricted due to the non-homogeneous characteristics of studies, mainly in terms of methodology, which did not allow us to draw comprehensive conclusions. Conclusions The comparison of available ML studies showed how promising risk factors can be combined within multivariate models to increase their predictive value. Future large-scale studies using multisource data may better define risk profiles to foster prevention strategies. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Author full names: Salon, Salim A. (59474419700); Sarmiento, Alfonso T. (23012990900); Mejía, Gonzalo E. (8364123900); López-Arboleda, Esteban (57209234122)
Title: Beyond Logistical Efficiency: How Social Conflict and Local Content Shape Siting Decisions for Shore Base Infrastructure in Offshore Energy Projects
Abstract: The strategic siting of shore bases, onshore facilities that support offshore energy operations, is traditionally approached as a problem of logistical efficiency, emphasizing distance, port capacity, and transport infrastructure. However, in emerging offshore frontiers, decision-makers must simultaneously balance logistical, social, and local content considerations that are difficult to incorporate into conventional location analysis. The objective of this paper is to quantify how these dimensions are traded off against one another by operationalizing shore base location decisions within a discrete choice framework. A stated preference experiment was conducted with 60 professionals from Colombia's offshore oil and gas sector, each completing eight binary choice tasks (480 observed choices), and analyzed through Multinomial Logit and Hierarchical Bayes models. Port infrastructure emerged as the most influential attribute: its absence carries a trade-off equivalent to 385 km of additional distance. Yet social conflict outweighed several traditional logistical considerations once explicit trade-offs were introduced, with respondents willing to travel on average approximately 250 km further to operate in areas of low social conflict, whereas local content attributes exerted limited influence on siting decisions. A preference-based segmentation via hierarchical clustering identified four distinct strategic profiles, revealing substantial heterogeneity behind these averages. By demonstrating how discrete choice methods can operationalize infrastructure location decisions that jointly involve engineering, social, and local content criteria, this study advances the facility location literature and provides a transferable framework for conflict-sensitive planning in emerging offshore energy regions. © 2026 Policy Studies Organization.

Title: A strengths-based resilience intervention for first-year nursing students: A mixed-methods quasi-experimental evaluation of short-term outcomes
Abstract: Background: Nursing students are highly vulnerable to stress, anxiety, and mental health challenges, particularly during their transition into academic and clinical training. Strengths-based resilience interventions have been shown to enhance coping and well-being in student populations but are underexplored in non-Western nursing education contexts. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and social ecological theory, this study aimed to examine the short-term outcomes of the Changing Minds, Changing Lives (CMCL) strengths-based resilience program among first-year nursing students in a non-Western context. Method: This mixed-methods quasi-experimental study included 53 first-year nursing students allocated to intervention (n = 27) or comparison (n = 26) groups according to their existing class sections; one section was assigned to each condition. The intervention group received a 10-session strengths-based resilience program over five weeks. Quantitative outcomes were measured pre- and post-intervention using validated instruments: the Thai Perceived Stress Scale (T-PSS-10), Thai Connor–Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC-25), Emotional Self-Awareness Scale (ESA), and Perceived Cohesion Questionnaire (PCQ). Outcomes were assessed immediately before and after the five-week program; no longer-term follow-up was conducted. Repeated-measures MANOVA with post hoc Bonferroni tests assessed group and time effects, and analyses of covariance adjusting for baseline scores were conducted as sensitivity analyses. Qualitative data were collected via reflective writings and final presentations and analyzed using conventional content analysis. Results: The groups were not equivalent at baseline: the intervention group reported higher perceived stress and lower resilience. Significant group × time interaction effects were found across all four outcomes, indicating that resilience, emotional self-awareness, and perceived university belonging increased, and perceived stress decreased, to a significantly greater degree in the intervention group than in the comparison group. Univariate interaction effect sizes were large (partial η2 =0.15–0.40), and all effects remained statistically significant after adjustment for baseline scores. Qualitative findings revealed four themes: focus on strength, not weakness; sharing, listening, and learning from each other; understanding yourself and understanding others; and transformational learning. Conclusion: Participation in the CMCL strengths-based resilience program was associated with short-term improvements in self-reported perceived stress, resilience, emotional self-awareness, and perceived university belonging. The translated and contextually adapted program was feasible to deliver within the first-year curriculum. Because allocation followed intact class sections, baseline differences were present, and no attention-matched comparison condition or longer-term follow-up was included, the findings should be regarded as preliminary. © 2026 The Author(s)
