Title: When social approach meets social avoidance: Social motivation and internet gaming disorder from variable-centered and person-centered perspectives
Abstract: Social motivations play a central role in driving individuals to engage continuously in online gaming. Prior research has documented separate associations of social motivations with Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD), but it remains unclear whether individuals exhibit distinct configurations of social motivations and whether these configurations are differentially associated with IGD. To address this gap, the present study employed an integrated variable-centered and person-centered approach to examine the joint associations of preference for online social interaction (POSI), social anxiety, and persistent gaming intention with IGD. Data from 1984 young adults were included in the analyses. Variable-centered analyses showed that both POSI and social anxiety were positively associated with IGD and had significant indirect associations with IGD through persistent gaming intention. Person-centered analyses identified latent social motivation profiles, with higher levels of persistent gaming intention and IGD observed among individuals with concurrently high POSI and high social anxiety. These findings are consistent with a more differentiated compensation account that considers both offline social difficulty and orientation toward online social interaction. More broadly, these findings suggest that the associations of social motivations with IGD vary across configurations of POSI and social anxiety. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhang J.; Boesen C.
Title: Analysis of public health influencers on social media
Abstract: This study aims to identify health-related themes on X, determine major public health influencers within each thematic category, analyze interrelationships among categories, and examine relationships among key platform variables. Social network analysis, inferential statistics, and visualization methods were used to achieve these aims. Subject analysis identified eight categories: Academia, Corporate, Government, Healthcare, Health Advocacy Program, Individual, Media, and Organization. Government and Health Advocacy Program were the most salient categories in both size and structural influence. Katz centrality was not significantly associated with either Following or Follower counts, whereas Following and Follower counts showed a moderate, statistically significant positive correlation. Katz centrality, Following and Follower counts also differed significantly across the eight categories. Accounts tended to follow Government and Organization accounts, whereas Individual accounts attracted fewer cross-category connections due to their lower structural visibility within the CDC-centered network. The results also indicated category-level homophily, with accounts tending to follow accounts in the same category. These findings have theoretical and practical implications. The identified subject schema provides a framework for guiding health information seeking on X and can help public health officials evaluate the reach and structure of their communication networks. The study also demonstrates a workflow for identifying structurally influential accounts and shows how Following and Follower counts, and Katz centrality reflect different aspects of health-related networks on X. Authors: Zhou Q.; Duan X.; Yu G.
Title: Beyond pairwise interactions: Investigating the impact of microlevel dynamic higher-order interactions on online rumor and debunking dynamics
Abstract: Prior research on rumor propagation and debunking dynamics has largely relied on pairwise interaction models with static network structures and Markovian assumptions. While analytically convenient, such models neglect key features of real-world diffusion, such as dynamic user participation, group interactions, and temporal dependence in propagation processes. Consequently, they may underestimate spreading speed and fail to capture bursty diffusion patterns. To address these limitations, this study develops a dynamic higher-order rumor propagation model based on simplicial complexes. By incorporating node activation and deactivation mechanisms, the model captures users’ dynamic participation and withdrawal behaviors, thereby representing the intermittent disruption and reconstruction of propagation chains. It further integrates higher-order interactions with user activity dynamics while accounting for quasi-non-Markovian processes and the influence of debunking agents. The model is evaluated using real-world data from Weibo and Douyin. A systematic analysis is conducted to examine network scale, structural complexity, the proportion of authoritative debunkers, and response speed. The results show that higher-order interactions significantly accelerate rumor diffusion. The introduction of 2-simplices increases transmission efficiency by approximately 20%. Regulating the formation and density of higher-order structures (e.g., disrupting clustered rumor groups) can effectively delay the onset of rumor propagation and suppress early-stage growth. Additionally, a 0.1 increase in the share of authoritative debunking nodes among all debunking nodes is associated with a 0.289% decrease in the average probability of rumor propagation. These findings highlight the importance of higher-order structures and provide actionable insights for mitigating viral rumor diffusion. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Shi J.; Yang L.; Yan Z.
Title: Combating mental health misinformation on social media: A knowledge-guided multimodal framework
Abstract: The proliferation of mental health misinformation on social media poses severe public health risks, necessitating automated detection systems. However, existing misinformation detection research remains limited in its ability to perform stance-aware evidence reasoning and robust multimodal analysis. In this study, we propose a Knowledge-Guided Mental Health Multimodal Misinformation Detection Network ((Formula presented) ). The framework contains three key modules: the Dual-Channel Attention Verification module differentiates supporting and contradictory evidence from knowledge graphs; the Statistical-Guided Attention Prior module uses statistical cues to guide attention over noisy multimodal representations; and the Directed Co-Attention Integration module hierarchically integrates verified knowledge with multimodal content. We conduct experiments on the MentalMisinfo dataset, including 2135 YouTube videos and 754 BitChute videos. (Formula presented) achieves the best overall performance on both datasets, improving F1-score by 0.0142 on YouTube and 0.0238 on BitChute over the strongest baselines, with statistically significant gains across 10 random seeds. Ablation analyses further confirm the contribution of each component. Our work advances knowledge-enhanced multimodal misinformation detection and provides practical implications for social media platforms and public-health stakeholders. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Roden A.; Urmee T.; Lund C.
Author full names: Roden, Andrew (60976727000); Urmee, Tania (23107679200); Lund, Christopher (58415024000)
Title: Waste mountains in developing countries: Impacts, barriers and pathways to sustainable solutions: A review
Abstract: This critical review examines the definition, impacts, underlying causes, and potential solutions for waste mountains in developing countries. The analysis highlights three major knowledge gaps: inconsistent terminology; the absence of reliable national inventories documenting the number, location, size, and composition of waste mountains; and limited information on sustainable waste-to-energy solutions. The findings reveal that waste mountains generate interconnected environmental, public health, social, and economic consequences, while the full economic costs of continued dumping remain largely unquantified. Rather than being primarily a technological problem, their persistence stems from systemic challenges, including weak governance, fragmented policies, insufficient financing, inadequate waste management infrastructure, and poor data availability. For existing waste mountains, waste mining combined with resource recovery and thermochemical waste-to-energy technologies offers a promising remediation pathway. However, the suitability of individual technologies depends on local conditions, including waste characteristics, moisture content, contamination levels, infrastructure capacity, financial feasibility, and environmental safeguards. Among available options, incineration remains the most widely established technology, whereas pyrolysis presents opportunities for resource recovery and circular economy outcomes through the production of valuable co-products. Nevertheless, its application to heterogeneous legacy municipal waste remains insufficiently proven at scale. The review concludes that effective management of waste mountains will require the development of comprehensive national inventories, risk-based prioritisation of remediation efforts, robust valuation of the costs of inaction, inclusive governance arrangements, and comparative techno-economic and lifecycle assessments to guide the selection of appropriate strategies. © 2026

Authors: Arena L.; Prescott M.P.
Title: Parental factors associated with US youth ultra-processed food outcomes: A systematic review
Abstract: Ultra-processed food (UPF) comprises 67% of the average US youth diet, among the highest rates globally. Health burdens associated with youth UPF intake include overweight/obesity, glucose dysregulation, poor cardiovascular health, liver disease, microbiome disruption, dental problems, DNA damage, mental health concerns, and lower cognitive and academic performance. This systematic review investigates parental factors associated with US youth UPF intake, preference, selection, or access. A comprehensive literature review was conducted using PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science databases were searched. Inclusion criteria required studies to examine youth (aged 0-19) UPF outcomes and parental factors. The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool assessed study bias and quality. PROSPERO registration number: CRD420251248701. The search yielded 1727 articles, 888 after duplicates removed. Full text review resulted in 11 extracted articles: 9 quantitative and 2 qualitative. Parental factors associated with child UPF outcomes included education level, gender (female), UPF intake, more frequent soda and fast-food intake, belief in food advertising, reward-based eating drive, allowing youth to watch greater hours of TV, and the home food environment. Mixed findings were found with parental substance use, depending on prenatal, maternal, and paternal use, cigarette, alcohol, or illicit drugs, and child age. Notable null findings included parent age, living with a partner, household income, shared family meals, human milk exposure, and parent motivation, attitude, and self-efficacy to limit junk food and eat more fruits/vegetables. Further research around parental factors and US youth UPF intake is warranted. Intervening in identified target areas may help mitigate youth UPF outcomes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Knowledge base on sustainability of land management practices and climate change resilience efforts
Abstract: This editorial introduces the Special Issue, Sustainability Dialogue: Land Management Practices and Climate Change Resilience Efforts, developed from a Summer School and journal call involving scholars and practitioners across the global sustainability community. Its articles provide multidisciplinary teaching and reference material linking land governance, ecological processes, climate risk, technology, and human behaviour across rural, urban, forest, agricultural, and river-basin settings. Governance studies show that resilience requires coordinated institutions, secure land access, and incentives for long-term stewardship. At the same time, social research explains how local knowledge, livelihoods, adoption, public services, and environmental justice shape intervention outcomes. Ecological studies examine biodiversity, wetlands, forests, soils, ecosystem services, carbon storage, and fragmentation, identifying practical pathways such as agroforestry, conservation agriculture, green infrastructure, nature-based solutions, urban forestry, and restoration, alongside trade-offs involving production, urbanisation, energy, property values, and carbon sequestration. Remote sensing, GIS, modelling, artificial intelligence, and scenario tools support hazard mapping, attribution, forecasting, and intervention planning. Evidence from Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas links diagnosis, prediction, governance, finance, and implementation, advancing place-based, socially accountable, climate-resilient land management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Krueanuan C.; Seemung J.
Title: Development and Dispossession: Land-Use Transformation and Conflict in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study examines conflicts arising from land-use reorganization in the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC), focusing on Chachoengsao province and the Chachoengsao-Chon Buri border areas. The analysis is grounded in the concept of accumulation by dispossession. The study employs qualitative methods, including documentary analysis, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussions. The findings show that land-use conflicts within the EEC constitute a complex arena involving state agencies, private capital, and civil society networks. These conflicts emerge from interactions between centralized legal mechanisms, land-use planning decisions, and development discourses. Land-use reorganization has transformed agricultural and community lands into industrial zones, leading to dispossession, livelihood insecurity, and unequal power relations. Conflicts unfold through negotiation, social mobilization, and legal contestation. Theoretically, this study contributes to debates on accumulation by dispossession by demonstrating how dispossession occurs through planning processes, land-use reclassification, and regulatory arrangements before direct land acquisition. The findings also extend debates on land conflict in the Global South by highlighting policy-driven forms of dispossession shaped through planning and development frameworks. The study recommends balancing industrial development with the protection of community resources through participatory planning and inclusive land-use governance. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Artificial intelligence (AI) in nursing education: An evolutionary concept analysis
Abstract: Background: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been explored for decades in nursing education, the existing body of knowledge provides no clear definition of the phenomenon. As technological advancements continue to shape teaching and learning environments, establishing a clear and robust definition of AI in nursing education is critical. Aim: To clarify the concept of AI in nursing education from an evolutionary perspective. Methods: We conducted a concept analysis following Rodgers' evolutionary method. The searches were performed in September 2024 in MEDLINE/PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ProQuest. Peer-reviewed English literature was included without time frame specifications. The components of Rodgers' evolutionary method (attributes, antecedents, consequences, surrogate terms, and related concepts) were identified and analysed using a deductive-inductive approach. Findings were synthesised into a conceptual model, supported by an illustrative exemplar of AI in nursing education. Results: Out of 1559 records retrieved, a total of 33 articles were included. Key attributes of AI in nursing education included computer systems and interdisciplinary knowledge. Antecedents included curriculum integration, workforce preparation, faculty preparedness, and ethical governance. Consequences were personalised learning and individualised feedback. Surrogate terms were generative AI models and machine learning systems. Related concepts included clinical simulation, and nursing informatics. AI in nursing education is defined as the application of intelligent computational systems to the teaching and learning process, augmenting the intelligence of nursing students and educators and enabling personalised teaching and learning experiences within technology-enhanced educational ecosystems. Conclusions: Our definition may contribute to a paradigm shift by embedding computational intelligence into nursing education. This is important in moving teaching and learning beyond the transmission of static content and toward adaptive and intelligent learning systems. Further research is warranted to advance conceptual development that can guide the evidence-informed integration of AI into nursing education. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Environmental Communication and Multi-Stakeholder Collaboration for Sustainable Fisheries Livelihoods and Coastal Resource Governance on Labengki Island, Indonesia
Source title: Journal of Global Innovations in Agricultural Sciences
Abstract: The goal of this study was to analyze multi-stakeholder collaboration in environmental communication in developing sustainable marine tourism in Labengki Island, North Konawe Regency, as a means of supporting coastal fisheries livelihoods and improving the social economy of Labengki Island’s small islands. A qualitative exploratory approach was used, with a case study design. Thematic analysis was conducted in NVivo using software, whilst Actor-Network Analysis (ANA) — an approach adapted from Actor-Network Theory (ANT) — was used to map relationships between human and non-human actors. Participative observation, in-depth interviews, Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), and document analysis were conducted to gather data from 20 informants including local government officials, tourism business actors, local communities, and tourists. The results show that collaboration among stakeholders is established but remains sectoral and has not yet integrated into a common governance framework. The main coordination mechanisms are social relations and informal communication structures such as village deliberation forums, tourism awareness group (Pokdarwis) meetings, and basic digital communication platforms. Although environmental communication plays a significant role in building collective awareness, its application remains insufficient, particularly in waste management and environmental conservation. A pattern of fragmented social-relational collaborative governance is evident, characterized by weak institutional integration, inequitable benefit sharing, and limited environmental management capacity. Beyond institutional fragmentation, the quality of environmental communication and social relations is crucial for the sustainable development of marine tourism in small island regions, as these constitute the primary coordination mechanisms. © 2027, Society for Innovative Agriculture, University of Agriculture. Title: Are maternal eating demonstrations associated with infant food acceptance? An observational study of solid food introduction in infancy
Abstract: Research with infants highlights an early capacity to learn from social partners, particularly about concepts that would be difficult to learn independently. However, scant literature examines social learning (such as the impact of demonstrations) on infants’ acceptance of foods, even though the timeline of solid food introduction (recommended to start at age 6 months) aligns with emerging capacities for infant social learning, making solid foods an ecologically valid category of unfamiliar stimuli. The present research examines whether infants eat more food at 6 (n = 103), 9 (n = 104), and 12 (n = 101) months when their mothers demonstrate eating and the factors that predict maternal eating demonstrations. Although the frequency of maternal eating demonstrations was positively associated with infant bites, we observed low levels of maternal eating demonstrations (fewer than 30% of mothers demonstrated eating at each infant age). Infants tended to eat more of familiar versus unfamiliar foods, yet mothers did not differ in their demonstrations of eating familiar versus unfamiliar foods. Mothers were more likely to demonstrate eating foods when the observations took place during shared meals (rather than individual infant feedings) and when feeding older infants, with more demonstrations occurring at the 9- and 12-month age points compared to the 6-month age point. Eating demonstrations are discussed as a potential target for intervention deserving further study given that we rarely observed spontaneous eating demonstrations in this study. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: König C.J.
Title: Who sends money home? Personality traits as predictors of remittance behavior in a longitudinal migrant sample
Abstract: Individual differences in migrants' remittance behavior remain poorly understood despite their economic and social significance. This study examines whether the Big Five personality traits predict remittance sending to family and friends, using prospective longitudinal data from two ethnic minority samples of Understanding Society: the UK Household Longitudinal Study (N = 2943). Personality was measured at baseline; remittance behavior was assessed one year later and at three further occasions spanning a decade. Conscientiousness was a positive predictor of remittance sending one year later, whereas Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness were negative predictors and Agreeableness showed no significant association. The Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, and Extraversion associations replicated four years after the personality assessment, the Neuroticism association additionally held a decade later, and the Openness association was confined to the initial occasion. These findings establish personality as a meaningful predictor of transnational financial behavior. That duty-related Conscientiousness predicted sending while prosociality-linked Agreeableness did not is consistent with the view that remittance sending reflects duty fulfillment more than general prosocial orientation; transfers may be harder to sustain for migrants who engage strongly with the host society, as extraverted and open individuals tend to do, and for those prone to worry and financial anxiety. © 2026 The Author.

Title: First-year international students’ experiences of loneliness and social isolation: The role of social support from family, friends, and romantic partners
Abstract: First-year international students face significant social challenges , including potential reductions in social support and difficulties in forming friendships. A nuanced examination of these social challenges is important because they may contribute to experiences of loneliness and social isolation, and in turn, have a negative impact on mental health and academic performance. While quantitative research has established the prevalence, predictors, and outcomes of international students’ loneliness, a qualitative approach can provide a richer, more in-depth account of their lived experiences. As such, we interviewed 15 first-year international students enrolled at a Canadian university about their loneliness and social isolation, the development and maintenance of their social networks, and the challenges they experienced when adjusting to a new cultural and academic environment. Key themes included the emotional and psychological toll of loneliness, especially during holidays, the benefits of solitude, difficulties in forming new friendships in Canada, the lack of opportunities to interact with classmates outside the classroom setting, as well as support from family, friends, and romantic partners from Canada or their heritage culture. Some participants reported feeling a lack of belonging after attending social events, realizing they did not share the same values as others. Family support (e.g., through video calling) was an important source of social support despite the lack of in-person interactions. These results may help to inform university initiatives for enhancing social support systems and assisting international students’ transition to life in Canada’s evolving sociopolitical landscape. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Liu T.; Qi X.
Title: Can property rights delineation incentivize farming households’ consumption? An analysis from the perspective of precautionary savings
Abstract: Property rights system reform is a crucial means to stimulate rural development vitality and facilitate the strategy of rural revitalization. However, there is still insufficient empirical evidence regarding whether property rights delineation can reduce farming households’ precautionary savings and thereby boost their consumption. To address this, this study takes China's new round of rural land rights confirmation (RLRC) as an example. It constructs a quasi-natural experiment based on data from the 2013 and 2015 China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) and the 2018 China Labor-force Dynamics Survey (CLDS). By comprehensively employing the Difference-in-Differences (DID) method, the Instrumental variable (IV) method, and the Mediation effect model, this study empirically investigates the causal relationship between RLRC and farming households’ consumption, with a particular focus on the mediating effect of precautionary savings. This study finds that the RLRC promotes the growth of farming households’ consumption, and this conclusion remains valid after undergoing various robustness tests. Mechanism analysis reveals that RLRC boosts farming households’ consumption by reducing their precautionary savings, and this mechanism remains robust and effective even after the implementation of the “separation of three rights” reform of rural land and the pilot programs for the mortgage loans of rural land management rights. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that for households with younger household heads and those possessing richer human capital and social capital, the stimulating effect of RLRC on their consumption is more pronounced. Further analysis shows that RLRC primarily promotes subsistence consumption among farming households, rather than developmental consumption, while also having a positive effect on their income improvement. This study not only provides a new explanation for the paradoxical phenomenon of “farming households having money but being reluctant to spend it” but also offers new empirical evidence for government departments to optimize or formulate consumption stimulation policies. © 2026

Title: Introducing improvised pragmatism of care: animal health, epistemic frictions, and veterinary governance
Abstract: This article introduces the concept of improvised pragmatism of care to analyze how Indigenous communities, living in and around protected areas navigate animal health amidst ecological disruption and limited institutional capacities. Drawing on focus group discussions conducted in 2024 in seven communities of the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Conservation Area in Mozambique, we show how livestock care emerges not as static tradition nor simple adoption of biomedical protocols, but as dynamic practices that combine embodied diagnosis, herbal repertoires, and selective engagement with veterinary interventions. These plural strategies constitute resilient responses to epistemic injustice and ontological displacement in a conservation landscape. Improvised pragmatism of care captures this mode of governance from below: an active reconstitution of knowledge and practice under conditions of uncertainty. Our analysis cautions against treating animal health as an abstract, detachable component independent of human–animal relations or as separable from historical trajectories and contemporary territorial and environmental management policies. By foregrounding community improvisation as both epistemic and political practice, this study contributes to veterinary anthropology and health social sciences, highlighting how Indigenous actors can sustain multispecies health in contested landscapes marked by displacement and inequality. Title: Does disfluency affect social judgments and decisions? Evidence from spontaneous speech
Abstract: Disfluency in speech (e.g., English um and uh, also known as filled pauses) has long been argued to have social costs for the speaker. However, this conclusion is based on a limited set of measures obtained for scripted, lab-recorded speech. Here, using stimuli from spontaneous speech and an expanded set of social trait evaluations, we argue that phenomena typically described as “disfluency” are not always evaluated negatively. First, at the global person level, filled pauses did not affect the overall perceived competence, trustworthiness, or warmth of the speaker as a person (Experiment 1). However, at the local conversation level, filled pauses reduced perceived speaker trustworthiness within a conversation (Experiment 2). Furthermore, within a conversation, speakers who produced filled pauses were rated as less ready and less certain than speakers who did not (even though experts who used filled pauses were more likely to be considered careful than novices; Experiment 3). Finally, speakers using filled pauses were more likely to be avoided in future interactions (Experiment 4). Together, these data reveal flexible and detailed mappings of speech features such as disfluencies to social attributes and showcase the value of studying social meaning using speech generated beyond the lab. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Sun Z.; Gao W.; Yin P.; Li W.; Zhang M.; Chen Y.; Shu J.; Guo Y.
Title: Optimization of encrypted data poisoning defense strategies in Social Federated Computing: An evolutionary game approach
Abstract: Social Federated Computing enables collaborative computation over distributed user-held data in social systems while preserving data locality and participant autonomy. To mitigate gradient inversion-based privacy leakage, intermediate updates are commonly protected through encryption, which fundamentally reduces system observability and weakens conventional poisoning detection mechanisms. This loss of observability introduces new security risks, including ciphertext-level poisoning, while exhaustive cryptographic auditing and verification incur prohibitive computational and communication overheads at scale. These inherent conflicts lie between privacy preservation, detection capability, and operational efficiency in encrypted Social Federated Computing environments. In this paper, we propose an evolutionary game-theoretic defense framework for encrypted Social Federated Computing to model and regulate these inherent conflicts. The framework captures two defining characteristics of social federated environments: adversarial behaviors that propagate along social relationships and organizational constraints, and participants that operate under partial information and exhibit locally rational behavior rather than global rationality. Server-side detection intensity and client-side poisoning propensity are modeled as co-evolving strategies under partial observability, explicitly accounting for false positive penalties, external incentives that motivate poisoning, and practical deployment constraints such as energy budgets. Through equilibrium and stability analysis, we characterize how defense policies adapt to varying costs, incentives, and resource limitations, and we identify stable strategy regimes across representative deployment scenarios. The proposed framework yields deployment-oriented guidance for tuning server-side defenses, enabling adaptive and cost-aware mitigation of ciphertext poisoning in large-scale encrypted Social Federated Computing systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Evaluating the role of social capital in land reform: Empirical evidence from rural China
Abstract: Achieving effective land use is a key objective for national and local governments. This study, proceeds from the angle of social capital, demonstrates the impact of its different types, i.e., social networks, social norms, and trust on the efficacy of land-use policies with respect to China's recent 'Three Rights Separation' (TRS) reforms, evidenced by household survey data from six provinces in eastern, central, and western China. Unlike existing literature, we reconstruct the second-generation collective action framework, shedding light on the more complex role of trust with a new conceptual approach. Furthermore, we develop a multidimensional framework for measurement of social capital and policy effects and use a Structural Equation Model (SEM) approach to provide robust estimates of the relationships between these factors, attending to both economic and social outcomes. The findings reveal three key insights. First, social norms exert a direct effect on social performance of land-use policy, as measured by policy satisfaction, while also having indirect effects through the mediating role of trust. Trust proves to be not only a mere form of social capital but also a critical outcome and driver of effectiveness. Second, well-established social networks and norms significantly promote economic outcomes measured by land investments, with social networks producing a more pronounced effect. Third, building robust social networks enhances another aspect of economic performance, namely farmers' willingness to participate in land transactions and agricultural cooperation. These findings provide valuable implications for how policymakers can harness various forms of social capital to achieve various objectives. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhao H.; Cai M.; Kang X.; Zhang T.; Ke Y.; Liang B.
Title: Prolonged exposure therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
Abstract: This meta-analysis examined the efficacy of prolonged exposure (PE) therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Fifty-two randomized controlled trials were identified through systematic searches of five electronic databases through March 2026; 43 studies (54 comparisons; N = 4964) were included in quantitative synthesis. PE produced medium-to-large effects on PTSD severity relative to inactive controls (Hedges' g = 0.74, 95% CI [0.51, 0.98]; k = 20) and a small but significant advantage over active treatments (g = 0.24 [0.12, 0.36]; k = 34). This advantage was almost entirely attributable to comparisons with non-trauma-focused therapies (g = 0.40); PE showed no meaningful superiority over other trauma-focused protocols such as Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR; g = 0.04). Neither trauma type nor population (military vs. civilian) significantly moderated outcomes. Session number did not predict effect size; briefer protocols warrant evaluation. In an exploratory analysis, effect estimates for complex-presentation samples (k = 14, g = 0.50 [0.32, 0.68]) and unselected samples (k = 40, g = 0.37 [0.21, 0.52]) were not significantly different; however, the imprecision of the estimated contrast precludes conclusions of equivalence. Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) certainty was moderate for both primary comparisons, downgraded for inconsistency. These findings support PE as a first-line PTSD treatment while indicating that its efficacy is shared with other trauma-focused approaches. The exploratory subgroup finding requires confirmation in better-powered studies using prospectively specified classifications. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Balancing blue growth and the ecosystem approach: policy coherence in Sweden’s Marine Spatial Plan for the Baltic Sea
Abstract: There is growing expectation within the European Union (EU) that Marine Spatial Planning (MSP) – the public process for allocating marine space among competing uses – can support environmental restoration and economic development through the Ecosystem Approach (EA), which seek to balance ecological, social, and economic objectives. This article examines how effectively MSP implements the EA in practice, using Sweden’s Baltic Sea plan as a case study. Building on Malawi Principle 3 of the Convention on Biological Diversity, the analysis assesses policy coherence across governance levels (global and EU policies to national planning) and across key sectors (offshore wind, fisheries, and shipping). A qualitative document analysis is used to evaluate alignment in terms of rhetorical ambitions, planning procedures, and actual operationalisation. The findings show that Sweden’s MSP reflects EA principles in policy discourse but lacks strong procedures and tools to manage ecological trade-offs in practice. Monitoring systems remain weak, ecological targets are limited, and legal authority to reconcile sectoral conflicts is constrained. Across sectors, sustainability goals are articulated but coordination mechanisms are insufficient. Offshore wind benefits from strong political support but fragmented permitting. Shipping is promoted as climate-efficient, yet ecological impacts receive limited attention. Fisheries emphasise socio-economic resilience but are weakly integrated with spatial planning and conservation measures. Overall, Sweden’s MSP demonstrates rhetorical alignment with the EA but limited operational capacity to balance competing sectoral interests with ecosystem integrity. These challenges mirror broader EU trends, suggesting that MSP remains symbolic unless cross-sectoral coordination, adaptive monitoring, and legal accountability are strengthened. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Language mutations and the persistence of COVID-19 conspiracy theories on social media
Abstract: This study investigates how language mutations affect the persistent diffusion of COVID-19 conspiracy theories on social media. Drawing on a three-year dataset of conspiracy-related posts from X, and applying computational linguistic analysis alongside survival modelling, we find that conspiracy claims with greater semantic mutations have substantially longer lifespans. Mutations in psycholinguistic properties, including pronouns, social reference words, cognitive process terms, risk- and health-related vocabularies, are associated with extended lifespans. Mutations in actor, action and target (AAT) categories are associated with longer lifespans as well. Qualitative analysis identifies two predominant mutation patterns: simplification and assimilation, at both linguistic and AAT structural levels. Taken together, the results advance our understanding of the association between language mutations and conspiracy persistence online and shed lights on longitudinal content moderation strategies. We argue that content moderation should consider the mutability of conspiracy claims and focus on the core claims that can address their potential variations. © 2026

Authors: Holmes R.L.
Title: Ignorance by Design: Unmasking Our Unknowing in a World Shaped by Whiteness
Source title: Ignorance by Design: Unmasking Our Unknowing in a World Shaped by Whiteness
Abstract: When ignorance is woven into the stories, institutions, and practices of everyday life, it limits both what we know and what we are able to know. In Ignorance by Design, Ryan L. Holmes reframes ignorance as an active social force rather than a simple absence of knowledge, showing how, in certain forms, it is cultivated to uphold structures of white male supremacy. Moving across philosophy, race theory, and the sociology of knowledge, Holmes maps the ways "unknowing" is built into institutions, everyday language, and the stories people tell about themselves and others. What emerges is a portrait of a culture in which misunderstanding is not accidental but patterned, shaping perception while insulating dominance from meaningful challenge. Holmes identifies distinct modes of ignorance at work today and links them to forms of epistemic injustice, revealing how power is sustained not only through what societies remember but also through what they are conditioned to overlook. He examines Whiteness as an evolving epistemic social project that continually redraws the boundaries of belonging, authority, and credible knowledge. At the book's core is a sustained focus on storytelling: the dominant narratives that normalize inequality and the counter-narratives that make recognition - and transformation - possible. The result is a probing, accessible account of knowledge's blind spots - and an invitation to reshape the stories, relationships, and institutions through which we come to know one another. © Bloomsbury Publishing Inc, 2027.

Title: Smiling your way to happiness or misery? Experimental tests of competing perspectives [Registered Report - stage II]
Abstract: Researchers and lay people alike have long been interested in whether people can make themselves feel happier if they simply fake a smile. Thus far, two largely disconnected research communities have provided seemingly competing answers to this question, with (a) emotion embodiment researchers observing positive causal links in experimental contexts, and (b) emotion labor researchers observing negative associations in real-world work contexts. In the present work, we conducted a pre-registered conceptual extension of the largest experimental demonstration of the positive effects of posed smiles on mood, focusing on three factors that may explain why such effects fail to generalize to real-world work contexts. More specifically, we tested whether posed smiles fail to improve mood (1) in negative contexts, (2) when performed repeatedly, and/or (3) when performed to avoid punishment. Ultimately, results did not support any one hypothesis. In negative contexts, participants reported higher levels of happiness after posing a single smile (vs. expressing themselves naturally). However, such effects were (a) diminished when posing smiles repeatedly and (b) virtually nil with the additional threat of punishment. Furthermore, in positive contexts, posing smiles repeatedly or under the threat of punishment led to lower self-reported happiness. Taken together, results suggest that posed smiles can be mood-boosting in some contexts and mood-dampening in others — a potential source of both happiness and misery. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Student engagement at the heart of teacher well-being: A network analysis of teachers’ professional, relational, and health-related resources
Abstract: Teacher well-being is increasingly viewed as a multidimensional construct with implications for teacher retention, instructional quality, and professional learning. Guided by Viac and Fraser’s (2020) framework, this study examined the network of cognitive, social, subjective, and physical and mental well-being indicators among Portuguese teachers. Participants completed measures of motivation, commitment, purpose, emotions, resilience, self-efficacy, school relationships, and physical and mental symptoms. Title: Quantifying the influence of fire and social factors on pre-evacuation time: a VR study based on an editable Multi-player Desktop VR platform
Abstract: Pre-evacuation time is a critical determinant of life safety outcomes during building fires, yet the relative quantitative influence of fire-related and social factors remains poorly understood. This study quantitatively investigates the influence of fire and social factors on pre-evacuation time using an editable Multi-player Desktop VR platform. A total of 210 participants were recruited to participate in VR experiments across different fire location scenarios. A Random Forest model was further constructed to evaluate and rank the relative importance of these factors. Results show that pre-evacuation time follows a Weibull distribution. Despite similar overall distributions between scenarios, there are notable differences in spatial distribution. The relationship between proportion of fire visibility time and pre-evacuation time is non-monotonic. However, when proportion of fire visibility time exceeds 0.34, pre-evacuation times become consistently short. Social reference time emerged as the dominant influencing factor, accounting for 47% of the total explained variance in the Random Forest model, substantially exceeding all fire-related factors. Title: A CRITICAL PERSPECTIVE ON ECTHR JURISPRUDENCE ON RACIAL PROFILING IN POLICING: THREE PROPOSALS TO IMPROVE VICTIMS’ ACCESS TO JUSTICE

Title: Environmental sensitivity and perceived social support in relation to adolescent eating disorder symptoms
Abstract: Eating disorders (EDs) frequently emerge during adolescence and are influenced by both individual and contextual factors. Among these, perceived social support has generally been associated with better outcomes, although findings remain inconsistent and may depend on both the source of support and individual differences in responsiveness to environmental inputs. The present study examined the role of Environmental Sensitivity (ES) and perceived social support in adolescent ED symptoms, focusing on different sources of support and their potential interaction within a vantage sensitivity framework. A sample of 466 adolescents (51.61% female; M = 14.80) completed self-report measures of ED symptoms, ES, and perceived social support. At a bivariate level, higher perceived support from family, teachers, friends, and peers was associated with lower ED symptoms. In covariate-adjusted models, only teachers' and family's support remained a significant predictor, while peer-related sources were no longer associated with ED symptoms. Exploratory analyses suggested a sex-specific pattern, whereby the association between perceived social support and ED symptoms appeared to vary as a function of ES among males, but not females. These findings suggest that the association between social support and adolescent ED symptoms may depend on its source. Moreover, ES was consistently associated with ED symptoms. Title: Beyond the tragedy of the commons: Spiritual legitimacy, customary land governance, and community development in Northern Ghana
Abstract: Customary land governance is widely studied in Northern Ghana for its failures, yet its contributions to social cohesion, community development, and resource management are underexplored. This study bridges that gap using a qualitative case of the Bole Traditional Area in the Savannah Region of Ghana, where customary land governance remains active and legitimate despite pressures from land commercialisation, small-scale mining and urbanisation. Drawing on twenty key informant interviews (KII) with land custodians (tindanas), chiefs, and community members, with eight focus group discussions, two each across the four communities (Kalba, Gbeniyiri, Soma, and Datompilayiri). The study employed thematic data analysis to examine how traditional values shape land governance, conflict resolution, environmental stewardship, and access equity. This study builds on Ostrom's Common Pool Resource Theory, expanding it by showing how spiritual legitimacy is central and not periphery to effective customary governance, a dimension historically neglected by the framework. Authors: Liu N.; He H.; Kim S.; Li A.
Title: Being hopeful: How parenting motivation influences pro-environmental behavior
Abstract: How to encourage pro-environmental behavior has long been a great concern for both the environment and society. The present research aims to address this issue from a novel perspective by examining how individual differences in parenting motivation influence pro-environmental behavior. In four studies, we found that participants who experienced higher parenting motivation tend to engage in more pro-environmental behavior. The effect was driven by hope, a special adaptive emotion that empowers individuals with resilience and helps them overcome challenges. We further illustrated that the effect emerges when the perceived environmental threat was salient (vs. not salient), indicating the adaptive and evolutionary function of parenting motivation. This research not only contributes to the parenting motivation literature by advancing understanding of its influence on pro-environmental behavior, but also contributes to the pro-environmental behavior and the hope literature by identifying individual differences in parenting motivation as a key antecedent. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Federico G.; Osiurak F.
Title: Click, swipe & tap … how digital habits rewire cognition
Abstract: Digital technologies shape how people think, learn and act, yet evidence on neural mechanisms supporting their use remains fragmented across research domains. Here, we make the case for a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology: a mechanistic research programme that examines how technologies recruit, extend and reshape cognition across the lifespan. By situating digital interaction within the broader domain of human tool use, we synthesise behavioural and neuroimaging evidence using the recently proposed hub-and-processors model of technological cognition as an organising framework. This model links modality-sensitive neural systems (processors) to three integrative hubs: the area PF of the left inferior parietal lobule, which supports causal–mechanical inference; the anterior temporal lobe, which supports cross-modal conceptual knowledge; and the precuneus, which supports visuospatial processing. Flexible scheduling and executive control in the left inferior frontal gyrus coordinate the operation of these hubs. The programme also places social cognition at the centre of digital interaction. Technologies that communicate, personalise their responses or conceal their causal mechanisms—including recommender systems and conversational artificial intelligence (AI)—may engage processes involved in social learning, intention attribution and communication, prompting users to treat digital artefacts as partly agent-like. We set out a research agenda that integrates the physical and social dimensions of technological cognition and generates testable predictions for cognitive assessment, technological reserve across the lifespan, digital markers of neurodegeneration, neurorehabilitation and human–AI interaction. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wu Q.; Luo J.
Title: Artificial intelligence in child welfare and family services: a scoping review of applications and ethics
Abstract: Objective: This scoping review examined applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in child welfare and family services and synthesized associated ethical considerations. Method: Seven databases were searched for articles published between 2015 and 2025. Twenty-three articles met the inclusion criteria. Results: Most identified articles originated from the United States, used machine learning approaches, and relied primarily on administrative datasets, including child protection, health, and service records. AI was most often applied to risk prediction and early identification of child and family vulnerability, followed by decision support and administrative automation. Most applications remained in the development, testing, or validation stage, with limited evidence on real-world implementation or family outcomes. Ethical concerns extended across the AI lifecycle, from data preparation and algorithmic processing to human-AI interaction, institutional governance, and societal impact. Key concerns included bias, fairness, interpretability, transparency, surveillance, misclassification, accountability, and implementation challenges. Conclusion: AI has potential to support prediction and service efficiency in child welfare and family services, but ethical and practical challenges limit its implementation. Future research should prioritize implementation studies, evaluation of child and family outcomes, and governance frameworks that support responsible AI use while protecting vulnerable populations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Van Thao N.; Herman H.
Title: Mental Health Awareness Campaigns on TikTok: A Critical Multimodal Discourse Analysis of Digital Health Education
Abstract: Mental health awareness has increasingly expanded beyond traditional healthcare institutions into digital environments, particularly on social media platforms such as TikTok. As one of the most popular short-video applications among adolescents and young adults, TikTok has become an influential medium for disseminating mental health information, promoting awareness, and encouraging public engagement. This study investigated how mental health awareness campaigns on TikTok construct educational meaning through linguistic, visual, and multimodal discourse practices. This study employed a qualitative research design using Critical Multimodal Discourse Analysis (CMDA), integrating Critical Discourse Analysis, Multimodal Discourse Analysis, and the Health Belief Model. The dataset consisted of 35 TikTok videos, including 30 user-generated awareness videos and 5 sponsored mental health advertisements, selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed by examining the verbal content, visual representations, multimodal elements, and persuasive health communication strategies. Four dominant discourse themes emerged from the analysis: mental health as a personal struggle, self-care as a solution, peer-to-peer emotional support, and professional help-seeking awareness. Creators combined personal storytelling, visual symbolism, emotional framing, and interactive features to construct mental health awareness messages. Across the corpus, captions, imagery, music, facial expressions, and other semiotic resources worked alongside verbal language to frame mental health messages as accessible, emotionally resonant, and educationally oriented. The study concludes that TikTok functions as an emerging platform for digital health education, where users act as information consumers and informal educators. This analysis positions TikTok as a significant site for examining how mental health knowledge, experiential authority, peer solidarity, and professional guidance are discursively represented in English-language digital communications. Authors: Arndt M.; Helming K.
Title: Diversification and agricultural resilience – what determines success?
Abstract: Context: Agriculture today operates amid multiple crises, affecting its economic, social, and environmental performance. The resilience of agricultural systems – their ability to maintain main functions under stresses – is shaped by the three resilience capacities: robustness, adaptability, and transformability. Since the 1960s, Europe's agricultural focus was characterized by an emphasis on specialization and increasing productivity within the economic paradigm of economies of scale. However, large, specialized farming structures exhibit a lack of flexibility, which hinders their ability to adapt or transform. Objective: The objective of this study was to examine whether, and under which conditions, agricultural diversification measures can enhance resilience in organic agriculture. Methods: We conducted participatory research employing the Resilience Assessment Framework to organic farming systems for a case study in Brandenburg, Germany. Results and conclusions: Results showed that the success of diversification measures is influenced by numerous resilience attributes of the organic farming system, which can be categorized into personal factors, location-specific factors, governmental factors, and economic factors. While location factors are inherent and immutable, all other factors are influenced by policy decisions. Consequently, policy can be used to direct diversification. Significance: While economies of scope can provide an attractive alternative to economies of scale, the success of diversification strategies depends on appropriate timing and context-specific conditions. The Common Agricultural Policy Framework of the European Union could support their implementation not only through financial incentives, but also by fostering local development initiatives and advisory services that help shape social norms. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Liu J.; Li X.; Meng B.; Zhan D.; Liu X.
Title: Mapping public disability-inclusive awareness in Chinese cities: Insights from geotagged social media data
Abstract: Public disability-inclusive awareness is a critical yet underexamined dimension of inclusive urban development. While existing studies has extensively addressed physical accessibility, services, and institutional arrangements, far less is known about how disability is perceived and discussed in daily urban life. This study investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics of public disability-inclusive awareness across more than 300 Chinese cities using large-scale geotagged social media data. Drawing on nearly 700 million geotagged Weibo posts from 2016 to 2022, we identified 459,694 disability-related posts using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based model. City-level indicators were constructed to capture three interrelated dimensions of public awareness: attention, attitudes, and discourse. The results reveal substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in disability-inclusive awareness across Chinese cities. Contrary to conventional expectations, public attention and positive attitudes toward disability do not increase with city size. Instead, many smaller cities in central and western China exhibit higher attention levels and more positive attitudes, whereas several large eastern megacities show comparatively lower engagement. Nationally, disability-related discussions expanded over time in both intensity and thematic breadth, increasingly encompassing diverse disability types, social inclusion, and (in)accessible environments. However, local urban discourse became more concentrated around volunteering and service-oriented themes, accompanied by declining topic diversity across cities. By providing the first large-scale, city-level assessment of public disability-inclusive awareness in China, this study demonstrates the value of geosocial media data for capturing the socio-spatial dynamics of disability-related perceptions and contributes new empirical evidence to support more inclusive urban research and governance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Li Y.; Xie M.; Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Wang Y.; Qu X.
Title: Deep learning ensemble for capturing urban mobility dynamics: A review of big data and AI applications in traffic prediction
Abstract: Understanding travel demand dynamics in rapidly urbanizing environments requires analytical perspectives that transcend traditional disciplinary boundaries. As traffic systems evolve into intricate networks influenced by social interactions, technological innovations, and stochastic behaviors, capturing their non-linear and dynamic nature becomes critical for effective urban management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of ensemble deep learning frameworks and argues that they can serve not only as predictive tools but also as analytical approaches for understanding the complexity of modern mobility systems. Firstly, we synthesize the theoretical underpinnings of ensemble deep learning, highlighting how ensemble strategies (e.g., Bagging, Boosting, Stacking) mirror multifaceted decision-making processes by aggregating diverse model perspectives to handle data heterogeneity. Secondly, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art deep learning (DL) architectures (including CNNs, GCNs, RNNs and GRUs) and their integration strategies, examining their role in utilizing multi-source big data derived from vehicular sensing and environmental contexts to enhance prediction reliability. Furthermore, this review investigates how ensemble deep learning frameworks enhance system adaptability and generalization by synthesizing the complementary features of multiple models, thereby providing dependable analytical tools for advanced traffic management and planning. Finally, we identify critical challenges and future opportunities, particularly in multimodal data fusion and cross-domain learning, aiming to inform practical strategies for achieving sustainable and resilient intelligent transportation systems (ITS). © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Are you looking for secrets? How autonomy and norms shape concealment
Abstract: This paper examines why individuals conceal information from others. Drawing on a recent theory about the origins of concealment, we argue that concealment stems from two primary sources: the desire for autonomy and norms of concealment. Using a nationally representative probability survey, we find that a desire for autonomy in two different domains—intimate relationships and work—is associated with concealment from romantic partners and coworkers/clients in those contexts. We also find that concealment is correlated with a descriptive and moral norm of concealment, with the moral norm having a weaker effect at work than in intimate relationships. Title: Can large language models interpret unstructured chat data on dynamic group decision-making processes? evidence on joint destination choice
Abstract: Social activities result from complex joint activity-travel decisions between group members. While observing the decision-making process of these activities is difficult via traditional travel surveys, the advent of new types of data, such as unstructured chat data, can help shed some light on these complex processes. However, interpreting these decision-making processes requires inferring both explicit and implicit factors. This typically involves the labor-intensive task of manually reading and annotating dialogues to capture context-dependent meanings shaped by social and cultural norms. Against this background, this study evaluates the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate and complement human annotation in interpreting decision-making processes from group chats, using data on joint eating-out activities in Japan as a case study. We designed a prompting framework inspired by the knowledge acquisition process in Knowledge Graph (KG) construction. This framework sequentially extracts key decision-making factors, including the group-level restaurant choice set and outcome, individual preferences of each alternative, and the specific attributes driving those preferences. This structured process guides the LLM to interpret group chat data step-by-step, converting unstructured dialogues into structured tabular data describing decision-making factors. To evaluate LLM-driven outputs, we conduct a quantitative analysis using a human-annotated ground truth dataset and a qualitative error analysis to examine model limitations. Results show that while the LLM reliably captures explicit decision-making factors, it struggles to identify nuanced implicit factors that human annotators readily identified. We further pinpoint specific contexts where the LLM performs poorly, establishing a boundary for when LLM-based extraction can be trusted versus when human oversight remains essential. These findings highlight both the potential and limitations of LLM-based analysis for incorporating non-traditional data sources on social activities into activity-based models. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Authors: Zhang H.; Zhou K.; Wu J.; Gao X.; Qin Y.
Title: The brick-to-jade effect of AI hallucination: Evidence from chatbots in online communities
Abstract: In online communities, user participation behaviors (e.g., comments and likes) are the source of sustainable development for these communities. Community platforms are actively exploring measures to enhance user participation. Benefiting from generative AI technologies, online communities have begun to deploy intelligent chatbots. However, the content generated by these bots often suffers from the problem of AI hallucination. Prior studies indicate that AI hallucination exerts negative impacts in fields such as healthcare and tourism, yet there has been limited focus on its influence on user participation behaviors in online communities. This study employs a total of 161,130 chatbot records from Sina Weibo over one year. Based on the theory of prosocial behavior, we examine the impact of AI hallucination on user participation behaviors in online communities, as well as the moderating effects of day type and active period. The study reveals that AI hallucination exhibits a “brick-to-jade effect”, increasing comments from users while simultaneously reducing their likes. Additionally, the study also shows that the positive correlation between AI hallucination and users' comments is stronger during weekends and active period. Theoretically, this study examines the effect of AI hallucination from the perspective of users, expanding the scope of research on the effect of AI hallucination and proving that AI hallucination has a positive role on the comments of online community users. This breaks the common perception in existing research that AI hallucination is always negative. Practically, it has significant reference value for community managers to stimulate user participation behaviors and enhance their activity levels. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Park D.J.
Title: Crossing disciplinary boundaries: Interdisciplinary doctorates, field-of-study mismatch, and job satisfaction
Abstract: This study bridges research on interdisciplinary research and field-of-study mismatch to examine how interdisciplinary doctoral training is associated with early-career job satisfaction, and whether this association varies by field-of-study mismatch. Using linked data from the Survey of Earned Doctorates and the Survey of Doctorate Recipients, I analyze U.S.-employed science and engineering doctorate recipients who earned their first doctoral degree from U.S. institutions between 2010 and 2017. Doctorate recipients with interdisciplinary dissertations (hereafter, interdisciplinary doctorates) report lower overall job satisfaction than mono-disciplinary peers and are more likely to work in occupations outside their primary doctoral field (field-of-study mismatch). Field-of-study mismatch moderates the association between interdisciplinary doctorates and job satisfaction: the job-satisfaction gap between interdisciplinary doctorates and mono-disciplinary peers is smaller among those in mismatched jobs than among those in matched jobs. Working outside one's primary doctoral field is not uniformly associated with worse outcomes and may be linked to higher job satisfaction among some doctorate recipients, particularly interdisciplinary doctorates. These findings suggest that universities and institutions promoting interdisciplinarity should also strengthen interdisciplinary career advising, and that doctorate recipients with interdisciplinary dissertation research may benefit from exploring a wider set of career opportunities beyond their primary field. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Experience Modulates Visuocortical Reponses to Faces in 3- to 6-Year-Old Children
Abstract: Face processing is essential for social cognition, yet little is known about how race and gender biases in face processing develop as children encounter increasingly diverse social environments. This study investigated how preschool-aged children’s prior familiarity with race and gender groups influences neural responses during face processing. Children aged 3-6 years viewed a stream of face stimuli using a fast period visual stimulation (FPVS) technique to record steady state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs). In this task, images of different faces from one race/gender group were presented at 6 Hz (base category), with every fifth face presentation from a different race or gender, eliciting an oddball response at 1.2 Hz. Familiarity with different race and gender groups was determined by parental report. Robust frequency-tagged neural responses were observed across conditions, indicating reliable face processing responses. Faces from familiar race groups elicited larger general visual responses (6 Hz), whereas oddball responses (1.2 Hz) were enhanced for faces from unfamiliar race groups. These results suggest that children's prior familiarity with race groups biases visuocortical responses to faces and sensitivity to changes within the visual stream. No significant effects of face gender were observed. Topographic analyses revealed increasing right occipitotemporal activity with age, suggesting emerging lateralization of face processing networks. These findings demonstrate that experience with race groups, but not gender, modulates neural responses to faces in early childhood, and highlights the importance of real-world social exposure as a contributor to face-processing biases. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Incentive design in gamified cyber security training: the roles of loss aversion and fixed rewards
Abstract: Human cognitive vulnerabilities remain the primary attack vector in organisational cyber security, yet traditional security education, training, and awareness (SETA) often fails to address this due to repetitive compliance formats and subsequent knowledge decay. Although gamification is widely proposed as a strategy to mitigate this ‘advice fatigue’, many implementations treat points-based incentives as a uniform motivational mechanism. This study examines the learning effects of two psychologically distinct points-based architectures: loss aversion (LA), operationalised through punitive point and streak deductions, and fixed rewards (FR), operationalised through positive point and streak accumulation. Using a two-cycle design science research approach, we evaluated these competing architectures in a pilot study (n = 27) and a larger-scale evaluation involving online crowd workers recruited through Prolific (n = 128). The results suggest a trade-off between experiential flow and productive cognitive friction. While participants in the FR condition reported descriptively higher mean scores across user engagement scale (UES-SF) dimensions, these between-group differences were statistically non-significant, and translated into only modest overall knowledge gains (+4.65%). In contrast, the LA condition appeared to introduce a form of productive cognitive friction. Although participants perceived this condition less favourably, the prospect of losing points may have encouraged more effortful, reflective (System 2) processing, resulting in statistically significant overall knowledge gains (+10.71%). These results suggest that points-based gamification mechanisms should not be viewed as interchangeable motivational tools. We propose a potential design trade-off between maximising user engagement and promoting deeper cognitive processing to guide SETA developers in strategically incorporating friction and reward mechanisms. © 2026 The Authors

Title: What primates know about other minds and how often they use it: A computational approach to comparative theory of mind
Abstract: Can non-human primates (NHPs) represent other minds? Answering this question is difficult because primates can fail tasks due to a lack of motivation or succeed through simpler strategies. Here, we address these challenges through a computational theory-testing framework for NHP Theory of Mind. In this framework, each theory combines a proposed social representation with a parameter for how often it is used. Fitting these models makes explicit an assumption that existing accounts leave unstated: how often NHPs must rely on a posited representation for that account to fit the data. This allows us to move beyond dichotomous positions about the presence or absence of Theory of Mind and instead analyze graded patterns of behavior as a combination of cognitive representations and their use. We apply this approach to one of the most foundational and well-studied aspects of Theory of Mind: the relation between seeing and knowing. Our results show that only theories in which NHPs have some representation of other minds can capture the qualitative pattern of successes and failures across five classic perspective-taking paradigms. However, these theories vary in their reliance on their representations, each showing significantly lower reliance than a human baseline. These results suggest that human and NHP social cognition differ in terms of reliance and possibly also in terms of representational complexity. © 2026

Title: Demographic and religious correlates of prejudice across 66 countries: The moderating role of national human development
Abstract: Prejudice remains a persistent social issue, yet limited evidence exists on how its predictors differ across countries. Data from Wave 7 of the World Values Survey were used to construct a generalized prejudice index based on self-reported xenophobia, homophobia, and sexism in a sample of 97,220 adults from 66 societies (M age = 43.18, SD age = 16.58, 52.6% female). Age, gender, education, income, subjective social class, and religiosity were examined as predictors of prejudice, and it was assessed whether these associations varied according to national human development. Bayesian multilevel analyses indicated that higher national human development was associated with lower average levels of prejudice. In the pooled global sample, older age and greater religiosity were positively associated with prejudice, whereas being female and having higher education, income, and subjective social class were negatively associated with prejudice. These relationships were, however, contingent on societal development. Cross-level interactions showed that demographic and religious predictors were weak or negligible in low-development countries but became stronger and statistically significant in high-development countries. In less developed societies, these predictors were largely unrelated to prejudice, suggesting that individuals’ demographic characteristics and religiosity say little about their level of prejudice in such societies. These results suggest that many findings often assumed to be general are in fact more characteristic of high‑development than low‑development contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Exploring individual, interpersonal, community, and environmental correlates of active commuting to school among Spanish adolescents: the PACO study
Abstract: Objectives To identify and analyze the individual, interpersonal, community, and environmental factors associated with active commuting to school (ACS) among Spanish adolescents, and to examine the contribution of correlates from multiple ecological domains to ACS. Data on potential correlates of ACS were collected using validated questionnaires (individual and interpersonal levels), school and city information (community level), and GIS-based indicators and MAPS-Global audits (environmental level). Results At the individual level, ownership of two or more motorized vehicles, identified motivation, and perceived environmental/safety barriers were associated with lower odds of ACS, whereas independent mobility, perceived competence for ACS, and integrated motivation were associated with higher odds. At the interpersonal level, parental barriers were associated with lower odds of ACS, whereas greater perceived proximity to destinations was associated with higher odds of ACS. At the community level, attending high-SES schools reduced the odds of ACS compared with low-SES schools. Environmentally, shorter home-school distance, greater leisure-time PA opportunities around the school, and higher aesthetic and social quality of the home neighborhood were significant correlates. In the final multivariable model, ACS was positively associated with perceived competence, integrated motivation, aesthetic and social quality, and higher active transport score around the home, whereas motorized vehicle ownership, identified motivation, perceived environmental/safety barriers, destinations and land use score, higher home-school distance, and higher grand score for leisure PA for home were negatively associated. Title: Creating realities on trial: experimental organizational development for sustainability in public institutions
Abstract: This article explores how to use the Experimental Organization Development (ExOD) approach to transform higher education institutions (HEIs) and applies it to ecological and social sustainability. The study investigates learning processes within universities and experimental pathways toward transformation. This undertaking matters because top-down directives at HEIs often fail to achieve lasting changes. Practically, this research explores alternatives for initiating change. Theoretically, we examine organizational learning processes for sustainability in public administration systems through a case study approach. The article compares and synthesizes findings from two cases that applied the ExOD approach to sustainability challenges at two German universities. The study collected qualitative and quantitative data to identify transformational processes and the potential of the chosen approach. The results from the two cases show broad consensus among participants that changes toward sustainability are necessary. In both cases, issues of status and hierarchies play an important role in preventing change. The ExOD approach can mitigate these issues to some degree because its participatory principle fosters acceptance and voluntary commitment to institutional transformation. Nevertheless, ExOD has limited scope and impact, and it primarily produces pilot projects and proofs of concept. Overall, this study implies that low-risk experimentation can facilitate organizational learning for institutional sustainability transitions. © 2026 The Author(s).
