Title: Behavioral trade-offs and heterogeneity in passenger response to in-train alighting information
Abstract: Real-time passenger information is increasingly deployed as a low-cost tool for managing crowding in urban rail, yet whether guidance delivered inside the train can shift passenger movement remains limitedly understood. This paper examines the stated behavioural trade-offs that determine when in-train alighting guidance translates into passenger relocation. A stated-preference survey of 216 younger adult MTR passengers in Hong Kong (1944 choice tasks), combined with a validated nine-item Public Transport Social Coexistence Scale, is analysed using a mixed logit model with latent variables. Movement difficulty emerges as the binding physical constraint: a one-level increase reduces the predicted probability of relocation by 18.8 percentage points, approximately 1.4 times the effect of distance. Sensitivity to difficulty is heterogeneous while sensitivity to distance is homogeneous, indicating that the effort dimension, involving subjective judgements about crowding, physical capacity and social comfort, generates taste variation that the spatial dimension does not. Seat availability reveals the most striking heterogeneity: approximately 43% of respondents treat a nearby seat as a comfort buffer encouraging movement rather than a reason to stay, a pattern invisible in the conditional logit baseline. The perceived social environment measurably shifts willingness to relocate, with cooperative atmospheres facilitating movement and frustration motivating it through a distinct channel. These findings reframe in-train guidance as a behavioural intervention embedded in socio-physical context. Four design principles, including situational feasibility, social awareness, behavioural realism and distributive attentiveness, are developed to translate the empirical trade-offs into actionable constraints for metro operators and information system designers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Co-producing sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries on the MOSE megaproject: Media frames of continuity, stability and transformation in Venice
Abstract: In Europe, sea level rise adaptation is strongly reliant on technological and engineering solutions. Megaprojects such as Venice’s mobile floodgate system MOSE are meant to provide protection to coastal areas. Due to their complexity and sizeable impact, however, megaprojects tend to be highly contentious. This article explores the interplay of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries in MOSE and how they build a collective past, present, and imagined future. Using data from Italian media, we identify frames that combine sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries that co-produce a legitimation of MOSE through techno-optimistic ideas of uniqueness and innovation, thereby illustrating how cultural and historical values shape spatial and sociotechnical imaginaries to construct the acceptance of wide-scale megaprojects. However, imaginaries of megaprojects also reveal contradictions: when ecological issues are framed as invasive events, imaginaries reject techno-optimism and place nature at the top of the hierarchy of space and place. Our study helps to deepen the conceptual understanding of sociotechnical and spatial imaginaries by looking at how they intertwine with temporal and spatial-hierarchical dimensions. Authors: Sergi A.; Storti L.
Title: Recognizing La Cosa Nostra: The Enduring Saga of the Italian American Mafia in New York
Source title: Recognizing La Cosa Nostra: The Enduring Saga of the Italian American Mafia in New York
Abstract: Force may establish power, but recognition is what sustains it. This book offers a contemporary re-examination of La Cosa Nostra (LCN) in New York City, moving beyond outdated images of a monolithic criminal hierarchy to reveal startlingly flexible and adaptive social formations. Drawing on judicial records, investigative findings, and informal interviews, Anna Sergi and Luca Storti argue that the Five Families' continued relevance depends as much on symbolic resources as on material capabilities. Using a framework centered on social recognition and reputation, the book shows how LCN functions as a “heritage brand,” in which names, rituals, and circulating narratives operate as durable currencies that structure criminal relationships, regulate markets, and reproduce authority across time and space. The authors demonstrate how the families now operate through semi-autonomous crews and pragmatic cross-family collaboration, where formal membership enhances credibility without enforcing rigid command-and-control. Case studies-from gambling schemes to labor union infiltration-illustrate how selective territorial engagement, strategic visibility, and narrative management enable the mafia to extract value and broker protection while minimizing overt violence. The analysis also highlights enduring transnational ties between New York and Sicily, showing how shared rituals, migration narratives, and cross-border brokerage transform symbolic capital into operational capacity. These connections reinforce a mutually sustaining relationship between the American and Sicilian branches, anchoring contemporary practices in a transatlantic system of meaning and exchange. Recognizing La Cosa Nostra reframes the modern mafia as a system sustained by “soft infrastructure”-stories, reputations, and shared cultural knowledge-rather than brute force alone. In doing so, it invites scholars and practitioners alike to rethink organized crime as a form of governance rooted in recognition and legitimacy, not merely corruption and coercion. Authors: Li X.; Wang Y.; Wang H.; Yu M.
Title: Deconstructing the heterogeneity of adolescent social anxiety: A cognitive diagnostic approach from a sex perspective
Abstract: Background The cognitive vulnerability patterns of adolescent social anxiety are highly sex-specific. However, traditional data-driven subtyping approaches often overlook these sex-specific patterns due to a lack of direct theoretical mapping. This study introduces Cognitive Diagnosis Models (CDMs) to identify sex-specific cognitive subtypes, exploring how these cognitive patterns manifest within high-risk comorbid contexts. Methods A sample of 2005 Chinese adolescents (M age  = 12.9 years; 54.5% male) was assessed on four core cognitive attributes: post-event rumination, negative social interpretations, fear of negative evaluation, and public self-consciousness. Depressive (SMFQ) and anxiety (SCARED) symptoms were also measured. CDMs were fitted separately for males and females to derive cognitive profiles. Subtype distributions were then compared within high-depression ( n = 611; SMFQ ≥ 8), high-anxiety ( n = 408; SCARED ≥ 25), and high-comorbidity ( n = 312) subgroups. Results While a “Pervasive Cognitive Deficits” subtype was common, a significant sex-specific pattern emerged. Females were more likely to present with profiles high in post-event rumination and negative interpretations (an “internalizing-ruminative” pattern). In contrast, males were more likely to display profiles high in fear of negative evaluation and public self-consciousness (a “performance-monitoring” pattern). These sex-differentiated cognitive profiles were consistently observed across high-depression, high-anxiety, and high-comorbidity contexts. Conclusions As one of the first studies to apply CDM to adolescent social anxiety with sex-stratified analyses, our study extends the understanding of social anxiety heterogeneity beyond a uniform model. The identification of distinct, sex-specific cognitive subtypes suggests the potential value of developing targeted, sex-informed intervention frameworks, which represents an important direction for future clinical validation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Author full names: Bazouni, Ramona (60998032700); du Plooy, Daniel R. (57200277118); Karakas, Gabriella (58244350300)
Title: Cultural identity and well-being in migrant caregivers: A qualitative systematic review
Abstract: Informal caregivers from migrant communities face challenges navigating care responsibilities alongside cultural identity and acculturation pressures. This qualitative systematic review examined how cultural background and caregiver identity intersect to shape the well-being of informal caregivers from collectivist migrant communities living in individualist host countries. Following PROSPERO registration, a comprehensive search of four databases using the SPIDER framework identified 1433 records with 27 studies meeting inclusion criteria per PRISMA guidelines. The Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) assessed methodological quality while GRADE-CERQual determined confidence levels in the review findings. Five themes emerged. First, filial obligation revealed how cultural values provided moral meaning but guilt intensified when idealised care standards could not be met. Second, living between two cultures revealed role conflict and bicultural stress as caregivers navigated traditional versus host country values with intergenerational ambivalence between first- and second-generation migrants. Third, structural and cultural barriers explored how language barriers, acculturation gaps, culturally insensitive services, and stigma compounded caregiver burden and isolation. Fourth, faith and migration as dual sources of resilience and constraint. Fifth, the cumulative psychological toll documented distress, including chronic exhaustion, social withdrawal and in extreme cases suicidal ideation. Findings demonstrated cultural background and caregiver identity are deeply intertwined exerting both protective and risk related influences on well-being. Results highlight the need for culturally responsive assessments, service design, and policies supporting migrant caregivers. Future research should focus on longitudinal studies to track identity shifts and well-being across generations and care transitions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

(7006747503); Hellmann-Regen, Julian (55096975900); Roepke, Stefan (57213425403); Otte, Christian (56219197400); Wingenfeld, Katja (57207544363)
Title: Mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation effects on stress-induced cortisol and alpha-amylase in female patients with borderline personality disorder and healthy controls: A randomized placebo-controlled experimental study
Abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) has been associated with alterations in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, such as a blunted cortisol response to acute psychosocial stress. The mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) is involved in HPA-axis feedback regulation and plays a key role in stress regulation. In response to stress, pharmacological blockade of the MR leads to exaggerated cortisol release, but MR stimulation has not been investigated in BPD. This is of special interest as altered hippocampal feedback regulation, possibly due to MR dysfunction, has been suggested in BPD. In a double-blind, randomized design, 120 female patients with BPD and 120 healthy controls (HC) received 0.4 mg fludrocortisone or placebo. Two hours later, participants were exposed to the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) or a placebo version (pTSST). Salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase (sAA) were collected at baseline (T0), +120 min (T1, pre-(p)TSST), +135 min (T2) and + 195 min (T3) after drug intake. Despite reporting higher subjective affective response to stress, patients with BPD exhibited a blunted cortisol response to the TSST compared to HC after placebo. After fludrocortisone, cortisol values were diminished in both conditions and across groups. sAA increased in response to stress across groups and was not affected by MR stimulation. These findings demonstrate that BPD show a blunted cortisol response to stress. Because negative feedback through exogenous MR stimulation leads to comparable cortisol values in BPD and HC, these findings make it less likely that increased MR-mediated feedback is the primary mechanism underlying the blunted cortisol response to stress in BPD. Title: Walk Score® as a moderator of neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage and psychological distress
Abstract: Introduction Neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage has been consistently associated with poorer mental health outcomes, while greater walkability has been shown to be beneficial. This study examined whether walkability moderates the association between neighbourhood socioeconomic disadvantage and psychological distress. Methods Data were drawn from wave 5 (2016) of the How Areas in Brisbane Influence Health and Activity (HABITAT) study and included 3088 mid-older aged adults who resided at the same address since baseline (2007). Psychological distress was assessed using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K6); neighbourhood disadvantage was measured using a census-derived index, analysed in quintiles; and walkability was determined using Walk Score®. Results Participants in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods had greater psychological distress compared to those in the least disadvantaged neighbourhoods (β = 0.48, 95%CI 0.09, 0.87; p = 0.016), however, there was no evidence of moderation by Walk Score. Conclusion Although walkable neighbourhoods have demonstrated health benefits, the results suggest that walkability alone may be insufficient to buffer the structural and social challenges present in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Local Knowledge of Climate Change: Insights From Traditional Fishermen in Lampung Bay, Indonesia
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study aims to assess the knowledge and perceptions of traditional Bagan fishermen operating in Lampung Bay regarding the dynamics of climate change. Lampung Bay serves as a center of fisheries activity, making coastal communities, including traditional Bagan fishermen, highly dependent on fisheries for their livelihoods. However, this area is highly vulnerable and heavily affected by climate change. This study employs a qualitative approach, utilizing data collected through in-depth interviews and participatory observations involving the traditional Bagan fishermen community, formal institutions specifically the Head of Kota Karang urban village, Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Agency of Lampung, and Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics of the Republic of Indonesia (BMKG) and informal institutions socio-economic institutions consisting of fishery product processing entrepreneurs, pelele (fish trader), konca (captain) and pelimelime (crew). The results indicate that despite being aware of the impacts of climate change on Lampung Bay, most fishing communities employ diverse adaptation strategies to overcome their inherent limitations. A critical determinant in constructing social resilience is the optimization of informal institutions. Based on these results, it is recommended to implement an adaptive climate change impact management policy with a participatory approach. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Authors: Uziel V.; Yuval F.
Title: Endorsement of a public off-the-shelf management strategy for fair urban public transportation
Abstract: Local transportation policy has a strong impact on residents’ quality of life and their access to social services, education, healthcare, housing, and jobs. It affects women differently than men due to differences in when they travel, the length of their trips, and women's often being accompanied by children. However, municipalities rarely consider gender in their transportation policy. Relying on three distinct scholarships – local management and the policymaking process, public transportation, and gender theories, which are rarely combined – we examine how the perceptions that guide policymakers in formulating policy about public transportation affect the gender sensitivity of the policy. Drawing on the qualitative narrative analysis of the 82 participants’ interviews and observations with policymakers in the administration of the city of Tel Aviv and in the Israeli Ministry of Transport, we reveal that personal and latent organizational aspects of the policymaking process strongly affect the key professionals and administrators when formulating policy. Our results emphasize that being a female policymaker or having sufficient relevant information or awareness about gender dimensions in transportation, while necessary, are not sufficient to bring about change. The obstacles typical of the bureaucratic environment that our interviewees identified—time, budgets, the constant need to deal with urgent matters, the lack of multi-disciplinary knowledge, and the tendency to seek ready-to-use policy instruments to cope with problems—are daunting. Therefore, we propose a public off-the-shelf management strategy for overcoming some of these obstacles. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Psychological and environmental factors influencing urban cycling: Insights from a pilot study
Abstract: Introduction Urban cycling represents a key strategy for promoting sustainable mobility and helping reduce the negative externalities caused by road traffic. However, its adoption remains limited due to several factors, not only related to the lack of adequate physical infrastructure, but also to socio-psychological and environmental aspects. Methods This pilot study examines the role of perceived danger, discomfort, and social norms in influencing cycling intentions in Cagliari, Italy. A sample of 109 participants was exposed to immersive scenarios depicting different urban cycling conditions, including variations in traffic levels, bicycle lane presence, urban greenery, and street furniture. Results Statistical analyses, including non-parametric tests and moderation models, suggested the presence of associations between perceived discomfort, danger, and vehicular interaction with cycling intentions. Scenarios incorporating cycling infrastructure were associated with lower perceived danger and discomfort and with higher reported cycling intention compared with the baseline scenario. Additionally, perceived social norms were positively and significantly associated with cycling intention in the best-rated scenario; however, the moderation analysis provided no evidence that perceived danger moderated this association. Conclusions Overall, the findings tentatively highlight the potential relevance of both environmental and socio-psychological factors in shaping cycling intentions. However, given the pilot nature of the study, the non-probability sample, and the use of simulated scenarios, the results should be interpreted with caution. Further research, ideally involving real-world settings and behavioral measures, is needed to better understand these relationships. These preliminary insights may nonetheless inform ongoing discussions on sustainable urban mobility and the possible role of infrastructure and social factors in encouraging cycling. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Threshold concepts in Primary Health Care nursing education – What they are, why they matter and how to facilitate learning: A reflexive thematic analysis
Abstract: Aim: To identify threshold concepts encountered by undergraduate nursing students during Primary Health Care placements, examine influences and supports that help students master these concepts, and explore how addressing them may better prepare students for placement and future workforce. Background: Primary Health Care workforce shortages are a growing international concern, emphasising the need to better prepare nursing students for the complexity of Primary Health Care practice. Threshold Concepts provide a lens for examining how students develop new ways of thinking and learning; however, little is known about the threshold concepts encountered during Primary Health Care placements and experiences. Understanding these concepts may strengthen future workforce preparation. Design: A qualitative descriptive study. Participants: Eight undergraduate nursing students who had completed Primary Health Care placements. Method: Semi-structured interviews were conducted in 2026, via an online platform and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Two threshold concepts underpinning transformative learning during Primary Health Care placements were identified. The first transformed students' understanding of patients by shifting their perspective from illness- and procedure-focused care to understanding the person within the broader personal, social and environmental factors that shape health. The second transformed students' understanding of nursing by integrating previously fragmented knowledge to understand the whole clinical picture. Threshold concept mastery was facilitated through authentic Primary Health Care experiences, supervisor1 guidance and debriefing, with supervisors playing a critical role by making expert thinking explicit. Conclusion: These findings provide new insight into how transformative learning occurs during Primary Health Care placements. Identifying threshold concepts and the educational processes that support students to master them offers a theoretical foundation for intentionally designing learning experiences and supervision that better prepare graduates for contemporary nursing practice and the future Primary Health Care workforce. © 2026 The Authors

Title: A systematic approach to community of practice evaluation using the value creation framework
Abstract: Communities of Practice (CoPs) are widely used to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange across disciplines. However, systematic evaluations of them remain limited due to the dynamic nature of CoPs and the lack of tested methodologies. In this manuscript, we present the evaluation of a CoP conducted by pairing the Value Creation Framework with guidance developed by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Through qualitative analysis using a structured coding framework, we examine participants’ experiences in the CoP and assess how the CoP generated value for its members, the barriers that may have hindered value creation, and the perceived benefits of participation in the CoP at both personal and organizational levels. We explored two dynamic pairs of value cycles (i.e., immediate and potential; applied and realized), identified barriers (i.e., capacity) and facilitators (e.g., discussion-oriented atmosphere, relationship building, and trust) to value, and visualized how value flows across cycles to ensure CoPs meet members’ needs. Our findings demonstrate the utility of this systematic approach, highlighting the individual and organizational benefits of participation in a conservation-focused CoP while providing a concrete example of how the VCF can be operationalized in practice. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A cluster-randomized trial of a classroom-based narrative intervention for adolescent peer support
Abstract: Adolescents’ peer relationships are central to their flourishing, yet empirically validated, developmentally attuned interventions to support these relationships at school remain limited. This study evaluates Humans of Our Classroom , a classroom-based narrative intervention designed to strengthen adolescents’ peer connectedness through structured storytelling and reciprocal listening. Implemented in 46 classrooms across secondary schools in Spain and the United Kingdom, the intervention was evaluated using a cluster-randomized controlled trial with pre- and post-intervention surveys (N = 609). Intention-to-treat analyses showed a trend-level increase in Student Personal Support (β = 0.11, 95% CI: -0.01, 0.22, p = .067). Among classrooms that completed the full intervention, a per-protocol analysis found a statistically significant increase in Student Personal Support (β = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.25, p = .032); because per-protocol analyses do not preserve randomization, this finding should be interpreted as associational rather than causal. Further, exploratory subgroup analyses suggested larger associations for students with low social connectedness (e.g., high loneliness [β = 0.26, p = .008], low classmate support [β = 0.16, p = .050], low prosocial behavior [β = 0.18, p = .026]), low well-being (e.g., low meaning and purpose [β = 0.15, p = .048], or low flourishing [β = 0.21, p = .023]) at baseline, highlighting the intervention’s potential as a targeted protective factor for students with low social connection or wellbeing. Title: Conservation outcomes and human dimensions in semi-arid Africa: A review of the Save Valley Conservancy
Abstract: Conservation outcomes in semi-arid Africa are shaped by the interaction of ecological change, livelihood vulnerability and governance performance. This review synthesises 39 studies (1990–2025) on the Save Valley Conservancy (SVC) using an integrated Human Dimensions of Wildlife (HDW), environmental governance and Social–Ecological Systems (SES) framework. The analysis situates SVC within global debates on conservation in water-scarce landscapes, showing how climate variability, tenure insecurity and socio-economic precarity influence public attitudes, wildlife crime, restoration success and community agency. Biodiversity loss is greatest where land-use transitions, weak enforcement and climate-linked livelihood pressures converge while collaborative governance and targeted interventions have enabled local recoveries. Wildlife crime emerges both as a coping strategy and as a symptom of institutional fragmentation, reflecting broader patterns in climate-stressed rural economies. Restoration outcomes depend on equity, participation, and secure rights, underscoring that ecological recovery is a socio-political as well as a biophysical process. The review identifies climate-resilient livelihoods, inclusive and gender-responsive governance, integrated water management and participatory monitoring as universal requirements for sustainability in semi-arid conservation landscapes. By positioning SVC as a globally relevant case, the review demonstrates how conservation can evolve into a climate-resilient livelihood-enhancing system that aligns biodiversity protection with human well-being. © 2026

Author full names: Rodríguez, L.A. Oliveira (57649708600); Zapico, I. Benítez (60883040300); Palacio, D. Melendi (10739633200); Fernández, R. García (57189255259)
Title: Caller ID spoofing effectiveness: A socio-technical analysis of trust propagation and user behaviour
Abstract: Caller‑ID spoofing remains a critical enabler of telephone fraud and social engineering attacks across IP‑based and mobile telephony systems. While prior work has analysed signalling vulnerabilities and detection mechanisms, the combined influence of infrastructure-level trust models and human perception remains underexplored. This study presents a socio-technical analysis of caller‑ID spoofing by integrating an experimental evaluation of telephony infrastructures with a large-scale survey of user behaviour. We examine spoofing in three representative environments: VoIP systems and SIP trunk interconnections through controlled experiments, and mobile broadband networks using SIM Box devices through a trust-model-based analysis. Results show that spoofing feasibility depends primarily on implicit trust assumptions and validation policies rather than protocol weaknesses alone. Permissive identity validation in VoIP and SIP trunks allows manipulated caller identities to propagate across administrative domains, while SIM Box-based attacks exploit mobile broadband trust models using legitimate mobile identifiers. The user study (332 participants) reveals that decisions are heavily influenced by contextual cues such as institutional identifiers and number familiarity. The findings suggest that the perceived credibility and behavioural impact of spoofed caller identities arise from the interaction of infrastructure trust and human heuristics, highlighting the need for multi-layered mitigation strategies addressing signalling validation, trust relationships, and user awareness. Behavioural findings are based on self-reported intentions rather than observed real-world actions. Statistical results reveal a behavioural separation between call engagement and compliance, where contextual trust cues influence initial interaction, while knowledge and awareness primarily affect subsequent actions. © 2026 The Authors

Author full names: Quast, Pepijn (60748161100); Boon, Wouter (22733384300); Akerboom, Sanne (57214076685)
Title: Empowerment in EU energy law: connecting legal and sustainability transition perspectives
Abstract: The EU advances consumer empowerment as one of the pillars of energy legislation, aiming to transfer ownership of the energy transition to citizens. Rights and instruments have been introduced that offer citizens new ways of engaging with energy. However, EU energy legislation lacks a clear conceptual understanding of empowerment, which is required for crafting fit-for-purpose policy measures. We aim to provide a structured overview of current articulations of consumer empowerment in EU energy law by conducting a legislative analysis. To this end, we introduce a framework based on sustainability transitions theory that conceptualises empowerment according to four dimensions: 1) as identity-oriented or centred around resource-mobilisation, 2) more focused on autonomy or power-shift, 3) addressing the general public or specifically marginalised groups within society, and 4) more passive or more active. Application of the framework shows that EU energy legislation recognises consumer empowerment covering all four dimensions, and confirms the legislation’s ambition to provide a comprehensive empowerment agenda for citizens. Nonetheless, our findings also reveal limited reflection on the conceptual implications of such a broad empowerment agenda and the challenge of maintaining policies consistently. By drawing on insights from sustainability transitions we hope to encourage policy makers to strengthen conceptual clarity about the potential role and limitations of consumer empowerment in EU energy legislation. Conversely, we aim to raise awareness among transition scholars of the impacts of legislation on empowerment of actors in the energy transition by connecting legal and sustainability transition perspectives. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Kelebek-Küçükarslan G.
Title: Negotiating biological family contact in foster care: Practitioners’ experiences and challenges in Türkiye
Abstract: This study examines how practitioners in a foster care unit in Ankara, Türkiye, understand the role of biological families and how they carry out contact with them within existing professional and structural constraints. Data were collected via semi-structured interviews with 17 practitioners and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis in MAXQDA. The findings are organised into two main themes: professional and structural challenges in working with biological families, and balancing contact between children and their biological families. Practitioners reported substantial difficulties in engaging biological families, which they attributed to limited parental capacity, low levels of cooperation with services, and enduring psychosocial problems that restrict meaningful involvement in the foster care process. In accounting for these difficulties, practitioners frequently drew on stigmatising characterisations of biological parents, indicating how readily a vocabulary of individual deficit was available to them. Although practitioners strive to establish a child-centred equilibrium between children, their biological parents, and foster families, the findings revealed that these efforts are severely constrained by chronic staff shortages, heavy workloads, legislative ambiguities, and inadequate institutional capacity. Furthermore, family reunification was described as a rare occurrence, suggesting that, in this setting, foster care functions as a de facto long-term care arrangement. While regular and well-supported contact was perceived to enhance the emotional well-being of the children, irregular or poorly structured interactions were frequently associated with distinct emotional and behavioural challenges. Participants called for structured guidance and training programmes for biological families, improved physical and staffing capacity, and revision of the legislative framework governing contact. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Navigating tensions between community needs and research protocols: Lessons from a disrupted hybrid effectiveness-implementation study
Abstract: Effective implementation of evidence-based practices in community settings requires balancing scientific rigor with community partnership principles. While frameworks exist for documenting modifications to intervention delivery, no comparable approach addresses adaptations to research protocols themselves, particularly when community-based participatory research values are in tension with methodological ideals. We conducted a retrospective analysis of a disrupted hybrid effectiveness-implementation study of Prevent-Teach-Reinforce for Young Children within public early intervention services in Quebec, Canada. Using an adapted framework, we systematically documented 20 protocol modifications and adaptations, analyzed their rationale, related decision-making patterns, and consequences for implementation, research, and partnership outcomes. Three contextual factor clusters precipitated modifications: the restructuring of the provincial health system, the COVID-19 pandemic, and organizational instability in leadership and personnel. Adaptations and modifications fell into three thematic patterns: (1) strategic prioritization of immediate intervention delivery and project survival over research integrity (7); (2) participant-centered flexibility supporting accessibility (4); and (3) cumulative degradation through passive losses and structural failures (9). While many adaptations aligned with research-community partnership values by maximizing community benefit, they compromised research rigor (and sustainability) through losses in fidelity, internal validity, and data quality. We present our analytical approach building on several implementation science-based frameworks to systematically document research decisions, trade-offs, and gains/losses and share recommendations for responsive, transparent community-partnered research in similar contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Drivers of public and administrative perceptions on the transition toward biodiversity-friendly and sustainable urban green space management
Abstract: Urban green spaces are essential for maintaining biodiversity, mitigating climate-related impacts, and enhancing human well-being. Despite growing interest in biodiversity-friendly urban green space management, the socio-ecological factors associated with user support remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates users’ and administrative perspectives on biodiversity-friendly green space management at Justus Liebig University of Gießen, Germany, using an integrated socio-ecological approach. Survey data from 464 respondents were analyzed to examine biodiversity awareness, sense of responsibility, willingness to participate, and management preferences, as well as key barriers and facilitators associated with support for biodiversity-friendly management. Respondents showed high biodiversity awareness (96.5%) and sense of shared responsibility (74.7%), and favored semi-natural, multifunctional urban green spaces such as wildflower meadows (86.2%). These positive attitudes contrast with trends in green space availability, as contextual spatial per capita analysis (2010–2024) revealed a continuous decline in green space availability, underscoring increasing pressure on green infrastructure and the urgent need for management strategies aligned with the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 11.7. Exploratory structural equation modeling suggested that concern about climate change, recognition of habitat function, and social responsibility were positively associated with stated support for biodiversity-friendly management, whereas preferences for tidy lawns and perceived health risks showed negative associations with acceptance. This study contributes to broader discussions on socio-ecological urban transitions and suggests that participatory planning, best-practice examples, and communication strategies emphasizing ecological, climatic, and well-being benefits may help strengthen support for biodiversity-friendly management while aligning green space governance with biodiversity and sustainability objectives. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Addressing gender-based violence in disaster contexts: institutional, professional, and social responses to the 2021 La Palma (Spain) volcanic eruption
Abstract: This study explores the institutional, professional, and social responses to the gender-based violence that occurred in the wake of the 2021 volcanic eruption in La Palma, Spain. Using a qualitative methodology, it analyses the perspectives of 46 stakeholders—political decision-makers, technical staff, and social activists—acquired through in-depth interviews. The findings reveal that gender-based violence was initially overlooked during the crisis as emergency actions prioritised general safety and housing. The absence of gender-sensitive planning increased the vulnerability of women, particularly those already at risk. Although institutional efforts were later redirected to strengthen specialised services, the system remained strained owing to inadequate coordination, a lack of specific protocols, and insufficient professional training, reflecting a reactive, fragmented, and sector-specific approach. The study also highlights significant discrepancies between stakeholder groups, linked to their roles within the disaster management system. It underlines the urgent need for early-stage gender mainstreaming in disaster preparedness and response, including tailored protocols, continuous training of frontline personnel, and inter-institutional coordination. © 2026 ODI Global.

Title: Perceived time in the presence of others: Further arguments for an attentional view of social facilitation
Abstract: Although the effects of the presence of others on behavior constitute one of the oldest topics studied in social psychology, the reason why these effects occur is still the subject of scientific debate. Three hypotheses are commonly cited: (1) the presence of others facilitates dominant responses by increasing arousal, (2) it captures attention, or (3) it increases the efforts of those being observed. Few studies have attempted to distinguish between these explanations, and those that have done so have used a specific paradigm: the Stroop task. In the present study, we proposed an alternative approach based on the use of the temporal bisection task. In three studies, the bisection results showed a temporal shortening effect in social presence (that of an experimenter) consistent with an attentional distraction-related effect. Our results also provided the first evidence that this effect may be stronger when the attentional conflict between the task and the presence is unimodal (e.g., visual task and visual presence) rather than cross-modal (e.g., auditive task and visual presence). They also suggested that the social presence effect might be similar to that produced by a mechanical distractor, although the social nature of the distractor increased the attention-related effect. We discuss how variations in the presence and behavior of the experimenter could contribute to the difficulty of replicating certain studies in experimental psychology, given that the social presence of the experimenter is generally assumed to be innocuous. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Consumers’ psychological constructs regarding hybrid meat products: a scoping review
Abstract: Growing concerns about the health, social, and environmental impacts of high meat consumption have driven interest in plant-based diets and effective policies to reduce meat intake. Hybrid meat products, combining animal-derived ingredients and alternative protein sources, represent a promising strategy toward reduced meat consumption. This scoping review set out to systematically map and synthesise existing research on consumers’ psychological constructs and outcomes related to hybrid meat products. Using the Population, Concept, and Context (PCC) framework, this review focused on consumers of any demographic exposed to hybrid meat in various contexts, including retail, restaurant, and experimental settings. Seventy-nine peer-reviewed publications published up to December 2025 were included in the review after meeting the predefined inclusion criteria. Data extraction used a custom tool, and analysis involved frequency counts and descriptive summaries of key characteristics and themes. Across studies, hybrid meat products generally showed high consumer acceptance, liking, and preference, often exceeding expectations. Sensory appeal emerged as a strong predictor of liking and acceptance, and a wide range of ingredients and non-meat ratios (1% to 80%) were generally well accepted. Information provision could influence hybrid meat adoption, with environmental and health messages showing the greatest positive impact. “These findings contribute to understanding how hybrid meat products may fit within sustainable dietary transitions, while highlighting communication strategy and long-term behavioural adaptation as areas requiring further research.". © 2026 The Authors. Authors: SENGUL T.; SARIKOSE S.; GUL A.; MURAT N.
Title: The effectiveness of extended reality methods (augmented reality, virtual reality, and mixed reality) in enhancing clinical competency in nursing education: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Aim: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the overall effectiveness of extended reality technologies as a unified educational approach in supporting the development of clinical competency in nursing education. Design: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Methods: This review focused exclusively on randomized controlled trials to ensure methodological consistency and a high level of evidence. Articles were retrieved from seven major databases: PubMed, Cochrane Library, OVID, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and ScienceDirect. Searches were conducted using keywords related to extended reality technologies and nursing education, and the review was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 checklist. Results: The systematic review included 22 studies; 12 were included in the meta-analysis. The meta-analysis showed that extended reality technologies significantly improved exam performance and learning satisfaction compared with traditional educational methods. However, no significant effects were observed for communication skills, knowledge acquisition, self-confidence, simulation performance, or stress. High heterogeneity was identified for several outcomes, reflecting variability in intervention designs and participant characteristics. Conclusion: The findings suggest that extended reality technologies may support selected aspects of nursing education, particularly exam performance and learning satisfaction. However, the evidence does not consistently demonstrate significant effects across all domains of clinical competency, including communication skills, knowledge acquisition, self-confidence, simulation performance, and stress. Future studies using standardized protocols, validated measurement tools, and competency-driven outcome measures are needed to fully integrate extended reality technologies into evidence-based nursing education and practice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Approval mechanisms fueling digital hate: Online incivility and intolerance perpetration in four countries
Abstract: Xenophobic digital hate perpetration is a growing challenge across Europe, where heated debates over immigration have intensified recently. Understanding what fuels people's production and dissemination of digital hate from a trans-European perspective is crucial to successfully combating it. In response, this cross-sectional survey (total N = 4041) examines how perceived social norms against immigration are associated with online incivility and intolerance perpetration via approval of hateful anti-immigration content and contingent upon dispositional need for social approval in Austria, France, Hungary, and Sweden. Social norms refer to participants' perceptions of how widespread anti-immigration views are among the population in their country, among family and friends, and within their online network. Further, incivility refers to hostile content expressed in a rude or harsh manner, whereas intolerance captures exclusionary and dehumanizing language that can also be calm in tone. Path models revealed that content approval mediated relationships between social norms and both types of perpetration in all four countries. Importantly, need for social approval not only emerged as a robust predictor but also moderated links between content approval and both online incivility (except for Hungary) and intolerance perpetration. These findings deepen our understanding of digital hate perpetration and suggest actionable pathways for interventions. Addressing visible social norms on online platforms more directly may help reduce approval of hateful content, while minimizing social approval signals could limit the perceived rewards of perpetration. Since dispositional need for social approval was directly linked to perpetration, prevention efforts may benefit from promoting alternative routes. © 2026

Title: National trends in suicidal ideation, planning, and attempts among US adults aged 50 and older, 2021–2024
Abstract: Background Suicide rates among middle-aged and older adults in the US remain disproportionately high, yet recent national trends in suicidal ideation, suicide planning, and suicide attempts and their clinical correlates remain poorly characterized. Methods This serial cross-sectional study analyzed data from the 2021–2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, a nationally representative survey of 42,440 US adults aged ≥50 years. Logistic regression estimated temporal trends in suicidality; interaction terms tested differential trends by sociodemographic characteristics, past-year major depressive episode (MDE), serious psychological distress (SPD), substance use, prescription medication misuse, and chronic medical conditions for suicidal ideation and planning. Results From 2021 through 2024, suicidal ideation increased from 2.0% to 2.9% (p = 0.049), suicide planning from 0.3% to 1.1% (p ' 0.001), and suicide attempts from 0.2% to 0.6% (p = 0.02). Significant increases in ideation and planning were concentrated among those without MDE, while increases in ideation were also observed among those without SPD, alcohol use, and prescription medication misuse. Suicide planning increased more steeply among those with cannabis use than those without (449.9% vs. 188.3% increase; interaction p = 0.04). Conclusions Suicidality increased significantly among US adults aged ≥50 years from 2021 through 2024. While individuals with MDE and other traditional risk factors had elevated absolute risk, increases in ideation were concentrated among those without these factors, and planning increased broadly across most subgroups. These findings highlight potential gaps in prevention frameworks that rely exclusively on traditional risk factor screening and underscore the need for broader risk assessment in this population. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Shin J.H.; Chun H.; Kim J.
Title: Patterns of fairness perceptions and their associations with immigrant inclusion, willingness for redistribution, and overall social inclusion
Abstract: Fairness perceptions play a critical role in shaping social attitudes, particularly in societies facing heightened inequality and institutional distrust. Prior research has mainly treated fairness perception as a linear, unidimensional construct, offering limited attention to potential subgroup differences in perceptions across multiple societal aspects. The purpose of this study was to identify subgroups of fairness perceptions and to examine how these subgroups are associated with attitudes toward immigrants, redistribution, and overall social inclusion—three key indicators of social inclusiveness. Data from the 2023 Korean Social Integration Survey (n = 8221) were analyzed using latent class analysis, followed by multivariate regression analyses of the associations between subgroup membership and the outcome variables. Four subgroups were identified largely ordered along a low-to-high fairness gradient: Low Perception (14.62%), Medium-Low Perception (35.02%), High Perception (8.81%), and Medium-High Perception (41.55%). These subgroups showed differential associations with attitudes toward immigrant inclusion, redistribution, and overall social inclusion. While these three outcome variables were positively interrelated, individual heterogeneity remained across the sample. Overall, the findings suggest that fairness perceptions are associated with multiple dimensions of social inclusion, highlighting the importance of considering differences in perceived fairness when developing targeted social policy frameworks. Title: Unveiling the efficacy of the Kanyashree Prakalpa; A critical analysis of West Bengal’s initiative to enhance women’s education and diminish dropout rates; [یدماراکحرطیرشایناک؛اپلاکرپیلیلحتیداقتنازاراکتبا تلایالاگنبیبرغردیاقتراشزومآنانزوشهاکدصرد کرتلیصحت]
Abstract: Comparative public policy is a domain of interdisciplinary study that uses public policy as a unit of analysis for comparing different regimes. A crucial aspect of public policy is public policy evaluation, which must deal with the impact of the policy and not with policy output. Evaluating public policy is crucial for governments because the success or failure of a given policy directly influences the government’s image, impacting its likelihood of returning to power. In most cases, governments focus on highlighting policy outputs which consists of superficial statistical data. Such data may not be a proper representation of the actual impact of the policy. In this regard, this paper aims to evaluate the ‘Kanyashree Prakalpa’ of the West Bengal Government to promote women education and reduce dropout rates. Department of Women Development and Social Welfare, Government of West Bengal (DWD&SW) has designed the Kanyashree Prakalpa in 2012- a conditional cash transfer scheme with the aim of improving the status and well-being of the girl child in West Bengal by incentivizing schooling of all teenage girls and delaying their marriages until the age of 18, the legal age of marriage. Using Thomas R. Dye’s conception of public policy evaluation, this paper aims to study each indicator of the ‘Kanyashree Prakalpa’ to understand the actual impact of the policy in solving the problem it claims to address, and thereby mention ways to improve the policy to better address the pressing problems related to girl child education in India. The paper also addresses the compatibility of the policy in relation to certain SDGs. © 2027, University of Tehran. All rights reserved.

Title: Unlinked: Why alters reported in name generators cannot be used to estimate personal network size
Abstract: Personal network size is a versatile and fundamental structural network measure, capturing the total number of personal connections or specific subgroups within an individual’s social environment. In standard sociological methods, such as surveys, personal network size is often indirectly inferred from name generators, which are used to list alters from the respondents’ personal networks. Implicitly, a higher count of named alters is assumed to indicate a larger personal network. We explicitly test this common assumptionand address this imprecise association between network size and number of listed alters by comparing the results from two very distinct approaches to measuring personal network size: alter counts derived from name generators and size estimates obtained from the network scale-up method (NSUM). Using survey data from over 300 participants in Spain, we compute these two independent network measures for the same respondents and assess the strength, significance and robustness of their association, including potential question-order effects on personal network size. Our analyses conclude that the alter counts from name generators primarily reflect participants’ response behaviour and task constraints rather than the underlying personal network size. Finally, our findings highlight critical limitations in the use of free name generators as proxies for personal network size. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: The association between transportation insecurity and food insecurity among older adults in Clark County, Nevada
Abstract: Introduction As the population of older adults continues to grow, addressing social determinants of health that influence access to basic needs is increasingly important for supporting healthy aging. Transportation and food insecurity represent interconnected challenges that may limit older adults’ ability to live independently and access essential resources. The purpose of this study was to determine the association between transportation insecurity and food insecurity among older adults aged 60 and older residing in Clark County, NV. Methods A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was administered via telephone (n = 1,001) between November 2022 and February 2023 using random-digit dialing, yielding a 24.58% cooperation rate. Transportation insecurity was assessed using the Sixteen-Item Transportation Security Index, and food insecurity was measured using the USDA 6-item short form Food Security Survey Module. Demographic and socioeconomic variables were included as covariates. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate associations. Results Food insecurity was reported by 18.2% of participants, while 25.3% experienced transportation insecurity. A logistic regression model (ꭔ2 = 263.509, df = 19, n = 789, p < 0.001) indicated that transportation insecurity was significantly associated with food insecurity, with individuals experiencing transportation insecurity having 4.26 times the odds of being food insecure. Having a disability and lower income were positively associated with food insecurity, while older age (85+) was negatively associated with food insecurity. Conclusions Transportation barriers and food access challenges frequently overlap among older adults and should be addressed in tandem. Integrating transportation solutions into food access interventions may strengthen public health efforts to reduce disparities and support aging populations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Engaged but careless? The roles of online civic engagement, well-being, and information literacy in careless information sharing
Abstract: Civically active people online are usually more prone to careless information sharing. Thus, although usually framed positively, the youth civic engagement can also result in the sharing of potentially harmful content. However, the evidence on underage social media users is limited. This paper focuses on two factors that can potentially influence online behavior: one through well-being, and the second through information navigation and processing digital literacy. A three-wave random intercept cross-lagged panel model was employed, and the analyses were conducted on adolescents (Mage = 14.3; N = 2660) from Estonia, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Portugal. The data was collected between Spring 2021 and Spring 2023. Between-person associations between online civic engagement and well-being, and between online civic engagement and information navigation and processing literacy, were supported. This means more engaged adolescents are also more dissatisfied and have higher digital literacy, corroborating the existing literature. There were only limited within-person associations between careless sharing and information navigation and processing literacy; however, none of them supported the proposed associations. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Retrofitting strategies and related uncertainties in multi-story buildings: A critical review
Abstract: Retrofitting existing multi-story buildings (MSBs) to improve energy efficiency is a crucial strategy for achieving urban net-zero building objectives. The large-area characteristic of MSBs increases both the potential impact of building energy retrofits and the complexity of decision-making, introducing significant uncertainties that remain insufficiently addressed in existing research. Therefore, this study aims to explore retrofits applied in MSB and critically review current knowledge regarding evaluation criteria for retrofits, with a particular focus on the uncertainty associated with retrofitting projects. The retrofits are classified into three dimensions: envelope (77 studies), renewable energy technologies (93 studies), and indoor environment (81 studies). The findings reveal that the current research hotspot involves integrating passive, active, and renewable-energy-based retrofit strategies, and highlight a research gap in broader social dimensions. This review also examined three core dimensions of uncertainty: input variables (36 studies), analytical methods (32 studies), and fuzzy data processing techniques (6 studies). Under input variables, the application scenarios of 13 variable distribution types used in Monte Carlo are summarized, along with empirical recommendations for selecting appropriate distribution shapes. The insights from five commonly used uncertainty analysis methods are compiled for retrofitting contexts. Finally, fuzzy logic is found to play a control-oriented role in quantifying fuzzy behaviors data within indoor environmental control strategies. Overall, this review integrates fragmented knowledge on MSB retrofitting and provides a structured foundation, along with systematic research approaches and recommendations, to advance future research by synthesizing retrofit strategies, evaluation criteria, and uncertainty analysis, thereby supporting robust and inclusive decision-making for urban net-zero transitions. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Generative artificial intelligence scaffolding for statistical competence in graduate nursing education
Abstract: Background: Graduate nursing students often experience significant anxiety related to statistics and have difficulty applying quantitative knowledge to clinical research practice. Although generative artificial intelligence may function as a learning scaffold, evidence supporting its structured integration into pedagogy remains limited. Purpose: To evaluate the impact of a structured generative artificial intelligence-supported self-directed learning intervention on statistical competence, learning capacity, and motivation among graduate nursing students. Methods: This quasi-experimental study employed a single-group repeated-measures design and included 15 graduate nursing students enrolled in a master's program in Taiwan. The study was conducted from September 10, 2024, to January 15, 2025, with assessments performed at Weeks 1, 10, and 18. The 18-week intervention followed a five-stage scaffolding protocol: (1) instruction in fundamental statistical concepts with instructor-guided support and demonstrations using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, (2) independent drafting, (3) online peer collaboration, (4) generative artificial intelligence-assisted learning support, and (5) in-class metacognitive verification. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, generalized estimating equations, Pearson's correlation coefficients, and stepwise multiple regression analysis. Results: Overall learning capacity improved significantly over time (post-test estimate = 1.26, p < .001), with a very large observed effect size (Hedges' g = 3.75). Meaning construction, self-regulation, and interpersonal learning also improved significantly by the post-test (p < .001). Learning motivation increased slightly but was not statistically significant. In the stepwise multiple regression analysis, satisfaction was the only variable significantly associated with final statistics report scores (R2 = 0.61; adjusted R2 = 0.58, p = .001). Conclusions: Participants showed improvements in learning capacity following participation in the structured generative artificial intelligence-supported protocol. Learner satisfaction may be associated with higher statistical competence. These findings support the use of generative artificial intelligence as a guided educational scaffold rather than an unregulated shortcut. © 2026 The Authors

Title: A randomized trial of poverty reduction in the US and residential mobility to lower-crime neighborhoods
Abstract: Low-income families disproportionately experience higher neighborhood crime. When choosing where to live, families report neighborhood safety as a top priority. Yet, the role (if any) that income plays in promoting moves to safer neighborhoods remains unclear. In our paper, we leverage a social experiment of a randomized trial of unconditional cash transfers to understand whether the effect of increased net income led mothers to move to safer neighborhoods. We utilize the Baby's First Years randomized trial of ∼1000 families to test whether unconditional cash transfers promote residential mobility among low-income families to safer neighborhoods characterized by lower violent and/or property crime. We also test for heterogeneity by the number of children in the household. Our intent-to-treat results show no difference in families' neighborhood crime rates, by cash transfer group, over the four-year test period for any crime outcome. However, among mothers with at least two children at enrollment, the high-cash gift group moved to neighborhoods with lower crime rates compared to the low-cash gift group. Title: Non-pharmacological interventions for perinatal parental depression and anxiety: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
Abstract: Background Perinatal depression and anxiety exhibit significant partner interdependence and family-level ramifications, constituting a family issue concerning both parents. However, existing evidence syntheses have predominantly examined maternal or paternal mental health in isolation, neglecting the systemic integrity of the family unit. Objective To conduct the first Bayesian network meta-analysis to evaluate and rank non-pharmacological interventions delivered concurrently to both parents for perinatal depression and anxiety. Methods Seven databases were searched from inception to May 30, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in which both perinatal parents received the same non-pharmacological intervention and depression or anxiety was assessed. A Bayesian network meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PROSPERO: CRD420251048539. Results We included 36 RCTs involving 15,477 parents (51.8% mothers and 48.2% fathers/partners). For depression, multicomponent interventions (SMD = −0.34, 95% CrI [−0.60, −0.08]; SUCRA = 79.86%) and psychosocial interventions (SMD = −0.25, 95% CrI [−0.43, −0.07]; SUCRA = 60.83%) showed beneficial estimates. For anxiety, multicomponent interventions (SMD = −0.48, 95% CrI [−0.66, −0.29]; SUCRA = 98.12%) and parent-child interaction interventions (SMD = −0.19, 95% CrI [−0.36, −0.03]; SUCRA = 62.69%) showed beneficial estimates. Certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Conclusion Multicomponent interventions may be preferred across both symptom domains, while parent-child interaction and psychosocial interventions may offer symptom-specific benefits. Because the networks were sparse, comparisons were predominantly indirect, heterogeneity was substantial, and evidence certainty was low to moderate, these findings are provisional. They support family-centered care involving both parents and require further rigorous head-to-head trials. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Long W.; Ma R.
Title: Thinking fast and slow: How investor group thinking modes influence stock returns
Abstract: This study investigates the behavioral proxies for investor group thinking modes and examines their contemporaneous associations with asset pricing, as reflected in stock returns under different market and information conditions. Using a dataset of 10,451,366 daily user posts and 24,284,543 comments from Eastmoney Guba, China's leading financial social media platform, we construct behavioral proxies for fast and slow thinking modes. Our methodological approach constructs the fast thinking proxy through sentiment analysis via supervised fine-tuned large language models, while the slow thinking proxy builds on a multi-attribute decision method rooted in prospect theory. By employing regression models and robustness tests, our key findings show that both thinking modes are positively associated with stock returns. Our results show a synergistic relationship between the two modes, with fast thinking playing a dominant role. Interestingly, fast thinking is related to higher returns by increasing idiosyncratic risk, whereas slow thinking is associated with higher returns by promoting heterogeneous information exchange. Further, we explore the roles of specific conditions, including bull and bear markets and environments with conflicting sentiment between posts and news, in the relationship between thinking modes and stock returns. These findings provide new insights into investor information processing and group decision-making and highlight the applicability of dual-system theory in the context of financial social media. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: When social media memes become mean to peers: Discrimination recognition and group norms in adolescent bullying
Abstract: The widespread circulation of harmful memes on social media is increasingly recognized as a contributor to adolescent aggression, yet the mechanisms linking meme engagement to bullying behavior remain underexplored. Drawing on a neo-ecological framework that distinguishes physical and virtual microsystems, this study surveyed 1319 Chinese middle school students to examine how harmful meme culture is transmitted within adolescent communities and translated into bullying. Using structural equation modeling, we identified adolescents’ difficulty in recognizing discrimination as a key cognitive mediator linking harmful meme usage to bullying behavior. Peer-group subjective norms emerged as the strongest factor in cultural transmission, while parental opposition and restricted media access appeared insufficient and showed no protective association. This challenges the traditional focus on parental supervision and media use, highlighting the prominent role of harmful meme culture within adolescent peer groups. These findings reframe adolescent bullying as a culturally mediated phenomenon shaped by peer normalization processes and sustained by the gradual erosion of critical perceptual capacity, with important implications for the design of educational, parental, and platform-level interventions. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Exploring the impact of cultural and masculine norms on the mental health of Arabic-speaking migrant and refugee men in Australia: Service provider perspectives
Abstract: Background Arabic-speaking refugee and migrant men in Australia likely experience unique mental health challenges due to a complex interplay of migration, cultural factors, and acculturation. Understanding how acculturation-related stressors interact with traditional gender roles and familial expectations to influence mental health and help-seeking is crucial for developing culturally responsive mental health interventions. Methods Forty-one in-depth interviews were conducted via Zoom with community service providers, including settlement workers, mental health professionals, and religious leaders, from August to October 2023. Results . Service providers described men's post-settlement distress as arising through three related themes: acculturation challenges (cultural adjustment, identity disruption, stigmatising narratives of mental illness); shifting family dynamics (disrupted provider roles, eroded paternal authority); and struggles for belonging (social isolation, diminished recognition). Conclusion This study shows that providers linked these men's mental health to the pressures of settling into a new culture, the loss of their role as providers and authority figures at home, changes in family life, difficulty finding suitable work, and isolation from community. How much each of these affected a man depended on his work and standing before migration, his education, his religion, and how he came to Australia. Title: Exploring the Struggles of Caregivers of Children With Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia: Implications for Social Work Services in Malaysia

Abstract: Childhood cancer can cause extreme discomfort and stress for the caregivers of affected children. These challenges affect caregivers and their children and need to be recognized and addressed. This study used individual, in-depth interviews to explore the challenges faced by caregivers of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in Malaysia, to identify the social work services available to them, and to understand the support they need. The interviews with eight informants were transcribed, translated, and systematically analyzed using qualitative content analysis to identify emerging themes and patterns. The study highlights several issues and coping strategies: financial burdens from indirect treatment costs and job or income loss; medical caregiving responsibilities, including accompanying their child during admission, treatment, and prolonged hospital stay; difficulties in addressing and providing for their ill child’s emotional needs and those of their other children; social support received from close and extended family members, and friends. There are also coping strategies, such as comparing one’s child with other children in the ward who are in a more disadvantaged condition, talking to other caregivers, and sharing information and experiences. Title: Constructing cross-scale local carbon emission zones in four global metropolises: A city-specific framework for mitigating spatial scaling effects
Abstract: Accelerating the transition to low-carbon urbanisation was critical for climate change mitigation. The delineation of local carbon emission zones (LCEZs) offers a promising approach for integrating urban morphology with CO2 emissions patterns for targeted planning. However, existing LCEZs frameworks are affected by scale dependence and often provided limited, context-insensitive explanations of emission heterogeneity. This study developed a cross-scale LCEZs framework and applied it to London, New York, Paris, and Sydney. First, the collapse method, grounded in finite-size scaling, was used to identify morphology factors exhibiting cross-scale statistical regularity, thereby mitigating the scale effect of the modifiable areal unit problem. Second, an optimal parameter-based geographical detector (OPGD) model was used to identify city-specific combinations of morphology factors associated with heterogeneity in CO2 emissions to construct LCEZs. Eleven factors passed the collapse screening, including transport, building, and landscape factors. In the constructed LCEZs results of the four cities, at least one transportation-related variable was retained in every combination, while mean building volume (MBV) emerged as a core factor in three of the four metropolises, demonstrating high universality and influence. The resulting LCEZs were statistically validated by Kruskal-Wallis tests, with effect sizes ranging from 0.143 to 0.233, and intra-zone coefficients of variation were reduced by over 80% relative to the global baseline in each metropolis, confirming strong internal homogeneity. This framework provided an basis for comparing morphology–emission associations and informing low-carbon interventions. It offered a repeatable diagnostic procedure to quantify trade-offs and tailor measures to local contexts, bridging computational urban science with planning practice. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Liu J.; Li S.; Wu S.; Liu H.
Title: From state-led environmental management to hybrid governance: A county-level case study of Lake Fuxian, China
Abstract: High-standard environmental protection in China has improved ecological conditions in many strategic regions, but it has also generated growing pressure on local development and social sustainability. Focusing on the Lake Fuxian basin in Chengjiang, this study examines the staged transformation of county-level ecological governance and explains why prolonged state-led environmental management has increasingly created pressures for a shift toward hybrid governance. Drawing on a longitudinal case study, ecological governance is shown to have evolved from an economy-dependent model shaped by economic logic to an authority-led model driven by administrative integration and high-standard regulation. Strong state intervention has been effective in improving water quality and strengthening institutional capacity, yet it has also produced fiscal strain, livelihood disruption, and heightened social tensions at the county level. Relocation, the transfer of rural land-use rights, industrial contraction, and the expansion of regulatory boundaries have improved ecological outcomes while weakening the social and economic foundations needed to sustain long-term governance. The county emerges as a policy-conversion arena where national ecological mandates, local development constraints, and community adaptation intersect. Under these conditions, hybrid governance is better understood not as a normative ideal, but as a practical response to the structural limits of prolonged administrative dominance. Greater attention to locality, trust rebuilding, and benefit-sharing mechanisms is essential for reducing the social costs of ecological transition and supporting more sustainable forms of county-level green transformation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Developing a resource-based analysis of technological innovation systems: The case of digital innovation in Dutch processing industries
Abstract: Resource-based perspectives in Technological Innovation Systems (TIS) research offer new insights into innovation dynamics and address gaps in the traditional structure-function approach. We take stock of this perspective to develop a framework that enhances TIS in two ways. First, we improve the conceptual linkage between TIS elements and functions by focusing on innovation resources and their dynamics. Next, we offer a combined view of system-building and hindering processes by identifying and characterizing meso-level TIS mechanisms through micro-level resource changes. We apply our framework to a qualitative case study on the digital TIS within the Dutch processing industry. The analysis generalizes four system-building activities and four systemic problems, which emerge from the presence, accessibility, applicability, and scale of innovation resources. Additionally, four case-specific mechanisms are identified which illustrate tensions between positive and negative dynamics, revealing fundamental complexity underlying the overall TIS functioning. Our framework provides a basis for unpacking such tensions and identifying more targeted policy interventions, particularly for innovation systems of general-purpose technologies. © 2026 The Authors. Title: From participatory evidence to policy recommendations: protecting children’s right to education amid ongoing war: evidence from Gaza
Abstract: Prolonged war in Gaza has profoundly destabilized education systems, eroding children’s access to safe and meaningful learning and weakening policy accountability mechanisms. Although children’s right to participation is internationally recognized, it also functions as an enabling right that supports the realization of the right to education by ensuring that children’s perspectives inform educational decision-making. However, children lived experiences are rarely integrated into formal educational policymaking in contexts of extreme instability. This study examines how children experience their right to education during ongoing war and how their perspectives, together with those of their educational and social environment, can inform evidence-based policy recommendations for Gaza.The research was informed by the Lundy Model of Child Participation (space, voice, audience, influence) and the Advocacy Coalition Framework, which provided complementary foundations for designing data collection with children and key actors within their educational and social environment. Education was conceptualized as interdependent with protection, psychosocial well-being, dignity, and identity. Data were collected during 2025. A qualitative, policy-oriented research design employed four complementary methods to enable methodological triangulation: thematic analysis of 29 reflective letters written by children in Gaza; analysis of 33 publicly available video documenting educational experiences and the lived realities of children and their educational and social environments during the war on Gaza (7 October 2023–2025); four focus groups involving 5 children, 9 teachers, 2 parents, and 6 educational experts from Gaza; and four semi-structured interviews with educational experts from the West Bank.Findings were analyzed through the four dimensions of the right to education (availability, accessibility, acceptability, and adaptability) revealing systemic erosion across all domains. The study identifies policy gaps and advances evidence-informed recommendations: establishing alternative safe learning spaces and coordinated partnerships; ensuring equitable access through mobile and low-connectivity modalities supported by alternative energy; strengthening educational quality through blended models and psychosocial support for teachers; and developing flexible pathways integrating academic and psychosocial components responsive to diverse learner needs.
