Authors: Libbrecht M.-L.
Title: Evaluating reintegration effectiveness differently: A realist evaluation of sports programs in Belgian male prisons using the Capability Approach
Abstract: Reintegration of (formerly) incarcerated people is often assessed through narrow behavioral metrics such as non-recidivism or compliance with supervisory conditions. Such measures overlook crucial dimensions of reintegration – dignity, agency, and access to valued opportunities that shape how people rebuild meaningful lives during and after detention. This study addresses that gap by applying the Capability Approach within a Realist Evaluation of prison sports programs in Flanders (Belgium), examining how, why, and under what conditions sport contributes to reintegration. It focuses on prison sports programs, which are typically treated as peripheral or as ineffective for reintegration. The study combined a scoping review, longitudinal participant observation across three prison sites, and 141 semi-structured interviews with 71 respondents, including incarcerated and formerly incarcerated participants, prison and reintegration stakeholders, and broader justice-system stakeholders. Several incarcerated participants were interviewed repeatedly, including after release, adding a longitudinal component to the study. The analysis produced context–mechanism–outcome (CMO) configurations that identified enabling conditions and structural barriers, synthesized into a refined middle-range theory explaining how agency, social connection, and systemic context interact to shape reintegration effectiveness. Findings indicate that sport contributes to reintegration by fostering agency, relational recognition, and connection to the outside world; yet these effects depend on voluntary participation, institutional support, and the absence of structural barriers. While Realist Evaluation explains how outcomes emerge through context–mechanism configurations, the Capability Approach clarifies what should count as meaningful effectiveness, shifting attention from narrow behavioral endpoints (e.g., recidivism) to capability expansion within and beyond carceral settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Lévesque G.V.
Title: The relational structure of corporate ignorance production
Abstract: This study interrogates patterns of interaction through which corporate actors influence environmental knowledge production. I ask 1) How intensive are relationships between corporate actors and knowledge-producing organizations? 2) What types of knowledge-producing organizations are subject to most engagement by corporate actors? and 3) How do these patterns evolve over time? I answer these questions with the landmark case of lead in the United States (1924–2003). I rely on longitudinal network data built from the raw text of Toxic Docs, a database that comprises millions of previously classified corporate documents over eight decades. Using relational event modeling, I find that corporate engagement with scientific organizations is consistently more likely than with other types of actors. In contrast, corporate engagement with regulatory expert organizations is less so. I also find that corporate engagement with scientific organizations is responsive to growing federal interest in the lead problem and anticipates regulatory developments. This suggests that corporate engagement with scientists is best described not simply as reactive but also as preemptive. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V. Authors: Yang S.C.; Suwandi
Title: Social knowledge construction across metaverse and chat collaboration: An epistemic network analysis of sequential hybrid learning
Abstract: As immersive technologies and asynchronous communication tools are increasingly combined in collaborative learning, limited attention has been given to how synchronous and asynchronous phases are associated with different patterns of social knowledge construction (SKC). This study examined discourse patterns across synchronous metaverse and asynchronous chat phases in sustainable development goal-oriented collaborative learning. Seventy undergraduates from Taiwan and Indonesia, organized into 14 groups of exactly five students, participated in a four-week intercultural project. All groups sequentially completed metaverse-based collaboration using Gather Town or ZEP, followed by asynchronous LINE chat. Discourse was analyzed using a revised Interaction Analysis Model, epistemic network analysis (ENA), and group-level paired-samples tests. The metaverse phase showed significantly more information sharing, whereas chat showed significantly more negotiation and co-construction. Social and coordination-oriented discourse remained prominent in both phases. ENA identified stronger negotiation–application connections in chat and stronger social–information-sharing connections in the metaverse phase. The principal network pattern was retained in sensitivity models excluding the prevalent social and coordination-oriented category and expanding the moving stanza from two to four turns. Because the phase order was fixed, the findings represent joint order-and-modality-associated patterns rather than causal modality effects. The study demonstrates the value of examining both the frequency and connectivity of coded discourse moves in sequential hybrid learning. Pedagogically, the findings support temporal orchestration in which synchronous immersive interaction establishes social grounding and asynchronous discussion extends negotiation and application, provided that appropriate bridging supports connect the two phases. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Advancing equitable and safe access to care through pre-service telemedicine acceptability: a UTAUT guided pilot study
Abstract: The introduction of telemedicine services into healthcare’s daily work routines brings both new resources and challenges. To ensure the development of safe and accessible services, it seems fundamental to co-design services with end-users and, concurrently, evaluate their acceptability to enhance care compliance. The current pilot study aims to develop, validate, and test a context-specific measurement tool grounded in the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and its extensions. The main objective of the model is to evaluate end-users’ acceptability and its antecedents before they have any experience with telemedicine services, thereby enabling context-specific evaluations of the proposed telemedicine services and fostering interest among patients. The model included different variables from both the original theory (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence) and its proposed extensions (compatibility, personal innovativeness, and acceptability). In total, we asked 429 participants from different residential contexts (i.e., urban, peripheral, and rural) in northern Italy to complete our cross-sectional survey. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity, internal consistency, and full measurement invariance across gender and both educational and residential contexts. Structural equation modelling showed excellent model fit (CFI = 0.96; SRMR = 0.05). Performance expectancy (β = 0.50), compatibility (β = 0.35), and social influence (β = 0.22) significantly predicted telemedicine acceptability. In particular, the compatibility effect on acceptability was partially mediated by performance expectancy. Our research proposes a workflow that provides a practical framework for assessing preparedness and guiding communication strategies to promote safe and equitable telemedicine implementation. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Attrash-Najjar A.; Katz C.
Title: Peritraumatic responses as conveyed by ultra-Orthodox survivors of child sexual abuse
Abstract: This study examined the peritraumatic responses to childhood sexual abuse among Jewish ultra-Orthodox adult survivors. Studies on childhood sexual abuse among closed societies are scarce. However, recent studies have stressed the importance of examining peritraumatic responses to childhood sexual abuse by exploring the top-down processes often embedded in survivors’ socio-cultural and religious contexts. Forty-eight narratives provided by women and men who experienced childhood sexual abuse in the ultra-Orthodox society in Israel were analyzed using a qualitative inductive thematic analysis. Crucial gender differences were found between women and men, indicating how their socio-cultural and religious context, particularly norms of female purity, obedience to religious authority, and community insularity, shaped their peritraumatic responses. These factors led women to internalize the abuse and men to comply with abusive religious figures. Specifically, the women who experienced intrafamilial abuse shared several peritraumatic responses, such as ignoring the abuse, dissociation and having faith in the future. The men who experienced abuse, mainly by religious figures, described their limited ability to resist the abuse. Both the women and men described how family and family-community dynamics often shaped social expectations, which were central to their peritraumatic responses to childhood sexual abuse. The discussion highlights the central role of top-down processes with a unique focus on the role of family and family-community dynamics. Title: Social priming enhances young children’s trust in robots
Abstract: This study examined preschoolers’ selective trust in a robot versus a human informant, and whether social priming may increase trust by making the robot’s social characteristics more salient, using the word-learning paradigm. ToM related to trust only for judgment scores (which informant was correct), an association largely explained by age. Both age groups preferred learning new labels from the robot, suggesting that social characteristics support children’s trust in robot informants, particularly among younger preschoolers. ToM predicted children’s endorsement of the robot’s labels, although this effect was largely explained by age. Authors: Boullineau E.
Title: Moral violations are made, not found: A theory of motivated violation construction
Abstract: Moral psychology has largely treated moral violations as features of behaviour that observers detect and then evaluate. This paper introduces Motivated Violation Construction (MVC): the proposal that observers may classify ambiguous behaviour as morally wrong when that classification supports a prior negative evaluation. MVC shifts whether behaviour enters the moral domain, rather than merely intensifying evaluation after entry. Factors such as threat, dislike, envy/status resentment, or group allegiance are proposed to lower the classification threshold under negative motivation. Positive stances raise it. The paper focuses on violation construction under negative motivation, where moral content is added rather than withheld. MVC concerns the point at which behaviour is classified as wrong, before its severity is evaluated. MVC is distinct from motivated reasoning, which shapes how people judge behaviour already seen as wrong, and from moralisation, which concerns shifts in what a society treats as moral issues. Four predictions are advanced. Negative motivation increases, and positive motivation decreases, the frequency with which identical behaviour is classified as a violation. When the behaviour is genuinely ambiguous, this effect is strongest. It weakens where moral consensus is clear. Differences in classification track the observer's motives rather than the behaviour. Motivation affects classification more strongly than severity, and this asymmetry is moderated by ambiguity. Each prediction has operationalisations and procedural falsifiability conditions, with a registered manipulation check on the evaluative-stance induction. © 2026

Authors: Taktak F.
Title: Rethinking land readjustment governance: Comparative institutional perspectives on Turkey's 2025 reform
Abstract: Land readjustment (LR) and Transfer of Development Rights (TDR) are planning instruments used to reconcile private property rights with public land requirements, although their institutional design differs considerably across national planning systems. In Türkiye, the traditional Land Readjustment Contribution (DOP)-based model has been criticized for limited transparency, weak valuation safeguards, and insufficient citizen participation. The 2025 amendment introduced two institutional innovations: the integration of the Parcel Monitoring and Supervision System (PARSID) into the e-Government platform and the legal adoption of TDR as a compensation mechanism. This study provides a comparative legal and institutional assessment of Türkiye's 2025 land readjustment reform by integrating doctrinal legal analysis, comparative institutional benchmarking, and complementary bipartite Social Network Analysis (SNA). The network analysis is employed to visualize institutional relationships among governance dimensions rather than to evaluate implementation effectiveness. The findings identify effectiveness, institutional capacity, valuation, equity, and participation as the most influential governance dimensions across LR/TDR systems, while digitalization functions as a complementary governance dimension. Within this comparative framework, Türkiye's 2025 reform represents an emerging institutional framework integrating land readjustment, TDR, valuation safeguards, and digital governance. Because the reform has only recently entered into force, the findings should be interpreted as a comparative assessment of institutional design rather than implementation performance. The study contributes to the land governance literature by integrating legal analysis, comparative benchmarking, and network visualization within a transparent and transferable comparative framework that supports future empirical research on land governance reforms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Social representations of intercultural encounters among young people from Finland, the Middle East, and Ukraine
Abstract: This study examines young people’s social representations of intercultural encounters. The study is based on qualitative material collected in 2023 during researcher-facilitated arts-based workshops with 13- to 19-year-olds. The research was conducted in North Savo, Finland. The participants, residing in the Northern Savo area, represented three cultural backgrounds: Finnish residents and displaced people originating from the Middle East and Ukraine. In workshops, participants created 45 visual artworks accompanied by written reflections on their perceptions of meeting people from different cultures. We employed a content analysis to examine the drawings and texts from the perspective of the social representations approach. The analysis produced three distinct social representations reflecting young people’s perceptions on encountering people from different cultures: Positive Representations of Encounters, Apprehensive Representations of Encounters, and Idealized Representations of Encounters. The findings reveal how the social representations of intergroup encounters constructed by young people from different cultural backgrounds differ from each other. Finally, we discuss the importance of social representations of intercultural encounters in shaping the perceptions of past and potential future intercultural encounters. The study contributes to research on intercultural encounters by employing the social representations approach and shifting the focus from representations of groups to representations of the encounter itself. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Lim H.; Kim H.
Title: Psychological pathways to digital safety: A sequential model of attitudinal endorsement, environment cognition, and WTP for malicious comment prevention
Abstract: Malicious comments (MCs) are a pervasive digital threat that is associated with substantial emotional costs for users. However, empirical research on how these affective burdens translate into protective economic behavior remains limited. This study addresses this gap by drawing on the complementary roles of the I-PACE model, the General Process Model (GPM), and Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) to investigate the sequential psychological pathways from MC exposure to willingness to pay (WTP). Using a nationwide survey of 1000 adults in South Korea, we adopt a two-stage analytical design combining Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and a Contingent Valuation Method (CVM)-based Spike Model. Methodologically, we first estimate WTP using a CVM-based Spike Model and then incorporate the resulting individual-level WTP estimates as the behavioral-economic outcome in the SEM stage, without imposing cross-model estimation dependency. The findings suggest an emotion-first structure with dual affective pathways exerting opposing influences on threat appraisal. Emotional discomfort amplifies the perception of environmental toxicity, while attitudinal endorsement of MCs, including resonance with aggressors, systematically attenuates risk perception and protective commitment. This dual mechanism illustrates competing forces where visceral distress promotes protection, yet resonance with perpetrators leads users to legitimize digital violence, counteracting protective motivation even in toxic environments. The monthly economic value of digital safety is quantified at approximately 1,529 KRW, serving as a behavioral-economic indicator of perceived utility loss in toxic digital environments. These results advocate for safety by design and shared responsibility frameworks, urging platforms to integrate prevention services as core features. © 2026

Authors: Almog E.; Herbst-Debby A.
Title: Exploring the dynamic links between divorce initiatives and the social landscape
Abstract: Women frequently initiate divorce, yet their post-divorce experiences are shaped by gender norms and societal expectations surrounding marriage and motherhood. In Israel, where liberal-secular values coexist with familistic and religious norms, initiating divorce may be perceived as a deviation from the social order. This study examines how women who initiate divorce perceive societal attitudes toward themselves and their decision, and how these attitudes shape their post-divorce social position. Drawing on semi-structured in-depth interviews with 38 mostly secular, heterosexual, Jewish-Israeli mothers aged 25–70 who initiated divorce, this thematic analysis revealed five central themes: repositioning in the social arena: loss of belonging and social status; reconfiguring support networks from couple-based ties to alternative sources of support; navigating social norms as part of the complex journey of divorce initiators; the attribution of blame and responsibility to the initiator; and societal attitudes that foster self-blame and weaken the initiator's social confidence. The study demonstrates that stigma and moral judgment directed at women who initiate divorce function as informal sanctions that regulate gender norms, weaken women's social capital in the post-divorce period and sustain patriarchal power relations. The findings highlight the need for supportive frameworks that validate women's autonomy and mitigate post-divorce social exclusion. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Securing extractive futures: unpacking the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act
Abstract: In 2024 the European Union’s (EU’s) Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) entered into force, seeking to ensure access to a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials (CRMs). While nominally predicated on just transition and climate mitigation narratives, implementation relies heavily on increasing extraction, largely outside the EU. Drawing on poststructuralist discourse analysis, we examine how the discourse within and around the CRMA evolved over time, and what shifts in framing can be observed in the EU’s quest to secure access to critical raw materials. Analyzing the CRMA alongside 32 official EU documents, we show how shifting meanings contribute to mobilizing and legitimizing secure access to CRMs. Socio-environmental safeguards become repositioned as barriers to secure an EU-first agenda, justifying deregulatory measures. Access to CRMs becomes increasingly imperative for EU interests, specifically security, while potential harms continue to be externalized to extractive regions. Reinforced by intensifying militarized geopolitical agendas in the EUs quest to secure CRMs, this paper shows how just transition discourse can serve to justify the maintenance of a political and economic order that began during formal colonialism. This holds important insights for transition scholars about how just transition language can be leveraged to increase extraction and securitization while marginalizing hard-won social and environmental safeguards. This illustrates how green colonialism further disadvantages peoples and places where CRMs are extracted and adds a militarized layer to the analysis as resource-control is leveraged for warfighting purposes. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Schizotypy is associated with a fear-specific bias in recognising dynamic facial expressions
Abstract: Schizotypy describes personality traits and subclinical psychosis-related experiences that vary across the general population, yet their relationship with facial expression recognition across motion and intensity remains unclear. Examining these factors may reveal social-perceptual differences not evident with static or high-intensity expressions alone. We analysed data from 226 adults who identified six facial emotional expressions (anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise) displayed by static and dynamic faces at low, moderate, and high intensity. Subscale analyses were broadly consistent with the total-score findings but were less differentiated. These findings suggest that higher schizotypy is associated with a selective tendency to resolve ambiguous, dynamically unfolding expressions toward fear and threat. Understanding this tendency is important, because heightened sensitivity to subtle signs of threat may shape social interpretations, everyday interactions, and avoidance behaviours. © 2026 .

Authors: Sun Z.; Li X.
Title: Intellectual Landscape of Technical and Vocational Education and Training: Knowledge Bases, Fronts, and Global Collaboration
Abstract: Although knowledge of Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) scholarship has experienced an impressive growth since the inception of the 2030 Sustainable Development Agenda, an intellectual mapping of the area has been lacking to date. This study systematically analysed 3,655 TVET-related publications from 2016 to 2026, based on the Web of Science Core Collection. The co-citation analysis shows five knowledge clusters. The keywords co-occurrence analysis reveals four new fronts of research. The co-authorship analysis displays the networks of collaboration at the country and institutional levels. The research presents a systematic mapping of the intellectual landscape of TVET in the Sustainable Development Goals era, clearly revealing the fragmentation of the current theoretical framework and highlighting the significant implications for researchers, policymakers, and practitioners engaged in the development of this field. © 2027 FahrenHouse. Title: How the built environment shapes the residential satisfaction of on-demand platform workers: The mediating role of sense of place
Abstract: As the platform economy develops, the residential satisfaction of on-demand platform workers has become an important dimension of urban social integration assessments, shaping urban inclusion and rights realization. From a holistic built environment perspective, this study draws on a sample of 1588 male food-delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers, incorporating objective physical environment factors such as housing and locational conditions, and subjective environmental perceptions including livability and resilience, into a unified analytical framework. A conceptual model linking the built environment, sense of place, and residential satisfaction is proposed and empirically tested through structural equation modeling. The results indicate that (1) housing conditions are positively and indirectly associated with residential satisfaction through higher livability and resilience, whereas locational conditions are negatively and indirectly associated with residential satisfaction through lower resilience; (2) livability shows the strongest positive association with residential satisfaction and is positively associated with sense of place, while resilience is also positively associated with both sense of place and residential satisfaction; and (3) sense of place constitutes a pathway through which livability and resilience are associated with residential satisfaction, playing a significant mediating role. Overall, the built environment is associated with male on-demand platform workers’ residential satisfaction through two dimensions of the objective physical environment and subjective environmental perceptions, with sense of place serving as an affective bond. By highlighting people-place interactions, this study offers an integrated lens for understanding residential satisfaction among male food-delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers, and provides context-specific implications for more inclusive urban planning and community governance. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Ogwu, Matthew Chidozie (57204350388); Aliu, Olugbemiga Ojo (59723318600)
Title: Silent environmental conflicts and pathways to armed conflict
Abstract: Environmental change is increasingly recognized as a contributor to conflict, yet scholars often examine its role only after violence becomes visible. This paper advances the concept of silent environmental conflict to capture latent, slow-moving socio-ecological tensions that accumulate beneath formal peace and may precede armed conflict. Drawing on insights from environmental security, political ecology, and climate-conflict research, the paper argues that environmental stress does not directly cause war but interacts with governance failures, inequality, and livelihood insecurity to amplify conflict risk. Silent environmental conflicts unfold through processes such as resource exclusion, ecological degradation, institutional neglect, and climate-induced livelihood decline, and may remain politically under-recognized unless addressed or made visible through protest, coercion, or violence. The paper synthesizes key mechanisms linking environmental stress to conflict, highlights climate change as a context-dependent risk multiplier, and examines how war itself generates new environmental grievances, creating recursive cycles of instability. By proposing an integrative framework that traces environmental stress, social mediation, political accumulation, possible escalation, and recursive feedback, this Perspective reframes conflict as a temporally extended and structurally embedded process without treating violence as inevitable. The paper concludes that recognizing and addressing silent environmental conflicts can support conflict prevention, climate adaptation, and sustainable development and calls for greater integration of environmental governance into peacebuilding and policy frameworks. © 2026

Title: Making goals visible: A feasibility study of co-designed visual goal sheets to support parent implementation in early autism intervention
Abstract: Background: Translating individualized intervention goals into everyday family routines can be challenging. This mixed-methods feasibility study examined the use/adoption and parent-reported acceptability/social validity of visual goal sheets embedded within routine Early Start Denver Model (ESDM) care. Methods: Ten families in a French university-hospital ESDM program used visual goal sheets for up to 36 weeks across two naturally occurring cohorts. The clinical team developed the initial visual-support framework, which was refined through parent feedback. Use/adoption was summarized using each family's final available assessment. Acceptability/social validity was assessed with a project-specific questionnaire comprising 13 four-point items, with weekly scores averaged within families. Home-practice frequency was reported separately as contextual information. Open-ended comments underwent descriptive content analysis. Results: Eight families completed 36 weeks and two ended participation after 12 weeks. At their final available assessment, all ten families reported using the visual goal sheets at least weekly: five daily, four several times per week, and one approximately weekly. The mean participant-level acceptability/social-validity score was 3.6/4 (SD = 0.3). Qualitative findings described perceived improvements in clarity and recall, easier prioritization, integration into everyday routines, communication across caregivers and settings, reassurance and support, and contextual barriers. Conclusions: Participating families reported regular use and positive acceptability/social-validity ratings of visual goal sheets embedded within routine ESDM care. The small uncontrolled sample and reliance on parent-reported data limit interpretation. Future studies should distinguish the contributions of visual representation, simplified language, clinician guidance, and parent-informed refinement while incorporating objective indicators of use and more diverse service and cultural contexts. © 2026

Title: Re-centering the user in recommender system research: Preface to the special issue
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Recommender systems increasingly shape what people watch, read, buy, and learn, yet their success has too often been assessed through system-centric objectives and proxy metrics. In this editorial introduction to the Special Issue on “Re-centering the User in Recommender System Research,” we argue for a sustained shift toward user-centered, value-sensitive recommender research that foregrounds user agency, transparency, fairness, privacy, and long-term welfare, while acknowledging the multi-stakeholder nature of many recommendation ecosystems. Building on perspectives from recommender systems, human–computer interaction, behavioral science, and responsible AI, we first synthesize key conceptual and methodological developments that motivate placing users at the core of design and evaluation. We then introduce the papers collected in this issue, which collectively examine the benefits and risks of persuasive explanations, frameworks for designing effective explanatory interfaces, user-calibrated approaches to mitigating popularity bias, preference conceptualization and modeling in specific domains, user experience in conversational recommenders powered by large language models, and methodological lessons for evaluating group recommenders. We conclude by outlining open challenges–including measuring long-term outcomes, balancing personalization with risks of manipulation, and developing ecologically valid, stakeholder-aware evaluation protocols–and by pointing to promising directions for future research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Author full names: Straffon, Larissa M. (57200247704); Dudojć, Olga (57208397628); Jordan, Fiona M. (7102620650)
Title: Maths and crafts: embodied mathematical knowledge in fibre technologies
Abstract: Mathematical reasoning, often treated solely as an abstract cognitive achievement, may emerge within the embodied, technical, and socially transmitted practices of material production. Here, we examine the relationship between mathematical ideas and material culture through a cross-cultural study of fibre technologies, including netting, basketry, and loom weaving. By analysing the operations involved in fibre crafts, we identify a range of actions that correspond to foundational numerical and geometric concepts, including grouping, ordering, pairing, counting, sequencing, memory, cardinality, and proportional reasoning. The material properties of threads, knots, and looms enable quantities and spatial relations to be stabilised, visualised, and manipulated, thereby externalising and scaffolding both arithmetic and geometric thought.Across techniques, these operations appear in nested and overlapping ways: the iterative loops of netting, the geometric constraints and symmetries of basketry, and the binary and algebraic structures of loom weaving each reorganise shared procedures into increasingly structured systems without implying a linear progression. Linguistic and symbolic evidence further suggests that weaving has shaped the conceptual vocabulary of mathematics, serving as a source of conceptual metaphors for space, time, and cosmology, and as a medium through which patterned knowledge is memorised and transmitted.Drawing on evidence from anthropology, linguistics, and cognitive science, we argue that fibre technologies afford and stabilise mathematical ideas, situating the development of mathematics within processes of embodied action and cultural evolution. Textile practices thus provide a bridge between cognition and culture, showing how mathematical knowledge is enacted, materialised, and historically accumulated through craft. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Livelihoods after resettlement: women's work, collective care, and solidarity in disaster recovery
Abstract: This paper critically examines livelihood recovery in the peripheral resettlement sites of Chennai, India, following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Despite the implementation of various gender-inclusive livelihood programmes as a part of disaster recovery, our longitudinal empirical research reveals a persistent gap between formal recovery measures and the everyday conditions required for livelihoods to become gender-inclusive and sustainable over time. Drawing on in-depth fieldwork, we explore how women respond in the long term to these limitations: not simply through individual coping strategies but also by developing and maintaining collective, care-centred practices, including adapting domestic spaces to work, sharing childcare responsibilities, and building networks of mutual support. These practices are often invisible in official recovery frameworks, yet they serve as critical choices for women both to sustain their livelihoods and perform their care roles. We build on Joan C. Tronto and Berenice Fisher's (1990) theory of caring to conceptualise these acts as forms of ‘caring with’, where care becomes a collective, political, and relational response to systemic exclusion. In doing so, we reposition disaster recovery not merely as a return to normalcy or economic productivity but also as a deeply social and gendered process that is shaped by care and solidarity. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Effects of paid partnership disclosures on responses to oral nicotine pouch advertising: a randomized psychophysiological study of oral nicotine pouch use-status
Abstract: Objective Social media marketing of oral nicotine pouches (ONPs) has expanded rapidly since their U.S. introduction in 2016, particularly among young adults. It remains unclear whether ONP use-status influences cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses to influencer-generated ONP marketing, including ONP interest and comparative harm perceptions. Methods A 2 (ONP use-status: people who use ONPs vs. people who do not use ONPs) x 2 (paid partnership disclosure: present vs. absent) between-participants experiment was conducted with young adults (N = 193; M age = 20.19 years). Participants viewed a TikTok influencer advertisement promoting ONPs while psychophysiological responses were recorded, followed by self-report measures. Results Paid partnership disclosures increased ONP interest among both people who use ONPs and people who do not use ONPs (p ' 0.001, ηp2 = 0.07), with people who use ONPs reporting greater overall interest than people who do not use ONPs (p ' 0.001, ηp2 = 0.53). Controlling for baseline comparative harm perceptions, disclosure effects varied by baseline comparative harm perceptions and ONP use-status (p ' 0.001, ηp2 = 0.14). Compared with people who do not use ONPs, people who use ONPs allocated fewer cognitive resources to the ONP advertisements over time (b = 0.01, p = 0.03), exhibited greater physiological arousal over time (b = 0.0084, p = 0.04), and showed less negative emotional responding when disclosures were present (b = -0.53, p = 0.02). Conclusions Paid partnership disclosures increased ONP interest but produced divergent effects on comparative harm perceptions, cognitive processing, physiological arousal, and emotional responding according to ONP use-status. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Early maladaptive schemas and four problematic excessive behaviors: Cross-sectional indirect associations involving desire thinking and craving
Abstract: Problematic gambling, problematic gaming, problematic social media use, and problematic pornography use differ in nosological status but may share some psychological correlates. The present cross-sectional study examined associations between early maladaptive schemas (EMSs) and these four problematic excessive behaviors, and compared theory-informed serial and parallel indirect-effect specifications involving desire thinking and craving. A community sample of 811 Iranian adults (43.4 % males; mean age = 27.70 years, SD = 9.00) completed self-report measures. Desire thinking and craving were assessed with reference to the same personally selected activity, although the selected activity was not recorded. Item-level confirmatory factor analyses supported a relative distinction between desire thinking, craving frequency, and craving strength, although substantial overlap remained. The parallel specification showed poor fit, whereas the serial specification showed acceptable fit (χ2(38) = 227.97, CFI = 0.967, TLI = 0.943, RMSEA = 0.079, and SRMR = 0.028). In the serial specification, EMSs were positively associated with desire thinking, desire thinking was strongly associated with craving, and serial indirect associations were observed for all four problematic excessive behaviors. EMSs also remained directly associated with the outcomes. Craving was positively associated with all four behavioral severity outcomes. However, because the selected activity was not recorded, these associations cannot be interpreted as behavior-matched craving–severity associations. The findings suggest possible cross-domain relevance of EMSs, desire thinking, and craving, but do not establish temporal or causal ordering, diagnostic equivalence, or a single underlying addiction process. Because the referent of the desire-thinking and craving measures was not recorded, behavior-specific interpretation of these associations remains limited. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Returning network findings: An art gallery as a report-back in a rural community
Abstract: In health research, communities rarely receive findings in a form they can use. This problem is more complex in social network research, where findings are both relational and individual. The challenge compounds in rural, underserved settings, where low health literacy and limited exposure to scientific visualization severely constrain how results can be communicated. As part of a longitudinal personal network project on primary cancer prevention in rural areas, we developed an art gallery to return findings to the community. The installation was framed as a performative intervention that made relational structures visible, inviting awareness and reflection. It comprised seven digitally printed canvases and a three-dimensional network sculpture. Each item presented a level of social organization (personal network, household, community structure, socio-spatial concentration, and food culture) through designs intended for non-specialist viewers and supported by facilitation. The three-day exhibition attracted 103 visitors, all of whom rated its utility highly. It also revealed how the community reacted to findings about their rural context. This exploratory single-site study supports three lessons: linking each canvas to a single analytical level aided reading, the order of presentation helped viewers build a basic vocabulary for network visualization, and facilitation, more than the canvases alone, carried the interpretive work. Limitations include a single installation and ratings that seem to reflect acceptability and acquiescence rather than comprehension. Future work should directly evaluate understanding, compare reception across sites, and test refinements such as written legends. We describe a working approach, not a validated framework. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier B.V. Author full names: Steenson, Áine (61014118100); Booth, Nichola (57226378141); Roulston, Audrey (55344838000)
Title: Pathological demand avoidance and schooling experiences: A scoping review examining the experiences of children and their families
Abstract: Pathological Demand Avoidance (PDA) is widely depicted to be a profile that lies within the autistic spectrum; its salient feature being a strong resistance to demands due to heightened anxiety or an intolerance to uncertainty, which arguably creates a significant conflict with a schooling environment. Alternatively, there are others who argue that there is growing evidence that a PDA profile can be observed outside of the autistic spectrum (Woods, 2022). This scoping review's objective was to explore the current available research pertaining to PDA and schooling experiences. A number of databases including Scopus, PsycInfo, Child Developmental and Adolescent Studies and the Social Science Citation Index were searched, and nine articles were selected for review based on the inclusion criteria. Analysis of the extracted data found three main themes; barriers that exist within the education system, characteristics of the PDA profile that prevent engagement in education and characteristics, approaches and interventions that help to improve schooling experiences. The findings of this review suggest that a substantial number of children and young people who present with the profile are experiencing extreme distress within their schooling environment, which is impacting their ability to learn, and contributing to exclusion and poor mental health. There are major gaps and methodological flaws that exist within the PDA literature; further research is urgently needed to address these and to help advance knowledge of the profile and assist in improving outcomes for this group of children and young people (CYP) within education. Recommendations for support to help these young people have been included. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Hu L.; Su S.; He S.
Title: Unravelling intra-urban spatiotemporal disparities in housing price dynamics: An infrastructural approach using interpretable machine-learning methods in Shenzhen, China
Abstract: Housing inequalities have long been a pressing global issue, particularly in the context of rapidly transforming urban housing markets. However, intra-urban spatiotemporal disparities in housing price dynamics remain insufficiently understood. By developing an infrastructural approach operationalized through interpretable machine-learning methods that explicitly incorporate spatiotemporal heterogeneity, this study examines the complex capitalization of key infrastructures into housing prices, drawing on 288,570 second-hand housing transactions and multi-source geographic data from 2010 to 2023 in Shenzhen, one of the largest and most dynamic urban housing markets in China. The results reveal increasingly intensified housing price disparities, which are particularly pronounced within school catchment areas and 15-minute infrastructure-accessible neighborhoods. Compared with physical infrastructures, as well as structural and locational attributes, social infrastructures—especially public schools—are more decisively and consistently associated with housing prices. Their spatiotemporally heterogenous capitalization and increasingly salient threshold effects highlight the agency of social infrastructures in leveraging urban development and (re)shaping social inequalities, thereby advancing the understanding of housing price disparities. Finally, this study provides dynamic, fine-grained evidence to support locally calibrated and stage-sensitive urban planning and housing policies. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Decriminalizing suicide in Uganda: Legal reform and public health imperative
Source title: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
Abstract: Uganda criminalizes attempted suicide, exposing survivors to prosecution and imprisonment while mental health legislation requires assessment and care. This study examines the consequences of criminalization for access to care and the protection of health and dignity in Uganda. We conducted a comparative legal and policy review of legislation, constitutional adjudication, national reports, and published research through September 18, 2026. India, Ghana, and Kenya provided comparators. Uganda's 2016–2017 surveillance analysis reported attempted-suicide prevalence of 7.1 per 100,000 among males and 6.7 among females. It reported approximately 38 deaths per 1000 recorded male cases. The Ministry of Health recorded 616,175 mental-health outpatient attendances in 2023/24, including 96,277 for unipolar depressive disorders. Ugandan accounts describe imprisonment after treatment and threats of prosecution during recovery. Mental health workers differed over punishment as deterrence, while survivors described both punitive police encounters and referral for care. Fear of legal consequences can discourage disclosure, delay help-seeking, and impede accurate reporting. Constitutional protections and judicial recognition of health rights support scrutiny of this penal response. The Mental Health Act's treatment duties leave criminal liability for the attempt intact. The evidence supports repeal alongside funded crisis services, clear referral responsibilities, and continued clinical and social support. Decriminalization should remove punishment for surviving a suicidal crisis while making timely care and recovery the purpose of the public response. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Transport cost-benefit analysis: critical evaluation and improvement
Abstract: Cost–benefit analysis (CBA) remains the dominant framework for the ex ante evaluation of transport policies and infrastructure investments, grounded in welfare economics and aimed at maximizing aggregate social welfare. However, a growing body of literature questions whether CBA adequately captures the multidimensional objectives of contemporary transport policy, including effectiveness, efficiency, and equity. This paper addresses this debate by systematically identifying and structuring criticisms of CBA in transport, drawing on a scoping review of 75 publications and insights from two expert workshops involving 16 specialists from multiple disciplines. The analysis categorizes criticisms into four groups: (1) fundamental limitations of CBA; (2) shortcomings in practical application; (3) issues related to debatable policy questions; and (4) decision-making challenges. Building on these insights, the paper discusses potential avenues for improvement, including better integration of distributional and accessibility effects, refinement of valuation methods, and alternative approaches. The results suggest that many shortcomings attributed to CBA stem from how it is applied within policy processes. The continued use of CBA in transport policy contexts requires an understanding of inherent weaknesses, their improvement, and appropriate use. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Du Y.; Cao Y.; Cheng Z.; Zhu X.; chen T.; Liu H.; Zhang F.
Title: Trajectory of maternal perinatal negative psychological states and its association with early offspring neurodevelopment: A longitudinal cohort study
Abstract: Background Existing studies often examined single psychological states in isolation (depression, anxiety, stress) or used static assessments, limiting the understanding of dynamic trajectories and synergistic effects of co-occurring psychological states. The study was designed to tackle both major limitations. Methods 609 pregnant women in their third trimester were enrolled. Maternal depression, anxiety, and perceived stress were repeatedly assessed at the third trimester and 1, 3, and 6 months postpartum using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, and Perceived Stress Scale. Infant neurodevelopment was evaluated at the same postpartum timepoints using the Ages and Stages Questionnaire-Third Edition. Group-based multi-trajectory modeling (GBMTM) was used to identify joint developmental trajectories of three negative psychological states, and multilevel models assessed their association with neurodevelopmental outcomes. Growth mixture modeling was applied to identify independent trajectories for each psychological state. Results A total of 417 mother-infant dyads completed the longitudinal follow-up. The GBMTM identified three distinct trajectories: Stable Low Negative Psychological State Group (29.9%), Stable Moderate Negative Psychological State Group (55.2%), and Unstable High Negative Psychological State Group (14.8%). After adjusting for confounders, maternal negative psychological states were significantly correlated with poorer offspring neurodevelopment, including communication, gross motor, fine motor, problem solving, personal-social skills. Stratified analysis revealed sex-specific effects of negative psychological states. Conclusion Maternal perinatal negative psychological states were significant risk factors for adverse early infant neurodevelopment. These findings highlight the importance of screening for and addressing co-occurring maternal negative psychological states during perinatal period. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Brief social contact videos to promote treatment seeking among young adults with depressive symptoms: Intention change, suicidal ideation, and treatment use in a randomized controlled trial
Abstract: Background Young adults with depression often avoid mental health care. Social contact videos may increase help-seeking intentions, but whether intention change leads to treatment use remains unclear, especially among those with suicidal ideation. We examined whether change in help-seeking intentions accounted for treatment use after social contact videos versus a written vignette, and whether this pathway differed by suicidal ideation. Methods In this randomized controlled trial, 1545 young adults (aged 18–25 years) with depressive symptoms were recruited via Prolific and randomized to one of three brief videos featuring personal recovery stories or a written vignette with identical content, yielding a 3:1 video-to-written comparison. Help-seeking intentions were measured before, after, and at 30-day follow-up. Treatment use at 30-day follow-up was modeled using structural equation modeling. Suicidal ideation was tested as a moderator of the association between intention change and treatment use. Results Participants assigned to video showed greater change in help-seeking intentions, and intention change was associated with treatment use. The indirect association through intention change and the total effect were significant. Treatment use was greater with video than with vignette. Conditional indirect effects did not differ by suicidal ideation. However, the association between intention change and treatment use was stronger among participants with suicidal ideation than those without. Conclusions Change in help-seeking intentions partially accounted for the association between intervention assignment and treatment use. Brief social contact videos may represent a scalable approach to treatment seeking among young adults with depressive symptoms, including those with suicidal ideation. Title: NIMBY to YIMBY: Towards a Better Neighbourhood
Abstract: ‘Not in my backyard’ (NIMBY) resistance to eco-economic technologies often reflects rational self-interest, escalating into NIABY (‘not in anybody’s backyard’) movements against inequality. While municipal solid waste (MSW) projects frequently face opposition, some communities adopt collaborative ‘yes, in my backyard’ (YIMBY) approaches. This study examines Beijing’s Anding Town, where landfill leachate treatment (reducing CH4) transitioned to waste incineration (producing grid electricity), fostering equitable urban sustainability. A ‘niche-nexus-nodes’ (3N) framework explains synergies in a ‘pilot-park-port’ complex. Niche—A rural homestead (zhaiji di) reform pilot relocated 1925 households into new residential zones, paired with a circular economy industrial part (waste incineration plant and environmental education hub). Nexus—the Lifang Mechanism—a governance model led by neighbourhood leaders (fang: 20 households; li: 10 fangs)—enhanced post-relocation community belonging, optimising public services. Nodes—integration with Daxing International Airport’s commercial zone expanded local networks through jobs, tourism and infrastructure, transforming residents into active governance participants. By aligning policy, technology and community agency, Anding Town redefined waste management as a collective asset, offering a replicable model for a greener neighbourhood, converging technologies with institutional innovation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Finn H.
Title: Material meanings of ‘transformative learning’ among sustainability educators in universities
Abstract: Prominent calls have been made to radically shift current teaching provision in higher education towards critically ‘transformative’ pedagogies that align with the pressing imperatives of sustainability. Yet much uncertainty remains over how educators envision the notion of ‘transformative learning’ and their possible role in supporting it. In this study, 21 interviews were conducted with specialist UK-based academics in which they were asked to bring a physical object to represent what ‘transformative learning’ might look like in the context of their sustainable development-focused curricula. Narrative thematic analyses indicated that while transformation cannot be directly brought about by the actions of educators, they can nonetheless indirectly help to support it by enabling students to encounter diverse perspectives, to acquire novel appreciations for relational thinking and to actively participate in social change. Such practices were found to enable a generative balance between the initiatives of the educator and the agency of the student. Title: Implementing peer-assisted learning in the clinical environment for undergraduate health sciences students: A scoping review
Abstract: Background: Peer-assisted learning (PAL) has been shown to provide a supportive learning environment, motivate students, and increase students' self-efficacy. Although PAL has been formalised in some training institutions in developed countries, its implementation in clinical practice still exhibits design shortcomings. This scoping review maps evidence on how PAL was implemented in undergraduate health sciences programmes. Method: The scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Manual for Evidence Synthesis and reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Six databases – MEDLINE, Academic Search Ultimate, CINAHL with Full Text, Education Source, PsycINFO, and African-Wide – were systematically searched from September 2024, with an update completed in January 2025. The search initially identified 894 articles. The research team resolved any discrepancies through discussion. Our study used a two-phase analytical process, utilising descriptive numerical analysis followed by qualitative content analysis and inductive category development. Results: The 20 reviewed articles were published between 2010 and 2024, with the majority originating from Sweden (n = 5). PAL was predominantly applied within the medical profession (n = 10). Near-peer teaching emerged as the most common approach (n = 12), followed by horizontal peer teaching (n = 7), while reciprocal peer teaching was the least frequent (n = 1). Our findings categorised the organisation and characteristics of PAL implementation into three themes: planning, implementation, and evaluation. Conclusion: The study findings identify implementation considerations that may inform future guideline development. Key factors for effective PAL include well-trained peer tutors, strong support systems, a mix of peer- and expert-led activities, and close collaboration with clinical staff. Although PAL is commonly used in healthcare training, nursing education requires specific, evidence-based guidelines for successful implementation. Moreover, more research is needed in low-resource settings to better understand PAL's applicability and challenges in these environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Jia C.; Huang S.; Xu Z.; Wang J.; Li T.; Xiao Y.
Title: A predictive model of derived topic propagation based on multi-task learning and group identity-confrontation
Abstract: With the rapid development of social media, predicting derived topic propagation faces three core challenges: data sparsity, high-dimensional noise, and complex group interactions. To address these in a coherent manner, this paper proposes an integrated framework that sequentially tackles each challenge. First, to combat data sparsity, a multi-task learning (MTL) mechanism is introduced. It enables knowledge transfer from data-rich original topics to sparse derived topics by learning shared feature representations, effectively augmenting the training signal for derived topics. Building on this, to handle the resultant high-dimensional and noisy feature space, a sparse representation module is applied. It performs low-rank and sparse coding to distill essential propagation features and eliminate redundancy, producing a purified and robust input for the final stage. Finally, to model the strategic group interactions that drive propagation, we quantify intra-group identity and inter-group confrontation using evolutionary game theory. These dynamics are embedded into a novel Identification–Confrontation Graph Convolutional Network (IC-GCN), which explicitly captures strategy-aware social influences for precise behavior prediction. Extensive experiments on four real-world derived topics from Weibo and Twitter demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The complete IC-GCN model consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating that the logical integration of MTL (for sparsity), sparse coding (for purification), and game-theoretic GCN (for interaction modeling) substantially enhances prediction accuracy. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Kruse, Felix (58982473200); Nagel, Arvid (60415689300); Nabi, Robin (6701455407)
Title: Erosion or protection? Testing directionality between problematic social media use and mindfulness over one year using a latent cross-lagged panel model
Abstract: Background Problematic social media use (PSMU) and mindfulness are consistently negatively associated, but longitudinal evidence on their directional relationship remains limited. This study examined whether mindfulness prospectively predicts lower later PSMU (protection pathway), whether PSMU predicts lower later mindfulness (erosion pathway), or whether their longitudinal association is bidirectional. Methods Participants were 246 early adolescents from German-speaking Switzerland (48.4 % girls), aged 10 to 13 years (M = 10.93, SD = 0.51), assessed approximately one year apart in spring 2024 and spring 2025. After establishing longitudinal measurement invariance, a two-wave latent cross-lagged panel model was estimated to examine temporal stability and prospective associations between the constructs. Results PSMU and mindfulness were moderately and negatively associated within both waves, and both constructs showed temporal stability. Cross-lagged effects were asymmetric: baseline mindfulness did not predict later PSMU, whereas higher baseline PSMU predicted lower mindfulness at follow-up (β = − 0.188). Supplementary analyses showed no evidence of sex differences, and sensitivity analyses supported the same directional pattern. Conclusions Findings suggest that, in early adolescence, PSMU may be more likely to undermine later mindfulness than mindfulness is to protect against later PSMU. This pattern provides initial support for an erosion pathway during an early phase of social media uptake and highlights mindfulness as a possible outcome of digital behavior. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Alchin N.
Title: Connection: A Year of Great Conversations with Your Teen
Source title: Connection: A Year of Great Conversations with Your Teen
Abstract: An insightful guide for parents to cultivate meaningful conversations and connections with their children. When today's world, and certainly tomorrow's world, looks so different from the world we grew up in, as parents we grapple with complex and urgent questions: How do we talk with our children so that we nurture resilience in an age of uncertainty? How do we prepare young people for an uncertain future while grounding them in a strong sense of purpose and values? How can we help our teenagers flourish and stay strong mentally when so many are struggling? In Connection: A Year of Great Conversations with Your Teen, Nicholas Alchin helps parents reflect on and talk about these matters with their kids, especially pre-teens and teenagers. It bridges the gap between mundane realities (kids going to school, being on social media, arguing with parents, falling out with friends) and timeless philosophical inquiries (who we are, who we aspire to be, how we find happiness and fulfilment), while challenging parents to reflect on their role in shaping their children's values, growth, and futures. With an inquiring, philosophical stance on growing up, parenting, wellbeing, achievement, and careers, Alchin offers specific, practical guidance to support parents in their journey to finding a deeper connection with their kids through intentional conversation. Open-hearted discussions can invigorate any relationship. But especially during the pre-teen and teenage years, being able to discuss the rocky parts of growing up is particularly impactful. Connection is born of this need, offering a map of ideas, conversations, and tools that enable families to have deep, meaningful conversations together. © Nicholas Alchin, 2027.

Authors: Yang X.; Xu X.; Zhang X.; Zhang S.; Zhang F.; Bao W.; Chen L.; Ge H.; Fu K.; Feng H.
Title: Career uncertainty, professional identity, and future workforce intention among students in ageing care-related majors: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study
Abstract: Aim/objective: To examine the relationships among social support, career clarity, career uncertainty, professional identity, anxiety, and future workforce intention among students enrolled in ageing care-related majors in China, with particular attention to how professional identity and career uncertainty were associated with anxiety and intention to work in ageing care after graduation. Background: Population ageing has increased the demand for a sustainable ageing-care workforce. However, evidence remains limited on the psychological and career-development factors associated with students' preparedness for and intention to enter ageing-care professions. Design: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1342 students from five educational institutions in China, followed by semi-structured interviews with 23 students. Anxiety and intention to work in ageing care after graduation were the primary quantitative outcomes, with professional identity and career uncertainty as the principal explanatory variables. Multivariable linear regression was used to examine associations with anxiety, and cumulative ordinal and multinomial logistic regression models were used for career intention. Qualitative interviews provided context and further insight into the quantitative findings, which were integrated with the qualitative findings through a joint display. Results: Overall, 45.6% of students reported at least mild anxiety symptoms. Stronger professional identity was associated with lower anxiety and greater intention to work in ageing care. Because the proportional-odds assumption was not supported for several predictors of career intention, category-specific multinomial estimates were also examined. In the multinomial model, professional identity was positively associated with the willing and very willing categories relative to the very unwilling category, although these estimates did not establish differences in the magnitude of associations between career-intention categories. Greater career uncertainty was associated with higher anxiety and lower career intention in the ordinal model, although the association with career intention was not consistently supported by category-specific multinomial estimates. Career clarity was independently associated with lower anxiety. Overall social support was not independently associated with anxiety or with career intention in the adjusted ordinal model. However, the multinomial model identified an association for the unwilling versus very unwilling comparison (OR = 0.429, 95% CI 0.196 to 0.940), which should be interpreted cautiously given the multiple category-specific comparisons. Qualitative findings contextualised these patterns, highlighting uncertainty about career pathways, concerns about professional recognition and working conditions, meaningful practical experiences, and perceptions of the professional value of ageing-care work. Participants also described educational and interpersonal support as important in shaping their career experiences, despite the absence of consistent adjusted associations between overall social support and the primary outcomes. Conclusions: Professional identity was associated with lower anxiety and greater career intention, although the multinomial estimates did not establish differences in association strength between career-intention categories. Career uncertainty was strongly associated with higher anxiety, whereas its association with career intention was less consistent across modelling approaches. Overall social support was not associated with anxiety or career intention in the adjusted linear and ordinal models, respectively, although one category-specific association was observed in the multinomial model. The findings highlight the importance of clearer career pathways, meaningful practical exposure, and opportunities to develop professional identity within ageing-care education. Longitudinal research is needed to determine whether these associations persist over time and are reflected in subsequent workforce entry and retention. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Fishman S.H.; Brewer M.; Andersson M.
Author full names: Fishman, Samuel H. (57202689169); Brewer, Mackenzie (56294441700); Andersson, Matthew (60215347100)
Title: Debt and early midlife substance use and suicidal ideation
Abstract: The article tests a common model of how different types of debt relate to substance use and suicidal ideation in early midlife. Drawing on data from US adults age 33 through 43 from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, we model how consumption and investment debt relate to four outcomes: opioid painkiller misuse, other drug use, frequent binge drinking, and suicidal ideation. While educational and mortgage debt do not predict higher risk of these outcomes, consumption debt, incurred from sources other than education or housing, is consistently associated with increased risk across all four outcomes. Sensitivity tests do not isolate any compelling evidence of reverse causality, but we cannot conclusively determine that indebtedness causes increased risk of substance use or suicidal ideation. We contend, however, that high levels of consumption debt are consistently associated with behaviors and ideations that are associated with elevated health risk. © 2026

Authors: Chung S.; Talebpour A.; Hamdar S.H.

Title: Characterizing lane-changing behavior in mixed traffic
Source title: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
Abstract: Characterizing and understanding lane-changing behavior in the presence of automated vehicles (AVs) is crucial to ensuring safety and efficiency in mixed traffic. Accordingly, this study aims to characterize the interactions between the lane-changing vehicle (active vehicle) and the vehicle directly impacted by the maneuver in the target lane (passive vehicle). Utilizing real-world trajectory data from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD), this study explores patterns in lane-changing behavior and provides insight into how these behaviors evolve under different AV market penetration rates (MPRs). In particular, we propose a game-theoretic framework to analyze cooperative and defective behaviors in mixed traffic, applied to the 7636 observed lane-changing events in the WOMD. First, we utilize k-means clustering to classify vehicles as cooperative or defective, revealing that the proportions of cooperative AVs are higher than those of HDVs in both active and passive roles. Next, we jointly estimate the utilities of active and passive vehicles to model their behaviors using the quantal response equilibrium framework. Empirical payoff tables are then constructed based on these utilities. Using these payoffs, we analyze the presence of social dilemmas and examine the evolution of cooperative behaviors using evolutionary game theory. Our results reveal the presence of social dilemmas in approximately 4% and 11% of lane-changing events for active and passive vehicles, respectively, with most classified as Stag Hunt or Prisoner’s Dilemma (Chicken Game rarely observed). Moreover, the Monte Carlo simulation results show that repeated lane-changing interactions consistently lead to increased cooperative behavior over time, regardless of the AV penetration rate. © 2026 The Author(s). Author full names: Castaldo, Romina (57194282513); Capiotto, Francesca (58193597300); Bari, Stefania (56973745300); Keller, Roberto (36454980400)
Title: Changes in social functioning and emotional well-being following an integrated social skills training programme in autistic adults: A pre–post study
Abstract: Social skills training (SST) is widely used to improve interpersonal functioning in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet evidence in autistic adults remains limited, particularly with regard to emotional outcomes. This study examined changes in perceived social functioning and emotional well-being following participation in a group-based SST programme integrating behavioural techniques with components targeting emotional awareness and metacognitive reflection. Sixty-eight autistic adults participated in a pre–post design. Perceived social functioning was assessed using the Social Responsiveness Scale–Second Edition (SRS-2), while anxiety and depressive symptoms were measured using the State–Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) and the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). After correction for multiple comparisons, significant pre–post changes were observed in social motivation, state and trait anxiety, and cognitive depressive symptoms. Changes in social communication did not meet the corrected significance threshold. Exploratory analyses indicated that greater reductions in perceived social difficulties were associated with lower post-intervention depressive symptoms and trait anxiety, but not state anxiety. An association between reductions in perceived social difficulties and reductions in trait anxiety also emerged in a separate model adjusted for baseline scores. Taken together, these findings provide preliminary evidence that participation in an integrated SST programme may be associated with concurrent improvements in perceived social functioning and emotional well-being in autistic adults. Given the pre–post design and reliance on self-report measures, results should be considered preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The impact of hunger and resource scarcity on children’s fairness judgments and behaviors: A developmental cross-national investigation
Abstract: This study investigated how hunger and poverty influence children’s willingness to share resources with a hungry recipient, as well as how these factors interact across development. Participants included 918 children aged 5 to 8 years from Bolivia, Haiti, and Cambodia, who were recruited from neighborhoods within each country varying in socioeconomic status. Children completed sharing tasks both before and after lunch. Linear mixed model analyses revealed that neighborhood poverty and acute hunger jointly influenced children’s sharing behavior towards hungry recipients, but only when both factors and age were considered. These findings illuminate the developmental integration of socioeconomic and contextual cues in shaping children’s social decision-making. Public significance statement: This study demonstrates how children consider both their own hunger and the availability of resources in their environment when deciding to share. The findings highlight the significant role that hunger plays in social cognitive development during middle childhood. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Yasa R.; Dogruyol Aladak K.B.
Author full names: Yasa, Rozerin (59732765100); Dogruyol Aladak, K. Begum (60888276700)
Title: Mansplaining and the marginalisation of women academics in Turkey
Abstract: This study investigates the systematic marginalisation of women academics in Turkish universities through the lens of ‘mansplaining’, using a phenomenological design and interviews with 13 women academics, and situates these dynamics within a centralised, politicised higher education system that shapes women's epistemic authority. Mansplaining emerges not as a communicative annoyance but as institutional violence and epistemic silencing that enforces a ‘masculinised’ identity performance and reinforces vertical discrimination—symbolised by the ‘men are deans, women are assistants’ hierarchy—particularly in regional settings. Participants' selective reticence about the political context reflects institutional caution and self-censorship. The study proposes concrete interventions—defining ‘epistemic violence’ in university codes, ‘interruption audits’ in academic boards, and peer-solidarity networks—underscoring the need for systemic transformation toward a more equitable academic culture in Turkey. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Zhang Y.; Zhong X.; Ahn S.; He Z.; Zou Y.
Title: Interaction-enhanced lane-change early warning in congested traffic: a spatial risk propagation-aware approach
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: This paper presents an interaction-enhanced Lane-Changing Early Warning (LCEW) system designed to issue reliable early warning signals through a spatial risk-propagation-aware approach. The system is built upon interpretable multi-vehicle trajectory predictions and collision risk identification within an extended LC zone, including multiple downstream and upstream vehicles. We first investigate the stochasticity and hazardousness of LCs, characterized by (i) variable-size multi-vehicle interactions within the LC zone and (ii) the resulting risk propagation from downstream to upstream traffic. To model these stochastic interactions, a Social Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Neural Network framework informed by mutual information (social STGCNN-MI) is introduced to predict multi-vehicle trajectories. By leveraging a mutual information-based kernel function, the framework enhances trajectory prediction accuracy while providing interpretable representations of vehicle interactions. Then, oriented bounding box detection is employed on the predicted trajectories to identify direct collision risks between the LC vehicle and adjacent vehicles and indirect risks among non-adjacent vehicles. These components jointly quantify and characterize how risks originating from downstream interactions influence LC behavior and subsequently propagate to upstream traffic. Finally, awareness of this spatial risk propagation enables the generation of an early warning signal that informs the LC decision-making with potential collision locations within the predicted time window. Traffic simulation experiments conducted in SUMO demonstrate that the proposed LCEW effectively improves vehicle-level safety and comfort, while maintaining system-level traffic safety and efficiency. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
