Authors: Hudson P.; Okitasari M.; Suzuki M.
Author full names: Hudson, Paul (55436620700); Okitasari, Mahesti (57211606574); Suzuki, Masachika (56113344300)
Title: An Introduction to Equitable and Sustainable Cities—Economics and Disruptive Technologies
Abstract: Sustainable development has been a key global policy goal, as reflected in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 11. Cities are central to this agenda, as they are home to over half of the global population—a figure projected to surpass 70 per cent by 2050. Despite occupying only 3 per cent of the Earth’s surface, urban areas are responsible for a disproportionate share of environmental, social and economic impacts. They account for up to 80 per cent of global GDP, but also contribute significantly to carbon emissions, energy consumption and vulnerability to climate change and natural disasters. Rapid urbanisation, particularly in developing regions, poses challenges related to infrastructure, housing and essential services, often exacerbating inequalities and urban poverty. More than one billion people currently live in informal settlements, a number expected to triple by mid-century. Achieving sustainable urban development requires balancing social justice, environmental responsibility and economic viability, necessitating transformative approaches to city planning, governance and resource management. This book explores multiple pathways towards equitable and sustainable cities, examining how novel technologies, social innovations and institutional frameworks can drive meaningful change. Some chapters focus on technological advancements, such as environmental monitoring and disaster risk insurance, while others examine alternative social and economic structures, such as housing cooperatives. Recognising that technology alone is insufficient, the book emphasises the need for socially responsible innovation and governance to ensure that urban development aligns with long-term sustainability goals. While some chapters address urban sustainability directly, others engage with broader socio-environmental challenges that ultimately intersect with cities. As hubs of economic activity, population growth and governance, cities serve as ‘living laboratories’ where solutions to global crises—climate change, social inequality and economic instability—are tested and implemented. By integrating diverse perspectives and interdisciplinary insights, this volume highlights the complex but crucial role of cities in shaping a sustainable and equitable future. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Rahmatian A.
Title: David Hume and Adam Smith on Law and Justice
Source title: David Hume and Adam Smith on Law and Justice
Abstract: Analyses the legal and jurisprudential writings of David Hume and Adam Smith * First comprehensive study of the legal aspects within Hume's and Smith's writings * Discussion of Hume's and Smith's moral philosophy, concept of justice, and, in connection, law * Examination of property and contract law within Hume's and Smith's understanding of moral philosophy and of law * Discussion of Hume's and Smith's political theory, moral philosophy and law: family and government, and trade Andreas Rahmatian presents the first comprehensive study of the legal aspects of Hume's and Smith's writings. The Scottish Enlightenment was considerably legal or jurisprudential in its moral and social or political philosophy. Yet until now, David Hume and Adam Smith's considerable body of legal texts - both with regard to technical (private) law and legal and political philosophy - have been neglected by lawyers and philosophers, political theorists and historians of political thought. By focusing on the legal aspects in relation to the works of Hume and Smith, this book connects Hume's and Smith's legal thought with their moral philosophy and shows the relevance of their moral philosophy to their legal writings. It completes the analysis of Hume's and Smith's moral philosophy by focusing on what they had to say about law, by comparing and contrasting these two thinkers and putting them into context with Scottish Enlightenment thought generally. Hume and Smith's different views in relation to the origin of justice, of morality and of other foundational conceptions of the law are compared and contrasted and also considered in relation to other thinkers of the Scottish Enlightenment and beyond. © Andreas Rahmatian, 2026.

Authors: Vargas-Chaves I.; López-Oliva J.
Title: The Precautionary Principle as a Constitutional Imperative in Traditional Agricultural Knowledge; [El principio de precaución como imperativo constitucional en los conocimientos tradicionales agrícolas]
Abstract: The dominant agricultural paradigm, while having increased food production, has provoked a crisis by undermining biological and cultural diversity, which threatens the resilience of food systems and violates interdependent human rights, such as adequate food and a healthy environment. In response to this problem, the objective is to analyze how the precautionary principle can be operationalized to protect this interdependence, defending traditional agricultural knowledge and democratizing food governance. To meet this objective, a documentary analysis methodology was employed, systematically reviewing academic literature, legal documents, and international treaties. The results demonstrate the interdependence of the rights to food and the environment as a foundation for biocultural protection, analyze regulatory threats, and examine the scope of the precautionary principle in international and constitutional law. It is concluded that the application of this principle is an essential governance strategy for building just and resilient food systems, with its main contribution being the operationalization of a legal principle for the defense of biocultural interaction, grounded in the interdependence of human rights. Authors: Liu S.; Gibbons R.D.
Title: Greenspace and suicide rate: comparing and contrasting the U.S., England & Wales
Abstract: Suicide claims more than 720,000 lives each year. Reducing suicide requires targeted policy interventions, underscoring the need to identify potential protective factors. Although greenspace has been proposed as a protective factor, empirical findings remain inconsistent. A comparative analysis that accounts for spatial scale, greenspace diversity, and contextual differences is therefore needed to investigate whether the relationship between greenspace and suicide varies across countries and to better understand how social and environmental inequalities shape suicide risk. Specifically, we examined four measures of urban greenspace: regional park count, regional park area proportion, local park proximity, and average park size. Using suicide data from 2019 to 2023, we performed a cross-sectional ecological study across all urban counties in the U.S. and all urban local authorities in England & Wales to study the associations between greenspace and suicide rates. By comparing two national contexts at similar administrative levels, we investigated whether the associations differ across social contexts and how these relationships change before and after adjusting for socioeconomic disadvantage. In the U.S., park availability stood out as a strong protective factor, with counties having at least one open park exhibiting an estimated 19% lower suicide rate (incidence rate ratio (IRR) = 0.81). In England & Wales, significant nonlinear association between suicide and park counts was detected, suggesting potential heterogeneity across local authorities, particularly those with a large number of parks. These findings underscore the need for context-specific approaches to urban greenspace planning and public health interventions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: See what you see, hear what you hear: Theorizing AI Device Embodiment (ADE) and its effects on well-being, perceived social support, and adoption
Abstract: AI glasses share sensorimotor coupling with users and represent a form of embodied AI, marking a fundamental shift in the human–AI relationship compared with other AI devices. This study theorizes AI Device Embodiment (ADE) and develops an ADE model by validating a newly developed ADE scale. We define ADE as the perceived degree of sensorimotor coupling between an AI system embedded in AI devices and human users. A 3 (device: AI glasses, mobile phones, laptops) between-subjects design experiment with 153 participants showed that users of AI glasses reported greater ADE than users of mobile phones and laptops. Indirect analyses further revealed that AI glasses increased subjective well-being, perceived social support availability, and intentions to adopt AI through higher levels of ADE. ADE captures the unique integration of AI systems with users’ perceptual and sensorimotor processes, representing a novel mechanism through which AI glasses influence user experiences. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Reid S.F.; Xue M.
Title: ‘Stop Banning Books’: A Multimodal Analysis of Two Fifth-Grade Students' Co-Authored Protest Comic
Abstract: This study draws from qualitative multimodal content analysis and interpretive research methods to examine how two elementary students in the midwestern United States co-authored an anti-censorship comic during a summer literacy programme focused on social justice and civic engagement. This study is rooted in critical and multimodal approaches to literacy education and draws upon recent scholarship responding to the current increase in censorship and book banning across the United States. The findings share a panel-by-panel analysis, demonstrating how the two students constructed a sophisticated comic that engages reader-viewers in meaningful socio-political critique. Students used a variety of multimodal resources as meaning-making tools to represent the significance of both individual and collective social action. Thus, the comics medium's sequential design gave these young composers room to ask not only what is wrong, but what might be, narrating a pathway from individual grievance through collective action to reconciliation. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that young students are capable of engaging with justice issues and offering hopeful visions for unity and resolution through images and words. This analysis of two students' protest comic testifies to what becomes possible when children are trusted as capable thinkers, multimodal composers and civic participants. © 2026 United Kingdom Literacy Association.

Title: Embedding professionals in place: The community connector program as a rural workforce retention strategy
Abstract: Globally, the sustainability of rural communities is increasingly threatened by professional workforce attraction and retention challenges, with cascading negative effects on service provision, economic viability, and community vitality. While traditionally addressed through siloed, profession-specific approaches, these challenges are complex socio-spatial phenomena that also require place and community-grounded responses. This article examines the Community Connector Program, a community-led, place-based initiative involving eight rural communities across Australia and Aotearoa/New Zealand. Drawing on two rounds of interviews with 14 Champions and Community Connectors conducted two years apart and analysed through a narrative, feminist-informed approach, we examine the conditions of possibility for community-led workforce retention programs. Our analysis is organised around three constructs—the conditions of community uptake, connection work as brokered embedding, and structural conditions and the boundaries of community agency—that were identified through iterative engagement between participants' accounts and theory. We find that communities able to take up the Community Connector Program exhibit strong self-determination, strategic leadership, and fluency in community development. The program's functioning depends on its community-level positioning and on the multilayered connection work of community connectors; stalled and faltering cases reveal the conditions under which it does not take root. The limits communities encounter—diffuse responsibility, insecure funding, and the siloed governance of publicly funded health systems—mark the boundaries of community agency. By specifying these conditions and limits, we demonstrate that community-led action can intentionally build belonging-in-place for newcomer professionals, while the principal drivers of workforce sustainability remain structural and, in significant part, lie beyond local control. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The indirect city: transport, environment, and perceived livability as pathways to subjective well-being
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Transport shapes daily life in dense cities by exposing residents to noise, pollution, and insecurity as they travel. Drawing on a 2023–2024 household survey of 2,448 adults around a high-demand corridor in Bogotá, we examine how the perceived livability of this travel-and-residential environment relates to subjective well-being (SWB). We model livability as a second-order construct reflected in five domains (transport, environment, neighborhood, local services, and security) and estimate an SEM-MIMIC linking it to SWB through perceived health and social capital. Livability shows no direct association with SWB and instead operates through better health and stronger social capital, with health the strongest predictor. Conditions of the travel environment, such as harassment, crime, noise, and pollution along the corridor, are among its strongest manifestations. Livability is most strongly reflected in security and environmental quality. Transport and environmental policies may raise SWB most when they reduce chronic stressors such as insecurity, noise, and pollution, and strengthen social resources, with implications for equity-oriented planning in Global South cities. Title: Education programs on emerging and reemerging infectious disease outbreak management for pre-registration Nursing and Medical Students: A scoping review
Abstract: Introduction: Preparing the future healthcare workforce in managing emerging and reemerging infectious disease (ERID) outbreaks is critical. However, knowledge gaps remain in education programs for ERID outbreaks for pre-registration nursing and medical students. Aim: To comprehensively identify existing ERID outbreak education programs for medical and nursing students, summarizing evidence on program design, curriculum content, learning outcomes, and student experiences. Methods: A scoping review was conducted using the Arksey and O'Malley framework. Eligible studies were searched from inception to 1st November 2025 across nine databases (Cochrane, CINAHL, Embase, MedNar, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, ProQuest). Two reviewers screened for eligible studies and appraised the quality of included studies independently. This was followed by data charting and narrative synthesis of findings. Results: Among the 38 included studies, ERID outbreak management programs for medical (n = 16) and nursing (n = 22) students predominantly targeted COVID-19 and involved short-duration (1 to 5 h) online or simulation-based methods. Curriculum content of these programs included fundamentals of infectious diseases, epidemiology and surveillance, clinical management of infected persons, infection prevention and control and public health and pandemic preparedness. Nursing curricula emphasised infection prevention and control while medical programs prioritised epidemiology and clinical patient management. Most programs reported improvements in knowledge and clinical procedural skills, particularly via simulation. Non-procedural skills (e.g., critical thinking) and psycho-emotional outcomes (e.g., anxiety, fear and preparedness) yield inconsistent results. Students favour experiential learning but highlighted gaps in interdisciplinary collaboration and stress management. Conclusion: This review identified curriculum design gaps in ERID outbreak management education programs and provided future pedagogical directions to prepare a pandemic-ready healthcare workforce. Key strategies include scaffolding ERID content across pre-registration training, incorporating interprofessional education, and leveraging blended pedagogies to balance theoretical and experiential learning. Future programs should integrate realistic scenarios to simulate emotional stressors, foster resilience, and evaluate knowledge and skill retention. © 2026

Title: Dispositional mindfulness as moderator between Big Five personality traits and social media addiction
Abstract: We analyzed the associations between dispositional mindfulness, the Big Five personality traits, and social media addiction, while investigating whether dispositional mindfulness acts as a moderator in these relationships. The research sample comprised 692 nonclinical French young adults (18–30 years old). The following measurement tools were used: the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire-Short Form, the Big Five Inventory-Fr, and the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Results demonstrated that neuroticism and extraversion had a significant positive association on social media addiction, while conscientiousness had a significant negative association. Agreeableness and openness had no significant associations with social media addiction. Dispositional mindfulness moderated the relationship between neuroticism and social media addiction. It also moderated the relationship between conscientiousness and social media addiction. Specifically, higher levels of dispositional mindfulness buffered the positive association between neuroticism and social media addiction and strengthened the protective effect of conscientiousness. The authors discussed the protective potential of dispositional mindfulness as a self-regulatory mechanism that can mitigate personality-related factors. These findings suggest that dispositional mindfulness is a valuable target for both the prevention and treatment of social media addiction. Integrating mindfulness-based strategies could help young adults navigate social media more intentionally, thereby reducing addictive behaviors and associated psychological distress. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Can electric buses encourage greater public transport use? The role of the green halo effect
Abstract: The electrification of urban bus fleets is widely promoted as a strategy to reduce emissions and enhance the sustainability of public transport systems. Beyond environmental benefits, electric buses may also influence user perceptions and travel behavior. This study investigates how the introduction of electric buses in Thessaloniki affects both actual public transport usage and intentions to increase future use, adopting a holistic approach that considers both users and non-users. Building on existing electric bus adoption models, we extend the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) by introducing the green halo effect, capturing the positive spillover of electric bus deployment on the overall image of public transport. The framework also incorporates green self-identity, attitudes, social norms, and satisfaction-related perceptions. Data were collected through an online survey of Thessaloniki residents (N = 474), including both electric bus users (N = 323) and non-users (N = 151). For users, the model examines changes in usage frequency, while for non-users it analyzes intentions to adopt public transport. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) is applied to test relationships among psychological constructs and behavioral outcomes, complemented by Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) to identify critical limiting factors for intended modal shift. Results indicate that for current users, physical ride quality is a necessary condition for satisfaction, while the green halo effect independently increases usage frequency. For non-users, exploratory findings suggest that the green halo effect emerges as the strongest model-based predictor and primary limiting factor for future adoption within this sample, overriding general attitudes toward public transport. These findings highlight the potential of fleet electrification to act as a facilitator for behavioral change regarding increasing public transport use. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Household-level flood vulnerability in a changing climate: An indicator-based assessment in the Upper Jhelum Sub-catchment, India
Abstract: Climate change induced floods have become more frequent and widespread posing growing challenges to communities worldwide. The Upper Jhelum Sub-catchment located in the Kashmir Himalayas of India was selected as the study area due to its high flood vulnerability, fragile ecology, recurrent flood events and livelihood vulnerability. We constructed the composite flood vulnerability index (CFVI) by integrating nine domains of vulnerability (social, economic, climate change and environmental, ecosystem, flood exposure, early warning system, local community adaptation, post flood adaptation and flood protection) at the household level. A total of 66 indicators of these domains were selected based on literature survey and expert knowledge. The data on the indicators were collected through a survey of 480 households from 24 villages using questionnaire. Most of the sampled villages experienced high and moderate flood vulnerability. Low socio-economic conditions, climate change and environmental, high ecological impact, high flood exposure and low adaptation strategies aggravated moderate to high flood vulnerability in these villages. The regression analysis revealed that the degree of vulnerability was most influenced by the climate change and environmental followed by the ecosystem and flood exposure domains. Raising awareness, local adaptation strategies, effective early warning systems and flood protection measures may help the communities for enhancing their adaptive capacities. Thus, CFVI has proved an effective not only in prioritizing villages but also helped in identifying domain areas where the efforts could be made for lessening flood vulnerability. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Zou Y.; Xu X.; Zhao L.
Title: The differences in adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making across different socioeconomic statuses: Evidence based on delay discount rates of healthy and unhealthy foods
Abstract: Adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making not only affects current learning adaptation but also influences development potential in adulthood. However, there is a lack of sufficient empirical evidence regarding whether socioeconomic status, which is an important background factor reflecting the availability of resources and future expectations, influences adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making. Based on life history theory, our study conducted three studies to examine the differences in adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making across different socioeconomic statuses. Study 1 consisted of two sub-studies: Studies 1A and 1B recruited 90 and 84 adolescent participants, respectively, from northwestern China. Based on objective and subjective socioeconomic status scales, the participants were divided into high- and low-score groups to examine the differences in adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making across different socioeconomic statuses. Study 2 recruited 110 adolescent participants from northwest China and used an income feedback comparison paradigm to manipulate subjective socioeconomic status, thereby examining the relationship between the two through experimental manipulation. In all three studies, the main effect of socioeconomic status on health intertemporal decision-making was not significant. However, exploratory analyses consistently indicated that the impact of socioeconomic status on adolescents' health intertemporal decision-making might vary depending on the food context. The results of Study 1 showed that adolescents in the low-score groups for objective socioeconomic status and subjective socioeconomic status exhibited a higher time discount rate when faced with unhealthy food. The results of Study 2 showed that adolescents in the low subjective socioeconomic status group exhibited a higher time discount rate when faced with unhealthy food. The present findings provide preliminary evidence for the association between socioeconomic status and health-related intertemporal decision-making among adolescents. Moreover, they offer a reference for future research aimed at developing interventions to promote healthy behaviors in adolescents from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, including goal-setting training, future self-imagination, and food environment optimization. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Perceptions of risk and investment in wind energy in rural communities
Abstract: This study examines whether individual risk attitudes, investment preferences and socio-economic characteristics are associated with stated willingness to invest in onshore wind-energy projects among rural respondents in Tanzania, with Ireland retained as a complementary case from a more established wind-energy market. Using ordered and generalised ordered logistic regression models, the Tanzanian results reveal substantial investment interest, with approximately half of respondents indicating willingness to invest. However, neither self-rated nor assessed risk consistently predicts investment propensity, while most financial, attitudinal and socio-demographic variables show weak or threshold-specific associations. In the complementary Irish sample, self-rated risk is positively and consistently associated with investment propensity, whereas assessed risk is substantially weaker. Required returns and selected individual characteristics are also associated with particular investment thresholds. Overall, the findings suggest that individual risk attitudes alone provide an incomplete explanation of prospective wind-energy investment in Tanzania. Policies should therefore consider accessible investment structures, credible information and greater opportunities for exposure to wind-energy projects, while future research should directly examine financial, institutional and project-level factors not captured in this study. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Seo J.; Li Y.; Song R.
Title: Comparative effects of activity-based interventions on quality of life among community-dwelling older adults: A systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
Abstract: Background: Meaningful activity participation may support healthy aging and quality of life (QoL) in community-dwelling older adults. We compared interaction-based social, exercise-based physical, and self-directed individual activities. Methods: Thirteen English- and Korean-language databases were searched through May 2026 for RCTs of community-dwelling older adults with a study-sample mean or median age ≥65 years. Interventions were classified using a theoretically informed operational framework. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2. Pairwise and Bayesian network meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences (SMDs); certainty was assessed using GRADE, with SUCRA rankings considered secondary. Results: Seventy-one RCTs (12,159 participants) were included. The overall pairwise effect favored activity-based interventions (SMD=0.59, 95% CI 0.45–0.73), but heterogeneity was substantial and the prediction interval crossed the null; certainty was very low. Category-specific pairwise estimates were 0.68 (0.27–1.08) for self-directed, 0.61 (0.43–0.78) for physical, and 0.46 (0.21–0.72) for social activities, all with very-low-certainty evidence. In the network meta-analysis, low-certainty evidence suggested that all three categories may improve QoL versus no treatment: self-directed SMD=0.78 (95% CrI 0.25–1.32; SUCRA 82.5%), physical 0.73 (0.46–1.00; 79.6%), and social 0.40 (0.11–0.69; 37.6%). Excluding high-risk studies yielded an overall pairwise estimate of 0.53 (0.37–0.69); the estimate for physical activities remained 0.61, whereas the estimates for social and self-directed activities were 0.43 and 0.45. Conclusions: Evidence does not establish superiority of one activity category. Findings remain limited by heterogeneity, risk of bias, potential publication bias, and sparse direct active comparisons. Comparative rankings should be considered hypothesis-generating, and higher-quality head-to-head trials are needed. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: DiMatteo D.F.
Title: Academic Protest Literature in the U.S., 1985–2015
Source title: Academic Protest Literature in the U.S., 1985-2015
Abstract: Through close readings of university fiction, college films, sculptures, and life writing by academics, Derek F. DiMatteo defines a distinct genre of academic protest literature that reveals how contemporary scholars and artists confront the increasing corporatization of higher education in the USA. This book analyzes representative works by Mohsin Hamid, Jane Smiley, Alex Kudera, John Singleton, Justin Simien, Margaret De Lima, and Michael Dubson among other writers that protest against academic capitalism's deleterious effects on the public good, BIPOC students and faculty, contingent faculty, and international students. DiMatteo argues that these works should be categorized as protest art within the cultural arm of a long-simmering higher education protest movement. Using protest literature as a lens to argue for a re-evaluation of university fiction as a serious contribution to the higher education reform movement, Academic Protest Literature in the U.S., 1985–2015 adds a cultural dimension to the field of critical university studies and defines the characteristics of academic protest literature, creating a space for education protest within the larger field of American social protest literature. Title: “We Know What We Don't Know” a reflexive synthesis of research and lay knowledge regarding group decision-making in mountaineering
Abstract: Groups navigating dynamic and hazardous mountain environments must continuously engage in collective decision-making. However, the assumption that groups naturally make better decisions than individuals is misleading. Groupthink, group polarization, and other social dynamics can impair judgement and lead to sub-optimal or even dangerous outcomes, making group decision-making a critical factor for safety in mountaineering. This scoping review maps the existing research on group decision-making in mountaineering using a systematic literature search complemented by reflexive thematic analysis. From 107 identified articles, we derived 14 themes, subsumed within six layers of influence, including factors benefitting group-decision making, authenticity, social influence, external pressure, expertise and contextual dynamics. Together, these themes underscore the complexity of group decision-making in the high-stakes environment. Our findings highlight its central role in mountaineering and provide useful directions for future research and practice. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Meng X.; Zhou S.
Title: Fatalistic and disengaged: How perceived cross-platform data flow and privacy boundary turbulence are associated with emotional distress
Abstract: This study examined the social and psychological impacts of perceived cross-platform privacy flow and addressed an important gap in privacy research by shifting the focus from privacy management within single platforms to user experiences in interconnected data ecosystems. Drawing on Communication Privacy Management (CPM) theory, this research examined how perceptions of cross-platform data flow predict privacy boundary turbulence, the emotional disruption associated with perceived privacy loss, and how this turbulence subsequently correlates with distinct psychological coping strategies, notably privacy fatalism and privacy disengagement. Using a survey-based design informed by prior qualitative interviews, including in-depth interviews with 33 young adults and a large-scale survey of 1419 respondents, the results indicated that perceived cross-platform data flow positively predicted emotional distress, which in turn was associated with these maladaptive coping mechanisms. The findings contribute to theoretical advancements in privacy management and offer practical insights for policymakers, platform operators, and users to navigate privacy risks and enhance protection frameworks in the digital age. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yang Z.; Tang J.; Cui Q.; Lin P.; Chen Z.; Koppel S.
Title: Available but avoided? How infrastructure perception, perceived safety and perceived risk relate to e-bike riders’ intrusion into motor-vehicle lanes
Abstract: Introduction A substantial proportion of e-bike injuries and fatalities occur in motor-vehicle lanes, where riders are exposed to mixed traffic and higher crash risk, potentially offsetting the health benefits of e-bike use. Notably, many riders still enter motor-vehicle lanes even when dedicated bicycle lanes are available. Such lane intrusion increases exposure to hazardous interactions with vehicles and diminishes the safety benefits of cycling infrastructure. Therefore, identifying psychological factors associated with lane intrusion is important for informing injury-prevention interventions. Methodology An online survey of 729 e-bike riders (650 valid for analysis) assessed self-reported e-bike lane intrusion behaviour (e-bike LIB) using a newly developed Riding Lane Intrusion Behaviour Questionnaire, and assessed infrastructure perception, perceived safety, perceived risk, and Theory of Planned Behaviour constructs. We combined multi-group structural equation modelling with explainable machine learning to examine theory-informed associations among infrastructure perception, key psychological constructs, and e-bike LIB, and to explore potential non-linear patterns. Results Attitude, perceived behavioural control, and subjective norms were positively associated with self-reported lane intrusion, with attitude showing the strongest association. Infrastructure perception was negatively associated with self-reported lane intrusion and exhibited a possible non-linear pattern, with larger marginal reductions at higher levels of infrastructure perception. As infrastructure perception increased from low levels, perceived safety increased while perceived risk decreased, and these perceptions were further associated with e-bike LIB primarily indirectly through attitude and perceived behavioural control. Conclusions E-bike LIB should be understood as a preventable mixed-traffic exposure rather than a neutral lane-choice decision. The findings suggest that infrastructure provision should be complemented by behavioural measures targeting favourable attitudes, overconfidence, and permissive social norms. In poorer riding environments, stricter enforcement and improvements to the perceived usability and visibility of existing facilities may help discourage non-compliance with available bicycle lanes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Tian J.; Shen X.; Li N.; Wu C.; Hu Y.; Teng M.; Tan M.
Title: Beyond efficiency: A meta-synthesis of nursing students' experiences with generative AI in developing clinical judgment and ethical reasoning: A qualitative systematic review
Abstract: Background: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping nursing education, yet its impact on students' clinical judgment and ethical reasoning remains multifaceted and complex. Objectives: To synthesize qualitative evidence exploring nursing students' experiences with GenAI in developing core clinical and ethical competencies. Review methods: A systematic meta-synthesis was conducted following ENTREQ guidelines. Five major databases (Cochrane, CINAHL, PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase) were searched up to February 2026. Data were synthesized using Thomas and Harden's thematic synthesis approach, and confidence in the findings was assessed with GRADE-CERQual. Results: Eleven studies were included, yielding four meta-themes: (1) personalized support versus the risk of dependency, (2) developing clinical judgment through simulation and verification, (3) ethical reasoning and the human element, and (4) the need for institutional guidance and literacy. Conclusions: Nursing students use GenAI for support, simulation, and feedback, but they also report risks of over-reliance, weak verification, and unclear ethical responsibility. Nursing programmes should teach students how to question AI outputs, protect patient data, and retain human clinical judgment when using GenAI. Title: A cluster-randomised controlled trial of Ahead of the Game: Mental health literacy and resilience in organised youth sport
Abstract: Organised sport provides an accessible environment for mental health promotion, particularly for adolescent males. The aim of this study was to conduct a cluster-randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of Ahead of the Game, a sport-based mental health literacy and resilience program, compared to an active control who received promotional materials. Forty-four Australian community sport clubs were stratified by sport and block randomised, in varying sizes, to receive either Ahead of the Game (n = 20) or the active control (n = 24). A total of 704 adolescent males aged 12-21 years (n = 349 intervention, 14 clusters; n = 355 active control, 18 clusters) completed surveys at baseline and follow-up, approximately 6 weeks post-intervention. Intention-to-treat analysis using mixed-effects modelling was used to account for clustering at the team level. The findings showed that compared to the active control, Ahead of the Game participants demonstrated significantly greater increases in resilience (differential change = 1.60, 95% CI 0.47 - 2.74, p = .005) and intentions to seek help from formal sources (differential change = 0.50, 95% CI 0.20 - 0.80, p = .001). Significant improvements were also observed for secondary outcomes, confidence to provide help and reduced endorsement of mental illness stereotypes. These findings extend those of the previous Ahead of the Game matched-control trial in providing evidence that the program produces benefits beyond low-cost social marketing approaches, despite modest engagement with the intervention components (∼55% attended at least one workshop). Future research is needed to examine the longer-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness of the program. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: A preference for sameness and associated positive emotions in interindividual discrimination, even when based on chance
Abstract: It was recently demonstrated that people allocate more money to another person when they both demonstrate the same outcome versus a different one, even when the outcome is based on chance. Different theoretical frameworks predict whether this effect reflects a preference for sameness, a derogation of difference, or both. Across three preregistered online experiments, we employed dot estimation (Exp. 1, n = 75), painting preference (Exp. 2, n = 75), and coin flip (Exp. 3, n = 84) versions of the sheer difference paradigm, while introducing a condition that lacked congruency information to distinguish these effects. Additionally, in the coin flip task, we explored retrospective emotional responses (using a self-report rating scale and the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule-Short Form). We found that: (1) allocations in the sameness (congruent) condition were significantly higher than in the congruency-unknown and difference (incongruent) conditions (Exp. 1–3); and (2) participants reported more positive emotions in the congruent condition than in both the congruency-unknown and incongruent conditions (Exp. 3). Notably, the congruency effect in retrospective positive emotion ratings was also significantly correlated with the congruency effect in allocation measures. We discuss the use of congruency-unknown conditions in this study and in the wider literature to disentangle preference for sameness from derogation of difference. This study provides a clearer understanding of unequal allocation following interpersonal sameness versus difference, while also offering preliminary evidence for their relationship with emotions. Authors: Dayot J.
Title: Asymmetrical dilemmas and oil compromises on an extractive frontier
Abstract: Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork with Quichua communities along Ecuador’s Lower Napo River, this article examines local engagements with the Ishpingo–Tambococha–Tiputini (ITT) oil project. It argues that acceptance of extractive projects is best understood as a response to asymmetrical dilemmas in which impacts, benefits, and opportunities are unevenly distributed through time and space. While oil extraction may indeed constitute a local dilemma, it is a highly asymmetric one. First, the benefits associated with oil development – employment opportunities, indemnización payments, and social compensation – are rendered necessary by broader socio-economic and environmental pressures that often predate the project itself. Second, the impacts of extraction frequently extend beyond the communities entitled to compensation, while access to benefits remains conditional upon incorporation into the project. Third, extraction may be perceived simultaneously as a source of environmental harm and as a means of addressing both anticipated impacts and pre-existing unmet needs. These asymmetries become visible only when oil decisions are approached as dynamic processes unfolding through time and across space rather than as discrete moments of consent or refusal. By reconstructing this process ethnographically, the article shows that responses other than resistance can emerge from the unequal distribution of risks, benefits, and opportunities through which extractive development is experienced. Under such conditions, local debates may shift from whether extraction should occur to what communities should demand in exchange for it. The article contributes to debates on extractivism, environmental justice, and Indigenous politics by shifting attention from extractive decisions alone to the uneven conditions under which acceptance comes to appear necessary, logical, or unavoidable. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Unpacking AI–education discourse: Topic modeling and fsQCA of Technology–Resilience dynamics in pedagogical perceptions
Abstract: This study investigates public discourse on AI in education by integrating Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to connect semantic patterns with configurational associations. Drawing on 28,137 anonymized comments from Douyin, Weibo, and Bilibili, eight latent topics were extracted and systematically aligned with theoretical constructs—technological capital penetration, micro-pedagogical resilience, and functional transformation at the discourse level—through Jaccard coefficient analysis. Sentiment classification further quantified emotional orientations, producing a dataset combining topic distributions, sentiment scores, and theoretical mappings for configurational modeling. The fsQCA results revealed a Technology–Resilience Co-Evolution Model, in which five sufficient configurations were interpreted as four broader synergistic evolutionary pathways—comprehensive stress, dual-cycle cognition, substitutional restructuring, and multimodal adaptation—that are associated with the discursive reconfiguration of pedagogical perceptions in media contexts. These findings suggest that AI is discursively framed as co-constructive rather than purely facilitative or disruptive, underscoring the asymmetric and multifaceted nature of public interpretations of its educational role. Methodologically, the study establishes a novel bridge between semantic clustering and configurational analysis, advancing innovation in educational text mining. At both the theoretical and practical levels, the study provides a multidimensional framework for understanding AI-related transformations in pedagogical perceptions within social media discourse. It also offers tentative implications for future research and practice on technological investment with human resilience. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Zhang M.; Li Y.
Title: The coordination between opportunity equality and procedural consistency in the social inequality contexts: evidence from middle childhood
Abstract: Due to disparities in family socioeconomic background and resources, equal procedures and standards for individuals from different social classes in society may always lead to unequal opportunities. This study examines whether children value equal opportunity over equal procedure when the two cannot both be achieved in contexts of social inequality. A total of 373 Chinese children aged 8–11 (167 girls, 206 boys) evaluated the fairness of two situations: an equal-procedure condition in which children from different resource backgrounds were treated identically despite unequal opportunities, and an equal-opportunity condition in which the procedure was adjusted to favor children from disadvantaged backgrounds to compensate for unequal opportunities. They were also asked whether they would adjust the procedure to favor children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Among 8- to 11-year-old children, younger children judged adjusting the procedure to benefit the disadvantaged group as fairer than maintaining an equal procedure and were more willing to do so, whereas this tendency decreased with age. For 11-year-old children, explicit assurance that the proposed adjustment would effectively ensure equal opportunity increased both fairness judgments of the equal opportunity condition and willingness to adjust the procedure. This research reveals children’s preference for equal opportunities and their willingness to support compensatory policies for those with fewer opportunities. These findings have implications for promoting social equality of opportunity. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: A socially informed optimization framework for rural electrification planning across alternative electricity demand scenarios: A case study in Bolivia
Abstract: Achieving universal electricity access remains a global challenge, particularly in remote rural areas where grid extension is technically or economically unfeasible. Existing approaches provide cost-optimal and technically feasible solutions for decentralized energy system design, but often fall short in delivering context-sensitive electrification strategies that combine microgrids and stand-alone systems while accounting for social and operational constraints. This paper proposes a socially informed optimisation framework for rural electrification planning, capable of generating alternative system configurations across different electricity consumption scenarios. The framework integrates solar PV generation, battery energy storage, and diesel backup, and incorporates hourly demand profiles together with socially informed constraints to enhance system manageability and reflect the electricity adoption process in rural areas. Methodologically, the proposed planning framework is built around a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) optimization model, integrated within a heuristic procedure to efficiently generate near-optimal electrification layouts and system designs under different social and operational preferences. The approach is applied to the rural community of Molle Orcko in Raqaypampa, Bolivia. Results demonstrate the framework's ability to adapt electrification strategies to varying community priorities and highlight the importance of jointly considering technical and social dimensions in decentralized energy planning. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Identity fusion in children: A validation of the Dynamic Identity Fusion Index
Abstract: Identity fusion is a strong form of group alignment, in which individuals experience a visceral sense of oneness with the group, motivating extreme forms of pro-group action. However, little is known about the emergence and development of identity fusion across the lifespan, largely due to the absence of validated assessment tools for children. The Dynamic Identity Fusion Index (DIFI) has proven to be an effective and efficient measure of identity fusion in adults and the present study aims to validate its use in children. Our findings indicate that fusion with ‘own family’ versus an unfamiliar family can be reliably measured in children aged 6 to 10 years. Criterion validity was supported through correlations with other measures of identity fusion, and discriminant validity from social desirability and personality traits was also established. However, results for temporal stability after three months were inconclusive, and evidence for convergent and predictive validity could not be confirmed. Potential methodological explanations for these limitations are discussed. Overall, this study is a first and important step toward understanding the development of identity fusion in childhood and provides a foundation for future research. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Everyday conceptualizations of patience
Abstract: People routinely use patience to interpret their behavior and the behavior of others, but the structure of these conceptualizations remains unclear. Across four studies (N = 1989), we mapped the cognitive prototype of patience and tested its robustness and consequences. Study 1 identified six definitive features falling under the categories of temporal tolerance, emotional composure, and self-governance. Study 2 found substantial relative convergence in multinational English-language definitions and in Spanish-language ratings and definitions from Mexico and Argentina. In Study 3, central features produced more false recognition and a more liberal response criterion. In Study 4, participants described a recent episode before seeing any mention of patience. Ratings of temporal tolerance, emotional composure, and self-governance jointly predicted subsequent patience judgments, and the combined prototype index predicted patience beyond practical success, overall handling, and context. Self-governance was more characteristic of self-control, whereas emotional composure was more characteristic of patience. Together, the studies identify a graded lay representation that recurs across different samples and organizes recognition and retrospective self-judgment. Title: The impact of disability onset on depressive symptoms: Longitudinal evidence from South Korea
Abstract: Depressive symptoms are a major mental health concern among people with disabilities in South Korea, yet little is known about how depressive symptoms change before and after disability onset, or how their levels differ between people with and without disabilities. Thus, we (a) examined changes in depressive symptoms before and after disability onset within people with disabilities, (b) compared their pre-onset levels with the levels of depressive symptoms in people without disabilities, (c) compared their post-onset levels with the levels of depressive symptoms in people without disabilities, and (d) examined changes in depressive symptoms associated with disability duration. Using the Korea Welfare Panel Study, we analyzed 152,152 person-wave observations from 13,643 individuals. Disability onset was identified using retrospectively reported onset age. We used linear mixed-effects models approximating a hybrid specification, with participant-level random intercepts. The levels of depressive symptoms among people with disabilities were higher after disability onset than before onset ( β = 0.06, p = .015). Pre-onset depressive symptoms among people with disabilities were elevated relative to those of people without disabilities ( β = 0.12, p < .001), as were post-onset depressive symptoms ( β = 0.18, p < .001). Depressive symptoms did not differ significantly across years since disability onset. We suggest integrating mental health screening into disability diagnosis processes, particularly at early stages for individuals with progressive health decline. The persistent gap in depressive symptoms between people with and without disabilities underscores the need for stronger systemic support. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Evidence for ideological confirmation, or how to politicize color intensity perceptions
Abstract: Political groups may form based in genuine differences between people, but once formed, these groups and their associated identities can influence people's views and behavior. In line with social-constraint models, we tested whether liberals and conservatives would report arbitrary perceptual experiences because those experiences were situationally framed as signals of political identity. Participants completed a bogus diagnostic task in which perceiving colors as becoming either more or less intense ostensibly signaled possession of a liberal or conservative brain type. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants were told which intensity experience signaled brain possession prior to completing the task; findings showed that liberal and conservative participants provided reports of color intensity in ways that confirmed their ideological identity. In Experiment 3, participants were told which intensity experience signaled brain possession only after a trial on the task; still, participants reported experiencing color in identity-confirming ways. These effects occurred in college and online adult samples, among participants who indicated unbiased responding, and the effects could not be attributed to left- or right-wing authoritarianism; moreover, the effects were associated with self-judgments and evaluations of others. Political identities do not merely bias how people feel about value-laden political information; rather, they can influence people to adopt arbitrary social symbols that, once adopted, may create the perception of real divides. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Internal Bayesian precision modulates the neural representation of social attention: Disentangling implicit and explicit components via model-informed multivariate EEG analysis
Abstract: Social attention integrates sensory cues with high-level cognitive expectations, yet the generative mechanisms through which implicit orienting and explicit belief-driven modulation interact remain poorly understood. This ambiguity complicates the distinction between specialized social modules and domain-general attentional processes. We combined a dynamic cueing task with hierarchical Bayesian modeling and model-informed multivariate EEG decoding to address this. Behavioral results revealed a computational double dissociation: symbolic arrow cues elicited heterogeneous strategies, whereas averted gaze recruited a consistent, surprise-driven computational phenotype. At the neural level, time-resolved decoding and temporal generalization revealed a critical representational shift starting approximately 400 ms post-cue. Initial activity related to physical cue features was rapidly replaced by stable neural templates of predicted spatial intent. Crucially, topographical activation patterns showed that this intentional template, characterized by a lateralized temporo-occipital distribution, emerged exclusively under high internal certainty. Furthermore, partial representational similarity analysis demonstrated that late-stage neural manifolds were overwhelmingly organized around integrated spatial goals rather than isolated sensory or motivational signals. These findings suggest that social attention is a specialized generative process, where internal certainty modulates the transformation of social perceptions into actionable top-down intentions. © 2026

Authors: Das B.
Title: Citizenship on Trial: The NRC, Exclusion, and the Making of Foreigners in Assam, India
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This paper examines the evolution and enforcement of the ‘foreigner’ category in Assam, India, focusing on how the National Register of Citizens (NRC) has produced exclusionary citizenship and statelessness. It asks how and why the notion of the ‘foreigner’ has taken shape in Assam, and what sustains its persistence in contemporary state practice. The study shows that citizenship in Assam is determined less by legal rights than by descent, ethnicity, and documentary proof, resulting in the disproportionate exclusion of linguistic, religious, and gender minorities. Drawing on documentary analysis and ethnographically inspired fieldwork that foregrounds lived experiences, the paper traces how colonial, Partition, and post-Partition anxieties have crystallized into a regime of suspicion and surveillance. It demonstrates that bureaucratic discretion, legal ambiguity, and inconsistent NRC procedures have institutionalized widespread legal limbo and arbitrary exclusion, producing deep social and psychological harm. Assam’s experience illustrates how securitized citizenship regimes erode the “right to have rights” and signal broader patterns of democratic erosion in India and South Asia. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Author full names: Alberto, Pedro Miguel (60520937300); Baltazar, Maria Emilia (57192007902)
Title: Permanent unfitness for flight among cabin crew: residual risk governance and the human consequences of preventive safety decisions
Abstract: Commercial aviation is a high-reliability sociotechnical system in which medical fitness constitutes a central mechanism of risk governance. Yet the human and organisational consequences of permanent unfitness decisions remain insufficiently integrated into dominant safety assessment models. This study examines permanent unfitness among cabin crew following occupational accidents as a post-decision governance problem in a safety–critical context. An interpretive, multilevel qualitative design was adopted, informed by a multiple case study approach. Twenty-four semi-structured interviews were conducted in Portugal with fifteen cabin crew members declared permanently unfit and nine specialist participants, including occupational physicians, aeromedical examiners, a regulatory authority representative, organisational and trade union representatives, and legal experts. Thematic analysis, supported by documentary and legal–regulatory triangulation, identified recurring patterns across micro, meso and macro levels. The findings suggest that the system ensures normative coherence and high operational safety standards. However, the management of the human consequences of unfitness decisions is marked by institutional fragmentation, weak follow-up, and frequent externalisation of protection to trade unions and labour courts. In the analysed cases, permanent unfitness emerged as a mechanism of social redistribution of risk, whereby the reduction of collective operational risk shifted identity-related, professional and socioeconomic costs onto affected workers, weakening perceived procedural justice, institutional legitimacy and organisational responsibility. The study conceptualises permanent unfitness as a sociotechnical governance problem of residual risk, showing how preventive safety decisions may redistribute human, professional and institutional burdens beyond the operational perimeter. It further proposes post-decision continuity as a neglected dimension of SMS maturity in safety–critical contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Ananiadou I.; Papacostas D.
Title: From technical viability to bankability: An integrated assessment of gigawatt-scale solar PV under compound uncertainty, evidence from Nigeria
Abstract: Utility-scale solar PV deployment in emerging electricity markets turns on whether policy and institutional arrangements make projects financeable, not on irradiation and hardware prices alone. This paper develops an integrated assessment framework linking four dimensions usually treated separately, namely technical performance, grid deliverability, financial viability, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG). The framework is applied to Abuja Solar One, a proposed 1 GW PV project in Nigeria, using feasibility-study data, comparative benchmarks, and a new compound scenario model. The case shows strong technical fundamentals, including a reported post-tax levelised cost of electricity of USD 0.0663/kWh from the feasibility study. Technical viability alone does not ensure bankability. A compound uncertainty analysis spanning 81 deterministic combinations of generation, curtailment, tariff, and CAPEX, to which no probabilities are assigned, shows that 6 combinations return an unlevered project IRR at or above an illustrative 15% cut-off, 54 fall between 12% and 15%, and 21 fall below 12%. Curtailment is the dominant single downside driver, while tariff compression and CAPEX escalation add to the downside additively, not through interaction, since the two-way curtailment and tariff interaction term is negligible. The threshold structure survives a complete change of the national fiscal incentive regime and the introduction of debt, although leverage relocates the binding constraint from the return test to debt service coverage. The findings suggest that in high-risk electricity markets the central assessment question is not whether gigawatt-scale solar can be built, but under what institutional conditions it can attract capital and remain investable. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Exploring group cohesion dynamics and the role of regulation in collaborative problem-solving using multimodal learning analysis
Abstract: In collaborative problem-solving (CPS), group cohesion is widely regarded as an important contributing factor, yet its underlying processes remain insufficiently understood. Traditionally, cohesion has been treated as a static construct, assessed primarily through self-report measures. In contrast, theory conceptualizes cohesion as a dynamic and emergent state, pointing to the need for temporally sensitive approaches that consider self-report evidence alongside process data. This exploratory study examined how post-task survey-based cohesion, selected socially shared regulation (SSR) discourse indicators, and synchronized leaning forward as a behavioral cue can be interpreted in relation to one another across CPS phases. Specifically, we investigated how selected SSR discourse indicators and synchronized leaning forward were configured in relation to survey-based dimensions of cohesion, including task, social, perceived, and emotional cohesion. We also conducted an in-depth qualitative analysis of selected groups differing in knowledge-construction quality to examine how SSR discourse and synchronized leaning forward appeared in interaction. The analysis is intended as an exploratory and interpretive account: synchronized leaning forward is treated as a context-dependent behavioral cue, and the observed patterns are interpreted as descriptive configurations rather than validated, causal, predictive, or generalizable relationships. The findings suggest that post-task survey-based cohesion can be descriptively interpreted alongside phase-specific discourse and behavioral configurations. In particular, early synchronized leaning forward appeared more meaningful when situated within elaborative and regulatory discourse in the selected cases. Overall, the study presents an exploratory and phase-sensitive interpretation of how survey-based cohesion, selected SSR discourse indicators, and context-dependent behavioral cues can be jointly interpreted to understand cohesion-related processes in CPS. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Fahmy R.
Title: From displacement to home: A systematic review on research streams, gaps, and directions in refugee integration and homemaking studies (2020–2026)
Abstract: Since 2020, forced displacement has been aggravated by overlapping crises like climate change and armed conflicts. While refugee integration has attracted growing scholarly attention, the relationship between structural integration processes and the lived experience of homemaking - how access to accommodation, urban space, and social environments enables or obstructs a genuine sense of belonging and integration - remains underexplored. This review addresses this gap through a systematic review of 60 impactful articles published between 2020 and 2026, identified through a comprehensive Scopus search and refined using bibliometric analysis in RStudio following PRISMA guidelines. The review identifies eight thematic streams through bibliometric and qualitative content analyses, covering (1) research methods, (2) the concept of home and belonging, (3) refugees’practices for integration, (4) social capital and networks, (5) policy responses and governance, (6) challenges and vulnerabilities, (7) the role of host communities and institutions, and (8) digital practices and literacies. The following gaps were revealed: limited longitudinal research on integration and place attachment, institutional actors and governance decisions that shape spatial conditions, and under-exploration of intersecting identity dimensions, such as age, sexuality, race, and disability, in relation to homemaking , and the underexplored role of settlement and trajectory in shaping whether homemaking is experienced as temporary adaptation, resistance to insecurity, or the gradual construction of belonging. The quality of environments as spaces affecting mental health and belonging also needs greater attention. These gaps highlight the need for a research agenda that prioritizes longitudinal studies, critical engagement with local governance, comparative research across settlement contexts, and greater attention to the diversity of refugee populations and experiences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Correspondence between daily decision-making and preferences for leisure activities
Abstract: This study examined whether individuals' willingness to engage in new leisure activities is systematically related, across activities, to activity-specific mean daily decision-making states. Decision-making was conceptualized along two dimensions: orientation (reflecting a reliance on System-1 versus System-2 processing) and intensity (reflecting the degree of cognitive engagement in judgment and choice). Because new leisure activities provide limited evaluative anchors, we tested whether their perceived cognitive characteristics show complementary correspondence with activity-specific mean decision-making states among participants highly willing to engage in them despite limited experience. In an online survey of 600 adults, participants reported their daily orientation and intensity and evaluated leisure activities in terms of their own willingness to engage in them, their experience, and activities' perceived activity-level orientation and intensity. Treating leisure activities as the unit of analysis, we found systematic complementary patterns. Activities perceived as more System-1-oriented were associated with more System-2-oriented activity-specific mean daily states among high-willingness inexperienced participants, whereas activities perceived as more System-2-oriented were associated with more System-1-oriented activity-specific mean daily states. Activities perceived as low-intensity were associated with higher activity-specific mean daily intensity among high-willingness inexperienced participants. Our findings suggest structured activity-level correspondences between perceived activity characteristics and activity-specific mean daily decision-making states. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: More walking and less driving since COVID in Denmark, England, Germany, and the Netherlands: Evidence from national travel surveys disaggregated by socioeconomic groups
Abstract: Introduction This paper analyzes the national travel surveys of Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, and England to compare travel behavior before and after the COVID pandemic. We focus on walking and car use because, as our analysis shows, they exhibit large changes over that period. Methods We base our graphical analysis on cross-sectional national travel surveys that are representative for each of the 4 countries in the years before and after the COVID pandemic: 2017-2019 and 2023-2024. We present trends in the number of trips by mode per year, total time traveled by mode per year, and modal-split share of trips over time. We disaggregate our analysis of modal shares by gender, age, income, car ownership/access, employment status, and population density. We calculated Pearson's chi-square tests to assess whether the proportion of trips made by walking or driving differed significantly between 2017-2019 and 2023-2024 for each country. Results We find that walking increased in all four countries between 2017-2019 and 2023-2024 according to all three of the measures we used. Even disaggregated by socioeconomic characteristics, the modal share of walking increased for almost all groups in all countries. By contrast, the car mode share decreased for almost all socioeconomic groups. Most chi-square tests showed statistically significant (p < .05) differences between 2017-2019 and 2023-2024. Conclusion The increase in walking, combined with the reduction in car use, may have generated considerable physical, mental, social, and environmental health benefits. That provides a rationale for better infrastructure and policies to encourage more walking. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: A predictive geospatial engine for city-wide pedestrian-centric urban regeneration
Abstract: Predicting pedestrian activity across unmonitored urban space from sparse sensor data remains a fundamental challenge for evidence-based policy and decision-making. Effective urban regeneration depends on understanding mobility patterns that shape accessibility, vitality, and social equity, yet limited monitoring infrastructure creates spatial blind spots that undermine investment decisions, risking misallocation toward low-activity areas while neglecting underserved neighbourhoods. This paper introduces the Geospatial Pedestrian Activity Engine (GPAE), a GeoAI framework that bridges human activity patterns, emerging sensing technologies, and urban planning by learning non-linear relationships between the built environment and pedestrian activity. Applied to Loughborough, UK, GPAE fuses WiFi sensor data and computer vision-derived video counts (29 monitoring points) with engineered spatial context features, deploying LightGBM gradient boosting to predict city-wide, high-resolution pedestrian activity data. Model performance was validated using Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation against raw observation points (R2 = 0.89, MAE = 400 pedestrians/day). Feature importance analysis reveals that pedestrian activity is associated with the combined contribution of social amenities, daily necessities, and residential density rather than transit infrastructure alone, directly informing active travel and public realm policy. The resulting intelligence, when combined with infrastructure provision data, supports a Policy Decision Framework which is designed to classify urban areas into four actionable intervention typologies: overburdened, underutilised, neglected, and effectively supported, enabling planners to target infrastructure upgrades, active travel investment, and equity-informed regeneration based on predicted activity rather than reactive observation. Beyond prediction accuracy, GPAE shows how existing pedestrian data can be transformed into decision-ready evidence for sustainable mobility and pedestrian-focused urban planning supporting modal shift to walking and contributing to sustainable urban mobility goals. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Aberrant amygdala subregion volumes in youth at high risk for bipolar disorder predict antidepressant-induced adverse events
Abstract: Youth with familial risk for bipolar disorder (BD) and current depression/anxiety are vulnerable to antidepressant-induced adverse events (AE), including mania. The amygdala, implicated in the pathophysiology of mood disorders, may play a key role in these AE. 105 youth with at least one first-degree relative with BD-I and a current depressive/anxiety disorder (high-risk) and 51 healthy controls (HC) underwent baseline MRI to investigate neurostructural risk factors for antidepressant-induced AE. High-risk youth were randomized to either psychotherapy plus escitalopram or psychotherapy plus placebo (2:1) for up to 16 weeks. Clinical efficacy was assessed using the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised and Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale, and AE were assessed using the Pediatric Adverse Events Rating Scale and Treatment-Emergent Activation and Suicidality Assessment Profile. Baseline amygdala subregion volumes and their associations with the rates of change in clinical symptoms and AE over time were evaluated using linear regression models. Compared to HC, high-risk youth had reduced volumes in left lateral and medial nuclei, bilateral central and cortical nuclei, and bilateral corticoamygdaloid transition area and increased volumes in bilateral basal and accessory basal nuclei. In escitalopram-treated youth, but not those receiving placebo, smaller baseline volumes in bilateral cortical nuclei and left medial nucleus were associated with fewer arousal-related AE. Additionally, larger bilateral basal nuclei volumes at baseline were associated with more arousal-related AE. Widespread amygdala volume abnormalities provide insights into neurobiological mechanisms underlying the development of BD in high-risk youth, and specific subregion volumes may serve as neurostructural markers for predicting antidepressant-induced AE. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Associations of sensory processing sensitivity with cannabis motives and consumption in young adults
Abstract: Sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) is a personality trait characterized by heightened responsiveness to both internal and environmental stimuli. Because substances can be used to reduce overstimulation, it has been hypothesized that SPS may correlate to cannabis use. Limited research has examined these associations, finding no relationship with cannabis abuse. Beyond levels of use, SPS could be associated with motives for using cannabis, but this has yet to be examined. The present study examined concurrent associations of SPS with cannabis use frequency, cannabis abuse symptoms, and cannabis use motives in young adults. Participants were 195 23-year-olds from Québec, Canada who self-reported SPS and cannabis measures. Path analyses indicated that SPS was not related to cannabis use frequency or abuse symptoms. Further, SPS was related to social, coping, and expansion motives for cannabis use. When examining SPS subscales, low sensory threshold/ease of excitation was associated with social and conformity motives for cannabis use, while aesthetic sensitivity was associated with enhancement and expansion motives. These results suggest that SPS is related to diverse cannabis motives, rather than only to coping as hypothesized in previous literature. Motivations for cannabis use could inform intervention strategies that are implemented when individuals high in SPS seek treatment for cannabis use problems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: TransMoE: Multimodal traffic prediction with large language model and mixture of experts
Source title: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
Abstract: Traffic prediction plays a crucial role in intelligent transportation systems, especially given the challenges posed by complex spatiotemporal dynamics and the integration of multimodal data. To address this, our work introduces TransMoE, an innovative framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) in combination with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to forecast traffic from heterogeneous data sources. Specifically, we propose a novel adapter, MixLoHa, designed for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and capable of modeling spatially heterogeneous contextual patterns and temporal dynamics across multiple modalities for grid-wise traffic forecasting. Using real-world datasets that incorporate social media streams, real estate information, and points of interest, TransMoE demonstrates significantly improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing methods, achieving a substantial reduction in Mean Absolute Percentage Error. This research underscores the potential of multimodal fusion technologies in advancing traffic prediction, offering new possibilities for real-time urban traffic management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The paradox of supervision - A study of students’ agentic opportunities
Abstract: The current study offers a framework for analysing systematic efforts to foster graduate student agency. The framework identifies key agentic opportunities during students’ research process. Based on qualitative interviews with graduate thesis supervisors in three very different cultural, social and institutional contexts, findings show considerable shared normative assumptions and taken-for-granted practices related to the supervision process as embedded in a research logic—despite attempts to structure and professionalise supervision as an educational process. A key feature in our data were the many opportunities that existed for students’ agency, the high level of flexibility shown by supervisors in the process and their willingness to be adaptive to student needs. In the discussion, a paradox related to supervision is identified, addressing how the qualities associated with developing student agency are inevitably linked to the quality risks of a less efficient and streamlined supervision process. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Ciudad Constitución: Urban utopia and sustainability in the peruvian Amazon; [Ciudad Constitución: Utopía urbana y sostenibilidad en la Amazonía peruana]
Abstract: Ciudad Constitución was founded in 1984 as part of the Special Project Pichis-Palcazú, conceived by the Peruvian State to integrate the Amazon through infrastructure, directed colonization, and new economic dynamics. The study evaluated urban sustainability over four decades by analyzing documentary records, expert opinions, and selected demographic, socioeconomic, and physical-environmental indicators. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) was applied to construct a sustainability ranking considering conflicting objectives. Three stages of urban evolution (foundational, intermediate, and current) were compared against the objectives of the original plan. Although informal urban growth, low population density, increasing deforestation, and social vulnerability are evident, the city shows positive indicators: sustained population growth, a proportion of urban population that shows its temporal persistence, a reduction in poverty rates, and improvement in the Human¨Development Index. To enhance its sustainability, the city requires greater attention from the State, under a renewed approach of citizen participation and interculturality. © Roger Eduardo Martínez Rivas, Rosario Beatriz Santa María HuertDaniela Ingrid Quispe Quispe, Ángel Robles Suaña, Vilma Gladys Vásquez PraManuel Villena Mavila, 2027.
