Title: Do words shape who can do what? How subtle linguistic cues can influence children’s categorization and ability judgments
Abstract: A central question in children’s social and cognitive development is how they represent people as belonging to one or more domains of activity and how they judge those individuals’ capabilities within those domains. The present research examines whether category-focused language (e.g., “scientist”), which marks domain membership as a bounded identity, versus action-focused language (e.g., “someone who does science”), which frames participation as non-exclusive, influences children’s and adults’ categorization, cross-classification, and ability judgments of others and themselves across science, arts, and sports. In Study 1, children and adults categorized and judged others’ abilities. In Study 2, children and adults did so for themselves. Study 1 showed that language had minimal impact on categorization and ability judgments about others; age group was the primary factor. Study 2 revealed that language was related to self-relevant categorization and ability judgments, with effects differing across children and adults and across the type of response. Category-focused language was associated with children more likely to classify themselves into a single domain and adults more likely to endorse cross-classification. Action-focused language was associated with children’s lower ability judgments within a single domain but more positive ability judgments across two domains. These findings show subtle linguistic cues can shape beliefs about category membership and ability, particularly in self-relevant contexts, and underscore the need to examine categorization and ability judgments across domains. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Li K.; Wu W.; Li J.; Li Z.; Wu Y.; Li L.; Sun Y.
Title: Conservation outcomes and heterogeneity of China's national protected areas in conserving terrestrial vertebrates
Abstract: Amid global change and increasing anthropogenic pressures, evaluating biodiversity outcomes associated with protected areas (PAs) has become a major challenge in conservation science. However, many previous assessments have not adequately accounted for spatial bias in PA placement and differences in landscape context. Here, we evaluated conservation outcomes associated with China's national PAs for terrestrial vertebrates using an integrated counterfactual framework that combines propensity score matching and generalized additive models, thereby reducing bias associated with non-random PA placement. Our results showed that national PAs were associated with higher terrestrial vertebrate species richness than matched unprotected areas, and substantial variation existed among taxonomic groups. Amphibians, despite having the lowest spatial representation within the PA, exhibited the largest biodiversity advantages relative to matched unprotected areas. In contrast, birds showed comparatively smaller advantages despite broad PA coverage. Biodiversity outcomes also varied among PA types: ecosystem and wildlife PAs generally showed positive conservation outcomes, whereas natural relic PAs showed no apparent advantage based on terrestrial vertebrate richness. Further analyses revealed significant nonlinear associations between matched biodiversity differences and environmental conditions. These positive outcomes declined with increasing human footprint, suggesting that anthropogenic pressures may limit biodiversity advantages within PAs. Climatic conditions were associated with spatial variation in biodiversity advantages for threatened species. Overall, our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity in conservation effectiveness across taxonomic groups, PA types, and environmental gradients. These results provide a counterfactual-based assessment of biodiversity conservation outcomes within China's national PA and highlight the importance of species-specific conservation strategies and landscape-scale management in future conservation planning. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Bimodal emotion decoding: When faces and voices diverge
Abstract: It is well established that people infer emotions from both faces and voices, yet how they integrate these cues when the two modalities convey conflicting emotions remains unclear. Evidence for facial dominance has typically come from studies contrasting facial and vocal expressions of anger and happiness, often using binary response formats that require observers to choose between face-consistent andvoice-consistent emotion labels. These findings, however, fail to inform us whether facial dominance reflects a general principle of bimodal emotion perception or whether these results are shaped by the specific emotion pairing and response format. Across six preregistered experiments (total N = 359), participants judged dynamic face–voice expressions spanning three incongruent pairings: anger–happiness, anger–sadness, and happiness–sadness. Experiments 1–3 used multidimensional ratings, and Experiments 4–6 used open-ended descriptions. The results revealed a pairing-dependent pattern: anger–happiness pairings showed robust facial dominance effects, anger–sadness pairings showed vocal dominance effects, and happiness–sadness pairings produced more heterogeneous impressions, including blended responses and third-category interpretations (i.e., anger or disgust for sad face–happy voice pairings). Together, these findings challenge a single-modality dominance view and suggest that bimodal emotion decoding depends on the specific emotions being integrated. To explain these pairing-dependent patterns, we propose and provide initial support for an emotion-similarity account, in which the relative influence of faces and voices depends on how distinguishable the competing emotions are within each modality. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Identification of priority areas for inclusive automated vehicle infrastructure investment
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Highly automated vehicles (AVs) have the potential to improve mobility for older adults and people with disabilities. Planning for AVs requires substantial infrastructure investments, but limited resources make simultaneous upgrades impractical. Understanding how potential mobility gains differ by locations is useful for targeting investments, yet little is known about these differences. To address this gap, this study uses propensity score matching with moderation analysis to examine how built environment characteristics moderate the potential impacts of AVs on trip frequencies of older adults and people with disabilities using two Australian datasets. Findings suggest that potential mobility gains vary by location. Potential mobility gains for people with disabilities are larger in areas with low density, public transport accessibility, diversity, and high cumulative accessibility; whereas those for older adults are greater in areas with high cumulative accessibility and road connectivity. These findings provide guidance for prioritising AV-related infrastructure investments to promote social inclusion. Title: Embodied strategic coupling: highland bodies, global production networks, and the 2026 TCS London Marathon
Abstract: Elite distance running concentrates value in bodies formed in a few highland geographies, yet firms and institutions elsewhere control how that value is recognised and rewarded. This article asks how value is created, enhanced and captured in elite marathon running, and what the case reveals about the limits of global production network (GPN) theory. Reading the 2026 TCS London Marathon as a paradigmatic case, it advances the concept of embodied strategic coupling, a reformulation of strategic coupling in which the regional asset is a social field’s capacity to form bodily capital, and the bodily capital it forms is the mobile product through which value is realised. The substitutability premise of strategic coupling fails for this asset, because firms substitute among athletes and among highland fields but have not formed equivalent capacity inside programmes of their own. The formed body travels while the field that forms it does not. Firm and field therefore depend on each other, and capture proceeds through positioning at the interfaces between training, competitive and commercial fields rather than through control of production. The article specifies a two-scale temporal fix spanning athletic careers and the intergenerational reproduction of highland fields, imports bodily capital, feminist social-reproduction theory and sport mobilities into GPN analysis, and shows through the two podiums how equal placement awards coexist with unequal calculated totals under time-bonus rules. Title: Socially mediated safety technology adoption in pesticide-intensive greenhouses: integrating social amplification of risk and planned behavior perspectives
Abstract: The adoption of safety technologies in pesticide-intensive greenhouse systems remains persistently low despite well-documented occupational and environmental risks. Existing studies have primarily emphasized technical, economic, and informational barriers, offering limited insight into the socio-psychological mechanisms shaping resistance to protective innovations. This study attempted to address this gap by developing and empirically testing an integrated framework combining the Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to explain greenhouse operators’ intentions to adopt safety technologies in Iran. Survey data were collected from greenhouse producers across five major producing provinces (n = 198). Results indicated that attitude toward safety technologies was the strongest predictor of adoption intention. However, attitude formation was influenced by deeper psychosocial processes: institutional trust and perceived risk significantly enhanced positive attitudes, while information sources affected adoption indirectly by strengthening trust rather than through direct persuasion. Importantly, social processes functioned both as amplifiers and attenuators of risk. Social attenuation reduced perceived pesticide risk, thereby weakening motivation to adopt safety technologies. Conversely, perceived social pressure increased both risk awareness and institutional trust, underscoring its dual influence. These findings demonstrated that safety technology adoption is a socially mediated process shaped by trust, risk perception, and collective meaning-making. The study contributes to the literature by extending SARF to technology adoption, explicitly modeling risk attenuation as a barrier, and positioning institutional trust as a central causal mechanism. Policy implications highlighted the need for trust-centered risk communication and interventions that counteract socially embedded risk attenuation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Meyer M.; Lucrezi S.
Title: Clustering tourists’ perceptions of Marine Protected Areas: A comparative study in Southern Africa
Abstract: Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) are essential for mitigating human pressure and conserving marine ecosystems, but their success in developing countries often depends on balancing conservation with socio-economic development, which requires users’ support. This study assessed and compared tourists’ perceptions of MPAs with case studies in South Africa and Mozambique, where nature-based tourism is vital for local economies. Using a quantitative, descriptive approach, data were collected in 2023 and 2024 from 504 tourists and recreationists at the Ponta do Ouro Partial Marine Reserve in the Maputo National Park, Mozambique, and the Table Mountain National Park MPA, South Africa. Results indicated that while participants generally recognised the ecological value of MPAs, they held more positive views toward conservation benefits than socio-economic outcomes. Cluster analysis identified two primary stakeholder groups: Informed Supporters, who prevailed in the South African sample, and Sceptical or Passive Users, who prevailed in the Mozambican sample. The findings highlighted a critical need for management to implement communication strategies emphasising the social, economic, and cultural value of MPAs. Based on these insights, recommendations are provided for marketing, management, and future research to foster stakeholder support and sustainable social licence for marine conservation in Southern Africa. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The hidden redundancy in psychological trait measures: A general factor of personality (GFP) perspective
Abstract: In psychology there is a plethora of different measures and constructs. However, the literature also shows that many of these measures overlap and may even sometimes be redundant. Recognizing such overlap in measures is essential for consolidation and for moving the field forward. Accordingly, we suggest a role herein of the General Factor of Personality (GFP), which emerges from the correlations between specific personality dimensions and reflects a mix of desirable traits (e.g. being sociable, honest, and emotionally stable). It is argued and shown that the GFP is highly correlated with a wide range of psychological traits. We further postulate that this phenomenon provides a parsimonious way of looking at the overlap between many trait measures. This idea is discussed in light of the ongoing debate on the GFP in which some scholars suggest the general factor is substantive and relevant for understanding personality, whereas others consider it to solely reflect a measurement artifact. Irrespective of whether the substantive, artifact, or a mixed explanation of the GFP is adopted, overlooking the presence of a common general factor in psychological measures may, respectively, either impede the development of unifying theories of human behavior, or otherwise compromise measurement validity. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Feng D.; He S.Y.
Title: Modeling acceptance of shared and private autonomous vehicles with social-media-informed psychological variables
Source title: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are emerging rapidly in the AI era, and many countries are actively advancing AV pilot tests and regulations in metropolitan cities. Despite numerous studies exploring factors influencing public acceptance of AVs, few have proposed a comprehensive framework that integrates social media insights into survey design. This study develops a modeling framework to examine the joint effects of psychological and observed factors on AV acceptance using social-media-informed psychological variables. Comments on Douyin videos are collected to capture public perceptions of AVs, and a survey is subsequently designed and deployed in Shenzhen, China. Structural equation modeling is used to identify five latent factors (e.g., task–technology fit, attitudes, technology adoption propensity), followed by a discrete choice model to examine acceptance of private and shared AVs. Results show that technology adoption propensity, trust in AV performance, and attitudes directly affect acceptance, while trust in AV institution and technology adoption propensity indirectly influence acceptance through attitudes and trust in AV performance. AV exposure emerges as a significant antecedent of both perceptions and acceptance. We further distinguish potential users of private and shared AVs based on their socio-demographic characteristics and travel behaviors. The findings offer theoretical contributions and practical implications for urban planners, policymakers, and AV operators, particularly in tech-forward urban environments with rapid AV deployment. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: How effective are interventions at enhancing preschool children's empathy? A meta-analytic review
Abstract: Empathy, defined as sharing and understanding others’ emotional experiences, is key to the formation of social groups and plays an important role in children’s social development. While enhancing this skill in early education has been a focus in the field, whether trainings employed succeed at enhancing children’s empathy, and what the mechanisms are behind their effectiveness, is still unknown. Importantly, understanding this is crucial to effective intervention. A meta-analysis of 30 studies (44 effect sizes) measuring empathy before and after a training, including 2,820 preschool children (Mage = 5.08, range 3.41 to 6.46), was conducted using robust variance estimation to account for multiple effect sizes within the same study. Results revealed that interventions had a small to medium-sized effect in improving children’s empathy (Hedges’s g = 0.49, CI: 0.32, 0.66; p < 0.0001). Further, the impact of interventions on children’s empathy was moderated by intervention leader and the size of intervention classes, with researcher-led interventions delivered in groups having a larger effect on children’s empathy development than other interventions ( g = 0.77, CI: 0.55, 0.98; p = 0.002 vs g = 0.34, CI: 0.14, 0.54; p < 0.0001) . Child age and intervention dosage (number of intervention sessions times the length of each session) did not moderate the effect of interventions on children’s empathy. Our in-depth results urge researchers to use a variety of empathy measures to gain a better understanding of empathy development in early childhood, and encourage practitioners to target empathy in small groups, performing activities linked to emotion understanding, or book-reading and discussing characters’ emotions. Further implications for future research and practice are discussed. © 2026 .

Authors: Aylı B.I.; Paksoy N.
Title: Declining fertility in Türkiye (2000−2023): A Kitagawa decomposition analysis interpreted through a gender lens
Abstract: Fertility decline is not merely a demographic phenomenon; it is a barometer of the structural conditions under which women negotiate reproductive decisions. In Türkiye, the total fertility rate (TFR) has fallen below the population replacement threshold of 2.1 since 2018, reaching 1.63 by 2023. This raises a question central to women's studies: does this decline reflect expanding reproductive autonomy, or is it a constrained response to failures in care provision and gender equity? This study examines the nature and sources of this decline between 2000 and 2023 to distinguish between demographic population structures and behavioural fertility components. Using data from the UN World Population Prospects 2024 and the Turkish Statistical Institute, this research employs Kitagawa decomposition analysis and age-specific fertility rate (ASFR) assessments at both national and provincial levels. The results reveal that while the female population of reproductive age grew by 29.7%, annual live births plummeted by 23.5%, and the TFR dropped from 2.49 to 1.63. Kitagawa decomposition indicates that changes in fertility behaviour accounted for 164.6% of the total decline, overwhelming the positive demographic contribution of population growth. Regionally, all 81 provinces experienced declines, with the most significant drops occurring in Eastern and Southeastern Anatolia. These findings suggest that Türkiye's fertility transition is driven by a fundamental shift in reproductive behaviour. Addressing this decline requires a policy shift toward accessible childcare, expanded parental leave, and genuine support for gender equality. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Li X.; Zhang H.; Ni P.; Wang S.; Qiu Y.
Title: How attack centers emerge and evolve in event-driven cyberbullying: A mechanistic study
Abstract: In event-driven cyberbullying, hostile attention can rapidly converge on identifiable targets, exposing them to repeated collective attacks. Existing research has advanced harmful-content detection and the analysis of online aggression, but offers limited insight into how such attacks become concentrated on particular targets. To address this gap, this study constructs event-level trajectories of attacks against specific targets and introduces Targeted Aggression Propagation, a mechanistic simulation framework for modeling how attack centers emerge and evolve. The framework links overall event dynamics with the uneven accumulation of attacks across targets. We evaluate this approach on five cyberbullying cases using public Sina Weibo posts and first-level comments. Empirical evaluation shows that the framework reproduces observed multi-wave comment dynamics and characterizes changes in target dominance. Across the five cases, attack centers take distinct forms, including stable single-target dominance, two-target concentration, and competitive allocation. Scenario simulations further clarify how different mechanisms shape these forms. Post-driven stimulation, comment-driven reinforcement, and cooling mainly regulate the scale and persistence of targeted exposure, but their effects weaken after the main activation period. By contrast, mechanisms at the target layer shape how exposure becomes concentrated, stabilized, or redistributed under similar levels of overall aggression. These findings show that cyberbullying events should be examined not only by harmful-content occurrence or aggregate aggression, but also through the targets repeatedly exposed to collective attacks. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Changchang W.
Title: An unfinished gender revolution? Li Jinming, reality TV show, and the rise of urban feminism
Abstract: The article starts with the social controversy over the Chinese actress Li Jinming, who gained brief but notable prominence through her leading role in iPartment (2009–2014), a Chinese urban sitcom widely regarded as the dometic adaptation of Friends. In September 2023, archival footage of her ostensibly ‘tragic’ entanglement in a rural, patriarchal household from the 2014 reality TV show Celebrities Come to My Home , which had aired nearly a decade prior, resurfaced and went viral on Chinese social media. Rather than focusing on the social controversy sparked by Li regarding the family pressures faced by urban women who marry below their social status, this article points out that the binary epistemology, educated women versus rural (single) men implicit in the controversy, represents a mode of cognitive warfare imbued with a teleological belief in progress, which the paper theorizes as ‘urban feminism’. To trace this volatile field, the study examines multiple texts illustrative of fictional television dramas, high-profile digital controversies, state-sanctioned broadcasting, and reality shows, along with participatory digital remixes and the cascading online disputes erupting across the cyber-sphere, in an attempt to probe into how gender antagonism is transformed into a digital spectacle rooted in the urban-rural divide. While reclaiming narrative power, urban feminism operates primarily on an epistemic approach that prioritizes visibility over structural critique or offline solidarity. Ultimately, by excluding rural women's struggles and avoiding systemic intervention, urban feminism risks reducing cognitive warfare to performance, leaving the broader gender revolution unfinished. Authors: Öz G.Ö.; Günbayi İ.
Title: Theory-informed storytelling for leadership learning in undergraduate nursing education: A qualitative study of first-year nursing students
Abstract: Background: Leadership is increasingly recognized as a core competency in nursing practice and education. However, leadership education is often introduced in the later stages of undergraduate nursing programs, leaving students uncertain about how leadership applies to clinical practice. Innovative pedagogical approaches are therefore needed to support early leadership development. Storytelling may provide opportunities for students to engage with authentic professional experiences, reflect on leadership behaviours, and connect leadership concepts with future nursing practice. Objectives: This study aimed to explore first-year nursing students' learning experiences following participation in a theory-informed storytelling-based leadership education session, with particular attention to how they understood nursing leadership and reflected on leadership in their future professional roles. Method: A qualitative descriptive design was used to evaluate a storytelling-based leadership learning activity implemented in an undergraduate nursing program. The intervention consisted of a two-hour face-to-face educational session in which two nurse academics shared their professional leadership experiences through structured storytelling and discussion. Storytelling was used as the pedagogical strategy, with experiential learning theory informing the reflective learning process and social learning theory informing the role-modelling component of the session. Data were collected from 58 first-year nursing students through a written questionnaire consisting of nine open-ended questions and analysed using thematic analysis. Results: Four main themes emerged from the analysis: (1) reframing leadership perceptions through leadership stories, (2) leadership as a learnable and developable competency, (3) leadership readiness for future professional roles, (4) translating leadership learning into nursing practice. Students described leadership as extending beyond formal managerial roles and recognized its relevance to clinical practice, teamwork, and patient care. Students also identified leadership as a competency that can be developed through experience and professional learning. Conclusion: Storytelling-based educational interventions may support nursing students' understanding of leadership by connecting leadership concepts with authentic professional experiences. Such approaches may foster early leadership awareness and help students consider how leadership relates to their future professional nursing roles. © 2026

Title: From graphical design to digital learning: One hundred years of the McCabe-Thiele method
Abstract: This article commemorates one hundred years of the McCabe-Thiele method by examining its origins, assumptions and subsequent trajectory, and by asking what function it still performs. Physical copies of the principal textbooks, monographs and handbooks published since 1922 were examined to establish how successive authors weighted the method against the enthalpy-concentration construction: balanced treatment of the two persisted for four decades beyond the last of the classical methods and ended in the late 1980s, earliest in works addressed to practice rather than to instruction. The tools now available to a student are compared by level of rigor and by barrier to access, from browser-based calculators to rate-based simulation, and are shown to trade transparency for computational power. What no higher level supplies is diagnosis: a converged simulation returns a valid result for a design operating close to its pinch or with a mislocated feed and reports neither, whereas both are evident on the diagram. On this reading the method persists not as a design procedure, which it ceased to be, but as the representation against which computed output is interpreted and audited. Title: Validity and reliability of children's eating behaviour trait questionnaire tools adapted for use in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review
Abstract: The reliability and validity of children's eating behaviour trait questionnaires is critical for accurately measuring and understanding children's eating behaviours among diverse populations and for developing targeted nutritional and behavioural interventions, especially in low- and middle-income countries. This review was conducted with the aim of investigating current evidence on the validity and reliability of child eating behaviour trait questionnaires, initially developed or used in high-income countries, when adapted for use among children aged 2 to 12 years in low- and middle-income countries. Systematic literature searches were conducted in MEDLINE Complete, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Global Health, and PsycINFO. Studies investigating the validity and reliability of the most commonly used children's eating behaviour questionnaire tools in low- and middle-income countries, and conducted from January 2001 were considered for inclusion in the review. Title and abstract screening of the studies was followed by full text screening by two independent reviewers. 24 studies were included in the review. A majority of the studies (n = 13 studies) examined the Children's Eating Behaviour Questionnaire, with fewer studies investigating the psychometric properties of the other child eating behaviour trait questionnaire tools. The evidence for the validity and reliability of the questionnaires in low- and middle-income countries was mostly limited to construct validity (n = 18 studies) and internal reliability (n = 24 studies) analysis. Future studies should conduct more comprehensive psychometric evaluations of other adapted questionnaires and develop new instruments tailored to assessing children's eating behaviour traits in low- and middle-income countries. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Liu Y.; Liu H.; Zhang H.
Title: Linking waterscape features to restorative emotional responses: Insights from LLM-based analysis of social media comments
Abstract: Waterscapes play an important role in enhancing residents' physical and mental wellbeing through their restorative effects. However, systematic comparisons across different waterscape types and integrated examinations of their material, immaterial, and temporal characteristics remain limited. To address these gaps, this study employs socially expressed emotional responses, characterized by both valence and arousal dimensions, as indicators of restorative experience. Using a large language model (LLM) to perform emotion analysis and waterscape feature extraction on social media comments, combined with objective built-environment indicators, the study systematically examines how diverse waterscape features are associated with restorative outcomes across spatial and temporal contexts. The results indicate that lakes, rivers, and fountains all exhibit relatively high valence levels, with fountains showing stronger associations with higher-arousal emotions. Both valence and arousal levels peak in spring and are lowest in winter. Among the identified features, natural atmosphere, sky, flowing water, and flowers, many of which possess an ephemeral aesthetic quality, are consistently associated with moderately activated positive emotions. Urban-related features and waterscape-related activities exhibit more context-dependent patterns, associating with higher-arousal positive emotions as well as stress-related responses. In contrast, objective waterscape indicators show weaker and nonlinear relationships with high valence. SHAP interaction analysis revealed that restorative associations emerged primarily from combinations of natural features with activities, facilities, and environmental atmospheres, rather than the accumulation of natural elements alone. Overall, this study enriches the theoretical and methodological scope of restorative environment research and provides practical insights for the design and management of restorative urban waterscapes. © 2026

Title: Official or Influencer? An AI-Enhanced Analytical Framework for Decoding Multimodal Persuasion in Government Marketing Videos
Abstract: Local officials increasingly use short-video platforms for direct-to-consumer marketing, creating tension between bureaucratic identity and platform logic. This multimodal persuasion context is difficult to analyze at scale without losing theoretical depth. To address this gap, we propose and validate an AI-enhanced analytical framework centered on a "Human-AI Dynamic Cognitive Dialogue" protocol, which turns the Multimodal Large Language Model (MM-LLM) from an automated "black box" into a theory-guided analytical mechanism and reduces the text-centric bias of traditional computational methods. Crucially, it uses theory-driven human oversight to guide AI-assisted induction, preserving methodological transparency while eliciting strategy configurations beyond researcher priors. Based on 779 Douyin videos from Chinese officials, the study identifies a "bifurcation of authority": authority cues are differentially associated with engagement depending on personified presentation (e.g., official attire) rather than institutionalized context (e.g., a government office). Engagement-cost differentiation is also evident: higher-cost actions such as sharing correspond to a synergy of personified authority, narrative resonance, and high cognitive value. Smaller accounts show a "legitimacy compensation" pattern, with strong authority signals associated with higher engagement among accounts lacking established social capital. The study establishes a replicable protocol for decoding unstructured video data and offers a bounded extension of the Elaboration Likelihood Model by showing how dynamic multimodal cues correspond to differentiated engagement patterns in algorithmic short-video environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Adults’ perceptions of rising food price and their impact on food purchasing: findings from the 2022 international food policy study
Abstract: Rising food prices reached record levels in 2022, raising global concern. This study examined consumer perceptions of food price increases in 2022 and their perceived effects on food purchasing in five countries, as well as differences by socio-demographic characteristics and household food security status. Despite some cross-country differences, respondents in all countries reported reductions in purchasing of non-core foods, such as desserts and non-alcoholic beverages, but also of core foods, such as fruits and vegetables. In all countries, reported reductions in core food purchases were associated with lower perceived income adequacy and household food insecurity. Authors: Shapiro P.
Title: Good inventions, not good intentions: technological displacement of animal use and the drivers of social change
Abstract: Throughout history, reductions of animal use in the economy have rarely resulted from moral awakening. Instead, just as new inventions have enabled many forms of animal use (e.g., harpoons, battery cages), new technological innovations have also frequently rendered long-entrenched forms of animal exploitation obsolete. This Commentary examines a series of cases–including but not limited to the replacement of whale oil by kerosene, ivory by plastics, goose quills by metal pens, horses by engines, and guano fertilizer by synthetic nitrogen–to illustrate how new inventions, rather than humane sentiment or philosophical arguments, have produced substantial and enduring reductions in animal use. While ethical arguments have driven personal, corporate, and public policy reforms, new technologies’ superior utility, scalability, or cost-efficiency has generally accelerated the abandonment of animal use altogether. Using Peter Singer’s Animal Liberation Now (2023) and its assessment of the limited progress since Animal Liberation (1975) as its starting point, this commentary examines historical cases in which technological substitution reduced institutionalized animal use. The Commentary argues that efforts to reduce animal exploitation should place greater emphasis on developing, scaling, and deploying alternatives that can outperform animal-based products in utility, affordability, or convenience. This approach has implications for how the public and private sectors fund, regulate, and prioritize innovation. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Lin J.-H.T.
Title: Pieces of me: Theorizing affordance-based social media usage styles and their impact on social capital and well-being
Abstract: People use multiple social network sites (SNSs) to interact and present different facets of themselves. However, existing studies often focus on a single platform, lacking a holistic view of users' behavior across multiple SNSs. Drawing on signaling theory, an affordance-based social media usage framework is proposed, incorporating three affordances: network structure, anonymity, and visual presentation. The framework contrasts honest signals with conventional signals, theorized as ego-centric versus interest-based networks, low versus high anonymity, and self-included versus non-self-included visual presentations. These six affordances-based behaviors were operationalized using a national representative sample of 1549 participants from the Taiwan Communication Survey. The latent class analysis (LCA) identified six latent user styles: ego-centric networkers, anonymous hobbyists, public social butterflies, cross-platform masqueraders, relationship maintainers, and lurkers. Title: Structural conditions for working-time reduction as an eco-social policy: stakeholder assessments across European welfare regimes
Abstract: Working-time reduction (WTR) has reemerged as a prominent eco-social policy proposal in debates on how to enable 1.5 °C-compatible lifestyles. While a growing literature documents its potential benefits for well-being and sustainability, less is known about the political conditions under which WTR becomes acceptable and implementable across different welfare regimes and positions in the global political economy. This article examines how stakeholder acceptance of WTR is assembled, contested, and constrained in practice, and what this implies for its political feasibility as an eco-social transition policy. Drawing on a hybrid Policy Delphi and Stakeholder Thinking Lab conducted in Sweden, Germany, and Latvia, we analyze how stakeholders embedded in distinct welfare-state and work-regime formations reason about WTR’s desirability, feasibility, and political possibility. The findings show widespread support for WTR on well-being grounds, but highly conditional acceptance when assessed as an ecological and political intervention. Perceived political feasibility depends on income security, labor-market institutions, coordination capacity, and countries’ positions within European and global core-periphery relations. Where welfare institutions buffer individuals from labor-market risks, WTR becomes a negotiable reform; where working time functions as a survival imperative, it remains politically fragile. We argue that WTR operates as a diagnostic “stress test,” revealing where societies can translate support for well-being into coordinated redistribution of time and where the social and institutional preconditions are missing. WTR debates in Europe are not only nationally differentiated but also globally situated, exposing the temporal and political-economic constraints that condition Europe’s 1.5 °C transition strategies. © 2027 The Author(s). Title: University students’ perceptions of ai-generated deepfakes: The case of Grok; [Percepciones del alumnado universitario sobre los deepfakes generados mediante inteligencia artificial: El caso de Grok]

Title: Italian Brainrot and Generative AI: Algorithmic Absurdity and Hyper-Engagement on TikTok; [Italian Brainrot e Inteligencia Artificial Generativa. El hiperengament de lo absurdo en TikTok]
Abstract: Introduction: This study focuses on the analysis of Italian Brainrot, a universe of absurd characters created and animated using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), which emerged in mid-January 2025 and achieved unprecedented levels of notoriety, engagement, and virality among Generation Z and Generation Alpha. Methodology: A sample of 300 short TikTok videos was viewed, 30 for each of the 10 most popular characters (including Ballerina Cappuccina, Tralalero Tralalá, and Tung Tung Tung Sahur). Data on likes, comments, share, and views were collected, and the Engagement Rate was estimated. Both the characters, examined from the aesthetic perspective of the absurd, and user comments were qualitatively described. Results: The main finding is an Engagement Rate above 25% and an emotional connection far stronger than that observed in other viral digital phenomena. Discussion: The exponential productivity of random meanings enabled by GenAI, together with the fascination with the absurd generated by Italian Brainrot, would explain, along with the TikTok algorithm, the high levels of emotional engagement among adolescents and preadolescents, hence the notion of hyperengagement. Conclusions: The Italian Brainrot phenomenon exhibits unprecedented levels of engagement, far exceeding those of previous viral phenomena, ushering in a new era of algorithmic popular culture 100% made by GenAI. © 2027, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Authors: Xie G.; Bao Q.; Chen Y.; Fu Q.; Jia F.; You F.
Title: The affective Human–AI Co-Flow model: an interaction design study of commuter behavior in AI navigation
Abstract: Navigation service providers are shifting from functional tools toward intelligent agents with social roles and affective influence. Existing technology adoption research emphasizes cognitive and utilitarian dimensions, offering limited explanations of how AI develops from a tool into an affective partner during stressful commuting. This study proposes the Affective Human–AI Co-Flow (AHCF) model to explain how affective processes relate to navigation behavior through a sequence connecting AI Role Discourse, Affective Vulnerability Context, and Collaboration Fit with Affective Appraisal, Affective Regulation, and Affective Attachment. Using Amap's “Gao Laoshi” AI agent as the empirical context, we collected data from 280 commuters and tested the model through structural equation modeling (SEM), artificial neural networks (ANN), and multi-group analysis (MGA). Collaboration Fit emerged as a key gateway in the affective sequence. After its inclusion, the direct effects of AI Role Discourse and Affective Vulnerability Context on Affective Appraisal became marginally significant or nonsignificant. Affective Appraisal was strongly coupled with Affective Regulation, which had significant positive structural relationships with both Behavioral Response and Affective Attachment. Differences in predictive rankings and group comparisons further indicated that AI's affective influence varies with role perceptions, contextual pressure, and usage experience. AHCF thus reconceptualizes technology adoption as an affective co-flow process characterized by gating, amplification, and shifts across user groups. It provides a theoretical framework for understanding AI's development from a functional navigation tool into a relational collaborator and offers emotion-centered implications for AI navigation and intelligent mobility. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Authors: Greitemeyer T.
Title: When darkness overrides partisanship: Psychopathy and sadism predict support for violence on both sides of the Israel–Hamas conflict
Abstract: Support for political violence is often shaped by ideological alignment, with individuals tending to endorse aggression by actors perceived as ideologically similar while rejecting violence by opposing actors. However, some individuals may show a broader tendency to endorse violence across opposing sides of a conflict. Two studies examined whether Dark Tetrad personality traits—narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism—are associated with support for violent actions by both Israel and Hamas ( N s = 257 and 470). Across both studies, support for violence by Israel and Hamas was negatively correlated, indicating actor-specific endorsement patterns. Psychopathy and sadism were consistently associated with support for violent actions by both actors, whereas narcissism and Machiavellianism showed weaker and less consistent associations. Interest in militarism and moral disengagement partially accounted for the associations between psychopathy and sadism and support for Israeli violent actions, but not for Hamas-related outcomes. Overall, the findings suggest that while ideological alignment structures actor-specific support for political violence, psychopathy and sadism are associated with a broader tendency to endorse violence across opposing actors. These results highlight the importance of considering both ideological and dispositional factors in understanding support for political violence. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Marine protected areas and maritime spatial planning integration dynamics across Europe
Abstract: Maritime Spatial Planning (MSP) has emerged as a central governance tool to balance ecological, social, and economic uses of marine space, while Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) remain essential for biodiversity conservation and ecosystem resilience. Effective integration of MPAs into MSP can enhance conservation outcomes and reduce conflicts with human activities, yet the degree of integration across the European Union (EU) remains highly uneven. This study examines how MPAs are embedded within national MSP frameworks in 20 EU Member States, aiming to classify, compare, and explain differences in integration levels. A typology of four integration levels is introduced, ranging from MPAs as primary drivers of MSP to their treatment as passive spatial layers. The methodology combines the development and application of a set of questions directed at MSP experts with the use of a decision tree and allocation criteria designed to assess responses and classify countries according to their level of MPA–MSP integration. Results reveal substantial disparities across EU Member States. Belgium, Germany, Latvia, Slovenia, Sweden and the Netherlands showed the strongest degree of integration, with conservation objectives embedded in MSP provisions and influencing cross-sectoral planning decisions. In contrast, most countries incorporated MPAs mainly through environmental assessment instruments or treated them as existing spatial layers, environmental constraints, or separate legal instruments. Key barriers include fragmented governance structures, limited translation of environmental assessments into binding spatial decisions, weak links between MSP and MPAs management, uneven monitoring and enforcement capacity, and limited mechanisms for stakeholder coordination. Advancing MPA–MSP integration requires stronger legal frameworks, adaptive management strategies, ecological connectivity, and inclusive governance processes. By providing a systematic comparison and highlighting best practices, this study provides recommendations to foster more cohesive, resilient, and biodiversity-informed marine governance. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Islam M.
Title: Solving Extreme Water Crisis Through Community-Driven Ice Stupa Project in Ladakh
Abstract: This chapter outlines the progression of the Ice Stupa Project in Ladakh, a landmark initiative in climate-adaptive water management practices in northern India. The Ice Stupa Project integrates environmental management and economic development objectives with local social, cultural, and religious values, creating a multifaceted approach to addressing water scarcity in the region. Ladakh, a cold desert with harsh climatic conditions, rugged terrain, and minimal precipitation, faces considerable challenges in securing adequate water supplies. The water crisis in Ladakh is different from the rest of the world; winters become extremely severe, with temperatures dropping below −30 degrees Celsius. Most of the population relies on water coming through the stream from melting glaciers. The entire community faces great difficulties in obtaining sufficient water for growing crops, livestock, and personal use in summer and spring, as Himalayan glaciers are receding at a rapid pace. Additionally, a substantial amount of water is wasted through glacier streams, as the severe cold conditions prevent crop cultivation. Despite confronting severe climatic challenges and water scarcity, the people of Ladakh have found adaptive strategies to address the water crisis by using traditional yet effective methods of water management through the formation of ice stupas, a type of artificial glacier or ice reservoir. This chapter examines the methodological framework for constructing ice stupas, drawing on observations made by the author at various ice stupa sites. It also inspects the successes and limitations of the project, alongside its global implementation and recognition. Furthermore, the chapter explores different water and ice harvesting methods used to address acute water scarcity in the villages of Ladakh. The findings suggest that the ice stupa methodology can be replicated in other regions facing similar challenges and could contribute to the development of broader climate change mitigation and adaptation strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Wang C.; Zhu W.
Title: A corpus-based study of disciplinary identity in economics lectures: Combining corpus linguistics, systemic functional linguistics and discourse-historical approach
Abstract: This study investigates how economics instructors construct disciplinary identity in the neglected register of the university lecture. Corpus Linguistics (CL) describes statistically salient features, Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) interprets their clausal function, and the Discourse-Historical Approach (DHA) explains them as identity strategies embedded in the field's epistemology. It tracks the markers I, we, you, economist(s) and economics, their process configurations and the salient semantic domains of each subcorpus across 288 lectures (≈1.83 million tokens) from elite universities and open online course series. Three findings emerge. First, the markers fall on three distributional planes: pronouns are densest in evaluative and applied subfields, whereas economics and economist(s) co-vary closely (r = 0.85) and peak in foundational courses, where the field must still be defined and its practitioners introduced. Second, they realise a three-way grammatical division of labour: pronouns co-occur across mental, material, verbal and relational processes, casting instructor and student as thinker, doer, sayer and identifier; economist(s) with verbal and mental processes (43% and 28% of subject-position cases); and economics with relational processes (76%), abstracting the field as an entity that is, not an actor that does. Third, in the three subfields examined for epistemic modulation, what distinguishes them is less the content of claims than the force with which they are made. Tracing the recontextualisation of labels such as the dismal science further shows how the lecture socialises novices into the insider-outsider boundary. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Ghatode J.; Nimbarte G.
Title: Performance Analysis and Science Mapping of Agricultural Research Within the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework: A Bibliometric Analysis Using the Scopus Database
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were established to eradicate poverty, achieve food security, promote sustainable agriculture, and develop resilient communities, making sustainable livelihoods a global priority. As a key livelihood sector, agriculture plays a central role in advancing these goals, particularly for vulnerable populations in the Global South. While agricultural sustainability has been widely studied through various lenses, there is growing interest in using the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (SLF) to explore the complex interplay among social, economic, and environmental factors shaping rural livelihoods. This study contributes to the literature through a comprehensive bibliometric analysis that maps the evolution of agricultural research within the SLF. Drawing on 1,977 documents indexed in the Scopus database (1960–2023), it employs performance analysis to identify influential authors, institutions, countries, and journals. It further applies scientific mapping to trace thematic shifts and collaboration networks. The thematic analysis reveals that clusters such as livelihood–resilience–sustainability occupy a central position, indicating their role as the primary drivers of contemporary sustainable livelihood scholarship. In contrast, themes such as climate change, adaptation, vulnerability, sustainable livelihoods, and livelihood assets, particularly in lower-income contexts like Ghana, appear as basic yet underdeveloped, signaling critical research gaps. By identifying these uneven thematic trajectories, the study offers new theoretical insights into how the SLF has been operationalized in agricultural research and provides evidence-based guidance for policymakers and researchers seeking to strengthen livelihood resilience and sustainability in vulnerable agrarian contexts. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Authors: Sasani M.S.; Shaghaghi S.
Title: Iranian women in sugar dating: An analysis of telegram users’ experiences
Abstract: This study explores the lived experiences of Iranian women involved in sugar dating and elucidates the structural, field-based, logical, and experiential dimensions of this phenomenon in Telegram. Employing a qualitative approach grounded in an interpretivist-constructivist paradigm, the study uses semi-structured interviews with five with direct experience with such relationships. The findings indicate that participation in sugar dating constitutes an “innovative” response to the gap between culturally prescribed goals of financial success and structural limitations in access to legitimate means. The body, as a form of physical capital, becomes a tool for negotiation and for acquiring economic, symbolic, and social capital. These relationships, situated in liquid modernity, have functional, temporary, and consumerist features that reproduce emotional-supportive functions and a sense of security. The participants' lived experiences reveal a strategic yet constrained form of agency, bounded by cultural limitations and social stigma, in which the management of the body and digital identity forms the intersection between social structure and individual agency. This study conceptualizes sugar dating as a structural-cultural phenomenon that necessitates supportive interventions, economic policymaking, and nonjudgmental social education. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: When does perspective-taking predict coalition success? The interplay of propensity, accuracy, and social predictability
Abstract: Theories of coalition formation assume that coalition outcomes are determined by static features of the game (e.g., players' resources), because these features are thought to elicit universal allocation norms that allow players to anticipate each other's demands. Yet the same structural features can carry different social meanings depending on what players want, expect, and consider fair. Perspective-taking helps players navigate this social information, but its importance may depend on how predictable the social context is. We examined whether perspective-taking predicts coalition success more strongly when allocation norms are difficult to anticipate, than when norms are clear. We tested this hypothesis in two experiments using a real-time three-person coalition paradigm, in which we manipulated the predictability of allocation norms (High-Predictable vs. Low-Predictable). In Experiment 1 (N = 851), perspective-taking predicted greater inclusion and higher payoffs only in the Low-Predictable condition. In Experiment 2 (N = 1206, preregistered), we replicated the main effect of perspective-taking across conditions, but not its moderation by norm predictability. Exploratory analyses distinguishing the propensity to take perspective from the accuracy of doing so found that in the Low-Predictable condition propensity translated into coalition success only when paired with accurate inference of partners' norms; in the High-Predictable condition, propensity predicted success independently of accuracy. These findings showed that socio-cognitive processes play a relevant role in coalition formation, and that accuracy adds value beyond propensity only when allocation norms are less predictable. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Xu K.; Wu B.; Zhao Z.; Shao Y.; Li L.; Jia Z.
Title: Stage-dependent gray matter morphological alterations across the clinical spectrum of depressive disorder
Abstract: Background Previous studies have reported gray matter volume (GMV) deficits in different illness stages of depression; however, whether patients at different stages show shared or distinct GMV abnormality patterns has not been systematically characterized. Methods We conducted a quantitative voxel-wise meta-analysis of whole-brain voxel-based morphometry studies in individuals with subthreshold depression (STD), first-episode drug-naïve depression (FEND), and long-term major depressive disorder (MDD). Separate, pooled and comparative meta-analyses were performed using the seed-based d mapping (SDM) toolbox. Meta-regression analyses were conducted to explore age- and disease-related alterations in depression. Results Twelve studies including 467 individuals with STD, 19 studies including 854 patients with FEND, and 14 studies including 525 patients with long-term depression were included. Compared with controls, STD and FEND exhibited mixed patterns of GMV increases and decreases predominantly involving key emotional and default mode network regions. In contrast, long-term MDD showed consolidated GMV reductions confined to the paracingulate gyrus and left middle temporal gyrus extending to insula. Direct comparisons across stages confirmed that GMV alterations in prefrontal and temporal regions showed progressive divergence from early to chronic depression. Meta-regression analyses revealed stage-specific associations between clinical characteristics and GMV changes. Conclusions This meta-analysis reveals stage-specific GMV abnormalities across depression. GMV changes shift from mixed alterations in early stages to purely atrophic reductions in chronic MDD, supporting a progressive model. Fronto-limbic deficits at the subthreshold stage may serve as early vulnerability markers, while GMV consolidation in long-term MDD underscores the importance of early intervention. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Evaluating the socio-economic determinants of housing affordability within the context of Egypt’s 4th generation cities; [Evaluación de los determinantes socioeconómicos de la asequibilidad de la vivienda en el contexto de las ciudades de cuarta generación en Egipto]
Abstract: As Egypt develops its 4th generation cities, housing affordability remains a critical determinant of urban well-being. This paper evaluates the relationship between housing affordability, socio-economic variables, and housing determinants across three housing mixes in and near the New Administrative Capital (NAC): middle-income housing (R3), luxury housing (R5), and social housing (Capital Gardens City: CG). The paper assesses the effect of nine independent variables on housing affordability by using multiple linear regression (MLR). The results demonstrate that affordability was most strongly associated with cost reduction and payment facilities across all housing levels. However, localized drivers emerge: the ownership system is pivotal in R5 and CG, while household size and employment type are significant in R3. In CG, marital status and income provide additional layers of influence. These findings underscore that affordability is a multidimensional, varied, local-context phenomenon. Finally, policy implications are proposed to enhance the sustainability of new urban housing markets. © Rola Kamal Ali, Sherief Ahmed Sheta, Esraa Mohamed Elazab, Ahmed Mohamed Thabet Alieldin, 2027. Abstract: This study investigates the representation of Brazilian police officers in recent academic literature. Authors: Pasanen A.; Matschoss K.
Title: From coal dependency to coal phase-out: Empirical multi-level policy examination in an urban energy system
Abstract: Research on the politics and governance of coal phase-out has primarily concentrated on national-level policymaking and the role of coal in electricity generation. This study examines an urban transitions and multilevel policy mix impacting the Finnish energy company Helen’s transition away from coal, leading to a coal phase-out in the City of Helsinki. Heating presents a major challenge in the shift toward renewable energy sources due to long heating seasons and district heating relying on coal. We integrate a co-evolutionary framework of policy subsystems and socio-technical change with a framework of policy mixes. Our empirical investigation focuses on the effects of multi-level policies that accelerated energy transitions from 2016 to 2021. Through semi-structured interviews with municipal decision-makers, company representatives, and stakeholders, as well as document analysis, we examine the policy instrument mix to better understand multi-level policies and the political environment influencing the energy company. Our analysis points toward four key issues that jointly made a coal phase-out achievable despite significant challenges, and can act as lessons of transitions in other contexts. First, a robust mix of strong destructive policies at various levels rendered coal burning economically unfeasible, while innovative measures created a path forward. Second, personnel changes facilitated the transition. Third, viable technological alternatives to coal were emerging. Fourth, public demand for climate action was intensifying. Our findings suggest that the credibility and comprehensiveness of the policy mix are more crucial than coherence or consistency. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: Teaching social and structural determinants of health in nursing: A comparative analysis of microlearning, problem-based learning, and gamification
Abstract: The Issue: Pre-licensure nursing programs are accountable for preparing nurses who can recognize and address social and structural determinants of health (SSDOH), yet nursing faculty have limited evidence to guide the selection of active-learning strategies that develop this competency. Since the pandemic, microlearning, problem-based learning (PBL), and gamification have been increasingly incorporated into health professions education programs; however, limited guidance exists regarding their relative contributions to SSDOH competency development. This contemporary issue uses Bereday's comparative method to interpret and compare health professions education literature (2022–2025) across five criteria aligned with SSDOH competency frameworks. We argue that these strategies serve distinct educational purposes rather than interchangeable ones: microlearning builds foundational knowledge and shared language, PBL develops systems thinking and ethical reasoning, and gamification promotes engagement with the lived experiences that shape health outcomes. We propose a scaffolded, blended sequence in which microlearning, PBL, and gamification develop complementary dimensions of SSDOH competence that no single strategy can achieve on its own. © 2026

Title: Enhancing the social innovation ecosystem: university-led incubation pathways for rural sustainability
Abstract: Universities are increasingly called upon to contribute to sustainability transitions, yet their roles as active intermediaries within social innovation ecosystems remain under-theorised. This study examines how universities can incubate social innovations that advance rural sustainability. Using an exploratory, theory-building case study, we draw on interviews, documents and observational materials from multiple rural revitalisation initiatives led by The University of Hong Kong to identify how incubation processes configure relationships, mobilise resources and reshape institutional environments. Our analysis reveals three distinct incubation pathways, stewardship, platforms and communities, which differ in their locus of intervention, the types of social capital they generate and the institutional roles the university performs. Stewardship initiatives cultivate bonding capital by transforming individuals into rural change agents through experiential learning and place-based engagement. Platform initiatives build bridging capital by providing shared infrastructures that connect rural and urban actors, lowering market and regulatory barriers. Community-focused initiatives mobilise linking capital, enabling collective governance arrangements and facilitating negotiation across local and institutional boundaries. Synthesising these findings, we develop a configurational framework of university supported social innovation incubation that elucidates how these pathways operate through different forms of institutional work across community and institutional boundaries. The framework demonstrates how universities, when locally embedded and institutionally trusted, can orchestrate multiple, complementary pathways that cumulatively reshape social innovation ecosystems. We discuss implications for sustainability transitions scholarship and for designing context-sensitive incubation strategies in underserved or peripheral regions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Xu X.; Deng X.; Chen C.; Dou B.; Wang L.; Xia J.; Sun J.
Title: Cognitive flexibility mediates the association between gross motor skills and Level-2 visual perspective taking in preschool children
Abstract: Understanding how children represent others’ visual perspectives is fundamental to early social-spatial cognition. Level-2 visual perspective taking (VPT) requires children to transform their own spatial reference frame to represent how a scene appears from another viewpoint—a process that places substantial demands on executive function (EF). However, the cognitive mechanisms through which bodily experience relates to children’s performance on Level-2 VPT tasks in early childhood (i.e., which specific EF components mediate this association) remain poorly understood. The present study examined the embodied account of Level-2 VPT that gross motor skills are associated with Level-2 VPT through one or more EF components—inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. Participants were 213 Chinese preschool children aged 3–6 years who completed standardized assessments of gross motor skills, EF components, and Level-2 VPT. Parallel multiple mediation analyses were conducted controlling for child age, gender, and family socioeconomic status. Results showed that gross motor skills were positively associated with all EF components and that cognitive flexibility, but not inhibitory control or working memory, mediated the association between gross motor skills and Level-2 VPT. These findings highlight gross motor skills as an important embodied context for children’s Level-2 VPT performance and provide evidence that cognitive flexibility constitutes the primary executive mechanism underlying Level-2 VPT in early childhood. Authors: Buzurukov B.; Zakirova M.
Title: Irregular Migration Through the Lens of Migration Theories: Testing Classical Theories in Explaining Visa Overstay in South Korea
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: The Republic of Korea presents an interesting case for testing the predictive power of migration theories in explaining a specific group of undocumented migrants: visa overstayers. Studies of irregular migration often overlook the potential of migration theories to explain migrants’ decisions to overstay their visas. Against this background, this study attempted to contribute to understanding the main drivers of irregular migration to the Republic of Korea from 143 countries between 2003 and 2013. Building on a synthesis of existing migration theories and their testing in the context of U.S. irregular migration, we replicated the analysis for the Korean case using five prevailing migration theories. The findings suggest that the neoclassical theory of migration, segmented labor market theory, and social capital theory are the most effective in explaining variations in irregular migration. Overall, our results are consistent with the predictions of international migration theories, except for social capital theory. Contrary to the generally accepted hypothesis, this study found that greater social capital among Korean migrants is more likely to facilitate legal migration, thereby reducing the need for undocumented stay. Owing to differences in how men and women decide to overstay their visas, we also conducted a gendered analysis. Strict measures against migrant violations, such as deportation, have a deterrent effect on female visa overstays, but do not affect their male counterparts. On the other hand, a strong driver of both female and male undocumented migration remains the labor demand for cheap, low-skilled foreign workers. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Authors: Li Y.; Wang F.; Jin J.; Pan Y.
Title: How conversation content and style shape service evaluations: Evidence from a dual-pathway mediation model and neural processing
Abstract: Chatbots are increasingly deployed in service interactions, yet users may evaluate them less favorably than human agents. This research develops an integrative conversational processing (ICP) perspective to examine how conversation content (tailored vs. generic) and conversation style (varied vs. non-varied) jointly shape service evaluations. It also investigates the social-cognitive appraisals and neural activity associated with different content-style configurations. Across a scenario-based experiment, an interactive behavioral experiment, and a within-subjects EEG experiment, tailored responses received more favorable evaluations than generic responses under both style conditions, but this advantage was consistently larger when responses were varied. Study 2 provided evidence consistent with conditional indirect effects through warmth and competence perceptions, both of which were stronger under varied-response conditions. An exploratory bootstrap contrast further showed that the overall indirect effect through competence perception was larger than that through warmth perception. Study 3 revealed a corresponding neural pattern: tailored responses elicited lower high-alpha activity than generic responses under both style conditions, with a larger difference under varied-response conditions, consistent with greater cognitive engagement. Together, the findings support a configurational account in which stylistic variation reinforces tailored content, while its independent influence may vary across evaluation formats. In the task-oriented service contexts examined, organizations should prioritize contextual tailoring and apply stylistic variation selectively. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Toward a Canadian agenda for sustainability transition research
Abstract: Sustainability transitions research has expanded well beyond its original empirical settings, yet questions remain about how transition perspectives can be meaningfully translated across political economies with distinctive configurations of institutional, geographic, environmental, and historical characteristics. In Canada, these questions are especially salient, as political-economic particularities both complicate the application of transition frameworks and create opportunities for theoretical and practical advance. In response, this perspective develops a Canadian agenda for sustainability transition research grounded in an iterative co-development process involving scholars and practitioners from across the country. Through this process, we identify four interrelated themes based on the above particularities that structure this agenda: federalism, regional cleavages, geography, and environment; resource- and energy-intensive political economies; Indigenous sovereignty and reconciliation; and relations with and proximity to a global power. These themes not only capture central features shaping transition dynamics in Canada but also offer opportunities to advance broader debates in the field. For each theme, the paper illustrates how engagement with Canadian particularities can help illuminate extant research debates and areas of fruitful exchange, from the role of Indigenous leadership to geopolitical and economic dependencies. The perspective also identifies how these themes come together as a configuration, raising promising directions for the study of transitions. In this fashion, the central contribution of the perspective lies not in proposing a transition theory tied to national exceptionalism, but rather in showing how sustained engagement with Canadian particularities (and their interrelations) can generate opportunities for mutual enrichment through the translation and extension of transition ideas. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Han R.
Title: Cognitive friction in AI use and emotional exhaustion: The mediating role of cognitive exploitation and the moderating role of fear of missing out
Abstract: Cognitive friction, defined as the mental effort required to overcome interaction obstacles with AI, and the subsequent awareness of being cognitively exploited may be key drivers of emotional exhaustion in human-AI interactions, a phenomenon that remains inadequately explained by existing technostress frameworks. To empirically test this possibility, we integrate conservation of resources theory with the digital labor perspective to examine how cognitive friction in AI use leads to emotional exhaustion. Using a three-wave longitudinal survey of 480 Chinese AI users, we constructed a moderated mediation model in which cognitive exploitation served as the mediator and fear of missing out (FoMO) as the moderator. The results reveal that: (1) cognitive exploitation mediates the relationship between cognitive friction and emotional exhaustion, and this indirect effect is significant across all FoMO levels, while the direct effect is fully mediated only at the average level of FoMO; (2) FoMO moderates the direct path, creating a “dual-pressure” effect for high-FoMO individuals while showing a negative direct effect for low-FoMO individuals; (3) AI usage frequency has no direct correlation with emotional exhaustion, suggesting that psychological risks are more closely associated with social-psychological variables than with usage intensity. These findings challenge purely technical explanations of AI-related stress and advance theoretical understanding by reconciling the tool-centric and social-actor views of AI through the integration of COR theory and the digital labor perspective. The study offers crucial insights for designing psychologically sustainable AI interfaces, developing targeted mental health interventions, and formulating organizational policies to prevent the transformation of technological divides into psychological health disparities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: An embedding-based approach for measuring science–technology topic linkages using LLMs
Abstract: Traditional citation- and keyword-based methods struggle to capture science–technology (S–T) topic linkages owing to data sparsity, citation bias, and substantial linguistic differences across publication and patent corpora. To address these limitations, we propose a novel embedding-based approach that integrates large language model (LLM) embeddings with the neural embedded topic model (ETM). The approach comprises four steps: (1) encoding a union vocabulary from publication and patent corpora into a unified semantic space via LLM embeddings, (2) extracting science and technology (S&T) topics via ETM within this shared space, (3) quantifying S–T topic linkages via cosine similarity between topic embeddings, and (4) comparing against keyword- and citation-based approaches. When applied to 79,997 3D printing publications and 100,786 patents with a lexical overlap of only 26.43%, the method improves topic coherence via Qwen3 embeddings. The resulting S–T linkages (mean = 0.148) are significantly higher than the keyword-based measures (mean = 0.058), correlating positively with both keyword-based (r = 0.425) and citation-based (r = 0.271) linkages. Expert evaluation confirms that the generated S&T topics are interpretable, complete, informative, and with low bias, while the embedding-based linkages align with real-world knowledge relatedness. These findings demonstrate that the proposed approach transcends the structural sparsity of citations and the lexical limits of keywords, offering a more robust, interpretable, and comprehensive measurement of S–T topic linkages. It also provides evidence-based tools for key stakeholders in innovation systems to monitor translational research impacts and identify innovation opportunities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Interpersonal emotion regulation and emotional adjustment among Chinese early adolescents: Within-person associations with depressive symptoms and life satisfaction
Abstract: Background Previous theories and empirical studies suggest that interpersonal emotion regulation (IER) and specific IER strategies are closely linked to emotional adjustment. However, reciprocal associations among these constructs have rarely been examined while accounting for the temporal stability, and the existing evidence remains mixed. Using random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM), this study examined within-person bidirectional associations between IER and emotional adjustment (depressive symptoms and life satisfaction) among Chinese early adolescents. This study then investigated whether these associations differed across four specific IER strategies: enhancement of positive affect, perspective taking, soothing, and social modeling. Methods Data were collected from 795 adolescents (56.7% boys, M age = 13.38, SD = 0.72) at a secondary school across three time points over six months. Results IER was positively associated with life satisfaction, and negatively associated with depressive symptoms at the between-person level. At the within-person level, IER and its specific strategies showed heterogeneous prospective associations with life satisfaction across measurement intervals; Depressive symptoms showed marginal negative associations with subsequent engagement in IER, particularly for soothing. Conclusions These findings extend prior literature by suggesting that IER and its specific strategies may be more closely linked to life satisfaction, but not to depressive symptoms. Instead, depressive symptoms may also be associated with reduced subsequent engagement in IER, particularly for soothing. These results highlight the importance of considering directionality in the association between IER and emotional adjustment. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.
