Title: Minds in motion: The theory and practice of empathy as embodied joint action towards shared goals
Abstract: This article presents the enactive social empathy model (ESEM), which conceptualizes empathy along four types (from individual to social) as an embodied social process reciprocally linked with joint action undertaken through shared commitment to concordant goals. In this model, empathy is the prerequisite capacity enabling coordinated interaction, while the embodied experience of joint action dynamically refines mutual understanding. This framework integrates cognitive, affective, and sensorimotor dimensions often studied in isolation; clarifies empathy's function in cooperation; reframes empathic distress as often stemming from commitment breakdowns; and offers a pragmatic lens reconciling self/other interest. By centering interaction and commitment, this model provides a theoretically grounded and ecologically valid foundation for new empirical research using interactive methodologies and for developing more effective interventions in fields such as public health, contemplative science, education, and conflict resolution. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Parallel development and maturation of GABAergic interneurons and corticotrophin-releasing factor signaling within the amygdala complex
Abstract: The amygdala complex is known to play a critical role in supporting adaptive behaviors in response to environmental stimuli, particularly during sensitive periods of brain development. Through its connections, the amygdala modulates hippocampal and striatal-dependent memories and shapes distinct cortical function within the emotional and cognitive domains. Major neural circuit remodeling is known to occur in the amygdala during postnatal development through adolescence, which includes the maturation of its excitatory connectivity and the progressive organization of local GABAergic inhibitory interneurons. Thus, the goal of this paper is to review current knowledge on how developmental trajectories of distinct GABAergic interneuron populations within the amygdala are temporally staggered to enable successive sensitive periods during which environmental input impacts amygdala-dependent emotional learning, threat processing, and social behavior. This review will discuss the early emerging somatostatin and neuropeptide Y interneurons, later maturing parvalbumin-positive interneurons, and developmental changes in stress-responsive corticotrophin-releasing factor signaling. We examine how these trajectories may shape age-appropriate behavior and sensitivity to early life adversity as GABAergic circuits within the amygdala mature. Title: Integrating trauma-informed and culturally responsive practice in schools: A qualitative ecological analysis of educator sense-making under structural constraints
Abstract: Trauma-informed practice (TIP) and culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP) are frequently advanced as complementary equity approaches in schools, yet the practice-level interface between them remains under-specified—particularly in communities shaped by poverty, displacement, racism, and intergenerational trauma. This qualitative study examined how 26 primary school educators in a culturally diverse, socioeconomically disadvantaged Australian school described adapting trauma-informed practices to students' social and cultural contexts. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with ecological systems theory providing an interpretive framework. Three themes captured educators' sense-making: (1) Prioritising safety and belonging , reflecting microsystem practices addressing basic needs shaped by socioeconomic adversity; (2) Navigating cultural complexity , illuminating mesosystem negotiations between institutional expectations and family cultural practices; and (3) Seeking deeper understanding , capturing educators' recognition of exosystem gaps between available professional learning and the intersecting realities of trauma, culture, and disadvantage. Findings highlight the interpretive labour educators undertake when adapting standardised frameworks to local contexts, while revealing tensions between individualised trauma responses and structural inequities. Implications for culturally responsive professional development, institutional policy reform, and educational practice are discussed. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Exploring students' cognitive interactions with their past and future learning experiences during professional socialisation: A focused ethnographic study
Abstract: Background: Becoming a professional is a complex psychosocial learning process usually framed in a period of formal education. The social-relational dimension of students' learning has been predominantly examined with a view of learning as a linear socialisation process. However, the underlying cognitive mechanisms that make learning a temporally dynamic process are underexplored. Aims: To explore the complex cognitive mechanisms by which nursing students mentally interact with past and future learning experiences during their professional socialisation. Design: A focused ethnographic study. Methods: A pluralism of methods was used. Eight nursing students were observed in their university activities in 2019, and seven students were followed in their final year using personal audio diaries in 2020. Finally, twelve students were interviewed in 2021 to refine the analysis. The data analysis considered inductive and abductive phases, framed in constructivist grounded theory strategies. Results: Students construct dynamic learning experiences by constantly revisiting past experiences and simulating future experiences. We identify descriptive forms of retrospection and prospection (evocative and imaginative, respectively) and cases where the mental move is deliberately interpretative. We bring insights from cognitive and memory studies to analyse this temporally dynamic facet of learning. Conclusions: This study offers a characterisation of the mechanisms of retrospection and prospection concerning professional learning. It also provides a framework for understanding learning as a dynamic process rather than a linear one, as personal experiences are constantly (re)constructed via mental faculties encompassing the student's biography and projected expectations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Soft Skills in Editorial and Communicational Management of Scientific Journals; [Habilidades blandas en la gestión editorial y comunicacional de revistas científicas]
Abstract: Introduction: In the context of the digital economy, the editorial management of scientific journals combines technical and normative demands with constant interaction among authors, reviewers, and editors. Although indexing metrics and prestige have been widely studied, there remains a gap regarding the influence of soft skills on perceived quality and the international positioning of journals. Methodology: This was a quantitative, descriptive, correlational, and cross-sectional study. An online survey was administered to faculty-researchers with recent experience in publication processes. The questionnaire included nine descriptive questions, sixteen Likert-scale items measuring soft skills, and one open-ended question. Frequencies, Spearman’s correlation, and the Kruskal–Wallis test were applied. Results: A total of 394 researchers participated. Most reported favorable perceptions across the four dimensions, although variations emerged according to indexing level. Correlations between soft skills and indexing were negative and significant, and the Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed differences in mean ranks. Discussion: Higher prestige and indexing were associated with lower perceptions of human engagement in editorial management, aligning with studies that highlight the divergence between technical excellence and relational quality. Conclusions: A higher perceived level of soft skills is associated with a more favorable author evaluation of the editorial experience and process. Title: Pedagogical patterns in science and mathematics classrooms of Pakistan: an observation-based study
Abstract: The persistent learning crisis in science and mathematics across countries of the Global South raises critical questions about the quality of classroom instruction. While participatory pedagogy is widely advocated for promoting cognitive engagement, inclusion, and student agency, large-scale empirical evidence on how practices are enacted, and the conditions that enable them, remains limited in contexts such as Pakistan. This study develops a national profile of participatory practices in elementary (Grades 5, 6, and 8) science and mathematics classrooms in Pakistan and examines the predictors of these practices. Grounded in the dynamic model of school effectiveness and constructivist theory, participatory pedagogy is conceptualised as teaching that promotes collaboration, student voice, shared decision‑making, and meaningful cognitive engagement. Using a large‑scale cross‑sectional design, the study reports findings from structured observations of 436 classrooms in 96 public and private schools across 16 districts. Classrooms were assessed using an adapted Classroom Observation Scale‑Revised (COS‑R), measuring the physical environment, classroom interactions, and teaching practices. Results indicate that instruction remains largely teacher‑centred, with limited student participation and weak cognitive engagement, although teacher–student interactions were generally positive. Peer interaction and formative feedback were minimal. Multivariate analyses show that class size and the effective use of allocated instructional time are key determinants of participatory practices. The study contributes large‑scale empirical evidence from the Global South, introduces a contextually grounded observation tool, and offers scalable insights for strengthening participatory pedagogy in pursuit of equitable learning outcomes aligned with SDG4. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Perceived descriptive norms and longitudinal change in conspiracy beliefs
Abstract: Belief in conspiracy theories represents a common and potentially rigid belief system that may be influenced by perceived social consensus. It remains unclear whether perceived social norms predict changes in personal conspiracy belief, or whether such associations reflect projection processes whereby individuals infer consensus from their own views. In a two-wave study of UK adults ( N = 1430) conducted six weeks apart, we examined whether perceived conspiracy belief norms prospectively predicted residualised change in conspiracy belief. Hierarchical regression analyses controlled for baseline belief levels and demographic covariates, and reciprocal analyses tested whether beliefs predicted subsequent norm perceptions. Parallel analyses were conducted for paranormal beliefs as a secondary test of domain generality. Conspiracy beliefs demonstrated high temporal stability. However, perceived conspiracy norms at Time 1 predicted increases in conspiracy beliefs at Time 2, even after accounting for baseline beliefs. Reciprocal effects were observed but were smaller in magnitude. Normative effects for paranormal beliefs were substantially weaker. These findings suggest that even relatively stable belief systems remain partially responsive to perceived social consensus, highlighting the potential value of normative feedback interventions aimed at correcting exaggerated perceptions of conspiratorial consensus. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Sunstein C.R.
Title: Animals Matter: the case for a kinder world
Source title: Animals Matter: The Case for a Kinder World
Abstract: In Animals Matter, Cass Sunstein offers a pathbreaking new argument for why we must change our practices to reduce the unjustified suffering of animals. This surprisingly personal book offers a simple proposition: The interests of animals count, and we should work to promote their well-being, just as we should work to promote the well-being of humans. Drawing on psychology, behavioral economics, and his White House experiences, Sunstein reveals why people are likely, in time, to increase their support for the legal protection of animals and why, ultimately, we should adopt a Bill of Rights for animals that affirms their right to live free from cruelty and deprivation. Applying his research on “social cascades,” Sunstein compares the animal rights movement to previous causes such as civil rights that exploded in size once they passed a threshold moment. But this change won’t happen on its own. Sunstein demonstrates that we need to overcome deliberate ignorance about the mistreatment of animals, to make their suffering conspicuous and visible, and to create animal welfare cascades. Our governments need to recognize benefits and harms to animals in their policymaking. We need to give political and legal representation to animals who are being mistreated, and we need to use “nudges” to increase their well-being. Animal rights are not radical or utopian; they are rooted in widespread moral judgments. Sunstein shows how we can eventually create a world in which most people will come to embrace rights for animals. Copyright © 2027 by Cass R. Sunstein.

Title: A pilot feasibility study of a brief psychoeducational intervention for caregivers following a child's autism spectrum disorder diagnosis
Abstract: Background: Caregivers of children recently diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) face challenges in understanding their child and adapting parenting approaches, yet structured post-diagnostic support is often limited. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and preliminary outcomes of a brief psychoeducational group program delivered after ASD diagnosis in a routine outpatient setting. Methods: A total of 119 caregivers of school-aged children (6–12 years) with newly diagnosed ASD participated in a single-arm pilot study. The intervention consisted of three 90-minute group sessions covering neurodevelopmental characteristics, structured teaching strategies, and social resources. Feasibility was assessed through completion rates, attendance, and satisfaction ratings. Primary outcomes included caregiver depressive symptoms (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale), parenting behaviors (Positive and Negative Parenting Scale), and caregiver-perceived child behavioral difficulties (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire). Results: The program completion rate was 65.5% (78/119), and attendance at the core psychoeducational sessions addressing neurodevelopmental understanding and structured teaching exceeded 84%. Participant satisfaction was high, with 96% of respondents reporting satisfaction or partial satisfaction. No significant changes were observed in primary outcomes. Exploratory analyses indicated modest increases in Respect for Autonomy (dz = 0.28) and reductions in Harsh Discipline (dz = −0.32). Conclusions: This brief psychoeducational intervention appears feasible and acceptable within routine outpatient care. Although primary outcomes did not change significantly, exploratory analyses suggested modest changes in selected parenting domains without correction for multiple comparisons. Given the single-arm uncontrolled design, these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and warrant further evaluation in controlled studies with longer follow-up. © 2026

Authors: Parcha S.K.
Title: Ladakh: A Tapestry of Geological Legacy, Cultural Heritage, and Environmental Transformation
Abstract: Ladakh, nestled in the Trans-Himalayan region of India, is a remarkable convergence of dramatic geology, ancient culture, and evolving socioeconomic dynamics. Often referred to as the “Land of High Passes,” this high-altitude cold desert, shaped by the ongoing India–Eurasia continental collision, presents a rare geological cross-section through major tectonic zones, including the Indus Suture Zone, Ladakh Batholith, and the Karakoram Range. These features offer critical insights into the tectonic evolution of the HimalayaHimalayas, past oceanic closures, and subduction-related magmatic events. Covering approximately 98,000 square kilometers in the northwest Himalaya, Ladakh encompasses all key tectonic subdivisions-from the Tethyan sedimentary sequences of the Zanskar Zone to the Indus and Shyok Suture Zones, and finally the Karakoram Batholith marking the Eurasian Plate’s southern margin. The iconic Ladakh Batholith, formed via subduction-zone magmatism, provides vital clues to arc-related processes preceding continental collision. Additional geodynamic features, such as the Dras and Khardung volcanic remnants and the ophiolitic mélanges of Nidar and Zildat, further enrich Ladakh’s geological narrative. Despite its arid, barren appearance, Ladakh supports intricate hydrological systems centered on the Indus River and its tributaries—Zanskar, Shyok, Nubra, and Shingo—which carve fertile valleys vital for agriculture. Glacial meltwaters, traditionally managed through terraced irrigation and innovations like ice stupas, sustain livelihoodLivelihoods during a short summer season. High-altitude wetlands and saline lakes such as Pangong Tso, Tso Moriri, and Tso Kar serve as critical ecological refuges and climate indicators. Culturally, Ladakh represents a rich tapestry of Tibetan Buddhist, Dardic, and nomadic traditions. From cliffside monasteries to vibrant festivals like Hemis, Losar, and Dosmoche, Ladakh showcases deep-rooted spiritual resilience and human adaptation. While Buddhism predominates in central and eastern regions, western Ladakh—especially KargilKargil and Dras— is home to a strong Islamic heritage rooted in seventeenth-century conversions among the Dardic people. The region’s ecological fragility is heightened by climate change, which has intensified glacial retreat, water scarcity, and extreme weather. Unregulated tourism, infrastructural pressures, and inefficient irrigation practices further strain Ladakh’s delicate ecosystems. However, sustainable traditions such as communal resource sharing, passive solar architecture, and high-altitude organic farming offer valuable models for resilience. Economic diversification through practices like sea buckthorn cultivation and vegetable cash cropping is also gaining momentum. Ladakh’s future hinges on balancing development with conservation. Priorities include climate-resilient infrastructure, renewable energy (particularly solar and geothermal), sustainable tourism, and inclusive education. Preserving Ladakh’s geoheritage is critical, as the region serves as a living laboratory for Earth system science. Traverses such as Sabu-Khardung-Hunder and Nyoma-Hanle-Tso Kar exemplify magmatic arcs, suture zones, metamorphic exhumation, and paleolake formations. The Tso Morari Crystalline Complex and Sumdo preserve high-pressure eclogites and schists, providing evidence of deep subduction and tectonic uplift. Sedimentary archives along the Indus and Shyok rivers are invaluable for paleoclimate reconstruction and geohazard assessment. Ladakh stands as both a geological crown jewel and a resilient cultural landscape. As modernization unfolds, careful stewardship is essential to preserve its unique legacy and promote a sustainable model for high-altitude regions worldwide. This chapter underscores the significance of Ladakh as a living laboratory for Earth system science. It highlights the urgent need to balance heritage conservation, geological research, and sustainable development. As Ladakh embraces modernization, it remains a testament to the resilience of both land and people in one of Earth’s most fragile yet profound environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Intergenerational eco-craft, women's agency, and climate adaptation in Telaga Biru Coastal Village, Madura, Indonesia
Abstract: This study examines how coastal women in Telaga Biru Village, Madura, Indonesia, use natural-dye batik as an everyday practice of livelihood adaptation, ecological knowledge transmission, and community sustainability. Rather than treating women only as vulnerable subjects of climate and coastal change, the article asks how women's craft labour enables them to negotiate socio-ecological uncertainty within unequal gender relations, unstable markets, and limited institutional support. Based on feminist ethnography, the study draws on participant observation, in-depth interviews with 15 women batik artisans, and supplementary interviews with the village head and a local batik business owner. The findings show that women's natural-dye batik work operates as intergenerational eco-craft: it sustains household livelihoods, preserves coastal motifs and natural-dye knowledge, supports small-scale waste management, enables limited digital marketing, and anchors community-based environmental care through women's informal and organisational networks. At the same time, the article cautions against romanticising women's resilience, as their adaptive labour remains under-recognised, poorly supported, and shaped by patriarchal household and community structures. By conceptualising natural-dye batik as intergenerational eco-craft, this study contributes to feminist climate scholarship by showing how women's craft labour connects ecological knowledge, livelihood adaptation, cultural continuity, and coastal sustainability in the Global South. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: When “they” is singular: The interplay between cognitive and social factors predicts pronoun misinterpretations in bilingual English speakers
Abstract: Language change is shaped by cognitive biases as well as by sociolinguistic perceptions of linguistic innovation. Although the use of they as a singular pronoun to refer to a generic referent is not new in English (e.g., “An employee can file a complaint if they need to”), a recent innovation extends this usage to refer to known individuals of non-binary gender. This type of socially motivated language change allows speakers to position themselves relative to linguistic innovation. Using the self-paced reading paradigm, we examined the processing of non-binary singular they across unambiguous (one-referent) and temporarily ambiguous (two-referent) contexts. We report on a processing experiment with second-language English speakers from Spain who, by virtue of their bilingual experience, are skilled at language learning and regulating activation of competing representations through cognitive control. We investigate how variability in the adoption of the pronominal innovation is influenced by sociodemographic and cognitive factors. We find that seemingly at-chance group-level performance in resolving temporary ambiguities is the product of bimodal distributions in interpretation within the population. Lingering misinterpretations in some speakers are predicted by a combination of sociodemographic and cognitive factors. Critically, we find that even among participants willing to adopt non-binary language, accurate interpretation of the non-binary singular they is mediated by cognitive resources. The findings bear implications for accounts of language change and the adoption of non-binary pronouns in bilingual communities as a result of individual variability. We outline a proposal for a conceptual Integrated Model of Adaptation to Grammar In Evolution (“IMAGINE”). © 2026

Authors: Pühringer S.; Bäuerle L.
Title: The economics of socio-ecological transformations: introducing a conceptual framework
Abstract: This article introduces the SETER framework, a conceptual tool for analyzing the interplay between socio-ecological transformation (SET) and economic reasoning (ER). In the context of global crises and the contested nature of sustainability discourses, the framework identifies nine key categories (economic goals, decisive economic institutions, role of the state, spatial scope, role of technology, economy-nature-nexus, socioeconomic cohesion, transformative dynamic, and transformative agency) to systematically compare diverse SET narratives and their basic underlying economic imaginaries. Drawing on insights from social studies of economics (SSE) and different strands of SET literature, the framework highlights how ER shapes SET discourses and potential pathways, influencing both diagnoses of socioecological crises and proposed solutions. The SETER framework also enables typifying antagonistic narratives opposing SET, such as techno-libertarianism or fossil modernization. While the framework offers a useful tool for categorizing and comparing SET narratives, integrating it with power-focused analytical tools is necessary to assess the performative influence of these narratives. By offering a flexible, cross-sectoral, and longitudinal approach, the SETER framework provides a robust methodology for navigating the complexities of SET-related discourses, current counter-developments, and the critical role of economic imaginaries. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Immovilli M.; Büscher B.
Title: Beyond ‘diversity of values’: power, pluralism and transformative change in biodiversity conservation
Abstract: The concept of value has, again, become a major bone of contention in biodiversity conservation. Responding to natural capital approaches that aimed to illuminate natures economic value, critics argued that this economic emphasis not only ignores but strengthens the root causes of the ecological crisis. These criticisms have not gone unheard. While attempts to uncover the economic value of nature continue, important biodiversity conservation actors like the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services and others have started taking issue with this narrow focus, too. Instead, they advance a pluralist conservation agenda where transformative decision-making promotes a broad diversity of values of nature beyond economic valuation. This article critically-constructively engages with this value pluralist turn. We describe how the debate got to this point, reveal the dangers of this turn vis-à-vis current changes in capitalism and aim to (re)direct it towards more radically transformative possibilities. We do so by 1) showing how capital could exploit a diversity of values agenda for its own reproduction; 2) how capital is historically objectified into material realities and 3) how the outcomes of this process are protected by powerful class interests that need to be acknowledged and confronted. We conclude that value pluralism needs to be embedded in a struggle against capitalism. Title: Maternal depressive symptom trajectories in the first 12 postpartum months and the associated risk correlates
Abstract: Postpartum depression has been known to emerge during the peripartum period or within the first 4–6 weeks of childbirth. However, its long-term progression and the underlying mechanisms of its different trajectories remain poorly understood. This longitudinal study examined the diagnostic stability and changes in 191 mothers who were non-depressed (ND), depressed, or had an adjustment disorder (AD). Fine-meshed repeated measures of depressive symptoms from childbirth through 12 months, along with assessments of mother-infant attachment and perceived stress, revealed distinct trajectories reflecting recovery, persistence, or new onset of depression. Approximately half of the postpartum depression (PPD) cases were found to recover, showing improvement within six months, with no recovery seen in the rest of the cases. Among the initially healthy participants, 4.7% developed major depressive disorder (MDD) within the first postpartum year, while 25.6% of those with early AD developed depression in the same period. Persistent PPD was found to be characterized by the strongest negative affective burden, low attachment, and an accumulation of characteristics including premenstrual syndrome (PMS), prior depression, childhood maltreatment, and low social support. In contrast, the recovering cases reported frequent baby blues and PMS, which can be understood as proxy indicators of a heightened hormonal sensitivity. These findings reveal that, rather than being a static condition confined to the early postpartum period, PPD is a heterogeneous and dynamic process. Close monitoring of new mothers in the first postpartum year combined with robust social support may help improve maternal and infant mental-health outcomes. Copyright © 2026. Authors: Li Y.; Liu Y.; Liu Y.; Li X.
Title: Alleviating urban heat exposure through green space optimization: A multi-objective framework using cellular signaling data
Abstract: Extreme heat events significantly threaten public health and urban sustainability. Traditional urban green space (UGS) optimization often relies on static census data, failing to capture spatio-temporal variations in human activity and associated thermal risks. This study proposes a spatially explicit multi-objective optimization model to mitigate heat exposure in Xuzhou's central urban area. Integrating hourly cellular signaling data from three representative time points (08:00, 14:00, and 20:00), the optimization framework utilizes a heuristic search strategy to simultaneously optimize four critical objectives: reducing heat exposure, minimizing conversion cost, enhancing spatial equity, and improving morphological compactness. Three policy-oriented scenarios—balanced development (BD), cost-effective (CE), and social equity (SE)—were simulated to explore the trade-offs between fiscal constraints and climate benefits. The main findings are as follows: (1) The proposed framework effectively captures the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of population heat exposure and generates differentiated UGS layouts under varying policy priorities. (2) The CE scenario achieves the lowest conversion cost, whereas the SE scenario yields higher cooling effectiveness and lower Gini coefficients through dispersed micro-scale green interventions in densely populated areas; the BD scenario provides a balanced compromise among the four objectives. (3) Spatial overlay analysis further identifies no-regret intervention zones that remain stable across scenarios and time periods, which are mainly concentrated on public service land, warehousing land, rural homesteads, and vacant land. This study advances UGS optimization from static, land-oriented planning toward multi-temporal, people-centered climate adaptation, providing practical support for heat mitigation and resilient urban planning in high-density cities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Chiriani, Ilaria (60110813900); Fiorillo, Iolanda (57207925957); Song, Wolf Yu (60172697100); Vink, Peter (7006242402); Naddeo, Alessandro (54970665800)
Title: Identifying the most comfortable interpersonal distances for autonomous vehicles’ passengers
Abstract: The evolution of autonomous vehicle interiors presents both opportunities and challenges in optimizing space for Non-Driving Related Activities (NDRAs). Previous research explored the reconfiguration of interiors in autonomous vehicles to support key activities such as reading, working, relaxing, and conversing. Building on this foundation, the present study examines how seating arrangements and interpersonal distances influence passenger comfort and conversational quality. Drawing on proxemics theory, the investigation considers the impact of gender, age, and nationality on interpersonal spatial preferences within vehicle cabins. Thirty-seven participants (aged 23–33) experienced three seating configurations -alpha (side-by-side), beta (opposite directions with parallel axes), and gamma (face-to-face)- in a virtual environment developed using Unity and accessed through HoloLens 2. Participants selected their preferred interpersonal distance from five predefined options while interacting in Augmented Reality (AR) with a virtual mannequin. Objective measurements were supplemented with subjective feedback from a post-test questionnaire. This study addresses the following research questions: 1) Which seating configuration is most comfortable for passengers during a conversation? 2) What are the ideal seating distances in each configuration? 3) How does gender influence interpersonal space requirements? 4) How does ethnicity impact interpersonal space preferences? Findings show no significant difference in distances chosen when conversing or not. Distance varied significantly with social relationships. Gender, body size, and culture influenced preferences. Results suggest the need for adaptable interior layouts that can accommodate diverse interpersonal spacing needs. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Hu B.; Huang Z.; Huang M.; Teng F.
Title: The vicious cycle: Effect of sexual objectification on women's retaliatory dehumanization of men
Abstract: Research on gender relations has documented reciprocal antagonistic attitudes and behaviors between men and women. The present study examined hostile intergender relationship through the perspective of sexual objectification and dehumanization, specifically we investigated the hypothesis that men's sexual objectification of women will incur women's retaliatory dehumanization of men and its potential mechanism as well as boundary condition across four studies. Employing large-scale social media data ( N = 127,975) and regional search behavior, Study 1 found that provincial levels of men's sexual objectification of women predicted women's dehumanization of men. Moreover, chronic (Studies 2 and 3; N = 121 for Study 2 and N = 235 for Study 3) and experimentally induced (Study 4, N = 270) experiences of sexual objectification led women to dehumanize men, either as a group (Studies 2 and 3) or as an individual perpetrator (Study 4), manifesting in perception (Studies 2–4) and behavioral responses (Study 4). We further found that meta-dehumanization served as a unique mediating mechanism of women's sexual objectification experience and their dehumanization of men and enjoyment of sexualization moderated this process. Among women who reported greater enjoyment of sexualization, the relationship between women's sexual objectification and reciprocal dehumanization of men was less prominent. These findings contribute to the literature on intergender interaction and relationships. Implications are discussed. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Chng E.; Schneider B.
Title: Using computer vision to support formative assessment in science experiments: An investigation into the suitability of action recognition models
Abstract: Providing feedback to move learners forward (i.e., feed-forward feedback) is one of formative assessment's key strategies (Black & Wiliam, 2009; Hattie & Timperley, 2007). Yet, within the context of science experiments, teachers lack adequate information on students' experimental conduct to be able to provide feed-forward feedback that is timely, structured and individualized. In this regard, we can leverage computer vision to detect student actions during science experiments for feedback, thereby creating an additional source of information to support teachers in implementing formative assessment. This study aims to investigate the construction of action recognition models using data collected from 140 ninth grade students as they conduct a science experiment in school laboratories. In two separate model investigations, we 1) compared model performance of various action recognition architectures (C2D, I3D, and SlowFast), and 2) inspected confusion matrix of the best fine-tuned action recognition model. Our results indicate that 1) SlowFast architecture is most suited for recognizing student actions in school laboratories and 2) similar and consecutive student actions, as well as uneven training data distribution, generate confusion for action recognition models. Further review of these findings allowed us to 1) explore suitability of using computer vision as an added information source for formative assessment and 2) consider details of implementing computer vision for formative assessment support. Overall, this study represents a preliminary investigation that uncovered intricacies of building action recognition models in a real-world setting and unveiled the ways in which computer vision can support teachers in implementing formative assessment in science experiments. © 2026

Title: Why are most people more creative than others? Exploring the better-than-average effect in creativity
Abstract: People tend to rate themselves as more creative than average, but how this better-than-average effect (BTAE) generalizes across creativity aspects and which individual differences predict it remains unclear. In two online studies ( N = 700), participants evaluated themselves relative to others on various traits (e.g., openness) and behaviors (e.g., creative writing). An independent sample rated the traits for social desirability and the behaviors for typical engagement frequency. The BTAE replicated for global creativity and most traits, but weakened or reversed for behaviors. Trait self-evaluations were primarily predicted by social desirability, whereas behavior self-evaluations were predicted by engagement frequency. Creativity self-assessments were further related to creative activity, self-esteem, and life satisfaction. Thus, the BTAE in creativity is predictably shaped by item- and person-level factors: it is robust for high-value traits but diminishes for rare, difficult behaviors, consistent with self-enhancement theory. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Salivary oxytocin and testosterone in empathic stress responding: a pilot study
Abstract: Suffering the stress of others (termed empathic stress or stress contagion) may affect an individual’s health and well-being. To understand the underlying hormonal processes of empathic stress, N = 108 opposite-sex dyads were tested, with one dyad partner passively observing the other undergoing a standardized psychosocial laboratory stressor. A positive link between oxytocin release and empathic stress response was hypothesized, while a negative relationship was expected for testosterone release. Associations of observer oxytocin and testosterone levels with two components of empathic stress were examined: stress resonance (i.e. synchronized observer–target responses) and vicarious stress (observer responses independent of target stress). During the passive observation of a stressed target, salivary oxytocin and testosterone levels increased by 16.64% and 23.00%, respectively, followed by a drop back to baseline levels. Supporting our hypotheses, increased observer oxytocin reactivity was linked to greater stress resonance in HF-HRV reactivity. This association was reversed in low oxytocin responders. Further, testosterone reactivity was negatively associated with stress resonance in heart rate activity. However, testosterone also showed a positive association with vicarious cortisol activity, which resembles the response pattern seen in first-hand stress exposure. We conclude that stress resonance may be the more empathy-dependent component of the empathic stress construct, aligning with previous work on the involvement of oxytocin and testosterone in empathy. To draw further conclusions about the role of oxytocin and testosterone in empathic stress response, future studies including a control group and hormone stimulation are needed. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Xing W.; Li Y.; Zhao Z.
Title: HAT-KI: A Hierarchical Auxiliary Task framework with asymmetric Knowledge Injection for early rumor detection
Abstract: Automated rumor detection on social media is crucial for curbing the spread of misinformation, yet most existing approaches rely heavily on extrinsic propagation structures unavailable in early detection scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose HAT-KI, a novel text-centric Hierarchical Auxiliary Task framework with Knowledge Injection for robust early detection. Our model introduces two key innovations: (1) a deep multi-view feature fusion mechanism that integrates pre-trained semantic features with refined emotion and topic knowledge distilled from teacher models; and (2) a hierarchical auxiliary learning architecture where coarse-grained detection guides the primary fine-grained verification task through asymmetric knowledge transfer. This design enables HAT-KI to capture both high-level semantic cues and subtle textual patterns indicative of rumors, even in information-sparse regimes. We evaluate our approach on three real-world datasets — Twitter15 (1490 posts), Twitter16 (818 posts), and PHEME (5802 posts) — and demonstrate that HAT-KI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art graph-based and content-only baselines, achieving accuracy scores of 92.0% on PHEME and 88.6% on Twitter, relying solely on intrinsic textual cues. These results underscore the effectiveness of our method in early-stage rumor detection and highlight its practical value for timely misinformation mitigation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Social feedback informs generalisation of control beliefs
Abstract: Perceived control in one context can affect behaviour in novel contexts. One potentially important variable determining generalisation is how perceived control in one context shapes beliefs about the self. Typically, learned helplessness studies do not control or manipulate beliefs about the self. Here, we test whether observing others' ability to exert control helps to inform inferences about whether the controllability is primarily due to one's own ability or a feature of the current environment, and thereby determines the degree of generalisation. In an initial study (N = 200) and pre-registered replication study (N = 436) we used comparative social feedback about performance in a novel task (the Wheel Stopping task) to assess how self- or environment-specific inferences shape control beliefs. Linear mixed effects models in both studies revealed that both task controllability and social feedback uniquely predicted participants' local control beliefs (trial-by-trial), after accounting for perceived task difficulty. Additionally, in Study 2, there was a significant decrease of internal locus of control in the group given low relative feedback in the low control condition, suggesting that in low control, social feedback impacts global control beliefs. Study 2 further revealed that task controllability and feedback were not related to changes in reported self- versus task-specific attribution of control. Social feedback generalised to influence behaviour in a second task in terms of the number of actions performed but not the time taken to escape or the proportion of those who learned to escaped. These results suggest that comparative social feedback shapes local control beliefs, global control beliefs in low control scenarios, and generalises to some aspects of behaviour in a second task, but does not change reported self- or task-attribution of control. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Cocaine profiling: Implementation of MCR-ALS for adulterant identification using ATR-FTIR in forensic analysis
Abstract: Cocaine stands out due to its significant social problems stemming from trafficking, leading to increased violence and detrimental effects on the physical and mental health of its users. Brazil serves as a transit route for cocaine produced in Colombia, Peru, and Bolivia to Europe, with Paraná being a strategic region due to its border with Paraguay and the second-largest port in Brazil. Cocaine is gradually adulterated with cutting agents along the distribution chain, altering its chemical profile. Paradoxically, these components can create a unique chemical signature, enabling the tracing of the drug's origin and distribution routes. This study analysed 298 mid-infrared spectra of cocaine samples seized in Paraná and applied Multivariate Curve Resolution with Alternating Least Squares (MCR-ALS) to identify and characterise the main adulterants and diluents present. MCR-ALS was chosen due to its ability to decompose overlapping spectra into individual component contributions, making it ideal for analysing complex mixtures. Five distinct chemical profiles were identified, and based on their spectral interpretation and the most reported adulterants and diluents in cocaine samples, the five components were defined as: cornstarch, cocaine, caffeine, sodium bicarbonate, and creatine. The concentration profiles of the components were clustered using Hierarchical Cluster Analysis, and seven profiles of cocaine samples were identified based on the amount of cocaine and the presence of adulterants and diluents. The MCR-ALS method proved effective in identifying cocaine cutting agents via ATR-FTIR, offering a fast and reliable approach for forensic analysis that can help to identify commercial routes. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Wang M.; Siller R.; Breuste J.; Gan J.
Title: Biodiversity of domestic gardens: Design, management, and perception in a case study in Salzburg, Austria
Abstract: Domestic gardens are pivotal yet underleveraged components of urban green infrastructure, where biodiversity outcomes depend on aggregated household decisions. This mixed-methods study of ninety private gardens in Salzburg, Austria, integrated field assessments with owner interviews to test four hypotheses: (H1) management intensity drives habitat function more than garden area; (H2) aesthetic preference for tidiness, rather than self-reported ecological knowledge, is the dominant social barrier to biodiversity-supportive management; (H3) management input and garden area interact compensatorily; and (H4) perceived habitat quality is predicted primarily by visible structural diversity. Habitat function was operationalized via an indirect indicator framework for wild bees, butterflies, birds, and hedgehogs. Results supported H1 and H2: management intensity, garden area, and weekly time investment were the strongest predictors of habitat function, with tidiness preference the sole significant social barrier. H3 was not supported; we found no evidence of a compensatory interaction, with area and management acting additively. Owner perceptions exhibited systematic, taxon-specific overestimation, 91 % for birds, 84 % for butterflies, 81 % for wild bees, but only 49 % for hedgehogs, and structural diversity was their only significant predictor, corroborating H4. These findings reveal a critical gap in urban biodiversity planning: biophysical metrics alone cannot account for the social filters, particularly aesthetic norms, that mediate on-the-ground implementation. We argue for an intervention logic combining structural, perceptual, and normative instruments in place of information-deficit approaches, and for matching the scale of intervention to taxon mobility, offering a transferable framework for medium-sized temperate cities seeking to reconcile aesthetic norms with biodiversity outcomes. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: An integrated cost–benefit assessment of invasive Acacia dealbata Link. restoration in Galicia (Northwest Spain): Combining remote sensing and contingent valuation to support decision-making
Abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) are linked to the extinction of numerous organisms, being a problem for which urgent measures must be taken. Their management requires robust decision-support tools capable of integrating ecological, economic and social impacts. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA) has been highlighted by bodies such as the European Union as an important tool for making sound decisions in IAS management. This study focuses on the restoration of plots invaded by Acacia dealbata in the SAC Sil Canyon (NW Spain), using a novel integrated assessment framework that links remote sensing and contingent valuation (CV) within an extended environmental CBA. Sentinel-2 data and a Random Forest algorithm were used to map Acacia plots with an accuracy of 98%, given that no data on the occupancy of the species were available for this location. Knowing the Acacia distribution made it possible to characterize the slope and location of the plots in order to estimate the restoration costs. The intervention yields benefits in terms of timber from native species and non-market benefits, which were monetized by CV, obtaining a median willingness to pay of 6.31 €/year over 50 years. All costs and revenues were incorporated into the CBA to assess the feasibility and impact of the project. After a sensitivity analysis using a Monte Carlo simulation, the restoration was found to produce a net present value (NPV) of 2,793,476.09 € over a 120-year horizon, with the non-market goods contributing most to this amount. The results demonstrate that integrating remote sensing and stated preference methods within an extended CBA provides a sound basis for evaluating IAS management alternatives, supporting transparent and evidence-based environmental decision-making in protected areas. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Classroom desertification: Understanding university attendance through students' perspectives using a mixed-methods approach
Abstract: Student absenteeism in higher education is associated with poorer academic outcomes, weaker social integration, and increased dropout risk. Beyond individual motivation, attendance decisions are increasingly understood as dynamic evaluations influenced by pedagogical practices, structural constraints, and students’ lived experiences. Within this broader perspective, and drawing on embodiment and power-oriented perspectives, this study examines how physiotherapy students experience the classroom, make attendance decisions, and interpret their presence or absence. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data were collected through surveys and attendance records from 184 physiotherapy students (2022–2023). The qualitative phase included five focus groups with 35 students (2024–2025). Data were analysed descriptively and through abductive thematic analysis informed by sociological theory. Quantitative findings showed that evaluative activities, practical exercises, and doubt resolution were primary motivators, while lectures were least valued. Non-attendance was influenced by the perceived efficiency of independent study, preparation for other courses, limited exam relevance, and external commitments. Recorded sessions (n = 91) showed average attendance of 63.7 % in the first half of the class and 57.8 % in the second half, with lower participation in theoretical courses and higher participation in practical subjects. Qualitative analysis revealed that absenteeism arises from interactions among structural conditions, relational experiences, pedagogical strategies, and personal agency. Three themes emerged: modes of engagement (responsive vs. non-responsive students), power and emotional climate, and relational misalignments. Findings suggest that attendance is a situated and strategic decision rather than a simple indicator of motivation or disengagement. Students weigh the academic, relational, and personal value of attending, while pedagogical design and classroom climate influence engagement. However, many determinants of attendance extend beyond instructors’ control. Understanding these interacting factors may support more realistic, equitable, and effective approaches to student engagement. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Processes of multi-system co-evolution: Insights from carbon capture and storage in Norway
Abstract: Net-zero solutions such as carbon capture and storage (CCS) require the creation of whole new clusters of innovations rather than “merely” a transition in existing systems or the diffusion of single technologies. While prior work highlights negative cross-system interdependencies (e.g., chicken and egg problems), this paper presents a theorization and an empirical study of the processes of multi-system co-evolution that contribute to the formation and development of multi-system complexes. To do this, a framework that integrates the concepts of a meta-rule, structural couplings (institutional, technological, organizational) and complementarity formation mechanisms — synchronization, amplification, and integration — is developed. The framework is illustrated through a qualitative case study of two Norwegian carbon capture and storage projects, Mongstad (2006–2013) and Longship (2016–), drawing on a broad range of media and documentary sources, including policy documents and funding agreements, and 20 interviews. The analysis shows how, in Longship, actors have sought to realize CCS by, for example, (i) fostering coordination and simultaneous co-development between CCS systems via contracts and standards, (ii) enabling CCS systems to expand and diffuse via a scalable ship-to-terminal transport design; and (iii) creating robustness in CCS multi-system complex by involving multiple actors, user sectors and business cases. This differed from Mongstad, where actors failed to prioritize the management of CCS system couplings and related uncertainties. The paper proposes how the processes of multi-system co-evolution can be conceptualized, and explores how actors may seek to deal with the issue of system interdependencies in sustainability transitions. © 2026 The Authors. Title: A two-stage diagnostic classification framework integrating heart rate variability and clinical features to identify recent suicide-related status in psychiatric inpatients
Abstract: Background Accurate identification of recent suicide-related risk remains challenging in psychiatric settings. Although clinical assessment is essential, objective physiological indicators such as heart rate variability (HRV) may provide complementary information. This study developed a two-stage machine-learning framework integrating clinical features and HRV to identify recent suicide-related status among psychiatric inpatients. Methods This retrospective study included 619 psychiatric inpatients who underwent standardized clinical assessment and 5-min resting HRV recording. Patients were classified as no suicidal ideation or behavior (no SI/SB; n = 416), suicidal ideation without suicidal behavior (SI; n = 137), or suicidal behavior (SB; n = 66) based on suicide-related information within the month before admission. Stage 1 classified patients with any recent SI/SB versus no SI/SB, and Stage 2 further classified recent SB versus SI among patients with suicide-related risk. Demographic-clinical, demographic-HRV, and combined feature sets were evaluated using multiple machine learning algorithms with repeated nested cross-validation. Results The combined feature set achieved the best overall performance. In Stage 1, the best combined model showed good discrimination (AUC = 0.894; AUPRC = 0.831). In Stage 2, the best combined model showed moderate performance (AUC = 0.778; AUPRC = 0.686). Depressive symptom severity, self-harm, past suicide attempt, younger age, diagnosis, and reduced vagally mediated HRV contributed to identifying any SI/SB, whereas past suicide attempt was the leading predictor of SB. Conclusions Integrating clinical and HRV features may support the identification and stratification of recent suicide-related status in psychiatric inpatients. HRV provided modest complementary information, particularly for broad SI/SB identification, but external prospective validation is required. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Satumanatpan S.; Pollnac R.
Title: Conservation attitudes among small-scale fishers: Governance implications from an industrialising coastal region in the Global South
Abstract: Small-scale fisheries support coastal livelihoods and food security across the Global South but increasingly operate in industrialising coastal environments marked by environmental degradation and governance complexity. Understanding fishers’ conservation attitudes is therefore important for context-responsive governance. This study examined 898 small-scale fishers in Rayong and Trat, Thailand, across three domains: psychological orientations toward nature, environmental knowledge and issue awareness, and perceived ecological change. Survey locations were classified as industrial or non-industrial according to their proximity to industrial facilities. Associations were examined between eight conservation-attitude measures and socio-cultural identity, socio-demographic and life-course factors, livelihood dependence, and spatial context. Spatial context and religious affiliation were each significantly associated with six measures. However, the two largest effect sizes among categorical comparisons were observed for spatial context, while religious differences were small. The spatial categories differed in selected value orientations and perceptions of changes in fish catch, whereas MPA awareness showed no statistically significant spatial difference. Gender and livelihood dependence showed limited, measure-specific associations, while life-course factors showed weak correlations. MPA awareness therefore did not necessarily vary in parallel with value orientations or perceptions of changes in fish catch. Integrating value orientations, policy awareness, and perceived ecological change helps explain why standardised approaches may not suit heterogeneous coastal communities. Governance responses should be based on local diagnosis rather than fixed policy packages and adapted to social–ecological and institutional conditions. Engaging with fishers’ experiential knowledge may help align conservation interventions with locally perceived environmental change in comparable industrialising coastal regions. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Satoh S.; Matsui H.
Title: Why are embodied social signals concentrated towards the rostral region? — The rostrum concentration principle
Abstract: Although frequently embodied, the relationship of animal social communication with body layout has rarely been investigated from a unified cognitive perspective. Across animal taxa, socially relevant signals, ranging from facial expressions and gaze to colouration and morphology, tend to be concentrated towards the anterior region of the body. Here, we propose the Rostrum Concentration (RC) principle, an empirically motivated hypothesis suggesting that social signals tend to evolve and become concentrated along the rostral body axis across bilaterian animals. We argue that this pattern does not reflect shared anatomical homology, but rather emerged from convergent interactions among body layouts, sensory organ concentrations, attentional biases and socio-ecological demands. Drawing on evidence from various taxa spanning from primates to insects, we suggest that the rostral concentration of social signals reflects the coevolution of signal production and receiver cognitive mechanisms. By reframing ‘facial’ communication as a broader organizational principle of the body layout, the RC principle reduces the risk of anthropomorphic interpretation and bridges research across behavioral ecology, cognitive science, sensory ecology and evolutionary biology. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Hussain Z.; Meng C.; Xia Y.
Author full names: Hussain, Zulfiqar (60703394200); Meng, Chen (60969510100); Xia, Yunjiao (60703197500)
Title: Judicial pathways to sustainable environmental development: Integrating jurisdictional oversight, legislative frameworks and adaptive governance
Abstract: Environmental degradation and climate-related risks continue to intensify, particularly in rapidly industrializing and urbanizing regions, while enforcement of environmental protection policies remains constrained by institutional, administrative, and governance barriers. These challenges weaken environmental compliance mechanisms and hinder progress toward sustainable development and social equity. This study examines the role of judicial institutions in strengthening environmental governance and fostering sustainable environmental development through enhanced policy implementation and institutional coordination. Drawing upon Adaptive Governance Theory and Transformative Governance perspectives, the study develops an integrated framework to investigate how judicial oversight interacts with environmental agencies and policy systems to address enforcement barriers. Empirical evidence was collected through a survey of 250 experts from higher courts and environmental agencies in Pakistan. Hypotheses were tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by an integrated Machine Learning (SEM-ML) approach to examine latent relationships and visualise institutional interactions. The findings reveal that governance and enforcement barriers significantly shape judicial engagement, explaining 89.2% of the variance in judicial involvement. Judicial oversight emerges as a critical mechanism for strengthening environmental governance, improving institutional accountability, and advancing socially equitable and sustainable policy outcomes. By linking judicial action with environmental policy implementation and adaptive governance processes, this study contributes a transdisciplinary perspective with relevance beyond Pakistan, offering practical and policy insights for strengthening environmental governance systems and supporting progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Author full names: Pavez-Fox, Melissa A. (56719717100); Schweinfurth, Manon K. (57188872950)
Title: Cooperation beyond the dyad: The emergence and stability of animal societies
Abstract: Cooperation is a fundamental driver of social evolution, yet we still lack an integrated framework explaining how interactions among individuals scale up to the formation and long-term stability of animal societies. Although major advances have been made, research has often focused on a narrow set of model taxa and on individual mechanisms in isolation, hindering a comparative understanding across species and theoretical approaches. In this review, we synthesise theoretical and empirical work to link the processes that initiate group living with those that sustain cooperation once groups are established. We first examine how cooperation promotes the emergence of social groups through byproduct benefits, mutualistic interactions, and population viscosity, highlighting their differing dependence on relatedness and their potential to operate simultaneously in nature. We then review mechanisms that maintain cooperation within established groups- including reciprocity, assortment and population structuring, division of labour, policing and punishment- and consider how their importance varies across socioecological contexts and levels of relatedness. Finally, we outline how emerging tools, such as long-term behavioural datasets, social networks, comparative analysis, simulations and experimental manipulations, can expand research beyond a small set of well-studied systems and support comparative tests to improve our understanding of the processes shaping cooperation and social complexity across diverse taxa. Title: Colonizing futures: A case study on the interplay between responsibilities and anticipation in energy policy-making processes in the Netherlands
Abstract: Actors use future perspectives as guidelines for action in practice, aiming to transform society into a 'better' future. In governing such transformation processes, decentralization and the inclusion of local stakeholders is often seen as part of the solution. The Dutch national government established a decentralized Regional Energy Strategy across 30 regions in a collaborative process involving government entities, water authorities, grid operators and societal stakeholders to develop energy transition strategies. To better understand decentralized governance dynamics within societal transformations, in this paper we examine the concept of anticipation in relation to responsibilities. The research question is: How does anticipation play a role in practised responsibilities in the organization of a just decentralized energy transition? To unravel anticipation, we distinguish the making of futures, acknowledging that every action we take has an impact, and the use of futures, referring to future expectations informing present actions. The use of futures can be both explicit, referring to certain targets, aims or imaginaries, and implicit, for example based on social or cultural assumptions. Studying documents and holding stakeholder interviews in one case study region, three policy process mechanisms were identified: (1) explicit futures were prioritized over implicit policy goals, (2) the lock-in of responsibilities via the implicit expected impact of certain responsibilities, (3) and the lock-in and colonization of futures via implicit use of futures. These findings highlight the need for deeper insights into the dynamic interplay between responsibilities and anticipation, especially into the role of explicit and implicit use of futures. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Shukla U.; Bajpai M.
Title: Clean energy financing and forest dependence: A socio-ecological perspective on the clean energy–forest degradation paradox in rural India
Abstract: The expansion of decentralized solar photovoltaic (PV) systems has become central to India's rural electrification and clean energy transition. However, in forest-fringe rural regions, solar adoption often occurs under conditions of livelihood insecurity, limited formal credit access, delayed subsidy support, and continued dependence on forest-based income. This paper conceptualizes the Clean Energy–Forest Degradation Paradox in the Indian context by examining how clean energy adoption may remain embedded within forest-dependent livelihood systems. Unlike generic accounts of renewable energy transition, the study highlights how the Indian manifestation of this paradox is institutionally and economically mediated through Forest Rights Act (FRA)-linked forest governance, non-timber forest product (NTFP)-based cash economies, and subsidy-driven but credit-constrained solar adoption pathways. Using a conceptual and theory-building approach, the paper synthesizes literature on rural solar PV adoption, sustainable livelihoods, forest dependence, energy stacking, and socio-ecological systems. Building on this synthesis, it proposes the Rural Energy–Environment–Livelihood Integration Model (REELIM–India), which integrates three subsystems: energy access, livelihood financing, and ecological–environmental outcomes. The framework proposes that solar PV adoption may reduce kerosene dependence and improve household welfare without necessarily eliminating biomass use, forest-based income dependence, or extractive livelihood practices. Under conditions of weak financing and livelihood vulnerability, forest-derived income may contribute to the purchase, repayment, maintenance, or replacement of solar systems, while continued forest-resource dependence may contribute to localized ecological degradation. The study contributes to energy justice and sustainability-transition literature by integrating technology adoption, livelihood financing, and socio-ecological feedbacks within an India-specific framework. It highlights the need for forest-sensitive clean-energy financing, livelihood diversification, and integrated energy–forest governance to support rural energy transitions that are both socially inclusive and ecologically sustainable. © 2026 International Energy Initiative

Authors: Pistocchi V.; Agneessens F.
Title: Mechanisms reinforcing and countering segregation: How existing friendship and dislike ties impact friendship homophily and dislike heterophily among Muslim and non-Muslim students in German schools
Abstract: Homophily is an important social force in many social networks. While homophilous tendencies among positive relations (such as friendship) and heterophilous tendencies in negative tie networks (such as dislike) have been extensively studied, less is known about how such tendencies might become stronger or weaker as a result of past experiences. Focusing on homophilous and heterophilous tendencies between non-Muslim and Muslim students in schools, this paper explores whether, in line with Intergroup Contact Theory, existing friendship connections with outgroup members will reduce their inclination to dislike outgroup peers compared to ingroup peers (i.e., reduce dislike heterophily), and reduce their preferences for ingroup friendships over outgroup friends (i.e., reduce friendship homophily). On the other hand, in line with Attribution Theory and Social Identity Theory, we propose that existing dislike connections with outgroup members are likely to strengthen dislike heterophilous tendencies and friendship homophilous tendencies, thus further reinforcing religious segregation in schools. To test these hypotheses, we apply Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs) to the friendship and dislike networks of 1678 Muslim and non-Muslim students (FIS data) across 17 German school settings where this religious divide is particularly salient. Contrary to what we expected based on Intergroup Contact Theory, our study shows that prior interreligious friendships do not weaken a person’s tendency for friendship homophily. However, it does seem to reduce heterophily in dislike, but only because it makes students more likely to dislike ingroup peers. On the other hand, prior interreligious dislike ties are found to amplify dislike to outgroups, while not affecting friendship homophily. Surprisingly, our study also shows that ingroup friendships reduce dislike for outgroup members. We explore the implications of the findings that friendship homophily appears unaffected by prior interreligious contacts, while dislike heterophily is strengthened by existing negative outgroup ties, but reduced by both outgroup and ingroup friendships. Title: Adverse childhood experiences and multidimensional frailty transitions in later life: evidence from three national aging cohorts
Abstract: Objectives: To examine whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with distinct multidimensional frailty patterns and transitions across frailty states in later life. Methods: We used harmonized longitudinal data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, the Health and Retirement Study, and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. The analytic sample included 10,643 adults aged ≥50 years who were free of multidimensional frailty at baseline. ACEs were assessed across eight childhood adversity domains and modeled as binary, categorical, and continuous exposures. Multidimensional frailty was defined as frailty in ≥2 physical, psychological, or social domains. Cox and multi-state models assessed incident frailty patterns and transitions, respectively, with adjustment for age, sex, and educational attainment. Results: Overall, 61.9% of participants reported at least one ACE, and 61.8% developed multidimensional frailty during follow-up. ACE exposure was associated with increased risks of all four incident frailty patterns, with hazard ratios ranging from 1.15 to 1.32. Cumulative ACE exposure was associated with higher risks across all four frailty patterns (3%-12% per additional ACE). In multi-state models, ACEs were associated with most transitions to multidimensional frailty (per-ACE HRs, 1.00–1.15). Sensitivity analyses were generally consistent, although associations were attenuated after excluding participants with frailty in any domain at baseline. Conclusions: ACEs were associated with a higher risk of multidimensional frailty in later life, including distinct frailty patterns and transitions across frailty states. These findings support a life-course approach to frailty prevention, with attention to early-life adversity and multidimensional vulnerability. © 2026

Title: Exposure to rising societal economic inequality reduces the misperception of racial economic equality
Abstract: People in the U.S. generally overestimate racial economic equality in contemporary society. A growing body of research suggests that the belief that the world is fair and just—i.e., belief in societal fairness—is a reliable predictor of the magnitude of these overestimates. The present work examined whether disrupting individuals' belief in the meritocratic opportunity structure in the U.S., via exposure to evidence of rising economic inequality, can subsequently reduce their tendency to overestimate contemporary racial economic equality. Across four studies (N = 4512), including one high-powered, pre-registered replication with a nationally representative sample, we found that reminding people of rising societal economic inequality, compared with control information, led them to generate more accurate estimates of the current state of racial income and wealth equality (Studies 1–4). Further, restoring individuals' faith in U.S. meritocracy by informing them that social mobility in the country is still possible, despite rising economic inequality, reduced the effect of rising inequality information on racial wealth gap perceptions (Studies 3 and 4). We discuss the implications of our findings for both theory and social policy. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Inc. Title: Multi-layer network analysis of deliberation in an online discussion platform: The case of Reddit
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-layer network model to study deliberation in online discussion platforms. The model comprises two layers: a discussion layer, which represents as a hierarchical tree the comment-to-comment replies within a given post, and an actor layer, which represents the actor-to-actor reply interactions. The interlayer links represent user-comment ownership. We use this network model to extend González-Bailón et al. (2010)’s foundational network analysis of argumentation and representation in discussion, by proposing two network metrics to measure the potential for deliberation in discussion threads. We also propose a new approach for identifying the boundaries that determine whether a given post is identified as deliberative, and for comparing the level of deliberation of collections of posts. We apply our new approach to a large Reddit dataset containing posts from 72 subreddits focused on different topics and demonstrate that our new metrics have construct validity in that observed differences in measured deliberation across categories of subreddits can be explained by the topics and purpose of the subreddits. While we find that some political subreddits exhibit high levels of deliberation thus indicating that online political talk can meet the prerequisites for deliberation, the level of deliberation in regional and sports subreddits was even higher. Analysis of the actor layer shows correlations between the deliberation measured on the discussion layer, and classical network metrics of the actor layer including degree distribution, assortativity, and the global clustering coefficient. These correlations reveal important insights into how the aggregate behaviour of users is related to deliberation. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Authors: Wang L.; Zhang Y.; Zhou M.; Ma Z.; Cheng X.
Title: Victim vs bystander: balancing a transgressor’s intention and apology in Chinese children’s forgiveness
Abstract: Forgiveness plays a crucial role in social functioning, particularly in collectivist cultures such as China, where relational orientation and group harmony are highly valued. Children’s forgiveness is shaped by multiple social cues, including the transgressor’s intention, apology, and the social perspective from which the transgression is evaluated. However, how these cues jointly influence forgiveness in a collectivist context remains underexplored. This study employed scenario-based experiments to investigate how Chinese children aged 4–6, assigned to either a victim or a bystander perspective, integrated transgressors’ intentions and apologies in forgiveness. Experiment 1 (N = 136) examined the effects of transgressor intention (intentional, unintentional) and social perspective (victim, bystander) on children’s forgiveness. Experiment 2 (N = 313) further explored the interaction between intention and apology (apologetic, unapologetic) across perspectives. The results showed that children were more likely to forgive unintentional and apologetic transgressors, and that bystanders showed greater forgiveness than victims; apologies moderated the influence of intention on children’s forgiveness; perspective further influenced how children balanced intention and apology in their forgiveness. Overall, this study represents an initial step toward understanding children’s forgiveness in a collectivist cultural context. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: Strategic Insights and Trends in Population Data Security for Urban Demography in Smart Cities
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study examines how scholarship on population data security has evolved within urban demography and smart city research. Using a scientometric and bibliometric design, the study analyzed Scopus-indexed publications from 2014 to 2023 with RStudio/Bibliometrix and CiteSpace to map publication growth, international collaboration, keyword trends, citation bursts, conceptual clusters, and thematic evolution. The findings show rapid publication growth, with a marked increase in 2023, and identify China, India, and the United States as major collaboration hubs. Topic mapping indicates a shift from general smart city and Internet of Things security concerns toward blockchain, machine learning, privacy by design, advanced analytics, and decentralized data governance. The conceptual structure reveals three interconnected knowledge clusters: information security governance, technical cybersecurity implementation, and urban infrastructure management. This study contributes to population and social studies by clarifying how data protection, demographic governance, and digital urban infrastructure intersect in smart city development. Rather than proposing a new framework, it synthesizes the intellectual structure of the field and offers evidence-based insights for strengthening privacy protection, institutional coordination, and adaptive cybersecurity governance in future smart cities. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research.
