Title: Gaming Motives and Impulsivity in Gaming Disorder: Additive or Interactive Effects?
Abstract: Background The Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution model suggests that impulsivity and specific gaming motives contribute to the development of gaming disorder (GD). However, it remains unclear whether these factors interact synergistically or operate independently. This study investigated the additive versus interactive effects of specific impulsivity facets, gaming motives, and behavior automatization on GD symptom severity. Method A sample of 377 adult gamers (338 male, 38 female, 1 diverse; age 18-58 years, M = 25.44, SD = 5.51) was assessed using the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale, Motives for Online Gaming Questionnaire, and the Assessment of Criteria of Specific Internet-use Disorders (ACSID-11) screening for GD symptom severity. Depression and anxiety were also assessed via self-report. We conducted hierarchical moderated regression analyses and exploratory cluster analysis. Results The non-planning impulsivity dimension significantly predicted GD symptom severity in the final models. Escape motive and behavior automatization emerged as robust predictors, explaining substantial additional variance. Contrary to initial hypotheses, no significant interaction effects were found. Depression and anxiety served as strong covariates across all models. Cluster analysis identified four distinct profiles: Unproblematic-Adaptive, Social-Recreational, Impulsive-Automatical, and Problematic-Clinical. Conclusion The findings support a predominantly additive model, indicating that impulsivity traits, maladaptive motives (specifically escape), and automatization contribute cumulatively to GD severity rather than through complex interactions. The identification of distinct gamer profiles suggests a need for personalized clinical interventions: the Impulsive-Automatical cluster may benefit from interventions targeting planning deficits and behavioral disinhibition, while the Problematic-Clinical cluster requires comprehensive treatment addressing comorbid affective psychopathology alongside gaming behavior. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Exploring the relationship between avoidance coping and cannabis use among black pregnant women
Abstract: Objectives This study examined the association between avoidance coping and prenatal cannabis use among Black pregnant women and explored whether perceived stress mediated this relationship. Methods: Data were drawn from the Biosocial Impact on Black Births (BIBB) study, a prospective cohort that enrolled Black pregnant women (18–45 years) with singleton pregnancies from prenatal clinics in Detroit (MI), Columbus (OH), and Orlando (FL) between 2017–2022. Participants completed a validated measure of the Revised Prenatal Coping Inventory for avoidance coping and self-reported ever use of cannabis during pregnancy. Logistic regression was used to adjust for maternal age, household income, education level, marital status, social support, gestational age at enrollment, and state of residence. Mediation analysis assessed perceived stress as a potential mediator using regression-based path models and the Sobel test. Results: Among 1,066 participants with cannabis use data, 21.3 % reported using cannabis during pregnancy. After adjustment, avoidance coping strategy was significantly associated with prenatal cannabis use, suggesting that individuals who rely more on avoidance coping are more likely to use cannabis during pregnancy. Compared to the lowest tertile, the odds of prenatal cannabis use were 1.80 (95 % CI: 1.19–2.76) in the second tertile and 2.45 (95 % CI: 1.61–3.76) in the third tertile of avoidance coping. Mediation analysis showed that perceived stress mediated this relationship (p ' 0.05), accounting for 36.4 % of the total effect. Conclusions: Findings underscore the importance of promoting adaptive coping strategies and addressing psychological stress in culturally responsive health interventions to reduce reliance on prenatal cannabis use. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: “Sailing Two Boats” the fragmented identity of working women and the hidden labor of infertility: a qualitative analysis
Source title: Journal of Psychosomatic Obstetrics and Gynecology
Abstract: Objective: To explore how professional women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART) experience and manage conflicts between treatment demands and professional identity; and to identify ways healthcare professionals can support them. Methods: Following COREQ guidelines, semi-structured, in-depth interviews were conducted with 18 professional women undergoing ART in a tertiary care hospital. Reflexive Thematic Analysis bolstered by interdisciplinary investigator triangulation (clinical and basic science) ensured thematic confirmability. Results: Analysis revealed Gendered Occupational Asymmetry (female occupational burden regardless of clinical aetiology), the Insider Paradox (the role reversal for healthcare professionals) and the Workplace Panopticon (constant self-surveillance to preserve professional authority). Interestingly, work simultaneously often acted as a Sanctuary of Competence, providing psychological respite. Finally, narratives exposed an Existential Rumination (mourning past personal-professional decisions) and permanent temporal career stalling. These themes were further mapped onto a ‘A Day in the Life’ structural framework to illustrate compounding daily burdens. Conclusions: Current clinical lifestyle directives inadequately account for the rigid psycho-socioeconomic structures governing professional women. Based on identified themes, we propose targeted measures for healthcare professionals to deliver patient-centric care by integrating occupational awareness and identity-sensitive counselling into routine ART practice, thereby potentially reducing distress and improving treatment experience. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A systematic review of electrophysiological markers of reward processing in addiction
Abstract: Prevalence of addictive behaviors is commonly associated with alterations in the brain’s reward circuitry, leading to the upholding of a maladaptive pattern of reward-seeking behavior despite aversive consequences. The main objective of this systematic review was to provide a broad overview of the literature on electrophysiological correlates of anticipation and reward processing in addiction, including substance use disorders (SUD), as well as behavioral addictions. Reward processing in addiction has been investigated using electroencephalography (EEG) studies employing a cue-reward experimental design, with event-related potentials (ERPs) as the outcome measure. Relevant studies were identified by searching scientific databases: PubMed, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus in April 2026. The terms used to search the databases covered EEG/ERP markers of reward processing in substance and behavioral addictions. The inclusion criteria comprised peer-reviewed ERP studies employing a cue-reward paradigm in adults with addictive behaviors and healthy controls, published in English between 2000 and 2026. Forty-two studies were reviewed (SUD: 23; behavioral addictions: 19). Reward anticipation was indexed by cue-P300, contingent negative variation (CNV), and stimulus-preceding negativity (SPN). Reward processing was examined in distinct early (feedback-related negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (RewP)) and late (P300 and late positive potential (LPP)) reward outcome phases. Altered neural responses were observed across multiple stages of reward processing in both substance and behavioral addictions, consistent with disruptions in the generation, evaluation, and updating of reward expectations. Despite these convergent patterns, methodological heterogeneity limits the strength of current conclusions and highlights the need for greater standardization in future research. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Understanding social-cognitive-norm mechanisms driving disinformation verification among Indonesian young adults on social media
Abstract: This research aimed to develop an integrated theoretical model to explain the factors influencing verification behavior regarding social media disinformation among young adults in Indonesia. The model combined the Stimulus–Organism–Response (SOR) framework with the Norm Activation Model (NAM) and the Social Identity Theory (SIT) to examine the collective effects of social, cognitive, and moral processes in shaping responsible information behavior. An online cross-sectional survey was conducted with 746 respondents, who actively used social networking sites to obtain and share information. The results showed that verification behavior was primarily driven by information skepticism and personal norms, emphasizing the importance of critical thinking and moral obligation for responsible engagement. In the Organism stage, awareness of fake information, perceived deception, and critical consumption enhanced moral sensitivity and analytical reasoning. At the social level, factors such as collective memory, parasocial interaction, and status-seeking were reported to be significant identity-based stimuli in shaping cognitive and moral responses, with gender found to moderate these effects. Thematic analysis suggested that most young adults verified information through cross-checking and peer consultation, but were influenced by social validation. Theoretically, this research contributed to disinformation research by framing verification as a cognitive-normative process rather than a reactive behavior. Different initiatives were recommended by educational institutions, governmental bodies, and community organizations to strengthen moral reasoning, digital literacy, and civic responsibility in combating disinformation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Street view video for urban sensing: Potential for measuring urban vitality
Abstract: Urban vitality is a key quality of the livability and attractiveness of a city, with street-level social dynamics recognized as a central representation. However, existing approaches to capturing such dynamics, primarily through pedestrian volume, rely on static imagery, location-based proxies, or custom sensors. Such methods are typically discontinuous, limited in spatio-temporal resolution, costly, and overlook the role of sound in shaping environments. To address these gaps, this study explores the feasibility of using Street View Video (SVV), a novel, promising, yet under-utilized data source, for capturing street-level dynamics. Leveraging widely available crowdsourced city tour videos as a representative form of SVV, we develop an automated and scalable framework for high-precision geo-localization of SVV by extracting textual and depth information. Further, we propose a visual–auditory pipeline that integrates continuous pedestrian activity and sound environments as complementary dimensions that reveal street-level social dynamics. Using Melbourne as a case study, we identified 892 high-quality and geolocatable videos totaling over 542 h and achieved an accuracy of 77% for geo-localization. We generated spatio-temporal maps that not only reproduced well-studied pedestrian volume patterns, but also previously neglected aspects, including human actions (walking, standing, sitting), sound intensity, and sound types (speech, music, vehicle). Correlation and quadrant analyses further explored the relationships among these vitality dimensions, revealing distinctive street characteristics and highlighting the limitations of conventional road classifications. Title: Changes in neural activation and in functional connectivity during affective memory recall after six months of psychotherapy: An fMRI study of individuals with depression
Abstract: Background While psychotherapy is established as an overall effective treatment of depression, a significant proportion of patients do not achieve adequate response. Understanding the neurobiological mechanisms underlying psychotherapeutic change may inform intervention optimization. This study examined changes in neural processing of personally relevant affective memory in individuals with depression following psychodynamic psychotherapy. Methods Twenty-five individuals with depression and 28 healthy controls underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanning at baseline and after six months. Depressed participants received weekly psychodynamic psychotherapy. During fMRI, participants recalled idiosyncratically meaningful affective memories cued by pictorial cues. Region-of-interest analyses examined therapy-related changes in neural activation across areas involved in emotion and memory processing, and social cognition. Seed-to-voxel analyses assessed changes in functional connectivity between those areas. Results Following six months of psychodynamic psychotherapy, depressed individuals showed significantly increased activation in the right temporoparietal junction (TPJ) when recalling personally relevant affective memories compared to controls. Functional connectivity analyses revealed decreased coupling between bilateral amygdala and bilateral TPJ in the depressed group post-treatment. Conclusions Psychodynamic psychotherapy may increase neural processing in regions supporting mentalizing and the evaluation of personally relevant relational memories. Decreased amygdala-TPJ connectivity suggests reduced automatic affective response during affective memory processing. Title: Is honesty the best policy? Why people prefer false empathy over truthful unempathy
Abstract: Literature of person perception suggests the primacy of morality over sociability in interactions. While theories of emotion highlight the importance of adhering to socially acceptable display rules, a contentious debate surrounds whether individuals prioritize moral or sociable communication of emotions. We investigated how people perceive and respond to others who falsely communicate empathic versus truthfully communicate unempathic emotions related to others' (mis)fortunes. Across five preregistered studies (N = 1305), we examined participants' perceptions (sociability, morality, intent) and behavioral responses in a resource-allocation task using multiple paradigms (vignette, retrospective recall, and real-time interaction) and contexts (e.g., promotion, education, and lottery scenarios). Consistently, participants perceived targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions as lower on morality but higher on sociability and having more positive intent than those who truthfully communicated unempathic emotions. Moreover, despite the mixed findings regarding overall impressions, participants were consistently more willing to interact with and allocate resources to targets who falsely communicated empathic emotions. This preference was primarily driven by perceived sociability attributed to the targets. Together, these findings suggest that false empathic communication is favored over truthful unempathic communication, highlighting the relative primacy of sociability (and perceived intent) over morality in shaping responses to emotional communication in the context of others' (mis)fortunes. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Factors contributing to the dropout of undergraduate nursing curricula according to the year of attendance: A mixed-methods systematic review
Abstract: Background: The global nursing shortage poses critical challenges for healthcare systems. Understanding nursing student dropout, particularly which factors contribute to this process and when they emerge during the curriculum, is crucial for developing timely and effective retention strategies that support workforce sustainability. Despite growing concern, no systematic reviews have examined the reasons for dropout through a time-sensitive approach. Aim: To understand the factors contributing to dropout from undergraduate nursing curricula with specific attention to the year of attendance. Design: A mixed-methods systematic review was conducted following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology, adopting a convergent segregated approach. Methods: Data Sources: PubMed, CINAHL, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and Scopus databases were searched from October 2023 to March 2025, according to PRISMA guidelines, without date restrictions. Results: Sixteen articles were included. Thirteen examined early dropout (588 students), mainly during the first year, while three explored addressed late dropout (37 students, third-fourth year). Across 36 primary findings, six overarching factors emerged, supported by qualitative and quantitative evidence: individual, lack of preparedness, unmet student expectations, negative emotional experiences, structural characteristics of the course, and political/professional. Negative emotional experiences and structural characteristics of the course were the most consistent contributors to both early and late dropout. Conversely, factors specific to the early years included family commitments, financial difficulties, low self-efficacy or self-esteem, poor academic performance, unmet expectations regarding clinical placements, course content and workload, restricted social life, and commuting distance. Conclusions: The six identified factors confirm the multifaceted nature of dropout, offering insights to design tailored, time-specific strategies and structural reforms. Rationalising course curricula and strengthening tutor support may enhance engagement and reduce the theory-practice gap. Reinforced orientation could support students' evolving needs, fostering retention and transition to the profession. Future research should explore longitudinal predictors of dropout, particularly the roles of tutorial support and clinical placements. © 2026 The Authors

Title: A systematic multi-criteria risk assessment modelling for safety–critical emergency shipboard operations
Abstract: Safety-critical shipboard operations involve complex socio-technical interactions where rapid and well-informed decisions are essential to prevent cascading failures, injuries, and environmental damage. Conventional occupational risk assessment approaches, such as the Fine–Kinney method, provide structured hazard evaluation but remain limited in incorporating expert-driven prioritization and multi-dimensional factors. This study proposes a hybrid multi-criteria risk assessment framework integrating the Fine–Kinney method with the Best–Worst Method (BWM) and the Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), enhanced by fuzzy logic to address uncertainty in expert-based evaluations. Title: Evac‑cast: an interpretable machine‑learning framework for evacuation prediction across hurricanes and wildfires
Abstract: Evacuation is one of the most decisive protective actions in natural hazards, yet agencies still lack fast, accurate, and transparent tools for predicting the number of residents who will evacuate. This study introduces Evac‑Cast, an interpretable machine‑learning framework that predicts tract‑level evacuation rates and reveals their underlying drivers by fusing four routinely available data dimensions, namely, hazard intensity, community vulnerability, evacuation readiness, and the built environment. Gradient‑boosted models are trained on anonymized mobility traces, census data, and hazard information from two U.S. hurricanes (Hurricane Ian in 2022 and Hurricane Milton in 2024), and two wildfires (the Kincade Fire in 2019 and the Palisades–Eaton Fires in 2025) and perform well in retrospective held-out evaluation. Crucially, the models achieve this performance without explicit psychosocial variables, indicating that macro‑level proxies, such as income, tenure status, and hazard proximity, implicitly encode much of the behavioral signal traditionally captured through time‑consuming surveys. Model interpretation further reveals a stable hierarchy across the studied hurricane and wildfire events, in which hazard intensity is the dominant driver of evacuation rates, followed by community vulnerability, built environment, and evacuation readiness factors. Title: The gap of psychological perspective in high-containment lab training — An exploratory systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: High-containment laboratories (HCLs) depend on sustained human performance to maintain biosafety and biosecurity, yet training primarily emphasizes technical competence and regulatory compliance while giving limited attention to human factors. We conducted an exploratory systematic review and meta -analysis to examine how laboratory personnel (LP) psychology can inform HCL training. Prevalence and odds ratios were pooled using random-effects meta -analysis (REML with Knapp–Hartung adjustment). Sixty-five studies met the inclusion criteria (38 HCL training; 27 psychology). Training literature was dominated by institution-specific programs, with limited international harmonization, inconsistent certification, infrequent incident-reporting frameworks, and minimal integration of psychological human factors. Leadership emerged as a recurring organizational factor influencing safety and well-being. Pooled prevalence estimates were 73% for stress (95% CI 51–88%), 45% for depression (27–65%), 44% for anxiety (22–68%), and 56% for burnout (31–78%). Title: Paid attention: Mapping political and news advertising strategies on social media across Europe
Abstract: We investigate the structure and dynamics of paid visibility on social media platforms by analyzing the advertising behavior of political parties and news outlets across six European countries (France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, and the United Kingdom) from 2019 to 2024. (2) Posts exposure grows rapidly with low levels of advertising expenditure but saturates beyond moderate thresholds, suggesting the presence of bounded attention markets. (3) Advertising spending is positively associated with overall page performance. Furthermore, when addressing the challenging task of comparing paid and organic visibility, we observe a positive increase in the spending coefficient, particularly for political parties, which consistently generate more impressions than news pages. These results offer empirical evidence that visibility operates as a platform-mediated market, shaped by algorithmic constraints, economic incentives, and strategic competition. Title: Stakeholder attention to advanced air mobility reveals worldwide disparities
Abstract: Advanced air mobility (AAM) has garnered escalating attention from academia, government, business, and the general public. Previous studies tended to investigate these main stakeholders separately, failing to identify their various attentions, attitudes and focus areas. This research employs bibliometric and social media large language model (LLM) text mining methods to explore the perspectives of main stakeholders on AAM for a decade (2015-2024), with approximately 300,000 texts in total. Our findings show a consistent rise in text volume across all key stakeholders, with government stakeholders demonstrating the fastest growth rate. Globally, the text sentiment is predominantly either positive or neutral, with negative sentiment being the least prevalent. The topic analysis reveals stakeholders have heterogeneous priorities, with businesses and governments tending to emphasize AAM-related infrastructure, the general public focusing more on end-user experiences and air mobility infrastructure and integration, while academia concentrating on aerodynamics and safety concerns. This research seeks to inform actionable policy formulation and air-transport planning, thereby facilitating AAM integration into urban and regional transportation systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Strengthening collective identity and psychosocial adaptation: A career intervention with MENA migrant women in Türkiye
Abstract: Migration constitutes a profound intercultural transition in which individuals renegotiate identity, belonging, and perceptions of group value within new social contexts. For migrant women, these processes are further shaped by gendered inequalities and constrained access to opportunity. Drawing on social identity and empowerment perspectives, this mixed-methods longitudinal study examined whether a short-term, skill-based psychosocial career intervention could reshape group-based beliefs associated with a shared migrant identity among university-educated MENA migrant women living in Türkiye. Across two cohorts ( N = 21), participants completed the Individual–Group Belief Inventory at pre-test, post-test, and three-month follow-up, complemented by a reflection-based focus group. Quantitative findings revealed a selective pattern of change: beliefs related to vulnerability, injustice, distrust, and helplessness remained largely stable, whereas superiority beliefs—conceptualized as perceptions of collective capability, value, and contribution—increased significantly following the intervention and remained elevated at follow-up. Qualitative analyses indicated that these changes were grounded in personal empowerment, collective solidarity, and gendered expressions of group pride, rather than in intergroup hostility or dominance. Together, the findings demonstrate that empowerment-oriented psychosocial interventions can selectively strengthen internal components of collective identity that function as resources for intercultural adaptation and agency, even when broader structural constraints remain unchanged. Title: Predicting sparse OD flows of perishable agricultural products in logistics and transportation networks: a socioeconomic-enhanced spatiotemporal graph model
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: Accurate origin–destination (OD) prediction for perishable agricultural products (PAP) is crucial for enhancing the resilience of the agricultural supply chain and improving social welfare. However, most existing studies focus on passenger or general freight OD prediction, while little attention has been given to PAP. Compared with traditional OD prediction tasks, PAP freight forecasting faces unique challenges: (1) PAP transport has strong time sensitivity, frequent disturbances, nonlinear decay, and high value loss. The related factors are complex and change over time. (2) OD flow data are highly sparse and follow a long-tail distribution, making it difficult to capture complex spatiotemporal patterns effectively. To address these issues, this study proposes a Decoupled Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network (DST-GNN) model. It integrates PAP freight big data with regional, socioeconomic, and dynamic disturbance features. The model has two main modules: spatiotemporal feature extraction and multi-task prediction. The first module uses a multi-graph learning mechanism to describe inter-city spatial interactions and adaptive spatial dependencies. A Transformer-based encoder captures long-term temporal dependencies from multi-source dynamic data, including historical flows, weather, and holidays. The second module divides the prediction into two tasks: classifying OD activity and regressing flow magnitude. A composite objective function combining mean squared error, cross-entropy classification loss, Focal Loss, and Tweedie loss is designed to jointly optimize point prediction accuracy, OD activity identification, class-imbalance mitigation, and probabilistic distribution fitting. This objective helps alleviate data sparsity, zero inflation, and long-tail effects, improving model robustness and generalization. Experiments on PAP freight data from 333 Chinese cities show that the proposed method outperforms mainstream baselines across four product categories. Further ablation and SHAP-based interpretability analyses confirm the effectiveness of key modules and highlight the importance of macroeconomic and infrastructure factors for prediction accuracy. Title: Psychometric evaluation of a child adaptation of the Tromsø Social Intelligence Scale in an Italian primary school sample
Abstract: Social intelligence is a multidimensional construct that plays a central role in children's peer relationships and school adjustment, yet validated measures for primary school children remain scarce. The present study examined the psychometric properties of a child-adapted version of the Tromsø Social Intelligence Scale (TSIS-kids) in an Italian sample of 669 primary school children aged 7 to 12 years. Confirmatory factor analyses indicated that a refined 20-item version excluding TSIS05r provided a more parsimonious and psychometrically cleaner solution while preserving the multidimensional structure of the scale. Reliability was satisfactory for Social Information Processing and Social Skills, and somewhat lower for Social Awareness. Convergent validity with trait emotional intelligence was supported by positive and moderate associations, strongest for the total TSIS-kids score and Social Skills. Measurement invariance across sex and grade was also supported, and percentile-based descriptive norms and preliminary percentile-based reference were derived. Overall, the findings support the TSIS-kids as a promising measure of social intelligence in primary school children, while highlighting the importance of developmentally appropriate wording in childhood assessment. Title: Protected areas: questioning the development-conservation system. A socio-political-economic and ecological framework for a bottom-up approach
Abstract: Despite repeated calls for urgent action to address biodiversity loss, the resounding verdict is that most conservation policies, in particular their main policy measure, Protected Areas (PAs), have failed to halt environmental degradation and achieve meaningful social outcomes. Yet, the international community has committed to extending PA coverage to 30% of the planet by 2030, and with one-third of the Global South's population already living in or near a PA, this proportion is set to become a majority. In view of this, the current practice, which is supposed to promote sustainable development but is problematic, consists of juxtaposing socioeconomic policies and environmental policies, often regarded as mutually antagonistic, without considering a comprehensive view of governance issues. This article reviews the impact of PAs on biodiversity and the populations’ living conditions and identifies the knowledge gaps, before looking into why biodiversity conservation has been prioritised, inconclusively, to the detriment of local sociopolitical and economic dynamics and why the narrow principle of ‘inclusive governance’, more words than deeds, falls far short of the mark. The traditional approach, which is blind to the fact that conservation and development objectives are embedded within power relations and a broader sociopolitical dynamic, dominated by extractivist and capitalist logic, should be challenged. We propose a novel analytical framework with an operational methodological approach grounded in critical political ecology in order to take a bottom-up approach rooted in a territory and improve our understanding of the complex interactions between local socioecological, socioeconomic and sociopolitical concerns. Title: Who perceives access? Disparities in satisfaction with public transport availability and associations with perceived accessibility in the Netherlands
Abstract: Accessible public transport is important for meeting daily mobility needs and supporting activity participation, particularly among vulnerable groups. Linear regression models were conducted to examine these relationships using empirical data collected from a sample of 3378 respondents from the Netherlands. Our findings indicate that frequency of public transport use moderates the association between satisfaction with public transport availability and overall perceived accessibility, with frequent public transport users reporting higher overall accessibility with higher levels of satisfaction with public transport availability. Additionally, low-income individuals, having mobility restrictions and residing in rural areas are negatively associated with satisfaction with public transport availability and overall perceived accessibility. These associations are especially pronounced among low-income occasional users, who report lower levels of satisfaction with public transport availability. Title: Psychological capital among undergraduate nursing students: A systematic review and meta-analysis of levels and correlates
Abstract: Aims: To synthesize instrument-specific levels of psychological capital (PsyCap) among undergraduate nursing students and examine its correlates and preliminary evidence concerning potential mediating pathways. Design: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Data sources: CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PubMed, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, CNKI, and WanFang Data were searched for studies published from January 2000 to June 2026. Methods: Random-effects meta-analyses were used to estimate instrument-specific pooled PsyCap scores and correlation coefficients. Subgroup analyses and exploratory univariable meta-regression were conducted to examine between-study heterogeneity. An exploratory two-stage meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) analysis was conducted when sufficiently comparable correlation data were available. Results: Thirty-four studies involving 15,705 nursing students were included. The pooled item-level mean was 4.235 for the Psychological Capital Questionnaire (PCQ; k = 13; 95% CI: 4.080–4.390; I2 = 98.80%) and 4.459 for the Positive Psychological Capital Questionnaire (PPQ; k = 13; 95% CI: 4.252–4.667; I2 = 99.42%). PsyCap was positively associated with professional identity, academic engagement, and self-directed learning, and negatively associated with stress-related and maladaptive outcomes. Exploratory meta-regression identified study-level female composition as a potential source of heterogeneity, although substantial residual heterogeneity remained. Conclusions: PsyCap was consistently associated with psychological and academic outcomes among undergraduate nursing students, although pooled levels varied substantially across studies and measurement instruments. Title: Stage- and context-dependent modulation of fear memory by oxytocin: Neurobiological mechanisms and implications for PTSD
Abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a multifactorial psychiatric condition characterized by re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and disturbances in social and emotional functioning. Within this broader clinical syndrome, persistent traumatic memories and excessive fear generalization represent important mechanistic and therapeutic domains. Despite substantial advances in understanding its neurobiological basis, current treatments remain suboptimal, with limited efficacy and high dropout rates. The neuropeptide oxytocin (OXT), a key modulator of social behavior, stress regulation, and memory, has been investigated as a potential therapeutic target. Accumulating evidence indicates that severe trauma profoundly disrupts endogenous OXTergic signaling, whereas pharmacological studies suggest that exogenous OXT can modulate fear-memory processing through region-, dose-, route-, and context-dependent mechanisms. Evidence from fear-conditioning indicates that across acquisition, consolidation, retrieval, reconsolidation, and extinction, the direction of OXT’s effects is heterogeneous rather than uniformly anxiolytic and pro-extinction. OXT may influence threat discrimination, fear expression, memory updating, and extinction by modulating specific neural circuits and neurochemical pathways. However, most preclinical models capture selected dimensions of PTSD rather than the full clinical disorder. Human studies further indicate that intranasal OXT can modulate neural, physiological, and social-cognitive processes relevant to PTSD, although evidence for consistent clinical efficacy remains limited and heterogeneous. This review synthesizes current findings on OXT and its synthetic analogs within a stage- and context-dependent framework to better investigate their heterogeneous effects and assess their potential relevance and translational limitations in PTSD. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Chowdhury S.A.
Title: The promise and paradox of a just energy transition in Bangladesh: Governance deficits, justice gaps, and the architecture of an equitable transition
Abstract: Bangladesh confronts an acute and multi-dimensional tension between formal commitments to clean energy transformation and the entrenched structural realities of a fossil-fuel-dependent economy. This paper offers a theoretically grounded and empirically situated analysis of Bangladesh's just energy transition (JET) deficit, conceptualizing the gap between the state's declared ambition of 100% renewable energy by 2050 and an energy system in which fossil fuels account for over 85% of electricity generation and renewables contribute less than 3% of total supply. Drawing on secondary data, policy documents, and a four-pillar energy justice framework encompassing recognition, procedural, distributional, and remedial justice, the study systematically interrogates the structural, institutional, financial, and normative barriers that constitute and reproduce this deficit. The paper advances three original contributions: it theorizes Bangladesh's transition condition as a ‘compulsory transition trap’ in which resource depletion and international trade conditionality drive energy system change in the absence of governance capacity and social protection mechanisms; it applies a disaggregated justice audit to demonstrate systemic failures across all four justice dimensions; and it documents an emerging contradiction between the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and Bangladesh's readymade garment (RMG) sector's energy supply constraints, with implications for 4.4 million workers. The paper evaluates Bangladesh's exclusion from the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP) architecture and develops evidence-informed policy recommendations addressing both the pace and equity architecture of transition. The analysis demonstrates that Bangladesh's transition deficit is not primarily technological but reflects deeper failures of governance, institutional coordination, climate finance access, and political inclusion. © 2026 International Energy Initiative

Title: Revealed preferences of residential decarbonization: Real estate agents and marketing sustainability amenities

Title: Can ecological compensation encourage participation? The heterogeneous patterns of ecological reserve policies and villagers' participation in public governance
Abstract: Although considerable attention has been devoted to the pollution-control effects and economic costs of environmental regulation, much less is known about its political consequences, particularly whether it encourages public participation in governance. Mechanism analysis indicates that, relative to ERN, ERC promotes villagers' participation by strengthening trust in local government and fostering decision-making preferences characterized by lower risk aversion and a longer time horizon. The heterogeneity analysis further shows that ERC has a significant positive effect among residents and farmers but no significant effect among migrants or non-farmers. By contrast, ERN significantly reduces PPG among residents and also discourages participation among both farmers and non-farmers, while its negative effect is concentrated among villagers with higher perceived levels of local governance. These findings suggest that the design of ecological reserve policies should give greater consideration to protecting villagers' economic interests, strengthening trust in local government, and cultivating decision-making orientations that support sustained and proactive participation in public governance. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Visual perspective-taking and image-like representations: we can see it

Title: Low Self-Control and Its Relationship to Deviant Behavior Among Incarcerated Women in Jordan

Abstract: This study investigates the relationship between low self-control and deviant behavior among incarcerated women, focusing on negative emotions, fear of victimization, exposure to violence, and demographic factors. Title: Collaboration fails to promote sharing behavior but both collaborative and parallel play boost friendship in young children aged 4 to 6
Abstract: Prosocial behaviors like collaboration and sharing are key to early childhood development. This study examined how collaboration, sex, and friendship influence sharing and perceived friendship among 48 dyads (96 children) aged 4–6. Participants were recruited from primary schools and paired into same-sex or cross-sex dyads. They were randomly assigned to either a collaborative or parallel play condition involving a cheese board game. In the collaborative condition, children worked together on one board, whereas in the parallel condition, they played individually on separate boards. After the game, children faced unequal rewards hidden under cups—one child received three candies (“lucky”), the other one candy (“unlucky”). Children then had the opportunity to share their rewards during a one-minute period without adult supervision. Friendship levels were assessed using a visual scale before and after the game. Children shared rarely, and contrary to our predictions, sharing behavior was not affected by collaboration, sex, dyad composition, or friendship level. However, both collaborative and parallel play led to increases in friendship ratings, suggesting that engaging in a shared activity and spending time with a peer may be associated with more positive evaluations of the relationship. No differences emerged between collaborative and parallel play in terms of this increase. Title: Growing appetites: the impact of vegetable-rich school meals on child nutrition, cognition, and well-being
Abstract: Typical lunch meals consumed by Dutch children fall short of national dietary guidelines. The average vegetable intake during lunch is around 8 g, contributing to inadequate overall vegetable consumption in over half of children under 12. A school-based lunch programme offering vegetable-rich meals may improve vegetable intake and potentially lead to other benefits. In the current controlled quasi-experimental study, such programme was assessed. Children aged 7-13 years at three primary schools received lunch on 3 school days per week, while three other schools served as controls. Pre- and post-intervention assessments measured cognition, well-being, food neophobia, food literacy, and skin carotenoid status using the Veggie Meter (VM). Post intervention, meal liking was assessed. 2 x 2 mixed ANOVAs were run (group x time). No significant differences were observed between groups and over time for any of the variables, but a decrease in food neophobia over time in the control group, but not in the intervention group, was observed. Exploratory analyses revealed positive associations between VM score and well-being, and between meal liking and VM score, while meal liking was negatively associated with food neophobia. Title: Impacts of decarbonisation policies on transport-poor households in Austria and possible mitigation strategies
Abstract: Decarbonising the transport sector is a critical goal for achieving climate neutrality, yet the disproportionate impacts of climate policies on transport-poor households are often overlooked. This study examines the effects of transport-related climate policies in Austria on transport-poor households with a focus on affordability. Using a combination of macro-level backcasting simulations and micro-level assessments, the research identifies policy measures necessary to achieve full decarbonisation of passenger transport by 2040 while ensuring social equity. Key findings reveal that approximately 7% of Austrian households experience transport poverty, characterised by high mobility costs and limited access to alternatives. Scenarios demonstrate significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and mobility expenditures but highlight the need for compensatory measures to mitigate adverse effects on these households. Recommendations include expanding public transport services, reducing fares, and providing financial support to ensure a fair transition to sustainable mobility. Title: Using social license to operate to understand social outcomes in ethnic tourism communities: Lessons from Yotkan Ancient City, China
Abstract: Tourism development in ethnic minority communities can generate both benefits and disruptions, yet the management of negative social impacts remains underexplored. This paper uses the Social License to Operate (SLO) framework to understand social outcomes of tourism projects, taking the Yotkan Ancient City, China, as a case study. Drawing on Thomson and Boutilier's (2011) model, we evaluate three SLO dimensions (legitimacy, credibility, and trust) through semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and field observations. The results show that the developer has achieved legitimacy, in terms of improved sanitation, roads, and local employment, but lacks credibility due to inconsistent information, rigid compensation, and insufficient consideration of local tradition. Trust, particularly among vulnerable groups, remains unestablished. The community's overall SLO level currently resides between acceptance and approval. Although tourism development has visibly improved the living conditions of the local community, critical local values, needs, and expectations remain insufficiently addressed. Rather than tailor planning to local cultural dynamics, the development approach relied on standard regional templates, resulting in a misalignment with traditional Ayiwang architectural features, daily living habits, and the distinct needs of vulnerable groups such as seniors and women. Furthermore, impact history is found to be a critical but under-theorized factor shaping trust. By extending the SLO framework from extractive industries to “socially friendly” ethnic tourism in a non-Western, state-led context, this paper offers actionable strategies for equitable benefit-sharing, culturally respectful design, and inclusive governance. © 2026

Title: Suboptimal but intact integration of reward information during perceptual decision-making in autism
Abstract: Alterations in reward processing have been proposed as a contributing factor to social and communication symptoms in autism. However, the nature of these alterations remains unclear, and it is debated whether autism is characterized by reduced sensitivity to reward. Evidence for general reduced reward processing in autism primarily comes from neurobiological studies, yet it remains uncertain how these findings translate to autistic behavior. A key challenge in addressing this question lies in the quantitative assessment of behavioral responses to reward. Here, we addressed this issue by investigating the integration of monetary reward information into behavior through the framework of Bayesian perceptual decision-making, enabling a quantitative evaluation of the direct contribution of reward to decision-making. Autistic (n = 32) and non-autistic (n = 48) participants performed an orientation categorization task, while the monetary reward given per correct answer varied across categories. Using signal-detection theory, we estimated decision boundaries while accounting for sensory uncertainty and prior expectation. Both groups comprehended the reward contingencies similarly and showed comparable perceptual sensitivity. Importantly, autistic individuals adjusted their decision boundaries in response to monetary reward in a suboptimal yet similar manner to that of non-autistic individuals. Integration of monetary reward during perceptual decision-making is intact in autism. These findings challenge the view of general reduced reward processing in autism and are inconsistent with accounts proposing enhanced rationality in autism. © 2026

Authors: Angın E.; Durak Batıgün A.
Title: Predicting social media addiction symptoms: The role of vulnerable narcissism and depressive affect
Abstract: Social media addiction (SMA) symptoms are increasingly linked to personality vulnerabilities, yet the specific factors contributing to these symptoms remain poorly understood. Grounded in the I-PACE framework, the present study examined the associations between vulnerable narcissism, depressive symptoms, social comparison, and SMA symptoms in a community adult sample recruited during the COVID-19 pandemic (N = 456; 69.5% female; M age = 31.97, SD = 13.27; age range: 18–64). A single direct entry regression analysis revealed that the model accounted for 39.8% of the variance in SMA symptoms (Adjusted R 2 = 0.390, F (6, 449) = 49.47, p < .001). Vulnerable narcissism emerged as the strongest predictor (β = 0.397, p < .001), followed by age, depressive symptoms, and social comparison. Sex and social-emotional loneliness were not significantly associated with SMA symptoms. These findings suggest that vulnerable narcissism represents a robust risk factor for problematic social media use, with depressive affect and diminished social standing as additional contributors. Clinical assessment of SMA may benefit from screening for narcissistic vulnerability and depressive symptomatology as interrelated factors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Optimizing multi-agent workflows via heterogeneous graph learning
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have shown promise for complex task solving, yet effective workflow design remains challenging due to poor scalability, limited use of historical context, and insufficient modeling of agent tool interactions in existing methods. To address these limitations, we propose Heterogeneous Graph-based workFlow optimization (HeGFlow), which models agents, tools, and the execution topology between agents and tools as interconnected graph components, transforming the design of MAS workflow into a heterogeneous graph adjacency matrix optimization problem. To efficiently explore the vast search space, HeGFlow introduces a two-stage matrix training process guided by a subgraph sampling strategy. Extensive experiments across six complex domains show that HeGFlow improves the average score of smaller LLM (e.g., Qwen3-8B) by 12.4%, enabling it to match or even surpass the performance of much larger models. Furthermore, HeGFlow achieves the best average performance of 79.7 on four widely-used benchmarks, which consistently outperforms existing manually design methods by an average of 3.7∼[jls-end-space/]7.8%, and surpasses the state-of-the-art automated workflow optimization methods by an average of 0.9∼[jls-end-space/]6.7%. Further experiments demonstrate that our graph-based approach achieves strong performance while maintaining low token consumption, establishing a new paradigm for scalable and effective MAS workflow generation. Title: Artificial intelligence as a decision partner in food choice: Typology and research agenda
Abstract: Research examining artificial intelligence's (AI) role in food choice largely asks whether AI helps people make better decisions, treating it as an information source that improves the accuracy or personalization of recommendations. We suggest that this framing captures one point on a broader continuum of how AI impacts food decisions. AI can act, often simultaneously, as an advisor consulted for information, a decision partner that actively shares in constructing the choice, or an ambient influence that shapes what appears desirable and available before deliberate choice begins. As AI becomes more conversational and more embedded across the food environment, this continuum is increasingly populated in less visible regions, yet the field remains concentrated on the advisor role. We focus on the decision-partner role, where AI participates in value construction, goal clarification, attribute weighting, and choice justification, raising questions about agency, responsibility, and delegation. We articulate four mechanisms that describe this participation, namely preference offloading, responsibility reallocation, confidence calibration, and food-decision skill erosion. Because food choice is frequent, often habitual, and commonly involves trade-offs among hedonic and utilitarian goals, it is an ideal domain in which these process-level effects can compound. We draw on evidence from consumer psychology, automation research, and cognitive science, noting where boundary conditions remain untested in food contexts, and close with a research agenda organized around agency, reliance, responsibility, confidence, and cognitive effort. When AI shares in constructing a food choice, the values being optimized may no longer be entirely the consumer's own. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Recovering from inauthenticity: Counterfactual thinking and the consequences of feeling inauthentic
Abstract: Counterfactual (i.e., “If only…”) thinking allows individuals to compare what has happened to what might have been, and may imbue both positive and negative events with meaning. Given authenticity's importance for well-being, we examined whether counterfactual thinking shapes affective and meaning-related responses to authentic and inauthentic experiences. Across four samples (N = 1359), participants recalled authentic and inauthentic events (order randomized), generated either counterfactual or factual details, and reported event-induced meaning in life and affect. In primary analyses on the combined samples, inauthenticity experiences elicited lower positive affect, greater negative affect, and lower meaning in life. Event type interacted with thought type, such that these affective and meaning in life differences by event were attenuated when participants thought counterfactually in the combined sample. Furthermore, affect significantly mediated the moderation of event and thought type on meaning in life, such that affect was a stronger mediator when participants thought factually than counterfactually. Findings were less consistent by individual sample, particularly regarding the interaction effects. This is discussed as an important limitation in conversation with robustness checks on the combined analyses. These findings provide preliminary evidence that counterfactual thinking may regulate emotional responses to authentic and inauthentic experiences, thereby weakening their association with meaning in life. However, effects on meaning were less robust and should be interpreted cautiously. Counterfactual thinking may therefore function as a double-edged sword when it comes to affect and authenticity, softening the negative impact of inauthentic reflection while dampening the positive impact of authentic reflection. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: Acculturation fit matters: Perceived acculturation discordance across work and family contexts differentiates majority threat perceptions and anti-migration attitudes
Abstract: Objective This study examined whether perceived acculturation fit between majority-group members’ own acculturation preferences and the acculturation orientations they attributed to refugees differentiated anti-migration attitudes and perceived intergroup threat, and whether these patterns differed across family and work domains and between Syrian and Ukrainian refugees. Methods Drawing on the Concordance Model of Acculturation and the Relative Acculturation Extended Model, we distinguished between consensual and discordant perceived acculturation fit in the family and work domains. A sample of N = 352 German majority-group members evaluated both Syrian and Ukrainian refugees. Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) were conducted to examine mean differences in antimigration attitudes and perceived threat as a function of perceived acculturation fit. Results Perceived acculturation fit significantly differentiated anti-migration attitudes and several dimensions of intergroup threat, although patterns varied across domains and refugee groups. For Syrian refugees, family-domain discordance differentiated anti-migration attitudes and most forms of perceived threat, whereas work-domain differences were more selective. For Ukrainian refugees, significant differences were more limited and varied across domains and outcomes. Exploratory analyses further indicated that participants perceiving discordance in both family and work domains reported highest levels of several negative intergroup responses regarding Syrian refugees. The broad pattern of findings was supported by alternative operationalizations of acculturation discordance. Conclusion These findings suggest that majority-group evaluations vary systematically according to perceived acculturation fit across social domains and refugee groups. Perceived discordance differentiated intergroup evaluations in a domain- and group-specific manner, underscoring the importance of considering both domain-specific expectations and group-specific perceptions in contemporary acculturation research. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Meelen T.; Dool T.
Title: How socio-political streams shape sustainability transitions: the case of a European rail network
Abstract: In current times of deep socio-ecological crises, political-economic governance of key infrastructural sectors such as energy and mobility is reconsidered by society, politics and academia alike. This paper explores how the dynamics of political economies influence sustainability transitions. Beyond static country comparisons, we develop a processual perspective on political economy that better resonates with the long-term nature of sustainability transitions. To analyze struggles over political directionality, we draw on literature on political ideologies and introduce the concept of socio-political streams. Socio-political streams refer to actor coalitions and their interrelated sets of goals, beliefs, practices and affects. Conceptually, our study provides insight in how political-economic debates about the role of state and market, as well as international integration, shape sustainability transitions. Empirically, we conduct a case study of international rail connections in Western Europe. Recent years have seen a push for rail revival, but developments seem to have stalled. We analyze 25 years (2000–2024) of media, sector and policy documents from seven countries (Germany, The Netherlands, France, Belgium, Austria, Switzerland and the United Kingdom) and conduct interviews with 26 sectoral informants. We study socio-political dynamics using qualitative content analysis and socio-technical configuration analysis. The results reveal how socio-political streams shape international rail in divergent ways, influencing policy choices, financing models, and creating barriers such as high track access charges under market-based approaches. Overall, the coexistence of conflicting socio-political streams without prioritization has stalled progress, with a potential path forward emerging through stronger coordination by the European Union. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: The role of pitch in the vocal communication of intentions
Abstract: Intonation, the variation of pitch in speech, helps listeners understand speakers' communicative intentions. This study examines the role of pitch information at different levels of granularity—spanning specific (discrete contours), more flexible (general contour shape), and general (averaged pitch)—in communicating intentions. We first used a reverse correlation approach to identify people's mental representations of two contrasting intentions – criticism and suggestion – when listening to the word “beer.” In a second experiment, listeners rated how much each resulting pattern sounded like criticism and suggestion. Statistical models revealed that listeners rely on the shape of the pitch contour in terms of its spikiness and overall pitch direction, in addition to mean pitch, while precise contour plays a minor role, supporting the relevant role of pitch dynamics as well as the inferential (rather than referential) role of intonation in communicating intentions. Notably, we found distinct groups of listeners who use pitch characteristics in different ways, highlighting both shared understanding (within groups of listeners) and substantial interindividual differences in processing social pragmatic cues. These findings clarify the role of pitch in intention communication, reveal its complexity, and highlight the potential for miscommunication in everyday interactions. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The convergence of traditional Chinese medicine and artificial intelligence: A bibliometric study on the development of neural networks in traditional Chinese medicine
Abstract: Neural networks have become increasingly integral to traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) research in recent years. To map the evolution of neural networks in TCM, this study conducted a bibliometric analysis of publications from 2013 to 2025, sourced from Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure). Our results revealed a striking growth in annual publications, from 32 articles in 2013 to a peak of over 240 articles in 2024, representing about 8-fold increase. This growth exhibited a pronounced acceleration after 2018, with annual publication volume entering a phase of rapid and sustained expansion. Algorithmically, ANN (Artificial neural network, 25.71%), DNN (Deep neural network, 14.29%), and CNN (Convolutional neural network, 11.43%) were the most prevalent architectures. Title: Driver-initiated takeover in highway tunnels: effects of non-driving-related tasks on driving workload and takeover risk
Abstract: Advances in automated driving technology have facilitated the commercial deployment of Level 3 systems. Complex traffic scenarios still require drivers to resume vehicle control before full automation is realized. Assessment of driver takeover performance and associated risks is essential for enhancing automated driving safety. Current literature focuses primarily on system-initiated takeovers. Research on driver-initiated takeovers remains limited. This study addressed this gap by investigating driver-initiated takeovers triggered by traffic pressure within highway tunnels. The experimental design included four non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs) and a no-task condition. Visual, physiological, and behavioral data were collected from 28 drivers across five experimental conditions using a high-fidelity driving simulator. An evaluation index system was established based on the takeover behavior from three dimensions: takeover performance, driving workload, and risk level. A quantitative grading model for driving workload level (DWL) was developed using kernel principal component analysis and fuzzy C-means clustering. Additionally, a cloud entropy-optimized extension cloud model was used to comprehensively evaluate the risk of driver-initiated takeovers. The results indicated differences in takeover performance, driving workload, and model-derived risk assessment results across the tested task conditions. Significant differences in driver-initiated takeover time were observed across task conditions, reflecting variations in the timing of driver-initiated intervention. Short-term speed compensation was generally observed after takeover and was more pronounced under the visual and multimodal task conditions. DWL values were higher under all NDRTs than under the no-task condition, with the highest value observed under the multimodal task condition. DWL was classified into three levels: low [0, 0.537), medium [0.537, 0.816), and high [0.816, 1]. Within the relative risk classification for the current sample and experimental scenario, the no-task condition was classified as low risk; the auditory, visual, and social task conditions were classified as medium risk; and the multimodal task condition was classified as high risk. The THW results provided preliminary convergent evidence for these risk classifications. Title: Context-sensitive learning analytics in open and distance education: Identifying students' online learning behavior patterns in a large-scale Indonesian context
Abstract: Learning analytics has been widely applied to examine student engagement and academic performance in online learning environments, yet most existing frameworks treat engagement–performance relationships as context-independent. This study challenges that assumption by adopting a context-sensitive learning analytics perspective, empirically demonstrating that engagement patterns and their academic consequences are systematically shaped by course-level contextual configurations. An explorative, correlational, and comparative design was employed, using LMS log data from one of Southeast Asia's largest open and distance education institutions. Data from 52 courses involving 5044 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and a General Linear Model-based one-way Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA). An Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC = 0.343, 95% CI [0.325, 0.361]) confirmed that 34.3% of variance in academic performance is attributable to between-class factors, providing substantial empirical support for a context-sensitive analytical approach. The findings reveal three novel patterns: (1) the direction of discipline-based engagement differences reverses as a function of course size; (2) tutor discussion activity and student discussion scores are systematically decoupled in large courses; and (3) course category exerts a significant contextual effect on final performance (Pillai's Trace F(15,14,334) = 5.208, p < .001; Final Score: F(5,4778) = 4.121, p = .001; post-hoc: social science courses in large and middle-size settings outperform STEM-oriented courses across all three simultaneous performance outcomes). Title: Long-term associations of pandemic depression symptom trajectories with post-pandemic depression score in times of contemporary mental health stressors

We applied a negative binomial regression model to examine the association of post-pandemic DASS-21 derived depression scores obtained in 2023/2024 (outcome) with depressive symptom trajectory clusters derived from densely spaced questionnaires answered during the pandemic. Models were adjusted for principal components of worries (individual, climate, social, war, migration). Title: Facility, community, and state-level correlates of overdose education and naloxone provision in substance use treatment facilities in the United States
Abstract: Background This study examined which characteristics of substance use disorder (SUD) treatment facilities and their surrounding areas are associated with offering overdose education and naloxone (OEN). Methods We linked data from eight national sources regarding 12,146 SUD treatment facilities (from the 2024 National Directory of Drug and Alcohol Use Treatment Facilities) and the communities and states where they operate. Title: Sequential and parallel prompt engineering on research article topic mining
Abstract: The rapid growth of research articles has intensified demand for scalable and interpretable topic mining methods. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising generative alternative to traditional approaches, their application to large-scale topic mining lacks methodological grounding, particularly regarding how prompt design and input preparation shape output quality. While structured metadata produced higher coherence under the sequential strategy, narrative abstracts yielded superior coherence and diversity under the parallel strategy, demonstrating the assembling resilience of the parallel strategy to input complexity. Benchmarked against LDA, BERTopic, and Top2Vec under both default and hyperparameter-optimized configurations, the parallel strategy with structured metadata achieved competitive performance across multiple evaluation dimensions. Title: Food noise: A theoretical review
Abstract: Food noise has emerged as a new term to describe a preoccupation with food that can be persistent, intrusive, and unwanted. The term has become popular on social media platforms like TikTok and Reddit, typically alongside discussion of the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist medications (e.g., semaglutide, tirzepatide). Specifically, people report that taking a GLP-1 medication can dampen or substantially reduce their food noise. Qualitative research describes how this effect is welcomed and can allow people more control over their eating habits. However, although reductions in food noise appear to be a promising impact of treatment with a GLP-1 medication and may help to explain disordered eating behaviours, little is known about what exactly food noise is, what causes it, and how any remediation of distressing thoughts might work. As such, this narrative review critically discusses existing research into food noise, including proposed definitions and existing qualitative findings, to better understand the conceptualisation of the construct. Based on current understandings of food noise, we present five potential theoretical explanations for food noise: homeostatic theory, food cue reactivity, food addiction, thought suppression, and memory inhibition. We end by synthesising these five theories and providing suggestions for future research. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: The hidden curriculum in health professions education: Associations with clinical competencies among nursing and allied health students
Abstract: Introduction: The hidden curriculum, which includes implicit messages and norms within educational environments, plays a significant role in shaping professional development in health professions education. This study examines associations between the hidden curriculum and clinical competencies, focusing on nursing care planning and educational leadership skills among nursing and allied health students. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study with 263 undergraduate nursing, operating room, and emergency medicine students at Ardabil University of Medical Sciences in Iran. Participants were selected via stratified random sampling. Data were collected using the Hidden Curriculum Evaluation Scale (HCES-N), the Student Survey on Writing Nursing Care Plan (SSW-NCP), and the Educational Leadership Scale for Nursing Students. Hierarchical multiple regression was used to examine factors associated with hidden curriculum perceptions. Results: The mean hidden curriculum score was 93.10 ± 9.33, indicating a moderate-to-high level. Significant positive correlations were found between the hidden curriculum and nursing care planning (r = 0.43, p < 0.001) and educational leadership (r = 0.18, p < 0.01). Hierarchical regression analysis revealed that satisfaction with patient care performance (β = 0.485, p < 0.001), nursing care planning competencies (β = 0.267, p < 0.001), and educational leadership skills (β = 0.107, p = 0.040) were significant positive associations with hidden curriculum perceptions. Collectively, these variables explained 34.5% of the variance in hidden curriculum scores. Conclusions: The hidden curriculum is associated with clinical competencies and leadership attributes among nursing and allied health students. These findings suggest that students' perceptions of the hidden curriculum are associated with important professional competencies; however, due to the cross-sectional design, causal relationships cannot be inferred. Longitudinal and multi-institutional studies are needed to further examine the direction and nature of these associations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Policy-as-practice: exploring the ‘hidden sides’ of policy-making in sustainability transitions
Abstract: While research on the politics of transitions has examined power dynamics, coalitions, and value contestations, the ‘hidden’ sides of operational governance, such as micro-political dynamics, strategies and tensions within decision-making spaces, remained largely underexplored. Considering the increased attention to politics in the governance of sustainability transitions, we argue for a better understanding of the complex, often messy policy processes behind the scenes. Drawing on insights from political science and policy studies, we propose a ‘policy-as-practice’ perspective for transition studies to explore how actors shape and negotiate the content of policies, and the often concealed arenas in which they operate. We discuss the roles of state and non-state actors, interest groups, policy advisors and experts, and how their day-to-day practices shape policy outcomes. Furthermore, we discuss hidden processes such as nondecisions, policy inaction and watering down of policy initiatives as research topics that highlight how a policy-as-practice perspective can provide valuable insights. These aspects of policymaking are difficult to observe from the study of policy documents, decisions or instruments, and require studying policy processes up-close and immersively. We also outline important ontological and methodological implications of our micro-political perspective for the field of transition policy studies. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: The role of epistemic and normative similarity in inter-organizational online relations: a self-categorization perspective on the bioplastics field
Abstract: Sustainability transitions unfold through the interactions of heterogeneous actors, yet the discursive mechanisms that structure inter-organizational affiliation remain poorly understood. This study examines whether organizations' publicly articulated epistemic and normative positioning is associated with the formation of inter-organizational ties and the emergence of coherent relational communities in the bioplastics field. Drawing on self-categorization theory, we advance a multilevel perspective in which organizations are treated as socially recognizable collective actors whose public positions provide categorical cues for affiliation, community formation, and differentiation. Conceptualizing epistemic and normative similarity as two dimensions of symbolic proximity, this perspective extends proximity-based accounts of inter-organizational relations by linking dyadic similarity to the emergence of internally coherent and comparatively differentiated communities. We reconstruct a hyperlink network of 4161 organizations across all world macro-regions, connected by 28,151 hyperlink ties, and derive their epistemic and normative positioning from web content using a transformer-based topic model and an automated UN SDG classifier. Dyadic logistic regression shows that epistemic and normative similarity positively predict tie formation, net of geographical, institutional, and social proximity, with a significant positive interaction between the two dimensions. At the community level, OLS regression and permutation tests show that greater relational density is associated both with higher internal epistemic and normative coherence within communities and with stronger differentiation from other communities in the field. These findings suggest that the relational architecture of sustainability transitions is partly constituted by the symbolic positioning organizations publicly display, shaping how coordination, fragmentation, and transition governance unfold across heterogeneous organizational fields. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Wan P.; Sun S.; Lan J.; Chen Y.; Qin S.
Title: Collaboration and competition in trending topics: A fractional dynamic evolutionary perspective
Abstract: In online social networks, the rapid diffusion of trending topics can significantly influence public discourse and social stability, especially in extreme or conflict-driven scenarios. Existing models often overlook the co-evolution of cooperative and competitive behaviors and the memory effects in user participation, which limits their ability to capture realistic propagation dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose a unified framework integrating evolutionary game theory, fractional order dynamics, and optimal control. Evolutionary game theory is used to model the interaction between cooperative and competitive behaviors, while a fractional differential equation formulation captures temporal dependence and long-range memory in user participation. In addition, three intervention strategies are incorporated into a fractional optimal control framework to suppress the diffusion of extreme topics while minimizing overall system loss. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is supported by theoretical analysis and experiments using the Facebook and PHEME datasets. Results show that the fractional order model better captures peak intensity, response timing, and decay patterns than the corresponding integer order model. Moreover, the combined control strategy reduces system loss by 58.8% relative to the uncontrolled scenario. These findings improve the understanding of the roles of behavior, memory, and control in information diffusion and provide practical insights for topic governance and public opinion management. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.
