Author full names: Zhang, Xiaojing (57214095336); Rezhaguli, Kamalebieke (61020093100); Liu, Yiting (60346878600); Xie, Jingchao (53985779800); Wargocki, Pawel (6602149538)
Title: Resolving inconsistencies in experimental studies of the effects of pure CO₂ on cognitive performance: a systematic review and meta‑analysis of existing evidence
Abstract: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is widely used as an indicator of ventilation adequacy, yet its direct effects on cognitive performance remain unclear. Most studies have treated CO₂ as a proxy for indoor air quality rather than an independent exposure, and existing findings remain inconsistent due to substantial methodological heterogeneity. This study systematically evaluates experimental evidence on the cognitive effects of controlled exposure to pure CO₂ and assesses the adequacy of current indoor concentration thresholds. Through a comprehensive search of databases including Web of Science and Scopus, 35 experimental studies were identified that examined the impact of pure CO₂ exposure on cognitive domains including attention, perceptual-motor function, executive function, language, learning and memory, and social cognition. The vote-counting analyses using exact binomial tests of significant outcomes suggest that at conventional environmental CO₂ concentrations in buildings (≤5000 ppm), evidence for negative cognitive effects is inconsistent. CO₂ appears to exert some effects on higher-order executive functions (e.g., complex decision-making) but has limited or no influence on language tasks or social cognition. Inconsistencies across studies may stem from variations in experimental design, task types, and individual tolerance. A meta-analysis of these data confirmed these observations. Current evidence remains insufficient to classify pure CO₂ as a cognitively harmful pollutant at commonly occurring indoor concentrations (≤5000 ppm). Although some laboratory studies reported statistically significant changes, generally above 2500 ppm, isolated findings at approximately 1000 ppm require further investigation and should not be interpreted as establishing a cognitive-effect threshold or recommended exposure limit. Moreover, laboratory findings may not directly translate into meaningful changes in real-world productivity or learning outcomes. Future research should prioritize ecologically valid field studies, long-term exposure effects, individual variability, underlying mechanisms, and interactions between CO₂ and other indoor pollutants. © 2026

Title: Who benefits from parental intervention programs in youth sport? A systematic review
Abstract: Despite growing recognition that parental behavior shapes athlete outcomes, evidence on whether structured intervention programmes effectively change parental conduct, and whether those changes reach athletes, remains scattered. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of parental intervention programmes in youth sport, positioning athlete outcomes as primary endpoints alongside parental behavior and mental health outcomes. Search was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO up to May 2025. Quantitative and qualitative designs were included, as the systematic search identified 2188 records, of which 14 studies met eligibility criteria, regarding parents or caregivers of youth athletes involved in sport-based intervention programmes (PROSPERO: CRD420250651529). Methodological quality was appraised using JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. Quantitative and mixed-methods findings were synthesized using a Level of Evidence framework, and qualitative findings were synthesized through Thematic Synthesis. Findings were considered “Inconclusive” for both parental behavior and mental health (59% consistency) and athlete well-being and stress (70% consistency). Thematic synthesis identified three analytical themes: Developing Sport Parenting Competence: Knowledge, Self-Awareness, and Confidence; Relational and Behavioral Change in the Parent-Athlete Dyad; Athlete Growth: Social Skills, Psychological Well-Being, and Coping Development, which gather outcomes such as gains in knowledge and awareness, relational and behavioral change in the relationship, and developmental and well-being gains in athletes. Parental intervention programs show promise in producing relational change in parents, with emerging evidence that these changes reach athletes through a relational pathway. Rigorous controlled trials and dyadic designs are needed to establish causal mechanisms and inform evidence-based programme development. Title: Reinforcement sensitivity and the association between exposure to racialized stressors and internalizing psychopathology among Black young adults
Abstract: Black Americans face frequent exposure to racialized forms of stress directly through interpersonal discrimination experiences and indirectly through racialized social contexts that are shaped by structural factors (e.g., exposure to community violence). Research findings link chronic stress exposure to increased risk for internalizing psychopathology, yet internalizing outcomes among Black Americans are varied. Reinforcement sensitivity theory (RST) describes two systems, the behavioral inhibition system (BIS) and behavioral activation system (BAS), which are thought to shape individual differences in behavior and sensitivity to external cues. To better understand factors associated with individual differences in Black mental health outcomes, this study examines the BIS and BAS as potential moderators of the relationship between exposure to racialized stressors and internalizing symptoms (i.e., anxiety and depression). Participants were 329 Black American young adults ( M age = 22.84 years, SD = 1.122; 55% female) who reported on levels of BIS/BAS, experiences of racial discrimination, community violence exposure, and anxiety and depression symptoms. Regression analyses revealed both interpersonal racial discrimination and community violence exposure predicted increased symptoms of anxiety and depression. Additionally, BIS and BAS measures moderated the association between community violence exposure and anxiety symptoms, with greater exposure to community violence predicting increased anxiety symptoms for individuals with relatively lower levels of BIS and low levels of BAS-reward responsiveness. BIS and BAS did not moderate the association between interpersonal racial discrimination and internalizing symptoms. These results suggest exposure to community violence may differentially impact mental health outcomes for Black individuals based on BIS and BAS differences. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Zhou M.; Wang P.; Han X.; Liu G.; Li L.
Title: All Is Heard: Mitigating conformity bias via dual-branch collaboration in group recommendation
Abstract: Group recommendation aims to integrate members’ preferences for consensus-aligned recommendations. However, conformity bias often leads to a “pseudo-consensus” where active members dominate the aggregation process, suppressing the latent preferences of inactive members. To address this, we propose VAPrompt, a dual-branch collaborative framework that unifies member-level variational debiasing and group-level prompting consensus. Specifically, the member-level variational debiasing branch utilizes a variational hypergraph encoder and an efficient variational attention mechanism to capture member preference diversity and prevent active members from dominating the group representation. Furthermore, the group-level prompting consensus branch introduces a heterogeneity-aware prompt to guide a multi-view gating fusion mechanism, dynamically balancing contributions from different views to focus on the intersection of members’ real intentions. We evaluate the proposed method on four real-world datasets: Mafengwo, Mafengwo-S, Weeplaces-S, and CAMRa2011. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VAPrompt outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all evaluation metrics. In particular, compared with the best baseline, VAPrompt achieves average improvements on the Weeplaces-S dataset, with gains of 18.26% in HR@10 and 16.84% in NDCG@10. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in mitigating conformity bias and improving group recommendation accuracy. Author full names: Eriksson, Mollie J. (57765435700); Schmidt, Louis. A. (7401563996)
Title: Neurovisceral model of social anxiety disorder: An integrative review
Abstract: Social anxiety involves persistent fear of negative evaluation that causes significant distress or avoidance in social situations and, when lasting at least six months with meaningful impairment across life domains, meets diagnostic criteria for social anxiety disorder (SAD). The origins and maintenance of SAD have been described by disparate models as dysregulation of central and peripheral networks involved in emotion regulation and threat appraisal. However, studies integrating central and peripheral levels of analysis remain scarce and lack integration, leaving our understanding of the neurobiology of SAD fragmented. Here we review these models and extant evidence. This review proposes an integrated neurovisceral model in which SAD reflects context-sensitive dysregulation among cortical regulation, limbic threat signaling, insular interoception, vagal and autonomic regulation, cardiac flexibility, HPA-axis output, and behavior. Genetic liability and behavioral inhibition are conceptualized as probabilistic influences on threat sensitivity and regulatory capacity. While environmental experience, developmental timing, sex-related factors, and stress sensitization shape the calibration of these systems. The model predicts heterogeneity along activation threshold, response magnitude, recovery, and central-peripheral coordination, which may give rise to acute hyperreactive, persistent sensitized/inflexible, and compromised/blunted SAD configurations. The model also generates testable predictions for longitudinal, multimodal research, and supports profile-sensitive approaches to assessment and treatment. Authors: Guerrero-Pérez E.; Diego P.
Title: Emotional Design in Fiction Series: Sentiment Analysis of the Script and Audience's Emotional Response; [El diseño emocional de las series de ficción: análisis de sentimientos del guion y respuesta emocional de la audiencia]
Abstract: Introduction: This article addresses the application of sentiment analysis to fiction series scripts to design content tailored to audience sensibilities, thereby improving content quality and production sustainability. The hypothesis is that emotional gratification optimizes audience engagement through the proper development of plots and characters. Methodology: A case study of the Spanish thriller Ana Tramel. El juego is conducted, triangulating three analyses: the pilot script using R, messages on Twitter/X during its premiere on television, and a questionnaire administered to an audience sample after a private screening of the pilot episode. Results: The results reveal that the script's emotional design is effectively transmitted (the main emotions align: trust, sadness, and fear), but the audience unconsciously reinterprets it, prioritizing fear. The reaction on social media is more polarized and negative, while the conscious analysis highlights surprise and anticipation as keys to engagement and validates the effectiveness of complex characters who generate positive feelings through trust and empathic sadness. Discussion: The comparison between the intention of the writing and production teams, the unconscious audience reaction on social media, and the conscious assessment by the public demonstrates the suitability of these studies as complementary tools in creative processes to align narrative design with the audience's emotional reception. Conclusions: It is concluded that this methodological triangulation is suitable for understanding the viewer's experience and that the emotional design of characters and plots is a fundamental element for achieving audience engagement, offering guidelines to optimize the efficiency and sustainability of audiovisual productions. © 2027, HISIN (History of Information Systems). Authors: Perez C.; Sokolova K.
Title: The reciprocity gap: How autonomous AI agent networks challenge platform ecosystem design
Abstract: We analyze the social networks of 13,298 autonomous AI agents on Moltbook, the first large-scale public platform dedicated to AI-to-AI communication, comprising 22,577 posts, 141,494 comments, and 11,326 communities. Constructing directed communication networks and comparing them against five human benchmarks, we find that AI networks reproduce human-like structural properties (clustering, degree distribution, average path length, small-world topology) but exhibit a pronounced reciprocity gap: binary reciprocity of 0.011 versus 0.396–0.841 in human networks (Cohen’s (Formula presented) ), with 99.43% of connected dyads asymmetric. This gap persists across four reciprocity operationalizations and robustness checks. Agent-based simulations confirm that even minimal behavioral strategies produce reciprocity approximately 30 times higher than observed. These patterns are consistent with a violation of social exchange theory’s memory assumption: current large language model (LLM)-based agents process interactions statelessly, without tracking prior interactors. We derive three design propositions (memory augmentation, reputation systems, hybrid governance) for platform architects integrating AI agents into digital ecosystems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Yu J.; Wang S.
Title: From awareness to adoption: modeling consumer readiness for urban drone delivery from a stage-change perspective
Abstract: Drone delivery, as a low-altitude logistics application of urban air mobility (UAM), may reshape last-mile distribution and urban service accessibility. However, its societal diffusion cannot be fully understood through conventional binary acceptance models, because consumers may differ substantially in their readiness to progress from awareness to repeated use. This study investigates heterogeneous consumer readiness for drone delivery using 1,018 valid survey responses collected in Shenzhen, China, where urban drone delivery has entered early deployment. Drawing on the Transtheoretical Model, adoption is conceptualized as an ordered five-stage readiness process: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance. An integrated framework combining the Technology Acceptance Model and the Theory of Planned Behavior, extended by environmental concern and perceived risk, is used to identify attitudinal latent constructs. A hybrid model integrating a Multiple Indicators and Multiple Causes model and a Partial Proportional Odds Model examines how socio-demographic attributes and psychological perceptions shape stage-specific readiness, with marginal effects quantifying heterogeneous influences across stages. Results show that drone delivery adoption is not a linear extension of general acceptance but a staged readiness process shaped by different psychological mechanisms. Socio-demographic attributes mainly explain baseline differences in adoption propensity, while attitudinal constructs exert stronger and more stage-dependent effects. Early-stage readiness is constrained by perceived risk and uncertainty, but is also sensitive to social influence and environmental concern; progression toward action and maintenance is more closely associated with perceived usefulness, ease of use, perceived behavioral control, attitude, and behavioral intention. This pattern indicates a pathway from risk reduction and cognitive activation to technology evaluation, experiential confidence, and behavioral consolidation. Findings provide behavioral evidence for stage-targeted risk communication, service design, and demand cultivation strategies in early urban drone delivery deployment. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Measuring the state of open science in transportation using large language models
Source title: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
Abstract: Open science initiatives have strengthened scientific integrity and accelerated research progress across many fields, but the state of their practice within transportation research remains under-investigated. Key features of open science, defined here as data and code availability, are difficult to extract due to the inherent complexity of the field. Previous work has either been limited to small-scale studies due to the labor-intensive nature of manual analysis or has relied on large-scale bibliometric approaches that sacrifice contextual richness. This paper introduces an automatic and scalable feature-extraction pipeline that combines full-text extraction and human agreement analysis in order to measure code and data availability in transportation research. We employ Large Language Models (LLMs) for this task and validate their performance against a manually curated dataset and through an inter-rater agreement analysis. We applied this pipeline to examine 10,724 research articles published in the Transportation Research Part series of journals between 2019 and 2024. Our analysis found that only 5% of quantitative papers shared a code repository, 4% of quantitative papers shared a data repository, and about 3% of papers shared both, with trends differing across journals, topics, and geographic regions. We found no significant difference in citation counts or review duration between papers that provided data and code and those that did not, suggesting a misalignment between open science efforts and traditional academic metrics. Consequently, encouraging these practices will likely require structural interventions from journals and funding agencies to supplement the lack of direct author incentives. The pipeline developed in this study can be readily scaled to other journals, representing a critical step toward the automated measurement and monitoring of open science practices in transportation research. Title: Blame the bot or the human: How do misinformation-generating anthropomorphic AI streamers influence purchase intention?
Abstract: Anthropomorphic AI streamers have been deployed by live-streaming merchants to promote product sales. Although prior research has investigated anthropomorphism and AI-generated misinformation, separately, limited attention has been paid to their intersection—misinformation-generating anthropomorphic AI streamers (hereafter, MGA-AI streamers). Drawing on attribution theory and the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, this study examines how MGA-AI streamers influence purchase intention for products they sell. More importantly, we investigate the spillover effects of MGA-AI streamers on consumers’ intention to purchase products from subsequent human streamers affiliated with the same merchant (hereafter, subsequent human streamers), and reveal their underlying mechanisms. Across five between-subjects online experiments (N = 1,142) with varying degrees of anthropomorphism, our analyses (independent-samples t-test and PROCESS Model 4) show that MGA-AI streamers lower purchase intention for the products they sell while increasing the intention for products sold by subsequent human streamers. Using consumer gender as a boundary condition, we find that this effect holds for female consumers but becomes insignificant for male consumers. Mechanism analyses indicate that this spillover effect on subsequent human streamers is driven by increasing internal attribution to these anthropomorphic AI streamers and decreasing external attribution to the merchants. This study advances research on anthropomorphism and AI misinformation, providing strategic guidance for the deployment of anthropomorphic AI streamers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The production of an eco-city forest as a socio-ecological fix to pollution and development in Rayong, Thailand: populism and post-politics in Thailand’s Community Forests
Abstract: This paper examines how a socioecological fix is produced within an urban community forest, focusing on Ban San Chao Community Forest in Rayong Province, Thailand. We argue that state and industrial actors, operating through Thailand’s Eco-Industrial City policy, mobilised populist postpolitical tactics to restructure the ideological, governance and political spaces of the forest in response to a legitimacy crisis generated by decades of industrial pollution. This crisis exemplifies capitalism’s second contradiction: the systemic degradation of the ecological and social conditions on which accumulation depends, politicised through sustained public protest and civil society activism. We show how the fix was produced through three interrelated mechanisms: the discursive homogenisation of the forest under populist ideals of coexistence and multi-sector cooperation; the hegemonic restructuring of Community Forest governance under municipal and industrial oversight; and a technocratic assessment cycle through which this restructuring is annually certified and reproduced. Together, these mechanisms temporarily restore institutional legitimacy for ongoing accumulation while depoliticising contestation over industrial pollution and deferring its material causes. Theoretically, the paper establishes populist postpolitical tactics as an operational mechanism through which socioecological fixes are produced at the local scale. Empirically, it identifies a form of eco-city fix, the absorption and restructuring of existing community-constituted green spaces, contributing to understanding of forest governance under green neoliberalism in Southeast Asia. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Zhai J.; Qu J.G.
Title: From “cost of asking” to “fit of asking”: How seeking help with AI shapes employees’ indebtedness and autonomy in different workplace helping contexts
Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into workplace processes has transformed organizational communication, yet little is known about how AI reshapes employee help-seeking behaviors. Leveraging on the social exchange perspective, this research examines how help source (human vs. AI colleague) and help context type (autonomy-oriented vs. dependency-oriented) influence employees' mechanisms to seek help in working contexts. Across two experiments, Study 1 investigates the psychological mechanisms underlying help-seeking from AI versus human, focusing on perceived autonomy and perceived indebtedness as mediators. Study 2 extends this framework by testing the moderating role of help context type on the proposed direct and indirect effects. Results indicated that employees perceived higher autonomy and lower indebtedness when receiving dependency-oriented help from AI compared to human colleagues, which in turn increased their willingness to seek help. The findings advance understandings of AI-mediated workplace interactions, offering theoretical and practical insights into the “help-seeker's dilemma”. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Prediction of Pedestrian-Vehicle Near-Crash Events during Turning Maneuvers at Signalized Intersections
Source title: Journal of Transportation Engineering Part A: Systems
Abstract: Urban road intersections are among the most critical locations for road safety because they involve complex interactions among multiple road users, particularly during turning maneuvers, where conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles frequently occur. This study adopts an observational approach to develop four statistical models for identifying the factors that significantly influence pedestrian-vehicle interactions during both right- and left-turn maneuvers. The study contributes to the existing literature by explicitly incorporating left-turn maneuvers and proposing a practical simplification of social force variables into directly observable indicators. These simplified indicators proved to be statistically significant and effectively captured the dynamics of pedestrian-vehicle interactions, enabling safety analyses in environments where advanced sensing technologies or automated traffic-monitoring systems are unavailable. The proposed simplification of the social force methodology incorporates variables such as pedestrian direction change, pedestrian conflict, crossing behavior, crossing speed, trajectory within the intersection, and the pedestrian paths. Vehicle-related surrogate safety measures, including crossing time and vehicle speed, were also incorporated into the analysis. Specifically, near-crash events were defined using the post-encroachment time (PET) indicator, linking conflict-based safety measures with behavioral and geometric explanatory variables. Predictive performance was further evaluated through receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. The final specification (Model 4) demonstrated excellent predictive accuracy, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.992. Traffic conditions, geometric characteristics, and the simplified social force variables emerged as the strongest predictors of near-crash occurrence. Title: Moral surgery: Negative revelations differentially alter retrospective evaluations of creators and creations
Abstract: When individuals learn of a moral transgression committed by a creator they once admired, they face psychological tension: How do they reconcile their positive prior evaluations with this newly acquired negative information? While existing literature has primarily examined how such revelations alter current attitudes, we investigate how they trigger the differential reconstruction of past attitudes. Across five preregistered experiments, we reveal a robust pattern showing that individuals reconstruct their prior evaluations by separating the art from the artist. Specifically, although the revelation of a transgression prompts a significant downward revision in individuals' recalled evaluations of the creator, their recalled evaluations of the creation remain relatively resistant to the negative information. This differential memory reconstruction occurs for both experimentally induced and pre-existing positive evaluations, across multiple creative domains, and for varying levels of transgression severity. Furthermore, through targeted stress tests, we demonstrate that this observed phenomenon reflects a genuine psychological process rather than a methodological artifact. The effect is robust across incentive-compatible, multi-wave longitudinal, and separate measurement designs that rule out potential alternative explanations such as low cognitive effort, temporal proximity, and demand characteristics. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: Walking in her shoes: Virtual embodiment of a famous female scientist reduces implicit gender–science associations
Abstract: Gender disparities in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) persist despite decades of intervention efforts. A key contributing factor is implicit gender–science bias, an automatic association of science with men, which undermines women's participation and progress. We examined whether immersive virtual reality (VR) embodiment of a counter-stereotypical role model—a famous female scientist—can reduce these associations. Participants (n = 253) embodied either a female scientist (Marie Curie), a male scientist (Albert Einstein), or a gender-matched control avatar depicting a peer. We assessed implicit gender–science associations one week before, immediately following, and one week after the VR experience, and we explored the moderating effects of participant gender. As hypothesized, the Marie Curie condition reduced implicit gender–science bias. This effect persisted after one week, and further analyses revealed that it was driven primarily by women. The Albert Einstein condition produced no changes. Unexpectedly, the control condition also reduced bias, with effects persisting for men but not women. These findings suggest that virtual embodiment of counter-stereotypical role models can produce durable shifts in implicit gender–science associations and highlight the importance of participant characteristics, task design, and context in bias-reduction interventions. This research advances the literature on implicit bias, role models, and virtual embodiment, and highlights immersive, first-person experiences as a promising avenue for reducing gender bias in STEM. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Family migration and gender inequality in housework: Evidence from China
Abstract: While the impact of family migration on paid work is well-documented, its potential influence on housework remains largely unknown. This study examines the effect of couple migration on the division of housework in China, focusing on changes in housework hours for both female and male partners. Using panel data from the 2014 and 2016 waves of the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), we examine whether and how housework hours change following couple migration, and whether these changes correspond with shifts in employment conditions and family structure. Drawing on three theoretical perspectives, our analysis identifies couple migration as a significant life-course transition influencing domestic labour patterns. Results reveal only an increase, around 2 h per week, in women's housework time post-migration, even after accounting for shifts in employment status, working hours, and family structures. This gendered increase may reflect persistent traditional gender views and the social isolation experienced by migrant families, who often face challenges integrating into local communities. Our findings contribute to the literature on gender inequality by highlighting how couple migration can reinforce traditional gender roles, especially under conditions of limited social support. The study offers novel insights into the mechanisms underlying shifts in housework division during migration, utilising high-quality longitudinal data to capture actual behavioural changes among Chinese couples. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Unlocking the potential of green development: Can intelligent manufacturing improve corporate environmental performance?
Abstract: Amid the global wave of digital and intelligent transformation, intelligent manufacturing (IM) is bringing new potential for enhancing corporate environmental performance (CEP). However, systematic evidence on whether and how IM delivers environmental effects at the firm level remains limited. This study treats China's Intelligent Manufacturing Pilot Demonstration Project (IMPDP) as a quasi-natural experiment and employs a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) design to examine whether and how IM impacts CEP. We find that IM leads to a statistically and economically significant improvement in CEP, and the basic conclusion is robust across a wide range of tests. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the positive effect is stronger for non-state-owned enterprises (NSEs), firms with better corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance, high-technology (HT) firms and firms located in regions with a higher level of digital infrastructure (DI). Mechanism tests show that IM enhances CEP through two complementary channels: (i) strengthening internal capacity building and responsiveness, and (ii) increasing external market attention and supervision. Extended analysis finds that production-oriented IM projects exerts stronger effects on CEP than coordination-oriented ones. It further provides evidence from economic dimensions that IM can deliver tangible value to firms. Overall, our findings provide empirical evidence that IM can serve as an effective pathway toward green and high-quality industrial development and offer policy insights for China and other emerging economies pursuing a joint transition toward digitalization, intelligentization, and greening of enterprises. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Building infrastructure and cohesion through locally embedded institutions: Evidence from a field experiment in War-torn Eastern Congo
Abstract: A defining feature of many Community-Driven Development (CDD) interventions in wartorn countries is their pursuit of transformative objectives, seeking to (re)shape local decisionmaking institutions in the process. In recent years, there has been a push to overhaul CDD approaches, with a focus on more realistic objectives aimed at providing infrastructure and building capacity of existing local institutions. We investigate, through a large-scale field experiment involving 400 communities in eastern Congo, the effects of a CDD program that embodied this new focus. Our strategy allows us to identify causal impacts of the CDD intervention, in its basic form consisting of a US$100,000 envelope to finance an infrastructure project with an emphasis on ‘local content’, as well as when augmented with a complementary conflict mitigation component. While the intervention successfully delivered visible infrastructure projects, we find no detectable effects on social cohesion, (violent) conflict, or economic welfare. We conclude discussing policy implications. © 2026

Title: Resources reconsidered: A network perspective on multi-system interactions in the underground
Abstract: Due to growing resource demands in sustainability transitions, multi-system interactions (MSI) increasingly extend into extreme environments, such as the deep sea, outer space, and the underground, which harbour vast but largely untapped resource reservoirs. Access to these resources drives new interactions among systems, yet MSI research has paid limited attention to how the pursuit of these resources transforms sectoral dynamics and redefines system boundaries. We address this gap conceptually and empirically. Conceptually, we develop a resource typology distinguishing place-bound from transportable and renewable from finite resources. We argue that these material properties shape whether interactions between systems tend towards symbiosis or competition. Empirically, we investigate the underground as one such environment using 25 expert interviews, Social Network Analysis, and two in-depth case studies of interactions among the energy, mobility, water, and carbon management systems in Switzerland. Our findings show that underground resources are more often associated with conflict than synergy, largely due to finite availability and regulatory constraints. Groundwater emerges as the most conflict-prone resource in the network, given its strict regulatory protection, whereas transportation infrastructure and pipelines display the greatest potential for collaboration. The case studies further illustrate how regulatory uncertainty constrains symbiotic arrangements despite technical feasibility for resource flows. System entanglers attempt to bridge boundaries and enable collaboration but face institutional barriers that hinder system couplings. Our approach of combining network analysis with case studies provides a practical tool for identifying intervention points for symbiosis in complex multi-system contexts, offering insights for integrated resource governance and sustainable management. © 2026 The Authors. Title: “Horizontal violence among nursing students and newly graduated nurses: A systematic review”
Abstract: Background: Workplace violence is prevalent among healthcare professionals. Horizontal violence, defined as aggression between individuals of equal hierarchical status, is a significant issue in nursing. Nursing students and newly graduated nurses are particularly vulnerable due to inexperience, lack of coping strategies, and personal risk factors such as young age. Objective: To synthesize current literature on horizontal violence experienced by nursing students and newly graduated nurses, determining prevalence, manifestations, consequences, and intervention strategies. Method: A systematic-narrative hybrid review was conducted PRISMA 2020 and SWiM guidelines. Primary studies published between 2015 and 2025 were searched across CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, DIALNET, and LILACS databases. Study quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Tools. Results: The review included 34 articles. Horizontal violence prevalence ranged from 11.8% to 91.5% among nursing students and from 54.8% to 60% among newly graduated. Manifestations included disrespect, public humiliation, excessive demands, verbal insults, social exclusion, and sexual harassment. Consequences encompassed psychological and physical distress, decreased job satisfaction, burnout, increased turnover intention, and compromised patient safety. Proposed interventions highlighted simulation-based training, conflict management and integrating resilience training into nursing curricula. Discussion: Horizontal violence is a multifactorial issue rooted in clinical learning environments and professional hierarchies, deeply impacting nurse wellbeing, professional development, and patient safety. Conclusions: Prevention and early intervention are essential fosters safe educational and clinical environments where early career nurses can reach their full potential, ultimately reducing attrition and ensuring high quality patient care. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Psychological needs and collective capabilities in interprofessional education: A sequential mediation of healthcare students' interprofessional learning readiness
Abstract: Background: Interprofessional education (IPE) is essential for healthcare collaboration, yet the psychological mechanisms influencing students' readiness remain underexplored, leaving teachers with limited guidance on how to effectively foster student engagement and collaboration. Objective: Guided by self-determination theory, this study explored the mechanism through which satisfaction of basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) promotes students' readiness for interprofessional learning (teamwork and collaboration, professional identity) via collective capabilities (team cohesiveness and collective efficacy). Method: A total of 222 undergraduate students from different health and social care, as well as legal-related disciplines participated in this study. These students represented diverse disciplines including Medicine, Nursing, Social Work, Chinese Medicine, Pharmacy, Speech and Hearing Sciences, and Law. To examine the fit of the hypothesized model, sequential mediation analysis was employed. Results: Results indicated that autonomy, competence, and relatedness had significant total effects on teamwork/collaboration and professional identity dimensions of IPE readiness, with distinct mediation patterns. Team cohesiveness and collective efficacy served as significant mediators, with varying patterns across needs. For autonomy, partial mediation was observed with indirect effects accounting for 49.7% of the total effect on teamwork/collaboration. For competence, full mediation was evident with indirect effects explaining 87.5% of the total effect on teamwork/collaboration, with the sequential pathway through both mediators contributing 45.0%. Relatedness showed partial mediation with strong direct effects on professional identity (80.6% of total effect). Conclusion: Distinct patterns of mediation reveal that autonomy and relatedness shape IPE readiness through both direct and team-level pathways, whereas competence operates primarily via team cohesiveness and collective efficacy. Targeting both individual psychological needs and collective capabilities may enhance the effectiveness of interprofessional education programs. © 2026

Title: Power in sustainability transitions research: A scoping review of conceptual views and methodological patterns for newcomers
Abstract: Power has become a central theme in sustainability transitions research (STR) since the field’s political turn in the 2010s. Yet this literature remains difficult to navigate because it draws on diverse conceptualisations whose differences are not always made explicit. Readers may therefore struggle to identify how power is understood and how it is traced empirically. This article addresses this problem through a scoping review of 57 peer-reviewed journal articles that explicitly engage with power, combining a systematic Scopus search, backward and forward snowballing, and thematic analysis. The review identifies three broad analytical views of power centred on agency, structure, and their interaction. It also develops two practical tools. The first is a glossary that introduces recurring power-related concepts and points readers towards further reading. The second is a reading template that helps identify how studies define, locate, and operationalise power through their conceptual views, units of analysis, methods, adjacent traditions, and empirical signals. Together, these contributions provide an accessible entry point into power research in STR, while supporting experienced researchers in reflecting on their approaches and their dialogue with other conceptualisations in the field. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Yang J.; Lin S.; Liu Q.
Title: Parenting stress and picky eating severity in preschoolers: An exploratory cross-sectional analysis of potential pathways via parental self-efficacy
Abstract: Background: Parenting stress links to preschoolers’ picky eating, yet underlying pathways via parental self-efficacy (PSE) dimensions remain underexplored. This study examined whether general parenting self-efficacy, comprising efficacy and satisfaction dimensions, statistically mediates the association between parenting stress and picky eating severity, acknowledging that the measure assesses overall parenting competence rather than domain-specific feeding self-efficacy. Methods: This cross-sectional study involved 459 parent-child dyads from Urumqi, China. Using two-phase data collection, we assessed parenting stress, general PSE (efficacy and satisfaction), and picky eating. Hayes’ PROCESS macro (Model 4) explored parallel mediation, adjusting for child age, caregiver education, and family type. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness across bootstrap specifications. Results: Parenting stress correlated negatively with efficacy and satisfaction, which inversely associated with picky eating severity. Total association between stress and picky eating was significant (b = 0.047). Direct association remained significant but attenuated after mediation (b = 0.023). Both efficacy (b = 0.008) and satisfaction (b = 0.016) showed significant indirect associations, jointly explaining 51.24% of the total relationship. Notably, satisfaction's indirect pathway was approximately twice as strong as efficacy's (contrast analysis confirmed this difference was statistically significant). Conclusions: Parenting stress associates with picky eating partially through dual general PSE pathways, with emotional satisfaction being the stronger link. Effect sizes were small and may be partly attributable to the large sample size (N = 459), warranting cautious interpretation of practical significance. Findings support social cognitive theory, highlighting affective pathways in feeding. Interventions should enhance both parental competence and caregiving fulfillment. Longitudinal research is needed to validate these exploratory pathways. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Reevaluating the empirical support for a lens-based account: dissecting comparative fit and reconstructive category guessing
Abstract: The lens-based account of intersectional stereotyping (Petsko et al., 2022) proposes that perceivers put on social “lenses” for categorizing their environment that exhibit comparative fit with observed behavior in a given situation. Support for this claim comes from studies using the Who-Said-What paradigm (Taylor et al., 1978), in which category membership was manipulated to covary with speakers' pro versus contra positions in a discussion along one of two crossed social dimensions. However, as noted by Klauer et al. (2014), this paradigm is vulnerable to a critical limitation: when category membership can be inferred from statement content, apparent categorization effects may reflect reconstructive category guessing rather than genuine category memory. Across three experiments (N = 764), we tested whether comparative fit modulates social categorization beyond such reconstructive processes. We replicated strong comparative fit effects when category membership was inferable from discussion statements, yielding large effects comparable to those reported by Petsko et al. (2022). Crucially, when participants responded to discussion-unrelated statements that no longer allowed inference of category membership, these effects disappeared, indicating that prior findings were substantially inflated by reconstructive guessing. In a final experiment, we introduced an alternative source of situational fit by spatially aligning speakers with opposing discussion positions during encoding of discussion-unrelated statements. Under these conditions, a significant but markedly smaller comparative fit effect emerged. Our findings suggest that comparative fit can enhance social categorization along the fitting dimension beyond reconstructive guessing. However, this situational lens is rapidly “put off” once the fit is no longer present. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Inc. Title: Insurance and land-use permanence in natural rubber: Implications for land transitions and carbon dynamics from Hainan, China
Abstract: This study evaluates how China's price-index insurance policy affects natural rubber land transitions in Hainan Province. We utilize satellite imagery to classify natural rubber land based on its unique phenological characteristics, specifically the leaf-off and refoliation signals. We then conduct a village-level analysis using a 2018–2021 panel of 719 villages to study the impact of insurance coverage on these land transitions. To establish causality, an instrumental variable (IV) strategy is introduced. Our results indicate that a 1% rise in the insured share causes a 0.055–0.237% increase in next-year rubber acreage. At the grower level, higher premiums and rubber prices reduce insurance take-up, whereas subsidies increase participation. Policy simulations show that a 1% increase in total subsidy expenditure raises insured acreage by approximately 0.29%, translating into a 0.016–0.069% increase in rubber acreage. The estimated carbon benefits exceed fiscal costs when valued using the social cost of carbon, although not at prevailing domestic carbon-market prices. Future climate projections further indicate the need for dynamic subsidy adjustments to sustain insurance participation under increasing climate risk. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Perceived social norms and video gaming in emerging adults: A cross-sectional investigation
Abstract: Background Problematic video gaming is a growing concern among emerging adults. While perceived social norms are well-established predictors of substance use, their role in problematic gaming remains understudied. This study examined whether descriptive norms (estimates of others’ gaming frequency) and injunctive norms (estimates of others’ approval of gaming) were associated with gaming frequency, duration, and problem gaming severity across three reference groups: typical students, same-gendered students, and close friends. Method Participants were 1,295 Canadian undergraduates recruited from five universities who reported past-12-month video gaming. Participants completed self-report surveys of normative gaming perceptions, personal gaming behaviours, and gaming-related problems. Path models tested whether perceived norms were associated with problem gaming severity via personal past-30-day gaming frequency and average daily duration. Results As hypothesized, participants estimated that peers gamed more often than themselves, with the largest estimations for more distal groups. Descriptive norms were positively associated with personal gaming frequency across all three groups, and with duration for the same-gender and close-friend groups; both were associated with greater problem gaming severity. Injunctive norms were associated with personal gaming frequency, duration, and problem gaming severity only for the close-friend group. Effect sizes were strongest for close friends, then same-gendered peers, then typical students. Conclusions Findings extend the social norms literature to problematic gaming and identify perceived norms as a correlate of problem gaming in emerging adults. Longitudinal/intervention research is needed to clarify the direction of these associations and evaluate whether personalized normative feedback may help reduce problem gaming. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Schröder M.; Yastrebov G.
Title: Postmaterial emancipative values emerge over time rather than solely through generational succession
Abstract: Value change is often attributed to generational replacement. Modernization theory has popularized the idea that as younger generations expand in the population, their postmaterial emancipative values come to dominate, while more conservative values fade away with older generations. Yet this cohort-centered view discounts that contemporaneous period effects can shift the values of all cohorts simultaneously. Using data on postmaterial emancipative values from the Integrated Values Survey (1981–2022), covering 122,205 respondents in 13 countries, we conduct a bounding age–period–cohort analysis. The analysis leverages modernization theory's own assumption that age effects on emancipative values are not positive. Under this constraint, period effects are positive in seven countries and exceed cohort effects in four throughout the admissible age-effect range. In the remaining nine countries, cohort effects exceed period effects under zero or sufficiently weak negative age effects. Assuming more negative age effects mechanically strengthens period effects while weakening cohort effects. These results challenge cohort replacement as a sufficient general account of long-term value modernization, showing that the relative importance of period and cohort effects depends on the country and assumptions about aging. © 2026 The Authors

Title: JustGreen: Health impact assessment of urban vegetation across the 200 most populated US cities
Abstract: Urban vegetation provides substantial health benefits in US cities, yet the protection that existing green cover delivers has not been quantified across a broad national sample. We conducted a census-tract-level health impact assessment across the 200 most populated US cities, estimating premature deaths, stroke cases, and dementia cases attributable to current greenness and the additional burden preventable through a 10% greenness increase. Using peak-greenness Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) values derived from Sentinel-2 satellite imagery at 10 m resolution, population attributable fractions applied to county- and state-level baseline disease rates, and dose–response functions from published cohort studies and meta-analyses, we estimated that existing urban vegetation is associated with 133,698 fewer premature deaths annually (95% uncertainty interval [UI]: 97,056 to 214,462), 24,721 fewer stroke cases (95% UI: 11,700 to 31,784), and 16,349 fewer dementia cases (95% UI: 10,609 to 22,403). A 10% vegetation increase would be associated with an additional 18,100 fewer deaths, 3,288 fewer strokes, and 2,125 fewer dementia cases. Per-capita benefits vary 14-fold across cities, driven principally by vegetation level. Equity analysis using the CDC Social Vulnerability Index across 28,620 census tracts shows that the most socially vulnerable neighborhoods have 18% lower vegetation and receive 20% fewer mortality benefits per 100,000 adults than the least vulnerable. These estimates represent the statistical burden attributable to current vegetation exposure rather than individually identifiable prevented events, and they quantify what is at risk when existing urban green space is removed. We identify 4,185 doubly burdened tracts as priority targets for equitable greening investment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: How children and adults judge retaliation in socio-moral contexts
Abstract: Our study examined how children and adults evaluate retaliatory transgressions, with particular attention to whether a retaliatory act matched or mismatched the domain of the initial provoking act. Children ages 4–9 and adults (n = 153) judged the seriousness and punish-worthiness of moral and conventional transgressions that were either unprovoked or retaliatory. Across ages, moral transgressions were judged as more serious and more deserving of punishment than conventional transgressions, and unprovoked acts were often judged more harshly than retaliatory ones. Adults were generally more lenient than children, although over-retaliations did not receive much leniency from any age group. Developmental differences emerged primarily in judgments of conventional transgressions, with younger children judging retaliatory acts more leniently than unprovoked acts, whereas older children and adults did not. These findings suggest that the role of provocation in moral judgment changes across development and depends on the relationship between the provoking and retaliatory acts. Participants also judged victims as feeling better after retaliating, with this pattern strongest among adults. Together, these findings suggest that judgments of retaliation are shaped by developmental and contextual considerations, while perceptions of retaliation as emotionally beneficial increase with age. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Peer bullying victimization and psychological well-being among Turkish and Syrian adolescents: The mediating roles of school adjustment and belonging
Abstract: Using a cross-sectional quantitative design, this study examined academic adjustment, social adjustment, school acceptance, and school exclusion as statistical indirect associations linking peer bullying victimization with psychological well-being among Turkish and Syrian middle school students attending Turkish-medium public middle schools in Kilis, a setting shaped by the long-term presence of Syrian families. Grounded in Ecological Systems Theory, the Need to Belong Theory, and the Risk and Resilience Framework, data were collected from 290 students (165 Turkish, 125 Syrian) in Kilis, Türkiye, using researcher-supervised paper-based self-report questionnaires. Multi-group structural equation modeling showed that victimization was negatively associated with academic adjustment, social adjustment, and school acceptance and positively associated with school exclusion. Victimization remained directly associated with lower psychological well-being, and all four school-related variables showed significant indirect statistical associations, with school exclusion showing the largest specific indirect association. Ordinal multi-group CFA using WLSMV supported configural, metric, and scalar/threshold invariance across nationality groups, allowing latent mean comparisons. Structural invariance further indicated that the regression pattern was statistically comparable across groups. Syrian students showed higher latent means for victimization and school exclusion and lower latent means for academic adjustment, social adjustment, school acceptance, and psychological well-being than Turkish students. The findings indicate that differences in average school experiences can coexist with statistically comparable patterns of association among Turkish and Syrian students in Kilis. The cross-sectional design and absence of direct measures of language proficiency, acculturation, and discrimination limit causal interpretation and explanations of the group differences. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: (Un)polarized forests? Disentangling drivers of polarization in the public debate around German forests affected by climate change
Abstract: Polarization is an increasingly prevalent issue in environmental conflicts, often simplified as two opposing arguments. However, most studies lack theoretical conceptualizations of polarization to reveal its complexity, drivers, and effects. By combining concepts of polarization with discourse analysis, this study provides a nuanced perspective on the social construction of land-use conflicts and their surrounding polarization. It demonstrates how disentangling underlying drivers and power relations enhances the understanding of conflicts, considering their context-specificity. To this end, I empirically scrutinize the factors of the deep-rooted conflict between forestry and nature conservation in Germany. The analysis focuses on public and political debates between 2018 and 2020 on forests affected by climate change. Large-scale forest damage has sparked controversy over whether to actively adapt forests or rely on the ecosystem's self-regulation. While both sides instrumentalize climate change to emphasize the urgency of their measures to ‘save’ the forests and make them climate-resilient, the results demonstrate the entanglements of narratives and subject positions beyond this dichotomy. Rather than being issue-related, polarization is mainly driven by affective sentiments toward pre-constructed actor groups that are discursively reproduced. Polarization is further reinforced through perceived polarization, expressed through simplifications, generalizations, misconceptions, and dismissive reframing of opposing arguments. Instead of taking the negative effects of polarization for granted, the discussion highlights the need for research to critically reflect on the dynamics of polarization and the ways in which it manifests. This understanding is crucial for resolving entrenched debates, unfolding the generative potential of conflict, and allowing alternative solutions to emerge. © 2026 The Authors

Title: From occurrence to consequence: Unraveling urban building fire risk
Abstract: Building fires remain a major public safety concern in U.S. cities, threatening lives, property, and critical infrastructure. Despite substantial investments in fire protection, significant disparities persist, underscoring the need for a holistic, data-driven understanding of fire risk. In this work, we analyze more than one million fire incident reports and integrate them with community-level socioeconomic indicators, building inventories, weather conditions, and incident-specific characteristics. Our study makes two key contributions: a comprehensive framework that traces fire risk from occurrence to consequence, and a detailed city-level fire risk ranking system for U.S. cities. By examining the full progression of fire events, we identify structural, environmental, and social drivers that disproportionately endanger communities with older infrastructure and economic disadvantages. Socioeconomic disparities intensify both the frequency and severity of fire incidents, while incident-specific factors, such as ignition sources, ignition locations, and the presence of detectors or automatic extinguishing systems, substantially influence fire outcomes. Lower-risk cities generally exhibit more favorable socioeconomic conditions and a higher prevalence of fire safety features. By pinpointing high-risk communities and targeting critical vulnerabilities, this framework supports strategies that further improve fire safety and foster more resilient cities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Towards socially acceptable XR agents: A modular approach for user interaction
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Recent advancements in eXtended Reality (XR) technologies have opened new opportunities for integrating virtual and physical environments, enabling natural immersive user experiences. This paper addresses the challenge of developing socially acceptable XR agents that can engage in complex, meaningful interactions across various social and public settings. Specifically, we propose a modular architecture for enhancing user-XR agent interaction, integrated into the framework of the Horizon Europe project “Socially-acceptable Extended Reality Models And Systems (SERMAS)”. The architecture is designed to ensure adaptability, scalability, and the integration of diverse communication modalities, including verbal and non-verbal cues. Its main components work together to enable seamless user detection and communication. In particular, the Detection module plays a key role in managing the agent’s awareness of the surrounding environment. Its functions include identifying user intentions, monitoring group dynamics, and inferring emotional states, thereby increasing responsiveness and enabling more contextually grounded behavior. In contrast, the Communication module employs Large Language Models for personalized verbal responses, and recognizes gestures and body language for enriched non-verbal communication. Together, these approaches guarantee contextually relevant, personalized, and emotionally intelligent interactions. The architecture supports scalability and the flexible integration or replacement of modules, fostering socially acceptable user-XR agent interactions. Its real-world applicability is demonstrated across three deployment scenarios, including a digital receptionist integrated with a physical robot, an XR-based security training system for journalists practicing safety-critical procedures, and a digital assistant supporting customers in a post-office environment. The functionality of the proposed system is presented through the implementation of the XR Agent interacting with users. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems
Abstract: Artificial systems increasingly behave in ways that resemble humans. But is that sufficient to make us see them as conscious, or as having related mental states? We contrast two broad possibilities. People may rely on a single general principle: the more appropriately an agent responds to its environment, the more conscious it is, whether human or artificial. We call this a functionalist attribution. Alternatively, people may reserve consciousness for certain kinds of beings: even an artificial system that behaves just as responsively as a human is judged less conscious. This is an essentialist attribution. A further question is whether this pattern is unique to consciousness or extends to closely related constructs such as awareness. In two pre-registered sets of studies (five experiments, N = 1092), UK participants read scenarios describing human or artificial agents whose responsiveness to spatial, social, and temporal features of the environment varied, and rated the agents' consciousness and awareness, either separately or in conjunction. Attributions of consciousness followed an essentialist logic: at similar levels of responsiveness, participants consistently attributed greater consciousness to humans. Attributions of awareness followed a functionalist pattern: for both humans and artificial agents, awareness increased steadily with responsiveness, although humans were rated more aware at the highest levels. These findings suggest that people use different inferential rules for different mental concepts. Consciousness is treated as depending on what an agent is; awareness largely on what an agent does. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Singhal I.; Yang F.
Title: Living beyond duty: People see meaning and happiness in supererogation
Abstract: In the timeless human quest for meaning and happiness, living a moral life has long been viewed as essential. But how do people determine which actions are most fulfilling? We find that when people evaluate the worth of morally good acts, it is not only what we do, but how society views our actions that matters. Five studies (N = 1800) across three cultures (U.S., China and India) examined if and how framing societal beliefs about actions as obligatory (fulfilling moral duty) versus supererogatory (exceeding moral duty) shaped people's judgments of meaning and happiness from moral actions. In Study 1, participants recommended greater behavioral prioritization and weekly time allocations to supererogatory (versus obligatory) actions, when giving advice intended to enhance meaning and happiness both for themselves and others. In Study 2, perceiving the same actions as more supererogatory was associated with greater meaning and happiness. Studies 3 (within-subjects) and 4 (between-subjects) experimentally demonstrated that framing identical moral actions as supererogatory rather than obligatory led to higher meaning and happiness judgments. These effects were mediated by inferring greater perceived choice and moral goodness from supererogation (Studies 3–5), and moderated by participants' own beliefs about the actions (Studies 5a and 5b). Similar mediation and moderation mechanisms were observed across the U.S., China, and India, except Indian participants associated even greater meaning with obligations. Together, these findings suggest that going beyond the call of moral duty is not just beneficial for society, but seen as rewarding in people's own lives too. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: “To be a personal trainer, you have to look like 4% body fat”: How online personal trainers negotiate social media and body image
Abstract: The online personal training industry is continuing to increase in popularity. Sociocultural pressures for personal trainers to maintain a certain physique to be deemed credible and marketable to consumers are well-documented, however no studies have qualitatively explored this in online personal trainers. Whilst previous research has highlighted that consuming certain types of fitness content may negatively impact body image, there is a paucity of research exploring the relationship between content creators and body image.This study aimed to examine how online trainers navigate social media as a digital workplace and their perceptions of its influence on their body image. 17 online coaches (Mage = 33.5; S.D. = 7.4 years), 58.8% female, participated in semi-structured interviews in which they discussed social media, body image and self-selected online content. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Overall, trainers viewed maintaining a social media presence as non-negotiable for business. However, participants also experienced pressure to uphold unrealistic standards online, including showcasing a lean physique and presenting an image of authenticity online whilst concealing body image struggles from consumers. Whilst some trainers rejected these industry standards, other trainers leveraged these norms by utilising their physique to gain traction on social media and enhance perceived desirability and competence to consumers. Findings contribute to improved understanding of appearance-pressures and highlight the need for greater education and support around body image within the online fitness industry. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Developing a competency model for clinical nurse educators to support nursing career ladder advancement: A grounded theory study
Abstract: Background: Clinical nurse educators greatly impact the development of high-quality clinical learning experiences. However, globally, the role remains inconsistently defined, and competency frameworks are rarely integrated with structured career ladder systems, limiting professional development and workforce sustainability. Objective: This study aimed to develop an empirically grounded competency model for clinical nurse educators integrated with a structured career ladder to support progressive professional development in clinical education settings. Methods: A qualitative study using a Straussian grounded theory approach was conducted in two teaching hospitals in Indonesia. Data were collected through focus group discussions with 16 clinical nurse educators, in-depth interviews with 9 clinical education coordinators, and participant observations. Initial purposive sampling was followed by theoretical sampling. Data were analyzed concurrently using open, axial, and selective coding and the constant comparative method. The competency subdomains generated from the grounded theory findings were subsequently validated through a two-round Delphi process involving 28 experts. Experts rated the subdomains using a 4-point Likert scale, with consensus predefined as ≥70% agreement. Results: Six overarching themes were identified: qualifications for becoming a clinical nurse educator; specialized competencies; lack of clarity in nurse mentoring programs; regulation of student clinical guidance by higher education institutions; limited managerial support; and expectations for clearer role definitions and career pathways. These themes were synthesized into five core competency domains: Ethical, Legal, and Cultural Clinical Practice; Leadership and Clinical Education Management; Clinical Teaching Competencies; Research and Evidence-Based Practice; and Social Competence. The two-round Delphi process with 28 experts established consensus for 171 competency subdomains across these five domains and informed a four-level career ladder. Conclusion: The resulting model integrates pedagogical, clinical, ethical, managerial, research, and social competencies with progressive career development. It provides an empirically grounded and expert-validated framework to clarify the clinical nurse educator role and support structured career development in hospital-based clinical education. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Karthik Rajan, C.S. (57940465600); Jayaraman, Senthil Kumaran (61024691800)
Title: From prediction to preference: Algorithmic incentive sensitization and the neurocognitive shaping of desire
Abstract: Predictive algorithms are commonly understood as tools that infer and respond to user preferences, implicitly assuming that the informational environment is independent of the user's learned behavior. This paper departs from that assumption, arguing that in algorithmically mediated environments, exposure is recursively shaped by prior behavior, creating policy-dependent conditions that existing models do not adequately capture. We introduce Algorithmic Incentive Sensitization (AIS), a constrained theoretical framework specifying conditions under which learning becomes self-referential, describing how recursive algorithmic feedback may influence motivational salience and desire over time. AIS proposes that engagement with predictive systems recruits three established neurocognitive mechanisms: (1) Predictive Coding, through which algorithms curate low-surprise informational environments that progressively constrain users' internal models of value; (2) Incentive Salience, whereby algorithmically amplified cues disproportionately engage dopaminergic “wanting” systems independent of hedonic liking; and (3) Reinforcement-Driven Neuroadaptation, whereby repeated engagement strengthens cortico-striatal pathways associated with algorithmically predicted rewards. Together, these mechanisms form a self-reinforcing loop through which algorithmic systems may bias reward learning and motivational sensitivity. Under such conditions, learning processes operate on behavior-contingent exposure, generating systematic biases that standard formulations of reinforcement learning, predictive coding, or incentive salience do not explicitly address. Rather than framing algorithmic personalization as a deterministic or intentional manipulation, AIS conceptualizes influence as an emergent property of recursive human–algorithm interaction in which exposure distributions are endogenously shaped by prior behavior. The paper concludes by outlining testable hypotheses and interdisciplinary research directions for empirically evaluating AIS across computational, behavioral, and neuroscientific settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Moore, Jared (57211010986); Choi, Yejin (36172231400); Levine, Sydney (57202333145)
Title: Intuitions of compromise: Utilitarianism, egalitarianism, contractualism
Abstract: What is the best compromise in a situation where different people value different things? The most common method for answering this question is to look at all the options, add up the utility per person associated with each, and pick the option with the largest sum. This approach seems like the obvious, theory-neutral solution, though, in fact, it relies on substantive utilitarian commitments. A second, quite common approach, involves integrating egalitarian concerns, and picking an option that trades off maximizing utility with equalizing outcomes. But there is an important, though often-ignored, third approach as well: a contractualist approach, which models what rational actors would agree to. In this paper, we test the proposals of these three competing preference aggregation algorithms in social decision-making contexts that are systematically sampled across a wide range. While the dominant approach to value aggregation up to now has been utilitarian, we find that participants strongly prefer the aggregations recommended by the contractualist algorithm, which also dominates the egalitarian approach across a range of parameterizations. Finally, we compare the judgments of large language models (LLMs) to those of our (human) participants, finding important misalignment between model and human preferences. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Bridging the detection-to-action gap with CLARITY: a scoping review and safety architecture for medication safety clinical decision support systems
Abstract: Detecting risk is not the same as preventing harm. This distinction is central to medication safety clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where artificial intelligence (AI) may improve risk detection yet still produce alerts or recommendations that are difficult to interpret, prioritize, or act on during routine care. We examine this problem as the Detection-to-Action Gap, in which recognized medication risk does not become a context-sensitive and accountable clinical response. Unlike capability-focused reviews, this scoping review examines the workflow, uncertainty, and governance conditions that determine whether detection leads to safer action. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2015 to January 2026. Eligible studies included direct medication-safety studies and a restricted set of adjacent studies reporting transferable safety mechanisms. Fifty studies were charted and synthesized thematically: 25 provided direct medication-safety evidence and 25 provided transferable mechanism evidence. Medication-specific evidence showed movement beyond rule-based alerting toward machine-learning, LLM-based, and knowledge-augmented approaches; retrieval-grounded and agentic mechanisms were supported mainly by adjacent-domain evidence and require medication-specific validation. Safety gains remain constrained by limited longitudinal awareness, poorly managed uncertainty, and governance added after deployment rather than embedded in system logic. We therefore propose CLARITY, a safety-control architecture linking longitudinal modeling, evidence-constrained reasoning, confidence-aware action routing, human oversight, and auditability. CLARITY supports anticipation, proportionate response, and governance-controlled refinement, providing a pathway from alert-centric tools toward governed decision systems. The Detection-to-Action Gap may inform safety–critical domains where automated systems convert risk signals into accountable action. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Jiang H.; Wang H.; Su Y.; Niu Z.; Xu L.
Title: Distributed anonymous authentication and privacy-preserving intelligent recommendation system in vehicular networks
Abstract: The rapid advancement of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) necessitates robust solutions that balance user privacy with efficient service delivery, particularly for personalized charging station recommendations. This paper proposes a lightweight anonymous authentication and secure computing service integration scheme based on distributed center architecture. By leveraging a distributed dual-cloud architecture, the scheme ensures secure and traceable anonymous authentication while facilitating efficient vehicle-to-service communication. Vehicle users encrypt their preference data, which is processed using matrix factorization and secure multi-party computation to deliver accurate, privacy-preserving charging station recommendations. The quick reconnection mechanism we established reduces re-authentication time costs by roughly 53 percent, while the dual-server architecture supports privacy computing for vehicles after authentication. The framework integrates multi-source heterogeneous data, such as real-time traffic and charging station status, to enhance recommendation accuracy and timeliness. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong anonymity, traceability, and low-latency performance, offering a practical and scalable solution for secure, intelligent IoV services. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Eggestrand H.
Title: Mobilising values in municipal governance? A case study of Gothenburg’s sustainable lifestyles strategy
Abstract: Sustainability transitions research has increasingly “turned to values” as central to shaping and legitimising transformative change, often implying a reorientation away from dominant logics of individualism and economic growth towards sustainability-aligned values (SAVs) such as collectivism, care, and justice. Yet empirical accounts of how such values are mobilised through governance arrangements and practices remain limited.This article examines how SAVs are mobilised through municipal strategy work, drawing on an in-depth qualitative case study of the City of Gothenburg’s Sustainable Lifestyles Strategy. The article operationalises four modes of value mobilisation (enabling, including, shifting, and reflecting) through an interpretive analysis of municipal transition governance, understood as co-constituted through everyday governance practices.Empirically, the analysis draws on policy documents, observations, and group interviews with public officials involved in the strategy’s development and implementation. The findings show how different modes of value mobilisation operate in tandem in practice, unfolding through processes of coordination, deliberation, and experimentation, while simultaneously being shaped by institutional constraints that limit more far-reaching value shifts. In this sense, the strategy functions as a performative and exploratory governance device, altering the conditions under which actors interpret and negotiate responsibility, agency, and possibilities for change.The article contributes to sustainability transitions research by foregrounding value mobilisation as a constitutive dimension of transition governance. By showing how governance arrangements reshape both the material and interpretive conditions for action, and thus which values become actionable in practice, the study advances understandings of how sustainability transitions are governed, negotiated, and sometimes circumscribed. © 2026 The Author.
