Authors: Suk K.
Title: Convergent microglial and astrocytic responses across diverse stress paradigms: Integrating inflammation, metabolism, and behavior
Abstract: The central nervous system responds to diverse challenges through convergent glial mechanisms, yet most reviews examine single stressor paradigms in isolation. This review uniquely integrates current knowledge across five major stress categories (psychosocial, immune/inflammatory, infectious, injury/damage, and metabolic), revealing both shared pathways and stimulus-specific glial responses that have not been systematically compared. Because microglia and astrocytes are the principal immune-metabolic sensors mediating these responses, this review is centered on these two cell types, while acknowledging that oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and ependymal cells also participate in stress-related glial pathology, particularly with respect to white matter and cerebrospinal fluid homeostasis. While all stressors activate common inflammatory cascades including NF-κB signaling, complement activation, and inflammasome assembly, they elicit distinguishable molecular signatures. For instance, psychosocial stress uniquely engages type I interferon responses driving microglial synapse elimination. Viral infections produce severe metabolic reprogramming, hijacking host metabolism to support viral replication while depleting cellular NAD + and ATP. Autoimmune inflammation generates lipid-laden disease-associated microglia with upregulated cholesterol metabolism genes. Unlike previous reviews focusing solely on inflammation or metabolism, we emphasize their bidirectional integration as a unifying principle. Inflammatory signals trigger metabolic shifts toward aerobic glycolysis, generating lactate serving dual functions as neuronal fuel and inflammatory mediator. This metabolic reprogramming, orchestrated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, and mTOR, creates feedback loops linking glial dysfunction to neuronal alterations. Complement-mediated synaptic pruning, disrupted neuron-glia metabolic coupling, and impaired neurotrophic support converge to produce depression, cognitive impairment, and sickness behaviors. Individual variability reflects interactions among genetic factors, sex, age, and blood-brain barrier integrity. This cross-paradigm comparative approach identifies high-value therapeutic targets applicable across multiple conditions rather than single diseases. We propose integrated intervention strategies simultaneously targeting inflammatory and metabolic pathways, guided by single-cell profiling for personalized medicine tailored to individual patient molecular signatures. We further discuss the conceptual overlaps inherent to the five-category classification scheme adopted here and outline the limitations of extrapolating across heterogeneous stress paradigms, glial cell types, and species. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Addressing Energy Poverty in the Developed Countries: A Case Study from Japan
Abstract: The United Nations outlines the alleviation of energy poverty within the Sustainable Development Goals. In the developing parts of the world, the focus of energy poverty is placed on the lack of accessibility to energy. In the developed parts of the world, on the other hand, it is due to the lack of affordability to pay energy or utility bills. As the understanding of the situation of energy poverty in small or rural communities is still missing in many developed parts of the world, this chapter explores who is energy poor, who is feeling energy poor, and what factors lead to energy poverty. The research is based on the analysis of the data collected through a survey study conducted in Japan. The results of the analysis confirm that there are different levels of energy affordability in different living environments, with the level of income and the level of education both associated with the levels of energy affordability in Japan. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors: Chatzi A.V.
Title: Evaluating healthcare professionals’ perceptions of medicine risk communications: A survey with Quantitative and Qualitative Analyses
Abstract: Background Effective medicine risk communication is a cornerstone of patient safety. Although safety information is routinely disseminated to healthcare professionals (HCPs), limited evidence exists on how these communications are perceived and acted upon in clinical practice. Objective To assess how national medicine risk communications are distributed and utilized by doctors and pharmacists, and to explore key behavioural and perceptual factors influencing engagement with these communications. Methods A cross-sectional mixed-methods study employed the DENS (Distribution, rEach, coNtent, utiliSation) questionnaire. The survey was distributed online to all registered doctors and pharmacists in Ireland via regulatory mailing lists. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, non-parametric tests, and exploratory factor analysis; qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Results Of 622 responses (431 complete), most participants trusted the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA). Direct Healthcare Professional Communication (DHPC) was preferred over and Drug Safety Newsletter (DSN) as a communication channel. Engagement was shaped by trust, relevance, clarity, and format, while barriers included time constraints, perceived impracticality, and habitual practice. Digital formats were strongly favoured for accessibility. Subgroup analyses revealed differences by gender, clinical setting, and professional role in preferences and compliance behaviours. Conclusions Medicine risk communication must extend beyond information delivery to become concise, role-relevant, and behaviourally informed. Tailoring content to professional contexts and addressing barriers such as time pressure and entrenched habits can improve uptake and patient safety outcomes. Findings highlight the need for adaptive, user-centred communication strategies integrated into safety management systems. © 2026 The Author.

Title: Reconstructing flood-induced human mobility using LLM agent with disaster context adaptation
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Understanding human mobility during extreme flood events is critical for emergency evacuation and resilient transport planning, yet flood-induced behavioral heterogeneity remains difficult to characterize. Progress has been constrained by data scarcity and the inherent complexity of emergency decision-making, which often induces abnormal travel behaviors and anomalous mobility fluxes. We propose the Disaster-aware Trajectory Generator (DTG), integrating Large Language Model (LLM) agents into an agent-based framework to generate individual-level mobility trajectories under evolving urban flood conditions. Validated against 1.32 billion mobility records from the 2021 “7.20” Zhengzhou flood in China, DTG outperforms all traditional and LLM-enabled baselines, achieving a flood-induced inflow-shift prediction accuracy of 0.713 with outflow and OD distribution JSD of 0.069 and 0.047 during the disaster period. By combining accessibility-constrained disaster context reasoning with the representation of heterogeneous socio-demographic responses, DTG reveals critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and abnormal behavioral patterns, offering actionable insights for flood-resilient transport planning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Patchwork integration: Adaptation challenges of Ukrainian refugee children in Polish schools through the eyes of their mothers
Abstract: Schools have become central sites for the integration of Ukrainian refugee children in Poland, yet formal access to education does not necessarily ensure meaningful participation, belonging, or psychological well-being. This study examines how Ukrainian caregivers make sense of their children’s school adaptation as part of broader integration processes, focusing on children’s sociocultural and psychological adjustment. We conducted 26 interviews with Ukrainian refugee women caring for preschool- or school-aged children enrolled in Polish educational institutions. Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, we developed Patchwork Integration as the overarching theme, reflecting the fragmented and uneven nature of school-based integration, which depended heavily on individual actors rather than coordinated system-level support. Five themes were identified: (1) positive surface narratives masking psychological distress and challenges (All is good, or so it seems); (2) individuals stepping in to compensate for systemic gaps (Forced to step in when the system fails); (3) pressure on children to conform culturally and linguistically (Assimilation in the guise of integration); (4) language as a marker of belonging but also psychological distress (More than a language barrier); and (5) the crucial but inconsistent role of relationships and agency in supporting adaptation (Connected and capable: More than the systemic minimum). Findings underscore the urgent need for coherent, system-level support that goes beyond well-meaning but improvised individual efforts. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Lin B.; Xu J.
Title: How energy transmission infrastructure affects production strategy? Evidence from China’s UHV projects
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Ultra-High Voltage projects represent a critical shift in energy logistics from physical fuel transport to efficient “power-by-wire” transmission. Using UHV construction as a quasi-natural experiment and matching the National Tax Survey with China’s Customs trade records, this paper examines how improved electricity transmission reshapes firms’ production and product portfolios. The results show: (1) UHV operation significantly increases firms’ electricity use and output; (2) greater electricity reliability induces firms to drop non-core products, narrow their product range, and concentrate resources on core products; and (3) production gains occur in both electricity-sending and electricity-receiving regions and are stronger in electricity-dependent industries, whereas product-range adjustment is more pronounced in receiving regions and among firms with lower electricity dependence. Further analyses show that product adjustment is concentrated among non-state-owned, large, and export-intensive firms. These findings provide micro-level evidence that clean energy transmission infrastructure improves resource allocation and supports sustainable industrial development. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Digital Learning Platforms and Language Skills Development: The Mediating Roles of Student Engagement and Self-Efficacy across Educational Levels
Abstract: The growing adoption of digital learning platforms has transformed language education by creating interactive and flexible learning environments. This study examines the influence of digital learning platform use on language skills development while investigating the mediating roles of student engagement and student self-efficacy and the moderating role of educational level. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 412 students through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using correlation, regression, mediation, and moderation analyses. The findings revealed that digital learning platform use positively affects student engagement, self-efficacy, and language skills development. Student engagement and self-efficacy were also found to significantly enhance language skills development. Furthermore, educational level significantly moderates the relationship between digital learning platform use and language skills development, indicating that the effectiveness of digital platforms varies across educational stages. Mediation analysis demonstrated that both student engagement and self-efficacy serve as significant mechanisms through which digital learning platforms improve language learning outcomes, with self-efficacy exhibiting a stronger indirect effect. The study contributes to the understanding of technology enhanced language learning by integrating technological, behavioral, psychological, and contextual factors within a single framework and offers practical insights for educational stakeholders seeking to improve language proficiency through digital learning environments. © 2027 FahrenHouse. Authors: Luu S.T.; Vo T.; Nguyen L.-M.
Title: M-RAV: Multimodal retrieve-augment-verify framework for boosting zero-shot fact verification system with large language models
Abstract: The rapid spread of multimodal content, combining text and images, has fueled the rise of misleading information online, making multimodal fact-checking increasingly vital. However, large language models (LLMs) often struggle with cross-modality reasoning to verify claims directly. To address this, we introduce M-RAV, a portable multimodal fact-checking framework that enhances LLMs’ reasoning capabilities. M-RAV operates in four key steps: it Multimodally Retrieves relevant evidence, Augments alignment between text and images by explaining their consistency, assigning the relevance score for each evidence explanation, and Verifies claims using this augmented evidence. By clearly explaining the relationship between text and image evidence in a way that guides LLMs, M-RAV significantly improves fact-verification accuracy. Evaluated on three benchmark multimodal fact-checking datasets, M-RAV demonstrates efficiency even in zero-shot settings. Title: Flexibility of hierarchical reasoning across age and species
Abstract: Hierarchical reasoning underlies complex abilities such as language, mathematics, and tool-use. In this study, we examined how hierarchical reasoning flexibly varies in adults across cultures, children, crows, and monkeys. We also tested hierarchical reasoning across varied task complexities and with stimuli from both visual-perceptual and semantic-conceptual relational domains. We conducted Bayesian modelling analyses with both previously published data (Ferrigno et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2022) and newly collected data. These data were cumulatively from US adults, Tsimane adults from an indigenous community at a field location in Bolivia, 3-to-6-year-old US children, rhesus monkeys, and carrion crows. We found evidence for hierarchical reasoning across age and species, though with much individual and cross-population variation. Adults exhibited the most consistent reliance on hierarchical mechanisms, while children and non-humans showed graded performance influenced by task complexity and stimulus type. In summary, the deployment of hierarchical mechanisms varies across contexts rather than operating as an all-or-none capability. These findings suggest that hierarchical reasoning may be a flexible ability—not necessarily unique to humans, but rather emerging through incremental increases in cognitive capacities across development and evolution. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Zhang Y.; Li M.; Li J.; Wu J.; Wang L.
Title: Is the will to learn sufficient for a deep approach? Longitudinal relationships between achievement goals and approaches to homework and the moderating role of perceived teacher autonomy support
Abstract: Achievement goal theory and the student approaches to learning framework constitute two core perspectives for explaining student motivation and behavior. However, there remains a dearth of longitudinal evidence as to whether goals drive learning approaches or learning approaches shape goals. To address this gap, the present study tracked 2108 middle school students over a one-year interval, assessing their achievement goals, homework approaches, and perceived teacher autonomy support in the context of mathematics homework. This investigation aims to uncover the longitudinal predictive relationships between these constructs and the moderating role of perceived teacher support. The findings indicate that initial goal orientations failed to longitudinally predict the adoption of a deep approach to homework. Conversely, the actual application of a deep approach reversely predicted both mastery-approach and performance-approach goals. Furthermore, a negative reciprocal relationship emerged between these approach goals (mastery-approach and performance-approach) and a surface approach: mastery-approach and performance-approach goals negatively predicted the surface approach, which, in turn, negatively predicted both goal orientations. Additionally, the results reveal that a high level of perceived teacher autonomy support in homework serves as a crucial external condition for translating motivation into deep approaches. Taken together, these results suggest that a deep approach functions more as an antecedent to achievement goals rather than a consequence. Moreover, adequate teacher autonomy support can enhance the translation of mastery-oriented goals into deep homework behaviors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wei X.; Kong Y.; Zhen F.
Title: Exploring the non-linear effect of street-scale built environments on short-distance travel of the elderly: A case study in Nanjing, China
Abstract: Understanding the short-distance travel patterns of the elderly and their relationship with street-scale built environment is of great significance for addressing the challenges of population aging and promoting the development of age-friendly cities. However, existing studies mainly focus on travel frequency, ignoring other travel characteristics. Moreover, there remains limited understanding of how the street-scale built environment influences short-distance travel through non-linear mechanisms. Using Nanjing as a case study, this study integrates mobile signaling data and street-view images to quantify the frequency, proportion and spatial extent of short-distance travel for the elderly. A machine learning framework combined with SHAP interpretation is employed to identify the non-linear effects of multidimensional built environment. The results show that: (1) Short-distance travel of the elderly exhibits a core-periphery spatial pattern. Central areas are characterized by high frequency, larger spatial extent, and higher proportion of short-distance travel, while mobility in peripheral areas is generally constrained. (2) Sky view index and building-to-road ratio have a significant influence on all characteristics of elderly travel behaviour. Green view index affects travel frequency and travel proportion, while safety factors such as sidewalks and traffic lights play a role in travel proportion and spatial extent. (3) Street-scale environment demonstrates non-linear and threshold effects. This study confirms the effectiveness of optimizing street-scale built environment within life circles in enhancing travel vitality, reshaping mobility structure, and expanding the activity space, and it provides empirical evidence to support the construction of 15-minute elderly-friendly life circles. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Explanation generation: Questions direct exploration in semantic space
Abstract: In everyday reasoning and scientific inquiry, explanations help people make sense of their experiences and observations. We investigate how people generate new possible explanations. Specifically, we study how the phrasing of “why” questions shapes exploration of the space of possible explanations. We hypothesized that rephrasing a question comparing two keywords to make one or the other more focal would guide people toward explanations that are more closely related to the focal word. Using a pre-trained machine learning model, we measured how closely each explanation aligned with the comparison words. In Study 1, we manipulated the order of the two keywords and found that explanations aligned more strongly with the earlier words. However, this design did not distinguish whether the effect was driven by the primacy of the words or the pragmatics of the question. In Study 2, we then independently manipulated which word appeared first and which word served as the grammatical subject, and found that participants were more likely to generate explanations related to the subject. These findings highlight how the phrasing of a question can shape explanation generation, demonstrating that pragmatic understanding influences how people explore a conceptual space. © 2026

Authors: Topcu M.; Akbulut N.
Title: Who bears the burden? Age dependency and gender employment gap
Abstract: As demographic structures change, demographic pressures increasingly threaten labor market inclusivity and sustainability. Age dependency, traditionally defined as the proportion of the population younger than 15 or older than 64 relative to the working-age population, is expected to place a greater burden on women, particularly in relatively low-income countries where caregiving responsibilities disproportionately fall on female workers. Given this expectation, this study investigates the impact of age dependency on the gender employment gap across 20 OECD countries from 2010 to 2021. Our analysis confirms the widening effect in lower-income members, while increasing age dependency does not affect the gender employment gap in higher-income members. Focusing on lower-income OECD countries, we find that institutional quality helps counter the impact of age dependency on the gender employment gap. Even when the gender wage gap narrows, an outcome often seen as progress, our results show that the widening effect of age dependency on the gender employment gap becomes stronger. Nonetheless, high institutional quality continues to counter this impact. These findings highlight the importance of institutional readiness in addressing the intersection of demographic change and labor market inequality, with direct implications for policy agendas related to inclusive growth, aging societies, and the Sustainable Development Goals. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Kang Y.-J.
Title: Experiential stability and mobility justice: A qualitative study of accessibility and uncertainty in the Seoul Metropolitan Area
Abstract: Background Many high-income metropolitan regions appear to provide extensive accessible transport infrastructure for people with disabilities. However, proximity-based and infrastructure compliance indicators may overestimate accessibility by overlooking how systems perform. This gap is particularly important in dense transit-oriented cities where formal provision coexists with lived uncertainty. This study examines how accessibility is experienced beyond visible built environment investments. Methods Twenty-two semi-structured interviews and three go-along observations were conducted with adults with visual, mobility, and hearing impairments in the Seoul Metropolitan Area between 2022 and 2023. Participants were predominantly adults with visual impairments (n = 17 of 22), with smaller numbers of participants with mobility and hearing impairments; findings should therefore be read primarily as reflecting visual impairment experience rather than the full range of disability groups. Iterative thematic analysis was used to examine how uncertainty emerged across stages of the travel chain and how individuals adapted to transport delivery conditions. Results Despite extensive infrastructure provision, participants consistently characterized accessibility as conditionally reliable rather than structurally dependable. Elevator breakdowns, inconsistent accessibility information, environmental obstructions, variable assistance practices, and unpredictable paratransit waiting times generated cumulative instability. Participants engaged in temporal buffering, vigilance, and selective avoidance to manage institutionalized uncertainty. These adaptations mitigated immediate risks but constrained spontaneity, increased cognitive load, and limited participation. Conclusions Visible accessibility infrastructure does not guarantee experiential accessibility. This study proposes experiential stability as a sensitizing framework for conceptualizing accessibility as sustained reliability across time and interaction, rather than as a generalizable theory of disability and transport. By framing transport instability as experiential exposure, this study contributes to transport-health research by highlighting performance variability and psychosocial burden as dimensions of lived mobility. Stability-oriented indicators may complement existing compliance metrics in policy evaluation, particularly in dense, transit-oriented urban settings where infrastructure provision is high but service reliability remains uneven. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Murillo-Jiménez, Tamara (59736585800); Remesal, Manuel (61007719900); Carpio Camargo, Antonio J. (55644240300); Serrano Rodríguez, Rocío (57220058392)
Title: A multidimensional analysis of children’s connection with nature: Associations with age, gender, and frequency of nature contact
Abstract: Connection with nature (CN) is increasingly recognised as a key construct in environmental education and a predictor of pro-environmental behaviour. However, empirical evidence on age-related patterns in CN during childhood and its associations with sociodemographic and contextual factors remains inconsistent. This study examines the affective, behavioural, and cognitive dimensions of CN in a sample of 1375 children aged 6–11 years from Córdoba, Spain. A validated multidimensional instrument was administered, and data were analysed using beta-binomial Generalised Linear Mixed Models, with school-level random intercepts to account for the clustering of pupils within schools. Age-related patterns were examined using spline-based modelling to capture potential non-linear associations. Findings revealed dimension-specific patterns. Affective CN was lower among older children, whereas behavioural CN was higher in early and middle childhood, showing only a slight attenuation at the oldest ages in spline-based estimates. Cognitive CN showed a positive overall age-related association, particularly among boys in the oldest age group. Because the design was cross-sectional, these findings describe age-related differences within the sample rather than intra-individual change over time. Gender differences were slight in the affective and behavioural components. Frequent contact with nature was strongly and consistently associated with overall, affective and behavioural CN, with a weaker association for the cognitive dimension. No robust differences were found between urban–rural places of residence. These results support a multidimensional understanding of CN. The findings have implications for environmental education policy and practice, suggesting the need for sustained and structured nature-based learning opportunities during middle childhood. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: The restorative value of urban environments: A systematic review of quantitative evidence, methods and data
Abstract: Amidst ongoing urbanisation, understanding how various urban elements contribute to stress reduction and well-being is increasingly crucial. However, existing research has prioritized natural elements, reinforcing a nature-urban dichotomy that overlooks the restorative potential of the built environment itself. This systematic review examines the restorative value of urban environments through quantitative studies from 2010 to 2024, exploring the effects on cognitive, affective, and physiological outcomes. Following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) reporting guideline, it narratively synthesises findings from 50 quantitative human studies, identified through PRISMA-referenced screening of peer-reviewed articles that report associations between urban environmental characteristics and restorative outcomes. Results indicate urban spaces with integrated greenery are more often linked to higher perceived restorativeness and short-term psychological benefits than predominantly grey comparators. Several built environment characteristics, including architectural façade design, design quality, service facilities, and street-scale vegetation, were positively associated with restoration. Psycho-environmental characteristics (e.g., serenity, prospect, refuge) and person–place relationships further shape restorative experiences. Future research should focus more on various urban settings—high-density neighbourhoods, historical districts, and waterfronts—and compare similarities and differences in their restorative mechanisms. The review identifies emerging neuro-urbanism and big-data approaches as transformative tools; despite current methodological limitations, they radically expand the potential to clarify mechanisms and enhance generalisability. Based on the evidence extracted from the 50 studies, an evidence-informed, hypothesis-generating conceptual framework is proposed to map the observed associations between urban environment attributes, restorative value, and health and well-being. The framework organises current associational evidence and identifies testable pathways for future research rather than depicting confirmed causal chains. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Tao X.; Ma W.; Shi S.; Liu J.
Title: Assessing accessible facilities for pedestrians with disabilities in Beijing, China
Abstract: Background China has invested heavily in accessible facilities, but research on their effectiveness is limited. Methods This study randomly sampled street view images in Beijing, analysing 6904 images to assess accessibility, usability, and observed use rates of tactile paving and curb ramps for pedestrians with disabilities. On-site observations of tactile paving and standardized wheelchair-based assessments were also conducted. Results The findings reveal that tactile paving and curb ramps are widely available in Beijing. However, over 10% of these facilities are either damaged or obstructed, suggesting their poor usability. Moreover, the study identified low observed use rates for tactile paving and wheelchair-accessible facilities in Beijing. The Capability Approach and Person-Environment fit theory suggest this may stem from a fragmented accessible environment, where coverage does not translate to effective real-world use. Conclusions Despite widespread availability, discontinuous, non-compliant, and poorly maintained accessible facilities lead to their poor usability and low observed use rates in Beijing, highlighting the need for cohesive accessible environments. Limitation and implications This study is limited by its focus on Beijing, reliance on static street-view images that cannot capture temporal patterns of facility use, and the absence of participants with disabilities. Nevertheless, the research advances the understanding of the accessible environment, illustrating the significant potential for using street view photos combined with complementary data sources to provide extensive, readily understandable data for future accessibility studies. Title: The digital mindfulness scale: Development and longitudinal validation in the workplace
Abstract: Digital mindfulness (DM) refers to the capacity to engage with digital technologies in a deliberate, attentive, and non-reactive manner. As digital work intensifies, DM has shown early promise as a protective factor for employee well-being. However, a domain-specific mindfulness measure grounded in the secular mindfulness tradition (Kabat-Zinn, 1994) and designed to capture a resource that is protective of well-being in digitally mediated work contexts is currently lacking. This study reports the development and validation of a 15-item Digital Mindfulness Scale (DMS) grounded in Shapiro et al.’s (2006) Intention–Attention–Attitude (IAA) framework. Scale development involved expert panel review (N = 12; 10 retained for analysis) of a theoretically developed item pool (N = 30) followed by exploratory factor analysis (EFA; N = 398) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; N = 336). Results supported a stable three-factor structure reflecting intention, attention, and attitude. The DMS demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α =.90–.91), good test–retest reliability (ICC =.77), and evidence of convergent and criterion validity. Using longitudinal data, DM predicted lower technostress and exhaustion and higher well-being over a month, over and above demographic variables, technology use, and extant mindfulness measures. These findings support the DMS as a psychometrically robust, context-specific instrument for assessing mindful engagement with digital work and contribute to theory and practice by distinguishing dispositional mindfulness from its behavioural expression in digitally mediated environments. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Yu H.; Dai S.
Title: Rural e-commerce and land-augmenting technological progress: Empirical evidence from China
Abstract: With the continuous advancement of digitalization, rural e-commerce has emerged as a burgeoning phenomenon. This study explores the impact of rural e-commerce on land-augmenting technological progress—a specific form of biased technological progress focused on enhancing land productivity while controlling for other inputs—using China's county-level data from 2010 to 2021. Taking the establishment of “Taobao Villages” as a proxy for rural e-commerce development, we employ a combination of empirical methods, including difference-in-differences, random forest, threshold regression, and mediating effect models, to analyze the relationship, its heterogeneity, and underlying mechanisms. The findings reveal that rural e-commerce significantly enhances land-augmenting technological progress. Notably, such technological progress led to a reduction equivalent to 0.35% of commonly cultivated arable land in 2021, highlighting its tangible contribution to land-use efficiency in the face of mounting environmental and demographic pressures. This positive impact is further amplified by improvements in knowledge production efficiency. The mechanisms driving these effects include promoting urbanization, labor mobility, and creating local non-agricultural employment opportunities. Moreover, the study underscores the vital role of land-augmenting technological progress in fostering sustainable local agricultural development, which includes increasing per capita agricultural production value and productivity, as well as narrowing the urban-rural income gap. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Anaya Ortiz B.
Title: Beyond Culture: Towards a Contractual Theory of Indigenous Corporate Identity in Mexico; [Más allá de la cultura: hacia una teoría contractual de la personalidad jurídica indígena en México]
Abstract: This article analyzes the philosophical and legal challenges in defining Indigenous people's legal personality in Mexico. Drawing on democratic theory and its analysis of the "boundary problem", I examine possible strategies for defining indigenous peoples as collective legal subjects. I argue that the criteria currently used to define these collective entities—such as qualified self-identification or shared culture—are either ambiguous or unduly exclusionary. In response, I propose a contractual model that would allow each community to incorporate as a legal entity by filing articles of incorporation before a public authority such as the INPI. This approach would provide legal certainty to persons contracting with indigenous communities, facilitate political representation, and streamline collective action, ensuring autonomy without falling into cultural essentialism or institutional ambiguity. Title: The legacy of redlining: Unveiling the impact on natural hazard risk and community resilience
Abstract: Historical redlining represents a foundational injustice in American urban development, yet its contemporary manifestations in natural hazard vulnerability remain inadequately addressed in disaster risk frameworks. This study treats the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's neighborhood grades as an institutional spatial artifact and asks how far that classification remains legible in present-day patterns of environmental risk. Integrating HOLC maps, FEMA's National Risk Index, and American Community Survey data, spatial Durbin models (SDMs) were employed across the full national set of HOLC-graded areas in the United States. Kruskal-Wallis tests reveal systematic disparities across 11 hazard types, with risk increasing progressively from grade A through D. However, the redlining gradient reverses for wildfire, a hazard outside the scope of 1930s appraisal. Strong spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = 0.67-0.85) indicates geographic vulnerability clustering. SDM estimates demonstrate that historically redlined neighborhoods (HOLC grades C and D) exhibit significantly higher risk index scores, expected annual losses, and community risk factors than grade A neighborhoods, with disparities widening from grade C to grade D and most pronounced for community risk factors. Impact decomposition further shows that the association with community risk extends into adjacent neighborhoods. Because expected annual loss is asset-based, it understates risk where property values were suppressed by disinvestment. Persistent spatial disparities aligned with historical segregation and sustained disinvestment underscore the need for targeted urban planning prioritizing low-asset, high-vulnerability neighborhoods through green infrastructure, resilience hubs, and adaptive capacity building. Authors: Kuhn D.
Title: The territorial power of appearing and disappearing groundwater conflicts
Abstract: This article aims for an enhanced understanding of groundwater conflicts. Worldwide, people compete over groundwater. However, this rarely leads to manifest conflicts. Whether a groundwater conflict remains latent or turns manifest, i.e. into an open, direct and hence visible confrontation, relates to hydrogeological processes as well as societal power relations. This article investigates how manifest groundwater conflicts appear and disappear and with which effects for whom. The conceptual lens of hydrosocial territories applied to a groundwater conflict in the Südharz region, Germany, and the Júcar river basin, Spain, enables the deep investigation into the visible and invisible contestations around groundwater quality and quantity. In Südharz, a toxic event co-produced by uranium and a citizen initiative turned long-looming tensions around water supply into a manifest conflict. In Spain, a drought event co-produced by groundwater-river interaction and downstream users led to a manifest conflict between two regions. In both cases, the power of existing large water infrastructures and institutions contributed eventually to the disappearance of the manifest conflict by re-scaling the respective systems of water supply. Thereby, conflicts about the fundamental relations between societies and groundwater have been kept under the surface – for now. In the future, they are very likely to appear somewhere in the newly established hydrosocial territories. © 2026 The Author. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Undesired body orientations in competitive pedestrian evacuations
Abstract: We report time-resolved experimental measurements of human body orientation in extremely dense crowds during highly competitive evacuations. By comparing different scenarios, we find that as competitiveness increases and contact forces among pedestrians build up, orientational order deteriorates and undesired rotations emerge. This effect is markedly amplified when an obstacle is placed in front of the exit door; in some cases, this even causes individuals to rotate by 180°, forcing them to exit backward (i.e., facing away from the door). Title: Integrating perceived coolness and emotional attachment: how K-POP shapes Chinese KFL learners’ willingness to communicate
Abstract: In an era of accelerating globalization and frequent cross-cultural contact, willingness to communicate (WTC) in a second language is widely recognized as a critical predictor of successful language acquisition. To deepen the understanding of cultural influences on the formation of language-related behaviors, this study examines how Chinese learners of Korean as a Foreign Language (KFL) perceive the coolness of Korean popular music (K-POP) culture and how such perceptions influence their WTC in Korean. Structural equation modeling using partial least squares (PLS-SEM) was conducted on survey data from 360 Chinese KFL learners recruited online via Wenjuanxing. The analysis employed 5000 bootstrap samples to test the measurement and structural models, including bias-corrected confidence intervals for mediation effects. All four dimensions of perceived K-POP coolness significantly predicted emotional attachment, which in turn strongly enhanced willingness to communicate (WTC) in Korean. Emotional attachment mediated the relationships between perceived coolness and WTC. Title: Eating green together: A qualitative study to explore children's motivations and role in household decision making for environmentally sustainable diets

Title: Beyond factual events: Evaluating LLMs’ capability of cognitive processes understanding in narratives
Abstract: Understanding cognitive processes embedded within narrative texts — such as characters’ thoughts, perceptions, and mental states — is fundamental to human narrative comprehension capabilities. Existing benchmarks for narrative text understanding primarily focus on factual events extraction, overlooking the critical ability to identify cognitive processes that could greatly influence the development of factual processes. To address this gap, we introduce CogNarr, a comprehensive benchmark comprising cognitively rich narrative texts with 980 factual events and 601 cognitive processes including perception and imagination. Evaluations on 20 diverse LLMs using our benchmark revealed that while the most advanced models demonstrate strong performance in event recognition, they frequently failed to recognize cognitive processes, achieving only 0.4–0.7 F1, substantially lower than that for factual events, with particularly poor performance in imagination recognition. Qualitative analysis uncovered systematic biases across models, highlighting issues such as confusion between imagined and factual events and excessive reliance on lexical cues of mental activities. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Assessing coordinated multi-pollutant mitigation and balanced economic development in urban agglomerations using a hierarchical multi-objective optimization model
Abstract: Urban agglomerations face growing pressure to reconcile economic growth with coordinated control of multiple pollutants. Based on life cycle assessment, production-stage carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus (CNP) emissions were quantified for major products and linked to city-level production activities. By integrating regional aggregated control, urban internal allocation, intercity adjustment, and rolling-horizon optimization, TMHOM was used to evaluate long-term emission-reduction pathways together with intercity development equity. Results showed that emissions peaked around 2023 and declined thereafter under the optimized pathway. By 2030, total output value increased by 51.06%, while total CNP emissions decreased by 20.23% and emission intensity declined by 47.19%, indicating a decoupling of economic growth from environmental pressure. Beyond emission control, the optimized pathway suggested that conditional reallocation of energy-related and industry-related production from core cities to mid-sized cities could improve regional balance and reduce the concentration of environmental burdens, subject to adequate receiving-city capacity. Scenario comparison further showed that the full three-stage framework provided a more balanced performance across emission reduction, output growth, and regional equity, while sensitivity analysis confirmed its robustness under plausible market fluctuations. Title: Brief video-feedback training enhances childcare professionals’ interaction skills: A cluster randomized controlled trial

Title: Stakeholder attributes in maritime logistics ecosystem: a policy perspective for small island states
Abstract: Transport policies should aim to integrate the demands and expectations of all stakeholders, even in maritime logistics contexts where a mix of private and public interests play out, sometimes in conflicting situations. The added value of an ecosystem for transport policy largely depends on how effectively coordination amongst its stakeholders is managed. The study aims to define stakeholders’ attributes within a small maritime logistics ecosystem, using the case study of Malta, by analyzing how power, legitimacy and urgency are relationally constructed and hierarchically distributed. This is grounded in the Stakeholder Salience Theory and distinguish ecosystem participants based on the attribute positioning derived from individual traits. Data is collected through interviews with the stakeholders and analysed qualitatively using thematic analysis . The results show how legitimacy emerges as a key attribute; power is developed by inter-organizational relationships and urgency plays a more limited role. In aggregate, salience attributes are pivotal in building the ecosystem collective identity and when the ecosystem orchestrator lacks legitimacy in constrained environments, the overall ecosystem stability is affected. Policies should therefore focus on the understanding of stakeholder salience and dynamics, as well as the need for effective coordination in maritime logistics ecosystems to guarantee stability and collective value creation. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Mirrors of the Future: Ethical and Societal Reflections in Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun (2021) and Dave Eggers's The Every (2021)
Abstract: This article examines Kazuo Ishiguro's Klara and the Sun and Dave Eggers's The Every, analyzing how both authors investigate the human experience amidst rapid technological progress. Authors: Yu P.; Chen Y.; Li Z.; Leng A.; Wang Z.; Deng X.
Title: Assessing the impacts of cropland physical fragmentation on abandonment: The institutional moderating role of rural cooperatives in China
Abstract: Cropland abandonment is increasingly prevalent in rural areas, posing risks to food security. Although the importance of spatial structure in shaping land use decisions is widely acknowledged, empirical understanding of how physical forms of cropland fragmentation contribute to abandonment remains limited. Thus, this study introduces an institutional moderator to enhance understanding of how different physical forms of fragmentation influence abandonment in China. Specifically, abandonment is identified using a temporal filtering process to detect plots left uncultivated for at least two consecutive years. Cropland fragmentation is assessed using patch density, split index, and division index, capturing internal, shape, location and extensive fragmentation forms. The effects of cropland physical fragmentation on abandonment are assessed using a fixed-effects model, and the moderating role of rural cooperatives is explored through interaction terms. Abandonment and cropland physical fragmentation in China showed marked regional variation, with particularly high levels observed in the Northern Arid and Semiarid Region and the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau. The results showed that higher fragmentation was significantly associated with increased abandonment, with the division index demonstrating the strongest effect. Cropland area, cropland production potential, household size and mechanisation level were significantly and negatively associated with abandonment, whereas the urbanisation rate exhibited a significant positive association. Notably, the analysis identified rural cooperatives as potentially important institutional moderators that alleviate the negative effects of fragmentation by reducing operational barriers and making it more feasible to cultivate fragmented plots. These insights highlight the need for region-specific consolidation and sustainable cropland management. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Sociodemographic and generational correlates of women's attitudes toward intimate partner violence in Türkiye
Abstract: Gender norms and sociodemographic resources shape women's perceptions of intimate partner violence (IPV). Understanding these factors within primary care settings is essential for implementing context-specific screening and counseling practices. To examine the sociodemographic and generational correlates of women's gender role and IPV-related attitudes, and evaluate the predictors of actual lifetime IPV exposure, this study included 1091 women aged 18 years and older registered at training family health centers in Türkiye. Lifetime IPV exposure rates were substantial. More egalitarian and anti-violence attitudes were associated with higher education, formal employment, and younger generations. Lower education, low income, and relationship separation were stronger predictors of victimization than individual attitudinal scores, with older generational cohorts facing a much higher risk of economic violence. Women's attitudes toward IPV and actual vulnerability are grounded in generational shifts and individual-level resources that dictate relational power. In primary care, the high sub-clinical burden of non-physical violence emphasizes the need for proactive, direct questioning strategies to improve disclosure. Copyright © 2026. Title: Integrating severity and diagnosis in needs assessment: A participatory framework
Abstract: Background: Needs assessment is widely acknowledged as a cornerstone of program planning, yet it is often treated as a compartmentalized, pre-evaluative exercise. In complex and inequitable contexts, this fragmentation can undermine the development of grounded program theory. Purpose: This article proposes an integrated, beneficiary-centered framework for needs assessment that specifically combines severity documentation and causal diagnosis into a single participatory inquiry that directly informs program theory development. Methods/approach: Building on Davidson’s (2005) three-phase model, we developed a five-step framework comprising: (1) orientation and stakeholder engagement; (2) integrated severity–diagnosis inquiry; (3) participatory data analysis and prioritization; (4) co-development of program theory; and (5) validation and advocacy with wider stakeholders. Findings: We found the application of the framework useful in simultaneously generating evidence of the severity of need (widespread, high-intensity care burdens) and causal mechanisms (structural, spatial, and gendered drivers). This culminated in a collaboratively developed program theory linking multi-sectoral strategies to desired outcomes. Implications for evaluation & program planning: The framework reduces disunity across need assessment phases, strengthens alignment between evidence and program theory, and creates stronger pathways for stakeholder engagement and program design. It offers evaluators a practical approach for integrating beneficiary perspectives and systemic diagnosis into theory-driven program design. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: DDMCL: Meta-path diffusion denoising and multi-view contrastive learning for recommendation
Abstract: Existing meta-path-based recommendation systems suffer from noise interference and intent fusion, which distort high-order semantic relationships and consequently degrade recommendation performance. To tackle these challenges, we propose meta-path Diffusion Denoising and Multi-view Contrastive Learning for recommendation (DDMCL), which enhances representation learning from three perspectives: (1) Dual-graph diffusion denoising: we employ diffusion model to simultaneously reconstruct the latent semantic distributions of two meta-path graphs on the user (item) side, achieving joint optimization through a shared-parameter network with graph-specific identifiers to enhance denoising performance while preserving semantic consistency. (2) Intent attention fusion: we extract path semantic representations based on graph convolutional networks, design an attention mechanism to dynamically aggregate intent features, and use the embedding of the user–item graph as a structural guide to capture the multi-dimensional preferences of users and items. (3) Multi-view contrastive optimization: we perform intent-aware contrastive learning in the meta-path semantic space and structure-enhanced contrastive learning in the user–item interaction space, jointly optimized with the main recommendation objective to improve robustness and generalization. Extensive experiments on six benchmark recommendation datasets demonstrate that DDMCL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving the NDCG@20 on the Amazon and Yelp datasets by 3.27% and 3.70%, respectively. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Climate-induced migration or immobility? Evidence from Nigeria
Abstract: The complex relationship between climate shocks, adaptation, and migration hinders a rigorous understanding of the heterogeneous mobility outcomes of farm households exposed to climate stress. To unpack this heterogeneity, we couple causal machine learning methods, tailored to a conceptual framework bridging economic migration theory and the poverty traps literature, with longitudinal multi-topic household data from Nigeria. This approach allows us to produce fine-grained, non-parametric evidence that identifies the factors driving divergent mobility outcomes across different household groups affected by the same shocks. The estimated conditional average treatment effects suggest that key variables—pre-shock asset levels, in situ adaptive capacity, and weather exposure during the previous survey period—shape not only the magnitude but also the sign of the impact of agriculture-relevant weather anomalies on the mobility outcomes of farming households. While in situ adaptation serves as an alternative to migration, the role played by wealth constraints and multiple shock exposure is consistent with the existence of climate-induced immobility traps. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: The effect of conversational style on children’s self-reporting: Evidence from a field study with an LLM-powered voice diary
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Sustaining children’s engagement and response quality in self-reporting diaries is a longstanding challenge, as repetitive tasks often reduce compliance and motivation. While conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) offer a promising solution, most designs for children emphasize semantic adaptation (e.g., phrasing, wording) and leave underexplored the sound-pattern form of language (e.g., rhyme/rhythm) that may shape children’s enjoyment. We conducted a seven-session field study with 32 children (aged 7–13) using an LLM-powered voice-based chatbot that supported two conversational styles: a prose baseline and a phonologically enriched (rhyming) style. Children selected their preferred style before each session, allowing analysis of behavioral preferences, compliance, response quality, and perceived enjoyment. Results show that younger children strongly preferred the rhyming style, whereas older children exhibited more varied preferences, and rhyming preference attenuated over sessions. Session-level rhyming choice was associated with higher completion, fewer skipped days before returning, and higher response quality. Mediation analyses were consistent with enjoyment as a candidate pathway linking style choice to response quality. Title: How language conveys emotion through sound: A review of affective iconicity
Abstract: Traditionally, the lack of association between the form of a word and its meaning (i.e. arbitrariness) has been considered a fundamental aspect of language. However, this idea has recently been challenged by growing evidence of form-meaning relationships in words from different conceptual domains, such as size, shape, motion, and colour. More recently, several studies have provided evidence of non-arbitrary associations between the acoustic or phonological forms of words and their meanings when conveying emotional concepts. This phenomenon is referred to as affective iconicity. These effects are evident within and across languages through the over-representation of certain phonemes in words denoting positive or negative emotions (e.g., the phoneme/i/tends to occur in positive words in several different languages) or through statistical regularities in the phonetic features of emotional words (e.g., in English, German and Spanish, sibilant sounds tend to be associated with a high degree of emotional activation of a word’s referent). In this article, we review the literature on affective iconicity. Overall, the current findings suggest that non-arbitrary relationships between word forms and affective meanings may have evolved from the capacity to integrate multimodal inputs with affective experiences. This ability could have been advantageous for communicating information relevant to an individual's survival through language. We argue that affective iconicity effects arise from a link between phonetic and phonological forms and schematic representations of affective experiences and states during the lexicalisation of emotional concepts. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Chen Z.; Tan Z.; Luo P.
Title: Mitigating psychological discomfort during automation error: A mixed methods research
Abstract: Automated driving errors can threaten occupants’ psychological comfort, creating a need for effective in-vehicle recovery communication. Recovery strategies refer to communicative system responses delivered after automation errors to mitigate negative impacts and restore positive interaction. This mixed-methods study examined how four recovery strategies (explanation, apology, promise, and denial) and two speech styles (machine-like and human-like) influence occupants' psychological comfort, operationalized as perceived safety and pleasure, after an automation error. Thirty-four participants completed a within-subjects driving simulator experiment and semi-structured interviews. Explanation and promise most effectively improved both dimensions, whereas denial impaired occupant experience. Apology showed a style-dependent reversal: human-like apology increased pleasure but reduced perceived safety. Machine-like delivery produced stronger overall benefits for perceived safety, but speech-style effects depended on strategy content. These findings suggest that recovery communication should align strategy content with the informational demands of the event and the expressive register of delivery. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Joint word recall and functional limitation among selected SHARE participants with prior survey-identified stroke versus a stroke-free reference group
Abstract: Background: Joint word-recall and everyday-function patterns after stroke require comparison with older adults without prior stroke. We compared survey-observed distributions while retaining longer-term observation limitations. Methods: We analyzed SHARE Waves 1, 2 and 4–8. T1 was the first post-stroke-positive assessment with valid recall and function, selecting survivors who remained observed and measurable. One country-wave-aligned pseudo-index with valid measures was selected per eligible, explicitly stroke-negative reference participant with no recorded stroke-positive response at or before that assessment. Overlap weighting balanced country-wave, age, sex and education. Four states combined low relative word recall and ADL/IADL limitation; four-year outcomes were secondary. Results: Among 2470 stroke and 83,767 reference participants, overlap-weighted proportions were 57.1% versus 74.4% for neither state (difference −17.3 percentage points, 95% CI −19.3 to −15.3), 7.2% versus 6.8% for low relative recall only (0.3, −0.7 to 1.4), 26.4% versus 15.0% for functional limitation only (11.4, 9.6 to 13.1), and 9.4% versus 3.8% for both (5.6, 4.4 to 6.8). In the secondary 778-person subset with full potential four-year coverage, 28.1% were unavailable. Title: The Manchester Clinical Supervision Scale-26 as a Measure of Perceived Clinical Supervision Effectiveness: A Systematic Review
Abstract: Aims: To assess the properties of the Manchester Clinical Supervision Scale-26 (MCSS-26) as a measure of perceived clinical supervision effectiveness in healthcare student and professional populations. Design: Systematic review of assessable measurement properties (content validity, structural validity, internal consistency, cross-cultural validity/measurement invariance, reliability, and hypotheses testing for construct validity) across MCSS-26 components using Consensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN). Data sources: Embase, PubMed, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to September 2025. Google Scholar and backward and forward citation tracking were used to identify additional studies. Review methods: Eligible studies examined at least one property of at least one component in healthcare student or professional populations. Study quality and results were appraised using COSMIN methodological standards and measurement property criteria. Appraised evidence was synthesised by property, and certainty was graded using the COSMIN-modified Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Results: 29 articles were included. Most studies were conducted in nursing-related samples. Evidence for content validity was limited or insufficient, and for structural validity indeterminate. Evidence for internal consistency was inconsistent, although findings for the Formative domain and the Supervisor Advice/Support subscale were supportive. Evidence for cross-cultural validity was inconsistent and for reliability indeterminate. Hypotheses testing for construct validity was favourable for workplace satisfaction, intention to remain in the workplace, emotional intelligence, burnout, and perceived skilfulness. Conclusions: The MCSS-26 cannot yet be regarded as a well-supported measure of perceived clinical supervision effectiveness. Although evidence for construct validity was supportive, evidence of other measurement properties was insufficient, inconsistent, or indeterminate. The instrument appears most defensible as a broad indicator of perceived clinical supervision rather than a precise measure of distinct effectiveness. Future work should prioritise revision of the instrument around a more clearly specified construct or development of context-sensitive alternatives. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: An agentic framework for reference integrity assurance via multi-source verification and topology-constrained citation consistency
Abstract: Accurate reference integrity is critical for ensuring the reliability and traceability of scholarly communication. Existing approaches typically focus on isolated subtasks, such as bibliographic field extraction or heuristic citation checking, but rarely provide a unified mechanism for ensuring document-level coherence in the presence of noisy or inconsistent metadata. This issue is particularly prevalent in modern publishing workflows, where poorly formatted or automatically generated references often lead to both local metadata errors and global citation-reference mismatches. To address this challenge, we propose an agentic multi-source verification framework for reference integrity assurance. The framework integrates uncertainty-aware reference extraction, adaptive canonical alignment against external knowledge sources, and topology-constrained citation-reference consistency validation within an iterative decision-making process. Through coordination between reasoning-oriented and tool-oriented agents over a shared structured state, our approach enables evidence-grounded correction, bounded refinement, and auditable resolution of reference errors at the document level. Experiments on a large-scale dataset comprising 5000 scholarly manuscripts demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Compared to the strongest retrieval-augmented LLM baseline, our method improves the overall integrity score by 4.7%, exact-match correction accuracy by 4.9%, reduces the residual reference mismatch rate by 27.0%, and increases citation-reference alignment accuracy by 4.4%. These results show that the proposed framework effectively balances local metadata correction with global citation consistency, offering a robust, practical, and human-supervisable solution for scalable reference integrity assurance in editorial environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The effect of positive emotions on psychophysiological recovery and performance in athletes - investigating the undoing-hypothesis
Abstract: Athletes have to cope with psychosocial and physiological stressors, requiring recovery to ensure subsequent performance. According to the undoing-hypothesis, positive emotions (PE) may enhance psychophysiological recovery. After a combined psychosocial-physiological stressor, participants either completed a five-minute PE induction (music; imagination exercise) or were assigned to a resting condition. Emotions, perceived stress-recovery, and physiological parameters (e.g., heart rate, heart rate variability, cortisol) were assessed. In Study 1, inhibition and cognitive flexibility were measured once. In Study 2, hand force and jump height were measured using a pre-posttest design. Due to the lack of psychological stress responses and successful PE induction, no conclusions could be drawn regarding the undoing hypothesis. Nevertheless, the present study provides valuable methodological insights into the challenges of testing the undoing hypothesis in athletes. These insights can inform the design and implementation of future studies and thereby contribute to advancing research on the undoing hypothesis in athletic populations. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Large language model counterarguments in older adults: Cognitive offloading or susceptibility to moral persuasion?
Abstract: This study examined whether counterarguments generated by large language models (LLMs) influence the moral judgments of younger and older adults, and whether these effects vary by dilemma type, cognitive functioning, trust in AI, and prior LLM experience. In the emotionally aversive footbridge dilemma, older adults with lower cognitive functioning were significantly more likely to align with the LLM-generated counterargument. General trust in AI and prior LLM experience did not predict judgment reversal, whereas lower initial confidence and higher perceived task difficulty were associated with greater susceptibility to LLM influence. Title: Rural policy between exploration and exploitation: Comparing Italy's SNAI and France's Agenda Rural
Abstract: Rural territories in Europe face challenges of access to services, depopulation, and limited administrative capacity. Governments respond with national policies driven by a strong push for institutional innovation, redefining which territories count as marginal and rural and how the State organises its support. This article compares two policy responses: Italy's National Strategy for Inner Areas (SNAI) and France's Agenda Rural. Both policies address the same problem, rural marginality, but treat it differently: for SNAI, it is a constitutive criterion for selecting target territories, while for Agenda Rural, it is an unequal condition within a broader rural population. Building on Hartley's (2005) typology of innovation and March's (1991) exploration-exploitation dilemma, we analyse how five dimensions of innovation, in each policy, combine into a cognitive-symbolic component, which produces discursive recognition of marginality or rurality, and an operative-technical component, which organises the support needed to translate that recognition into capacity for action. The analysis draws on policy documents, evaluation reports, semi-structured interviews, and observation of thematic forums. The research shows that SNAI is predominantly exploratory, introducing criteria, bodies, and methods that are largely unprecedented, amid implementation frictions. Agenda Rural, by contrast, is hybrid on the cognitive-symbolic component and exploitative on the operative-technical one, relying on pre-existing administrative networks. The article contributes to rural studies and to the comparative analysis of rural policies, examining on one hand the concepts of rurality and marginality, and on the other how exploration and exploitation combine in forms of institutional innovation. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Unpacking two sides of empathy in friendships: Understanding and feeling understood as resources for sociocultural adaptation and psychological well-being
Abstract: Cross-group friendships can help young immigrants and refugees adapt within the receiving culture. But how can these friendships facilitate sociocultural adaptation and psychological well-being? Prior research has investigated the beneficial role of showing empathy (perceived understanding), and – less intensely studied – receiving empathy (feeling understood) in intergroup relations. We expected to find a positive association between the number of cross-group friendships and sociocultural adaptation, and for the overall number of friendships on psychological well-being. We hypothesised to find an indirect effect via perceived understanding and feeling understood within friendships on the two outcomes. In line with our expectation, there was a significant positive association between intergroup friendship and sociocultural adaptation in both samples. We found small yet significant indirect effects via perceived understanding in cross-group friendships on sociocultural adaptation in Sample 1, and via feeling understood in Sample 2. We further detected a positive link between feeling understood in friendships and psychological well-being in Sample 2. Title: Professional regulation in nursing education: Cultivating ‘critical polyvocality’ in regulator-educator relationships
Abstract: Professional regulation aims to assure the public that nurses are educated to minimum standards of competency and safety. Yet, assurance is not reducible to the existence of written standards alone. It also depends on the quality of the relationship between regulators and educators through which standards are developed and enacted. Imbalance in this relationship is evident within international debates around issues such as clinical practice hours, simulation pedagogy, board governance, graduate mobility, and the perceived extension of regulatory authority into curriculum design. This asymmetrical relationship may encourage defensive compliance, risk aversion and self-limiting behaviours among educators that potentially constrains pedagogical innovation and the development of person-centred and place-sensitive curricula that are responsive to local population need and uncertain future practice contexts. In this paper, we argue that the perceived inequality in the regulator-educator relationship is neither inherent nor inevitable. Drawing on Foucault's concept of governmentality, we suggest that through challenging perceptions of regulator dominance, educators have more influence on curriculum design than perceived. This point is developed using Lefebvre's rhythmanalysis to characterise the current regulator-educator relationship as arrhythmic, marked by often unspoken discomfort and disagreement. Recognising that conflict-free alignment between regulator and educator (eurythmia) is an unattainable and unwanted end, we argue instead for a polyrhythmic relationship sustained through what we call 'critical polyvocality'. Cultivating critical polyvocality requires opening positively disruptive dialogical spaces characterised by constructive tensions, mutual respect and shared responsibilities between people. Far from weakening public assurance, we conclude that this constructive disagreement and debate can enable co-production of future-focused, living statements of shared professional expectations that enhance public protection through genuine regulator-educator partnership. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Can combined goal prioritization and implementation intentions promote adherence to the Mediterranean Diet? A randomized controlled trial
Abstract: Adherence to the Mediterranean Diet (MD) requires the simultaneous regulation of multiple distinct dietary behaviors, often creating a significant intention-behavior gap. Title: Does the impact of calorie (energy) labelling on food purchased in worksite cafeterias differ by food category? A mega-analysis of field trials

Title: Resilience and empathy dimensions in undergraduate nursing education: A multicenter structural analysis in Latin America
Abstract: Background: Empathy is a core competency in undergraduate nursing education and is closely linked to quality of care. Its expression may be influenced by individual regulatory traits such as resilience, particularly in emotionally demanding academic clinical contexts. However, the dimensional associations between resilience and empathy remain insufficiently explored in nursing students. Objective: To examine structural associations between resilience and empathy dimensions among undergraduate nursing students from multiple Latin American countries. Methods: A cross-sectional multicenter study was conducted with 3611 undergraduate nursing students from five Latin American countries. Participants completed the Jefferson Scale of Empathy-Health Professions Student version (JSE-HPS) and the Resilience Trait Scale (RTS). Confirmatory factor analyses and reliability analyses were performed for both instruments. Measurement invariance across countries was evaluated for the resilience scale. Structural associations between resilience and empathy dimensions were estimated using structural equation modeling and interpreted as theoretically guided exploratory approximations. Results: The structural model showed inadequate incremental fit (CFI = 0.83; TLI = 0.81), despite comparatively more favorable RMSEA and SRMR values. Consequently, the individual path coefficients cannot be regarded as stable or well-supported structural associations. Within this misspecified model, the estimated coefficients suggested heterogeneous patterns across resilience and empathy dimensions; however, their magnitude, direction, and statistical significance may be sensitive to model specification. These results should therefore be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than as reliable estimates of dimensional relationships. Conclusions: The inadequate incremental fit of the structural model precludes firm conclusions regarding the dimensional associations between resilience and empathy. Title: Power, expertise, and policy shifts: Governance of karst resources by Indonesia’s geological agency
Abstract: State scientific agencies occupy an ambiguous position in environmental governance: formally mandated to deliver impartial expertise, they are simultaneously embedded in political-economic systems that press technical judgments toward developmental ends. This paper examines how that tension shaped Indonesia’s Geological Agency (GA) in its governance of karst resources at the Watuputih Groundwater Basin, North Kendeng Mountains, a case in which the Agency moved from a conservation-oriented stance to one that authorised continued limestone extraction. Drawing on multi-sited ethnography (29 semi-structured interviews, observation of a public scientific examination, and documentary analysis) and deploying Svarstad, Benjaminsen and Overå’s (2018) pluralistic power framework, we trace the mechanisms through which this institutional shift was produced. The GA’s repositioning was not reducible to leadership change or procedural irregularity. Three interlocking mechanisms were at work: the discursive reclassification of spring typology, which narrowed the definition of hydrological risk and sidelined competing academic assessments; the structural realignment of the Agency’s mandate within Indonesia’s infrastructure-led development apparatus; and actor-level networks connecting GA personnel to cement industry interests, which constrained the institutional space for precautionary judgment. The contribution is theoretical: it extends capture theory in political ecology by showing industry alignment produced without capture, through networks and ministry structures that already blur public and private interest. The analysis points to the need for institutionalised independence, mandatory conflict-of-interest disclosure, and community-accessible audit mechanisms in state bodies whose technical assessments determine the fate of ecologically sensitive territories. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Evaluating desired outcomes of peatland management
Abstract: Peatlands are globally important habitats, covering an estimated 4.23 million km2 worldwide. The significance of peatlands to climate change, and across ecosystem services, makes their protection a key policy area across Europe. The large areas and long timescales needed for peatland management means that both private and public funding is required. Additionally, links with society, development, and culture mean that stakeholder involvement in decision making is central to the success of peatland policy. To ensure that peatland policy and management is legitimate and able to persist in the long-term, understanding individual preferences for outcomes is therefore vital. To this end we carried out a choice experiment in Scotland, UK, supported by a literature review and expert workshop. We build on previous choice experiments to investigate preferences for outcomes of management, including: climate change, impacts on drought and flood risk, timber restocking and wind farms. Final analysis included 762 valid responses, which showed no significant difference to the characteristics to the Scottish population for all demographic variables measured with the exception of education. Our sample under-represented those with education below secondary level, and above bachelors level. All choice experiment attributes were significant, with the exception of community owned timber. A positive willingness to pay for management in general was estimated. Value was not impacted by familiarity with peatlands, but higher willingness to pay was associated with more positive environmental attitudes. Overall, our results support the Scottish and global policy agenda on peatland management to combat climate change. However, preferences are also shown for both wind farms and timber restocking, which may run counter to this. © 2026 The Authors
