Authors: Di Nallo A.
Title: Women's job market outcomes around live births and pregnancy losses
Abstract: Up to one in five or six recognised pregnancies ends in an involuntary loss, yet what follows for women's working lives is largely undocumented. In fifteen waves of the UK panel Understanding Society, this event study follows 2654 women whose first reported pregnancy ends in a live birth or a loss, each against her own pre-pregnancy baseline. After a loss, the hourly wage declines by 6 to 7% in the first year, with no detectable change in employment or hours. Employment and hours fall from the second year, and earnings decline by about £760 per month after five years, concentrated among the women who later become mothers, unlike the wage decline. Human capital, subsequent childbearing, career characteristics, and health account for only part of these gaps. Women whose pregnancy ends in a live birth show the well-documented child penalty. A pregnancy loss, then, carries labour-market costs in its own right. © 2026

Authors: Rapp A.; Fiore E.
Title: How do senior qualitative researchers perceive the risks and opportunities of using large language models in qualitative analysis? An exploratory study
Source title: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into research practices due to their ability to simplify knowledge-intensive tasks. Although qualitative research is often seen as difficult to automate, qualitative scholars have begun exploring LLMs for analytical support. Even though existing work highlights concerns about depth, transparency, and responsibility, little is known about how senior qualitative researchers perceive these tools. In this article, we present an exploratory study that investigates the attitudes of 19 senior researchers in psychology, sociology, and anthropology toward the actual or potential use of LLMs in qualitative analysis. Findings show that participants view qualitative analysis as a subjective endeavor and are reluctant to delegate it to LLMs. This resistance stems primarily from anxieties about AI, including fears of losing control and authorship over their work and of being replaced as researchers. Moreover, we show that senior researchers tend to devalue LLM technology when they feel their scientific identity is threatened. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Perceived authenticity and evaluative asymmetry in judgments of AI-generated product designs: An eye-tracking and behavioral study
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) increasingly produces visual content for human evaluation, understanding how people evaluate machine-generated outputs has become a critical behavioral issue. This study examines how individuals evaluate AI-generated versus human-designed product concepts, focusing on associations among creativity ratings, visual attention, and individual differences. Using a mixed-methods approach combining subjective ratings, eye-tracking, and retrospective interviews, we examined responses to chair designs across multiple evaluative dimensions. The results extend prior findings on novelty–usefulness tradeoffs in machine-generated outputs by showing a similar evaluative imbalance in AI-generated product design: AI-generated concepts were perceived as more novel and visually distinctive, but less authentic and, particularly compared with ordinary human-designed counterparts, less useful. Eye-tracking data provided exploratory evidence that novelty judgments were associated with visual fixation patterns, although these effects should be interpreted cautiously. Individual differences were also relevant: self-reported creative design experience was positively associated with usefulness and authenticity judgments, whereas openness to experience showed only a weaker, exploratory association with usefulness judgments. Overall, the findings suggest that evaluations of AI-generated design are related to stimulus characteristics, visual attention, and user traits. The study contributes by identifying perceived authenticity as a distinct plausibility-related criterion in AI-mediated creativity evaluation, while treating evaluative asymmetry as a descriptive pattern and outlining design propositions for future empirical testing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Islamic scholarly perspectives on mental health: implications for care, ethics, and regulations

Abstract: Background The interplay between Islamic teachings and interpretation of mental health disorders is currently unclear, despite Islam's Shariah principles pertaining to humanitarianism and care of vulnerable individuals. Aim To explore authentic Islamic beliefs pertaining to mental health disorders. Title: Sustainable rural settlements in question: Testing synergy and processes within the agricultural transition–human capital–amenities nexus in Northeast China
Abstract: Enhancing rural sustainability has become a prominent issue in the global academic debate, calling for a synergistic framework that integrates multiple dimensions of rural development. Therefore, this study develops the Agricultural Transition- Human Capital- Amenities (ACA) nexus model to explain how these three dimensions jointly contribute to and advance the theoretical framework of Sustainable Rural Settlement (SRS). Agricultural transition creates economic opportunities and supports human capital development, which in turn improves rural amenities and living conditions, ultimately promoting SRS. This research focuses on Heilongjiang Province in Northeast China, a key region for food security that faces several challenges. It examines the contradiction between agricultural modernization and sustainable rural development using panel data from 2003 to 2022. The Coupling Coordination Degree Model (CCDM) is used to measure synergy within the ACA nexus, while Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MM-QREG) identifies the heterogeneous drivers of SRS across different levels of development. The results demonstrate a convergent yet uneven sustainability trajectory across regions, with SRS scores increasing from 2003 to 2022. Despite overall progress, persistent disparities remained, as Mudanjiang consistently outperformed Heihe throughout the study period. This convergence was primarily driven by agricultural modernization after 2012, whereas improvements in amenities and living conditions lagged, revealing structural imbalances within the ACA nexus. Quantile regression results highlight mechanization, education, and village planning as key determinants, with education's effect strengthening and planning's diminishing along sustainability gradients. Rural income exhibited only negative associations rather than causal impacts, while Granger tests indicated limited short-term causality. This highlights the necessity of incorporating place-based rural policies that should no longer be sectoral to tackle multifunctional rural challenges. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Li B.; Huang C.-M.; Lin Q.; Huang H.-W.
Title: Openness to experience modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing
Abstract: Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to experience (Openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across the four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes becoming more negative as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Generative AI-supported peace pedagogy in higher education: A two-wave quasi-experimental study of AI literacy, intercultural sensitivity, and empathy
Abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but its value for humanistic learning depends on pedagogical designs that preserve learner judgment and require critical evaluation of generated content. This two-wave quasi-experimental study examined a six-week GenAI-supported peace-pedagogy module in 522 Saudi higher-education students (intervention n = 276; waitlist n = 246). Primary analyses used linear mixed-effects models for Time × Group interactions, with baseline-adjusted posttest ANCOVA models as sensitivity analyses; network analyses were secondary and exploratory. The intervention group showed a larger increase in intercultural sensitivity (interaction b = 0.699, 95% CI [0.524, 0.875], BH-adjusted p < .001), and the baseline-adjusted posttest difference remained substantial (b = 1.042, 95% CI [0.918, 1.165], BH-adjusted p < .001). Authors: Tschäschke N.; Thielsch M.T.
Title: Motivation under pressure: a systematic review of psychological and organizational factors in emergency volunteering
Abstract: Emergency services worldwide rely heavily on volunteers, yet high-risk organizations such as fire, civil protection, and disaster response services struggle with member demotivation and dropout. This systematic review integrates psychological and organizational perspectives to identify factors that sustain or erode volunteers’ motivation in high-risk environments (HREs). Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a preregistered, protocol-driven search in seven international databases, screened 3,684 records, and included 87 empirical studies from 24 countries covering volunteer fire services, emergency medical services, search and rescue, and civil protection units (N_total = 8,162). Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), we mapped our findings to need-supportive and need-thwarting conditions at individual and organizational levels. Across contexts, the most consistent positive driver of retention was relatedness, operationalized as team cohesion, identification, and mutual trust. Individual competence was fostered by clear roles, realistic preparation, high-quality training, and constructive feedback; autonomy was fostered by meaningful voice and local discretion. Demotivation and withdrawal were associated with chronic overload, work–family conflict, burnout and secondary trauma, high alert load, poor leadership and communication, and perceived lack of fairness and recognition. Overall, the evidence suggests that retaining volunteers in HREs is primarily an organizational design outcome rather than an individual resilience trait. We outline two practice-oriented implications, namely “trust and risk resilience” and “expectation-to-experience alignment” which translate SDT-based insights into actionable levers for designing safer and more reliable volunteer systems under conditions of growing societal risks. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: A representation-explanation framework for flow-based border effects on intra-urban commuting using geographically weighted additive gravity model and machine learning
Abstract: Border effects suppress cross-boundary flows of people and goods, and it is precisely this suppression that drives the gradual divergence of built environment and socioeconomic conditions on either side of a boundary. Measuring border effects from flows is therefore more proximate to the border effect itself than inferring them from downstream outcomes such as housing price differentials or service provision gaps. To address the challenge that flow-based border effects are inherently unobservable and thus unable to be systematically characterized, this study proposes a representation-explanation framework. In the representation stage, a flow-based geographically weighted additive gravity model (FB-GWAGM) that treats each border crossing as an additive increment to physical distance is adopted. In the explanation stage, reliability-weighted random forest models with SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis identify the built environment and socioeconomic factors affecting border thickness. On the basis of the modeling results, the spatial heterogeneity of border thickness is identified and quantified in distance-equivalent units, and the contributions of built environment and socioeconomic factors to this heterogeneity are decomposed in the same metric, enabling direct comparison across border types and factor dimensions. These findings demonstrate that the representation-explanation framework provides a replicable and physically interpretable approach to quantifying flow-based border effects, advancing the understanding of how borders shape spatial interaction within cities and revealing the socioeconomically contingent nature of border thickness heterogeneity. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: An integrated safety framework for human-informed learning and injury-aware evaluation of autonomous driving

Title: Blame, trust, and public cooperation in child protection: a comparative compositional survey analysis of nine societies

Title: Wind energy and protected areas on islands: Scaling, spatial intensity, inequality, and licensing outcomes across an archipelago

Title: What creates safe and efficient pedestrian–vehicle interactions? a naturalistic study to design human-like behaviour for automated vehicles

While vehicle speed and acceleration are vital communication signals for this interaction, the ways in which human drivers use these kinematic communication signals remain under-explored. To design motion-based communication for AVs, this study aims to explore how drivers control their speed as a function of initial interaction conditions, and how this translates into more or less successful interaction outcomes. We analysed naturalistic trajectory data of vehicles and pedestrians from two zebra crossings in Leeds, UK, comprising 981 interactions. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) was applied to quantify the mediating effect of vehicle kinematics on the relationship between initial time gap and interaction outcomes (crossing order, efficiency, and safety). Based on these models, vehicle speed profiles associated with optimal and worst outcomes were identified and compared using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE). PLS-SEM results confirmed that vehicle kinematics significantly mediate interaction outcomes, exerting a strong influence on efficiency and safety, and a weaker influence on crossing order. Minimum vehicle speed in particular exerted a strong influence on crossing order and safety, suggesting that the speed to which the driver drops is a key communication signal to pedestrians. The mediation results and trajectory analysis revealed that drivers used different strategies to achieve balance between their efficiency and interaction safety: in yielding scenarios (time gap > 3 s), they decelerated early and softly to maintain a low non-zero speed (∼1 m/s) at a far distance (>10 m) to ensure safety while conserving momentum to ensure efficiency; in ambiguous non-yielding scenarios (time gaps ∼ 1 – 3 s), they employed a two-stage strategy: a proactive initial deceleration to prepare for potential danger and reduce uncertainty, followed by an assertive acceleration for efficiency; in unambiguous non-yielding scenarios with a narrow time gap (< 1 s), they sacrificed a small amount of efficiency and adopted proactive deceleration before pedestrians displayed a clear crossing intention to ensure safety. This study expands the understanding of interaction beyond binary yielding choices, offering new insights into the proactive strategies human drivers use to negotiate right-of-way safely and efficiently. Emulating these kinematic strategies can support better integration of AVs into human traffic. Title: Exploring pro-environmental behavior of urban green spaces’ visitors through the information-motivation-behavioral skills model
Abstract: Pro-environmental behavior of citizens in utilizing urban green spaces is a critical factor in the sustainable management and effective use of services provided by these areas. In the context of factors influencing this behavior, there exists a research gap regarding the impact of informational, motivational, and behavioral skills factors. Authors: Wunderlich F.; Reis M.
Title: Studying trust in AI in sports: An interdisciplinary primer
Abstract: The increasing use of AI in daily life has not only changed society, but also research on AI. The focus has broadened from methods and problem-solving ability towards consideration of legal, ethical or psychological aspects, investigating how AI is perceived, used and affects human behavior. Rapid developments in AI technology and conflicting theories on the extent of human trust in AI-based decision aid have made trust in AI a much-discussed topic. Inspired by the increasing importance of AI-tools in sports and the role of sports as a well-established environment to study psychological phenomena, we review the current state of research on trust in AI in sports. Moreover, drawing on existing research from other domains, we explore the potential of sport to expand our theoretical understanding of trust in AI. Through a literature search, we find that sport has been mainly ignored in the literature so far. At the same time, reviews from other domains have highlighted open research questions, for which sports would be the predetermined research environment. We particularly identify sports as a domain where behavioural measures are easy to assess, where field studies are possible, where reliable and objective skill assessments exist and with high availability of individual-level data. This article intends to serve sports psychologists as a starting point to assess existing evidence in this large, interdisciplinary and rapidly growing research field and to stimulate more studies on trust in AI in sports. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Rapa C.; Busayo E.T.
Title: Global paradigms of sustainable urban mobility: Towards just transportation transitions
Abstract: The transition towards low-carbon and inclusive urban mobility has become increasingly important as cities seek to reduce transport-related greenhouse gas emissions while addressing congestion, road safety, pollution and unequal access to mobility. This study systematically reviews sustainable urban mobility (SUM) research to examine the implementation of electrification, active mobility and mass transit, the barriers affecting their implementation, and their implications for just transportation transitions. The review synthesizes evidence from 75 peer-reviewed articles published between 2009 and 2024, complemented by relevant grey literature. Three dominant paradigms emerged: electrification of mobility, active mobility, and mass transit, particularly Bus Rapid Transit (BRT). The findings indicate that the implementation of these pathways varies substantially across urban contexts, reflecting differences in infrastructure, financial capacity, institutional arrangements, governance, technological readiness and socioeconomic conditions. While electrification and active mobility are increasingly prominent in many higher-income contexts, mass transit remains an important transition pathway in many cities of the Global South, including African cities. Across contexts, however, implementation is constrained by recurring challenges, including financing limitations, infrastructure gaps, fragmented governance, policy inconsistency, technological constraints and behavioural barriers. The review demonstrates that sustainable mobility transitions cannot rely on the direct transfer of policy models but require adaptation to local institutional, spatial and socioeconomic conditions. It further highlights the importance of equity, accessibility, participatory governance and integration with broader urban and energy systems in achieving just transportation transitions. The study contributes a comparative synthesis of global mobility pathways, implementation barriers and justice considerations, providing policy-relevant insights for context-sensitive sustainable mobility transitions in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Deng H.; Xin S.
Title: From growth machine to integration machine: A historical-institutional perspective of Chinese statecraft under rural revitalization
Abstract: This study analyses the transition trends of China’s spatial governance from a growth machine to an “integration machine,” from an institutional reconfiguration perspective. We propose that while the urban growth machine has dominated spatial politics in China, its institutional foundations also provide the conditions for the emergence of an integration machine. This integration machine reflects a path-dependent logic rooted in the historical Chinese statecraft of integrating fragmented grassroots communities into cohesive territorial governance — an alternative logic to capital-driven growth. Drawing on China’s Rural Revitalization, including its strategic position, policy initiatives, and local implementation, this article reveals how the integration machine is underpinned by the reconfiguration of party, bureaucratic, and fiscal institutions. Meanwhile, new challenges have emerged from the intensifying interplay between institutions and actions during implementation. By conceptualizing the integration machine, the study introduces a new perspective on territorial governance by emphasizing the institutional foundations of statecraft. Title: Patterns of kindergarten mathematics instructional content in the United States’ classrooms and associations with children’s academic gains
Abstract: While most prior research has used variable-centered approaches to examine how mathematics instructional content relates to children’s academic outcomes, we extend the literature by applying the latent class analysis to classify patterns of teacher reported mathematics instructional content in 2,800 classrooms at the spring of kindergarten and investigate their associations with children’s (Child N = 12,290) academic gains from fall to spring. Moreover, children with initially low mathematics skills in Pattern 2 classrooms showed higher mathematics gains than those in Patterns 3 or 4. Title: Global patterns of marine protected area downgrading, downsizing, and degazettement (PADDD) and offshore infrastructure development
Abstract: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are key to conserving ocean biodiversity and regulating extractive uses. However, legal rollbacks to MPAs, known as protected area downgrading, downsizing, and degazettement (PADDD) events, threaten the durability of these protections, especially when authorizing activities incompatible with conservation objectives. To examine these links, we collected new and existing PADDD data from 1975 to 2025 and assessed satellite-based detections of infrastructure from Global Fishing Watch. Detections focused on large, persistent offshore infrastructure located more than 1 km from shore, including oil platforms. A total of 64 oil and gas developments and 12 unknown infrastructure developments intersected 9 unique MPAs across 10 PADDD events in 6 countries. Of these 9 MPAs, 90% had infrastructure detected after establishment, and 44% had detections following the PADDD event. MPAs with PADDD events were twice as likely to have overlapping infrastructure point compared to MPAs without PADDD events (9.5% vs. 5.0%). Such MPAs occurred in China, Venezuela, Jamaica, Peru, Australia, and the United States. Case studies from China, Venezuela, and Australia show how PADDD enables industrial development via legal reclassification and rezoning. These findings indicate that PADDD in marine systems is not the result of isolated decisions, but rather a manifestation of deeper governance phenomena and competing development priorities. Stronger legal safeguards, and improved implementation and enforcement are needed to ensure the durability of MPAs under accelerating industrial pressures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Early educator depressive symptoms and responses to challenging behaviors
Abstract: Educator wellbeing has received increased attention as a critical factor in early care and education (ECE) quality, yet little is known about how depressive symptoms impact classroom practices, particularly responses to challenging behaviors. We use data from a community sample of toddler and preschool teachers working in publicly funded ECE settings in Louisiana to document the prevalence of depressive symptoms and examine their relationship to educators’ reported behavior management strategies. Consistent with previous findings in Louisiana, our study revealed elevated rates of depressive symptoms across the workforce. Title: Understanding the temporal dynamics of user experience in VR gaming: Evidence from large-scale game reviews
Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) challenges static views of user experience (UX), yet little is known about how evaluations shift over time. This study investigates the temporal dynamics of VR UX by focusing on three factors: playtime, post-release time, and Early Access (EA) status. We analyze 351,432 Steam reviews across 334 VR titles (2016–2024), applying transformer-based classifiers to detect sentiment for seven UX dimensions (immersion, presence, engagement, achievement, embodiment, controllability, and physical discomfort). Using the Cognitive-Affective-Behavioral (CAB) framework, we assess how these dimensions shape recommendations under varying temporal conditions. Results show distinct temporal patterns. Longer playtime shifts attention from pragmatic concerns to hedonic aspects, while sentiment becomes more positive overall. However, extended play reduces the weight of every single UX factor in recommendation decisions. In contrast, reviews of older games mention fewer UX dimensions and display more negative sentiment, though sentiment for specific dimensions becomes more predictive of recommendation. Finally, EA reviews are more positive, mention more UX dimensions overall but tend to downplay physical-discomfort concerns, and exhibit weaker links between sentiment and recommendation, reflecting tolerant, forward-looking evaluations. Authors: Spencer D.
Title: Form and Fetish: Architecture, the commodity, and the ends of capitalism
Source title: Form and Fetish: Architecture, the Commodity, and the Ends of Capitalism
Abstract: For more than half a century, critical theory has seen architecture as an ideological tool of capitalism. Form and Fetish confronts this assumption – developing a new form of critique to fundamentally rethink the relationship between architecture and capitalism at a time of economic crisis and environmental breakdown. Douglas Spencer, author of the critically acclaimed The Architecture of Neoliberalism, introduces contemporary Marxist theories of value, commodity fetishism, and economic compulsion to examine architecture as a vehicle for accumulation and a means of subjectification. From architectures of luxury in Seoul, Bangkok, and London to climate-controlled enclaves in Singapore, from billionaire real estate in Los Angeles through to Saudi Arabia's NEOM, Spencer explores how architecture has shaped itself to these ends through its disdain for everyday use and its fetishization of form. As capitalism buckles under the weight of its own contradictions, Form and Fetish is an appeal to de-fetishize, dis-alienate and re-collectivize the design and construction of the built environment. With its capacity to protect and to shelter, to articulate and mediate our relationships to others and our environments, architecture, Spencer argues, is too essential to be treated as exceptional, too important to be determined by exchange value. This book is a must-read for architects, architectural theorists, critical theorists and philosophers – all who wish to seize the opportunity to rethink design and building activity as a means to realize collectively conceived ends. © Douglas Spencer, 2027.

Title: Isolating task-related, low-level, and high-level influences on interobserver congruency of eye movements in scene viewing
Abstract: When different individuals view the same image, their eye movements are often similar. The degree of this similarity is called interobserver congruency (IOC). We investigated how IOC is determined by three factors that impact gaze control: the visual features of an image, its semantic content, and the task observers perform when viewing it. We first quantified the low-level physical features and semantic complexity of images using a well-established measure of visual clutter and a novel measure based on a distributional semantic model, respectively. Then, we selected an image set in which these two measures were uncorrelated and used it in an eye-tracking experiment, in which observers either freely viewed the images or memorised their content. We assessed IOC using four metrics: two capturing purely spatial IOC and two sensitive to spatiotemporal IOC, i.e., considering both the locations and order of fixations. The values of the two spatial metrics decreased with increasing clutter and remained insensitive to the remaining factors we investigated. The two spatiotemporal metrics were sensitive to both clutter and semantic complexity, but, interestingly, in different ways. Specifically, according to a metric that was insensitive to the presence of objects in images, IOC decreased with clutter and increased with semantic complexity, while the metric sensitive to objects showed the opposite pattern. Additionally, we found that the memorization task rendered oculomotor behaviour more exploratory, which had modulatory effects on spatiotemporal – but not spatial – IOC. Authors: Nie X.; Huang Z.; Yu G.
Title: The proximity–access paradox in Medicaid administrative services: Transportation barriers and spatial inequalities in the United States
Abstract: Health equity depends not only on insurance eligibility, but also on access to the administrative system that enables coverage. Using Medicaid administrative offices in the United States as a case, we assess accessibility from over 80,000 census tracts to the nearest Medicaid office across driving, public transit, bicycling, and walking using distances and travel times. We identify a proximity–access paradox: while geographic distances to offices are broadly similar across modes, functional accessibility diverges sharply once translated into time and transportation feasibility. Multilevel analyses further show that accessibility varies systematically with neighborhood income, racial composition, age structure, disability prevalence, and state context. These findings highlight transportation barriers as an important structural determinant of administrative access to health insurance coverage and suggest that improving health equity requires policy attention not only to eligibility and coverage expansion but also to the transportation systems that enable people to reach the administrative institutions of health systems. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Modeling and simulating human behavior in large-scale emergency evacuations: A comprehensive review
Abstract: Disasters pose persistent threats to human life and infrastructure, making evacuation planning vital for disaster risk reduction. The effectiveness of such efforts depends on understanding and accurately modeling human behavior. This study reviews 479 peer-reviewed articles on large-scale evacuation planning and management, classifying them along two dimensions: behavioral factors influencing key authority-issued decisions and modeling approaches incorporating these dynamics within optimization, simulation, and simulation–optimization frameworks. While demographic and route-choice behaviors are extensively studied, mode selection and road-segment designation remain largely unexplored. Optimization models commonly assume full- or non-compliance, with limited research that considers partial-compliance, leading to more realistic solutions. On the other hand, simulation-based studies capture dynamic and uncertain conditions more effectively but are dominated by rule-based behavioral proxies, particularly for departure timing and route choice, and typically limit dynamic feedback to route choice alone. Simulation–optimization approaches, while increasingly adopted, remain largely reliant on parameter-based behavioral representations rather than empirically calibrated, behavior-oriented coupling. Emphasizing the importance of embedding behavioral heterogeneity in model structures, this review develops a taxonomy, highlights research gaps, and outlines future directions for behaviorally realistic evacuation models that enhance the effectiveness and practicality of evacuation strategies in real-world crises. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From coast to cost: Mispricing and reform scenarios in Italy's coastal concession system

Title: Development and psychometric evaluation of the parent-report preschool defending behaviors questionnaire in Chinese preschoolers
Abstract: Although defending behaviors represent early-emerging prosocial responses that can effectively counter peer aggression or bullying, age-appropriate measures for preschoolers remain scarce. Title: Southern roots abroad: The long-run impact of the Confederate migration to Brazil
Abstract: This paper examines the long-term economic and cultural impacts of the postbellum migration of Southern white individuals to Brazil. Following the U.S. Civil War, thousands of individuals from the former Confederacy settled in a relatively poor region of São Paulo, contributing to its transformation into one of Brazil's wealthiest areas. Title: Who plans and who sticks to it? The travel plan-generation gap and forecasting long-holiday trip generation

Title: The dual-path mechanism underlying the influence of negative workplace gossip on receivers' thriving at work

Title: Behavioral nudges and feedback lead to improved pre-primary teacher practices in Kenya

Title: Transportation convenience perceptions, travel modes, and migrants’ settlement decisions in urban China
Abstract: Rapid urbanization and unprecedented population mobility in China have intensified the need to understand the drivers of migrants’ settlement decisions. Title: Cross-typology positive energy district pathways in Mediterranean Southern Italy: harmonised district energy modelling and urban-scale life cycle assessment
Abstract: Reducing carbon emissions is a central EU objective, and Positive Energy Districts (PEDs) are increasingly recognised as a practical pathway for urban decarbonisation. Both post-retrofit configurations achieve full electrification, completely phase out natural gas, and consequently shift final energy use towards electricity, partly compensated by rooftop PV generation. However, introducing electric cooling alongside full HVAC electrification further increases electricity demand, and PV covers 45% of annual post-retrofit electricity demand. Authors: Fernandez Escobar R.; Font S.
Title: Children's educational outcomes: Variation by children's living arrangements and exposure to maternal criminal legal system involvement
Abstract: Maternal involvement with the criminal legal system (CLS) often leads to changes in children's living arrangements, reorganizing family roles, authority and daily routines. Drawing on family systems theory, we argue that these living arrangements function as emergent responses in the context of adversity that can either be protective or disruptive for children's educational outcomes. Using longitudinal administrative data from the Wisconsin Administrative Data Core (WADC), we follow a cohort of 129,139 children from Wisconsin born in 2000-2002 across grades 3-11. We examine how living arrangements (with biological parents, grandparents, other relatives, or nonbiological family) shape educational outcomes (reading and math test scores; attendance rates) across varying levels of early-life maternal CLS involvement (none, CLS contact without incarceration, incarceration). Specifically, we leverage hybrid mixed effects models that decompose associations into within- and between-child components. Attendance rates were higher during years children lived with grandparents, other relatives, or nonbiological family than during years with a biological parent, across all CLS groups and robustness checks. Test-score associations were more modest, heterogeneous, and CLS-dependent. Overall, alternative living arrangements were associated with small increases in test scores in the context of prior maternal incarceration but were associated with decreased test scores among children with no maternal CLS involvement. Supplemental analyses highlight that the duration spent in alternative living arrangements and institutional support may be more important correlates of children's educational outcomes than caregiver type. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Dolker P.; Sharma S.
Title: Indigenous Mountain Farming in Nubra Valley: Diversification in Cropping Pattern
Abstract: This chapter delves into the intricate dynamics of indigenous mountain farming in Ladakh’s Nubra Valley, emphasising the multifaceted interplay between agriculture, pastoralism and economic transformations. Focused on five strategically chosen villages, the study employs a mix of primary data gathered over 8 months, including household interviews, group discussions and participant observations. The research unfolds the historical, socio-economic and cultural significance of agriculture in the region, shedding light on traditional farming practices and the unique challenges imposed by the harsh climate. The chapter also explores the prevalent cropping patterns in the valley and the transition marked by a decrease in traditional crops and a rise in horticulture farming. The emergence of vegetable cultivation, driven by factors such as tourism and military demand, for both local consumption and commercial purposes, is highlighted. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Personality meta-traits are associated with neural control regimes governing the persistence–flexibility trade-off
Abstract: Human personality is highly structured, yet the mechanisms giving rise to this structure remain poorly understood. Although the Big Five framework provides a robust descriptive taxonomy, it offers limited insight into why personality traits cluster into higher-order dimensions or how these dimensions relate to adaptive behavior. Here we address this gap by linking personality meta-traits to neural dynamics governing the stability–flexibility trade-off in cognitive control. Using electrophysiological recordings and latent-variable modeling ( N = 160), we show that individual differences in metacontrol adjustment—indexed by variability in the aperiodic component of EEG activity—predict the Big Five meta-traits of Stability (Persistence) and Plasticity (Flexibility). Critically, these associations emerge at the neural level but not at the behavioral level, indicating that domain-general control dynamics provide a more direct window into personality structure than task performance alone. These findings suggest that personality meta-traits reflect enduring biases in a neural control regime that regulates how humans balance persistence and adaptability across contexts. By linking personality structure to a mechanistic principle of neural control, our results move beyond descriptive trait models and offer a unified account of individual differences in human behavior. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Ross A.G.
Title: From transient shocks to unexpected outcomes: Disruptive drivers in scenario pathways
Abstract: Scenario pathways (e.g. for the energy transition) often use a single trajectory or a band. That is not sufficient when one needs to understand not just that outcomes differ but what drives those differences, whether a transient shock, a different storyline, or uncertainty about how factors interact. Doing so requires tracking disequilibrium along pathways, comparing runs across “worlds” or storylines, and surfacing outcomes that are unlikely under a central view but plausible when how factors interact is uncertain. Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) is a well-established method for generating pathways. This paper extends CIB to formalise and implement disequilibrium, extremes, and unexpected outcomes in pathway runs, and defines four run types that respectively emphasise one-off shocks, extremes under alternative regimes, influence-structure uncertainty that widens over time, and exogenous shocks as a baseline for comparison. The approach is applied to a socio-technical decarbonisation pathway for illustration. Together, these extensions support stress-testing, comparison across storyline or regime assumptions, and exploration of rare or surprising futures, and help analysts distinguish results that are stable across those assumptions from those that depend on structural uncertainty about the influence table. © 2026 The Author

Title: The dynamic relationship between intern nursing student's transition shock and job retention intention: A dual trajectories longitudinal study
Abstract: Background: The global shortage of nurses underscores the critical need to understand intern nursing students' willingness to persist in the profession. The transition shock commonly encountered by intern nursing students significantly impact their job retention intention and career choices, making it essential to understand the dynamic relationship between these factors. Aim: This study aims to investigate the developmental trajectories of transition shock and job retention intentions among intern nursing students during their clinical placements. It will assess the interrelationships between these phenomena and identify relevant influencing factors. Design: A prospective cohort study Methods: A prospective cohort study was conducted in Chengdu, China, from July 2024 to May 2025. Data were collected three times during the nursing students' internship period using the Social-demographic information questionnaire, Transition Shock Scale of Undergraduate Nursing Students(TSS, Chinese version)and the Questionnaire for Nurse Intention to Remain Employed. The analysis utilized Group-Based Dual Trajectory Modeling (GBDTM) and multiple logistic regression. Results: The study included 211 intern nursing students. Transition shocks were classified into four trajectories: Low-flat (9.9%), Low-to-Middle (9.9%), Middle-stable (37.4%), and High-to-Middle (42.8%). Job retention intentions showed four trajectories: Low-flat (16.1%), Middle-stable (50.2%), High-stable (22.3%), and High-curved (11.4%). Group-Based Dual Trajectory Modeling (GBDTM) identified 16 co-occurrence patterns, the most prevalent being the “High-to-Middle transition shock and Middle-stable job retention intention” (28.43%) and the “Middle-stable transition shock and Middle-stable job retention intention” (26.81%). Factors such as job retention intention, education, Internship hospital is the first choice, and satisfaction with the internship environment were identified as risk factors for transition shock among intern nursing students. Additionally, transition shock, being an only child, Preference for the nursing profession, and the relationship with the preceptor during the internship emerged as significant predictors of job retention intention. Conclusion: We identified distinct trajectories, co-occurrence patterns, and influencing factors related to transition shock and job retention intentions among intern nursing students. Nursing educators can utilize these findings to design personalized intervention strategies aimed at mitigating transition shock and enhancing job retention intentions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Cannabis use and subsequent onset of manic symptoms and bipolar disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Background Bipolar disorder is a disabling psychiatric condition affecting approximately 2% of the population, for which identifying modifiable risk factors prior to illness onset is a research priority. Cannabis use is highly prevalent, yet its role in the development of bipolar-spectrum outcomes remains unclear. Previous reviews have included few studies or combined distinct bipolar-spectrum outcomes, limiting outcome-specific inference. Aims To evaluate the association between cannabis exposure and subsequent incident BD and manic/hypomanic symptoms separately and examine potential moderating factors. Methods Registered ( https://osf.io/s38x4/ ), PRISMA/MOOSE-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of PubMed and Web of Science from inception to October 2025. We included longitudinal observational studies comparing cannabis-exposed and unexposed individuals without prior BD and assessing subsequent bipolar-spectrum outcomes. We meta-analysed studies with extractable data, calculating the unadjusted risk ratios (RRs) for incident BD and manic/hypomanic symptoms. Random-effects meta-analyses, heterogeneity analyses, subgroup analyses and meta-regressions were performed. Study quality was appraised using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). Results Nineteen studies were included (total N = 6,960,517; mean age 23.8 ± 11.8 years; 49% female). Cannabis use was associated with increased risk of BD (RR = 2.46, 95% CI = 1.57–3.84; k = 8; N = 206.572) and manic/hypomanic symptoms (RR = 2.11, 95% CI = 1.07–4.18; k = 6; N = 57,243). Moderator analyses identified significant clinical and methodological sources of heterogeneity. NOS scores ranged from 6 to 9, indicating good to high methodological quality. Title: Does it matter how we measure family complexity? Sequence-based indices and children's educational outcomes
Abstract: Objective: The association between a wide range of family complexity indicators and children's educational outcomes was assessed. Background: Previous research documented the negative impact of disadvantageous family transitions and family instability on children's educational outcomes. However, theoretical and empirical debates continue on how to measure family complexity during childhood. Method: We are the first to combine dynamic sequence analysis with fixed-effects models: using UK linked survey–register data (UKHLS and the National Pupil Database for England), we construct eight family complexity measures including novel indices weighted by three theoretical perspectives and estimate within-child associations with math and English test scores, separately by child and parental gender. Results: Family complexity measures are largely negatively associated with children's academic performance, but strength and even direction vary across measures, subjects, and parental gender. The number of transitions and the badness measures are most consistently associated with children's test scores. Associations are often stronger for boys compared to girls. Crucially, the conventional number-of-transitions measure blurs — and in some cases reverses — gender differences that the theory-driven measures reveal: boys are most affected by measures capturing parental absence in mothers' partnership histories (consistent with the same-sex hypothesis), while girls tend to be more affected by disruption and favorability perspectives. Conclusion: Findings highlight the importance of theoretically derived measures of family complexity. Measures associated with family instability and parental absence were shown to be most often linked with children's educational outcomes. However, relying on family instability may conceal gender differences and their theoretical drivers, which are more effectively captured by the new family complexity measures suggested in this study. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Yang Y.; Zhang Y.; Xia H.; Liu X.; Li J.
Title: Food go/no-go training changes food wanting in women: Behavioral, brain activity, and choice outcomes
Abstract: Food evaluations can be altered by associating mere action versus inaction with these foods. In this study, we examined how food go/no-go training influences food wanting and its brain correlates using functional magnetic resonance imaging in a sample of women (N = 85). During the training session, participants learned to consistently respond to go foods while suppressing responses to no-go foods. Food wanting was assessed through a rating task in which participants reported how much they wanted to eat the go and no-go foods before and after training. The results revealed that wanting ratings for no-go foods declined significantly after training. Functional magnetic resonance imaging data indicated that the devaluation effect was associated with lower blood-oxygen-level-dependent responses in the middle frontal, middle occipital, and inferior occipital gyri. Exploratory dynamic causal modelling was used to characterize post-training modulation of effective connectivity among these three regions, with the strongest effects involving bidirectional middle frontal gyrus-inferior occipital gyrus connectivity. Statistical mediation analysis suggested an indirect association between the inferior occipital gyrus-to-middle frontal gyrus modulatory effect and post-training food choice through food wanting, although this same-session analysis involved closely related preference readouts and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Overall, the findings suggest that simply responding or not responding to certain foods can alter subjective food evaluation, and that these evaluation changes may be related to immediate post-training food choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Reassurance without onboard staff: System cues, positive travel experience, and intention to use GoA4 unattended metros
Abstract: Introduction Grade of Automation 4 (GoA4) unattended metros remove onboard staff from routine journeys, so passengers must judge whether a staffless trip feels manageable, supported, and useable. This study examines how system cues are associated with intention to use GoA4 unattended metros. Methods We integrated TAM with SDT and service/automation perspectives. System autonomy support (SAS) and system relatedness support (SRS) were modeled as cues for independent trip management and the visible availability of help. Cross-sectional online survey data from four Chinese megacities (N = 347) were analyzed using covariance-based SEM and exploratory multigroup analysis with false discovery rate adjustment. Results Behavioral intention was positively associated with PEOU (β = 0.446, p < .001), perceived enjoyment (PEN; β = 0.382, p < .001), and PU (β = 0.140, p < .05). PEN was positively associated with PEOU (β = 0.192, p < .05) but not PU. SAS and SRS were positively associated with PU, PEOU, and PEN. After adjustment, experience-based differences remained for the PEN-PU and PEN-PEOU associations; among self-reported gender groups, only the PU-BI difference remained significant. Conclusions Intention to use GoA4 unattended metros was associated mainly with ease of use and anticipated positive travel experience, with a smaller association for usefulness. System cues such as clear wayfinding, visible help resources, remote-support information, and fallback procedures may help make unattended journeys feel more manageable. Direct health outcomes were not measured; the findings indicate acceptance mechanisms related to perceived safety/security, travel stress, accessibility, and willingness to use sustainable mass transit. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Design as a Means of Valuing Heritage and Sustainable Regional Development

Title: Determinants of Maternal Adaptation to Childhood Vaccination in 21st-Century Southernmost Thailand
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study investigates maternal behavioral adaptation toward childhood immunization within the sociocultural context of Southernmost Thailand, evaluating how individual capacities and contextual correlates influence vaccination completion. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,200 mothers of children aged five years or older in Pattani, Yala, and Narathiwat. Using a three-stage, stratified, multi-stage random sampling technique, geographic and demographic representativeness was ensured. Data were collected via structured interviews using a validated instrument (IOC ≥ 0.60), and binary logistic regression was employed to identify significant predictors of immunization adherence. Results indicated a childhood vaccination completion rate of 63.7%. Multivariate analysis revealed that maternal adaptation was strongly driven by socio-economic stability and modern health literacy. Mothers with stable socio-demographic profiles, particularly government officials (OR = 7.98; 95% CI [2.67, 23.81]) and business owners (OR = 6.74; 95% CI [2.54, 17.87]), had significantly higher odds of completing. High service satisfaction (OR = 4.39; 95% CI [3.09, 6.23]) and maternal COVID-19 vaccination history (OR = 3.28; 95% CI [1.53, 4.22]) emerged as robust positive predictors. Conversely, specific contextual determinants, including paternal decision-making authority and vaccine safety anxiety, significantly hindered adherence, reflecting the enduring influence of traditional patriarchal structures. Strictly medical or economic approaches are insufficient to address this variation in uptake, as barriers are deeply rooted in the region’s unique sociocultural and structural scaffolding. Title: Perceived environmental qualities and purpose-specific walking across neighborhoods: Evidence from working-age adults in a second-tier city in China
Abstract: Introduction Walkable neighborhoods are central to public health agendas, yet how neighborhood environments shape everyday walking remains inconsistently understood and unevenly evidenced. Existing research relies mainly on objective spatial indicators, concentrates on well-studied megacities, and overlooks working-age adults. This study addresses these gaps by examining perceived qualities and purpose-specific walking among working-age adults in a non-western and non-mega context. Methods A questionnaire survey was conducted across four purposively selected residential communities in Ningbo, a second-tier city in eastern China. A total of 811 adults aged 19-59 were recruited. Ordinal logistic regression was used to identify associations between perceived built-environment qualities (26 items in four dimensions: accessibility, comfort, aesthetics, and safety) and three walking purposes (commuting, household errands, and leisure). Results Distinct patterns emerge across walking purposes. Perceived comfort and aesthetics show context-dependent associations with commuting walking, while perceived accessibility is positively associated with household walking, with limited evidence of contextual variation in the association with perceived safety. Leisure walking is most consistently associated with perceived accessibility and aesthetics. Notably, residents in the newly-built and relatively well-served community report lower levels of leisure walking despite higher perceived environmental ratings, suggesting a perception-behavior discrepancy within modern gated developments. Conclusions This study offers a comparative and perception-based approach, which provides transferable insights to other mid-sized Asian urban settings where megacity evidence may not hold. The findings suggest that urban planning should move beyond uniform infrastructure standards and physical provision, toward more diagnostic and trip-purpose-specific interventions that address the contextual constraints of different neighborhood environments. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Core attributes of nursing disciplinary leaders in higher education: A modified Delphi study
Abstract: Background: The Australian and New Zealand Higher Education sectors have been subject to many challenges over the last decade. Methods: A modified e-Delphi, inclusive of an Expert Advisory Group, was used to identify an evidence-based set of core attributes. Title: Employee knowledge and smart technology adoption: Evidence from the E-waste sector
Abstract: Smart technologies are increasingly introduced in workplaces, yet employees do not always translate positive evaluations into technology adoption. This study examines how different forms of employee knowledge shape persuasion toward smart technologies and how employee engagement conditions the relationship between persuasion and technology adoption, an area that has received little attention. However, persuasion alone does not directly lead to the adoption of smart technology in the e-waste sector businesses. Instead, employee engagement positively moderates the persuasion–smart technology adoption relationship, suggesting that engagement helps explain when favourable evaluations are more likely to translate into adoption behaviour. Therefore, mediation analysis indicates a more complex pattern: persuasion showed a negative direct association with smart technology adoption, and the indirect effects suggest a possible context-specific discontinuity between persuasion and reported adoption behaviour rather than a straightforward knowledge-persuasion-smart technology adoption pathway. Title: Unlocking hidden demand: Reconstructing bus OD flows by integrating mobile trajectories and Map API
Abstract: Accurate Origin-Destination (OD) data are essential for understanding complex travel behavior and advancing sustainable, equitable urban bus systems, yet remain globally scarce. It also yielded strong correlation with official ridership data (R2 = 0.786). The reconstructed OD flows revealed demand complexities invisible to boarding-only data, including stop-level functional imbalances between trip generators and attractors, and Pareto-distributed ridership concentration. An illustrative network optimization application further quantified planning value. Title: Task-based functional connectivity in striato-motor-cortical system in autism: Associations with sex and executive function
Abstract: Previously we found that female autistic youth (Aut-F) showed reduced brain response in dorsal striatum (putamen) when viewing human motion, alongside larger rare copy number variants that included genes expressed in early striatal development. Thus, striatal differences may characterize Aut-F, but broader systems-level and behavioral implications of these differences remain unexplored. Title: Police violence against women during protest gatherings in eight countries
Abstract: This article focuses on the gender-specific forms of police violence against women during protests and the institutional and discursive mechanisms that legitimize such violence. The reviewed cases suggest that police violence may function not only as a means of public-order control but also as a mechanism for disciplining, delegitimizing, and intimidating women whose political participation challenges established gender norms and political authority. The article underscores the need for systematic and institutionally independent documentation to clarify the forms, scope, and distribution of police violence and gender-based repression and to challenge the institutional impunity that permits such practices to persist. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Exploration and modeling of a longitudinal cross-sector telemedicine and ambulatory wound care intervention in Norway – The CROSTAI model

Title: A decision-centric framework for timing and intensity of recommendation interventions
Abstract: This study reframes interventions in short-form video recommendations as an operational decision-making problem. Title: How public health perspectives can influence risk management practices of OHS professionals
Abstract: This study explores how occupational health and safety (OHS) professionals can rethink and expand their usual risk management approaches by employing public health perspectives. Drawing on a focus group and interview study conducted in Australia between October 2024 and March 2025, this study reveals a positive trend: OHS professionals exposed to public health courses start to shift their thinking about risk management. Results show four areas of risk management. First, broader determinants of health emphasised in public health courses encourage OHS professionals to extend risk management beyond traditional risk control and to consider upstream, midstream, and downstream factors in a tailored approach. Second, OHS professionals’ strong grounding in tangible risks, engineering- and technology-related training, and practical experience serves as a hidden strength that may equip them well to acquire public health logic. Third, public health perspectives enhance holistic and inclusive risk management-related consultation and support more effective collaboration with occupational health professionals. Fourth, public health training fosters reflective practice, enabling OHS professionals to recognise their knowledge gaps and seek additional expertise when managing complex risks. Overall, the findings suggest that OHS professionals’ practical grounding in risk management provides a robust foundation for integrating human‑centred, health‑focused approaches, highlighting a promising and important opportunity to enhance modern workplace risk management through public health education. Title: Nursing students' critical engagement with generative AI in evidence-based practice education: A qualitative descriptive study
Abstract: Background: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into nursing education presents both opportunities and challenges, yet empirical evidence on students' critical engagement with AI-generated content within assessment contexts remains limited. Aim: To examine undergraduate nursing students' reflections when comparing their own evidence-based summaries with AI-generated outputs in response to the same clinical research questions. Methods: A qualitative descriptive design was employed using retrospective analysis of 497 assessment submissions from an undergraduate nursing cohort at an Australian university. Students formulated a research question, synthesised peer-reviewed evidence, submitted the same question to an AI tool, and critically reflected on the comparison. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis and thematic analysis. Results: Four themes were identified: 1. Credibility, quality of evidence and academic rigour. Students identified fabricated references, outdated information, and absence of peer-reviewed sourcing as key limitations. Additionally, students reflected on algorithmic limitations and the challenge of verifying AI outputs without prior topic knowledge; 2. Critical thinking, depth of analysis, and human intelligence. AI was perceived as unable to replicate contextual reasoning or multi-source synthesis; 3. Efficiency, accessibility, and practical utility. AI's speed and clarity were valued for brainstorming and initial scoping; and 4. Student identity, learning, and professional development were shaped by the view that engaging in manual, hands-on research was integral to forming a safe, evidence-informed nursing identity. Conclusion: This study suggests that structured AI-comparison tasks offer the opportunity to develop AI and digital health literacy in nursing students. Students are neither naively accepting of AI nor reflexively dismissive but are actively working to understand its place within the ethical frameworks of nursing education. These findings contribute to AI integration in nursing education and offer practical guidance for educators seeking to support graduates to be AI-critical and well-equipped to leverage the efficiencies of these tools. © 2026

Title: India's electric vehicle transition: Regional disparities, infrastructure deficits, and pathways for sustainable development
Abstract: India's electric vehicle transition is one of the world's most dynamic automotive transformations, driven by emission regulations, policy interventions, and environmental awareness. Annual EV registrations grew from fewer than 25 thousand in 2014 to more than 2 million in 2025. However, systematic understanding of state-level adoption disparities, charging infrastructure adequacy, and regional heterogeneity across India's 36 states and union territories remains limited. This study addresses that gap through a simultaneous, longitudinal, state-level analysis of EV adoption dynamics and public charging infrastructure adequacy. Using 11 years of administrative data (2014–2025) covering 7+ million EV registrations and 25,000+ public charging stations, we apply hybrid forecasting (ARIMA, Prophet, scenario modeling), k-means clustering, Haversine spatial proximity analysis, S-curve saturation modeling, and LASSO-regularized regression. Results reveal exponential acceleration, with year-on-year growth of 166% (2021) and 209% (2022), moderating to 31% by 2024. National S-curve saturation reaches 35.6%, a measure of progress along each state's own diffusion trajectory rather than actual fleet penetration, masking extreme state-level variation (0.2%–90.4%). ARIMA and Prophet trend extrapolation projects 3.2–4.8 million annual EV sales by 2030. A separately framed, illustrative probability-weighted scenario estimate across four policy trajectories indicates 16.8 million annual sales by 2030, requiring infrastructure expansion from 25,000 to about 43,000–47,000 stations under baseline-to-optimistic conditions. The national sales-per-station ratio (93:1) masks sharp disparities: Bihar (337:1) versus Karnataka (35.7:1). Tier 3 cities show 13.5× station deficits and 3.2× greater inter-station spacing than Tier 1 metros despite comparable adoption. Regression identifies a Northeast regional dummy with the largest coefficient magnitude among predictors. Given its borderline significance (p = 0.050) and the small state-level sample, this is best interpreted as suggestive, directional evidence of structural geographic barriers rather than a strong confirmatory finding. GDP shows a positive effect, while population density is non-significant after controls, challenging conventional urbanization narratives. Findings inform a differentiated policy framework: tier-specific infrastructure targets indexed to local adoption; geographically calibrated subsidies for laggard states; a shift from upfront purchase incentives toward usage-based mechanisms (charging tariff discounts, toll exemptions, preferential financing) as markets mature; and federated coordination protocols for interoperable charging networks. This integration of domain knowledge with quantitative rigor offers a replicable template for EV market analysis and policy evaluation in developing economies, where infrastructure constraints and regional disparities shape technology diffusion. © 2026 International Energy Initiative

Title: “Mary thinks that John thinks that…” Developmental change and individual stability in attributing second-order mental states in 5 to 7-year-olds
Abstract: Second-order understanding of mental states develops during middle childhood. However, due to the limited number of longitudinal studies on this topic, the timing of developmental changes and the stability of individual performance remain insufficiently explored. The current study examined the development of recursive theory of mind abilities, namely second-order ignorance and false-belief understanding, between the ages of 5 and 7. Using the Ice Cream Task and the Birthday Puppy Task, we longitudinally tested 166 Polish children at three time points (mean ages: MT1 = 5.64 years, SDT1 = 0.23; MT2 = 6.69, SDT2 = 0.11; and MT3 = 7.63, SDT3 = 0.13). Although we observed overall growth in second-order mental state understanding, understanding of ignorance emerged two years earlier, showing smaller gains between ages 5 and 7 compared to false-belief understanding. Moreover, most children demonstrated consistent developmental trajectories in individual performance. These findings provide a comprehensive developmental overview of second-order mental state attribution, suggesting that, alongside gradual improvement, the observed rank-order stability in rToM may reflect partially stable individual differences over time. Title: SQ-DMVGNN: Decoupling asymmetric technological relationships and fusing semantic-quality representations for dynamic collaboration forecasting
Abstract: Technological collaboration has become an important means of sharing technological risks and advancing key technological breakthroughs. However, existing studies often overlook patent value heterogeneity in technology representation and insufficiently integrate multiple technological drivers of collaboration, while also lacking effective modeling of their dynamic evolution. This study proposes a Dynamic Multi-View Graph Neural Network model based on Semantic and Quality fusion (SQ-DMVGNN). A semantic-quality fusion module is designed to project applicants’ textual semantic features and multidimensional quality attributes into a unified high-dimensional vector space, thereby capturing both technological semantics and patent quality. Then, the proposed framework constructs a dynamic multi-view graph structures to systematically decouple and integrate technological similarity, complementarity, and strategic trend, while modeling their evolution across time slices. Through the proposed framework, SQ-DMVGNN more accurately captures the multidimensional technological relationships underlying collaborations driven by high-quality technological resources, thereby improving both the performance and interpretability of collaboration prediction in dynamic environments. This study selects the representative semiconductor industry as empirical data, obtaining a total of 668,790 non-duplicated invention patents. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating patent quality into technological portfolios enables a more precise differentiation of technological heterogeneity among organizations. Compared with baseline methods grounded in different principles, the proposed model generally achieves near-optimal performance across major evaluation metrics, particularly in AUC, AP, MRR, and Hits@K. Ablation studies not only validate the effectiveness of each auxiliary view, temporal module, and patent quality, but also investigate model substitutions. Moreover, our work conducts parameter sensitivity analyses across different modules, verifying the stability of technological knowledge extraction and collaboration prediction. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Multidimensional energy poverty in Indonesia: Urban-rural perspectives
Abstract: Energy is essential for human welfare and development, and the inability to meet basic energy needs adversely affects household welfare. Households deprived of access to energy services such as clean cooking fuel, lighting, adequate electricity, refrigeration, space cooling, entertainment and education, and communication are considered multidimensionally energy poor. Without effective policy intervention, energy poverty may worsen during the energy transition. Therefore, reliable empirical analysis is required to support the development of appropriate policies. This study measures energy poverty in Indonesia using the Multidimensional Energy Poverty Index, with particular emphasis on differences between urban and rural households. The results show that the average national level of energy poverty between 2022 and 2025 was classified as moderate, with a gradual reduction over this period. Energy poverty was classified as low in urban areas and moderate in rural areas. Electricity adequacy, measured by household electricity connection capacity, contributed the largest share of deprivation intensity, while lighting contributed the least. This indicates that although most households have electricity connections, basic energy needs are not necessarily met when electricity connection capacity is limited and modern appliances are unaffordable. At the provincial level, most rural areas were classified as moderate, while a clear regional disparity was observed in urban areas, with western Indonesia generally classified as low and eastern Indonesia classified as moderate. Overall, the findings highlight the need for institutionalised policies that address energy poverty, increase minimum household electricity capacity, and ensure equitable access to essential energy services, particularly in rural areas and eastern Indonesia. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Moreira L.M.
Title: Divide and Rule: Border and Identity in Late Nineteenth-Century Portuguese Cartography
Abstract: In 1864, the need to define the precise boundary between Portugal and Spain—the Raia—prompted the production of specific topographical maps, under the supervision of the Corpo do Estado-Maior (General Staff Corps). The main objective of this initiative was to define the jurisdictions of the two states and put an end to legal ambiguities and conflicts. This process required scientific cartographic mapping, and to achieve this, the Comissão Internacional de Limites (International Boundary Commission) produced and published three general map series of the border, at different scales. For the first time, the frontier was clearly defined, demarcated and systematically documented. The main aim of this analysis is to compare the way the border was depicted in these first official maps, which were produced for political and diplomatic negotiations, with other more widely circulated maps, such as military and civilian topographic series. It considers how these representations adopted and/or conveyed geopolitical narratives, with regard to the quantity, quality and consistency of information included; identifying evidence of conflict, state presence, or local cooperation and determining the usefulness of the data presented and the intended users. Once the boundary line was drawn, central government authority extended along the border. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Acute stress experiences as markers of temporal risk for near-term suicidal ideation: Examining the roles of tonic and phasic impulsivity and emotion dysregulation
Abstract: Stressful experiences are a well-established risk factor for suicidal ideation. Yet, it is imperative to develop a granular understanding of when acute stressors increase risk and which person-level markers exacerbate this risk relationship. The current study evaluated the joint moderating effects of impulsivity and emotion dysregulation on the relationship between the frequency of acute stressful experiences throughout the day and momentary concurrent and prospective suicidal ideation (i.e., 3-way interaction). Impulsivity and emotion dysregulation were evaluated as both tonic (trait) and phasic (state) measures. A community sample of 103 adult participants with a recent (i.e., past 6 months) and repeated history of suicidal ideation completed a virtual baseline session and 30-day ecological momentary assessment period ( M age = 33, SD = 11.7; 63.1% female, 15.5% non-binary, 15.5% transgender; 20.4% racial minority; 62.1% sexual minority). Findings indicated a significant two-way interaction between the frequency of acute stressful experiences and phasic impulsivity, after controlling for momentary stress intensity: stressful experiences were associated with concurrent momentary suicidal ideation when an individual's phasic impulsivity was higher-than-usual (i.e., within-person above average). No other 3-way or 2-way interactions emerged. Also, main effects of tonic emotion dysregulation and phasic emotion dysregulation emerged as risk factors for concurrent and prospective momentary suicidal ideation. These findings highlight that moment-to-moment fluctuations, not stable dispositions, are most relevant for understanding how stressful experiences translate into immediate risk for suicidal ideation. This study has the potential to inform the development of effective just-in-time interventions. © 2026 The Authors.
