Authors: Lee
Title: Rethinking anticipation in the age of generative AI: Toward a theory of hybrid anticipation
Abstract: Anticipation has long been understood within futures studies as a human capacity: individuals, organizations, and societies construct representations of possible futures and use them to guide present action. The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence does not overturn this understanding, but it does change the conditions under which anticipation is exercised. Large language models are now used to scan for weak signals, synthesize strategic intelligence, generate scenario variants, and draft future-oriented narratives, activities that the field has treated as core anticipatory functions. This paper develops Hybrid Anticipation Theory, which conceptualizes anticipation as a socio-technical process through which human actors perceive, generate, interpret, and mobilize representations of possible futures within anticipatory systems increasingly mediated and reconfigured by generative AI, data infrastructures, organizational arrangements, and governance mechanisms. The theory attributes no anticipatory agency, intentionality, or future-directed purpose to AI; it explains how AI-enabled resources alter the systems and process frames through which human anticipation becomes possible. The argument rests on four assumptions: anticipation is socially organized; it depends on epistemic infrastructures; generative AI reconfigures those infrastructures; and changes in infrastructures transform anticipatory capacity. It specifies the boundary conditions under which these effects are most pronounced, and it identifies five mechanisms that connect the assumptions to observable transformations: epistemic delegation, algorithmic mediation, human-AI epistemic interaction, anticipatory capacity transformation, and adaptive governance, each linked to a corresponding proposition. Drawing on the distinction between anticipation for the future and anticipation for emergence, the paper argues that AI-mediated systems operate first on perception and only subsequently on judgment and choice. The argument extends, rather than replaces, anticipation theory, futures literacy, and anticipatory governance, and it carries a central governance implication: as the systems through which futures are perceived and imagined become hybrid, governing AI increasingly means governing anticipation itself. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Comparative analysis of machine learning and transformer models under class imbalance for sentiment prediction toward edible insect products
Abstract: While sentiment analysis is critical for monitoring the market adoption of novel foods, its practical application is often hindered by severe class imbalance and prohibitive costs of manual annotation. This study developed a data-centric machine learning (ML) framework for sentiment analysis using 4,616 online product reviews. To address severe class imbalance and high manual annotation costs, we compared self-labeling and clustering-based labeling schemes. Hybrid resampling strategies were applied across five ML algorithms (logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost) and two fine-tuned transformer models (KcELECTRA, KoELECTRA) for binary (positive/negative) and ternary (positive/neutral/negative) classification. While KcELECTRA performed exceptionally well under ideal self-labeling conditions (Macro F1 0.83), the performance gap between deep learning and machine learning narrowed significantly in practical, automated scenarios. Under the clustering scheme, resampled ML models (CatBoost) achieved a Macro F1 of 0.69, effectively matching or even surpassing the fine-tuned large language model (Macro F1 0.65), which proved more sensitive to label noise. These results demonstrate that a well-calibrated ML pipeline, enhanced by hybrid resampling, offers highly competitive predictive power with only a fraction of the computational cost and manual labor. Consequently, this study suggests that for domain-specific sentiment analysis, where expert labels are scarce, the robustness–efficiency trade-off of the proposed ML framework provides a more viable and sustainable alternative to heavyweight transformer architectures. This data-centric approach democratizes large-scale, real-time consumer-perception monitoring for resource-constrained emerging food sectors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Early and late adoption and appropriation of LLMs differs by gender, age, and technology education

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly integrated into critical activities of daily life. This raises concerns about equitable access and utilization across diverse demographics. This study investigates the adoption and usage of LLMs in two waves of a survey with a quota-based U.S. sample (n2023=1495[jls-end-space/], n2025=970[jls-end-space/]). The share of respondents who reported utilizing an LLM rose from 42% in 2023 to 82% in 2025. We found a gender gap in early LLM adoption (more male than female users) with complex interaction patterns regarding age and technology education as a mediator. Over time, the gender gap in usage disappeared, but male users were still more frequent users and rated their perceived competence as higher. Common usage scenarios show an increase in information search and editorial use as opposed to a decrease in entertainment purposes and experimental use. Title: Using Exploratory Factor Analysis to Explore Writing Test Anxiety Factors Among EFL Learners
Abstract: Writing test anxiety is prevalent among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners and may negatively affect their writing performance. However, the dimensional structure of writing test anxiety remains under-investigated in EFL contexts. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the underlying factors of writing test anxiety among EFL learners. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from 375 EFL learners using a writing test anxiety questionnaire. The questionnaire responses were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). The data were suitable for factor analysis (KMO = 0.913; Bartlett’s test of sphericity, p < 0.001). Six underlying factors were identified: Writing-Induced Emotional Strain (WIES), Cognitive Strain in Writing (CSW), Writing Accuracy and Evaluation Stress (WAES), Performance Evaluation Anxiety (PEA), Time-Pressure Writing Anxiety (TPWA), and Sociocultural Feedback Response (SFR). Together, these factors explained 60.420% of the total variance. The findings contribute to the understanding of the multidimensional nature of writing test anxiety and suggest practical implications for language teachers and curriculum designers to develop instructional strategies and supportive learning environments that may help reduce anxiety and enhance EFL learners’ writing performance. Title: How are language and culture considered in workplace OHS practices and interventions? A scoping review
Abstract: Language proficiency and cultural background influence how immigrant workers access, understand and apply occupational health and safety (OHS) information, as well as how they perceive and respond to workplace risks. While existing literature has documented OHS disparities among immigrant workers and their association with language and culture, less attention has been paid to how workplaces design or implement linguistically and culturally responsive OHS practices. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on how language and culture are considered in workplace OHS practices (routine processes) and interventions (deliberate programs). Guided by Arksey & O’Malley’s methodological framework, we screened 9,965 articles, of which 32 articles covering 31 independent studies, met the inclusion criteria. The findings indicate that workplace OHS practices often lacked the effective communication of safety information to immigrant and low-literacy workers, underscoring persistent challenges in conveying occupational risks to diverse workforces. Workplace OHS interventions incorporated some culturally and linguistically tailored approaches, such as bilingual materials, visual tools and peer mentoring, and generally reported positive outcomes, such as increase in safety knowledge compared to pre-intervention. However, important gaps remain. The review identified a critical disconnect between workplace OHS practices and research-led OHS interventions, raising concerns about the feasibility and sustainability of the latter in real-world, resource-constrained workplaces. The majority of studies were conducted in industrialized and wealthy countries, limiting their applicability across diverse cultural and economic settings. Finally, there is a need to address broader system-level barriers that compound language and culture to better support OHS of immigrant workers. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Reconfiguring online–offline shopping during the early COVID-19 public health shock: Evidence from mobile phone signaling and app usage data in Shenzhen
Abstract: Public health shocks can reshape shopping behavior through mobility disruptions, perceived infection risk, retail restrictions, delivery-capacity limits, and wider disruptions to daily routines. While previous studies have explored the relationship between online shopping and travel behavior, less is known about how these relationships are reconfigured during acute public health shocks and how urban environments influence such adjustments. Using anonymized mobile phone signaling data with individual spatiotemporal trajectories and monthly app-usage duration for the same analytical samples in Shenzhen, China, this study models online engagement, offline shopping activity, and shopping-related travel as an integrated individual-level behavioral system and compares its configuration between the pre-shock period (December 2019) and the early-shock period (February 2020) using an MGSEM. The results show that offline shopping duration, travel distance, and travel time declined sharply, while online shopping-app engagement also declined. The conditional association between offline shopping and online shopping engagement shifted from a substitution-like to a weak complementarity-like association, indicating that residents may have drawn on both channels under constrained retail access and delivery conditions rather than that online shopping replaced in-store shopping. The association between offline shopping time and offline shopping travel distance strengthened and the association between offline shopping travel distance and offline shopping travel time weakened. Males, young individuals and those living in dense neighborhoods with high levels of walkability, street connectivity, and accessibility to regional shopping facilities can better moderate the impact of mobility disruption. These findings highlight the context-dependent nature of online–offline shopping relationships, caution against assuming that digital channels automatically substitute for constrained in-store shopping during acute shocks, and show the value of jointly observing mobility and app-usage measures from the same anonymized MPS dataset when examining rapid behavioral change. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Unpacking the development of digital competence in Irish primary initial teacher education: A mixed-methods study
Abstract: Education policy mandates that pre-service teachers (PSTs) develop digital competence. Grounded in DigCompEdu and the Theory of Planned Behaviour, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigated the self-reported digital competence of 300 Irish primary PSTs and factors influencing their intention to use digital technology (DT). While PSTs felt competent sourcing and creating digital resources, they reported lower proficiency in areas involving active use of DT by learners. Qualitative findings revealed that Higher Education tutor modelling was prominently reported to have influenced PST intentions. This modelling focused on resource sharing and presentation, with pedagogical use of DT by learners reportedly modelled less frequently. The study identifies a mismatch between policy expectations and PST readiness. We conclude that initial teacher education must intentionally model diverse, pedagogically integrated DT use to bridge the gap between generic and professional digital competence. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Transparency or obscurity: Privacy information disclosure strategies for generative artificial intelligence enterprise
Abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created a critical tension between technological progress and privacy protection, making it a key challenge for both industry and government regulation. From the perspective of information disclosure, this study develops a signaling game model to analyze the strategic interactions between GenAI firms and governments in the context of information asymmetry. The results indicate that both separating and pooling equilibria in the model can be sustained only under multiple condition constraints, including disclosure costs, regulatory costs, policy incentives, and privacy breach probability, highlighting the complex strategic adjustments between enterprises’ privacy information disclosure and government regulation. Additionally, numerical simulations based on the OpenAI case demonstrate that external mechanisms (e.g., penalties and incentives) and internal interventions (e.g., transparent privacy disclosures and compliance reviews) can mitigate disclosure dilemmas and promote a shift from pooling to separating equilibria. This research provides a theoretical explanation for the disclosure behavior of GenAI firms and offers actionable insights for governments seeking to design more effective and nuanced regulatory policies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Public acceptance of autonomous vehicles after firsthand riding experiences
Abstract: Public acceptance of autonomous vehicles (AVs) often depends on media exposure rather than direct experience, leading to a significant perception-actuality gap. This field study investigates how actual AV experience influences user acceptance, comparing pre-exposure expectations with post-experience evaluations. Through a longitudinal field experiment involving 306 participants in Changsha, China, who experienced SAE Level 4 AVs (Baidu Apollo) on urban roads, we examined shifts in perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PeoU), trust, perceived risk (PR), behavioral intention (BI) and general acceptance (GA) using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Results indicate that the firsthand AV exposure significantly enhances BI and GA of adopting AVs, while significantly increasing PeoU and trust, while decreasing PR. After the experience, the extended TAM explained 79% of the variance in BI and 75% of the variance in GA. Notably, the strongest predictor, trust, mediated the effects of PeoU and PU. These experiences also significantly increase acceptance among non-drivers and women. These results imply that real-world AV riding experiences for groups of women without driver's licenses should be a priority for automakers. Title: DiffMBR: diffusion-guided GCN for multi-behavior recommendation
Abstract: Current multi-behavior recommendation methods are often sensitive to noise and sparsity in auxiliary behaviors and comprehensively model users’ intrinsic behavioral habits. To address these limitations, we propose a diffusion-guided graph convolutional framework for robust multi-behavior recommendation, named DiffMBR. DiffMBR first introduces a dual-level structural diffusion mechanism to denoise and enhance both behavior-specific and unified interaction graphs. This process recovers reliable latent connections while suppressing noisy signals. These complementary representations are further aligned through cross-view contrastive learning to obtain a unified and robust embedding. Title: The effect of the flipped learning model on fifth graders’ conceptual understanding, retention, and engagement in decimal fractions
Abstract: This study examined the effects of flipped learning (FL) on fifth-grade students’ conceptual understanding of decimal fractions, retention, and mathematics engagement. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was used with 98 students in western Türkiye (FL: n = 50; control: n = 48). The FL group watched instructional videos before class and engaged in teacher-guided collaborative activities during class, whereas the control group received conventional instruction instead. Data were collected using the Decimal Conceptual Understanding Test (DCUT) and the Mathematics Engagement Scale (MES). Independent-samples t- tests, a 2 × 3 mixed-design ANOVA, and a 2 × 2 × 4 mixed-design MANOVA were conducted. The FL group showed significantly greater improvement in conceptual understanding across the pretest, posttest, and retention tests, with a large Group × Time effect (ηp² = .199). Between-group effects were large at posttest ( d = 0.93) and retention ( d = 1.06). Title: Postural configurations as micro-ecological constraints: How embodied arrangements shape the emergence of bodily-visual communication
Abstract: How do embodied configurations shape the emergence of communication? By contrast, seated-at-table interaction promoted more compact movements and digital specialisation, whereas standing-open interaction involved larger movements and progressive brachiomanual specialisation. Title: Exploring trajectories of physical functioning by transport mode, neighbourhood environment, and self-selection among mid-to-older adults: A multilevel longitudinal study in Brisbane, Australia
Abstract: Physical functioning is a key determinant of quality of life and healthy ageing in mid-to-older adults; however, little is known about how transport mode and neighbourhood environmental features jointly shape trajectories of physical functioning. Additionally, potential confounding for self-selection bias for living in neighbourhoods that support preferred behaviours has been insufficiently addressed in prior research. Multilevel linear regression analyses were used to examine associations between neighbourhood walkability and public transport accessibility accounting for residential self-selection, with changes in self-reported physical functioning across primary transport modes. Results indicated that self-selection weakened the association between active transport users and improvements in physical functioning, rendering it non-significant. Neighbourhood walkability and public transport accessibility were not associated with changes in physical functioning in the fully adjusted model. However, transport mode use moderated the association between neighbourhood features and change in physical functioning. Significant interaction effects indicated that higher residential density, greater street connectivity, higher walkability, and closer proximity to bus stops were associated with greater improvements in physical functioning among public transport users, compared with private transport users. Title: Distributive equity and wellbeing implications of catch shares: Bayesian influence diagram of the US IFQ scallop fishery
Abstract: Catch shares have been shown to have many benefits, including eliminating the race to fish, increasing profitability, and supporting stock sustainability. However, without express measures to prevent inequities, catch shares may result in socially undesirable outcomes. Currently, data and methods to evaluate equity and wellbeing outcomes are lacking, contributing to questions about if and how outcomes may be improved. Based on a review of US catch share programs and using the US Atlantic sea scallop individual fishing quota program as a case study, we developed a Bayesian belief influence diagram to evaluate management options to improve distributive equity and associated wellbeing outcomes. The influence diagram evaluated an intervention to expand community quota ownership, which was deemed the most desired and plausible option through expert interviews, on eight wellbeing-related dimensions. The model and the intervention scenarios were developed and evaluated by fishery management and industry stakeholders and utilized a combination of existing and new data obtained from a harvester survey. Findings suggest that an expansion of community quota ownership can improve several dimensions of wellbeing but may not improve access and affordability of quota shares; suggesting the central roles played by quota lease and transfer markets. Title: Gendered horizontal stratification in public universities in Türkiye
Abstract: This study examines the reproduction of gender-based horizontal stratification in income-generating research centers of public universities in Türkiye. Drawing on structural inequality theories and the gendered organization approach, universities are conceptualized as segmented labor markets in which revenue-producing units are marked by status and economic value. Using a dataset covering 130 public universities and 2451 research centers, the analysis compares the distribution of gender across research centers and between universities founded before and after 2000. Chi-square tests show that men are concentrated in high-status, revenue-oriented units, while women are more represented in pedagogically and communication-oriented centers associated with traditionally feminized organizational functions. Findings show that gender-based horizontal stratification persisted despite the formal legal equality reforms introduced after 2000; universities established after this period exhibited even higher levels of gendered segmentation than those founded earlier. These patterns suggest that managerial positions in income-generating institutional units remain characterized by pronounced gender disparities and that formal legal equality, defined here as the removal of discriminatory provisions from law, has not on its own translated into substantive equality within institutional practice. Title: Can individual differences in developmental changes be explained by processual dispositions? The sample case of accommodative adaptation
Abstract: Piaget’s theory of cognitive development posits the accommodation of schemata as a central process when information cannot be incorporated (assimilated) into existing schemata. Interindividual variance in actually responding accommodatively to specific information is usually attributed to special conditions (e.g., task or context of assessment). The possibility of considering a relatively stable individual tendency to respond accommodatively as an explanation for interindividual variance has not yet been systematically investigated. The present study (N = 47 children at preoperational stage) shows variance with respect to accommodative responses across four different cognitive tasks (domains): Actually, 16 of the children showed accommodative responses across all tasks. As expected, this general tendency towards accommodation correlated neither with (nonverbal) intelligence nor with age (as a proxy variable for developmental maturity). Authors: Bhattacharya S.; Kesar S.
Title: Development economics and the colonial encounter: Informality, caste, and postcolonial capitalist development in India
Abstract: This article posits the contradictory relation between capitalist and non-capitalist segments of an economy as a key dimension of the colonial encounter and as a critical and constitutive element in the contemporary process of postcolonial capitalist development. It points to the obfuscation of this contradiction in the prevalent theoretical approaches in development economics, particularly focusing on the discourse on informal economy and the role of identity. It then foregrounds an emerging theoretical framework on postcolonial economic dynamics — and its key methodological tenets — that frames the development process as being marked by this on-going and ever-occurring contradiction. The article, however, highlights a key gap in this framework to grapple with the role of identities in these development dynamics, and points to some critical methodological approaches to identity that may be productively integrated to further develop it. Finally, the article provides empirical illustrations from the Indian context that underscores the constitutive role of caste in shaping both the reproduction of non-capitalist informal enterprises that sustain the working populations excluded from the capitalist segments, as well as the selective inclusion of parts of this population into capitalist segments as informal wage labor — processes that can be generatively interpreted through the above theoretical framework. Through this intervention, the article aims to clear grounds towards formulating a pathway to build a decolonized approach to contemporary processes of economic development. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Summer heatwave travel behaviour adaptations vary across purposes, modes, space, and time
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: During summer heatwaves, travel modes and trip timings provide insights into heat exposure and adaptive responses; however, the moderating roles of trip purposes, space, and time remain underexplored. This analysis links England’s National Travel Survey with ERA5 climate reanalysis data, defining heatwaves using a heat index (‘feels like’ temperature). Probit discrete choice models of travel modes and Cox proportional hazards models of departure times assess differences across trip purposes and spatio-temporal factors. The models estimate population-level associations for trips longer than one mile and provide limited evidence of uniform differences during heatwaves; both travel behaviours vary widely across space and time. The relationships suggest that typically cooler locations exhibit travel behaviours consistent with heat-avoidance during extreme heatwaves, urbanization is associated with greater public transit usage and heat-avoidant departure timing, and over 15 years, there are tendencies towards typically more sheltered modes for commuting and heat-avoidant departure timing during extreme heatwaves. Authors: Iranmanesh A.; Kamalipour H.
Title: Configurational morphogenesis under rapid expansion: Access network adaptations in Kutupalong refugee camp, Bangladesh
Abstract: This paper presents a multi-temporal, multi-layered analysis of the configurational morphogenesis of Kutupalong refugee camp in Bangladesh as a critical case study. In particular, it investigates the configurational adaptations of the access network from incremental growth to rapid expansion, and the extent to which topography has enabled or constrained the network's spatial transformations over time. The study adopts an exploratory approach and engages with a range of interconnected spatial variables. Using Space Syntax angular segment analysis at local and global radii, six time slices (2002–2025) are analysed for integration, choice, and intelligibility. A slope-range index from SRTM data quantifies terrain engagement at the segment level. The relationship between terrain and configuration is then interrogated at the level of individual access network segments through bivariate correlation, multivariate regression, and spatial autocorrelation diagnostics. The findings illustrate how the 2017 major influx marks a configurational rupture: local and global integration cores diverge, global choice axes reorient, and intelligibility falls significantly by 2025. Terrain associations with syntactic measures are statistically detectable but substantively negligible: elevation and slope add negligible explanatory power once segment length, building density, water, and road density are controlled for, and model residuals remain strongly spatially autocorrelated, so terrain effects are interpreted as exploratory rather than causal. The study shows how topography constrains but does not deterministically shape the network's evolution under crisis conditions. The findings also suggest that as flatter terrain became saturated first, expansion increasingly encroached into steeper, more topographically challenging areas. Presenting a novel exploration of the dynamics between topography and configurational morphogenesis in a significantly large settlement, this study offers insights to inform more spatially grounded and contextually tailored upgrading interventions in displacement contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Fang D.; Kwan M.-P.
Title: Are urban residents trapped by high temperatures? A travel-based heat segregation analysis
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Rapid urbanization has profoundly reshaped urban thermal environments and mobility patterns. While socioeconomic segregation has been widely studied, it remains unclear whether daily mobility connects places with similar or dissimilar thermal conditions. This study proposes a travel-based heat segregation index and applies it to dockless bike-sharing trips and diurnal land surface temperature data in Shenzhen, China. Spatial analysis and explainable machine learning reveal widespread heat segregation, with high-temperature and high-segregation clusters concentrated mainly in peripheral districts. Inflow-based segregation varies more between daytime and nighttime, whereas outflow-based segregation differs more between weekdays and weekends. Mobility features are the strongest predictors: greater mobility diversity, more variable flows, and greater spatial extent of OD flows are generally associated with lower heat segregation. Urban environmental factors also show nonlinear, context-dependent effects. These findings support spatially targeted and temporally adaptive heat-mitigation strategies, particularly where high LST coincides with strong OD-based heat segregation. Title: From kindergarten to second grade: Socioeconomic pathways to academic performance in South Korea
Abstract: Grounded in the Family Stress and Investment Models, this study examined how family SES during age 5 (kindergarten age) relates to teacher-rated academic performance at age 8 (second grade; G2) through two primary pathways: family dynamics at age 5 (home learning environment [HLE] and parenting stress) and child developmental factors at G1 (language skills and parent-reported executive functioning [EF] difficulties). This nationally representative secondary study used data from the Panel Study on Korean Children (PSKC; N = 1,304). The results from longitudinal path analysis showed that higher family SES at age 5 was not directly related to a latent construct of G2 teacher-rated academic performance (comprising Korean, math, and overall performance). Instead, its effects were mediated through higher concurrent HLE and, separately, through lower G1 EF difficulties. In addition, higher SES at age 5 was significantly related to higher G2 teacher-rated academic performance through two indirect pathways: (a) higher SES was associated with higher concurrent HLE, which in turn was linked to stronger G1 language skills, and (b) higher SES was associated with lower concurrent parenting stress, which in turn predicted fewer G1 EF difficulties. These findings indicate that both family dynamics and child developmental factors serve as key mediators, explaining how early family SES links to teacher-rated academic performance during the early elementary years. Our findings highlight the complex pathways through which SES advantages are linked to school-age educational outcomes, contributing to the literature with evidence from a South Korean sample. Authors: Chen W.
Title: When blame meets fate: cultural attribution and safety risk judgment after fire-related accidents in China
Abstract: Public judgments after accidents are shaped not only by technical and regulatory explanations, but also by culturally resonant interpretations that circulate in public discussion. This study examines how culturally grounded attribution affects safety risk judgment in China. Focusing on the Red Horse Year narrative, which links fire-related accidents to a temporal and cosmological cycle, we conducted a 2 × 2 survey experiment (N = 600) varying event type, a fictional fire versus a real explosion, and comment environment. Compared with accountability-only comments, mixed comments combining accountability claims with cultural attribution reduced personal risk perception. Accountability demand and institutional attribution remained largely unchanged. Traditional cosmological beliefs were positively associated with risk perception, indicating threat sensitivity rather than fatalistic disengagement. The findings show that culturally resonant attribution can attenuate prospective vulnerability judgments after accidents without displacing expectations of institutional responsibility. The study contributes to safety risk communication by distinguishing public concern about future exposure from retrospective judgments of accountability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Trends and Determinants of Condom Use Among Indonesian Adolescents: Evidence from 2007–2017 IDHS

Abstract: Adolescent sexual and reproductive health remains a significant public health concern in Indonesia, particularly amid increasing reports of unprotected premarital sex. In 2022, adolescents accounted for approximately 50% of new HIV cases, underscoring the need for improved protection and education. This study aimed to examine trends in condom use among Indonesian adolescents from 2007 to 2017 and identify factors associated with protected sexual behavior. Data were drawn from three waves of the Indonesian Demographic and Health Surveys (IDHS) conducted in 2007, 2012, and 2017 using a two-stage stratified sampling design. The proportion of adolescents reporting protected sex increased from 11.8% in 2007 to 20.6% in 2012, followed by a slight decline to 18.1% in 2017. Title: Naming the one to save the many: The effect of animal identifiability on children's reduced meat preference

Title: Neural dissociation between liking and wanting in successful versus unsuccessful restrained eaters: Brain responses to wanting are associated with daily dietary control
Abstract: This study aimed to explore the differences in reward processing between successful (SREs) and unsuccessful restrained eaters (UREs) within the ‘liking–wanting’ framework, and to examine how these neural differences are associated with daily dietary control in the real world. Fifty-eight restrained eaters were classified into 28 SREs and 30 UREs based on the Dutch Eating Behavior Questionnaire. During a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scan, participants rated high- and low-calorie food images for liking (hedonic value) and wanting (incentive value). Subsequent real-world eating behaviors were tracked over one week using ecological momentary assessment (EMA). Behaviorally, SREs reported lower wanting ratings for foods compared to UREs, as supported by a significant rating type×group interaction, with no group difference in liking ratings. The findings suggest that heightened wanting-related brain activity which distinguishes UREs from SREs correlates with poorer dietary control at the individual level. Title: Age-Specific Patterns and Dual Economic Burden of Dyadic Chronic Disease Combinations Among Older Inpatients in Inner Mongolia, China

Title: BiHoG-ERC: Dual-channel hypergraph convolutional network embedded with large-language-model knowledge for emotion recognition in conversations

However, existing ERC studies often extract multimodal features in isolation before fusion and fail to fully leverage speaker and topic dynamics, potentially leading to a loss of cross-modal semantic consistency. Third, modality-aware and structure-aware channels are designed in parallel, incorporating contrastive learning at the node level to enhance cross-channel representational consistency and robustness. On the interactive emotional dyadic motion capture dataset and multimodal emotion lines dataset, BiHoG-ERC improves the strongest baseline by 1.18 and 0.84 percentage points in accuracy, and by 1.22 and 0.49 percentage points in weighted F1, respectively. Title: Psychological need experiences inside and outside gaming as predictors of adolescent problematic gaming and well-being: A longitudinal test of the Need Density Hypothesis
Abstract: Video games are a widely valued activity because they are densely packed with elements that can satisfy one's basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness and can, as such, support healthy development. However, drawing on Self-Determination Theory, the Need Density Hypothesis posits that a lack of need satisfaction outside of video gaming in combination with need satisfaction inside of gaming may render adolescents vulnerable to gradually disengage from less satisfying domains, fostering obsessive gaming patterns and poorer mental health. Because empirical support for this hypothesis has been largely cross-sectional, this one-year longitudinal study investigates whether discrepancies in adolescents' psychological need experiences inside versus outside of video gaming predict changes in problematic gaming behavior and associated outcomes over time. We surveyed 661 adolescents (Mean age = 14.36; 55.98% boys) who played video games in two waves conducted one year apart. Results of polynomial regression analyses found partial evidence for the Need Density Hypothesis: Adolescents scoring higher on inside gaming than on outside of gaming need satisfaction showed increases in problematic video gaming, and mental health problems over time, while no interactive effects of need satisfaction inside gaming and need frustration outside of gaming were found. Moreover, low need satisfaction outside of video gaming was identified as a robust standalone predictor of increases in problems. These findings highlight that adolescents' vulnerability to problematic video gaming, as well as to associated mental health problems, is shaped by the interplay between need-satisfying experiences outside and inside the gaming world. It suggests that prevention efforts need to shift from focusing narrowly on gaming behavior toward addressing the broader ecological contexts of adolescents' daily lives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Bai W.; Ye X.; Zhang W.; Ye Y.; Newman G.; Song Y.
Title: Interpreting human responses to urban scene composition with EEG: A framework for lab-to-urban transfer
Abstract: The visual characteristics of urban scenes can shape emotional and cognitive responses and contribute to how environmental quality is perceived. Understanding these responses is increasingly important for the human-centered evaluation and spatial interpretation of urban visual environments. While these responses are often assessed through self-reported perceptions or visual indicators, electroencephalography (EEG) offers a complementary way to capture rapid neural responses to environmental stimuli. However, its application in urban research remains constrained by the scarcity, small sample sizes, and variability of urban scene-based EEG data. To address this gap, this study develops the Urban-Ready EEG Emotion Framework (UREEF), a lab-to-urban-scene representation framework that learns Emotional Neural Signature (ENS) templates from a laboratory emotion EEG dataset and projects EEG responses from an urban scene-based appraisal dataset into a shared ENS representation space. Methodologically, UREEF provides an interpretable way to connect structured laboratory-derived neural knowledge with urban scene analysis. Empirically, the transferred ENS space retained interpretive value in the urban scene-based context: vegetation was associated with stronger threat-related and arousal-like neural tendencies, sky visibility with greater happy-related similarity, road proportion with weaker positive-bias, and building proportion with lower threat-related tendency. The framework therefore extends urban scene analysis beyond visual description or subjective appraisal alone by adding a laboratory-informed neural perspective. These findings show that laboratory-derived neural representations can reveal structured relationships between urban visual composition and affective tendencies, providing an interpretable neural layer for the human-centered evaluation of urban visual environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Huang W.; Chai S.; Gao A.; Duan Y.; Chen Y.
Title: Crossing safety of school-age pedestrians: An evolutionary game analysis in autonomous driving scenarios
Abstract: With the popularization of autonomous driving, the interaction mechanism between child pedestrians and autonomous vehicles (AV) in school zones has become a new governance challenge. Due to immature cognitive development, school-age pedestrians (SAP) exhibit significant differences from adults in their street-crossing decision-making behaviors and are more likely to trigger severe traffic conflicts. To investigate the street-crossing safety of school-age children in school zones under autonomous driving scenarios, a SAP-AV evolutionary game model (SAP-AV EGM) was established by introducing a cognitive level factor on the basis of the traditional evolutionary game framework, taking into account the limited cognitive abilities of SAP and the algorithm-driven decision characteristics of AV. First, the replicator dynamics equation was revised by quantifying SAP's cognitive limitations in risk perception, benefit judgment, and strategy learning, while the decision-making of AV was dominated by objective cost parameters and algorithm rules without emotional interference of human drivers. Then, combined with stability analysis of system equilibrium points and phase diagram simulation, the influence mechanisms of key parameters such as cognitive level, conflict loss, and waiting loss on the evolutionary path and stable state of the system were explored. The research results show that SAP are involved in significantly more high-risk crossing conflict scenarios than adult pedestrians. Accordingly, targeted optimization strategies are proposed, including delineating school low-speed buffer zones, establishing punishment mechanisms to curb competitive passing of AV, and implementing hierarchical safety education to mitigate the irrational crossing tendency of SAP. This study expands the quantitative analysis framework for SAP traffic interaction and delivers targeted quantitative references for refined school traffic governance under autonomous driving scenarios. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Hu Y.; Bhatia S.
Title: Adaptive judgment in the cognitive reflection test: A computational analysis
Abstract: The Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) is widely used in reasoning and decision making research, but it lacks a formal cognitive foundation. As a result, debates persist over why CRT scores correlate with mathematical ability, why some individuals solve CRT problems easily while others struggle, and which mental processes drive observed patterns in data. We use an ecological perspective combined with computational cognitive modeling to address these questions, focusing in particular on the bat-and-ball problem. First, we specify the learning environment by assembling a large dataset of grade school verbal math problems. Second, we specify a formal learning mechanism that selects the arithmetic operation most likely to be applied to a novel problem based on the linguistic association of the problem with learned exemplars. Our model generates the intuitive errors elicited by the bat-and-ball problem (as well as other CRT items) and explains why these errors can be seen as byproducts of adaptive cognition. It also makes new predictions about the effect of environmental structure and problem wording on strategy selection and downstream performance, and we validate these predictions in two new preregistered experiments. Overall, our work provides theoretical clarity and quantitative rigor to our understanding of intuitive judgment, and shows how such judgments can be understood as rational adaptations to the learning environment. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Socio-environmental assessment of vulnerability to mining in the Brazilian Amazon
Abstract: In Brazil, the Amazon biome concentrates the country's greatest biological diversity and is home to extensive Conservation Units, Indigenous Lands and Quilombola Territories. In recent years, the expansion of legal and illegal mining has intensified environmental degradation, increased territorial conflicts and exposed institutional limitations on control and enforcement. Few studies to date have investigated the multidimensional nature of threats posed to indigenous community. Thus, this study aimed to assess the spatial distribution of vulnerability to mining across the Amazon biome using an integrated index that combines environmental sensitivity, exposure, and adaptive capacity. The study methodology comprised five phases: 1) Geospatial database Consolidation; 2) Reclassification of mining mapping; 3) Adaptation of the IPCC Theoretical Vulnerability Model; 4) Calculation of the Vulnerability to Mining Index (VMI); and 5) Spatial analysis of critical areas in the biome. High and very high vulnerability categories were mainly found in the states of Pará, Amazonas, Roraima and Mato Grosso, especially in cells overlapping socio-environmentally sensitive areas such as the APA do Tapajós, FLONA do Jamaxim, FLONA do Crepori, the Munduruku Indigenous Land, Kayapó Indigenous Land and the Quilombola Territories of Oriximiná. These regions coincide with recent records of accelerated deforestation, mercury contamination, invasions of garimpo, and federal operations against illegal mining, reinforcing the consistency of the VMI with independent evidence. The study is an initial tool for understanding how mining pressures interact with ecological fragility and institutional capacity, generating key information to guide monitoring strategies, territorial planning, and environmental protection policies in the Brazilian Amazon. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Thianthai C.; Mai-Ngam N.
Title: ‘Please Let Me Breathe’: A Case Study of Digital Parenting Beliefs and Fears Among Middle-Class Thai Generation Y Parents in Bangkok
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: In Thailand’s hyperconnected society, middle-class Thai Generation Y parents—raised alongside the internet—are now navigating parenting in a digital age where screens are ever-present. This qualitative study examines how Generation Y parents of children aged 3–6 integrate digital technology into their parenting, the fears they associate with its use, and the belief systems that shape these perceptions. Based on in-depth interviews with fourteen Bangkok-based parents, the data were thematically analyzed to uncover key patterns. The findings reveal that digital technology serves multiple roles in daily parenting: as a caregiver, a pacifier, an educator, and a surveillance tool. Parents expressed seven core fears, including exposure to harmful content, emotional disturbance, developmental delays, pseudo-autism, attention deficits, vision problems, and poor socialization. These fears reflect a hybrid belief system shaped by Western medical knowledge, Buddhist morals, Eastern family norms, and parental intuition. Thus, daily parents of this generation act like negotiators and protectors, balancing institutional guidance and personal judgment. In conclusion, the study moves beyond binary views of techno-optimism and techno-fear, revealing how culturally embedded belief systems shape digital parenting. These insights offer a valuable foundation for reflecting on digital parenting frameworks that are more nuanced and that recognize the various layers that respond to local realities. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Tactile exposure as a strategy for shaping food texture preferences in preschool children – a mixed-methods pilot study
Abstract: Food texture, such as the presence of lumps or pieces, is a common reason for food rejection among children. Yet, few strategies exist to support children with narrow texture preferences. This pilot study explored whether tactile exposure to food stimuli could improve children's preferences for food containing particles. Twenty-four children aged 3-6 years with an initial low preference for particulate textures, screened using a validated forced-choice questionnaire, participated in three tactile activities over one week. These included (1) searching for hidden objects in muesli and yoghurt, (2) preparing a yoghurt-fruit mix by cutting and smashing fresh fruits, and (3) matching foods to texture vocabulary in a semantic task. Texture preferences were assessed immediately before and after the activity week using paired preference tests comparing smooth yoghurts with yoghurts containing fruit pieces, and at a one-week follow-up by repeating the questionnaire. Parents were also interviewed regarding their perceptions of the activities. Paired preference tests showed no significant change in children's preference for yoghurt with fruit pieces. However, children's self-reported preferences for foods containing particles increased significantly at follow-up (p = 0.032). Parents responded positively to the activities, and about half reported positive changes in their child's eating behaviours, such as being more explorative, increased acceptance of foods with particles and willingness to try new foods. Overall, these findings support the feasibility of texture-focused activities within this pilot sample and provide examples that could inform future interventions in home or childcare settings. Larger controlled studies are needed to determine their effectiveness. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Career guidance and investments in education: Experimental evidence from Cambodia
Abstract: Students in low-income contexts often lack guidance in their career decisions, which can lead to a misallocation of educational investments. We report on a randomized field experiment conducted with 1715 students in rural Cambodia and show that a half-day career guidance workshop designed to support adolescents in developing occupational aspirations on average increased educational investments. We document substantial heterogeneity in treatment effects by baseline student performance. While the workshop increased schooling efforts of high-performing students, treated low-performing students reduced their educational investments. We develop a simple model that explains this treatment effect heterogeneity by baseline performance. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Thayansin S.; Phuphaibul R.
Title: Family Well-Being, Hardiness, and Coping Under Socioeconomic Disruption: Evidence From Thai Families Raising Young Children Exposed to Adverse Childhood Experiences During the COVID-19 Pandemic
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic intensified vulnerabilities among families raising young children, particularly those exposed to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs). Evidence remains limited on how family well-being, resilience orientations, and coping interact under sustained structural constraint in middle-income contexts. This mixed-methods study examined family well-being, family hardiness, and family coping among 212 Thai families raising children aged 0–6 years with ACE scores ≥ 2 in Bangkok, of whom 26.9% had ACE scores ≥ 4. Quantitative analyses used descriptive statistics and Pearson’s correlation, complemented by qualitative interviews. Overall family well-being was moderate (M = 3.38), with stronger relational and value-based domains but weaker economic conditions. Families demonstrated high family hardiness (M = 42.32), particularly in cohesion and commitment, alongside limited perceived control. Family well-being was strongly associated with family hardiness (r = .64) and moderately associated with family coping (r = .46). Qualitative findings highlighted self-reliance and emotional endurance amid economic insecurity. These findings suggest that families sustain relational well-being through internal resilience orientations despite structural constraints. Family hardiness serves as a foundational resource, while coping operates within bounded conditions, underscoring the need for policies that address material vulnerability, including income security and accessible childcare support, particularly among single-parent and skipped-generation households. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: The effect of AI-based linguistically tailored health messages on plant-based lunch choices of adolescents: A randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Adolescents are a notoriously difficult audience to engage in digital health communication. While many tailoring strategies focus on tailoring what is communicated, far less attention has been paid to how messages are expressed. Addressing this gap, we examined automated AI-based linguistic tailoring as an innovative approach to personalised health communication. Using large language model–based text style transfer, we tailored health messages to adolescents’ individual communication styles to examine whether linguistic tailoring enhances persuasive responses and dietary behaviour. To this end, we conducted a preregistered two-week randomised controlled trial with 587 adolescents (Mage = 13.09) in the UK and Ireland. Participants were assigned to four arms: no messages, non-tailored messages, linguistically tailored messages, or a tailored–non–tailored crossover arm. The primary outcome was the choice of a plant-based lunch; secondary outcomes assessed evaluations of the message and source. Bayesian mixed-effects analyses showed that adolescents receiving daily health messages (tailored or not) increasingly chose plant-based lunches over time (from 44% to 59%; OR = 1.06 per day; BF10 = 35.39), whereas choices remained stable in the passive control group (45–46%). This effect was comparable for the tailored and non-tailored message conditions, indicating no additional short-term behavioural benefit of linguistic tailoring. However, exploratory analyses showed higher ratings of message relevance (BF10 = 3.50), perceived personalisation (BF10 = 4.93), and source liking (BF10 = 3.38) for linguistic tailoring in the second week of the intervention. These exploratory findings suggest that LLM-based linguistic tailoring may enhance the persuasive appeal of dietary health messages, particularly following repeated exposure. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Developing the emotion regulation skills of autistic pupils in education settings: A case study of a residential special school in England
Abstract: Emotion regulation skills enable individuals to manage how they express their emotions, but little is known about how to support the development of these skills within educational practice. Therefore, this nested case study explored how a residential special school supported autistic young people to develop emotion regulation skills. The school is graded ‘Outstanding’ by the inspection system in England and so this study was focused on exploring good practice. The study focused on four young people, and data was collected over eight months from staff who supported them. Staff members were involved through providing written reflections about facilitators and barriers to emotion regulation (n = 50), being observed in classrooms and homes (n = 8) and undertaking semi-structured interviews (n = 9). Transcripts of reflections, observations and interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Four main themes were generated to characterise the main principles and practices that underpinned good practice: (1) evolutionary ethos, (2) reciprocal relationships, (3) communication: attuning, asking, and adapting, and (4) everyone expresses emotions every day. Overall, interpersonal factors were considered by the school staff to be foundational for supporting the development of autistic young people's emotion regulation skills. Recommendations for practice and future research are considered. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Long Y.; Jiang H.; Hong S.; Yuan B.; Chen X.; Xing X.
Title: A city-level assessment framework for intercity mobility resilience in China
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: Aggregate mobility recovery provides incomplete information about changes in intercity connections. We examine this distinction using 230.8 million Amap migration-index records spanning the Wuhan lockdown, Zhengzhou flood, Shanghai lockdown and New Ten policy transition. Daily response curves describe trough retention, cumulative loss, rebound and later levels; monthly origin–destination (OD) comparisons describe network change. Results show that: (1) Wuhan experienced the deepest trough, Shanghai the largest cumulative loss and Zhengzhou the mildest decline; (2) later city-level index levels and monthly OD changes were not consistently associated, while network-loss rankings depended on reference months; and (3) regional background, socioeconomic conditions, built-environment features and network position showed nonlinear, event-specific predictive associations with cumulative loss. New Ten followed a separate release-and-overshoot trajectory. The study identifies the limits of aggregate recovery as evidence of restored intercity relations and supports interpreting daily responses alongside monthly network observations within China’s intercity mobility system. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Schultz H.; Benoit R.G.
Title: It's about time: Specific and unspecific effects of episodic future thinking on farsighted decisions
Abstract: Humans tend to discount the value of delayed rewards. As a consequence, they forego larger long-term benefits (e.g., €29 in 91 days) in favor of smaller short-term gains (e.g., €20 now). Episodic future thinking (EFT) attenuates such delay discounting. That is, people are more likely to choose a larger but delayed reward after imagining an episode at the future time point (e.g., a café visit in 91 days). We here elucidate the underlying mechanism by examining the temporal specificity of this effect. Does EFT foster farsighted decisions in general by shifting the mental focus towards the future, or does it specifically influence decisions in favor of the imagined time point? In two experiments (n = 84 total) we systematically varied the concordance between the imagined time point and the delay at which the larger reward could be received. When these time points matched, we replicated the beneficial effect of EFT (Experiments 1 and 2). Critically, when the imagined time point matched the sooner of two delayed choice options, the effect was reversed: Choices became more short-term (Experiment 1). When the imagined delay was double the delay of the larger option, the effect was not significant and numerically lower than when the delays matched (Experiment 2). Notably, more vivid imaginations were associated with more farsighted choices at longer delays, irrespective of whether the imagined time point matched the delayed choice. Together, the data demonstrate that both temporally specific and unspecific mechanisms contribute to the impact of EFT on delay discounting. © 2026

Authors: Schürer D.
Title: The (tedious) making of change: investigating agency dynamics in the sustainable mobility transformation of Wuppertal, Germany
Abstract: This study addresses the need for a deeper, more empirically grounded understanding of agency dynamics in processes of change by examining successful sustainability-related projects in the mobility domain of the medium-sized German city of Wuppertal in the early stages of its sustainability transformation. Using a grounded-theory approach, based on document analysis and 15 semi-structured interviews, the article analyzes the general mobility development as well as three cases: the construction of a 23-kilometer (km) multifunctional path for cycling, walking, and recreation (Nordbahntrasse), the implementation of a neighborhood mobility station/hub (MiQ), and the pedestrianization of a city square (Laurentiusplatz). The results conceptually describe the continuous agentic making of change under challenging circumstances and particularly suggest the importance of proactive, persistent, and resilient leading agents. Key agents completed the project through strategies of communicative pragmatism to mobilize and secure additional resources, as well as intentional spatial management to curb and prevent the emergence of destructive conflicts. While the article shows how individuals can initiate and drive substantial change in the mobility development of a constrained city, it also points out how intensive, demanding, and often tedious the process can be. Conceptual findings are critically discussed in relation to four key literatures on individual agency and agency dynamics: institutional/transition work, intermediation, the trinity of change agency, and urban transformative capacity. This comparative inquiry highlights the advantages of conceptual integration, as well as the need to advance theorization by linking the explicit study of individuals’ agency and their constitution to the collective making of change. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Lu Q.; Yao Y.; Zhu X.; Xiao L.; Yin H.
Title: More externalization, but less inference? Exploring changes in young learners’ critical thinking during conversational AI bot-supported multimodal writing practice
Abstract: Conversational AI bots are increasingly integrated into writing instruction. However, little is known about how these tools may function as multimodal learning partners in writing activities, especially among younger learners. This study examined changes in primary school students' critical thinking during and after a conversational AI bot–supported multimodal writing practice and explored students' experiences to contextualize the observed changes. A mixed-methods design was employed with 60 Grade 5 students in a Chinese primary school. Over an eight-week intervention, students transformed their narratives into multimodal representations using a conversational AI bot and created short videos combining images and narration. Quantitative data were collected at three time points (pre-intervention, post-intervention, and one-month follow-up). Semi-structured interviews with nine students explored their perceptions and experiences. Quantitative results showed significant increases in interpretation, analysis, evaluation, and explanation from pre-intervention to post-intervention and follow-up. Inference showed no significant increase, while self-regulation showed a short-term increase that was not sustained at follow-up. Qualitative findings suggest that conversational AI bot-supported multimodal composing helped students to externalize ideas through visual representations, which they associated with processes such as idea verification, gap detection, and revision. However, explicit multimodal representations may have reduced the need for inferential reasoning, while peer collaboration appeared to create complementary occasions for students to infer others' interpretations and reconsider their own texts. These findings suggest the potential of conversational AI bots as multimodal learning partners, while highlighting the need for continued instructional scaffolding to help sustain observed increases in students’ critical thinking. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Public transport for people with hearing impairment: A scoping review
Abstract: Introduction Mobility is an important aspect of daily life, yet people with disabilities often encounter barriers when using public transport. In this paper, we reviewed the literature on accessibility in public transport for passengers with hearing impairment and identified several recurring challenges. Methods To structure the material, we grouped the findings into four areas: access to information, environmental conditions, vehicle design, and interactions with staff. Within these areas, the studies describe a range of practical measures, such as clearer high-contrast visual signage, real-time information displays, tactile guidance, visual emergency alerts, and more targeted staff training. Results Recurring challenges for people with hearing impairments include difficulties accessing important information, barriers in the surrounding environment, limitations in vehicle design, and gaps in staff training. Across studies, these barriers were linked to reduced participation and, in many cases, lower perceived quality of life. Conclusions The scoping review points to the need for transport systems that combine universal design principles with digital and assistive technologies and indicates that relatively few studies have examined the specific transport and mobility needs of passengers with hearing impairment. This suggests a need for further research, particularly in relation to how emerging transport systems and services, including automated and digitally supported travel, can be designed to support this group. Addressing the identified issues is likely to improve access, independence, and the mobility of passengers with hearing impairment, and contribute to more inclusive and useable public transport systems. Authors: Boger T.; Amir D.; Yousif S.R.
Title: Near-random behavior in strategic games
Abstract: Humans struggle to produce random behavior when asked to do so, leading some to suggest that our ability to randomize is attenuated (or even absent). Here, we demonstrate that the capacity for random behavior is much greater than previously acknowledged: Humans can behave in (near) optimally random ways when the context demands it. We created a custom, online version of the game Battleship in which participants competed against one another. On each turn, one player chose a tile on a 3 × 3 grid to place a ship, while the other player tried to guess the ship's location. Across six preregistered studies, this strategic context led to dramatic increases in random behavior relative to closely matched non-strategic tasks. Such random behavior was also remarkably flexible and optimal depending on context; both players readily incorporated varying information about the game (e.g., that tiles can differ in value) while simultaneously accounting for their opponents' knowledge of that information. A computational model validated these findings and revealed nuanced differences across contexts. Contrary to decades of work finding that humans fail to randomize, we find that strategic games promote highly flexible, near-random behavior. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The structural fragmentation of energy poverty metrics limits global comparability and policy targeting
Abstract: Energy poverty (EP) measurement has expanded from affordability-based indicators to increasingly complex multidimensional frameworks. However, this diversification has also generated a fragmented measurement landscape, marked by uneven dimensional coverage, weak methodological integration, and a strong reliance on context-specific assumptions. This study examines the structural organization of EP metrics by analyzing 25 widely used indices through a standardized coding of variables into 18 dimensions and seven methodological approaches. Using network analysis, similarity metrics, and coverage assessment, we identify systematic imbalances in how EP is conceptualized and operationalized. Results show that most indices capture less than 35% of the total dimensional space, while approximately 96% rely on only one or two methodological approaches. In parallel, around 92% of indices are developed within specific national or subnational contexts, limiting their transferability across climatic and institutional settings. These patterns reveal a structurally fragmented system dominated by a narrow set of economic and technical dimensions, with limited incorporation of contextual and structural drivers. The network structure further shows that measurement outcomes emerge from the interaction between variables, methodological choices, and analytical scale, rather than from the inclusion of individual dimensions. Based on these findings, the study reframes EP metrics as integrated evaluation frameworks rather than isolated measurement tools and proposes a three-layer conceptual structure that distinguishes between core outcome, determinant, and structural vulnerability dimensions. This approach provides a basis for improving comparability, interpretability, and policy relevance, supporting the development of more coherent and context-sensitive energy poverty assessments. © 2026

Authors: Wolpert M.; Chen Y.; Ding N.
Title: Phrase-level speech timing preferences predict synchronization in joint reading
Abstract: For rhythmic motor activities, such as tapping, walking, and playing music, individuals often show preferred timescales, and differences between individuals' timing preferences impact how well they can synchronize. Speech is only quasi-periodic, but previous studies have suggested that it also exhibits preferred timescales for linguistic units, e.g., syllables and intonational phrases. The present study provides a direct test of whether individual speech timing preferences at syllable and phrase boundaries constrain synchronization in joint speech. We recorded Mandarin speech while participants read aloud lists of short, regularly structured sentences in solo and joint reading tasks. Syllable-level timing was measured with inter-syllable onset interval, and phrase-level timing was indexed by phrase-final lengthening and inter-phrase pause. Participants (N = 88) completed an at-home solo reading task; a subset (N = 32) participated in an in-lab session with solo and paired joint reading. Results show that mean syllable duration is highly aligned in joint reading, regardless of individuals' preferred syllable duration during solo speech. In contrast, mismatches in individuals' phrase-level, but not syllable-level, timing preferences during solo speech significantly predicted syllable onset asynchrony during joint reading. These findings suggest that syllable timing is adaptable in speech synchronization, while final lengthening and pauses between intonational phrases show stronger individual preferences that impact synchronization performance. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Yun Y.; Zhang M.
Title: The economic effects of interregional transport infrastructure: A meta-analysis
Abstract: Improving interregional transport infrastructure is vital for regional growth, yet governments face considerable challenges in prioritizing transport policies, as existing studies show varied effects in both size and direction. This paper compiles 95 studies with 225 estimates published or circulated between 2000 and 2022 and employs a multilevel random-effects model to examine the characteristics associated with heterogeneity from both contextual and methodological perspectives. Our results show that the pooled estimate indicates a modest positive average association, but its prediction interval spans zero and the topic-specific mean effects differ. The reported harmonized effect size varies with functional form, data structure, infrastructure measurement, and spatial scale. We also find small-study effects, with less precise estimates tending to report larger estimates, particularly in studies of economic growth. Title: Post-Brexit fisheries policy and marine conservation in England and Scotland: Trajectories towards policy coherence and fisher wellbeing
Abstract: This article presents a comparative study into what governance-contextual factors shaped trajectories towards policy coherence in two marine policymaking processes in England and Scotland: post-Brexit fisheries policy and the contemporary debates over the introduction of Highly Protected Marine Areas (HPMAs), a new category of MPA. To this end, we conducted a qualitative study using official documentation and document-guided, semi-structured interviews which were interpreted through established, state-of-the-art analytical frameworks grounded in recent conceptual literature. Our analysis brought to light different dynamics driving policy outcomes in each country. Firstly, it became evident from developments in Scotland that, even in the absence of one integrated marine policy deliberation process, overarching objectives at the political level can ensure coherence in policy outcome. Secondly, in the absence of strong overarching objectives, developments in England demonstrated how local interest groups can influence policy processes towards coherent outcomes. In the light of calls for a reorientation of fisheries policy towards more holistic wellbeing objectives, we argue that such objectives can be brought about through different pathways, but that trade-offs between objectives can exist in practice. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Xie Z.; Liu W.
Title: Exploring undergraduates’ interpersonal emotion regulation in thesis supervision: a qualitative study of relationship-oriented strategies and motives
Abstract: Supervisor-student relationships are fraught with emotional interactions that exert profound influences on thesis progress and the psychological well-being of both parties. Nevertheless, students’ proactive agency in shaping these relationships through interpersonal emotion regulation remains largely understudied, particularly in undergraduate thesis supervision contexts. Drawing on semi-structured interviews and digital artifacts, this study examined ten Chinese undergraduates’ relationship-oriented interpersonal emotion regulation strategies and the motivational drivers. Data analysis yielded nineteen interpersonal emotion regulation strategies grouped into three categories: intrinsic, extrinsic and dual-target strategies. Supplementing the conventional binary intrinsic-extrinsic classification, the newly-identified dual-target interpersonal emotion regulation strategies captured students’ efforts to simultaneously influence both their own and their supervisors’ emotional experiences. These strategies were underpinned by distinct yet interrelated motives including navigating students’ own emotional struggles, promoting supervisors’ emotional well-being and exercising relational agency. Building on these findings, an integrative framework was developed to delineate the cyclical process in which students’ interpersonal emotion regulation efforts foster constructive supervisor-student relationships via three emotional-relational pathways, which in turn reshape their subsequent interpersonal emotion regulation practices. By repositioning undergraduates as proactive relational agents, this study challenges prevailing supervisor-centric interpretations of interpersonal emotion regulation within supervisory interactions and advances our understandings of student agency in hierarchical academic relationships, with implications for undergraduate thesis supervision. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhou L.; Li Y.; Sun Y.; Hu L.; Li A.
Title: Transboundary cascading economic impacts and efficiency dynamics of power shortages induced by extreme heatwaves: An integrated weather-shock input-output data envelopment analysis framework for China
Abstract: Efficiency analysis is critical for evaluating economic impacts of extreme heat-induced power shortages. It detects inefficient sectors and resource misallocation to boost economic resilience. However, existing studies only examine associated economic losses, ignoring post-shock efficiency analysis. This limitation impedes the full assessment of cascading socio-environmental risks and the design of targeted resilience policies. This study constructs an integrated Weather-Shock Input-Output Data Envelopment Analysis framework. Empirical results reveal: First, macroeconomic risks triggered by heatwaves stem from two sources: the direct physical impacts of heatwave shocks and the institutional rules that shape power rationing schemes. Under our baseline scenario where energy-intensive industries bear priority cutbacks, indirect economic losses are roughly twice as high as direct losses; however, both the scale and composition of total losses vary significantly when adopting alternative power rationing policies. Second, this study differentiates the functional roles of various sectors in risk transmission. While agricultural and financial sectors act as passive absorbers, sectors like food & tobacco processing and leasing & business services are identified as key amplifiers that propagate supply-chain shocks. Third, power shortages widen disparities in efficiency, with more than 90% of this inequality attributable to within-group heterogeneity, a pattern prominent in western China and secondary industries. The findings support a transition from “one-size-fits-all” energy rationing toward supply-chain-based strategies that protect loss transmission pathways and optimize cross-regional resource reallocation. © 2026

Title: Cognitive control, the broad autism phenotype, and everyday participation
Abstract: The broad autism phenotype (BAP), a continuum of subclinical autism-related traits, has been linked to cognitive control (CC) difficulties and to poorer everyday participation. These constructs have rarely been examined together, and whether the BAP-CC association depends on how CC is assessed remains unclear. This cross-sectional study examined how self-reported and task-based CC relate to BAP traits in non-clinical young adults, and how CC and BAP traits jointly relate to distinct facets of everyday participation. A non-clinical community sample (N = 177; ages 18–40) completed the Broad Autism Phenotype Questionnaire (BAPQ), the Adult Executive Functioning Inventory (ADEXI), a battery of CC tasks (ACE Explorer), and the Young Adults' Daily Participation Scale (YADAPS). FDR-corrected correlations and a path model with bootstrapped indirect effects examined how CC and BAP traits jointly account for variance in participation outcomes. Self-reported CC difficulties were substantially associated with BAP traits (ADEXI Total with BAPQ Total, r = .54, p < .001), whereas task-based CC showed little association. Participation performance was independently associated with both self-reported CC and BAP traits, which together accounted for a quarter of its variance. BAP traits were the only consistent correlate of the pleasure facets, whereas self-reported CC showed no association with either pleasure outcome and task-based CC showed weak and inconsistent associations. Subclinical autism-related variation is tied to self-reported rather than task-based CC, and the performance and pleasure facets of participation have distinct correlates. These findings position the BAP as a meaningful dimension of daily functioning beyond diagnostic thresholds. © 2026 The Authors
