Authors: Yi W.; Wu W.
Title: Pedestrians as obstacles in dense crowds: Local encounters and collective motion
Source title: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
Abstract: Understanding how different pedestrian movements relate to crowd dynamics is an important topic in pedestrian and evacuation research. However, direct comparisons of pedestrians who remain stationary, move against the main flow or cross it remain limited, particularly regarding their local interactions and relationships with collective motion. Here, we use trajectory data from the Festival of Lights in Lyon to classify pedestrians by walking speed and direction and examine the associated local interactions and crowd-level motion. Counterflow encounters show shorter times to closest approach among approaching pairs and greater local velocity variance than encounters involving stationary or crossing pedestrians. After accounting for density, a higher proportion of these non-mainstream pedestrians is associated with lower corridor-axis alignment and greater crowd-level velocity variance, predominantly in the longitudinal component, whereas associations with mean walking speed are less consistent across recordings. An idealized continuum model further illustrates how prescribed differences in walking direction and speed contribute to these crowd-level responses. These findings provide a clearer understanding of how heterogeneous pedestrian movements reshape local interactions and the organization of dense flow in public spaces. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: “As long as it tastes good”: Students’ perceptions of climate-friendly school meals in a mixed-methods study
Abstract: Shifting toward sustainable diets is key to reducing the environmental impact of food systems. In school meals, this often involves meat reduction through strategies such as all-vegetarian days and lower-carbon recipe reformulation. Yet students' perceptions of such concrete menu changes have received little attention. This convergent mixed-methods study examined students’ perceptions of climate-friendly school meals and their interpretations of meat reduction. Quantitative survey data from 1268 students across six Swedish schools were analyzed using multiple regression, alongside qualitative data from student discussions analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Both quantitative and qualitative findings suggested that lower-carbon recipe reformulation was more acceptable to students than vegetarian-only days. Quantitative analysis showed that more positive attitudes toward climate-friendly school meals were associated with perceiving climate considerations as important in food choice, more frequent selection of vegetarian meals at school, and being female. Students also showed clear awareness of the relative carbon footprint of red meat and plant-based foods across support levels. Qualitative findings, however, highlighted that the acceptability of climate-friendly meals depended strongly on perceived taste and satiety. Meat was positioned as a normative component of a meal, while acceptance of vegetarian meals was more conditional on familiarity and palatability. These findings corroborate earlier research showing that taste, familiarity, and meal norms shape acceptance of meat reduction in school meals more strongly than sustainability concerns alone. They also indicate that lower-carbon recipe reformulation may complement vegetarian-only days as a practical strategy for supporting acceptance and intake of climate-friendly school meals. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Barriers to quality mental health services for youth in foster care: a systematic review
Abstract: Objective: The US foster care system oversees the care of over 400,000 children at any given time. The rates of mental health diagnoses within foster youth is over double that of non-foster youth. Over 58% of children stay in care for over one year, resulting in a substantial number of mental health care visits taking place during the placement. However, access to quality mental health care to meet the needs of these children remains a concern. The goal of this paper was to review and critique the literature examining barriers to quality mental health care for youth in foster care. Methods: The search was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Studies including youth currently residing in US foster care which identified at least one barrier to quality mental health services were included. The NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies was used to evaluate and compare study quality ratings across manuscripts. Results: A systematic search of the literature returned nine studies to include in the review. Studies identified numerous barriers to quality mental health care (e.g. provider adherence to treatment protocols, problems with care coordination, long wait times) and received input from participants who spanned a range of key contributors to the system (e.g. former foster youth, foster parents, case workers, providers). Conclusions: The reviewed studies suggest that youth in foster care face numerous barriers to receiving quality mental health care. Clinical implications and future directions for improving access are discussed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: The politics of environmental peacebuilding: global agendas, advocacy networks, and domestic policy arenas
Abstract: This article examines how environmental conflict narratives emerge and are used in peacebuilding policies. It advocates for a multi-level perspective that systematically connects global intervention agendas to political struggles in domestic policy arenas. Through a comparative analysis of four case studies—Liberia, Colombia, Côte d'Ivoire, and Lebanon—it investigates how environmental considerations are framed as security issues and incorporated into peacebuilding agendas. It explores how actors construct causal stories linking environmental issues to conflict, and how these narratives shape policy design, implementation, and resistance to change. It highlights how environmental conflict narratives are shaped by security concerns and donor-recipient relationships. While such narratives can support policy change by providing advocacy coalitions with a platform, their effects vary significantly depending on the domestic political context. This article contributes to environmental peacebuilding research by highlighting the strategic and contested nature of how environmental concerns enter peacebuilding discourse and practice. © 2026 The Author(s)

Authors: Wu Z.; Zhu S.; Tan Y.; Yu X.; Zhong S.; Wu X.; Fang K.
Title: Expanding e-commerce logistics but unequal spatial accessibility: evidence from the spatial distribution of express delivery points in Chinese megacities
Abstract: The boom in e-commerce activities has raised demands for express delivery services and driven the rapid growth of delivery networks in megacities. However, whether this growth has translated into more balanced spatial accessibility remains unclear. Here, we examine the spatial accessibility to express delivery points in Chinese megacities from 2012 to 2023. Using the Dagum Gini coefficient to measure spatial inequality in accessibility and a two-way fixed effects model to identify its associated factors. The findings reveal the following: (1) the coverage and spatial accessibility to express delivery points have improved over time, while spatial equality in accessibility has worsened; (2) urban areas exhibit the highest spatial accessibility but face greater spatial inequality compared to suburban and exurban areas; (3) intra-regional disparities are the primary contributor to overall spatial inequality, though inter-regional disparities are gradually increasing; (4) improvements in spatial accessibility coincide with increasing spatial inequality; (5) reduced spatial inequality is mainly associated with population concentration and tertiary industry growth. These results suggest that policymakers should reduce spatial inequality in urban areas while improving spatial accessibility in suburban and exurban areas, and also offer a lens for the express industry and urban planning in defining better transport policies to promote a more balanced and efficient logistics network in Chinese megacities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Lhardy S.; Guillet-Descas E.; Martinent G.
Title: The relationships between subjective mental load, cognitive appraisals, and cognitive biases of risk-taking, depending on firefighters’ personality: a longitudinal hierarchical linear modelling approach
Abstract: This study investigated the relationships among subjective mental load, cognitive appraisals, and five cognitive biases related to risk-taking, as well as the mediating role of two personality profiles derived from the Five Factor Model. The research followed 95 firefighters (mean age = 41.73 years, SD = 8.36) over 10 weeks of operational activity. Each week, participants completed a 22-item self-assessment on a 10-point Likert scale measuring the perceived number of high-demand interventions, subjective mental load, cognitive biases in risk-taking, regulation strategies, cognitive appraisals, and self-regulation. Personality profiles were first identified through Latent Profile Analysis based on the firefighters’ five personality traits. Hierarchical Linear Modelling was then used to examine how mental load and cognitive appraisals predicted risk-taking-related cognitive biases. Finally, Monte Carlo simulations were performed to test mediation pathways. The results showed that subjective mental load was positively associated with cognitive appraisals for two personality profiles, labelled resilient and higher-neuroticism/high-agreeableness. Cognitive appraisals were also linked to cognitive biases in risk-taking, with both relationships moderated by these profiles. Monte Carlo analyses further revealed specific mediated pathways for the resilient and higher-neuroticism/high-agreeableness profiles, involving subjective mental load, threat appraisal, and two biases: optimism and overconfidence. Overall, these findings suggest that professions exposed to sustained mental workload, such as emergency services, should pay particular attention to cognitive biases influencing risk-taking. They also underline the importance of considering personality differences when assessing risk perception, decision-making, and safety-related behaviours in high-demand operational contexts. Authors: Bigliassi M.; Antonio D.S.
Title: The inhibitory control epidemic: A new framework for chronic disease prevention
Abstract: Inhibitory control failure is an emerging neurobehavioral epidemic contributing to the growing global burden of chronic disease. This narrative review integrates findings from neuroscience, psychophysiology, and public health to examine how modern environments may progressively erode inhibitory control capacity and increase risk for chronic disease development. Modern lifestyles characterized by hyperstimulation, hyperpalatable foods, reduced physical activity, digital overexposure, and chronic psychosocial stress diminish adaptive stress exposure and weaken inhibitory control. Impaired inhibitory control contributes to behavioral dysregulation underlying obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and sedentary behavior. Traditional public health approaches, which emphasize individual motivation and education, may not sufficiently address the neurobiological basis of self-regulatory failure. Emerging interventions that strengthen inhibitory control capacity include structured physical exercise, behavioral therapies, cognitive training, stress inoculation protocols, and environmental redesign. These antifragility-based strategies aim to progressively rebuild adaptive stress regulation mechanisms and restore neurobehavioral resilience. Inhibitory control failure may represent an underrecognized but modifiable population-level risk factor for chronic disease. Public health strategies that target inhibitory control capacity through progressive adaptive stress exposure may offer novel opportunities for preventing chronic diseases and promoting long-term health. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Acceptance of blind spot monitoring among older drivers: A structural equation modelling study in Hohhot, China
Abstract: Introduction Rapid population ageing has drawn increasing attention to the relationship between older drivers' well-being and independent driving. Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) may help support older drivers, but their benefits depend not only on technical availability but also on user acceptance. This study examines factors associated with older drivers’ acceptance of blind spot monitoring (BSM), a key ADAS function, as reflected in their behavioral intention to use it. Methods A questionnaire-based survey was conducted in Hohhot, China. Drawing on an integrated framework combining the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), this study incorporated three context-specific constructs: perceived barriers to use, perceived functional decline, and perceived cost. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was used to test the proposed relationships. Results The SEM showed good model fit. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were positively associated with behavioral intention to use BSM, with perceived usefulness showing the strongest direct association. Perceived cost was negatively associated with behavioral intention to use BSM. Subjective norms and attitude toward using BSM were positively associated with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, while perceived barriers to use were negatively associated with both constructs. Perceived functional decline was positively associated with perceived usefulness. The model accounted for 45.6% of the variance in behavioral intention to use BSM among older drivers. Conclusion These findings provide preliminary implications for improving communication, user guidance, and affordability-related considerations for age-friendly ADAS. In particular, they suggest that clearer communication about BSM functions, targeted user guidance, and attention to cost-related concerns may be relevant to improving older drivers’ self-reported behavioral intention to use BSM. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Core Competencies, Challenges, and Predictive Factors in Health Service Management: A Study of Transferred Sub-District Health Promoting Hospitals in Phitsanulok
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: The transfer of Subdistrict Health Promoting Hospitals to the Provincial Administrative Organization aims to improve primary care but faces management and workforce challenges, particularly in core competencies. This study assessed core competencies among staff of SHPHs transferred to the Phitsanulok PAO, identified related factors and challenges, and proposed policy recommendations. A mixed-method approach was conducted across 47 decentralized SHPHs, including qualitative interviews with 16 executives and staff and a quantitative survey (n = 141). Results showed high competency levels across all eight domains, with mean scores (M) ranging from 3.82 to 4.06 and standard deviations (SD) ranging from 0.609 to 0.764 on a 5-point scale. Personal factors, including job position, age, and work experience, were significantly associated with specific domains. Organizational factors, such as workforce development support, participation support, internal communication, resource management, and PAO support, were positively and significantly correlated with all domains. Predictive analysis indicated that these factors (β = 0.034–0.123) significantly enhanced competencies, with participation support identified as the most significant predictor, followed by internal communication. This suggests that policy-makers should prioritize inclusive governance and effective communication to enhance workforce readiness. Qualitative findings highlighted challenges of limited access, staff shortages, and outdated systems, whereas enablers included community engagement, leadership, integrated data, and professional development. While high competencies reflect strong workforce resilience, overcoming the resilience–infrastructure paradox through systemic and technological upgrades is essential for sustainable decentralized health management. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Transitions in state limits on local smoke-free authority: adult smoking patterns across sociodemographic groups
Abstract: Introduction State smoke-free indoor air (SFIA) preemption laws can restrict smoke-free protections by limiting local authority. This study evaluated whether ending binding SFIA preemption was associated with adult smoking prevalence across sociodemographic groups. Methods We analyzed 1996–2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data from states with SFIA preemption histories. Outcomes were respondent-level current and everyday smoking. The exposure was ending venue-specific binding SFIA preemption through repeal or comprehensive statewide smoke-free coverage. We used a staggered-adoption two-stage difference-in-differences quasi-experimental design adjusting for state- and year-fixed effects, respondent characteristics, and time-varying state covariates across workplace, restaurant, bar, and combined-venue regimes. Results Ending binding SFIA preemption was associated with lower current smoking prevalence across all six regimes (workplace, restaurant, bar, workplace-and-restaurant, bar-and-restaurant, and combined workplace, bar, and restaurant). Average treatment effects for the treated (ATTs) for current-smoking ranged from −0.0080 (95% CI: −0.0123, −0.0002) for workplaces to −0.0118 (95% CI: −0.0177, −0.0073) for the combined workplace, bar, and restaurant regime. Current-smoking ATTs ranged from −0.0181 to −0.0218 among adults aged 18–24 years and from −0.0215 to −0.0357 among respondents with less than a high school education. Conclusions Among states with SFIA preemption histories, ending binding SFIA preemption was associated with lower current smoking prevalence among adults. Title: Combined WhatsApp and Face-to-Face Intervention Improves Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) Practices in Indonesia: A Longitudinal Quasi-Experimental Study

Title: An LLM-based approach for quantifying regulatory intensity of ecological and environmental zoning policies in China
Abstract: Environmental regulations are increasingly fine-grained and spatially differentiated, but the resulting text-intensive and largely unstructured policy documents make regulatory measures difficult to interpret consistently. Here, a regulatory intensity evaluation framework based on Large Language Models (LLMs), combining policy authority, target stringency, and measure clarity was developed to quantify China's Ecological and Environmental Zoning-based Regulation (EZR). The average regulatory intensity across all IEEUs is 4.16, with pronounced heterogeneity across control types and dimensions: critical regulatory units (5.10) and the spatial layout constraint dimension (7.26) exhibit the strongest intensity. A clear east–west gradient is observed, with Shanghai (6.70) and Beijing (6.26) at the upper end, while provincial-level scores extended down to 1.68. Response surface methodology (RSM) further shows that regulatory intensity reflects a joint configuration of regional development and environmental pressure, featuring nonlinear and interaction effects. Title: Eventful migration and intercultural self-formation: Ethical selves among Indonesian returnee migrant workers
Abstract: This article examines how returned Indonesian female migrant domestic workers retrospectively interpret the intercultural encounters they experienced during overseas employment. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 24 returnees from Cilacap, Indonesia, it explores how some encounters came to be understood as ethically significant after migration rather than merely as instances of cultural adaptation. Title: Young children can infer what speakers know based on their causal influence over listeners
Abstract: A causal, mentalistic understanding of communication—a process by which a speaker's mind causes a change in a listener's mind—can support powerful inferences that go beyond observable data. If A struggles to activate a toy but succeeds after B whispers to A, you can infer that B knew how to activate it even without hearing what was said. Although humans are precocious communicators, much remains unknown about how we come to understand communication as a process by which speakers causally influence listeners. Extending prior work on children's forward inferences about communication—from speakers to listeners—the current work examined how children reason backwards from listeners’ behaviors to recover speakers’ knowledge. Children viewed two scenarios where a listener failed to activate a toy twice before finally succeeding. In one scenario the speaker communicated before a listener's success, whereas in the other scenario the speaker communicated before a listener's failure. Even 3-year-olds chose the former speaker as the one who knew how the toy works (Exp.1). However, when communication always preceded success but the scenarios differed in what would have happened without communication (i.e., the listener was poised to fail or succeed), a preference for the former speaker did not emerge until later (Exps.2–3). Importantly, across all experiments, children held no preference when speakers produced non-speech vocalizations. These results suggest that even young children have an abstract understanding of communication as a causal, mentalistic process, but their inferences are constrained by the causal cues available in context and continue to develop throughout early childhood. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Kai Wai: Enacting Resilience and Negotiating Governance of Voluntary (Im)mobility in Oceanic Worlds
Abstract: Dominant climate governance frameworks, including planned relocation policy, remain underpinned by Western, state-centric, modernist ontology. Indigenous Pacific communities challenge this when resisting relocation, adapting instead in place through complex, place-based governance systems across interconnected land-sea worlds. The choice to stay thus offers an opportunity to reground dominant frameworks in Indigenous governance systems and strategies that have long guided island communities.We respond to this by engaging with processes of resilience and adaptation governance guided by Pasifika relational philosophies in a community resisting relocation. We ask: ‘How are processes of resilience in voluntary (im)mobile communities revealing and renegotiating adaptation governance?’. Drawing on the Vanua Research Framework (Nabobo-Baba, 2006), the research engages in oral narratives and storytelling emerging from 25 talanoa sessions and ethnographic fieldwork in Qoma island, Fiji.Narratives from Qoma reveal a relational Oceanic cosmology underpinning community life and governance, informing resistance to relocate and strategies to stay in place. Strategies include forms of mobilising through collectivist practices of the Vanua and through relations across scales, linking communities, ancestors, islands, the state, and transnational actors across the seascape. Relations extend across a ‘sea of islands’, through ancestral agreements of care between kin, that enable micro-mobilities. Insights from Qoma reveal a renegotiation of state-centric governance frameworks towards approaches that centre the Vanua. We conclude that climate adaptation is about more than protecting the individual. It is about restoring and maintaining relationships connecting past, present and future members of a collective oceanic community. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Integrating Circular Economy Principles into Financial Risk Management: A Strategy for Growth and Sustainability of Rumah Dangke, an Indonesian MSME
Source title: Journal of Global Innovations in Agricultural Sciences
Abstract: Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) play a vital role in Indonesia’s economy but often face significant financial risks due to volatile input costs, limited access to financing, and market uncertainty. This study examines the case of Rumah Dangke, a traditional dairy based food MSME in South Sulawesi, to identify internal and external factors influencing its business sustainability and to formulate strategic financial risk management approaches. Using a qualitative case study design, the research employs SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) and QSPM (Quantitative Strategic Planning Matrix) analyses. Internally, Rumah Dangke demonstrates strengths such as an organized financial system, diversified capital sources, stable market demand, and efficient production processes. However, it faces weaknesses including limited financial literacy, inconsistent documentation, dependence on local raw materials, and restricted access to external financing. Externally, opportunities include growing market demand, government and institutional support, digital market access, export potential, and collaboration with other MSMEs and the culinary sector. Key threats involve raw material price volatility, rising production costs, competition from substitutes, regulatory changes, and shifting consumer preferences. A key strategic approach identified is the SO (Strengths–Opportunities) strategy, which integrates circular economy (CE) principles into financial risk management. Rather than replacing fresh milk, the primary raw material CE practices aim to buffer financial volatility by generating additional value from by–products (e.g., repurposing whey into secondary food products or animal feed) and reducing operational costs (e.g., using biogas from dairy waste for energy). These measures enhance cost efficiency, reduce exposure to milk price fluctuations, and improve long–term business resilience. Implementing CE not only strengthens Rumah Dangke’s competitiveness but also aligns its operations with environmentally responsible and sustainable business practices. Specifically, repurposing whey a by–product of dangke’s papain–based coagulation process into value added products offers a practical circular economy entry point that improves cost efficiency and reduces environmental impact. © 2027, Society for Innovative Agriculture, University of Agriculture. Authors: Shi L.; Wu S.
Title: Whom and when to deport and punish: Experimental evidence on Americans’ attitudes toward immigrants in the criminal legal system
Abstract: Across many immigrant destination countries, recent immigration law enforcement has expanded in scope and salience, intensifying public debate over deportation, criminal punishment, and the treatment of immigrants in the criminal legal system. Drawing on focal concerns theory, the current study uses the U.S. as an empirical case and a 4 (country of origin: Syria, China, Russia, or Mexico) × 2 (crime severity: felony drug offense or misdemeanor trespassing) × 2 (possibility of judicial error: certain or uncertain witness) × 2 (legality: valid work visa or expired tourist visa) online survey experiment with a national sample of U.S. adults to examine public preferences for deportation and criminal punishment of immigrants arrested for non-immigration offenses. Results indicate that legality is significantly associated with both deportation and imprisonment preferences, and that respondents rely on overlapping considerations when evaluating immigrants’ deportability and criminal culpability. Although the uncertainty of evidence reduces imprisonment preferences, it has no effect on deportation preferences, suggesting greater public tolerance for errors and mistakes in the context of immigrant removal. Together, these findings suggest that punishment decisions involving immigrants are shaped in part by concerns about undocumented status, even when individuals are formally processed through the criminal legal system. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Dai Y.; Ding Y.; Zeng K.; Li N.
Title: Guard your mind: Mind manipulation detection via multi-agent interaction and fine-grained stepwise reasoning
Abstract: Mind manipulation in dialogue exploits emotional vulnerabilities via covert tactics and hidden goals. We present a fine-grained framework that (i) detects turn-level manipulation tactics and (ii) infers dialogue-level intent before issuing a final manipulation judgment. To support training and evaluation, we curate a balanced dataset of 776 dialogues (388 manipulative, 388 non-manipulative; 15520 dialogue turns) generated via a three-phase multi-agent simulation with dual verification. On this benchmark, our model achieves 84.01% accuracy for dialogue-level manipulation detection, outperforming the strongest baseline by +6.83%. It further attains 76.25% accuracy on tactic detection and 79.53% BERTScore for intent prediction. A user study on forward-simulatability shows +11.0% accuracy improvement when the tactics and intent detected by our model are provided as rationale for dialogue manipulation detection results. These results indicate that explicit, stepwise reasoning over tactics and intent yields both higher performance and actionable interpretability for proactive monitoring of manipulative conversations. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zheng Q.; Hu Y.; Lai Y.; Yang Y.; Zhou X.; Yuan Y.; Sun Z.; Wen P.; Fu J.; Yang M.
Title: Effects of an embodied micro-film intervention on ethical sensitivity, compassion, and ethical decision-making in nursing students: A mixed-methods study
Abstract: Background: Bridging the “knowing-doing gap” remains a central challenge in nursing ethics education. Traditional didactic methods often position students as disembodied observers, limiting the transformation of ethical knowledge into practical competence. Objective: To address the “knowing-doing gap” in ethics education, this study aimed to develop and evaluate an innovative micro-film intervention, guided by embodied cognition theory, and to assess its impact on key components of nursing ethical competence. Design: A mixed methods study employing a two-arm cluster-assigned quasi-experimental design with an embedded qualitative component. Setting: A nursing school at a medical university in China. Participants: A total of 282 third-year undergraduate nursing students were cluster-randomised into an experimental group (n = 142) and a control group (n = 140). Methods: A 16-week embodied micro-film intervention was administered to the experimental group, and traditional lecture-based instruction was delivered to the control group. Validated instruments, including the Ethical Sensitivity Questionnaire for Nursing Students, the Compassionate Love for Humanity Scale, and the Judgments about Nursing Decisions questionnaire, were administered at baseline and post-intervention. Qualitative data were collected from reflective journals submitted by the experimental group. Data were analysed using SPSS version 26.0, with paired and independent t-tests and mixed-design ANOVA for quantitative directed content analysis for qualitative responses. Results: Compared with the control group, the experimental group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in ethical sensitivity (t = 8.741, p < .001, d = 1.04), compassionate tendency (t = 4.663, p < .001, d = 0.56), and overall ethical decision-making ability (t = 6.634, p < .001, d = 0.79). In addition, a significant reduction in the knowing doing gap of the JAND was observed only in the experimental group (p < .05). Qualitative findings revealed four interrelated mechanisms underpinning these changes: transforming abstract ethical principles into embodied understanding, cultivating empathy through simulated lived experience, strengthening ethical decision-making in contextualized dilemmas, and showing preliminary potential in narrowing the knowing-doing gap through bodily rehearsal and anticipatory reflection. Conclusion: An embodied micro-film–based pedagogy represents an effective and theory-informed innovation in nursing ethics education. By integrating bodily engagement, situated interaction, and reflective learning, this approach facilitates the internalisation and enactment of ethical competence, offering a promising strategy for narrowing the knowing–doing gap in undergraduate nursing education. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Castulo N.J.; Marasigan A.C.; Congman R.
Author full names: Castulo, Nilo Jayoma (59355509600); Marasigan, Arlyne C. (57209750058); Congman, Rao (58035663100)
Title: Teach by all means: Evidence of university-community-school partnerships through the Bayanihan spirit
Abstract: Promoting partnerships between universities, communities, and schools helps address challenges within the school system, particularly the theory‑practice nexus. This study investigates emergency remote teaching (ERT) in a disadvantaged area of Mindanao (Philippines) towards learning recovery through a university‑community‑school partnership animated by the Filipino cultural value of Bayanihan – collective solidarity, resource pooling, and reciprocal obligation. A descriptive qualitative approach was used, collecting data through interviews and online diaries from 16 teachers affected by armed conflict and the COVID‑19 pandemic. Thematic analysis revealed that teachers employed multimodal instruction (radio‑based learning, modular learning, digital platforms) sustained by relational presence and collective responsibility. Community partnerships exemplified the Bayanihan spirit by addressing the digital divide and resource constraints. Despite challenges such as increased workload, stress, and student‑engagement gaps, ERT fostered technological skill development, sustainable resource mobilization, and enhanced community engagement. This study contributes an empirically grounded framework showing how Bayanihan mediated university‑community‑school partnerships during ERT. While scholarship on culturally embedded disaster response exists, this study provides one of the first detailed accounts of Bayanihan’s role in educational emergency response, offering a model adaptable to other collectivist cultural contexts. Findings are geographically and socioeconomically specific to Mindanao, limiting generalizability. Further research is recommended to expand and adapt the proposed partnership model to diverse settings in the Philippines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Zhang X.; Lin X.; Wang Y.
Title: Mapping the school factors that shape teachers’ career commitment: A network analysis
Abstract: Teacher career commitment is essential for organizational sustainability, yet prior research has often examined it through isolated predictors. Using TALIS 2018 data from 261,426 teachers across 48 countries, this study applied network analysis to model the interdependencies among career commitment and 22 school-level factors across four domains. The sample was drawn predominantly from lower secondary schools serving students aged approximately 11 to 15, with a sampling criterion requiring a minimum of 20 teachers per school. Results show that commitment emerges from a complex system of mutually reinforcing influences rather than linear causes. School autonomy over instructional policies was the most influential node, followed by school size (number of enrolled students), school autonomy over curriculum, and school autonomy over budgeting, suggesting that teachers’ career commitment is most strongly shaped by their meaningful influence over instruction, the organizational scale of the school, and control over what is taught and how resources are allocated. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Angles of trust in transboundary water cooperation: Capturing the multidimensional and dynamic nature of trust in the Sava and Syrdarya river basins
Abstract: Trust is frequently invoked to explain cooperation or conflict in interstate relations over shared water resources. Drawing on qualitative research in the Sava River Basin in Southeastern Europe and the Syrdarya River Basin in Central Asia, this article suggests three key dimensions through which trust can be better understood – its sources, levels, and intensities. We combine these three dimensions, or angles, into a Trust Angles Framework that builds on existing conceptualisations and provides an empirically grounded analytical lens for examining trust as a multidimensional and dynamic process. Our findings indicate how different sources of trust (risk-minimising, value-shaping, and psychosocial), governance levels (interpersonal, interorganisational, interstate), and varying intensities (from mistrust to high trust) interact unevenly over time. The Sava case illustrates how cooperation can emerge through strong interorganisational and interpersonal trust despite persistent interstate mistrust, while the Syrdarya case reveals how high-level rapprochement may not translate into stronger interorganisational or interpersonal trust when institutional reliability remains weak. By foregrounding trust as a relational, historically embedded, and spatially differentiated practice, the article contributes to scholarship on transboundary water governance and debates in international relations. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Zhe C.; Zhang L.
Title: A mixed method quasi experimental study: Teachers' perspectives and student outcomes of innovative mathematics teaching through project-based learning, digital tools, peer collaboration, mathematical experiments, and interdisciplinary teaching
Abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of innovative teaching methods in improving the mathematical skills and literacy of middle school students. A mixed-method quasi-experimental design was used that included 310 middle school students, who were split into experimental groups (n = 155) and a control group (n = 155). The quantitative data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics and SmartPLS 4, while the qualitative data obtained from 19 mathematics teachers were analysed using QDA Miner software based on thematic analysis. The results showed that innovative methods in learning mathematics have positive effects on students' mathematical competencies and mathematical literacy. The positive influence of project-based learning on mathematical modeling skills was observed (β = 0.570, p < .001), whereas digital tools had a positive effect on imagination and data analysis skills (β = 0.579, p < .001), peer collaboration had a positive effect on logical reasoning abilities (β = 0.598, p < .001), mathematical experiments had a positive effect on procedural fluency (β = 0.526, p < .001), and the interdisciplinary approach positively influenced mathematical literacy (β = 0.179, p = .001). The mediation analyses confirmed significant indirect effects on mathematical literacy through procedural fluency (β = 0.094, p = .003), imagination and data analysis skills (β = 0.087, p = .004), mathematical modelling skills (β = 0.108, p = .001), and logical reasoning abilities (β = 0.065, p = .027). Qualitative results confirmed quantitative results, and teachers emphasized that innovative teaching methods were effective in stimulating learners' active involvement, conceptual development, and meaningful learning of mathematics. The findings suggest that the innovative mathematics teaching methods are effective for developing mathematical competence and literacy in middle school students with a learner-centered teaching model. The results provide implications for enhancing mathematics instruction and curriculum development using innovative pedagogical practices, grounded in constructivist learning theory. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: “I've let screens take over”: Maternal guilt about media and relations to children's problematic media use
Abstract: Parents today face increasing challenges in managing children's media use, which are often accompanied by intense feelings of guilt. This study examines the prevalence and predictors of mother's parental media guilt surrounding their own and their child's media use. Using structural equation modeling, we analyzed data from 474 U.S. mothers (65% White, M child age = 7.48 yrs). Approximately half of mothers endorsed moderate or higher levels of guilt on several media guilt related items. Maternal guilt about their child's media use was significantly associated with higher maternal depression, lower media efficacy, and greater child problematic media use (PMU). In contrast, mothers' guilt over their own media use was associated with maternal depression and child PMU. Media content and screen time did not predict guilt levels. Younger maternal age predicted both types of guilt. Findings suggest that maternal media guilt is both common and complex and may be more closely tied to perceived parenting ideals and emotional well-being than to actual media behaviors. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Liu Y.; Liu J.; Xu K.; Sun X.; Xu S.
Title: Who do national logistics hubs really serve? A multi-spatial-scale analysis of logistics-industry coordination in China
Abstract: China's National logistics hubs (NLHs) are pivotal nodes intended to form a nationwide logistics network, facilitate industrial upgrading and optimise economic distribution, which makes their spatial relationship with industries crucial. Using employment data of 313 Chinese cities across 19 industries from 2011 to 2019, this study proposes a multi-spatial-scale coupling coordination model based on the metacoupling framework and compares coordination between logistics in national logistics hub cities (NLHCs) and industries at local, urban agglomeration (UA) and national scales. Logistics-industry coordination varies across spatial scales: Logistics-operation-oriented industries mostly follow a Hub-Embedded pattern, including utilities, construction, wholesale, information, finance, business, and technology, whereas manufacturing and mining exhibit a Hinterland-Anchored pattern. Logistics-enabled industries demonstrate more diversity: education, healthcare, and public management exhibit a Node-Radiating pattern, while agriculture, hospitality, and household services show weak coordination. Logistics in 40 of the NLHCs has not achieved advanced coordination with industries, especially in the Central Plains and Chengdu-Chongqing UAs. Results of explainable machine learning further show the predictive contributions of industrial characteristics, logistics and transportation, foundations, and policies to coordination across industries and spatial scales. The findings inform optimising the spatial layouts of logistics hubs according to industries, deepening logistics coordination within UAs, and extending the radius of public services by leveraging national-level logistics hubs. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Wang Y.; Wu S.; Guo K.; Li H.; Xu Y.; Qiu M.; Si J.
Title: Developmental trajectories of children’s academic self-handicapping: role of academic self-efficacy and outcomes in mathematics achievement
Abstract: The present study examined the developmental trajectories of children’s academic self-handicapping and the role of academic self-efficacy. A total of 1285 children (770 boys; M T1age = 9.47 ± 0.59) were assessed four times from the 3rd to 6th grades. The overall trajectory followed a quadratic curvilinear pattern, characterized by an initial increase from Grade 3 to Grade 4 followed by a gradual decline through Grade 6. Three distinct trajectories were identified: the low increase-decrease group (48.9%), the moderate slowly-decreasing group (40.0%), and the high quickly-decreasing group (11.1%). Academic self-efficacy significantly predicted the initial level of academic self-handicapping and increased the likelihood of belonging to the low increase-decrease group. Moreover, significant group differences were found in Grade 6 mathematics achievement after controlling for Grade 3 mathematics achievement, with the low increase-decrease group outperforming the moderate slowly-decreasing group. These findings highlight the heterogeneous developmental patterns of academic self-handicapping and underscore academic self-efficacy as a protective factor, providing educators with prospective indicators for identifying at-risk children and informing early intervention efforts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Tiznado-Aitken I.; Soza-Parra J.
Title: Setting boundaries and thresholds in transportation research and policy: Between principles of sufficientarianism and limitarianism
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: This paper rethinks transport research and practice by integrating two distributive justice principles: sufficientarianism and limitarianism. While sufficiency has shaped debates on minimum accessibility, basic needs and mobility rights, the notion of upper thresholds or limits, central to limitarian thinking, remains underexplored. Drawing on transport, environmental, and political philosophy scholarship, we propose a normative mobility-accessibility-wellbeing corridor that guarantees accessibility to fulfill basic needs while curbing resource-intensive travel that exacerbates environmental degradation and undermines collective wellbeing. Combining features of a narrative and critical review, we examine cross-disciplinary frameworks on boundaries, critically discuss the main challenges when defining and navigating trade-offs between lower and upper thresholds in transportation, and illustrate how these principles are associated with established and emerging transport policies. We conclude with a discussion of further conceptual, empirical, and policy-oriented research directions opened up by this approach. Title: Delegating (or not) to machines: How role expectations shape leaders’ willingness to use AI for communication
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly capable of replacing people in interpersonal communication, yet it remains unclear how willing leaders will be to delegate communication to AI. Four preregistered studies examine leaders' willingness to delegate specific employee interactions to AI and explore the underlying psychology behind these preferences. Results indicate that leaders are reluctant to rely on AI assistants to automate employee interactions (Studies 1–4). This reluctance is consistently driven by leaders' role-based expectations to signal care to employees, while leaders' desire to maintain control over interactions with employees plays a more context-dependent role (Studies 2–3). Importantly, we find that leaders’ reluctance to delegate communication to AI is specific to AI and not merely a reluctance to delegate communication in general (Study 3). Finally, building on these findings, we show that leaders are most reluctant to delegate communication to AI assistants when interacting about sensitive issues (i.e., issues that heighten the need to signal care and maintain control), in contrast to operational issues (Study 4). Practical and theoretical implications are discussed. © 2026

Authors: Bolz S.
Title: Do local energy agencies accelerate the solar expansion in Germany?
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of a specific district-level measure, local energy agencies (LEAs), on solar PV adoption in Germany. These agencies, founded since 1992, serve as contact points for citizens, municipalities, and companies, focusing on consultancy and networking for renewable energy and energy efficiency. Using data from the Core Energy Market Data Registry and an originally compiled dataset on LEAs, the analysis utilizes augmented synthetic controls to account for staggered agency adoption. A significant effect of the foundation of LEAs on new solar adopters, measured as the number of actors installing solar PV for the first time per 10,000 inhabitants, cannot be established. The result holds for different subgroups of new adopters, model specifications, and dependent variables. Effect sizes are generally small and standard errors are large. A positive or negative significant effect cannot be established for LEAs in general or for LEAs with certain characteristics. © 2026 The Author. Published by Elsevier B.V. Authors: Şahin M.K.; Uluışık İ.
Title: Learning with playful maps: The role of orienteering on problem-solving skills and environmental awareness of preschool children
Abstract: This study examined how an eight-week orienteering training affected preschoolers' problem-solving abilities and attitudes toward their environment. An explanatory sequential mixed-method design was used and involved 40 children in a public preschool in Afyonkarahisar, Türkiye, ages 5 to 6. The Children's Attitudes Towards the Environment Scale - Preschool Version (CATES-PV), the Problem Solving Skills Scale (4-7 years) (PSSS), a demographic information form, and an open-ended questionnaire were used as data collection tools. The dependent-groups t-test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test were used to determine the difference between pre-test and post-test scores. Descriptive analysis was applied for the qualitative part. Children's problem-solving abilities significantly improved throughout the training, according to the findings. The training was not generally associated with improvements in scores on the Children's Attitudes Towards Environment Scale, but it did improve the living habits dimension of the scale. Both parents and teachers have noted positive changes in children's problem-solving, environmental awareness, map-reading skills, and nature sensitivity. These results show that orienteering training is associated with promising changes, particularly in ​​problem-solving. The study presents orienteering as an encouraging pedagogical approach for improving problem-solving skills in daily routine and contributes to the expanding literature on outdoor learning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Travel socialization within households: A longitudinal analysis
Abstract: While transport research has shown that individual attitudes and subjective norms affect travel behavior, most studies overlook how household-level travel socialization processes (i.e., how attitudes and behaviors are transmitted between members) affect these patterns over time. The current study examines socialization processes in two household types, two-partner and family households, focusing on how fathers (or male partners), mothers (or female partners), and children influence each other's travel attitudes and behaviors over time. Using a two-wave cross-lagged panel model from the Netherlands Mobility Panel, we test the directionality of these effects. Results indicate that (i) in two-partner households, sustainable modes show more bidirectional effects between partners, though train use remains asymmetrical; (ii) in family households, the socialization process is largely parent-driven, with mothers playing a central role in influencing sustainable travel attitudes/behaviors of both children and partners; (iii) car use shows bidirectional effects between children and parents; and (iv) in both household types, individual travel behaviors are also highly stable over time, indicating the importance of behavioral consistency in addition to socialization processes. Mode-specific strategies targeting influential household members; mothers for cycling, parents for train use, and children for car reduction; can more effectively promote sustainable travel. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Assessing inter-rater agreement among large language model judges: Evidence from persona evaluation across varying educational risk contexts
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as automated judges for evaluation, yet their reliability remains unclear. This study examines the inter-rater agreement of three LLM judges (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Gemini 1.5 Pro) when evaluating fairness, lack of stereotypicality, and diversity in user personas across varying educational risk contexts. We analyzed 60 individual personas and 12 persona sets to assess whether these judges demonstrate sufficient consistency to function as reliable evaluators. Although inter-rater agreement was moderate at the individual persona level, three critical limitations emerged. At the set level, agreement ranged from .39 to .63 across persona generators and therefore did not show a uniform decline relative to individual-level agreement. Mean dimension-support scores were 41% to 61% lower, although the individual- and set-level tasks are not directly comparable. Second, non-compliance rates, where judges could not provide textual justification for their ratings, ranged from 9.6 to 26.7% at the individual level and increased to 34% to 49% at the set level. Third, agreement differed across the three educational scenarios classified by risk: individual-level agreement declined from the lower- to higher-risk scenarios, while set-level agreement showed no monotonic pattern. We conclude that, under the tested protocol, current LLM judges demonstrate poor-to-moderate inter-rater agreement for persona evaluation. These findings contribute a descriptive characterization of LLM evaluation behavior across risk contexts and provide a foundation for future validation studies comparing LLM agreement against human judgment. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Wang Z.; Wang J.
Title: Task-aware modality configuration in personalized health information systems: Evidence from multi-attribute task contexts
Abstract: This study investigates how multi-attribute health-related tasks shape users’ observed choices among single-modal and multimodal information combinations. It examines modality configuration as a task-triggered, micro-level instantiation of task–technology fit in personalized health information systems. Grounded in task facet classification theory, the study conceptualizes health tasks along three dimensions: task type, task complexity, and topic group. These effects are examined through a quasi-experimental design based on simulated work task scenarios. A total of 120 participants were recruited, yielding 25,000 valid health information records selected and saved in a researcher-supervised controlled live-web SWTS setting. Distributional differences in modality choices across task configurations are examined, and the findings are triangulated using descriptive odds ratios and multinomial logit models to assess the consistency of effect direction and relative strength in task–modality relationships. The results show that users’ observed modality choices are highly concentrated in a small number of dominant text-centered single-modal and multimodal formats, indicating a clear distributional concentration pattern rather than indiscriminate multimodal use. Systematic distributional differences are observed across task configurations in the selection proportions of key modality combinations, including text-only, text–voice, text–image, text–image–video, and text–video formats, suggesting that task attributes are associated with observed modality choices in multimodal information system use. By translating task attributes into implementable modality configuration logic, this study operationalizes modality configuration as a task-triggered, micro-level instantiation of task–technology fit and provides actionable principles for adaptive and risk-sensitive modality design in personalized and generative AI–enabled health information systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Yang Y.; Xu M.; Zhan J.; Zhang Z.; Liu Y.; Qu X.
Title: Public acceptance of autonomous flying cars in urban air mobility: The mediating role of trust
Abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Authors: Awaekachi F.; Laeheem K.
Title: Youth and Stakeholder Perspectives on Depression Literacy and Game Design in Thailand’s Southern Border Provinces
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This formative qualitative study examined how youth and stakeholders in Thailand’s Southern Border Provinces understand depression and what they would require of a board game intended to promote mental health literacy. It formed the needs-assessment phase of a larger research and development project. Eighteen key informants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling: two psychiatrists, two board game experts, 10 youth volunteers aged 15–24 years, and four mental health personnel. In-depth interviews were analyzed through qualitative content analysis. Four themes were constructed. Informants perceived youth knowledge of depression as limited and closely tied to fear of stigma. Stigma and religious misattribution were described as delaying help-seeking. Religious practice was reported both as a valued source of comfort and, when depression was equated with weak faith, as an interpretation discouraging professional help; concealment and withdrawal were described alongside it. All groups considered a board game acceptable and specified design requirements: expert-verified information; locally familiar situations and language; a clear position that religious practice supports rather than replaces professional care; and mechanics that allow responses through characters rather than personal disclosure. Because no game was developed or tested, these findings describe perceived acceptability and proposed design requirements and point to the need for co-design and evaluation. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research. Title: Consumer preferences for vehicle types informed by direct and indirect emission estimates
Source title: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
Abstract: As financial incentives for EVs wane and price parity approaches, engaging mainstream adopters is critical to sustaining market growth. While early adopters are driven by environmentalism and proactive information-seeking, the broader market remains hesitant due to knowledge gaps regarding EV benefits. We evaluate how communication of state-specific emission estimates for five vehicle types (ICE, HEV, PHEV, BEV, and FCEV) influences vehicle perceptions, rankings, and fleet composition. Surveying 908 participants across four states (CA, FL, PA, TX), we find that, while emissions information shifts vehicle rankings, political identity and charging feasibility remain the primary determinants of top preferences. Furthermore, participants favor fleets with a diverse composition over a single technology. Our findings suggest that providing state-level emission estimates effectively reshapes consumer preferences and reduces the desired share of high-emission vehicles. This research provides a strategic framework for policymakers and manufacturers to sustain market momentum through transparency and targeted communication. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Iqra S.H.; Saphores J.-D.
Title: Still walking, still cycling? Post-pandemic active travel and healthy mobility in Southern California
Abstract: Introduction The COVID-19 pandemic, together with the rise of remote work and e-shopping, substantially altered travel behavior. Whether these changes persisted for active travel, and how they reshaped access to health-promoting mobility opportunities, remains unclear. This study examines how the determinants of walking and cycling changed between 2019 and 2023 across the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) region, a highly diverse region comprising six counties, 191 cities, and more than 18 million residents. Methods We estimate generalized spatial regression models on StreetLight InSight® active transportation data to compare pre- and post-pandemic associations between active travel and sociodemographic, built environment, safety, and crime-related factors at the census-tract level. Results We find that average daily walking trips declined across most of the SCAG region between 2019 and 2023, whereas cycling trips increased. Most pre-pandemic correlates persisted; formal between-year comparisons identified several meaningful changes for walking but none for cycling. For walking in 2023, tracts with more residents outside the labor force and more workers with short commutes were associated with more walking. For cycling, tracts with more residents outside the labor force were positively associated with cycling in 2023, whereas a larger share of tract area classified as urban remained negatively associated with cycling. Conclusions Our findings indicate substantial continuity in active-travel correlates, with selective between-year changes concentrated in walking that are consistent with more flexible and localized activity patterns. To support healthy, sustainable, and inclusive mobility, investments should prioritize safe neighborhood-scale connectivity, low-stress walking and cycling networks, and equitable access to everyday destinations, particularly in communities where safety, infrastructure, and vehicle-ownership constraints may limit active travel. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Trends in cannabis use disorder among adults in the United States, 2021-2024
Abstract: Background The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with disruptions to mental health and substance use behaviors in the United States (U.S.), alongside continued changes in cannabis policy. While increases in cannabis use during the early pandemic are documented, less is known about more recent trends in cannabis use disorder (CUD). Methods We used repeated cross-sectional data on adults (aged 18 +) from the 2021–2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (n = 186,823). We used survey-weighted logistic regression to model past-year cannabis use disorder (CUD; DSM-5 yes/no) as a function of survey year, sociodemographic characteristics, and state medical cannabis law (MCL) status. Overall and subgroup-specific adjusted marginal linear trends were estimated by including year-by-covariate interaction terms. Results The proportion of CUD was 5.9% (2021), 7.0% (2022), 6.9% (2023), and 7.4% (2024), with an average of 6.8%. Increasing survey year was associated with greater odds of CUD (AOR: 1.09, 95% CI: 1.06–1.13). Average marginal effects showed higher annual percentage point (pp) changes in CUD overall (pp = 0.54) and among all age groups (pp range = 0.35–0.89); males (pp = 0.69) and females (pp = 0.40); Hispanic (pp = 0.27), non-Hispanic White (pp = 0.68), and non-Hispanic Black (pp = 0.90) adults; across all educational attainment (pp range = 0.35–0.76), annual household income (pp range = 0.49–0.63), employment (pp range = 0.44–0.60) statuses; metropolitan status subgroups (pp range = 0.52–0.63; and among residents of states with and without MCL coverage (p = 0.54 for both). Conclusions CUD prevalence was higher in recent years, with consistent upward trends observed across sociodemographic subgroups, including historically disadvantaged populations. These findings underscore the need for continued policy attention to address rising CUD risk. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Yu Y.; Gao W.; Ren Y.
Title: Effects of green travel creation initiative on carbon mitigation: Evidence from China
Abstract: As countries pursue carbon neutrality, green travel has become an important means of advancing low-carbon transport transitions in developing economies. Treating China's green travel creation initiative (GTCI) as a quasi-natural experiment, we estimate its carbon mitigation effects using multiple causal inference frameworks. The results show that the GTCI significantly reduces transport-sector CO2 emissions, and this finding remains robust to endogeneity tests, alternative estimation methods, and model specifications. The GTCI has stronger carbon mitigation effects in coastal cities, resource-based cities, cities with stronger environmental regulation, and non-old industrial base cities than in their respective comparison groups. Mechanism analysis suggests that enhanced public transportation input, green technological innovation, and green infrastructure development may serve as potential channels. Additional spatial analyses indicate that the carbon-reduction effects of the GTCI are largely confined to the pilot cities, with no robust evidence of cross-city spillovers. These findings provide evidence on the environmental effectiveness of the GTCI and offer policy implications for advancing sustainable transport development in emerging economies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Kocanci, Mustafa (57224140676); Aksoy, Beyhan (59717668200); Cetınturk, Veli Ercan (60836854000)
Title: Seeing gender inequality through glass metaphors: Epistemic power and blind spots
Abstract: This study examines the glass ceiling, glass cliff, and glass escalator in terms of their explanatory power, the conceptual frameworks they generate, and the solutions they establish. A comparative critical thematic analysis of 15 high-impact peer-reviewed reveals three patterns. First, metaphors name structural inequalities, but the conclusions and recommendations of the reviewed studies frequently shift the horizon of possible solutions toward individual strategies. This points to the risk of relocating responsibility from institutions to individuals. Second, metaphor-based explanations often rest on an implicit assumption of a “universal woman” and engage with intersectional differences only in limited ways. This limitation stems both from authorial choices and from the simplifying tendencies of metaphorical framing. Third, metaphors do not always operate as substantive explanatory tools; in some texts, they reduce inequality to discursive labels. The study argues that glass metaphors function as selective epistemic apparatuses that make certain inequalities visible while obscuring others and shaping the repertoire of possible solutions. These metaphors reveal distinct organizational logics, including exclusion, risk delegation, and the invisible circulation of rewards. Accordingly, the article calls for a more critical, reflexive, and intersectional approach to the use of metaphors in gender studies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The mediating role of palatable eating motives in the associations of problematic digital technology use with body mass index and Mediterranean lifestyle in young adults
Abstract: The problematic use of digital technology is closely related to a sedentary lifestyle and unhealthy eating habits; however, the underlying mechanisms of these associations are unclear. It is believed that problematic use of digital technology may increase motives for eating palatable foods through changes in the reward system and exposure to food cues in digital environments, and that this may be associated with unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. The aim of this study was to investigate the mediating role of palatable eating motives in the relationships between problematic digital technology use, body mass index (BMI), and Mediterranean lifestyle (MEDLIFE) among young adults. This cross-sectional study analyzed data obtained from 610 young adults. The data collection tools included Descriptive Information Form, Digital Addiction Scale (DAS), Palatable Eating Motives Scale (PEMS), BMI and MEDLIFE index. The mean age of participants was 21.6 ± 1.7 years. In the mediation model between DAS and BMI, the total (β:0.215, 95%CI:0.586; 1.237), direct (β:0.167, 95%CI:0.365; 1.051) and indirect effects of PEMS (β:0.048, 95%CI:0.074; 0.346) were all statistically significant. In the mediation model between DAS and MEDLIFE index, the total (β:-0.456, 95%CI:-2.212;-1.603), direct (β:-0.424, 95%CI:-2.101;-1.451) and indirect effects of PEMS (β:-0.032, 95%CI:-0.251;-0.024) were all statistically significant. Findings suggest that higher digital addiction is associated with higher BMI and lower MEDLIFE, and these relationships are partially mediated by palatable eating motivations. Notably, the mediating effect was more pronounced in the association with BMI, whereas it was comparatively limited in the association with MEDLIFE. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Driving Simulation Methods for Assessing Post-Injury Driving Performance After Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Scoping Review
Abstract: Driving is a cognitively demanding task that involves the continuous integration of attention, executive control, visual processing, and motor coordination. Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) may disrupt these functions and affect driving performance during recovery. Driving simulation is increasingly used to examine post-mTBI driving performance, yet substantial heterogeneity exists in simulator platforms, task designs, and outcome selection. This scoping review characterized driving simulation methodologies used to assess post-mTBI driving performance and examined patterns of mTBI-related findings across reported outcomes. A systematic search of seven electronic databases identified 12 eligible publications between 2017 and 2026. Publications were synthesized by participant characteristics, time since injury, simulator platform, task demands, and outcomes. Across publications, mTBI-related findings were most frequently reported for vehicle control metrics, particularly lane position variability and speed regulation. mTBI-related differences were most often condition-specific, including differences during curves, hazard events, and manipulated cognitive load or dual-task conditions. Cognitive measures also demonstrated mTBI-related differences and associations to driving performance, particularly those assessing executive functioning and processing speed domains. Differences were observed across all post-injury intervals, including ≥ 15 days, with a small number of related publications reporting performance differences after symptom resolution. However, the predominantly cross-sectional evidence does not establish whether these differences persist over time within the same individuals. Findings suggest that driving simulation can provide a useful controlled method for examining functional driving performance following mTBI across varying road environments and task demands. Future work should prioritize standardizing simulator outcomes and validating simulator performance against on-road, naturalistic-driving, and crash-related outcomes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Ha T.
Title: Household income heterogeneity across employment type and sub-region: Evidence from Seoul and Busan, 2018–2022
Abstract: This study examines household income heterogeneity across employment types, sub-regions, and income quantiles in Seoul and Busan. South Korea's two largest metropolitan cities have followed contrasting demographic and economic trajectories. Using the Seoul and Busan Welfare Condition Surveys, unconditional quantile regressions examine employment-related and sub-regional income differences in 2018 and 2022. Bootstrap-based coefficient-difference tests assess changes between the two survey years. The results reveal distinct distributional patterns. In Seoul, significant changes were observed in several sub-regional income differences relative to the Central area, whereas in Busan, significant changes were concentrated in employment-related income differences, particularly among temporary employees in sales and service occupations. Income measures including and excluding public transfers yield broadly similar patterns. In both cities, income increased significantly at the 75th percentile but not at the 25th percentile. Overall, the findings demonstrate substantial employment-related, spatial and distributional heterogeneity and highlight the value of examining within-city and distributional variation beyond metropolitan averages. © 2026 Akademikerförbundet SSR (ASSR) and John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Author full names: Stewart, Eric (59565689300); Gallegos, Erika E. (58662448400); Conrad, Steven A. (36801865200)
Title: Paying for autonomous vehicle instructure and effective oversight: Preferences for funding methods
Abstract: The emergence of self-driving vehicles (SDVs) introduces not only technological and regulatory challenges, but also fiscal ones. Ensuring the safe and effective integration of SDVs into existing transportation systems will require new infrastructure investments and oversight mechanisms, prompting governments to seek sustainable and publicly acceptable funding strategies to cover these additional costs. These revenue streams, likely coming from taxes or fees, must not only offset costs, but also represent methods that face minimal public resistance. To identify which funding approaches are least opposed by the public, an anonymous online survey was conducted in the United States using a sample that roughly matched the demographic characteristics of the general population. Respondents completed a discrete choice experiment featuring 62 unique funding profiles that combined different forms of taxes (fuel, mileage, and vehicle) and fees (subscription service and increased vehicle price) as revenue sources. In addition to completing the choice experiment, respondents also provided information on vehicle ownership and demographics, and completed assessments measuring their risk tolerance, familiarity with self-driving vehicles, and trust in SDVs. Analysis of the survey results revealed a strong preference for funding SDV related costs through fees specifically applied to autonomous vehicles, alongside general opposition to increased fuel or mileage taxes. Significant predictors of funding preferences included the type of vehicle currently owned, education level, average number of miles driven annually, and level of trust in SDVs. These findings provide insight into the public's willingness to support different funding mechanisms as SDV adoption expands. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Quantifying internal and external heterogeneous effects of bus drivers’ personality traits and driving behavior on bus crashes: Insights from questionnaires and NDS data
Abstract: Existing studies about bus accident analysis have examined the impacts of internal or external heterogeneity from multiple perspectives, highlighting the multifaceted nature of accident risk factors. However, there are core limitations still to be addressed: reliance on single-type physiological, psychological or driving behavior data, neglecting group classification stability in accident heterogeneity analysis, and insufficient guidance for bus on-board Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) and Driver State Monitoring System (DSM) applications, resulting in incomplete crash mechanism interpretation, reduced intervention specificity, and inadequate tailored monitoring system adaptability. To address these gaps, a hybrid analytical framework (K-means-RPBLM) based on multi-source operational data and driver data was proposed in this study to quantify the internal and external heterogeneous impacts of personality traits and driving behavior on bus crashes. First, bus drivers were categorized into Robust, Ordinary, and Anxious personality trait groups through the K-means clustering algorithm. Subsequently, random parameter binary logit models (RPBLM) were estimated for the overall bus driver sample and each personality subgroup, and pairwise Wald tests were conducted for selected cross-group coefficient comparisons. The results revealed distinct subgroup-specific association and random-parameter patterns. Pairwise Wald tests showed significant cross-group coefficient differences for 20-30 years of driving experience across all three pairwise comparisons and for speeding-warning frequency between the Robust group and the other two groups, whereas no significant cross-group difference was detected for distracted-driving warnings. These findings provide partial, factor-specific evidence of personality-related heterogeneity in crash-risk mechanisms and support differentiated safety management for bus drivers. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: An Integrated Community-Based Model for Chronic Disease Care in a Community in the Lower Southern Peninsular Thailand
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: Effective chronic disease management requires community-based approaches tailored to local contexts. This study sought to develop an integrated community-based model for chronic disease care in a community in the lower southern peninsular Thailand. It was a research and development (R&D) study consisting of three phases: Phase 1 identified situational factors through focus group discussions; Phase 2 produced a model validated by three experts using the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation II (AGREE II) instrument; and Phase 3 employed a one-group pretest-posttest design to implement the model and evaluate outcomes over three months. Key informants included 30 patients with non-communicable chronic diseases and 15 healthcare professionals. Data analysis used descriptive and inferential statistics, paired-samples t-test, and content analysis. The study found that the integrated community-based model for chronic disease management consisted of three main components. First, individual participation (focusing on shared goal setting and risk awareness); Second, interpersonal participation (involving peer support and structured information/feedback exchange); and finally, community participation (including positive motivation, community-based healthcare activities, and surveillance). The results show that after the patients were taken care of with the integrated community-based model for three months, the average HbA1C (glycated hemoglobin) levels among chronic disease patients had significantly decreased by 0.10 (95% CI [0.04–0.16]), and the average systolic blood pressure had significantly decreased by 4.70 mmHg (95% CI [2.32–7.07]). Chronic disease clinics in comparable rural settings can adopt this three-tiered participation structure within existing services, with village health volunteers and community groups recognized as partners in care. © 2027 Mahidol University, Institute for Population and Social Research.
