Title: What you foresee isn't what you forget: No evidence for the influence of epistemic states on causal judgments for abnormal negligent behavior
Abstract: Why are agents who act abnormally considered more causal than agents who act normally? Kirfel and Lagnado (2021) claim that agents who act abnormally are better able to foresee the outcomes of their abnormal behavior, giving them an epistemic advantage over agents who act normally. On their view, this advantage explains why people attribute more causality to agents who act abnormally. We tested an extension of this view to cases of negligence. Across three experiments (N = 1713), we found that epistemic advantages are not necessary for inflated attributions of causality to abnormally acting agents. In Experiment 1, participants attributed more causality to an agent who is abnormally negligent relative to an agent who normally does not act, even though they attributed equal degrees of foresight to both agents. In Experiment 2, participants attributed more causality to statistically abnormal negligence relative to statistically normal inaction without any corresponding difference in attributed foresight to either agent. In Experiment 3, we replicated the pattern of results from Experiment 2 and found that people attribute equal degrees of desire and intentionally to normal and abnormal omitters. We argue that Kirfel and Lagnado's epistemic explanation of the abnormal inflation effect in causal judgment does not extend to abnormal negligence precisely because people attribute causality to outcomes that an agent neither foresees nor expects. © 2026

Title: Challenges in exfiltration, evasion, and behavioral sequences in malicious insider threat: Evidence from a live behavioral experiment
Abstract: Insider risk and threat detection have several well-meaning assumptions that are difficult and rarely tested using scientific methods. For example, exfiltration is often seen as a “smoking gun” of malicious insider activity. This study drew on data from a live behavioral experiment in which 154 employees searched for, collected, and exfiltrated sensitive information from a real corporate network under benign, malicious, and super malicious task conditions. Endpoint- and network-based cyber sensors collected over 7000 separate types of user activity resulting in over 10 terabytes of logs before, during, and after the task, and employee participants completed interviews and questionnaires describing their actions and reasoning. Two analyses identified valuable indicators and/or detectors for insider threat or risk programs. First, qualitative content analysis identified 13 exfiltration techniques with 11 sub-techniques, and 76 evasion techniques categorized in 14 types. Malicious and super malicious intent participants used a broad range of exfiltration and evasion techniques, many relying on ordinary workplace tools and workflows rather than advanced tradecraft. Most techniques were observable in cyber logs in some form, but were difficult to distinguish from benign intent employee activity. Second, sequential analysis of cyber logs produced 5957,005 permutations of malicious cyber activity yet all but 13 had limited practical value. The study's findings indicate that insider risk detection should focus less on employee exfiltration and more on earlier patterns of search and collection behavior, and that sequence-based analytics should not be a core feature required for insider threat detection. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Post-pandemic changes in nursing careers choice: An exploratory qualitative study
Abstract: Background: Understanding the factors influencing individuals' choices to pursue a nursing career is essential for creating effective recruitment and retention strategies, particularly in the aftermath of pandemics. Title: Reducing sectarian prejudice through virtual reality in the post-conflict context of Northern Ireland
Abstract: Virtual reality (VR) offers a promising platform for intergroup contact, yet the conditions under which it effectively shapes attitudes remain poorly understood, particularly in post-conflict contexts. This study examined human-steered avatar contact among Catholic and Protestant participants in Northern Ireland (N = 72), testing three contact models that varied the salience of group identity — common ingroup, intergroup differentiation, and decategorized — alongside manipulations of outgroup helping behavior and the Proteus effect as a theorized moderator. Title: The state-led reproductive boundary: Divisions and income disparity in mainland China's paid care work
Abstract: This study examines how the state and the market shape income divisions among paid care workers in China's domestic service economy. We develop the concept of the state-led reproductive boundary to examine how state intervention, through certification, training, work arrangement, and long-term care insurance, redraws the lines along which reproductive labour is valued, financed, and protected. Drawing on a 2021 survey of 919 domestic workers in Shanghai, the first Chinese city to implement a municipality-wide long-term care insurance scheme, we distinguish maternity-infant care, eldercare, and non-nurturant work, and model both monthly and hourly income. We compare a purely cultural account of care valuation with one that incorporates the state. Cultural valuation alone cannot explain the wage divisions within paid care. The division between nurturant and non-nurturant work in China is organised less through race than through human capital, certification, and market recognition. Within nurturant work, the maternity-infant care advantage holds in monthly but not hourly terms, since live-in arrangements obscure the low hourly returns of feminised, time-intensive care. The culturally anticipated eldercare penalty does not materialise. Eldercare workers absorbed into the hourly-priced, state-financed insurance scheme are no longer disadvantaged relative to non-nurturant workers, showing that state intervention can partially insulate a culturally devalued form of care from market discounting. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Emotional and physical burdens of water poverty: evidence from the drinking water service ladder in Mozambique
Abstract: Access to safe and reliable drinking water remains uneven across sub-Saharan Africa, yet existing evidence largely focuses on health outcomes and binary measures of access, overlooking how different service levels affect everyday well-being. This study examines how the water service ladder shapes the emotional and physical burdens of water poverty and whether these effects differ by household head gender in Mozambique. Results show that limited services, i.e., improved sources located more than 30 min away, do not significantly reduce water-related distress relative to unimproved sources. In contrast, both basic and safely managed services substantially reduce emotional and physical burdens, with no additional gains from on-premises access beyond the 30-minute accessibility threshold. Female-headed households are more likely to access improved services, but the well-being benefits of improved water access do not differ by household head gender. These findings highlight the importance of service proximity rather than source type alone and suggest that progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 6 may be overstated when measured using binary indicators of improved access. Title: Occupational Mismatch and Income Effects in Indonesia’s Gig Economy: A Gender Perspective

Abstract: This study examines the relationship between occupational mismatch and income in Indonesia’s gig economy, with particular attention to gender differences. Using nationally representative data from the 2020 Indonesian National Labor Force Survey, gig workers are identified based on self-employment status and digital engagement in work activities. To address potential endogeneity, this study employs a treatment-effects model using district-level mismatch rates as an instrumental variable. The results show a negative association between occupational mismatch and income, indicating that mismatched workers have lower income than their well-matched counterparts after accounting for selection bias. This finding is consistent across ordinary least squares (OLS), propensity score matching (PSM), and treatment-effects models, supporting the robustness of the results. Gender-disaggregated analysis further shows that the negative effect is statistically significant for male workers but not for female workers, indicating important gender heterogeneity. Quantile regression results show that income penalties are present across the income distribution for male workers and become more pronounced at higher income levels. In contrast, the estimated effects for female workers remain statistically insignificant across quantiles. These findings suggest that occupational mismatch in digitally mediated labor markets reflects structural constraints rather than efficient skill allocation. This study contributes to the literature by providing evidence on the distributional and gender-specific effects of occupational mismatch. Title: Fisher-led ecological monitoring for adaptive FRA design and OECM-relevant governance: The AMORGORAMA case in the Aegean Sea
Abstract: Fisher-led area-based fisheries measures require ecological and socio-economic evidence that is scientifically robust, locally legitimate and usable for policy design. The AMORGORAMA initiative on Amorgos Island, central Aegean Sea, addressed this through a fisher-led quadruple-helix partnership among fishers, scientists, NGOs and public authorities, formalized in a 2021 Memorandum of Understanding. This study combined year-round ecological monitoring of small-scale fisheries with a parallel full-census socio-economic survey of the island's 21 active vessels to inform fisher-proposed areas later established as Fisheries Restricted Areas through Presidential Decree P.D. 73/2025. Standardized fishing with gillnets, trammel nets and longlines recorded 3181 individuals from 123 species. Biodiversity peaked in spring, while density was highest in summer, reflecting reproduction and recruitment dynamics. Title: Time perspective and gambling behavior: A systematic review of temporal influences on risk, cognition, and decision-making
Abstract: Background Time Perspective (TP) has emerged as a relevant construct for understanding decision-making processes underlying gambling behavior. Objective This systematic review synthesized empirical evidence examining associations between TP and gambling-related outcomes. Data sources Searches were conducted across six databases (e.g., PsycINFO, MEDLINE) and supplemented with Google Scholar. Eligibility criteria Quantitative and mixed-method studies published post-1994 assessing TP and gambling in adolescent or adult populations were included. Study selection 49 studies were identified across all databases, which were then screened. After removing two duplicate studies, 18 additional studies were excluded. Participants/design 29 observational and experimental studies involving community, student, and clinical samples were reviewed. Appraisal/synthesis Study quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool; narrative synthesis was conducted. Results Past Negative, Present Hedonistic, and Present Fatalistic TPs were consistently associated with greater gambling frequency, severity, and risk-taking, whereas Future TP was generally protective. Limitations Evidence was predominantly cross-sectional and relied on convenience samples, limiting causal inference and generalizability. Conclusions TP provides a distinct framework for understanding gambling vulnerability through temporal organization of cognition and preference for immediate rewards. Authors: Jonason P.K.; Gruda D.
Title: Sex, love, and work: What you do is not whom you want
Abstract: Interest theory treats vocational interests as broad dispositions that shape behavior beyond the workplace, and the people–things dimension is among the more stable and sex-differentiated of them. We tested that generalization claim in the most demanding domain available. In seven countries, 1974 adults (968 men, 982 women) completed a forced-choice task indexing revealed preferences for five partner traits (i.e., physicality, compassion, competence, compatibility, and character) across long-term and short-term relationship contexts, and were classified by current sector, a proxy for orientation, as people-oriented (n = 746), things-oriented (n = 289), or abstract-oriented (n = 710). Orientation, sex, and context were estimated in one model per trait. Occupational orientation had almost no bearing on partner choice. Choices for competence and compatibility were statistically equivalent between the people and things poles in both contexts, as were character choices in the long-term context, against a smallest effect size of interest of d = 0.20. The one association to emerge, more frequent compassion choices among people-oriented workers, was small, confined to men, and absent among women. Participants' sex and relationship context reorganized the same choices far more powerfully than orientation did. Vocational interests appear to organize what people do, not whom they want. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: De la Fuente Stevens D.
Title: Compulsory education, life trajectories, and intergenerational mobility: evidence from Mexico's 1993 schooling reform
Abstract: Mexico's 1993 reform extended compulsory schooling from six to nine years, creating a birth-cohort discontinuity in educational exposure. This paper exploits that discontinuity to identify the causal effects of schooling expansion across the life course. Using a regression discontinuity and instrumental variable strategy applied to the 2020 Mexican Census, it traces the reform's consequences from educational attainment through fertility, child mortality, labour market participation, and geographic mobility, and into the schooling outcomes of the next generation. The reform raised educational attainment across all groups, but its effects were concentrated among Indigenous communities and rural populations, where baseline attainment was lowest and barriers to secondary schooling were greatest. For Indigenous individuals, literacy rates increased by 4.5 percentage points and lower-secondary completion by 3.8 percentage points, from baselines of 78 and 29 per cent respectively. These gains translated into lower fertility, reduced child mortality, higher employment, and a reallocation of workers out of low-productivity agriculture into higher-productivity sectors. Using census household identifiers to link parents to children, the analysis further finds that an additional year of parental schooling raised the probability of children's secondary school enrolment by 3 to 4 percentage points and upper-secondary enrolment by 5 to 8 percentage points. Together, the results show that a single compulsory schooling reform generated a sustained, multi-domain shift in life trajectories that extended across generations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Do coupled population, economic, and land use dynamics explain household energy transitions in Malawi?
Abstract: In sub-Saharan Africa, population growth coupled with weak or missing markets for clean energy means that the absolute number of people relying on woodfuels for cooking is growing. Charcoal, which has distinctly different environmental and economic implications from firewood, has become one of the most consumed fuels in the region. However, among rural populations, the drivers and consequences of charcoal use remain under-studied. We examine rural woodfuel dynamics in Malawi, a majority rural country with high poverty, rapid population growth, lagging economic development, and abundant but rapidly declining forest resources. We examine how household energy transitions are influenced by concurrent demographic, economic, and land use changes. Using four waves of national household surveys and satellite-derived forest cover datasets, we investigate trends in household energy consumption, identify factors driving rural household fuel choices, and characterize geographic patterns of forest cover loss during 2004–2020. During this time, the share of rural households using charcoal grew from 3.9% to 13.4%. Rural households that are smaller, headed by younger individuals, and are asset-rich but land-poor had greater odds of using charcoal compared to firewood, indicating that rural livelihood dynamics have important consequences for household energy transitions. Several protected areas have experienced > 20% forest cover loss since 2001, characterized by geographic patterns consistent with unsanctioned woodfuel extraction. These findings emphasize a renewed need for integrated natural resources, energy, and livelihoods management strategies. Our insights provide information for policy makers to better predict and understand the continued growth of charcoal's popularity in Malawi and similar contexts. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Emotion regulation strategies as mediators in the relation between Big Five personality traits and achievement emotions: Cross-cultural evidence from university students
Abstract: Personality traits and emotion regulation (ER) are key antecedents of emotions in learning contexts. Nevertheless, little is known about the possible mediating role of ER in the relation between the Big Five (BF) traits and achievement emotions (AEs). Considering the Control-Value Theory as the main framework, we examined the mediation of behavioral (Actively Approaching, Withdrawal) and cognitive (Refocus on Planning, Catastrophizing) ER strategies in the relation between the BF traits and 10 study-related AEs. We recruited 754 university students from Italy and the United Kingdom. Using path analyses (PAs), we found that Actively Approaching mediated the relation of Extraversion, Agreeableness, Negative Emotionality, and Open-Mindedness with pride and relaxation. Withdrawal mediated the relation of Extraversion and Negative Emotionality with boredom. Catastrophizing mediated the relation between Negative Emotionality and hope, anxiety, anger, and hopelessness. Through multi-group PAs, we observed some country differences in the relation of the BF traits with, respectively, Actively Approaching and Catastrophizing, and three negative emotions. These findings can serve as the basis for developing evidence-based interventions that take into account personality differences and/or influence ER strategies to improve students' AEs. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Uyan M.
Title: Spatial structure of land value potential after land consolidation using spatial econometric modelling
Abstract: Land consolidation (LC) is a widely adopted land management instrument for improving agricultural efficiency through parcel restructuring and reducing land fragmentation. However, how LC reshapes the spatial distribution of land value remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the spatial determinants of post-consolidation land value potential (LVP) using parcel-level data from an agricultural LC project in Türkiye. The analysis examines the effects of changes in parcel compactness (ΔCI), fragmentation, and pre-consolidation LVP within a spatial econometric framework. The average LVP increased from 0.491 before LC to 0.737 after LC, representing an improvement of approximately 50%. OLS residuals exhibited significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = 0.198, p < 0.001), confirming that conventional regression was inadequate. Model comparison identified the Spatial Error Model (SEM) as the most appropriate specification (AIC=-510.51), indicating that post-consolidation LVP is primarily influenced by spatially structured contextual factors rather than direct parcel-to-parcel interactions. The findings demonstrate that LC reshapes rather than eliminates inherited spatial value structures and highlight the importance of accounting for spatial dependence when evaluating rural land management interventions. Methodologically, the study provides a reproducible spatial econometric framework that can support more robust and equitable evaluations of LC programmes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: More vs. less cognitive offloading from ai assistants: impacts on novices’ collaborative performance and skill development
Abstract: Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly deployed as professional teammates. However, it remains unclear how they can enhance collaborative performance without hindering human skill development, particularly for novices in high-stakes domains. Cognitive offloading, using external resources (in this case, AI assistants) to reduce one’s own cognitive effort, is central to this tension.We conducted a controlled experiment using a custom platform and the CAIL 2018 dataset. 130 participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: a no-AI control, high-offloading AI (which provided direct recommendation), moderate-offloading AI (which provided analytical support), or low-offloading AI (which provided evaluative feedback). The results reveal a fundamental trade-off. The high-offloading condition achieved the highest decision accuracy at 68.8% and the shortest decision time (37.55s). However, it diminished skill development, showing a 7.1% lower accuracy improvement than the control. In contrast, moderate- and low-offloading conditions fostered skill gains of approximately 5.5%. Mediation analysis indicated that this impeded skill development was associated with metacognitive miscalibration (a gap between perceived and actual ability) rather than merely reduced behavioral engagement. These findings extend the “AI Competency Paradox” by revealing a critical offloading threshold below which AI can enhance collaborative performance while supporting skill development, and by identifying metacognitive miscalibration (not reduced effort) as a mechanism underlying skill impairment, suggesting that AI assistants for novices should prioritize adaptive cognitive friction and real-time competence calibration over full automation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Little time travelers: Future thinking and temporal language in the second year of life
Abstract: Episodic future thinking—the ability to anticipate and prepare for future events—is a central component of mental time travel. Although most research on episodic future thinking has focused on preschool-aged children, much less is known about its earliest emergence in toddlerhood. The present study investigated whether precursors of episodic future thinking, such as future-oriented object selection, can be observed in the second year of life and whether this ability is associated with temporal language use beyond general vocabulary. Eighty-one typically developing Polish toddlers ( M = 22.04 months, SD = 2.24; range = 17–26 months) participated in an adapted Rooms Test. The task required children to select an object needed to solve a previously encountered problem after a 3-minute delay and a change of context. Parent-report measures assessed children’s temporal term use and general vocabulary. Among children included in the main analyses ( N = 74), 55% selected the target object without prompting, significantly exceeding chance performance (33%). Children who passed the task used more temporal terms and had larger general vocabularies than children who failed. Temporal term use was strongly correlated with general vocabulary and did not explain additional variance beyond age and general vocabulary. These findings indicate that precursors of episodic future thinking may already be observable during the second year of life when experimental paradigms are developmentally appropriate and employ salient, motivating task structures. They also link future-oriented task performance to emerging language abilities, while leaving the specific association between temporal language and early future-oriented behavior open for future research. Title: No glue, no scissors: Bridging parental mental health, parenting activities, and the early home learning environment
Abstract: Research has linked poor parental mental health to lower engagement in parent–child activities within the home learning environment (HLE). Drawing on parenting, family stress, and depression research, impaired mental health may disrupt cognitive and affective regulation processes important for parenting, including engagement in educational and leisure activities. However, prior research has largely focused on single activity domains and data from only one parent. Addressing these limitations, the present study compares mothers’ and fathers’ engagement across global and domain-specific activities within a unified framework. Multilevel regression analyses based on cross-sectional data from 1,582 children showed that poorer maternal and paternal mental health was associated with less frequent engagement in developmentally beneficial activities, such as outdoor walks and sports. Poorer maternal mental health was additionally linked to less shared reading. Although causal conclusions cannot be drawn, the findings suggest that maternal and paternal mental health are associated, partly differently, with the frequency of everyday learning-related activities. Reduced engagement in these activities may weaken children’s early home learning environment. Overall, the study extends previous research by jointly examining maternal and paternal reports across multiple activity domains and highlights the importance of supporting both parents’ mental health to sustain early home learning environments. Title: An Analysis of Mobility Styles and Carsharing Adoption Intentions in Major Urban Areas of Japan: Evidence from Tokyo, Osaka, and Kanagawa
Abstract: This study links mobility styles with carsharing intentions and next-generation vehicle preferences in urban Japan. An online survey of licensed drivers in Tokyo Metropolis, Kanagawa Prefecture, and Osaka Prefecture captured mode use frequencies and stated preferences by travel purpose. Cluster analysis identified three mobility styles: private-car users, public-transport users, and a diversified, high-carsharing group. For daily and business trips, most respondents prefer carsharing stations within 400 m and short distances; for tourism and hometown visiting, they accept longer access to carsharing stations and longer trips. Compact and Kei cars (Japanese light vehicles) in Japan dominate daily use, while minivans and SUVs gain importance for leisure. Title: Exploring adverse childhood experiences among students of tertiary care hospital of India: prevalence, impact on mental health, coping strategies and resilience

Title: Self-assessment bias and airline Pilots’ safe operational behavior: the roles of risk perception and crew climate
Abstract: Accurate self-appraisal may be as important as technical competence for aviation safety. Title: Emotionally vulnerable subtype of internet gaming disorder: Measuring and exploring the pathology of problematic generative AI use
Abstract: Concerns over the potential over-pathologization of generative AI (GenAI) use and the lack of conceptual clarity surrounding GenAI addiction call for empirical tools and theoretical refinement. Title: The impact of industrial land use policy on urban innovation: Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment in China
Abstract: Promoting innovation through land-use governance has become increasingly important for urban development, yet the role of industrial land use policy in shaping urban innovation remains relatively underexplored. In China, the New Industrial Land Use Policy (NILUP) has emerged as a key local policy instrument for optimizing land use and fostering industrial innovation. Employing a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) model and an instrumental variable (IV) approach, we analyze data from 281 cities over the period 2008–2022. Title: From “Aha!” to “Haha!”: Humour processing and insight problem-solving in autism

Title: Towards understanding the benefits of shellfish aquaculture for U.S. coastal communities: Demographics, spatial concentration, and localness of leaseholders

Title: A structuration approach to theorizing cybersecurity practice: The STARC model

Title: Refugee immigration and natives’ fertility

Authors: Liu K.; Wang E.; Xu Y.
Title: Enhancing older adults’ healthcare accessibility and equity in the 15-minute city: An O2O model to overcome spatial mismatch
Abstract: Introduction Building on an assessment of the evolution in spatial accessibility to community hospitals for older adults (2012–2024) within the 15-min city framework, this study proposes and evaluates an integrated online-to-offline (O2O) model to enhance healthcare accessibility and equity. Methods Using Nanjing, China, as a case study, an Enhanced Two-Step Floating Catchment Area (E2SFCA) method was applied to assess the spatial accessibility of community hospitals for older adults (stratified into age groups of 60–69, 70–79, and ≥80) from 2012 to 2024. A counterfactual analysis decomposed the effects of infrastructure expansion and demographic change. Furthermore, an “online diagnosis + 15-min medication delivery” service was integrated into the model to evaluate the proposed integrated O2O approach, with a sensitivity analysis conducted on the online service allocation parameter (θ). Results Despite a 24% net increase in community hospitals between 2012 and 2024, spatial accessibility for older adults declined, a trend disproportionately affecting the oldest-old (aged ≥80). Counterfactual analysis attributed this paradox to a significant spatial mismatch between infrastructure development and demographic shifts. The proposed integrated O2O model substantially improved both accessibility and equity. Sensitivity analysis identified an optimal online service allocation (θ = 0.1), which more than doubled accessibility for the most vulnerable group (≥80) and reduced the Gini coefficient by up to 25.8%. Conclusions The findings demonstrate that equitable and resilient urban health systems for aging populations require not only physical infrastructure expansion but also strategic digital integration, reframing the 15-min city as a conditional benchmark that demands age-sensitive calibration rather than a uniform spatial standard. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Berdida D.J.E.
Title: The commodification of nursing education: A discursive paper on academic identity, faculty work, and the future of nursing knowledge
Abstract: Background: The nursing and midwifery educator workforce is increasingly seen as key to sustaining healthcare, driving professional education, and shaping nursing knowledge. However, debates often focus mainly on numbers, such as shortages, recruitment, and expanding capacity. Less attention is given to the institutional and epistemic factors impacting academic nursing work. Aims: To critically examine how commodifying nursing education affects academic identity, faculty work, educator sustainability, professional formation, and the future of nursing knowledge. Design: Discursive paper. Methods: This discursive paper draws on literature about neoliberal higher education, commodification, academic identity, student consumerism, faculty workload, nurse educator sustainability, and nursing knowledge. Through critical synthesis, it examines how market reforms, performance metrics, managerial control, teaching-heavy contracts, and student-consumer expectations reshape nursing education. Results: The discursive analysis shows that commodification recasts students as consumers, curricula as products, faculty as service providers, and nursing knowledge as measurable outputs. These shifts narrow nurse educator identity and increase both visible and invisible labour. They also weaken scholarly capacity and reduce professional formation to technical skills, satisfaction metrics, and workforce output. The paper contends that the educator workforce crisis is more than a shortage; it is also an ideological, institutional, and epistemic crisis. Conclusion: Nursing education should be reclaimed as a public, professional, and epistemic good. Protecting its future requires more than hiring educators; it demands transforming academic environments so nurse educators can fully teach, mentor, research, lead, critique, and sustain the profession's knowledge and traditions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Estimating visible deprivation through the analysis of street view image embeddings
Abstract: Material deprivation is often visible in the physical fabric of neighbourhoods in the form of litter, graffiti, abandoned buildings, etc. Recent advances in vision transformers and the widespread availability of street-level imagery make it possible to analyse these features systematically at scale. This paper assesses the extent to which area-level material deprivation, measured using the 2025 English Indices of Multiple Deprivation (IMD), can be estimated from visual imagery alone. Using Greater Manchester, UK, as a case study, CLIP embeddings are computed for approximately 75,000 Street View images and AlphaEarth embeddings are obtained for the corresponding satellite imagery. XGBoost models are trained on each source to predict LSOA-level IMD rank, and the street-level embeddings are further partitioned by k-means clustering to examine whether particular kinds of scenes carry stronger predictive signal. The street-level model explains approximately 68% of the variation in IMD rank, substantially outperforming the satellite model (33%). Importantly, the predictive signal is highly uneven across image types: residential scenes are considerably more informative than images of roads, greenery, or commercial and industrial areas. With the exception of the Barriers to Housing and Services domain, the signal is broadly similar across individual IMD domains, consistent with deprivation being spatially concentrated and the visual character of a neighbourhood appearing to act as a proxy for multiple dimensions of disadvantage simultaneously. Together, these results provide a quantitative measure of how much of an administrative, multi-domain deprivation index is recoverable from imagery alone, and identify the kinds of scenes – and the dimensions of deprivation – for which this visual signal is strongest. © 2026

Title: Anticipating the movement of football (soccer) goalkeepers
Abstract: The outcome of a penalty kick can pivot the fate of a football match. While previous research has mainly examined how goalkeepers anticipate shot direction, little is known about how penalty takers anticipate goalkeeper movements when using a keeper-dependent strategy. The current study examined how temporal constraints shape the penalty takers' ability to anticipate the movement direction of the keeper, and whether expertise plays a role in such anticipation. Participants (N = 253; 130 experts; 123 novices) completed a temporal occlusion task in which they viewed 64 penalty kicks filmed from the taker's perspective. On each trial, participants indicated whether the goalkeeper would dive left or right. Videos began 4 s before simulated foot-ball contact and were occluded at four time points (0, 200, 400, 600 ms before contact). Overall accuracy decreased as occlusion occurred earlier, from 95% at 0 ms to 51.9% at 600 ms. Performance was reliably above chance at 0 ms, 200 ms, and 400 ms, but not at 600 ms, indicating that penalty takers could anticipate goalkeeper movement direction before foot-ball contact, but not at the earliest occlusion time. Furthermore, experts outperformed novices across occlusion times. Additional analyses showed that this effect was more closely related to years of football experience than to frequency of football watching. Together, these findings quantify perceptual constraints on anticipating goalkeeper movements and suggest that passive and active forms of experience contribute differently to anticipatory performance. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Akanji A.A.; Hudson P.
Title: Housing Cooperative: A Force to Be Harnessed for Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation
Abstract: Housing cooperatives offer a community-driven approach to addressing the twin challenges of climate change mitigation and adaptation, particularly in rapidly urbanising regions like Nigeria. As urban populations grow and housing demand increases, conventional housing models often contribute to rising greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, environmental degradation and heightened climate vulnerabilities. This chapter explores how housing cooperatives can serve as a potential solution by fostering sustainable building practices, energy efficiency and collective climate resilience. We examine the role of cooperatives in promoting low-carbon housing, enhancing adaptive capacity and integrating novel financial and governance mechanisms to support climate action. However, the expansion of housing cooperatives in Nigeria faces significant challenges, including financial constraints, unclear legal frameworks and governance complexities. To maximise their potential, targeted policy support, access to green finance and the integration of digital innovations such as blockchain for property rights and smart housing technologies are crucial. By embedding sustainability within cooperative housing models, Nigeria can leverage these structures to create more climate-resilient, socially inclusive and environmentally sustainable urban futures. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Night-time demand-responsive transport in seasonal tourism contexts: Evidence from Hakuba, Japan
Abstract: This study investigates the behavioural and operational dynamics of a night-time demand-responsive transport (DRT) system in the alpine resort of Hakuba, Japan, within a digitally mediated service environment, with particular attention to the temporal and spatial patterns of seasonal tourism. Using a dataset of 5,232 completed trips, the analysis identifies the key drivers of demand intensity in a low-density mountainous context. The findings reveal a dispersed hub configuration, defined here as notable demand concentration at a limited number of functional stops combined with low geographic clustering and scattered local hotspots. This pattern reflects the role of DRT in connecting physically fragmented activity nodes. Moreover, the results highlight a distinct seasonal tourism rhythm: demand is shaped by month-to-month variation within the winter season and short-term temporal persistence, rather than conventional weekday–weekend cycles. The scale of passenger-carrying service delivery provides a baseline for understanding the operational demands of night-time DRT in rural, seasonally intensive tourism settings. The findings from the study suggest that DRT planning in such contexts should move beyond rigid, calendar-based approaches towards seasonally adaptive strategies that account for temporal persistence and spatial fragmentation in tourism-driven mobility systems. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Title: Reducing antibiotics? experimental evidence from poultry farmers in China
Abstract: Antibiotic overuse in the livestock sector has negative environmental implications and leads to bacterial resistance. We set up a randomized controlled trial in two locations in China among poultry farmers to evaluate the effects of a two-pronged approach: Providing micro- subsidies for alternative production methods and exposing farmers to differential norms through role models. These interventions, alone or combined, resulted in no detectable effects on antibiotic use and profits. However, in the wealthier location, the combination of the two interventions prompted the use of alternative technologies. However, the degree of take-up was limited, and the recommended accompanying changes in sanitation measures were not fully implemented (although sanitation measures improved, possibly due to the information campaign, which was delivered to all farmers at the start of the study). No such behavioural changes were observed in the poorer location (although this lack of effects might also be partially due to supply constraints in the poorer location). © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Understanding driver responses to automated traffic enforcement systems: a qualitative analysis of behavioral adaptation and traffic safety perceptions
Abstract: Driver perceptions of automated traffic enforcement systems and intelligent transportation technologies are of critical importance for achieving sustainable improvements in traffic safety. This study examines the psychological and behavioral effects of Automated Traffic Enforcement Systems (ATES) and Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) on driver behavior within an interpretivist paradigm using a qualitative approach. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 37 drivers and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings show that drivers interpret traffic safety through three main motivational structures: internalized safety awareness, enforcement-based compliance, and ethical responsibility. It was also determined that traffic violations are shaped by multidimensional factors such as time pressure, perceived legitimacy of traffic rules, and the normalization of risk through habit. The presence of ATES leads to significant improvements in behaviors such as speed control and self-regulation; however, this effect largely depends on external motivations—particularly the expectation of punishment—and has limited capacity to produce long-term behavioral change. The increase in violation tendency when enforcement is absent reveals the fragile nature of deterrence-based compliance. In contrast, ITS technologies provide a more proactive contribution by increasing driver awareness, regulating traffic flow, and offering real-time information. The integration of ATES and ITS presents a holistic framework that combines deterrence with behavioral guidance, enabling not only the reduction of violations but also the development of more sustainable behavioral compliance. This study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that the effectiveness of automated traffic enforcement systems depends not only on technological capabilities but also on drivers’ motivational structures and perceived legitimacy levels. From a policy perspective, the findings indicate that sustainable improvements in traffic safety require enforcement mechanisms to be supported by real-time feedback systems, driver education, and interventions aimed at the internalization of traffic norms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Exercise to enhance antipsychotic effectiveness and mitigate metabolic harm: systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: Objective Antipsychotics are first-line treatments for schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders but are frequently accompanied by cardiometabolic adverse effects (weight gain, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, hyperglycaemia). We assessed whether supervised exercise interventions enhance psychopathology outcomes and reduce antipsychotic-related metabolic harm in adults receiving antipsychotic treatment medication. Design Systematic review and meta-analysis. Data sources We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420251139904). Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) published since 2000 that tested supervised exercise in people receiving antipsychotics were eligible. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies Two reviewers selected studies using PICOS criteria, assessed methodological quality with the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomised trials (RoB 2), and pooled effects with random-effects models, expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE. Results Twenty-eight studies (n = 1119) and four additional analyses met inclusion criteria. Exercise significantly improved negative symptoms (MD −3·078, 95% CI −4·457 to −1·699; p < 0·001), general psychopathology (−2·178, −4·140 to −0·216, p = 0·034), and PANSS total score (−7·069, −13·290 to −0·849; p = 0·030). Effects on positive symptoms were not significant (−1·220, −2·462 to 0·022; p = 0·053). Exercise reduced body weight (−1·620, −3·080 to −0·159; p = 0.034), body fat percentage (−1·250, −2·174 to −0·327; p = 0·020), and waist circumference (−1·420, −2·646 to −0·195; p = 0·032), with no material change in BMI. No significant effects were observed for systolic, diastolic blood pressure or fasting glucose. Lipid outcomes were largely null, with limited and inconsistent evidence, including a small increase in total cholesterol. Based on GRADE assessment, the certainty of evidence was moderate for negative symptoms, general psychopathology, body weight, body fat percentage, and waist circumference, with low to very low for the remaining outcomes. Conclusion Supervised exercise may be a beneficial adjunct to antipsychotic treatment, improving core psychopathology, particularly negative symptoms, and favourably shifting body composition by reducing adiposity and central fat, although the magnitude of change did not reach clinically meaningful thresholds. High-quality, adequately powered RCTs using multicomponent exercise and comprehensive metabolic endpoints are needed to determine effects on blood pressure, lipid profile, and glucose regulation. Authors: Yang Q.; Tan C.K.K.
Title: The post-feminist healthism of female fitness enthusiasts in Kunming, China
Abstract: Recently, China witnessed a rapidly growing interest among urban women in bodybuilding and fitness. They made up nearly 62% of gym members nationwide by 2022 (Santi Yundong Shuju Zhongxin, 2023), and more than 13,000 women had competed in professional bodybuilding contests by 2023. With slightly plump slenderness being a traditional marker of feminine health and beauty (Jung, 2018), what motivates women to take up strength-training? What bodies do they consider “beautiful”? Using the concept of post-feminist healthism (Evans et al., 2018) to frame ethnographic fieldwork data gathered in Kunming, we maintain that socio-economic anxieties about the “disordered body” drive urban women to epitomize the bodies of Western-style fitness competitors as “healthy beauty.” Contrary to the individualistic neoliberalism embedded in post-feminist healthism, however, the Chinese iteration is also strongly shaped by the family, the nation-state, and pre-existing ideals of femininity and bodily restraint. As much as advertisements sell the hope of achieving the desired “healthy beautiful” body, most women cannot attain it unless they too restrict their diets and train like professional fitness athletes. Thus, our research highlights how post-feminist healthism needs further qualification in China. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Age 70 as a threshold for vulnerable road user case fatality: A population-based study of older drivers in Taiwan
Abstract: Age-based licensing renewal policies are implemented in aging societies to protect vulnerable road users (VRUs), yet the rationale for selecting age thresholds remains uncertain. This study examined whether age 70 represents a threshold for VRU case fatality among crash-involved older drivers and whether license status modifies this association. This population-based cross-sectional study analyzed Taiwanese police-reported crash data from 2011 to 2024 involving nonprofessional car drivers aged ≥ 50 years and VRUs. Driver age was modeled categorically and continuously using restricted cubic splines (RCSs). License status was examined as an exploratory effect modifier. A prespecified primary linear-spline analysis directly tested for a change in slope at age 70, while supporting RCS analyses evaluated overall nonlinearity. Multivariable logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors estimated adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 602,782 crash-involved VRUs, 2,789 sustained fatal injuries (0.46%). The prespecified analysis did not detect a change in slope at age 70 (change-in-slope AOR per year, 1.001; 95% CI, 0.977–1.025; P = 0.95), and the selected 3-knot RCS specification provided no evidence of overall nonlinearity (P = 0.24). Compared with drivers aged 50–64 years, odds of VRU case fatality were higher among drivers aged 65–69 years (AOR 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03–1.28) and ≥ 70 years (AOR 1.14; 95% CI, 1.01–1.29). However, among drivers aged 65–99 years, age ≥ 70 years was not independently associated with VRU case fatality (AOR 1.08; 95% CI, 0.93–1.25; P = 0.32). Unlicensed driving was associated with higher odds of VRU case fatality (AOR, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.62–2.28). Overall, the prespecified analysis did not detect a change in slope at age 70, while the association with unlicensed driving highlights a potentially important correlate of VRU case fatality among crash-involved older drivers. Title: Children’s thinking about asymptomatic carriers of disease
Abstract: Prior research has examined children’s understanding of disease transmission between people who demonstrate illness symptoms or are labeled as sick (Blacker & LoBue, 2016; DeJesus et al., 2021). The present studies examine North American children’s thinking about illness carriers with varying symptoms in terms of the likelihood and severity of disease transmission (Study 1) and moral judgments about disease transmission (Study 2). In Study 1, we tested 6- to 12-year-old children on Zoom (n = 108, 42 % female, 59 % White). Children were introduced to one character that was symptomatic, asymptomatic, or did not have a novel germ (“Germ X”) inside them (the carrier). After the carrier interacted with their friend (the recipient), participants were asked if the recipient caught Germ X and how they would feel later. Children rated the recipient as feeling worse if the carrier had Germ X and was symptomatic. In Study 2, we tested 5- to 10-year-olds at a children’s museum (n = 96, 53 % female, 54 % White). Here, the carrier was symptomatic or asymptomatic and shared an apple with the recipient, who later became symptomatic or asymptomatic. Children were asked before and after learning about the recipient’s symptoms if the interaction was okay. Children provided worse ratings if the carrier felt sick, and adjusted their ratings based on recipient status after the interaction. Across studies, we observed limited age effects. These findings suggest that children consider the severity of illness as part of its transmissibility and by age 5 negatively view interacting while sick. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Binge drinking inequities patterned by grade, race/ethnicity, sex, and sexual identity among U.S. high school students: An application of intersectional MAIHDA
Abstract: Introduction Binge drinking among U.S. adolescents varies by developmental stage, race/ethnicity, sex, and sexual identity. However, few studies have examined how these positions/identities intersect to shape drinking patterns. This study examined inequities in binge drinking among U.S. high school students using an intersectional multilevel analysis of individual heterogeneity and discriminatory accuracy. Methods We used data from 88,291 students who participated in the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System. Multilevel logistic regression models were fitted with students nested within 224 intersectional strata defined by grade, race/ethnicity, sex, and sexual identity. We calculated the variance partition coefficient (VPC), proportional change in variance, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Results Approximately 10.4% of students reported binge drinking. The null model VPC was 10.7%, with grade, race/ethnicity, sex/gender, and sexual identity explaining 79.6% of the between-stratum variance in binge drinking. Higher grades (12th: odds ratio [OR]: 3.18, 11th: OR: 2.20, and 10th: OR: 1.44 vs. 9th), girls (OR: 1.15 vs. boys), and gay/lesbian (OR: 1.77) and bisexual identities (OR: 1.34 vs. heterosexual/straight) were associated with greater odds of binge drinking. Asian (OR: 0.52) and Black (OR: 0.63) students had lower odds, whereas Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander students had higher odds (OR: 1.41) than white students. Predicted probabilities of binge drinking ranged from 1.96% to 30.49% across strata, with 12th-grade, white, heterosexual girls and boys exhibiting the highest positive departures from the predicted probabilities. Conclusion Binge drinking inequities were largely explained by grade, race/ethnicity, sex, and sexual identity, although intersectional interaction effects remained. Findings call for proportionate universal public health interventions with a focus on high-risk groups. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: How negative life events and emotion regulation difficulties are associated with non-suicidal self-injury in adolescents: A dimension-level network analysis and the role of physical activity
Abstract: Background and objective Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is prevalent during adolescence and is associated with an elevated risk of subsequent suicide. Guided by the integrated theoretical model of NSSI and the cross-stressor adaptation hypothesis, this study constructed a unified dimensional network incorporating negative life events (NLEs), emotion regulation difficulties (ERD), physical activity (PA), and NSSI. The study aimed to identify nodes with high overall and cross-community connectivity, dimensions exhibiting the strongest direct conditional associations with NSSI, and the connectivity patterns of PA. Additionally, network structures were compared across sex and age-defined adolescent groups. Methods A total of 4427 students aged 10–19 years were recruited. Data were collected using the Deliberate Self-Harm Inventory (DSHI), Adolescent Self-Rating Life Events Checklist (ASLEC), Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale–16 Item Version (DERS-16), and Physical Activity Rating Scale–3 (PARS-3). Gaussian graphical models were employed to estimate the network structure and evaluate network stability. Network comparison tests were conducted to examine differences in network structure and global strength across sex groups and age-defined adolescent groups, including early adolescence (10–12 years), middle adolescence (13–15 years), and late adolescence (16–19 years). Results The mean age of participants was 14.31 years (SD = 2.85). Overall, 28.87% of participants reported NSSI, with proportions of 28.17%, 30.09%, and 28.38% in early, middle, and late adolescence, respectively. Punishment-related stress, academic stress, and limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies exhibited the highest expected influence. Lack of emotional clarity, interpersonal stress, and academic stress demonstrated the highest bridge expected influence. NSSI showed the strongest direct conditional associations with punishment-related stress and limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies. Network structure and global strength did not differ significantly by sex or developmental stage. Conclusion These findings suggest that early identification and prevention of NSSI among adolescents should consider both external stressors, such as punishment-related stress, and internal regulatory vulnerabilities, particularly limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies. Physical activity, as a potentially modifiable health behavior resource, warrants further investigation through longitudinal and intervention studies. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: “Oops! That was my fault, I am so sorry for sudden braking”: using voice assistants to repair trust after automated driving failures
Abstract: Automated vehicle failures can undermine drivers’ trust and increase the risk of automation misuse or disuse. This study investigated the effects of vehicle voice assistant (VA) messages on trust repair following an automated-driving failure. Thirty-four drivers were categorized into two groups based on their initial Trust in Automated Driving (TiAD): Trustful (high TiAD) and Distrustful (low TiAD). After each automated-driving failure involving delayed pedestrian detection and abrupt emergency braking, participants received one of four repair strategies (apology, explanation, promise, or denial), delivered with or without interjections (e.g., wow, oops, hmm, oh), resulting in eight distinct VA messages (2 × 4). Trust ratings were collected across four driving scenarios, and participants also reported their preferences for the VA messages. Results showed that explanation was the most effective strategy for repairing trust, while denial was the least effective. Interjections alone did not directly facilitate repair trust. Distrustful participants demonstrated greater trust repair gains, suggesting a stronger need for corrective feedback. In preference ratings, the explanation strategy with interjections was selected as the most preferred among all VA messages. These findings provide practical guidance for designing VA trust-repair messages following automated-driving failures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Does green design improve environmental performance? Evidence from Chinese Mobile phone and tablet computer industrial chain enterprises
Abstract: Amidst the pursuit of sustainable development and China's dual carbon goals, green design has attracted significant attention as a tool for improving environmental performance and reducing resource use. Using data from listed companies in China's mobile phone and tablet industrial chain between 2015 and 2024, this paper combines text mining information from corporate annual reports with objectively disclosed quantitative data of enterprises. It constructs an indicator system for the level of corporate green design. The study delineates the influence of green design development on environmental performance and examines the causal pathways involved. The relevant results are fivefold. (1) The green design performance of enterprises in China's mobile phone and tablet industrial chain shows a consistently upwards annual trend. There are significant differences in green design levels across enterprises. Meanwhile, disparities also exist among different dimensions of green design and across different links of the industrial chain. (2) Green design enhancement improves corporate environmental performance, and this finding withstands a battery of robustness and endogeneity tests. (3) Green design enhances corporate environmental performance by promoting internal attention and external attention mechanisms. (4) Artificial intelligence strengthens the improvement effect of green design on corporate environmental performance. (5) Further analysis reveals that the environmental performance improvement of green design varies markedly across its dimensions and industrial chain segments. Green materials, green use and green recycling yield the strongest effects at the dimension level, while supporting component enterprises dominate at the chain segment level. These findings have important implications for policymakers crafting green design policies and corporate managers developing green and low-carbon transition strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: A framework for defining, quantifying and implementing a noise footprint approach
Abstract: The noise footprint is emerging as a framework for assessing and communicating the impacts of noise. Although footprint terminology has been used across diverse areas of environmental acoustics research, its meaning, definition and application vary across fields. This research aims to provide a consensus-based noise footprint definition, identify the conceptual and methodological requirements that should guide future quantitative implementation and establish its basic operational characteristics. An adjusted Delphi process was conducted with a panel of 8 experts spanning two domains, namely acoustics and Life Cycle Assessment & environmental footprinting. The process combined semi-structured interviews and two rounds of questionnaires to establish consensus on the conceptual definition and quantitative characteristics of the noise footprint and thematic analysis of the collected material. The outcomes were subsequently synthesized through a SWOT analysis to identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with the proposed framework. In contrast to most existing noise footprint applications, the proposed framework suggests a life cycle perspective and supply chain attribution. The noise footprint is proposed, on the basis of expert consensus, as a measure for assessing and comparing noise, applicable to products and adaptable to individual and societal activities. Title: Where to start with urban Digital Twins? Backward-chaining key indicators for cross-sector water, heat, and housing impact analysis
Abstract: Digital planning for urban systems can benefit from integrated frameworks that capture cross-sectoral dependencies, impact assessment, support causal reasoning, and adapt to diverse data sources. We present a methodological approach for Digital Twinning that combines backward-chaining analysis with Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) to identify, decompose, and interlink key performance indicators across three critical planning domains: drinking water supply, urban heat stress, and housing provision. Building on a comprehensive indicator review, we selected key targets and traced each to its fundamental components using the DPSIR framework (Driving Forces, Pressures, States, Impacts, Responses). We quantified relational dependencies and network centrality metrics to construct sector-specific DAGs, then merged overlapping elements into an integrated cross-sector model, revealing critical causal pathways. This enables scenario testing across diverse drivers, including climate change, demographic shifts, and credit conditions. Our results demonstrate how infrastructural and natural system interventions propagate through water reliability, thermal comfort, and housing affordability. The framework clarifies data requirements and analytic workflows for Digital Planning tools while offering a scalable template for cross-sectoral impact analysis. Authors: Yang S.; Yokoyama S.
Title: Resettlement and spatial transformation: reconstructing sacred space in Wa homes in Yunnan, China
Abstract: Development-induced resettlement has become an increasingly prominent form of spatial restructuring across the Global South, yet the spatial transformations it produces at the household scale remain empirically underexplored. Using an integrative spatial–ethnographic approach that combines ethnography, architectural analysis, and 3D documentation, this study examines the production of space and place-making through sacred space in the homes of a resettled Wa community in Yunnan, China, tracing the place–placelessness–re-placing process unfolding at the domestic scale. Resettlement housing disrupted the spatial order through which cosmology and hierarchy had been materialized, eroding shared spatial perceptions and cultural meanings, and producing placelessness. Through embodied spatial practice and the material reorganization of the home, Wa residents restored symbolic meaning, reaffirmed household authority and reverence, and transformed their new houses into places of Wa identity and emotional attachment. This re-placing process reveals Wa residents’ cultural spatial agency—their capacity to actively reshape space and sustain cultural identity through vernacular beliefs and spatial practices, fostering collective belonging and cultural resilience. At the same time, the growing diversification of spatial patterns risks weakening shared spatial perceptions over time. By extending the analysis of spatial production to the household scale and foregrounding the materiality of domestic space in post-resettlement home-making, this study highlights resettlement as both a spatial and an existential process, contributing to broader debates on the production of space, place-making, and cultural transformation in development-induced resettlement. Title: Returns to Caring? Health and Well-Being Effects of Subsidized Long-Term Care
Source title: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management
Abstract: We estimate the health and well-being effects of subsidized access to long-term care (LTC). Our analysis exploits the staggered implementation of Spain's 2007 System of Autonomy and Care for Dependent People (SAAD), which expanded publicly funded and universal LTC subsidies and supports, as well as its subsequent reform. Using two decades of administrative and survey data and leveraging exogenous regional and individual-level variation in program exposure, we find that access to SAAD benefits reduces the care receiver's depressive symptoms by approximately 10 percentage points, increases its survival probability by 2.6–3 percentage points, and raises its life satisfaction by 0.24–0.50 scale points. Title: Experiences, Challenges, and Practices in Accessing Digital Health Services Among Manipuri Indigenous Older Adults in Bangladesh: A Qualitative Study

Abstract: Employing a qualitative design, this study investigates how indigenous Manipuri older adults in Bangladesh access and use digital health services to manage their health needs. Authors: Lee S.J.; Kwon J.; Lee J.H.; Kang B.
Title: Barriers to inclusive subway station use for older adults: An age-comparative video-stimulated recall study identifying universal and age-specific discomfort
Abstract: Background Subway stations are essential but demanding environments for older adults, yet how their experiences differ from those of younger users remains qualitatively underexplored. Prior work has examined older passengers in isolation, leaving it unclear which barriers are age-specific and which reflect universal design failures. Methods We compared 30 older adults (aged 65+) and 30 younger adults (aged 20–39) navigating a major multi-line transfer station in Seoul, South Korea. Non-participatory behavioral observation was paired with video-stimulated recall (VSR) interviews using first-person wearable camera footage. Thematic analysis was applied to 1,831 coded segments, with an exploratory gender comparison. Results Five discomfort themes were identified: Stairs, Escalator and Elevator, Signage, Crowding, and Station Infrastructure. Factors were universal when participant reach was comparable across groups and age-specific when one group's reach was at least twice the other's. Stair descent, elevator access, and handrail discomfort were older-adult-specific; being slowed by pedestrians ahead was younger-adult-specific; and stair ascent, crowding, and signage complexity were universal. Older adults generated 4.4 times as many high-level discomfort mentions, mainly in vertical circulation. Universal factors differed in meaning: crowding was a safety threat for older adults but a flow disruption for younger adults. Younger women had more high-level crowding mentions than older women. Conclusions The same station environment was associated with differing forms and levels of discomfort across groups; comparable participant reach did not imply comparable burden. Authors: Giugni L.
Title: Women and men against Camorra: urban (un)safety, cross-gender collaborations, and collective courage in a mafia-affected city
Abstract: Research on responses to gendered urban (un)safety and its spatial implications has largely focused on either individual coping strategies or planning and design interventions. Less attention has been paid to how subjects across gender groups may collaboratively respond to their distinctive experiences of insecurity and create shared safety through collective action. This article addresses this gap through a qualitative case study of Ercolano, a Southern Italian city historically shaped by mafia territorial control. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, ethnographic observation, and documentary materials, it examines how self-identifying women and men collectively confronted gender-differentiated fears associated with mafia violence and criminal territorial governance. These dynamics are interpreted through the feminist-informed concept of collective courage. The findings identify three interrelated, recursive socio-spatial practices through which collective courage emerged and shaped the production of space in Ercolano: recognising shared yet unequal urban vulnerabilities; establishing localised, gender-aware forms of mutual support; and anchoring enhanced feelings of communal safety in specific sites. Based on this analysis, the article further develops and geographises the theorising of collective courage, making two key contributions to debates in human geography, urban studies, and feminist theory. First, it conceptualises how collective courage is (re-)produced and becomes operative, and how its entanglements with socio-material environments enable collective action and spatial transformation. Second, it sheds light on how shared urban safety can be generated through grassroots cross-gender mobilisations that restructure both gender power relations and spatial arrangements. Authors: Zhang M.
Title: Professional identity under constraint: An autoethnographic study of an English teacher in Chinese private higher education
Abstract: This autoethnographic study traces one English teacher's professional identity trajectory in Chinese private higher education from 2009 to 2025. The study draws on autobiographical narratives and documentary materials and uses timeline construction and thematic analysis. Across this period, professional identity was ruptured by classroom non-recognition, provisionally repaired through institutionally valued reform work, held in suspension during caregiving, and carried forward through imagined exits. The analysis suggests that autonomy deprivation functioned as a recurrent mechanism of identity erosion in the context of institutional and disciplinary positioning, the organisation and valuation of academic labour, and gendered care responsibilities. It develops four linked concepts—rupture, substitute professional value, identity suspension, and imagined exits—to explain how professional identity can be damaged, temporarily stabilised, held in suspension, and sustained through future-oriented possibility. The study extends teacher identity scholarship into Chinese private higher education and offers a structurally situated account of identity under constraint. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Inferring activity semantics from mobile phone signalling Data: An LLM framework for Activity-Based travel behaviour analysis
Abstract: Mobile phone signalling and other passive-sensing mobility data offer population coverage at low cost, but they record where people are rather than what they do. This semantic gap limits their value for activity-based travel behaviour analysis and planning diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose UrbanAct-GPT, an evidence-constrained and task-adapted LLM framework that converts location-only signalling records and POI information into period-level activity types and day-level behavioural roles through Context-constrained Chain-of-Thought prompting, closed activity and role taxonomies, and QLoRA fine-tuning. On an independent test set, UrbanAct-GPT achieves 0.95 activity accuracy and 0.70 role accuracy. Benchmarking against both general-purpose LLMs and conventional activity-inference baselines shows that UrbanAct-GPT's advantage lies mainly in category-balanced inference for context-dependent activities such as eating, shopping, leisure, care, and fitness, rather than routine home and work recognition alone. Applied to approximately 2.1 million anonymised users in Shanghai, UrbanAct-GPT transforms passive mobility traces into activity-specific and time-sensitive evidence. In Shanghai, the inferred activity semantics show that mobility concentrations can reflect different urban demands, including peak-period commuting around employment centres, late-return trips along cross-district corridors, and evening non-work activities in residential communities. In this sense, the model links mobility intensity to the urban functions supported by different places at different times of day. By distinguishing activity purposes across locations and time periods, the results support targeted transport service adjustment, community-facility provision, night-time amenity planning, and jobs–housing diagnosis. Overall, UrbanAct-GPT provides a pathway for recovering activity semantics from passive-sensing mobility data and supporting city-scale planning diagnosis. © 2026 Hong Kong Society for Transportation Studies

Authors: Stephens M.
Title: The Fracture–Strategy–Distortion model: The developmental architecture of compensatory high performance
Abstract: This paper advances a single theoretical claim: that high-performance behaviour can be understood as an adaptive response to early relational fracture that, through the compounding mechanisms of strategic recursion and cultural amplification, comes to be misrecognised as authentic identity, by the individual, by their relational environment, and by the cultural systems that reward and reproduce it. This misrecognition is not incidental but structural: it is the condition that makes compensatory high performance self-sustaining and resistant to transformation. The paper introduces the Fracture–Strategy–Distortion (FSD) Model to account for this structure. Fracture refers to early relational conditions of conditional worth, safety, or belonging, in which the developing self learns that approval is contingent on performance rather than inherent in being. Strategy describes the adaptive identity configuration assembled in response. Distortion names the consolidation of strategy into a fixed identity structure experienced as selfhood rather than adaptation. The model's central contribution is to explain why this misrecognition persists despite insight, achievement, and environmental change, through strategic recursion, by which the distorted configuration actively generates the conditions that confirm its own necessity, and through cultural amplification, by which high-performance environments reward the precise traits that emerge from fracture, rendering the strategy's compensatory function structurally invisible. The paper situates the FSD Model within constructive-developmental theory, self-determination theory, and attachment research, and advances an integrative theoretical contribution that explains not merely the existence of compensatory high performance but the structural conditions under which it persists and resists transformation. Implications for developmental theory, practice, and future empirical research are identified. © 2026 The Author

Title: Who invests matters: A multimodal contrastive learning approach to successful startup-investor matching
Abstract: Startup success depends not only on startup characteristics but also on alignment with investors. Yet most data-driven models for startup-investor matching focus on whether an investment link will occur, leaving post-investment outcomes and bilateral compatibility underexplored. This study introduces MCL-Invest, a multimodal contrastive learning framework for success-oriented startup-investor recommendation. Compared to the best traditional classifier, it improves PR-AUC from 0.3458 to 0.4158 (+20.2%) and achieves substantially higher NDCG@K scores. Compared with the hybrid baseline, it improves PR-AUC from 0.2620 to 0.4158 (+58.7%) and ROC-AUC from 0.5699 to 0.6994 (+22.7%) while doubling NDCG@1 to 0.1143. Title: Exponential-family random graph models in resident-healthcare provider networks: An application using data from long-term healthcare facilities in the United States
Abstract: Infectious pathogens have a high burden in long-term care facilities [LTCFs]. Using multilevel exponential-family random graph models [ERGMs] applied to bipartite graphs, in one of the first applications of these models to healthcare contact data, we investigate network structures associated with resident cohorting based on resident-level characteristics. Methodologically, the fitted pooled bipartite ERGM uses mode-specific, mean-centered log-size interactions and combines Monte Carlo maximum likelihood estimation [MC-MLE] point estimates with stochastic approximation [SA] bootstrap inference, a combination that makes these models practical when the pooled networks differ widely in size. In contrast, no evidence of cohorting-like HCP sharing was found for measured resident clinical characteristics, including Multi-Drug Resistant Organism [MDRO] status. Title: Mitigating shortcut learning in multimodal misinformation detection via LLM-guided orthogonal disentanglement
Abstract: Multimodal misinformation detection is often prone to “shortcut learning,” where models rely on spurious correlations from entangled feature representations rather than learning intrinsic semantics. Title: Resisting the move? Anchors of rural staying among youth and young adults in the Western Balkans
Abstract: Across the world, many young people are leaving rural areas in search of better opportunities, yet others resist the move and choose to stay. Understanding why some remain despite strong incentives to leave has become a central question in contemporary migration and rural studies. The cluster analysis identifies four anchoring profiles that range from symbolically attached younger respondents to occupationally anchored young adults and deeply rooted adults characterised by family, work, property, routine, and belonging. Inertia is the strongest and most consistent correlate of staying intentions across all age groups. Sunk costs and livelihood anchors, particularly paid work and property-related commitments, are more prominent among older respondents. Title: Neural correlates of achievement motivation and their associations with happiness: A connectome-based predictive modeling study
Abstract: Achievement motivation is a fundamental personality trait that robustly predicts happiness, yet the large-scale functional brain networks that give rise to individual differences in achieving tendency and its two core facets—the motive to achieve success (MAS) and the motive to avoid failure (MAF)—remain poorly understood. Critically, the two networks were differentially associated with the subcomponents of achievement motivation: the positive network correlated positively with MAS and negatively with MAF, whereas the negative network showed the opposite pattern. Finally, both the overall network strengths and these subcomponent-specific patterns showed modest associations with happiness.
