Title: Psychiatric evaluation of non-responsibility and diminished responsibility in criminal law: A scoping review
Source title: International Journal of Law and Psychiatry
Abstract: Background The assessment of discernment is central to the evaluation of criminal responsibility in forensic psychiatry. However, its conceptual ambiguity and methodological variability raise concerns regarding the reliability and consistency of expert assessments. Objective This scoping review aims to map how discernment is defined, assessed, and interpreted in the literature, and to identify the main conceptual, methodological, and contextual challenges associated with its evaluation. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR; Tricco et al., 2018 ). A total of 41 records were identified through database searches and additional sources; after removal of duplicates, 29 records were screened by title and abstract, and 26 reports were assessed for full-text eligibility. Seventeen studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Data were extracted using a structured framework covering conceptual definitions, methodological approaches, reliability, contextual factors, and normative implications. Results The findings reveal that discernment is conceptualized as a multidimensional and heterogeneous construct, lacking a consensual definition. Assessment practices rely predominantly on unstructured clinical judgment, leading to methodological variability. Inter-expert disagreement emerges as a recurrent finding, particularly in cases involving partial impairment. Structured tools may improve consistency but do not fully address underlying conceptual ambiguity. Legal and institutional contexts significantly influence both evaluation practices and their outcomes. Conclusions The assessment of discernment appears as a structured yet inherently interpretative process shaped by the interaction between conceptual, methodological, and contextual factors. Title: The role of early parenting practices in preschool children's school liking and pre-academic skills
Abstract: The present study examined the longitudinal pathways linking early parenting practices, children’s school liking, and pre-academic skills among Hong Kong Chinese families during the preschool years. Using a two-wave longitudinal design, this study analyzed multi-informant data from 307 parent–child triads recruited from five local kindergartens following invitations to a randomly selected pool of schools. At Time 1 (T1), when children were nearly 4 years old, both fathers and mothers reported on their parenting practices (i.e., positive, inconsistent, and punitive behaviors) using the Alabama Parenting Questionnaire–Preschool Version. Two years later (T2), when children were approximately 6 years old, parents rated children’s school liking using the School Liking and Avoidance Questionnaire, and children completed direct assessments of oral vocabulary and numeracy skills. Specifically, early positive parenting significantly predicted higher levels of children’s school liking (β = 0.43, p < 0.001), whereas inconsistent parenting predicted lower school liking (β = –0.29, p < 0.05). Title: Joint production, externalities, and terrace conservation strategies
Abstract: Multifunctional agriculture jointly produces commodity and non-commodity outputs, yet many non-commodity benefits are underprovided due to insufficient economic incentives. This challenge is amplified in the agriculture-tourism nexus, where tourism depends on agricultural landscapes while potentially contributing to their degradation, creating interconnected externalities that distort benefit distribution and undermine joint production efficiency. The results show that achieving optimal multifunctionality requires balancing the benefits and costs of externality internalization across agricultural and tourism activities. Failure to do so may reduce joint production efficiency by distorting factor income distribution. Multi-stakeholder collaboration improves benefit allocation and lowers internalization costs, enabling the socially optimal provision of agricultural non-commodity benefits. Title: Political economy of scaling education reforms with equity in Pakistan: Political leadership, bureaucrats, and donors
Abstract: This paper examines the political economy dynamics behind scaling of education reforms in Pakistan, with particular attention to equity. Drawing on documentary analysis and 12 key informant interviews, the study uses Hickey and Hossain's (2019) Domains of Power framework, to examine scaling within Pakistan’s fragmented hybrid-clientelist political settlement. Political leadership emerged as the strongest influence on scale, with politically visible reforms more likely to receive sustained championing. Institutionalisation, however, also depended on bureaucratic support, administrative feasibility and integration into government systems. Donors provided financing, evidence and technical support and were stronger advocates of equity, but their influence depended on domestic ownership. Equity remained secondary where it was less aligned with political and administrative priorities. Title: “United in diversity?” A comparative study of initial midwifery education and practice in 30 European countries
Abstract: Aim: To explore initial midwifery education and scope of professional practice across Europe. Shortfalls were addressed through simulation or clinical placement solutions. Conclusion: European midwifery education has advanced considerably since the introduction of the European Directives. Title: Using anti-Western perceptions to frame anti-feminist discourse on the Chinese TikTok
Abstract: This article examines how anti-Western tropes are mobilized to construct anti-feminist discourse in Douyin video commentaries. Drawing on a critical discourse analysis of 54 short videos, the analysis identifies a recurring problem–effect–solution pattern realized through three interrelated strategies: spatialization, which constructs “western feminism” as a destabilizing force in Western societies; securitization, which criticizes “western feminism” as ideological brainwashing in China; and legitimation, which extols China's state feminism as the authentic model of gender equality. This study expands scholarship on overtly misogynistic and gender-nationalist anti-feminist backlash by drawing attention to a more “authoritative” mode of anti-feminist argumentation, whose legitimacy derives from intertextual resonance with state-sanctioned narratives, the socialist legacy of state feminism, and the misappropriation and refunctionalization of Euro-American alt-right and far-right anti-immigration disinformation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Author full names: Apatinga, Gervin Ane (57211990848); Tenkorang, Eric Y. (57216997115)
Title: Economic abuse and food insecurity among women living with HIV in Ghana
Abstract: Economic abuse has recently gained recognition as a distinct form of intimate partner violence in sub-Saharan Africa, with women disproportionately affected. However, limited research has explored its consequences, particularly its impact on food insecurity among women living with HIV, who face compounded vulnerabilities due to stigma, poverty, and health challenges. This study addressed this gap by conducting 39 in-depth interviews with women living with HIV in Ghana who had experienced economic abuse, to understand how this abuse influenced their experiences of food insecurity. Using inductive thematic analysis, we identified critical connections between economic abuse and food insecurity. Participants shared narratives of financial withholding, income sabotage, and coercive control that prevented them from meeting their food needs and those of their children. Many described experiences of self-sacrifice, hunger, and dependence on kinship or religious networks as coping mechanisms. Addressing economic abuse requires stronger legal protections, increased public awareness, and tailored support for women living with HIV. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Griffin B.; Abed R.
Title: The aetiological role of cumulative cultural evolution in eating disorders and muscle dysmorphia
Abstract: Dual inheritance theory posits that human behavior is shaped by the interplay of two distinct inheritance systems, genetic and cultural evolution. This framework has become a theoretical cornerstone for a range of disciplines seeking to understand the unique evolutionary trajectory of Homo sapiens, emphasising that cumulative culture has co-evolved with species-specific psychological mechanisms that facilitate its transmission. The burgeoning field of evolutionary psychiatry seeks to bring the powerful theoretical insights of evolutionary biology to bear in the study of mental disorder, yet no existing accounts draw explicitly upon the principles of dual inheritance theory. This paper aims to address this gap, breaking new ground theoretically. The significance of dual inheritance theory for evolutionary psychiatry is discussed, then its practical utility is demonstrated through presentation of the Extended Sexual Competition Hypothesis of eating disorders and muscle dysmorphia. By integrating cultural and biological evolution, this novel hypothesis offers a unified perspective on these debilitating and often treatment-refractory conditions, pointing to testable predictions that, if validated, could inform early interventions and targeted public health strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Li Z.; Shen G.; Wang K.; Ru X.; Hong T.; Xu Z.; Chen L.; Gu Y.; Han J.; Guo Y.
Title: Health perception biases among rural Chinese adults: Differences in structural, behavioral, and nutrition-related correlates across subtypes
Abstract: Health perception bias (HPB), defined as a mismatch between subjective health perception and objective health risks, may conceal accumulated risks among rural residents. Using survey data from 1539 middle-aged and older rural residents in eastern China, this study measured objective health risk using a biomarker-based objective health risk score (BIO), constructed from 15 physiological indicators and blood biomarkers. A finite mixture model was used to identify HPB subtypes based on the joint distribution of self-rated health (SRH) and BIO. Regression analyses examined their associations with structural characteristics, health-related behaviors, and nutrition-related awareness and engagement, with additional comparisons of correlate patterns across mismatch subtypes and by gender. Three HPB subtypes were identified: PCT characterized by relatively consistent subjective and objective health assessments, MPBT characterized by moderate subjective-objective mismatch and relatively high BIO, and SPBT characterized by favorable SRH despite elevated BIO. HPB was associated with gender, education, income, alcohol consumption, unhealthy diet, and nutrition-related awareness and engagement, with lower nutrition-related awareness and engagement more consistently observed in SPBT. Behavioral and informational correlates differentiated MPBT from SPBT more clearly than structural factors, while evidence of systematic gender heterogeneity was limited. These findings highlight heterogeneity within subjective-objective health mismatch among rural residents and show that different mismatch subtypes are linked to non-uniform behavioral and informational correlate patterns. Rural health promotion should combine objective risk assessment, clear interpretation of examination results, alcohol-risk communication, and differentiated nutrition and health information support to improve early risk recognition and targeted health management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Exploring differentiated instruction as a mechanism of pre-k score convergence: Descriptive evidence from a study of kindergarteners from low-income backgrounds
Abstract: Some evidence indicates that pre-k score convergence (also known as pre-k fadeout) may occur because kindergarten teachers focus instruction on children furthest from meeting end-of-year benchmarks, or those with weaker behavioral skills, bringing pre-k attenders and non-attenders closer to parity over the course of the year. To examine this possibility, we conducted path analyses using data from a study of kindergarteners from low-income backgrounds with and without pre-k experience. 975 children (59.6% Hispanic, 15.2% Black, 11.8% Asian, 10.3% White, and 3.1% other races/ethnicities; 50% with pre-k experience) were individually observed during kindergarten to determine how much time they spent in teacher-led individual work and small group instruction. Children were assessed in the fall and spring on language, literacy, and mathematics achievement and were rated by teachers on task orientation and disruptive behaviors in the fall. Descriptive path analyses illustrate that pre-k attendance was associated with higher school entry academic skills and task orientation as well as elevated disruptive behaviors. Stronger academic skills, higher task orientation, and lower disruptive behavior problems were associated with children spending less time with teachers. However, time spent with teachers in small group or individual work was largely not associated with achievement gains. Results suggest a need for more research on individual classroom experiences that may explain pre-k score convergence. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Time-varying mediation effects of health warning labels on smoking cessation-related cognition and behavior: Evidence from a randomized trial using ecological momentary assessment
Abstract: Introduction Health warning labels (HWLs) on cigarette packs influence risk perceptions and cessation behaviors, but their effects diminish over time. Time-varying mediation modeling can uncover when and how HWLs affect cessation-related cognitions and behaviors. Methods As part of a two-week randomized trial, US adult daily smokers (N = 179) received cigarette packs with either control HWLs or HWLs plus inserts containing rotating efficacy messages about quitting benefits and cessation tips. Using time-varying mediation models with ecological momentary assessment data, we examined how inserts (vs control) influenced daily cognitive elaboration of cessation benefits and subsequent forgoing of cigarettes (i.e., next day) and whether those effects changed over time. Results Over two weeks, inserts progressively increased cognitive elaboration, reaching statistical significance around day 6. The association between cognitive elaboration and forgoing a cigarette the next day was significant across the study period, peaking mid-study. Direct effects of inserts on forgoing behavior emerged in the first week and stabilized after day 7. The indirect (mediated) effect of inserts on forgoing via cognitive elaboration increased during the first week and declined slightly in the second week. Conclusions Inserts gradually increased both cognitive elaboration of quitting benefits and forgoing cigarettes, with mediation of insert effects by cognitive elaboration peaking after one week, then declining. These findings suggest that additional communication strategies, perhaps using different channels, may be necessary to boost HWL effects on cessation-related behaviors that are mediated through the pathway of cognitive elaboration of cessation benefits. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: The ludic paradox: Why behavioral change through games requires agency, not control
Abstract: Games engage more than three billion players worldwide, and the interventions that seek to harness them for behavioral change, from gamification to serious games, produce strikingly heterogeneous results: meta-analytic syntheses report effects ranging from negligible to moderate, with a dispersion that the game elements treated as active ingredients by design-centered accounts explain poorly. We take this heterogeneity to be the phenomenon that a theory of behavioral change through games must explain. Our proposed hypothesis is that the relevant explanatory variable is controlling regulation, understood as the degree to which a design displaces the player's own reasons for acting, whereas instrumental purpose as such, which many effective interventions openly declare, carries no comparable explanatory weight. Drawing on motivational psychology, cultural economics, and game studies, we develop a four-pole framework that reconceptualizes gameplay as cultural meaning-making, identifying games as designed artifacts, play as evolved behavioral disposition, gameplay as situated experience, and re-play as reflective cultural practice, whose dynamic interaction generates behavioral transformation across extended temporal scales. Central to our analysis is the ludic dilemma, which we locate in the metacommunicative frame that constitutes an activity as play rather than in reward contingency alone, and which therefore predicts a discontinuity where accounts grounded in the overjustification effect predict a gradient. We specify what the framework adds to meaningful gamification, situated motivational affordances, Self-Determination Theory, and the debriefing tradition in simulation research, and we derive predictions, each with operational indicators and falsification conditions, that discriminate cultural meaning-making from these alternatives. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Parental self-efficacy to reduce internalising problems in autistic children: Scale development and validation
Abstract: Background: Autistic children commonly experience internalising disorders, such as depression and anxiety disorders, that significantly impact child and parent quality of life. Parents play an important role in supporting their child's mental health and reducing their risk of internalising disorders. Parental self-efficacy (PSE), that is parent's confidence to engage in preventive parenting practices, is a key factor in this role. To measure domain-specific PSE to reduce internalising problems in autistic children, we developed and initially assessed the psychometric properties of the 14-item Parental Self-Efficacy Scale - Autism version (PSES-Autism) and identified parent-reported contributing factors to PSE. Methods: A sample of 123 parents of autistic children aged 5–12 completed the PSES-Autism, as well as measures of parenting practices, parent mental health, child psychosocial functioning, and general PSE. Results: The PSES-Autism demonstrated good internal consistency reliability, construct validity, and test-retest reliability. Higher PSES-Autism total scores were associated with increased preventive parenting practices and better parent mental health and general PSE in parents of autistic children, but were not associated with child psychosocial functioning. Contributors to PSE, as reported by parents, included support from family and friends, parental mental health, and the child's care team. Conclusions: The PSES-Autism has clinical and research utility as a measure of PSE to reduce internalising problems in autistic children. The present study provides insight into the factors related to PSE in parents of autistic children, highlighting potential targets for interventions to better support parents. © 2026 The Authors

Title: A collaborative learning framework for predicting the structure and spreading dynamics of multiplex networks
Abstract: Structure and dynamical prediction are two core tasks in multiplex network research, yet they are often investigated separately. However, in real-world scenarios, the structural and dynamical information is typically simultaneously available but incomplete, which makes these tasks more challenging. Therefore, a natural idea to utilize such incomplete information for collaborative modeling of the two tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a data-driven collaborative learning framework (Multi-CoLF) that integrates incomplete structural and dynamical information for predicting network structure and dynamical evolutions of multiplex networks. The framework consists of a structure prediction learner and a dynamical prediction learner. Specifically, the structure prediction learner employs the Gumbel-Softmax technique to infer missing links in each layer and constructs an extended graph. Based on this extended graph, the dynamical prediction learner develops an extended graph neural network to model spreading dynamics and capture the underlying evolution rules. An alternating optimization strategy is further designed to enable collaborative optimization between the two learners, facilitating collaborative prediction of structure and dynamics. Experiments on three synthetic and five real-world networks demonstrate that our method outperforms baseline approaches on both tasks under different types of spreading dynamics, with structure prediction accuracy improving by more than 10% on certain datasets. Moreover, extensive experimental results reveal that the structure and spreading dynamics in multiplex networks are complementary: the learned network structure enhances the accuracy of dynamical prediction, while the learned spreading dynamical rules improve the accuracy of structure prediction. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: How does adolescent neurodevelopment impact substance use? The substance use neuroplasticity and peer (SNAP) model: A novel neurodevelopmental model of adolescent substance use
Abstract: Substance use among adolescents age 13–18 remains a significant societal concern, yet contemporary neuroscience models of addiction have been grounded in the chronic, cyclic stage model developed for adult presentations of substance use disorder (SUD). Relative to adults, adolescents exhibit distinct patterns of substance use, and many structural and functional findings garnered from studies of addiction in the adult brain have not been reliably observed or replicated in adolescent samples. Thus, contemporary models of adult addiction do not readily translate to adolescents, resulting in downstream developmental incongruities in how substance use is conceptualized, measured, and treated in this age group. Here, we present a review of the current state of human and preclinical models of neurobiological risk factors and mechanisms specific to substance use in adolescents. Grounded in this literature, we present the Substance use Neuroplasticity And Peer (SNAP) model, a novel neurodevelopmental model of adolescent substance use that captures the differentiated nature of substance use initiation and escalation in this high-need, yet undertreated population. Title: Land price stabilization under Japan's LocatIon Optimization Plan: A propensity score matching analysis of Hachioji City
Abstract: This study uses propensity score matching (PSM) to quantitatively evaluate the impact of Japan's Location Optimization Plan (LOP) on residential land prices. Despite the growing attention given to compact city development policies, rigorous empirical evaluations of the effectiveness of the LOP using causal inference methods remain limited. Stable land prices are crucial for sustainable urban development. Stable land prices ensure fair property valuations and promote investment confidence. Land price stability also affects infrastructure planning. The analysis uses data from Hachioji City, where the LOP has been implemented for over a decade, and compares it with data from other densely populated areas within Tokyo Prefecture. By applying nearest neighbor and kernel matching techniques, the study isolates the effects of the policy from confounding variables. The results demonstrate that land prices in Hachioji City decreased by approximately 6701.32 JPY/m2 compared to other areas in Tokyo. The results suggest that LOP implementation is associated with more moderate land price changes in Hachioji than in comparable areas. The findings contribute to our understanding of how spatial planning policies influence land markets in the context of demographic decline. The findings also offer methodological foundations for future policy assessments in similar contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Xu Z.; Liu J.
Title: Toward equitable carbon reduction: Quantifying household emission profiles and community-scale interventions for urban neighborhood regeneration
Abstract: Households contribute a substantial share of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet their carbon footprints are uneven due to socio-economic, spatial, and behavioral factors. However, quantifying carbon reduction potential remains difficult due to complex household activity patterns. This study investigates how equitable carbon reduction can be achieved through community-level interventions targeting high-emission households for neighborhood regeneration. Drawing on household survey data from Chongqing, China, this study estimates carbon emissions from household energy, vehicle use, commuting and facility-related travel. A mean squared error-based threshold detection classifies households into high- and low-emission groups in each domain. Under thirteen proposed intervention scenarios, three reduction indicators (R1-R3) are calculated to capture equity, domain-specific, and system-wide mitigation potential respectively. Results reveal that spatial-economic, socio-demographic, transport mode, and facility accessibility factors jointly shape carbon inequality. Household mitigation should move from identifying high emitters to distinguishing responsibility-based, welfare-based, and accessibility-based measures. Self-investment retrofitting owns the highest absolute potential for spatially advantaged households, while welfare-oriented measures are more important among single-occupant vulnerable households of older adults. Facility-related measures are effective among households with children facing unmet needs for accessing nearby parks and sports areas. These findings offer broader implications from a life-cycle perspective for cities undergoing drastic demographic and economic changes. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Lan W.; Tian X.; Zhao W.; Zhao Y.
Title: Occupational Safety and Health Status of Food Delivery Drivers: Current Challenges and Enhancement Strategies
Abstract: The rapid growth of the global platform economy has given rise to a sizable workforce of gig workers, represented by food delivery drivers, whose occupational safety and health (OSH) protection has become increasingly pressing concerns. The present study adopts an integrated policy and institutional analysis combined with a questionnaire-based case study to examine the current challenges and improvement pathways for the OSH protection of food delivery drivers. Specifically, the study analyzes and compares existing policies and institutional arrangements related to occupational safety protection for food delivery drivers. Taking Beijing, China, as a case study, a questionnaire survey was conducted among 100 food delivery riders (effective participants) to examine the current state of occupational safety within this workforce, forming the basis for targeted mitigation strategies. Policy analysis indicates that the current labor protection system exhibits significant gaps and misalignments. On the one hand, existing regulations do not clearly define the substantive employment relationship between platforms and food delivery drivers, resulting in ambiguous labor status under flexible employment models. Consequently, some food delivery drivers are excluded from the traditional labor protection framework, limiting their access to comprehensive labor rights. On the other hand, pilot policies have a narrow scope and insufficiently address the high-risk characteristics of this workforce. Platforms frequently externalize risks to third parties, leaving well-documented occupational hazards such as traffic accidents and overwork-related injuries insufficiently covered by institutional safeguards. The survey results further reveal that food delivery drivers commonly experience excessively long working hours, relatively low earnings per unit of time, and a weak sense of job belonging. Delivery platforms generally demonstrate insufficient investment in safety measures and inadequate training efforts. In response to these issues, this study proposes targeted countermeasures from three dimensions. These include legislative and institutional development, government and industry regulation, and corporate management. Together, they form a systematic framework to improve occupational safety protection for food delivery drivers. The findings offer new insights for enhancing the OSH of this workforce and provide a useful reference for advancing protection mechanisms for other forms of emerging employment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Governing the unpriced hazard: A land-use policy framework for spatially concentrated seismic risk when markets do not capitalise it
Abstract: Hazard policy relies, often tacitly, on property prices to warn households away from danger and to reward mitigation. This paper develops a land-use policy framework for the case in which that mechanism fails. Drawing on neighbourhood-level evidence from post-2023 Istanbul, where any capitalisation of expected earthquake mortality is smaller than the smallest discount that would matter in either the sale or the rental segment, and where ten per cent of neighbourhoods carry more than half the city's expected casualties in a single contiguous belt, we argue that the conjunction of non-pricing and spatial concentration defines a distinct governance problem that market-reliant approaches cannot reach. We set out a diagnostic typology classifying hazards by whether the market prices the risk and whether exposure is diffuse or concentrated, together with the tests that assign a case to a cell: equivalence testing on the price axis, and local spatial association with a concentration-magnitude criterion on the spatial axis. Istanbul occupies the most demanding cell, which we term silent systemic exposure. We then specify a four-layer framework whose organising principle is that policy must substitute for the missing signal rather than wait for it: dual-market risk disclosure, cluster-scale renewal sequenced by concentration, a layered risk-financing architecture with a public tail, and tenure and equity safeguards. Comparison with four other seismic settings indicates that non-capitalisation is institutionally produced and therefore reversible. We illustrate sequencing and fiscal scale on Istanbul's central-western cluster and specify the scope conditions for transfer. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: REASSESSING THE REASONABLE SUSPICION: THE JUDGMENT OF HC 208.240/SP BY THE BRAZILIAN SUPREME COURT (STF) AND ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR POLICE STOPS AND SEARCHES; [REAVALIANDO A FUNDADA SUSPEITA: O JULGAMENTO DO HC 208.240/SP PELO STF E SEUS REFLEXOS SOBRE AS ABORDAGENS POLICIAIS]
Abstract: In April 2024, when judging Habeas Corpus 208.240/SP, the Brazilian Federal Supreme Court (STF) established the doctrine that police stops and searches must be based on objective criteria, holding it unlawful for such measures to be based on race, sex, sexual orientation, skin color, or physical appearance. The ruling, however, proved controversial with respect to its practical effects, since in the case at hand the court denied that the stop had in fact been driven by racial profiling. Against this backdrop, this article seeks to reflect on the ruling and its possible practical repercussions. Drawing on a literature review and an examination of the term “reasonable suspicion,” the normative category used to assess the lawfulness of a police stop and search, the article discusses the potential implications of the decision for the institutions of the criminal justice system. The findings suggest that, while the ruling marks an important milestone in addressing racial profiling, it also raises doubts about the capacity of the courts to identify and confront such situations in practice. © (2026), (Forum Brasileiro de Seguranca Publica). Authors: Vahedi L.; Logie C.
Title: Fragile against what? Imagining climate change resilience by unmasking governance fragility
Abstract: Since the 1990s, fragility has been used to describe low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with limited ability to respond to external threats in ways that ensure citizen safety, security, and welfare. Fragility challenges us to engage with governance, including why and how many institutions (including those in high-income countries) fail to protect citizens during climate change. We ask the question: how can state fragility be applied, critiqued, and expanded when considering climate change, including anthropogenic drivers, extreme weather events, mitigation, and adaptation? We present a globally applicable framework of governance fragility and emphasise the role of institutional-level gaps in motivation/willingness to act, evidence uptake, and implementation in creating fragilities that inhibit climate resilience. Using the United States as a case study, we apply the framework to identify the political ideologies that inform institutional-level motivations, shape evidence uptake, and moderate implementation capacity. This expanded notion of governance fragility (beyond conflict-affected LMICs) offers a globally-relevant lens to imagine possible solutions, including a research-to-practice agenda that contends both with ideology/willingness to act and decentralised forms of climate governance in the face of national-level fragilities. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Outcome severity increases verbal probabilities used in dyadic communications
Abstract: Verbal probability expressions (VPEs) are interpreted as denoting higher numerical probabilities where they describe severe events, as compared to more neutral events (all else equal). Previous research suggests that this effect represents the correction of a perceived tendency for communicators to downplay the likelihood of more severe events, consistent with a rational speech act. We tested whether communicators really do downplay the likelihood of more severe events in four studies (total N = 2210). In each study, participants read four to six scenarios including a numerical probability of either a severe or non-severe negative outcome, and were asked to communicate this probability ‘to a friend’ with a VPE. Our results did not show that communicators downplayed the likelihood of more severe events. Participants typically provided higher VPEs to communicate the same numerical probability when that probability referred to a severe versus a non-severe event. This result was observed when participants communicated about events for which explicit actionable protective actions were highlighted (Study 1), where such actions were stated not to be possible (Studies 2 & 3), and where this was not specified (Study 4). Similar results were observed when participants chose a VPE from a pre-specified list (Studies 1, 2, & 4), and where they chose their communication freely (Study 3). The finding, coupled with those of past research, suggests that severity has a two-fold effect on subjective probability: VPEs are increased, and numerical interpretations of these VPEs are also subsequently increased. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Audrin C.; Hascoët M.
Title: Revisiting control-value theory: A network analysis of parental aspirations, students' control-value appraisals, and their homework emotions
Abstract: Emotions experienced in academic settings play a crucial role in students’ motivation, learning, and overall well-being. Among these, achievement emotions (such as boredom, anxiety, and enjoyment) are particularly relevant as they directly relate to students’ engagement with learning tasks and academic outcomes. Achievement emotions have largely been assessed in the context of the classroom. However, there are less studies focusing on homework emotions. In this work, we are interested in how subjective control and value are related to achievement emotions during homework. We are further interested in assessing how parental aspirations may intervene during the emergence of homework emotions. Using a theory-informed exploratory approach, we aim to uncover the links between emotions, appraisals and parental aspirations and provide new insights for homework achievement emotions literature. 392 students from 7th and 8th grade completed self-reported questionnaires focusing on homework achievement emotions, subjective control, subjective value and parental aspirations. To capture the complexity of these interactions, we perform network analysis, an analytical approach that models the structure of interrelated psychological constructs rather than assuming unidirectional causal chains. Results from the network analysis emphasize that enjoyment and boredom are close to each other despite being negatively related, that control is close and negatively related to anxiety, and that parental aspirations are positively related to anxiety and boredom but not to enjoyment. We discuss the relevance of including parental aspirations to better understand the emergence of achievement homework emotions. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Hydrogen-natural gas blends in pipelines: A review of challenges and opportunities for India
Abstract: Hydrogen blending with natural gas offers a promising way to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through existing pipeline systems, advancing India's shift towards a low-carbon energy system. Including hydrogen in natural gas pipelines offers an approach for long-term emissions reduction while accelerating market development of hydrogen technologies, including electrolysers. The current development of this technique has reached an affordable stage that enables its application at a large scale through existing pipeline infrastructure. According to scientific studies, blending Hydrogen with natural gas substantially cuts down carbon dioxide emissions. Regular blending of hydrogen with natural gas reduces CO2 emissions and can cut down emissions by 11.11% at a 20% hydrogen blend fraction under the specific combustion conditions. The review evaluates different worldwide techniques for blending hydrogen and natural gas. A thorough analysis explores the economic feasibility of hydrogen blending opportunities in India. The present study includes a detailed exploration of natural gas‑hydrogen blends, which explains both the advantages and technical problems and the broad implementation aspects. Authors: Kihara T.
Title: Constrained occupational pathways: Historical ethnic penalties in career mobility among Japanese immigrants in the United States, 1920–1940
Abstract: Racial and ethnic stratification was a persistent feature of the early 20th-century U.S. labor market. While acknowledging structural barriers such as organized exclusion, studies of Japanese immigrants have typically emphasized their upward mobility from laborers to independent farmers or small-business owners before World War II. Yet, few studies have examined how such barriers shaped Japanese mobility relative to that of contemporaneous immigrants from Europe, as well as Canada and Mexico. Using linked 1920–1940 U.S. census panel data, this study compares occupational mobility between first-generation Japanese immigrant men (born 1881–1900) and other immigrants by educational attainment. Findings indicate substantial ethnic occupational penalties for Japanese immigrants, particularly pronounced at higher levels of education, where they ranked below even their similarly educated Mexican counterparts. Whereas European and Canadian immigrants frequently ascended into managerial, professional, and skilled or semi-skilled blue-collar occupations, upward mobility among Japanese immigrants remained largely confined to small-business ownership and farming. Such an absence from mid-tier occupations is consistent with historically documented patterns of organized exclusion from labor unions and labor market discrimination. Title: Can nurse education foster professional authenticity? Four tensions within a regulated profession
Abstract: Professional authenticity has recently been positioned as a form of resistance to restrictive understandings of professionalism (Melino et al., 2025). This commentary positions professional authenticity as ethically accountable, context-responsive practice rather than a personality trait or unrestricted expression of a ‘true self’. The paper also examines four tensions that complicate professional authenticity in nurse education: personal values versus professional obligations; openness and vulnerability versus boundaries and safety; consistency versus context-sensitive adaptation; and self-knowledge versus the socially constructed and partially unknowable self. Nurse educators can foster professional authenticity by employing ethically challenging cases that include situations in which responsibilities are genuinely complex, critical reflection, bounded self-disclosure, and psychologically and culturally safer dialogue. Title: Spatial Epidemiology of Infectious Diseases in Indonesia: Patterns, Clusters, and Environmental Determinants
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: Indonesia’s vast geography, high population density, and environmental diversity contribute to uneven patterns of infectious disease transmission. This study aims to explore the spatial distribution and environmental influences of seven key infectious diseases—acute respiratory infections (ARI), pneumonia, tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis, diarrhea, malaria, and filariasis—across the country's 34 provinces. Spatial statistical techniques—including the Variance Mean Ratio (VMR), Moran’s I, Moran Scatter Plots, and Spatial Autoregressive (SAR) modeling—were applied to detect spatial clustering, spatial autocorrelation, and neighborhood effects. We also examined the role of environmental quality in shaping disease patterns. Strong spatial correlations were observed among ARI, pneumonia, TB, hepatitis, diarrhea, and filariasis. In contrast, malaria displayed a distinct, uncorrelated pattern. SAR modeling revealed positive spatial spillover effects, indicating that neighboring provinces influenced disease occurrences in the province under study. Moreover, provinces with higher EQI scores tended to have lower rates of ARI, TB, diarrhea, and other diseases—except for malaria, which followed a different pattern. Title: Engaging with ChatGPT: A qualitative meta-synthesis of nursing students' experiences and perceptions
Abstract: Background: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, ChatGPT, as an interactive large language model, is increasingly entering higher education settings and influencing how students access information and engage in learning activities. As both important users of digital technologies and future nursing professionals, nursing students' experiences, perceptions, and reflections regarding ChatGPT are essential for understanding how this technology may be incorporated into nursing education. Aim: This study aimed to systematically synthesize qualitative evidence on nursing students' experiences of ChatGPT, explore their perceived benefits and challenges, and provide an evidence base to inform the development of nursing education practice. Methods: 11 databases were searched for relevant articles, with searches conducted up to May 2026. Two researchers independently performed literature screening, quality assessment, and data extraction. The Joanna Briggs Institute's qualitative research appraisal tool was used to evaluate the methodological quality of the included studies and the ConQual approach was applied to assess confidence of the synthesized findings. Results: Ten studies were included and synthesized into three core themes and ten sub-themes. The core themes were: benefiting from human-AI collaboration, reflecting on application dilemmas and rebuilding the educational ecosystem. The sub-themes comprised: optimizing information acquisition, empowering academic research, gaining emotional support, over-dependence tendencies, information quality concerns, limitations in professional suitability, academic integrity and ethical concerns, updating the curriculum system, innovating teaching methods, and improving practice guidelines. Conclusion: ChatGPT presents both advantages and limitations in nursing education. The synthesized findings suggested that nursing students' experiences of ChatGPT were diverse, may shaped by individual, technological, and institutional factors. Nursing educators and institutions may therefore consider complementing technical training with greater attention to develop a comprehensive educational support system that promotes more cautious and responsible use of ChatGPT in nursing education. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How users interpret AI-assisted reviews: Disclosure design and authenticity perceptions
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly involved in digital content creation, disclosure messages play an important role in shaping how users interpret human–AI collaboration. Drawing on cue utilization theory, this study examines how two dimensions of AI disclosure—authorship dominance (human-centered vs. AI-centered) and AI role framing (logical, emotional, or integrity enhancement)—influence the perceived authenticity of online reviews across search and experience goods. A 2 × 3 × 2 mixed-factorial experiment was conducted with 272 Korean online shoppers. Linear mixed-effects analyses showed that human-centered disclosure produced higher perceived authenticity than AI-centered disclosure overall. However, AI role framing did not have a uniform main effect; instead, its influence depended on authorship dominance and product type. For search goods, human-centered disclosure enhanced perceived authenticity when AI was framed as supporting integrity, whereas for experience goods, this advantage emerged when AI was framed as supporting logical organization. No significant authorship-dominance difference was found under emotional-expression enhancement. Product-specific Bayesian mediation analyses further showed that disclosure configurations influenced purchase intention through perceived authenticity and platform trust, although the relative serial indirect effects differed across product types. For search goods, all comparison conditions produced lower serial indirect effects than the human-centered integrity-enhancement condition, whereas for experience goods, a significant difference emerged only for the AI-centered logical-enhancement condition. These findings demonstrate that AI disclosure functions as a set of interdependent interpretive cues through which users infer human agency, the nature of AI involvement, and the authenticity of AI-assisted reviews. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Teacher agency in student learning outcomes–based curriculum reform: perspectives from federal and provincial secondary schools in Pakistan
Abstract: International education research foregrounds the contextual and relational dimensions of educational change, shaped by global and local policy pressures and structural constraints (Bromley & Meyer, 2023). Rather than treating comparison as a methodological device, the paper engages with the process of change itself, a process in which teachers continually compare current practice with what the reform intends it to become in order to enact it. The findings indicate that teachers' enactment of SLO-oriented reforms is shaped by persistent, systemic and classroom-level realities, and demonstrates individual resilience within constrained conditions. By situating teachers' experiences within global-local policy dynamics, and across two differently resourced sites, the paper contributes to ongoing debates on teacher agency and policy enactment in resource-constrained settings. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Associated factors of anxiety symptoms among reproductive married women in Bangladesh: Using a structural equation model with decomposition analysis
Abstract: Background Anxiety symptoms can undermine women's wellbeing and family functioning. This study examines the associated factors with moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms and wealth-related inequalities among currently married women of reproductive age in Bangladesh. Methods This cross-sectional study analyzed 13,438 currently married women aged 15–49 years from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey, 2022. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression was used as the primary analytical model, supplemented by exploratory path analysis for assessing direct and indirect associations. Wealth-related inequality in anxiety symptoms was evaluated using concentration indices and decomposition analysis. Results The weighted prevalence of moderate to severe anxiety symptoms among currently reproductive married women in Bangladesh was 4.1% (95% CI: 0.04–0.05). Survey-weighted regression indicated that high endorsement of attitudes justifying intimate partner violence, older age, sexual inactivity, pregnancy termination, and having no children were associated with higher odds of anxiety symptoms. Title: A comparative analysis of the drivers and outcomes of work, location and commuting choices of the office only, hybrid, and home/other location only workers
Abstract: Hybrid work has become a mainstream work pattern in addition to only working in the office or working from home (WFH). This paper compares the three work groups within a framework covering drivers and outcomes for work, location and commuting choices, using survey data of 981 randomly sampled employees in Australia. A discrete choice model for the three groups suggests that commuting and work patterns for each day of the week (DoW) and time of the day (ToD), together with roles in the organisation, enable us to predict whether employees are likely to belong to one of three work-location alternatives. The research goes beyond the traditional socioeconomic characteristics of employees to examine more in-depth reasons why the three groups choose the way they work and commute, and their work-related motivation, performance and wellbeing. The research identifies the following key findings: 1) Having the highest level of work-related motivation drives hybrid workers to work hard with more working hours than other groups. The long working hours, however, have a detrimental effect on their wellbeing and job performance, despite the highest level of job satisfaction. 2) The WFH only group has the healthiest wellbeing and the least counterproductive work behaviour on job performance. This suggests that work location is not the key reason for poor job performance. 3) The office-only workers have the best task performance as well as the second-best performance for contextual performance where more responsibilities and challenges are required. Title: Flourishing profiles and associated factors among undergraduate nursing interns: A cross-sectional study using latent profile analysis
Abstract: Background: As clinical nursing practice continues to evolve, undergraduate nursing interns face substantial psychological challenges during the transition from students to healthcare professionals. Flourishing, a key indicator of positive psychological functioning, encompasses positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment, and overall well-being. Despite growing interest in positive psychology within nursing education, the flourishing profiles of undergraduate nursing interns and the factors associated with these profiles remain insufficiently explored. Aim: This study aimed to identify latent profiles of flourishing among undergraduate nursing interns and examine the factors associated with these profiles. Design: A cross-sectional study using latent profile analysis. Setting: The study was conducted across multiple universities and teaching hospitals in Zhejiang and Shanxi provinces, China. Methods: Participants completed the PERMA-Profiler and a General Information Questionnaire. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was employed to identify distinct flourishing profiles. Univariate analyses and multinomial logistic regression were conducted to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results: Latent profile analysis of 315 undergraduate nursing interns identified a three-profile solution comprising a low flourishing group (29.8%), a moderate flourishing group (54.0%), and a high flourishing group (16.2%). Multinomial logistic regression identified several factors significantly associated with flourishing profile membership, including family relationship quality, attention to job recruitment information, career planning, student leadership experience, and prior internal medicine internship experience. Conclusion: Flourishing among undergraduate nursing interns is heterogeneous, and both individual and environmental factors are associated with profile membership. Title: Intergenerational sustainability: Overcoming barriers via participatory governance, regenerative economics and cultural preservation
Abstract: Intergenerational sustainability represents a significant socio-ecological concern of the twenty-first century, requiring governance frameworks, economic models, and cultural practices to account for the interests and well-being of future generations. Existing literature remains fragmented across disciplinary silos, often failing to reconcile technocratic policy interventions with Indigenous custodial epistemologies. This study addresses this gap by synthesizing 41 comparative cross-sectoral cases from peer-reviewed qualitative secondary literature spanning diverse contexts in 18 countries. Building on these cross-case patterns, we construct an Integrated System Model for Intergenerational Sustainability, conceived as a conceptual heuristic rather than a predictive or empirically validated model. This model articulates the systemic interactions across three core dimensions: Economic (regenerative models vs. market hegemony), Governance (future-generation representation vs. presentist electoral bias), and Cultural (Indigenous knowledge systems vs. epistemicide). Furthermore, we propose an operationalization framework for the ‘future ancestors bias' not merely as a normative critique, but as a structural governance failure described through four proposed observable indicators: Temporal Liability Transfer Ratio, Intergenerational Discount Rate Asymmetry, Representation Deficit Indicator, and Epistemic Exclusion Indicator. We also advance three testable theoretical propositions governing inter-dimensional nexuses—including the Water-Energy-Food-Forests (WEFF) nexus and institutional path-dependency. Our comparative synthesis indicates that addressing intergenerational equity may require moving beyond Western-centric sustainable development toward a ‘custodial ethic of sustainable coexistence.’ Such a transition would involve institutionalizing future-generation ombudspersons, enacting reparative land tenure redistribution, and developing pluriversal governance frameworks that recognize the legal personhood of nature. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Preparing teachers for multigrade classrooms: An action research study of a preservice teacher education curriculum

Title: Daily associations among protective behavioral strategies, alcohol use, and consequences in a sample of adolescents and young adults: The influence of drinking context and neighborhood disadvantage

Title: The impact of urban greening policies: Evidence from China's National Garden City Program
Abstract: Urban greening has become a widely adopted policy strategy for improving environmental quality and urban livability. However, the effectiveness of large-scale government-led greening programs and their ecological outcomes remain insufficiently evaluated, particularly in rapidly urbanizing countries. China's National Garden City Program (NGCP), implemented nationwide for more than three decades, represents one of the world's most extensive urban greening policy initiatives. Title: Negotiating relational goals in PhD vivas: A multimodal, interpersonal-pragmatic analysis of how examiners manage supervisors’ face
Abstract: In PhD vivas, examiners are often confronted with the challenge of meeting expectations as ‘gatekeepers’ and managing the face needs of candidates’ supervisors (whose supervisory expertise also indirectly comes under scrutiny) without sacrificing rigour. This notwithstanding, virtually none of the limited research on relational work in PhD vivas in English for academic/specific purposes (EAP/ESP) has investigated how examiners negotiate such critical moments successfully to maintain healthy interpersonal relationships with candidates’ supervisors. Moreover, with few exceptions, most studies on PhD vivas have focused solely on linguistic features, although communication is often conceptualised as a multimodal phenomenon among many applied linguists. Analysis foregrounds relational strategies that examiners in the context of the study employ to manage supervisors’ face—affirming the supervisors, shifting responsibility away from them, and strategically realigning with them. Analysis also highlights examiners’ use of embodied communicative resources to perform interactive, pragmatic and modal functions, the latter of which intensify both face-enhancing and face-aggravating speech acts. Findings demonstrate that, in such high–stakes interactions, examiners employ rapport strategies to manage not just the supervisors’ quality and identity face, but also the intergroup face of the panel and faculty. Title: Exploring periodic and temporal association in crime incidents using time-constrained geographically weighted colocation quotient analysis

Title: A comparative study on textual and multimodal PII detection using large language models

Title: The effects of AI-based research ethics education program on academic ethical awareness, attitudes toward plagiarism, and research ethics knowledge among nursing students: A quasi-experimental study

Title: Psychometric evaluation of the hypersexual behavior inventory in a Brazilian sample of gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men: Bifactor structure, item response theory, and preliminary classification indicators

Title: A CCTV based early warning framework for crowd safety in high density religious events
Abstract: Crowd disasters at large religious gatherings continue to cause fatalities, particularly in high-density events where crowd management relies on reactive monitoring rather than anticipatory safety control. Although CCTV surveillance is widely deployed, it rarely provides advance warning of escalating crowd risk. Most existing crowd forecasting studies rely on simulated data or low-density environments, limiting their applicability to real, high-density religious gatherings. There is a lack of validated early warning frameworks that operate on real CCTV data and generate actionable risk alerts suitable for operational use. This study develops an integrated early warning framework that forecasts crowd parameters, density, flow, and entropy, using time-series modelling applied to CCTV footage from the 2016 Kumbh Mela in India. Forecasted parameters are converted into location-specific risk levels through a classification module and visualised using graded warnings designed for control-room deployment. Model performance and transferability are evaluated across two spatially distinct locations within the same event venue. The forecasting model achieved R2 values between 0.70 and 0.92 and mean absolute percentage error values of 0.8–33.6% across the three parameters, providing reliable 10-minute advance forecasts. The model generalised effectively to a secondary study location without retraining. The risk classification system achieved 93–98% recall in distinguishing Low- and Medium-risk conditions. Authors: Wang Y.; Chen K.; Miao Q.; Liu C.; Li Y.
Title: Self-balanced information bottleneck for few-shot multimodal information extraction
Abstract: Few-shot multimodal information extraction (FMIE) seeks to recognize named entity pair and their corresponding relation from scarce annotated multimodal instance. Existing methods primarily leverage external knowledge generated by large language models to compensate for the lack of supervision in few-shot learning. However, knowledge over-injection tends to introduce task-irrelevant knowledge, which interferes with effective representation learning. In addition, a knowledge imbalance between task-irrelevant and task-relevant knowledge can induce overfitting, ultimately impairing prediction results. In this paper, we propose a novel self-balanced information bottleneck (SBIB) model for solving the aforementioned FMIE challenges. Specifically, SBIB model consists of a compact knowledge injection (CKI) module and a self-balance knowledge (SBK) module that collaboratively learns compact and meaningful knowledge to obtain optimal multimodal representations. The CKI module introduces a mutual information minimization–maximization strategy to effectively compress task-irrelevant knowledge while preserving task-relevant knowledge. Then, the SBK module incorporates a novel heuristic strategy that adaptively achieves a trade-off between task-relevant and task-irrelevant knowledge. Finally, we integrate the two modules into deep IB framework to enhance the performance of FMIE task. Experimental results on three benchmark few-shot datasets show the superiority of the SBIB model. Referring to the representative Macro F1 score metric, SBIB model outperforms the strongest baseline, KECPM, by 3.12% on FS-JMERE dataset. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Association between abnormal theta oscillation-default mode network functional connectivity and internet addiction behavior in adolescent depression patients: a resting-state EEG study
Abstract: Background Major depressive disorder (MDD) and internet addiction (IA) are closely linked in adolescents, yet the neurobiological mechanisms underlying their relationship remain unclear. This study aimed to explore the role of abnormal functional connectivity (FC) between theta oscillation and the default mode network (DMN) in IA development among adolescent MDD patients. Methods A total of 183 drug-naive first-episode adolescent MDD patients and 93 healthy controls (HC) were enrolled. Clinical assessments were conducted using the HAMD-24, HAMA, and Young Internet Addiction Scale, with MDD patients divided into IA and MDD subgroups. Resting-state EEG data were collected for time–frequency analysis, brain electrical source reconstruction, and FC analysis, with statistical tests performed via SPSS 22.0. Results The IA group had higher scores in depression, anxiety, anhedonia, and IA severity than the MDD and HC groups. Theta band power spectral density (PSD) was lower in the IA group than in the MDD group, while both MDD groups exhibited higher theta PSD than HCs. IA was associated with abnormal intra-DMN connections; theta oscillation mediated the relationship between anhedonia and IA severity. HC subjects had stronger DMN FC across Delta, Theta, Alpha, and Gamma bands than MDD patients, and the MDD group showed stronger theta-band DMN FC than the IA group. Conclusions Abnormal theta oscillation-DMN network correlates with IA in adolescent MDD patients, and the mediating role of theta oscillation provides a new perspective for understanding the neural mechanism of this comorbidity. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Yu R.; Su J.; Fan Z.; Weng M.; Yin X.; Gong Y.
Title: Dynamic interactions between depressive and somatic symptoms following a positive psychology intervention: Evidence from a cross-lagged panel network analysis
Abstract: Aims To investigate the dynamic relationships between depressive and somatic symptoms among perinatal women and to explore the potential influence of a positive psychology intervention on symptom network evolution using a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) approach. Methods This exploratory secondary analysis used data from a community-based randomized controlled trial. A total of 687 women received a positive psychology intervention and 735 received usual care, with assessments at baseline (T1), 1 month postpartum (T2), and 3 months postpartum (T3). Depressive-related and somatic symptoms were assessed using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) and Somatic Symptom Scale-8 (SSS-8), respectively. CLPN models were estimated separately by group. Results Depression-related symptoms, including anhedonia, reduced enjoyment, self-blame, difficulty coping, sadness, and crying, remained prevalent, while anxiety and panic were also frequently observed as anxiety-related manifestations within the EPDS. Fatigue or low energy was the most frequent somatic symptom. Network patterns differed between groups across T1-T2 and T2-T3. In the control group, anxiety, panic, and difficulty coping showed cross-lagged associations with dizziness during T1-T2, while anxiety and panic and panic and sadness showed bidirectional associations during T2-T3. The intervention group showed fewer network connections and cross-domain associations, with anxiety linked to gastrointestinal discomfort, back pain, headache, and dizziness during T1-T2, and back pain occupying a prominent predictive and bridging position during T2-T3. Conclusions Depression-related and somatic symptoms showed distinct temporal network patterns across the perinatal period. These exploratory findings provide a basis for further validation of symptom network patterns and their relevance to perinatal psychological interventions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Imagining transformation across systems: institutional logics and their dynamics within a cross-sectoral food-health pilot
Abstract: We examined the Food Pharmacy in Rotterdam as a hybrid food-health pilot. Designed as a food-based intervention for patients with type-II diabetes, the pilot offers an insight into how institutional boundaries between agrifood and health are reconfigured in practice. We analyzed how institutional logics interact within the Food Pharmacy as well as its transformative potential and perceived pathways for scaling.Building on the institutional logics perspective, multisystem transformation, and debates on scaling, the analysis shows that transformation arises not from replacing old logics but from their tension and blending. Early relational practices created openings for experimentation, yet institutional pressures around efficiency and standardization repeatedly narrowed this space, prompting actors to engage in reactive blending. These oscillations shaped how respondents envisioned scaling: scaling deep drew on relational foundations, scaling out on cross-sector improvisations, and scaling up on alignment with formal structures.The study draws on interviews, observations, and documents, identifying four logics: State, Market, Professional Biomedical, and Community. Each shaped the pilot in dynamic and contested ways. State and Market logics provided resources and legitimacy but often imposed bureaucratic and profit-oriented frames. Community and Professional logics sustained engagement by stressing belonging, fairness, and rights to healthy food.The findings highlight how relational, culturally embedded practices remain difficult to institutionalize within governance frameworks privileging measurable outcomes. The Food Pharmacy illustrates both the promise and fragility of cross-sectoral innovation: new practices and connections can emerge, but their realization depends on governance systems capable of supporting relational work over time. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Wang M.; Li X.
Title: Differentiated associations between urbanization structure and asset wealth inequality in Africa
Abstract: Understanding the relationship between urbanization and inequality is critical for explaining regional disparities in developing countries. However, existing studies often treat urbanization as homogeneous, and the associations between urbanization structures and asset wealth inequality in Africa remain underexplored. To address this gap, this study integrates high-resolution asset wealth and urbanization data to examine associations between urbanization structures and inequality across Africa from 2000 to 2024. The results indicate that asset wealth growth in Africa exhibits pronounced urban–rural divergence, with rural areas experiencing less than half the growth observed in urban areas, corresponding to persistent regional disparities. Asset wealth growth also differs markedly across urbanization structure transition pathways, with regions transitioning toward higher levels of urbanization demonstrating faster wealth accumulation. Further econometric analysis reveals significant structural heterogeneity in the associations between urbanization and inequality: urbanization patterns characterized by suburban expansion and dense urban development are associated with higher inequality, whereas urban centre development is associated with lower inequality. Conditional scenario simulations further suggest that future urbanization pathways characterized by greater urban centre development may potentially correspond to lower levels of asset wealth inequality in Africa, although the magnitude of these changes remains uncertain. By adopting an urbanization structure perspective, this study highlights that the relationship between urbanization and inequality depends not only on the extent of urbanization but also on its spatial structure, providing new evidence for understanding urbanization–inequality dynamics and informing more inclusive urban development strategies in developing countries. Authors: Tao R.; Yu J.; Zhao Z.
Title: Race-to-the-bottom dynamics in industrial land pricing: Asymmetric effects of China's 2009 price floor adjustment policy
Abstract: Minimum price floors are a common but understudied instrument for regulating industrial land markets in developing economies. We exploit China's 2009 adjustment of minimum industrial land prices, which lowered the minimum land price in some counties and raised it in others. Combining parcel-level land transactions with county characteristics in a difference-in-differences design, we find a striking asymmetry: easing counties experienced a 9.15% decline in industrial land prices and a 23.12% expansion in transferred area, whereas tightening counties showed no detectable change. The asymmetry reflects the floor's initial binding status: it was binding in easing counties, where competition for mobile manufacturing capital pushed prices down and expanded land supply, but non-binding in tightening counties, where the raised floor either stayed below market prices or was offset through rebates and subsidies. Easing counties also gained 15.53% more large-scale industrial enterprises relative to the sample mean and 7.90% in fiscal revenue, yet new land sales concentrated in low- and medium-low-tech, land-intensive sectors, a pattern that persisted through 2022 with no shift toward higher-tech industries. Relaxing a binding industrial land price floor thus brings short-run gains in firm entry and fiscal revenue but leaves these counties specialized in low-tech industries, consistent with race-to-the-bottom competition operating through industrial land pricing. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: OmniTraj: Pre-training on heterogeneous data for adaptive and zero-shot human trajectory prediction
Source title: Transportation Research Part C: Emerging Technologies
Abstract: Accurate trajectory prediction of vulnerable road users is a cornerstone of safe autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems. While large-scale pre-training has advanced this field, achieving robust zero-shot generalization remains a critical challenge for real-world deployment, particularly when vehicles encounter unseen environments and heterogeneous sensor configurations (e.g., varying frame rates and observation horizons). In this work, we revisit zero-shot trajectory prediction from the perspective of distribution shifts and distinguish three transfer settings: temporal transfer, scene transfer, and joint scene–temporal transfer. Through systematic experiments, we show that temporal mismatch is a key source of failure in current pre-trained models. By isolating temporal configuration from dataset shift, we demonstrate that explicitly conditioning on temporal metadata provides a simple and highly effective solution. Building on this insight, we propose OmniTraj, a Transformer-based framework pre-trained on large-scale heterogeneous data with explicit temporal-aware design. OmniTraj is designed to handle omni-generalization in trajectory prediction, namely adaptability across temporal configuration and scene shifts. It achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization under joint scene–temporal transfer, reducing prediction error by over 70%. Furthermore, it exhibits exceptional robustness in safety-critical edge cases with severely limited observations and maintains high few-shot data efficiency, paving the way for scalable, dataset-agnostic deployment in real-world autonomous systems. Authors: He Z.; Zhao W.; Rui J.
Title: Seeing prosperity, confronting crime: Infrastructure inequality and perceived wealth in Chinese cities
Abstract: Cities increasingly rely on infrastructure investment and streetscape upgrading to improve urban conditions, yet how macro-scale infrastructure inequality and micro-scale street environments relate to different dimensions of urban experience remains insufficiently understood. This study develops a geospatial learning framework to examine their associations with two distinct outcomes across Chinese cities: recorded crime rates and perceived wealth. The framework combines network-based accessibility measures for infrastructure systems, within-city inequality indicators, street-view-derived environmental and perceptual measures, and interpretable machine-learning analysis. The results reveal divergent spatial patterns. Recorded crime rates are most strongly associated with inequalities in telecommunications and educational infrastructure accessibility, together with selected streetscape characteristics. Telecommunications accessibility inequality shows a strong positive association with recorded crime rates, with its contribution becoming more pronounced at higher levels of inequality. By contrast, perceived wealth is explained predominantly by directly visible streetscape characteristics, particularly greenness, complexity, and openness, while infrastructure, socioeconomic, and security-governance variables contribute less. These findings show that recorded crime and perceived wealth capture different dimensions of the urban environment: the former is more closely associated with infrastructure accessibility inequality and selected street conditions, whereas the latter is primarily structured by visual streetscape cues. This distinction highlights the need to consider both spatial inequality and street-level environmental quality in evaluating urban conditions. For urban policy, strategies focused on beautification alone may overlook underlying vulnerabilities, while more equitable infrastructure provision may better address persistent spatial disparities in recorded crime rates. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Striving for excellence or chasing perfection? Differential associations with test anxiety for students in tertiary education
Abstract: Past studies have found an unexpectedly small and inconsistent association between perfectionistic standards and test anxiety. One plausible explanation is that the measurement of perfectionistic standards did not differentiate between the pursuit of excellence and perfection. Our primary goal across two studies was to examine the unique associations of excellencism and perfectionistic standards (controlling for each other) with test anxiety among tertiary education students. Consistent with the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism, the results of Study 1 (N = 273) showed a positive association between perfectionistic standards and test anxiety. A positive association was also observed for secondary outcomes, including fear of failure and mistake rumination. Results of Study 2 (N = 248) replicated these findings for test anxiety and fear of failure. Also, perfectionistic standards were positively associated with catastrophizing about small mistakes, use of reassurance-seeking safety behaviors, and lower self-reported academic performance. When separated from excellencism, perfectionistic standards showed a positive link with test anxiety and variables from its nomological network. Title: Organizational control outside of work: a multi-method investigation of an emerging psychosocial hazard
Abstract: Theory and research have documented the ways in which organizations control workers during work hours. However, with new technical possibilities and societal trends towards greater integration between work and home, some organizations have adopted practices that control workers outside of primary work contexts, a phenomenon that is less commonly researched. Focusing on fly-in-fly out (FIFO) camps in Australia, and drawing on total institution (TI) theory, we explore the nature of organizational control practices in employer-provided camps and investigate how they affect worker identity and mental health. Combining qualitative (i.e., interviews, n = 24) and quantitative (i.e., surveys; n = 479) approaches, our results show that control practices manifest in FIFO camps in profound ways via stringent rules, surveillance, and treating everyday aspects as privileges. These practices encroach on workers’ identity through identity suppression and identity duality. Our results further indicate that the control practices are overall detrimental to worker mental health, and that this impact operates mostly through identity suppression and less through identity duality. We advocate for further research to explore the impact of these sorts of organizational control practices on outcomes beyond mental health as well as within other non-work contexts. Practically, we encourage organizational leaders to balance control practices alongside safety and productivity interests in ways that safeguard worker mental health. Copyright © 2026.
