Authors: Sharma Pathak J.
Title: The Sorcerer’s apprentice and riverine publics: hydrosocial assemblages, disasters and political responses from below in the Brahmaputra River Valley of Assam
Abstract: Despite being subjected to escalating levels of engineering interventions to control and harness rivers, the Brahmaputra Valley of Assam is among the worst flood-and-erosion-affected areas globally. This article develops the concept of riverine publics to theorize politics from below in response to the inability of the state and its engineering endeavors to manage rivers, whose volatility and disastrousness are in part a paradoxical outcome of their designs.This paper uses the assemblage analytic and draws together scholarship on critical water studies, disaster studies, and publics. Utilizing the hydrosocial lens, I analyze how fluvial disasters and their governance represent complex entanglements of rivers, the environment, the state, infrastructure, and people. I track these relationships through a case study of embankment breaching and avulsions along the Nonoi and Kulsi Rivers, two north-bank tributaries of the Brahmaputra River.The paper argues that flood and erosion events are emergent outcomes of hydrosocial assemblages. Further, I argue that hydraulic actions of rivers within hydrosocial assemblages and the consequent spatial patterns of vulnerability they generate spark the formation of riverine publics, which respond to the threats posed by floods and erosion to protect their land, lives, and livelihoods. Despite the absence of formal mechanisms of participation, riverine publics play an integral, albeit unacknowledged, role in river management and the governance of fluvial disasters.Through an examination of the socio-material and emergent dynamics of fluvial disasters and public formation, the paper studies why, where, how, and with what kinds of demands and sociotechnical imaginaries, publics assemble to modulate their riverine environments. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
Abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the strength of the relationship between trait narcissism and emotion dysregulation. PsycINFO, MEDLINE Complete, Scopus, Embase, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global databases were searched on 7 January 2026 for two concepts: narcissism and emotion dysregulation. Included studies were written in English, included adult samples, used validated self-report measures of narcissism and emotion dysregulation, and reported their relationship. Further moderator analyses revealed significant, weak, positive correlations between narcissism and specific emotion regulation difficulties (i.e., non-acceptance of emotions, impulse control difficulties, and limited access to emotion regulation strategies). Title: Expectations, emotional responses, and early experiences with a newly introduced autonomous metro
Abstract: Rapid advances in automation are transforming transport systems worldwide, with autonomous technologies increasingly being deployed in public transport. This study examines public perceptions of a newly introduced autonomous metro system during its initial phase of operation in Thessaloniki, Greece. Title: Childhood loneliness and deficit-accumulation frailty progression in mid-to-late life
Abstract: Background: Adult loneliness has been linked to various age-related conditions, yet the long-term consequences of childhood loneliness remain poorly understood. This study examined the association between childhood loneliness and frailty progression in mid-to-late adulthood. Methods: We analyzed data from 13,643 participants in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study from 2011 through 2018. Childhood loneliness was defined based on self-reported frequent feelings of loneliness and the absence of close friendships before the age of 17. Frailty, defined using a 40-item deficit-accumulation frailty index (FI), was repeatedly measured. Linear mixed-effect models were used to evaluate the associations between childhood loneliness and frailty progression. Results: Of 13,643 participants (mean [SD] age, 58.48 [9.42] years; 6445 [47.2%] male), 561 (4.1%) reported definite childhood loneliness, while 6580 (48.2%) reported possible childhood loneliness. Compared with people without childhood loneliness, those with definite loneliness had higher baseline FI (β = 1.740; 95% CI: 0.903 to 2.576) and faster frailty progression (β = 0.289; 95% CI: 0.145 to 0.433). Possible childhood loneliness was also associated with accelerated frailty progression (β = 0.153; 95% CI: 0.095 to 0.210). These associations persisted after adjusting for adult loneliness, and no significant interaction between childhood and adult loneliness was observed. Childhood loneliness remained significantly associated with faster FI progression among individuals without adult loneliness Conclusions: In this national cohort, childhood loneliness was associated with accelerated frailty progression in adulthood, independent of adult loneliness. Title: Does sustainability enhance or compromise aviation safety? A systematic review
Abstract: Aviation is pushing hard towards net-zero, yet what this means for safety remains poorly understood. This systematic review analyses 129 studies (2015–2025), coded into 451 excerpts across nine types of aviation organisation, to ask whether, where, and how sustainability initiatives affect safety. Sustainability initiatives are neither good nor bad for safety in themselves. They improve safety when built into everyday operations and management, through clearer procedures, stronger governance, and better decision support. They harm safety when procedures are immature, infrastructure is not ready, or oversight is weak. Building on this evidence, this paper develops the sustainability–safety nexus, a new framework that treats safety as a core part of sustainability. It rests on Safety-II thinking and four pillars: technology, management commitment, adaptive safety management systems, and international regulatory collaboration. This study translates it into three practical levers, including integrated ESG/CSR–SMS governance, sustainability management of change, and Safety-II learning loops. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Deconstructing and evaluating China's land consolidation from the dual perspective of quantity and quality
Abstract: The spatiotemporal patterns of land consolidation in China have undergone profound reshaping, exerting significant impacts on socioeconomic development. Based on land use data from 2000 to 2024, this study analyzes the multi-scale spatiotemporal evolution and multidimensional effects of Chin's land consolidation from the two dimensions of quantity and quality, specifically through cultivated land conversion area and cultivated land fragmentation. Significant spatial heterogeneity is identified. Four governance modes emerge: a “high-quantity-high-quality” synergistic improvement in the Northeast Plain; a coexistence of “high-quantity-low-quality” in the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau; a “low-quantity-high-quality” optimization in the Huang-Huai-Hai Plain; and a “low-quantity-low-quality” lag in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Markov-chain forecasts indicate that cultivated land conversion is mobile under policy intervention and spatial spillovers, whereas cultivated land fragmentation remains rigid and stable due to natural constraints and spatial lock-in. Using the High-Standard Farmland Construction Policy as a quasi-natural experiment, land consolidation is found to have significantly increased grain production capacity and agricultural net carbon sequestration, while its effects on land transfer exhibit marked regional heterogeneity. Stronger policy responses in yield improvement and carbon-sink gains are observed in central western regions and major grain-producing areas, whereas land-transfer markets in eastern China are more sensitive to policy shocks. Title: How to deal with AI technology anxiety and its negative consequences? The role of strengths-based leadership
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into hospitality operations, employees’ AI technology anxiety has emerged as a salient managerial concern. Drawing on social information processing theory, this study examines the effect of strengths-based leadership on AI technology anxiety and the subsequent influence of this anxiety on employees’ social loafing behavior. Across a time-lagged field study and an experiment, the findings reveal the following key results. First, strengths-based leadership effectively alleviated hospitality employees’ AI technology anxiety, thereby reducing their social loafing behavior. Second, job automation weakened the negative effect of strengths-based leadership on AI technology anxiety. Title: When AI ads violate expectations: the interplay of AI character, product type, and advertising appeal of AI ads on consumer attitudes

Abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping video advertising production. Using expectancy violations theory as an interpretive lens, this study develops a framework in which ad appeal (rational vs. emotional), product type (high-tech vs. low-tech), and AI character embodiment (no character vs. animal-like vs. human-like) jointly relate to ad attitude and to two appraisals: perceived novelty and perceived uncanniness. Novelty is positively and uncanniness negatively associated with ad attitude, and the indirect effects through both appraisals are consistent with the proposed process. Title: Ensuring eco-resilience in Physical Internet-enabled production routing problem under ripple effect: a scenario-based robust possibilistic flexible programming approach
Abstract: Abstract: Resilience and eco-friendliness have emerged as two pivotal objectives for modern supply chains facing increasing disruptions and sustainability demands. Title: When AI wears a face: How AI appearance shapes intentionality attributions in service success and failure
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Customer-facing AI agents are becoming frontline service interfaces, yet firms still face a consequential design question: should these agents look human-like or robot-like? This research examines how AI agent appearance shapes consumers' intentionality attributions in AI-mediated service encounters and how these inferences translate into satisfaction and future AI use intention. Title: Why they come (back): Motive clusters of seasonal employees and their multiple workplace commitments

Authors: Fang J.; Pan Y.
Title: Not alone: How group photos enhance audience responses to virtual influencers
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Although marketers increasingly use virtual influencers to engage consumers, concerns about authenticity continue to limit their effectiveness. This research examines whether group photos can make virtual influencers appear more socially connected and authentic, thereby improving audience responses. We propose that, compared with no-person images or solo photos, group photos provide visual social cues that place virtual influencers in recognizable interpersonal contexts and make them appear more socially connected in shared experiences. Title: Cultural value configurations and guests’ evaluations of AI-enabled service technologies
Abstract: As Artificial Intelligence reshapes hospitality service delivery, understanding how culturally diverse guests evaluate AI-enabled encounters is critical. Title: What drives versus what is required: Sufficient and necessary conditions for consumer intention in an unfamiliar wellness service
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Despite the growing importance of wellness and health tourism, little is known about how individuals who have never experienced thermal spa treatments form intentions toward such services. Title: When does inconsistency help? The nonlinear effect of AI summary-rating inconsistency on consumer purchase intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in e-commerce platforms, AI-generated review summaries have emerged as an important information source for consumers. Title: What Strategies Can Payers Use to Negotiate Medicine Prices Globally? Insights and Lessons for Low-Income Countries from a Scoping Review
Abstract: Objectives No comprehensive global review has synthesized mechanisms, strengths, limitations, and implementation challenges of pharmaceutical pricing policies. This scoping review aimed to examine global pharmaceutical pricing policies and generate policy-relevant insights, particularly for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Methods Electronic searches were conducted in Medline, CINAHL, EconLit, and Embase using predefined inclusion criteria. Gray literature was identified through government publications and World Health Organization reports, and reference lists of relevant studies were screened. The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute scoping review framework and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews guidelines. Results Searches conducted up to May 2024 and updated in February 2026 identified 88 eligible studies. Reference pricing was the most commonly reported strategy, used in 85% of identified countries, offering simplicity and transparency through price benchmarking. Value-based pricing was widely adopted in high-income countries, aligning prices with health outcomes but requiring strong health technology assessment infrastructure. Managed entry agreements were reported in 56% of countries and were used to improve access to new medicines while mitigating financial risk. Indication-specific pricing was implemented in 9 countries but faced operational challenges. Compulsory licensing in several LMICs improved access to essential medicines at lower cost, although concerns regarding impacts on pharmaceutical innovation were noted. Most countries combined multiple pricing approaches to balance affordability, access, and innovation. Conclusions Although value-based pricing and managed entry agreements are common in high-income settings, simpler approaches such as reference pricing and compulsory licensing may be more feasible in LMICs. Context-specific strategies are needed to balance access, affordability, and sustainability. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: AI for guilt, human for encouragement? The interaction effects of creator type and emotional appeal on green purchase intention

Abstract: Green advertising inherently embeds emotional appeal to drive consumer responses. Title: Entropy as a diagnostic for time-related constraints on circular transition: Evidence from plastic waste management in the OECD–EU countries

Title: Simulation-Based Assessment of Business Process Robustness

Abstract: Business process robustness describes a process’s ability to meet performance targets despite variations in parameters such as arrival rates or resource availability. Assessing business process robustness quantitatively is challenging because dependencies between process parameters and performance are complex and stochastic. Business process simulation avoids the need to specify those dependencies by simulating the process and observing the resulting behavior. Our evaluation demonstrates that the proposed approach substantially reduces assessment complexity compared to our baselines while accurately identifying parameter combinations under which a process remains robust. Title: Navigating travel paradoxes: Gen Z coping responses and implications for destination management
Source title: Journal of Destination Marketing and Management
Abstract: Paradoxes involve contradictory yet interdependent poles that persist rather than disappearing when one side is chosen. Tourism routinely exposes travelers to such tensions, but traveler-level paradoxes and the responses used to navigate them remain underexamined. Using the early tourism-recovery period of 2022 as the empirical context, this study examines paradoxical tensions perceived by young adult Gen Z student travelers and how they respond to them. A two-stage qualitative design was employed. Study A recruited 98 Norwegian Gen Z student travelers, of whom 95 provided useable responses; Study B recruited 48 Gen Z student travelers from the United Kingdom and the United States, of whom 46 provided useable responses. Online open-ended essays were analyzed using thematic analysis, with constant comparison used as an iterative coding technique. Title: Too much of a good thing? The curvilinear effects of job clarity on career satisfaction and creativity among hospitality employees

Title: FDI spillovers in history: Interwar Japanese “Zaikabo” investment in China's cotton spinning industry
Abstract: We estimate productivity spillovers from Japanese cotton-spinning firms in China (known as Zaikabo,"在華紡") to local Chinese cotton-spinning mills based on plant-level data for 1925 to 1938. We also find some evidence in line with the idea that these gains are larger for Chinese mills with higher initial productivity, consistent with a role for absorptive capacity. Title: Ethics, economics, and environmental stewardship: Religious moral frameworks as constraints for rational policy choice
Abstract: Environmental policy often embeds ethical judgments implicitly in discount rates, welfare weights, prices, or informal constraints. This paper develops a constraint-based framework that makes major ethical commitments explicit before economic optimization begins. Drawing on convergent principles in Jewish, Islamic, Christian, Indigenous, Buddhist, and secular traditions, it identifies stewardship, restraint of waste, intergenerational responsibility, ecological limits, and institutional responsibility as candidate non-compensatory constraints. Economic analysis then compares costs, trade-offs, and institutional feasibility only among policies that satisfy the adopted constraints. Applied water-policy illustrations show how this approach can clarify minimum access, pricing, desalination, and wastewater-reuse choices without claiming that these policies were historically caused by the ethical framework. The contribution to ecological economics is methodological: moral commitments define the admissible policy space, while economics identifies efficient pathways within it. This division of labor improves transparency under moral pluralism and environmental scarcity. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Impact of substitution on product families’ competition in networked markets
Abstract: The competition among product families supplied by different firms in networked markets is constructed as a bipartite graph model. Title: Accounting for the risk of restoration failure in ecosystem service valuation
Abstract: While ecosystem recovery is widely recognized to vary, valuations of ecosystem services often assume guaranteed outcomes. Further, we examine how two personal attitudes (connectedness to nature and place attachment) influence risk perception. Title: Footwear waste recycling: material complexity, technological barriers, and pathways to circularity
Abstract: The global footwear industry produces >20 billion pairs annually, yet post-consumer recovery rates remain below 5%, with the vast majority landfilled or incinerated. This review focuses on non-leather footwear, the dominant category in mass-market production. Unlike packaging plastics or single-polymer waste streams, non-leather footwear is an engineered multi-material composite that incorporates crosslinked polyurethane foams, ethylene-vinyl acetate, vulcanised rubber, thermoplastic polyurethane, polyester textiles, and permanent adhesive systems, whose structural complexity places it beyond the reach of conventional recycling strategies. This review critically examines footwear as a polymer waste stream from a materials, processing, and resource-systems perspective. Pre-consumer and post-consumer waste generation pathways are analysed, and the technical feasibility and economic viability of mechanical, chemical, and hybrid recycling routes are evaluated against the key barriers of multi-material integration, crosslinking, adhesive bonding, and additive contamination. Footwear recycling initiatives such as large-scale mechanical programs, automated sorting, and chemical pretreatment-led delamination are critically assessed. The review finds that no single recycling route adequately addresses the structural complexity of footwear, and that the most promising pathway lies in integrated frameworks that combine selective chemical pretreatment with polymer-specific downstream valorisation. Pre-consumer manufacturing waste is identified as the most immediately actionable entry point for circularity, offering compositionally defined, minimally contaminated feedstocks with substantially lower technical and economic barriers than post-consumer streams. Policy enablers, including Extended Producer Responsibility and design-for-disassembly, are discussed as necessary complements to technological advancement. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Multinational dynamic capabilities: How multinational, how dynamic, how capable?
Abstract: The dynamic capabilities perspective is a central framework used to explain how firms adapt, sustain competitive advantages, and/or create new competitive advantages in changing environments. Despite more than three decades of research, important questions remain about the nature, development, deployment, modification, and effectiveness of dynamic capabilities, particularly in multinational contexts. These questions are increasingly salient as multinational enterprises confront technological disruption, geopolitical fragmentation, institutional volatility, and other manifestations of an expanding global polycrisis. Drawing on our review of the evolution of the dynamic capabilities perspective and its extension into international business research, we argue that future research can advance our understanding of the dynamic capabilities construct by addressing three fundamental questions: How multinational are multinational dynamic capabilities? How dynamic are dynamic capabilities? And how capable are dynamic capabilities? Answering these questions requires greater attention to capability configurations and hierarchies, managerial and organizational microfoundations, heterogeneous multinational contexts, capability evolution, and capability measurement. The articles in this special issue advance our understanding of capability development, deployment, orchestration, and reconfiguration across a variety of international settings. They also highlight the importance of context-dependent capability systems and multilevel adaptation. Integrating these insights, we develop a framework for understanding multinational dynamic capabilities and identify directions for future research. We conclude that future progress will depend on developing more precise theories of multinationality, richer explanations of capability evolution, and more rigorous approaches to measure and evaluate multinational dynamic capabilities across contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Heuristic approaches for a new variant of the team orienteering problem

Title: Can the European recycling target for plastic packaging be met? A scenario analysis for Finland
Abstract: The European Union’s plastic packaging recycling target for 2025 is unlikely to have been met by most member states, so to achieve the more ambitious 55% target for 2030 will require significant changes to existing waste management and recycling practices. This study examines the factors affecting plastic packaging waste recycling and assesses, using 13 waste collection and recycling efficiency scenarios, the conditions under which Finland could meet the 2030 target. The findings indicate that the target is a multidimensional challenge shaped by multiple factors along the plastic value chain. At present, a substantial proportion of packaging waste is incinerated instead of material recovery. Priority should be given to business packaging by substantially improving the separate collection rates, with material recovery from mixed waste streams as a complementary measure. The paper also suggests targeted policies and interventions for improving plastic packaging recycling in Finland and beyond. Authors: Tiwari V.
Title: Reframing artificial intelligence as an observable market signal: Extending Signaling Theory in luxury fashion retail
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming luxury fashion retail; however, existing research primarily views AI as an operational technology that enhances efficiency and personalization. Less attention has been given to how consumers interpret AI-enabled marketing applications as signals of luxury brand meaning. Drawing on Signaling Theory, this study conceptualizes AI-enabled marketing applications as market signals through which consumers infer luxury brand attributes. Using a multi-method design comprising survey-based structural equation modeling (n = 362), exploratory consumer segmentation (n = 101), and sentiment analysis of 193 online reviews, the study examines how AI shapes perceptions of exclusivity, authenticity, innovation, and responsiveness and how these perceptions influence luxury brand performance. The findings reveal that AI-enabled marketing applications do not show a statistically significant direct effect on brand performance; instead, their effects operate through these four signaling dimensions. The exploratory segmentation identifies three consumer profiles with different signaling perceptions, while sentiment analysis reveals generally positive evaluations alongside concerns about excessive automation and diminished human interaction. Title: Reputation and value signals as moderators of advertising spend efficiency in E commerce search advertising
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: China hosts the world's largest e‑commerce search advertising market, yet merchants persistently misallocate advertising budgets by treating ad spend as a monotonic driver of sales efficiency. Drawing on the Resource‑Based View (RBV) and Information Overload Theory, this study investigates how advertising spend intensity (ASI) affects two core efficiency metrics—the Ad‑to‑Sales Ratio (ASR) and Return on Ad Spend (ROAS), as well as the moderating roles of two structural market factors. Keyword Specificity (KS) reflects the semantic breadth of keywords ranging from generic terms to long‑tail queries, whereas Category Competition Intensity (CCI) captures the density of competing products within each keyword market. Based on keyword‑level panel advertising data from a home appliances and household goods retailer operating on China's leading business‑to‑consumer platform, alongside supplementary observational data on competing products, this study identifies an inverted‑U‑shaped relationship between ASI and both ASR and ROAS: advertising efficiency improves with greater spending initially but declines after crossing a category‑specific threshold. KS shifts the efficiency peak toward higher spend levels, meaning long‑tail keywords can maintain efficiency under greater advertising investment. Title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
Abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. The findings of this study will help academics and policy makers to design institutional arrangements which are fit-for-purpose for bringing accountability for nature. © 2026 The Authors. Title: A dynamic, physics-driven life cycle model for citrus supply chain: Evidence from a South Africa–Netherlands maritime trade route
Abstract: Agri-food chains, especially fruit, produce about 10% of global GHG emissions, with more than half arising after harvest. Yet current methods, such as life cycle assessment (LCA), lack the spatial, temporal and physiological detail needed to resolve stage-specific drivers of environmental impact. The proposed framework is demonstrated using a case study of the citrus supply chain connecting production in South Africa to consumption in the Netherlands. We show that variability among fruits and between shipments substantially alters CC and RU,f impact outcomes, demonstrating the need for dynamic rather than static supply-chain assessment. Stage-specific interventions, such as reducing field heat prior to forced-air cooling or increasing shipping temperatures from −1 °C to 1–3 °C under validated phytosanitary conditions, can meaningfully lower impacts. Title: Sourcing strategies for mixed-component products considering the risk of external procurement and consumer information perception
Abstract: Manufacturers employing dual-sourcing strategies produce mixed-component products, leading to consumer unawareness about these products. It also explores the impact of information transparency, specifically blockchain adoption, on these sourcing strategies. Notably, the findings reveal that blockchain adoption broadens the applicability of dual sourcing. The effect of increasing brand value differences on the preference for dual-sourcing procurement varies depending on the presence of blockchain. Title: Measuring success: A refined methodology for estimating long-term continuous improvement
Abstract: Successful resource management systems require current and detailed feedback on operational and corporate-level performance. Authors: Kambala M.I.
Title: Early-life adversity and long-term outcomes: evidence from the cocoa swollen shoot virus outbreak in the Gold Coast
Abstract: How do early-life economic shocks that do not directly affect human biology shape long-term development outcomes? While a large body of work documents persistent effects of early-life exposure to health crises, famines, and natural disasters, much less is known about shocks that operate through economic disruption. This study addresses this gap by examining the long-term effects of the Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus Disease (CSSVD), an agricultural epidemic that devastated cocoa production in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) during the 1940s. Combining historical data on climatically suitable cocoa-growing areas with georeferenced household survey data, I exploit variation in exposure across birth timing and space to estimate the epidemic's long-term effects. The results show that exposure during early childhood and school-going years led to substantial and persistent human capital deficits. Individuals exposed during early childhood lost about one year of schooling and were 8.5 percentage points (pp) less likely to obtain formal education, while those exposed during school-going years lost about 0.8 years of schooling and were 7.0 pp less likely to obtain formal education. Exposure is also associated with worse health outcomes, increasing morbidity by 6.2–8.5 pp and disability by 5–7.5 pp. In contrast, there is no systematic evidence of long-term effects on employment type or labor supply. Evidence on potential mechanisms points to both educational and occupational channels. Conditional on ever attending school, exposed individuals completed fewer years of schooling and were more likely to have incomplete primary education, indicating disruptions to both school progression and initial access to schooling. In addition, exposed individuals are more likely to work in the agricultural sector in adulthood, consistent with reduced educational attainment having narrowed their occupational options. These findings demonstrate that industry-specific economic shocks can generate long-term human capital deficits, even in the absence of direct biological exposure. © 2026 The Author

Title: Mechanisms for digital business model innovation in international new ventures from developing economies
Abstract: Digital international new ventures (DINVs) increasingly leverage ecosystem partnerships to drive digital business model innovation (DBMI) and navigate global markets. Moreover, foreign market turbulence tends to positively moderate the relationship between ecosystem partnerships and digital learning capability. In addition to demonstrating how DINVs build innovation capacity under volatile conditions, findings help to extend perspectives on capabilities, learning, and ecosystems. Leveraging ecosystem partnerships, digital learning, and digital business model innovation appears to enhance the performance of DINVs. Ecosystem partnerships appear to be especially valuable to DINVs when market turbulence is high. Title: Beyond landlockedness: transit structure, infrastructure, and the geography of trade costs
Abstract: This paper examines how geographic disadvantage and infrastructure shape bilateral trade flows, with a particular focus on landlocked countries. Using a global panel dataset covering 2007–2019, the paper moves beyond the conventional binary classification of landlockedness by decomposing the geographic disadvantage into coastal accessibility and transit structure. The empirical strategy combines an augmented gravity model with the Hausman–Taylor estimator to address endogeneity while retaining time-invariant geographic variables, and is complemented by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood (PPML) estimation and extensive-margin analysis to account for zero trade flows, heteroskedasticity, and trade participation. Second, the negative effect of landlockedness is largely driven by coastal accessibility: once distance to the nearest coast is accounted for, the estimated penalty of being landlocked declines substantially. Third, and most importantly, the structure of transit access matters. Landlocked countries that depend on a single coastal neighbor experience significantly lower trade, highlighting the importance of competition among transit routes. The findings are robust across alternative estimators, including fixed effects, Hausman–Taylor, PPML, and extensive-margin models. These findings suggest that the disadvantages faced by landlocked countries are multidimensional, reflecting not only geography and infrastructure but also regional political economy. Title: Optimizing equity and efficiency in the aerial firefighting resource allocation problem

Title: A game-theoretic approach for the retailer-third party multiple market-site capture competition in an end-of-life product collection system

Title: Your recommendation and my choice: The impact of algorithmic recommendation convergence on consumers’ algorithmic recommendation aversion

Abstract: Personalized recommendation features launched by integrated online shopping platforms with multi-brand competition trap consumers in the dilemma of product choice constrained by algorithmic recommendation convergence, and induce consumers' algorithmic recommendation aversion. Title: Beyond sales: Seller explanation, product availability, and returns in livestream commerce

Title: Reframing destination stability: how scale reshapes tourism volatility in the Balearic Islands
Source title: Journal of Destination Marketing and Management
Abstract: Tourism destinations are often described as spatially differentiated systems, with coastal areas portrayed as more stable and inland areas as more volatile. Title: Shared but feared: A vulnerability-sensitive account of consumer responses to post-crisis service environments

Title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees

Title: From cox to DeepHit: A comprehensive analysis of aircraft longevity using time-varying and machine learning models
Abstract: Estimating the economic useful life (EUL) of commercial aircraft is governed by extreme right-censoring: with over 70% of 35,212 aircraft still in service, retired-only analysis underestimates longevity through exclusion bias, while full-fleet analysis must work from relatively few observed retirements. Leasing is associated with later retirement (24.2% lower estimated hazards for passenger aircraft and 42.6% lower estimated hazards for cargo aircraft), and, in pooled passenger-aircraft models, the estimated Airbus–Boeing contrast reverses over the lifecycle, with Airbus aircraft facing higher early but lower late retirement risk; this contrast may partly reflect differences in the manufacturers’ model composition. Title: Terrorism and altruistic giving: Evidence from child sponsorship

Title: Student perceptions of generative AI in accounting education: A thematic analysis
Abstract: Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. Title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy

Title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics

Title: Self-built or retailer-based? Online direct-to-consumer channel introduction strategies for the fresh producer under retailer competition and disruption risk
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services

This study examines rater-side psychological antecedents of appraisal rigor among hospitality managers, focusing on how managers’ positive attitudes toward the job and the organization drive appraisal quality and whether that relationship is disrupted by the managers’ own turnover intention. Because job satisfaction and organizational commitment were empirically indistinguishable in the sample (r = .976), a higher-order Managerial Attitudes factor was specified to test the two attitudinal hypotheses jointly. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to estimate direct and moderating effects. Common method variance was addressed procedurally and through a marker-variable technique combined with an unmeasured latent method construct. Findings: Managerial Attitudes had a strong positive relationship with self-reported appraisal quality (β =.71 in the method-adjusted model). Contrary to the “withdrawal–negligence” prediction of Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, turnover intention showed a small but significant positive direct association with appraisal rigor, and its interaction with attitudes was not statistically significant. The pattern is consistent with a “Lame Duck Objectivity” account in which anticipated exit releases managers from certain political constraints on evaluative candor, but reverse causality, statistical power, and measurement limitations remain plausible alternatives that the design cannot rule out. Title: Micro-foundations of destination supply: A configural analysis of herders’ livelihood strategies in grassland tourism

Abstract: Based on the revised Sustainable Livelihoods Framework, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis was used to investigate the combinatorial effects of social, human, cultural, policy, physical, natural, and financial capital on herders' livelihood strategies in Chen Barag in the Hulunbuir Grassland, to identify the key drivers of herders’ adoption of a tourism livelihood. Conversely, mixed livelihoods are associated with configurations involving productive resource release, locational advantages, cultural commodification, and intergenerational labour division, while governance tensions between institutional arrangements and diversified livelihood needs may create additional constraints. Title: Leaning into risk: How slanted typeface logos increase perceived risk of efficacious products
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Marketing practice commonly uses slanted typeface logos on product packaging to convey movement and vitality, yet existing research has paid limited attention to the potential conflict between this low-level visual feature and the core claims of specific products. Drawing on the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), this research examines when and why slanted typeface logos on packaging increase consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products, revealing the underlying mechanism and boundary condition. Across three controlled experiments and one incentive-compatible experiment, this research manipulates the form of typeface logos on packaging and evaluates its effects and subsequent behavioral responses. Study 1 shows that, compared with an upright typeface logo, a slanted typeface logo increases consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products. Study 2 supports the mediating role of design instability: a slanted typeface logo triggers a visually perceived sense of imbalance, which further induces consumers’ risk inferences about the product; meanwhile, arousal, perceived movement, and perceptual fluency do not emerge as significant mediating mechanisms. Study 3 identifies the moderating role of cognitive load, showing that high cognitive load amplifies the effect of a slanted typeface logo on perceived risk. Study 4 further provides behavioral evidence through an incentive-compatible experiment, showing that consumers are less likely to choose the product in the slanted typeface logo condition. Overall, this research reveals a boundary of the visual marketing principle that “slanting implies vitality” in the context of efficacious products. Title: Transforming hospitality and tourism services through artificial intelligence: The influence of experiential dimensions on user satisfaction, continuance intentions, and word-of-mouth

Title: Inner-supportive destinations for psychologically vulnerable solo travelers: A framework of narrative reconstruction and reintegrative stabilization
Source title: Journal of Destination Marketing and Management
Abstract: This study examines how inner-supportive destination experiences support psychological reconstruction among solo visitors reporting self-identified emotional disruption. Inner-supportive affordances, including temporal deceleration, sensory softness, perceived safety, and supported solitude, reduced defensive pressure and created conditions for regulated emotional exposure. This exposure enabled narrative re-authoring, through which distressing experiences were reinterpreted and integrated into a more coherent self-understanding. Based on these accounts, the study proposes the inner-supportive destination framework, explaining how destination affordances, regulated emotional exposure, narrative re-authoring, participant-attributed reintegrative stabilization, and boundary conditions relate within a contingent process. Theoretically, the study extends destination marketing and management by distinguishing narrative reconstruction from restoration, healing, or emotional elevation. Practically, it offers guidance for designing vulnerability-sensitive destinations that support autonomy, low-pressure engagement, and safe solitude without making therapeutic claims. Title: From airplanes to classrooms: A cross-domain literature review of seating assignment models and methods
Abstract: Seating assignments play an important role in customer-focused managerial decisions, yet existing studies are frequently limited in scope to isolated application domains. Our cross-domain synthesis identifies technique transfer opportunities previously invisible due to research silos, such as applying restaurant group-seating strategies to airline passengers traveling together or entertainment venue considerations to dining table assignments. Title: THE VALUE OF RECOMMENDATIONS FROM SOCIAL MEDIA ANALYSTS IN ONLINE INVESTMENT COMMUNITIES
Abstract: This study examines the informational value of stock recommendations issued by social media analysts through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using comprehensive data from Seeking Alpha, we demonstrate that these recommendations significantly predict abnormal stock returns over a two-month horizon, with no subsequent reversal, suggesting that they convey incremental information not captured by sell-side analysts or textual sentiment. Guided by SDT, we further show that predictive accuracy varies systematically with analysts’ motivational contexts. Recommendations are more informative when issued by analysts identified as traders, whose direct financial stakes deepen the internalization of extrinsic incentives, and by analysts with high comment-section engagement, where interactive feedback supports needs for competence and relatedness. Conversely, predictive ability declines with longer platform tenure, consistent with motivational saturation as psychological needs become satisfied, and with higher posting frequency, where cognitive overload undermines need satisfaction. Finally, we find that both editorial selection and user-driven engagement effectively identify recommendations with greater ex-post informativeness. In an era of information abundance in online investment communities, our SDT-grounded analysis offers investors guidance for signal extraction and provides platform designers with principled insights for fostering higher-quality content ecosystems. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. Title: An EOQ model with green degree and population size sensitive demand under pentagonal intuitionistic cloudy fuzzy environment
Abstract: This proposed study represents an EOQ (economic order quantity) model concerning the population size, which is an important factor in any inventory management system. Here, demand is assumed to be dependent on the selling price, the green level, and the size of the population. The holding cost is a time-dependent quadratic function. At the start of the cycle, the customers buy the items according to their choice. After a certain time, the deteriorated and overall less preferred items are sold to customers at a discount. In this period, demand may increase, decrease or remain unchanged. Some people will buy the items because of their low prices. However, some customers may not be interested in buying them, thinking that the items are very low-quality products. As a consequence, a study is proposed, developed and solved in a crisp environment. Then, the model is transformed into a fuzzy model by using a pentagonal intuitionistic cloudy fuzzy number. The carbon tax is included, and the development cost is used for preservation technologies for storing decaying items like vegetables, fruits, etc. The computer-based algorithm is used for the solution of the proposed study. Title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. Building on control theory, this study investigates how and when GenAI usage is related to employees’ corner-cutting behavior (CCB). Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. Title: An investigation of the neglected serial mediators and moderators of green inclusive leadership in the hospitality industry

Title: Where AI enters the product development process: Task orientation, human identity threat, and purchase intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Title: Smart and green solutions in the catering and hospitality: A review of the existing literature
Abstract: The integration of digital technologies and sustainability practices is reshaping the catering and hospitality industry, yet research on smart and green solutions remains fragmented. Title: When AI shops for me: How agentic retail representation turns assistance into purchase delegation

Title: Corporate strategy for the green transition: Are executive incentives effective?
Abstract: This paper examines whether green incentives embedded in executive compensation schemes are associated with a reorientation of firms' innovative activities toward environmentally sustainable technologies. Title: Hotel resilience to prolonged uncertain disruptions: A business model dynamics analysis
Abstract: This study examines how hotels adapted their business models to sustain operations during the prolonged uncertainty of COVID-19. Title: When service environments signal ideology: Customer responses to ideological cues

Abstract: Service environments increasingly contain visible cues that communicate political engagement, religious identities, LGBTQ + affiliation, environmental advocacy, and other collective values. Title: From LinkedIn to labor statistics: Using Revelio microdata for labor market research in developing economies

Title: Bridging the implementation gap in MCABC inventory management: from a taxonomy to practical archetypes

Title: Survival analysis of U.S. regional airline routes during and after the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, U.S. regional airlines have faced substantial operational challenges, including reduced flight activity, fleet restructuring, rising labor costs, and persistent pilot shortage. Using airline-route panel data for 2017–2024, we estimate Cox proportional hazards models with time-varying route-performance covariates. The results show that routes operated by independent regional airlines face significantly higher discontinuation hazards than those operated by wholly-owned subsidiaries of mainline carriers. Support through the U.S. Essential Air Service (EAS) program is also associated with greater route survival, while larger aircraft are linked to improved route persistence, consistent with post-pandemic upgauging and capacity consolidation. The analysis also accounts for market demand conditions and operational characteristics, including population, per capita income, unit cost, stage length, and aircraft size. Title: Go local or global? How consumers’ response to charity locality shapes checkout charity outcomes

Title: When products speak: The effects of product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication on consumer responses to carted products

Abstract: Shopping cart abandonment is a pervasive challenge in e-commerce, with more than 70% of online shopping carts failing to convert into purchases. Title: Data-center expansion and the dynamic regional redistribution of the water-energy-food stress in Texas
Abstract: Data centers are Texas's fastest-growing electricity and water claimants, with interconnection requests exceeding 400 GW against an 86 GW peak. Results showed that local siting restraint never relieves nexus pressure. It displaces the buildout into water-scarce agricultural regions in a closed state, or exports the industry once demand turns footloose. Under a drought of record, irrigation absorbs nearly all shortage, accumulating 6.3 million acre-feet of foregone Panhandle supplies, while an 80% irrigation-protection reservation changes nothing. Title: Diversification or concentration? Supply chain configuration responses to decoupling risk
Abstract: This study investigates corporate supply chain configuration strategies in the context of perceived decoupling risk. Further analysis reveals that this negative association is attenuated by both executive risk preference and the level of corporate investment irreversibility. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the reduction in supply chain concentration is more pronounced for firms with high overseas revenue exposure, those in strategic emerging industries, and small-scale enterprises. Additionally, this impact is amplified during periods of heightened geopolitical tensions, particularly following the U.S.-China trade frictions in 2018, and is more pronounced in the upstream ends of supply chains. Title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms

Abstract: Amidst the crowded media environment and growing consumer disconnection from nature, leveraging biophilia - the innate human tendency to connect with nature - offers a compelling way for service firms to attract and engage consumers. Title: From eco-signals to green trust: How tourists evaluate sustainability credibility through online reviews
Source title: Journal of Destination Marketing and Management

Authors: Merveille N.
Title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
Abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate. © 2026 The Author. Published by Elsevier B.V. Title: When stigmatized workers become consumers
Abstract: Existing research on occupational stigma has focused primarily on workplace consequences, with less attention to how stigmatized service workers respond to service failures as consumers. Title: Examining perceptual spillover effects in social media influencer marketing effectiveness: A PLS-SEM and fsQCA approach

Title: When passion breeds silence: How coworkers’ work passion elicits envy and employee silence in hospitality workplaces

Title: Investigations of the cascading effect of hotel entrepreneur's optimism on employees’ work behaviors and customers evaluations in small and medium hospitality enterprises

Title: Augmented reality as a digital scaffold for slow travel: The roles of cultural competence and tourist engagement at a heritage site

Title: Consumers and local short food supply chains: Critical purchasing factors

Title: Operational constraints in professional kitchens: A theory of constraints perspective on food waste reduction

Title: The dark side of AI customer service: How service failures damage consumer-brand relationships

Title: Lost in the narrative: How embedded content reduces sales on short video commerce platforms

Title: Paying for the future? Cross-season pre-sale product launch strategy in hotels
Abstract: Traditional hotels face persistent seasonal demand imbalance, with weak off-peak demand and constrained peak-season capacity. Drawing on Contingency Theory, this study examines cross-season pre-sale as a context-dependent hotel revenue management configuration and investigates how different configurations (i.e., no pre-sale, self-run pre-sale, and platform-based pre-sale) fit varying operating conditions. Results show that cross-season pre-sale does not universally outperform conventional practices; its value depends on the balance among incremental demand, impacts on existing demand, and implementation costs. Moreover, neither self-run nor platform-based pre-sale always dominates, as their relative effectiveness depends on the trade-off between platform-enabled market reach and channel costs. The study identifies boundary conditions for effective cross-season demand coordination and offers practical guidance for configuration choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Driving impact? How imperfect displacement shapes heterogeneous rebound in carsharing
Abstract: Green technologies, products, and services, such as carsharing, are commonly promoted as pathways to lower environmental impacts by increasing efficiency. Yet rebound effects, behavioral and economic responses to improved efficiency, may erode these environmental impact reductions. Many rebound studies assume perfect displacement, where a new technology or mode of service provision fully replaces an existing service on a one-to-one basis. While analytically convenient, this assumption overlooks real-world complexity and consumer heterogeneity. Using survey data from nearly 4500 Belgian carsharing users, we compare rebound estimates under perfect displacement with those based on reported shifts in mobility. Under the perfect displacement assumption, we find a 53% rebound effect. When accounting for imperfect displacement, however, rebound effects vary widely across users. While median effects remain positive (20%–46%), at the individual level rebound effects range from substantial net benefits to strong rebound (5th–95th percentile: −331% to 147%). A cluster analysis further reveals distinct user groups with systematically different impacts, underscoring that displacement patterns vary not only in scale but also in direction. These findings suggest that carsharing's environmental impact is highly user-dependent, and that relying on a single aggregate estimate may mask critical behavioral variations. As this case study demonstrates, accounting for imperfect displacement in rebound analysis is critical for advancing theory and for tailoring more effective policy interventions. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Wei S.; Hu Z.; Zhang D.; Liu X.
Title: Too personal to be accepted? How personalization visibility drives perceived surveillance and advertising intrusiveness
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: A central challenge in digital advertising is that firms seek to increase relevance through personalization, yet visibly signaling the use of personal data may provoke consumer discomfort and resistance. Guided by privacy calculus theory and communication privacy management theory, this research develops and tests a model in which personalization visibility shapes perceived intrusiveness through perceived surveillance, with data sensitivity and prior brand trust as boundary conditions. Across five studies, including four controlled online experiments and one real-world field experiment using personalized watch advertisements, we examine how explicit versus implicit personalization cues affect consumers’ privacy-related responses. Study 1 shows that explicit personalized visuals, relative to implicit personalized visuals, increase perceived intrusiveness. Study 2 validates this main effect in a live platform-based advertising environment, showing that explicit personalized visuals increase self-reported intrusiveness and produce directionally consistent behavioral ad-dismissal responses under naturally occurring exposure conditions. Study 3 replicates the effect and demonstrates that perceived surveillance partially mediates it, whereas perceived ad relevance does not account for the effect. Study 4 shows that the positive effect of explicit personalization visibility on perceived intrusiveness is stronger when the advertisement is based on sensitive rather than general consumer data. Study 5 further demonstrates that prior brand trust weakens both the direct effect of explicit personalized visuals on perceived intrusiveness and the indirect effect through perceived surveillance. These findings contribute to consumer behavior theory by identifying personalization visibility as a distinct antecedent of advertising intrusiveness and by clarifying the surveillance-based process through which visible targeting cues trigger privacy-related reactions. By combining controlled experimental evidence with field-based validation, the research also strengthens the ecological validity of the personalization visibility account. Managerially, the results suggest that firms should avoid overly conspicuous personalization cues, especially when sensitive data are involved or brand trust is weak. © 2026

Authors: Feng M.; Sun L.; Xiao S.; Zhang R.
Title: When virtual falls short: How influencer type and message congruence shape green purchase intentions
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The rise of virtual influencers has reshaped digital marketing, yet their efficacy in promoting sustainability-related products remains underexplored. Building on the persuasion knowledge model, this study investigates whether and how virtual versus human influencers differ in shaping green purchase intentions through perceived moral authenticity—the extent to which consumers perceive an influencer's environmental advocacy as reflecting the influencer's own underlying values. Through five experiments (total N = 1184), we found that exposure to virtual (vs. human) influencers generally resulted in lower green purchase intentions. This relationship was mediated by perceived moral authenticity, with virtual endorsers viewed as less morally authentic than their human counterparts. Additionally, influencer–message congruence moderated this indirect effect: higher congruence attenuated the difference between virtual and human influencers in perceived moral authenticity and, consequently, the indirect effect of influencer type on green purchase intention. These findings extend research on influencer marketing and sustainable consumption by identifying perceived moral authenticity as a crucial psychological mechanism and influencer–message congruence as a boundary condition of this mechanism in consumer responses to virtual versus human influencers in green marketing contexts. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Discount display in tiered pricing: Nudging subscriptions in online healthcare services
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Discounts are increasingly embedded within tiered pricing to encourage larger purchases or longer service commitments. However, such discounts are often implicit and embedded across the price options, heightening consumers’ cognitive burden of cross-tier comparisons. How platforms display these discounts and whether salient discount display in tiered pricing can drive consumer demand remain largely unclear. Drawing on nudge theory, we conceptualize discount display as a digital salience nudge and examine its effect on consumer subscription demand in online healthcare settings. We leverage a quasi-natural experiment on a leading Chinese online healthcare platform, which redesigned its subscription interface to render implicit savings across tiers salient to patients. Using an intensity-based difference-in-differences approach, we find that discount display significantly increases patient subscriptions. Further analyses suggest that this effect is unlikely to stem from physician-side price reductions or concurrent platform-side changes and is instead consistent with the informational effect of discount display. Moderation results further show that the promotional effect of discount display strengthens for physicians treating a higher share of chronic conditions and becomes statistically insignificant in predominantly episodic care. This study contributes to discount promotion literature by offering robust empirical evidence on the positive effect of salient discount display in tiered pricing contexts and provides managerial implications for interface design and promotion management in digital retailing markets. © 2026

Title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers) unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposing AI-decision checkpoints: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organisational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a BPM Teaching Case, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module’s output serving as the next module’s input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Lee S.; Choi N.
Title: Club research: A review and research agenda
Abstract: Private clubs constitute a distinctive hospitality context defined by membership-based governance, shared authority, and long-term relational exchange, yet existing scholarship remains theoretically fragmented. This study systematically reviews 67 SSCI-indexed journal articles published through 2025 to examine the thematic evolution, theoretical foundations, and methodological patterns of club research. Using multi-layered bibliometric and content-based analyses, the review shows that research has expanded from managerial competency and member satisfaction toward innovation, governance, and digital engagement, but remains divided between consumer-experience and organization-centric management perspectives. This fragmentation under-theorizes clubs as hybrid governance-service institutions, especially at the member–management interface where authority, legitimacy, accountability, and value co-creation intersect. Methodological reliance on cross-sectional quantitative designs, U.S.-centric samples, and single-stakeholder perspectives further constrains cumulative theory building. Grounded in an institutional governance lens, the review advances a hybrid governance perspective and proposes future research on member–management dynamics, multi-role members, and access-sensitive, multi-stakeholder methods suited to private club settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Tong X.; Ma B.
Title: Talking to the screen: Influencer nonverbal cues and observed platform engagement in Douyin travel short-form videos
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Short-form travel videos have become important digital service touchpoints, yet little is known about how influencers' auditory and visual nonverbal cues jointly relate to cumulative observed likes. Drawing on processing fluency and cognitive load theory, we computationally extracted acoustic and gestural features from 495 Douyin travel videos posted by 60 influencers and estimated Poisson fixed-effects models of within-creator variation. Harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR)-based acoustic signal quality exhibited a U-shaped association with observed likes, with the fitted minimum occurring at an intermediate HNR level. Faster speaking was associated with fewer likes. Illustrator gestures had no uniform main association, but their association with likes became less favorable at higher vocal pitch and faster speaking rates, with the latter pattern showing greater sensitivity across robustness checks. Highlighter gestures were more favorably associated with likes at higher vocal intensity, although this evidence was comparatively limited. Overall, audiovisual moderation was selective across cue combinations rather than uniform. These observational findings identify bounded associations between nonverbal cues and cumulative observed likes and provide empirically grounded hypotheses for controlled experiments on audio-gesture combinations. © 2026

Authors: Zhu S.; Nuruzzaman N.; Hashai N.; Han X.
Title: Geopolitical tensions and foreign R&D subsidiaries’ innovation performance: Evidence from emerging economy MNEs
Abstract: In an era of intensifying geopolitical rivalries, emerging economy multinational enterprises (EMNEs) face unprecedented challenges in sustaining cross-border innovation, particularly as technological competition becomes increasingly entangled with national security agendas. Integrating the literature on geopolitics in international relations with EMNE subsidiary innovation, this study investigates whether and to what extent inter-country geopolitical tensions influence the innovation performance of EMNEs’ R&D subsidiaries in advanced economies. Using a sample of Chinese listed firms’ foreign R&D subsidiaries, we find that escalating geopolitical tensions between home and host countries significantly reduce the innovation output of these subsidiaries. Furthermore, the number of host-national innovation partners of a foreign R&D subsidiary can help mitigate the negative effect of geopolitical tensions on its innovation pursuits, while its local same-parent sisters can exacerbate this adverse impact. Our study enhances the understanding of how international politics affect EMNE subsidiary innovation and advances the political risk literature by revealing the role of subsidiary-level networks in shaping firm vulnerability to geopolitical disruptions. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Truden C.; Gansterer M.
Title: Assessing second-price auctions for parcel exchanges in last-mile logistics
Abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has led to multiple carriers operating in the same regions, creating opportunities for collaboration. However, logistics companies typically operate independently, leading to inefficiencies. Horizontal cooperation, where carriers share resources and infrastructure, can improve efficiency and reduce costs. This study explores the requirements for a parcel exchange framework through a game-theoretic lens. We focus on auction-based mechanisms to facilitate horizontal cooperation, optimize exchanges, and minimize delivery costs and emissions. Our approach prioritizes ensuring that carriers report accurate marginal delivery costs while maintaining business privacy. First, we define the key properties of an exchange mechanism for redistributing parcels among carriers. Our analysis reveals a conflict between incentive compatibility and budget balance when non-free disposal is enforced. Among the mechanisms considered, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism is the most suitable, though it tends to overpay carriers. The rationale for using VCG is that we consider incentive compatibility and allocation of all parcels more important than budget balance to ensure long-term participation of carriers and delivery fulfillment. In a computational study, we analyze a VCG-based parcel exchange under realistic settings. The experiment considers several parcel carriers within a region with heterogeneous market shares. In the simulated auctions, carriers compute marginal costs for the parcels, and the winner determination problem is solved via a linear program. A random parcel assignment serves as proxy for noncooperative behavior. The results demonstrate that second-price premium reward payments are typically moderate and that second-price compensation for allocated parcels remains superior to noncooperative last-mile parcel logistics. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Is sustainable design effective? An empirical life cycle assessment of environmental impacts in basketball footwear production
Abstract: The footwear industry is characterized by labor-intensive and resource-consuming production. Sustainable design provides a pathway for reducing the environmental burdens of footwear manufacturing, yet its benefits may vary across production processes and impact categories. This study conducts a high-resolution cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment of basketball footwear by linking upstream material acquisition with seven manufacturing processes and compares eight prospective sustainable design scenarios. Environmental hotspots are evaluated using ReCiPe 2016 at midpoint and endpoint levels. Results indicate that raw material acquisition dominates impacts related to toxicity, land use, and resource consumption, while manufacturing dominates global warming potential (GWP) and water consumption potential. At the process level, blanking of upper materials and sole manufacturing are major contributors to endpoint damage, mainly due to textile inputs, petroleum-based polymers, and manufacturing energy demand. Scenario analysis reveals that the reduction scenario (S7), which combines a 3D-printed TPU upper, adhesive-free sole joining, and packaging reduction, provides a relatively balanced environmental response, reducing GWP from 6.44 to 5.90 kg CO₂-eq without the pronounced cross category burden increases observed in the combined scenario (S8). Although S8 achieves the greatest GWP reduction (5.41 kg CO₂-eq), it increases freshwater eutrophication and ecotoxicity burdens. Monte Carlo simulation confirms the robustness of these carbon reductions and the persistence of several trade-offs. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating sustainable design across multiple environmental impact categories rather than carbon reduction alone. High-resolution modeling can support process optimization and sustainable design decisions through precise identification of environmental hotspots. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Filling in the gaps: Digital platform economies and the agglomeration of urban consumption amenities
Abstract: The spatial agglomeration of restaurants and retail establishments provides a physical platform for consumers searching for differentiated local goods and services. However, the rapid penetration of digital platforms, such as Yelp and Meituan, has substantially lowered search frictions and fundamentally changed the search behavior of consumers. This paper establishes a directed consumer search model to investigate the impact of the introduction and merger of digital platforms on urban agglomeration and provides empirical evidence with novel datasets on merchant relocation, platform registration, and consumer reviews. It is found that (1) digital platforms drive merchants to locate in cluster locations with lower horizontal and vertical accessibility; (2) digital platforms complement urban agglomerations regarding business density, diversity, and clustering patterns. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Bridging game-theoretic modeling and Artificial Intelligence for fast policy recommendations in multi-channel retail
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Emerging-market milk retail is increasingly split across General Trade, Modern Trade, and E-commerce, where pricing and advertising are strategically interdependent through cross-channel substitution, advertising spillovers, and trust-sensitive demand. Yet decision support is challenging: game-theoretic models capture these interactions but are costly to solve repeatedly, while standard machine learning approaches typically require rich quantitative data, often unavailable in fragmented markets where key drivers (e.g., “low trust”) are qualitative. This paper bridges this gap by proposing a hybrid simulation–surrogate decision-support framework that operationalizes omnichannel theory into rapid decision support. First, a tri-channel game-theoretic simulator incorporating trust, advertising spillovers, and cost heterogeneity generates constrained solver benchmark pricing and advertising decisions. Second, to reduce repeated equilibrium-solving costs during scenario evaluation, a lightweight policy network is trained to approximate this structural mapping, providing feasible scenario-based recommendations at low computational cost. A rule-based natural-language descriptor layer operationalizes qualitative managerial inputs by mapping predefined cues into parameterized intervals. Across 10,000 simulated market states, the trained surrogate policy closely approximates the solver-generated benchmark decisions, with evaluation on the held-out test set yielding a mean profit ratio of 1.001, a trimmed profit ratio of 0.999, and mean economic regret of 0.40%.
