Authors: Park C.; Cho M.
Title: The storyteller matters: How mega- and micro-influencers shape narrative and emotional engagement in luxury user-generated content
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Luxury brands increasingly employ experiential marketing through branded cafés and restaurants that serve as immersive storytelling spaces. Within these contexts, user-generated content (UGC) plays a pivotal role in shaping consumer engagement. This study conceptualizes and empirically tests how five UGC qualities—imagery fluency, comprehension fluency, informativeness, entertainment, and authenticity—affect narrative transportation, positive affect, and electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM) intention, and how these effects vary by influencer type (mega vs. micro). Across two studies combining structural equation modeling and an experiment, informative content was found to be more persuasive when delivered by mega-influencers, whereas authenticity exerted stronger effects for micro-influencers. The impact of entertainment varied by platform affordances, highlighting the importance of format-specific expression. Overall, the findings provide theoretical and managerial insights into how narrative-driven UGC can be strategically tailored across influencer types to enhance consumer persuasion in luxury marketing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Gaan N.; Gursoy D.
Title: Effects of leader greenwashing on employee eco-voice: The role of trustworthiness, gender, and social norms
Abstract: This study examines the conditional indirect effect of perceived leader greenwashing on employees’ eco-voice behavior and explores the mechanisms through which this effect unfolds. Eco-voice, a discretionary form of pro-environmental action, is critical for translating organizational sustainability goals into frontline practices, yet remains highly sensitive to leadership authenticity and trustworthiness. Data were collected in three phases from 318 full-time employees across 98 green certified hotels and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings reveal that leader greenwashing negatively influences eco-voice both directly and indirectly by eroding trust in leaders’ ability and integrity. Gender differences were observed. Male employees’ eco-voice was more strongly shaped by competence-based trust, whereas female employees were more sensitive to integrity-based trust. Additionally, descriptive social norms moderated these relationships, strengthening the translation of trust into eco-voice. These findings highlight the interplay between leadership authenticity, trustworthiness, and workplace norms in shaping employees’ willingness to raise environmental concerns, and they underscore the fragile yet vital role of eco-voice in advancing organizational sustainability. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Bao J.; Pan J.; Ai S.
Title: The algorithmic bias in creative legitimacy attribution
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly involved in producing consumer-facing outputs, consumers may evaluate otherwise identical outcomes differently depending on whether they are attributed to AI or to human creators. However, the psychological process underlying this attribution bias and the conditions under which it becomes stronger remain underexplored. Drawing on attribution theory and the creativity-evaluation perspective, this research examines how creator attribution influences perceived creative legitimacy through perceived creative effort and identifies contextual and identity-based boundary conditions. Studies 1 and 2 provide preliminary evidence in a relatively analytical travel-platform pricing context. Study 1 shows that an identical pricing outcome receives higher legitimacy evaluations when attributed to a human pricing team rather than to an AI-driven pricing system. Study 2 demonstrates a significant indirect effect through perceived creative effort, whereas perceived professionalism does not statistically mediate the attribution effect. Studies 3 and 4 then test the framework using a fully rendered travel advertisement, representing a more prototypically creative consumer-facing output. Study 3 examines display context as a second-stage moderator of the effort-based process. Study 4 distinguishes temporary creative-identity salience from chronic creative identity and examines both as first-stage moderators. Together, the findings identify perceived creative effort as an important, although not necessarily exclusive, pathway linking creator attribution to creative-legitimacy judgments and clarify the conditions under which the disadvantage associated with AI attribution becomes more pronounced. Practically, communicating meaningful human oversight and deliberate human involvement in AI-assisted production may strengthen legitimacy evaluations, particularly in design-oriented contexts and among consumers for whom creativity is personally salient. © 2026

Author full names: Cipollina, Maria (24376256000); De Pascale, Gianluigi (57197717357); Romagno, Anna (58944760600)
Title: Digitalisation as a push or pull factor for foreign direct investments: a meta-analysis
Abstract: The empirical literature on digitalisation and foreign direct investment (FDI) reports heterogeneous findings. We interpret this evidence through two complementary mechanisms: digitalisation may act as a pull factor for inward FDI by improving infrastructure and market accessibility, or as a push factor for outward FDI by strengthening firms’ technological capabilities and facilitating international expansion. We conduct a meta-regression analysis of 56 primary studies comprising 959 estimates to examine the sources of heterogeneity, accounting for publication bias, methodological choices, and study characteristics. The synthesised evidence indicates a small but statistically significant average association between digitalisation and FDI. However, results differ substantially across mechanisms. After accounting for publication bias and study characteristics, push-factor studies report positive associations with outward FDI, whereas pull-factor estimates are more heterogeneous and sensitive to study characteristics and empirical context. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between push and pull mechanisms when interpreting the digitalisation–FDI relationship. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: The double-edged sword of referral rewards: How metacognitive inferences and community structure shape crowding-out patterns in high-involvement markets
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Referral reward programs (RRPs) are widely used to mobilize consumer advocacy in social commerce and retail service systems, yet their effectiveness in high-involvement retail contexts remains theoretically ambiguous. Drawing on Social Capital Theory and the Persuasion Knowledge Model, this study examines when referral rewards strengthen consumer advocacy and when they may undermine it. Study 1 uses a field survey of New Energy Vehicle (NEV)-related community members (N = 408) to establish the social and motivational baseline of referral intention. The results indicate that referral intention is shaped by social interaction ties, trust, shared vision, and a higher-order Prosocial Motivation construct composed of reciprocity and altruism/helping, whereas perceived reward magnitude has no significant direct effect. Study 2 uses a supplementary 2 × 2 scenario-based analysis (N = 160; n = 40 per condition) to examine reward–context fit. Kruskal–Wallis tests and non-parametric pairwise comparisons identify a crossover pattern: high rewards increase referral intention in weak-tie interest communities but reduce it in strong-tie social networks. Supplementary moderated mediation analysis provides mechanism-consistent evidence that motive skepticism is associated with this pattern. The findings contribute to RRP research by shifting attention from reward magnitude to reward–context fit and by extending the application of persuasion knowledge to recommender-side metacognitive inference in high-involvement retail services. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Mamudu A.; Syed R.
Title: “Are BPM Graduates Future-Ready?” Reframing BPM Competencies for the Future-of-Work
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Business Process Management (BPM) is at the forefront of digital transformation, yet it remains an open question whether BPM graduates are equipped for this role. This study conducts a thematic discourse analysis to examine how BPM competencies are discursively constructed in academic literature and how they align with emerging skill demands in the World Economic Forum (WEF)’s Future of Jobs reports published between 2016 and 2025. The analysis shows that BPM competency is progressively framed as a hybrid profile spanning process, digital, analytical, social, and adaptive domains, with process and analytical capabilities dominating. This profile is broadly congruent with future-of-work skill projections. In contrast, social, adaptive, and sustainability-related competencies are less strongly foregrounded, despite their growing importance in future-of-work narratives. The study contributes a competency-skill alignment matrix and argues that BPM’s challenge is not a lack of relevant competencies, but uneven emphasis on how they are taught, assessed, or resourced. For educators, the key task is to identify ways to orchestrate BPM curricula that integrate process foundations with digital fluency, learning agility, social capability, and transformational leadership competencies, which are increasingly central to the digital transformation of work environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: The Opportunity Alignment Canvas: Operationalizing Founder Fit Within Entrepreneurial Life Design
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: The Opportunity Alignment Canvas (OAC) facilitates a student-centered conversation about self-authorship (Baxter-Magolda, 2004) and responds to the challenge of operationalizing Entrepreneurial Life Design within classrooms and coaching scenarios using a practical visual canvas-type framework for educators, coaches, and institutions to explore Entrepreneurial Life Design principles with a student-centered approach. The OAC draws upon entrepreneurial and effectual theory and practice as to how an individual creates value in their own life through “micro-adventuring” and creating linkages or recognizing gaps between their internal ambitions and external contexts (Jones, 2019). The OAC emerged from both practice and scholarship; from the author’s own conversations with founders and would-be founders wrestling with how they personally aligned with the demands of their (emerging) venture opportunities within the context of their lives, and with elements of scholarship that highlight the role of founders’ resource profile (Jones, 2011) and effectual strategies for the creation of value (Sarasvathy, 2001). © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Zhang X.; Zhu J.J.
Title: How can the tourism short videos shaping destination emotional attachment?
Abstract: Drawing on constructivist grounded theory and in-depth interviews with 32 Chinese users of Douyin (TikTok China) and Xiaohongshu (Rednote), this study constructs an integrated “Attraction–Alignment–Commitment” model to elucidate how tourism short videos cultivate destination emotional attachment. The findings reveal that multisensory immersion initiates tourists’ emotional engagement, while algorithmic relationality, defined as a platform-driven mechanism that reinforces affective bonds through iterative personalization and social interactivity, sustains and deepens attachment by regulating exposure cycles and affirming users’ emotional investment. This research advances theoretical understanding of technology-mediated attachment by conceptualizing algorithmic relationality as a distinct, context-specific process that extends beyond conventional notions of algorithmic curation. Practically, the study offers valuable implications for destination marketers seeking to foster emotional resonance in algorithmically mediated digital ecosystems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Operationalizing Entrepreneurial Life Design Through Career Crafting, Job Crafting, and Intrapreneurship: Insights from Higher Education
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: How individuals shape their professional lives is increasingly defined by uncertainty, rapidly shifting work environments, and rising expectations for meaningful and sustainable careers. However, higher education and organizational development lack approaches to translate these challenges into actionable learning experiences. Existing concepts such as career crafting, job crafting, and intrapreneurship offer promising mechanisms for proactive career and work design. Nevertheless, they remain largely disconnected in theory and difficult to operate in practice. This chapter proposes an integrative approach that combines these three mechanisms into a coherent model of Entrepreneurial Life Design (ELD). We introduce a practice-oriented framework that links long-term career navigation, day-to-day work design, and entrepreneurial behavior within and outside organizations. The framework is supported by structured design loops that enable learners to explore personal values, redesign daily work practices, collaborate effectively in teams, and experiment with intrapreneurship initiatives. Drawing on insights from higher education and applied teaching formats, we demonstrate how this model can be implemented through experiential learning and reflective development tools. The contribution of this chapter lies in offering a concrete didactic pathway that makes ELD teachable, measurable, and actionable, empowering not only to craft meaningful careers but also to contribute to well-being and positive change within and beyond their organizations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: The performance effects of attentional focus, vigilance, and switching
Abstract: While prior research has examined the relationship between the three attention dimensions and firm performance, none has analyzed all three simultaneously. We also show how the effects of these organizational attention patterns are shaped by five organizational factors. Taken together, these findings extend existing understanding of organizational attention by illustrating how organizational attention patterns relate to a broad range of performance outcomes within particular organizational contexts. Title: Integrating sustainability and customization in retail: A cost-benefit analysis of dual-channel strategies
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The rapid evolution of the retail landscape has forced companies to redefine conventional supply chain structures to meet customers' requests for customisation and sustainability. This study provides a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of dual-channel retail strategies across both physical and digital (e-commerce) channels through the lens of sustainable operations and mass customisation. Drawing on transaction cost economics, the triple bottom line framework, and channel coordination theory, this paper constructs an analytical model that quantifies the trade-offs among the costs of environmental compliance, the costs of personalisation, and long-term profitability across demand elasticity scenarios. The analytical model is validated and refined through an iterative qualitative multiple-case study of four retail organisations, analyzed using NVivo, which together constitute a pragmatic mixed-methods design. The findings indicate that dual-channel configurations can yield tangible benefits in terms of operational efficiency, customer lifetime value, and carbon footprint, especially when combined with green logistics and modular customisation architectures. The findings show that significant cost differences due to reverse logistics, technological integration, and regulatory compliance limit the scalability of sustainable customisation in a resource-constrained retail environment. The results have implications for supply chain managers, policymakers, and investors who seek to balance economic sustainability with environmental care. The paper proposes an innovative decision-support framework that combines sustainability and customisation, offering actionable insights for dual-channel retailers facing more complex market dynamics. © 2026

Title: Corporate hype behavior and stock price crash risk
Abstract: We examine whether corporate hype behavior, the pattern of simultaneously adopting trending themes and shedding fading ones in annual report disclosures, predicts future stock price crash risk. Using textual analysis of MD&A sections from 33,590 firm-year observations of Chinese A-share listed firms over 2011–2024, we find that hype behavior predicts higher subsequent crash risk. We document two potential channels: hype increases investment inefficiency as firms misallocate capital toward theme-aligned projects, and hype erodes the firm's media sentiment environment as journalists discount the credibility of trend-chasing firms. Institutional ownership attenuates the hype-crash relationship. Cumulative abnormal returns reveal deferred market discipline: prices do not react at disclosure but correct downward over the subsequent months, concentrated among firms adopting outdated rather than genuinely emerging themes. Our findings complement conventional crash risk models by documenting a predictor that is observable in public filings. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: From Seizure to Social Value: Descriptive Evidence on the Management and Reuse of Confiscated Assets
Abstract: The social reuse of assets confiscated from organized crime has become an increasingly important instrument for promoting social justice, inclusion, and territorial regeneration. Title: Process Binoculars: Resilient Log Generation from Multi-video Sources
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Process mining links event data to process models, typically assuming structured logs. However, many actual processes do not leave digital traces and need to be discovered in the field. Existing approaches mitigate this by integrating logs with multiple sources, including observations of actual processes. Recent works have pioneered process discovery methods from video sources, but these methods often require manual labeling and produce brittle logs dependent on a single viewpoint, risking incomplete capture of activities. Learned representations over event windows improve robustness to camera errors, while clustering and abstraction yield human-readable activities. Evaluation on a large-scale assembly dataset shows that Process Binoculars produces accurate process models and remains resilient under controlled noise. Authors: Aldemir A.A.
Title: Comparative Analysis of Accounting Education in Different Countries
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: Accounting education, as a critical subfield within business and management studies, reflects not only technical and professional competencies but also deep-rooted cultural, institutional and pedagogical dimensions. The diversity observed in accounting education systems across countries stems from variations in cultural values, educational philosophies and socio-economic environments. In this regard, examining accounting education through a cross-cultural perspective offers a valuable lens for understanding how cultural and institutional contexts shape accounting knowledge, teaching methods, and professional orientation. Title: Human touch in an AI world: How coaching leadership mitigates burnout in the hospitality sector

Title: Mobilizing ecosystem support for architectural innovation: Broker-mediated expectation formation

Title: Too much memory, too little trust? How AI customer service memory depth violates relational boundaries in retail service

Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in retail service, AI customer service is becoming more capable of drawing on historical records to provide continuity and personalization. Title: Evaluating LLM-Generated Conceptual Models: A Theoretical Approach for Formalizing the Calculation of Metrics on the Meta Level
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: The generation of conceptual models using large language models (LLMs) for supporting information systems engineering is today being widely discussed. Title: When AI ads backfire: Deconstructing consumer backlash to GenAI advertising

Title: The expert's edge? Bank lending specialization and informational advantages for credit risk assessment

Title: Blockchain E-invoicing adoption and corporate vertical integration: Evidence from transaction cost theory

Title: Exploring the Impact of Soft Preventive Judicial Measures on Business Resilience and Performance Under Organised Crime Infiltration: Evidence from a Multi-Case Analysis
Abstract: Organised crime infiltration in legitimate businesses threatens market functioning, firm governance and local economic development. Title: Status without cost: how color darkness can increase preferences and perceptions of status

Title: Evaluating service quality and customer loyalty in robot-serving restaurants: A DINESERV-based approach

Title: Competing against whom? Competitor identification and opportunity belief revision

Title: Who Gains from creative destruction? Evidence from high-quality entrepreneurship in the United States

Title: A Systematic Review of Accounting Culture Research: Mapping the Literature

Abstract: As a social science discipline, accounting reflects the characteristics of its field, being both influenced by and influencing the surrounding socio-economic context. Title: A Meta-model for Integrated Management of Quality and Risk in Organizational Change

Title: Government policy incentives: Premium subsidy and risk compensation in credit guarantees
Abstract: In the manufacturing sector, micro and small enterprises (MSEs), which are generally associated with higher default risk, often rely on credit guarantee institutions (CGIs) to obtain bank financing. However, as CGIs have limited risk-bearing capacity, they are generally reluctant to provide guarantees for these MSEs. By contrast, the relative advantage of the two policies in terms of CGI profit and the total profit of the firm and the CGI depends on the firm’s default risk; premium subsidy performs better when default risk is low, whereas risk compensation performs better when default risk is high. Title: Configuring and Diagnosing Conversational Agents for Process Mining Tasks

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer process mining questions about event logs, models, conformance, performance, fairness, and redesign. Title: The judgment-based approach to entrepreneurship: The uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus
Abstract: The judgment-based approach (JBA) has emerged as an important contemporary perspective in management and entrepreneurship research. Because judgment is subjective, tacit, and difficult to communicate or contract upon, entrepreneurs must rely on ownership and residual control rights to create value, linking judgment to the combination and deployment of resources, profit and loss, and organizational structure. The purpose of this article is threefold. First, we provide a systematic statement of the JBA as a theoretical framework, clarifying its core constructs, causal mechanisms, and domain of application. Second, we engage with key critiques and distinguish the JBA from related approaches, including opportunity-based, effectuation, and bricolage perspectives. Third, we outline directions for future research that build on the JBA's emphasis on judgment, ownership, and the organization and deployment of heterogeneous resources under uncertainty. This research examines how tourism and hospitality businesses should respond to different types of unfair reviews through three scenario-based experiments. The findings reveal a congruity effect: rational responses are more effective in improving third-party consumers’ purchase intentions for low-arousal unfair reviews, while emotional responses are more effective for high-arousal ones. The results further show that social distance mediates this effect. In addition, in high-arousal cases, weak victimization responses are more suitable than strong reprimands. These findings enrich theories related to Communication Accommodation Theory and contribute to the literature on unfair negative reviews. They also provide practical guidance for tourism and hospitality businesses on how to effectively handle online consumer unfair reviews. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: If you don't care about me, I become lazy: A multilevel model of despotic leadership and employee procrastination
Abstract: Grounded in the social distance theory of power, this study examines the direct and indirect effects of hotel-level despotic leadership on individual-level factors, including emotional contagion, psychological distance, and employee procrastination. A three wave research design was adopted to collect data from the Malaysian hospitality industry and multilevel modeling was used in Mplus to analyze the data. The results confirmed existence of positive correlation between hotel-level despotic leadership and individual-level emotional contagion, psychological distance, and employee procrastination. Emotional contagion was also found to be positively associated with psychological distance, which, in turn, exhibited a positive relationship with employee procrastination. Furthermore, emotional contagion and psychological distance sequentially mediate the nexus between hotel-level despotic leadership and employee procrastination. Overall, this study extends the social distance theory of power by elucidating the multilevel mechanisms through which despotic leadership influences employee procrastination in the hospitality context. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From family obligation to organizational behavior: A comparative study of filial piety in Asian and Asian American employees
Abstract: Drawing on social cognitive theory, acculturation theory, and paternalistic leadership theory, this study examines how filial piety, perfectionism, and paternalistic leadership affect work outcomes among Asian and Asian American employees. Data was collected via online surveys from 340 hospitality employees in India and the United States. Structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis revealed that reciprocal filial piety leads to higher organizational citizenship behavior, while authoritarian filial piety increases counterproductive work behavior. The relationship between reciprocal filial piety and organizational citizenship behavior is further strengthened by all three dimensions of paternalistic leadership: authoritarianism, benevolence, and morality. However, only moral leadership moderates the link between authoritarian filial piety and counterproductive work behavior. Overall, the proposed relationships were stronger for Asian employees than for their Asian American counterparts. Authors: Ogu N.C.; Antipenko V.
Title: Toward a Layered Model of Security Risk Management Artefacts in Organisational Cybersecurity
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Organisations increasingly rely on security frameworks, standards, and methods to manage cybersecurity risks, yet the relationships between these artefacts remain conceptually fragmented. Existing literature frequently uses these concepts interchangeably, while the growing complexity of cyber threats continues to expose gaps between compliance-driven governance and operational resilience. This paper addresses these issues through a systematic literature review of 23 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026 following the Kitchenham methodology. The study examines how organisations select security artefacts, how these artefacts evolve, and what organisational impacts they produce. The findings reveal that security risk management artefacts operate within a layered governance structure consisting of strategic frameworks, compliance-oriented standards, and operational methods. To explain this relationship, the paper introduces the Cascade of Implementation Model. In addition, the study proposes a four-level Hierarchy of Evolution Maturity to classify how security artefacts evolve through adaptation, fusion, and layering. The review shows that while more than half of the analysed studies propose evolved or hybridised artefacts, none demonstrate long-term empirical validation in operational organisational environments. The findings also highlight tensions between compliance and agility, as well as limited integration of socio-technical factors within current security governance research. The paper identifies the gap between conceptual innovation and operational validation as a major challenge for future cybersecurity governance research. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Firms reap what they sow: Leadership and green intentions in a cross-national context
Abstract: Our paper develops and tests a novel moderated serial mediation model of environmental transformational leadership (ETL). Title: Alleviating user anxiety towards AI health assistant platforms: integrating HAII-TIME and perceived control perspectives
Abstract: This study addresses the critical yet under-researched area of user anxiety alleviation in artificial intelligence (AI) healthcare services. Drawing on the Human-AI Interaction model based on the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII-TIME) and perceived control theory, we develop and test a framework that matches specific design interventions—message interactivity (action route) and visual nonverbal cues (cue route)—to distinct user anxiety types: technology use anxiety, privacy leakage anxiety, and individualized service anxiety. The findings were consistent across both studies: (1) technology use anxiety was most effectively mitigated by high message interactivity (action route), which restores users’ sense of behavioral control; (2) privacy leakage anxiety was best alleviated by strong visual nonverbal cues (cue route), which restore cognitive control; and (3) individualized service anxiety, which involves a dual deficit in both behavioral and cognitive control, required the synergistic combination of both routes for effective mitigation. Authors: Yan X.; Lv Y.; Chen H.Y.
Title: Product essence in avatars: How visual attribute mapping influences avatar effectiveness in online product displays
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As brands increasingly use digital avatars to present products online, understanding how to enhance avatar effectiveness has become increasingly important. Yet evidence regarding avatars' effectiveness in shaping consumer responses remains mixed. Moving beyond the traditional use of avatars as static endorsers, this research examines how visual attribute mapping, a design strategy that projects product attributes onto avatar appearance, enhances avatar effectiveness in product displays. Across seven studies (N = 2120), we demonstrate that visual attribute mapping increases consumers’ purchase intentions and willingness to pay. Perceived brand authenticity, particularly perceived originality, mediates this effect, while ruling out the confound of mere visual variation. Moreover, the effect is moderated by growth creativity mindset and brand personality. Specifically, the effect is attenuated among consumers low in growth creativity mindset. In terms of brand personality, the effect remains positive for exciting brands but is attenuated for sincere brands. Authors: Shan L.; Jin Y.; Xu Y.; Xu L.; Liu X.
Title: Loss or gain? Examining the intervention and spillover effects of message framing on restaurant food waste behavior
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: In recent years, China has actively promoted initiatives such as the “Clean Plate Campaign” to encourage food conservation; however, food waste in the restaurant sector remains a serious issue. Against this backdrop, the present study develops a theoretical framework for intervening in consumers' food waste behavior in dining contexts, drawing on Appraisal Theory of Emotions, Message Framing Theory, and Behavioral Consistency Theory. Using consumers from two emerging first-tier Chinese cities, Ningbo (eastern Zhejiang) and Hangzhou (western Zhejiang), as research samples, this study employs two experimental investigations to examine the effects of different message framing strategies on consumers' restaurant food waste reduction behavior. Furthermore, it explores the behavioral spillover effects from restaurant contexts to household contexts. Specifically, Study 1 employed cross-sectional data with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine the associations among variables, supplemented by Artificial Neural Network (ANN) for predictive analysis. Study 2 employed a randomized controlled trial to provide more robust causal evidence. The findings indicate that, compared with a gain-framed message, a loss-framed message is more effective in reducing consumers' food waste behavior in restaurant contexts. Both anticipated guilt and anticipated pride significantly associate with restaurant food waste reduction behavior. In addition, the study reveals that consumers’ restaurant food waste reduction behavior positively spills over into household food waste reduction behavior. These findings provide both a theoretical foundation and empirical evidence for the development of cross-context intervention strategies aimed at reducing food waste. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Ownership attribution and consumption objects evaluative bias: The role of female intrasexual competition in consumer evaluation
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Ownership cues are pervasive in consumer environments, yet little is known about how the relational meaning between an owner and an evaluator shapes consumer judgments. Drawing on female intrasexual competition and self-threat theory, this research examines how female consumers evaluate consumption objects attributed to female intrasexual competitors. Across five studies comprising seven experiments, we show that products or creative outputs attributed to female competitors are evaluated less favorably than identical objects attributed to non-competitive female others. Studies 1a and 1b establish this ownership attribution effect in clothing and advertising evaluation contexts. Studies 2a and 2b identify self-threat as the underlying mechanism and show that this process remains robust after accounting for alternative explanations, including envy, affect, perceived stress, and perceived attention-seeking motivation. Study 3 provides causal evidence by manipulating self-threat. Studies 4 and 5 identify two boundary conditions: the effect is strengthened for highly attractive competitors but reverses for low-attractiveness competitors; it emerges for appearance-enhancing products but disappears for non-appearance-enhancing products. Theoretically, this research identifies owner-evaluator relational meaning as a source of evaluation bias and shows that female intrasexual competition can extend to objects attributed to competitors. Practically, this research provides guidance for brands and retailers in managing product presentations that attribute products to specific female owners, particularly when the owner is highly attractive or the product is appearance-enhancing. © 2026

Title: Information sharing and procurement strategies in agricultural supply chains under retailer competition
Abstract: This study examines the interaction between information sharing and procurement strategies in agricultural supply chains with competing retailers. To do so, we establish a game-theoretic model consisting of one farmer cooperative and two brand retailers that differ in both brand strength and access to market information. The strong-brand retailer holds more accurate demand signals, while the farmer cooperative sets the wholesale price, and both retailers decide their procurement quantities either from self-operated production bases or from the cooperative for resale in the end market. The analysis first explores how different information-sharing structures affect procurement decisions and supply chain performance, and then derives the optimal information-sharing strategy under various cost and information conditions. The results indicate that the interaction between information sharing and procurement decisions significantly influences wholesale pricing, order quantities, and profit allocation. When the sourcing cost or signal precision reaches certain thresholds, the strong-brand retailer chooses to share demand information with the cooperative, while the cooperative decides whether to pass this information to the weak-brand retailer based on its profit trade-offs. Overall, procurement and information-sharing strategies are closely interrelated, and their interaction jointly determines the equilibrium sourcing structure and overall performance of the agricultural supply chain. This study provides actionable managerial insights for farmer cooperatives and retailers on how to align pricing, information sharing, and procurement decisions to enhance competitiveness and achieve mutual benefits. © 2025 International Federation of Operational Research Societies.

Title: From Event Logs to Process Performance Indicators via Declarative Process Mining
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Organizations increasingly rely on event logs to monitor and improve business process performance, yet identifying meaningful and measurable Process Performance Indicators (PPIs) remains a challenging and largely manual task. Recent work has shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process by suggesting, operationalizing and computing PPIs against an event log based on process descriptions and business goals. However, such approaches depend heavily on user input quality and are not explicitly grounded in observed process behavior. In this paper, we present Declare2PPI, a fully automated pipeline for generating PPIs directly from event logs. Our approach follows a bottom-up strategy in which declarative process mining extracts behavioral constraints that guide LLM-based generation. The resulting PPIs reflect process-wide execution patterns and are automatically translated into executable definitions and computed to ensure measurability. The approach also supports the exploration of multiple PPI sets and prioritizes indicators based on their relevance and variability. We evaluate the approach through a qualitative comparison with a state-of-the-art top-down method and a quantitative analysis of correctness and robustness. The results show that grounding PPI generation in observed behavior leads to more relevant, non-redundant, and consistently computable PPIs, supporting data-driven performance analysis with minimal effort. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Kurt Y.
Title: Accounting Fraud: Comparative Analysis by Country
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: Accounting fraud was first encountered in ancient Sumerian tablets and has persisted to the present day. While the purpose of manipulating financial realities has remained unchanged, the methods of accounting fraud have evolved from simple to increasingly complex over time. In this study, between 2000 and 2025, four countries with large, active economies from each continent were selected, and the accounting fraud cases with the highest monetary value in each country were analyzed. The findings reveal that the largest fraud by monetary value occurred in the United States, followed by France and Germany. Countries with the highest perceived tendency toward fraud include Denmark, Finland, Singapore, and New Zealand, whereas Syria, Venezuela, Somalia, and South Sudan have the lowest corruption perception scores. A significant relationship was observed between Hofstede’s cultural dimensions and the perception of fraud tendency. Specifically, countries with lower corruption perception scores tend to exhibit more egalitarian cultures and stronger long-term orientations, which enhance transparency and serve as deterrents to fraud. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: From symbolic gestures to substantive reform: how ethics shape the diffusion of gender quota responses

Title: Buffer or burden? The role of corporate reputation in the market valuation effects of suppliers’ human rights controversies

Title: Linking multiple sources of performance feedback to firm behavior: the combined effect of technological and financial performance on innovation

Title: The Effect of Cultural Dimensions on Independent Audit Reports: A Study on BIST30 Companies in TÜRKİYE

Title: Designing Futures: Entrepreneurial Life Design for Agency, Self-Efficacy, and Career Planning

Title: The Transformation of Accounting Culture in the Digitalization Process: A Comparative Examination of Türkiye and Northern Europe Within the Framework of Gray’s Accounting Values

Title: Building brand awareness or driving sales? How influencers’ campaign intent shapes consumer engagement with sponsored posts
Abstract: Brands increasingly rely on influencers to reach and engage target consumers. Title: U-shaped versus linear? The impact of trajectory-based price reduction visualization on consumer purchase intention

Abstract: As competition for consumer attention intensifies on e-commerce platforms, retailers increasingly deploy diverse promotional displays. Title: Aspirations in duality: how upward social cohesion shapes the social fabric of the bottom of the pyramid consumers

Title: From Human-AI Task Allocation to Accountable Process Design:: Modelling Concerns for Responsible Hybrid Intelligence

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly sub-symbolic AI (e.g. Large Language Models, and Generative AI), is increasingly integrated into knowledge-intensive business processes. Title: Defining family firms: A survey of empirical criteria

Title: Scaffolding the void: Digital platforms as intermediaries in supply chain traceability
Abstract: In response to the escalating regulatory and normative demands for supply chain traceability and transparency, digital platforms offer a novel solution that overcomes the limitations of the conventional, siloed approach to managing opaque, multi-tiered supply networks. Employing an abductive, multiple-case study approach, we analyze four use cases of traceability-oriented platforms within the garment and footwear sectors. Our findings first reveal that traceability challenges constitute an institutional void, a space where rapid legislative advancement outpaces existing norms and shared understandings in the industry. This in turn creates architectural, cognitive, and relational deficits that hinder traceability efforts. Title: Beyond the green purchase: How emotional decay reshapes the dual pathways from eco-product experience to repurchase loyalty and prosocial engagement

Abstract: Converting first-time green buyers into loyal repeat customers, and channeling green consumption into broader prosocial engagement, remain pressing yet unresolved challenges for retailers of eco-friendly products. Title: Who will I be? Refugee entrepreneurship and founder identity
Abstract: We conducted a 27-month field study of 23 North Korean Defector (NKD) founders. Title: The paradox of algorithmic disclosure in prosocial campaigns: how utilitarian and deontological moral frameworks divide consumer support

Title: The e-CNY and corporate tax avoidance: Evidence from China

Title: Lease governance and comparability in the Korean Air–Asiana merger: A four-dimensional framework under IFRS 16 and ASC 842

Title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered personalisation in service industries: An integrative review and future research directions
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming service industries by enabling personalised experiences that enhance customer satisfaction and operational efficiency. Title: Capital structure adjustments of Hotel SMEs in Portugal's hospitality industry during the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented economic shock, disrupting business operations and demand across sectors. Supported by human oversight and organisational support, these responses foster responsible AI use and enhance perceived organisational legitimacy. The results identify shadow AI as a double-edged mediator: it exerts a negative direct effect on responsible AI use while generating a positive indirect effect through adaptive governance. Title: Does AI Improve BPMN Modelling? Evidence from Iterative Assignments and Critical Verification Practice

Abstract: This paper investigates whether and under what conditions AI assistance improves BPMN modelling in higher education. Error frequencies decreased across most categories, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured scaffolding for guiding iterative improvement. The comparison of V2 and V2–AI reveals heterogeneous outcomes: while some students benefited from AI support, others introduced new inconsistencies when relying uncritically on AI-generated suggestions. Title: Gender Equality in Governance and Social Topics of Italian Sustainability Reports. First Evidence Under the CSRD
Abstract: Gender equality is a key driver in addressing inequalities in business and society while creating value for the broader ecosystem. Title: Commercial or relational cues: how information salience in project titles affects crowdfunding performance
Abstract: Scholars have paid considerable attention to factors that could influence crowdfunding performance. However, whether or how the salience of information in project titles may affect crowdfunding performance remains unknown. Specifically, projects will more (less) likely be funded when entrepreneurs provide information that is congruent (incongruent) with stereotypes associated with their gender. Author full names: Wegener, Kristian Hilmar Mikkelsen (61025189900); Breunig, Karl Joachim (54580596200)
Title: Configuring innovation portfolio management practices in an era of emerging digital technologies
Abstract: Organizations that innovate with emerging digital technologies increasingly manage portfolios in which activities differ not only in risk and maturity, but in the kind of management they require. Research on innovation portfolio management has often approached the portfolio as a managerial object whose practices can be optimized, offering limited guidance for managing heterogeneous portfolios in contexts shaped by emerging digital technologies. Drawing on interviews with 26 informants in seven incumbent Scandinavian organizations, this study explores how organizations differentiate and configure their innovation portfolio management practices. Through an abductive analysis, we develop a taxonomy comprising three innovation portfolio management practice configurations: the product-developing, platform-mediating, and problem-solving configuration. The taxonomy helps explain portfolio heterogeneity by showing how qualitatively different innovation activities correspond to different configurations of innovation portfolio management practices. By reconceptualizing portfolio heterogeneity as the coexistence of qualitatively different practice configurations, the study extends innovation portfolio management theory and offers a practical framework for managing innovation portfolios in contexts shaped by emerging digital technologies. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Marketing strategy and firm value under commoditization
Abstract: This paper examines how firms’ emphasis on different areas of marketing strategy contributes to firm value in the face of increasing product market similarity. We argue that tangible and intangible strategic differentiators of marketing play asymmetrical roles. Intangible differentiators (i.e., promotion and customer relationship management (CRM) features) are primarily non-transactional and more difficult for rivals to replicate. In contrast, tangible differentiators (i.e., product, price, and place features) are largely transactional and may not provide a sustainable competitive advantage in markets with high product similarity. To test these predictions, we develop and validate textual measures of each marketing strategy area. Consistent with the predictions of the contingency framework, the results show that greater emphasis on promotion and CRM has a stronger value-enhancing effect when the firm’s product space is characterized by high versus low similarity, whereas no such effect is observed for product, price, and place features. However, an important boundary condition exists: the stronger value-enhancing effect of intangible differentiation in high-similarity industries is attenuated when firms face high financial distress, which tends to increase uncertainty about the future benefits of these differentiators. Our findings provide new insights into the complex and dynamic nature of investors’ valuation of firms’ marketing strategies amid accelerating commoditization. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Wang S.; Li P.; Ao X.; Fan R.
Title: Honest words may sound harsh: Research on the differentiated effects of negative workplace gossip on targets
Abstract: Despite the growing body of research on negative workplace gossip (NWG), its outcomes remain insufficiently understood in a comprehensive and systematic manner, particularly regarding its double-edged effects on gossip targets. Grounded in social information processing theory and attribution theory, we adopted a sequential mixed-methods approach to explore the differentiated effects of NWG on targets in the hospitality industry. Study 1 employed semi-structured interviews with 52 employees to develop a theoretical framework of NWG's differentiated effects. Specifically, NWG prompted self-reflection and support seeking, facilitating self-improvement and work crafting, while also inducing negative emotions, psychological and physical strain, and job insecurity, which in turn led to self-doubt, work withdrawal, and interaction tension. Employees’ attribution styles were identified as a key influencing factor in these processes. Study 2 validated the core findings of Study 1 through a time-lagged questionnaire survey of 302 hotel employees. Results showed that NWG positively predicted both emotional exhaustion and self-reflection. Emotional exhaustion mediated the relationship between NWG and work procrastination behavior, whereas self-reflection mediated the relationship between NWG and self-improvement. Furthermore, positive attribution moderated the relationships between NWG and both emotional exhaustion and self-reflection, weakening the indirect effect of NWG on work procrastination behavior via emotional exhaustion while strengthening the indirect effect on self-improvement via self-reflection. By examining the differentiated impacts of NWG and its underlying mechanisms, this study advances a more comprehensive and systematic understanding of the consequences of NWG. Its theoretical implications and managerial insights are particularly applicable to hotel work contexts in which employee interactions are mainly based on interpersonal communication. This provides a basis for hotel managers to develop a comprehensive and accurate understanding of NWG and to guide and respond to it at different stages. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Family ownership, performance below aspiration levels and signaling strategies in emerging markets
Abstract: Advertising and CSR constitute the two key signaling strategies for family firms in emerging markets to attract new stakeholders and investors and to retain existing ones. We combine Signaling Theory with the Behavioral Theory of the Firm to examine how family ownership influences these strategies and whether these preferences shift when firms perform below aspiration levels. On a sample of Indian firms over the 2006–2019 period, we find that family ownership is positively related to signaling through both advertising and CSR investments. However, when the performance of the firm falls below aspiration levels, family owners invest more in CSR and less in advertising. Title: Serendipity and innovation in new ventures: The moderating role of primary investor type
Abstract: Rather than pure luck or a fully planned search, opportunities in new ventures frequently emerge from serendipitous discoveries. While research has emphasized the antecedents of serendipity, empirical evidence on its innovation outcomes remains scarce. Analyzing survey data from 386 founders and CXOs of new ventures in Western and Northern Europe, we find that serendipity is positively associated with innovation radicalness and speed. These relationships are contingent on investor type: Compared with bootstrapped ventures, the positive associations are weaker in ventures backed by venture capitalists, business angels, or family and friends. Authors: Merli M.; Roger T.
Title: Environmental values, climate awareness and willingness to pay for green savings: The direct and moderating effect of perceived greenwashing
Abstract: The transition to a low-carbon economy depends critically on mobilizing household savings toward green financial products. Using a survey experiment on a representative sample of 1061 French adults, we examine how perceived greenwashing shapes willingness to pay for a green savings account and whether environmental impact disclosures influence it. We find that individuals are, on average, unwilling to pay a premium to green their savings, and that willingness to pay does not increase when the stated environmental impact is scaled up. Perceived greenwashing plays a dual role: it directly reduces willingness to pay and moderates the relationship between pro-environmental attitudes and financial behavior. Green consumption values raise willingness to pay only when sustainability claims are perceived as credible; climate awareness follows the same pattern. When perceived greenwashing is high, these relationships become statistically insignificant, even among environmentally motivated individuals. At the individual level, willingness to pay declines with subjective financial literacy, whereas climate-related emotions play no robust role. These results suggest that impact disclosure alone is insufficient to shift household financial behavior, and that the perceived credibility of environmental claims is a necessary condition for translating pro-environmental values into green financial choices. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Huang X.; Qu X.; Cao X.; Wei M.
Title: Perceived financial constraints and consumer responses to anthropomorphic service robots
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Anthropomorphic service robots have become a visible feature of contemporary commercial service environments. At the same time, many consumers are experiencing growing financial strain. Although both trends are increasingly salient, prior research has paid limited attention to whether and how perceived financial constraints shape consumer reactions to anthropomorphic service robots. Drawing on a social comparison perspective, social interaction anxiety theory, social observability perspective, and tight–loose culture theory, this research develops and tests a framework that explains why perceived financial constraints can undermine consumer responses to anthropomorphic service robots and identifies when the effect is more or less likely to occur. The operation of this mechanism, however, varies across interaction and cultural contexts. Specifically, the indirect effect is observed when human–robot interaction occurs through voice, but not through touchscreen, and it appears in tight cultures, but not in loose cultures. By uncovering the role of perceived financial constraints in shaping responses to anthropomorphic service robots, this research contributes to both literature streams and provides guidance for marketing managers on when the use of anthropomorphic service robots is likely to be most effective. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: IFRS Compliance Debates From A Cultural Perspective: A Comparative Analysis Based On Selected Country Examples
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: International Financial Reporting Standards are widely accepted as globally applicable financial reporting standards used by or committed to adoption/convergence by numerous jurisdictions. However, discussions continue regarding the impossibility of achieving uniformity in reporting on a global scale despite legal adoption. Culture, as an important environmental factor influencing the accounting practices and institutions of nations, is at the center of these debates. This is because national culture influences the shaping of accounting practices and institutions. In this study, the debates surrounding the IFRS adoption process are examined from a cultural perspective, and the cultural incompatibilities that arise during the implementation of International Financial Reporting Standards in countries with different cultural structures are analyzed using the Hofstede-Gray model. Using a combination of quantitative and comparative qualitative analysis methods, the study found that full compliance, where both a cultural profile conducive to IFRS and actual compliance exist, was only observed in developed countries. Title: Data Chameleon: Biological-Inspired Contextual Privacy for Automated Compliance Evaluation in Trustworthy Data Sharing
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Data sharing has become a key factor in data analytics, as it allows organizations to operate on others’ data for secondary usages. At the same time, when sharing datasets, due to privacy reasons, some transformations are required to the shared datasets to limit the visibility according to an agreement between a consumer and the data provider. Usually, upon this agreement a specific access control setting is established to ensure the data privacy protection. However, when data sharing occurs at scale, reconciling the conceptual discrepancy between data sharing and privacy protection requires automated mechanisms to evaluate whether the shared data is compliant with the data sharing agreement. In this work, inspired by the biological mechanism by which chameleons adapt their coloration in response to environmental stimuli, we propose an automated, context-aware compliance evaluation mechanism for data sharing. This mechanism characterizes how the privacy level of data can vary across interaction contexts, such as access roles and query content, thereby providing interpretable decision support for compliance evaluation and fine-grained governance throughout the data-sharing process. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Redesigning Lives and Sustainable Careers for a Complex World with the Inner Development Guide

Title: Modularization Barriers and Barrier Breakers in Capital Projects
Abstract: Modularization is an execution strategy that transfers work from the project site to an offsite location for improved project performance. It is expected to have significant growth and wide acceptance, leading to enhanced productivity and competitiveness of capital projects. However, many practitioners in capital projects are still unfamiliar with modularization and resist changing from a traditional approach. The implementations have been limited to lower levels of modularization (e.g., prefabs or pipe racks) and lower extents of modularization. Although previous research has investigated barriers to modular/offsite construction in residential and commercial sectors, there is a lack of studies identifying barriers specific to capital projects (including but not limited to petrochemical plants, manufacturing plants, power generation facilities, and mining operations). Thus, this study focuses on identifying barriers to modularization implementation and proposing solutions to break these barriers in capital projects. First, 33 barriers were identified through iterative sessions with the Construction Industry Institute (CII) Research Team (RT-396), a panel of 15 subject matter experts averaging more than 15 years of modularization experience and 28 executed modular studies/projects. Subsequently, a survey based on these barriers was distributed to CII member companies, gathering data from experts affiliated with globally leading owner and contractor organizations, who possess an average of 23 years of industry experience and 11 years of specific modular expertise. The results identified nine top-rated barriers: (1) requirement of early scope/design freeze; (2) unavailability of vendor data; (3) noncompelling business cases; (4) exclusion of modularization from initial design; (5) incompatible project delivery methods; (6) owner reluctance; (7) lack of final drivers; (8) insufficient early fabricator involvement; and (9) lack of project standardization. These findings contribute to the management-in-engineering body of knowledge by showing that modularization adoption in capital projects is constrained primarily by front-end managerial and organizational conditions rather than by technical concerns alone. The comparative analyses and expert-derived specific "Barrier Breakers"strategic solutions developed to overcome each of these nine top-ranked barriers provide actionable guidance for diverse practitioners regarding early decision making, project delivery alignment, and supply-chain integration.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: The gendered glass of wine: Making sense of Chinese women's professional identity in wine sector
Abstract: This study examines how the intersection of gender and non-Western cultural backgrounds shapes professional identity formation among early-to-mid career Chinese women in the wine sector. Title: CSR focus under competitive pressure: The role of national institutions

Title: Adjustment and pivoting in tandem: The evolution of EMNEs in CoPS industries under geopolitical tensions

Title: Signaling for success in university research funding applications
Abstract: Signaling theory explains how organizations convey credible information under conditions of information asymmetry. Yet, while recent work highlights that signals often interact—reinforcing or substituting—most studies have treated signals as independent and additive, and empirical evidence of configurational interaction patterns remains limited. This study addresses this limitation by examining how multiple institutional signals jointly shape evaluators’ judgments in peer-reviewed university research funding. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), we identify distinct configurations of capability, reputation, and status signals that lead to both high and low funding success. The findings reveal that no single signal ensures success; rather, outcomes emerge from specific portfolios of signals whose effects depend on their combinations. We extend signaling theory by demonstrating that signals can also suppress or neutralize one another, and by introducing a configurational perspective that captures synergy, substitution, and suppression within signal portfolios. © 2026 The Authors. Authors: Li W.; Lin Y.; Yi J.; Zhang H.
Title: Dual-track in the family: How spousal state employment fuels entrepreneurship
Abstract: China's rapid growth alongside extensive state ownership challenges theories of state-sector inefficiency. This paper identifies a novel micro-level channel: “dual-track in the family,” whereby one spouse's stable state job enables the other to pursue private entrepreneurship. Using a triple-difference design that exploits the 1993 market reform, we find that spouses of state employees were 9.8 percentage points more likely to become entrepreneurs after the reform. Mechanism evidence suggests that spousal state employment may promote entrepreneurship by insuring the family against risk. The findings reveal how a gradualist, dual-track transition can succeed partly by leveraging state-sector stability to underpin private-sector dynamism. © 2026

Title: Representing BPMN Choreographies in OCEL 2.0
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Inter-organizational business processes describe the interaction between distributed parties. BPMN choreographies offer a modeling notation for business interactions between participants, setting aside their internal behaviors. In process mining, existing literature views choreographies through a single-case notion lens, attempting to fit interaction data involving several business entities into a flat event log format. In this paper, we investigate how the object-centric event log format OCEL 2.0 can be used to express choreography data. To that end, we present a mapping between the BPMN choreography metamodel and OCEL 2.0 elements. The mapping enforces BPMN choreography semantics by defining data constraints. We demonstrate and evaluate the approach with 19 datasets from different domains. We provide implementations to extract choreography data, validate choreography event logs, and convert them to BPMN choreography diagrams. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Zheng C.
Title: Cross-Channel effects of online reputation and offline event participation in B2B Platforms: Synergy or Attenuation?
Abstract: This study examines how online reputation and offline event participation jointly relate to seller performance on B2B platforms. Although omnichannel research often predicts online–offline synergy, the interaction between these channels remains underexplored in B2B platform settings. Drawing on media richness theory and anchoring logic, we view both channels as distinct yet potentially overlapping credibility cues. Using 30 months of operational data from sellers on a leading Chinese B2B platform, we find that both are positively associated with seller performance, but their interaction is negative: the conditional association of each mechanism weakens as the other strengthens. Online reputation also has a stronger average association with performance. These findings identify cross-channel attenuation as a boundary condition of omnichannel complementarity, suggesting that one salient credibility cue may reduce the other’s incremental informational value. The study contributes to B2B omnichannel research and informs online–offline investment allocation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Yang J.; Ji Q.; Lu D.; Lv P.
Title: Data assetization, information asymmetry, and digital technology innovation: Evidence from China
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of data assetization on enterprise digital technology innovation, focusing on the role of information asymmetry and the moderating effect of data intellectual property protection. Using data from Chinese listed companies, we find that data assetization significantly promotes digital technology innovation, with internal-use data assetization exerting a stronger effect than transactional data assetization. Mechanism analysis indicates that data assetization alleviates information asymmetry in product, financial, and innovation markets, thereby strengthening innovation incentives, easing financing constraints, and promoting collaborative innovation. Further analysis reveals that data intellectual property protection strengthens the innovation effect of data assetization, particularly through its role in reducing information asymmetry in financial and innovation markets. However, it weakens this effect in product markets by restricting consumer data feedback and information flows. These findings provide insights into how firms can leverage data as a strategic asset to overcome information frictions and foster innovation, while offering policy implications for the design of data governance and intellectual property institutions. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Human vs AI-generated advertisements: What converts tourists into destination evangelists
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is fundamentally reshaping the planning, development, and execution of advertising campaigns. Despite the growing application of GenAI in advertising and scholarly interest, research findings on the effects of AI-generated ads on consumer-related outcomes are mixed and rapidly evolving. In particular, the extant literature does not provide sufficient insight into how consumers process cognitive (informativeness and credibility) and affective (creativity and entertainment) values delivered by AI-generated advertisements compared with human-generated advertisements. To fill this gap, the present research used two scenario-based experiments to collect data from 405 (study 1) and 602 (study 2) tourists by randomly exposing them to human and AI-generated advertisements. Data was analyzed in two stages. First, tourists' perceptions of advertising values were compared using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), and then the impact of advertising values on outcome variables was measured using structural equation modeling (SEM). The findings indicate that tourists perceive human-generated advertisements as slightly more informative, credible, creative, and entertaining than AI-generated advertisements. However, the SEM results indicate that the effects of advertising values on tourists' self-expression, attitudes toward the destination, and destination evangelism do not differ significantly between the two advertising formats. These findings are particularly noteworthy, as they suggest that advertising values that emerge from AI-generated advertisements positively influence tourists' attitudes and self-expressive responses. Consequently, the results support tourism marketing professionals in strategically leveraging emerging GenAI tools to develop advertising content that fosters favorable destination attitudes, enhances tourists’ self-expression, and ultimately stimulates destination evangelism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The voting behavior of women-led mutual funds
Abstract: This paper explores the interplay between female representation in mutual funds’ management teams and their voting behavior. We find that women-led mutual funds are more likely to support environmental and social (ES) proposals, but not governance ones. This result is robust to excluding sustainable funds, alleviating concerns that the findings are driven by the self-selection of female fund managers into sustainable funds. While women-led mutual funds are also more likely to vote with management in firms headed by female CEOs, this does not conflict with their greater support for ES shareholder proposals. Overall, our results suggest that female representation in fund management teams is related to their voting behavior on ES issues. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Lubbe J.; Smuts H.
Title: The Dual Identity Dilemma: A Multi-Level Framework for Understanding Platform-Dependent Entrepreneurship
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Entrepreneurship has fundamentally been transformed by the platform economy. However, this transformation carries a paradox that remains undertheorized: the same platforms that empower individual entrepreneurs simultaneously constrain them through asymmetric governance structures designed to extract value whilst simultaneously locking in their users. This concept paper advances a multi-level framework to address this paradox, through combining three analytical levels into an integrated explanation of platform-dependent entrepreneurship. The dual identity dilemma emerges as the core theoretical puzzle – how do platform-dependent entrepreneurs maintain legal autonomy whilst being operationally dependent on the platform and its governance? This paper makes three contributions. First, it adapts the established concept of the dual identity dilemma to platform-dependent entrepreneurship, defines it as the tension between legal independence and operational platform dependence that is operationalised with four observable markers, and embeds it within a process model of platform dependence. Second, it positions the dilemma as the psychological mechanism driving entrepreneurial behaviour across the Platform Dependency Lifecycle. Third, it identifies adult platforms as an illustrative extreme case where the dilemma is most observable and where innovations diffuse to mainstream platforms. The framework provides a roadmap for empirical investigation and offers actionable insights for platform-dependant entrepreneurs, platform designers and policymakers. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Liu S.; Jiang W.; Stark A.W.
Title: Media reach and the market reaction to negative ESG media stories: do industry affiliation and ESG performance matter?
Abstract: Using an event study of U.S.-listed firms, we examine how media reach conditions the stock market reactions to adverse environmental, social, and governance (ESG) news across firms with different ESG performance and industry affiliations. On average, we find that a one-unit increase in media reach is associated with a decrease of 0.13 percentage points in cumulative abnormal returns, indicating an economically meaningful valuation effect. Further analysis shows that this effect is mainly concentrated among low-ESG firms in controversial industries. For high-ESG firms in these industries, media reach makes stock price declines significantly less severe than for low-ESG firms, indicating a media reach insurance effect. However, unless adverse news receives the highest-reach media coverage, we do not find evidence that high ESG performance provides an overall insurance effect. By identifying media reach as a key moderator, this study refines the ESG insurance hypothesis and clarifies when markets value ESG performance. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Inc. Authors: Wu Y.-L.; Yan H.; Xu H.; Xu W.
Title: Legal enforcement and the governance role of underwriter reputation: Evidence from China's securities law reform
Abstract: Ineffective legal enforcement undermines the enforceability of debt contracts (Diamond, 2004). For a long period, however, inadequate enforcement of China's Securities Law failed to effectively constrain opportunistic behavior in the corporate bond market. Taking the 2020 revision of the Securities Law as an exogenous shock, this study finds that the reform strengthens the governance role of underwriter reputation in the corporate bond market. Mechanism analyses indicate that the revision operates by enhancing legal enforceability in the bond market. Heterogeneity analyses show that the effect is more pronounced among low or unrated bonds and unsecured bonds. With respect to underwriter characteristics, the effect is more pronounced for bonds underwritten by a single (non-joint) lead underwriter and by non-IPO lead underwriter. Overall, the effect is mainly observed in bond subsamples where alternative governance mechanisms are relatively weak. This study deepens the understanding of how the legal environment shapes financial markets and sheds light on the complex interaction between formal and informal institutions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Data-driven comparison of airline passenger flight supply using optimal transport theory
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: This study develops an optimal transport (OT) framework for measuring pairwise airline supply dissimilarity across heterogeneous route networks. By representing each airline as a distribution of seat capacity or flight frequency across routes and defining route-level transportation costs, the framework provides a flexible and interpretable approach to comparing carriers beyond traditional measures based on multimarket contact or aggregate concentration. To illustrate its versatility, three OT-based dissimilarity indices are introduced to capture differences in seasonal supply positioning, geographic market proximity, and route-length structure. The framework is applied to European scheduled passenger flights for 32 airlines between 2016 and 2025. The empirical results show that airline relationships are multidimensional, with different patterns of similarity emerging across carrier types and network characteristics. A longitudinal analysis relative to the 2016 baseline reveals heterogeneous adjustment trajectories across airlines and indicates post-pandemic convergence in some dimensions of network organization alongside persistent differentiation in others. Overall, the proposed OT framework provides a general tool for inferring airline similarity from transport distances, assessing resilience and recovery following shocks, and examining structural change over time. The framework can also support the construction of airline peer groups for benchmarking, and the medium- to long-term monitoring of structural network recovery following major market shocks. © 2026 The Author(s).
