Authors: Revoredo K.; Santoro F.
Title: Towards Ethics into BPM Research Through Ethical Dilemmas Assessment
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Business Process Management (BPM) research increasingly influences organizational decision-making, automation, and human work practices, raising important ethical concerns about fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, and societal impact. Despite their growing importance, ethical aspects are often addressed only implicitly or considered in isolated stages of BPM research projects. In this paper, we argue that ethics should be integrated throughout the BPM research lifecycle. To support this goal, we propose a framework that identifies potential ethical dilemmas at different research stages, and outlines possible strategies to address them. The framework is grounded in perspectives from Philosophy and Information Systems ethics, emphasizing the socio-technical implications of BPM technologies and methods. We demonstrate its applicability through an analysis of three papers published at the BPM 2025 conference, selected as representative cases of BPM research projects. The analysis illustrates recurring ethical gaps and highlights the need for more structured ethical reflection during the design, development, evaluation, and deployment of BPM solutions. The paper contributes a practical and reflective instrument for supporting ethically aware BPM research and provides initial directions for strengthening the role of ethics within the BPM community. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Fan X.; Tao W.
Title: To show or not to show? how human vs. digital entrepreneur streamers shape brand attitudes through trust mechanisms
Abstract: Live streaming is reshaping business development, with entrepreneur live streaming emerging as a prominent trend. Despite the growing impact of digital human entrepreneurs, the effects of varying live streamer types on consumer outcomes remain underexplored. This study investigates how entrepreneur live streamer typologies (Real human vs. Digital human) and influence levels (High vs. Low) interact to affect brand attitudes. Grounded in non-evaluative meaning transfer theory and the ELM, we identify distinct mechanisms through which different streamer characteristics enhance brand attitudes. Analyzing 7,631 social media comments and conducting two situational experimental studies (N = 1004), we provide empirical support for our hypotheses. The results indicate that high-influence real-human entrepreneurs boost brand appeal by fostering affective trust, while low-influence digital entrepreneurs enhance communication effectiveness by strengthening cognitive trust. This research broadens the understanding of the live streaming ecosystem and offers insights for businesses to develop strategies optimizing entrepreneur live streaming effectiveness. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Joining schools of thought on value propositions: a review and research agenda
Abstract: The value proposition (VP) is foundational to business research, yet literature devoted to it remains fragmented, hindering the theoretical development and practical application of this key concept. To consolidate and unify the field, the current article presents an analysis of its conceptual and intellectual structure, which distinguishes two dominant schools of thought: a strategic school and a service school. Building on this analysis, the authors propose an integrative framework to bridge these perspectives, which in turn reveals how they can be mobilized jointly to address complex, multilevel, value co-creation dynamics. Finally, a research agenda outlines key questions and thematic priorities—particularly related to sustainability, technology, and innovation—to guide further theoretical integration and the continued evolution of VP scholarship. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

Authors: Sui J.; Li C.; Chen H.Y.
Title: Delays before shipment: How seller fulfillment time shapes consumer return behavior
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Waiting time is a central feature of online shopping, yet prior research has paid limited attention to seller fulfillment time—the seller-controlled period between order placement and handoff to a third-party logistics provider. We propose that longer seller fulfillment time increases product return behavior because it lowers consumers’ shopping experience satisfaction and perceived product quality. Across six studies, combining analyses of large-scale transaction data from a Chinese watch retailer with controlled experiments, we find consistent evidence that longer seller fulfillment time increases product returns. We further show that shopping experience satisfaction and perceived product quality mediate this effect, and that seller fulfillment delay has a stronger negative effect on perceived product quality than courier delay. This effect is weaker when product functionality is emphasized, stronger among consumers who pay greater attention to shipment updates, and weaker in tighter cultural contexts. These findings identify seller fulfillment time as a distinct, seller-controlled driver of product returns and offer practical guidance for managing the pre-shipment stage of online shopping. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Roth K.; Leitner J.
Title: Invisible Entrepreneurs: How Life Design and Systemic Coaching Reveal Unimagined Career Futures
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: In mid-career transitions, many professionals begin to question their career paths. While Life Design offers a structured, creative process to navigate such transitions, it often falls short when individuals are confronted with deeper limiting beliefs, unacknowledged fears, or systemic constraints. This chapter first draws on career construction theory, research on self-efficacy, and identity narratives as the theoretical foundation for Life Design. It then presents a three-month training program that combines Life Design, value-based systemic coaching, and behavioral nudging. Structured across five workshops and one individual coaching session, the program follows a two-tiered intervention logic: first building confidence and agency through small, low-risk routine experiments, then expanding into broader career and identity exploration. Drawing on experience-based insights from two program cohorts, the chapter shows that the program can prompt participants to consider entrepreneurial careers, even when this was not an initial intention. The findings suggest that whether participants move toward entrepreneurial or remain in corporate pathways is influenced by three interrelated factors: their initial career situation, their engagement in experimentation, and how they interpret these experiences in relation to their identity. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Spahic-Bogdanovic M.; Hinkelmann K.
Title: Modelling Professional Experience for Career-Aware Academic Planning: A Weighted Occupation Profile Approach
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Professional experience can shape course relevance for postgraduate students, especially in flexible programmes where many study while working. Academic planning systems rarely treat work history as a structured input. When considered, it is often reduced to free-text job titles or flat role lists that ignore duration, recency, employment intensity, employment type, and overlap. This paper presents JobRanking, a deterministic method that takes job episodes assigned to ESCO occupations, computes monthly full-time-equivalent contributions from employment intensity and type, caps overlapping exposure, applies duration and configurable recency weighting, and normalises the result into an explainable occupation profile. The profile provides a professional-background signal for downstream occupation–course scoring. Controlled profile variants verify design-conformant behaviour for recency, overlap handling, intensity, employment type, and boundedness. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Chang H.; Wu K.-S.
Title: Does ESG reduce hospitality firms’ cost of debt? Roles of information asymmetric and internal control quality
Abstract: Sustainability is increasingly vital for hospitality firms whose operations depend on natural and social resources. However, the financial consequences of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices—particularly their effect on the cost of debt (COD)—remain inconclusive and even contradictory. Using panel regression based on Chinese listed hospitality firms (2010–2023), this article proposes and empirically confirms a U-shaped ESG–COD nexus. The robustness of this U-shaped pattern demonstrates the double-edged nature of corporate sustainability initiatives: debt costs initially decline with ESG engagement; however, beyond a critical threshold, the effect turns upwards as ESG over-investment entails potential trade-offs. Further, mechanism analyses reveal the information asymmetry (IA) mediates this nonlinear relationship, while internal control quality (ICQ) moderates it. Practically, hospitality managers should recognize the U-shaped nature of ESG investments and the underlying mechanisms, through which lower information asymmetry and higher internal control quality weaken the adverse effects of ESG over-investing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Navigating the paradox: Empowerment and power dynamics in international social entrepreneurship
Abstract: Social entrepreneurship (SE) often seeks to empower marginalized beneficiaries by reshaping unequal power relations and promoting more enduring forms of social change. Yet efforts to empower others inherently involve the exercise of power and may therefore reproduce the very asymmetries they seek to overcome. While this “empowerment paradox” has primarily been conceptualized through discrete empowerer-empoweree relationships, considerably less is known about how it unfolds across broader relational systems, particularly in international social entrepreneurship (ISE), where organizations operate across institutional contexts characterized by Global South-North asymmetries. Drawing on a qualitative multi-case study of six ISE ventures, informed by 45 interviews and extensive archival data, we develop an integrative model explaining how the empowerment paradox is structured, experienced, and navigated in these settings. We show that empowerment is organized through multilevel relational chains spanning ecosystem, organizational, and operational levels, that the paradox is experienced differently depending on actors’ positions within these chains, and that organizations navigate persistent tensions through the recursive interplay of relational and structural mechanisms. Building on these findings, we introduce ethical ambidexterity, the capacity to integrate pragmatic and critical orientations toward the use of power, as a means of engaging with rather than resolving the empowerment paradox. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Hemmati Y.
Title: A Bounded-Autonomy Multi-agent Architecture for Policy-Constrained Data Governance
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Enterprise data governance teams enforce a complex ecosystem of roles covering stewardship, quality, traceability, policy, and audit, yet no technical architecture operationalizes these roles as autonomous, collaborating agents. This thesis proposes AGORA (Accountable Governance with Oversight and Role-bounded Autonomy), a governance-oriented multi-agent system (MAS) whose primary contribution is a formally verified, role-bounded enforcement mechanism coupling a Governance Role Ontology (GRO) with a Bounded Autonomy Model (BAM) to make every governance decision deterministically auditable and policy-constrained. Five role-specialized agents operate through a three-layer decision engine separating a role-specialized Large Action Model (LAM) core from a deterministic GRO rule engine and a BAM checkpoint handler—ensuring probabilistic reasoning is always constrained by deterministic enforcement. Supporting this core are a role-specialized training pipeline demonstrated on two pilot agents, and AGORABench. Phase 1 (field study and GRO construction) is complete. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Motivated by differentiation or assimilation: How consumer motives shape luxury channel use
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The rapid digitization of luxury retail has changed how consumers interact with luxury products and services, expanding the range of both online and offline channels. In this evolving landscape, understanding the factors that can influence consumers' online channel use is critical for luxury businesses. This research explores the role of two core social identity motives in luxury consumption, differentiation (the desire to stand out) and assimilation (the desire to fit in), in shaping consumers' luxury channel choices. Using a proprietary dataset of 1,879 verified luxury consumers from eight major Chinese cities, we provide empirical evidence that differentiation reduces exclusive online channel use, whereas assimilation increases it. Additionally, we demonstrate that status signaling amplifies the negative effect of differentiation on exclusive online channel use, whereas social engagement strengthens the positive effect of assimilation. These findings offer novel insights by applying social identity motive theory to the context of digital luxury consumption and examining luxury channel choice, an understudied aspect of luxury behavior. This study highlights the importance of symbolic and identity-driven motives in shaping luxury channel usage, providing practical guidance for multi-channel retailers to align channel strategies with consumers' diverse identity needs. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Balancing risk and opportunity: Digital transformation, cybersecurity investments, and export performance in low-tech firms
Abstract: This study examines whether investments in digital technologies raise export sales among low-tech firms, and whether cybersecurity spending conditions these returns. Reading the Resource-Based View through resource orchestration, we frame digital technologies as enabling resources and cybersecurity as a protective commitment securing their value but competing for the investment budget under scarcity. This competition is sharper in low-tech firms, with thinner slack. Using Bank of Italy data (2016–2023), we find digital investment positively associated with export sales where cybersecurity spending is absent. This association is negative in the highest protective-spending brackets, and a specification imposing no functional form locates the reversal at the top of the distribution. The pattern is clearer among SMEs and manufacturing firms; among larger firms, digital investment shows no association with exports, while protective spending is associated with higher export volume. This is a cyber-risk paradox: under scarcity, protection substitutes for, rather than complements, digital expansion. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier Inc. Title: Digital platform selection and decision optimization for service-oriented manufacturing
Abstract: Digital platforms present great opportunities for companies to transform their operations. However, platform selection is both critical and complex, especially in service-oriented manufacturing (SOM), where after-sales service is as important as production. In practice, manufacturers often face resource constraints that prevent them from adopting multiple digital platforms simultaneously, making it important to determine which type of platform should be prioritized. This study develops an analytical framework of an SOM supply chain with one manufacturer and multiple heterogeneous operators, and compares three platform-adoption scenarios: no digitalization platform (NDP), a production digitalization platform (PDP), and a service digitalization platform (SDP). The results provide clear guidance for manufacturers: platform choice depends on the relative benefit–cost ratio of PDP versus SDP and the equipment's per-use price, and it shapes key decisions by both manufacturers and operators. Manufacturer and operator preferences may diverge in certain cases, underscoring the need for coordination within the supply chain. As an extension, we further examine a full-process digitalization platform (FDP), in which the manufacturer adopts both PDP and SDP, and show how full-process digitalization changes the benchmark comparison. This study contributes an integrated framework for analyzing digitalization platform selection in SOM supply chains and offers actionable insights for manufacturers considering digital platform adoption. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Agag G.
Title: From eco-certification to market value: How green innovation drives sustainable advantage in the global hospitality industry
Abstract: This study explains when eco-certification creates firm value in hospitality and why similar certification programmes generate different outcomes across institutional settings. Using a balanced panel of 50 listed hospitality firms from the United Kingdom, the United States, and Egypt (2015–2025; 550 firm-year observations), the study combines staggered difference-in-differences estimation with implementation-alignment analyses. Results show that eco-certification intensity increases both firm value and green innovation, while green innovation transmits most of the valuation effect. Additional analyses identify a certification-translation gap, whereby firms with extensive certification coverage but limited innovation receive significantly lower valuation benefits. Certification effects are nonlinear and delayed, becoming stronger only after certification reaches meaningful portfolio breadth. Regulatory stringency and environmental norms mainly stimulate implementation, whereas sustainable finance depth and governance quality facilitate and capitalise innovation. The study reconceptualises eco-certification as a translation-governance mechanism whose value depends on implementation alignment, scale, timing, and institutional support. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Exploring the Cultural Foundations of Trust and Accountability in Accounting: A Hofstede-Based Analysis
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: Cultural values profoundly influence organizational behaviors and accounting systems, shaping how trust and accountability are perceived and enacted across societies. Hofstede’s cultural dimensionsCultural dimensions provide a widely recognized framework for understanding how societal values influence business conduct across cultures. Given accounting’s central role in transparency, governance, and decision-making, understanding the interplay between culture and accounting practices is critical for multinational organizations and policymakers. Title: Too smart for comfort? How neural inference depth shapes consumer adoption of brain–computer interfaces
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As firms increasingly introduce consumer-facing neurotechnology products and services, such as brain–computer interface (BCI)-enabled applications, understanding how consumers respond to varying levels of personal data inference becomes critical for market success. This study examines how neural inference depth—defined as the extent to which a technology infers psychologically sensitive information about users—shapes consumer adoption intention in retail and digital service contexts. Across three between-subjects experiments (total N = 1547), results reveal an inverted-U relationship between inference depth and adoption intention, with moderate levels of inference maximizing consumer acceptance. We further identify a dual-path mechanism underlying this effect: whereas the self-insight value exhibits diminishing returns at higher levels of inference, perceived creepiness increases at an accelerating rate, leading to a systematic shift in pathway dominance. Perceived data control mitigates the negative effect of creepiness without enhancing perceived benefits. Importantly, a design intervention in the form of modular disclosure, which staggers the activation of advanced features, reduced perceived creepiness and increased adoption intention under conditions of deep inference without compromising self-insight value, although it operated only partly through the creepiness pathway. Based on experimental evidence from adult online consumers in China responding to hypothetical BCI scenarios, these findings contribute to the retailing and consumer services literature by conceptualizing consumer data inference as a continuous hierarchical construct and offer directional guidance for firms designing privacy-sensitive, technology-enabled service experiences, pending cross-cultural and field-based replication. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Entrepreneurship Education in Action: Preventing the NEET Phenomenon. Lessons from La Paranza Case Study

Title: Toward Hybrid Agile Teams: Enhancing Collaboration in Agile Projects by Exploring Traditional and AI-Based Tools for Process Optimization and Best Practices

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of agile teams and is increasingly shaping how collaboration takes place in software development environments. Although some human-AI collaboration supports have been proposed in the literature, the use of process mining techniques in agile and collaborative settings remains relatively unexplored. Title: Increasing the Efficiency of Using the Energy Potential of Wood: Solutions for Ukraine
Source title: Studies in Systems, Decision and Control
Abstract: The aim of the research is to develop directions for increasing the efficiency of using wood as an energy source in Ukraine. The state of global forestry and the use of the energy potential of fuel wood from 2013 to 2023 is assessed on the basis of data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The analysis of global trends in logging, wood processing, and the use of wood as fuel revealed discrepancies in global trends regarding the rates of change in the share of fuel wood production, wood pellets, and briquettes. Significant growth rates in the production of wood agglomerates worldwide indicate an intensification of the use of energy potential of wood driven by ecological and economic factors. With one of the highest shares of fuel wood in total wood volume, Ukraine produces nearly 7 times less wood pellets than Germany. Based on the developed regression models, a scenario has been elaborated to enhance the efficiency of utilizing the fuel potential of wood in Ukraine. It has been demonstrated that there are reserves in Ukraine for processing fuel wood and waste from both wood processing and saw-milling industries into more efficient products in terms of energy production and compliance with environmental conditions, namely pellets, briquettes, and so on. It is concluded about advisability to process wood waste directly at the sites of logging or wood processing, using technologies and equipment for collecting and sorting the waste from saw-milling and woodworking production and by-products. Title: Judicial delocalization and corporate cash holdings: evidence from China
Abstract: This paper examines how local judicial governance shapes corporate cash holdings by exploiting the staggered implementation of China's judicial delocalization reform as a quasi-natural experiment. The reform shifted personnel, fiscal, and material control over local courts from same-level local governments to provincial authorities, thereby weakening local judicial protectionism. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2007 to 2023, we find that the judicial delocalization reform significantly reduces corporate cash holdings. Channel analyses show that the reform weakens firms' precautionary demand for cash by reducing litigation risk and improving external capital availability, while also mitigating agency-related cash retention by lowering managerial agency costs and rent-seeking expenditures. Cross-sectional evidence indicates that the impact is more pronounced among non-state-owned enterprises that rely more heavily on judicial protection, firms located in regions with more abundant judicial resources, and firms situated farther from local courts. Furthermore, we find that the reform accelerates firms' adjustment toward target cash levels. Overall, this study enriches the literature on the judicial determinants of corporate cash holdings and offers policy insights into the corporate financial consequences of reducing local judicial protectionism. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Bridging Accuracy and Interpretability in Business Process Simulation via Knowledge Distillation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Business Process Simulation (BPS) is widely used to analyze and optimize processes in a controlled environment. Recent advances integrate AI models to improve the simulation accuracy of process perspectives such as control-flow and time. However, BPS-based improvement requires testing alternative what-if analyses. This can only be achieved through white-box models, where analysts can inspect and modify the underlying decision logic. Purely black-box models, although often highly accurate, lack transparency and limit configurability. However, traditional white-box models (e.g. decision trees) provide explicit and interpretable rules but may struggle to capture complex dependencies, leading to lower predictive accuracy, hampering the BPS realism. This paper proposes a distillation-based approach to bridge the gap between predictive accuracy and interpretability in BPS. We first train black-box predictive models (referred to as teacher models) to learn complex temporal and behavioral patterns from event logs. We then extract the knowledge captured by the teacher models and transfer it into probabilistic decision trees, obtaining interpretable surrogate white-box models (referred to as student models). The distilled models approximate the learned behavior of the teacher while offering a white-box representation and maintaining competitive predictive performance. Experimental results in four case studies, using four alternative teacher models, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The findings show that distillation is able to improve the accuracy of simulation models, compared to standard decision trees without distillation, while maintaining interpretability and supporting reliable what-if analyses. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: BPMN-Based RPA Projects Modeling and Analysis Method
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: During the last decade, RPA (Robotic Process Automation) has gained significant popularity as a transformative force in enterprise digitalization projects. However, the practice has been largely platform-driven and detached from traditional business process management, the BPM lens being applied rather retrospectively. In the authors’ regional outsourcing hub, RPA projects are defined around the licensed platform that facilitates the actual development of bots. This pragmatic view is based on the RPA promise of reduced operational costs, but not all business processes are suitable for this transformation. Elements of the traditional BPM lifecycle return in specific forms, e.g. new approaches to process querying and reporting. The transition from identifying a potential RPA candidate project to a successful and scalable one can be complex, relying on traceable semantics that consider both the process structure and key performance indicators - these can be integrated by means of domain-specific conceptual modeling, extending process modeling standards that lack the specificity needed to support the phases of the RPA project lifecycle. This paper proposes a BPMN extension in tandem with Generative AI recommendations, tailored to bridge the gap between traditional business process modeling and RPA project management. The work follows a metamodeling approach and a Design Science process to produce a hybrid BPMN-RPA modeling method informed by the concrete needs of RPA practice as well as by the design-oriented research tradition on BPMN extensions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Connecting the Dots: Path-Based Entity Linking in Object-Centric Event Data
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: How long does it take from placing an order to its full delivery, and does the number of packages it was shipped in affect this duration? In object-centric event data, answering such questions requires connecting objects and events that have no direct relationship but are linked through chains of intermediate entities. Existing techniques analyze control flow within individual object types yet provide no systematic means to discover or quantify these cross-type connections. We introduce path schemas: type-level descriptions of how any two entities (events or objects) can be connected through the data graph. We automatically enumerate path schemas from a compact type graph and rank them by metrics such as selectivity and coverage to separate meaningful connections from noise. Path schemas enable end-to-end performance analysis across object types (e.g., order-to-delivery throughput) and structural connection discovery (e.g., tracing how orders relate to packages through items). We evaluate our open-source implementation on five datasets, including two real-life ones, and show that path schemas uncover process structure often overlooked by existing techniques and that targeted analysis scales to logs with over a million events. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Test of a triple serial mediation model of green ethical leadership: Empirical research in two countries
Abstract: Our study developed and tested a triple serial mediation model of green ethical leadership (GEL). The study relationships were gauged via time-lagged data collected from hotel frontline employees (FLEs) in Türkiye (Study 1) and Ireland (Study 2) using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The following findings are valid for two studies. GEL fosters green creativity, while anticipated pride mediates the linkage between GEL and said outcome. Anticipated pride and green work engagement (GWEN) serially mediate the connection between GEL and green creativity. This is also true for job embeddedness (JEM) and GWEN as the serial mediators relating GEL to green creativity. More importantly, anticipated pride, JEM, and GWEN serially mediate the influence of GEL on FLEs’ green creativity. Our paper fills in research lacunas by reporting the outcomes and multiple/triple mediators of GEL simultaneously that have not been gauged in the pertinent literature so far. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Non-deceptive counterfeiting with brand dilution and network externalities: Beyond conventional beliefs
Abstract: Non-deceptive counterfeiting involves producing and selling counterfeit products without misleading consumers about their authenticity. This practice intensifies price competition for genuine brands while contributing either to brand dilution or network externalities. Using a two-period game modeling approach, we analyze how genuine products should adjust their advertising and pricing strategies in response to non-deceptive counterfeiting. Our findings reveal that in the presence of brand dilution, manufacturers should reduce advertising investments and prices to remain competitive. However, when counterfeiting generates network externalities, the optimal response depends on market conditions and managerial effectiveness. In some cases, a survival strategy (reducing advertising and/or prices) may be necessary to maintain profitability. In other cases, a differentiation strategy (raising advertising and prices) can lead to profit gains. Regardless of the approach adopted, manufacturers must improve the targeting, content, and effectiveness of advertising to further differentiate their offerings and reduce positive spillover effects to counterfeit products. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: From trash to treasure: How exclusivity influences quality perception across different recycled materials in luxury fashion
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Luxury fashion brands increasingly respond to corporate social responsibility expectations by integrating recycled materials into their products to reduce environmental impact. However, little is known about how these brands should communicate their use of recycled materials on social media without compromising product evaluation. To address this issue, through two between-subjects experimental studies, this paper examines whether and how luxury fashion products crafted from different types of recycled materials (natural vs. synthetic) affect product evaluation on social media, and whether exclusivity moderate this effect. Study 1 (N = 149, 63.09% male, Mage = 41.12, SDage = 13.48) shows that luxury fashion products made from recycled synthetic (vs. recycled natural) materials significantly reduce product evaluation, an effect fully mediated by perceived product quality. Study 2 (N = 199, 59.30% male, Mage = 35.64, SDage = 12.30) further indicates that this negative indirect effect through perceived product quality emerges under high exclusivity, and is not significant when exclusivity is attenuated. These findings contribute to sustainable luxury fashion literature by identifying material type as the key dimension differentiating consumer evaluations of recycled materials in luxury fashion. The findings also show that exclusivity is the critical contextual trigger that activates this material-driven effect through perceived product quality. Managerially, luxury fashion brands are advised against pairing exclusivity cues with their products made from recycled synthetic materials on social media, while such cues remain viable for recycled natural materials. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Attention constraints and the limits of clustering benefits for operational efficiency
Abstract: Spillovers from geographic clustering have received considerable attention, yet there is an implicit assumption that firms can effectively process all available information in clustered environments. This study examines how clustering affects firms’ operations and is constrained by the informational environment. We draw on the attention-based view (ABV) and propose that the operational benefits of clustering are bounded by firms’ attentional capacity, creating an inverted U-shaped relationship in which efficiency gains initially increase with cluster density but diminish when information volume exceeds capacity. We test these predictions by analyzing how proximity to same-industry firms affects operational efficiency in resource utilization. Leveraging power consumption data from 2317 privately owned Canadian firms (2012–2016), we find that while initially beneficial, clustering benefits plateau and decline when processing demands exceed capacity. These constraints are less pronounced in mature, financially stable firms and in those with top management teams appropriately sized for their clustering environment. Our findings identify boundaries to the benefits of clustering and clarifying when attention becomes a binding constraint. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: From Dreams to Entrepreneurial Actions and Life Design: Creating Flourishing Students through Vision Boosts in Higher Education
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: This chapter examines how students can transform their lives by taking control of their dreams and actively working to bring them to fruition. The transformation begins with the Vision Boost teaching tool. Vision Boost creates a framework for conversations focused on entrepreneurial life design and career development. The chapter demonstrates how structured reflection formats can support entrepreneurial orientation, identity development, and future-oriented sensemaking in higher education. The Vision Boost method involves three distinct staged steps: 1) identifying dream(s), 2) reflecting on personal competencies, skills, and knowledge, and 3) recognizing and generating opportunities to take next steps. The study draws on qualitative semi-structured interviews with female students and graduates from a university of applied sciences who have participated in Vision Boost sessions. The findings show that students see a strong connection between their future aspirations and their disciplinary skills. They also reflect on how to act immediately to achieve their goals and dreams, both in the near and distant future. An important outcome is the boost in motivation to engage in their current educational programs. The study provides new insights into promoting women’s empowerment to see themselves as entrepreneurial in their personal and professional futures. It also helps students view their professional identities more broadly, beyond traditional career paths, and consider future entrepreneurial opportunities, such as starting their own ventures. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Hurt at home, loafing at work: Spillover effect of family ostracism on hospitality employees’ cyberloafing and its mitigation through self- and others’ care
Abstract: In the hospitality industry, employees’ cyberloafing is more visible to customers, potentially harming key business outcomes such as customer experience and satisfaction. Given these detrimental effects, it is critical to examine the underlying drivers that trigger cyberloafing behavior among hospitality employees. From this perspective, this study examines the influence of interpersonal stressor in the home domain—specifically, family ostracism—on cyberloafing among hospitality employees. Guided by the work-home resources framework, the present study explores a spillover process whereby family ostracism exacerbates hospitality employees’ cyberloafing via family emotional exhaustion. Additionally, it explores how these adverse effects can be mitigated through self-care efforts (self-compassion) and others’ care (family-supportive coworker behavior). Data were obtained from a three-wave survey involving 291 employees and their coworkers at two five-star hotels located in Southeastern China. The results confirm an indirect spillover effect wherein family ostracism leads to cyberloafing via family emotional exhaustion. However, this effect becomes insignificant when employees demonstrate high self-compassion or benefit from family-supportive coworker behavior. This study discusses both the theoretical implications derived from the findings and the practical contributions to the hospitality industry. © 2026

Title: Hidden in plain sight: service quality gaps in retail self-service systems
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Retail self-service systems (RSSS) fundamentally challenge established assumptions of service quality research by redistributing service delivery from frontline employees to consumers interacting with technologically mediated service systems. Extant service quality gap models are anchored in employee-mediated interaction and offer limited insight into how service quality emerges once adaptive frontline mediation is substantially reduced or absent. Addressing this research gap, we develop a socio-technical reconceptualization of service quality in RSSS grounded in socio-technical systems theory. Empirically, we draw on a sequential qualitative study combining interviews with managers responsible for RSSS development and in-situ consumer interviews conducted immediately after system use. Our findings identify six interdependent service quality gaps that collectively form the socio-technical alignment cycle (STAC), a recursive framework explaining how service quality stabilizes across repeated interactions through alignment between service configurations and heterogeneous consumer capabilities, expectations, and perceptions. The findings further reveal an efficiency paradox in which design choices intended to maximize scalability and operational efficiency simultaneously generate socio-technical frictions that destabilize service quality. By shifting service quality research from an interpersonal toward a systems-centered perspective, this study reconceptualizes service quality in technologically mediated retail environments as a dynamic socio-technical process continuously fostered by system-consumer misalignments. The study advances service quality, socio-technical systems, and smart retailing research while providing retailers with a framework for managing socio-technical tensions in RSSS. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Civardi C.; Moro A.
Title: Promotion and prevention regulatory focus in equity crowdfunding reinvestment decisions
Abstract: Using qualitative comparative analysis, our study draws on regulatory focus theory to examine how chronic promotion and prevention foci and situational factors are associated with reinvestment decisions in equity crowdfunding. Evidence suggests that both chronic promotion and prevention foci are sufficient conditions for reinvestment and that situational factors, particularly the absence of inhibitors related to information asymmetry, valuation difficulties, and exit constraints, play an important role. We also identify configurations incorporating the presence of inhibitor factors, which we interpret as consistent with investors adopting a speculative, bet-like approach. Our study offers practical insights for platforms and entrepreneurs by emphasising how transparent communication and risk disclosure can build investor trust and encourage continued investments. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Güleç Ö.F.
Title: Global–Local: Exploring the Cultural Dimension of Sustainability
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: Sustainability reporting is a multi-dimensional communication and management tool that complements a company’s full set of financial statements in the context of environmental, social and governance, and is critical for companies to survive and create value. The plurality of practices and differences in formats in sustainability reporting raise various issues regarding reporting quality and comparability. The lack of standards in the voluntary reporting environment can lead companies to disclose only selective information and engage in “greenwashing.” In this context, the primary goal of standardization is to increase the consistency and comparability of sustainability-related information required by global capital markets. Standards and guidelines aim to reduce such opportunistic disclosures and increase the legitimacy of reporting by specifying what and how to report. The purpose of standards is to help establish a common language for sustainability reporting for both organizations and stakeholders. While standardization for sustainability practices is important for building a common language, it can cause companies to overlook issues and demands in cultural contexts. Thus, global standardization should not be seen as absolute target in sustainability reporting and attention should be paid to the role of cultural context in sustainability reporting. The motivation to ensure that reporting is meaningful and legitimate in the eyes of local stakeholders makes the cultural factor an important issue in the standardization process. In this study, the concept of sustainability, its historical development process and the transformation of standards are discussed and the role and impact of culture in global sustainability standards and sustainability reporting practices are examined from the perspective of cultural dimensions (Hofstede) and various theories. The purpose of this compilation study is to reveal how cultural dimensions and culture-related theories affect the understanding of sustainability by reviewing the fundamental studies in the literature. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Extending sustainable consumption after EV purchase: Green signals and purchase intention toward green EV insurance
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Green consumption in the electric vehicle (EV) market increasingly extends beyond vehicle ownership to services that shape driving, repair, claims and renewal decisions. Green EV insurance is a credence service because consumers cannot easily verify its environmental value before purchase. Across markets, similar functions appear in telematics pricing, driving feedback, green repair, battery support and carbon or resource disclosure, even though they are not usually packaged under one label. Using China as a policy driven setting where these functions are becoming more visible, this study examines how EV owners judge whether green insurance signals are credible and worth acting on. Drawing on signaling theory and an extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), we analyze survey data from 758 Chinese EV owners. Structural equation modeling (SEM) is the main method, with necessary condition analysis (NCA) and fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) used as complementary tests. The results show that policy and corporate green signals do not directly increase purchase intention. Instead, they work through attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, green perceived value and green trust. Attitude is the strongest pathway. Price sensitivity strengthens the signal intention relationship, suggesting that cost conscious consumers respond when signals clarify value. Consumers with low climate concern show little response. The study extends sustainable consumption research to services after EV purchase and shows how green signals can turn fragmented insurance functions into clearer consumer value. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Why consumers disengage from DTC brands: A stressor–strain perspective on mental fatigue and purchase avoidance
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) brands have expanded their presence in digital retail, particularly in the apparel sector, and a substantial proportion of consumers browse these platforms without completing a purchase. Existing research has largely explained this shopping disengagement through transactional barriers and user experience issues, leaving the psychological processes that drive purchase avoidance on DTC platforms inadequately understood. Drawing on Expectancy Violation Theory and the Stress–Strain–Outcome framework, this study proposes that when DTC brands fail to meet the ease and efficiency consumers expect from large online marketplaces, consumers experience unmet expectations as shopping stressors that give rise to mental fatigue and drive purchase avoidance. A sequential mixed-methods design was adopted. In the qualitative phase, critical incident interviews identified the principal stressors experienced during DTC apparel shopping and informed the development of a conceptual model. In the quantitative phase, the model was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling with survey data from 569 Indian consumers. Shopping stressors significantly intensify mental fatigue, which in turn drives purchase avoidance. Consumer frugality moderates the stressor–mental fatigue relationship, with frugal consumers exhibiting heightened strain responses under equivalent stressor levels. Stressors also exert a direct effect on purchase avoidance beyond the mediating role of mental fatigue, indicating that the strain mechanism does not fully absorb the influence of shopping stressors. This study contributes to consumer behaviour literature by introducing mental fatigue as a theoretically specified mediating construct linking shopping stressors to purchase avoidance in DTC retail. It also offers practical guidance for managers seeking to reduce cognitive load in DTC shopping, thereby improving consumer engagement and purchase conversion. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How regulatory focus shapes consumer spending under threshold promotions
Abstract: Minimum purchase requirement deals, such as “$10 off when you spend $50”, represent a common form of threshold promotion and are widely used in everyday retail contexts. However, little is known about how consumers adjust their spending once they have decided to redeem such deals. This research examines how consumers’ regulatory focus shapes their spending behavior when using such deals. Across field and experimental studies, we demonstrate that prevention-focused consumers consistently spend less than promotion-focused consumers after committing to a minimum purchase requirement deal because they show greater persuasion knowledge and suspicion toward the marketer’s intent. This suspicion is amplified when the deal benefit is uncertain, for example, in offers such as “up to £100 off”. Our findings offer actionable guidance for retailers. By identifying consumers’ regulatory orientation and tailoring message framing accordingly, retailers can enhance the effectiveness of minimum purchase requirement deals and meaningfully influence consumer spending. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Inc.

Title: Bridging accounting and AI: A sentiment-enhanced analytical framework for forecasting hotel profitability from customer reviews
Abstract: This study examines how customer-generated reviews complement accrual-based financial indicators in analyzing short-term financial performance in the hotel industry. It develops a sentiment-enhanced framework that integrates unstructured customer feedback with structured accounting data. Using natural language processing (NLP) and ensemble learning, the analysis aligns review-based sentiment with quarterly financial records to examine their temporal interaction. Drawing on signaling theory, customer sentiment functions as an external signal that reflects perceived service quality and evolving demand conditions. The findings indicate that certain accrual-related accounts, particularly unearned revenue, move in patterns associated with shifts in customer feedback. Negative sentiment aligns with periods of financial pressure, while themes related to comfort and service quality correspond with changes in financial outcomes. This approach offers an additional interpretive perspective for examining the relationship between market perception and accounting-based performance in service-oriented settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Curcio V.; Le Van O.
Title: Agency Perceptions and Trust in Generative AI: A Longitudinal Study on Software Engineers
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Generative AI tools are reshaping software development, yet the mechanisms through which developers build or lose trust in these tools remain poorly understood. Vanneste and Puranam posit that perceiving an AI as agentic affects trust through three mechanisms: enhancing perceived ability, shifting the locus of trust from designer to AI, and amplifying betrayal concerns. This model remains untested, and treats agency as a unitary construct—an assumption not yet examined empirically. To address this gap, we test the three-mechanism model and examine whether agency functions as a unitary construct through a mixed-methods longitudinal field study with 107 software professionals using AI coding assistants (four survey waves; nine semi-structured interviews). The survey confirms the first two mechanisms: agency correlates with perceived ability and trust progressively shifts from the designer to the AI as the primary trustee. The third mechanism, however, is reversed: betrayal cost is positively associated with trust, contradicting the predicted negative relationship. The interviews reveal why: professional users do not perceive agency as unitary. They grant the AI autonomy but deny it intentionality and free will, a distinction drawn by 7 out of 9 interviewees. Because users do not attribute intentional action to the AI, they assign errors to their own prompting and describe potential AI loss as functional dependency rather than betrayal. Agency decomposition thus emerges as a boundary condition for trust models in AI: mechanisms requiring only perceived autonomy (ability enhancement, locus shift) operate as predicted, while betrayal aversion, which presupposes perceived intentionality, is structurally neutralized. These findings suggest that treating agency as unitary may lead to incorrect predictions in populations that differentiate its facets. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Accounting Culture and Sustainability: “A Transdisciplinary Framework for Global Practices”
Source title: Accounting, Finance, Sustainability, Governance and Fraud
Abstract: As sustainability emerges as a dominant paradigm in global governance and corporate accountability, the role of accounting is being redefined through the lenses of culture and interdisciplinary integration. This study explores the intersection of sustainability accounting and accounting culture by employing a transdisciplinary framework. Drawing on Hofstede’s cultural dimensions and Gray’s accounting values, the research highlights how cultural and institutional contexts shape the interpretation, application, and evolution of sustainability practices across different countries. It argues that sustainability accounting must go beyond technical compliance and engage with the ethical, cultural, and social dimensions of corporate behavior. The paper also critiques the limitations of standardized ESG frameworks in culturally diverse settings and underscores the need for culturally sensitive policy development. By positioning culture as a potential “fourth pillar” of sustainable development, the study calls for an integrated approach that incorporates education, governance structures, and organizational culture. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of how cultural foundations can enable or constrain the implementation of global sustainability goals within accounting systems. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Integrated production planning, berth allocation, and time-variant quay crane assignment scheduling problem
Abstract: This paper addresses integrated production planning, multi-quay berth allocation, and quay crane assignment scheduling problems. The results show that the MILP-ALNS approach performs better than existing iterative local search procedures reported in the literature. Title: Place-Based AI policy and corporate green transformation: Evidence from China’s National AI pilot zones

Abstract: Advancing corporate green transformation constitutes a critical avenue for realizing China’s high-quality development and long-term sustainable economic growth. Title: Multiple Criteria Group Decision as a Rule-Based Ensemble Classifier
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: In this paper, we consider a multiple-criteria group classification decision-making (MC-GCDM) problem as a rule-based ensemble classification task, where individual decision makers are modeled as expert classifiers induced from diversified subsets of data. A group of experts assigns a set of objects, evaluated on multiple criteria, to predefined and ordered decision classes. Each expert expresses their preferences by classifying a subset of reference objects that are well known to them and reflect their expertise. Based on this preference information, a set of “if–then” decision rules is derived for each expert using the Variable Consistency Dominance-based Rough Set Approach (VC-DRSA). These rule sets serve as base classifiers in an ensemble classifier designed to classify all objects in the decision problem. In addition to this straightforward ensemble construction, we propose an alternative approach. The rule sets obtained by VC-DRSA are aggregated into a joint pool, from which several diversified subsets are generated by solving a series of integer linear programming problems. These subsets cover all reference classifications with minimal rule sets and form the base classifiers of a second ensemble. In both ensembles, the base classifiers vote on the final classification. Computational experiments on several classification datasets demonstrate a clear superiority of the optimized ensemble classifier. Moreover, the diversified rule sets better capture the different preference perspectives within the group than classifiers constructed separately for individual experts. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Commons without borders: How entrepreneurs can engage local actors into collective action for the governance of supra-local common-pool resources
Abstract: Based on 41 interviews across three UK-based commons enterprises, this study addresses one of the most pressing challenges of our time: encouraging local actors to contribute to the sustainable governance of supra-local common-pool resources (CPRs)—shared resources whose use and impacts extend beyond community boundaries. While existing research has focused on locally bound natural CPRs, we lack understanding of how entrepreneurial ventures can mobilize the members of local communities to govern resources that span multiple jurisdictions. Our findings reveal a two-step process through which entrepreneurs first embed their commons enterprises in the local community, using asset locks and diversified engagement strategies to involve citizens, local businesses, and public authorities. Building on this embedding, three commoning practices emerge: collective learning about the CPR, collective action and capacity building for CPR stewardship, and collective institutionalization of CPR governance. Around these practices, a community of commoners emerges that is nested within the local community and increasingly sustains collective action independently of the entrepreneur. These practices anchor the supra-local CPR within the local community through three mechanisms: resource proximization, local conditionality, and bonding as a selective incentive, thereby overcoming the collective action barriers arising from lacking resource proximity and perceived responsibility. Our study contributes to research at the intersection of entrepreneurship and the commons by demonstrating the strategic role of common property regimes, shifting attention from the resource to the commoning practices and communities that form around it, and specifying the mechanisms that enable local collective action for supra-local CPR governance. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Author full names: Igboanua, Chukwuka (59395639700); Siefkes, Meike (58609464800); Schillebeeckx, Simon J.D. (55255151800); Hakala, Henri (36915070700)
Title: Between mission pull and governance burden: Geographic distance and deal realisation in impact investing
Abstract: Impact investing is widely expected to direct capital to locations where social and environmental challenges are most severe. Yet such opportunities are often found in places geographically distant from major pools of investment capital. We examine how geographic distance affects the realisation of impact investment deals and how host-country conditions alter that relationship. Integrating transaction cost economics with the location logic of the eclectic paradigm, we argue that impact investment decisions reflect the joint consideration of anticipated transaction value and governance costs. Distance raises the costs of screening, contracting, monitoring, and supporting ventures, while severe sustainability challenges can increase a location's mission-specific attractiveness by signaling greater unmet need and potential scope for additionality. By contrast, trade and investment risk increases transaction hazards that make distant deals harder to execute. We test these arguments using PitchBook data on 3126 impact deals closed in 2022–2023. We analyse 3606 realised investor–venture ties against matched unrealised alternatives in a choice-based sampling design. Distance reduces the likelihood of deal realisation. Challenge severity modestly weakens the distance penalty for a subset of sampled dyads, whereas trade and investment risk strengthens it across most observations. Abstract: The accounting profession is not limited to the preparation and reporting of financial information; it is also an important tool that lays the groundwork for businesses to make sound decisions during times of crisis. Title: Meta-analysis of antecedents and consequences of customers’ perceived advertisement value
Abstract: The literature has frequently studied the effect of privacy concerns, irritation, trust, incentives, enjoyment, innovativeness, usefulness, ease of use and subjective norms on mobile advertising value. Abstract: The fuel consumption emissions caused by maritime transport present challenges to sustainable development. Title: Bridging the experience gap: cognitive biases and heuristics in the internationalization of small firms
Source title: International Journal of Entrepreneurial Behaviour and Research
Abstract: Purpose – Research on early internationalization in smaller firms has primarily focused on initial market entry, often neglecting responses to adverse post-entry events. This paper addresses the gap between entrepreneurial internationalization and small business survival by examining both initial and post-entry stages through decision-maker cognition. Design/methodology/approach – This conceptual paper develops a cognition-based decision framework that explains how cognitive biases influence pre- and initial entry decisions, and evolve in response to post-entry negative events. It introduces the “experience gap paradox”- a misalignment between personal experience and required international market experience – as a key driver of biased judgment. The framework links non-contextualized pre-entry experience with post-entry decision-making, offering testable propositions on the dynamic interplay between biases, heuristics, and internationalization decisions. Findings – This model supports the argument that heuristic decision-making is contingent upon context-specific prior experience, which leaders of small firms typically lack pre-entry, causing them to develop and rely on decision biases. Originality/value – This article contributes by exploring how cognitive heuristics and biases evolve in decision-making across the pre-entry and post-entry stages of internationalization, with a focus on smaller firms-particularly International New Ventures (INVs). It provides a comprehensive understanding of the “experience gap paradox” and its influence on entrepreneurial internationalization, offering insights relevant to small firms' adaptive decision-making and survival. © 2025 Anisur R. Authors: Qu J.; Solinger O.N.; Shi J.
Title: Creative nonetheless: performance avoiders maintain creative performance through bootlegging under team culture tightness
Abstract: Research suggests that the performance-avoid goal orientation trait inhibits radical creativity by prompting individuals to avoid rejection in social situations. We extend this conclusion by investigating bootlegging as a means of developing creative output, especially under tight team cultures. Drawing on trait activation theory, we propose that under tight team cultures, employees high in performance-avoid goal orientation uphold their creative output by engaging in informally innovative efforts away from the scrutinizing eyes of others and outside visibility of formally authorized programs. This behavior is known as bootlegging. Hypotheses surrounding this phenomenon were supported in a scenario experiment involving 279 employees and in a multi-wave, multi-source field survey involving 318 employees across 63 work teams. Our findings challenge the prevailing assumption that performance-avoid goal orientation is necessarily detrimental to creativity, increase the understanding of a bootlegging pathway toward radical creativity for these employees, and emphasize the importance of team culture tightness. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Author full names: Salatiello, Emma (57926003100); Papa, Francesca (59965359000); Vespoli, Silvestro (57200013194); Grassi, Andrea (55828149363)
Title: Dynamic lead time coordination in supply chains under bilateral operational information asymmetry
Abstract: Coordinating modern supply chains (SCs) is hindered by market volatility and, critically, by bilateral operational information asymmetry, where partners hold private, unverifiable information about their real-time capabilities. This study addresses this challenge by developing and testing a novel coordination framework for a dyadic SC, centered on a dynamic lead time negotiation coupled with an adaptive revenue-sharing mechanism. A comparative simulation analysis reveals that while lead time negotiation alone enhances responsiveness by significantly reducing delivery times, it can paradoxically destroy total SC profit in decentralized settings due to uncompensated operational costs. However, the proposed integrated framework – combining negotiation with adaptive revenue sharing – proves highly effective. It not only fosters cooperation but also recovers nearly all profit losses from decentralization, while ensuring an equitable profit distribution. Furthermore, the study uncovers a critical insight into pricing power: a leader’s ability to charge for faster service is fundamentally limited by the partner’s economic viability, with a clear threshold beyond which an aggressive pricing strategy becomes value-destructive for the entire SC. This research contributes a novel operational contract that effectively mitigates the impacts of information asymmetry and enhances system-wide efficiency by explicitly linking dynamic operational decisions (lead time) to their shared financial consequences, offering a practical path toward resilient and profitable SC collaboration. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Infrastructuring socio-ecological stewardship: accounting, governance and circular economy transitions in construction
Abstract: Purpose – This study examines how accounting, adaptive governance and financial infrastructures interact with circular economy (CE) initiatives in the construction industry. It explores how product-as-a-service (PaaS) business models challenge conventional assumptions around ownership, valuation and accountability, foregrounding accounting’s infrastructural role in shaping socio-ecological stewardship and long-term material commitments. Design/methodology/approach – This is a qualitative exploratory study of two PaaS cases (“Road-as-a-Service” and “Façade-as-a-Service”) incorporating eleven focus groups with 45 professionals from financial, legal and technical domains. Data are thematically analysed through a framework integrating corporate biosphere stewardship, adaptive governance and radical traceability, while remaining open to emergent institutional tensions. Findings – The findings highlight frictions between CE aspirations and linear infrastructures underpinning organisational practices. Participants surfaced challenges around residual value estimation, intertemporal accountability, financing adaptability and governance flexibility. These challenges crystallised into three interconnected themes – transition accountability, adaptive governance and material stewardship – which structure the analysis of how circular economy principles encounter existing institutional arrangements. Accounting emerged not merely as a reporting function but as a dynamic, contested site where ecological, material and financial futures are recursively negotiated and reconfigured. Socio-ecological stewardship emerged as a situated practice requiring continual realignment of valuation, governance and traceability infrastructures across institutional and temporal boundaries. Originality/value – This study contributes to understanding accounting as constitutive infrastructure for sustainability transitions, moving beyond instrumental approaches to accounting for sustainability. It provides empirical insights into how accounting, legal and financial infrastructures might be reconfigured to support more adaptive and ecologically attuned business practices, offering a situated perspective for enabling socio-ecological stewardship in construction. © Diane Zandee, Kristian Rotaru, Andrew Creed and Ambika Zutshi

Title: Head-and-shoulders patterns in the Taiwan stock market: A comprehensive analysis of predictive ability, profitability, and decision making factors
Abstract: This paper studies the predictive content and implementation choices associated with mechanically detected head-and-shoulders (HS) patterns in the Taiwan equity market. Rather than treating HS recognition as a single unconditional trading rule, we examine how event-level performance varies with two economically interpretable decision parameters: the profit-target multiple η and the historical price-percentile threshold ψ. The evidence shows that HS bottom patterns display stronger and more persistent directional information than HS top patterns, particularly when the detected head occurs in more extreme low-price regions. We further show that strict Bry-Boschan turning-point alignment improves average event-level performance, suggesting that independent turning-point confirmation helps filter weaker pattern signals. To address concerns about data snooping, risk normalization, and implementability, we report multiple-testing diagnostics, event-level mean-to-volatility ratios, and transaction-cost sensitivity analyses. The results should be interpreted as mechanism-consistent event-level evidence on HS decision rules, rather than as a direct test of investor sentiment, market frictions, or fully risk-adjusted calendar-time portfolio alpha. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Authors: Pang H.; Jin C.; Ruan Y.; Wang T.; Yan X.; Zhu Y.
Title: From sociotechnical affordances to sustained engagement: Unraveling the sequential mediating roles of online flow state and virtual community experience on China's barrage video platforms
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Barrage video platforms have transformed digital media consumption into a participatory and socially embedded experience. Exemplified by platforms like Bilibili, these sites have evolved into cultural hubs fostering collective engagement among youth subcultures. Despite their cultural and commercial significance, academic research on user retention in such contexts remains fragmented. Existing studies have primarily examined isolated technical features, ignoring how the interplay between technological affordances (human-computer interaction, HCI) and social interactions (human-human interaction, HHI) jointly shapes continued engagement. To bridge this gap, the present study develops a Cognition-Affect-Conation (CAC) framework that decomposes perceived interaction into HCI dimensions (perceived control, responsiveness, personalization) and HHI dimensions (perceived entertainment, sociability, connectedness). Employing structural equation modeling (SEM) on data from 1015 Chinese users, the study examines how these interaction dimensions influence continuance intention through two sequential mediators: online flow state and sense of virtual community. The results reveal that both HCI and HHI positively associated with users’ online flow state and sense of virtual community. Specifically, technological attributes foster immersive experiences through immediate system feedback and personalized adaptation, whereas social interaction dimensions exert stronger effects on communal attachment by fulfilling emotional and relational needs. Furthermore, these affective experiences, specifically online flow state and sense of virtual community, function as both direct antecedents of continuance intention and sequential mediators transmitting the effect of perceived interaction to sustained use. These findings extend the CAC framework to barrage video contexts, suggesting that operators could refine technical responsiveness to facilitate flow and strengthen social connectivity to support community, which may contribute to sustainable growth in the attention economy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Li L.; Li X.; Xiang J.
Title: The effects of aggregate and local extreme weather on financial distress risk: Evidence from China
Abstract: This paper constructs both aggregate and local Extreme Weather Indices (EWI) to measure the severity of extreme weather events from 2000M01 to 2022M12 in China. Evidence from a Structural Vector Autoregressive (SVAR) model reveals that aggregate EWI shocks trigger a significant and persistent rise in financial distress risk. Firm-level evidence shows that both aggregate and local EWI increase financial distress risk, with aggregate EWI having a more pronounced effect. Firm-level mediation analysis further shows that the heightened financial distress risk resulting from extreme weather is accompanied by higher operating cash outflows, increased firm-specific uncertainty, and more limited access to credit. Title: Beyond the meal: How restaurant health positioning and language–platform context shape the relationship between sensory language and restaurant ratings
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Prior research shows that sensory cues are closely linked to food evaluation, yet it remains unclear how sensory language is associated with post-consumption restaurant ratings across different market contexts. This study examines how five sensory sentiments (visual, gustatory, olfactory, tactile, and auditory) relate to online review ratings across restaurant health positioning and language–platform context. Analyzing over 130,000 bilingual reviews from Dianping and Yelp, we model sensory sentiment–rating associations while controlling for price level, per-sense cue counts, and restaurant-level clustering. All five sensory sentiments were positively associated with ratings, but the strength of these associations varied across restaurant positioning and language–platform contexts. In healthy-positioned restaurants, taste and visual sentiment showed weaker rating associations, whereas tactile, auditory, and olfactory sentiment showed stronger associations. Across language–platform contexts, gustatory and visual associations were stronger in the English/Yelp context. These findings suggest that sensory language is systematically associated with post-consumption evaluation and offer implications for restaurant positioning, review communication, and sensory marketing across digital markets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wang W.; Du Q.; Zheng M.
Title: International sanctions and the dynamics of cross-border capital flows in emerging markets
Abstract: This study investigates the effect of international sanctions on cross-border capital flows in emerging markets. Using panel data covering 35 countries between 2005 and 2022, this research takes a worldwide view to explore the relationships between international sanctions and cross-border capital flows. This paper finds that international sanctions significantly reduce cross-border capital flows in sanctioned emerging countries, and unilateral sanctions as well as trade sanctions generate largest negative impact. The negative impact is attributed by the increased financial risk and the reduced interpersonal globalization. The paper also finds that better domestic institutional quality can alleviate the negative effect of international sanctions on capital outflows. This study provides useful insights for policy design in combating international sanctions. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Author full names: Lee, Kyounghun (57210433537); Oh, Frederick Dongchuhl (55349391500); Park, Junghum (57192105511)
Title: Corporate disclosure, government bailout, and liquidity crisis
Abstract: This study examines the effects of a government bailout on corporate disclosure when a firm is exposed to the risk of investors withdrawing their investments from the firm. The government bailout affects the behavior of investors, which, in turn, alters the disclosure behavior of the firm. We find that the firm discloses less (more) than the case without a bailout when investors have pessimistic (optimistic) beliefs about the firm. These changes in disclosure decision reduce investors’ expectations about the firm's fundamentals. Therefore, the government bailout can increase the likelihood of the firm facing a liquidity crisis if it distorts the disclosure behavior of the firm. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Li D.; Xie L.
Title: Authentic or cool? The paradoxical impact of robotic chefs on consumers’ willingness to pay for restaurant meals
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) enabled robotic chefs are increasingly integrated into back-of-house restaurant operations, yet research remains inconclusive regarding whether, and if so, when and why they influence consumers’ willingness to pay for meals. To offer practical insights into managing AI-driven culinary experiences, this research investigates the competing mechanisms through which robotic chefs influence diners’ willingness to pay. Across seven experiments, we find a paradoxical effect: robotic (vs. human) chefs decrease willingness to pay through an authenticity-suppressing mechanism but increase it through a coolness-enhancing mechanism. The authenticity-suppressing mechanism outweighs the coolness-enhancing mechanism, leading to an overall decrease in willingness to pay. We also identify boundary conditions by showing that chef-related cues (i.e., working experience) and restaurant-related cues (i.e., third-party certification) moderate these processes. These findings reconcile prior inconsistencies in evidence of consumer responses to robotic chefs and provide actionable guidance for deploying robotic chefs in restaurant settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
