Author full names: Lim, Edwin KiaYang (57200888508); Luo, Kun (57223002014); Mihret, Dessalegn (55662971000); Wong-Lim, Christina Shuet (57883354400); Zhang, Xuan (57192504131)
Title: The role of foreign directors from positive peace culture in advancing environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance: evidence from China
Abstract: Purpose – This study investigates whether foreign directors from positive peace cultures enhance a firm’s environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance. Grounded in Social Learning Theory, we argue that such directors facilitate the diffusion of ethical values and sustainable governance practices in boardrooms. Design/methodology/approach – Using a sample of 26, 744 firm-year observations of Chinese firms listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges from 2009 to 2024, we construct a novel board-level Positive Peace Index (PPI) based on the PPI scores of foreign directors’ countries of origin obtained from the Institute for Economics and Peace (IEP). We then estimate a lead-lag OLS model, regressing ESG performance, measured using the Huazheng ESG composite score, on PPI alongside relevant control variables. Findings – Firms with foreign directors from stronger positive peace cultures (i.e. a higher average of positive peace level on the board) demonstrate superior ESG performance, particularly in product quality, corporate governance, and environmental protection. The positive effect of PPI is more pronounced in firms with less government intervention, lower CEO power, and more frequent board meetings, reflecting conditions that foster open dialog and social learning. Importantly, PPI provides explanatory power beyond Hofstede’s cultural dimensions and generic board diversity measures. Originality/value – This study introduces positive peace culture as a novel, values-based lens for examining the cultural influence of foreign directors on ESG, addressing prior mixed findings in the literature. By moving beyond Hofstede’s framework, we respond to calls for more nuanced, context-sensitive cultural metrics (Chanchani and MacGregor, 1999; Doupnik and Tsakumis, 2004). Our findings carry practical implications for firms, investors, and policymakers in emerging markets, advocating for thoughtful board composition strategies that prioritize cultural values such as positive peace that are aligned with ethical and sustainable business practices. © 2026 Edwin KiaYang Lim, Kun Luo, Dessalegn Mihret, Christina Shuet Wong-Lim and Xuan Zhang

Authors: Gao Q.; Ma Y.; Yang B.
Title: Production complementarity, 52-week high, and cross-firm return predictability
Abstract: Using Chinese A-share data, we study whether the 52-week high changes the way return information travels across firms linked by production complementarity. Returns of strong complementors forecast the subsequent returns of focal firms: a long-short portfolio formed on lagged complementor returns earns a monthly alpha of 114 basis points under the Liu et al. (2019) Chinese four-factor model. This predictability is materially stronger when a focal firm's price is close to its prior 52-week maximum, consistent with anchoring slowing investors' response to signals originating from complementors. The interaction survives controls for the focal firm's own past news and is not attributable to lower investor attention. It is more pronounced in high-sentiment and rising markets, and the main inference is unchanged under fixed WH cutoffs, alternative reference-price horizons, macroeconomic controls, and different sample windows. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Fostering competitiveness through knowledge management and sustainability-oriented resources: insights from manufacturing industries
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to examine the relationships between sustainability-oriented resources, innovative capabilities and competitiveness, accounting for the mediating roles of responsible innovation and organisational support. Design/methodology/approach – The authors used a cross-sectional research design during the fiscal year 2023. Data were gathered from a sample of 493 manufacturing small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across the European Union (EU), the UK and the USA. Mediation effects were tested using the causal steps approach and path analysis. Findings – The empirical evidence proves that both direct and indirect pathways enhance competitiveness, with responsible innovation and organisational support acting as key mediators. Practical implications – This research suggests that SME managers should deepen their commitment to responsible innovation by embedding sustainability into business models and daily routines. Furthermore, policymakers should encourage targeted initiatives, such as grants or incentives, to support sustainable transitions and bolster long-term competitiveness. Originality/value – Unlike prior research, this study’s dual-path model elucidates how these sustainability-oriented mechanisms enable SMEs to convert internal resources into competitive performance. By adopting a context-sensitive approach across different geopolitical environments, this research offers new insights into how firms can strategically leverage both tangible and intangible resources within diverse institutional frameworks. © 2026 Mauro Romano, Antonio Netti, Marika Intenza and Christian Favino.

Title: From proposed to realized narrative: tracing the application of service-dominant logic’s foundational premises as theory travelling
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how the foundational premises (FPs) of service-dominant logic (SDL) have been applied and interpreted in scholarly research. By distinguishing between SDL’s proposed and realized narratives, the study advances understanding of how SDL has evolved through cumulative use and interpretation, and proposes directions for future research and theory development in marketing. Design/methodology/approach – Using a data set of 4, 371 papers published between 2004 and 2019, complemented by a qualitative analysis (2020–2025), the authors combine quantitative mapping and interpretive analysis to trace how SDL as a theoretical framework has travelled through the literature and how its meanings have shifted over time. Findings – Results show a consistent yet evolving application of the FPs across journals, disciplines and ranking levels. While SDL remains a cohesive theoretical framework, its use reveals increasing conceptual variety, reflecting both stabilization and drift in its realized narrative. Recent developments highlight stronger ecosystem and institutional orientations, marking SDL’s continuing theoretical maturation. Research limitations/implications – The study provides a lens for examining how marketing theories evolve through cumulative scholarly use and adaptation. It underscores the need to balance theoretical coherence with interpretive flexibility. Practical implications – The overall message of the framework for managers is in its advocacy of a company’s service orientation. The essentials of such a service orientation lie in the company’s proactive stance vis-à-vis its business context and its capability to identify and seize emerging opportunities for service provision. Originality/value – To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study offers the first large-scale, longitudinal analysis of SDL from 2004 to 2025, revealing how its FPs have travelled from a proposed to a realized narrative in scholarly discourse. © 2026 Hannu Makkonen, Matti Mäntymäki, Jaakko Aspara and Valtteri Kaartemo.

Authors: Oskan S.; van Hugten J.
Title: What motivates leaders to engage in strategic renewal behavior? Examining effects of career development motive and strategy implementation motive
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to examine whether leaders' proactive personality leads them to pursue self-oriented career development and organization-oriented strategy implementation motives, which in turn influences their strategic renewal behavior, with perceived career success acting as a boundary condition in this process. Design/methodology/approach – This quantitative study examines the empirical data gathered from 13 business units of a Dutch private organization, involving 263 leaders and 1, 296 direct reports. Findings – Leaders’ proactive personality is associated with their strategic renewal behavior, and this relationship is mediated by their organization-oriented strategy implementation motive. Perceived career success moderates this relationship such that the negative relationship between self-oriented career development motive and strategic renewal behavior is stronger for leaders with high levels of perceived career success, while the positive relationship between organization-oriented strategy implementation motive and strategic renewal behavior is stronger for leaders with low levels of perceived career success. Research limitations/implications – These findings highlight that leaders' proactive personality does not uniformly translate into strategic renewal behaviors but is shaped by their motives and career perceptions. Originality/value – This study contributes to leadership and organizational change research by revealing why and when leaders’ strategic renewal behavior is driven by self-oriented and organization-oriented motives, which is an area with limited prior exploration. © Selen Oskan and Joeri van Hugten

Author full names: Wojciechowska-Dzięcielak, Paulina (57212608013); Arduin, Pierre-Emmanuel (55855332700); Merad, Myriam (8960435400)
Title: When Fake News Sounds Right: Assessing Message Credibility in AI-Generated Misinformation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) enables the large-scale production of fluent and coherent content that mimics legitimate news, raising critical challenges for how credibility is assessed in digital information systems. While “fake news” dominates public discourse, this study adopts the broader and analytically more precise concept of “misinformation” to describe false or misleading content regardless of intent. Although empirical research on GenAI’s impact on credibility judgments is growing, findings remain fragmented across disciplines and system contexts. This paper provides a preliminary critical synthesis of empirical and conceptual studies on AI-generated misinformation, focusing on two outcomes central to information systems research: perceived credibility and detection accuracy. To enable meaningful comparison, findings are synthesized descriptively along two informational dimensions (source and structure) which are the only cues users can realistically access when evaluating AI-generated content. Results show that AI-generated misinformation tends to be perceived as more credible and is less accurately detected than comparable human-written content. Disclosure labels indicating AI authorship have negligible effects on credibility judgments, underscoring the limited efficacy of transparency-based interventions. Theoretically, the paper contributes to Information Systems research by clarifying how GenAI shifts credibility heuristics away from source-based evaluation toward structurally optimized content. Practically, it highlights the limits of content-level countermeasures and points to the need for system-level, user-centered design interventions that restore epistemic salience and foster reflective trust. Overall, the study reframes AI-generated misinformation not simply as a new type of falsehood, but as a structural transformation of the credibility landscape. It calls for a reconceptualization of credibility as a dynamic process shaped by interaction design, interface cues, and evolving epistemic norms in AI-mediated environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Review of the External Processes Related to Assessing Quality of New Undergraduate Academic Programming in Canadian Universities
Source title: Canadian Journal of Educational Administration and Policy
Abstract: Quality assurance (QA) processes oversee programmatic creation and cyclical reviews to ensure the quality of academic programming for students. In Canada, university oversight, including funding and QA, takes place at the provincial level. Oversight of quality varies dramatically across regions in Canada, from government ministries to arm's-length quality assurance agencies to internal university governance. Our research compares the guiding documents of Canadian QA agencies from across Canada to answer the questions: (1) How do external QA procedures vary in provinces across Canada, and (2) Is financial viability considered in QA? Our results suggest a distinct lack of specificity in multiple areas, most profoundly in the financial considerations. Consequently, in the fifth section, and based on our findings, we propose a Financial Viability and Sustainability Framework for Quality Assurance (FVSF-QA) as a tool for supporting consideration of financial viability and stability in quality assurance. Title: A supply chain digital twin for adaptive master planning under multi-source disruptions: Evidence from a dual-channel manufacturing case
Abstract: Conventional Supply Chain Master Planning (SCMP) approaches are poorly suited to environments characterized by simultaneous supply, demand, and sales-channel disruptions particularly in dual-channel supply chains where asymmetric shifts between online and offline demand can create inventory misallocation, service deterioration, and cost escalation. Although Supply Chain Digital Twins (SCDTs) are increasingly discussed as enablers of disruption-aware planning, limited evidence exists on how SCDT frameworks support adaptive SCMP in multi-echelon dual-channel settings. This study develops a SCDT framework for adaptive SCMP that integrates demand forecasting, machine learning-based disruption detection, discrete-event simulation, and multi-objective optimization to dynamically revise sourcing, production, and inventory decisions in response to evolving system states. The framework is instantiated in a television manufacturing supply chain and evaluated against static and rolling-horizon planning approaches under supplier, demand, and channel-shift disruptions. Results show that the proposed SCDT improves service-cost performance, supports more balanced channel-level fulfillment, and enhances adaptive recovery behavior under disruption relative to benchmark approaches. The findings further show that channel-aware SCMP is especially important when demand shifts asymmetrically across sales channels. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Authors: Alter S.; Eshuis R.
Title: Analyzing increasingly digitalized knowledge-intensive processes
Abstract: Purpose – Knowledge-intensive processes (KiPs) are typically viewed as business processes performed by knowledge workers making complex decisions. Increasing digitalization of KiPs through AI and other means reduces the adequacy of that view. This conceptual contribution proposes and illustrates an updated view of KiPs based on a work system perspective (WSP) that expands the scope of BPM. Design/methodology/approach – Three WSP approaches are proposed to analyze KiPs. First, work system models are used with different degrees of specificity to support different stakeholders. Second, continuous design dimensions are proposed for visualizing important KiP issues and challenges. Third, the roles and responsibilities of digital agents in relation to different facets of work are analyzed. The three approaches are introduced using a running example and are evaluated using a real-world KiP involving diagnostic radiology. Findings – The three WSP approaches help to analyze KiPs and attain a greater understanding by offering an integrated view of KiPs that spans management and technical viewpoints. Originality/value – This conceptual contribution shows how ideas and models related to the WSP provide paths for integrated visualization and analysis of KiPs. The paper extends Business Process Management (BPM) by providing approaches that stakeholders with different concerns and interests can use for describing and analyzing KiPs that may be automated to varying degrees. Authors: Jin L.; Shan X.; Zha Q.
Title: Active Preference Elicitation with Temporal Weighting for Linguistic Multi-attribute Decision Making
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: In linguistic multi-attribute decision making (LMADM), evaluation terms carry varying meanings for different decision makers (DMs). However, DMs often have limited cognitive capacity, and their internal evaluation standards may evolve during interaction. This research proposes an interactive preference elicitation framework that accounts for the transition from initial cognitive ambiguity toward subsequent clarity. The model infers the evolution and gradual stabilization of the DM’s preference pattern from observed behavior. Specifically, a temporal weighting mechanism is integrated into the personalized individual semantics (PIS) model to capture this evolution. This mechanism assigns lower weights to early evaluations while focusing more on consistent feedback from later stages. Title: From Acts to Chances: Measuring Participation and Inequality of Opportunity

Title: Does positive attribute framing work better in promoting AI-powered services? Boundary conditions of the valence-consistent shift effect

Abstract: The Valence-Consistent Shift (VCS) effect–a foundational principle in framing theory–holds that consumers generally respond more favorably to positively framed information than to negatively framed information. Title: What is fair? Balancing performance metrics for multiple stakeholders in disruptions and reduced service capacity
Source title: Research in Transportation Business and Management
Abstract: Reduced capacity to operate services presents significant challenges for infrastructure management during disruptions and maintenance. Dispositions and procedures minimizing inconvenience for passengers or operators may not guarantee – or even hinder - the equitable treatment of all the stakeholders. Furthermore, accounting for different stakeholder roles and multiple solutions can complicate decision-making. This paper addresses this topic with three main contributions. Title: To charge or to transfer? Coupled scheduling in smart operating rooms with reinforcement learning-based neighborhood search
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: Powered patient-transfer beds and smart transport systems are increasingly being introduced in hospitals to reduce the manual-handling burden and support patient movement. Authors: Güven G.
Title: A fair share of the sky: How tradable baggage rights reallocate scarce payload capacity
Abstract: Airline baggage policies generally rely on uniform weight allowances combined with excess-baggage fees. From a payload-allocation perspective, this design may obscure the scarcity value of the aircraft payload and generate implicit incidence patterns across passengers. We study a Total Weight Allocation (TWA) benchmark in which passengers receive tradable baggage rights derived from a fixed per-passenger payload allowance net of body weight and trade these rights in a competitive market. When the payload capacity binds, the TWA implements a payload-efficient allocation by equalizing the marginal valuations of discretionary baggage capacity, exactly under quasi-linear preferences. Efficiency is independent of the initial assignment of rights, whereas incidence depends on endowments: conditional on baggage demand and travel needs, lower-body-weight passengers tend to be net sellers and higher-body-weight passengers tend to be net buyers. A non-tradable seating baseline preserves feasibility without changing the tradable baggage margin. The theoretical results extend to convex weight-cost formulations and multidimensional payload constraints. An illustrative numerical exercise based on assumed parameter distributions reports model-implied efficiency gains relative to non-tradable uniform baggage allowances and the transfer patterns implied by tradable rights; it is not an empirical calibration or a route-specific prediction. A per-kg fee equal to the payload shadow price can replicate the benchmark trading allocation while transferring scarcity rents from passengers to the airline, highlighting the efficiency–incidence trade-off in baggage-policy design. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Private communication between managers and financial analysts: evidence from taxi-ride patterns in New York City
Abstract: Private communications between managers and sell-side analysts are widespread yet are largely unobservable to outside market participants. At the firm level, companies with greater taxi activity by forecast-issuing analysts exhibit stock prices more reflective of future earnings and larger reductions in forecast dispersion and bid-ask spreads. Title: Bank enforcement actions, supervisory deterrence, and corporate maturity mismatch
Abstract: Using penalty announcements disclosed by China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, we examine whether and how bank supervisory enforcement shapes corporate maturity mismatch through shifts in bank behavior. Title: Measuring Compromise in Voting Rules Under Polarization
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: We study how voting rules behave under polarization when the aim is to select not only a popular option, but also a compromise. We compare standard rules with two parameterized compromise-oriented families and with fallback bargaining as a high-compromise reference point. Title: Transport capital and regional economic performance in Korea: Implications for balanced regional development under the public investment appraisal system

Abstract: In 1999, Korea introduced the Preliminary Feasibility Study (PFS), a mandatory appraisal framework for large-scale public investment projects that designates balanced regional development as a core policy objective. Title: When humor beats believability: How AI-generated imagery shapes pet-inclusive restaurant choice

Abstract: This chapter proposes a holistic reconceptualization of Entrepreneurial Life Design (ELD), advancing the paradigm beyond its predominant “first-person” perspective (individual-level focus) to encompass both organizational and societal transformation. Drawing on Sara Ahmed’s theory of affective economies, the manuscript foregrounds the vital role of emotion and relational affect in shaping not only personal trajectories but also the collective aspirations and values driving organizations and communities. Ahmed’s framework, which positions emotions and affects as circulatory dynamics embedded within social and political structures, provides a critical lens for understanding how entrepreneurial mindsets and life designs “stick” to particular social projects, communities, and institutional practices. Furthermore, this chapter brings decolonial knowledge systems into dialogue with ELD, demonstrating how alternative epistemologies and communal approaches to learning, agency, and value creation enrich and challenge Eurocentric models of entrepreneurship education. Decolonial perspectives foreground fundamental questions of whose knowledge counts, which futures are imagined, and how power circulates in shaping entrepreneurial agency. By centering Indigenous, Afrocentric, and other non-hegemonic models of knowing and doing, the chapter champions a pluralistic and emancipatory understanding of ELD—attentive to contexts of marginalization, cultural resilience, and collective flourishing—and thereby enhances the international applicability of the concept. Central to this chapter is the development of the concept of progressive affectivity: the generative force that emerges when individual sense-making, purpose, and action resonate outward, catalyzing organizational culture, systemic change, and societal well-being. It is shown how a holistic approach, weaving affective economies and decolonial practices into ELD, can produce ripple effects that foster not only self-efficacy and resilience but also solidarity, ethical innovation, and sustainable futures at scale. At the societal level, affective economies intersect with moral and economic decision-making, suggesting that broadening the affective scope of ELD has substantial implications for equity, justice, and social innovation (McGregor & Pouw, 2016). This points to the need for transdisciplinary frameworks that integrate affect, ethics, and systemic thinking to address contemporary challenges and cultivate meaningful impact both within and beyond the entrepreneurial sphere. In sum, the chapter articulates a holistic ELD paradigm—grounded in progressive affectivity and decolonial epistemologies—that journeys from the individual to the organizational and radiates into the social. By designing for societal resonance, ELD becomes a vehicle for collective empowerment, transformational leadership, and the creation of just and flourishing futures. Title: Financial disclosure under regulatory fragmentation
Abstract: Regulatory fragmentation occurs when multiple agencies promulgate overlapping rules on the same policy topic, requiring firms to coordinate compliance across regulators and reconcile potentially inconsistent requirements. Title: AI washing in technology markets: The divergent roles of patient capital in innovation signaling distortion
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes a central driver of innovation and competitive advantage, firms increasingly rely on AI-related narratives to signal technological capabilities to external stakeholders. In contrast, debt-type patient capital (PCD) is positively associated with AIwash, and this association is related to earnings management. The decomposition of disclosure–activities divergence indicates that PCS is primarily associated with lower levels of AI over-claiming, whereas PCD is associated with higher levels of over-claiming. Moreover, financing constraints positively moderates the relationship between PCD with AIwash. Heterogeneity analyses show that the negative association between PCS and AIwash is stronger in high-technology industries, star firms, and firms in mature and declining stages, whereas the positive association between PCD and AIwash is primarily concentrated in non-high-technology industries, non-star firms, and growth-stage firms. Title: Assessing the monetary and fiscal policy in India: coordination or conflict
Abstract: This study examines whether fiscal and monetary policies in India are coordinated or conflicting in maintaining macroeconomic stability. We estimate a Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) model using quarterly data from 1997 to 2025. The results show fiscal expansions temporarily increase economic activity but raise public debt. Title: A multi-objective humanitarian aid distribution problem with experts’ preferences

Title: Efficiency of the Wind and Solar Power Plants Regulation According to Traditional Schemes
Source title: Studies in Systems, Decision and Control
Abstract: The modern development of the electric power industry is characterized by a rapid increase in the share of renewable energy sources (RES), among which wind (WPPs) and solar power plants (SPPs) occupy a key place. Their widespread introduction is associated with environmental safety, low operating costs and a gradual decrease in capital intensity. However, the integration of WPPs and SPPs into power systems faces a number of challenges due to their variable and hard-to-predict output, as well as limited opportunities to participate in traditional regulatory processes. This chapter discusses the technical and economic characteristics of WPPs and SPPs when they are operated under traditional power control schemes. It is shown that the installed capacity utilization factor for WPPs averages 0.25–0.45, and for SPPs—0.12 to 0.20, which reflects the significant dependence of their operation on natural conditions. At the same time, the range of power regulation can formally reach 0–100%, but in fact, the reduction in generation is often carried out by forced curtailment, which leads to losses of 5–15% of the annual output. From an economic point of view, WPPs and SPPs are characterized by a relatively low level of operating costs: for WPPs they are 20–35 €/kWh year, for solar—10 to 20 €/kWh year. At the same time, capital costs are in the range of 1200–1600 €/kW for WPPs and 500–900 €/kW for SPPs. The cost of generated electricity (LCOE) averages 40–60 €/MWh for wind and 30–50 €/MWh for solar generation. However, under traditional regulatory schemes, part of this economic benefit is offset by additional system costs for balancing the power system, which can reach 15–25 €/MWh. Particular attention is paid to the system limitations of traditional regulation, which does not allow WPPs and SPPs to fully participate in primary and secondary frequency control, ensuring system reliability and covering abruptly alternating loads. This leads to an increase in the role of reserve capacities based on hydro and thermal power plants, which reduces the overall efficiency of renewable energy integration. Thus, the analysis shows that when operating WPPs and SPPs under traditional control schemes, there is a contradiction between the low cost of electricity and additional system costs to ensure the stability of the power system. Title: Customer-perceived supplier innovativeness in B2B services: evaluative cues across ecosystem interactions

Abstract: Purpose – In business-to-business (B2B) contexts, innovativeness is often conceptualized as a firm-internal capability reflected in research and development investment, technological advancement and process improvements. Data were analyzed through iterative coding and comparison within an abductive analytic logic. Service-dominant logic and service ecosystem theory are used as sensitizing lenses. These evaluations draw on three interrelated cue clusters: (1) credible enactment of innovation intent, (2) transparency in resource integration and coordination and (3) contributions to ecosystem arrangements that support customer value creation. Authors: Ezekoye G.
Title: When Does FX Intervention Work? A State-Dependent Analysis of Inflation and Volatility Regimes in Emerging Markets
Abstract: Under the right conditions, foreign exchange intervention (FXI) plays an important role in stabilising currencies in emerging markets. Using a panel smooth transition regression model for 20 emerging economies and an instrumented FXI measure to address endogeneity, the paper finds that central banks lean against the wind of currency depreciation and appreciation and respond to deviations from long-run exchange rate targets. The effectiveness of FXI is state-dependent and varies with prevailing macroeconomic conditions, particularly exchange rate volatility and inflation differentials. FXI is not statistically significant in low-volatility regimes but becomes effective in high-volatility regimes, suggesting that intervention has a stronger influence on exchange rates when market pressures are elevated. Similarly, FXI is effective in high-inflation regimes, where it helps counteract inflation-induced depreciation pressures. These findings highlight the need for central banks to tailor the size and timing of FXI to prevailing economic conditions. In high-volatility environments, intervention can play an important stabilising role, while in high-inflation regimes its signalling channel can communicate a credible commitment to currency stability and help anchor market expectations. Central banks should also balance the frequency of interventions, using clustered actions where appropriate to reduce operational costs. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: In-house or outsourced: The online trade-in option considering acquisition and disposition
Abstract: Online trade-ins confront dual challenges: trust cultivation in acquisition processes and efficient disposition of collected products. Third-party-led acquisition erodes consumer trust more than manufacturer-led acquisition, while manufacturer-led disposition may lack objectivity due to new product cannibalization concerns. This study proposes three models to examine the extent of online trade-in outsourcing between a manufacturer and a third party: in-house operations, partial outsourcing (acquisition only), and full outsourcing (acquisition and disposition). Specifically, we investigate trust-building in the acquisition process and the allocation between reselling and recycling in the disposition process. Our findings indicate that manufacturers favor partial outsourcing over full outsourcing when consumer trust discrimination toward third parties is low, whereas they opt for in-house operations when the trust gap is significant. Furthermore, manufacturers may strategically underutilize resources by recycling only a subset of resale-eligible products when new product production costs are low. Notably, the resource underutilization does not always harm the environment. By contrast, third parties prioritize truthful resale decisions to maximize disposal profits rather than focusing on trust-building. Consequently, compared with partial outsourcing, third parties invest less in trust-building in full outsourcing. Additionally, manufacturers in the in-house model tend to be more proactive than third parties in the other two outsourcing models when unit collection costs are low. This study provides valuable insights for manufacturers in making informed trade-in outsourcing decisions, while addressing critical issues such as trust-building and the selection of disposition methods. Title: Assessment of the Level of Soil Cover Pollution by Petroleum Products and Strategies for Reducing the Content of Heavy Metals in Agroecosystem Soils

Title: Mental Time Travel in Entrepreneurial Life Design: Neurocognitive Foundations and Practical Implications
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: Imagination is the core cognitive mechanism through which individuals envision, evaluate, and shape future life and career trajectories. The findings suggest that imagination-based ELD methods, such as Three Future Lives or Future-Self Journaling, can be interpreted as targeted training for these neural systems, even though their specific neural effects have not yet been directly tested. Recent large-scale empirical research demonstrates that dynamic switching between DMN, SN, and ECN reliably predicts creative performance (Chen et al., 2025), offering empirical support for the neuroscientific basis of ELD practices. Title: Post-adoption interaction burden and selective avoidance intention in autonomous delivery services: A stressor-strain-outcome perspective

Abstract: Autonomous delivery services (ADS) can reduce physical pickup effort, but their use requires consumers to coordinate digital information, verification, and physical retrieval. Title: Strategic inventory holdbacks: Managing waste and backlog in humanitarian operations
Abstract: Humanitarian organizations distributing relief supplies must allocate limited inventory across multiple locations under uncertain demand, donation-constrained replenishment, heterogeneous lead times, and operational losses such as theft, displacement, and handling damage. Performance is evaluated using waste, fill rate, backlog age, and retailer-level fairness measures. Results show that the holdback policy substantially reduces waste while maintaining competitive service and fairness performance. Title: Willingness-to-pay for bacteriophage-treated rainbow trout: A comparative study of Denmark and Germany
Abstract: The use of antibiotics in aquaculture contributes to the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), which poses serious public health risks. Title: Do textual attributes of management commentary matter for analyst coverage and information quality: evidence from the United Kingdom
Abstract: Purpose – This study examines whether the readability of management commentary is associated with analysts' coverage and the precision of analysts' information sets. Title: Enhancing Gen Z Employee Retention in Islamic Banking through Gamification and Employee Recognition: The Mediating Role of Work Enjoyment

Title: The political economy of regional development: Evidence from the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno
Abstract: Institutional design can shape the political economy of regional development programmes, ultimately affecting their overall efficacy. We test this hypothesis in the context of the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno, a large-scale place-based policy aimed at fostering industrial development in Southern Italy (1950–1984). In the long run, aligned municipalities received a greater number of smaller projects, predominantly public works. This pattern intensified in municipalities characterised by higher pre-reform corruption, lower industrial capacity, and larger electorates, consistent with a logic of broad electoral coverage rather than developmental targeting. We also show that the positive association between funding and long-term employment growth weakens substantially after the reform, particularly in aligned municipalities. Title: ESG performance and supply chain risk: A partner management perspective
Abstract: A focal firm depends on trading partners it does not control, whose disruptions interrupt its own operations. Based on resource dependence theory, we argue that a firm's ESG performance reflects the routines, assessment capability, and incentives with which it selects and develops partners on their ESG performance, so that it holds a stronger partner portfolio and can spread its dependence across more partners and regions. Reductions in partner composition and geographic concentration each carry part of the effect, and the composition channel is broader where more qualified candidates are available. Title: Communicating the Boundaries of Sustainability Assurance under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive: Evidence from Independent Auditors’ Reports on European Electricity Producers
Abstract: This study examines how independent auditors' reports communicate the scope, uncertainty, liability, double materiality, and limitations of sustainability assurance during the early implementation of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). Interpreted through the SEGAP, these patterns are consistent with an increasing risk-communication function alongside assurance's traditional risk-reduction function, helping to explain how procedural standardisation can coexist with limited substantive accountability. Title: Macroscopic modeling and optimization of mixed-autonomy traffic in general road networks: A comprehensive and critical review

Title: A latent class approach to estimate passengers’ air itinerary preferences in Indian domestic aviation market
Abstract: Numerous studies have analyzed airline itinerary choice behavior to understand passenger preferences and the trade-offs they make among key flight service attributes such as total elapsed time, number of connections, and fare. However, limited attention has been given to evaluating the influence of latent attitudinal constructs on itinerary choice decisions. This study examines the influence of latent attitudes and demographic characteristics on passengers' itinerary choice behavior and identifies distinct patterns of preference heterogeneity among air travelers. Two modelling approaches using stated preference data collected from 614 respondents are employed. We begin by estimating a multiple indicators multiple causes (MIMIC) model, which incorporates latent attitudes identified through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. The model reveals three latent attitudinal factors, viz “comfort and hygiene conscious”, “in-flight service seeking” and “time and punctuality-oriented”. To capture heterogeneity in preferences, we extend our analysis using a latent class choice model (LCCM), incorporating socio-demographic characteristics and latent variables as class membership covariates. The LCCM results reveal two distinct flyer segments, each exhibiting different sensitivity to airline itinerary attributes. Class 1 accounts for approximately 78% of the sample, while Class 2 comprises the remaining 22%. The first segment (Class 1) displays high preference for reduction in connection time and elapsed time while the second segment (Class 2) reflects greater sensitivity to service quality (legroom and meals). Besides, Class 1 flyers display a strong inclination to nonstop itineraries, while Class 2 flyers show increased reception for connected itineraries. The willingness to pay for connection time and elapsed time reductions are $14 and $16, respectively, for Class 1 air travelers. While flyers falling under Class 2 are willing to pay $10 and $13, respectively, for 1 h reduction in connection time and elapsed time. Moreover, elasticity analysis indicates that Class 1 passengers exhibit a strong aversion to extended connection times on direct itineraries. Additionally, a unit fare increase on direct flights leads to a 2.33% shift toward nonstop options. Females and highly educated individuals are slightly more represented in Class 1, indicating demographic influences on latent class membership. The findings demonstrate variations in flyer preferences especially in the context of latent attitudes of individuals. Title: Navigating institutional terrains: home-country institutional agent boundary spanning and brokerage in SME B2B internationalization

Abstract: Purpose – Grounded in the theoretical foundations of institutions, boundary spanning and brokerage and SME internationalization, the purpose of this paper is to examine how home-country institutions (HCIs) facilitate the post-entry internationalization of small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) through home-country institutional agents (HCIAs) in a business-to-business (B2B) context. This study explores how HCIAs influence the type and nature of institutional support for post-entry internationalization of SMEs from the home country of New Zealand to the two large emerging host markets, China and India. They offer a novel perspective by investigating the role of HCIAs, representing institutions at the micro level and operating in both home and host country, in supporting the internationalization of SMEs. Findings – The findings of this study demonstrate that HCIAs, working in both home and host country locations, assume boundary spanning and brokerage roles when connecting SMEs with relevant actors to supply the requisite knowledge for successful post-entry internationalization. Key findings highlight how specific HCIAs, representing a range of HCIs, facilitate institutional support to SMEs in their post-entry development. This study explores the mechanism of boundary spanning and brokerage used by these agents in connecting relevant actors involved in the internationalization of SMEs from New Zealand to China and India. This study demonstrates how specific HCIA types, different boundary spanning activities and the home or host country location of the agents of the HCIs facilitate this process. Originality/value – The authors offer a novel micro-level examination of institutional support for SME internationalization, focusing on the activities of specific agents representing their respective HCIs. This study shows that these HCIAs use boundary-spanning and brokerage activities to connect and facilitate key interactions between SMEs and relevant actors in the host market. Further, the authors highlight the little explored roles and activities of HCIs located in the host market in the context of SME internationalization. Specifically, they show different contributions by home and host-based institutional agents and differentiate between the types of boundary spanning objects used and the associated outcomes for the SMEs. Title: Integrating knowledge management and digital product passports to foster sustainable and collaborative ecosystems
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to explore the potential of the digital product passport (DPP) to support circular and collaborative ecosystems within the fashion and cosmetics industries. Findings – The results demonstrate that the DPP contributes to the circularity of raw materials, enhances supply chain resilience and facilitates the dissemination of shared knowledge. Successful DPP implementation depends on aligning its technical capabilities with both organizational readiness and consumer engagement. Title: Joy of Missing Out (JoMO), Voluntary Simplicity, and Responsible Consumption: Examining Direct and Indirect Associations in an Emerging Market Context
Abstract: This study examines the direct association between the joy of missing out (JoMO) and responsible consumption behaviour, and tests whether this association is channelled indirectly through voluntary simplicity. Drawing on self-determination theory and the digital well-being perspective, the study explores whether a disposition toward positive solitude and digital disengagement (JoMO) is associated with sustainable consumption. Turkey constitutes a theoretically meaningful setting for this inquiry, as it combines rapidly expanding digital consumption habits and status-oriented purchasing patterns with an emerging, yet still limited, culture of sustainability awareness and simple living, creating a distinctive tension between consumer culture and voluntary restraint. Data were collected through an online survey from 1,015 participants using a geographically distributed, quota-based online convenience sample structured according to the Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics. Structural equation modelling was employed for analysis. The findings indicate that JoMO is associated with responsible consumption (RC) orientation primarily indirectly, through the simple living philosophy dimension of voluntary simplicity; the direct JoMO–RC association was only marginal in the baseline model and did not survive a robustness check controlling for demographic covariates (gender, age, income). The overall mediating role of voluntary simplicity was not statistically confirmed. Additionally, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses reveal an empirically two-dimensional structure of voluntary simplicity in the Turkish context, comprising CC and SLP. As the JoMO measure showed limited convergent validity and its retained items reflect a positive-solitude/autonomy orientation rather than digital disconnection per se, findings involving JoMO warrant cautious interpretation. The findings contribute to sustainability, slow marketing, and digital well-being literature by positioning JoMO as a psychological correlate of responsible consumption. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: From Social Participation to the Civic Gift: The Geography of Blood Donation in Italy
Abstract: This chapter examines the relationship between social participation, social capital and blood donation as a form of civic engagement in contemporary Italy. Drawing on the civic tradition of social capital, participation is conceptualised as a socially embedded process shaped by organisational infrastructures, institutional arrangements and territorial contexts. Within this framework, blood donation is interpreted as a paradigmatic form of organised altruism and as an empirical expression of a “civic gift”. In the Italian context, it represents a link between associative participation and individual civic action, translating organisational infrastructures into repeated practices of giving. Unlike other forms of volunteering, donation involves a tangible contribution to collective well-being, mediated by institutional systems ensuring equitable redistribution. The empirical analysis, based on secondary data from the National and Regional Blood Centres, highlights territorial differences in donation patterns, reflecting uneven civic infrastructures and associational capacity. Title: A trade-off between monetary policy transmission and systemic risk
Abstract: We study how interbank funding links monetary policy transmission to systemic risk in a banking system with heterogeneous access to deposit funding. Using bank-level data from China, we show that monetary policy easing reallocates liquidity through the interbank market: large banks raise household demand deposits and lend in the interbank market, while small banks expand loans through interbank borrowing. During economic downturns, greater reliance on interbank funding is associated with higher systemic risk. To interpret these facts, we build a structural model with deposit-rich and deposit-poor banks and interbank rollover risk. The model shows that monetary policy easing reallocates liquidity and boosts lending, but also raises run risk. It reveals a macroprudential trade-off: a regulatory limit on interbank funding weakens monetary policy transmission but reduces systemic risk. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Stock mispricing and myopic marketing management
Abstract: We examine whether stock mispricing affects firms’ likelihood of adopting myopic marketing management. Drawing on myopic marketing management theory (Mizik, 2010), we argue that when stock prices deviate from fundamentals, managers adjust marketing and R&D expenditures in response. Using 34,302 firm-year observations from 1980 to 2016, we find an asymmetric effect where overpricing decreases the likelihood of myopic marketing management more than underpricing increases it. Equity issuance weakens this relationship, whereas firm growth strengthens it. Our research extends myopic marketing management theory by showing that the direction of mispricing changes managers’ incentives to maintain or reduce short- and long-term marketing expenditures. The findings also provide guidance for CMOs and CFOs. Title: Organisational performance and value (OPV) tool: an analytic autoethnographic study
Abstract: Purpose – Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) often lack decision-support tools that support context-sensitive real-time prioritisation. Existing models, frameworks and tools primarily focus on performance measurement and management rather than guiding individual-level decision-making. These systems are often too generic, technocentric and burdensome to implement, especially in environments where decisions are intuitive, time-pressured and owner-driven. In response to this gap, this study introduces the organisational performance and value (OPV) framework, a structured yet flexible personal decision-support tool designed to help SME owner-managers identify and act on high-impact priorities aligned with their unique organisational contexts. Design/methodology/approach – This study is guided by Anderson's (2006) five principles of analytic autoethnography, and data sources include recorded reflexive conversations, email exchanges with the practitioner and beta testing results of the developed tool. Using an iterative narrative interpretation, excerpts were selected based on their conceptual richness and relevance to the tool's evolution. This approach supports a layered, reflexive analysis that elevates the study from personal reflection to a theoretically grounded scholarly contribution. Findings – The analysis of Beta test feedback identified five main themes covering platform and report-level matters: navigation, user interface and functionality; required time and effort; relevance and question design; design and experience suggestion; and engagement and consolidation potential. These insights reveal that SME decision-makers assess tools not only by usability but also by how well they match their expectations and strategic thinking needs. Perceived time burden reflected an expectation-experience mismatch, highlighting the importance of managing cognitive load and aligning design with user assumptions. More broadly, the findings show that tool development in SME contexts functions as an entrepreneurial negotiation, balancing user input with business model realities rather than the linear application of user experience (UX) design principles. Finally, the study underscores the importance of emotional design, as SMEs seek tools that foster trust, legitimacy and reflective engagement alongside functional efficiency. Practical implications – Decision-support tools should help owner-managers think, prioritise and act, not just complete tasks efficiently. They should also promote emotional engagement and build trust. Future research should explore the impact of diagnostic tools on strategic action and organisational adaptability, entrepreneurial constraints and tensions on SME tool development and design approaches for managing SMEs' expectations. By improving reflective prioritisation under constraint, such tools may also contribute to more resilient small businesses and local entrepreneurial ecosystems. Originality/value – This study presents the OPV framework as a practitioner-informed, context-sensitive contribution to SME strategy support tools. It is distinct in translating the lived consulting experience of advising SME owner-managers into a practical, structured tool for prioritisation. Unlike traditional large-firm-based frameworks or performance measurement systems, the OPV framework reflects the cognitive demands, intuitive styles and adaptive needs of SME decision-makers. It offers a timely and relevant model for real-time, capacity-conscious decision-making, bridging a critical gap between academic insight and practical application in the SME domain. © John Downes and Chamindika Weerakoon

Title: Technology acceptance, multidimensional experience and disability sensitivity: a critical review
Abstract: Purpose – Although various disciplines have explored technology use by people with disabilities (PwDs), business and management studies have rarely addressed how they accept and use these technologies. This is partly because existing technology acceptance frameworks often rely on complex, normative assumptions that overlook the diverse abilities of users. Consequently, this study questions the inclusivity of technology acceptance frameworks by examining whether the items used to measure relevant variables are grounded in assumptions that exclude users with specific needs. Title: Does the climate-adaptive city pilot policy exacerbate urban sprawl? Evidence from a quasi-natural experiment in China
Abstract: Although climate-adaptive policies are primarily designed to enhance urban resilience, they may also generate unintended consequences for urban spatial development. Results show that pilot policy significantly promotes urban sprawl, a conclusion validated by robustness tests. Fiscal resource allocation and green infrastructure expansion are plausible potential pathways behind this effect, while land use efficiency and intensity show no significant impact. Noticeable heterogeneity exists across city characteristics; the policy generates a stronger sprawl effect in non-central cities than in central cities, and its impacts increase with city size. Along the urbanization gradient, the policy effect follows a U-shaped pattern and is most prominent in highly urbanized areas. Title: How consumers construct dining experiences through sensory language: Evidence from Xiaohongshu posts on Michelin-starred restaurants in Macau
Abstract: Online restaurant reviews are crucial sites where premium hospitality experiences are narrated, evaluated, and culturally circulated. Semantic clustering further identifies culturally meaningful sensory groupings related to freshness, balance, layering, refinement, intensity, and texture-based pleasure. These patterns suggest that sensory expressions operate as evaluative templates through which consumers make fine-dining experiences recognizable, persuasive, and culturally meaningful in digital word-of-mouth. Title: Helpful or hollow? fit-to-feel alignment in proactive AI travel communication

Abstract: How do users evaluate proactive AI communication when functional actions and empathic expressions co-occur? Across three studies using an exploratory sequential mixed-method design (Study 1: qualitative interviews, n = 36; Study 2: pilot experiment, n = 162; Study 3: main experiment, n = 480), we show that users assess whether signals follow a shared underlying logic: utilitarian PSR aligns with cognitive empathy, whereas symbolic PSR aligns with emotional empathy. Title: Group Assessment of Overall Airline Customer Satisfaction from Online Reviews: A B-TOPSIS Approach
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Online review platforms provide a rich source of passenger feedback, enabling airlines and researchers to evaluate service quality across multiple dimensions. This paper aims to assess the service quality of 25 Star Alliance airlines using the B-TOPSIS method and to demonstrate a robust approach for analyzing group online reviews. Unlike conventional average scoring, B-TOPSIS accounts for the full distribution of ratings, including variability and extremes, as well as ordinal-scale perceptions that simple averages cannot reflect. Three selected variants of different utility functions were tested within the B-TOPSIS routine, showing potential vulnerability of airline rankings to scoring function shape. Therefore, we proposed using simulation-based sensitivity analysis to produce a final airline ranking and classification. As a result, Air New Zealand, ANA – All Nippon Airways, EVA Air, and Asiana Airlines consistently ranked highest. In contrast, Air India, TAP Air Portugal, LOT Polish Airlines, and Air Canada ranked lowest. Three clusters of airlines representing excellent, good, and medium quality were identified. Title: Retail investor heterogeneity in the Korean stock market
Abstract: This study investigates heterogeneity in informativeness among retail investors in the Korean stock market using high-frequency transaction data. We use cross-sectional variation in brokerage advertising expenditures to distinguish retail investors who trade through aggressively advertising brokerages from those who do not. Consistent with the hypothesis that aggressive marketing attracts relatively naïve investors, investors trading through high-advertising firms contribute less to efficient price discovery and incur substantial trading losses against all counterparty types, including other retail investors. Their trading nevertheless improves market liquidity, and additional analyses indicate that this liquidity-provision role remains resilient during periods of market stress. The lower price-discovery contribution and trading losses persist after controlling for brokerage service quality, when brokerages are classified using advertising predicted by lagged retained earnings, and under alternative brokerage classifications. Title: Impact of carbon emission trading on airline operations: Organizational structures and pricing strategies under the carbon abatement consensus
Abstract: The global carbon abatement consensus, particularly on the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), has effectively overturned the realistic basis of airlines' revenue management, including capacity pricing and seat allocation. This has created a novel scenario for studying airline operation management under the carbon reduction consensus. In this analysis, we consider an air-transport service supply chain consisting of two airlines and a downstream travel agent under the carbon emission trading system (ETS). The present study examines the impact of carbon emission trading and pricing strategies within two distinct organizational structures: the parent-subsidiary structure and the independently operated structure. The results demonstrate that the organizational structure of airlines does not influence the correlation between operational decisions and the carbon emission allowance allocation scheme, as well as the carbon emissions trading price. Incentivizing airlines to reduce emissions is advantageous for both increasing ETS activity and for airlines when a lenient allowance allocation scheme is adopted for low-emission airlines and a strict allowance allocation scheme is adopted for high-emission airlines. The independently operated structure is more conducive to encouraging airlines to invest abatement technology. With regard to the potential for abatement technologies, there is a possibility of a rebound effect for high-emission airlines under this organizational structure, whereby they may invest in abatement technologies. Furthermore, the ETS has a crowding-out effect on high-emission airlines, as a high carbon emission trading price will result in a reduction in their capacity inputs. Title: Competence cues drive engagement with food posts on Facebook: Convergent multimodal evidence from the field

Title: Letting go to taste more: Navigating the role of food goal disengagement in travel

Title: Non-linear and interaction effects of causation and effectuation on new venture performance: the role of ecosystem support

Title: Assessing climate action plans and emission reduction challenges: evidence from Tasmanian local governments on the path to net zero

Title: When industrial companies implement circular business models, what do they really do?

Finally, the scaling phase focuses on market expansion and digital integration to enhance circular operations. Title: Personalized pricing with asymmetric information: A supply chain perspective

Title: Strategies for enhancing construction digitalisation: a machine learning-based sensitivity analysis
Abstract: Purpose – To achieve digitalisation, construction organisations need strategies to help align existing business structures with emerging digital technologies. To this end, this paper presents the findings of an assessment of the strategies required for construction digitalisation using South Africa as a point of reference. Design/methodology/approach – The study adopted a mixed-method design using a Delphi and questionnaire survey, while the critical strategies for digital construction were identified using three different machine learning (ML)-based sensitivity analyses. Findings – The study, through factor analysis, found five major groups of strategies: (1) understanding the construction market, (2) creating a digital culture, (3) technology deployment and assessment, (4) communication management and (5) finance. However, the three ML-based sensitivity analyses all revealed that technology deployment and assessment, as well as understanding the construction market, are the two most important strategies for construction digitalisation in South Africa. Originality/value – The paper offers practical guidelines for construction organisations to be digitalised. It also offers methodological contributions to using ML in survey studies within construction. Theoretically, the study provides a foundation for future studies on strategies for construction digitalisation – an aspect that has received less attention in the current construction digitalisation discourse. © 2026 Douglas Aghimien, Emmanuel Imuetinyan Aghimien, Clinton Ohis Aigbavboa, John Ogbeleakhu Aliu, Ayodeji Emmanuel Oke and Daniel W.M. Title: Dining with dogs or doubts? Understanding customers’ perceptions of pet-friendly restaurants through perceived risk and protection motivation theory
Abstract: In response to the trend of pet-friendly foodservices, drawing on perceived risk theory and protection motivation theory, this study identified domain-specific risks associated with pet-friendly restaurants through a qualitative approach (Study 1). Then, a quantitative approach (Study 2) was employed to examine how these risks influence customers’ threat and coping appraisals and behavioral outcomes, as well as the moderating role of customers’ political identity. The findings revealed that customers primarily perceive health, environmental, and psychological risks when dining at pet-friendly restaurants. These perceived risks significantly shape their threat and coping appraisals, which subsequently influence visit intentions and vigilance behaviors. Moreover, customers with conservative political identities were found to be more sensitive to perceived psychological risks. This study extends the application of protection motivation theory to innovative foodservice contexts and offers practical insights for industry practitioners seeking to design inclusive yet safe dining environments. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Tao C.; Cheng P.
Title: Who designs what matters: How design task allocation affects consumer attitude towards Human-AI collaborative design?
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into design practice. Consumers increasingly encounter products created through human-AI collaboration across various domains. Understanding how consumers respond to products designed collaboratively by humans and AI has become increasingly important. Drawing on design theory, this research distinguishes two types of human-AI collaborative design according to whether AI is assigned to process-oriented or outcome-oriented activities. Building on attribution theory, this research further proposes that different human-AI collaborative design types influence consumers' inferences about firms’ motives for involving AI, particularly motives related to quality improvement and cost reduction. Across five controlled experiments (N = 1163), together with additional pilot and pretest studies, this research this research provides initial evidence that different human-AI collaborative design types are associated with differences in consumer attitudes. Study 1 (N = 150) found that consumers responded more favorably to AI-process & human-outcome (vs. human-process & AI-outcome) and Study 2a (N = 199) provided evidence consistent with the mediation roles of quality improvement and cost reduction. Study 2 b (N = 243) extended these findings using a more realistic disclosure format. Study 3 (N = 278) and study 4 (N = 293) provided preliminary evidence these effects may vary depending on product information complexity and collaboration dominance. The findings offer a preliminary theoretical understanding of how and why consumers respond differently to distinct types of human-AI cooperation design. These findings may also inform future research and offer tentative implications for firms communicating AI involvement in product design. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Fostering employees' adoption of machine learning-enabled technologies in asset pricing
Abstract: Purpose – This research aims to explore how financial professionals perceive and apply machine learning (ML) in asset pricing, identifying key determinants of its adoption by examining the role of institutional pressures, individual and organizational factors. In addition, the study examines the moderating roles of technology interconnectivity and technology interoperability in the association between employees' ML adoption intention and actual usage behavior. Design/methodology/approach – Using a quantitative approach, data were gathered from 689 financial professionals in Vietnam through an online survey targeting those with experience or knowledge in asset pricing. The research model was analyzed using structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4 software. Findings – The results indicate that ML knowledge, perceived cognitive capabilities, personal innovativeness and leadership vision positively influence employees' intention to adopt ML. However, contrary to expectations, concerns about job displacement and organizational innovativeness were found to negatively affect ML adoption. Moreover, adoption intention strongly predicts the actual use of ML in asset pricing practices. Originality/value – This study pioneered insights into how individual and organizational factors, such as leadership vision and cognitive abilities, shape ML adoption in finance. It highlights the interplay between digital transformation, employee perceptions and organizational culture in emerging markets. Policymakers and businesses can use these findings to drive innovation and enhance competitiveness in the ML-driven financial sector. © Khoi Minh Nguyen, Minh Tran Dang, Linh Dan Nguyen Thi, Han Gia Nguyen, Thanh Nguyen Hoang Hung, Dung Phan Thi Minh and Ngan Thanh Nguyen

Title: Dynamic responses of clean energy markets to trade uncertainties and partisan conflict: Evidence from a TVP-local projection framework
Source title: North American Journal of Economics and Finance
Abstract: The study examines how Partisan Conflict (PC), World Trade Uncertainty (WTU), and Trade Policy Uncertainty (TPU) influence clean energy market (CEM) indices from 2010 M11-2024 M06 using Time-Varying Parameter Local Projection (TVP-LP). Analysing eleven sub-indices – BIO, SOLAR, WIND, and others – results show that these uncertainties vary significantly across energy sectors and macroeconomic conditions. During economic booms characterized by low global unemployment, some sectors – SMART GRID and ENERGY STORAGE – are sensitive to TPU and PC, while others – WIND and BIO – show delayed but persistent effects. Conversely, during uncertainty periods, negative impacts on investment are severe and enduring. These underscore that clean energy sector vulnerability depends on source and shocks timing, emphasizing tailored policies to promote resilience and investment under different economic regimes. The study offers a nuanced, disaggregated, and state-dependent framework for understanding how uncertainty propagates through CEM, with broader macro-financial, political, and energy policy implications. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Beyond promotions: business model innovation in everyday low pricing grocery
Abstract: Purpose – This paper seeks to conceptualise an integrated, dynamic, everyday low-price (EDLP) retail business model (EDLP-RBM) and understand how retailers revitalise their EDLP business model in today’s hypercompetitive environment. The qualitative approach adopts an exploratory grounded theory perspective to build an interpretive theory for EDLP-RBM and BMI. Findings – The paper proposes an extended representation of the EDLP-RBM, highlighting the interlocking elements that collectively renew the BM to create, capture and deliver value in a competitive context characterised by significant discontinuities for the retailers. Research limitations/implications – The main limitation is related to the qualitative nature of the research, which reduces the opportunity for generalising the results. Practical implications – The case studies reveal that the BMI can serve as a redefinition of the value proposition currently offered within the industry (i.e. conventional EDLP, HILO and discount retailing) and how the operating model delivers it. Authors: Liu X.; Song X.; Nguyen M.
Title: When AI disclosure makes charities seem less communal: The downside of disclosing AI-generated suggested donation amounts
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Charitable giving depends not only on how much donors are asked to give, but also on how they interpret the charity behind the ask. As charities increasingly use data-driven systems to personalize suggested donation amounts, disclosure decisions become increasingly consequential. We propose a relational transparency paradox: in charitable giving, AI-personalized source disclosure does not merely inform donors that a suggested amount was generated by AI using personal data; it changes how they interpret the charity's relational orientation. Because donor–charity relationships are expected to be communal, AI-personalized source disclosure can make the charity appear less caring, less donor-oriented, and more exchange-like. Four primary experiments and one incentive-compatible behavioral extension support this account. Study 1a shows that, holding the suggested amount constant, AI source disclosure lowers donation intention and trust in the charity relative to a no-source control condition and a social-norm source condition. Study 1b extends this effect to a real bonus-allocation decision: participants donated less of an additional bonus when the recommended amount was described as AI-personalized. Study 2 shows that lower net communality accounts for these effects beyond perceived autonomy. Study 3 identifies effectiveness-focused appeal framing as a boundary condition: the penalty associated with AI source disclosure is weaker when the appeal emphasizes measurable impact rather than human need. Study 4 shows that a donor-care explanation attenuates the downside of AI source disclosure by increasing net communality and restoring a more communal interpretation of AI use. Together, these findings extend suggested-donation research by identifying AI-personalized source disclosure as a distinct feature of the ask, contribute to AI and personalization research by specifying a relational pathway for disclosure effects, and show charities how to communicate transparent AI use in ways that preserve donor support and trust in the charity. © 2026

Title: Macroeconomic policy sensitivity and mutual fund performance: Evidence from Five-Year Plans of China
Abstract: The effect of market-wide macro information on asset returns is a topic with substantial research interest, while not enough evidence supports how firm- or industrial-specific macro information influences investor behaviors. Grounded in China's Five-Year Plans, this study investigates whether and how mutual funds benefit from incorporating industrial policy signals into portfolio decisions. Using mutual fund holdings data covering the policy cycles of 2006, 2011, 2016, and 2021, we construct a novel measure of industrial policy sensitivity and find that funds with higher sensitivity consistently achieve superior performance. Further analyses show that this effect is strengthened by stronger stock-picking ability, greater industry research intensity, and consistency between disclosed policy views and portfolio adjustments, but weakened by market-timing behavior. The effect also varies with institutional and industry environments. These findings highlight the investment value of industrial-specific information and underscore the importance of contextual factors in shaping mutual fund performance in policy-intensive markets. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Ethnic Capital in AHP-Driven Preference Elicitation and Public Policy Negotiation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: The research concerns interstate negotiations. The perspective of negotiation theory is adopted and the AHP method is used to analyze the role of ethnic capital in this process. The example of peace negotiations between Ukraine and Russia illustrates the general argument. The resulting negotiation support system – a peace negotiation map – uses a formalized protocol for option generation, pair comparisons, concession rates, and mediation steps. The AHP method assists in aggregating the parties’ priorities in the areas of security, sovereignty, economics, procedural parameters, etc. Extended ethnic capital is introduced as a separate criterion influencing conditions for the compromise. The results of the analysis and simulation of negotiation procedures reveal the impact of the structure of the protocols on the outcome of the process. The presented proposals treat negotiations as a formalized analytical process with clearly defined procedures considering cultural background and communicative aspects. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From scores to decision: Unveiling company maturity for Industry 4.0 using Benefit-of-the-Doubt models
Abstract: Digital maturity assessments are essential for guiding industrial firms through their transformation toward Industry 4.0. This study proposes a novel composite indicator to evaluate digital maturity using a Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) approach grounded in robust and conditional efficiency techniques. Leveraging a unique dataset of 490 Portuguese firms that completed a self-assessment, following the IMPULS model adapted to the Portuguese context, we constructed firm-specific scores that account for performance heterogeneity and environmental factors. The empirical results show that firms exhibit low maturity in Smart Infrastructure, Smart Products, and Data-Driven Services, while Human Resources emerges as the comparatively most developed dimension, indicating that digital transformation remains at an early stage for most firms, especially SMEs. Importantly, this work pioneers the application of Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to explore the non-linear influence of contextual variables, such as firm size, sector, and region, on digital maturity scores obtained via the BoD methodology. We find that conditional BoD scores differ significantly from the standard BoD and the fixed-weight IMPULS-adapted index, and that firm age category and sector exert significant effects on digital maturity, whereas financial productivity indicators do not. This innovative use of GAMs provides richer and more flexible insights than traditional parametric methods, uncovering complex interactions that affect firms’ digital maturity. Our findings offer actionable guidance for policymakers and industry stakeholders, highlighting priority areas for tailored support and capacity-building interventions. The proposed framework contributes both methodologically and empirically to the evaluation of Industry 4.0 maturity and provides a replicable approach for assessing digital transformation in other national and sectoral contexts. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Bailly F.; Dubrion B.
Title: Work “as if people mattered”: Reassessing the contribution of E. F. Schumacher
Abstract: While academic literature has widely acclaimed E. F. Schumacher's work for its critique of the industrial production system and its contribution to the depletion of natural resources, it has downplayed the author's reflections on work. This article aims to reassess Schumacher as a genuine theorist of work. By conceptualising ecological and work issues as two sides of the same productive reality, we demonstrate that Schumacher emerges as a proponent of the thesis of the centrality of work in human life, outlining concrete pathways to strive towards what he terms “Good Work”. Schumacher's reflections on work thus serve not only to critique the manner in which mainstream economics apprehends the nature and purposes of work, but also to more broadly question the conceptual and normative assumptions underlying that paradigm. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.
