Title: Exploring the Drivers of Circular Economy Implementation: Evidence from Bangladesh’s Manufacturing Sector
Abstract: This study examines the key drivers that helps in implementing Circular Economy (CE) in Bangladesh’s manufacturing sector by focusing on textile, pharmaceutical, food processing, and equipment industries. The study employed a quantitative research design using convenience sampling techniques to collect data from 218 survey responses from selected manufacturing industries and job positions. Data were collected using a validated questionnaire, and the interrelations among environmental awareness, resource availability, regulatory pressure, and organizational culture with the implementation of a circular economy were examined using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The findings indicates that environmental awareness and regulatory pressure have a considerable impact on circular economy implementation whereas resource availability and organizational culture also have an impact, but to a lesser extent. Notably, organizational culture does not substantially moderate the relationship between regulatory pressure and circular economy implementation. These findings support a multimodal approach to implementing circular economy through enhance legal frameworks and corporate commitment to sustainability. This study offers actionable insights for stakeholders to promote a sustainable industrial transition in Bangladesh’s manufacturing sector. Future research should focus on broader and more diverse samples including different industries and rural regions to improve generalizability moreover, mixed-method approaches may provide a deeper insight into Circular Economy implementation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Market coordination and structure of the roundscad (Decapterus spp.) value chain in the Philippines: Implications for sustainable fisheries development
Abstract: Small pelagic fisheries are central to food security and livelihood stability in the Philippines, with roundscad (Decapterus spp.) among the most consumed and economically important marine species nationwide. Despite its significance, the roundscad industry still has several opportunities to strengthen its structure and governance. Recent trade data show that roundscad imports increased from 53,566 MT in 2022–65,180 MT in 2023, indicating rising domestic supply gaps despite continued local production. These concerns highlight the need for an industry assessment. This study applied an industry assessment framework that integrated structural mapping, financial evaluation, and governance analysis across the Philippine roundscad industry. The results show that the industry is dominated by mid-aged, low-income actors, with women playing key roles in trading and processing. The chain involves diverse actors, with traders facilitating small-scale fishers’ access to capital and markets. Persistent constraints include high operational costs, limited postharvest infrastructure, and exposure to climate and price risks. Improving cold chain systems, strengthening cooperative-based market linkages, expanding financial access, and enhancing monitoring and enforcement mechanisms are necessary to increase competitiveness, livelihood security, and resilience. The findings provide timely evidence to support the enhancement of management plans and national strategies toward a more efficient, equitable, and sustainable roundscad industry in the Philippines. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Authors: Jo I.; Kwon S.
Title: Consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management considering consumer behavior toward sustainability
Abstract: As consumer attention to sustainability grows in response to climate change concerns, firms face increasing pressure to align their supply chain strategies with evolving market responses. This study aims to support managerial decision-making by examining how firms should strategically design and manage their supply chains when consumer demand is shaped by cumulative, multidimensional, and uncertain responses to sustainability performance. To this end, we develop a consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management framework, embedding a feedback loop between sustainability-driven operations and market demand. We formulate a multi-period mixed-integer linear programming model that links demand to consumers’ sustainability perception, which is formed cumulatively based on firms’ past sustainability performance. Sustainability performance is evaluated using carbon emissions, differentiated across emission scopes, and translated into an overall sustainability evaluation from the consumer perspective. To capture uncertainty in consumer behavior, the framework is extended to a two-stage stochastic programming model that reflects the evolution of sustainability-conscious consumers over time. Numerical experiments validate the proposed model and its internal feedback mechanism, illustrating how sustainability investments dynamically reshape consumer perception, demand realization, and subsequent supply chain decisions. The results show that incorporating consumer responsiveness can simultaneously increase profit and reduce total emissions, while sensitivity analyses reveal systematic shifts in optimal strategies with respect to consumer evaluation characteristics. Under uncertainty, the model favors precautionary sustainable capacity expansion and diversified parallel contracting as effective strategic hedges against evolving market conditions. These findings yield meaningful managerial implications and provide insights into how consumer-driven market mechanisms can support firms’ progress toward net-zero emission targets. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: How Brands Communicate Sustainability to Consumers: A Comparison Between Luxury and Fast Fashion Brands
Abstract: This study aimed to investigate the ways in which luxury and fast fashion brands were communicating sustainability to consumers via their e-commerce websites. Ten luxury and seven fast fashion brands were included in the research and Voyant Tools was utilized in the text analysis. There existed no significant differences in the length and readability of sustainability pages between the luxury and fast fashion brands. All fast fashion brands and 70% of luxury brands have sustainability pages accessible in one click from the homepage. Recommendations for brands included making text easy to read, using easily identifiable names for sustainability pages, locating the pages at the bottom of the homepage, and loading the page in one click. The similarities and differences in using sustainability terminology between luxury and fast fashion brands were identified and recommendations were made. This study was helpful for brands in preparation for sustainability legislation that requires consumer involvement. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Mapping the ESG Research Landscape and Its Consumer Behavior Gap: A Systematic Literature Network Analysis
Abstract: This study maps research at the intersection of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues and consumer behavior. Title: Cost awareness as a fundamental prerequisite of advanced manufacturing technology adoption in a supplier–OEM dyad
Abstract: Purpose – The article focuses on the limited cost awareness as a fundamental yet insufficiently understood barrier to advanced manufacturing technology (AMT) adoption and, consequently, enhanced business performance. Design/methodology/approach – The article utilizes a longitudinal, interventionist case study (2015–2021) of an AMT-based supplier and its manufacturer customer in Finland. Findings – The findings of this article show that decisions not to leverage the advantages offered by AMT may be based on inaccurate financial numbers, indicating limited cost awareness. Thus, considerable cost information asymmetry between an AMT supplier and their customer is problematic and hampers legitimizing AMT adoption decisions. Practical implications – Realizing the efficiencies offered by AMTs and their associated services requires a business model transition, which is often justified on economic grounds, particularly through cost savings. However, if cost awareness is inadequate, the business model transition may not be possible and the potential benefits remain unrealized. As a response, the article proposes a framework to analyze and develop the cost awareness of the stakeholders in a customer-supplier dyad. Originality/value – As a unique contribution to the AMT literature, the article argues the importance of utilizing truthful and up-to-date cost information to support the adoption of the AMTs and the benefits they potentially entail. The article brings together literature on value creation, AMT and digital servitization in a novel synthesis, paving the way for critical studies on costs in manufacturing technology adoption. © Kari Ingman, Jouni Lyly-Yrjänäinen, Teemu Laine and Tuomas Korhonen

Title: Problem-Based Learning for Enhancing Sustainability and Circularity Concepts in Fashion Design

Title: Conflict Analysis of China-US Trade Disputes Based on Quantitative Time-Varying Attitude Preferences

Abstract: To address the core issues in Graph Model for Conflict Resolution (GMCR) with time-varying attitude—specifically, the lack of representation of preference intensity and the insufficient efficiency and consistency in evaluating time-varying attitude toward large-scale events—this paper proposes a time-varying attitude preference quantification method based on news texts. Title: How team knowledge sharing drives employee service innovation in luxury hotels: A cross-level model
Abstract: Service innovation is a key source of competitive advantage in luxury hospitality, yet little is known about how team-level knowledge processes shape employee service innovation performance (ESIP). Drawing on the knowledge-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, this study tests a cross-level model using two-wave data from 422 employees nested within 60 teams across 33 five-star hotels in China. Multilevel structural equation modeling shows that team knowledge sharing (KS) is positively associated with knowledge orchestration capability (KOC), which in turn predicts ESIP. KOC mediates the cross-level relationship between KS and ESIP. Absorptive capacity (AC) further moderates the KS–KOC relationship in an inverted U shape: the positive effect of KS strengthens from low to moderate AC but weakens at high AC. These findings show that the innovation value of team knowledge sharing depends on effective knowledge orchestration and balanced absorptive capacity. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Human-Centric AI in Financial Management: Aligning Digital Transformation with Industry 5.0 Principles

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the manner in which we handle finances. Besides automation with artificial intelligence and predictive analytics and real-time decision-making, most companies are also starting to transition to a sustainable model (Industry 5.0). This research paper will look at how artificial intelligence can enhance financial processing including evaluating the risk, identifying fraudulent behaviour and also strategic predictions. It will also assess the ethical consequences of integrating artificial intelligence into financial processing, both the organisational as well as the technical consequences. According to this research and the existing literature, the research will show the growing role that AI is playing in the contribution of employees, the capacity of financial institutions to perform resilience and the degree of interaction that customers are having with their financial services providers. The research will also touch upon the issues of providing the privacy of the data utilised by AI, the clarification of the decisions made by AI and training financial professionals in AI. Lastly, the research will give recommendations on how to build a framework of the adoption of AI in financial management using the integration of digital transformation practices and Industry 5.0 principles. These results will be incorporated into the more general scholarly debate concerning sustainable innovations that will facilitate the close of the chasm between technological innovations and human values in the finance industry. In general, this paper will add to the existing literature by developing a highly considered conceptual framework that will integrate the concepts of Industry 5.0 in the context of AI-based financial management. Title: Strategic service network design for integrated road-rail express freight based on existing passenger train services and road service networks
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: Railway-based express transportation has become an important component of modern logistics systems, offering an alternative to express deliveries. To enhance coordination between road and rail transportation, this study investigates a strategic service network design and freight flow allocation problem for integrated road-rail express freight, in which shipments can be transported either entirely by road or through a combination of road transport and existing passenger trains equipped with attached parcel carriages. An integrated road-rail express service network is constructed to support flexible mode choice, road-rail transfers, and cross-line transshipment within the railway service network. Based on this network, an integer linear programming model is established to jointly optimize the design of the railway express service network and freight flow allocation, to minimize total system operating cost. To address the computational challenges in large-scale instances, a hybrid solution framework combining adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) with a commercial solver is developed. The effectiveness of the methodology is evaluated through numerical experiments of different scales and a case study based on a realistic service-network setting. The results indicate that the integrated road-rail express service network achieves a lower total system cost than a road-only transportation alternative and better accommodates degraded road operating conditions. Despite cost accounting being vital for company operations and life cycle many counties may vary making cost accounting applied voluntary or mandatory. This phenomenon may wholly affect formation of a cost-centric company culture. While corporate culture is the set of common values, behaviors, and practices that influence how work is done within an organization, cost accounting may be considered as one the essential components of corporate culture. In this research effects and reflections of cost accounting on corporate culture were examined. Title: Understanding Circular Economy Implementation in Apartment Building Projects: A Systematic Literature Review
Abstract: The construction and real estate sectors are major contributors to global environmental impacts, particularly through greenhouse gas emissions and high resource consumption. Title: Leader knowledge transformation and competence development: becoming-to-know and sensemaking through action learning
Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this paper is to explain how action learning and sensemaking can be utilised effectively as tools for knowledge transformation. The motivation for this study was to stimulate growth in smaller owner-managed/family businesses through use of action learning. However, as our participatory action research process unfolded, the overarching research problem was clarified as how does action learning enable smaller owner-managed/family business leaders to transform their knowledge and competence? Design/methodology/approach – The authors applied participatory action research with action learning as the intervention for leaders of six smaller owner-managed/family businesses. The intervention consisted of eight half-day sessions over a fourteen-month period, preceded by in-depth leader interviews and company case analyses. Process-as-withness, process-as-narrative and contextualized explanation are used to present the participatory action research analysis, results and discussion. Findings – The authors highlight the underutilized value of action learning as a detached-deliberate sensemaking process for unsticking leader assumptions and transforming knowledge and competence. Participatory action research as a form of representational sensemaking enabled the development of a framework that synthesizes how action learning facilitates sensegiving, sensetaking, sensebreaking and ultimately meaning making in a leader becoming-to-know process. This study responds to Jakubik’s request for a greater use and understanding of action-oriented and experiential approaches to understand how knowledge evolves. Originality/value – Action learning is not new but thus far researchers have not fully explained how this peer-supported process theoretically and practically facilitates effective individual and organizational change. Title: Student distrust of AI in entrepreneurship education contexts: development and validation of an empirical scale

Abstract: Purpose – As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more embedded into higher education, it is essential to understand why some students remain sceptical. Title: Unlocking air cargo demand: A novel predictive model selection framework based on data characteristics
Abstract: Air cargo transportation plays a key role in global trade, especially for time-sensitive and high-value products. Accurate prediction of air cargo demand is essential for informed decision-making on infrastructure planning, capacity management, and resource allocation across the air transport sector. While previous studies have largely advanced air cargo demand forecasting through model development and performance comparison, this study introduces a framework to explain and compare established predictive models based on data characteristic analysis (DCA). By examining key time series characteristics, such as stationarity, seasonality, and complexity, across statistical, machine learning, and deep learning approaches, this research examines how intrinsic properties of demand data are associated with forecasting performance. A rolling horizon design is also employed to evaluate how dynamic changes in data characteristics influence model performance over time. The findings reveal that statistical models are particularly sensitive to the mutability and complexity of air cargo demand data, whereas machine learning and deep learning models demonstrate stronger adaptability under diverse demand data conditions. Overall, this study shifts the emphasis from developing new forecasting models to explaining model suitability and supporting model selection, offering both theoretical insights and practical guidance for stakeholders by highlighting which models are best suited under specific data conditions. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Greenhouse Gas Mitigation Potential of Biogas in Boarding Secondary Schools: An Exploratory Multiple-Case Study in Dar es Salaam and Pwani, Tanzania
Abstract: Biogas offers a potential pathway for improving institutional cooking-energy systems, organic-waste management and greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation. This exploratory study assessed the theoretical biogas potential and modelled GHG-emission reductions in ten boarding secondary schools in two coastal regions of the United Republic of Tanzania in East Africa, with nine schools included in the comparable mitigation analysis. Survey data on cooking-fuel use and waste generation were combined with literature-derived parameters to estimate theoretical biogas production, fuel-substitution potential and associated GHG-emission reductions, alongside an assessment of institutional acceptability. The baseline assessment included cooking-fuel combustion, carbon-stock loss associated with non-renewable woody-biomass use and wastewater emissions. The modelled biogas system included residual use of existing cooking fuels, biogas combustion and fugitive methane leakage. Across nine comparable schools, baseline emissions were estimated at 832.10 t CO2-eq yr-1, dominated by wastewater emissions and carbon-stock loss associated with reliance on septic wastewater systems and widespread firewood use. Aggregate theoretical net GHG-emission reduction declined from 473.74 t CO2-eq yr-1 at 0% methane-leakage to 170.12 t CO2-eq yr-1 at 40% leakage, equivalent to 56.93% and 20.44% reductions, respectively. Of the ten surveyed schools, only one had adopted biogas; however, it was excluded from the comparative mitigation analysis because of insufficient technical and operational data on the biogas plant. The aggregate leakage break-even point was approximately 62%, while substitution potential varied markedly among schools. Institutional acceptance of biogas was generally favourable, but adoption remained conditional to technical reliability, financing and adequacy of institutional support. These findings highlight the importance of site-specific system design, effective methane-leakage control and sustained technical and financial support. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Green intellectual capital and organizational learning: pathways to sustainable innovation and firm performance in Pakistani SMEs
Abstract: Purpose – This study investigates the impact of green intellectual capital (GIC) on green innovation (GI) and firm performance (FP) in Pakistani manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Title: Property rights and market frictions: Evidence from the universe of land dispute files in China
Abstract: This research demonstrates how securing land property rights can mitigate frictions in rural land rental markets, specifically in the form of landlord-tenant disputes. Title: Taking the pulse of service ecosystems: exploring viability through valences and forms of becoming

Title: Asymmetric trust production in human–AI augmentation: the structural vulnerability of affected groups
Abstract: Human–artificial intelligence (AI) augmentation (HAA) is widely expected to enhance trust in AI-supported decision-making by combining algorithmic processing with human judgment. However, existing research on trust in HAA has focused primarily on AI users, providing limited insight into how trust is formed among affected groups that do not directly interact with the systems involved. This study develops a theory of asymmetric trust production, which proposes that, although HAA may strengthen trust among AI users, it can simultaneously constrain trust formation among affected groups by creating structural vulnerability, particularly in contexts characterized by equivocality and invisibility. This study employed a two-part design. Study 1 used a vignette experiment involving hiring, adjudication, and scholarship selection scenarios. The results showed that, under unfavorable outcomes, affected groups reported lower trust under HAA than under human-only decision-making. Higher perceived equivocality and invisibility were also associated with lower trust, particularly in pooled cross-scenario analyses. Study 2 used survey data from job applicants and structural equation modeling (SEM) to identify alternative trust pathways. Findings showed that institutional transparency and social influence shaped appealability, procedural fairness, and institutional accountability, which, in turn, supported trust in AI and HAA decisions, although several paths received only partial or no support. These findings extend research on trust in AI beyond direct users to structurally affected stakeholders by identifying both the conditions under which HAA can constrain trust and the institutional pathways through which trust may still be sustained. This study offers implications for the responsible design and governance of AI-supported decision-making. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: When wages rise, quality falls: Minimum wages and the hidden trade-off in competitive e-commerce markets
Abstract: We show that product and service quality serve as a hidden margin of adjustment to minimum wage hikes in hyper-competitive digital markets. Leveraging granular transaction data from 2628 Tmall stores in rural China from 2015 to 2020, combined with household surveys and firm-level data, we exploit staggered city-level minimum wage increases and find that in the short run, firms neither reduce employment nor significantly raise prices. Instead, they systematically degrade quality, as evidenced by worse product ratings, slower logistics, and poorer customer service, starting within two quarters and persisting over time. The reduction in intermediate inputs compromises product quality, while cuts to outsourced IT services undermine service quality by weakening operational efficiency. Crucially, this decline is driven by high-quality incumbents, whereas low-quality firms show no change but are more likely to exit the market following the shock. These results reveal a trade-off between labor income and consumer welfare, a cost that is invisible in traditional labor market evaluations but central to a complete welfare assessment. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: What drives environmentally friendly packaging choices? Evidence from an in-store field study of real shopping behavior and psychological determinants
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Single-use plastic packaging contributes substantially to global waste, and the transition to environmentally friendly packaging (EFP) depends on consumer acceptance. Title: Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
Abstract: Auctioning access rights to private providers through competitive tendering has become a central instrument for governments to regulate markets and public services. Title: Decomposing flight delay distributions: Tail, location, and center effects
Abstract: Flight delays impose substantial costs on airlines, airports, and passengers. While existing studies predominantly focus on predicting average delays, extreme delays cause disproportionate operational disruptions and passenger dissatisfaction. This study introduces a distributional sensitivity analysis framework to identify factors that specifically drive extreme flight delays. Using 2.08 million U.S. domestic flights from 2024, we employ quantile regression models combined with Global Distributional Importance and Tangent-SHAP to decompose factor contributions across the entire delay distribution. Summer months exhibit 2.04 times higher tail risk than fall. The estimated annual cost of delays exceeding 60 min is approximately 1.9 billion USD, with potential savings of approximately 1.0 billion USD through targeted interventions. These findings provide actionable insights for airlines and airports to prioritize interventions targeting extreme delay prevention rather than average delay reduction. © 2026 The Author.

Title: Impact of mortality salience on the citizenship behavior of hotel employees: A construal level theory perspective

Title: Background music as a cultural cue in ethnic restaurants: Evidence from different restaurant contexts

Title: Pass or fail? Modeling restaurant inspection outcomes through interpretable machine learning
Abstract: This study examines scores on U.S. restaurant health inspections through the lens of government data sources. We noticed comparable trends concerning the timing of inspections, whether across various seasons or on weekdays. Furthermore, we found that CatBoost and logistic regression offered different performance advantages. Title: From if to when: Timing hotel booking cancellations to improve demand management
Abstract: Booking cancellations distort hotel demand forecasts, pricing, and overbooking decisions. The dominant approach in the literature predicts whether a reservation will cancel. Title: Physical climate risk and inflation: evidence from 146 countries
Abstract: Using an unbalanced panel of 146 countries from 1993 to 2023, this study examines the effects of physical climate risk on consumer prices and the underlying transmission mechanisms. These findings provide empirical evidence for incorporating climate risk into price-stability and macroeconomic policy frameworks. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: The road to integration: mapping barriers and challenges in AI implementation processes within KMSs
Abstract: Purpose – Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into knowledge management systems (KMSs) offers transformative potential for organizations by enhancing knowledge-intensive business processes. Title: Optimal investment-based crowdfunding: Crowdblessing versus scale
Abstract: This paper examines crowdfunding of a risky, constant-returns project. The crowdfunder chooses a threshold and interest rate. Title: Airline-driven ground delay program with proactive slot reduction and airline precancellation

Abstract: Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) are widely used to mitigate demand-capacity imbalances in air traffic operations. Title: Application of Discrete Fourier Transform for Wind Speed Modelling

Abstract: In the context of energy transition and the growth of renewable energy sources (RES), especially wind power plants, there is an urgent need for accurate modelling of generation processes due to the stochastic nature of wind. Title: The role of sufficiency in aligning European sovereignty and sustainability in the lithium value chain

Title: Consumer psychological pathways to pro-environmental purchase of specialty freshwater fish: Mediating effects of risk perception and moderating effect of dietary cultural conservatism

Title: From bureaucracy to dashboard: How digital government reshapes corporate liquidity

Title: Dual-speed compliance in Nigeria’s anti-money laundering and counter-financing terrorism regime: understanding sectoral disparities in the implementation of FATF international standards
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to explain why the implementation of Financial Action Task Force (FATF) anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-financing of terrorism (CFT) standards vary significantly across sectors within the same national jurisdiction. Data were collected through 36 semi-structured interviews with regulators, financial institutions, designated non-financial businesses and professions (DNFBPs) and security agencies, supplemented by two focus group discussions. Title: Impacts of altruistic preferences on green innovation in a supply chain under uncertainty

Title: How chatbot eating-action language shapes food purchase responses?

Abstract: AI chatbots increasingly use vivid eating verbs to recommend food products, yet it remains unclear whether such language uniformly increases consumers' purchase intention. Title: From climate vulnerability to elite capture: the hidden pathways linking inequality to climate adaptation readiness

Title: The competitive role of returnless refunds in an E-commerce duopoly

Title: Beyond Single-Theory Explanations: A Dual-Capacity Model of Carbon Disclosure Effectiveness in Sustainable Finance
Abstract: Carbon disclosure has emerged as a central mechanism of sustainable finance, yet its effectiveness in influencing investor decision-making remains theoretically fragmented across legitimacy, signaling, stakeholder, and institutional theory. Applied in isolation, these frameworks generate contradictory findings and leave three gaps unresolved: the absence of integrative frameworks explaining simultaneous mechanism operation, the lack of dynamic models accounting for temporal strengthening, and insufficient boundary condition specification across contexts. This systematic literature review synthesises 44 empirical studies published between January 2015 and June 2025, identified through a Scopus search conducted in July 2025 following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with inter-rater reliability of k = 0.85 at screening and k = 0.82 at full-text assessment. Four mechanisms are identified: information asymmetry reduction (75% of studies; median b = 0.24), signaling of management quality (57%; b = 0.18 to 0.35), risk communication (50%; b = 0.08 to 0.35), and legitimacy building (39%; b = 0.06 to 0.28). These mechanisms operate simultaneously, with relative dominance shifting across sectors and contexts. Disclosure-investment relationships show temporal strengthening, with median effect sizes rising from b = 0.12 in 2015 to 2018 to b = 0.27 in 2022 to 2025. Three contributions are proposed: a dual-capacity extension of signaling theory suggesting that disclosure effectiveness may depend multiplicatively on information supply and market processing capacity, a cascading legitimacy theory offering one account of temporal strengthening through feedback loops between disclosure and infrastructure development, and boundary conditions specifying mechanism dominance across sectors. Findings carry implications for policymakers, managers calibrating sector-specific reporting, and investors building disclosure-informed portfolios aligned with net-zero objectives. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: An interdependency perspective on disruption: crossfield discussion and literature extension

Abstract: Purpose – This paper departs from how the literature is filled with partly contradictory notions on disruption, while lacking a perspective that interlinks disruption causes of technology, business model and mindset with disruption effects beyond focal firms and industries. Title: Negotiating the Small Stuff: AI Agents for Low-Stakes Group Decisions
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Everyday life is dominated by low-stakes decisions—such as choosing a restaurant for a group dinner, deciding which movie to watch, or scheduling a meeting—that are individually trivial but cumulatively consequential. These repeated choices shape cognitive load, decision fatigue, and social coordination, particularly when they must be made jointly. As LLM agents are increasingly used to support everyday decision-making, there is growing interest in delegating such low-stakes choices to assistants. Despite this interest, much existing research on negotiation by LLM agents has focused on economically structured, benchmark-style, or adversarial settings, leaving open how LLM agents negotiate in everyday coordination tasks characterized by mild preference conflicts and satisficing rather than strategic bargaining. To study this, we develop a controlled multi-agent negotiation environment in which three LLM agents, each representing a user with heterogeneous preferences, negotiate to select a single restaurant from a fixed set of alternatives. We compare two settings. In a baseline setting, LLM agents negotiate without convergence guidance and may fail to reach agreement. In a strategy-guided setting, LLM agents operate within an integrated negotiation design combining prompt-level behavioral guidance with platform-level coordination rules, including satisficing thresholds, fairness considerations, and convergence mechanisms. Holding the task environment, preferences, and communication protocol constant, we evaluate how negotiation design affects agreement rates, convergence speed, joint welfare, inequality, and perceived fairness. Our results show that negotiation design plays a critical role in enabling reliable, efficient, and acceptable delegation of low-stakes group decisions to LLM agents, highlighting the importance of coordination-oriented mechanisms in AI-mediated group decision-making. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: When reputational power shapes commitment: industry reputation, supplier adaptation and product quality
Source title: International Journal of Physical Distribution and Logistics Management
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how supplier behavior, specifically relationship-specific adaptation and product quality, shapes two forms of buyer commitment: affective and calculative. Drawing on social exchange theory, we investigate how reputational power, operationalized as the non-coercive influence a supplier derives from its industry reputation, moderates these behavioral effects. We treat industry reputation not as a behavioral act but as a reputational form of non-coercive power that alters how buyers interpret suppliers’ actions. Design/methodology/approach – Guided by social exchange theory, this manuscript employs two field studies targeting purchasing professionals. Study 1 investigates how relationship-specific adaptation affects affective commitment, while Study 2 examines the impact of product quality on calculative commitment. Both models assess the moderating effect of perceived reputational power. Psychometric validity was evaluated using covariance-based structural equation modeling in Analysis of Moment Structures, and hypotheses were tested using Hayes’ PROCESS macro in Statistical Package for the Social Sciences, employing moderated mediation models with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Findings – Relationship-specific adaptation increases affective commitment, while product quality drives calculative commitment. Reputational power strengthens the relational pathway but does not affect the economic one, indicating that buyers respond emotionally to reputation only when relational behaviors are present. Power's influence is thus relational rather than transactional. Practical implications – Suppliers with high power can reduce adaptation yet retain loyalty and performance benefits. Managers should thus invest in building strong brand recognition, balancing the trade-offs between meeting demands and leveraging reputational capital. Meanwhile, buyers must avoid over-reliance on powerful suppliers to preserve bargaining capacity. The findings highlight that intangible factors like reputation can be as critical as product or service quality. Suppliers must ensure responsiveness to maintain trust. Overall, managing power asymmetries is vital for sustaining healthy, performance-enhancing buyer-supplier relationships. Social implications – In highlighting how supplier reputation can tilt relationship power, the study's findings have broader societal implications around fairness and collaboration in business partnerships. When powerful suppliers leverage their industry status, it can create unequal power dynamics that may pressure buyers into unfavorable terms, potentially affecting employee welfare, local communities and smaller firms with fewer resources. Conversely, understanding these dynamics encourages transparent, equitable relationships, prompting businesses to adopt fair negotiation practices, share information and foster trust. Consequently, better-managed power imbalances can lead to more ethical business conduct, greater social responsibility and potentially more inclusive supply chain ecosystems for all stakeholders. Originality/value – This study introduces supplier industry reputation as a non-coercive form of power and shows how it differentially affects relational and economic forms of commitment. Guided by social exchange theory, we model relationship-specific adaptation and product quality as behavioral antecedents of affective and calculative commitment, respectively and test how supplier reputation – conceptualized as non-coercive power – moderates both pathways By distinguishing between affective and calculative commitment and modeling them in parallel, the study advances understanding of how social and economic value interact in supply chain relationships, re-centering power as a critical dynamic in an era dominated by relationship marketing. © Christopher D. Title: More than money: socioemotional wealth, rurality and small business owner exit intentions
Source title: Journal of Small Business and Enterprise Development
Abstract: Purpose – We examine how socioemotional wealth (SEW) and rurality influence small-business owners' exit intentions. With over 50% of US small businesses owned by individuals over 55 and most lacking succession plans, understanding how non-financial factors drive exit intention is critical for economic continuity. Findings – Business owners with high SEW were more likely to choose stewardship strategies rather than liquidating or selling to outsiders. Both older and younger rural business owners were less likely to sell their business to outsiders. Female business owners were less likely to sell to family members. Minority business owners were less likely than White business owners to choose liquidation. Practical implications – Results highlight the urgent need for succession planning education in rural communities. Policymakers and financial advisors could tailor succession resources by SEW score, provide more support for rural owners and design culturally responsive programs for minority owners. Title: Platform evolution for data-driven servitization: an affordance perspective

Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to investigate how manufacturing firms can leverage digital platforms to drive digital servitization by actualizing the action potential offered by data. Title: Value-in-context for digital servitization
Abstract: Purpose – Digital servitization (DS) is transforming value creation and appropriation for manufacturing firms. Title: Award competition and risk taking behavior: Evidence from the Chinese mutual fund industry
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of the Golden Bull Award—China's fund industry's most prestigious accolade—on the principal-agent problem between fund managers and investors, using Chinese actively managed open-end equity funds during 2015–2020 as the sample. Our findings extend the literature on the star effect in China's fund market, provide empirical evidence of managerial behavioral distortion from similar incentive mechanisms, and offer insights for regulatory oversight and industry incentive design. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Assessment of Service Quality of Online Fresh Food Service Platforms: Leveraging Large Language Model Information Extraction Technology and Trustworthy Knowledge Aggregation Algorithms

Title: Liquidity regulation and bank lending: Evidence from China

Title: The low human rights advantage and the failure of globalization: the challenge of China Inc.
Abstract: Purpose – We develop a framework of the low human rights advantage – labor repression, state discretionary expropriation and total control – that reduces factor costs and enables coordinated resource mobilization. These mechanisms generate economic advantage only when combined with access to global markets, which provide demand, capital and technology. By leveraging this low human rights advantage, the Chinese state has transformed China into a giant corporation that combines the agility of a firm with the resources of a nation, thereby reshaping global competition. Economic integration without corresponding political integration is a major contributor to the failure of the current wave of globalization. Design/methodology/approach – The study employs a conceptual and comparative political-economy approach. It integrates international business theory, institutional analysis, and historical analogy to develop two linked frameworks: the low human rights advantage and the China Inc. Model. Drawing on prior empirical research and historical comparison – particularly the antebellum USA and South Africa under apartheid – the paper theorizes how economic integration across incompatible political systems generates systemic instability. The analysis is theory-building rather than empirical testing. Findings – The paper finds that low human rights operate as an institutional subsidy when embedded in global markets, lowering costs of labor, land and capital, and mobilizing national resources. China's global competitiveness is shown to depend on the systematic suppression of rights. Given the low human rights conditions, the party-state has transformed China into a giant corporation with firm agility and state capacity, functioning simultaneously as both a regulator and a market actor, thereby enabling nation-level strategic mobilization and coordination. Globalization without political integration, therefore, produces asymmetric competition, industrial hollowing, dependency and rising geopolitical risk. Research limitations/implications – While providing a proposition that can be empirically tested, this study does not do econometric testing of the proposed mechanisms. Future empirical research could use cross-national indicators and firm-level data, and extend the analysis to other low human rights regimes. Practical implications – For policymakers, the findings suggest that economic openness without political conditionality is unsustainable. Trade, investment and supply-chain policies should account for institutional asymmetry and coercive advantages embedded in authoritarian systems. For firms, the analysis highlights heightened risks associated with dependence on low-rights regimes, including political exposure, regulatory uncertainty and supply-chain vulnerability. Strategic decisions should incorporate institutional risk alongside cost considerations. Social implications – The paper reframes human rights as a structural economic variable rather than solely a moral concern. It shows how the suppression of rights abroad can undermine employment, social stability and democratic norms in high-rights societies, while reinforcing authoritarian control domestically. Globalization without political integration shifts adjustment costs onto citizens in democracies and weakens the normative foundations of the liberal international order. Originality/value – This paper offers a novel framework linking human rights, political and economic organizational forms and global competition. By conceptualizing low human rights as a source of comparative advantage and modeling China as a Nation-as-Firm, it advances international business and emerging-market scholarship beyond distributional or geopolitical explanations. Title: What are safer streets worth? Bridging resident preferences and policy design in traffic calming
Source title: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
Abstract: Traffic calming is widely adopted, yet implementation is often contested, and little is known about which treatments residents prefer or whether they would support a funded traffic-calming program. We surveyed 1717 residents living within 650 feet of 19 corridors in Portland, Oregon. A best–worst scaling (BWS) task elicited relative preferences among eight treatments; a single-bounded contingent valuation (CVM) question elicited support for a funded traffic calming program at a randomly assigned monthly household contribution, from which willingness to pay (WTP) was derived. Median refuge islands were most preferred, followed by mini roundabouts, shared streets, and gateway treatments; diverters, speed humps, and pinchpoints ranked lowest, with diverters and speed humps the most polarizing. Support for the funded program was higher among residents who perceived nearby streets as busy, preferred walking or wished to bike more, or had young children, and lower among older residents and those concerned about crime. Derived WTP averaged US $34 per household per month (median $30). Relative design preference and support for funding did not always align: preference for median refuge islands was associated with lower support, whereas preference for shared streets and diverters was associated with higher support. The combined design is best understood as a low-burden instrument for prioritization and public engagement rather than for formal economic appraisal. © 2026 The Authors

Authors: Zhou S.; Yi N.
Title: How and when does occupational stigma perception undermine service employees’ proactive customer service performance? The role of core self-evaluation
Abstract: Frontline hotel employees are expected to notice changing guest needs and initiate service improvements before formal procedures can be adjusted, yet less is known about whether occupation-specific stigma constrains such proactive behavior. Using cognitive-affective personality system (CAPS) theory, this study examines how perceived occupational stigma undermines proactive customer service performance (PCSP) among frontline service employees. We propose two psychological routes—a cognitive route through organization-based self-esteem (OBSE) and an affective route through harmonious work passion (HWP)—and examine core self-evaluations (CSE) as a boundary condition. Across a scenario experiment, a 2 × 2 experiment, and a three-wave field survey, perceived occupational stigma consistently reduced PCSP. OBSE and HWP transmitted this effect, and CSE weakened the negative indirect pathways. These findings clarify how occupational stigma is processed in frontline hospitality work and offer guidance for sustaining proactive service behavior in stigmatized roles. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Food & beverage firms in the U.S. equity network: Connectedness, drivers, and portfolio implications
Source title: North American Journal of Economics and Finance
Abstract: Food-system firms face shocks uncommon in other equity markets, including those driven by biological production cycles, weather variability, and fluctuations in agricultural commodity prices. Despite these unique exposures, such firms remain integrated into the broader economy through input costs, logistics, financing, and final demand. The extent to which this duality confers a distinctive role in cross-sector shock transmission, and its implications for portfolio allocation, remain unresolved. This study investigates the role of food-system equities within the U.S. sectoral network using a time-varying parameter vector autoregression connectedness framework. Food-system equities, proxied by the S&P Food & Beverage Select Industry Index (FB), which spans production, processing, beverages, distribution, and retail, are benchmarked against the ten S&P 500 sector indices to situate FB within the broader U.S. sectoral landscape. FB ranks fourth in net return transmission, transmitting more price-relevant shocks than it absorbs, while its net volatility transmission remains close to neutral. Although returns in FB and Consumer Staples (CS) – the sector within which these firms are conventionally classified – are highly correlated (0.862), each index accounts for only approximately one-sixth of the other’s inbound connectedness, and their net transmission roles are uncorrelated throughout the sample period. FB’s net transmission increases with food price inflation relative to the headline rate and decreases with supply-chain, credit, and interest-rate pressures. Dynamic minimum-variance portfolios include both indices on 70% of trading days and, for 470 days, allocate nearly one-fifth of portfolio weight to FB. These findings suggest that food-system equities constitute a distinct segment within the sectoral network: they are informationally active, risk-balanced, and not substitutable with the aggregate index typically used to represent them. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Authors: Sandberg E.
Title: Linear retailers going circular: the logistics implications
Source title: International Journal of Retail and Distribution Management
Abstract: Purpose – This paper seeks to answer the question: What are the logistics implications when linear retail business models are complemented with circular ones? In particular, this research targets logistics implications perceived as critical for supporting circular business models (CBMs) that are economically viable. Design/methodology/approach – The study adopts a multiple case study design involving seven Swedish retail companies operating a total of eleven CBMs, including second-hand sales, rentals and repair services. Empirical data were mainly collected through semi-structured interviews, and the analysis followed a Gioia-inspired approach informed by a narrative literature review on logistics implications that arise when retailers combine their forward and reverse logistics operations. Findings – The study identifies 16 empirically grounded logistics implications across the four reverse logistics (RL) activities of collection, sorting, recovery and redistribution. The results reveal the coexistence of two overarching perspectives on logistics implications when combining forward and reverse logistics: an extension perspective emphasising challenges, and a design perspective highlighting various design areas for integration. Research limitations/implications – The study is limited to Swedish retailers. Further studies in other geographical contexts are suggested. Originality/value – The research goes beyond the existing, often generic and conceptual literature on barriers to RL operations and provides a more granular view of the role of logistics in retail CBMs. By articulating complementary analytical perspectives, the study advances theory on the integration of forward and reverse logistics in a retail setting. 2026 © Erik Sandberg

Author full names: Grebe, Leonard (58315866500); Santos, Beatriz (60261715000); Schiereck, Dirk (55883510000)
Title: Is AI really valuable for European companies? The market impact of AI project announcements
Abstract: Purpose – Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to disrupt international businesses processes. However, given the complexity and inherent risks associated with AI investments, it remains debatable whether such projects offer tangible benefits to firms. In the global discussion, this paper aims to add an European perspective for international businesses by analyzing the value effects of AI project announcements by European companies. Design/methodology/approach – This study is based on an event study methodology to test for abnormal market returns around the announcement of AI projects by European companies. The market perception is further controlled for differences in AI projects like additional strategic partnerships, industry-fixed effects and success in implementation. Findings – Contrary to expectations, this event study finds no significant abnormal market reactions to AI project announcements by European companies on general. Project-specific characteristics also do not appear to meaningfully influence investor perception. However, the authors observe clear industry-specific effects: the automotive sector exhibits a comparatively positive market response, while pharmaceutical and telecommunications firms also show above-average abnormal returns around the announcement date. These findings suggest that investors evaluate AI initiatives in Europe through a sector-specific lens, resulting in diverging market reactions. Overall, the results further challenge assumptions about the uniformly US-centric valuation of AI announcements. Practical implications – The findings suggest that European managers should align AI announcements with clear, sector-specific innovation strategies to enhance credibility and investor confidence. However, to ensure broader societal benefit, AI strategies must be inclusive, avoiding the concentration of value in select sectors. These insights highlight the need for context-sensitive approaches to AI communication and implementation across Europe independent from the US role model. Social implications – The findings highlight the heterogeneous interpretation of AI projects across sectors in Europe. The sector-specific nature of investor reactions suggests that firms must adopt tailored AI communication strategies that resonate with the expectations and realities of their respective industries. This underscores the broader societal importance of fostering public trust in AI, not just as a technological innovation, but as a tool for meaningful and inclusive social and economic progress. Originality/value – This study contradicts the common understanding of market perception on AI projects from the USA and adds a European perspective, which indicates that the value of AI projects differentiates geographically. © 2025 Emerald Publishing Limited

Title: Evaluation of positioning performance losses in European airspace due to the shutdown of the Ukrainian air navigation network
Abstract: War in Ukraine creates a significant impact on global air transportation system due to the wide area of involved airspaces. On February 24, 2022, Ukrainian air navigation service provider closed national airspace and suspended all navigation services. The ground network of radio navigation aids has been locked. Ukrainian network of radio navigation aids includes 16 Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) and 7 collocated VHF Omnidirectional Range (VOR) stations, which is also a part of the European radio navigation aids network. Service areas of Ukrainian radio navigation aids were provided in airspaces of neighboring countries that allow this equipment to participate in the pair formation process of the on-board positioning system. In the paper, we estimate the configuration of the European navigation aids network and study the impact of closed network on the performance of positioning by pairs of DME/DME and VOR/VOR in airspaces of neighboring countries: Poland, Slovak Republic, Hungary, Romania, and Moldova. Key performance parameters including availability, number of available pairs, positioning accuracy, and system reliability (mean time between failures and probability of failure-free operation) are used in area analysis to identify the impact of closing Ukrainian sub-network of navigational aids. Proposed methodological framework provides a systematic approach for assessing navigation network performance and highlights the implications of network disruptions for aviation safety in European airspace. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Leveraging machine learning to predict employee turnover in the service industry
Abstract: This study employed a machine learning approach to identify and predict the most influential determinants of employee turnover in the hospitality industry. Using archival HR records from 1419 full-time employees extracted from organizational systems, 122 potential predictors across demographic, job-related, behavioral, psychological, engagement-related, organizational, and external domains were evaluated. Feature ranking revealed ten salient predictors, including availability and quality of community support services, physical ergonomics, problem-solving demands, perceived career growth opportunities, career development participation, job satisfaction, recognition from supervisors, organizational commitment, and resilience. Logistic regression achieved the strongest predictive performance, outperforming decision trees and performing comparably to random forest and Naïve Bayes. The findings extend turnover theory by embedding community-level and personal resources alongside classical attitudinal and organizational factors, while also demonstrating the methodological value of predictive analytics. Practical implications highlight targeted interventions in ergonomics, recognition, career development, and resilience-building to reduce turnover. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Keling W.; Yap C.S.
Title: Entrepreneurial resilience and empowerment among rural indigenous women entrepreneurs
Source title: Journal of Small Business and Enterprise Development
Abstract: Purpose – This study explores the dynamics of entrepreneurial resilience and empowerment by examining the lived experiences of rural Indigenous Dayak women entrepreneurs in Sarawak, Malaysia. Focusing on this distinct group, the research investigates how access to resources, support mechanisms, and cultures and traditions shape the development of entrepreneurial resilience. The study further examines how such resilience facilitates personal, social, and economic empowerment among these women. Design/methodology/approach – A qualitative research approach was employed, involving semi-structured interviews with fourteen rural Indigenous Dayak women entrepreneurs. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis to identify key themes related to entrepreneurial resilience and empowerment. Findings – The findings reveal that the resilience of rural indigenous women entrepreneurs is shaped by a set of interconnected factors. Key challenges include balancing cultural values with business demands, coping with financial constraints, and navigating uncertainty in the business environment. At the same time, resilience is strengthened by access to financial and digital resources, strong family and community support, and supportive government initiatives. Cultures and traditions, particularly values emphasising sustainability, respect for the environment, and harmony with nature, play a critical role in guiding business practices and decision-making. Collectively, these elements foster personal growth, social recognition, and economic empowerment among the entrepreneurs. Originality/value – This research offers valuable insights into the intersection of entrepreneurial resilience and empowerment among rural indigenous women entrepreneurs. By illuminating the experiences of a distinct and under-researched demographic, it extends existing scholarship on gender, entrepreneurship, and rural development. The study also offers practical implications for policymakers and development agencies seeking to design context-sensitive interventions that promote gender equality, strengthen entrepreneurial ecosystem, and advance sustainable rural economic development. © William Keling and Ching Seng Yap

Authors: Cuevas L.; Li J.; Han H.
Title: How travel influencers persuade: The role of inspiration, emotional connection, and trust in shaping follower behavior
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Social media influencers play a critical role in building emotional connections between followers and brands, however evolving digital trends have reshaped what audiences value in online personalities. Grounded in persuasion theory, this study examines the characteristics of travel influencers that inspire followers’ decision-making process and enhance perceived value. A sample of 510 was collected from adults residing in the United States. Using PLS-SEM, the results showed that relatability and coolness simultaneously stimulate inspiration and strengthen emotional attachment, thereby shaping travel planning and visit intentions. Relatability exerts the strongest influence on emotional connection, while self-disclosure also positively affects attachment. Moderation analysis revealed that trust strengthens only the relationship between self-disclosure and emotional attachment; specifically, that self-disclosure is more influential when trust is low but less impactful once trust is established. Theoretically, the findings refined influencer models by positioning trust as an outcome of affective persuasion. Practically, the results can guide destinations in leveraging relatable, cool, and authentic influencers to engage audiences effectively. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Determinants of employer-provided training in construction firms: evidence from transition economies
Source title: European Journal of Training and Development
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to investigate the determinants of employee training provision in construction across Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Design/methodology/approach – Using Business Environment and Enterprise Performance Survey (BEEPS) 2019 data, the study analyses 1, 372 construction firms (1, 098 after listwise deletion) across 28 countries. A probit model with average marginal effects examines how managerial experience, perceived workforce education adequacy, innovation activity, firm size and locality size influence training provision. Institutional grouping controls and extensive robustness checks are reported. Findings – Training provision is predominantly reactive, driven by perceived skill deficiencies rather than strategic planning. Perceived workforce education inadequacy is jointly significant as a determinant of training (Wald test p = 0.011), though the graduated intensity pattern observed in point estimates is not statistically distinguishable from a simple binary effect. Manager experience, perceived education inadequacy, firm size, innovation activity and smaller locality size significantly increase training likelihood. Practical implications – Policy should address skill deficiencies through vocational partnerships and place-based strategies rather than relying solely on financial subsidies. If the association between managerial experience and training reflects a causal pathway, management development programmes can indirectly benefit workforce training. Training initiatives should target smaller localities, where firms demonstrate greater receptivity. Originality/value – The findings challenge the assumption that training decisions in construction follow the strategic optimisation logic of human capital theory, revealing a reactive pattern shaped by bounded rationality. The study provides sector-specific evidence from 28 transition economies. The finding that firms in smaller localities are more likely to provide employee training contributes new evidence on place-based workforce development. © 2026 Chloe Delaney, Marie Ryan and Eleanor Doyle.

Title: Ex-ante distributionally robust fleet deployment and slot allocation on liner shipping networks
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: We study ex-ante fleet deployment and slot allocation on fixed weekly liner networks. Before O–D demand, freight-rate coefficients, and deliverable capacity are realized, the carrier chooses vessel deployment, cadence, and baseline slot allocation; the fixed plan is evaluated for profit and reliability, with no scenario-dependent re-optimization. The central idea is to let one deployment-allocation plan carry three linked roles: it protects accepted O–D demand, prices accepted flows through offline conservative revenue coefficients, and enforces correlated deliverable-capacity safeguards over shared disruption regions. We formulate a mixed-integer conic model that links these three uncertainty blocks through common decisions, not one estimated joint ambiguity set. Demand and deliverable capacity receive moment-based distributionally robust safeguards: Cantelli lower-confidence caps and a Boole-based second-order cone approximation for protected capacity reliability. Freight rates enter only as fixed offline conservative revenue coefficients, not dynamic prices, recourse decisions, or an in-model pricing-optimization block. In this formulation, the fleet, cadence, and voyage decisions directly set how much correlated capacity loss each shared disruption region is exposed to. To keep the conic model tractable at network scale, a PCA-based outer-approximation layer reduces the covariance dimension in the capacity certificates, retaining the leading directions and bounding the residual tail. On LINER-LIB-derived instances, out-of-sample diagnostics, component ablations, a 21-point PCA threshold sweep, and a public-data calibration and holdout plausibility check show how the safeguards change deployment decisions and when PCA-OA improves tractability. The evidence supports internal consistency and plausibility, not operational validation on proprietary carrier data. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: I deserve better: beauty work increases consumer preference for advanced products
Abstract: Consumers often engage in beauty work to improve their physical appearance. Prior research has largely focused on how such efforts shape others’ perceptions and inferences about the focal individual. However, little is known about its impact on consumers’ self-perception, particularly how these shifts influence subsequent product preferences. This research demonstrates that beauty work increases consumers’ preference for advanced products by heightening their perceived deservingness. Specifically, after engaging in beauty work, consumers are more likely to choose products featuring premium packaging, upgraded hardware, advanced services, and superior auxiliary functions. This effect occurs because beauty work uniquely generates a sense of “I deserve better”, a mechanism not observed in a general self-improvement activity. Additionally, we identify three boundary conditions: the effect dissipates (1) when beauty work does not produce visible appearance enhancement, (2) among entity theorists, and (3) when consumers make choices for others. Together, this research contributes to the literature on beauty work and offers practical implications for promoting advanced products. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Assessing the impact of public–private partnerships and enabling factors on port efficiency: evidence from Latin America and the Caribbean
Source title: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
Abstract: In response to the challenges posed by outdated infrastructure and fiscal constraints, Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries initiated comprehensive port sector reforms during the 1990 s and 2000 s. At present, LAC is a global leader in the domain of private port operations, with 96% of container throughput—mostly through Public-Private Partnership (PPP) operators under the landlord model. While there have been over 150 PPP port projects implemented since 1990, there is a lack of empirical evidence regarding their impact on port performance. This study presents a longitudinal analysis of container-handling ports in 22 LAC countries, based on selected years between 2001 and 2024, depending on data availability. The findings indicate that PPP-operated ports demonstrate 4641% higher technical efficiency compared to state-run ports. A comparative analysis reveals that ports managed by global terminal operators demonstrate a 3129% higher performance than those managed by local operators. The efficiency gains observed are primarily concentrated among medium-sized terminals. Competitive selection processes have been demonstrated to enhance efficiency, with the impact intensifying as the number of bidders rises. The findings of this study underscore the critical role of regulatory and policy instruments in the design of PPP contracts and procurement processes to drive port performance and optimize investment outcomes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Comparative Annual Analysis of Therminol VP1 and Direct Steam Generation for Hybrid Solar-Geothermal Power at Cerro Prieto
Source title: Studies in Systems, Decision and Control
Abstract: The integration of complementary renewable energy sources represents a critical strategy for improving the stability, efficiency, and output of clean power generation. Geothermal energy supplies consistent baseload power, while concentrating solar thermal (CST) technology delivers high-temperature heat, creating a synergistic relationship ideal for hybridization. This approach proves particularly valuable for addressing challenges in aging geothermal fields where steam production and enthalpy are declining. This study tackles the essential problem of identifying the optimal solar field configuration for augmenting a geothermal facility—a decision with significant technical and economic implications. Through comparative thermo-hydraulic analysis, we demonstrate that a direct steam generation (DSG) system outperforms a conventional system using Therminol VP-1 at the Cerro Prieto geothermal plant in Mexico. The DSG configuration achieves higher annual energy efficiency (0.61 versus 0.49) and an increased solar fraction (29.13% versus 28.38%), all while requiring a smaller solar field area. This finding challenges the conventional preference for synthetic heat transfer fluids and confirms that the characteristically higher pressure drop in DSG systems remains operationally manageable within the annular flow regime and the plant's existing pressure limits. Our results deliver a validated framework for renewable energy integration, establishing direct steam generation as a new performance benchmark for solar-geothermal hybrids. This work advances the broader scientific objective of creating dispatchable, fully renewable power systems by optimizing the synergistic use of geothermal and solar resources. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Daniels S.O.
Title: DIAPROD: A Framework for Formal Consent Modelling, Dynamic Storage Limitation, Data Minimisation, and LLM-Assisted Compliance for Data Protection by Design
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Modern information systems process personal data across complex ecosystems where consent states change, purposes complete, and regulations evolve—all after deployment. Yet existing privacy engineering approaches remain static, with no formal mechanisms for dynamic runtime enforcement. An analysis of 29 named approaches from 73 primary studies confirms this gap. This research presents DIAPROD (DynamIc dAta PROtection by Design), a framework reconceptualising Data Protection by Design as a runtime capability through: (i) ConsentML, a formal modelling language with denotational and operational semantics for lifecycle-aware consent; (ii) a Certifying Kernel with an extensible constraint registry for consent, storage limitation, and data minimisation enforcement; and (iii) an LLM-assisted architecture where the LLM proposes and the kernel decides. ConsentML tool is implemented as a Secure Tropos add-on, verified via the MMQEF framework, and validated through a United Kingdom open banking case study. The remaining work extends the kernel to address storage limitations and data minimisation, with evaluation across healthcare and public sector domains. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: U.S. vs. China: Diverging spillover dynamics in the GCC financial system
Source title: North American Journal of Economics and Finance
Abstract: This study examines the financial stress connectedness and risk spillovers between the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and two major economies—the United States and China—utilizing the Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregressive (TVP-VAR) model to capture dynamic relationships over time. Authors: Zou W.; wan F.
Title: Can algorithms care? Algorithmic empathy and consumer trust in AI-mediated service encounters
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are reshaping service encounters across retail and consumer service industries, yet little is known about whether consumers perceive these systems as emotionally responsive during service interactions. As AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants increasingly handle customer inquiries, complaints, and service recovery processes, understanding how algorithmic systems communicate empathy has become important for building consumer trust and sustaining long-term service relationships. This study introduces the concept of algorithmic empathy, defined as consumers’ perception that an AI-mediated service interface recognizes, understands, and responds appropriately to their emotional states during service interactions. Drawing on service encounter theory and trust formation research, we propose that empathetic design elements embedded within AI communication, including emotion-sensitive language, adaptive response timing, and context-aware acknowledgment of consumer concerns, can substantially influence consumer trust and subsequent service loyalty. Across three empirical studies combining large-scale field data and controlled experimentation, we examine how algorithmic empathy shapes consumer responses in AI-mediated service environments. Study 1 analyzes over 120,000 real customer service interactions from a national online retail platform to identify linguistic and behavioral indicators of empathetic AI responses and their relationship with post-interaction satisfaction and repeat purchase behavior. Study 2 employs a randomized field experiment on an online travel booking platform to test how varying levels of AI empathy influence consumer trust, perceived service quality, and complaint resolution outcomes. Study 3 uses a nationally representative consumer panel survey (N = 1524) with structural equation modeling, confirmatory factor analysis, and reliability testing to examine the psychological mechanisms underlying these effects. The results show that AI systems capable of expressing empathetic cues significantly increase consumer trust, service satisfaction, and repurchase intentions. The effectiveness of algorithmic empathy is particularly pronounced in high-frustration service situations and among consumers with prior negative service experiences. These findings advance understanding of human-AI interaction in consumer service contexts and offer practical guidance for designing emotionally responsive AI service systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Human likeness and behavioral authenticity in virtual influencers: Effects on consumer responses and underlying mechanisms
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: With the growing popularity of computer-generated social media personas, known as virtual influencers, in brand communication, companies are gaining innovative marketing tools while simultaneously facing the challenge of understanding how consumers perceive these non-human endorsers. Drawing on the Uncanny Valley Theory, Parasocial Interaction Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model, this study develops a dual-cue analytical framework to systematically examine the joint effects of virtual influencers’ human likeness and behavioral authenticity on brand attitude.Based on three pre-registered randomized experiments (N = 374, 316, and 494, respectively), the study yields the following findings. First, human likeness exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with brand attitude, with a mediate level of human resemblance generating the most favorable evaluations. Second, parasocial interaction and perceived credibility sequentially mediate the effect of human likeness on brand attitude, while behavioral authenticity mediates this mediation process. Under conditions of low behavioral authenticity, the mediation effect becomes fully dependent on these two mechanisms. Third, consumers with higher AI readiness show greater acceptance of highly anthropomorphic virtual influencers; however, their sensitivity to insufficient behavioral authenticity does not diminish. Instead, they become even more critical of authenticity deficiencies. Furthermore, the effects of virtual influencers on purchase intention and positive word-of-mouth intention are fully mediated by brand attitude.The study makes several theoretical contributions. It extends the cross-cultural applicability of the Uncanny Valley Theory, reveals the threshold effect of behavioral authenticity, and identifies the multidimensional structure of AI readiness. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that brands should adopt a “mediate anthropomorphism–high behavioral authenticity” strategy, avoid the “high anthropomorphism–low authenticity” combination, and develop differentiated marketing approaches for consumer segments with diverse digital-cultural backgrounds. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
