Title: How online communities motivate gaming goal pursuit and recurring community visits
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Online forums serve as technological platforms that enable online communities to engage in the provision, sharing, and seeking of information. By providing valuable information services to consumers, online forums enable users to obtain knowledge from online forums to pursue their goals in target activities. For example, game players visit game forums to acquire knowledge that can help them achieve their gaming goals. However, the previous research has not investigated how goal pursuit affects target activities and shapes users' sustained revisits to forums. To address this gap, the present research employed goal-setting theory to identify how forum connection factors and gaming experience further influence users’ pursuits of mastery goals and performance goals, as well as their revisits. The present study used multiple-wave and multiple-source data—self-reported data and system-recorded data—derived from 1447 active users of gaming forums. Interestingly, we found that past visits significantly discouraged the pursuit of performance goals. Social connections with in-forum friends encouraged the pursuit of both mastery goals and performance goals. Gaming frustration reduced the pursuit of both mastery goals and performance goals. Surprisingly, mastery goals increased the number of revisits to the forum, whereas performance goals reduced the number of forum revisits. These new findings indicate that in-forum friends encourage users to pursue gaming goals, whereas gaming frustration and past forum visits discourage such goal pursuit activities. Moreover, the findings provide important practical implications for consumer services by informing forum managers that they should encourage mastery goals while discouraging performance goals, thereby better securing and increasing the rate at which users revisit forums. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Boardroom bridges: the impact of directors’ overseas experience on firm-level FinTech adoption
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how board directors’ overseas experience affects financial technology (FinTech) adoption in Chinese financial firms. Directors’ overseas experience is shown to enhance firm-level FinTech, particularly its technological application, with the effect operating through both independent and non-independent directors. The findings highlight the strategic value of overseas experienced directors in fostering financial innovation under the dual pressures of state-led regulation and BigTech competition. Title: Stock price synchronicity and internet penetration: International evidence
Abstract: Using a panel of 166,063 firm-year observations across 37 countries from 2001 to 2023, this paper provides, to our knowledge, the first large-scale cross-country evidence on the relationship between internet penetration and stock price synchronicity (SYNC). We document a robust negative association between internet penetration and SYNC, consistent with more efficient dissemination of firm-specific information. This relationship remains stable across multiple model specifications and is robust to controls for potential endogeneity. The negative relationship is stronger in developing markets and in environments characterized by more credible firm-specific information and greater investor sophistication. Together, these findings suggest that internet penetration reduces information frictions, particularly in developing markets, and enhances the incorporation of firm-specific information into stock prices when disclosures are credible and investors can effectively process information, offering important guidance for policymakers. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Navigating uncertainty: Supply chain risk exposure and corporate investment efficiency
Abstract: Supply chain risk not only disrupts operations but can also distort firms’ investment decisions, affecting long-term value creation. Using natural language processing on quarterly earnings call transcripts, we construct firm-level measures of supply chain risk exposure and examine its effect on investment efficiency. We find that higher supply chain risk primarily induces underinvestment, rather than overinvestment. Mechanism tests reveal that elevated risk increases financing constraints, leading firms to prioritize defensive investments, such as inventory and cash reserves, which reduces capital allocation efficiency. Moreover, this negative effect is stronger for firms with high operational environmental uncertainty, limited supply chain finance, or weaker ESG performance. Title: A Review of Human-Centric Construction Manufacturing: Current Practices and Research Opportunities
Source title: Journal of Construction Engineering and Management
Abstract: The industrialization of the construction industry has transformed traditional practices by streamlining construction processes in controlled, factory-based environments through construction manufacturing production systems, in which building components are produced in factories and assembled on-site. Beyond improvements in efficiency and environmental performance, this production paradigm establishes long-term relationships between workers and management, creating an opportunity for human-centric construction manufacturing that prioritizes workers' well-being as a core element of production within the Industry 5.0 paradigm. Human-centric construction manufacturing offers a practical means of integrating worker well-being, safety, mental health, inclusiveness, and skill development into construction production systems. Despite growing interest in human-centric considerations, existing research remains fragmented, loosely defined, and predominantly technology-driven. To address these gaps, this paper presents a scoping review on human-centric construction manufacturing that synthesizes key research themes, enabling technologies, emerging trends, research gaps, and future research directions within construction production systems. A total of 54 articles were included in the review, spanning three research areas examined from a human-centric perspective, i.e., ergonomics, safety, and workforce planning, each further categorized into subresearch areas. Workers' mental health, equity, diversity, inclusion, and holistic well-being in the construction manufacturing paradigm remain significant and underexplored research opportunities. Among the most prominent technologies were simulation, virtual reality, optimization, sensing technologies, and 3D modeling, while computer vision, machine learning, robotics, and digital twins were less frequently applied, despite their strong potential to support human-centric construction manufacturing. Overall, this review establishes a comprehensive foundation for understanding the current state of human-centric construction manufacturing, identifies critical research needs, and provides guidance for future efforts toward developing safer, healthier, and more productive factory environments that support resilient construction manufacturing systems.  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Corporate social responsibility and investors with multiple blockholdings: a monitoring capacity perspective
Abstract: Prior work shows that institutional investors with multiple blockholdings can be effective monitors of financial performance. I ask whether this conclusion extends to CSR, a governance domain whose informational properties differ sharply from financial performance. I further predict that this negative effect is amplified by blockholders’ portfolio industry dispersion and exogenous blockholder distraction. Title: Environmental protection through green innovation performance

Abstract: Purpose – Businesses focus on digital transformation (DT) to improve performance; hence, this study aims to examine the relationship between DT and green innovation performance (GIP) within small- and medium-sized enterprises. In line with stakeholder theory, the study investigated the mediating impact of absorptive capacity (AC) and the moderating role of competitive pressure (CP) and environmental regulations (ERs). Design/methodology/approach – Data were collected from 233 enterprises in China via an online survey and analyzed empirically. Findings – Outcomes explained the positive and significant impact of DT on GIP and highlighted the mediating role of AC. In addition, CP and ERs were found to be convincing moderators, modeling dynamics of GIP. Conclusions extend enterprises’ understanding of how to strategically control DT and emphasize AC linked with ERs and CP. Title: Clean job creation versus dirty job destruction: labor market dynamics and business cycles
Abstract: Purpose – This paper studies how the green transition affects labor-market reallocation, business-cycle dynamics and distributional outcomes. It focuses on the distinction between clean job creation and dirty job destruction and how these adjustment margins affect high- and low-skilled workers differently. Design/methodology/approach – We develop an environmental dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model with search-and-matching frictions, clean and dirty sectors, and high- and low-skilled workers. Transition risk is modeled through four skill-specific job-flow shocks, distinguishing clean job creation from dirty job destruction. Findings – The paper finds that job creation and job destruction are asymmetric channels of adjustment. Clean job creation supports sectoral reallocation but generates limited aggregate fluctuations. By contrast, dirty job destruction produces larger business-cycle effects, especially when it affects low-skilled workers. Low-skilled dirty job destruction generates the largest output losses, stronger inflationary pressures and the most severe distributional effects, widening both consumption inequality and the wage premium. Originality/value – The paper treats transition risk as a labor-market reallocation process rather than solely as a carbon-pricing shock. Authors: Cheer A.; Qian Y.
Title: Impacts of ending consumer purchase incentives on electric vehicle adoption: Evidence from interrupted time series analysis
Source title: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
Abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) markets mature and governments worldwide consider ending costly financial incentives, there is a lack of empirical evidence on the sustained effectiveness of these incentives once they are reduced or eliminated. Exploiting the sudden pause of the Canada iZEV purchase subsidy program as a natural experiment and using the quasi-experimental controlled interrupted time series approach, this nationwide study estimates the causal impacts of the purchase subsidy on the uptake of zero-emission electric vehicles (ZEVs) over the 7-year period from 2019 to 2025. The results show that after accounting for the pre-pause quadratic growth trend in ZEV adoption, ending the purchase subsidy in the first quarter of 2025 immediately reduced the new ZEV adoption rate by 10.2 percentage points, representing more than half (55%) of the adoption rate that would have been observed in the absence of the subsidy exit. Furthermore, the new ZEV adoption rate grew only linearly over time in the post-subsidy period, losing the quadratic growth enjoyed in the pre-pause period. Our analysis also reveals substantial heterogeneity in the impacts of ending the purchase subsidy across ZEV types (battery EVs vs. plugged-in EVs) and across regions with different population sizes and EV market maturity. These findings help inform the boundaries of subsidy effectiveness, the design of subsidy exit schemes, and the forecasts of policy impacts, thus supporting more efficient allocation of public resources. © 2026

Authors: Fan Z.; Chen Q.; Duan Y.
Title: Consumer or platform in control? Responsible AI governance and its unintended consequences in smart retail supply chains
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Smart retail platforms rely on AI recommender systems to improve search efficiency and matching quality, yet the same data and interface infrastructure can also be used for manipulative designs that interfere with consumers’ authorization and purchase decisions. Responsible AI governance therefore often advocates shifting algorithmic and data control from platforms to consumers. However, the consequences of such consumer-control regulation in vertically organized supply chains remain unclear. This paper develops a two-tier supply chain game consisting of an upstream brand manufacturer and a downstream smart retail platform. We decompose AI recommender systems into an algorithmic value-added effect and an algorithmic value-extraction effect, and compare equilibrium pricing, data authorization, manipulation intensity, deployment decisions, and welfare outcomes under platform-led and consumer-led governance. We find that, in the single-platform benchmark, the consumer-led regime blocks algorithmic extraction, expands authorization and demand, and improves consumer surplus, platform profit, and social welfare. In a manufacturer-led vertical supply chain, however, this welfare advantage may be reversed. The reason is that the upstream manufacturer captures part of the demand-expansion rent generated by AI through a higher wholesale price, while the consumer-led regime removes the financial buffer that the platform obtains from extraction revenue. When the platform's residual profit is insufficient to cover deployment incentives, the platform exits AI deployment earlier. We define this transmission mechanism as the deployment channel. Under specific market conditions, this channel causes consumer surplus, platform profit, and manufacturer profit to decline simultaneously, generating a simultaneous deterioration region. Extensions with wholesale-price bargaining and incomplete consumer control show that the mechanism is robust. The paper suggests that responsible AI governance should not be understood as an unconditional expansion of consumer control, but should be designed jointly with vertical supply chain structure, upstream extraction power, and technology deployment incentives. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: How body-shape diversity in virtual-fitting displays drives customization intention
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Online clothing customization platforms often fail to visually demonstrate how garments adapt to different body shapes, leaving consumers uncertain about whether a garment can be tailored to their own body. This limitation represents an important barrier to consumers' clothing customization intention. To address this issue, this research examines whether displaying customized garments on virtual models with diverse versus uniform body shapes increases consumers' intention to customize clothing. Across five experiments, we show that virtual model body-shape diversity significantly increases clothing customization intention and that this effect is mediated by perceived customization affordance. The indirect effect through perceived customization affordance is stronger for fitted rather than loose garments and for non-luxury rather than luxury brands. In addition, perceived customization affordance translates more strongly into customization intention when consumers perceive their body shapes as stable rather than changing. This research extends affordance theory to digital clothing customization by showing how body-shape diversity in virtual-fitting displays activates consumers’ perceptions of customization possibilities. It also offers retailers a scalable visual strategy for improving customization interfaces by displaying garments on virtual models with diverse body shapes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Beyond integration to validation: the differential impact of physicians’ knowledge collaboration behaviors on online medical team performance
Abstract: Online knowledge collaboration among physicians in team services has become the key to improving the quality of online healthcare services. However, existing research lacks a discussion of the classification of different types of knowledge collaboration behavior and their impact on team performance. To fill this gap, this study collected public data from China's leading online medical communities from December 2022 to October 2023, forming a panel dataset covering 510 teams, 2559 physicians, and 130,000 unstructured physician–patient interaction records. Based on the shared mental model, we first distinguished two modes of online knowledge collaboration: knowledge integration and knowledge validation. Second, our two-way fixed effects model revealed that both collaboration modes contribute to team economic returns, while knowledge validation is particularly important for enhancing online patient experience, especially when facing complex medical tasks. Furthermore, communication directionality strengthens the positive relationship between knowledge collaboration and team performance. This study provides valuable guidance for online medical teams to optimize their knowledge collaboration strategies based on specific performance objectives. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Towards a Conceptual Model for Evaluating Prospective Scenarios - A Case Study in Future Air Transport
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: In a context of growing uncertainty, prospective scenarios have become widely used across economic and geopolitical sectors as long-term decision-support frameworks. Over the years, a broad variety of methods and scenario types have emerged, ranging from quantitative models to expert-based narrative approaches, serving purposes as diverse as risk preparedness and policy justification, yet no unified framework exists to assess scenario quality systematically. Then a fundamental question remains: how can the quality of prospective scenarios be systematically assessed? This thesis proposes to address this gap by developing a unified conceptual model for prospective scenarios, designed to integrate all the elements required by existing evaluation metrics and to provide a foundation for building new ones. Through a systematic review following the PRISMA2020 protocol, existing criteria and associated metrics were first catalogued. A conceptual model will then be built, based on the scenario elements required by criteria metrics, and then validated against a corpus of existing and purpose-built scenarios. The formalism will be benchmarked against established approaches such as dynamic networks, combinatory optimization and morphological analysis. The proposed framework will be applied to the domain of future air transport, a field rich in projections from industrial, commercial, and institutional stakeholders, to demonstrate its relevance and versatility. Title: From Automation to Coevolution: A Systematic Review of Human-AI Interaction Hierarchies and Professional Implications in the Construction Industry
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping the construction industry, creating increasing reliance on human-AI interaction across project processes. Although previous research has made significant progress in applying AI across construction workflows, existing literature reviews lack a systematic analysis of human-AI interaction patterns, coupling depths, and the implications for professional competence. To close this gap, this study aims to (1) systematize the hierarchical levels of human-AI interaction in construction applications; and (2) identify the professional competence requirements corresponding to different interaction levels. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-guided systematic review was conducted, covering 57 peer-reviewed studies from 2016 to 2025, complemented by bibliometric mapping and thematic synthesis to identify patterns of interaction and competence demand in construction contexts. The review proposes a four-layer hierarchical framework of human-AI interaction: AI automation (Layer 1), AI assistance (Layer 2), AI-human coordination (Layer 3), and adaptive coevolution (Layer 4). Layers 1-3 emerged from empirical analysis of construction practice, and Layer 4 represents an emergent stage informed by nascent construction technologies and cross-domain coevolution frameworks. Each layer reflects distinct coupling intensity, interaction dynamics, and competence requirements. Building on these insights, this study proposes a human-AI interaction literacy matrix that systematically maps distinct levels of interaction depth to evolving professional competence requirements across technical-operational, analytical-evaluative, collaborative-interactional, and reflective-adaptive dimensions. These findings provide actionable guidance for construction organizations to design role-differentiated training programs aligned with interaction depth, assess workforce readiness for AI integration at specific project phases, and develop career pathways as human-AI interaction evolves from automation-dominant to collaboration-intensive configurations. The framework redefines AI adoption as a competence-driven progression rather than a purely technological implementation. © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Identification of Social Key Performance Indicators-A Case Study
Abstract: Social Key Performance Indicators (SKPIs) and the competitiveness they can bring is studied and applied to a case in the energy sector (district heating). A case study has limited generalizability, but we argue that the case serves as a critical case, informing other companies on actions to take for increasing their competitive advantage by social value inclusion. Results confirm that social sustainability generation is complex and needs to be planned for and applied across the process from pre-feasibility to ongoing activities. The study also confirms that social values are relevant both to companies and wider community. New results provide insights on the complexity of social value creation. Some of the complexity is related to the social values being either monetary, non-monetary or both. Furthermore, the values can develop and shift in importance over time and their importance varies to different stakeholders. An important conclusion is that the short-term ambition of setting a system up to deliver energy in an intended way (secure, affordable and sustainable energy; the energy trilemma) needs to be revisited by adding the dimension of what social values to generate, to whom and at what point in time (what we refer to as a “social value trilemma”). © DSRPT 2026.

Title: Household consumption and savings over the life cycle: The roles of demographics and durables
Abstract: The canonical prediction of life-cycle models, that individuals smooth consumption over their lifetime, has mostly been tested in developed countries and found little empirical support. We provide a novel developing-country perspective by analyzing patterns of life-cycle consumption, income, and savings rates in India. In contrast to the U.S., Indian households exhibit little growth in nondurable consumption expenditures after adjusting for family size. Surprisingly, this flat adjusted profile coexists with substantial income growth and a sharp rise in the savings/surplus rate over the life cycle. We show that lumpy non-housing durable accumulation is an important use of this life-cycle surplus, helping reconcile high savings rates with flat measured adult-equivalent nondurable consumption. Title: Integrating parking delay uncertainty in urban delivery tour planning
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: Securing curb space near a delivery location is a major source of uncertainty for urban commercial vehicle drivers. While tour planning tools increasingly account for time-dependent traffic conditions, they typically ignore parking delays, even though evidence shows they vary systematically across locations and times of day. This paper empirically examines how expected parking delays affect urban delivery tour planning. Using GPS data from real-world delivery operations, we estimate time- and location-specific parking delays and incorporate them into a Time-Dependent Traveling Salesman Problem with Time Windows. We compare conventional parking-blind planning, which considers only travel times, with parking-aware planning, which additionally accounts for expected parking delays. The results show that parking-blind planning substantially underestimates tour duration and overestimates schedule feasibility. When realistic parking conditions are considered, parking delays accounted for about 33% of total delivery tour duration and generate substantial increases in lateness and time-window violations. Parking-aware planning reduces tour duration by 3.4% on average (17.4 min), with some instances obtaining total tour duration reductions of more than 10%, by trading slightly longer driving times for lower parking delays, while reducing time spent in parking delays by 11% on average. More importantly, it substantially improves service reliability, reducing average lateness and greatly decreasing the frequency of time-window violations. These improvements are achieved primarily through small adjustments in stop sequencing and service timing that shift deliveries toward periods with lower expected parking delays. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Cyber Resilience in the Age of Digital Sovereignty: A Comparative Analysis of Assessment Frameworks for Sovereign Cloud Environments
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: This paper investigates the convergence of cyber resilience and digital sovereignty in cloud-dependent environments, with particular emphasis on the European regulatory landscape. As reliance on public and hybrid cloud services intensifies, concerns over data protection, jurisdictional exposure and strategic dependency transform cyber resilience from a predominantly technical concern into a broader governance and policy challenge. The paper traces the co-evolution of digital sovereignty and cyber resilience in European policy and scholarship and examines how it reshapes contemporary interpretations of cyber resilience. Using a qualitative, document-based comparative method, the study derives eight digital-sovereignty dimensions from EU legislation and peer-reviewed taxonomies and evaluates five widely adopted frameworks - NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 22301, CERT-RMM, COBIT 2019 and the MITRE Cyber Resiliency Engineering Framework/NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 - against them through transparent deductive coding. While the frameworks cover continuity, governance, assurance and third-party risk well, they systematically under-represent sovereignty-specific dimensions including jurisdictional control, portability and exit readiness, rights-aligned data governance and strategic autonomy. The paper concludes that existing frameworks require sovereignty-aware adaptation rather than wholesale replacement, and identifies an integrated assessment model as the principal direction for future work. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Policy strategies for improving multimodal freight transport: A two-stage framework for Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) project

Abstract: The multimodal transportation network is critical to a country's economic development, acting as a lifeline for containerized cargo flows from domestic to international destinations and vice versa. Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) has been designated to promote the country's investment in advancing innovation and technology for future generations. Title: Blockchain-driven subsidy mechanisms in green food supply chain: a comparative study of lump-sum and per-unit incentives
Abstract: This paper investigates how blockchain-enabled empowerment alters consumer trust mechanisms regarding food greenness, consequently influencing supply chain decisions and modifying the effectiveness of government green subsidy policies. Specifically, we examine the moderating role of blockchain technology on the performance of two alternative government subsidy schemes (per-unit and lump-sum) within a green food supply chain. The results indicate that government subsidies significantly stimulate green innovation among the green food producer and generate downstream benefits. The size of the subsidy coefficient has a dual effect: It simultaneously shapes stakeholders’ preferences between subsidy schemes and acts as a key determinant of blockchain adoption decisions. Under the per-unit subsidy, the extra revenue that a producer can obtain by misreporting green food output unintentionally becomes an implicit source of funding for quality investment, whereas the adoption of blockchain raises the likelihood that the lump-sum subsidy will outperform the per-unit subsidy. Furthermore, for the per-unit subsidy, the e-commerce platform as a retailer is more cost-sensitive toward blockchain application compared to the producer. Lower blockchain implementation cost can improve food greenness and freshness while achieving a Pareto improvement in overall supply chain environmental performance and social welfare. However, when the green Research and Development (R&D) costs are excessively high, blockchain adoption can actually reduce both the environmental sustainability and market demand. These findings offer policymakers valuable insights into how to leverage the synergy between technological empowerment and institutional innovation. © 2026 International Federation of Operational Research Societies.

Title: Governing Sustainable Digital Transformation: An Adaptive Architecture for Embedding Sustainability in Transformation Decisions
Abstract: Digital transformation creates opportunities for sustainable value creation but also generates complex governance challenges. This paper conceptualises Sustainability-Embedded Digital Transformation (SEDT) as a governance perspective and develops an Adaptive Transformation Governance Architecture (ATGA) that provides a mechanism for its implementation. Grounded in transformation governance, adaptive governance, and systems thinking, ATGA integrates governance actors, decision rights, sustainability-oriented principles, adaptive processes, organisational learning, and feedback mechanisms. The architecture explains how sustainability is embedded in transformation decisions and how governance arrangements are reconfigured through feedback, learning, and institutional change. In doing so, the paper provides a recursive and multi-level governance mechanism for sustainable digital transformation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Authors: Tanveer A.
Title: Does striking a balance between dynamic and enduring grit lead to new venture performance?
Source title: Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
Abstract: Purpose – New ventures in emerging economies like Pakistan encounter high failure rates due to volatility and limited resources. Grit – the perseverance in overcoming challenges while striving toward long-term goals – has been associated with enhanced venture performance. However, the absence of a validated firm-level grit measure limits our understanding of its antecedents and associated with on financial and non-financial outcomes. Consequently, this research aims to develop a firm-level grit scale and investigate its relationship with the performance of new ventures. Design/methodology/approach – This collaborative study aims to bridge the measurement gap in organizational grit by developing and validating a novel firm-level grit scale. It employed a rigorous five-step process to construct an 11-item instrument that captures grit’s dynamic and enduring dimensions. The final step utilized Hayes’ PROCESS mediation analysis in SPSS to test the study’s hypotheses. Findings – This study of 285 new ventures in Pakistan indicates that dynamic and enduring grit mediates the relationship among strategic orientation, bricolage and new venture performance. This equilibrium allows ventures to tackle immediate challenges while also pursuing long-term objectives. The findings show the significance of grit in aligning short-term adaptability with a long-term strategy, highlighting the necessity of strategic flexibility to mitigate the risks associated with excessive grit. Practical implications – The findings suggest that new ventures, entrepreneurs and business incubators use grit measurement tools to improve business outcomes and innovation, although excessive grit may cause missed opportunities. Originality/value – This study deepens the understanding of firm-level grit by harmonizing endurance with adaptability. It enriches the fields of entrepreneurship by conceptualizing grit as a resource-dependent, context-sensitive construct while offering actionable guidance for optimizing gritty behaviors to improve venture sustainability and performance. © 2026 Asif Tanveer.

Authors: Ma D.; Hu Z.; Li X.
Title: Incentivizing environmental public goods: Evidence from urban greening in China
Source title: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
Abstract: China’s recent surge in urban greening presents a puzzling deviation from global patterns. We document three empirical patterns. First, urban greening was stable from 2001 to 2013 but expanded rapidly afterward, coinciding with China’s air pollution control efforts. Second, more polluted cities experienced faster growth in urban greening. Third, greening expansion was disproportionately concentrated near air quality monitoring stations. These patterns suggest that urban greening expansion in China after 2013 was largely driven by political pressure induced by air pollution control. The economic benefits of the urban greening expansion exceed the associated costs. Our results suggest that top-down air pollution control reshaped local government incentives, thereby improving the provision of environmental public goods and social welfare. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Estimation of Stressed State of Nuclear Power Plant Structural Elements Under Emergency Loads
Source title: Studies in Systems, Decision and Control
Abstract: The purpose of this study is to develop methods of computational assessment of strength and safe operation of structural elements of nuclear power plants under emergency loads. The problems of safe operation of nuclear power plants are of great global importance. Nuclear power plants are objects of extremely high responsibility. Therefore, their design takes into account special impacts that are not usually considered for other civil and industrial facilities: earthquakes with very rare recurrence, industrial explosions, man-made accidents, airplane crashes, hurricanes, tornadoes. Such impacts are usually characterized by high intensity, which, however, is compensated by low probability of their realization. Due to the complexity and impossibility of experimental studies in real conditions (radiation hazard combined with high temperatures, low availability, high cost), the issues of modeling of structural elements of nuclear power plants in emergency situations become especially relevant. This work proposes an approach to modeling the response of nuclear power plant structures to the impact of aircraft and solid fragments. The results of computational studies make it possible to evaluate the strength of structures and select the most promising variants of their design. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Seeing is believing? How AI information disclosure and picture content shape tourist acceptance and visit willingness
Abstract: To delineate the cognitive mechanisms underlying tourist responses to AI-generated marketing pictures, this study adopts the Heuristic-Systematic Model (HSM) as its overarching theoretical framework. The theoretical model was validated in three core scenarios of tourism (destinations, restaurants, and hotels) through a three-stage contextual experiment, within the mixed methodology of ANOVA, Bootstrapping and SEM. Findings indicate that when the disclosure of AI prompts is detailed, scene-oriented pictures enhance tourists perceived intelligence, leading to increased acceptance and visit willingness. Conversely, with brief information disclosure, service-oriented pictures prove more effective by enhancing perceived authenticity. Furthermore, implicit biases were found to exert a significant moderating effect, particularly in the conversion pathway where perceived authenticity directly impacts visit willingness, bypassing picture acceptance. This study guided the application of AI-generated content within the realms of tourism and hospitality, emphasizing the importance of balancing disclosure strategies with tourist’ information processing in the era of intelligent marketing. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Yue Y.; Lin Y.; Wu M.; Zhang Y.; He Q.
Title: Credit risk early warning for SMEs from the perspective of supply chain networks
Abstract: This study examines how to improve credit risk identification for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) by incorporating network-based risk information from supply chain structures. Using Chinese A-share listed SMEs from 2000 to 2023, we develop a comprehensive prediction framework that integrates firm-level risk factors with a network-based risk exposure measure. First, at the firm level, a baseline credit risk indicator system for SMEs is constructed by integrating multisource heterogeneous data with principal component analysis (PCA). Second, drawing on upstream and downstream transaction relationships and complex network analysis, this study proposes a “network risk exposure” (ExRisk[jls-end-space/]) indicator to capture firms' structural positions and counterpart risk conditions. Finally, multilevel comparative analyses via various machine learning models demonstrate that the firm-level baseline indicators provide a robust foundation for credit risk prediction. More importantly, incorporating ExRisk significantly improves predictive performance across models, indicating that network-embedded risk information provides nonsubstitutable incremental information for credit risk identification. These findings remain robust under alternative credit risk classification criteria, highlighting the strong practical applicability of the proposed early warning framework. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Adaptation of UK airports to a changing climate: an evaluation of the Adaptation reporting Power Process (2011 – 2024)
Abstract: The Climate Adaptation Reporting Power (ARP) established adaptation reporting requirements for critical national infrastructure in the United Kingdom to inform the 5-yearly UK Climate Change Risk Assessment (CCRA). This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis of the reports submitted by ten airports across the four ARP rounds to date (ARP1- ARP4, 2011-2024). Classifying over 900 reported risks, it provides the first complete synthesis of the climate risks and adaptation actions reported by the airports and the first complete mapping of airport climate risks since the second UK CCRA in 2017. Findings demonstrate that the initial mandatory round catalysed engagement: all airports embedded climate risks into corporate risk registers, identified adaptation actions, and nine established monitoring processes. Subsequent voluntary rounds show sustained participation and improved reporting quality, although inconsistencies in timeframes, climate scenarios, and risk classifications hinder comparability. Four recommendations for the ARP fifth round are identified: (1) provide clear templates and guidance identifying what good-quality reports should contain; (2) adopt sector-specific risk classifications to support network-level comparability; (3) broaden reporting to a wider set of UK airports, particularly smaller regional and local airports; (4) consider a mandatory approach to ensure thorough identification of climate risks, adaptation actions and gaps, and interdependencies. The study demonstrates the clear value of regulatory mandates in driving climate adaptation at airports and highlights lessons for other countries considering similar initiatives: the need for strong support and guidance, and early standardisation of inputs such as timeframes, climate scenarios, and risk categories. Adopting comparable measures internationally would strengthen resilience across the global aviation network. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Zhang X.; Sun X.; Fu Y.
Title: Toward greener urban freight: The effect of China's green freight distribution pilot program on PM2.5 concentrations
Source title: Research in Transportation Business and Management
Abstract: The green transformation of urban freight distribution systems is essential to advancing the low-carbon transition of the transportation sector and improving urban air quality. Treating China's Green Freight Distribution Pilot Program (GFDP) as a quasi-natural experiment, this study uses city-level panel data and a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) framework to estimate its effect on urban PM2.5 concentrations. We further examine the underlying mechanisms, effect heterogeneity, and spatial spillovers. The results show that the GFDP significantly reduces PM2.5 concentrations in pilot cities, with the main finding remaining robust across a battery of robustness checks. Mechanism tests identify green transportation technology innovation and government attention to smart transportation as two important channels underlying the GFDP's pollution-reduction effect. These effects are stronger in cities with higher pre-policy levels of green transportation technology innovation and government attention to smart transportation. Heterogeneity analysis reveals stronger pollution-reduction effects in coastal cities, cities with greater attention to green and environmental issues, and non-national logistics hub cities. Spatial analysis further reveals that the environmental effects of the GFDP extend beyond pilot-city boundaries. Spatial exposure coefficients are significantly negative across all distance bands within 300 km, with a relatively large negative point estimate for the 100–150 km band; beyond 300 km, the estimated effects are no longer statistically significant. The estimated negative effect on PM2.5 concentrations in pilot cities also remains stable when potentially exposed non-pilot cities are progressively excluded from the control group. By documenting both within-city pollution reduction and cross-city spatial spillovers, this study provides new evidence on the environmental consequences of green freight policies and informs efforts to advance low-carbon freight transportation and coordinated regional air pollution control. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Passing the buck: How numerical information influences consumer food waste
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Food waste poses a severe threat to global food security and environmental sustainability. This problem is largely driven by irresponsible consumer behavior, which often results from a lack of awareness about the extent of food waste. Therefore, anti-food waste campaigns commonly present numerical information about the scale of food waste. However, the effectiveness of such information remains debated in the literature. This study examines whether two common numeric framing (individual vs. aggregate) differ in their effectiveness in reducing consumer food waste. The results of one field experiment (N = 267) and four laboratory experiments (Ntotal = 1024) show that individual numeric framing is more effective than aggregate numeric framing in reducing consumer food waste, with diffusion of responsibility mediating this effect. In addition, this effect is moderated by self-construal. These findings offer a theoretical explanation for the inconsistent results regarding the effectiveness of numerical information, and can help marketers use numerical information more effectively to enhance the persuasive power of anti-food waste communication. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wang D.; Zhang B.; Chen J.
Title: AI-driven “new migrants”: skill-spatial mismatch and out-migration intention
Abstract: While AI profoundly reshapes the labor market, its spatial impact remains under-researched. Addressing this, this paper uses data from the China Migrant Population Dynamic Monitoring Survey and the China Patent Database across 250 prefecture-level cities during 2014–2018 to examine AI's effect on labor out-migration intention. Findings reveal AI significantly increases out-migration intention, especially among women and in non-digital hubs or central/western regions. Mechanistically, the results are consistent with a displacement channel involving routine jobs and a restructuring channel involving industrial shifts. These channels can be understood through a “skill-spatial mismatch” resulting from the changing spatial distribution of tasks. Furthermore, regional aging and fiscal support amplify the positive relationship between AI and out-migration intention. The study concludes by emphasizing the need for a spatially inclusive employment policy framework as AI reshapes employment geography. The findings concern workers' stated propensity to leave, which may precede future mobility, rather than observed migration flows. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: The role of copper global price on long-term volatility: An asymmetric GARCH-MIDAS approach for NYSE assets
Source title: North American Journal of Economics and Finance
Abstract: Global commodity markets play an important role in shaping macroeconomic conditions and financial market dynamics, particularly in sectors that are closely linked to economic activity such as banking. Among commodities, copper is considered as a key indicator of global industrial activity and economic conditions, suggesting that its price dynamics may contain relevant information for financial market risk. This paper examines the relationship between global copper prices and the long-term volatility of U.S. banking returns using the GJR-GARCH-MIDAS framework. The model splits volatility into short- and long-term components while accounting for the asymmetric effects of positive and negative shocks. The empirical analysis is based on daily returns for four major U.S. banks listed on the NYSE (Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Wells Fargo) and monthly global copper prices over the period 2002–2026. The results show a negative relationship between copper prices and the long-term component of banking volatility, which is robust across specifications for Bank of America and Citigroup, and weaker and specification-dependent for JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo. Positive changes in copper prices, typically associated with stronger industrial demand and more favorable macroeconomic conditions, are associated with lower long-term volatility of bank stock returns. These findings highlight the role of copper as a macro-financial indicator and demonstrate the usefulness of mixed-frequency models in capturing the interaction between macroeconomic conditions, and financial market volatility. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Insider share pledging, information opacity, and stock price crash risk in emerging markets
Abstract: This study investigates the impact of insider share pledging on stock price crash risk. Using a large panel of listed firms, we employ heteroskedasticity-based instruments within the generalized method of moments framework to address endogeneity concerns and apply a Heckman two-stage selection model to mitigate sample selection bias. The empirical evidence indicates that insider share pledging significantly increases stock price crash risk, primarily through managers' bad-news hoarding behavior. Further analysis reveals that stock repurchase activity attenuates this effect, while the mediating role of bad-news hoarding fully explains the relationship between insider share pledging and stock price crash risk. In addition, we document a positive association between insider share pledging and stock price synchronicity, suggesting that pledging activities are associated with greater co-movement in stock returns. Collectively, these findings enrich the literature on crash risk and stock price synchronicity by identifying insider share pledging as a novel determinant. The results also have policy implications, highlighting the importance of regulating insider share pledging practices and strengthening disclosure requirements to mitigate potential destabilizing effects on capital markets. © 2026 Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: More innovative, more popular? The effect of amenity innovation on listings’ prospective booking performance in P2P accommodation
Abstract: In the peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation market, amenity innovation has emerged as an important strategy used for gaining competitive advantage, but how does amenity innovation affect listings’ prospective booking performance? Is it a case of the more innovative the popular? Based on resource orchestration theory, this study constructs econometric models to examine the effect of amenity innovation on listings’ prospective booking performance and investigates the moderating roles of host capabilities in leveraging amenity innovation. Using 44,057 listings from Airbnb as the research object, text mining methods are used to comprehensively identify amenity innovation that combines distinctiveness, scarcity, and novelty. Host capabilities are classified into two types: amenity information description and amenity reputation accumulation, which represent expressive capability and relational capability, respectively. The findings show that, from the resource-based view, amenity innovation has an inverted U-shaped effect on listings’ prospective booking performance. From the capability-based view, amenity information description enhances the inverted U-shaped effect of amenity innovation. Conversely, amenity reputation accumulation weakens the inverted U-shaped effect of amenity innovation. In addition, high-priced listings and listings operated by regular hosts exhibit a greater magnitude of marginal fluctuation in amenity innovation. This study enriches the understanding of amenity innovation in P2P accommodation and provides theoretical contributions and practical implications for hosts and platform managers to leverage amenity innovation for sustainable competitive advantage. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: The role of digitalized supervision in mergers and acquisitions: Evidence from the SOEs online supervision system in China
Abstract: This study investigates whether digital supervision technologies enhance the monitoring effectiveness of controlling shareholders in complex investment decisions. We exploit the staggered rollout of the SOEs Online Supervision System (SOSS) by China's State-Owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC), the controlling shareholder of state-owned enterprises (SOEs), across its central and 31 provincial offices from 2018 to 2021. Following SOSS implementation, SOE transactions exhibit shorter deal duration, fewer regulatory inquiries, lower goodwill impairment, greater withdrawal of low-quality deals, and improved target quality. These improvements in deal review efficiency and screening effectiveness translate into stronger announcement returns and long-run performance. The performance effects are more pronounced for acquirers with stronger technological infrastructure, in transactions characterized by lower transparency and weaker governance, and when SASAC offices face tighter capacity constraints. Overall, digital technologies relax information-processing constraints and strengthen shareholder monitoring in complex investment settings. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Board gender diversity heterogeneity and sustainability: a systematic literature review on multi-dimensional board diversity
Abstract: Purpose – This systematic review examines how within-gender heterogeneity in board gender diversity, variation in female directors' observable and underlying attributes, relates to corporate sustainability outcomes, captured as ESG performance and ESG reporting. Design/methodology/approach – Guided by stakeholder–agency theory and an adapted Milliken and Martins' (1996) framework, we systematically searched EBSCO Business Source Complete and Web of Science. We included 70 English-language, peer-reviewed archival studies that operationalise board gender diversity through multiple female-directors attributes and report associations with ESG performance and ESG reporting. We synthesise findings using vote counting and report simple summary statistics for the most frequently studied attributes. Findings – Evidence is most consistent for female non-executive directors, who are robustly associated with stronger ESG performance across governance systems and regulatory settings. Results for female executive directors are more context-dependent and frequently mixed. For other heterogeneity dimensions, the evidence base remains comparatively thin and inconclusive, particularly for ESG reporting, reflecting both limited study volume and measurement heterogeneity. Practical implications – Boards and regulators should treat gender diversity as a multi-attributed governance resource rather than a headcount metric. Emphasis on the composition and authority of female directors appears most consequential for sustainability performance, while disclosure-related effects require more consistent measurement and stronger identification. Originality/value – This review's contribution lies in systematically operationalising and coding within-gender heterogeneity by separating observable from underlying attributes and mapping them distinctly to ESG performance versus ESG reporting, thereby clarifying where evidence is comparatively consistent and where key gaps remain. © 2026 Jan Marvin Apel and Patrick Velte

Title: Navigating service recovery: a model for mobile ISPs in South Africa
Source title: International Journal of Quality and Service Sciences
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to address the lack of industry-specific service recovery frameworks for internet service providers (ISPs) in South Africa by identifying essential service recovery attributes and evaluating the impact thereof on customer satisfaction and customer behavior. Title: Reverse logistics contract design under market uncertainty: An analysis of value-preserving repurchase policy for electric vehicles
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: This study proposes a reverse logistics framework by introducing a value-preserving repurchase (VPR) policy for electric vehicle (EV) makers. Under VPR, users pay a service fee and retail price and can return EVs after a specified period. To motivate returns, EV makers guarantee refunds exceeding typical secondhand prices. EV makers can offer repurchase, exchange (crediting the refund toward a new EV), or mixed options. However, market uncertainty can inflate secondhand prices beyond contract refunds, driving users to sell directly in secondary markets instead of returning. This undermines EV makers’ value recovery and new-vehicle demand. While the existing literature focuses on post-purchase returns from valuation discrepancies, we integrate volatile secondhand market prices into the VPR design. Methodologically, we develop an analytical framework for the EV reverse logistics channel, characterize the participants’ utilities through three VPR modes, and derive how secondhand prices reshape optimal VPR terms under different market structures. Furthermore, the EV makers’ mode preferences across monopoly and competitive settings are identified, thereby providing a rigorous analytical foundation for when and why different VPR options are chosen. From a managerial perspective, the results offer actionable guidance for EV makers designing VPR contracts under uncertain resale values: in a monopoly, the exchange mode emerges as dominant, and the mixed mode exhibits subtle efficiency; whereas the mixed mode prevails under competition, even it does not dominate in a monopolistic market. Overall, the findings extend beyond EVs by offering a transferable framework for value-preserving trade-in policy design in other industries facing uncertain secondhand prices. Copyright © 2026. Title: Global airport connectivity and resilience: a data-driven approach and inverse-U relationship, 1996–2024
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: This study analyzes the long-run evolution of global airport connectivity from 1996 to 2024 and examines how resilience to major shocks varies across the connectivity distribution. Using an extended Global Airport Connectivity Index (GACI) panel covering 101,049 airport–year observations and 5428 airports, it documents steady expansion punctuated by crises, a redistribution of connectivity across continents, and an increasingly multipolar hub hierarchy. The paper then develops a reproducible, multi-crisis resilience index with three components: depth (magnitude of loss), speed (pace of recovery), and adaptability (post-shock upgrading in the global hierarchy). The index aggregates realized airport performance across multiple major shocks, applies empirical-Bayes regularization to improve comparability across airports with uneven shock histories, and filters micro-fluctuations below 1% to reduce noise. Relating resilience to connectivity uncovers a consistent inverse-U relationship: resilience increases with connectivity up to a mid-scale range and declines among the most globally connected hubs. This pattern is consistent with greater exposure to synchronized shocks and scale-related operational frictions, although the analysis identifies the relationship rather than its underlying mechanisms. Robustness checks include alternative component weightings, pre-COVID estimates, crisis-specific recovery horizons, alternative adaptability definitions, region-specific COVID timing, an alternative fixed-scale connectivity construction, and non-overlapping crisis windows. These checks confirm the stability of the pattern. By embedding airport-level recovery behaviour in a three-decade network context, the GACI–resilience framework provides a systematic basis for comparing hub types and benchmarking realized resilience, and for informing route-development, infrastructure-planning, and policy strategies during pandemics, geopolitical disruptions, and other major shocks. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Traffic forecasting considering burst disturbances based on spatial-temporal graph neural impulsive differential equations
Source title: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review
Abstract: Traffic forecasting, as a cornerstone task in intelligent transportation systems, plays a vital role in alleviating urban congestion, optimizing traffic management, and improving travel efficiency. However, in real-world traffic systems, smooth and continuous variations driven by routine commuting patterns often coexist with abrupt disturbances caused by accidents, signal transitions, and unexpected events. Although capturing such mixed dynamics is of significant practical importance, it has not been fully explored in existing studies. To address this challenge, we propose a spatial-temporal graph learning framework (ST-GINDE) incorporating an impulse-like modulation neural ordinary differential equation module. The model formulates traffic dynamics as a continuous-time evolution process on spatial-temporal graphs, enabling unified modeling of temporal evolution, spatial dependencies, and adaptive responses to significant traffic state variations. To capture abrupt disturbances, we introduce an impulse-like modulation mechanism that adaptively adjusts the continuous dynamics when significant traffic variations occur, without introducing discontinuous state jumps or explicit hybrid system assumptions. Furthermore, ST-GINDE integrates multi-scale temporal feature extraction and hybrid dynamic graph learning to jointly model short-term fluctuations, long-term periodic patterns, and time-varying spatial dependencies across traffic networks. Title: Social capital, knowledge sharing, and performance in family firms: the central role of absorptive capacity

Title: Dealing with Failure Through Individualized Self-Intervention: A Microintervention for Self-Management Based on Personality Systems Interactions Theory
Source title: FGF Studies in Small Business and Entrepreneurship
Abstract: Failures, setbacks, and negative feedback are unavoidable. Although such experiences often trigger threat reactions, they also hold significant learning potential. Research emphasizes that learning from failure requires a constructive attitude that views difficulties not as personal deficiencies but as opportunities for growth. This perspective is central to the entrepreneurial mindset, which involves recognizing opportunities, acting under uncertainty, and remaining adaptable and resilient even in the face of challenges. Entrepreneurial Life Design (ELD) builds on this idea by integrating innovation with self-development, encouraging individuals to reflect on challenges and identify the resources that support resilience. However, according to the theory of Personality Systems Interaction (PSI), failures induce a state of threat that inhibits access to the self, i.e., the system that encompasses one’s resources for coping effectively with failure. When self-access is blocked, individuals may struggle to identify or use their resources, despite ELD’s emphasis on precisely this process. In such situations, the key to managing challenging experiences lies in strengthening an individual’s self-management competencies, i.e., the competencies that enable effective dealing with failures and the restoration of access to personal resources. Drawing on ELD and PSI theory, we propose an individualized approach and introduce a practical tool designed to strengthen self-management competencies. Title: Understanding how supervisor feedback delivery style influences employee reactions: a dynamic affective perspective

Title: Aspiration, appearance, argumentation or attack? Reconstructing stakeholder engagement images of German industrial companies on social media
Abstract: Purpose – Social media platforms, such as Twitter, offer companies the opportunity to interact with their stakeholders, thereby explaining and legitimising their business activities and further developing their CSR practices. In reality, however, Twitter is often not used dialogically. While research on corporate stakeholder engagement online has provided several explanations for the absence of dialogue, the question arises as to what role commercial social media can play in engaging stakeholders in the context of CSR and how this role can be conceptualised. By adopting the perspective that “communication constitutes organisation”, this study seeks to answer this question and broaden the understanding of corporate stakeholder engagement on social media and legitimisation beyond the conceptual boundaries of “real” stakeholder dialogue. Design/methodology/approach – We apply qualitative analysis to tweets from companies listed on the German stock index (DAX) and analyse conversations containing key hashtags used by climate activists. The underlying assumption is that companies using hashtags that are “charged” with certain meanings on Twitter respond to social expectations by creating stakeholder engagement images. We develop an analytical framework that is based on, firstly, the openness of companies to interact with their stakeholders, as demonstrated by the use of elements that favour dialogue, and secondly, the characterisation of post contents as distancing from the societal expectations or confirming the societal expectations. Findings – We reconstruct four basic types of stakeholder engagement images: the “Aspiration”, “Appearance”, “Argumentation” and “Attack” images. The “Aspiration” image is mainly about what could be, which can have a performative and transformative effect even if aspirational talk is not fully translated into action. The “Appearance” image seems to be geared towards fixation and leaves little room for interaction, negotiation and change. The “Argumentation” image has the potential to challenge, influence and affect the boundaries of an organisation. The tweets under the “Attack” image contain one-sided conflicts that usually remain without interaction. Research limitations/implications – Due to the qualitative nature of the present study and its limitation to a specific sample, the developed framework cannot be generalised to other contexts without further research. Another limitation is the rapidly changing context of social media research. In our case, this is exacerbated by the change of ownership of Twitter and its transformation into X. This further limits the collection of data for scientific purposes, making it unlikely that a similar, information-rich sample of tweets could be created at a later point in time. Practical implications – The novel framework could be used by companies to assess their communication from a novel perspective. It might be interesting to review whether specific CSR topics influence the occurrence and frequency of certain images, if some images in general occur more often than others, and how images are distributed and developed over a longer period or related to certain occasions. Social implications – In a rapidly changing environment, effective stakeholder communication is crucial, yet companies face greater challenges and risks. This study aims to identify ways to analyse and facilitate productive stakeholder communication in a digital society. Originality/value – In this study, we empirically address the topics of stakeholder engagement and legitimisation in a digital society by offering an approach that recognises communication's constitutive role in engagement. Applying the novel framework we have developed and examining the performativity and impact of the reconstructed images – for instance, on the roles of dissent, struggle and aspiration – can provide a rich basis for further theoretical and practical insights into stakeholder engagement and legitimisation on social media. 2026 © Silke Niehoff, Malte Reißig and Grischa Beier

Title: Examining digital platform resilience: a social–ecological systems approach
Abstract: Purpose – We examined digital platform resilience through a social–ecological systems lens, treating platforms as socio–technical entities embedded in and interacting across, broader environmental scales. Findings – Socio–technical factors, namely innovation capacity, diversity, IT infrastructure (ITI) flexibility and ITI efficiency, along with a cross-scale interaction factor, sustainability positioning, serve as critical drivers of digital platform resilience. Title: A configurational view of the role of managerial cognition and Industry 4.0 in SME internationalization

Title: Obscuring tax avoidance by alternative interpretations in applying segment disclosure under IFRS 8
Abstract: Purpose – We examine whether firms concealing tax avoidance activities through lower effective tax rates (ETRs) are associated with the flexibility allowed on disclosing segments under the International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS) 8, Operating Segments. Title: Unpacking emotions in SME internationalisation: towards a multilevel theoretical framework and research agenda

Title: Why leader empathy backfires: relative LMX and leader work meaningfulness in predicting unethical pro-organizational behaviors

Abstract: Purpose - Although leader empathy has long been argued to enhance leader-member relationships (LMX) and promote positive employee behaviors, its potential negative consequences, such as promoting unethical behaviors, remain unexplored. Title: The hidden layers of knowledge management processes: a multidimensional framework for organizational KM excellence
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to address a persistent gap in the knowledge management (KM) field: the disconnect between conceptual models and the lived realities of KM implementation. While KM literature has advanced theoretically, existing frameworks often lack empirical grounding and fail to reflect the systemic, contextual and adaptive nature of KM in practice. Design/methodology/approach – Data were collected between 2020 and 2024 through in-depth interviews and two focus groups with 52 KM professionals from multiple sectors, complemented by 18 months of ethnographic fieldwork in three organizations (finance, government and digital services). Analysis employed grounded theory principles and thematic coding, guided by Gioia’s inductive methodology. Findings – The study identifies a multidimensional KM framework comprising seven interrelated components: (1) Knowledge Strategy, (2) Governance and Leadership, (3) Knowledge Flow Processes, (4) Content and Contextualization, (5) Technological Infrastructure, (6) People and Organizational Culture and (7) Measurement and Evaluation. KM is conceptualized as a dynamic system – structured yet adaptable – where each component reinforces and is reinforced by the others. The model evokes a navigation metaphor, positioning KM as a strategic enabler of innovation, resilience and alignment. Originality/value – The model offers a dual contribution to theory and practice. It reconceptualizes the underdeveloped “process” dimension of the People–Process–Technology framework as a systemic domain, enhancing its theoretical precision. Title: Socio-economic determinants of digital financial inclusion in SAARC countries

Abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of individuals’ socio-economic factors on digital financial inclusion in the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) countries. Besides, this study only considers a single period to identify socio-economic determinants of digital financial inclusion in SAARC countries. Besides, practitioners should also facilitate the execution of payments and the receipt of services through card-based, internet-based, and mobile-based financial transactions in remote areas. Furthermore, the findings underscore the necessity for broader participation of financial institutions and financial technology service providers in rural areas, owing to geographical inequities that lead to the financial exclusion of the marginalised rural individuals in SAARC countries compared to urban residents. Title: A prescriptive generative AI maturity model for new product development processes

Title: Bridging the gap between procedural and relational ethics in qualitative research: insights from the ethics review process
Source title: Qualitative Research in Organizations and Management
Abstract: Purpose – This paper aims to examine how ethics committee documents shape the negotiation of ethical dilemmas in qualitative management and organisational studies (MOS). Findings – Ethics documents enact three dynamics that constrain qualitative inquiry: epistemic risk (foreclosing knowledge by privileging immediate utilitarian benefit), political risk (sanitising critical terms such as “modern slavery”) and relational risk (neglecting harms that arise unpredictably in encounters). While committees seek to protect participants and researchers, these textual practices also channel ethics into compliance rituals and depoliticised categories. Originality/value – By analysing documents as the unit of study, this paper shifts debates from adversarial critique to constructive reform. We argue for a dialogic model of review that retains safeguards while recognising researchers as reflexive ethical agents. Title: Leaders' gossip as informal leadership communication: norms, strategy and ethics

Title: Non-predictive strategies for political risk management in international markets

Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine how Global South firms mitigate political risk when operating in armed conflict zones and politically unstable international markets. It addresses the limited understanding of how firms develop, mobilize and transfer institutional capabilities in highly unstable contexts, where traditional predictive approaches lose effectiveness. Specifically, it investigates how Brazilian firms mobilize immediate resources, relational networks and trust to transform uncertainty into opportunity, uncovering patterns of resilience, adaptability and organizational learning underexplored in the literature on the internationalization of Global South multinational enterprises. Design/methodology/approach – This study adopts a qualitative, multiple-case design grounded in an inductive approach, examining six Brazilian firms with operations in, or exposure to, conflict-affected or politically unstable environments. Primary data comprised seven semistructured interviews conducted between February and March 2023, complemented by documentary evidence including corporate documents, media coverage, export data and institutional reports. Data were analyzed through iterative open coding, second-order theming and cross-case pattern matching, with documentary triangulation enhancing construct validity. Findings – The findings highlight the central role of strategic partnerships in managing financial exposure, enabling market entry and navigating political uncertainty. Firms rarely rely on formal predictive models; instead, they combine commercial safeguards, trusted relationships, effectual reasoning and adaptive responses. Concrete mechanisms include trust-based distributor networks, advance-payment safeguards, institutional bricolage and rapid reconfiguration routines, alongside effectuation heuristics such as bird-in-hand and affordable loss. Networks function as relational infrastructure, providing critical information, local resources and logistical support that strengthen organizational resilience and enable firms to convert political shocks into opportunities. Research limitations/implications – The small case sample limits generalizability, calling for comparative studies across Global South regions and sectors and for investigating whether the findings extend to multinationals from developed economies. The durability and scalability of effectuation-based responses warrant longitudinal and mixed-method research, including whether non-predictive routines become institutionalized over time and the development of measures linking effectual reasoning to firm performance under political shocks. Practical implications – Managers of emerging multinationals and smaller exporters in fragile markets should cultivate diverse partnerships and strengthen local intermediaries, which provide legitimacy, market intelligence and operational capacity beyond what predictive models offer. Acceptable-loss rules, implemented through contractual clauses, payment safeguards or staged investments, preserve strategic flexibility and limit downside exposure, while rapid relocation routines and logistics reconfiguration enhance agility. Public policy and multilateral agencies can support these efforts through risk-mitigation instruments, internationalization programs and stronger intermediary networks. Social implications – By showing how firms sustain operations in conflict-affected and institutionally fragile regions, the study illuminates how continued trade and investment can preserve access to essential goods, employment and local economic activity in underserved markets often abandoned by established competitors. Cases such as engagement with international institutions to improve trade facilitation and participation in humanitarian reconstruction suggest that resilient Global South firms can contribute to post-crisis recovery. Strengthening intermediary networks and risk-mitigation instruments, as recommended to policymakers and multilateral agencies, may foster more stable trade links and reduce the economic isolation of politically unstable regions. Originality/value – By specifying the microfoundations of non-predictive strategy, this study extends effectuation theory to political-risk settings and advances debates on the interplay among effectuation, resilience and institutions in Global South internationalization. Title: Mandatory sustainability reporting and cost stickiness: empirical evidence from the EU directive
Abstract: Purpose – This study aims to examine the influence of mandatory sustainability reporting on the cost stickiness of companies. Design/methodology/approach – The study employs Anderson et al.’s (2003) cost stickiness model, using the difference-in-difference method, where the treatment and control groups comprise companies from 17 European Union (EU) countries and 11 non-EU Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries, respectively. The time period spans from 2013 to 2022, with 2017 being the year of the EU Directive’s implementation. The study uses various approaches in addressing endogeneity issues, including propensity-score matching, the multiple specifications method, parallel trend analysis, placebo variable and control variables. Findings – The results confirm a statistically significant increase in discretionary costs, i.e. selling general and administrative costs, for EU companies in the post-implementation period. The stickiness is more profound in companies demonstrating an annual improvement in sustainability performance. Stakeholder-oriented civil law countries exhibit an increase, while shareholder-oriented common law countries show a decrease in cost stickiness. Research limitations/implications – The study extends the literature on the economic effects of mandatory sustainability reporting by examining the novel aspect of cost behaviour, thereby revealing managerial perceptions about costs arising from compliance. Practical implications – The study provides insights for policymakers in terms of formulating future regulations.
